AEVEX shows off jet-powered Specter attack drone at AUSA
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
16:16:14 UTC
01:16:14 KST

- AEVEX is displaying a full-size model of Specter, a turbojet-powered one-way attack drone developed with Divergent Technologies, at AUSA 2026.
- The company has not released Specter’s speed, range or payload, and has introduced a maritime unit following its BlackSea Technologies acquisition.
AEVEX is showing a full-size model of Specter, its new jet-powered one-way attack drone, at the Association of the U.S. Army’s annual meeting in Washington this week, along with a maritime drone line built from its recent purchase of BlackSea Technologies.
The California-based company announced Specter on Sept. 23 as a high-speed, turbojet-powered autonomous strike platform under development with Divergent Technologies, a Los Angeles company that builds structures through additive manufacturing. AEVEX says Specter will come in ground-launched and air-launched versions and has a swappable nose section that can carry explosive warheads, electronic warfare equipment or surveillance sensors without redesigning the airframe.
The drone uses AEVEX’s CompassX autonomy software, which the company says is built to keep working when GPS and communications are jammed. AEVEX has not released Specter’s speed, range, size, payload weight, price or flight test schedule, and has not named a customer.
Divergent’s role is to make the drone easier to build in large numbers. Its DAPS production system designs and prints complex structural parts digitally, which AEVEX says lets it change the design quickly and plan for high-rate production from the start of engineering. The model at AUSA is the first time the company has shown Specter at full size.
AEVEX is best known for the Phoenix Ghost loitering munition, which the United States sent to Ukraine starting in 2022, and for larger Group 3 drones such as Disruptor. The company went public on the New York Stock Exchange this year. It also buys rocket-assisted takeoff motors for its drones from X-Bow Systems, which has delivered hundreds of them under a $12 million contract.
The company used AUSA to introduce AEVEX Maritime Systems, a new unit formed after it acquired BlackSea Technologies, a Baltimore-area maker of uncrewed surface and underwater vessels that supplies the U.S. Navy and other U.S. forces. The acquisition was valued at about $650 million. AEVEX says its portfolio now covers air, surface and subsurface drones, aimed at an army expecting to fight with jammed navigation, cut communications and supply lines under attack.

Zelenskyy: Ukraine skipped strikes on Russian energy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
16:12:37 UTC
01:12:37 KST

- Zelenskyy said Ukraine did not strike Russian energy facilities overnight into Oct. 12 after Trump announced an energy ceasefire.
- He said Russia kept attacking Ukrainian gas and power infrastructure, and Moscow has not confirmed agreeing to the ceasefire.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Ukraine did not strike any energy facilities inside Russia overnight into Oct. 12, after President Donald Trump announced an immediate halt to attacks on energy targets, but that Russia kept hitting Ukraine’s gas and power infrastructure.
Zelenskyy made the comments in a live interview with Fox News on Monday. Trump said on Truth Social on Sunday that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to stop attacking each other’s energy facilities. Moscow has not confirmed accepting any such deal, and the exact scope of the proposal is still unclear.
“We didn’t attack any energy objects on the territory of Russia because President Trump said that there will be an energy ceasefire between Ukraine and Russia. And we didn’t attack, but Russia attacked our gas stations, energy infrastructure, infrastructure and other things,” said Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
He said Kyiv was ready to observe the ceasefire but doubted Moscow was, describing the overnight strikes as Vladimir Putin’s answer to Trump and saying Russia had signaled it knew nothing about an energy ceasefire.
Ukraine’s charge d’affaires in Washington, Denys Sienik, said Russian forces hit a power plant in Kyiv, cutting electricity and water, and then struck a thermal power plant in Kharkiv after Trump’s announcement. Sienik said Russia had attacked electricity generation and transmission facilities more than 200 times over the past week. Russia has not commented on those claims.
A White House official told Axios that Trump’s proposal initially focused on stopping attacks on oil refineries, with a broader halt covering power plants and electrical grids possibly to follow. Ukraine’s long-range drone campaign against Russian refineries has been a point of friction with Washington, and Trump has argued the strikes push up fuel prices. Zelenskyy rejected a refinery-only arrangement, saying an energy ceasefire has to cover Ukraine’s power grid, and tied any pause on refinery strikes to Russia doing the same.
“If Russia will not attack our energy, we will not attack the energy,” said Zelenskyy.
He also disputed Trump’s view that Ukrainian strikes are behind higher diesel prices, pointing instead to disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz. On Friday, Trump announced a deal with Russia to release Russian diesel to the United States and global markets, which critics in Congress say gives Moscow more revenue for the war.
Zelenskyy also responded to Trump’s suggestion over the weekend that Ukraine needs a new president. He said he was ready to hold elections but that Ukraine would need at least 60 days of security for its infrastructure to prepare, given ongoing Russian drone and missile attacks. Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov rejected the idea of a 60-day pause on Monday, arguing that European countries would use it to rearm Ukraine.
“I don’t think he deserves a respite,” Lavrov said, according to the BBC.
Zelenskyy said he last spoke with Trump in person at the U.N. General Assembly in New York in late September. Russia has not said whether it will stop striking Ukrainian energy facilities.

Lockheed unveils longer-range Patriot missile, PAC-3 Edge
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
16:09:32 UTC
01:09:32 KST

- Lockheed Martin unveiled PAC-3 Edge, a longer-range, higher-altitude Patriot interceptor, as its entry in the U.S. Army’s Future Interceptor competition.
- Lockheed says the U.S. Army advanced it to the next stage and it is working toward an early operational capability by 2031.
Lockheed Martin has unveiled PAC-3 Edge, a new Patriot interceptor designed to reach higher, fly farther and maneuver harder than the PAC-3 MSE now in service. It is the company’s entry in the U.S. Army’s Future Interceptor competition.
The company debuted the missile on Oct. 12 at the Association of the U.S. Army’s annual meeting in Washington. Lockheed says the U.S. Army has moved it into the next stage of the competition and that it is working toward what the service calls a residual operational capability by 2031, meaning a small number of missiles ready for emergency use before full fielding. The company did not release range, altitude, speed or cost figures, and did not name the other competitors.
PAC-3 Edge builds on the PAC-3 MSE, the hit-to-kill missile that destroys targets by striking them directly and has been used heavily against Russian missiles in Ukraine and Iranian missiles in the Middle East. Lockheed says the new version adds a new seeker, an upgraded propulsion system and improved flight controls. The seeker was designed by the company’s Strigo Product Center, which Lockheed says it funded with $250 million of its own money.
The company says the missile is meant to counter a wide range of aircraft, missiles and hypersonic weapons at higher altitudes and longer ranges than current Patriot interceptors. In the U.S. Army’s layered missile defense, it would sit between the PAC-3 MSE and the THAAD system, which intercepts ballistic missiles at much higher altitudes.
The U.S. Army has tried before to field a next-generation Patriot interceptor. It ran a Lower-Tier Future Interceptor competition between Lockheed and Raytheon, then announced in 2024 that it would cancel the effort before reviving the idea as the Future Interceptor program. The U.S. Army has not published the program’s budget, the number of missiles it plans to buy or when it will pick a winner.
PAC-3 Edge becomes the fourth missile in Lockheed’s Patriot family, alongside the older PAC-3 CRI, the PAC-3 MSE and the lower-cost PAC-3 ACE the company announced in July for European customers.

From Diana to the ordinary citizen: How Britain lost its sense of duty - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
16:09:19 UTC
01:09:19 KST

In 1997, Princess Diana died in a Paris tunnel alongside Dodi al-Fayed, the son of an influential Egyptian businessman.
What followed was an extraordinary accusation: that Britain’s establishment had arranged her death because it feared that her relationship with a Muslim man – and the influence she wielded over millions – could change the country itself.
Dodi’s father, Mohamed al-Fayed, accused the royal establishment and British intelligence of orchestrating the crash. The allegations were investigated and rejected.
There was no established plot, and no proof Diana intended to convert to Islam. But the accusation mattered for what it alleged about the establishment’s priorities: that those at the top were prepared to sacrifice the mother of Britain’s future king rather than risk a profound change in British society.
Thirty years later, look at Britain.
A country once accused of being willing to sacrifice its crown jewel to stop a feared transformation now has leaders accused of refusing even the smallest political sacrifice to protect the ordinary citizen – the peasant.
That is the other side of the coin. The allegation then was that Britain would go too far to protect its identity. The indictment now is that its leaders have sold out the duty to protect it.
This is not a story about one demonstration, one election, or one religious community. It is about what happens when a government knows the dangers of extremism yet allows political calculation to outweigh its responsibility to confront them.
Britain was warned. Its own 2015 review described the influence of Muslim Brotherhood-associated organizations and recorded expressions of support for Hamas attacks among individuals linked to the movement. Islamist extremism was not a threat discovered yesterday. It was something Britain’s leaders had already examined in their own institutions.
Then came October 7. Hamas murdered civilians in Israel, and Gaza became a powerful force in British politics. Marches, campaigns and electoral pressure demanded a tougher posture toward Israel. Britain’s government made its own choices, and those choices – not the slogans on the street – are what its leaders must answer for.
In March 2026, London limited American use of British bases for offensive strikes against Iran, the regime that has armed and financed Hamas and Hezbollah.
US President Donald Trump publicly criticized the restriction. Britain later permitted specified defensive operations, but the dispute exposed how far London was prepared to distance itself from Washington on a central security issue.
Britain also imposed arms-export restrictions and sanctions relating to Israel, recognized Palestinian statehood and announced further measures involving Israeli settlements.
Israel closes Britain's Jerusalem consulate
The confrontation ended with Israel ordering the closure of Britain’s Jerusalem consulate. Its consular operations ceased in October, with 20 diplomats required to leave and a smaller British mission remaining.
No protester signed those orders. British ministers made those decisions. They may argue that each serves international law or British interests. They still owe their own citizens a convincing account of the priorities behind them – and of the consequences for the country’s security and alliances.
That is where the charge of a sellout comes from. Britain’s government has shown it can take hard positions when it chooses. Yet its critics see hesitation in confronting extremist intimidation at home, alongside a readiness to take measures against a democratic ally abroad.
British Jews face rising antisemitism; ordinary people are entitled to ask why protecting them is not met with the same resolve.
The controversy even reaches cultural partnerships. A Palestinian museum whose archives describe a perpetrator of the Coastal road massacre as a martyr has worked with British institutions.
That does not prove those institutions funded or endorsed the material. It does make the standards they apply a legitimate subject of scrutiny.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu called Britain the “Islamic Republic of Britain.” It was a political rebuke, not a literal description of the country. But his words captured the anger at a Britain whose foreign-policy decisions appear, to its critics, increasingly remote from the instincts of its traditional Western allies.
The real failure is not that Britain’s population or religious life has changed. It is the accusation that its leaders have traded the courage to defend their people and principles for the comfort of avoiding political confrontation.
A government is not judged by how firmly it speaks of its heritage, but by what it protects when protection becomes costly.
Diana’s death was not justified, and the murder allegation was not proved. The contrast is about the extremes Britain was accused of contemplating then and the resolve its leaders are accused of lacking now.
Once, the alleged sacrifice was the princess – the highest symbol of the nation. Now, critics say, its leaders will not risk their political standing for the peasant – the ordinary person who depends on the government for security and freedom.
That is how a country loses its way: not when its people change, but when those entrusted with protecting them stop putting them first.
The writer is the founder and CEO of the Orthodox Jewish Chamber of Commerce.

Transnational political actors, far Left networks capitalize on France's student riots
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
16:08:52 UTC
01:08:52 KST

A Fox News investigation has examined how recent student demonstrations across France over deteriorating educational conditions have been heavily capitalized on by an extensive network of far-left communist and socialist organizations.
Fox News said it “has found that a transnational network of far-left communist and socialist organizations is seizing on France’s fiery student protests to advance a wider political and ideological agenda, using tactics deployed in the United States over the past decade to amplify unrest, deepen divisions and project an image of chaos” and that throughout the world “adults with deep pockets are tapping France's school protests and turning a domestic education dispute into a platform for broader political and ideological confrontation.”
Fox News tracked how the local issue became co-opted by transnational political actors, radical trade unions, and foreign-funded media outlets, including New York City-based Break Through News funded by American-born, Shanghai-based tech tycoon Neville Roy Singham, alongside communist organizations and activists spanning from France to Greece, Britain, the United States, Brazil, and India.
The unrest began as localized, peaceful blockades organized by students in late September in the low-income Paris suburb of Seine-Saint-Denis. According to the investigation, adult-led political operatives quickly intervened to fan the flames and escalate the disruption.
French-Moroccan journalist Nora Bussigny stated that elected officials from the far-left party La France Insoumise worked to co-opt the student protests, writing that they risked seeing them spiral out of control by fanning the flames, discrediting institutions like the police, and legitimizing the principle of political violence.
Following these initial blockades, a wide network of far-left groups put out the call for tens of thousands of secondary school students and supporters to march through Paris on October 6, while demonstrations rapidly spread across the country.
Of 50 groups involved, only 15 were student, youth groups
To demonstrate how the movement expanded far beyond students demanding educational reform, Fox News conducted a digital analysis of scores of news articles, social media posts, and public statements. Fox News identified 50 organizations involved in the broader movement and its network of supporters, revealing that only 15 are student or youth groups.
The remaining 35 adult-led groups included a dozen labor unions, eight communist or socialist organizations, four political parties, specifically naming La France Insoumise and the French Communist Party, as well as civil rights and human rights groups, parents' associations, and a Palestinian advocacy faction. The network supporting the mobilization extended far beyond teenagers, with national labor federations and professional education unions calling on adult workers to join the mobilization.
Adult-led labor federations such as the Confédération générale du travail, Force Ouvrière, and the National Union of Autonomous Trade Unions joined alongside education-sector unions that called for strikes and demonstrations. Support also extended into parents' councils, human rights leagues, and antiracist organizations.
The on-the-ground involvement of communist groups was prominently on display during major demonstrations in Paris. Protesters marched behind a bright red banner carried by the Young Communists, associated with the Mouvement Jeunes Communistes de France, bearing the words Contre Les Guerres Impérialistes and Guerre De Classe! alongside images of the hammer and sickle.
Fabien Roussel, national secretary of the French Communist Party, joined demonstrators in Paris and posted on X/Twitter that he was standing alongside high school students in Paris, together with Communist elected officials and activists while campaigns online demanded an end to arms supplies to Israel.
Use of social media, global news outlets to amplify narratives
On Instagram, the Young Communists announced the launch of Democratic and Antifascist Vigilance Committees, declaring that high school students are neglected, pro-Palestinian activists are persecuted, and unionists are fired while state repression against democratic rights has intensified. Far-left lawmaker Louis Boyard was also seen waving a Palestinian flag while standing with students blocking Paris-Est-Créteil University.
Fox News detailed how international media networks and outside organizations plugged directly into this coordinated apparatus to amplify these narratives.
Central to this connection, according to Fox News, is Break Through News, which the report describes as a pro-communist media platform in New York City and financially backed by Neville Roy Singham, an American-born tech tycoon operating from Shanghai who Fox News said “has financed a network of communist and far-left groups in the U.S. that have capitalized on grievances to stoke similar street unrest for almost a decade.”
Fox News reported that Break Through News served to amplify these synchronized protests by immediately pushing out active alerts and used visual media to frame local law enforcement as aggressors, publishing an Instagram video of far-left Saint-Denis Mayor Bally Bagayoko physically shielding student demonstrators from police.
Links to Hasan Piker, far Left social media influencer
Fox News noted that among the accounts that liked the video was far Left Twitch influencer Hasan Piker; BreakThrough News editor Zoe Alexandra; the Houston chapter of the Party for Socialism and Liberation; the Pittsburgh chapter of Jewish Voice for Peace; and other groups alleged to be within the Singham network.
Fox News further highlighted Piker's ties to this apparatus, reporting that earlier in the year, Piker traveled to Cuba as part of a far-left "caravan" supporting the island nation's communist government, where he took a photo with Jodie Evans, Singham's wife and co-founder of CodePink, an organization that Fox News noted has received $1.33 million from Singham.
Additionally, Fox News reported that teleSUR, an international television network within the Singham network based in Latin America, frequently circulated material from left-wing media outlets like BreakThrough News and shared footage of French students clashing with police.
Fox News stated that this cross-platform amplification rapidly accumulated 346,000 likes in a single day on a Break Through News posted video driven by online figures like Piker and editors within the Singham network.
Fox News noted that the network extended further to organizations in Greece and India, with the Communist Youth of Greece issuing a statement declaring "Victory for the struggle of the school students in France!" which was quoted by Break Through News in its coverage.
Fox News concluded that the result is a "self-reinforcing cycle" in which far-left activist networks amplify protests around the world and then package the unrest as evidence of a growing global uprising. According to Fox News, on Thursday, after French students had headed home following their siege on Bastille, Break Through News posted a collage on Instagram featuring short video clips from the US, Spain, India, France, Brazil, Belgium, Chile, and Germany showing youth waving communist flags, clashing with police, and flooding the streets, accompanied by a headline in bold capital letters reading "YOUTH RISE UP AROUND THE WORLD."

Oct. 7 accusations and the manufactured crusade to bring down Netanyahu - opinion

The orchestrated storm of unconfirmed allegations surrounding Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s actions before and after the October 7 attacks has devolved into a transparent exercise in political warfare.
In recent weeks, the public square has been systematically flooded with self-serving leaks, retroactive warnings, and highly selective recollections. We are expected to blindly accept that United Arab Emirates President Mohamed bin Zayed (MBZ) magically warned Netanyahu of an impending offensive, and that Egyptian intelligence chief Abbas Kamel made a clandestine trip to deliver an identical alert.
Concurrently, a parade of defense and intelligence officials has stepped forward, audaciously claiming they systematically flagged a deteriorating security situation only to be ignored by the political echelon.
Attempts to sabotage Netanyahu, cover up military failures
Let’s inject some overdue reality into this narrative: The ongoing wave of unconfirmed accusations against Netanyahu is a desperate weaponization of institutional self-preservation and political timing, designed to cover up systemic military failures and sabotage his reelection.
To date, not a single one of these convenient external warning claims has been independently verified. More importantly, the forces peddling these assertions are far from neutral observers. The catastrophic failure of October 7 was, first and foremost, a colossal institutional collapse across Israel's military and intelligence apparatus. It is blindingly obvious that individuals within these very systems are highly motivated to leak curated narratives, shifting the blame from their own severe operational blind spots onto the prime minister.
Furthermore, the timing of these disclosures exposes their true intent. With shifting political horizons and the looming prospect of future elections, this sudden rush to air long-held grievances is a coordinated hit piece meant to destroy Netanyahu’s electoral viability. When accusations are deliberately timed to maximize political damage, their credibility evaporates entirely.
This pattern of selective narrative-building collapses under scrutiny, especially when examining the recent assertions made by Netanyahu’s former military secretary, Avi Gil. Gil claims that the prime minister bypassed critical "opportunities" to secure the release of hostages out of fear that his governing coalition would fall apart. This accusation completely divorces itself from reality. The American special presidential envoy for hostage affairs explicitly stated that during the time in question, Hamas was simply not interested in releasing any of the Israeli hostages.
This definitive assessment completely decimates the media's favorite lie that viable, realistic deals were sitting on Netanyahu's desk waiting to be signed.
The only "terms" Hamas ever seriously demanded centered on a total, permanent surrender – a comprehensive ceasefire and the mass release of high-profile security prisoners. Accepting these suicidal demands would have cemented Hamas's survival and rule in Gaza, delivering the terror group a total victory. Key coalition partners like Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich rightly vowed to leave the government if such a capitulation occurred.
While naive commentators argue that Netanyahu could have accepted Hamas's terms to return the hostages and subsequently wiped them out later, such a reckless gamble contradicts his historically cautious strategic doctrine. Confronted with a choice between political suicide or relying on a defense establishment hamstrung by decades of conceptual stagnation, the government faced an incredibly narrow operational path. The IDF’s initial challenges in securing a rapid, decisive victory point squarely to deeper institutional incompetence – including legacy doctrines associated with former chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot and restrictive rules of engagement that tied the army's hands – rather than simple political obstinacy.
Predictably, the mainstream media has completely buried alternative viewpoints that destroy their preferred anti-Bibi crusade. For instance, testimonies from hostage families revealing that Hamas was so heavily damaged that they were on the verge of cutting a deal far more advantageous to Israel have been met with total silence. Instead, it was the Israeli Left that rushed to Hamas's rescue, prioritizing an immediate hostage deal over the total destruction of the terror group, thereby granting Hamas vital strategic breathing room.
This disastrous approach was heavily championed by figures like Gadi Eisenkot, yet he and the other architects of this failure enjoy a striking lack of media accountability.
Instead, the media remains single-mindedly obsessed with Avi Gil’s baseless allegations. Yet Gil’s own credibility is entirely shot, given the glaring questions regarding his own failure to decisively alert the political leadership in the critical hours immediately preceding the October 7 assault.
As long as the national discourse relies on unverified leaks from desperate actors with everything to lose, the true history of this period will remain obscured by political warfare. It is time to look past the media consensus, ground ourselves in the external diplomatic reality that Hamas refused to deal, and reject this transparent hit job for what it is.

Israeli soldiers say ordered to drop heavy bombs on inhabited Gaza buildings without evacuation: Report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
16:08:15 UTC
01:08:15 KST

Four Israeli military intelligence soldiers acknowledged they received instructions to use “heavy bombs” against inhabited buildings in the Gaza Strip without evacuating residents first, in strikes that killed and injured hundreds of Palestinians, according to a media report on Monday.
The soldiers gave their accounts to the Israeli newspaper Haaretz, as Israel continues its genocide in Gaza, which began in October 2023.
The Israeli army has repeatedly claimed that it warns civilians in Gaza to evacuate before strikes, a practice Israeli officials, including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, have frequently boasted.
However, soldiers’ testimonies contradict these claims, as they revealed a complete change in open-fire regulations since the start of the war on Gaza, where approximately 2.4 million Palestinians live.
One intelligence soldier, identified only as A, who was tasked with tracking Hamas commanders in Gaza, said: “We knew almost nothing about Hamas and its military wing at the field level.
“In October 2023, we started almost from scratch to identify where their members and operatives were,” he said.
He added that the criteria for defining a target were quickly loosened, alongside “a sharp change in the concept of proportionality and the use of heavy weapons” and a significant easing of the policy governing the killing of civilians considered “collateral damage.”
Expanded targeting policy
Haaretz said the testimonies of the four soldiers portrayed “a fundamentally different concept of warfare, in which even relatively minor targets could be considered sufficient justification for attacks to harm civilians.”
The newspaper said the large number of civilians classified by the military as “collateral damage” was not simply the result of failures or mistaken identification, but stemmed from a policy of expanding the use of firepower “to the maximum extent.”
Haaretz said similar accounts had been presented during the three years of the war and that efforts to compensate for the intelligence failures of Oct. 7, 2023, “contributed to unprecedented tolerance for civilian casualties.”
The newspaper cited an Oct. 31, 2023 Israeli airstrike on a large residential complex in the Jabalia refugee camp in northern Gaza as one example. The stated target was Ibrahim Biari, a Hamas battalion commander in Jabalia.
“We knew Biari was underground, beneath large buildings, but we did not know beneath which building,” said a soldier identified only as D.
“So they chose buildings that were still inhabited and decided to destroy all the buildings above the tunnel where he was located. We did not carry out an evacuation because it was important to kill him without allowing him to escape,” he said.
Soldier A, who said he took part in the mission, said members of the targeting cell understood that the number of civilians likely to be harmed “was extremely high.”
“In the military intelligence estimates of potential collateral damage, there was talk of 250 to 300 people, so the decision was passed up for direct approval by the chief of staff,” he said.
“After the strike, as time passed, we understood that the number of dead was around 250,” he added, referring to Palestinian civilians.
“I remember being shocked when several densely populated buildings were flattened, killing hundreds, in order to kill a battalion commander who only a few weeks earlier would not even have been considered a target,” he said.
Responding to the Jabalia massacre, the Israeli army claimed that the strike had been “replanned several times to reduce harm to civilians,” saying the expected number of civilian casualties “was not in the hundreds.”
The army claimed that after the strike, “the damage was found to have exceeded its initial assessment.”
OPINION: Gaza’s displaced face a deadly choice: collapsing buildings or flooded tents
Civilian bloodshed
Nadav Weiman, executive director of Breaking the Silence, a left-wing Israeli organization, denounced the army’s conduct in Gaza.
“We cannot allow the killing of 300 civilians to assassinate a battalion commander,” he said. “Nor can we kill 20 civilians to kill every Hamas truck driver and then claim publicly that we did everything possible to prevent harm to innocent people.
“It is time for those who issued these orders to take responsibility instead of trying to get rid of the soldiers who courageously decided to tell the public the truth,” Weiman said.
In November 2024, the International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants for Netanyahu and former Defense Minister Yoav Gallant over war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza.
The International Court of Justice, the UN’s principal judicial organ, is also hearing a case brought by South Africa and joined by several countries accusing Israel of genocide against Palestinians in Gaza.
Haaretz said another case described by the soldiers involved the Oct. 13, 2023 targeting of Hamas commander Ali Qadi.
According to the newspaper, an intelligence soldier in the Gaza Division had warned that Qadi “was behaving unusually,” but the division’s intelligence officer disregarded the warning.
“A few days after the war began, Qadi became a target and was subjected to heavy fire,” soldier A said.
“He was in the house with his family, and they decided to kill him. The army quickly announced that he had been killed, but in reality Qadi was the only person who survived the attack. Everyone who was killed had no connection to the target,” he said.
Without evacuation
Another soldier, identified as B, who served in a drone unit, said that after the war began, the division was authorized to operate under expanded parameters, meaning attacks expected to injure up to 20 noncombatants “did not require approval from a senior official outside the targeting cell.”
A third soldier, identified as C, who served in military intelligence, said that several months after the ground offensive began on Oct. 27, 2023, his unit was asked to prepare an entry zone into Gaza City for a maneuvering division.
He said several high-rise buildings in the area were considered a threat to Israeli troops and that an intelligence assessment estimated that about 25% of residents were still inside their homes.
“When we tried to ask how many residents remained and whether that was reasonable, we were told that those residents were targets for the forces on the ground. I could not understand or believe that we were talking about such numbers,” he said.
He added that the forces planning to enter the area could have waited considerably longer before approving the attack.
“So in the early stages we attacked without a full evacuation. Defending the soldiers was given priority, which is understandable, but the numbers (of civilian casualties) kept growing and became unreasonable,” he said.
The Israeli army has killed more than 74,300 Palestinians and injured over 175,400 others in a brutal war since October 2023 that has left the entire enclave in ruins.

How would NATO defeat a Russian invasion? Its top commander envisions a wall of drones, a counteroffensive, and missile strikes deep behind Russian lines.

Unknown Publisher

01:07:59 KST

How would NATO defeat a Russian invasion? Its top commander envisions a wall of drones, a counteroffensive, and missile strikes deep behind Russian lines.
General Alexus Grynkewich, NATO’s Supreme Allied Commander Europe, said NATO forces would destroy “anything and everything” involved in any Russian attack on the alliance’s territory. He presented his “theory of victory” at a security conference in Warsaw.
Bloomberg reported a week earlier that Grynkewich would present a “quick victory” strategy for responding to a Russian advance on the alliance’s eastern flank. Reuters reported that he did not explicitly mention Russia in his speech, but his message was clearly directed at the Kremlin.
Grynkewich said NATO is a defensive alliance but will thwart, repel, and crush any attacks on its members:
If someone is foolish enough to attack us, we will fight. […] We will, in short, ensure any attack, against any ally, proves utterly futile.
In Reuters’ assessment, the general signaled to Moscow that, if necessary, NATO would launch large-scale retaliatory strikes against both the forces directly involved in the attack and facilities beyond the area under attack. “Should the adversary choose to press the attack or commit his reserves, we will break the warfighting system engaged against us,” Grynkewich said. “This includes not just the attacking force itself, but anything and everything that supports, sustains, and controls that force.”
He said that if NATO territory comes under attack, its forces would not allow the enemy to gain a foothold on the alliance’s territory. The aim, he said, is to reduce the enemy’s offensive capabilities until it can no longer continue fighting. Grynkewich believes this approach should underpin a deterrence strategy in which any escalation by the aggressor backfires.
Grynkewich said a key factor in deterring Russia is consistently and unambiguously showing that NATO is ready to repel any aggression.
The Wall Street Journal reported details of Grynkewich’s “theory of victory.” The plan calls for creating an extensive “autonomous zone” on the eastern flank, where drones and “ground robots” (probably ground drones) could hold back a Russian advance without heavy losses among NATO troops.
At the same time, long-range missiles would strike Russian command posts and air defense systems in the Kaliningrad region, near St. Petersburg, and in Belarus. The strikes are intended to undermine Russia’s ability to control the skies and allow the U.S. Army’s V Corps and other NATO ground forces to counterattack.
NATO aircraft would also need to strike Russian reinforcements quickly as they move toward the battlefield, along with other targets in the rear.
A system allowing NATO allies to share classified targeting data instantly through cloud infrastructure would make these strikes possible. Some elements of the system have already been tested in the Middle East during the U.S. attack on Iran.
The German tabloid Bild reported on a similar NATO plan in mid-August 2026. The article said NATO has a plan for a military response to a Russian attack on the Baltic states. Among other things, it calls for the alliance’s missiles and drones to disable Russian missile systems, including those in Kaliningrad.
The Wall Street Journal reported that while Grynkewich was speaking in Warsaw, more than 20,000 military personnel from various NATO countries were taking part in a 10-day command-post exercise called “Steadfast Duel.” The exercise was intended, among other things, to simulate one million NATO troops repelling an invasion from the east by an army of comparable size. The newspaper reported that other exercises also rehearsed strikes with ground-launched missiles to disable enemy command posts.
In late September, Russia’s embassy in Ireland claimed its diplomats were receiving information about NATO preparations for an air and naval blockade of the Kaliningrad region. The diplomats said that if this happened, Russia would be prepared to use any weapon, including nuclear weapons. The same warning appears in a document Russia sent to NATO that Reuters obtained. In it, Moscow accuses the alliance of pursuing a “dangerous and reckless course” that carries “high risks of the outbreak of a direct armed conflict.”
Vladimir Putin later made a similar statement:
If it comes to a direct attack on the Russian Federation — in this case, we mean Kaliningrad, perhaps other territories as well — then, of course, Russia’s use of all the weapons at our country’s disposal will inevitably and immediately be on the table. That is inevitable.
In its written response to the Kremlin, NATO said none of the alliance’s exercises or activities pose a threat to Russian territory.

General Dynamics shows Wolf XM30 at AUSA 2026
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
16:05:38 UTC
01:05:38 KST

- General Dynamics Land Systems displayed only a one-eighth-scale model of its Wolf XM30 at AUSA 2026, while its prototype undergoes U.S. Army testing.
- The U.S. Army expects to choose between the Wolf and American Rheinmetall’s Lynx in 2027 to replace the M2 Bradley.
General Dynamics Land Systems has brought its Wolf XM30 infantry fighting vehicle to the Association of the U.S. Army’s annual meeting in Washington, but only as a one-eighth-scale model, leaving the full-size vehicle out of public view while it undergoes U.S. Army testing.
The company is offering the Wolf as a replacement for the M2 Bradley Fighting Vehicle in the U.S. Army’s XM30 Mechanized Infantry Combat Vehicle competition.
In a social media post on Oct. 12, General Dynamics said the vehicle was designed from the start around the U.S. Army’s Modular Open Systems Approach, which uses common hardware and software interfaces so new sensors, weapons and electronics can be added without redesigning the vehicle. The company also said the Wolf was “born digital,” meaning its digital engineering model is used in testing, production and maintenance as well as design. It did not release new specifications, photos of the full-size vehicle or any test results.
General Dynamics delivered its first Wolf prototype to the U.S. Army at Aberdeen Proving Ground, Maryland, on Aug. 21. The only public photo since then has shown the vehicle wrapped in a black tarp on a flatbed trailer. The company has said seven more prototypes will go to the 1st Armored Brigade Combat Team, 1st Cavalry Division, at Fort Hood, Texas, where soldiers will put them through field trials. The Wolf is based on the company’s Griffin III demonstrator, itself derived from the ASCOD 2 infantry fighting vehicle, and its team includes GM Defense, AeroVironment and General Dynamics Mission Systems.
The other finalist, American Rheinmetall, is not showing its Lynx XM30 at AUSA at all. The company said its prototypes have gone straight to the U.S. Army for soldier evaluation. American Rheinmetall delivered the first of eight Lynx prototypes days after General Dynamics’ delivery in August.
The U.S. Army’s requirements for the XM30 call for an uncrewed turret armed with the XM913 50 mm cannon, a hybrid-electric drivetrain and room for six dismounted infantry soldiers. The vehicle would carry infantry squads and cavalry scouts into combat and support them with fire once they dismount, the same job the Bradley has done since the early 1980s.
The U.S. Army picked General Dynamics and American Rheinmetall as finalists in June 2023, with the design and prototype phase valued at about $1.6 billion between them. The U.S. Army expects to choose a winner in 2027, and its budget plans call for buying 108 vehicles by fiscal 2031 ahead of larger production later.

Scientists uncover a possible trade-off in how the hippocampus replays new memories
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
16:00:43 UTC
01:00:43 KST

When the brain rests after learning something new, it actively replays the recent experience to lock it into memory. A recent small study published in the Journal of Cognitive Neuroscience reveals that this mental replay involves a trade-off, where the brain prioritizes the general meaning of an event while weakening the memory of specific details. These biological adjustments suggest that false memories are a natural byproduct of how the mind extracts useful themes from the world.
Memory involves balancing two competing tasks. The brain must hold onto the specific details of a single event, but it also needs to find patterns across multiple events to predict what might happen in the future. If a person only remembers exact details, they might struggle to apply lessons from the past to new situations.
In traditional models of brain function, the hippocampus acts as a fast-acting recorder for new experiences. Over days and weeks, it slowly teaches these memories to the neocortex, the outer layer of the brain, which extracts statistical rules and overarching concepts. However, recent computational models suggest that this division of labor might also exist entirely within the hippocampus itself.
If the hippocampus manages both rapid recording and slow generalization, it must have a mechanism to edit memories shortly after they form. The biological principle of competitive plasticity suggests a possible method. When a person learns related concepts, the neural pathways sharing common features activate together and become stronger. Unique, isolated details that do not reactivate as often are competitively weakened.
To understand how the brain handles this balance, researchers Nicholas C. Hindy, Ryan Coleman, and Surya Rajan Meenakshi Selvam focused on specific sub-regions of the hippocampus. After a person experiences something, the hippocampus spontaneously reactivates the neural patterns associated with that event. The research team wanted to see if this reactivation process transforms a memory rather than just making a perfect copy of it.
They specifically looked at a sub-region called CA1. This area acts as a primary output hub, sending information to other parts of the brain. The structural position of CA1 allows it to resolve competition between specific episodic details and broader generalizations.
The experimental design aimed to see this competitive editing in action. The researchers conducted a small study with 24 adult participants using a classic psychological test known for reliably producing false memories. Participants heard word lists designed around a missing target concept. For example, a list might include the words bed, rest, and awake, but leave out the central theme word, sleep.
The words were read aloud by artificial voices, splitting the incoming information into two distinct channels. The semantic channel was the meaning of the words and their shared theme. The episodic channel was the specific sensory experience of hearing a male or female voice.
The research team used high-resolution functional magnetic resonance imaging to scan the participants. Standard brain scans often blur the tiny sub-regions of the hippocampus together. By using high-resolution techniques, the team could isolate the CA1 area, as well as neighboring regions known as CA3 and the dentate gyrus.
After listening to the words, participants spent 90 seconds performing a simple math task. This kept them distracted but allowed their brains to rest from active memorization. During this short rest period, the researchers used the brain scans to measure how often the hippocampus spontaneously replayed the neural patterns associated with the word lists.
Finally, the participants completed a memory test while still inside the brain scanner. They had to indicate whether they recognized words from the lists, and whether they falsely recognized lure words that fit the theme but were never actually played. They also had to recall which voice spoke the recognized words.
The researchers found that spontaneous brain reactivation during the rest period had opposing effects on the two types of memory. When the CA1 region replayed a memory more frequently, participants were more likely to confidently claim they had heard the lure words. At the same time, this increased reactivation predicted worse accuracy when participants tried to remember whether a male or female voice spoke a specific word.
This means the mental replay strengthened the overarching concept of the word list but weakened the memory of the exact sensory experience. The memory of the actual words that had been played remained unchanged by the reactivation process. The effect only influenced the broad themes and the specific voice details.
While the CA1 region showed the strongest evidence for a bidirectional trade-off, the other sub-regions displayed specialized roles. Reactivation in the CA3 area was linked exclusively to a higher rate of false memories for the overarching themes. Neuroscientists believe CA3 helps with pattern completion, a process where the brain rebuilds a full memory from a partial cue, which may naturally strengthen the broader concept.
Conversely, activity in the dentate gyrus was linked only to worse memory for the specific voices. The dentate gyrus is typically associated with pattern separation, the ability to tell similar experiences apart. When this region is forced to process overlapping themes, its ability to hold onto precise episodic details might be compromised.
The research team also noticed a spatial pattern along the length of the hippocampus. The front and middle sections of the structure were primarily linked to extracting general themes and falsely recognizing the related lure words. The rear section of the hippocampus was linked to the loss of specific source details, such as the voice of the speaker.
The study relies on correlational data, meaning the results show a relationship between brain activity and memory performance but cannot prove that the reactivation directly caused the memory changes. People might have processed the words differently while listening, which could influence both the brain replay and the later memory errors. The rest period was also very short, only capturing the earliest moments of memory formation.
The brain scans tracked activity linked to entire word lists rather than individual words. The researchers could not separate the replay of a single word from the general activity of the whole list. Future research will need to separate individual events with greater precision and track memories over longer periods to see how these trade-offs evolve.
The study, “Hippocampal Reactivation Trades Episodic Detail for Semantic Gist in Human Memory,” was authored by Nicholas C. Hindy, Ryan Coleman, and Surya Rajan Meenakshi Selvam.

Defence Readiness Bill to give government reserve powers
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
17:00:36 BST
01:00:36 KST

Legislation being developed to give ministers powers in reserve for escalation towards war will cover the Defence Nuclear Enterprise, and the government has committed to bring it forward within this Parliament, according to an answer given in Parliament.
Ben Obese-Jecty, the Conservative member for Huntingdon, asked what progress had been made on recommendation 33 of the 2025 Strategic Defence Review, which covers legislative reform that could direct industry to prioritise defence nuclear requirements in the sovereign supply chain, or enable compulsory acquisition of assets where necessary to protect national security.
Luke Pollard, Minister of State at the Ministry of Defence, said: “The Government has accepted the SDR recommendation to develop a ‘Defence Readiness Bill’ to ensure ‘the Government has powers in reserve to respond effectively in the event of escalation towards a war involving the UK or its allies’. Defence is working closely with the rest of government to develop detailed policy requirements, including for the Defence Nuclear Enterprise, and to establish what new legislation is required as part of the Government’s wider Home Defence programme.
“Defence Readiness legislation is being developed to ensure the Government has the powers it needs to keep the UK safe, both now and in times of heightened crisis or escalation towards war.”
The minister listed the measures under development as improving the ability to defend against sub-threshold threats; increasing industry preparedness, agility and resilience; expanding the supply of privately owned services to defence and access to and protection of critical national infrastructure; and strengthening the mobilisation of defence’s people, including the Reserves and civil servants.
Mr Pollard added: “The Government has committed to deliver this legislation within this Parliament. As is standard with the legislative process, any future legislation will be brought forward when parliamentary time allows.”
The answer does not say whether the powers to direct industry or compulsorily acquire assets that Mr Obese-Jecty asked about will appear in the Bill, and no date was given for its introduction.
A second question from the same member asked about progress on recommendation 30, which seeks to strengthen NATO and British led training and exercises addressing escalation and conflict scenarios with nuclear-armed states.
Louise Sandher-Jones, Parliamentary Under-Secretary and Minister for the Armed Forces, said: “The Government is implementing the recommendations of the Strategic Defence Review 2025, including Recommendation 30, which seeks to strengthen coherence between the conventional and nuclear elements of NATO’s deterrence and defence posture.
“The Ministry of Defence continues to strengthen UK and NATO-led training and exercises through a programme of national and multinational activity that improves readiness, interoperability and the ability of Allied forces to operate across the full spectrum of conflict. This includes participation in NATO’s exercise programme, including the Alliance’s flagship STEADFAST exercise series, which tests collective defence plans and strengthens Allied deterrence and defence.
“Through these activities, we are working closely with Allies to ensure NATO is better prepared to deter, defend against and, if necessary, respond to threats from capable and nuclear-armed adversaries.”
The latest instalment of that series, the annual nuclear deterrence exercise Steadfast Noon, begins in Italy on Tuesday with seventeen nations taking part.

IN BRIEF: Russian presidential aide’s statements at meeting with Chinese Foreign Minister

BEIJING, October 12. /TASS/. Expanding natural resource extraction requires Russia and China to jointly safeguard maritime shipping, Russian Presidential Aide and Chairman of the Maritime Board Nikolay Patrushev said during a meeting with Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi in Beijing, according to the Maritime Board's press service.
He emphasized that relations between the two countries have withstood the most challenging times. In Patrushev's view, Russia and China are capable of reshaping the global geo-economic map through joint efforts and protecting global maritime trade more effectively against external risks.
TASS has compiled the key statements made by the presidential aide.
Relations with China
"Relations between Russia and China have proven their resilience during the most challenging times. Today, our task is to make these relations even more multifaceted by adding a new, maritime dimension. I am confident that through joint efforts, based on trust and mutual respect, we will be able to open this new chapter of cooperation just as successfully as we have opened all previous ones. May our partnership continue to grow, strengthen, and serve as an example to the entire world," Patrushev said.
Shipping security
The growth of trade between Russia and China requires reliable transport corridors, including maritime routes: "The expanding trade volumes between our nations demand reliable transport corridors, a significant portion of which rely on maritime routes. Furthermore, deepening energy cooperation requires resilient logistics chains."
Russia and China must cooperate to ensure shipping safety: "The increasing development of resources, including in northern latitudes, demands joint efforts to ensure the safety of navigation."
Development of maritime trade
Russia and China should pool their strengths and potential in maritime trade: "Russia possesses an extensive maritime border, well-developed port infrastructure, and unique expertise in navigating northern seas. Meanwhile, China has a powerful shipbuilding and logistics sector, along with vast experience in managing maritime trade. Today, it is crucial to combine these advantages."
"Our countries have everything required to succeed in this area: complementary capabilities, extensive experience in joint projects, and, most importantly, a mutual interest in the results."
"We attach particular importance to the joint development of strategic logistics initiatives. China has been implementing its Maritime Silk Road concept for over a decade. Meanwhile, drawing on its vast experience in polar navigation and the operation of the Northern Sea Route, Russia has launched the Trans-Arctic Transport Corridor project."
Geo-economic map
By developing Russia’s Trans-Arctic Transport Corridor and China’s Maritime Silk Road initiative, the two nations can reshape the global geo-economic map and better protect global maritime trade against external risks: "By advancing these initiatives, our countries are capable of reshaping the global geo-economic map, making maritime trade less costly, more accessible, and better protected against all risks – including military escalation, piracy, and sanctions."

Scarred blood vessels may be one clue to APOE4’s Alzheimer’s risk
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
16:00:00 UTC
01:00:00 KST

Scarred blood vessels may be one clue to APOE4’s Alzheimer’s risk
The gene variant may alter cells that support the brain’s blood vessels
The gene APOE4 is the strongest common genetic risk factor for Alzheimer’s disease. But it’s still something of a mystery to researchers.
Now, new work suggests one way the gene variant does its dirty work. It influences the production of scar tissue throughout vital vascular connections carrying blood to and from the brain, researchers report September 24 in Cell. This process may also contribute to the buildup of the protein amyloid-beta, which is thought to be one of the first signs of Alzheimer’s disease in the brain.
APOE4 is an allele, one of three slightly different, common forms of the APOE gene, which makes a protein that helps carry fats in the bloodstream. The variant is common among people who have Alzheimer’s disease. “If you had a room of 10 people with Alzheimer’s disease, and you asked how many of those people have the APOE4 allele, six of them would,” says neuroscientist Joel Blanchard of the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai in New York City. Yet many people who carry APOE4 never develop the dementia-causing disease, leaving researchers trying to understand what the gene variant actually does to make the brain more vulnerable.
One clue came from people who seemed unusually resilient to that risk. In 2024, researchers examined more than 3,500 people, including some who carried two copies of APOE4 but had not developed Alzheimer’s. Genetic analysis showed that they had a mutation in their DNA that meant their blood vessels had far lower levels of a protein called fibronectin, a kind of cellular superglue that assists wound healing. The reserachers suggested that too much fibronectin could make it harder for the brain to clear amyloid-beta from the brain. A buildup of those plaques is a hallmark of the disease.
That result pushed Blanchard and his colleagues to look more closely at blood vessels. “The prevailing thought in the field is basically that the Alzheimer’s disease is so bad that the blood vessels break down,” Blanchard says. ”But we wanted to ask the question: Is it the other way around?”
Blanchard and his colleagues built an atlas that mapped gene expression — how DNA is read and converted into proteins — across the human brain vasculature at a cellular level. Stitching together data from three existing brainwide maps, their atlas represented 66,000 cells from 220 people. They team examined how this map differed in people with two copies of APOE4 compared with those with less harmful gene variants.
APOE4 carriers had fewer pericytes, starfish-shaped cells that wrap around and stabilize blood vessels. They also had higher numbers of myofibroblasts, cells normally formed during tissue injury that pump out fibronectin, the team found.
The map offered a snapshot, but it couldn’t show whether the missing pericytes were actually transforming into myofibroblasts. The researchers turned to 3-D models of human brain tissue grown from stem cells. In models carrying two copies of APOE4, pericytes began taking on the characteristics of scar-producing myofibroblasts. The transformation also offered a possible explanation for the earlier clue from resilient APOE4 carriers: Myofibroblasts produce large amounts of fibronectin. And when the researchers prevented cells in their models from producing fibronectin, amyloid accumulation dropped.
The researchers also found a possible trigger for the cellular switch. In the APOE4 models, signaling through the immune molecule TGF-beta helped drive pericytes toward the scar-producing state. Blocking that signaling in cell models and aged mice restored the proportion of blood vessels wrapped up by pericytes.
The TGF-beta data are “particularly interesting,” because inhibiting the protein reversed some of APOE4’s effects on pericytes, says Abdel Ali Belaidi, a neuroscientist at the Florey Institute of Neuroscience and Mental Health in Parkville, Australia. But TGF-beta performs many jobs throughout the body, he says, making it a difficult molecule to target safely with a drug.
And damage to the brain’s blood vessels is only one of the many ways APOE4 has been linked to Alzheimer’s. Other studies have shown that the gene variant alters inflammation and interacts with another Alzheimer’s-linked protein, tau. How all these changes lock together to link APOE4 so strongly to Alzheimer’s disease is a greater mystery than one study can solve. ”As a field, we’re all progressing toward an answer,” Blanchard says.

Did you solve it? The treacherous puzzle of the round table
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
16:00:00 UTC
01:00:00 KST

Earlier today I set you these six puzzles. Here they are again with solutions.
The round table
Three people sit at a round table, facing inwards, towards the centre of the table. No two of them are the same age.
Each of them says “I am younger than the person to my left.”
1. What is the greatest possible number of people telling the truth?
2. What is the smallest possible number of people telling the truth?
Solution
1. The oldest person must be lying, so the maximum is 2. Here is an example with 2 people telling the truth:
30-40-20 (Ages as you go clockwise around the table)
The answer is two.
2. The youngest person must be telling the truth, so the minimum is 1. Here is an example with 1 person telling the truth
40-30-20
The answer is one.
Seven people sit at a different round table, facing inwards, towards the centre of the table. No two of them are the same age.
Each of them says “I am younger than the person to my left, and I am younger than the person two places to my right”.
3. At this table, what is the greatest possible number of people telling the truth?
4. At this table, what is the smallest possible number of people telling the truth?
Solution
3. The two oldest people must be lying, so the answer cannot be six or seven.
It turns out that the answer cannot be five either. If five were telling the truth, the third oldest would be one of them, and so the three oldest people would have to be arranged in one of the two cases below (suppose the ages are 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70).
* * * 60 * 50 70 (Ages as you go clockwise around the table)
* * * 70 * 50 60
But now there is nowhere for the next oldest (the 40-year-old) to sit and be telling the truth.
It is, however, possible for four people to be telling the truth:
10 20 40 70 30 50 60
The answer is four.
4. The youngest person must be telling the truth, so the answer cannot be zero. If you order everyone in descending order of ages, no one is telling the truth apart from the youngest:
70 60 50 40 30 20 10
The answer is one.
999 people sit at a third round table, facing inwards, towards the centre of the table. No two of them are the same age.
Each of them says “I am younger than the person three places to my left, and older than the person three places to my right”.
5. At this table, what is the greatest possible number of people telling the truth?
6. At this table, what is the smallest possible number of people telling the truth?
Solution
5. We might think about this by colouring the seats gold, silver and bronze in a repeating pattern, like so (in the illustration there are only 21 people, but the idea works for 999 people as well).
It can now be seen that each person makes a statement about people sitting on seats with the same colour as them; in particular, the closest people on either side with the same colour seat.
Consider those 333 people sitting in gold. The youngest and oldest of these must be lying, so there cannot be 333 or 332 gold truthtellers. But, as the example below helps to illustrate, it is possible for every other gold person to be telling the truth, by seating them with age increasing as we move clockwise around the table. Applying the same reasoning to those seated on silver or bronze, we can have all but six people telling the truth.
The same idea with 999 people has 999-6=993 telling the truth.
The answer is 993.
6. If the people are sat with age decreasing as we move clockwise around the table, then everybody is lying.
The answer is 0.
Thanks to Daniel Griller for today’s puzzles. He is the author of the excellent puzzle books Elastic Numbers and A Ring of Cats and Dogs, and Other Curious Puzzles.
I’ll be back in two weeks.
I’ve been setting a puzzle here on alternate Mondays since 2015. I’m always on the look-out for great puzzles. If you would like to suggest one, email me.

Russia is building satellite network that could put all of Europe in reach, defense executive warns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
15:58:50 UTC
00:58:50 KST

Russia is building a satellite network that could soon put all of Europe within its reach. The “Rassvet” satellite system is an extraordinary threat, first to Ukraine and then to the rest of Europe, Oleksandr Danyliuk, the head of the private European aerospace and defense technology company Destinus, said at the Warsaw Security Forum, according to Ukrinform.
Rassvet is Russia’s answer to Starlink, a low-orbit satellite network built by Bureau 1440 to give Moscow’s forces communications that no one else can switch off. European states must invest more quickly in cheap, effective, mass-produced systems to counter it. 
“They will be able to navigate to any point in Europe without problems. This needs to be stopped,” said Danyluik, a former Ukrainian finance minister, said.
Cheap systems, made at scale
Danyliuk’s prescription is already being used on Ukraine’s front. Europe should invest in inexpensive, effective systems that can be mass-produced, he argues, the same approach Ukraine uses, and that Russia also turns against it.
“This gap needs to be filled as quickly as possible,” he said.
He urged allies not to overlook threats that might look secondary today, pointing to Rassvet as exactly that kind of slow-building danger.
Appearing strong is not enough to deter Russia, Danyliuk argued, because Moscow can gauge how ready European states actually are.
Ukraine races to catch up
Both sides are now scrambling to own the satellite link rather than rent it. Ukraine is building a satellite system of its own, similar to Starlink but beyond any single company’s control, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on 4 October.
He argued Kyiv should be free to turn Starlink on Russian military targets, warning that China and other states will share comparable satellite technology with Moscow within months.
By Ukrainian estimates, Russia still needs five to eight years to complete Rassvet, which so far reaches Ukraine only in brief passes. That window is the time Danyliuk says Europe must use.

Pakistan: Declaration of emergency must not be pretext to crackdown on human rights
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
15:53:34 UTC
00:53:34 KST

Responding to the declaration of a state of emergency in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, as well as the imposition of governor rule and the deployment of armed forces in the province, Babu Ram Pant, Amnesty International’s Deputy Director for South Asia, said:
“Reports of arbitrary detentions of key leaders – including the provincial chief minister – and internet disruptions across the province raise concerns about the proportionality of these emergency measures. While states may, in strictly limited circumstances, derogate from their human rights obligations to respond to a public emergency that threatens the existence of the nation, emergency measures are not a blank cheque to crack down on human rights, silence dissent, or concentrate power.
“Given the history of enforced disappearances and extrajudicial executions in counterterrorism operations by the armed forces, the deployment of the army further militarizes the province and could create conditions for unlawful use of force. Pakistani authorities must avoid using military personnel for ordinary policing tasks and ensure that military forces remain accountable and comply with international human rights law and standards.
Emergency measures are not a blank cheque to crack down on human rights, silence dissent, or concentrate power
Babu Ram Pant, Amnesty International’s Deputy Director for South Asia
“At this critical juncture, the federal authorities must ensure independent oversight of all actions taken under the emergency framework, and guarantee that any emergency measure is strictly necessary and proportionate to the situation.”
Background
President Asif Ali Zardari approved recommendations by the federal cabinet to impose a state of emergency and governor rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province under Articles 232 and 234 of Pakistan’s constitution respectively, citing an “unprecedented level of violent intensity of terrorist attacks” and a “breakdown of constitutional machinery” in the province on 11 October. A state of emergency allows the federal legislature (national assembly and senate) to pass laws regarding the province and allows the federal government to suspend fundamental rights such as the freedoms of assembly, association and expression.
The notification by the president stated that the powers of the provincial assembly will be exercised by the federal parliament and it was stated that the chief minister along with the provincial ministers, advisors, special assistants and advocate general would cease to hold office. Separately, the federal government deployed the Pakistan military “in aid of civil powers” in the province under article 245 of the constitution.
Former Prime Minister Imran Khan’s Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party has been in power in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province since 2013. PTI formed its latest government with a two-thirds majority after the 2024 general election.

Andy Burnham said Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps were “almost certainly” behind threats to RAF Fairford, the firmest attribution of responsibility made so far by the UK after an incident late last month.
The prime minister told MPs the UK would bring further sanctions against Tehran and the IRGC as a result, with more information to follow in an update from the home secretary, Shabana Mahmood.
Addressing parliament on Monday about events at RAF Fairford, Burnham said: “I can confirm our assessment that it is highly likely to have been coordinated in Iran, almost certainly directed by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guards.”
Five men from London drove to Whelford, a village next to a base used by the US air force, in three white vans shortly after midnight on 27 September. They were released on police bail a day later after no bombs or explosives were found.
However, the incident was followed by the withdrawal of 12 B-1 bombers a week later, amid reports that the US was concerned about a possible drone attack on a base it had used to attack Iran during the Middle East war in the spring and summer.
Burnham’s brief remarks were a step up from previous comments. The prime minister had said in the days after the incident that there were “strong indications” that Iran had played a part – but now appeared confident enough to apportion responsibility.
However, despite his statement, it remains unclear what the authorities think happened at Fairford. Some experts have speculated it was a “feint” to demonstrate that Iran could in theory attack a relatively open site.
British sources have repeatedly maintained that Iran lacks the capability to launch what would be a sophisticated drone attack, but the incident appears to have unnerved the US, which is worried about the security of its bases in Europe.

Hackers heat French supermarket fridges, sparking fires and food losses

Hackers heat French supermarket fridges, sparking fires and food losses
PARIS, Oct 12 - Hackers forced the temperature of many French supermarket fridges up to 50 degrees Celsius (122°F) overnight, causing fires and food losses at several hundred stores across the country in a major cyberattack.
The Paris prosecutor's office said a "large-scale" attack was "affecting connected refrigerators in several major food retailers across France" and reported damage included "food losses and fires".
Meanwhile, Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu instructed France's National Cybersecurity Agency ANSSI to investigate, a person in his office said.
They said France "was coordinating with its European counterparts, as other countries may also be affected," while also investigating whether any other French firms were at risk.
Les Mousquetaires, which owns retailer Intermarche, said around 150 of its stores had been hit, with fridges heated up to 50 degrees Celsius for six hours. It had thrown all the food away to avoid any sanitary risks, a spokesperson said.
And Cooperative U CEO Dominique Schelcher said his supermarket had also been hit by the attack.
"Targeting equipment essential to the preservation of fresh products and to the food supply of the French people is of extreme gravity and is unprecedented," he wrote on X.
Carrefour said 80 of its supermarkets had been hit but that the vast majority of its 6,000 stores had not been affected.
Several other supermarket chains, including Monoprix, E.Leclerc and Auchan, did not respond to requests for comment.
DUTCH SECURITY ISSUE
Dutch supermarket operator Ahold Delhaize, which operates the Netherlands' largest supermarket chain Albert Heijn and has substantial operations in the United States, said it was also dealing with a "security issue" in its network, and had taken several systems offline to protect them.
A smartphone app for the retailer told clients that due to a "cybersecurity incident" it was unable to deliver groceries.
Online orders represent around 10% of sales for Albert Heijn. Physical stores remained open and Dutch news agency ANP reported that rivals had seen an influx of delivery orders.
It was not clear if there was any link between the French supermarket attack and the problems flagged by Ahold Delhaize.
Ahold is the fourth-largest grocery retailer in the US, where websites for its Stop & Shop, Giant, Hannaford and Food Lion stores all had notices saying "site temporarily down".
It was unclear if other operations were affected.
The source close to Lecornu said ANSSI had identified a vulnerability in software supplied by Danish company Danfoss.
Danfoss said it was "aware of incidents in France affecting a limited number of refrigeration management systems".
The affected units "were running outdated firmware", Danfoss said, adding that it had "long advised customers to keep supported systems updated with the latest firmware and to migrate legacy systems to current-generation solutions". REUTERS

After a storm stranded an enormous cargo ship off Russia’s Baltic coast, locals turn it into a tourist attraction
A powerful storm swept through Russia’s Kaliningrad region on October 9. In Kaliningrad, gusty winds toppled trees and brought down power lines. Authorities put the city on heightened alert. Residents were advised to avoid going out unless necessary, and attendance at schools and kindergartens was made optional. The Kaliningrad Zoo closed, and flights were delayed at Khrabrovo Airport.
Near Svetlogorsk, the storm tore loose a lifting platform belonging to the company Geoisol. The company’s assets, including the platform, are under a seizure order. Regional authorities said there was no risk of water pollution. A criminal investigation was opened into the incident under a law covering violations of safety rules for maritime navigation and vessel operation.
In Yantarny, the storm drove the Bahamas-flagged dry cargo ship Sunny Faith ashore. The vessel had arrived in Kaliningrad from Algeria, stopping along the way at the Spanish port of Algeciras. The Kaliningrad regional government’s press office said the Sunny Faith had no cargo aboard and no fuel spill had occurred. The crew chose to stay aboard and wait for the weather to improve rather than evacuate.
The enormous cargo ship at the shoreline — 129.9 meters (about 426 feet) long and more than 23 meters (about 75 feet) wide — briefly became a tourist attraction. Residents of the Kaliningrad region and tourists posed for photos and filmed videos with the ship in the background. “There’s a huge ship right on the shore!” someone said in one such video, according to the news outlet Klops. Russian Industry and Trade Minister Anton Alikhanov, a former governor of the Kaliningrad region, was also photographed with the Sunny Faith in the background.
Visitors will be able to see the Sunny Faith for at least a few more days. As of October 12, the ship was still at the shoreline. Sources told Klops that further surveys involving divers would probably be needed to determine how to refloat it.

Children ran for cover at Joseph Lakanal Middle School in Aubagne on Monday after the suspect fired multiple shots. The student fired once or twice on the first floor of the school, injuring the principal and teacher in the legs before he continued to the second floor and opened fire again, twice, Marseille Public Prosecutor Nicolas Bessone said in a statement.
A staff member disarmed the teen before police arrived and took him into custody, Mayor Jean-Pierre Squillari told reporters.
A third person was grazed in the shooting in the southern town near Marseille, while the headmaster and teacher were not in critical condition after being hit with ammunition used in 12-gauge shotguns, police said.
One student told Reuters that her maths teacher had played down the bang of the first gunshot blast as noise from nearby construction. A subsequent blast was followed by an alarm and classes emptied into the corridors.
“We were panicking; we ran,” the student said. “There were two ways out: one passage to the sports hall and one passage to go outside. Survival instinct took over, and I ran towards the outside.”
France’s Education Minister Edouard Geffray took to X to comment on the event and wrote, “This unacceptable act is yet further evidence of the rise of unchecked violence in our society, against which we must all take a stand.”
Gun violence perpetrated by pupils in schools is rare in France. In 2017, a 16-year-old student armed with a rifle, pistols and a small grenade opened fire at a high school in southern France, and wounded three students and the principal.
The prime minister’s office said the interior and education ministers were heading to the scene.
There was no immediate information to suggest that the shooting was in any way connected to protests by high school pupils demanding better-resourced schools that have been shaking France for several weeks.
