A Ukrainian first-person-view (FPV) interceptor drone has brought down a Russian Molniya-2 attack drone using a net-launching system developed by Ukrainian manufacturer Ptashka Drones.
The company released footage of the interception, showing the Ukrainian drone deploying a net against a Russian UAV carrying two munitions.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Following the deployment, the Russian drone lost stability and began falling. Accordinfg to Militarnyi, he aircraft's descent may have been caused by a shift in its center of gravity or by the net becoming entangled in one of its propellers.
The interception demonstrated the use of a net-based system designed to disable hostile drones by physically disrupting their flight rather than destroying them with explosives.
The Ptashka Drones net launcher has a maximum projectile range of 30 meters when operated from a handheld launching device, Militarnyi reported. However, strong headwinds can reduce its effective range to approximately 27 meters.
The manufacturer identifies 20 to 25 meters as the optimal engagement distance for reliably intercepting FPV drones, with effectiveness decreasing at greater distances.
According to the outlet, the system deploys a net measuring 4 by 4 meters, designed to entangle an approaching drone and prevent it from maintaining controlled flight.

Russia Pulled Rare S-400 Launchers From Strategic Kapustin Yar Range—Ukraine Found and Hit Them
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
15:47:03 UTC
00:47:03 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russia Pulled Rare S-400 Launchers From Strategic Kapustin Yar Range—Ukraine Found and Hit Them
Ukrainian forces destroyed three and damaged five Russian Iskander and S-400 launchers used for ballistic missile attacks during September and early October 2026, according to Defense Minister Yevhenii Khmara.
New footage released by Ukraine’s Security Service also appears to support earlier assessments that the vehicles hit were rare 51P6A launchers pulled out of storage at the Kapustin Yar test range and reassigned for strikes against Ukraine, according to Defense Express on October 12.
OSINT researcher AS-22 examined satellite imagery of Kapustin Yar and found that roughly 30 such launchers were visible there in 2022, but only 14 remained by 2025. That would mean 16 had been removed from storage and likely reassigned to operational use.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
One of the easiest ways to distinguish the 51P6A from more common S-400 launchers is its chassis. The vehicle is mounted on the Belarusian-made MZKT-7930 Astrolog platform, while standard S-400 launchers more commonly use the Russian-built BAZ-64022 chassis.
Defense Express notes that the 51P6A launchers observed near Ukraine were reportedly moving individually, without the radar vehicles normally associated with S-400 air-defense batteries.
That pattern supports the theory that they were being used not in the system’s traditional air-defense role, but as launch platforms for PM-48U surface-to-surface ballistic missiles.
Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence had estimated by late August that Russia possessed up to 17 S-400 launchers specifically assigned to PM-48U operations.
The same 51P6A launchers had also appeared at Kapustin Yar when Russia first publicly discussed specialized ballistic missiles for the S-400 in fall 2023.
The PM-48U itself represents an unusual adaptation of Russia’s existing air-defense missile inventory for ground-strike missions.
The exact launch and guidance architecture used with the 51P6A remains unclear, but the absence of accompanying radar vehicles near some of the launchers suggests that Russia is operating them differently from a conventional S-400 battery.
Previously, reports emerged that Russia used its newest 9M723-2 ballistic missile, commonly referred to as the Iskander-1000, against Kyiv for the first time during a combined attack on the Ukrainian capital this summer.

The ICJ’s Rohingya ruling will test the OIC’s promises
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
15:46:05 UTC
00:46:05 KST

The ICJ’s Rohingya ruling will test the OIC’s promises
Muslim governments backed the genocide case against Myanmar. They must now show that their commitment to the Rohingya goes beyond words.
The Organisation of Islamic Cooperation (OIC) has made Muslim solidarity central to how it presents itself. Nine years ago, Myanmar’s military massacred Rohingya civilians and drove hundreds of thousands from their homes. The persecution has not ended: the Rohingya remain stateless, face continuing violence and risk death while fleeing by sea. Throughout those years, the OIC has held summits and passed resolutions. Yet it has failed to protect them.
When I founded the Burma Human Rights Network 14 years ago, I believed that if we gathered evidence carefully and put it before institutions with the power to act, they would act. We have gathered testimony from survivors of massacres. We have documented the systematic destruction of Rohingya villages, the denial of their citizenship and the deliberate starvation of a people. Yet despite all this documentation, the situation facing the Rohingya has mostly grown worse. The International Court of Justice is expected to rule later this year on whether Myanmar’s actions constituted genocide.
I have sometimes asked myself whether a ruling could help stop the atrocities. The Rohingya survivors who gave evidence in The Hague relived the worst moments of their lives before international judges because they trusted that their testimony would matter. Many of them are still in Bangladesh, still in limbo, dependent on food assistance worth as little as $7 per person per month. One in every seven Rohingya who attempted sea crossings last year was reported dead or missing. They are unprotected, and governments that could do more have not done so.
People often ask me why we continue. I have never had a satisfying answer. What I know is that without a record of these atrocities, it becomes easier to deny they happened. I continue because, after hearing these accounts and seeing the evidence, I do not know how to walk away from it.
We have published evidence that governments did not want to confront, and we have called the atrocities what they are: genocide. If the court finds that Myanmar committed genocide, it would be the first time in the International Court of Justice’s 80-year history that a state has been held responsible for the crime.
I now address the OIC foreign ministers who will gather in Baghdad on October 17. The OIC backed this case, and your governments supported the effort to hold Myanmar accountable for its treatment of the Rohingya. Many Rohingya, along with many of us who work with them, took those commitments seriously. When the ruling arrives, I expect statements welcoming it and renewed promises of accountability. But another communiqué will not protect anyone. OIC governments should refuse to forcibly return Rohingya to Myanmar, protect Rohingya who reach their territory, sustain support for refugees in Bangladesh and agree on diplomatic and economic measures against those responsible for their persecution. These are choices your governments can make.
The way Rohingya are treated across the region is hard to reconcile with those commitments. Some governments that speak about the Rohingya in international meetings do not offer the same protection to those who arrive at their borders. A government cannot demand accountability from Myanmar and at the same time send people back into danger.
Bangladesh hosts 1.2 million Rohingya and has faced years of pressure to send them back. The OIC must also challenge abuses against the Rohingya by governments outside its membership. In 2025, according to testimony documented by Amnesty International, Indian authorities forced at least 40 Rohingya from a naval vessel into the Andaman Sea, leaving them to swim towards Myanmar. If the OIC says nothing when governments expose Rohingya to that kind of danger, those governments have little reason to change course.
To the Rohingya community organisations that kept working, the journalists who reported despite restrictions on access, those who helped survivors bring their testimony to international forums, and the advocates who stayed with this issue when official attention moved elsewhere, I can only say this: you did work that governments with armies and treasuries should never have left to you. The evidence you preserved is now part of the record.
The 57 governments meeting in Baghdad have repeatedly pledged solidarity with the Rohingya and supported efforts to hold Myanmar accountable for genocide. But solidarity means little if it does not translate into action. A judgment from The Hague will not protect the Rohingya by itself. What those governments do after it will show whether their support for this case has consequences beyond the courtroom.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

2026-10-12
15:43:31 UTC
00:43:31 KST

Abductions and arbitrary detention of Palestinians by Israeli occupiers have increased across the occupied West Bank, particularly targeting farmers and rural communities, Palestinian officials and rights groups said Monday, Anadolu reports.
Salah al-Khawaja, director of the Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission’s office in the central West Bank, told Anadolu that such incidents were often accompanied by abuse and violence.
“Palestinians were being detained at makeshift checkpoints or seized during attacks on farmers and rural and Bedouin communities,” he said.
Amir Daoud, the commission’s documentation official, said the repeated attacks make farmers fear for their lives and freedom when accessing their land and could discourage them from reaching their fields.
“The impact of the attacks extends from the victim to the entire village and becomes a means of intimidating residents and weakening their connection to their land,” Daoud said.
The UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) said in May 2025 that it had documented around 36 incidents since October 2023 in which Israeli occupiers, some wearing military uniforms, abducted or detained at least 50 Palestinians, including three children.
Palestinian rights group Al-Haq also said in a Sept. 24 report that documented cases showed an “increasing pattern” of abductions and unlawful arbitrary detentions.
In the latest reported incidents, Israeli occupiers abducted seven Palestinians on Saturday, according to the official Voice of Palestine radio.
The outlet said three abductions were reported in Nahalin west of Bethlehem, three in Qaffin north of Tulkarem and a farmer in Beit Imrin near Nablus, adding that their fate was not immediately known.
Daoud accused the Israeli army of providing protection to occupiers during some incidents, saying the Qaffin attack took place under army protection.
READ: Israeli occupiers give 47 Palestinian families 24 hours to leave West Bank homes
Systematic policy
Settlement affairs researcher Jamal Juma said the abductions were part of a “systematic policy” targeting Palestinian presence in Area C, which makes up around 60% of the occupied West Bank and remains under full Israeli control.
Under the 1995 Oslo II Agreement, which was intended as a temporary arrangement, the occupied West Bank was divided into Areas A, B and C.
Area A is under full Palestinian civil and security control, Area B under Palestinian civil and Israeli security control, while Area C remains under full Israeli control and makes up around 60% of the West Bank.
The incidents have drawn particular concern during the olive harvest season, when Palestinian farmers face attacks including beatings, denial of access to fields, theft of crops and damage to trees.
According to the official Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission, more than 26,000 olive trees were cut down or damaged across the West Bank during the first half of 2026.
The olive harvest season began on Sept. 20 with olives intended for pickling, while harvesting varieties used for olive oil production is scheduled to begin on Oct. 15.
Since Israel began its genocide in Gaza in October 2023, attacks by the Israeli army and occupiers against Palestinians and their property have intensified across the occupied West Bank, including East Jerusalem.
The attacks include killings and arrests of Palestinians, the demolition of homes and structures, the burning of mosques and vehicles, bulldozing of agricultural land, preventing farmers from reaching their fields, stealing crops, displacement and illegal settlement expansion.
Palestinians warn that Israel is paving the way through such measures for the formal annexation of the West Bank, in a move that would undermine the possibility of establishing a Palestinian state as envisioned in relevant UN resolutions.

Exclusive: UK parliament refuses to release Arab Spring report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
15:39:24 UTC
00:39:24 KST

Breadcrumb
Exclusive: UK parliament refuses to release sensitive Arab Spring report
The British parliament has refused to release a confidential report examining the UK's relations with governments that came to power in Egypt, Tunisia and Libya following the Arab Spring uprisings, insisting the document must remain secret until 2046.
The House of Commons rejected a freedom of information request submitted by The New Arab seeking access to the findings of a parliamentary inquiry into British foreign policy towards the three countries.
The report, titled British Foreign Policy and the 'Arab Spring', was prepared by the House of Commons Foreign Affairs Committee following a series of hearings, some held behind closed doors, and visits to Egypt and Tunisia in 2015.
During those visits, committee members met the countries' leaders and senior officials to discuss human rights, political developments and Britain's relations with their governments.
The committee did not visit Libya because of security concerns and the closure of the British embassy there in 2014.
Although the committee published a brief summary of its findings in March 2015, the full report has remained confidential for more than a decade.
In its response to TNA, the House of Commons confirmed that the document would not be released until 1 January 2046, more than 30 years after it was prepared.
"The House of Commons Commission has decided to maintain the closure of the report until 1 January 2046," the response stated.
The commission said it had formally decided to maintain restrictions on archived parliamentary records and would not release them before their designated disclosure dates.
It also cited parliamentary privilege, which gives each house of the UK parliament the exclusive right to determine whether and when privileged information should be made public.
The House of Commons Commission is the body responsible for overseeing the administration of the Commons. It is chaired by the Speaker and includes the Leader of the House, an MP nominated by the leader of the opposition and three other MPs appointed by the House.
Public interest argument rejected
TNA argued that releasing the report would serve the public interest, given its examination of British policy towards countries that experienced major political upheaval during the Arab Spring.
However, the commission invoked Section 34 of the Freedom of Information Act, which protects information covered by parliamentary privilege.
The provision allows parliamentary authorities to withhold information relating to privileged parliamentary proceedings without having to conduct a public interest balancing test.
The Foreign Affairs Committee is responsible for scrutinising the work of the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office and its associated public bodies.
In February and March 2015, the committee conducted a follow-up inquiry into British foreign policy and the Arab Spring, building on its earlier examination of the uprisings that swept across the Middle East and North Africa from late 2010.
Committee members travelled to Egypt and Tunisia and subsequently heard oral evidence from Tobias Ellwood, then Britain's minister for the Middle East, as well as ambassadors, other officials and regional experts.
A short report was published on 24 March 2015, while the detailed final document was subsequently submitted to the House of Commons authorities.
British support for authoritarian governments questioned
The publicly available summary raised concerns about Britain's relationship with Egypt following the military's return to power under President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi.
The committee noted that discussions in Egypt and meetings with British Foreign Office officials had placed "particular emphasis on security cooperation and trade" in bilateral relations.
It also drew comparisons between Britain's relationship with Sisi's government and its earlier ties with Egypt under former President Hosni Mubarak, who was overthrown during the 2011 uprising.
The committee acknowledged the reputational damage Britain had suffered because of perceptions that it supported authoritarian governments.
It noted that Western countries, including the UK, had faced criticism for returning to policies that prioritised stability and strong leadership over support for emerging democracies, particularly in Egypt.
Those concerns were reinforced by reports of a serious deterioration in Egypt's human rights situation.
According to the summary, individuals who met the parliamentary delegation said human rights and those defending them were under severe pressure.
During the visit, committee members met Sisi, the Egyptian prime minister, former presidential candidate Abdel Moneim Aboul Fotouh, who is currently imprisoned, and Major General Mohamed al-Assar, then assistant defence minister.
They also held discussions with representatives of political parties.
Optimism in Tunisia, security fears in Libya
The committee's assessment of Tunisia was more optimistic, reflecting the country's relatively successful political transition following the uprising that began in late 2010 and triggered the wider Arab Spring.
The summary noted a generally positive outlook among those who met the delegation, although committee members expressed disappointment with the European Union's response to the uprisings.
They also voiced frustration that British efforts to support political and economic reforms were not widely recognised.
The committee highlighted projects undertaken by British organisations, including the British Council and BBC Media Action in Libya, describing some of their work as particularly impressive.
However, the summary did not address Tunisia's human rights situation.
During their visit, MPs met then-President Beji Caid Essebsi, the prime minister, the parliamentary speaker and Rached Ghannouchi, leader of the Ennahda party, who is currently imprisoned.
They also held talks with civil society representatives and parliamentarians.
The committee painted a considerably bleaker picture of Libya, saying conditions in 2015 were far less promising than they had appeared in 2012.
Its findings highlighted concerns about irregular migration through Libya and the possibility that militants could exploit migration routes to reach Europe and carry out attacks.
Although the delegation did not travel to Libya, it met the British, American, German, French and EU ambassadors to the country during its visit to Tunisia, alongside British officials involved in Libyan affairs.
The withheld report is expected to contain fuller details of the committee's findings, including discussions with leaders of countries affected by the Arab Spring and its assessment of Britain's response to the uprisings.

Syria's Shaibani meets Haftar's son in Libya over missing Syrians
Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani visited the eastern Libyan city of Benghazi on Sunday and met with Saddam Haftar, the son of Libyan General Khalifa Haftar, who commands the self-styled “Libyan Arab Armed Forces”.
The meeting reportedly discussed the issue of Syrian nationals missing in Libya, as well as strengthening security cooperation and opening a new Syrian consulate in Benghazi.
Al-Shaibani was accompanied by Abdul Qader Tahan, the director of Syrian intelligence, on his visit.
This is Shaibani’s second visit to Libya in less than two months. In late August, Shaibani visited the Libyan capital Tripoli and reopened the Syrian embassy there.
Libya is currently split between two rival administrations – an internationally recognised government which controls Tripoli and the west of the country and one close to Khalifa Haftar which controls Benghazi and most of the east and the south.
An estimated 16,000 Syrians are believed to live in Libya. Thousands of them, however, have tried to travel across the Mediterranean to reach Europe, making an extremely dangerous journey, and many have gone missing as a result.
Many Syrians are also believed to be held in Libya’s migrant detention centres, where detainees are subjected to torture and abuse.
“Dozens, perhaps hundreds of Syrians have gone missing in Libya. These, in most cases, have attempted to reach Europe through Libya. It’s a testimony to the disastrous situation in Libya that Syrians and many others – many sub-Saharan Africans – are being arrested and detained and tortured and sometimes killed by various militias,” Syrian author Robin Yassin-Kassab told The New Arab.
Libyan authorities in both the east and west of the country have received support from the EU for their efforts to stop migration to Europe. 
This has been condemned as “shameful” by human rights organisations including Amnesty International, given the torture, ill-treatment, and even killing to which migrants and refugees are subjected.
“The EU is turning a blind eye to this or even encouraging it by paying the Libyan government and others to keep refugees in Libya,” Yassin-Kassab said.
The issue of Syrians missing in Libya has returned to the spotlight in recent weeks, with families desperately seeking news of their loved ones and calling on Syrian authorities to do more to find out about their fate.
Last month, the families of around 200 Libyans missing in Syria protested outside the foreign ministry in Damascus, calling for information about their relatives, Arab News reported.
 Although Yassin-Kassab condemned the Haftar-led administration’s violations against migrants and refugees, he welcomed Shaibani’s meeting with them.
“It’s a good thing that Shaibani is going to Benghazi to talk to the Haftar dictatorship about [the issue of missing Syrians] because they are responsible for the detentions of lots of Syrians, including apparently Syrians who are legally residing in Libya,” he said.
Yassin-Kassab said that Syrians in the Haftar-controlled parts of Libya had been detained simply for celebrating the fall of the Assad regime in December 2024. 
Haftar is closely allied to the Assad regime’s former key benefactor, Russia, and had established cordial relations with the Assad regime before its fall.

NMT in minority languages and new rights for schools — the law on education in minority languages enters into force on Tuesday
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
18:39:08 EEST
00:39:08 KST

NMT in minority languages and new rights for schools — the law on education in minority languages enters into force on Tuesday
Kyiv • UNN
The law enters into force on October 13 and expands the use of the languages of Indigenous peoples and national minorities in education. Schools will be able to obtain the corresponding status.
President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy signed a bill on ensuring the educational rights of the indigenous peoples of Ukraine and persons belonging to the national minorities (communities) of Ukraine. The document was published in the Holos Ukrainy newspaper on Monday, October 12, UNN reports.
Details
Returned with the signature of the President of Ukraine
On October 12, the document was published in the Verkhovna Rada's official newspaper, Holos Ukrainy.
According to the transitional provisions, the bill "shall enter into force on the day following the day of its publication," that is, on Tuesday, October 13.
According to the adopted bill, the language of the educational process in educational institutions is the state language; however, in an educational institution where a class providing instruction in the language of an indigenous people of Ukraine or a national minority of Ukraine that is an official language of the European Union operates, the right to use the language of the respective indigenous people of Ukraine alongside the state language is guaranteed.
It is established that, at the students' request, the tasks of the multi-subject test/external independent evaluation shall be provided in the language of an indigenous people of Ukraine or a national minority, except for tasks in subjects of the linguistic and literary field.
At parents' request, schools will be able to determine a list of subjects that may be taught in the languages of indigenous peoples. However, the number of requests must exceed ⅔.
Schools in which more than 50% of students receive education in the language of an indigenous people will also have the right to be recognized as national minority general secondary education institutions.
Such schools will have the right to use the respective status in their names and founding documents in the corresponding language of an indigenous people.
Additional information
It should be noted that in November 1992, the European Charter for Regional or Minority Languages was signed to protect and promote historical regional and minority languages in Europe.
Ukraine ratified the Charter in 2003, and it entered into force in 2006.
Under the Charter, Ukraine applies its provisions to the following languages: Belarusian, Bulgarian, Gagauz, Hebrew, Yiddish, Karaim, Crimean Tatar, Krymchak, German, Modern Greek, Polish, Romani, Rumei, Romanian, Slovak, Hungarian, Urum, and Czech.
In June this year, Zelenskyy signed Bill No. 14120, which provides for the exclusion of the Russian and Moldovan languages from the list of those protected by the European Charter for Regional or Minority Languages.
Reminder
On October 7, EU ambassadors cleared the way for the start of negotiations within the accession process with Ukraine and Moldova on the single market and competitiveness. Budapest lifted its veto on the talks. Hungary had blocked this step since the summer, demanding that Ukraine adopt legislation concerning the educational rights of national minorities.

Russian diplomat expelled from Bulgaria in 2021 amid investigation into arms depot explosions now serves as assistant military attaché in Serbia, RFE/RL finds
RFE/RL’s Balkan Service and the investigative project Sistema have identified a diplomat at the Russian Embassy in Serbia who was declared persona non grata in Bulgaria in 2021 during an investigation into explosions at weapons depots.
Alexander Krasiy, an assistant military attaché, held the same position at the Russian Embassy in Bulgaria before moving to Serbia. In April 2021, Bulgaria’s Foreign Ministry said it was expelling a Russian diplomat but did not name him. The news agency Zona News and Bulgarian National Television identified him as Krasiy.
The decision came amid an investigation into explosions at four weapons depots and production facilities between 2011 and 2020. Bulgarian prosecutors suspected six Russians of involvement. According to prosecutors, the explosions may have been linked to the attempted poisoning of Bulgarian arms dealer Emilian Gebrev and were intended to “halt deliveries of military supplies to Georgia and Ukraine.”
After his expulsion, Krasiy resurfaced in Serbia. In 2021, he was photographed among instructors and participants in a professional development course at the University of Defense in Belgrade. He received accreditation as an assistant military attaché in 2026.
The journalists said Krasiy may have ties to Russia’s military intelligence agency, the GRU. Leaked records show that when he applied for a “COVID pass” during the pandemic, he listed his home address as a dormitory at the “Conservatory” — a nickname for the GRU’s Military Diplomatic Academy. Many graduates went on to become Russian intelligence officers and saboteurs, including Anatoly Chepiga.
According to The Telegraph, Russian intelligence services used Serbia as a base to prepare an unsuccessful sabotage attempt at Leipzig Airport in August 2026. The suspected organizer, Oleg Levushkin, left Europe through Serbia, while his accomplice, Maxim Lapunov, entered Europe through Belgrade. Investigators believe the explosives intended to blow up a Ukrainian aircraft may also have reached Germany through Serbia.
In September 2026, Agentstvo included Krasiy on a list of 29 Russian Embassy employees in Serbia with confirmed or possible ties to intelligence services. The outlet said Russia’s embassy and trade mission in Serbia employ a total of 78 people, while just 18 Russian diplomats work in neighboring Bulgaria, which has a comparable population.
Krasiy is not the first Russian diplomat to continue working in Serbia after being expelled from the EU. In 2023, RFE/RL found that at least three Russian diplomats expelled from the EU after the start of the war had received accreditation in Serbia. Two of them were found to have ties to Russian intelligence services.

2026-10-12
18:32:32 EEST
00:32:32 KST

The Ukrainian defense industry and business associations are urging the Cabinet of Ministers not to adopt a new draft resolution amending the procedure for reserving conscripts from mobilization, which provides for cutting quotas for the defense industry and other significant restrictions.
Serhiy Pashynsky, head of the National Association of Ukrainian Defense Industries (NAUDI), has appealed to Prime Minister of Ukraine Serhiy Koretsky to intervene and prevent a reduction in the reservation quota for conscripted employees of defense industry enterprises.
“I was forced to appeal to Prime Minister Serhiy Koretsky because of the ill-conceived attempt by the Ministry of Economy to reduce the percentage of reservation for defense industry workers. The literally few thousand people who would lose their reservation as a result of such actions will certainly not solve the problems of mobilization into the Defense Forces, but will definitely undermine our capabilities to supply weapons and ammunition to the army. And they will definitely hit not only Ukraine’s defense capability but also its economy,” Pashynsky said, urging that the decision, which he said bears signs of sabotage against national security, not be adopted.
He also stressed other systemic problems in the industry, in particular the lack of conditions for exporting defense products, currency restrictions on long-term contracts and joint ventures under the Build with Ukraine initiative, and the absence of a mechanism for insuring military risks. NAUDI stresses that the domestic defense industry supplies weapons worth more than $10 billion every year, that the supply of the military depends on specialists, and that defense industry workers make up no more than 10% of all reserved employees.
“If the defense industry collapses, the front will collapse,” the association said.
According to a statement by Tech Forces of Ukraine, any changes proposed by the state must strengthen defense capability, while stripping 15% of the personnel potential of reservation would jeopardize the fulfillment of defense orders.
The Gunsmiths Council also stressed that lowering the limit to 85% does not take into account the actual personnel needs of defense production, which is currently growing, mastering new technologies and needs additional specialists. The organization said that lowering the reservation limit would create additional uncertainty for enterprises that invest in training people and fulfilling state orders, and urged the Ministry of Economy to drop the initiative.
Meanwhile, the Union of Ukrainian Entrepreneurs (UUE) pointed out that the government had not officially announced preparation of such changes and had not involved the business community in working on them, so it sent an official request to the relevant ministry.
According to MP Yaroslav Zhelezniak, the draft government resolution provides for setting a maximum reservation limit of 85% (instead of 100%) for the defense industry and energy sector, and for utilities (heat and water supply, waste management) a reduction from 75% to 60%. In addition, employees with other grounds for deferment (students, caregivers, fathers of many children) would no longer be counted in the general base for calculating the 50% quota, which would force enterprises to leave a significant part of their staff with no protection from mobilization at all.
The draft also proposes creating a 17-member Coordination Center under the Cabinet (including representatives of the Security Service of Ukraine, the Defense Intelligence of Ukraine, the Foreign Intelligence Service and the National Police), without whose positive recommendation companies would not be able to obtain critically important status or a quota above 50%, and obliges ministries and regional military administrations to review sector criteria of “criticality” by October 20.

JOHANNESBURG, Oct. 12 (Xinhua) -- South Africa is releasing about 2.5 million hectares of state-owned land to black farmers, with title deeds, as part of efforts to address racial inequalities in agriculture and expand their participation in commercial farming, President Cyril Ramaphosa said Monday.
In his weekly newsletter, Ramaphosa said that despite significant growth in the agricultural sector since the end of apartheid, its benefits had not been shared equally.
South Africa's agricultural exports reached a record 270 billion rand (about 16.3 billion U.S. dollars) in 2025, but commercial farming remains dominated by white-owned farms, while black farmers account for only around 10 percent of commercial farming output.
Ramaphosa stressed that transforming the sector is essential to addressing historical inequalities and strengthening food security. "The first step in building a new generation of South African farmers is providing them with titled access to land," he said.
Through the Proactive Land Acquisition Strategy, the government is releasing the land with title deeds to black farmers, Ramaphosa said, adding that secure access to land needs to be accompanied by affordable financing, practical training, mentorship and access to technology and other resources.
"Far too often, emerging farmers are kept trapped at subsistence level because they cannot get the financing they need for farming inputs, infrastructure and additional land," he said.
The president noted the Land Bank and the Department of Agriculture have introduced a blended finance scheme combining government grants with loans, encouraging more commercial banks and agribusinesses to join the program and develop additional funding mechanisms.
"We can bring more land under cultivation, create a new generation of black commercial farmers and ensure that we grow enough not only to feed all our people, but to sell to markets across the world," Ramaphosa said. ■

Austrian judges, prosecutors go on strike over staff shortages
VIENNA, Oct 12 - Austria's judges and prosecutors went on strike on Monday over staff shortages among their ranks, demanding that the state fill the gap despite government efforts to shrink the budget deficit back to within the European Union's limit.
As in many European countries, Austria's judiciary is plagued by delays and backlogs as it struggles to cope with an ever growing number of cases. To draw attention to the problem, judges and prosecutors across the country have stopped handling non-urgent matters this week.
"Stop! We simply can't take this anymore," Anna-Maria Wukovits, vice president of the Austrian Prosecutors' Association, told a press conference marking the start of the protest week.
"Prosecutors cannot go on like this. We are at our limit," she added.
Austria's national judges' association estimates there is currently a shortage of more than 250 judges nationally, while Wukowits told national broadcaster ORF that for prosecutors the figure is around 70.
Workloads for prosecutors and judges have increased for various reasons, including ever more complex cases such as those involving cyber crimes, and many criminal complaints are now written using artificial intelligence but must then be reviewed manually by prosecutors, Wukowits said.
"Those often involve reams of pages that have to be read. One cannot ignore that," she said.
While the justice ministry has expressed sympathy with the prosecutors and judges, it has said the government's current priority is reducing the budget deficit, which came in last year at 4.1% of economic output, well beyond the EU limit of 3%.
"The rule of law cannot be maintained in the long term only because judges work unpaid overtime. For years, our colleagues have been making up for structural staff shortages by working on evenings, weekends and even on holiday," Austrian Judges' Association President Gerhard Karmuth said in a statement. Roundup: Bound by resolve, China and Lesotho mark national milestones, look to shared future
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
23:30:08 CST
00:30:08 KST

by Silence Charumbira
MASERU, Oct. 12 (Xinhua) -- Two distant nations, vastly different in geography, size and historical trajectory, reached major national milestones within days of each other this month.
On Oct. 1, the People's Republic of China marked its 77th anniversary. Three days later, the Kingdom of Lesotho celebrated 60 years of independence.
Despite their physical distance and different sizes, a common thread runs through both anniversaries: an unyielding resolve to chart an independent path toward development and modernization.
"Our two countries have different national circumstances," Chinese Ambassador to Lesotho Yang Xiaokun said at a cultural event in Maseru on Friday. "But these anniversaries remind us of the determination of our peoples to shape our own future, pursue development, and build a better life."
Both nations embarked on modern state-building from arduous beginnings. In 1949, the New China emerged as a war-torn, agrarian society. In 1966, Lesotho gained independence as a poor, landlocked kingdom surrounded by apartheid South Africa.
Since independence, Lesotho has sought a development path suited to its own conditions, working to strengthen economic resilience and governance. China's own transformation into the world's second-largest economy has likewise rested on a path tailored to national realities, built on self-reliance and long-term planning.
"Modernization does not equate to Westernization, and there is no single model for development," Yang emphasized, affirming the right of African nations to chart their own course.
Lesotho's recent experience underscores why economic self-determination matters. The kingdom's vital garment industry has faced severe disruptions due to shifting global trade environments, leaving factories vulnerable.
Having navigated similar uncertainties during its own growth, China has consistently offered stability to its African partners. Under the frameworks of the Forum on China-Africa Cooperation, China has extended zero-tariff treatment to all 53 African countries with which it has diplomatic ties, including Lesotho.
Practical cooperation between the two nations continues to yield tangible results, ranging from debt relief and streamlined trade in agricultural exports like wool and mohair, to human resource development initiatives that sent over 270 Basotho professionals to China for training this year alone.
Progress extends beyond economics into cultural exchanges and global governance, where China advocates equal rights, equal opportunities and equal rules for all nations regardless of size. On Friday, a Chinese artistic troupe performed traditional Wu Opera in Maseru to mark Lesotho's diamond jubilee, celebrating mutual learning between distinct civilizations.
"Sixty years is not only a milestone; it is a new starting point," Ambassador Yang said, closing his address with Lesotho's national motto: "Khotso, Pula, Nala" (Peace, Rain, Prosperity).
Standing at this historic juncture, China and Lesotho are moving forward as equal partners, bound by a shared resolve to turn bilateral cooperation into lasting prosperity for both peoples. ■

Deadly gold mine air strikes highlight Egypt-Sudan border insecurity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
15:30:08 UTC
00:30:08 KST

Deadly gold mine air strikes highlight Egypt-Sudan border insecurity
Repeated air raids targeting civilian gold miners reveal deepening regional instability as Sudan’s devastating conflict spills across porous borders.
An alleged air strike on a gold mining site in northern Sudan has killed at least 72 workers, according to a rights group, highlighting the severe security vacuum along the country’s increasingly lawless border with Egypt.
The Khartoum-based rights group Emergency Lawyers accused the Egyptian military of targeting civilian miners in the North Wadi area of Jabal al-Uqaydat, a mountainous border area between Sudan and Egypt.
Egypt has not commented on the incident.
Images allegedly from the site and shared by rights monitors showed chaotic scenes, with bodies wrapped in funeral shrouds.
A troubled border
The border region between Sudan and Egypt has a long history of tensions which continue to this day.
In 1899, the British and Egyptian governments designated the 22nd parallel north as the dividing boundary between Sudan and Egypt on maps.
But the absence of physical border demarcation along this line, coupled with the area’s gold wealth, has left the area open to dispute and lawlessness.
Abdul Kareem Al-Almin Ahmed, a specialist in Egypt-Sudan border affairs, said the Sudanese territorial borders have long been subject to historical negligence which still goes on.
“The presence of the Egyptian Border Guard forces near the region, amid a complete lack of Sudanese military or administrative presence, has left the Sudanese highly vulnerable to Egyptian violations and encroachment,” he told Al Jazeera.
“What is required now from the Sudanese state – if it exists – is to elevate and escalate this issue to the United Nations as an encroachment on Sudanese territory. This must be followed by the immediate physical demarcation of border points in this region and along the entire border strip, in addition to establishing border observation posts along the entirety of the borders.”
In June, another artisan gold mine in the Jabal al-Uqaydat region was targeted by drones and artillery, with a number of people killed. The Egyptian army said it carried out an operation “within Egyptian territory” and detained 223 people.
Egyptian security forces continue to conduct sweeps of the border to combat what they described as illegal migration, drug smuggling and illegal mining.
Historical border disputes
Egypt and Sudan have a long history of border tensions stretching back to the colonial period which goes beyond the Jabal al-Uqaydat area.
The Halaib Triangle, a 20,580sq km area on the African coast of the Red Sea, has been a flashpoint between Egypt and Sudan for over a century.
The dispute stems from conflicting colonial-era maps. An 1899 agreement between Britain and Egypt regarding Sudan and parts of Libya placed the triangle within Egyptian political boundaries. But a 1902 British administrative decree handed control to Khartoum because the area was closer to the Sudanese capital.
The triangle, home to the Bisharin tribe, is renowned for its fertile lands and rich mineral deposits, including uranium, granite, copper and gold.
Following clashes between the two militaries on the border in the 1990s, Sudanese forces withdrew from the area in 2000 and Cairo has maintained effective control over the territory since.
Security and sovereignty
The latest unrest follows the start of the civil war in Sudan in April 2023, which has pitted the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF), allegedly backed by Egypt, against the Rapid Support Forces (RSF).
The conflict has devastated the country and collapsed the economy. Abject poverty has forced many into dangerous methods of gold mining, including unregulated mines on the border. The collapse of central authority in Sudan has also allowed lawlessness to flourish in the borderlands.
Sudan’s gold has been a key source of financing for both sides, but there is no indication that the gold mine revenue in the border region is going to either party in the war.
Osama Ahmed Eidrous, a professor of strategic and security studies, told Al Jazeera that foreign powers have prolonged the conflict between the two sides.
“What is happening in Sudan is not a civil war; despite the presence of the Rapid Support Forces as one of the fighting parties in this war, this war is a war of external aggression within a large regional project,” Eidrous said.
“Everything that is happening in Sudan now in terms of effects on the Sudanese citizen, the weakness of the central government and the difficulty of controlling the borders, all these things are caused by this ongoing war in Sudan.”
He added that the miners posed no threat to neighbouring countries, such as Egypt, and were not involved in the war.
“We are talking about miners working in gold mining and we have not heard that there was an armed clash, or that they were carrying weapons, or that they were fighting the Egyptian government or the Sudanese government,” he said.
“They are Sudanese citizen miners who were suddenly attacked by the Egyptian aviation and struck for the second time, killing 85 of them.”

BANGKOK, Oct. 12 (Xinhua) -- Applications for intellectual property (IP) protection in Thailand rose 9.59 percent year on year to 61,288 in the first nine months of 2026, official data showed on Monday, reflecting the growing use of IP by Thai and foreign businesses to gain a competitive edge.
According to the Commerce Ministry's Department of Intellectual Property (DIP), registrations granted across trademarks, invention patents, petty patents, and design patents rose 6.34 percent from a year earlier to 43,379 during January-September.
Trademark applications, the largest category, climbed 10.76 percent to 45,696. Retail and marketing services, health and herbal products, and cleaning and beauty products led the filings. Thai applicants made up 56 percent of trademark filings.
Invention patent applications rose 3.98 percent to 6,483, and foreign firms filed 87 percent of them.
Petty patent applications jumped 18.16 percent to 4,313, with Thai applicants accounting for 94 percent, led by universities and state research agencies. Design patent applications were nearly flat at 4,796.
Voluntary copyright notifications surged 63.71 percent to 17,176 works, most notably literary works, including computer programs.
DIP Director-General Jittima Srithaporn said the department aims to make IP protection more effective and better suited to trade and investment needs, build confidence among applicants, and support the commercial use of IP.
The department will also keep improving its IP protection and services, using digital technology and artificial intelligence to raise efficiency, link up data, and make the system easier for the public and businesses to use, Jittima said in a statement. ■

ULAN BATOR, Oct. 12 (Xinhua) -- Facing oil supply constraints and fuel shortages, Mongolia is accelerating its transition to new energy vehicles (NEVs), as affordable, reliable Chinese NEVs rapidly gain popularity.
Mongolia is advancing its transition to electric mobility by incorporating the promotion of NEVs and the development of charging networks into its medium- and long-term national development plans. The country plans to establish around 500 electric vehicle charging stations, known as "green stations," in the capital, Ulan Bator, and other parts of the country over the next two years.
In the past, many local consumers had reservations about NEVs, with some concerned about their performance in Mongolia's harsh winter climate. However, as fuel supplies tighten and the cost of running conventional gasoline- and diesel-powered vehicles rises, Chinese NEVs have attracted growing interest.
Otgonbayar is among the early adopters of Chinese NEVs in Ulan Bator. "I bought a Chinese NEV in 2024, and after using it for more than two years, my perception of these vehicles has changed completely," he said.
Otgonbayar noted that a full charge costs just 20,000 Mongolian tugriks (about 5.6 U.S. dollars), more than sufficient for his daily commute, while offering a smoother driving experience.
Like Otgonbayar, an increasing number of local vehicle owners are recommending Chinese NEVs to their friends and family after experiencing their benefits firsthand. Choosing Chinese NEVs and embracing greener mobility are becoming increasingly popular among Ulan Bator residents.
At a Chinese NEV dealership in Ulan Bator, customers are regularly seen enquiring about vehicles, placing orders and collecting their purchases. Sales staff said sales had risen significantly in recent months, reflecting strong market interest.
In recent years, several Chinese companies have stepped up cooperation with Mongolia in the new energy sector. Zheng Dongdong, vice president of Zero Carbon Engine Technology Group Co., Ltd., said the company was working with relevant local authorities to develop supporting measures to facilitate the introduction and wider adoption of NEVs. ■

Adieu aux ‘Enfants Rouges’: Tears and shock as fire destroys Paris’s oldest covered food market
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
15:28:36 UTC
00:28:36 KST

Adieu aux ‘Enfants Rouges’: Tears and shock as fire destroys Paris’s oldest covered food market
A devastating blaze destroyed the French capital’s oldest covered food market in the early hours of Monday, stripping Paris of a cherished venue popular with locals and tourists alike. Traders and residents said the destruction of the Enfants Rouges market, named after a 16th-century orphanage, had left them feeling “orphaned” themselves.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
New Yorkers Lorrie and Ricky so enjoyed discovering the Marché des Enfants Rouges (Red children’s market) a few days ago, that they decided to pay another visit to its celebrated food stalls before leaving the French capital.
But when they approached the centuries-old venue on Monday morning, they were greeted by police cordons, fire trucks and a foul, acrid smell hanging over this picturesque neighbourhood in central Paris.
“It was such a lovely place, so charming – and now it’s gone,” said Ricky, gazing at the blackened entrance to the Enfants Rouges. “It’s tragic.”
Read moreFire destroys Paris's oldest covered food market
A spectacular blaze tore through the iconic covered market overnight, gutting its iron and glass roof and torching all 17 food stalls. Video footage on social media showed huge flames and billowing smoke rising above the venue, hemmed in between buildings on the northern edge of the Marais district popular with tourists.
After touring the site, Paris Mayor Emmanuel Grégoire said the market had been “completely destroyed”. He thanked firefighters who battled the blaze for over two hours – for ensuring that it did not spread to surrounding buildings in the densely populated area known for its cozy cafes and stylish boutiques.
There were no casualties aside from a firefighter who suffered “minor injuries”, Grégoire told reporters. It was the only consolation for shopkeepers huddled together on a sidewalk – many in tears as they listened to accounts of the devastation wrought by the flames.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
“We’re all a big family, and now we’ve been orphaned,” said Ahmed Ouaddi, whose Moroccan couscous stall had been a fixture of the market for decades. “Our livelihoods have gone up in smoke.”
‘Heart and soul’ of the neighbourhood
Founded in 1615 during the reign of Louis XIII, the Enfants Rouges was the oldest covered market still in operation in Paris. It owed its name to a nearby 16th-century orphanage whose young residents wore red clothing, a symbol of Christian charity at the time.
A buzzing hub for locals and tourists alike, the market offered fresh produce and specialties from around the world. The industry magazine Food & Wine ranked it fifth worldwide for street food this year, after other eating spots in London, Bangkok, Mexico City and France’s culinary capital – Lyon.
To those nostalgic for the Paris of old, it provided a small taste of what the historic Les Halles, the city’s sprawling central market, was like before it was gutted and turned into a giant mall in the 1970s.
In recent years, the Enfants Rouges had become too touristy – and pricey – for many Parisians, in step with the area’s rapid gentrification. But it remained “the heart and soul” of the neighbourhood, said Ouaddi.
“It was the oldest and prettiest market in Paris. We all loved it and we’re all in shock today,” said local pharmacist Virginie Prulhière, still shaken from the blaze, her voice breaking as she gazed at the fire truck parked where her partner’s stall would normally be standing.
“It was also a symbol of resistance, because people here fought to preserve it,” she added, referring to a grassroots campaign in the 1990s against plans to tear down the market and replace it with an underground carpark and housing units.
‘The Enfants rouges will survive’
Residents looked on in disbelief Monday morning as firefighters accompanied the Paris mayor and other officials to inspect the smouldering ruins. Some asked why it had not been possible to save at least part of the structure, noting that the nearest fire station is located just minutes away.
Local authorities said the fire broke out at 3am (01:00 GMT) but the fire brigade did not receive a call until over an hour later. More than 150 firefighters and dozens of vehicles were mobilised to battle the blaze. Their efforts were hampered by the layout of the market, surrounded by buildings on all sides and accessible only through alleyways too narrow for most vehicles.
The cause of the blaze is not yet known.
Read moreSounding the fire alarm: Why French firefighters are on strike
“Luckily, no one was hurt, and that’s the most important thing,” said Alexis Abbou, the market’s manager, striving to remain upbeat as he sought to console its shopkeepers and caterers. “We’ll start all over again and rebuild this wonderful place,” he added.
Paris Mayor Grégoire promised to find a temporary relocation for the traders “so they can resume their business as soon as possible”. In a post on X, Serge Papin, the minister for small businesses and tourism, said the French state would “stand alongside Paris City Hall to help with reconstruction”.
Ariel Weil, mayor of the third arrondissement (district) that housed the market, also recalled the fight to save the market in the 1990s, as he vowed to restore it to its former glory.
“The Enfants Rouges survived a threat to replace it with a carpark,” he said. “It will survive this fire, too.”

Journalists confirm 940 children killed in Russia’s war against Ukraine: 873 in Ukraine, 67 in Russia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
15:27:17 UTC
00:27:17 KST

At least 940 children have been killed as a result of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Meduza found after a study of open-source data from international organizations, Ukrainian and Russian authorities, reports from relatives of the dead, and other sources. They found that at least 873 children have been killed in internationally recognized Ukrainian territory, including regions occupied by Russia, and another 67 inside Russia. The researchers stress that this is a minimum estimate: the real number of fatalities is significantly higher, as many cases still cannot be verified.
For the count of the dead in Ukraine, the journalists took data from the UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission, which had confirmed the deaths of 835 children as of Aug. 31, 2026. Meduza additionally established another 38 cases that occurred or were identified after that date but before Oct. 9. Out of the total, the researchers established the names of 409 dead children: 372 in Ukraine and 37 in Russia.
Nearly all cases were checked against two or more independent sources, including reports from relatives, and publications by schools, hospitals, local authorities, law enforcement, and the media. Exceptions were made for hard-to-reach and occupied territories, where the only source was sometimes official reports specifying the exact place and date of a child’s death.
The journalists took into account the territory where a child died, not the child’s citizenship. Deaths that occurred in Crimea, Sevastopol, and the occupied parts of the Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia, and Kherson regions were included in the Ukrainian tally.
In Russia, almost half of child deaths occurred in 2026
Of the 67 confirmed child deaths on Russian territory, 32 occurred from January to September 2026 — nearly as many as the 35 confirmed killed in the previous four years of the war combined. For comparison, researchers confirmed eight cases in all of 2025 and 19 in 2024.
Child deaths were recorded in 13 Russian regions, with Belgorod Region at the top of the list with 30 cases, followed by Krasnodar Krai with 14 deaths, the Kursk Region with seven, the Bryansk Region with five, and another three in the Moscow Region.
Russia’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs had previously reported 264 children allegedly killed in Ukrainian attacks. However, Meduza was able to match only 99 of these cases to specific events. Of them, 44 occurred in Russia’s internationally recognized territory and were included in the outlet’s count, and another 55 happened in occupied Ukrainian territories. For the remaining cases, Russian authorities did not provide enough information to allow for independent verification.
Ukrainian authorities had reported 755 killed children as of Oct. 9. The differences between the estimates are explained in part by the lack of access to occupied territories and different counting methodologies. In particular, Russian authorities include in their statistics those killed in occupied regions of Ukraine.
The number of child victims continues to grow
In July 2026, the number of children killed and injured in Ukraine reached its highest level since April 2022, according to UN data. Over the month, the organization confirmed the deaths of 17 children and injuries to another 166.
One of the deadliest Russian strikes in terms of child deaths remains the attack on Kryvyi Rih on April 4, 2025, which killed nine children aged three to 17. Russia’s Ministry of Defense claimed the target was a meeting of Ukrainian military personnel and Western instructors, but surveillance camera footage published by France 24 did not confirm the presence of military personnel in the area of the attack.
The researchers separately note that the statistics remain incomplete due to a lack of access to cities captured by Russia. The UN confirmed the deaths of at least 120 children in Mariupol from February to April 2022, but the real number of victims may be significantly higher. For example, it is still unknown how many children died in the Russian strike on the Mariupol Drama Theater on March 16, 2022.
In addition to deaths directly linked to hostilities, Meduza found five more cases of children’s deaths that the researchers did not include in the main count because they did not fit the international criteria for counting war victims. Among them are three murders committed by Russian servicemen who had returned from the front. Two of the perpetrators received life sentences, and another was sentenced to 14 years in a penal colony.
The Insider earlier examined claims by Russian human rights commissioner Yana Lantratova that Ukrainian military personnel supposedly attack playgrounds on a daily basis and deliberately kill Russian children. Even the official statistics of Russia’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs did not confirm her claim of children dying daily.

EU agrees new security mission in Lebanon as UN peacekeepers prepare to leave
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
15:26:50 UTC
00:26:50 KST

EU foreign ministers approved a civilian-military mission to train Lebanon’s armed forces. It will not replace UNIFIL, whose mandate ends in December. Personnel numbers and participating countries are yet to be confirmed.
EU foreign ministers agreed on Monday to set up a new civilian and military mission in Lebanon to strengthen the country's security forces, as the United Nations prepares to end its long-running peacekeeping operation there.
The mission, which could deploy within months, will focus on border and maritime security, counter-drone operations and training Lebanese security forces. Its precise mandate, staffing and command structure have yet to be finalised.
Unlike the United Nations Interim Force in Lebanon (UNIFIL), whose mandate expires at the end of 2026, the EU mission will not be deployed in the south, where Israel is continuing its military campaign against the Iran-backed Hezbollah group.
“We will establish a new mission in Lebanon. It has a civilian and military pillar,” EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said ahead of the Foreign Affairs Council in Luxembourg on Monday.
“We hope that this mission will be ready to work on the ground already, in a couple of months. I was just in Lebanon last week. This is highly welcomed by the local authorities,” she added.
The decision comes as Lebanon faces an uncertain security future following the planned withdrawal of UNIFIL, which has served as a buffer between Israel and Lebanon. Lebanese President Joseph Aoun has called for the UN operation's mandate to be extended.
Israel has long criticised UNIFIL as ineffective in containing Hezbollah, while the United States has also questioned its role, favouring a security arrangement directly between Israel and Lebanon.
EU officials insist the new mission is not intended to replace UNIFIL, but to strengthen Lebanon's own security capabilities.
“It will have a number of tasks to carry out over a period of up to three years, namely strengthening border security, ensuring maritime security and combating drones. In both its military and civilian aspects, the mission will support the Lebanese police in their day-to-day duties,” said Jean-Noël Barrot, France’s Minister for Europe and Foreign Affairs.
Brussels is considering deploying around 150 personnel, a fraction of the roughly 7,500 peacekeepers currently serving with UNIFIL.
The mission is expected to operate under the EU's Common Security and Defence Policy (CSDP), with an initial mandate of up to three years, subject to renewal. Contributions of personnel and equipment by member states will be voluntary.
It remains unclear which countries will participate, although several existing UNIFIL contributors – including Italy, France, Spain, Ireland, Germany, Austria, Finland and Poland – have expressed interest in maintaining a presence in Lebanon.
The command structure is another unresolved issue. One proposal under discussion would see leadership rotate between Italy, France and Spain.
In June, French President Emmanuel Macron and Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni announced that their countries would jointly lead an international coalition to support Lebanon following UNIFIL's withdrawal. It is not yet clear whether that initiative will operate separately or be incorporated into the EU mission.
Ireland, which currently holds the rotating presidency of the Council of the EU, has also signalled its intention to participate.
Dublin is prepared to contribute to the civilian component, although its involvement in the military mission could be complicated by ongoing reforms to the legal framework governing overseas deployments of Irish troops.
“We have been there for decades. We have contributed to supporting the region, supporting the Lebanese Armed Forces, but in particular the civilian population for decades. And I would not like to see that being lost,” said Irish Minister for Foreign Affairs Helen McEntee.

AI could boost Asian growth but widen regional divide: IMF
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
15:25:53 UTC
00:25:53 KST

Mücahithan Avcıoğlu
12 October 2026•Update: 12 October 2026
Artificial intelligence could add as much as 1 percentage point to annual growth in advanced Asian economies over the long term but risks widening regional disparities, according to an International Monetary Fund study.
The IMF working paper, AI and Economic Divergence in Asia, examines how differences in capital, skills, productivity and digital infrastructure could affect countries’ ability to adopt the technology.
The study estimates that AI could raise average annual growth by 0.5 to 1 percentage point in advanced Asian economies and by 0.2 to 0.8 percentage point in emerging-market and developing economies, depending on the pace of technological progress.
Advanced economies such as Singapore and South Korea are positioned to adopt AI faster because of their strong digital infrastructure, skilled workforces and access to capital.
Many emerging Asian economies, however, could begin widespread adoption one or two decades later, with substantially longer delays possible in low-income countries.
Before adoption accelerates, emerging and developing economies could record annual growth about 0.5 to 0.6 percentage point lower than under a scenario without the global AI transition.
The divergence could become self-reinforcing as early adopters attract investment and accumulate capital faster. Stronger global demand for capital could also raise interest rates, making it more difficult for late adopters to finance the infrastructure needed to catch up.
The findings are based on model simulations rather than economic forecasts and depend heavily on the assumed speed of technological development.
The paper also found that AI could reshape employment because the technology is capital-intensive and favors skilled labor, potentially reducing labor’s overall share of income.
The study was highlighted as the IMF and World Bank opened their annual meetings in Bangkok, where AI’s effects on productivity, employment and inequality are among the main topics.

EU approves Lebanon mission despite 'US objections'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
15:25:42 UTC
00:25:42 KST

Breadcrumb
Lebanon's Aoun hails EU security mission amid 'US objections'
Lebanese President Joseph Aoun welcomed the EU's decision on Monday to establish a new three-year security support mission in Lebanon, amid reported US objections to the bloc's plans for a greater security role in the country.
The mission, approved by the Council of the European Union, aims to strengthen the Lebanese army and Internal Security Forces as the country prepares for the withdrawal of UN peacekeepers from its southern border with Israel.
The decision, announced on Monday, establishes the European Union Support Mission in Lebanon (EUSM Lebanon) for an initial three-year period, with the aim of supporting the country's stability, sovereignty and state institutions.
EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said the mission would provide advice and assistance to Lebanon's security institutions to strengthen their control over the country's territory, border security and internal security.
"Europe is investing in Lebanon's future," Kallas said, describing the mission as a significant upgrade in security relations aimed at helping Lebanese state institutions restore full sovereignty and build lasting stability.
The mission will include civilian and military components operating under a unified political mandate, providing training and advice on border surveillance, intelligence gathering, reconnaissance, counter-smuggling operations, maritime security and cybercrime.
The military component will focus on strengthening the Lebanese army's capabilities in land border monitoring and control, maritime security and operational coordination.
The civilian component will provide specialised training and advice to the Internal Security Forces, including on cybercrime and counter-smuggling, while helping develop sustainable training structures.
It will also support security management at Lebanese ports, including the Port of Beirut.
The mission will contribute to the implementation of UN Security Council Resolution 1701, which calls for the deployment of Lebanese government forces in southern Lebanon and the withdrawal of armed groups from the area.
It will also complement existing EU assistance through the European Peace Facility and coordinate with EU member states, the United Nations and other international partners supporting Lebanon's security sector.
The decision formally establishes the mission, although its deployment remains subject to further operational planning and a separate decision by the EU Council.
The announcement follows a visit to Beirut on 8 October by Kallas, who outlined plans for a European mission to strengthen Lebanon's security institutions.
Kallas stressed that the initiative was not intended to replace the United Nations Interim Force in Lebanon (UNIFIL), whose current mandate is scheduled to end on 31 December, with a phased withdrawal expected over the following year.
US objections to European security role
However, the Lebanese news website Al-Modon reported on Monday that Washington had expressed objections in principle to the proposed European mission, citing sources familiar with discussions over Lebanon's future security arrangements.
According to the report, the US opposes establishing another international military arrangement resembling UNIFIL, preferring existing coordination mechanisms and a greater security role for the Lebanese army.
The reported disagreement reflects competing approaches to the international presence in Lebanon, with European governments seeking to maintain a role in supporting the country's security institutions as UNIFIL prepares to leave.
The reported American objections have not been independently confirmed, and there has been no indication that Washington has formally opposed Monday's EU Council decision.
Al-Modon also reported that discussions were underway over a separate monitoring committee potentially involving Italy, Switzerland and Jordan, although its composition and responsibilities had yet to be finalised.
The proposed committee would address questions surrounding the verification of security commitments, including the deployment of Lebanese forces, the withdrawal of Israeli troops and the monitoring of violations.
Israel has also opposed the deployment of a new international force to replace UNIFIL, favouring direct security coordination with the Lebanese army through US-backed mechanisms, according to Al-Modon.
The future of southern Lebanon's security arrangements remains contentious as Israeli forces continue to occupy positions inside Lebanese territory and carry out military operations despite agreements intended to secure their withdrawal.
Lebanese officials have repeatedly called for an international presence capable of monitoring violations and supporting the army's deployment across the south.
UNIFIL, established in 1978, has played a central role in monitoring the border area, documenting violations and coordinating with Lebanese forces.
Its departure raises questions about who will independently monitor the situation along the Blue Line, particularly as disputes persist over Israeli military activity, Hezbollah's weapons and the implementation of existing security agreements.
While the newly approved European mission is intended to strengthen Lebanon's security institutions, it will not assume UNIFIL's peacekeeping responsibilities, leaving the future of international monitoring in southern Lebanon unresolved.

Bipartisan US senators say Trump’s Russian diesel deal conflicts with 2022 ban, as he presses Kyiv to spare Russian refineries
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
15:22:07 UTC
00:22:07 KST

Seven US senators from both parties said the Trump administration's decision to authorize Russian diesel imports conflicts with a 2022 law banning Russian energy imports and accused it of failing to consult Congress, in a statement on 11 October.
The dispute comes as the war with Iran drives up US fuel prices, which US President Donald Trump has blamed on Ukraine's strikes on Russian refineries. Trump says Russian supplies will help bring prices down, while lawmakers warn that purchases could provide Moscow with revenue to continue its war against Ukraine.
The senators—Republicans Susan Collins, Lisa Murkowski, Thom Tillis, and John Curtis, and Democrats Jeanne Shaheen, Richard Blumenthal, and Ron Wyden—called on the administration to reverse course, saying the US should not provide Russian President Vladimir Putin with “a financial lifeline.”
What the 2022 law requires before the ban can end
The law, signed on 8 April 2022, allows the president to end the import ban only after submitting a certification to Congress. The certification must find that Russia has agreed to pull out its forces and stop the fighting on terms Ukraine's free and independent government accepts, no longer poses an immediate threat of attack to any NATO member, and recognizes Ukrainians' right to pick their own government.
The law also requires consultation with four congressional committees and a report at least 45 days before certification. The termination takes effect 90 days after certification unless a joint resolution of disapproval is enacted into law during that period. The senators allege the administration failed to meet the consultation and reporting requirements. Their statement does not establish whether a certification has been submitted.
Treasury’s license cites sanctions rules, not the 2022 law
The Treasury Department's Office of Foreign Assets Control issued General License No. 135 on 9 October, authorizing certain transactions involving Russian-origin diesel that would otherwise be restricted under US sanctions regulations. It runs until 7 April 2027 and cites sanctions regulations, not the 2022 import-ban law.
EU blacklists 1,569 Russian arms suppliers and their bosses in its biggest sanctions round ever, as Trump eases up on Moscow
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent defended the deal on Fox News on 11 October, saying the administration would proceed under existing legal authority. He said lawmakers who argued that either the earlier law or the current Lindsey Graham sanctions law prohibited the deal were wrong, and argued the agreement would lower prices, Reuters reported.
How much diesel Trump says Russia will supply
Trump said on Truth Social that Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel to US and global markets, followed by 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons after that. He said Russia would deliver another 3 million tons “within a short period of time,” depending on the condition of its diesel refineries. The promised volumes have not been independently verified.
Russia partially lifted its diesel export ban on 10 October, allowing 500,000 tons onto the global market at this stage, the Russian government said, according to state news agency TASS.
A House bill to block Russian oil purchases
Pennsylvania Republican Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick plans to introduce the Ronald Reagan Peace Through Strength Act to block Russian oil purchases and use a discharge petition to force a House vote, Axios reported. The procedure can force consideration of a bill if 218 House members sign. Republican Rep. Don Bacon said he would support the bill and called Trump's decision a serious mistake, according to Ukrainska Pravda.
Barrasso defends the deal. Zelenskyy calls it an investment in war
On CBS's Face the Nation on 11 October, Senate Majority Whip John Barrasso, a Republican from Wyoming, called the deal “another point of leverage” for Trump to use against Putin. Asked whether the decision violated US law, Barrasso said the president was balancing competing priorities and had to make tough decisions.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy wrote on Telegram on 9 October:
“Allowing Russia to sell petroleum products is an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged.”
Trump also expects Ukraine to stop striking Russian refineries under his proposed energy ceasefire, a White House official told Axios. Zelenskyy said Kyiv would halt such strikes if Moscow did the same.
