Reservations under threat: the Cabinet of Ministers wants to reduce the limits and review the status of critically important enterprises
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
18:21:10 EEST
00:21:10 KST

Reservations under threat: the Cabinet of Ministers wants to reduce the limits and review the status of critically important enterprises
Kyiv • UNN
The Ministry of Economy proposes reducing reservation limits and changing the calculation of quotas. The draft has not yet been adopted, so the rules may change.
The Cabinet of Ministers of Ukraine is preparing changes to the procedure for reserving liable-for-military-service employees. For Ukrainians, this will mean the abolition of 100% reservations, particularly in the "defense industry" and energy sectors, UNN reports, citing a post by Member of Parliament Yaroslav Zhelezniak, which he published on his official Telegram channel.
Details
The draft also introduces a new approach to calculating the number of reserved employees and revises the criteria for a business’s critical importance. According to the parliamentarian, the document was prepared by the Ministry of Economy. It should be emphasized separately that it has not yet been adopted, so the rules described by the parliamentarian are not currently in effect and may change during the approval process.
Which enterprises will have their reservation quotas reduced
Under the changes proposed by officials from the Ministry of Economy, even enterprises whose operations are essential to the country’s defense capability or the functioning of vital infrastructure may lose the ability to reserve their entire staff.
The most significant restrictions are proposed for the defense-industrial complex and the energy sector. Instead of the current ability to reserve up to 100% of liable-for-military-service employees, the maximum limit for such enterprises would be 85%. This applies, in particular, to fuel and energy enterprises and contractors that ensure their operation.
For heat-supply enterprises, water utilities, and household-waste management companies, the share is proposed to be reduced from 75% to 60%. For all other critically important enterprises, the overall limit would remain at 50%.
How the calculation of the number of employees eligible for reservation will change
One separate innovation concerns the rules for enterprises that can reserve up to half of their liable-for-military-service employees. They are proposing to exclude from the calculation base employees who already have a deferment from mobilization on other legal grounds. This includes, in particular, students, caregivers, and parents of three or more children. Previously, such people were taken into account when determining the maximum number of reservations.
For example, if an enterprise has 100 liable-for-military-service employees, 20 of whom have deferments on other grounds, under the current approach it could expect to receive 50 reservations. Under the proposed mechanism, the quota would be calculated based on 80 people, leaving only 40 reservations available.
Who will decide whether an enterprise is critical
The draft resolution referred to by Yaroslav Zhelezniak also provides for the creation of a Coordination Center under the Cabinet of Ministers consisting of 17 people. It is to include representatives of the Ministry of Economy, the Ministry of Defense, the Security Service of Ukraine, the Main Directorate of Intelligence, the Foreign Intelligence Service, the National Police, and other agencies. According to the information released, without a recommendation from this center, enterprises will not be able to obtain critically important status or have a reservation quota above 50% approved. The center will also be able to recommend revoking a status that has already been granted.
At the same time, the draft does not establish clear deadlines for issuing recommendations, a transparent assessment procedure, or a separate mechanism for appealing such conclusions.
What is to change by October 20, 2026
Under the draft, by October 20, ministries and regional state administrations must review the sectoral and regional criteria under which enterprises are recognized as critically important. However, attention should be paid to the fact that, at this stage, the document does not explain what will happen to reservations already оформed above the proposed limits. Therefore, there are currently no grounds to speak of their automatic cancellation.
How society reacted to the changes in the reservation rules
The initiative has already prompted objections from representatives of the defense industry. In particular, Ihor Fedirko, executive director of the Ukrainian Council of Armaments Manufacturers, emphasized that the restrictions could complicate the fulfillment of defense contracts due to a shortage of specialists.
From paper lists to "Diia": how the rules for reservation from mobilization have changed since 2022
Since the beginning of Russia’s full-scale invasion, Ukraine has changed the rules for reserving conscripts for military service several times. Over four and a half years, the procedure has evolved from paper lists to processing through "Diia," while the requirements for enterprises have become stricter.
In March 2022, the government adopted Resolution No. 194, which established the procedure for reserving employees of government bodies and enterprises that met the needs of the military and the population. The lists were approved through government bodies, while the decisions were made by the Ministry of Economy. Deferrals were granted for up to six months.
In January 2023, Resolution No. 76 introduced a system of critically important enterprises. Companies that met economic and sectoral criteria were granted the right to reserve employees. For most, a basic limit of 50% of conscript-eligible personnel was established, while exceptions were provided for.
In 2024, the rules were changed in view of the needs of the defense industry and the energy sector. Certain enterprises were allowed to reserve up to 100% of their employees, and the reservation period was extended to one year. In July, the service became available through "Diia." At the end of the year, the authorities tightened inspections and introduced a salary requirement for most private companies, set at least 2.5 times the minimum wage.
In 2025, reservation opportunities were expanded for enterprises that support the Armed Forces of Ukraine and critical infrastructure facilities. A limit of up to 75% was established for water utilities, heat-supply enterprises, and waste-management operators. Critically important enterprises in areas of hostilities were allowed to reserve up to 100% of their personnel. The law also provided for a 45-day temporary deferral for certain new employees in the defense sector who had violations related to military registration.
In 2026, the government raised the salary threshold for most private enterprises from 2.5 to three minimum wages and provided for the repeated confirmation of critical status.
We remind you
From September 1, 2026, Ukraine raised the salary requirements for reserved employees to three minimum wages. In addition, employees working part-time for multiple employers and persons with another deferral began to be counted at only one place of employment.

For years, Hungary tied Ukraine’s whole EU course to ethnic Hungarians’ language rights. Kyiv has now passed the schooling law meant to lift the block
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
15:19:12 UTC
00:19:12 KST

Kyiv just cleared the important roadblock for Budapest, which stood between Kyiv and EU membership talks. Ukraine’s parliament has passed a bill on schooling in minority languages, meant to finally lift Hungary’s block on the country’s path toward EU membership, with 266 of the 450 lawmakers voting in favor, UNIAN reports.
Hungary has been the lone EU member blocking the opening of four of Ukraine’s negotiating clusters, stages of the membership process, over how Kyiv treats the Hungarian minority in Ukraine's Zakarpattia region. Roughly 80,000 ethnic Hungarians live in it, and Budapest had tied Ukraine’s entire EU course to their language rights.
Lawmakers have instructed the parliament’s speaker to sign the law without delay and send it to President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
What the law changes in schools
The bill keeps Ukrainian as the main language of education, but guarantees classes in minority languages where they exist. Minorities may study in the official languages of EU member states alongside Ukrainian, and pupils may use their language in other forms of communication on school grounds.
A school can gain the status of a national-minority institution if more than half of its pupils study in that minority language, provided that language is an official EU language. Parents of at least two-thirds of a minority class can also ask the school to expand the list of subjects taught in Ukrainian.
The dispute dates back years
Ukraine’s 2017 education law and 2019 language law narrowed minority-language schooling and required more Ukrainian in secondary grades, which then-Hungarian leader Viktor Orban treated as an attack on the Hungarians of Zakarpattia, blocking Kyiv’s NATO and EU steps for years, EUalive reports. Kyiv’s position was that the laws applied to all minorities and excluded Russian.
Hungary’s newer government, in office since spring 2026, inherited the veto. Budapest lifted it on the first cluster, which the EU opened in June, Ukraine’s first since gaining candidate status in 2022, but made the rest conditional on this law.
With the bill passed, Hungary is set to allow the EU to open two more clusters, on the internal market and competitiveness, at a Council meeting in Luxembourg on 13 October. Kyiv aims to open all its clusters by year’s end.

Far-right party Reform UK leader Nigel Farage pledged Monday to suspend the UK’s asylum system for up to five years if his party wins the next general election, including voiding outstanding applications, as part of a proposed crackdown on immigration.
Speaking at a news conference, Farage said a Reform government would end the asylum system for its first parliamentary term, arguing that the UK can no longer afford the security risks associated with its current arrangements.
“We will end the asylum system for up to five years,” he said.
“We literally have no idea who is here, and we frankly can't afford to take the risk. It's not as if we've been ungenerous over the course of the last decade,” he added.
Under his party’s proposals, suspending the system would also invalidate pending asylum applications.
Farage said a Reform government would seek to deport all foreign nationals convicted of crimes and people residing in the UK illegally.
He described the policy as an effort to restore national security and strengthen border controls.
He said he would prioritize making Britain “a country that puts national security at the top of the agenda, a country that does everything it can to protect its own citizens, and a country that detains and deports people that come illegally, as virtually every other country in the world does.”
Farage said the party also proposed imposing visa and flight restrictions, and potentially tariffs, on countries that refuse to accept the return of their nationals, citing Pakistan as an example.
The proposals would involve disapplying the 1951 UN Convention Relating to the Status of Refugees, to which the UK is a signatory.
The convention establishes international obligations to protect refugees, including the principle of non-refoulement, which prohibits returning people to territories where they face specified threats to their life or freedom. 
Farage accuses Burnham of lying over claims of Russian interference in Brexit referendum
At the same news conference, Farage accused Prime Minister Andy Burnham of lying over claims of Russian interference in the 2016 Brexit referendum, calling him “a liar. Yes, a liar.”
Citing remarks by former Prime Minister Boris Johnson, also formerly Britain’s top diplomat, Farage said: “Boris Johnson, when he became foreign secretary, one of the first questions he asked was: 'Was there seen to be Russian interference in referendum campaign?' And the answer was no.”
The UK left the EU in 2020, four years after a referendum in which about 52% of voters chose to leave.
At the ruling Labour Party’s annual conference last month, Burnham said Britain should look at different options for its relationship with the European Union, including possibly rejoining the bloc.

====================================================================================================

On Columbus Day, remember Abraham Zacuto, the Jewish astronomer history forgot - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
15:17:37 UTC
00:17:37 KST

Every October, Christopher Columbus returns not only as history but as controversy. The voyages associated with his name transformed the world, but their legacy is inseparable from conquest, coercion and the destruction that followed European expansion.
Yet the same Iberian age also produced a quieter and far less controversial revolution: advances in astronomy, mathematics, cartography, instruments and practical navigation that made sustained oceanic voyaging possible. Its protagonists included scholars, translators, mapmakers, instrument makers and pilots whose names are far less familiar than those of the captains who commanded the ships.
Among them, one figure deserves particular remembrance on Columbus Day: Abraham Zacuto, a Jewish astronomer born in Salamanca around 1452. Zacuto belonged to the same Iberian world as Columbus, but experienced its monarchies very differently. In 1492, Columbus sailed west under the patronage of Ferdinand and Isabella. That same year, the Catholic monarchs ordered the Jews of their realms to convert or leave. Zacuto left Castile and continued his work in Portugal. The celebrated maritime discoveries and the expulsion of Iberian Jewry were therefore not distinct historical worlds; they unfolded under the same rulers, at the same moment, within the same culture of ambition, knowledge and power.
Zacuto stands out within that larger scientific story. He was a rabbi, astronomer, mathematician and historian whose astronomical work helped give oceanic navigation a new degree of precision and practicality. His contribution belongs not at the margins of the Age of Exploration but within the scientific infrastructure that made long-distance navigation increasingly systematic.
Around 1478, Zacuto completed his great Hebrew astronomical work, “Ha-Hibbur ha-Gadol,” the “Great Composition.” Working within a long scientific conversation that included Greek, Islamic, Jewish and Christian astronomy, he refined and organized astronomical calculations in forms of exceptional practical value.
After the expulsion from Spain, Zacuto entered Portugal at precisely the moment when the kingdom was pushing maritime exploration farther into the Atlantic and down the African coast. Zacuto’s pupil, José Vizinho, a Jewish adviser to Portuguese King John II, was associated with the practical Latin and Castilian presentation of Zacuto’s astronomical material. In 1496, Zacuto’s Almanach Perpetuum was printed at Leiria in four known issues - three with Latin preliminary matter and one with Castilian.
Zacuto's research proved incredibly useful
The importance of those tables was intensely practical. They supplied precise, ready-to-use values for the changing position of the sun through the year. For a pilot on the high seas in daylight, far from recognizable coastlines, this meant that a noon observation of the sun could be combined with solar-declination data to determine latitude - the ship’s north-south position. The difficult astronomical calculations had already been embodied in the tables. What remained aboard ship was an operational procedure: Observe the sun, consult the appropriate value and calculate latitude. That combination of precision and usability greatly facilitated daytime position-finding at sea. Solar tables derived from Zacuto’s work entered early Portuguese navigational manuals and became part of the practical scientific culture of oceanic travel.
The clearest measure of Zacuto’s importance may be what happened next. The Almanach did not remain a local Portuguese publication. Its tables were reprinted repeatedly in Venice in 1498, 1502, 1525 and 1528. A work first printed in Leiria moved into one of Europe’s great publishing centers and continued to circulate for decades. That publishing history alone tells us something about the standing Zacuto’s astronomy acquired.
Its reach extended farther still. Zacuto’s astronomical material was translated and adapted into Arabic. One Arabic version was produced, likely in Istanbul, in 1505-06; another, associated with Ahmad ibn Qasim al-Hajari in Morocco around 1624, survives in several manuscripts. The work of a Jewish astronomer writing in Hebrew in 15th-century Salamanca had crossed into Latin, Castilian and Arabic scientific cultures.
Zacuto’s name also became entwined with the memory of the great navigators. Accounts have long connected his tables with Columbus and Vasco da Gama, including the famous 1504 lunar eclipse in Jamaica. In this episode, Columbus intimidated Indigenous Jamaicans by predicting the disappearance of the moon, relying on Zacuto’s almanac, which he had on board. A manuscript connected with the Almanach also survives in Seville’s Biblioteca Colombina, the library created by Columbus’s son Hernando. Taken together, these associations reveal the stature Zacuto’s work acquired in the historical memory of the Age of Exploration.
Exiled from Portugal as a Jew
Perhaps the most striking part of Zacuto’s story is what happened to the man himself. Portugal valued the kind of expertise he represented. Yet in December 1496, King Manuel I ordered Portugal’s Jews to leave unless they converted, and in 1497 the crown subjected the Jewish population to mass forced conversion. Zacuto left Portugal as well.
Exile did not end either his travels or his scholarship. From Portugal he moved through North Africa, including Tunis, before eventually reaching Jerusalem. There, late in life, he returned once more to the astronomical work that had made his name known across the Mediterranean, recalculating and updating his earlier tables for the Jewish calendar and the meridian of Jerusalem. The strongest recent reconstruction of his life places his death in Jerusalem in Tevet 5274, or late 1513 or very early 1514 - commonly given as 1514.
Zacuto’s story is therefore larger than a footnote to Columbus. It joins two strands of Sephardic history too often told apart: persecution and exile, and the transmission of knowledge, texts and technologies across borders.
Zacuto’s own tables and 15th-century procedures are now obsolete, but their underlying navigational logic endures. Modern celestial navigation still determines position by combining observations of the sun, moon, planets or stars with authoritative astronomical data. The US Naval Academy requires all midshipmen to study navigation, and its current curriculum includes celestial navigation alongside electronic methods. The US Naval Observatory still describes celestial navigation as a critical independent backup to GPS and other electronic systems. And the Nautical Almanac, first published in 1855, remains the standard US Navy resource for marine celestial navigation. The instruments and calculations have changed, but the essential logic remains: Observe the heavens, consult reliable astronomical data and determine position.
Zacuto’s scientific reputation also survives in an unexpected place. In 1935, the International Astronomical Union formally adopted the name Zagut for a lunar crater honoring Abraham ben Shmuel Zacuto. Modern astronomy has, quite literally, written his name onto the Moon.
Columbus remains a household name because voyages leave dramatic images: ships, landfalls, encounters and conquest. The calculations, tables, instruments, translations and printed books that made such voyages possible are easier to forget. Remembering Zacuto widens the story: His tables brought greater precision and practicality to daytime navigation; his work crossed languages and continents; and his life traced the routes of Sephardic exile from Iberia to Jerusalem. The age of maritime discovery was also an age of scientific discovery, and some of the knowledge that carried Iberian ships across oceans was created by scholars whose communities those same monarchies expelled.

Lithuanian lawmakers on Monday called for legal safeguards to protect people against artificial intelligence-generated voice cloning, according to broadcaster LRT.
Lawmakers proposed changes to the Civil Code to recognize a legal right to one’s voice, requiring consent for its reproduction, publication or other use amid rising concerns over AI-generated deepfakes.
The proposed safeguards would apply to recordings of a person’s real voice, as well as imitations and AI-generated voices capable of identifying them.

The government, meanwhile, said it would review whether existing Lithuanian legislation provides sufficient protection for individuals’ voices and digital likenesses.

Homeland Security Investigations, a division of the Department of Homeland Security, conducted the raid, Fox News reported. The Department of Justice later confirmed the raid after CNBC asked about it. DHS declined to comment.
A person familiar with the situation, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss the non-public investigation, told CNBC that the investigation into Omar is complex and has been going on for years.
MS NOW reported that a law enforcement source with direct knowledge of the raid said the investigation into Omar is based on allegations of fraud.
Omar, 44, was born in Somalia and brought to the United States as a child. She became a U.S. citizen in 2000 at 17. She was elected to Congress in November 2018 to represent Minnesota's 5th District, which includes all of Minneapolis.
She and Rep. Rashida Tlaib, D-Mich., became the first two Muslim women elected to Congress.
Omar has been a target of criticism by President Donald Trump, and heckled Trump during his State of the Union address to Congress on Feb. 24, which came on the heels of aggressive immigration enforcement actions in Minneapolis by federal authorities.
The Department of Justice, in a statement to CNBC when asked about the raid, said, "Today in the Washington, D.C., area, Homeland Security Investigations executed a judicially authorized search warrant secured by the Department of Justice."
"This enforcement action is part of an ongoing federal investigation," the statement said.
The raid comes less than a month before November's midterm elections. Omar is seeking another term as a representative for Minnesota's 5th District.
CNBC has requested comment from Omar's office.
In September, DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin told right-wing commentator Benny Johnson at the Republican midterm convention in Dallas that DHS was investigating issues around Omar and her family's immigration to the United States.
"There may be more to this, the whole family migration and possibly some illegal activity for them to come to the United States to begin with," said Mullin. He said the investigation could end with deportations.
The DOJ, for years, has had a policy regarding the announcement and initiation of federal investigations and prosecutions close to elections. The policy discourages beginning an investigation, taking investigative steps, bringing criminal charges, or making public statements for the purpose of affecting an election or to give a candidate an advantage or disadvantage.
A person familiar with the raid on Omar's home told CNBC on Monday that the DOJ does not consider that action to violate the policy because the raid was not meant to be public.
Republican John Nagel is running against Omar in a race the Cook Political Report with Amy Walter rates "solid Democrat." The general election is just over three weeks away on Nov. 3.
The Democratic leadership of the House of Representatives blasted the Trump administration for the raid.
"The Trump administration's raid on Congresswoman Ilhan Omar's home is deeply disturbing and raises serious questions about the continued corrupt weaponization of the federal government against Donald Trump's adversaries," said House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., Minority Whip Katherine Clark, D-Mass., and Rep. Egypt explores hydrogen tram for new capital amid cost-of-living pressures
Egypt is exploring a hydrogen-powered tram network for its New Administrative Capital, state media reported on Sunday, advancing another high-tech transport proposal for President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi’s flagship project as households face persistent cost-of-living pressures.
Egypt's National Authority for Tunnels signed a memorandum of understanding with South Korean manufacturer Hyundai Rotem on 7 October to examine a network comprising 44 tram trainsets along a route roughly spanning 28 kilometres.
The agreement remains at the feasibility stage, with the parties expected to assess how economically viable it is before deciding whether to proceed. The announcement did not disclose a project budget, financing arrangements or proposed passenger fares.
The trams would run on hydrogen fuel cells, avoiding the need for overhead electrical wires, according to Egyptian state-affiliated outlet Cairo24. Potential cooperation with Hyundai Rotem would extend beyond supplying vehicles to railway systems, operations and maintenance.
The proposal would bring another transport system to a city whose construction has been estimated to cost around $58 billion.
The development has become a focal point of scrutiny over Sisi’s infrastructure priorities and the economic consequences of large-scale construction projects. Analysts have argued that debt-fuelled, military-led megaprojects had contributed to Egypt’s economic troubles, challenging official claims that the new capital would not burden state finances.
The latest proposal comes as Egyptians continue to absorb the effects of successive price increases, even as the annual pace of inflation has eased slightly. Urban inflation stood at 13.9 percent in September, down from 14.5 percent in August, according to figures from the Central Agency for Public Mobilisation and Statistics. Consumer prices nevertheless increased 1.3 percent compared with the previous month.
Transport prices were 24.3 percent higher than a year earlier, while housing and utility costs rose 35.2 percent, according to CAPMAS figures compiled by Trading Economics. The increases underline the pressure on household budgets beyond the headline inflation rate.
In its October 2026 poverty brief, the World Bank estimated that 33.5 percent of Egyptians lived below the national poverty line in 2021/22, the latest survey period for which an estimate was available. Its April 2026 economic outlook warned that the socioeconomic damage from the 2023–24 inflation surge persisted, with double-digit inflation continuing to constrain purchasing power.

Antarctic sea ice records its third-smallest winter peak
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
15:11:09 UTC
00:11:09 KST

Antarctic sea ice records its third-smallest winter peak
Sea ice around Antarctica reached its largest extent of 2026, but coverage remained unusually low even at its seasonal peak. The winter maximum was the third lowest in the satellite record, Qazinform News Agency reports.
According to NASA and the US National Snow and Ice Data Center (NSIDC), sea ice reached its maximum extent on September 14, covering approximately 17.59 million square kilometers.
Sea ice around Antarctica expands each winter and retreats each summer. It usually reaches its greatest extent in September, at the end of the Southern Hemisphere’s winter, and its smallest in February. Scientists therefore compare both summer minimums and winter maximums. The latter show how far the ice cover has expanded during the colder months.
These measurements concern frozen seawater surrounding the continent, rather than glaciers on Antarctica itself.
For many years, Antarctic sea ice extent gradually increased. Between 1979 and 2014, it grew by about 1% per decade. From 2012 to 2014, winter sea ice extent set new records for three consecutive years.
The pattern then changed. Growth stopped in 2015, and significant declines began in 2016. Although sea ice partially recovered in some years, its extent generally remained below normal. In 2023, scientists recorded both the lowest summer minimum and the lowest winter maximum in the satellite record.
Special satellite instruments allow scientists to monitor the ice even through clouds. They detect natural microwave emissions from Earth’s surface, which differ between ice and open water. This helps researchers map the boundaries of the ice cover regardless of cloud conditions. Such observations have been conducted since late 1978.
Earlier, Qazinform News Agency reported that NASA scientists had developed a more precise method to track shifts in Earth’s center of mass.

SBU detains 19-year-old suspected of plotting bomb attack on bus full of soldiers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
15:07:14 UTC
00:07:14 KST

Ukraine's Security Service (SBU) has foiled an alleged Russian plot to bomb a bus carrying Ukrainian soldiers in the northwestern city of Rivne, detaining a 19-year-old student suspected of preparing the attack, the SBU and Rivne Regional Prosecutor's Office said on Oct. 12.
According to the SBU, the suspect planted an improvised explosive device under a bus transporting "an entire unit" of Ukrainian soldiers and installed a remotely accessible camera disguised in a juice box opposite the parking area to monitor the vehicle.
Russian intelligence operatives planned to detonate the bomb once the soldiers boarded the bus and were moving to their permanent deployment location, the SBU said.
The suspect acted in exchange for money after being recruited by Russian intelligence services through Telegram channels offering quick earnings, according to the SBU.
After arriving in Rivne, he allegedly collected the explosives from a hiding place designated by his Russian handler and planted the device under the military vehicle. The explosive device was reinforced with two glass bottles containing flammable liquid, the SBU said.
SBU officers discovered the plot, neutralized the explosives, and detained the suspect at the city's bus station when he attempted to leave for Kyiv. Investigators also seized his phone, which the SBU said he had used to report the planted device to his Russian handler.
The Rivne Regional Prosecutor's Office said the suspect had been formally notified of suspicion of an attempted terrorist attack. A court ordered his detention without bail. If convicted, he faces up to eight years in prison and possible confiscation of property.
The SBU said it had foiled a series of alleged terrorist plots prepared by Russian intelligence services in Rivne this year. Previous alleged plots targeted a park area and administrative buildings in the city center.

Zelenskyy signs law on educational rights of national minorities needed to open EU negotiation clusters
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
18:05:50 EEST
00:05:50 KST

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy signed the law On amendments to certain Laws of Ukraine regarding the Guarantee of educational rights of Indigenous Peoples of Ukraine and persons belonging to national minorities (communities) of Ukraine (Bill No. 16119), which is intended to unblock the opening of two negotiation clusters on Ukraine's accession to the European Union by lifting Hungary's veto.
According to the Verkhovna Rada's website, the law, which had been sent to the President of Ukraine for signature earlier on Monday, has already been returned with the head of state's signature.
The bill was supported by 266 members of parliament during Monday's plenary session.
It codifies the right of children from national minorities and indigenous peoples of Ukraine to study in their native language alongside the state language, rather than instead of it. "The Ukrainian language remains a guaranteed component of education for every child. No provision of the bill restricts the scope of the official language; on the contrary, it preserves guarantees for its study, free command, and use in the educational process… Important: The additional rights provided for in the bill apply exclusively to languages that are official languages of the European Union and to the languages of Ukraine's indigenous peoples, and do not apply to the Russian language," the Ministry of Education and Science said earlier.
For example, if an educational institution has a class where children are taught in Hungarian, they will be able to use the language of an EU member state (alongside Ukrainian) not only during lessons but also when communicating with teachers and other participants in the educational process.
The document also defines the concept of a general secondary education institution with the status of a national minority (community) institution, and in order to qualify for this status, the institution must have 50% plus one of its students studying in the language of the national minority (community).
According to estimates by the Ministry of Education, 149 schools – about 1.2% of all general secondary education institutions in Ukraine – will be eligible for this status. Separately, regardless of whether this status is granted, any school with at least one class (group) taught in a minority language is entitled to provide signs, educational documents (upon parents' request), and administrative documentation in that minority language – specifically for that class.
Institutions that receive this status as a result of the law's adoption must have at least 20% of their students studying in a minority language in order to retain it. If this percentage falls below 20%, the right to this status is revoked, subject to approval by the Ministry of Education.
In addition, according to the document, parents will be able to request an expansion of the list of subjects taught in Ukrainian. In other words, if a child is enrolled in a class or group taught in the language of an indigenous people or a national minority that is an official language of the EU, the number of subjects taught in Ukrainian may be increased. To expand the list of subjects, written support from at least two-thirds of the parents in the relevant class will be required.
It is stipulated that the reorganization or closure of municipal institutions with the status of "national minority/indigenous people's school" will require mandatory approval from the Ministry of Education. At the same time, the school's founder is obligated to ensure that students can continue their education, upon their parents' request, at an institution with the corresponding status within the same community.
According to the Ministry of Education's assessment, this provision may affect a maximum of 141 municipal schools in Zakarpattia, Chernivtsi, Odesa, and Lviv regions.
The law also clarifies the procedure for applying the requirement for a state certificate in the Ukrainian language to heads of private educational institutions that have a class or group taught in the language of a national minority or indigenous people. This applies only to heads who are already holding such a position at the time the law takes effect. Thus, for the duration of their tenure in these positions, they are exempt from the obligation to confirm their proficiency in the state language with a certificate. However, the obligation to know and use the state language remains in effect.
The Education Ministry said the provision has a specific and limited scope – it applies to the heads of 29 institutions nationwide.
Earlier, Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar responded to the submission of a draft law on the educational rights of national minorities to the Verkhovna Rada and expressed his expectation that such rights for the Hungarian national minority in Ukraine will be fully guaranteed in practice.
Ukraine's Deputy Prime Minister for European and Euro-Atlantic Integration Vsevolod Chentsov said negotiation clusters 2 and 3 ("Internal Market" and "Competitiveness and Inclusive Growth") regarding Ukraine's accession to the European Union could be opened as early as October 13, provided that the Verkhovna Rada passes the law on the educational rights of national minorities the day before.
In turn, on October 12, Hungarian Foreign Minister Anita Orbán confirmed that the Ukrainian parliament's adoption of the law on education for national minorities would allow the intergovernmental conference, scheduled for October 13, to open the following clusters for Ukraine as part of its EU accession negotiations.

Will Ukraine survive the winter?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
15:04:08 UTC
00:04:08 KST

Will Ukraine survive the winter?
Washington’s position on Ukraine remains ambivalent while losses mount and an energy crisis deepens.
As winter approaches, Russia has lifted its ban on exports of diesel and is preparing to sell hundreds of thousands of tonnes to the United States and other countries. The move is part of a deal negotiated between US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin, which resulted in the US Department of the Treasury issuing a sanctions waiver on Russian fuel.
The deal was struck amid a growing global crisis over energy supplies and prices. More importantly for Trump, he announced it just a few weeks before the US midterm elections, in which his Republican Party risks losing its majority in both houses of Congress.
The deal’s principal significance is political. Trump is in dire need of being seen by American voters as caring for them. The fact that Trump turned to Putin and the latter was in a position to oblige him reflects Russia’s crucial role in the global energy market. But it also revealed the White House’s willingness to dump a client at a time of weakness – Ukraine, in this case – to serve domestic interests.
Whether the deal constitutes a turning point in the US approach to the war in Ukraine is not clear yet. The fate of last year’s Anchorage understanding suggests it should be approached with caution. Trump’s sudden mention post-deal of an “energy ceasefire”, which is unacceptable to Russia, looks like the US president balancing a move towards Moscow with another one reassuring Kiev – and the Europeans.
In any event, the US’s ambivalent position is not helping Ukraine and its European allies as they struggle with an energy crisis and continuing losses.
The conflict, since its very start, has been about much more than what happens on the battlefield. When the US-led West in the spring of 2022, declared the “strategic defeat of Russia” as its top goal, it hoped that Western sanctions would “turn the rouble into rubble”, as then-US President Joe Biden famously said, and leave the Russian economy in tatters, all translating into Russia’s military collapse. This, as we know, did not work.
Now, Ukraine and its European allies face another difficult winter that will test their resilience to continue fighting a war of attrition.
Their strategy – to escalate through a heavy air campaign against targets deep in Russian territories – has not worked either. The expectation was that ordinary Russian citizens, once directly affected by the war, would rise up and compel the Kremlin to agree to a ceasefire that would give Ukraine much-needed respite. The result, however, was just the opposite: more support for the Kremlin’s policies, not less.
In retaliation for the campaign, which Putin admitted cost 1 percent of Russia’s gross domestic product, the Russian army has launched its own. It has dropped some of its self-imposed restraint and begun hitting the targets that heretofore it had avoided, such as ships carrying goods to and from Ukraine, bridges across the Dnieper River and data centres.
Some observers have wondered whether for Russia, this is a way “to escalate to de-escalate” – six to nine months of intense air war in combination with advances on the ground that could bring the conflict to an end.
Indeed, Ukraine’s economy is suffering severe damage. Its Black Sea ports can no longer handle its wheat exports; the country’s steel industry has halted production; rail logistics are disrupted by the lack of operable engines.
Meanwhile, Kiev is being subjected to not just daily but virtually round-the-clock drone and missile attacks. The Ukrainian capital’s outlook for the coming winter is dire. Local authorities have started calling on residents to leave as winter preparations, like heating backups and food and water stockpiles, may not be enough to pull through the cold months.
Yet, Ukraine’s leader Volodymir Zelenskyy is as defiant as ever. For him, there is no turning back. If he agrees to withdraw Ukrainian forces from the remaining part of Donetsk, as Putin has demanded, he has to fear for his life. If there is a new presidential election in Ukraine, he clearly will lose. Once he loses, his patrons will dump him: just like they did to the likes of Mikheil Saakashvili, Georgia’s ex-president, who is now serving time in a Tbilisi prison.
Ukrainian politicians have become more restive of late, but they are not breaking ranks with Zelenskyy on the issue of war and peace. Nationalists at home and donors in the West are adamant that the fight will go on.
For Europe in particular, this war is not about Ukraine. It is about Russia. The current opportunity of using what had been the second-largest republic in the former Soviet Union to weaken Russia, Europe’s historic adversary, is too good to be missed. Europe, which pays for half of Kiev’s budget, appears to think it can afford to continue fighting “to the last Ukrainian”, hoping that it can kill more Russians and thus cripple their country.
This is not to blunt the supposedly imminent Russian threat, which is a red herring. Russia is precisely the enemy at the door that the EU needs to keep itself together. Military Keynesianism is a way to relaunch the economy, and branding political competitors as “Putin’s agents” is convenient to the extreme.
Besides, a number of EU and NATO members are covertly seeking historical revanchism: Germany for Hitler’s defeat in 1945, Poland for its several partitions, Sweden for Russia ending its great power status, Britain for the loss of its empire and so on.
Finally, having invested hundreds of billions in Kiev, Europe will not call it quits in Ukraine until its financial and political losses begin to outweigh the usefulness of its Ukrainian proxy. Or until a version of the 1962 Cuban nuclear missile crisis brings them to their senses.
Russia’s tested resilience in this war is superior to Ukraine’s in material terms and to Europe’s in nonmaterial ones, which will likely determine what happens in the future.
Chances are that both Ukraine and Europe will survive this coming winter – all the losses, privations and sufferings notwithstanding. They will live to fight another day – meaning a year or two (or less, as Putin has recently suggested) – but in the end Kiev is bound to lose, and Europe will have to grudgingly accept its client’s defeat while pretending that existence of a rump Ukrainian state constitutes a victory of sorts.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

Chinese electric vehicles filmed military personnel and access codes during exercises in Norway

Deepal vehicles rented for the exercises stored footage of military personnel, routes, and access codes to facilities. The recordings were discovered after reviewing the\r\nsystem.
Chinese electric vehicles recorded military activities and access codes to secure facilities during military exercises in Norway. The cars were rented for the needs of the Norwegian army, and the stored footage was discovered by the military personnel themselves. Dagens Næringsliv reports, UNN writes.
Details
At least two of the vehicles were Deepal models, owned by the Chinese conglomerate Changan.
Five thousand territorial defense troops took part in the Øvelse Hovedstad exercise. One of their tasks was to guard Gardermoen Airport in wartime conditions. The recordings were discovered by servicemen who were browsing the onboard system’s menu "out of boredom." Exercise participant Lieutenant Fredrik Blank said:
You can see who gets into the car and who gets out, where we are going, whom we pick up, and how much time we spend at each location
According to Blank, the footage also captured codes that in some cases are entered near gates together with the use of key cards. Due to a shortage of transport, the unit used these vehicles until the end of the exercise, including on the premises of military facilities. The servicemen deleted the recordings only after the exercise and only in those vehicles where it was possible to do so. They reported the discovery to the command in a separate report.
The Norwegian Armed Forces did not answer DN’s questions, but the agency’s press secretary, Karoline Lisne, wrote that it is currently inappropriate to ban vehicles from particular countries on military premises. According to her, this would provide a "limited security gain" while causing significant practical inconvenience.
The vehicles were provided by First Rent A Car Norway, the main supplier under its contract with the army. According to the NTB news agency, the company’s ownership chain leads to China’s Zhejiang Geely Holding Group. The company said it complies with Norwegian and European law.
In February, Poland banned Chinese-made vehicles from entering guarded military facilities over concerns that their cameras and sensors could collect classified data, the American think tank FDD reported. Military personnel were also prohibited from connecting official phones to the multimedia systems of such vehicles.

Adel Abdelrheem, Rania Abushamala

Sudan’s Transitional Sovereignty Council Chairman Abdel Fattah al-Burhan on Monday ordered a fact-finding investigation into the reported killing of miners near the Egyptian border on Saturday.
The council said in a statement that the committee would include representatives of the Public Prosecution and relevant judicial and security bodies.
It will investigate the circumstances surrounding the incident and submit a report on its findings. No deadline was announced.
“Protecting the lives of Sudanese citizens and safeguarding their safety and dignity is a fundamental responsibility of the state,” Burhan said.
He stressed “the need to deal with the incident seriously, ensuring that the facts are uncovered and borders are protected and respected.”
“The leaderships of the two brotherly countries are in contact to establish the circumstances of the incident and make the facts public,” he added.
On Sunday, the independent Emergency Lawyers group said the death toll from an airstrike in the North al-Wadi area inside Sudanese territory had risen to 72 miners. It said Egyptian aircraft were suspected of carrying out the attack.
The announcement came hours after the independent Sudan Doctors Network reported that 13 miners had been killed and 28 injured in aerial bombardment near the Egyptian border.
There was no immediate comment from Cairo on the report.
Sudan’s artisanal mining sector employs more than 2 million people, often in harsh conditions, and accounts for around 80% of the country’s gold production.
The government permits artisanal mining while seeking to regulate the sector, which provides employment for large numbers of Sudanese.
Sudan relies on gold as a major source of foreign currency after losing three-quarters of its oil revenues following South Sudan’s secession in July 2011.
The country has been engulfed in war between the army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces since April 2023. The conflict has killed tens of thousands of people and displaced around 13 million, according to UN and international estimates.

Croatia Expands Probe Into Alleged Multi-Million-Euro Toxic Waste Scheme
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
15:02:00 UTC
00:02:00 KST

Reported by
Croatia's anti-corruption office, USKOK, expanded its investigation into an alleged international illegal waste dumping ring, arresting and questioning five new suspects and three companies over the suspected criminal disposal of hazardous materials near the town of Benkovac and inside the Velebit Nature Park near Senj.
The suspects were released after questioning, as USKOK stated there were no legal grounds to request pre-trial detention. Friday's action marks the third expansion of the sweeping environmental crime probe, which now targets a total of 14 individuals and four companies suspected of severe environmental crimes and falsifying official documents within a criminal enterprise.
The investigation, supported by Europol and law enforcement from Italy and Slovenia, became public in February 2025 with the initial arrest of 13 people. Authorities dismantled an alleged criminal network that is accused of orchestrating the illegal import of hazardous waste from Germany, Italy, and Slovenia into Croatia.
According to Europol, instead of properly treating the materials, the network allegedly buried or dumped at least 35,000 tonnes of waste across at least three locations, generating an estimated 4 million euros ($4.5 million) in illicit profits. To execute the scheme, suspects allegedly generated hundreds of falsified waste tracking sheets and fake construction diaries to disguise hazardous materials as municipal waste cover or legitimate building materials.
The severe environmental toll of the scheme became clear in early August, when USKOK released an expert report from the University of Zagreb's Faculty of Geotechnical Engineering, which concluded the local habitat was "partially irreversibly destroyed." Testing at an illegal landfill in Gospić revealed critical levels of heavy metals—including copper, zinc, lead, and antimony—and "forever chemicals," synthetic compounds that do not easily break down in the environment or the human body.
The report noted that downstream water samples showed high concentrations of the chemicals while upstream samples were clear, proving the landfill was the source. Experts warned there is a "high probability of further deterioration" if the waste is not immediately removed.
The latest USKOK findings reveal the destruction extends further. Between 2020 and 2024, the network allegedly dumped nearly 2,900 tonnes of hazardous plastic and industrial waste at the Senj site, and almost 6,500 tonnes of waste laced with heavy metals and microplastics into an inactive mineral field in Benkovac. Prosecutors warned the microplastics serve as a permanent pollution source that could easily leach into groundwater and the local food chain.
The revelations of widespread contamination and potential long-term health impacts sparked mass outrage. In September, tens of thousands of demonstrators took to the streets of Zagreb to demand stronger environmental protections, while local communities demanded strict sanctions against those responsible for the ecological damage.
Seeking to manage the ongoing political fallout and reassure the public, Prime Minister Andrej Plenković announced following a meeting with a scientific council that the government is initiating urgent remediation efforts in Gospić. Plenković stated Monday on X that surface waste will be removed in large bags and buried toxins temporarily covered, insisting that recent air and water tests show no deviations from permitted limits and that the public water supply remains completely safe.

====================================================================================================

'Scary' dementia modelling shows how cases will surge by 2050
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
15:01:28 UTC
00:01:28 KST

Dementia cases expected to soar to 'scary' highs, women will face more risk, study reveals
By 2050 an estimated 24.7 million people will be diagnosed with dementia each year and women will be disproportionately affected, according to a landmark new study.
The research found approximately 11.4 million people developed dementia globally in 2023 and that by 2050 that figure will double and demand for care will explode.
The study's authors said women's brain health needed to be prioritised and risk factors like hormonal changes and unequal education or job opportunities needed investigating.
"Understanding these differences is critical if we are to develop dementia prevention, diagnosis and care strategies that respond to the populations facing the greatest future risk," lead author Dr Ashleigh Vella said.
The research from the Centre for Healthy Brain Ageing (CHeBA) at the University of NSW analysed 38,418 people through population-based studies from 18 countries and territories.
It is one of the most comprehensive studies looking at the incidence rate of dementia. The study found cases were highest among women and people living in low income and middle income countries.
Nearly two thirds of current dementia diagnoses in Australia are women and this has long been considered a symptom of their longer life expectancy but researchers said there may be more at play.
The paper, published in the Journal of the American Medical Association Neurology, suggested the higher prevalence could be caused by other factors such as:
- Menopause
- Disproportionate educational and occupational opportunities
- Cardiometabolic factors such as body mass index and physical activity
Co-director of the CHeBA and Senior Australia of the Year Professor, Henry Brodaty, said historically women had less access to education and fewer career opportunities which could lead to poorer cognitive resilience.
"[Studies have shown] people who are in more complex occupations, particularly where they have complexity in managing people, they have a lower rate of cognitive decline and dementia," he said.
"Education has its most benefit in childhood and early development through to young adulthood but you can still build up your cognitive reserve or buffer against pathology building up in the brain throughout your life."
Higher rates of depression, anxiety and obesity among women could also be contributing factors, Professor Brodaty said, and more research was needed on the role menopause might play.
"Perhaps stopping oestrogen production may play a role but it's not established … and there's been conflicting results about whether hormone replacement therapy makes a difference."
Leading dementia researcher Matthew Pase at Monash University said the research was ambitious and provided important comparisons on dementia rates between low income and high income countries.
He described the figures as "scary".
"To see what rates are projected to be in low-income countries is alarming because they are less equipped to deal with this … so any solutions need to be scalable and not just be available for people who can pay to see an academic at a medical centre in Sydney or Melbourne."
Reducing dementia risk
Professor Brodaty, whose father passed away with Alzheimer's at just 52, said having a clear idea of what was coming meant there must be more investment in diagnosis, care and prevention.
Almost half of dementia cases could be prevented or delayed by addressing 14 risk factors.
Professor Brodaty urged Australians to "embrace" brain health by:
- Engaging in at least half an hour of physical activity five days a week
- Staying socially connected and "stretching the brain" by learning new things
- Eating a diet rich in vegetables, legumes and extra olive oil aka the Mediterranean diet
- Talking to their GP about brain health when they have their subsidised health check between the ages of 45 and 49
Professor Pase said given the high cost of the two dementia drug therapies approved in Australia, which are not subsidised through the Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme, prevention was still key.

====================================================================================================

Reform’s Zia Yusuf is sounding more and more like Trump every day | Zoe Williams
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
14:59:15 UTC
23:59:15 KST

Had Reform merely announced its intention to suspend the asylum system for an entire parliamentary term, I’d have just ignored it. Even to dignify its policy platform with a response is to enter its alternate universe, in which it’s preparing for government. I prefer, if only fractionally, this universe we’re in, where the party hangs by a thread on the results of a parliamentary inquiry into Nigel Farage’s £5m gift from a disinterested well-wisher.
Had Zia Yusuf, the party’s home affairs spokesperson, gone on BBC Radio 4’s Today programme merely promising a British version of ICE, I still would have ignored it, not due to complacency, more due to a bone-penetrating despair that anyone, even he, would look at the US’s shadow militia, performing staged acts of unfettered violence and inhumanity, and think: “That looks cool – I bet I could get some political capital out of that.”
However, as Yusuf laid out his arguments, they were so dumb, so random, disconnected, hammy and cliche-riddled, just so unremittingly stupid, that it turned out to be impossible not to react. I cannot let his nonsense slide. It would be an insult to words.
An elderly woman, he said, waited 23 hours for an ambulance and the coroner found this contributed to her death. A Welsh 15-year-old’s educational attainment is below the OECD average. Many young people have to live with their parents into their 30s and 40s because they can’t afford rent. How does any of this relate to asylum seekers? Are they displacing elderly people in ambulance-demand? It seems unlikely, although if they are an immediate fix would be to stop masked gangs surrounding their living quarters and scaring the hell out of them. Those are ethno-nationalist thugs, of course, and nothing to do with Reform.
High private rents, meanwhile, are not driven by asylum seekers, who have no right to work even if they arrive through a formal route, and as for Welsh 15-year-olds … well, we have some data here. They’re underperforming compared with English 15-year-olds, who are above the OECD average, indeed, above every other European nation, except Estonia and Ireland. If migrants destroy educational standards, how is Ireland managing to thrive? Why, with its very low number of asylum seekers, is Slovenia full of 15-year-olds who (no offence) suck at reading?
None of it makes sense because none of it was meant to. It’s bilge punctuated by soothing mantras (“Charity begins at home”, Yusuf repeated), aimed at the half-asleep mind dreaming of a whites-only yesteryear. It had that in common with a Trump rally, but lacked his pizzazz. Reform can’t even do neo-fascist mimicry right.
A word entered my social-media lexicon recently, which I wish I’d never had cause to look up, because I wish it wasn’t so useful: “agnotology” is the deliberate creation of ignorance, confusion and doubt. You can do it with misinformation and fake news, or you can do it with half-truths pouring out of bot factories, then leave an entire body politic tearing chunks out of itself as it seeks to establish whether the discursive environment has been deliberately polluted, or whether people are just mean and wrong nowadays. But you can also do it by simply talking nonsense, which we’ve seen writ large in party conference season and its aftermath.
“Let’s build an impenetrable and state-of-the-art defence dome for £10bn, and call it the Britannia Shield, even though that’s already the name of a Oxfordshire roofing company,” says the party that spent vastly more than that trying and failing to build the HS2 train line. “Let’s stop all refugees coming from everywhere, until the conditions for every single Briton at every conceivable stage of life have been improved,” from the party whose only discernible allegiance is to its billionaire donors.
The policies don’t even matter. Florid, premeditated stupidity is an end in itself, to clog the collective consciousness with nonsense, chase down every citizen who woke up in a good mood, with a scintilla of confidence about the future, and kill their mojo. The only defence is to hold your line. Insist on the difference between truth and untruth; guard your precious mojo with everything you’ve got.
Zoe Williams is a Guardian columnist

NATO commander unveils strategy to make any attack on alliance ‘utterly futile’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
14:59:01 UTC
23:59:01 KST

Alexus Grynkewich says the new strategy aims to deny adversaries a foothold and dismantle their warfighting capabilities, telling the Warsaw Security Forum that NATO is prepared to block, blunt and break any attack.
NATO's Supreme Allied Commander Europe (SACEUR) Alexus Grynkewich has unveiled a new defence strategy aimed at ensuring that any attack on an alliance member proves “utterly futile”, as countries on NATO’s eastern flank face sabotage, arson and drone incursions.
Speaking at the Warsaw Security Forum, Grynkewich said the strategy, known as the 'Theory of War,' was designed to deny adversaries the ability to penetrate NATO territory and sustain an attack.
“If attacked, we are ready to fight tonight,” Grynkewich told the audience to loud applause. “We will continue to prepare and rehearse each and every day, so we will be more ready tomorrow, and even more ready the day after that,” he added.
Grynkewich said the strategy was intended both to reassure the one billion people living under the NATO security umbrella, as well as adversaries such as Russia that the alliance was willing to respond to an invasion.
“Enemy formations will be starved of replenishment. Enemy commanders will be unable to control their forces. Enemy forces and support capabilities will be reduced and destroyed,” he said. “We will, in short, ensure any attack, against any Ally, proves utterly futile.”
Endorsed by all 32 NATO members, the plan combines conventional military capabilities, including ground forces, and military hardware, with advanced technologies such as drones, counter-drone systems and artificial intelligence.
It also draws on lessons from modern warfare, particularly the fighting on the ground and in the skies over Ukraine. “We're learning a tonne from Ukrainian partners,” Grynkewich told the forum.
Three stages of defence: block, blunt and break
The strategy rests on three principles — “block”, “blunt” and “break” — which Grynkewich described as simple but central to NATO’s approach.
“We will block the initial attack. If the attack persists, we will blunt it and prevent any enemy advance. And if required, we will break the enemy’s forces and the operational warfighting system arrayed against us,” he said.
Block: prevent an initial advance
The first phase would focus on stopping hostile forces from seizing allied territory.
NATO ground troops would engage advancing formations, contain their movements and destroy forces attempting to push into alliance territory.
“We will fix the enemy formations and deny the seizure of Alliance territory,” Grynkewich said. “Land-based forces will attack the enemy and destroy his advancing forces,” he added.
Blunt: stop further attacks
If an initial attack continued, NATO would deploy a broader range of capabilities to disrupt and overwhelm advancing forces.
These would include advanced sensors and autonomous systems, which can identify and assess threats with limited or no direct human intervention.
Grynkewich said the strategy would combine capabilities across multiple operational domains to prevent enemy forces from making further advances.
Break: disable the enemy’s ability to fight
The final phase would target not only enemy troops but also the systems that allow them to operate.
These would include command structures, supply networks and other logistical infrastructure, using capabilities such as long-range precision strikes and sensor networks.
The objective would be to disrupt the adversary’s overall military operations and leave its forces unable to sustain an attack.
“The approach also draws on lessons from modern warfare in Ukraine and the Middle East,” Grynkewich said.
NATO insists its strategy is defensive
Grynkewich stressed that NATO’s strategy was intended to protect allied territory rather than pursue territorial ambitions.
“We have no plans, no intentions, and no ambitions beyond the protection of our people and the defence of our territory,” he said.
He described the threat of an imminent attack on the alliance as low but warned that NATO would respond if an adversary chose to strike.
“If someone is foolish enough to attack us, we will fight,” he told the forum.
His remarks come amid growing security concerns among NATO members, particularly those on the eastern flank, where authorities have reported incidents involving sabotage, arson and drone incursions, some involving military-grade explosives.
Grynkewich said the increasingly challenging security environment underscored the need for NATO to demonstrate its readiness to defend allied territory.
US commitment to NATO
Asked whether the strategy remained viable amid concerns among some member states about the United States’ commitment to NATO, Grynkewich pointed to the alliance’s collective defence pledge.
He said Washington had agreed to a statement at the NATO summit in July reaffirming its “ironclad commitment to Article 5”.
Article 5 is the cornerstone of NATO’s collective defence principle, under which an armed attack against one member is considered an attack against all.

EU blacklists 1,569 Russian arms suppliers and their bosses in its biggest sanctions round ever, as Trump eases up on Moscow
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
14:58:45 UTC
23:58:45 KST

The EU adopted its largest-ever round of sanctions listings on 12 October, targeting the suppliers behind Russia’s war industry, the Council of the EU announced. The bloc acted as Russia keeps killing Ukrainian civilians every day, while US President Donald Trump eases sanctions on Russian diesel.
Russia’s planned winter campaign against Ukraine’s infrastructure depends on arms factories fed by a web of component suppliers and on oil revenue that still flows despite Ukraine’s refinery strikes, so every supplier cut off from that web raises the cost of waging it. As Washington eases off, Europe’s own pressure has a gap: its ports still take record volumes of Russian Arctic gas, and a full ban on long-term contracts starts only in 2027.
Missile suppliers top the list
More than half of the new listings hit the supply chain for ballistic missiles that Russia “uses to kill Ukrainian civilians every day,” EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said in the statement. Russian attacks killed more than 150 people in the past week, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on 11 October.
The list names 826 Russian companies, mid-level firms the Council calls the “core” of Russia’s arms industry, with at least €20 billion in yearly turnover, and 743 people who run them. They make parts for missiles, drones, and military aircraft, from semiconductors and radars to explosives and navigation systems. Their assets are frozen, EU firms may not finance them, and the executives may not enter the EU.
Foreign ministers ratified a deal EU envoys reached on 7 October. Ukraine’s sanctions commissioner Vladyslav Vlasiuk said 60% of the listings came from Ukrainian proposals.
Ministers reject the diesel deal
EU foreign ministers in Luxembourg vowed to keep the sanctions despite Trump’s diesel deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin, Euronews reported. Kallas addressed Washington directly as she arrived.
“The US is our biggest ally, but our message is clear: if we want to end this war, the only way we can do this is (by) putting more pressure on Russia,” Kallas said.
Irish Foreign Minister Helen McEntee called the deal “concerning,” and Lithuanian Foreign Minister Kęstutis Budrys said it was “not the European way.” Kallas warned that an energy truce covering only refineries would favor Russia, since Ukraine has one refinery and Russia “plenty.”
Trump announced the diesel deal on 9 October, and the US Treasury waived sanctions on Russian diesel until April 2027. Zelenskyy said the EU would provide about €3 billion more in military aid this week.
Washington presses Kyiv
Trump expects Ukraine to stop hitting Russian refineries under his proposed energy ceasefire, a White House official told Axios. Zelenskyy said Kyiv would halt such strikes if Moscow did the same. On 10 October, Trump told reporters it was time for Ukraine to get a new president. Germany’s foreign minister, Britain’s defense secretary, and a senior lawmaker from Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s party backed Zelenskyy, while the Kremlin sided with Trump.
Zelenskyy offered to hold elections after a 60-day ceasefire, and Kallas said elections are impossible while the war goes on. The Institute for the Study of War assessed that Russia exploits Ukraine’s legal ban on wartime elections to drag out the war.

Gaza war losses exceed $80bn amid infrastructure devastation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
14:56:51 UTC
23:56:51 KST

Breadcrumb
Gaza war losses exceed $80 billion as infrastructure devastation deepens
Direct losses from Israel's war on Gaza have exceeded $80 billion across 15 vital sectors, according to the territory's Government Media Office, as widespread destruction and restrictions on aid continue to deepen the humanitarian crisis.
Smail al-Thawabta, director general of Gaza's Government Media Office, told The New Arab that the destruction had extended beyond buildings and facilities to roads, water, electricity, telecommunications and sewage networks, as well as economic and public service infrastructure.
He said the Israeli military had dropped around 223,000 tonnes of explosives on Gaza and taken control of approximately 80% of the territory through bombardment and ground incursions, while the destruction had affected around 90% of the infrastructure essential to daily life.
The devastation has paralysed economic activity, severely weakened local institutions and left residents struggling to access food, clean water and other basic necessities.
Economic activity paralysed
Al-Thawabta said the cumulative losses had undermined local institutions' ability to provide services and brought much of Gaza's economic and productive activity to a standstill.
In the transport sector, he said the destruction had affected around 3,000 kilometres of roads, with preliminary losses estimated at $3 billion.
The damage has severely restricted movement across Gaza, hampering ambulances, civil defence teams and humanitarian workers trying to reach affected areas, while disrupting the transportation of goods and essential supplies.
Water and sewage infrastructure has also suffered extensive damage, with around 700 kilometres of water pipelines and an equivalent length of sewage networks destroyed.
A further 725 main water wells have been put out of service, while 134 freshwater projects have been destroyed, severely restricting access to clean water and increasing health risks linked to contamination and deteriorating sanitation.
"The water crisis is worsening alongside food shortages, as more than 200,000 families search daily for a single meal through community kitchens, amid declining aid and difficulties in providing necessities," al-Thawabta said.
He warned that thousands of families were struggling to feed their children, with even obtaining a loaf of bread becoming a daily challenge as living conditions deteriorate and dependence on humanitarian assistance grows.
More than 95% of Gazans rely on aid
According to al-Thawabta, more than 95% of Gaza's population now relies entirely on humanitarian aid and community kitchens to meet basic needs.
Restrictions on food supplies and funding shortages have forced some food programmes to suspend operations and others to close, further reducing relief organisations' ability to respond to growing demand.
He said the number of trucks entering Gaza amounted to no more than 35% of what was needed, including vehicles carrying humanitarian aid, food and commercial goods.
The shortfall has worsened supply shortages, leaving markets and humanitarian organisations struggling to provide residents with essential goods.
Al-Thawabta warned that the crisis extended beyond hunger to severe water deprivation, caused by the destruction of hundreds of wells and extensive damage to supply networks.
Delays in repairs and shortages of essential materials have compounded the damage, placing additional pressure on families and deepening the humanitarian crisis.
Electricity and communications networks devastated
Gaza's electricity infrastructure has also suffered extensive destruction, with around 5,080 kilometres of distribution networks, 2,285 transformers and 235,000 electricity meters destroyed, according to al-Thawabta.
He estimated preliminary losses in the electricity sector at approximately $2 billion.
The damage has severely affected hospitals, water pumping stations and sewage systems, making the restoration of essential services increasingly difficult.
Losses in the telecommunications and internet sector were estimated at a further $3 billion, with widespread infrastructure damage disrupting communications and complicating humanitarian coordination.
Al-Thawabta said the destruction had left residents struggling to communicate, access information and obtain essential services.
Meanwhile, losses to municipal and government services have reached an estimated $6 billion, with 253 government buildings destroyed.
He said 194 municipal employees, including four mayors, had been killed, further weakening local authorities' ability to maintain public services and respond to emergencies.
The destruction of civilian infrastructure, he stressed, could not be separated from its consequences for Gaza's population, as the collapse of essential networks undermined the foundations of daily life and made recovery increasingly difficult and costly.
Calls for urgent international intervention
Al-Thawabta called on the international community, United Nations agencies and humanitarian organisations to intervene urgently to provide food, clean water and other essential assistance.
He also urged immediate efforts to repair electricity, water and sewage networks, rehabilitate hospitals and restore vital public facilities to support recovery and reconstruction.
He warned that continued destruction, restrictions on aid and the declining capacity of local institutions would deepen Gaza's humanitarian and economic crisis and prolong the suffering of its population.
The Government Media Office's estimates come amid mounting concerns over the enormous cost of rebuilding the devastated territory.
A joint assessment by the World Bank, United Nations and European Union, published in April 2026, estimated direct physical damage in Gaza at approximately $35.2 billion, while recovery and reconstruction needs were projected to reach around $71.4 billion over the next decade.

EU Gives Final Approval to AGILE as Ukraine Gains Access to Defense Startup Funding
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
14:55:48 UTC
23:55:48 KST

- Category
- World
EU Gives Final Approval to AGILE as Ukraine Gains Access to Defense Startup Funding
The EU Council formally approved a new defense innovation program designed to accelerate emerging technologies from prototype to operational use, the European Council reported on October 12.
The Council formally adopted AGILE as a €115 million ($128.5 million) defense innovation instrument providing rapid financial support to SMEs, start-ups, and scale-ups developing emerging and disruptive military technologies. The program is designed to help companies move from prototype to operational capability more quickly.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The program is intended to help companies move technologies from development into military use more quickly, including by adapting civilian technologies for defense applications.
“Ukraine has shown us that innovation and cutting-edge technology can be decisive for defence preparedness and resilience,” Irish Defense Minister Helen McEntee stated. “AGILE gives SMEs an additional key instrument to do what they do best, innovate, only faster and at greater scale.”
According to the Council, companies supported through AGILE will be eligible for fast-track grants with a target approval time of four months. Relevant products and technologies are expected to reach defense forces within one to three years.
EU member states will help define specific capability challenges under the program, while participating companies will receive accelerated access to testing and experimentation facilities.
AGILE will also provide matchmaking between smaller companies and major defense manufacturers, while introducing simplified procurement procedures for products developed through the program.
The Council noted that the initiative was designed as a complement to existing EU defense-industrial instruments and is intended to address barriers that smaller companies face when moving new technologies into production and military deployment.
The regulation will now be signed by the presidents of the European Parliament and the Council before publication in the EU’s Official Journal. It will enter into force 20 days after publication, with the first call for proposals expected in early 2027.
In July, Babel reported, citing its sources in the European Parliament, that Ukraine would be integrated into the AGILE program without paying an entry fee, allowing Ukrainian defense developers to access its funding and support mechanisms.
The program also includes a dedicated RAZOM mechanism designed to give the Ukrainian Armed Forces access to weapons and technologies financed through AGILE and certified by the European Commission. Babel noted that some European Parliament officials considered the program’s limited budget its main weakness, while suggesting funding could be expanded if AGILE proves effective.
The EU’s new AGILE program forms part of a wider effort to close Europe’s defense production gap with Russia. In April, the European Commission proposed a $153.8 billion defense and space budget, with Commissioner Andrius Kubilius warning that Europe must “outproduce Russia” to strengthen deterrence.
