"Above all, they are fueling inflation that is beyond our
control yet weighs heavily on families, production systems, and
public finances.
                                    
"Europe cannot ignore this: when we approved our national budget
plans, we did so based on a projected inflation rate of 1.8%,
but today inflation is much higher.
                                    
"In Italy, as in other nations, a significant portion of
expenditure automatically adjusts to inflation by law.
                                    
"This means billions of euros in additional spending without the
government having made any new decisions, and for reasons beyond
our control; yet, that spending consumes the fiscal space
allowed by European rules, taking it away from everything
else—businesses, investments, and growth," she added.
                                    
"(Economy) Minister (Giancarlo) Giorgetti discussed this at the
ECOFIN meeting a few days ago, and I will personally raise the
issue again at the European Council scheduled for this Thursday
and Friday: it is a simple, common-sense proposal, as well as a
responsible one."
Meloni said the EU needs to change course on energy and that the
ETS system creates imbalances.
                                    
According to Meloni, "a change of pace is needed in Europe,
too," to contain energy costs.
                                    
"The ETS system," she explained at the Assolombarda assembly in
Milan, "inflates prices, creates imbalances among member states,
and harms our businesses, which face competitors not subject to
the same constraints."
"If a steel mill closes in Lombardy and we buy that steel from
the other side of the world—produced under lower environmental
standards—the planet loses rather than gains.
                                    
"We lose jobs and supply chains without reducing global
emissions," she emphasized.
                                    
"Strategic autonomy is built on steel mills, foundries, and
chemical plants. We are working on this in Europe; it won't be
an easy negotiation, but we will do our part, as always."

UK and EU agree to hold Brexit ‘reset’ summit on Nov. 20
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
14:55:39 UTC
23:55:39 KST

Andy Burnham and Ursula von der Leyen on the sidelines of the 81st United Nations General Assembly on September 22, 2026 in New York City. | Pool photo by Toby Melville/WPA via Getty Images
LONDON — Britain and the European Union will hold their annual leaders summit on Nov. 20 in Brussels.
U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham confirmed the date in a statement to the House of Commons on Monday afternoon.
Brussels and London want to use the meeting to sign off new agreements on agri-food trade, emissions trading, and a youth mobility scheme.
Advertisement
Burnham told the Commons he wanted to secure a deal on the agreements — begun by previous Prime Minister Keir Starmer — and then begin a “calm, clear-eyed, rational look” at even closer relations.
“If we are serious about promoting growth, controlling immigration, upholding our values and security, it is a conversation we must have,” he said.
“Sticking with the status quo is not good enough for Britain. Worse, it would be a major dereliction of duty to turn away.”
He added: “Our immediate priority is securing a successful outcome at the summit, and I believe we should then set up a serious dialogue about the different options for our relationship in the long term.”
The prime minister also said the meeting would nn opportunity to “raise our concerns about Made In Europe” — the EU’s program of protectionism which some countries want to exclude the U.K.
Burnham has previously suggested these future options could include rejoining the single market, customs union, or even the EU wholesale.
Advertisement
Kemi Badenoch, the leader of the opposition Conservative party, criticized the prime minister for focusing on the U.K.’s relationship with the EU.
“His exact words earlier this year were, ‘The last thing we should do right now is rerun those arguments,’” she said.
“And yet, here he is unpicking the deal this country signed with the EU a decade after the referendum. He is not going to get a better deal. The EU are tough negotiators.”
She added: “Just like some people thought all of Britain's problems would be solved by leaving the EU, some now think all our problems will be will be solved by rejoining. Neither of these are serious positions.”
In a statement issued while Burnham was speaking in Westminster, António Costa, president of European Council, which represents EU member countries, said improving cooperation was “essential.”
He said the three agreements under negotiation could be complemented by additional deals on a defence and security partnership, as well as on migration and law enforcement.
Advertisement
“The European Union and the United Kingdom are like-minded partners, united by common values and shared interests,” he said in a statement,” he said.
“Our security and prosperity are closely intertwined, making a strong partnership between us essential.
“By deepening our cooperation, we can strengthen our ability to address the challenges of our time, strengthen our resilience and promote stability in Europe and beyond.”
Costa and Burnham will be joined by European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen at the Nov. 20 meeting. Negotiations have been taking place since the previous summit in May 2025, which was attended by Starmer.
This year’s summit was intended to take place in July but was postponed following the collapse of Starmer’s administration.

Gaza’s displaced face a deadly choice: collapsing buildings or flooded tents
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
14:54:38 UTC
23:54:38 KST

With thousands of buildings damaged and the punishing winter fast approaching, displaced Palestinians sheltering inside Gaza’s ruins face two bitter choices: sleep beneath unstable concrete or risk having nowhere to stay at all.
Pieces of concrete sometimes break loose without warning, and stones tumble from damaged walls. Yet fear of the coming winter drives families to seek any shelter with a concrete roof, no matter how fractured it may be. They view these broken structures as their final line of defence against the looming winter storms.
However, this choice carries potentially catastrophic risks. Instead of keeping families warm and dry, cracked ceilings can let rainwater seep through, flooding their makeshift living spaces.
Displaced families are already making exhausting efforts to patch gaps and holes, using whatever remnants of plastic or cloth they can find to block the biting cold and winter winds. For many, even the short walk to collect water means passing beneath sections of a building that appear ready to collapse at any moment.
Families are trapped inside bomb-damaged houses, schools and universities. Cracked walls and weakened ceilings surround them, but leaving could mean returning to sodden tents, sleeping in the mud outdoors or beginning yet another agonising search for shelter.
Read: Gaza winter nears as 162,000 tents become unusable, raising fears of humanitarian crisis
“Unfortunately, whenever we sit here, stones fall on us,” said Maher Awad Khader, a displaced resident sheltering with his family at the Islamic University of Gaza. “Everything is in terrible condition, even when we go to carry water. I have been here for four or five months. This is the only place where we have been able to take shelter.”
For displaced families like Maher’s, finding a roof in Gaza no longer necessarily means finding safety.
“When we find a place to sit, we sleep there,” Maher said. “But the same stones keep falling on us from the rubble.”
Maher said he has no job or income to support his family, nor the means to set up even a small makeshift stall to earn a living. He added that no humanitarian aid organisations or institutions had reached them with assistance, leaving them to face the coming winter alone.
The danger has become more acute following a series of building collapses in Gaza City.
Last month, the Al-Saada residential building in the Sabra neighbourhood collapsed, killing 21 people, most of them women and children. Days later, another damaged building came down in the same area.
The incidents have renewed fears over thousands of structures weakened during the war but still being used as shelters by displaced families who have few, if any, alternatives.
For them, displacement is no longer only about escaping bombardment. It is also about deciding whether the building offering protection tonight could collapse before morning.
‘We have no choice’
A short distance from Maher, Taher Hajjo and his family are sheltering beneath what remains of another building at the Islamic University. He remembers the previous winter clearly.
Sections of the damaged structure repeatedly gave way, he said, while chunks of concrete and debris fell from different parts of the building almost every day.
Now, as another winter approaches, Taher is trying to reinforce the space around his family with whatever materials he can find.
Makeshift walls and basic supports have become a fragile line of defence around his children. They offer little reassurance.
Asked how he lives with the possibility that the ceiling above them could collapse, Taher replied: “Honestly, we have no choice. What can we do? May Allah bring relief to us and to everyone.”
That lack of choice has become a defining feature of life for many displaced families.
After repeated displacement and widespread destruction, moving again does not necessarily lead somewhere safer. For some, it simply means exchanging one danger for another.
A damaged concrete building may offer protection from rain and cold but carry the risk of collapse. A tent may remove the danger of falling masonry but leave families exposed to winter storms, flooding and freezing temperatures.
As the colder months approach, that calculation is becoming increasingly urgent.
Thousands of buildings at risk
The threat is not limited to the Islamic University.
Field assessments cited by Gaza’s Ministry of Public Works and Housing and engineering bodies have classified about 3,000 buildings across the Gaza Strip as highly dangerous and at risk of sudden collapse
Many remain occupied.
The danger is expected to increase during winter, when heavy rain, wind and severe weather can place additional pressure on structures already weakened by bombardment.
For families living inside them, a night of strong wind or heavy rainfall can bring fears that cracked walls will shift or damaged ceilings will finally give way.
The result is another form of displacement, driven not necessarily by a new attack or evacuation order but by the instability of what remains.
Gaza City officials have appealed to international organisations and UN agencies for urgent assistance, warning that winter could further endanger people sheltering inside unsafe buildings.
Municipal authorities say they lack the equipment and materials needed to secure or reinforce damaged structures on the scale required.
Gaza’s Civil Defence has also called for the entry of heavy machinery, rescue vehicles and concrete-cutting equipment, saying shortages make it far harder to reach people trapped beneath collapsed buildings.
Rescue operations are particularly difficult when large concrete slabs fall onto occupied rooms and teams lack specialised machinery to remove them
Officials have also called for prefabricated housing units and emergency shelter materials to provide alternatives for families living in buildings considered unsafe.
But for Maher and Taher, those appeals remain distant from the immediate question confronting their families each night: where else can they go
They know the buildings around them are damaged. They see the cracks, hear debris falling and remember the collapses elsewhere in Gaza.
Yet they remain.
In a place where displacement has already stripped thousands of families of their homes, even shelter has become another source of fear.
A roof, once the simplest symbol of protection, can now be the danger hanging directly overhead.

House prices continue to climb in Switzerland
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
14:54:00 UTC
23:54:00 KST

House prices continue to climb in Switzerland
Housing prices in Switzerland rose significantly again in the third quarter of 2026. Both single-family homes and flats saw sharp price increases compared with the previous quarter.
Prices for single-family homes rose by 2.0%, while those for flats increased by 1.7%, according to the Raiffeisen Transaction Price Index published on Monday. Compared to the same quarter last year, single-family homes became 3.6% more expensive and flats 5.9% more expensive.
+ Housing costs drive more French-speaking Swiss to emigrate
The rise in interest rates for fixed-rate mortgages has not yet slowed the price increase. According to Raiffeisen chief economist Fredy Hasenmaile, the moderate rise in interest rates is not enough to reverse the strong upward price momentum. The supply of residential properties remains too scarce for that.
Significant Regional Differences
Prices varied by region. For single-family homes, Zurich (+4.8 %) and Western Switzerland (+4.6%) recorded the strongest year-on-year gains. In Southern Switzerland (+3.3%) and Eastern Switzerland (+3.5%), the increase was somewhat lower.
For flats, Southern Switzerland led the way with a 7.4% increase. In the Lake Geneva region, however, prices rose by only 0.4%.
More
Buy or rent? Find out where you can afford to live in Switzerland
There are also differences among the various types of municipalities. Single-family homes saw the sharpest price increase (5.2%) over the course of a year in central municipalities. For flats, tourist municipalities recorded the largest price increase, at 7.9%. In central municipalities, the increase was significantly lower, at 1.6%.
The Raiffeisen Transaction Price Index measures the quarterly price trends of owner-occupied residential property in Switzerland. It is based on actual purchase prices derived from data provided by Raiffeisen and the Swiss Real Estate Datapool.

Among other things, the ministry added that it plans to digitize all bus routes within the next year.

EU approves €115m defence innovation grant programme open to Ukraine
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher

EU approves €115m defence innovation grant programme open to Ukraine
The European Union has set up the €115 million AGILE programme to fund innovative defence projects developed by small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). Ukrainian companies will also be eligible to participate.
Source: European Pravda, citing the European Commission press service
Details: The new €115 million funding instrument will provide targeted support to SMEs to develop innovative defence solutions and facilitate their deployment.
"The programme will operate with an unprecedented time-to-grant of just four months and for technologies to reach defence forces between 1-3 years. It will support between 20 and 30 projects, providing up to 100% funding for all eligible costs," the press service said.
The work programme will cover two main activities: the development of revolutionary defence products and technologies, and their introduction to the market.
The AGILE programme was adopted less than seven months after the European Commission submitted its proposal in March 2026.
"Russia's war in Ukraine has demonstrated that success on the battlefield relies on new technologies, from drones and autonomous systems to artificial [intelligence]. Europe's ability to develop, test, and deploy new technologies and cost-efficient solutions in weeks or months rather than years is now being tested," the European Commission stated.
The AGILE programme is expected to become fully operational in early 2027. Entrepreneurs from Ukraine and the European Free Trade Association (Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway and Switzerland) are eligible to participate.
Background:
- By the end of October, the European Commission plans to unveil a separate Security Strategy designed to complement NATO's Article 4.
- It was previously reported that the European Commission plans to allocate around €20 billion in unused loans to launch a call for defence projects for the EU and Ukraine.
- The European Commission is also allocating €325 million to support the establishment and implementation of five European Defence Projects of Common Interest (EDPCI), with Ukraine taking part in four of them.

====================================================================================================

Europe has 11 ways to choke Russia’s war. It doesn’t need Trump’s permission for any of them
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
14:50:00 UTC
23:50:00 KST

On 9 October, three weeks after signing the first major Russia oil sanctions in two years, Donald Trump agreed with Vladimir Putin to bring Russian diesel back to world markets. The US Treasury suspended its sanctions on that trade until April 2027 the same day. In the two days before, Russian strikes had killed more than 80 Ukrainian civilians.
Europe answered on 12 October with its largest sanctions package yet: nearly 1,600 new listings, almost all in Russia’s military-industrial complex. Its core, says Ukraine’s sanctions envoy Vladyslav Vlasiuk, is Russia’s missile program and the electronics inside it, from capacitors to semiconductors. Six in ten listings came from Ukrainian proposals, and Brussels adopted them within weeks.
That is the right reflex, and proof that Europe can move fast when it chooses. But the package names companies and people one by one. On the measures that cut whole sectors, the ones that would hurt Moscow most, Europe still waits for Washington.
It waits for Trump to decide whether to enforce the Graham Act he signed in September. It waits for him to decide whether to lean on Hungary and Slovakia or let them off. It waits for the G7 to rule on tanker services before touching its own ships. Europe keeps asking the Trump administration to decide things it is perfectly able to decide itself.
If the EU is serious about ending a war on its own continent, it does not need a miracle from Washington. It needs to pull the levers already in its hands. Here they are.
Strip Russian weapons of European parts
1. Fix export-control enforcement on dual-use goods. It is unacceptable that the newest Russian drones and missiles contain not only Chinese parts but American and European ones. The "War and Sanctions" portal logs what turns up. The EU should find and close the enforcement gaps in its own dual-use export law. Choking the supply to Russia's war industry serves Ukraine and Europe alike.
Cut Russia's energy money
2. Force Hungary and Slovakia off Russian oil. The EU banned Russian oil imports in 2022, with temporary exemptions for landlocked states: Czechia, Slovakia, Hungary. Czechia has since diversified and dropped Russian oil entirely. Slovakia and Hungary can do the same; the Czech case proves it is a question of will, not feasibility. Ending the exemptions would also make good on REPowerEU's central promise, phasing out Russian energy. The gas-import ban is already decided. Oil is the gap that remains.
3. Close the Greek and Maltese tanker loophole. Up to 40% of Russia's seaborne oil travels on European tankers, Greek and Maltese. The EU has banned maritime services for Russian oil since 2022, with one exception: cargoes sold below the price cap. This spring the Council discussed scrapping that exception, which would have meant a full ban, then made any change conditional on coordination with the G7. Once again, Europe is asking Washington to act for it. The EU should overcome Greek and Maltese resistance and ban every maritime service for Russian oil: transport, insurance, and the rest.
4. Stop the shadow fleet in European waters. Russia ships oil to India, China, and Türkiye through a shadow fleet of aging, often uninsured tankers. Europe can check their insurance and turn away any that lack EU or G7 cover, especially in the North Sea and the Baltic, where any spill would be an ecological disaster, and an uninsured operator would not pay for it.
Patrols in territorial waters and exclusive economic zones have to be reinforced. Russia also uses these ships for espionage, sabotage, and damage to undersea infrastructure. Strengthen NATO's Baltic Sentry. Consider adding a maritime operation by the UK-led Joint Expeditionary Force or the Coalition of the Willing across the North and Baltic Seas and the Skagerrak, before the Danish straits. If the Russian Baltic Fleet escalates, Europe should be ready for confrontation. Moscow should hear that it is not feared and that it will be stopped. At sea, it is weaker than even NATO's Baltic Sea states alone, never mind NATO's European members together.
5. Scrap the Lingen nuclear-fuel deal. In July, Lower Saxony approved a plan for the French state company Framatome to make nuclear fuel jointly with Rosatom, Russia's builder of nuclear weapons, at Lingen. It is dressed up as serving REPowerEU, since the venture lets Hungary, Slovakia, and Bulgaria buy fuel from a Franco-Russian joint operation instead of straight from Rosatom.
This is nonsense. Ukraine was once wholly dependent on Russian nuclear fuel and diversified fast; Finland and Czechia have done the same. Hungary, Slovakia, and Bulgaria can follow. Stretching the dependence out and hiding it behind a French partner is the opposite of what REPowerEU is for. Lower Saxony's own environment minister called the deal "grundfalsch," fundamentally wrong.
Fund Ukraine from Russia's own money
6. Build a Ukraine Fund from frozen Russian assets. Supporting Ukraine will cost more next year, not less, so it is time to get serious about Russia's frozen assets. Not confiscation, which European capitals still resist, and not a simple transfer to Kyiv, which amounts to the same thing, but a dedicated EU-run Ukraine Fund that could invest these assets and use them better than they are used now. ICUV has set it all out in a policy paper.
Isolate Russia further
7. Adopt the Graham-bill sanctions. Sanction every Russian state company (majority or controlling state stake) and every Russian oligarch who has not taken a public anti-war stand. Forbes counts 155 Russian billionaires.
8. Cut every Russian and Belarusian bank off SWIFT. Russia still has 301 operating banks, yet only 103 Russian banks and financial institutions sit under the EU's transaction ban, and just a handful of Belarusian ones. Gazprombank, which the US Treasury says pays Russia's soldiers, is still not on the EU list. Stop listing banks one by one: disconnect the entire Russian and Belarusian banking systems and put them under a full transaction ban, with narrow exceptions for food, medicine, and humanitarian trade.
9. End land transit to and from Russia, Kaliningrad included. Stop all overland freight, rail and road, between the EU and Russia. Baltic ports should carry no Russian trade at all, not just grain. Halt the gas transit to Kaliningrad through Lithuania's pipelines, too; let it arrive by sea, where Russia already runs an LNG terminal. Winters are mild now, so the real effect is mostly higher costs, and even that is worth doing.
10. Ban visas for Russian (ex-)servicemen and their families. The EU's 21st sanctions package laid the legal basis in July and then set no start date. Bring it into force, and extend it to the families.
Deliver accountability
11. Launch the Tribunal for the Crime of Aggression and the Claims Commission. Speed up the creation of, and accession to, the tribunal for the crime of aggression against Ukraine, and the convention establishing a Claims Commission.
The point
Europe cannot escape this burden. A Russian victory, even a partial one such as a peace on Moscow's terms, would cost it far more than helping Ukraine to a partial victory of its own, a peace along the line of contact. If Europe wants the war to end, it has to lead, alongside Ukraine, instead of waiting on a miracle from the Trump administration. The tools are already in its hands.

====================================================================================================

Russia can meet promised diesel exports to U.S. and global markets only at the expense of domestic strategic reserves, expert says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
14:49:59 UTC
23:49:59 KST

On Oct. 9, Donald Trump announced that he had reached an agreement with Vladimir Putin regarding the supply of Russian diesel fuel to the U.S. and global markets. The same day, the U.S. Treasury Department suspended sanctions on imports of Russian diesel. Russia, for its part, announced that it was lifting a ban on diesel exports imposed amid a domestic fuel crisis.
Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said Moscow was prepared to export 300,000 metric tons of diesel as early as October, 500,000 tons in November, and up to 1 million tons in December. “Over time, the volume could rise to 3 million tons a month,” he added.
George Voloshin, an international sanctions expert and specialist on the former Soviet states, told The Insider that the promised 3 million tons a month would restore Russian exports to pre-sanctions levels:
“The volumes of 300,000 to 500,000 tons a month being discussed for the coming weeks are relatively modest for the global balance. That is equivalent to several LR-class tanker loads or medium-sized MR cargoes, which the market can absorb without structural shifts. But the stated target of 3 million tons a month, or about 36 million tons a year, is already an enormous figure, comparable to nearly all of Russia’s historical seaborne diesel exports during peak pre-crisis periods. In effect, this would be an attempt to return Russian export flows to pre-sanctions highs — but this time under the umbrella of direct shipments to Western markets.
For the U.S. domestic market, this is more of a targeted logistical measure. U.S. refineries themselves produce huge volumes of distillates, but the Northeast traditionally faces shortages because of logistical constraints imposed by the Jones Act, so imported spot cargoes could ease local retail prices ahead of the winter season. Globally, the effect will depend on whether this represents a net increase in supply. In other words, if these barrels are simply redirected from Turkey, Brazil, or Asia, there would only be some reshuffling of trade routes without pressure on global prices. But if genuinely new physical volumes reach the world market, then refining margins (known as ‘crack spreads’) in Europe and Asia would inevitably fall.
Meeting the initial commitments of 300,000 to 500,000 tons would not create critical problems for Russia’s domestic market because autumn maintenance at most refineries is nearing completion and seasonal agricultural demand is beginning to decline. The main obstacle to reaching 1 million to 3 million tons a month lies in the technical condition of refining capacity and logistics, because continuing damage to primary processing units and secondary hydrocracking facilities at key refineries in European Russia is limiting output of winter-grade diesel. To export as much as 3 million tons without risking a fuel crisis and a sharp rise in wholesale prices on the St. Petersburg exchange, Russian oil companies would not only have to fully restore capacity but would in effect have to prioritize exports at the expense of building strategic reserves at home. That looks very difficult to achieve. Hence the market’s expected skepticism.”
Tatiana Mitrova, a research fellow at Columbia University’s Center on Global Energy Policy, said Russia has enough diesel to sell, but its export capacity will depend on the intensity of Ukrainian strikes on refineries and ports.
“I would say that despite the decline in refining, Russia can still export certain volumes of diesel. Because of the export ban, some refineries have already faced the risk of excess inventories. Additional flexibility comes from accumulated stocks, fuel imports — primarily from Belarus — and, if necessary, restrictions on domestic consumption.
Exports are possible not only through Baltic and Black Sea ports, but also through ports in the Far East, which are far less vulnerable to Ukrainian strikes. The main question is whether Ukraine will continue attacks on refineries, ports, and storage facilities despite pressure from Trump. In short, one-off shipments are entirely realistic, but sustained growth in exports is much more doubtful.”

Ramlila Maidan: The ground where protests dealt a blow to Congress government, twice
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
14:46:04 UTC
23:46:04 KST

Ramlila Maidan is best known as a venue for the annual staging of Ramlila, the traditional enactment of the Ramayana.
NEW DELHI: Delhi has a new map for protest, with Jantar Mantar losing its status as a designated venue for demonstrations on Monday. Delhi Police has named three alternative sites, including Ramlila Maidan in central Delhi, a ground that has witnessed political movements with far-reaching consequences for the Congress.The other two designated venues are Burari Ground in north Delhi and CBD Ground in east Delhi. The move comes amid protests against the Election Commission over alleged irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls. While Jantar Mantar's removal marks a significant shift in the capital's protest landscape, Ramlila Maidan brings its own political history to the fore.
A view of Ramlila Maidan, designated as a protest site along with two news venues,. (PTI photo)
The venue has a political legacy of its own: two major mass movements held there, decades apart, that became defining moments in the Congress’s political history.
Two protests that changed Congress's fortunes
Ramlila Maidan has been the stage for two major mass movements that challenged the Congress at crucial moments in its political history, decades apart.The first came on June 25, 1975, when socialist leader Jayaprakash Narayan addressed a massive rally at Ramlila Maidan against then Prime Minister Indira Gandhi's government, calling for resistance to the establishment.
Jayaprakash Narayan addressed a massive rally at Ramlila Maidan.
That night, Gandhi imposed the Emergency, suspending civil liberties and triggering a crackdown on the Opposition.
The Congress lost the 1977 Lok Sabha election, its first defeat at the Centre, as the Janata Party came to power.More than three decades later, the ground witnessed another movement that put the Congress-led government under pressure. In 2011, anti-corruption activist Anna Hazare launched a nationwide agitation demanding a strong Lokpal law. The protest began at Jantar Mantar before moving to Ramlila Maidan, where Hazare staged a high-profile hunger strike that drew widespread public attention.
Anna Hazare during the India Against Corruption (IAC) movement in 2011.
The agitation intensified the political pressure on the Congress-led United Progressive Alliance (UPA), already facing a series of corruption allegations. It also helped create the momentum for the emergence of the Aam Aadmi Party (AAP), which went on to challenge both the Congress and the BJP in Delhi and fundamentally alter the capital's political contest.Separated by 36 years, the two movements cemented Ramlila Maidan's place in India's protest history, with each marking a significant challenge to a Congress-led establishment.
History of Ramlila Maidan
Ramlila Maidan is best known as a venue for the annual staging of Ramlila, the traditional enactment of the Ramayana. According to historian Narayani Gupta, Ramlila was held on land near Ajmeri Gate as early as the 19th century. Historian Sohail Hashmi has said the early celebrations were supported by the Khatri community.The ground acquired a wider public role after Independence, hosting large gatherings and events involving national and international leaders.Soviet leaders Nikita Khrushchev and Nikolai Bulganin visited in 1955, US President Dwight Eisenhower addressed a gathering there in 1959, and Queen Elizabeth II spoke at a public event in 1961.Over time, the ground became a venue for political rallies, mass meetings and demonstrations, cementing its place in the capital’s public life.
How the protest site has shifted
Jantar Mantar was not always the designated site. The Boat Club lawns near Rajpath were used earlier, until a week-long farmers’ protest led by Mahendra Singh Tikait in 1988 raised security concerns. By 1993, protests had moved to Jantar Mantar, which was close to Parliament but easier to police.In 2017, the National Green Tribunal banned protests at Jantar Mantar, citing environmental and civic issues, and named Ramlila Maidan, nearly four kilometres away, as the official venue for sit-ins.However, the Supreme Court, while setting aside a blanket ban on protests at Jantar Mantar in a 2018 ruling, had held that the right to peaceful protest could not be completely extinguished and that the competing rights of protesters and residents had to be balanced through regulation.The Court had accordingly directed authorities to permit limited and regulated use of the area.With the Delhi Police now de-notifying Jantar Mantar as a designated protest site and shifting demonstrations to three other venues, the question is whether the decision is legally sustainable in light of the Supreme Court’s ruling.
The Supreme Court, in Mazdoor Kisan Shakti Sangathan v. Union of India, was dealing with a 2017 order of the National Green Tribunal (NGT) which had directed authorities to immediately stop dharnas, protests, agitations, public speeches and other such activities at Jantar Mantar Road and shift protesters to an alternative site.Protest groups have since argued that greater distance from Parliament reduces the visibility of their demands. Farmers who were denied permission even at Ramlila Maidan in 2020-21 camped instead at Delhi’s borders at Singhu, Tikri and Ghazipur.The latest order formalises a shift away from the central site, though it remains to be seen how the revised rules will affect where and how protests are held.
Rajeev Singh is a Digital Content Producer with The Times of India. He covers politics, policies, defence, and conflicts for readers curious to know their implications. He loves digging into legal maxims and political trivia. On off days, when not turning pages or learning русский, he lives in the reverie of “what ifs” and “how abouts.”

Russia’s military-industrial complex and those involved in the “elections” in TOTs — who is included in EU’s new sanctions package against Russia and Ukraine’s response

Russia’s military-industrial complex and those involved in the “elections” in TOTs — who is included in EU’s new sanctions package against Russia and Ukraine’s response
Kyiv • UNN
The EU imposed sanctions on 1,569 individuals and companies, more than half of them linked to the production of ballistic missiles. Separately, restrictions were imposed on 77 individuals for the “elections” in the TOTs.
Within the sanctions regime against the Russian Federation for Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine, the EU has approved its largest-ever package of sanctions, which covers nearly 1,600 individuals and entities in Russia’s military-industrial complex. In a separate decision, the Council of the EU imposed sanctions on 77 individuals involved in organizing and holding the illegal "elections" to the Russian State Duma in the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine. The Council of the EU listed what was included in the new package on October 12, UNN reports.
Details
"In response to the continuation and escalation of Russia’s aggression against Ukraine, including its recent brutal military campaign deliberately directed against civilian infrastructure and causing severe suffering to the civilian population, today the Council (EU) adopted additional restrictive measures against 1,569 individuals and entities in Russia’s military-industrial complex. The agreed lists include 826 Russian companies and 743 individuals who hold the positions of chief executive officers of these companies," the statement said.
This, it is noted, is the largest sanctions list ever agreed by the EU, and the total number of entities sanctioned under this sanctions regime is approaching 4,600.
"Today, the EU adopted its largest package of sanctions lists since 2022. Around 1,600 are directed against Russia’s military-industrial complex. More than half concern the production chain of ballistic missiles that Russia uses every day to kill Ukrainian civilians. The bombing of Kyiv’s bridges, vessels transporting grain, and the National Academy of Sciences are not the actions of a country seeking peace. Now is not the time to ease pressure on Moscow, but to increase it," said the EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy and President of the Council of the EU Foreign Affairs Council, Kaja Kallas.
What is included in the sanctions lists
Today’s sanctions package, it is noted, is "specifically targeting mid-level suppliers representing the ‘core’ of Russia’s military industry, generating an annual turnover of at least €20 billion and employing more than 250,000 people."
"The companies included on the list are suppliers of key components for some of Russia’s most advanced weapons systems, including missiles, unmanned aerial vehicles, and aircraft. Such key components include: electronics, including semiconductors, microchips, and computers; communications equipment, including radars, antennas, and receivers; aviation, satellite, and missile systems; explosives and ammunition, as well as optics and navigation systems," the statement said.
Those included under this sanctions regime, as stated, "are subject to an asset freeze, and the provision of funds or economic resources to them, directly or indirectly, or for their benefit, is prohibited. In addition, the individuals listed are subject to a travel ban to the EU."
The EU also imposed sanctions on 77 individuals under the sanctions regime for organizing the "elections" to the Russian State Duma in September 2026 by the Russian Federation in the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine. These include 74 "candidates" from various Russian parties in the temporarily occupied territories, as well as three members of the Central Election Commission of the Russian Federation.
The relevant legal acts, it is reported, were published in the Official Journal of the European Union.
Those sanctioned include, in particular:
-   Serhii Arbuzov, former Governor of the National Bank of Ukraine and former acting Prime Minister, who was a candidate from the A Just Russia party and took part in the illegal so-called "elections" to the Russian State Duma;  
-  Yanina Pavlenko, the so-called "mayor of Yalta"; a candidate from the United Russia party who took part in the illegal so-called "elections" to the Russian State Duma; former director of the Novy Svet sparkling wine factory; former production director of the Masandra agricultural union. 
The EU’s restrictive measures against Russia’s military-industrial complex also apply to:
-   Serhii Hureyev, General Director of the Joint Rocket and Space Corporation joint-stock company; 
-  Vasyl Burenok, who is the president of the "Russian Academy of Rocket and Artillery Sciences";  
-  Serhii Pitikov, CEO of the "Machine-Building Design Bureau Scientific and Production Corporation," which, according to HUR data, is a developer and manufacturer of 9M723 "Iskander-M" ballistic missiles and Kh-47M2 "Kinzhal" aeroballistic missiles, "Strela," "Igla," and "Verba" man-portable air-defense systems, the "Khrizantema-S" anti-tank guided missile system, "Ataka" guided missiles, the "Arena" active protection system, and the "Izdeliye 305" missile; 
-  Viktor Ivanov, CEO of the "Research Institute of Precision Instruments," which, according to EU data, operates in the space and military spheres and supplies Russia's Ministry of Defense with specialized equipment and services. The company is part of the state corporation "Roscosmos" and is working on a new satellite system for the Russian army — the Kasatka-R space-based synthetic-aperture radar; 
-  Dmytro Avtaikin, CEO of the "Russian Corporation of Rocket and Space Instrumentation and Information Systems," whose main areas of activity, according to HUR data, are the creation, development, and targeted use of the GLONASS global navigation satellite system. 
Ukraine's response
The Office of the President and Ukraine's Ministry of Foreign Affairs responded to the EU's expansion of sanctions against russia.
"This is a very powerful decision! Thank you, Council of the EU! Is there anything related to ending exports of alumina from the EU to russia in this package? In the next package?" — commented Serhii Kyslytsia, First Deputy Head of the Office of the President, on X.
Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha also welcomed the unprecedentedly extensive expansion of the EU's sanctions lists against russia — nearly 1,600 new sanctions listings targeting its military-industrial complex, more than half of which are linked to the production of ballistic missiles.
"Special thanks to the EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy, Kaja Kallas, for her determined leadership, as well as to all EU member states — for their unity and steadfastness. Against the backdrop of the latest brutal Russian strikes on Ukrainian cities, the timing and scale of this decision are particularly significant. moscow is intensifying its terror. Europe is demonstrating that its response can be just as resolute. The kremlin has been trying for years to divide Europe. Today, Europe is demonstrating why moscow fears its unity so much," Sybiha said.
The Foreign Minister emphasized that moscow must not be able to regard the cost of another attack as merely another acceptable expense. The cost of aggression must continue to exceed any calculations made by the kremlin.

The United States has deported Russian citizen Idris Makhmudov, one of the organizers of a mass hunger strike that took place earlier this month at an immigration detention center in Folkston, Georgia, according to a report by the independent investigative outlet Agentstvo, citing Makhmudov’s representative and a source familiar with the recent events at the facility. Makhmudov, who had sought asylum in the United States, spent nearly 27 months in custody. Shortly before his deportation, he helped organize a protest by at least 73 detainees over their prolonged detention and the poor conditions at the center. U.S. court records reviewed by The Insider show that on Sept. 28 a federal court denied Makhmudov’s petition challenging the legality of his detention.
According to Makhmudov’s representative, he was removed from the United States on a commercial flight through Morocco, where he waited for onward travel to Russia. During the journey, Makhmudov, who his representative said had refused food and water for four days, lost consciousness. The representative also said U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) told Makhmudov that his appeal would continue to be reviewed and that he would be returned to the United States if it succeeded. Those claims have not been independently verified.
Court rejects Makhmudov’s challenge to detention
Makhmudov filed a petition in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Georgia on Dec. 22, 2025, seeking review of the legality of his prolonged detention and seeking the opportunity to be released on bond. According to a Sept. 28, 2026, court ruling, a magistrate judge initially recommended granting Makhmudov an individualized bond hearing. U.S. District Judge Lisa Godbey Wood, however, upheld objections from the detention center’s administration and dismissed Makhmudov’s petition in full while still allowing him to appeal.
Makhmudov was initially detained in July 2024 after seeking permission to enter the United States at the Nogales border crossing in Arizona. Makhmudov is a Russian citizen who was born in Kazakhstan. Acquaintances say he is originally from Chechnya.
73 detainees join hunger strike, organizers placed in solitary confinement
A mass hunger strike began at the Folkston facility on Oct. 6. Several dozen people, most of whom had come to the United States seeking asylum, joined the protest. Participants included citizens of Russia, China, Sudan, Afghanistan, and other countries.
In June, Makhmudov prepared a collective appeal to U.S. authorities that was signed by 45 detainees, including eight Russians. They complained of prolonged detention without criminal charges, inadequate medical care, spoiled food, and the lack of any meaningful way to secure release while their immigration cases were pending.
Shortly before the hunger strike began, four detainees, including Makhmudov, recorded a video appeal from inside the facility. The Verge reported that the video was recorded using the center’s internal video communications system. In the video, Makhmudov said detainees were paid just $1 a day for work inside the facility — enough, he said, for about a 10-minute phone call with family members. He also said many asylum seekers had come to the United States fleeing political persecution but ended up behind bars for months or years. The Russian protesters were soon placed in solitary confinement.
The Folkston center is operated by the private U.S. prison company GEO Group under a contract with ICE. According to The Verge, the company earns substantial revenue from immigration detention. GEO Group has also contributed to political organizations that support Donald Trump.

Iran offers to mediate between its Houthi allies and Saudi Arabia
Erika Solomon
- Iran offered to mediate between Saudi Arabia and the Houthi militia, saying there is no military solution to conflicts in the Middle East.
- A Houthi strike on Riyadh airport killed at least 12 people and injured hundreds, followed by reported strikes on Sanaa and more drone and missile threats.
- The conflict has widened across Yemen and the Gulf, raising fears of fresh regional fighting as Iran warns it could target digital infrastructure if war resumes.
AI generated
TEHRAN – Iran has offered to mediate between Saudi Arabia and the Iran-backed Houthi militia in Yemen, after a string of deadly attacks on the kingdom, warning that overlapping conflicts in the region have no military solution.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi made the offer to his Saudi counterpart, Faisal bin Farhan, during a telephone call on Oct 11, according to a statement posted on social media by the Iranian minister’s office.
“Insisting on a military approach and ignoring a political solution will further complicate the current situation,” the statement, posted on Araghchi’s Telegram channel, said.
Araghchi said Iran stood “ready to provide any assistance to help initiate a dialogue” between the two sides.
The Saudi government said the two ministers spoke, though it made no reference to any mediation offer from Iran. The call was a day after the deadliest attack on a Persian Gulf country since the start of the US-Israeli war with Iran.
On Oct 10, a Houthi strike on an airport in the Saudi capital, Riyadh, killed at least 12 people, with hundreds injured.
That sparked an exchange of strikes with Saudi-led forces targeting the airport in Sanaa, Yemen’s Houthi-controlled capital, according to reports on Oct 11 in local news media affiliated with the group.
The Houthi-run health ministry said a child was also killed in a strike on a residential building in Sanaa.
Saudi authorities have not commented on those assertions, but reported another deadly Houthi attack on Riyadh’s airport on Oct 11.
On Oct 12, a state-owned Saudi television channel, Al Ekhbariya, warned that the Saudi-led military coalition in Yemen was fending off drones and cruise missiles headed toward Saudi Arabia. The Saudi authorities have not commented publicly.
Fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis rapidly escalated in September when Houthi forces seized Yemen’s Red Sea coast, taking territory that sits alongside a strategic waterway for global trade and a key export route for Saudi oil.
The militia has been fighting the internationally recognised government of Yemen, which is backed by Saudi Arabia, since 2014. A fragile truce agreed in 2022 has unravelled in recent months.
The conflict has stoked further upheaval in the oil-rich Persian Gulf region, which was already reeling from the economic fallout of the US-Iran war.
US and Iranian officials appear braced for the possibility that their stalemated regional conflict could spill back into the open, with the Pentagon drawing up new plans for strikes.
Iran’s national security adviser, Mohsen Rezaei, threatened on Oct 11 that if fighting were to resume, Iranian forces would target digital infrastructure in the Gulf, including data centres, cables, and artificial intelligence facilities.
The Houthis are one of several militant groups that Iran is allied with across the region, and part of what the Islamic republic calls its “Axis of Resistance”.
Though the Houthis have benefited from years of military and financial support from Iran, regional experts have long described them as among the most independent of these allied forces, with ambitions distinct from Iran’s. NYTIMES

Ten years on, Britain’s prime minister says Russia meddled in the Brexit vote—and warns Germany and France
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
14:43:39 UTC
23:43:39 KST

UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Russia interfered in the 2016 referendum that took Britain out of the European Union, in podcast excerpts released on 11 October, the Associated Press reported. His remarks are believed to be the first time a British prime minister has publicly acknowledged such meddling.
Russia’s information war keeps running through Europe’s ballots. German security sources said in August that Moscow was escalating disinformation before state elections, and Ukraine’s Center for Countering Disinformation found more than 200 Russian fake news sites aimed at France last year.
One question, one clear answer
Burnham told The Rest Is Politics podcast that he asked his advisers whether Russia had interfered in the 2016 vote. He asked after taking office in July.
“I’ve had the clear answer that yes, there was,” he said.
He argued that such things must now be put clearly on the record. He did not say how Russia interfered or offer evidence, and Moscow has long denied interfering in foreign votes.
Burnham said he had discussed Russian interference with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz in Berlin the previous week. “You know he was saying to me that the AfD are clearly linked to Russia, funded I believe,” Burnham said, referring to Germany’s far-right Alternative for Germany party. Putting such interference on the record would help “voters in Germany and France understand that some of this politics is instigated via our enemies, namely Russia,” he added.
Years of silence
In 2020, Parliament’s Intelligence and Security Committee found that the government had actively avoided investigating whether Russia meddled in the referendum. The report noted open-source signs of Russian attempts to sway the Brexit campaign. The government, it said, had never looked for hard evidence.
The government rejected the committee’s call for a review.
“We have seen no evidence of successful interference in the EU Referendum,” it said.
That same year, London said Russian actors had almost certainly tried to interfere in the 2019 general election. The government said they did it by amplifying leaked UK-US trade documents online.
From 2019 to 2016
Three weeks ago, Burnham stopped short of this. At the UN General Assembly on 22 September, he said the Kremlin spends around £1.3 billion each year on manipulating information. That is roughly $1.7 billion at recent exchange rates. He cited evidence that Russian agencies tried to interfere in the 2019 general election, but he did not mention 2016.
In the same speech, he said Britain had already helped Moldova protect its elections from Russian interference.

A woman’s eviction in Madrid brought down a government. What can Israel learn from it? - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
14:41:10 UTC
23:41:10 KST

At 87, wheelchair-bound Maricarmen Abascal was evicted from the Madrid apartment she had called home for more than 70 years.
Her story became a symbol of Spain’s housing protests, which brought down the government, showing that even a lifetime in the same home offers no guarantee of being able to stay.
For an Israeli family weighing whether to buy a home, her story may reflect the anxiety that comes with every lease renewal.
And when a 30-year mortgage starts to look like a way to stop worrying about next year, we should ask how much of the demand for housing is really a demand for peace of mind.
When a family takes out a mortgage because it can no longer bear the uncertainty of renewing its lease, someone gets to count another sale. Whether that counts as a success is another matter.
The family may have traded one kind of uncertainty for a financial commitment that will weigh on it for 30 years. This is where the neat distinction between “renters’ problems” and “buyers’ problems” breaks down.
Sometimes, they are the same family, before and after they have had enough of moving.
In Madrid, that insecurity acquired a human face. Maricarmen, an 87-year-old wheelchair user, was evicted from her apartment following a dispute over a rent increase. Her eviction became a symbol of the housing protests.
Today, Spain’s prime minister announced a snap election after demonstrations that brought hundreds of thousands of people onto the streets over the country’s housing situation.
Israel does not need to copy every provision of Spain’s housing policies to understand why this story matters to people saving for a down payment here. It is easy to tell a family that cannot afford to buy to keep renting.
It is harder to explain how they are supposed to plan their lives that way. Can they enroll their child in the neighborhood school? Is it worth investing in their home? Will they still be able to afford the rent next year?
When the answers depend on each lease renewal, buying a home can become less about improving a family’s financial position and more about escaping uncertainty.
That is why any program designed to help a family buy a home must also answer a less headline-friendly question: What options does that family have if it does not buy?
If the answer is another short lease and another possible move, assistance with buying addresses only half the problem.
Being able to stay in the same neighborhood and know how the rent will change should not be a privilege reserved for those who can afford a down payment.
Making life easier
Long-term rental housing already exists in Israel, but the government needs to continue expanding it and make it a viable option for more families.
That means encouraging the construction of homes specifically for rent and offering incentives to private landlords willing to commit to leases lasting several years.
Those incentives should come with clear conditions: a guaranteed tenancy period, an agreed formula for rent adjustments, and termination provisions that protect both parties.
Tenants could plan their lives, while landlords would have a financial reason to make a long-term commitment. As this option becomes more widely available, fewer families would feel pressured into buying.
Ultimately, stable rental housing does not promise an immediate fall in home prices, and protecting one tenant does not automatically protect another.
Housing supply must also grow, and progress should be measured by homes actually delivered and the real cost of living in them. The number of transactions alone does not tell us how many families have found a housing solution they can afford in the long term.
Success can also mean a family deciding not to buy this year without having to move to yet another rental as a result. As long as ownership is seen as the only route to stability, we should be cautious about celebrating every rise in home sales.
Behind some of those purchases may be someone who cannot necessarily afford the commitment over the long term, but is simply afraid of eviction, a rent increase, or a landlord’s decision not to renew the lease.
The writer is an international real estate expert and a former member of Israel’s parliament and its Economic Affairs Committee.

Israel is losing the war of narratives: Einat Wilf unveils plan to fight back

The Reservists-Economic Party unveiled a seven-point national policy plan on Sunday aimed at countering anti-Israel narratives internationally, calling for a major expansion of the Foreign Ministry's resources and the integration of what it terms the "war of consciousness" into Israel's national security decision-making.
The proposal, authored by former MK Dr. Einat Wilf, who is running third on the party's Knesset list, outlines measures ranging from establishing a centralized information and intelligence hub to building international political alliances and using diplomatic, legal, and economic tools against supporters of terrorism.
According to the party, Wilf would lead the plan's implementation in the next Knesset and government, should the party secure a role in either.
The proposal marks a shift from Wilf's previously stated arguments about Israel's failures in the international arena toward a formal policy platform setting out how the party believes the next government should address them.
At the center of the plan is a call to treat international public opinion and narratives as national security considerations, rather than issues handled primarily through public diplomacy after government decisions have already been made.
Seven-point plan calls for diplomatic overhaul
The first component would require Israeli decision-makers to consider the international narrative implications of diplomatic and security decisions as part of the decision-making process itself.
The second calls for shifting from a reactive posture to a proactive one, in which Israel seeks to shape the international debate rather than primarily respond to criticism and accusations.
The proposal also calls for transforming the Foreign Ministry into a professional institution with funding, resources, and standing comparable to those of the Defense Ministry.
Another central component is the establishment of a hub to coordinate reliable information and intelligence at the speed of social media, allowing Israel to respond more rapidly to developments in the international information environment.
The remaining measures focus on building strategic alliances with international opinion leaders and parliamentarians, deploying diplomatic, legal, and economic tools against supporters of terrorism, and establishing a new international agenda rather than operating within frameworks set by Israel's adversaries.
The party did not specify the proposed budget for these measures, the structure of the new coordination hub, or a timetable for implementation.
The proposal comes as the government has already increased its public diplomacy spending. In December 2025, Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar and Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich agreed on a NIS 2.35 billion allocation for Israel advocacy efforts in the 2026 budget, alongside plans to strengthen the Foreign Ministry's public diplomacy operations.
Wilf's proposal, however, calls for a broader transformation of the role that international narratives play in Israeli policymaking, rather than limiting the response to communications campaigns.
Wilf: 'This is not hasbara'
"The war of consciousness is just as important as the war on the battlefield. Hasbara is appropriate when responding to criticism of Israel. But we are confronting an ideology that is constructing a justification for the annihiliation of the Jewish people," Wilf said in a statement accompanying the plan.
She argued that hostility toward Israel and Zionism was increasingly being legitimized by international institutions, universities, and media organizations, creating consequences that extended beyond the country's reputation.
"This is not merely damage to Israel’s image. It lays the groundwork for attacks on Jews, sanctions, boycotts, on Israel’s freedom of action. Faced with such a threat, Israel must move beyond hasbara and begin conducting a national war of consciousness."
The position is consistent with arguments Wilf made in a recent conversation with The Jerusalem Post, in which she described the international battle over narratives as a central challenge facing Israel and the Jewish people.
In a separate discussion, Wilf also outlined her broader policy vision, including her approach to Gaza, the need to confront the ideology underpinning hostility toward Israel, and her ambition to serve as foreign minister in the next government.
The new platform places those positions within a series of proposed government actions, particularly concerning the Foreign Ministry's responsibilities and Israel's diplomatic strategy.
Yoaz Hendel, chairman of the Reservists-Economic Party, also backed the initiative, arguing that Israel had fallen behind its adversaries in shaping international perceptions.
"Qatar is an enemy state that finances our enemies," Hendel said, accusing Qatar and the Islamist axis of having gained the upper hand in the international battle over narratives while Israel and Diaspora Jewish communities concentrated on conventional public diplomacy.
"Just as we turned the tide on the battlefield, we must do the same in the war of consciousness."
The announcement follows renewed pro-Palestinian demonstrations and events surrounding the anniversary of the October 7 Hamas attacks, which the party cited as part of the backdrop for its initiative.

Russia is hacking cameras across Europe to track arms bound for Ukraine. At home, Ukraine has secured about 40,000 that could guide strikes — WSJ
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
14:41:02 UTC
23:41:02 KST

The ordinary security camera watching a street or a parking lot has quietly become a weapon of war. Ukraine’s Security Service has identified about 40,000 surveillance cameras since Russia’s 2022 invasion that Russian forces and spy agencies could have used to snoop, find targets and correct strikes, and has protected, reoriented or blocked them, The Wall Street Journal reported.
The discovered threat reaches well beyond Ukraine: Dutch intelligence warned in July that Russian state actors are systematically hacking cameras across Europe to track arms deliveries to Ukraine and the whereabouts of Ukrainian troops.
AI makes it faster
About 1.2 billion internet-connected cameras now watch the world, in doorbells, traffic lights, and baby monitors, and almost any of them can be hacked, the journalists found.
In Ukraine, the danger is lethal. In 2024, Russian hackers took over residential webcams in Kyiv, including one that a condominium association had installed, to find targets and adjust missile strikes on the capital, Ukraine's Security Service says.
Spying on Europe’s edge
Evidence of European reach keeps surfacing. Cybersecurity firm CloudSEK has recently uncovered an exposed server it suspects belongs to a Russian-speaking hacker, containing hundreds of webcam images of Ukrainian defense, government, energy, and communications sites, as well as scenes of daily life.
Many of the images came from locations near Ukraine’s border with NATO member Romania, CloudSEK says.
The Dutch warning and the server point the same way: cameras far from the front line are feeding Russia data on how the West arms Ukraine.
Ukraine turns the lens back on Russia
Ukraine also uses the same tactic inside the occupied territory. The international hacker group Team OneFist took control of a camera in Sevastopol, in occupied Crimea, and used it to watch Russian ships, submarines, and helicopters, spotting a previously unknown air base that Ukraine later struck, damaging planes and air defenses.
Team OneFist also reached cameras on the Kerch Strait Bridge, learning that Russia had installed motion sensors beneath the bridge to guard against waterborne attacks. Penetrating a well-placed camera gets analysts closer to targets at less risk than any secret agent.

====================================================================================================

Turkey’s historic bid to end the PKK insurgency hangs in the balance - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
14:40:57 UTC
23:40:57 KST

On August 10, 2026, the Turkish parliament passed, by 467 votes in the 600-seat legislature, a law putting into effect what Ankara calls the “Terror-Free Turkey” process – a euphemism for the disbandment and disarmament of the outlawed Kurdistan Workers’ Party (PKK).
The PKK is designated a terrorist organization not only by the Turkish government, but by the US and the EU.
The overwhelming majority by which the law passed was made possible because it was supported not only by President Recep Tayyip Erdogan’s AK Party and its political allies, but also, perhaps surprisingly, by that long-time thorn in Erdogan’s flesh, the pro-Kurdish DEM Party.
That unusual accord between long-time political opponents sealed a compromise that had been decades in the making: the dissolution of the PKK in exchange for unprecedented leniency for its former members.
The new law provides a mechanism for suspending certain prosecutions relating to PKK offences, and for deferring the execution of some prison sentences.
Most importantly, it establishes a framework intended to facilitate the reintegration of eligible former PKK members into civilian life. The Associated Press reported that the measure could potentially affect approximately 4,000 PKK members not directly involved in violent crimes.
The new law becomes operative only after Turkish security authorities have determined that the PKK and affiliated structures have indeed ended their armed existence and surrendered the weapons and ammunition under their control. This must then be confirmed by the National Security Council and published in the Official Gazette.
These requirements are not as oppressive as may first appear. The ground has been well prepared, and the PKK is ready and willing to comply.
The Kurds are an ethnic group of some 30-40 million people. They inhabit a contiguous mountainous area divided between Turkey, Iran, Iraq, and Syria. Most live in Turkey, where they constitute roughly one-fifth of the population.
Belief that Kurdish autonomy would weaken Turkey
For decades, Erdogan, together with many in the Turkish establishment, believed that granting their Kurdish citizens political autonomy could weaken the unity of the state.
Some feared it would be a first step toward an independent sovereign Kurdish state, particularly after the constitutional recognition of the autonomous Kurdistan administration in northern Iraq in 2005.
These fears were compounded during the Syrian civil war, starting in 2011. Kurdish forces established autonomous institutions in northern Syria, creating the possibility of a Kurdish-controlled zone along much of Turkey’s southern border. Links between the Kurdish forces in Syria and the PKK were perceived by Erdogan as a security threat.
He had already authorized military operations against PKK bases in northern Iraq. Turkish aircraft struck them in late 2007, and this was followed by a major ground offensive in February 2008. Subsequent PKK attacks on the Turkish military in 2011 led Erdogan to repeat air strikes against them, alongside intensified fighting in southeastern Turkey.
The current Terror-Free Turkey initiative is not the first time that Erdogan has attempted to hold out an olive branch to the PKK. In late 2012, when still prime minister, his government began a serious negotiation process with Abdullah Ocalan, the founder of the PKK, imprisoned on Imrali island since 1999.
The initiative produced a positive result in March 2013, when Ocalan issued a message calling for a ceasefire and the withdrawal of PKK fighters from Turkey. Armed resistance ceased for a time, but the ceasefire did not hold.
A historic moment came on February 28, 2015. At a joint press conference involving government representatives and leaders of the HDP (the Peoples’ Democratic Party), a message from Ocalan was read out calling on the PKK to take the “strategic and historical decision” to end the armed struggle.
It looked like a genuine call to transition from armed conflict to politics. Yet once again the ceasefire unraveled. During 2015, a series of incidents led Erdogan to resume airstrikes against PKK positions in northern Iraq.
The resulting fighting was extremely destructive. Almost 3,000 people were killed between July 2015 and July 2017. Overall, Reuters estimates that since 1984 the conflict has killed more than 40,000 people, including combatants and civilians.
This second attempt at resolving the PKK issue is quite different, triggered by a quite unexpected event.
In October 2024, Devlet Bahceli, leader of the Nationalist Movement Party (MHP) and Erdogan’s principal parliamentary ally, unexpectedly suggested that Ocalan be brought from prison to address parliament and call upon the PKK to dissolve itself.
The initiative was all the more startling because Bahceli had historically taken one of the hardest nationalist positions against the Kurdish political movement. Erdogan described the development as a potentially “historic window of opportunity.”
A dramatic address by Ocalan to the Turkish parliament – akin, perhaps, to that by Anwar Sadat to Israel’s Knesset in 1977 – never took place. But there was a series of meetings between DEM politicians and Ocalan at Imrali prison, and in February 2025 Ocalan issued a crucial statement.
He called upon the PKK to abandon the armed struggle and lay down its arms, to dissolve itself and pursue the Kurdish question through democratic politics.
The important difference from 2015 is that the current process does not seek yet another ceasefire, but explicitly envisages the end of the PKK as an organization – an outcome announced in May 2025, when the PKK said its 12th Congress had decided to dissolve the organization and end its armed struggle.
In July 2025, Ocalan appeared in a rare video and said the armed struggle was over. He called for a transition toward democratic politics and asked the Turkish parliament to establish a mechanism to oversee disarmament and the broader peace process.
The result is Turkey’s August 2026 law – a legal mechanism for implementing the PKK’s decision to dissolve and disarm. But its principal provisions are conditional on verified PKK disarmament, and that step has not yet been taken. The process is at its most delicate point.
Currently, the debate is focused heavily on where and how PKK weapons are to be surrendered and who verifies the operation. Reports indicate that Turkish intelligence and security officials have been dealing with counterparts in Iraq, the Kurdistan Region of Iraq and Syria over precisely these practical questions.
A terror-free Turkey is in the balance.
The writer, a former senior civil servant, is the Middle East correspondent for Eurasia Review. Follow him at: www.a-mid-east-journal.blogspot.com

23:40:31 KST

Comedian Giorgio Bracardi, whose surreal, over-the-top characters delighted generations of radio and TV audiences in Italy and who is perhaps best remembered for his appearances on mid-80s cult late-night variety show Quelli della Notte, has died at the age of 93, his family said Monday. 
Bracardi, who was also a musician and singer, was famous for characters such as the "Nicaraguan vulture" Scarpantibus and the pushy journalist Max Vinella from the cult 1970s radio show Alto Gradimento. 
He had been staying at a care home in Fiano Romano near his native Rome after breaking his femur last spring. 
Born in Rome on May 3, 1933, Bracardi grew up in the world of show business. 
His father was one of the first managers of Rome's Salone Margherita theater; his mother, Edvige, was a soprano, and his father, Glauco, was a tenor. 
All five of their children received a musical education and learned to play an instrument. 
Giorgio was a pianist who later became a composer, even participating in the Sanremo Festival as a songwriter. However, Bracardi rose to great popularity with Alto Gradimento, the radio program he co-created with Renzo Arbore, Gianni Boncompagni, and Mario Marenco. 
He later made the leap to television with Arbore in the 1985 show Quelli della notte, and also appeared on Pronto, chi gioca?, hosted by Enrica Bonaccorti and Giancarlo Magalli. 
In 1989, he hosted and starred in Chiappala chiappala on Rai 2. 
In 1995, he moved to Mediaset to join Striscia la Notizia, playing Lucio Smentisco, a fictional spokesperson for Silvio Berlusconi. 
In 2001, he was a featured performer on Marco Giusti's Rai 2 program Stracult. 
Bracardi also provided the voice for the character Cattivik in the animated series broadcast by Mediaset in 2008. 
With the surreal, chaotic characters created by Bracardi on Alto gradimento, his most famous catchphrases and character yells include: • "PATROCLOOO!" - His iconic, absurd shout performed as an unlikely Achilles wandering around looking for his lover/companion Patroclus. 
• "In galera! In galera!" (In jail! In jail!) - The signature aggressive chant of his character Ermanno Catenacci, a nostalgic, raging ex Fascist 'hierarch' (high-up official). 
• "Chettefrega!" (What do you care!) - A frequent, dismissive exclamation used across his sketches. 
• The screeching, bird-like squawks of Scarpantibus, a prehistoric, laceless-boot-wearing bird creature he created that spoke in chaotic noises.

Rostov Oil Terminal Burns for Third Day After Reported Ukrainian Drone Attack
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
14:40:24 UTC
23:40:24 KST

A fire at an oil terminal in the southern Russian city of Rostov-on-Don continued to burn for a third day Monday after a reported Ukrainian drone attack over the weekend, according to independent media and Ukrainian monitoring channels.
Footage published by Astra and Exilenova+ showed flames and thick smoke rising from the terminal’s fuel storage tanks. The facility, owned by the Novoshakhtinsk oil refinery, has a total storage capacity of 60,000 cubic meters and can handle 3.5 million metric tons of petroleum products a year, according to publicly available data.
Authorities had not announced that the fire had been extinguished as of midday Monday.
The Ukrainian monitoring channel Supernova said preliminary information indicated that seven of the terminal’s 12 tanks had burned and another showed signs of fire damage. Footage it published showed blackened tanks alongside others still engulfed in flames. The reported extent of the damage could not be independently confirmed.
The local Telegram channel Rostov Glavny also published footage of the blaze, saying the city had been shrouded in smoke for a second day. Its post suggested that reeds might be burning, citing rumors, but Astra’s analysis placed the fire at the oil terminal.
The facility, formerly known as Yug Rusi, was reportedly struck overnight into Saturday in Rostov-on-Don’s Zheleznodorozhny district. NASA’s FIRMS satellite monitoring system detected a fire at the site.
The terminal transfers petroleum products onto sea and river tankers for export and has reportedly been used to supply fuel to the Russian military.
Rostov region Governor Yury Slyusar said air defenses had shot down more than 100 drones over the region that night. He reported several fires following strikes and said six people had been injured, but did not mention damage to the terminal.
Ukraine had not publicly claimed responsibility for an attack on the facility.
The overnight attacks also damaged a railway drawbridge on the line between Rostov-on-Don and nearby Bataysk, causing lengthy delays to dozens of trains, according to Russian Railways.
Slyusar said two vessels were also damaged in the nearby city of Azov.

'Disclose EC files, set up audit panel': Rahul Gandhi, 10 INDIA bloc leaders move SC against CEC
