Rahul Gandhi, Priyanka Gandhi Vadra and other INDIA bloc leaders marched towards Supreme Court in Delhi to protest against the CEC. (PTI photo)
NEW DELHI: A Rahul Gandhi-led INDIA bloc march to the Supreme Court against alleged electoral irregularities encountered police barricades in central Delhi on Monday before the opposition leaders eventually reached the court and filed a joint petition against the Election Commission of India (EC).The march, dubbed "March for Democracy", brought together opposition leaders, MPs, party workers and activists, with Rahul Gandhi, Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge, Samajwadi Party chief Akhilesh Yadav, Congress leader Priyanka Gandhi Vadra and RJD leader Tejashwi Yadav among those who joined the procession.The march was initially halted at Bhagwan Dass Road, where police had erected barricades to prevent the procession from proceeding towards the Supreme Court. As the crowd swelled and the standoff continued, several leaders, including Rahul Gandhi, Priyanka Gandhi Vadra, Akhilesh Yadav and Tejashwi Yadav, climbed atop a vehicle as supporters raised slogans against the government and Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.As per Supreme Court website, their legal team had filed the petition against the EC as the leaders failed to reach on time.Subsequently they reached the Supreme Court premises and filed the petition in a show of strenght.
Visuals released by the news agency showed Rahul Gandhi, Kharge and other INDIA bloc leaders filing the plea.The march came after the Chief Justice of India refused to meet the opposition leaders who had sought an appointment to submit a memorandum over alleged electoral irregularities. CJI Surya Kant had said the matter was already before the court and advised the leaders to pursue the judicial route by filing a petition.ALSO READ: 'Ready to contest on ballot paper': Himanta lobs dare at Cong but with a big rider
11 leaders named in the petition
The petition names Rahul Gandhi as the lead petitioner, along with 10 other opposition leaders from INDIA bloc parties. The petitioners are:
Rahul Gandhi, Congress
Mallikarjun Kharge, Congress
Saugata Roy, Mamata-TMC
Akhilesh Yadav, Samajwadi Party
Tejashwi Prasad Yadav, Rashtriya Janata Dal
Sanjay Raut, Shiv Sena (UBT)
MA Baby, CPM
D Raja, CPI
Mahua Majhi, Jharkhand Mukti Morcha
Supriya Sule, NCP (Sharadchandra Pawar)
ET Mohammed Basheer, Indian Union Muslim League leader
The Election Commission of India has been named as a respondent. Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and the other two Election Commissioners, Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi, have also been named as respondents, according to the Supreme Court website.
What does the petition seek
The petition filed by Rahul Gandhi and 10 other opposition leaders in the Supreme Court has challenged the manner in which the Election Commission has taken decisions relating to the SIR of electoral rolls, news agency ANI reported.It seeks disclosure of the EC’s complete files, agendas, minutes, notings and objections concerning the disputed decisions, including the June 24, 2025 decision to commence the SIR, as well as ECINET and ERONET access logs.It also seeks a judicial examination of whether these decisions were taken in accordance with Article 324 of the Constitution, the 2023 law governing the Election Commission and the Supreme Court’s ruling in TN Seshan vs Union of India.The petition seeks several safeguards against voter deletions during the SIR, including a direction that no elector be removed from the electoral roll without prior notice and a reasonable opportunity to be heard.
It also seeks the booth-wise publication of deleted electors, along with the reasons for their deletion and demographic details.The petition further calls for an independent committee headed by a retired Supreme Court judge to audit deletions and modifications in electoral-roll databases, including ECINET and ERONET. It also seeks an interim suspension of the ongoing SIR until the court adjudicates the matter.Additionally, the plea asks the court to direct the Election Commission to ensure that “every decision of the Election Commission relating to the Special Intensive Revision is taken and duly minuted” in accordance with the 2023 Act.

Founder of pro-war propaganda project Rybar returns to Russia after being expelled from Montenegro
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
14:39:27 UTC
23:39:27 KST

Mikhail Zvinchuk, founder of the Russian pro-war Telegram channel Rybar, returned to Russia after being detained and expelled from Montenegro. He arrived in Moscow from Belgrade overnight Oct. 11 with his wife, Valeria, and three Rybar employees. Meanwhile, Montenegrin President Jakov Milatović demanded an explanation as to how the EU-sanctioned propagandist was able to enter the country and whether local security services had prior information about his trip.
Zvinchuk told reporters that the Russian government, Foreign Ministry, security services, and state defense conglomerate Rostec had been involved in securing his release, with Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova, former President Dmitry Medvedev, and RT editor-in-chief Margarita Simonyan also playing various roles. The U.S. has previously identified Rostec as one of Rybar’s sources of financing. The same claim appears in documents published by the UK Foreign Office.
“This is probably one of the few cases where both the state and private organizations worked in a coordinated way,” Zvinchuk told a correspondent for the Russian news channel RTVI at Moscow’s Sheremetyevo Airport. He also noted that Montenegrin police had not returned the filming equipment they seized, adding that of the equipment had been rented, and that Russian diplomats were now working to secure its return.
Zvinchuk also claimed that Montenegrin authorities had checked Interpol and Europol databases during his detention but found no basis for an international search warrant.
Montenegro president demands review of security agencies’ actions
On Oct. 10, the office of Montenegrin President Jakov Milatović issued a statement demanding that law enforcement agencies explain the circumstances of Zvinchuk’s entry into the country. The statement noted that the Rybar founder is under European Union sanctions, which Montenegro has aligned itself with as part of its EU integration policy.
The president’s office called for authorities to establish what information government agencies had about Zvinchuk, whether border procedures were followed, and whether there had been prior coordination with foreign intelligence services. Officials were also asked to explain whether they knew in advance that he was coming and what measures they took while he was in the country.
The Insider previously reported that Zvinchuk arrived in the Balkans from Germany. According to Bosnian investigative outlet Detektor, he and his team flew from the EU to Sarajevo on Oct. 2 and crossed the land border into Montenegro on Oct. 7.
Zvinchuk has been under EU sanctions since June 2023, and Brussels characterizes him as a member of a group created by Vladimir Putin to coordinate mobilization efforts for Russia’s war against Ukraine, in addition to his duties running the Rybar propaganda project.
His wife, Valeria, who was detained with him, has been under individual British sanctions since July 13, 2026. British authorities describe her as Rybar’s creative director. London sanctioned 10 other Rybar employees and managers at the same time.
When was Zvinchuk arrested?
Montenegrin police detained Mikhail and Valeria Zvinchuk, along with Sergei Belous, Pavel Lekatorchuk, and Kira Doroshenko, on the morning of Oct. 9 in the town of Risan on the Bay of Kotor. Montenegro’s National Security Agency took part in the operation. Officers seized cameras, a GoPro, a drone, and mobile phones from the group.
Dmitry Medvedev, deputy chairman of Russia’s Security Council, responded to the detention by suggesting that Russia expand its “exchange pool” with detained European and U.S. citizens. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Russian diplomats would work to protect Zvinchuk’s rights.
U.S. offered up to $10 million for information on Rybar employees
Since 2024, the U.S. State Department has offered a reward of up to $10 million for information about people linked to interference in U.S. elections, including Rybar employees. Mikhail and Valeria Zvinchuk are among those named on the department’s list.
U.S. authorities say the project was previously financed by organizations linked to Wagner Group founder Yevgeny Prigozhin and later began receiving money from Rostec. According to the State Department, Rybar employees created English-language information platforms aimed at interfering in the 2024 U.S. presidential election and deepening divisions in American society, including over immigration. In December 2025, Britain imposed sanctions on Zvinchuk and Rybar LLC.

Ukraine Passes Education Law to Unlock EU Talks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
14:39:11 UTC
23:39:11 KST

Ukraine’s parliament passed legislation on Monday, Oct. 12, expanding the educational rights of national minorities, fulfilling Hungary’s key condition for advancing two areas of Kyiv’s EU accession negotiations.
Bill No.16119 received 273 votes in its first reading and 266 votes in the final vote, lawmaker Yaroslav Zhelezniak said.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Parliament immediately instructed Verkhovna Rada Speaker Ruslan Stefanchuk to sign the legislation and send it to President Volodymyr Zelensky for approval, with Zelensky signing the bill into law hours later on Monday.
The measure is intended to clear the way for opening Cluster 2, covering the EU internal market, and Cluster 3, covering competitiveness and inclusive growth.
Hungary had repeatedly blocked the two clusters, arguing that Ukraine had not sufficiently protected the education and language rights of its ethnic Hungarian minority.
What changes under the new law?
The legislation introduces a special status for general secondary schools serving national minorities.
Schools where more than half of students receive instruction in a minority language that is also an official EU language will be eligible for the status. Parliamentary estimates suggest that 149 schools, or approximately 1.2% of Ukraine’s secondary schools, could qualify.
Ukrainian remains the primary state language of education. The legislation more clearly defines how the languages of Indigenous peoples and national minorities may be used alongside Ukrainian. Its provisions apply only to languages that have official status in the EU and therefore do not extend to Russian.
Russia Plots Assassinations of European Arms Executives – FT
Parents of at least two-thirds of the students in a relevant class or group may request that additional subjects be taught in Ukrainian.
Schools containing at least one minority-language class will also be permitted to duplicate signs, education certificates requested by parents, and certain administrative documents in the relevant minority language.
Students who received their education in an Indigenous or minority language may obtain translated external assessment materials and complete the tests in that language, except for examinations covering language and literature.
EU decision expected within hours
Hungary agreed to stop blocking the clusters only after Ukraine adopted the education amendments, according to European Pravda, citing EU sources.
The EU’s Committee of Permanent Representatives, known as Coreper, is expected to consider the common negotiating positions for Ukraine and Moldova on Monday evening.
All 27 EU member states must agree before the clusters can formally open.
If the ambassadors approve the documents, intergovernmental conferences with Ukraine and Moldova could take place on Tuesday, Oct. 13, formally launching negotiations under the two clusters.
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said Kyiv expected that decision after meeting his Hungarian counterpart, Anita Orban, in Luxembourg.
The negotiating positions have reportedly been ready since Friday, Oct. 9, with adoption delayed until the Ukrainian parliament completed its vote.
Part of Kyiv-Budapest minority agreement
The legislation follows an agreement reached between Kyiv and the new Hungarian government on the language, cultural, and educational rights of the approximately 100,000 ethnic Hungarians living mainly in Ukraine’s Zakarpattia region.
Budapest had previously linked progress in Ukraine’s EU accession process to the implementation of those commitments in Ukrainian law.
Hungary signaled earlier in October that it was prepared to ease its veto once parliament passed the minority education legislation.
The law’s adoption satisfies that condition, but the clusters will not be considered formally open until EU ambassadors approve the negotiating positions and the intergovernmental conference takes place.

Nuclear war and malicious use of AI could end humanity by 2100, scientists warn
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
14:39:04 UTC
23:39:04 KST

They are among 17 global threats to human health according to a new study by The Lancet which aims to drive global action to address them.
The malicious use of AI or nuclear war could end humanity as we know it by 2100, according to a new global health risk assessment.
They top a pyramid of 17 major threats to human health identified in a study published in The Lancet, including antimicrobial resistance, climate change, pandemics, income inequality and a range of health issues such as tobacco, obesity and mental health.
According to the study, nuclear conflict does not just cover the impact of the missiles but the consequences too, such as nuclear famine, while the malicious use of AI includes the use and development of bioweapons against us.
The research was conducted by the new Lancet Commission on 21st-century global threats to health, a group made up of 37 experts in health, economics, security and technology.
Together they used disability-adjusted life years, also known DALYs, as a metric to compare each threat from the year 2025 to 2100 from 204 countries and territories across age, sex and cause.
The research essentially shows how many healthy years of human life could be lost to each global threat, according to their best- and worst-case scenarios. This also gives an idea of how much of an impact humanity can have if it acts now or chooses to do nothing.
The 17 threats range from 1.02 billion DALYs to 23.1 billion DALYs. For comparison, the COVID-19 pandemic caused approximately 500 million DALYs. The largest cumulative expected amenable burden is from obesity.
The Commission's aim is to encourage and empower governments to act, by giving them the information and tools needed to prepare for these global threats and take decisive action now to avoid worst case scenarios.
However, they also make it clear that their work is not aimed at providing a ranking of threats or policy priorities, but to report and analyse global threats as part of a dynamic process, with findings changing over time as new evidence and data are collected.
While “malicious use of AI, including bioweapons, and nuclear conflict with nuclear famine carry risks of extinction in the next 75 years,” the experts warn that all the threats are interconnected and therefore they call for “holistic action framework grounded in science, human rights, and solidarity.”
The Commission first recommends national governments invest in building “threat-ready health systems,” to put them on the front foot when faced with global health challenges such as seen in the COVID-19 pandemic.
They also call for more investment in “breakthrough solutions,” such as nuclear fusion and carbon removal technologies that could radically affect climate change outcomes and other globally threatening issues, or the vaccines developed during the pandemic.
The Commission also calls for regular monitoring and risks assessments of these risks, with findings presented to international organisations such as the G20 and the UN to increase the urgency in addressing the issues before they escalate and become crises, and encourage wider action rather than individual countries going it alone.
Researchers believe the current “competitive approach” of tackling major challenges one by one is hindering humanity’s chances.
The Commission's findings were presented on Sunday at the World Health Summit in Berlin, Germany. Their assessment will be updated each year to re-evaluate each of the 17 threats identified, incorporating new data and any emerging challenges.

Bracardi an eclectic humorist with unique, unrepeatable talent says Arbore
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
16:37:59 CEST
23:37:59 KST

Giorgio Bracardi was an eclectic
humorist with unique, unrepeatable talent, the veteran showman
and presenter Renzo Arbore, who launched the comic genius on his
cult 1970s radio show Alto Gradimento, said after his death at
the age of 93 Monday.
                                    
"Giorgio Bracardi was a unique and unrepeatable talent—an
eclectic, instinctive humorist and improviser who defied
categorization and broke all the rules, yet was also an
intellectual in disguise," said Arbore.
                                    
From the microphone of that cult programme, Bracardi brought to
life characters who became legendary.
                                    
"There was the Fascist official Catenacci, the amateur
journalist Max Vinella. And then Patroclo (Patroclus), the
Cinecittà extra who would shout to summon other extras for films
set in antiquity," Arbore recalls.
                                    
"He also told curious stories about characters from the fringes
of society, adopting the persona of a scholar of bizarre
traditions—covering people, animals, and inventors. We never
engaged in topical satire or impersonations; our hallmark—and I
include Mario Marenco here—was inventing characters of pure
fantasy, surreal figures born of the wholesome, good-natured,
and tasteful high-spiritedness of those years—a spirit that
still lives within us: that ability to joke about low-brow
subjects while remaining cultured."
Those characters "have all remained in the memory of a
generation; even today, people who listened to the show back
then speak of them as if they were still on the air when they
meet me.
                                    
Fortunately, there are clips on YouTube that still hold up
remarkably well."
Not to mention catchphrases like "Chettefrega!" (Who
Cares)—shouted at his students by Professor Aurelio Ovidio
Marcellini, a staunch monarchist patriot—which were later
brought together in the shout "In Galera!" (In Jail).
                                    
Arbore and Bracardi first crossed paths through music.
                                    
"I saw him at a festival in Venice—I heard him at a piano bar,
performing the odd little vocal tics and noises characteristic
of Scarpantibus, another of his bizarre characters—and I
immediately invited him to the studio to join Marenco.
                                    
Together with them and Gianni Boncompagni, we formed a quartet
that has absolutely no equal."
He would later reunite with Bracardi on television for the show
Quelli della Notte.
                                    
"Giorgio would improvise impressions of characters created on
the fly, day by day, following the rules of a sort of homegrown,
playful camaraderie—like having fun at home: everything
instinctive, everything in the moment."
Although a lawsuit regarding the authorship of Alto Gradimento
had driven a wedge between them in recent years, today Arbore
had no reluctance in paying tribute to the comic.
                                    
"He was truly a magnificent comedian, the kind who leaves an
indelible, inimitable mark; today, I cannot say there is a new
Bracardi, just as there is no new Marenco." 
                                    
ALL RIGHTS RESERVED © Copyright ANSA

Pope Leo to go to hospital Tuesday for lung nodule surgery

Pope Leo to go to hospital Tuesday for lung nodule surgery
Pope Leo XIV will be admitted to the hospital on Tuesday, days after he shared he would undergo surgery to remove a lung nodule discovered during recent medical tests, the Vatican announced.
The Holy See press office didn't say when the operation itself would take place, but said it will require a weeklong recovery in the hospital.
The U.S.-born pontiff revealed the discovery of the nodule during his Sunday noon prayer and said he was following doctors' advice to have it removed.
He said it was found in an early stage and was "circumscribed."
"The doctors believe it's best to take action, so, following their advice, I've decided to have surgery to remove it," Leo, 71, said Sunday. "Thank you for your spiritual support, and I entrust myself to your prayers."
He will be treated at Rome's Gemelli Hospital, which has a special apartment for the pope.
The Vatican press office said Monday that no particular issue precipitated the tests, denying Italian media reports suggesting an inflammation had prompted Leo to undergo the checkup.
The pope's surgery marks the first major health event of his 17-month pontificate. It was significant because the pope himself revealed the news, in perhaps the most public way possible: at the end of his Sunday noon blessing with thousands of people in St. Peter's Square.
The Vatican has for centuries zealously guarded the pope's health and has often sent out confusing information, or none at all, about papal illnesses. Pope Francis tried to change that by being upfront about his frailties and musing on his eventual death. But even during his pontificate, information was tightly controlled.
Leo's decision and reveal suggested an unusual level of transparency by the American pope.
A lung nodule is a small abnormal area measuring less than 1 inch that sometimes appears on a CT scan of the chest or abdomen, according to the American Cancer Society. Often, the scans are done to investigate trauma or a lung infection, unrelated to a lung cancer screening.
On Monday, it was business as usual at the Vatican. Leo presided over an audience with members of a Rome-based charity, the Circolo San Pietro, and received a donation from them. He spoke in a strong, clear voice, praising their service and sacrifice. The crowd gave him a rousing round of applause afterward.
He had six other private audiences, made three appointments and the Vatican released a letter he had penned to the outgoing dean of the College of Cardinals, thanking him for his service. The letter was signed on Sunday.
In the afternoon, he was expected to continue his audiences and, if time, rejoin a weeklong conference he convened on ministering to families.
The pope has a major trip planned Nov. 6-17 to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru. It's unclear whether the planned surgery and recovery would affect the itinerary.

NATO's top military commander outlines 'block, blunt, and break' strategy to counter potential attacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
14:34:03 UTC
23:34:03 KST

Melike Pala
12 October 2026•Update: 12 October 2026
NATO's top military commander on Monday outlined a three-stage military strategy to counter a potential attack against alliance territory, saying the bloc would first block an initial assault, then blunt any continued offensive, and, if necessary, break the enemy's forces and warfighting capabilities.
Speaking at the Warsaw Security Forum 2026 during a panel titled "Theory of Victory: How Do We Achieve Military Success Against Russia in Deterrence and Defense?" Gen. Alexus Grynkewich, NATO's supreme allied commander Europe (SACEUR), said the strategy is designed to deny an adversary the ability to seize and hold NATO territory.
"My theory of victory is simple: we will block the initial attack. If the attack persists, we will blunt it and prevent enemy advance. And if required, we will break the enemy's forces and the operational warfighting system that is arrayed against us," he said.
He stressed that NATO does not consider a conflict "imminent or inevitable," describing the alliance as defensive and emphasizing that its primary objective is to deter aggression and preserve peace.
"Our alliance exists to preserve peace, but let there be no doubt: should war come, we will block, blunt any attack, and then if it does not cease, we will break the forces conducting aggression against us," Grynkewich said.
He explained that the first stage, blocking an attack, would involve forward land forces preventing enemy formations from advancing and seizing allied territory, supported by air, naval, space and cyber capabilities.
If an offensive continued, NATO would seek to blunt it through advanced sensors, autonomous systems, and coordinated multi-domain operations, denying the adversary the ability to gain momentum or seize the initiative.
In the final stage, the alliance would target not only enemy forces but also the systems supporting and sustaining them, including command structures, logistics, and replenishment capabilities. 
Ukraine will get through winter with 'more resolve and more fight'
He said NATO would combine high-end precision weapons with large numbers of affordable and scalable systems, applying sustained military pressure across land, air, sea, space, and cyberspace.
The objective, he added, would not be to inflict a strategic defeat on an adversary but to render its forces incapable of continuing an attack against alliance territory.
"We are not seeking to impose a strategic defeat on our adversary, nor do we need to do so. Rather, we are only seeking to stop any attack in its tracks, to deny the ability to seize and hold our territory," he said.
Grynkewich said this approach would also help NATO maintain an advantageous position in terms of escalation, stressing that the alliance would act only against the forces and systems involved in attacking it.
He said NATO is working to translate the strategy into operational readiness through exercises, forward deployments, and investments in both advanced military capabilities and more affordable systems.
Asked about the possibility of a simultaneous conflict in Europe and the Asia-Pacific, Grynkewich said NATO's planning takes such a scenario into account.
Turning to Ukraine, he warned that continued attacks on energy infrastructure would make the coming winter particularly difficult for civilians.
"They're going to get through this winter. They're going to come out of it with more resolve and more fight," Grynkewich added.
On concerns about NATO members’ political commitment to collective defense, Grynkewich said he has confidence in the alliance's commitment to Article 5, which treats an armed attack against one member as an attack against all.
He also rejected doubts about the US commitment to NATO, noting that American troops are already deployed in Poland and across the alliance's eastern flank.

Starlink India launch: Why Elon Musk is still waiting
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
14:33:00 UTC
23:33:00 KST

Starlink India launch: Why Elon Musk is still waiting
October 12, 2026
Elon Musk, the CEO of SpaceX, has escalated his criticism of the delay in launching Starlink in India. Last week, he sarcastically referred to Mukesh Ambani, one of India's richest people and chairman of Reliance Industries, as "Prime Minister Ambani" and accused his supporters of protecting a monopoly.
"Would you nonetheless consider allowing Starlink to compete?" Musk wrote on X, arguing that the service could bring internet access to underserved communities across India.
Rahul Gandhi, a leader of the opposition Indian National Congress, joined the discussion, writing: "Welcome to India, Elon. Wait till you discover the other guy." Musk replied: "Thank you, Rahul. This is indeed troubling."
A delayed launch and a war of words
Prime Minister Narendra Modi's ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) accused Gandhi of championing Musk's interests, while party leaders defended the government's handling of the issue.
Speaking during the India Mobile Congress 2026 in New Delhi last week, Reliance Jio chairman Akash Ambani declined to comment on Musk's remarks. He said: "I have no comments to make. We want to keep our heads down and deliver value to our Indian consumers."
Akash, Mukesh Ambani's eldest son, also noted that Jio was progressing on its own end-to-end indigenous satellite broadband technology stack.
Meanwhile, Starlink — despite securing key approvals and signing distribution agreements with Reliance Jio and Bharti Airtel — has yet to begin commercial operations in India.
Its low-earth-orbit satellites could provide internet access in remote villages, hilly regions and border areas where fiber-optic networks and mobile towers are expensive to build.
But the service would enter a market where mobile data is inexpensive and established telecom operators have extensive networks.
India's Ministry of Communications says security assessments for all three licensed satellite operators are under way and that they are at broadly the same regulatory stage.
In a statement, the ministry said every licensee must meet security conditions intended to protect users and their data. Once an assessment is completed, an operator can seek spectrum assignment. It described allegations that the framework was unfair or discriminatory as "baseless and misconceived."
Legitimate security concerns?
Starlink secured a satellite communications licence from the Department of Telecommunications and authorization from the Indian National Space Promotion and Authorization Center in 2025. These approvals do not automatically permit commercial operations, however.
The security debate surrounding Starlink has intensified following remarks by BJP leader Nishikant Dubey, who chairs a parliamentary committee. In a post on X on October 11, Dubey said the panel had examined Starlink's security challenges.
"As the chairman of the parliamentary committee, our committee has understood the challenges facing the country's security agencies through Starlink," he wrote in Hindi.
Responding to Musk's criticism, Dubey added, "India is a healthy democratic, sovereign nation, and it does not change its security policy under pressure from social media or external figures."
Dubey did not specify the security risks or regulatory requirements holding up the launch.
Former intelligence officer and national security expert Yashovardhan Jha Azad said the impasse reflected commercial competition, regulatory uncertainty and legitimate security concerns.
"The central question is: who retains effective control over an essential communications service during a crisis?" Azad told DW.
He said India needed safeguards covering traffic routing, lawful interception under due process and cybersecurity.
"The existence of security requirements, however, does not establish why Starlink's application remains pending," Azad said. He pointed out that the government has not publicly detailed which specific conditions, if any, the company still needs to satisfy.
Investment, manufacturing and affordability
The delay in Starlink's launch has raised questions about the predictability of India's investment environment.
Economist Lekha Chakrabarty, who has studied the issue closely, said the problem was not that India was shutting its doors to foreign investment, but that companies could not plan around an open-ended approval process.
"The Starlink impasse is best read not as India closing its door to foreign investment, but as a failure to make an already open door predictably passable," Chakrabarty told DW.
She said security reviews were necessary given the sensitivity of satellite communications, which involve critical infrastructure, cross-border data, gateway control and lawful interception.
But the problem, she said, was the lack of transparency around approval criteria and timelines.
"Investors can price known rules, they cannot efficiently price discretionary, multi-agency processes with uncertain endpoints," Chakrabarty added.
Pankaj Mohindroo, chairman of the India Cellular and Electronics Association, said Starlink's entry could create opportunities for Indian electronics manufacturers in satellite terminals, antennas, communication modules and network equipment.
"India already has a strong trusted electronics manufacturing base, which provides an opportunity for global technology companies to develop local partnerships and strengthen domestic supply chains," he told DW.

Fridges in French supermarkets hit by cyber attack
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
15:30:09 BST
23:30:09 KST

Fridges in French supermarkets hit by cyber attack
- Published
Hundreds of French supermarkets have been hit by a cyber attack that caused their fridges and freezers to heat up, spoiling fresh and frozen food estimated to be worth millions of euros.
Hackers gained control of the software that regulates the temperatures of the refrigeration units, forcing some to warm to 50C (120F) overnight.
The chief executive of Coopérative U said several of its supermarkets had been hit by the "extremely serious and unprecedented" attack.
More than 100 of the chain's supermarkets were targeted, while at least 300 stores from Intermarché and its Netto brand were affected, according to the AFP news agency.
Other major food retailers including Carrefour, Monoprix and E.Leclerc were also hit by the attack, which targeted software provided by Danish engineering firm Danfoss.
The software allows retailers to manage their cold units remotely.
Normally, supermarket freezers go through a short period of defrosting overnight, in which temperatures rise slightly. But here, the hackers ordered the units to heat up and stay hot.
Danfoss said the affected cold units were older models whose security software could not be updated to ward off a risk they had identified.
The full scale of the attack is unclear, but figures supplied by individual chains suggest about 500 stores were affected out of 15,000 or so overall in France.
Carrefour said fridges in 80 of its 6,000 stores were hacked, while Monoprix said 5% of its more than 400 stores had been hit, with food removed from sale if its condition could not be guaranteed.
In a statement to the BBC, Mousquetaires Group - which owns Intermarché and Netto - said some fresh and frozen food display units remained out of service on Monday afternoon.
The stores had "taken all necessary precautions to remove the products from these units", it said, adding that staff were working to restock the shelves "as soon as possible".
Intermarché said its fridges had heated up to 50C for six hours overnight into Monday, and the retailer had thrown away all the affected food to avoid health risks, the Reuters news agency reported.
As a result of the attack, managers arriving at branches of several supermarket chains on Monday morning were hit by a wave of hot air from the freezers. In some places there were even small fires.
French broadcaster BFMTV published an image showing a freezer in an ice cream aisle displaying a temperature of 26.5C.
Two supermarkets in the Alsace region reported losses of €270,000 (£228,000) between them, the broadcaster added, meaning the nationwide total could run into the millions.
French prosecutors have opened a specific cyber-crime investigation into the incident, which the Paris prosecutor's office called a "large-scale cyber-attack affecting the refrigerators of several major food retail chains across France".
European Food Commissioner Christophe Hansen condemned the hack in a post on X and added: "Food security requires more attention at all levels. Because the weaponisation of food has become a reality."
In a post on X, Coopérative chief executive Dominique Schelcher said staff were "fully mobilised, in co-ordination with refrigeration specialists, to restore the situation as quickly as possible".
He called for an investigation into the hack and said targeting equipment essential to the French food supply was "unacceptable".

"And, of course, this will also affect the pace of the Russian army’s advance along the line of engagement. Given the critical situation Zelensky is facing both on the front line and inside the country, particularly in the energy sector, things will only get worse for Kiev and the Ukrainian armed forces," the expert said.
Yesterday, US President Donald Trump said elections needed to be held in Ukraine. The Wall Street Journal noted that the US leader’s remarks indicated that relations with Zelensky had deteriorated to their lowest point since the winter of last year. Meanwhile, the Financial Times reported, citing unnamed European officials, that the US administration was threatening to halt its weapons procurement program and the provision of intelligence to Ukraine.
Earlier, Axios reported, citing White House sources, that US President Donald Trump was angry with Ukraine’s Vladimir Zelensky and expected Ukraine to stop attacking Russian oil refineries. Trump believes the strikes are driving up US gasoline prices, the news outlet reported. He is also angry that Zelensky takes Washington’s support for Kiev for granted.

Iran-Saudi talks on Yemen’s Houthis: What’s in it for Tehran?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
14:27:49 UTC
23:27:49 KST

Iran-Saudi talks on Yemen’s Houthis: What’s in it for Tehran?
Tehran seeks dialogue in the Yemen conflict, warning that a military solution risks complicating a volatile regional situation.
Iran has offered to facilitate talks between Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Houthi group after a series of deadly attacks on the kingdom, raising questions about Tehran’s diplomatic calculations as fighting intensifies across the region.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi spoke with his Saudi counterpart, Prince Faisal bin Farhan Al Saud, on Sunday, in their first publicly reported contact since the Iran-aligned Houthis stepped up attacks on Saudi Arabia.
The diplomatic outreach comes after strikes on Riyadh’s international airport over the weekend killed 14 people and wounded hundreds, while Saudi-backed forces continued their offensive against the Houthis, also known as Ansar Allah, in Yemen.
The talks also come against the backdrop of the wider US-Israel war on Iran, with Tehran potentially seeking to avoid being dragged into another confrontation.
“Tehran is an ally of Ansar Allah and has influence with the movement, although it does not control its decisions,” Negar Mortazavi, senior fellow at the Washington, DC-based Center for International Policy, told Al Jazeera.
“By offering to facilitate talks with Riyadh, Iran is positioning itself as an indispensable party to a broader regional settlement.”
So what discussions are happening between Riyadh and Tehran, and why is Iran offering to facilitate talks?
What did Iran and Saudi Arabia talk about?
According to the Saudi state news agency, the two foreign ministers discussed the recent escalation in the region and efforts to reduce tensions. Iran’s Foreign Ministry also confirmed the development.
Following the discussions, Araghchi on Sunday warned against pursuing a military solution to the conflict and offered Tehran’s assistance in facilitating dialogue between Saudi Arabia and Yemen.
“Insisting on a military approach and disregarding a political solution would only further complicate the situation,” Araghchi said, according to Iran’s Foreign Ministry.
On Monday, ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei reiterated Tehran’s willingness to mediate, saying Iran was deeply concerned about developments in the Arabian Peninsula.
“We absolutely do not want hostilities and war to continue between two Islamic countries,” Baghaei said, urging dialogue to resolve the conflict.
What is Iran’s stance on the war in Yemen?
Iran has repeatedly called for a diplomatic settlement to Yemen’s conflict and says it supports a political solution rather than continued military action.
Tehran backs the Houthis, who control Yemen’s capital, Sanaa, and other parts of the country.
The armed group forms part of the Iran-aligned “axis of resistance”, which also includes Lebanon’s Hezbollah and armed groups in Iraq.
Saudi Arabia, meanwhile, has led a military coalition supporting Yemen’s internationally recognised government since 2015.
Baghaei said on Monday that the conflict served Israeli interests, framing a negotiated settlement as preferable to further fighting.
What is the latest in the Yemen fighting?
Fighting has intensified in Yemen, after the internationally recognised government’s forces announced Operation Dawn of Yemen on October 4 to reverse recent Houthi territorial gains, including the capital, Sanaa.
Government forces, backed by Riyadh, have reported advances near the strategic Bab al-Mandeb strait, a vital international shipping route. However, competing battlefield claims remain difficult to independently verify.
The Houthis have responded with missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, energy infrastructure and other targets.
Two strikes on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport on Saturday and Sunday killed 14 people and wounded more than 300. The casualties included foreign nationals from Bangladesh, Pakistan and Palestine.
The escalating violence has also disrupted commercial flights, businesses and schools in Riyadh, underlining the growing economic and civilian consequences of the conflict.
UN Special Envoy for Yemen Hans Grundberg warned on Friday that Yemen had returned to “full-scale war”, with civilians bearing the brunt of the attacks.
Why is Iran willing to facilitate talks between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis?
Iran’s offer to facilitate talks between Riyadh and the Houthis could be an attempt to strengthen Tehran’s diplomatic position and secure a wider regional agreement that extends beyond Yemen.
“I think Iran is trying to turn Yemen from a military liability into a diplomatic asset,” Andreas Krieg, a Middle East security analyst at King’s College London, told Al Jazeera.
He said Tehran recognises that Saudi Arabia is struggling to reverse Houthi territorial gains, particularly around Taiz and Bab al-Mandeb, despite intensifying its military campaign.
“Araghchi’s offer is an attempt to position Iran as part of the solution to a crisis in which it has also helped sustain the problem,” Krieg said.
Analyst Mortazavi, meanwhile, said Iran’s diplomatic outreach is part of a broader effort to link the conflicts unfolding across the region.
“The larger political objective is an informal non-aggression arrangement between Iran and its allies on one side and the United States and its regional partners on the other,” she said.
Such an agreement, she argued, would require an end to hostilities across multiple fronts, including Yemen and Lebanon, rather than a settlement confined to the US-Iran conflict.
Moreover, academic Krieg said there was also an important “Saudi dimension” to the discussions.
“Riyadh is increasingly uncomfortable with its dependence on Washington, frustrated by the limited American willingness to intervene in Yemen and reluctant to become dependent on the UAE again,” he said.
“Iran sees an opportunity to demonstrate that engagement with Tehran can deliver something Saudi Arabia’s traditional security partnerships have struggled to provide.”
There are also economic considerations, the analysts noted. Iran is under significant pressure from the US blockade, while Gulf countries are gradually recovering their energy exports to pre-war levels despite Iranian disruptions.
“Offering Riyadh a way out of Yemen potentially gives Iran leverage well beyond the Yemeni theatre, particularly in negotiations over Hormuz, sanctions relief and the wider regional security architecture,” Krieg said.
However, Krieg cautioned against overstating Iran’s influence over the Houthis, who have their own political ambitions and demands.
“Ansar Allah is not simply an Iranian proxy awaiting instructions,” Krieg said. “Its leadership has its own political ambitions, increasingly sees itself as a regional military actor and believes its recent territorial gains have strengthened its negotiating position. Iran can facilitate talks and potentially influence the intensity of escalation, but it cannot simply order the Houthis to surrender their gains around Mocha or Bab al-Mandeb.”
For Mortazavi, the broader message is that regional security cannot be addressed in isolation.
“Ultimately, Tehran’s message is that regional security cannot be divided,” she said. “Saudi Arabia cannot obtain security from attacks, while Iran and its allies remain under military and economic pressure.”

EU establishes new security support mission in Lebanon
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
14:26:03 UTC
23:26:03 KST

Melike Pala
12 October 2026•Update: 12 October 2026
The European Union on Monday established a new support mission in Lebanon to strengthen the country’s defense and security institutions, reaffirming its commitment to Lebanon’s stability, sovereignty and state institutions.
The EU Council adopted a decision establishing the EU Support Mission in Lebanon (EUSM Lebanon), with an initial mandate of three years, according to a statement.
The mission aims to contribute to peace and security in Lebanon, strengthen state institutions and promote lasting stability in line with UN Security Council Resolution 1701.
It will focus on enhancing the capabilities of the Lebanese Armed Forces and the Internal Security Forces, as well as supporting maritime security governance.
EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said foreign ministers had agreed to launch the new mission, which will advise and assist Lebanon’s armed forces and internal security forces in strengthening territorial control, border security and internal security.
“With this new mission — a major update of our security ties — we continue to support the country’s institutions in restoring full sovereignty and building lasting stability for the Lebanese people,” she said.
The mission will operate through two pillars, military and civilian, under a unified political mandate, with each carrying out complementary tasks within its respective area of responsibility.
The military pillar will provide advisory support and training to the Lebanese Armed Forces, focusing on border and maritime security, land border surveillance and control, intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance, counter-smuggling and operational coordination.
The civilian pillar will support the Internal Security Forces through advisory assistance and specialized training to strengthen operational capabilities and develop sustainable training structures.
Following the EU Council’s decision, operational planning will continue ahead of the mission’s deployment.

Iran sets crosshairs on ‘US-UAE’ oil shuttle out of Strait of Hormuz
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
14:25:55 UTC
23:25:55 KST

Iran sets crosshairs on ‘US-UAE’ oil shuttle out of Strait of Hormuz
The IRGC is hitting more ships allegedly part of a shuttle operation to move crude oil beyond the Strait of Hormuz.
Tehran, Iran – Iranian authorities have signalled they intend to disrupt an Arab-operated and United States-assisted shuttle system that has enabled more energy exports through the Strait of Hormuz during the US-Israel war on Iran.
With the US naval blockade of Iran’s southern ports in place and sanctions tightening, Tehran has said it will pursue military and diplomatic efforts to put pressure on Washington to submit to its demands regarding reopening the Strait of Hormuz.
This strategic waterway, through which roughly a fifth of global oil and gas flowed before the war, has been largely closed to shipping following Iranian attacks since the US and Israel launched strikes on Iran on February 28.
But the US Navy has reportedly opened up a route so Gulf states can export oil and other commodities amid an energy crisis.
Iran’s security chief Mohsen Rezaei responded on Sunday night, saying the shuttle system is now an explicit target for Tehran.
Rezaei claimed that the US Central Command, with the assistance of the United Arab Emirates military, was using smaller vessels to transfer oil to larger tankers. He claimed Iran had been striking five or six participating vessels nightly for weeks.
“You are smuggling, but the strait is under Iran’s control, and we manage it,” he asserted.
This appeared to be a taunt aimed at US President Donald Trump, who has hailed energy exports at times reaching pre-war levels over recent weeks.
Rezaei appeared to give the impression that Iran wants to have lasting authority over Hormuz, and promised a harsh response if Iran’s energy and civilian infrastructure were attacked again.
His threats appeared aimed at Arab regional states, with a warning that digital infrastructure could be targeted. Rezaei threatened US-linked cables, data centres and artificial intelligence facilities in the UAE and around the Strait of Hormuz.
Rezaei also accused Saudi Arabia of helping the US move oil around Iran’s restrictions. But he did not threaten a direct attack against Riyadh – which is currently being targeted by Yemen’s Tehran-aligned Houthis.
In early September, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) threatened tankers at ports and anchorages in Kuwait and Bahrain, citing US attacks on Iranian tankers. It accused both countries of complicity through hosting US armed forces.
Iran has claimed the US accepted some of Tehran’s seven conditions for the full reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and ending the war. But Tehran insists that a deal will only materialise when all its demands are met.
Hamidreza Azizi, a senior Iran analyst at the Crisis Group, said this reflects Tehran’s apparent assessment that it is under no immediate pressure to reach an agreement with the US since its pressure in the Hormuz has a global impact.
“The question, however, is whether Tehran is overestimating its ability to sustain this pressure, given the growing economic costs of the confrontation for Iran itself,” Azizi wrote on X.
Transfer system
The system involves very large crude carriers (VLCCs) and smaller vessels coordinating with the US military to load crude oil at Arab ports and use southern corridors near the coast of Oman to exit the strait.
Vessels often switch off their transponders and travel at night to minimise the risk of being targeted by the Iranians. After ship-to-ship transfers in the Gulf of Oman, some of the shuttles come back to load more.
Multiple vessels were targeted overnight Sunday to Monday, including two outbound tankers and one in anchorage near Oman’s port city of Sohar, where ship-to-ship transfers are allegedly being conducted.
Other vessels were targeted by projectiles last week, indicating that attacks have extended beyond the Strait of Hormuz to target the shuttle system.
The IRGC has also increasingly driven a narrative that naval mines, believed to have been planted across the Strait of Hormuz since the start of the war, pose a serious threat to vessels attempting to navigate the waterway without coordinating with Iran’s Persian Gulf Strait Authority.
The IRGC said three tankers suffered major damage over the weekend after being struck by mines. It also released footage of one ship ablaze that is said to have been struck by a mine, although the footage did not appear to show a mine going off.
‘Cascading impact’
The shuttle system has provided Arab national oil companies with a way out of Hormuz via the southern corridor near Oman.
Michelle Wiese Bockmann, a London-based senior maritime intelligence analyst at Windward, said this system has proven highly effective.
“Under international maritime law, which underpins 11 billion tonnes of seaborne trade annually, vessels have what’s called the right of transit passage,” Bockmann told Al Jazeera. “So, what Oman has done is allow vessels to go through under international maritime law, but they have had US military assistance.”
Tehran says shipping will be disrupted so long as the US continues its choking naval blockade against Iran, which has also stepped up its efforts to counter efforts by Arab states to export oil. At least 15 ships are believed to have been targeted in October so far, according to Winward.
“The more effective the route has become in facilitating the transport of oil and gas, the less leverage Iran has over Hormuz, and more attacks we are seeing on vessels that are using that southern corridor,” Bockmann said.
Windward’s data shows 31 ships transited the Strait of Hormuz daily in the final week of September. This was considerably lower than the 138 before the war.
Eighty-seven percent of the 45 ships targeted by Iran during the third quarter of 2026 were tankers.
Around 47 percent belonged to Gulf Arab energy companies’ national shipping fleets, Windward noted, and 93 percent of the strikes took place in the Strait of Hormuz. Most attacks targeted vessels transiting the southern corridor with their transponders turned off.
These attacks have contributed to a massive increase in freight costs. Freight represented 25-30 percent of Gulf crude’s cost, versus just 1 to 3 percent before the war, according to Windward. National oil companies have resorted to offering discounts of up to $35 per barrel below official selling prices.
The main reason for the rise is a shortage of tankers willing to make the dangerous crossing. Between 15 and 20 percent of very large crude carriers (VLCCs) are tied up with an inefficient logistics system that relies on shuttle transfers, complicated by escalating attacks and exposure at loading ports and anchorages.
“This is having cascading impacts for all vessel classes on freight and values across the world,” Bockmann said.

U.S. federal agents searched on Monday the home of Democratic Rep. Ilhan Omar, a Muslim lawmaker for the state of Minnesota and frequent target of Trump administration criticism, as part of a criminal investigation, media reports said.
Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) agents conducted the search, said the sources, who were not authorized to publicly discuss an ongoing investigation and spoke to The Associated Press (AP) on the condition of anonymity.
More details about the investigation were not immediately clear, although Vice President JD Vance has in the past accused Omar of committing immigration fraud – an allegation she has denied – and has said he and a top White House official were trying to figure out how to investigate the Minnesota congresswoman.
The Justice Department said in a statement Monday that HSI agents executed a judicially authorized search warrant secured by the department in the Washington, D.C., area, but provided no other details. The street was blocked off on Monday morning as HSI agents remained near the home.

The raid followed a criminal fraud investigation into the Somali-born lawmaker's immigration paperwork, which was filled out by her late father when she was a child, Fox News Digital reported, citing unidentified sources.

Republicans have raised questions about Omar's past since before she was even elected, including asserting that she had married her brother and committed immigration fraud. Omar has broadly denied the allegations as "disgusting lies."
"It certainly seems like something fishy is there, but everybody's entitled to equal justice under the laws," Vance told reporters in May.
"So we're going to investigate it. We're going to take a look at it. If we think there's a crime, we're going to prosecute that crime."

"This is a ridiculous lie and desperate attempt to distract from the pedophile protection party’s unpopular war of choice, increasing gas prices, and rapidly dropping polling numbers," McNutt said of the vice president’s allegations and comments.
Omar, an outspoken critic of Trump, has called his focus on her an "unhealthy and creepy obsession."
Last week, Trump also criticized the Democratic candidate for U.S. Senate from Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed, who is Muslim, while offering support for the Republican candidate, Mike Rogers.
Civil rights advocates have criticized the Republican president's rhetoric towards minorities and immigrants, including when he previously called Somalis "garbage."
Trump in February said that Omar and Democratic Rep. Rashida Tlaib of Michigan, who is also Muslim, should be "institutionalized" and sent back to "where they came from."

Ukraine knocked out key Yandex data centers. The fallout is being felt across Russia.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
14:24:49 UTC
23:24:49 KST

Ukraine knocked out key Yandex data centers. The fallout is being felt across Russia.
Ukraine has struck three of the six data centers belonging to Yandex, a Russian technology company, in Sasovo (Ryazan region), Kaluga, and Vladimir. Kyiv called the strikes a response to Russian attacks on Ukrainian data centers, which Russian forces have been striking lately. The infrastructure of the company’s “iron heart,” as Yandex calls its data centers, has been damaged. Operations at two of them — in Sasovo and Vladimir — have been halted. At the data center in Kaluga, “several modules have been completely knocked out.” Outages have plagued the Russian internet since the strikes began: not only Yandex’s services but also the websites of other companies and even media outlets have been operating with restrictions. Users abroad have also complained about problems with Yandex’s apps. As of October 12, the company had not managed to restore their operation. Here’s a look at the consequences of the Ukrainian strikes that Yandex and its users have faced.
How the strikes on the data centers affected the company and its users
- Since the first attack on Yandex’s data centers on October 8, users have complained about outages in the company’s services, including Mail, Pay, Disk, Go, and others. The strikes also disrupted Yandex Cloud for its clients. In recent days, there have been reports (1,2,3) of problems accessing other companies’ websites and services: the app for the cafe chain Vkusno i Tochka, media websites, the Pulkovo airport, and continuous glucose monitoring services used by people with diabetes.
- Russians have been especially vocal in their complaints about problems with Yandex Pay, after some users reported on social media that all their funds had been frozen. “All my money’s on Yandex, so I have no money for food,” one affected user said. Yandex tried to reassure users, saying their funds were safe, though the company could not say when everything would be working again.
- The outages affected Yandex users outside Russia as well. People in Kyrgyzstan, Kazakhstan, and Uzbekistan were unable to order taxis and food, and similar problems were reported in Armenia, Belarus, and Serbia.
- Three of Yandex’s supercomputers are located in the data centers hit by the strikes. The company uses them, among other things, to train its artificial intelligence models, and their fate remains uncertain.
- Cybersecurity experts said Russian bot traffic dropped by almost half, to 49% of its usual level, after the strikes on Yandex’s data centers. According to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, there has been “less hatred and provocations” on social media since the strikes because there are fewer bots.
How Yandex responded
- After the first strike, Yandex warned users of possible outages. On October 11, the company announced it had restored access to Alice (its AI assistant), Search, Maps, Mail, and other services, though not all features were working again.
- Yandex restricted downloads from its Yandex Disk cloud storage to “maintain the functionality” of other services, as engineers focus first on restoring the most popular services.
- After navigation outages, Yandex Pro advised drivers working with Yandex Taxi to use Google Maps or the navigation app Waze, which is also owned by Google.
- Yandex arranged to move customer data and services to data centers operated by cloud providers VK Cloud, Selectel, and K2Cloud.
- After the strikes, Yandex added a clause to its user agreement exempting the company from liability in cases of force majeure, including attacks by Ukrainian drones.
What company employees, analysts, and market participants are saying
- “Things are bad. I don’t think we’ll come out of this night without losses. Some [of the capacity] definitely won’t be restored at all,” one of The Bell’s sources at Yandex said after Ukraine’s first attack on the Sasovo facility.
- Replacing the damaged equipment is expected to take about six months, and Yandex will have to buy new equipment “on the most expensive market in recent years.” The additional cost will ultimately push up prices for customers’ cloud services.
- After the first strikes, Yandex shares on the Moscow Exchange fell more than 7.6%. Experts say the company’s business has a sufficient margin of safety, but its main risk is rising spending on protection, backup capacity, and infrastructure redistribution if the strikes continue. A second risk is disruption to Yandex’s cloud infrastructure and corporate solutions, which could affect customers’ businesses.
- Amid the attacks on Yandex, other data center owners have begun taking measures to protect their infrastructure, including purchasing equipment to defend against drones. Those added costs could make data center services even more expensive.
- Yadro, an X Holding subsidiary, could profit from protecting Russian data centers from drones. The holding’s deputy general director is Boris Korolev — the son of Sergei Korolev, first deputy director of Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB). Yadro supplies mobile data processing centers, demand for which has grown since late summer, as the industry has discussed the inevitability of Ukrainian attacks on Russian data centers since around that time. Russia has more than 250 data centers in total, a significant portion of which are located in Moscow and neighboring regions.
What authorities and propagandists are saying
- The Kremlin has not commented on the strikes on Yandex. Russia’s digital development minister called the attack on Yandex “unprecedented,” and the ministry is discussing data center protection with the Defense Ministry. The State Duma, the lower house of Russia’s parliament, said the responsibility for protecting data centers lies with the companies themselves.
- Margarita Simonyan, editor-in-chief of RT, a Russian state propaganda outlet, complained on her Telegram channel about outages at Yandex. “They won’t stop sending me requests and confirmations to prove I’m not a robot. I’m not a robot!” she explained. Simonyan threatened to switch back to Google or move to China’s DeepSeek. She soon deleted the post.

14:24:31 UTC
23:24:31 KST

Children and mothers would not be exempt from plans by Reform UK to immediately deport 90,000 asylum seekers and impose a five-year ban on people being granted asylum.
The party’s most hardline immigration policies to date were condemned by refugee charities and others as “unworkable” and an abandonment of Britain’s tradition of helping victims of war after they were announced by Nigel Farage on Monday.
New claims would be automatically rejected and failed applicants would be returned either to their home countries or a safe third country while a Reform government would impose tariffs, visa bans or airspace restrictions on countries refusing to accept the return of asylum seekers.
Asked if children would be exempt, Farage told a press conference in Kent: “If you allow Palestinian or Afghan women to come as well as children, that may well sound compassionate given the circumstances in that country. However, as soon as you do that you open the door to family reunions, to husbands coming, to partners coming, before you know it you have plenty of young men coming as well.”
The home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, said last month that approximately a quarter of arrivals under the reopened UK Resettlement Scheme (UKRS) will consist of Afghan women and girls fleeing Taliban rule and Palestinians who have fled Gaza. A Home Office source said Farage was mistaken in his claim as those coming under the scheme will not have reunion rights.
Appearing in front of a replica of the type of inflatable boat that he said was now being used to cross the Channel, Farage said a Reform government would also review the status of anyone granted asylum since 2024.
Those coming from countries deemed safe by a Reform home secretary would lose their permission to remain in the UK, while all legal resettlement routes would also be abolished, except for those set up for Ukrainians in the wake of the full-scale Russian invasion in 2022.
A 17-page document published by the party on Monday envisages the “embedding” of immigration enforcement throughout the state, and effectively society, by including immigration checks in food safety, housing and licensing inspections. People targeted for deportation would be identified from data on water or electricity usage, “aerial imaging” and complaints from neighbours.
Zia Yusuf, the party’s would-be home secretary, said Reform planned to deport “north of 1 million people” but insisted the party was “not in the business of sending people to be killed or tortured”, telling the press conference there would be “third-country options” for “edge cases”.
However, the Refugee Council said that closing Britain’s asylum system would “cause chaos” and desperate people who would still arrive on the country’s shores would be driven underground instead of entering an orderly system.
Jon Featonby, the chief policy analyst at the charity, said: “These unworkable proposals would see us abandon our proud tradition of offering safety to victims of war, which our ancestors established in response to the horrors of world war two.”
The Labour party’s chair, Bridget Phillipson, said the Reform UK leader was “casting around for more and more extreme policies” as he faced questions about his own finances and the threat posed by rivals Restore Britain, which appeared to have cost his party the opportunity of finishing third in the St Pancras and Holborn byelection.
Phillipson said that Labour could “control immigration and get numbers down with serious action, not by abandoning the asylum system altogether”.
The new Reform policy was described by Luke Tryl, the UK director of More in Common, as an “eye-catching” move that was perhaps aimed at stemming the growth of Rupert Lowe’s Restore Britain party on Farage’s right.
Tryl added that a policy to stop asylum entirely ran contrary to the desire of a majority of Reform voters, of whom only 14% wanted to see a cessation of Britain welcoming people fleeing persecution and war.

Pope lung nodule: Could it be cancer?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
14:24:00 UTC
23:24:00 KST

Pope lung nodule: Could it be cancer?
Published October 12, 2026last updated October 12, 2026
It often takes a chest X-ray or CT scan to spot small lung (or pulmonary) nodules, especially when a patient is asymptomatic.
At less than 3 centimeters (1.1 inches), lung nodules are less likely to press against your airway and cause any chest pain or shortness of breath or wheezing.
In the case of Pope Leo XIV, who told a gathering at the Vatican on October 11, 2026, doctors had found a nodule on his lung, it is unclear exactly how large that nodule is.
What we know so far
All we know (at time of writing on October 12, 2026) is that it was "detected at a very early stage," and that it was "well localized."
That suggests it has not spread or metastasized, although its full status is not publicly known. Doctors advised the pontiff to have his lung nodule removed.
Whether his was a chance finding — or whether the pope had presented with symptoms — we do not know.
But "incidental findings of lung nodule(s) in asymptomatic individuals" is considered an "increasingly common clinical dilemma," according to a 2019 paper published in the Annals of Thoracic Medicine.
This "dilemma" rests in part on the fact that biopsies — removing a small sample of tissue from the spot or nodule to determine whether it's malignant (cancerous) — are difficult to perform on small nodules.
The risks involved in a surgical diagnosis are considered "excessive compared to the relatively low prevalence of malignancy in the small nodules."
That's according to a 2017 paper published in the European Respiratory Review. And that may also be the dilemma that Pope Leo's doctors have faced.
Fortunately many — if not most — early-stage lung nodules are benign. It is also possible to have more than one nodule at a time, and they can all be benign.
It's said the pope will need a week to recover after his operation to remove the lung nodule. He is due to travel to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru between November 6-17.
What are lung nodules?
Lung nodules are generally defined as a white spot or lesion on the lung. They have a rounded or irregular shape.
Radiologists refer to their "opacity" because, compared to the surrounding air-filled lung tissue, lung nodules appear as white or gray spots on a CT scan — that is, they have a certain density.
Causes and symptoms of lung nodules
Lung nodules can be caused by old lung infections, foreign particles that are inhaled and get lodged in the lung, inflammation, scar tissue and indeed the onset of cancer.
At more than 3 centimeters, the nodule is defined as a mass. The bigger it gets, the greater the chance that it will obstruct your airway and the lung's ability to function.
Symptoms may start with chest pain, shortness of breath and wheezing. They may then progress to a chronic cough or coughing up of blood, fatigue, hoarseness, loss of appetite, unexplained weight loss and recurring respiratory infections like bronchitis or pneumonia.
What makes lung nodules cancerous?
It is hard to determine when lung nodules become life-threatening cancer. But one indicator of a lung nodule's malignancy is its size.
At 2 milimeters or smaller, the risk of cancer is very small and remains so up to a nodule size of about 6-7 milimeters.
The risk of cancer becomes 9%-10% at about 8 to 10 milimeters. And at larger than 1 centimeter, the risk of cancer is about 15%.
The density of a lung nodule is also a vital indicator of malignancy.
There are two main categories of lung nodule density: solid and subsolid. Subsolid nodules are further divided into pure ground-glass (nonsolid) and part-solid nodules.
According to a 2026 review article published in the New England Journal of Medicine, subsolid nodules are less prevalent than solid nodules, but they have "a higher likelihood of being malignant."
Lung nodules and lung cancer are common
It is said that radiologists see lung nodules in about 30% of chest CT scans. But that number may be rising.
A Dutch study published in 2023 cited an increase in lung nodule detections from 38% of scans in 2008 to 50% in 2019. The same study said "the proportion of patients in whom significant new nodules (≥ 5 mm) were reported increased from 9% in 2010 to 17% in 2017."
However, this may also be a result of the development of better scanning technology in recent years and the use of artificial intelligence to spot tumors.
Bearing in mind that most lung nodules are benign, lung cancer does tend to start with a lesion or nodule. And lung cancer remains the most common type of cancer and the most common cause of cancer death in the world.
The World Health Organization's International Agency for Research on Cancer says that in 2024 almost 2.65 million people were diagnosed with lung cancer and more than 1.8 million people died from the disease.

Ukrainian defense technology company Phantom Defense specializes in creating an integrated ecosystem for countering unmanned threats, including electronic warfare, target detection systems, kinetic weapons and a situational awareness and combat management platform.
Karakurt is a Ukrainian team of specialists that supplies, configures and maintains modern drones and unmanned solutions.

Why are the Houthis striking Saudi airports?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
14:23:20 UTC
23:23:20 KST

Why are the Houthis striking Saudi airports?
The attacks mark one of the most significant disruptions to Saudi civil aviation in years and the deadliest assault on Saudi soil in more than a decade
Yemen’s Houthis have claimed responsibility for Sunday’s attack that killed one person and injured nearly a dozen others at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh – the day after another attack killed 13 people and wounded more than 300.
The attacks mark one of the most significant disruptions to Saudi civil aviation in years and the deadliest assault on Saudi soil in more than a decade, as Yemeni government forces are also targeting airfields in Houthi-controlled territory.
The sharp escalation in the war’s new front comes amid fighting between the Iran-aligned Houthis and Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces, following the collapse of a United Nations-brokered ceasefire largely in place since 2022.
Which Saudi airports have the Houthis hit?
- King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh: The airport in the Saudi capital has been struck four times in the past five days. Saudi authorities reported that one person was killed and eight wounded on October 7 . The following day, a raid killed an airline pilot and two other Saudi citizens, with several others wounded.
- King Fahd International Airport in Dammam: Houthis claimed an attack on the airport in Dammam, the industrial port city on the Gulf coast, on Sunday.
- Abha International Airport: On October 7 , two people were killed and 28 wounded in an attack on facilities at the airport, the civil aviation authority said.
- King Abdullah bin Abdulaziz International Airport in Jazan: On October 6 , Saudi authorities reported attacks on the southern airport that injured three people.
- Najran Airport: The same day, Saudi authorities said Najran Airport was hit and reported minor injuries.
Have Yemeni forces hit Houthi-held airports too?
Yes. Houthi-run media on Sunday reported “Saudi” air strikes targeting areas in Yemen’s capital Sanaa, held by the Iran-backed armed group.
The reports said the attacks targeted the Airport Road area of Sanaa’s al-Thawra district, as well as the Hamdan district. There was no information on the results of those attacks.
Yemeni government forces backed by Saudi Arabia also hit Sanaa airport on July 13 with at least five munitions in a series of air attacks, three of which directly struck the only working runway.
The Houthis have controlled Sanaa and parts of northwestern Yemen since 2014. Battles are raging around the southern cities of Mocha and Dhubab, which are on the Red Sea coast and strategically important for control of the Bab al-Mandeb strait.
The vital shipping chokepoint has become an important alternative to the Strait of Hormuz, where Iranian attacks have raised the costs and risks for oil tanker operators.
Why are Houthis attacking Saudi airports?
The attacks have emptied skies over the Saudi capital Riyadh, as authorities extended the suspension of operations at the city’s international airport, the second-busiest after Jeddah.
Lufthansa has cancelled all flights to Riyadh until October 16 , while Air France-KLM extended its previous suspension of services to and from the Saudi capital until the end of the month. The UK, France and Germany have warned their citizens to avoid Riyadh.
The disruption comes as the country hosts two major Saudi energy and investment conferences.
Organisers of the World Petroleum Congress (WPC), set to host top global oil executives and policymakers from Sunday to Thursday, said it was proceeding as planned. The Future Investment Initiative, launched by Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman as the kingdom’s flagship investment conference a decade ago, would also proceed as planned from October 26-29 .
Saudi Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman told the WPC that the kingdom’s resilience had been put to the test, but sought to reassure attendees at the high-profile conference that its response would be “equally serious”.
The kingdom, which is preparing to host the 2032 FIFA World Cup, has long sought to market itself as a secure destination for major events, global tourism and investments.
Hisham al-Omeisy, a conflict analyst and adviser at the European Institute of Peace, predicted that the Houthis would escalate attacks to include oil pipelines and energy facilities – and continue attacks on airports because of the strong “public response” to hitting such targets.
“Houthis have escalated massively, they’ve crossed that line… they have their own frameworks, their own calculations and stopping at attacking a civilian airport is not one of those calculations,” al-Omeisy told Al Jazeera.
“They are a maximalist group and they’re there to do whatever they need to do to get to what they want,” the analyst said, including “more concessions from the Saudis.”
Why are Yemeni forces attacking Houthi-held airports?
The Yemeni capital hosts the only airport providing international flights to and from Houthi-controlled territory, where the majority of Yemen’s population lives.
The Houthi-run broadcaster also reported attacks on Thursday on Hodeidah International Airport on the Red Sea coast, without specifying the extent of the damage.
Yemeni representatives at the UN have claimed that those airports are being used to shuttle Houthi delegations to and from Iran, which backs the group. According to the government of Yemen, the attacks have hit airport facilities to prevent Iranian flights from landing there.

The distinction is between supporting a cause and joining a particular protest platform.CJP legal head Ratna Singh said the invitation remained open to all parties.“If the Congress is willing to come forward and join the protests, it is most welcome. Not just the Congress, but other parties too. Everyone should come together,” she said.“This is not the time to look at different groups protesting separately. We must see this as a unit, as a team effort, with people raising their voices against the wrongs happening in this country,” she added.Her appeal raises a question that extends beyond Congress: What does solidarity mean when parties agree on an issue but differ over how a protest should be organised, represented and politically sustained?
The Anna Hazare lesson
The tensions around CJP have echoes of the 2011 India Against Corruption movement. The BJP publicly backed Anna Hazare's anti-corruption agitation against the Congress-led UPA government. Congress later accused the BJP and RSS of exploiting the movement to undermine its government.
The movement's political afterlife was significant. Arvind Kejriwal, one of its prominent figures, went on to form the Aam Aadmi Party in 2012.
Anna Hazare, Arvind Kejriwal, Kiran Bedi during India Against Andolan movement, 2011
The parallel is relevant to the present Congress-CJP friction. Congress spokesperson Reetam Singh has alleged that CJP's Assam outreach was viewed as an AAP initiative, accusing the party of “piggy riding and hijacking issues of others”.The allegation raises a question about whether Congress sees CJP not simply as a citizens' movement, but as a platform whose political associations and future trajectory matter.

Her work brings together reportage and analysis, tracking developments in India and abroad while examining the broader social and economic currents shaping public discourse.
