Greece's social media ban for under-15s: What you need to know
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
14:20:16 UTC
23:20:16 KST

The government argues that setting a clear age limit, combined with reliable age checks, will help protect children from potential risks associated with social media usage.
Greece is moving to ban children under the age of 15 from accessing social networking services, introducing a new regulatory framework that is expected to come into force on 1 January 2027.
The main provisions of the bill were presented on Monday by Minister of State Akis Skertsos, Health Minister Adonis Georgiadis, and Digital Governance Minister Dimitris Papastergiou, with a focus on protecting minors from the risks linked to the use of social media, as well as safeguarding users' privacy.
The bill will be tabled before the parliamentary committees on 13 October, while debate and the final vote in the plenary have been scheduled for 22 October.
The new framework is due to apply from 1 January 2027, giving platforms time to prepare for the changes.
Skertsos referred to the responsibility of the state and technology companies to protect children online, stressing that the bill sets a clear age limit at 15 and places the burden of verifying users' age on platforms.
He noted that parents need real support in the face of algorithms designed to keep children constantly connected, underlining that technology must be regulated with people in mind and, in particular, the health and development of minors.
At the same time, he pointed out that the Greek initiative is moving forward in parliament and feeds into a common European response to protecting children in the digital world.
Age limit
The central provision of the reform is a ban on access to social networking services provided by online platforms for minors who have not yet reached their 15th birthday.
The measure covers services such as Instagram, TikTok, and Facebook and is accompanied by an obligation on platforms to apply appropriate, proportionate, and reliable age-verification methods.
Kids Wallet and Gov.gr Wallet are expected to play a key role in implementing the measure.
Companies will also be able to choose different technical solutions, provided that these meet the requirements of European law. The aim is to ensure the effective enforcement of the age limit without imposing a single technology across all services.
Papastergiou said Gov.gr Wallet and Kids Wallet are tools for verifying age that are designed to protect privacy and minimise the amount of data collected.
Digital 'age tokens'
The options presented are based on the use of digital "age tokens," which make it possible to confirm whether the age threshold has been met without requiring the disclosure of more personal data than is strictly necessary.
In this way, a platform can obtain the necessary confirmation that a user meets the prescribed age limit without needing access to full identity details or other sensitive personal data about the minor.
Under the specifications outlined, age-verification mechanisms must rely on robust and accurate techniques, work effectively in real-life usage conditions and offer sufficient safeguards to prevent circumvention.
The bill forms part of the European regulatory framework for digital services and the Digital Services Act. A key reference point is Article 28 of the DSA, which concerns the protection of minors who use online platforms.
Supervision will not take place solely at national level, but through the existing DSA mechanism, which provides for cross-border cooperation between the competent authorities and the European Commission.
In Greece, the main authority is the National Telecommunications and Post Commission (EETT), which acts as Digital Services Coordinator. Within their respective remits, the National Council for Radio and Television (ESR), for oversight of the relevant provisions, and the Hellenic Data Protection Authority (HDPA), for personal data issues and the DSA's related requirements, are also involved.
How the enforcement process is triggered
The enforcement process can be triggered by a user complaint or by information passed to the EETT from another authority or body.
If the case concerns a platform supervised by another member state, it is forwarded to the competent authority in the country where the platform is established.
Protecting the mental health of minors
The initiative is part of a wider debate on the impact of social media use in childhood. Concerns are centred around pressures on mental health, symptoms of anxiety and depression, cyberbullying, and effects on concentration.
The government argues that setting a clear age limit, combined with reliable checks, will help protect children from such risks. At the same time, the effectiveness of the measure will depend on platforms fulfilling their obligations.

Hundreds of French supermarkets hit by cyberattack on refrigeration systems
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
14:19:31 UTC
23:19:31 KST

Several supermarkets were forced to discard fresh and frozen food, Intermarché said, and have yet to estimate the losses. The Paris prosecutor has opened an investigation.
Hundreds of French supermarkets belonging to the Intermarché and Coopérative U chains have fallen victim to a cyberattack targeting their refrigeration systems, the two retail giants said on Monday.
Around 150 to 200 Intermarché stores were hit, along with nearly 100 Coopérative U outlets, they added. The Paris prosecutor's office confirmed the cyberattack, which is also thought to have affected other major chains.
BFM TV reported that France's largest supermarket chain, E. Leclerc, had also been targeted, with the hackers managing to trigger the defrost cycle on its refrigeration systems. Contacted by AFP, E. Leclerc did not immediately confirm the report.
The affected stores will have to "throw away all their products", fresh and frozen, Intermarché told AFP.
The specialist French retail news website jebosseengrandedistribution.fr (source in French) said that other retail heavyweights, Carrefour Market and Monoprix, had also been hit, although the companies have yet to confirm this.
An "unprecedented" attack
The chief executive of Coopérative U, Dominique Schelcher, described the attack as "unprecedented" and confirmed that the cyberattack had been affecting refrigeration systems since Sunday evening.
"Targeting equipment that is essential for preserving fresh products and for the food supply of people in France is extremely serious and without precedent. It is unacceptable", he wrote on X.
He added that the company is "fully mobilised" to resolve the situation as quickly as possible. "A full investigation will be needed to shed complete light on this attack", he said.
Investigation opened
The Paris prosecutor's office confirmed to AFP that an investigation had been opened into "the large-scale cyberattack affecting the cold rooms of several major food retail chains across France".
The investigation aims "to identify the victims and establish a link with the damage they have reported, in terms of losses of foodstuffs and the triggering of fire alarms", the prosecutor's office said.
Intermarché condemned the food waste and financial losses resulting from the attack, without providing figures, and warned that there could be problems with insurance policies, which do not "cover this type" of incident in stores.
The incident comes against a backdrop of growing concern about the devastation that cyberattacks by malicious actors could cause across all sectors in Europe.
President Emmanuel Macron, a staunch supporter of Ukraine in its fight against the Russian invasion, last month ordered the implementation of measures to protect France's critical infrastructure against Russian "hybrid attacks".

Man jailed for $8 million AI music scam
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Man jailed for $8 million AI music scam
Michael Smith, 54, of Cornelius, was also ordered to forfeit $8,091,843.64 and serve two years of supervised release, the U.S. Department of Justice said. He pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit wire fraud on March 19, 2026.
The scheme operated from 2017 to 2024 across platforms including Spotify, Apple Music, Amazon Music and YouTube Music. Smith uploaded hundreds of thousands of AI-generated songs and used as many as 10,000 automated accounts simultaneously to inflate their listening figures.
He spread fraudulent streams across numerous tracks to avoid triggering detection systems.
In April 2023, his accounts generated 80.9 million YouTube Music family-plan streams, compared with 9.3 million for Taylor Swift’s entire catalogue through family plans.
“Smith robbed millions in royalty payments from genuine artists and their fans,” U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald said.
Prosecutors said manipulated streams diverted payments from musicians and songwriters with real audiences. The conviction concerned fraudulent royalty collection rather than the creation of AI music.
The case comes as technology companies expand tools for identifying synthetic media. On October 7, Google announced that its SynthID Detector was becoming available to everyone globally in English, following an earlier version intended for media professionals.
Users can check whether images, videos or audio contain SynthID watermarks associated with AI tools from Google and partners including OpenAI, NVIDIA and Kakao. Apple is expected to join.
Google said it had embedded the imperceptible watermarks in more than 180 billion images and videos, alongside the equivalent of 240,000 years of audio.
The detector complements verification features in Search, the Gemini app and Chrome, which Google says collectively handle more than one million requests daily.
These tools provide information about how content was created. Smith’s prosecution highlights the need for streaming services to ensure that listening figures reflect real audiences and royalty payments reach legitimate rights holders.

Swiss swimming pools and saunas warn against use of smart glasses
Regulations at municipal and local swimming pools must prohibit the wearing of glasses fitted with a camera, according to a warning issued by public swimming pools on Monday.
In German-speaking Switzerland, the Swiss association of swimming instructors, the association of swimming pools and the Swiss sauna federation have responded to the growing use of eyeglasses fitted with built-in cameras. They have warned against taking photographs and making video recordings without the knowledge of those being filmed.
As these devices are difficult to distinguish from ordinary eyewear, privacy in swimming pools and changing rooms is under threat, the associations said in a joint statement on Monday. The wearing of optical devices with a recording function will now be prohibited throughout all swimming pool premises.
More
Smart glasses ban in swimming pools debated in Switzerland
The associations are advising towns and local authorities to amend their regulations. To help staff enforce this ban, they have produced a guide and an information poster for bathers.
Pressure on the authorities has intensified in recent months: in Bern, Zurich and other cities, motions have been tabled calling for a ban on smart glasses in municipal swimming pools and sports facilities.
In French-speaking Switzerland, the association of swimming pools in French-speaking Switzerland and Ticino (APRT) is not taking any measures for the time being, it told the news agency Keystone-SDA. The association has not received any specific reports regarding the relatively new phenomenon of smart eyeglasses, but staff have been trained and made aware of the issue.

As a scientist, here's what worries me about the suspected Russian plague victim | Devi Sridhar
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
14:12:58 UTC
23:12:58 KST

In pandemic preparedness work, scientists like to focus on the technical challenges: identifying pathogens, diagnosing infections, understanding their effects and developing vaccines and treatments. Each step promises progress through human innovation, investment and planning. The World Health Organization (WHO), for example, brings experts together to identify and prioritise emerging disease threats and collect the evidence needed to prepare for them. But preparedness depends on more than scientific innovation.
As the past week has shown, politics is the elephant in the room in all of this. No one could have predicted we would be talking about pneumonic plague, and that the death of a single lab worker in Russia would cause global headlines. It might feel like an overreaction: the WHO deals with thousands of potential disease signals worldwide every month. But the circumstances of this case are unusual given the lack of transparency from Russian authorities on what happened – and ongoing concern about biological weapons research.
The 28-year-old lab worker died after developing severe pneumonia. She worked at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute, established in 1934, which studies plague and other dangerous pathogens including anthrax and cholera, and is rumoured to be involved in biological weapons research. Prof Ashish Jha, who was the US White House Covid-19 response coordinator, and who co-chaired an Ebola commission with me, wrote on social media: “US intelligence assess that Russia’s scientists continue developing biological weapons capabilities. Those programmes operate in secret. Nobody outside inspects them and nobody inside has much incentive to admit when something goes wrong.”
On top of that, initial local media coverage suggested that she had died from pneumonic plague after a lab accident, possibly a broken test tube. Pneumonic plague is caused by a bacterium (Yersinia pestis), and can spread through respiratory contact and is always fatal if untreated. If antibiotics are given in the first 24 hours after symptoms, or even before onset of symptoms post-exposure, it is largely treatable. If she knew she had been exposed, why was treatment not given in time? (Pneumonic plague is a different disease to the more common bubonic plague, which transmits through flea bites.)
Despite Russian health authorities denying that it was a case of plague and insisting it was pneumonia of unknown origin, they quickly placed about 200 contacts of the lab worker under quarantine. The authorities reported that no high-threat pathogens were detected and monitoring had ended. The WHO released a statement noting a potential second linked case, but Russia denied this. The cause of death remains unconfirmed.
The WHO has pushed the Russian government for more information – including confirmation of the diagnosis and details of the investigations, the reason why it put so many people in quarantine and more information on the second case – but it has not yet received this information.
On the one hand, if this infection was spreading further, additional cases would have emerged by now. The lab worker died on 2 October, and the testing of contacts and release of those in quarantine indicates that any spread has been contained so far. However, given that the incubation period can be one to three days, continued monitoring is important.
There are three hypothetical scenarios if we assume the illness was pneumonic plague. The first is that the lab worker was accidentally exposed to the bacterium while doing research, and either didn’t know, or didn’t tell anyone out of fear – and therefore didn’t ask for treatment immediately. So when she became sick, her window of treatment had been missed.
Second, the lab worker was exposed to an antibiotic-resistant strain. This may sound like a conspiracy theory, but senior academics have raised concerns given the history of the Soviet biological weapons programme and the potential for pathogens to be engineered for hostile purposes.
Third, Dan Singer (the former White House director for countering biological threats) has suggested that this lab worker might have been given an outdated vaccine, which is only available in Russia as it is not approved by the WHO or most other countries. This is a live-attenuated vaccine, meaning a weakened version of the bacteria is given, but it doesn’t always provide protection and sometimes can cause disease.
In short, we don’t know what happened because there is insufficient information from the Russian authorities. To understand what happened, investigators would need access to laboratory and clinical evidence, including genomic sequencing, pathogen identification and details of the worker’s research. Without this, we are left with speculation when only scientific certainty will do.
As a member of the WHO, Russia has an international legal obligation to share information with the agency. The WHO’s health regulations specifically cover “unusual and unexpected” events, as well as those with serious public health impact and with significant risk of international spread, or that risk affecting trade or travel. But unfortunately, as with most international law, there’s no real enforcement mechanism. There is a reliance on broad cooperation across countries, with the understanding that sharing information on disease spread is in all nations’ best interests.
The US government has also put pressure on Russia for answers, with Donald Trump saying he would speak to Putin about the situation. The US state department also formally requested further information under the international health regulations – the irony being that the US withdrew from the WHO in January 2026, but is now invoking the international framework it left behind.
As a scientist watching this unfold, I’m reminded that while we can have research and expert conferences into better diagnostics, faster genomic sequencing, more effective vaccines and accessible treatments, none of these advances can compensate for a failure to share the information needed to identify a pathogen in the first place. Preparedness is a political challenge as well as a scientific one. And without transparency, it will be a case of one step forward, two steps back.
- Prof Devi Sridhar is chair of global public health at the University of Edinburgh

Dozens of possible dinosaur footprints emerge in Iran, researcher urges urgent documentation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
14:12:51 UTC
23:12:51 KST

Dozens of possible dinosaur footprints emerge in Iran, researcher urges urgent documentation
TEHRAN – A rock surface bearing dozens of possible dinosaur footprints has been exposed in Iran following a landslide, prompting a paleontologist to call for urgent scientific investigation and documentation to protect the traces from weathering and erosion.
Erfan Khosravi, a paleontologist and zoologist, announced the discovery in a post on his personal account on the social media platform X, the Iranian Students’ News Agency (ISNA) reported on Sunday.
Khosravi said the footprints had emerged from beneath sediment deposits after a section of a mountain collapsed. He warned that exposure to the elements could damage or destroy the traces if they were not documented promptly.
The proposed research program includes surveying and investigating the site, making casts of the footprints and recording their three-dimensional structures. These measures could help preserve fine details and provide researchers with material for more detailed scientific analysis.
Khosravi, a graduate of the University of Tehran, said the work was being pursued independently, without government funding. The scope and methods of the documentation would depend on available resources, with different practical approaches considered as the project progresses.
He emphasized that the footprints’ three-dimensional features could provide important clues about how the animals’ feet contacted the ground and how they moved. Preserving these details could help researchers investigate the traces beyond their visible outlines.
Khosravi invited people interested in paleontology and natural heritage documentation to contact him through direct messages on X for further information.
He said the findings would be compiled into a scientific paper and submitted to specialist journals for publication. Financial supporters would be acknowledged in the relevant section of the paper in accordance with journal requirements and agreements with the sponsors.
Dinosaur footprints are known as trace fossils, geological records of animal activity rather than preserved body parts. They form when animals walk across soft sediment that later hardens and is buried, preserving impressions that may survive for millions of years. Their shapes, depth and spacing can help researchers investigate the animals’ movement, foot structure and interactions with their environment.
Iran has a documented record of dinosaur tracks, although such discoveries remain relatively limited. A scientific study published in 2022 described a dinosaur tracksite in the Farrokhi Formation near Khur in central Iran, dating to about 70 million years ago. The researchers said the site added to knowledge of dinosaur activity in Iran and the wider West Asia. The newly reported footprints will require their own geological and paleontological assessment to establish their authenticity, age and scientific significance.

NATO general sets out tough military response to any ‘foolish’ Russian attack
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12

NATO general sets out tough military response to any ‘foolish’ Russian attack
BRUSSELS/WARSAW – NATO’s top commander warned Russia on Oct 12 that his forces would destroy “anything and everything” involved in any attack if Moscow was “foolish enough” to launch an assault on alliance territory.
Speaking at the Warsaw Security Forum, US Air Force General Alexus Grynkewich stressed that NATO was a defensive alliance. But he outlined a three-pronged approach of blocking, blunting and breaking enemy forces to make any attack “utterly futile”.
His remarks come amid heightened tensions between Europe and Russia and lingering concerns among European allies over US President Donald Trump’s commitment to NATO’s mutual defence pact.
Trump recently announced a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin allowing Russia to supply diesel to global markets and renewed his criticism of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky.
European governments accuse Moscow of stepping up a campaign of sabotage, drone incursions and cyberattacks against them, while Russia warned last month it could use nuclear weapons if NATO attempted to cut off its Kaliningrad exclave.
Grynkewich did not mention Russia by name but much of his message was clearly directed at Moscow. NATO’s 2022 Strategic Concept describes Russia as the alliance’s most significant security threat.
“If someone is foolish enough to attack us, we will fight,” he said. “We will, in short, ensure any attack, against any ally, proves utterly futile.”
NATO would strike beyond front lines
Grynkewich said NATO’s response would not be limited to forces involved in an initial attack.
“Should the adversary choose to press the attack or commit his reserves, we will break the warfighting system engaged against us,” he said.
“This includes not just the attacking force itself, but anything and everything that supports, sustains and controls that force.”
Putin said in October that Russia had no plans to attack any European country and wanted to co-exist peacefully. Such declarations have not reassured European leaders, given that Russia made similar statements before the 2022 invasion of Ukraine.
Russia has also repeatedly denied involvement in sabotage and other hybrid operations.
Commander seeks to reassure allies
Grynkewich said he had decided to talk publicly about NATO’s plans because recent acts of sabotage and arson had made people around the alliance nervous.
“What I want to do is assure the one billion citizens of our alliance that we’ve got this. We know what we need to do. We know how we would do it,” he said.
He said he also wanted to send a message to anyone considering harming NATO members.
Grynkewich sought to downplay concerns about Washington’s commitment to the alliance, recalling that Trump spoke of “love” at a NATO summit in Ankara in July.
“I was in the room and I felt the love,” he said. REUTERS

South Africa, India share common vision for medicinal plant conservation: Minister
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
14:10:01 UTC
23:10:01 KST

India and South Africa are joining forces to protect medicinal plants and ensure future biodiversity. (https://en.wikipedia.org/)
India and South Africa have similar views on the need to protect medicinal plants and preserve biodiversity, South African deputy minister of forestry, fisheries and the environment Narend Singh said at a symposium in Durban.Organised by the Indian consulate in Durban, the event brought together experts in AYUSH — Ayurveda, Yoga and Naturopathy, Unani, Siddha and Homeopathy — from both countries to explore opportunities for stronger collaboration in traditional and alternative medicine.Addressing the gathering as the keynote speaker on Saturday, Singh said the two nations had worked together to promote systems that uphold rights, ensure fairness and facilitate the equitable sharing of benefits derived from genetic resources and traditional knowledge.He stressed that the current generation has a responsibility to safeguard biodiversity so that future generations can continue to benefit from it.According to the South African National Biodiversity Institute, 262 indigenous plant species are used in traditional medicine in the country, accounting for approximately one-tenth of its total plant species.Singh warned that rising demand for medicinal plants in urban areas, coupled with unsustainable harvesting, climate change, drought, poverty and illegal trade, was putting growing pressure on these natural resources.
“Town and city demand for these plants has outpaced what the wild can supply. Harvesting has become increasingly difficult and, at times, irresponsible. Drought and climate change are worsening the situation, while poverty encourages people to collect whatever they can sell. Some of this trade is also illegal,” he said, referring to the findings of South Africa’s 2024 red list of endangered plants.
Highlighting the risks of excessive harvesting, Singh said 154 medicinal plant species commonly used in traditional practices were facing the threat of extinction, putting their distinctive genetic resources at risk, according to the news agency PTI.He emphasised that the loss of medicinal plants would also endanger the traditional remedies and knowledge associated with them. Singh called for greater efforts to cultivate medicinal species, replenish depleted resources and ensure their sustainable use.He said traditional knowledge could not be genuinely protected while the natural resources supporting it continued to be depleted. Responsible management of genetic resources and gene pools, he added, was essential to preserving medicinal plants for future generations.India’s Deputy high commissioner to South Africa, Banu Prakash, noted that South Africa possessed a rich legacy of traditional knowledge linked to medicinal and aromatic plants.“We were surprised to see the number of herbal products that are popular and being used here,” she said.
While appreciating the South african government’s efforts to plant millions of trees in recent years, Prakash called for greater emphasis on planting species associated with Ayurvedic medicine.Another speaker, Shobhit Kumar, research officer (ayurveda) in the health and family Welfare vertical at NITI Aayog, said India did not view traditional medicine and modern medicine as competing approaches.Instead, he said, the focus was on finding ways for the two systems to complement each other for the wider public good.Kumar said traditional medicine could work alongside allopathic treatment to help advance the goal of universal health coverage.

Russia’s Retreat Leaves a Hidden Battlefield—1,739 Ukrainian Civilians Killed or Injured
A total of 1,739 civilians, including 178 children, have been injured or killed by mines and explosive remnants of war in Ukraine since Russia’s full-scale invasion began in 2022.
This was reported by ArmyInform on October 12, citing data from the Main Directorate for Mine Action, Civil Protection and Environmental Safety.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The figures show that farmers, unemployed people, pensioners, and critical infrastructure workers were among the groups most frequently affected.
The recorded casualties included:
- 306 farmers;
- 256 unemployed people;
- 170 pensioners;
- 166 critical infrastructure workers;
- 112 drivers;
- 171 school students.
The directorate collects, analyzes, and verifies information on incidents involving mines and other explosive remnants of war. Data is supplied by regional military administrations, State Emergency Service units, and the National Police before being entered into a centralized information system.
Ukrainian law enforcement agencies open criminal proceedings over civilian mine incidents as possible violations by Russia of the laws and customs of war. The collected information is also used to identify victims’ needs, conduct mine-risk education, and coordinate assistance for people with blast injuries.
Ukraine continues large-scale clearance operations across liberated territories as mines and unexploded ordnance remain a persistent threat. In September alone, Ministry of Defense units surveyed and cleared 1,347 hectares, including nearly 340 hectares of agricultural land, and destroyed 364 explosive objects.
The scale of contamination has also prompted Kyiv to seek compensation from Moscow for the cost of cleanup. On August 14, the Register of Damage for Ukraine began accepting claims for demining, explosive ordnance clearance, specialist training, and mine-risk education, as well as a separate category for humanitarian spending.
Almost 23% of Ukraine's territory remains contaminated by mines and unexploded ordnance, with roughly 128,000 square kilometers considered potentially hazardous. Full clearance is expected to take at least ten years, and clearing a single hectare of farmland can cost at least $1,400.

Meet Steelfin—Anduril Says It Can Deliver 80% of PAC-3 Capability for Less Than Half the Price
Unknown

- Category

Meet Steelfin—Anduril Says It Can Deliver 80% of PAC-3 Capability for Less Than Half the Price
Anduril Industries has unveiled Steelfin, a new family of air and missile defense interceptors designed to offer a significantly cheaper alternative to Patriot’s PAC-3 missiles while remaining compatible with existing US air defense infrastructure, The War Zone reported on October 12.
The company is developing a Steelfin configuration specifically for launch from the M903A2 launcher already used with PAC-3 interceptors.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Steve Milano, an Anduril representative, told The War Zone that the version intended to perform PAC-3-type missions could deliver roughly 80% of the interceptor’s capability for less than half the cost.
That price difference is central to Anduril’s pitch. Modern air defense systems face growing pressure from large missile and drone salvos, making the cost and availability of individual interceptors increasingly important.
Anduril says it intends to manufacture several thousand Steelfin missiles annually, using a common production base for multiple variants rather than building each configuration around an entirely separate industrial line.
Steelfin is being designed as a modular, two-stage weapon. The first stage will act as a booster and determine much of the missile’s range and flight performance, while the second stage will serve as the interceptor itself.
Different versions could use alternative motors, seekers, and other components depending on whether the target is a cruise missile, ballistic missile, or higher-speed threat.
Anduril is also looking beyond Patriot. The company is studying integration with the Mk 41 vertical launch system used aboard US and allied warships, as well as the land-based Typhon missile system, potentially allowing the same interceptor family to operate across several existing launch architectures.
More powerful Steelfin variants are being developed for higher-end missile defense missions, including ballistic and hypersonic threats. Milano told The War Zone that one configuration could eventually perform missions comparable to the THAAD missile defense system at a substantially lower cost.
The company has already carried out ballistic testing of demonstration hardware, while flight tests of different Steelfin configurations are scheduled to begin in 2027.
Earlier, Ukrainian missile maker Fire Point has updated its FP-7.x Freyja interceptor with a combined infrared and radar seeker. The revised specification replaces the infrared-only seeker previously described for the missile.

Comedian Giorgio Bracardi dies at the age of 93
Italy

Comedian Giorgio Bracardi, whose
surreal, over-the-top characters delighted generations of radio
and TV audiences in Italy and who is perhaps best remembered for
his appearances on mid-80s cult late-night variety show Quelli
della Notte, has died at the age of 93, his family said Monday.
                                    
Bracaro, who was also a musician and singer, was famous for
characters such as the "Nicaraguan vulture" Scarpantibus and the
pushy journalist Max Vinella from the cult 1970s radio show Alto
Gradimento.
                                    
He had been staying at a care home in Fiano Romano near his
native Rome after breaking his femur last spring.
                                    
Born in Rome on May 3, 1933, Bracardi grew up in the world of
show business.
                                    
His father was one of the first managers of Rome's Salone
Margherita theater; his mother, Edvige, was a soprano, and his
father, Glauco, was a tenor.
                                    
All five of their children received a musical education and
learned to play an instrument.
                                    
Giorgio was a pianist who later became a composer, even
participating in the Sanremo Festival as a songwriter. However,
Bracardi rose to great popularity with Alto Gradimento, the
radio program he co-created with Renzo Arbore, Gianni
Boncompagni, and Mario Marenco.
                                    
He later made the leap to television with Arbore in the 1985
show Quelli della notte, and also appeared on Pronto, chi
gioca?, hosted by Enrica Bonaccorti and Giancarlo Magalli.
                                    
In 1989, he hosted and starred in Chiappala chiappala on Rai 2.
                                    
In 1995, he moved to Mediaset to join Striscia la Notizia,
playing Lucio Smentisco, a fictional spokesperson for Silvio
Berlusconi.
                                    
In 2001, he was a featured performer on Marco Giusti's Rai 2
program Stracult.
                                    
Bracardi also provided the voice for the character Cattivik in
the animated series broadcast by Mediaset in 2008.
                                    
With the surreal, chaotic characters created by Bracardi on Alto
gradimento, his most famous catchphrases and character yells
include:
• "PATROCLOOO!" - His iconic, absurd shout performed as an
unlikely Achilles wandering around looking for his
lover/companion Patroclus.
                                    
• "In galera! In galera!" (In jail! In jail!) - The signature
aggressive chant of his character Ermanno Catenacci, a
nostalgic, raging ex Fascist 'hierarch' (high-up official).
                                    
• "Chettefrega!" (What do you care!) - A frequent, dismissive
exclamation used across his sketches.
                                    
• The screeching, bird-like squawks of Scarpantibus, a
prehistoric, laceless-boot-wearing bird creature he created that
spoke in chaotic noises.

Russia’s New 6,500-Km Missiles Could Target NATO as Moscow Prepares 32 for Strategic Bombers
Unknown

- Category

Russia’s New 6,500-Km Missiles Could Target NATO as Moscow Prepares 32 for Strategic Bombers
Russia is expanding its long-range strike capabilities with plans to acquire 32 Kh-BD cruise missiles, each capable of traveling up to 6,500 kilometers (4,039 miles).
The weapons could allow Russian strategic bombers to target NATO countries from launch areas in the Arctic, potentially expanding Moscow’s long-range strike capabilities while raising questions about whether the missiles are intended for use against Ukraine or reserved for a possible confrontation with the Alliance.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Defense Express on October 11, citing a new report by the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI), the Kh-BD missiles are intended for Russia’s Tu-160M and Tu-95MS strategic bombers. The report, authored by defense researcher Sidharth Kaushal, examines Russia’s nuclear arsenal and its efforts to modernize strategic delivery systems.
The Kh-BD, also known as Izdeliye 506, is designed to extend the strike range of Russia’s existing bomber fleet. Its development comes as Moscow continues to struggle with its next-generation PAK DA bomber program, originally intended to replace the aging Tu-95MS and Tu-160 aircraft.
Russia’s Kh-BD could strike US from the Arctic
According to Kaushal, the missile’s claimed 6,500-kilometer range could allow Russian bombers to launch attacks against US territory from the Arctic, potentially using Alexandra Land Island in Russia’s far north as a launch area.
Such a capability could expand Moscow’s strategic strike options and complicate American air defense planning. However, the Kh-BD’s actual performance and ability to penetrate US missile defenses have not been independently verified.
The RUSI report also highlights a significant vulnerability in Russia’s strategic aviation operations.
US intelligence capabilities reportedly allow Washington to detect preparations for missile strikes involving Russian Tu-95MS and Tu-160 bombers. In a scenario involving direct nuclear escalation, this could leave major Russian strategic aviation bases, including Engels and Olenya, vulnerable to potential preemptive NATO strikes.
Defense Express noted that Russia first publicly unveiled the Kh-BD in September 2023, when Russian officials disclosed its claimed range and identified the modernized Tu-160 as a potential launch platform.
The missile is reportedly larger than Russia’s existing Kh-101 air-launched cruise missile, requiring additional modifications to the Tu-95MS and Tu-160 bombers before they can carry it.
32 Kh-BD missiles for Ukraine or NATO?
Details about Moscow’s procurement plans emerged in 2025, when Ukrainian defense outlet Militarnyi published leaked Russian documents indicating that the Russian military was scheduled to receive 16 Kh-BD missiles in 2024 and another 16 in 2026.
Each missile was reportedly valued at approximately $4.5 million, bringing the estimated cost of the planned 32-missile acquisition to $144 million.
If Russia fulfilled the procurement schedule, its military could have received up to 32 Kh-BD missiles by 2026. However, there is no independent confirmation that all planned deliveries have been completed.
According to Defense Express, Moscow faces two potential options for deploying the new weapons.
One possibility is that Russia could use the Kh-BD in strikes against Ukraine, testing the missile under actual combat conditions. Alternatively, the Russian military could retain the limited stockpile as a strategic reserve for a possible direct confrontation with NATO.
The development reflects Moscow’s broader effort to modernize its strategic aviation capabilities without introducing an entirely new bomber platform.
With the PAK DA program still unrealized, Russia remains dependent on upgraded versions of its existing long-range aircraft, making advanced cruise missiles such as the Kh-BD an important component of its future strike capabilities.
Earlier, Russian officials and state propagandists issued a series of threats against NATO countries, including Poland, Lithuania, Germany, and Norway. Russian state television host Vladimir Solovyov declared, “We don’t need their love. We need their fear,” while European officials warned that Moscow was attempting to intimidate NATO allies and weaken their support for Ukraine.

Network data do show Yandex’s automated traffic collapsing after the strikes. Disinformation researchers say that traffic is search crawling, not trolls. A Ukrainian social media monitor told Euromaidan Press its own data show no clear drop in bot activity either.
Russian influence operations are a live threat to European votes. In August, the Matryoshka network fabricated news clips aimed at Sweden’s general election. German and French authorities flagged the same network targeting Germany’s local votes and French presidential hopeful Gabriel Attal. A way to switch such networks off would hand allies a new tool, which is why the claim needs testing.
The president’s claim
Addressing the Warsaw Security Forum by video link, Zelenskyy said that once Ukraine began answering Russia’s operation against Ukrainian data centers and its strikes reached Yandex, many social media platforms suddenly became a little easier to breathe on.
Many people noticed less hatred, discord, and provocation because there were fewer bots, he said. It was quite clear where those bots came from, he noted. Their disappearance once Yandex went down proves again that Europe is not the source of the problems, he added.
Lithuanian Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius said at the same forum that allies should ask Zelenskyy to strike more data centers in Russia, answering a question on how to protect their elections from interference.
Three data centers in four days
Drones first hit Yandex’s data center in Sasovo, Ryazan Oblast, on 8 October. Yandex said it shut the site down completely. The next day, a strike on its Kaluga site completely disabled several modules, the company said. Yandex calls Kaluga its largest data center, Russian science outlet T-Invariant noted.
Ukrainian drone maker Fire Point said its FP-1 long-range drones carried out that strike.
After the first strike, on Sasovo, a source at Yandex summed up the mood for The Bell: “Things are rotten. We keep working.”
Overnight on 11 October, drones hit the third site, in Vladimir. Yandex said it fully halted that data center too. Vladimir Oblast Governor Aleksandr Avdeev acknowledged an attack on “infrastructure” near the city. It started a fire and cut power to two substations serving 5,000 residents, he claimed.
What the traffic data show
Automated web requests from Yandex’s network fell to 0.4% of their two-week peak after the third strike, Cloudflare Radar data showed, Cybernews reported. That chart counts automated requests to websites, mostly from Yandex’s own search crawlers. It does not count social media posts.
The chart “has nothing to do with social media,” the Russian opposition analysis group Antibot4navalny wrote.
Russia’s overall bot traffic last week looked much like any other week. Yandex’s own figure began recovering on Sunday. Covert troll farms usually hide behind residential proxies, hacked devices, virtual private networks (VPNs), and Western cloud providers, the outlet added.
What Ukrainian social media shows so far
Yevhen Luzan tracks Ukrainian social media sentiment as an analyst at the Ukrainian nonprofit CAT-UA. Its daily reviews sample about 500 random posts. On 11 October, that sample showed an unusually small share of posts criticizing Ukraine’s authorities, he told Euromaidan Press. Accounts showing signs of bot activity made up only a few tenths of a percent of that criticism. That is within the margin of error.
The same day, though, US President Donald Trump’s deal for Russian diesel supplies dominated Ukrainian feeds. Luzan said a rally-around-the-flag effect could explain the shift, as outrage at Washington crowded out domestic stories.
“To state it definitively and draw a cause-and-effect link from this correlation would be too bold,” he said.
Across the wider pool of about 10,000 daily mentions, CAT-UA sees no significant drop in posting activity in recent days. The curve shows only the usual rises and dips around the start and end of the week, Luzan said.
“For now, even a hypothetical drop in bot farm activity dissolves entirely in the natural fluctuations of the information space,” he said.
How a crawler chart became a bot story
The claim that Russian social media bots fell by half is unproven and built on a misread chart, disinformation analyst Joohn Choe concluded in a fact-check. It traces back to an 8 October post by security researcher Jeremiah Fowler. That post said Russian bot traffic had dropped to 49%. On 11 October, radio reporter Jamie Dupree spread it on X. Tom’s Hardware then ran it under a headline calling the crawler traffic “Russian disinformation bot traffic,” wording it has since changed.
Ukrainian military analyst Tatarigami claimed that Texas separatist accounts with identical “Veteran, Christian, Father, MAGA” bios had gone quiet. He said Quebec separatists and Polish anti-EU accounts went quiet alongside them.
Polish military analyst Jarosław Wolski claimed that AfD’s online support fell 56%, posting a chart without naming its source. Another X user said “Polish” bots had vanished.

Two-thirds of women in NL feel unheard by healthcare workers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
14:05:37 UTC
23:05:37 KST

Two-thirds of women in NL feel unheard by healthcare workers
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Two-thirds of women in the Netherlands say they don’t always feel heard by healthcare professionals, for example when describing symptoms, asking for referrals or discussing treatment options, according to a new report by polling company Kieskompas.
The findings were sent to MPs today and drawn from a survey of 14,000 women aged 16 and over. Only one in five women in the survey said healthcare professionals listen well to women.
Women aged 25 to 54 and women with unexplained symptoms were the most likely to say they felt misunderstood by consultants, and fewer than half of women with a condition or disability said the care they received helped them sufficiently.
Women also said they felt less well informed about topics that only affect women, such as menopause, than about general health issues. Women of all ages said they wanted that information, and would like to see more research on it.
According to ZonMw, a research funding body behind the report, girls would like to know more about how hormones can impact mental health for example.
Nearly two in three women said they thought women did not feel comfortable discussing health problems at work. Of women with health problems, 63% said these had affected their work, mainly through stress and lower productivity, and over a quarter had stopped working earlier than planned.
A second report, also presented on Monday, analysed the experiences of women who have got stuck in the healthcare system because of long-term, unexplained symptoms. The analysis, carried out by health research institute Nivel for the Voices for Women foundation, was based on surveys and accounts that women submitted themselves, which the researchers note it is not representative.
A lack of recognition came up in almost every account, ANP reported, and only one in four women said they felt heard by their care provider. According to ZonMw, almost 90% did not feel taken seriously, and 65% said they often got a psychological diagnosis when they came in with a physical complaint.
“The two new reports underline the urgency of the message ZonMw and others have been spreading for some time: more attention for women’s health is needed,” ZonMw said in a statement.

Ukraine “De-Russifies” Internet: Russian Disinformation Machine Plunges
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
14:04:56 UTC
23:04:56 KST

Ukrainian drones struck three Yandex data centers between Oct. 8 and 11, shutting down two facilities and damaging a third before automated traffic from the Russian technology giant’s network plunged.
The attacks hit Sasovo, Kaluga, and Vladimir, disrupting cloud computing and consumer services used across Russia. Yandex acknowledged the damage, while Kyiv Post reported that the outages affected databases, applications, and businesses relying on its servers.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The disruption also prompted reports of a quieter political internet, with commentators in Poland and Israel describing fewer inflammatory accounts and less apparent support for some Kremlin-friendly movements.
President Volodymyr Zelensky linked the strikes to that change on Monday, Oct. 12, saying there was “less hatred, less discord, and fewer provocations because there were fewer bots,” according to Interfax-Ukraine.
Concurrently, Cloudflare Radar recorded a sharp fall in automated requests from Yandex’s network.
How Moscow turns divisions into influence
Russia’s online campaigns seek to make Kremlin-friendly messages look like the opinions of ordinary voters, using fabricated identities, imitation news websites, and coordinated posting to amplify existing grievances.
A US Justice Department investigation in 2024 identified 968 accounts in an AI-assisted bot farm developed by an RT employee and backed by an FSB (Russian Federal Security Service) officer. Many posed as Americans while distributing pro-Russian material.
Zelensky Warns China Is Helping Russia Develop Starlink Rival
In a separate action against the Doppelganger operation, US authorities described cloned news sites and fictitious profiles used to weaken support for Ukraine. Together, those methods disguise who produced a message and manufacture the appearance of public agreement.
The political consequences have already reached national elections.
In Romania, the Constitutional Court annulled the 2024 presidential election after intelligence documents alleged Russian interference and coordinated online promotion of far-right candidate Calin Georgescu, who opposed military aid to Ukraine and unexpectedly won the first round.
The European Commission subsequently opened proceedings against TikTok, examining risks involving its recommendation systems, coordinated manipulation, and paid political content.
Britain has meanwhile returned to the question of Moscow’s role in Brexit. On Sunday, Oct. 11, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he had received confirmation that Russia interfered in the 2016 referendum after seeking answers on entering Downing Street.
His acknowledgment followed a 2020 parliamentary intelligence report criticizing the failure to assess possible interference. Burnham did not disclose the underlying evidence or establish how it affected the result.
Poland and Israel report a quieter internet
In Poland, Russian campaigns have exploited disputes over refugees, history, and military aid to intensify anti-Ukrainian sentiment online.
An August assessment by the Polish Institute of International Affairs reported 364,000 Polish-language posts containing extremely hateful terms directed at Ukrainians in its May-July analysis, generating 1.2 million reactions, comments, and shares. The researchers described Russian amplification of existing tensions, rather than attributing all hostility to Moscow.
After the Yandex attacks, military commentator Jarosław Wolski described a “de-Russified internet,” reporting fewer purportedly Polish accounts attacking Ukrainians and fewer purportedly Ukrainian accounts attacking Poles.
He also claimed a 56% decline in online support for Germany’s far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD), attaching a graph showing sharp falls in daily activity. While the screenshot provides the general observable trend, it does not feature an identifiable data source or account sample. Besides, activity cannot be equated with voter support.
Meanwhile, former Ukrainian lawmaker Borislav Bereza reported that accounts posting aggressive political comments in Russian and Hebrew had fallen silent, citing Israeli observers.
As the country is approaching its Oct. 27 election, Ynet reported that the Shin Bet had established a dedicated election-security team, with foreign cyber operations and political bots among the threats being monitored.
Kyiv Post has previously examined how Russian propaganda combines anti-Israel and anti-Ukrainian narratives, including antisemitic conspiracies and attempts to depict both countries as fascist.
France’s next election is already in the crosshairs
France, which holds pivotal presidential elections next year, is likewise in the focus.
Ahead of the election, Russia-linked campaigns have targeted Edouard Philippe, Gabriel Attal, and Raphael Glucksmann with fabricated health claims and scandals, sometimes impersonating established French news outlets.
As Kyiv Post’s analysis of Marine Le Pen’s presidential bid explained, divisions among pro-Ukraine candidates could benefit her and reshape French policy toward Kyiv. Le Pen has since ruled out further financial assistance to Ukraine if elected, while leaving room for military assistance and training.
Yandex turns to rival providers to restore services
While acknowledging immediate impact, Yandex is already arranging for affected customers to move their data and applications to competing cloud providers while engineers assess the damaged facilities.
The company said it had reached agreements with Selectel, K2Cloud, and VK Cloud to accelerate those transfers, providing additional technical teams, simplified onboarding, and flexible financial terms.
Yandex said rehearsals for the prolonged loss of an entire data-center zone had helped it switch critical workloads after the attacks.
In its own statement, Yandex said teams were working around the clock to restore services and assess the infrastructure, but could not give a timetable for bringing the damaged equipment back online.
Moving customers elsewhere can restore access before the damaged facilities are repaired, meaning that malign online operations may resume soon.

A university student lay in wait for his housemate to return home before stabbing him 30 times, a murder trial has been told.
Zack Coughlan, 23, dressed in black and wore a mask and gloves to ambush Jamie Collins, 21, in the garden of their home near the University of West England in Bristol, where both were studying robotics.
Collins was attacked shortly before 6pm on 8 April after returning from campus on his bike, Bristol crown court heard.
Coughlan then allegedly cycled away on the bike, dumped it at a nearby retail park, bought a change of clothes and threw his bloodstained clothing into a pond.
He returned to the house they shared in Filton, south Gloucestershire, at about 9pm, put a pizza in the oven and did some online gaming with friends, the court was told.
Adam Vaitilingam KC, prosecuting, said: “A few hours later he decided it was time to call the police and pretend that he had just found his friend’s body in the garden.
“At about 2am, eight hours later, the defendant called 999. He said that his friend had been stabbed. They told him to do CPR until paramedics arrived and he told them that he was.”
He told police he had noticed the back gate was open, went outside and found Collins’s body.
The court heard the attack was caught on CCTV installed at the house, which Coughlan showed officers, who initially treated him as a witness.
Coughlan had injuries to his hands but he said he had hurt himself when he fell while climbing trees.
Vaitilingam said that as the evidence against Coughlan mounted, he went from being a witness to a suspect. He now accepted he had killed Collins but denied murder. He said he “lost his self-control” when he carried out the attack, the barrister said.
The jury was told that Coughlan and Collins were final-year students and lived together in a house owned by the defendant.
Vaitilingam said there had been disagreements between the pair about rent and whether Coughlan was charging too much, but they appeared to have been resolved.
“There was nothing that any friends were aware of that seemed to be a significant problem,” he said. “They hung out together, both in person and online, they did gaming together, they went out together; entirely normal student life.”

Microsoft to rely more on homegrown AI chips, reducing dependence on Nvidia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
14:04:16 UTC
23:04:16 KST

Microsoft will ramp up use of its homegrown artificial intelligence chips after years of reliance on Nvidia's graphics processing units, as the software giant attempts to bolster its AI stack.
Starting with its third-generation Maia AI accelerator, unveiled on Monday, Microsoft said it will mainly rely on its own silicon to handle incoming requests.
Microsoft's greatest strength in AI has been its Azure cloud, which runs a series of models for clients. Its Microsoft 365 Copilot and GitHub Copilot offer AI-powered services to software engineers and other office workers. And the company develops in-house models, though they've yet to make a big splash in a market dominated by OpenAI, Anthropic and Google.
The emerging opportunity in chips stems from unrelenting demand for advanced processors and a desire in the market for choice. Nvidia's GPUs have been the standard for AI workloads and models, and they fill Microsoft's existing data centers, while also serving to train models from OpenAI and Anthropic.
But as demand keeps growing, the model leaders have embraced a variety of silicon from companies including Amazon, Advanced Micro Devices, Cerebras, Google and, in recent months, Microsoft.
For general-purpose use, Microsoft already taps its own central processing units as well as silicon from Intel and AMD. Finance chief Amy Hood said at a Goldman Sachs conference last month that use of its own chips has helped with "margin improvement over the course of a decade."
Microsoft introduced its inaugural AI chip, the Maia 100, in 2023. It touted the Maia 200 this past January, and CEO Satya Nadella told analysts in July that Maia 200 "delivers 30% better performance per dollar than the latest generation hardware in our fleet" and said it was handling OpenAI models.
Production of the Maia 300 starts in 2027. Microsoft is targeting multi-gigawatt deployments of chips in the Maia family, according to a blog post from Executive Vice President Scott Guthrie. But Alistair Speirs, a general manager, declined to provide a timeline.
"We reserve a little bit of optionality there, because this is an industry that's changing very fast, and we want to deploy the right silicon for the right models that we're using at the right time as well," Speirs said.
Microsoft expects to pack 96 Maia 300 chips into each data center rack, double the number for the Maia 200. The new version can run through up to seven times more AI tokens per rack, with 40% more tokens per megawatt when compared with GPUs.
"We need new architectures that will give us essentially better performance, better use of the power that we have," Speirs said. "You can think of power translating pretty directly into operational cost for something like a data center as well."
Parts of Microsoft 365 Copilot should speed up with Maia 300, said Jim Kleewein, a technical fellow at the company.
In a note distributed to clients on Wednesday, Evercore ISI analysts estimated that Maia will represent about 10% of Microsoft's spending on AI chips by the first quarter of 2027. The analysts recommend buying Microsoft shares.
Nvidia will still be a big part of the equation. CEO Jensen Huang spoke at an event last week where Microsoft announced a Surface laptop containing an Nvidia processor. And when it comes to training models, Microsoft partners with Nvidia and AMD, Speirs said.
Unlike Google's tensor processing units or Amazon's Inferentia and Trainium, Microsoft's accelerators can't be rented by the hour to other companies.
"Nobody has tested them outside of Microsoft yet," said Patrick Moorhead, CEO of advisory firm Moor Insights and Strategy.

South Korea opens military’s 1st AI base to train robots for hazardous missions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
14:04:06 UTC
23:04:06 KST

Faisal Mahmud
12 October 2026•Update: 12 October 2026
South Korea’s Defense Ministry on Monday opened the military’s first artificial intelligence (AI) transformation base to develop robotic systems capable of performing dangerous military operations.
The facility, located in Pangyo, south of Seoul, will train humanoid and multi-legged robots using physical AI data and advanced AI models, Yonhap News Agency reported, citing the ministry.
Around 150 officials, including representatives from the science and industry ministries, attended the opening ceremony.
The robots will be trained to transport supplies into hazardous areas, dispose of explosive ordnance and clear land mines, reducing soldiers’ exposure to potentially fatal missions.
The ministry said the initiative aims to establish a world-leading defense hub specializing in physical AI, which enables machines to interact with real-world environments.
Under the program, South Korea will establish five AI transformation bases nationwide involving individual military branches and the Joint Chiefs of Staff.
One facility will be located at the Joint Chiefs of Staff headquarters in Seoul’s Yongsan district.
The ministry also plans to strengthen cooperation with private technology companies to integrate commercially developed AI systems into military operations.
The initiative comes as South Korea increasingly turns to automation to address military personnel shortages caused by its declining birth rate. Anadolu previously reported that the military has been expanding AI adoption to maintain operational readiness with fewer troops, including trials of humanoid robots aboard naval vessels.

Estonian grain farmers have reason to be happy with the summer
This past summer was the best in years for grain growers, but a good harvest does not necessarily translate into strong financial results. The outlook for grain prices remains uncertain.
According to the Ministry of Regional Affairs and Agriculture's food security report, grain quality was poor last year due to excessive rainfall. Low prices also weighed on producers' profits. This year, however, was one of the strongest harvest years in recent memory for Estonian grain growers.
According to Statistics Estonia, the total grain harvest reached nearly 1.55 million tons this year, while wheat yields were the highest in 14 years. Ants-Hannes Viira, head of agricultural policy at the Estonian Chamber of Agriculture and Commerce, said that when grain, pulses, rapeseed and turnip rape harvests are combined, this summer was the third most productive in Estonia's history.
"We were lucky with the weather this time. In the spring, there were fears that it would be a very dry year. There was very little rainfall until May, but after that, precipitation was above average. The grain will be sold, of course. Fortunately, prices are better this year than last year," Viira said.
Viira added that the grain sector's financial results are positive. Looking ahead to next year, the key factors will be the same as this year.
"We don't know what the weather will be like. Fertilizer prices will remain high next year, just as they have been this year, and there is uncertainty about grain prices. It depends on the situation in the Black Sea and whether the Ukrainian and Russian grain harvests, which have also been good this year, can reach the global market," Viira said.
The difficulties Ukrainian and Russian grain face in reaching global markets are helping support grain exports and prices elsewhere, but that may not be the case next year.
Estonian grain is exported to the Middle East and North Africa, while peas are shipped to Spain and Norway for use in animal and fish feed. Grain growers would welcome the opportunity to expand their farmland, but subsidy policies limit their ability to do so.
"For more than 20 years, we've been in a situation where permanent grassland must remain permanent grassland and arable crops cannot be grown on it. This has prevented the expansion of grain-growing areas. Ultimately, the soils and fields suitable for grain production are already being used for that purpose. There isn't much room for a major expansion in cultivated land. Arable crops cover around 400,000 to 500,000 hectares. The area has gradually increased, yes, but not significantly," Viira explained.
The more difficult years have also affected investment. According to Bank of Estonia statistics, the agricultural sector's leasing portfolio has fallen from approximately €370 million in September 2023 to around €305 million today. Marjan Savtšenko, head of business banking at Luminor, said farmers should avoid drawing up overly optimistic budgets for next year based on a single exceptionally good year. There are already signs that purchases of new machinery, for example, have declined.
"Farmers would be wise to remain conservative and build up financial reserves. Most investments go into machinery because it is essential for harvesting crops. If a neighboring property comes up for sale, farmers take the opportunity to expand their farmland," Savtšenko said.

Dystopian and dehumanising: that’s what it felt like when I was interviewed by an AI assistant
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
14:00:57 UTC
23:00:57 KST

Over the past 15 years of my working life, I’ve done a lot of interviews for a lot of different jobs and industries: call centre operator, social media manager, bookseller, copywriter, library worker. Recently, after completing my first year of a masters degree in early childhood and primary teaching, I applied for a preschool education role and experienced a first: being interviewed by AI.
I’d heard of this practice and was aware of its shortcomings, from how demoralising it is to the risk of discrimination.
Yet I still wasn’t prepared for how dystopian and dehumanising it felt to be in the situation myself.
I had applied for the role with great interest – it was at a sessional kindergarten managed by a not-for-profit. My initial excitement at being shortlisted soon faded as I realised I would be speaking with an “AI assistant”. Nevertheless, she persisted: I dressed as I would for any other job interview, shooed my cats out of the room, sat down at my laptop and clicked to enter the interview.
A disembodied voice greeted me by name and the interview began. I found it disconcerting to see myself in the little video window with no one else visible, but I pushed through the discomfort to answer the questions. At one point the AI asked me a question that I needed time to consider. I’ve previously been told it’s acceptable to pause during job interviews to think through a particularly tricky question, so I did just that – and I was booted off the interview entirely. As I clicked the link once more to restart the interview, I could feel a guttural scream rising in my throat.
At the end of the interview, the AI asked if I had any questions about the role. I did, but they were all answered with regurgitations from the job ad. For any clarification, the AI said, I would need to have a conversation with a manager. I stifled a laugh at the irony.
The AI thanked me for my time and said that my video would be reviewed by the company, which would be in touch. I closed the browser window and stared at my blank laptop screen and my own reflection. I had been alone the entire time, after all.
In the following days, I could not stop thinking about this experience. I posted on early childhood forums asking if anyone had gone through the same thing. I was met with a ripple of shock from industry peers, including senior people, who couldn’t believe this was happening. I couldn’t either – it’s demeaning enough to put any job-seeker through AI interviews, but the profession of caring for and educating children is surely one of the most human that still exists. Especially in light of the ongoing childcare crisis in Australia, outsourcing recruitment of this essential role to a machine seems lazy at best and negligent at worst.
Still, I tried to bargain with myself: maybe the experience will be worth it. Surely this is only the first stage of the recruitment process and the next interview will be with a person? I really want to contribute positively to my community! This is the future, right?
But that little voice in my head was only getting louder. I felt degraded: I’d put effort into my application and interview, so why shouldn’t I receive effort back? I noticed, too, that the organisation’s website had AI photos of “educators”. Was the interview a sign of labour erasure to come?
I ultimately decided to withdraw my application and emailed the organisation to tell them precisely why. It has been over a month and I have received no response, no acknowledgment whatsoever. I still haven’t spoken to a single human being.
I think of those sweet little children I could have taught, learning about the world, each other, themselves. They don’t know what an AI interview is yet, but if things continue this way, one day they will. I want better for them. I want better for all of us.

Is fatness a feminist issue?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
14:00:42 UTC
23:00:42 KST

Recent research published in Sex Roles suggests that while many fat women identify as feminists, they do not consistently view their body size as a feminist issue. The study highlights a divide in how women understand their bodies, with some pointing to gendered double standards and societal discrimination, while others view their weight as a matter of personal responsibility.
Anti-fatness refers to the systemic and interpersonal prejudice directed at people with larger bodies. Feminist scholars have often linked this anti-fat stigma to traditional gender roles and patriarchal beauty norms. This perspective argues that societal pressure to be thin falls especially hard on women, creating toxic environments that negatively impact their body image, mental health, and social standing.
“American society is often fixated on how women look,” lead author Breanne Fahs, a professor of women and gender studies at Arizona State University and author of Fat and Furious: Igniting Radical Fat Resistance, told PsyPost. “Women are often told to be young, pretty, and skinny by their parents, partners, classmates, and strangers. Psychological research has often shown the problems with ‘thin idealization’ and living for a male gaze. In particular, women are criticized about having defective bodies, and they consequently fear gaining weight, try dangerous diets, and/or loathe their own bodies.”
“In the 1970s, second wave feminists warned that the fixation on slender bodies seriously hurt women and the slogan of ‘fat is a feminist issue’ was born,” Fahs added. “In the last twenty years there has been a growth of social movements that challenged the sexist assumptions of fat stigma, with the group called National Association to Advance Fat Acceptance (NAAFA) leading the way.”
Research has shown that fat women generally face harsher social and economic consequences for their body size than fat men. In one study, fat women were 16 times more likely than fat men to report weight-related job discrimination, and other studies have found that fat women receive harsher judgments of their parenting and are more often denied loans, promotions, or apartments. Fat men, on the other hand, tend to face less stigma and fewer everyday indignities for similar body sizes.
Despite these documented disparities, it has remained an open question whether fat women themselves view their physical experiences through a political or feminist lens. Fahs and her colleague Eric Swank, a professor of social and cultural analysis at Arizona State University, sought to understand how fat women talk about this connection and whether they recognize the gendered dimensions of weight stigma that academics often discuss.
“Lots of research has looked at the causes and consequences of fat hatred among women of all body sizes,” Fahs explained. “Some studies have even looked at the reasons for being a fat activist, but the way fat women view feminism has mostly been overlooked.”
Fahs’s own work helped motivate the project. She has written about women’s dread of gaining weight, anti-fat bias in health care, and the relationships between fat therapists and fat patients. Her experience as both a professor and a practicing clinical psychologist left her curious about whether fat women see anti-fat stigma through a feminist lens.
To investigate this, the researchers interviewed 20 women living in the United States who self-identified as fat or overweight. The participants were recruited through local classified advertisements on Craigslist, allowing the research team to reach a geographically diverse group. The women ranged in age from 27 to 66, with an average age of 40. Half were women of color, 40 percent identified as bisexual or lesbian, and their body weights ranged from under 200 to over 300 pounds.
All 20 interviews were conducted by Fahs over video calls and lasted about 90 minutes each. She asked the women questions about their bodies, their social experiences, and their political perspectives. Two key questions guided the core of the analysis: whether the participants considered themselves feminists, and whether they believed fatness was a feminist issue. The researchers did not provide a definition of feminism, allowing each participant to respond according to her own understanding.
The participants’ responses pointed to a complex divide between personal identification and political frameworks. Thirteen women explicitly identified as feminists, three said they might use the label for certain issues, and four rejected it entirely. When asked if fatness was a feminist issue, the group was evenly split: eight said yes, four said maybe, and eight said no. Several self-identified feminists insisted that fatness was not a feminist issue, while one woman, identified in the study as Marge, firmly rejected the feminist label but still stated that it was.
The researchers identified six distinct themes in how the participants evaluated the issue. Three of the themes supported a connection between weight and feminism. Four women highlighted gendered double standards, observing that society readily accepts fat men as funny or relatable, while fat women face intense social disapproval for the same size. Three women described fatness as a central way women are judged, explaining that a woman’s social worth remains tied to physical appearance.
Overt discrimination, tied for the most common theme linking the two concepts, was raised by four participants. These women cited institutional obstacles in hiring, healthcare, and media representation as evidence of a broader feminist problem. When discussing these barriers, Fahs noted that participants “elaborated how workplaces, hospitals, schools, and families discriminate against women who are fat.”
The remaining three themes rejected the connection between body size and feminism. Three women stated that fatness has nothing to do with feminism, arguing that body weight is an individual matter of personal responsibility and lifestyle rather than gender politics. Two women maintained that fatness has nothing to do with gender, arguing that weight stigma affects people of all genders equally and should not be framed as a women’s issue.
In the final theme, three participants argued that fat women deserve ridicule, framing teasing as a natural consequence of body size or a motivator to lose weight.
Describing these women, Fahs said, “They thought fat women were supposed to be ‘made fun of by someone who is not fat’ and fat people ‘should lose weight’ if they do not want to be teased. This diversity of perspectives shows how fat resistance and feminist fat liberation perspectives still diverge from narratives of self-blame and ridicule.”
The findings point to an uneven alignment between feminist theory and the everyday perspectives of fat women. While some participants expressed an awareness of gender inequality, others expressed anti-fat attitudes, which the authors say could reflect internalized stigma or a form of anti-feminism, or viewed their struggles as entirely personal. The researchers noted that framing fatness through a political lens rather than individual failure could help people challenge anti-fat bias and reduce feelings of personal self-blame.
As with all research, there are some caveats to consider. The study relied on a small group of 20 women recruited through Craigslist during the COVID-19 pandemic, so the sample does not reflect the full population of fat women in the United States. In addition, the questions about feminism came after about an hour of discussion focused on fatness, which may have influenced the way participants answered.
The study also asked participants whether they identified as feminists rather than measuring specific feminist beliefs, and several women appeared to associate feminism primarily with the #MeToo movement or perceived extremes. Both researchers identify as fat feminists, and Fahs conducted all 20 interviews herself, which could have shaped how participants discussed sensitive topics. Future research using standardized surveys could help clarify how widespread these viewpoints are across the broader population.
The study, “Does Fatness Politicize Women? Fat Women’s Narratives on Whether Fatness is a Feminist Issue,” was authored by Breanne Fahs and Eric Swank.
