Europe still divided on buying locally for defence, MBDA CEO says
Oct 12 - The head of European missile maker MBDA said on Monday that efforts to steer more defence spending towards European suppliers faced political hurdles, with EU governments still divided over how much to rely on US security guarantees.
Washington has been pressing European NATO allies to increase defence spending, while France has led calls to buy more European-made weapons amid questions over the US commitment to Europe's security.
"Do we want as Europeans to really take our own fate in our hands and then bring our European capabilities to the NATO alliance, or are we simply increasing our capabilities by buying outside?" MBDA CEO Eric Beranger asked the Warsaw Security Forum.
"There are some different attitudes between the various governments. I think the jury is still out," Beranger said, adding: "There is still some way to go".
DETERRENCE
Beranger, who steps down next month, was among several speakers debating European strategic autonomy at the forum, which is taking place amid heightened tensions over the war in Ukraine.
Several European countries, including conference host Poland, Germany and the Netherlands, have turned to US suppliers for equipment such as F-35 fighter jets.
"Limiting American defense industry in European procurement programs threatens that partnership and weakens our mutual security", the US mission to the European Union said in February.
Nuclear deterrence was also a focus of the discussion, with Russia recently renewing warnings that it could use nuclear weapons to defend itself.
"Of all the events at this conference that the Russians will be most interested in hearing ... it will be this one", former British defence minister Ben Wallace said, referring to Europe's ability to strengthen its nuclear and conventional deterrence.
"Deterrence is not only capabilities; deterrence is also perceptions. Do we believe our American allies will come? Does Russia believe our American allies will come?" said Claudia Major, senior vice president for transatlantic security at the German Marshall Fund.
"I don't say give up on the US. I just say don't blind ourselves", Major added, citing recent friction with the US over Greenland, Russia and Ukraine.
NATO members, including the US, reaffirmed their commitment to collective defence in the Ankara Summit Declaration in July, repeating that "an attack on one is an attack on all".
Stressing that credibility is central to deterrence, Beranger said Europe already had the industrial base it needed to strengthen its defences. REUTERS

The Verkhovna Rada adopted a law on workplace safety — what it provides for
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
17:00:04 EEST
23:00:04 KST

The Verkhovna Rada adopted a law on workplace safety — what it provides for
Kyiv • UNN
Bill No. 10147 was supported by 246 lawmakers. It introduces European rules for managing occupational risks and recording incidents.
The Verkhovna Rada adopted on second reading a bill that brings Ukrainian legislation closer to European standards and reforms the national occupational safety and health management system. UNN reports this, citing a parliamentary session.
Details
Bill No. 10147, “On the Safety and Health of Workers at Work,” was supported on second reading and as a whole by 246 members of parliament.
Under the bill, guarantees, benefits and compensations may be established for employees engaged in work under conditions of increased danger and/or involving harmful occupational factors, including, but not limited to, free provision of therapeutic and preventive nutrition and water, paid breaks when maximum permissible temperature levels are exceeded, reduced working hours, additional paid leave, preferential pension benefits, and remuneration at an increased rate.
The bill establishes an obligation for employers to keep records of all incidents, determine the causes of their occurrence, and document information about them.
The procedure for recording incidents is determined by the employer, taking into account the model regulation approved by the Ministry of Health and the State Service of Ukraine on Labour.
The employer must also report the occurrence of accidents, occupational diseases and emergencies, keep records of them, investigate them, and provide information on the results of such investigations.
Information on occupational diseases is entered into the electronic epidemiological surveillance system and transferred to Ukraine’s public health information platform.
The Verkhovna Rada said that this bill is a “European integration” bill and provides for the introduction in Ukraine of a new system for preventing occupational risks based on the principles of risk assessment, control and management defined by Council Directive No. 89/391/EEC.
Previously
The Cabinet of Ministers adopted a resolution that relieved the State Service of Ukraine on Labour of functions not inherent to it. Instead, the State Labour Service will focus more on people’s safety at work, compliance with labour rights, and supporting fair rules in the labour market.

When climate change brings the heat, what happens to a mighty redwood?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
14:00:00 UTC
23:00:00 KST

Towering coast redwoods are known for their resiliency, withstanding fire, fungus and rot to survive for centuries. But these ancient trees now may be vulnerable to a relatively recent foe: heat waves.
As temperatures climb, photosynthesis slows in these iconic trees, researchers report September 22 in the Journal of Geophysical Research: Biogeosciences. Lab experiments show the rate of the sunlight-driven food making process in its needles roughly halves when temperatures rise from 30° to 40° Celsius.
Such a change usually indicates “severe levels of stress,” says Lily Klinek, an ecophysiologist at the University of California, Davis. That vulnerability can cause tree deaths that may jeopardize one of California’s largest stores of carbon, a shield against climate change.
Coast redwoods (Sequoia sempervirens) live only in a narrow strip of coastal habitat from central California to southern Oregon, where temperatures are mild and fog is abundant. But recent heat waves have spiked temperatures in parts of their range to over 40° C.
The impact of heat waves on photosynthesis has been studied in other tree species, with some faring better than others. But this is the first study to investigate how coast redwoods respond to the heat, says Troy Magney, an ecophysiologist at the University of Montana in Missoula.
From July 2022 to October 2024, Klinek, Magney and colleagues repeatedly measured the performance of needles from redwoods in California’s Mendocino County. That period included two heat waves.
Typically, trees stay cool when small porelike openings called stomata allow water to evaporate, taking heat with it, similar to how sweat cools humans. But when conditions get too hot and dry, stomata close, retaining a plant’s moisture. Under extreme heat, the team found that needles reached up to 10 degrees C hotter than the surrounding air due to the dark needles absorbing ample sunlight. That suggests that the stomata were at least partially closed.
Those same pores are crucial for photosynthesis; it’s where the trees take in carbon dioxide — used to make food — and release oxygen. “They could essentially starve if they don’t have access to enough carbon,” Klinek says.
It’s hard to investigate the impact of heat on photosynthesis in the field, though. That would take building a “heat chamber around a real-life branch or wait[ing] for a heat event to happen,” Klinek says. Instead, she climbed onto the roof of her car with a pole pruner and collected samples from about five meters high, in the lower canopy.
In the lab, the researchers subjected the samples to increasing heat to match the heat waves seen in recent summers and measured the resulting photosynthesis rates. Even though the samples were submerged in water, so had their stomata open and had full access to the ingredients for photosynthesis, the rate still declined. “They weren’t slowing their photosynthesis because of carbon starvation,” Klinek says.
For practical reasons, the study focused on younger coast redwoods, not the old growth giants. It’s difficult to reach even the lowest branches on trees more than 100 meters tall. “There are just fundamental limitations on what you can sample if you don’t have a jetpack,” says Christopher Still, an ecophysiologist at Oregon State University in Corvallis who was not associated with the study. Even so, the team’s results show that coast redwoods are “really temperature sensitive. You don’t see this as much with other species necessarily,” Still says.
In the field, Klinek observed trees closing their stomata to preserve water. This suggests that in more realistic conditions, where a heat wave and drought hit simultaneously, lack of heat and water could make the slowdown “even more intense.” But more work needs to be done, she notes. “We still don’t know what the threshold is for irreversible damage.”

Ukraine Adapts Air Defense to Counter Faster Russian Jet Drones
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
13:57:49 UTC
22:57:49 KST

Ukraine is fielding new ways to intercept Russia’s jet-powered drones, the country’s defense ministry said on Monday in its September air defense report.
The ministry said Russia is sending small groups of several jet drones into different regions, which Ukraine counters with aircraft and what it called innovative interception, according to RBC-Ukraine, though the ministry provided no specifics.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
It added that ballistic missiles remain a challenge, while jet drones flying at about 400 kmh (249 mph) shorten the time available to detect and intercept them.
The new Russian drones are already having an effect. On Oct. 10, turbojet loitering munitions damaged power distribution facilities in the Kyiv region, injuring four people, causing voltage drops that shut down all three metro lines, and knocking out municipal water pumping stations.
How Kyiv is responding
While the ministry has been tight-lipped about its innovations, recent reports suggest a combination of efforts.
The most immediate is the F-16 fighter jets. Pilots have already used the jets’ 20mm cannons against jet drones, and Kyiv wants tens of thousands of rounds as a cheaper alternative to air-to-air missiles.
The second track focuses on dedicated interceptors, with the defense ministry testing and codifying various models that can down jet-powered drones. Arms makers are also working with the military to test new models, such as the Griffen jet-powered drone, which is said to have successfully intercepted a target in July.
Ukraine’s TENCORE Bundles 4 Ground Drones in Single AI-Powered Ecosystem
A third track is a small-missile program that President Volodymyr Zelensky said is expected to show results in the second half of the month, with production scaling up if it works.
The last would be AI-powered gun turrets, deployed around Kyiv in October after Russia began targeting bridges across the Dnipro River. Reports suggest 12 are in place, with eight more planned, though a defense adviser cautioned they are only a last line of defense and cannot protect the entire city, despite reported successes against jet-powered drones.
And scaling the new systems remains the main obstacle.
The Associated Press reported that ramping up interceptor production and training pilots could take three to six months, well beyond the end-of-October target. RBC-Ukraine has reported that technical complexity and high component costs, especially for engines Ukraine largely buys abroad, limit how quickly Ukraine can produce jet interceptors.
From experiment to mass use
Jet-powered drones are not new.
In February 2025, Ukraine’s military intelligence warned that Russia had begun domestic production of the jet-powered Geran-3, a variant of the Iranian Shahed design. Ukraine officially confirmed its inclusion in mass airstrikes in July 2025.
For months, use remained limited. Russia launched about 1,400 jet-powered Gerans in the first months of 2026, compared with 180 recorded in all of 2025, according to defense outlet Militarnyi.
Russia began launching the newer Geran-4 in May, and in August, the Ukrainian Air Force said up to two-thirds of the drones in some strikes were jet-powered, with around 2,850 launches documented in a single month, rising to nearly 3,500 by September.
Why they are harder to stop
Speed and altitude are the main advantages. Jet drones fly faster and higher than propeller-driven Shaheds, making them harder for mobile fire groups and existing interceptor drones to hit.
Defense Minister Yevhen Khmara has framed the shift as a change in the nature of the threat.
“The effectiveness of countering standard ‘Shahed’ drones already exceeds 90%,” he said. “The key challenge now is jet-powered drones, which require different interception speeds.”

U.S. court allows airBaltic to continue its critical aviation contracts, insurance coverage, and customer loyalty programs  - The Baltic Times

RIGA - The Southern District of New York Bankruptcy Court has approved several uncontested motions filed by Latvian national airline airBaltic, allowing the company to continue critical aviation contracts, insurance coverage, customer loyalty programs, payments to certain foreign suppliers, tax payments, and its employee compensation system during the Chapter 11 proceedings, according to the court's statements.
Although the court hearing on the remaining EUR 35 million debtor-in-possession (DIP) financing to airBaltic has been postponed to October 19, airBaltic informed the court that no objections had been received to six important motions concerning continuation of the company's day-to-day operations during the Chapter 11 proceedings.
Among other things, the U.S. court has allowed airBaltic to maintain its critical aviation contracts, fulfill its obligations under these contracts, and enter into new contracts necessary to ensure the company's continued operations during the Chapter 11 proceedings. At the same time, the company will be required to report on a regular basis to creditor representatives on major payments made under these contracts.
Similarly, the U.S. court has definitively authorized airBaltic to continue its existing insurance policies, purchase new insurance coverage, and fulfill its insurance-related obligations during the Chapter 11 proceedings.
In accordance with the court's decision, airBaltic will also be able to pay certain claims from foreign suppliers and other creditors that arose prior to the Chapter 11 proceedings, as well as continue to perform contracts entered into with them to ensure continuity of the airline's operations during the restructuring process.
At the same time, the airline will be able to continue its customer loyalty programs, issue refunds to customers, and maintain its obligations under gift card and loyalty programs.
airBaltic has also received court approval confirming that the airline may continue to pay taxes and duties, including adhering to existing payment schedules with the State Revenue Service and, if necessary, enter into new tax payment arrangements during the restructuring process.
The court has also definitively authorized airBaltic to continue paying salaries, maintain employee benefits and social programs, and fulfill obligations to employees that arose prior to the Chapter 11 proceedings. Furthermore, the court ruled that any significant changes to compensation or bonus systems must be agreed upon in advance and disclosed to creditors' representatives.
airBaltic had also requested permission to maintain its bank accounts, payment systems, and cash management procedures during the Chapter 11 proceedings, however, this matter has been postponed until the October 19 court hearing.
The Southern District of New York Bankruptcy Court earlier said that its hearing during which a decision would be made on remaining portion of the first DIP financing to airBaltic, amounting to EUR 35 million, had been rescheduled for October 19.
If necessary, the hearing will continue on October 20.
As reported, the preliminary order of the court states that the first tranche of airBaltic’s DIP financing is EUR 175 million out of a total planned amount of EUR 350 million; of which airBaltic has received EUR 140 million, while the remaining EUR 35 million will be disbursed to the company after the court issues its final order.
Furthermore, upon achieving certain reorganization targets, airBaltic will be able to receive up to EUR 125 million in the second tranche of financing and up to EUR 50 million in the third tranche.
LETA also reported, airBaltic has begun restructuring its financial obligations in accordance with the Chapter 11 procedure set forth in U.S. law.
In total, airBaltic has received binding commitments from financiers to provide up to EUR 350 million in DIP financing to ensure the company’s liquidity and operations during the Chapter 11 process. Currently, airBaltic has received the first tranche of financing in the amount of EUR 140 million, of which EUR 78.925 million will be used to repurchase eight aircraft and seven engines.
The financing was arranged by SVP, and Barclays, Hayfin Capital Management, Morgan Stanley, Oaktree Capital Management, and Strategic Value Partners have committed to providing it. The interest rate is SOFR +8 percent, or approximately 12 percent at present; however, this transaction will also involve additional fees totaling up to EUR 52.5 million.
Consequently, the previous plan to raise up to EUR 257 million at an annual rate of 25 percent from bondholders will not be implemented.
Chapter 11 protection shields airBaltic from creditor claims until the restructuring of its liabilities is completed.
The company also reports that flights and customer service will continue as usual. All flights will operate according to the scheduled flight plan; existing tickets and reservations remain valid, and passengers can continue to purchase tickets and travel with airBaltic as before.
Upon completion of this process, the final outcome will be a so-called reorganization plan, which must be approved by the court. The process is expected to be completed by mid-2027.
It was also reported that airBaltic bondholders supported in August the capitalization of the next two bond interest payments, as well as several other measures that provide the airline with additional flexibility in implementing its revised business plan.
Bondholders supported the capitalization of interest payments due on August 14 and November 14 of this year, adding them to the principal amount of the bonds rather than paying them out in cash. A decision was also made to grant a temporary exemption from minimum liquidity requirements until November 2026.
The airBaltic Group’s revenue last year increased by 4.2 percent compared to 2024, reaching EUR 779.344 million. Meanwhile, the airBaltic Group’s losses last year totaled EUR 44.337 million, which is 2.7 times less than in 2024. The airline carried a total of 5.2 million passengers in 2025, which is 1 percent more than in 2024.
Last summer, Germany’s national airline, Lufthansa, became a shareholder in airBaltic. Currently, the Latvian government owns 88.37 percent of airBaltic’s shares, Lufthansa holds 10 percent, the company Aircraft Leasing 1, owned by Danish businessman Lars Thuesen, a financial investor, holds 1.62 percent, and 0.01 percent is held by others. The company’s share capital is EUR 41.819 million.

Top 10 Benefits of Digital Payment for Business  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
13:56:39 UTC
22:56:39 KST

An invoice can be paid on time and still create work for finance. The recipient receives less than expected, or the receipt sits unmatched in the ledger. Digital business payments give finance transaction records it can use to trace transfers and match receipts to their invoices.
The convenience of digital international payments is hard to overstate, especially if your company has to manage two currencies, collecting euro revenue and paying dollar invoices. Railor can provide this convenience by combining multi-currency accounts with SEPA, SWIFT, and local payment routes for international business payments, consolidating customer receipts and supplier transfers onto a single platform.
Here is exactly what you get from digital payment platforms.
1. Faster access to usable funds
Within ten seconds, a successful euro transfer on a supported SEPA Instant route makes the money available, even outside business hours. The new balance can cover a supplier invoice holding up an order.
2. Better control of payment costs
The sending fee is only the first number in a quote. Finance can compare the total debit with the invoice amount once the exchange rate and other charges are visible, and any extra transfer needed to cover a shortfall at the supplier’s end belongs in the same calculation.
3. Fewer unnecessary currency conversions
Dollar receipts can fund dollar invoices directly from a supported currency balance. For USD 12,000 converted through euros and back, a hypothetical 0.4% charge deducted at each conversion leaves the following amounts, assuming an unchanged exchange rate and no other charges:
The round trip costs USD 95.81, which remains available for the supplier when the dollars are held without conversion.
4. Less repeated data entry
With verified beneficiary details already saved, staff update the amount and invoice reference without retyping the supplier’s account details. So, they reduce opportunities for entry errors.
5. More efficient batch payouts
A monthly run of 60 contractor payouts becomes one submission through batch upload. Individual transfer statuses keep exceptions visible while the team reviews the run together; the time saved on repeated submissions can go into resolving payments that need attention.
6. Easier invoice reconciliation
Two open invoices for EUR 2,000 each leave an amount-based match unresolved when the customer pays just one without specifying which invoice it covers. With a unique invoice reference in the transfer record, finance can identify the paid debt. This reduces investigation and makes the customer less likely to receive another reminder for an invoice already settled.
7. Stronger payment approval controls
An employee authorized to prepare business payments can leave release to a separate approver, giving an incorrect amount or changed account details another chance to be spotted before funds move.
8. Better visibility of payment status
The supplier says nothing has arrived. If the status still shows processing, finance has a starting point for tracing the transfer with support. A credit confirmation establishes receipt. With the transfer’s tracking reference attached, support has a specific transaction to investigate.
9. More convenient international collections
Local receiving details simplify international payments for business by letting an overseas customer pay through a familiar domestic route. No international wire is needed for that invoice.
10. Clearer cash planning
A EUR 20,000 available balance leaves EUR 4,000 to allocate once EUR 16,000 is committed. The planning figure is the remainder. With expected receipts shown separately, finance can schedule the next supplier run against spendable funds and avoid allocating the same money twice, even when the customer has already marked an invoice paid. A customer’s promise to pay tomorrow remains a future receipt.
Fewer repeated tasks mean finance can spend more time resolving payment exceptions as the volume of global business payments grows.

Madise gives her first speech as president in the Riigikogu  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
13:56:32 UTC
22:56:32 KST

TALLINN – Ülle Madise delivered her first speech as the President of the Republic of Estonia in the Riigikogu on Monday, after President Alar Karis handed over the office to her. BNS is publishing Ülle Madise's speech in its entirety.
Honorable Riigikogu, Presidents, Prime Minister, Ministers, constitutional officials, Your Excellencies, guests. Honorable people of Estonia!
On September 2, I spoke before you about how Estonia's greatest treasure is its people. That we must do everything possible to ensure there are many carriers of the Estonian language and culture. That Estonia should be the best place to raise children and grow old; to invent and create; to conduct science and business. That our children should be among the world's smartest, most balanced, and happiest. That the joy of life should not be lost as a family member or a worker, nor because of age or health.
Clean nature, roaring forests. The sea, lakes, rivers. Birds and animals. Plants, mushrooms, bees. Fish and dragonflies. In just a generation, our nature here will be an even greater wonder of the world than it is now! If we know how to preserve it.
Estonia is indeed one of the most pleasant places in the world to live. With mosquitoes and puddles, with good and bad skiing weather. Everyone here in Estonia must be able to feel that they themselves, as well as their lives, work, and creations, are valuable. That we can all fit here comfortably – as different as we are.
With our own interests, views, lifestyles, tastes, and mother tongues. High and pop culture, alternative culture and underground, this whole vibrant palette. Practicing for the Song and Dance Festival doesn't interfere with hip-hop or a midnight rave. And vice versa! Estonia is free, exciting, lively, developing, and diverse. Can we maintain and continue building such an Estonia? That depends on trust, hope for the future, and courage.
Perhaps we don't notice every day, or have forgotten, that in most parts of Estonia, kindness, simple work, common sense, and helping neighbors are still held in high regard. A car stuck in the snow is pulled out by a neighbor; an old person freezing at the bus stop gets a ride to where they need to go; another family's children get a ride home from practice with one's own; fresh cucumbers and tomatoes are shared with neighbors, or apples are put out for everyone to take. Let us notice this, acknowledge it, and participate in it.
In my work as the Chancellor of Justice, I unfortunately saw all too often how a person gives their best, dedicates themselves to others, but is not treated in kind. Yet they could be. They should be. For example, a mother who, by a twist of fate, is raising a child alone, works, studies for a profession so necessary for society, and volunteers where she can; yet when she herself needs help, she encounters administrative harassment and cold arrogance in her search for support. My colleagues and I in the Chancellor of Justice's office always stood against soulless proceedings. What is the point of a system where one can coldly shrug and state that 'clients did not receive the service,' instead of regretting that a child and their mother were left in distress?
Fortunately, there are those who solve problems. But do we know how to notice and recognize them? A police officer who saves the life of a child speeding on a scooter-shaped electric vehicle and hears from the parent in response... I won't even repeat it. How can anyone think that a highly trained officer leaves their family in the evening to go to work simply to harass decent people? Or a teacher who carries concern for their students in their heart, looks for opportunities for them to spread their wings, opens their computer – and there it is! No, not expressions of gratitude.
We need much more trust and warm recognition. A doctor, a journalist, a police officer, a teacher, a farmer – each of us in our profession – is a trained expert who gives their best. And trust must indeed be earned. By giving one's best. All of us, in our lives and our work.
The attempts in recent decades to re-educate people, to prescribe the one right way to live, think, feel, or speak, have resulted in a strong backlash. The lesson has been learned by all; now credibility must be restored. Especially in people with experience of the occupation, all sorts of ideological propaganda provoke contempt, which can lead even the best person to write or do things they would not otherwise even consider. And to vote simply... against everything. Eventually, resentment transforms into an election result.
Everyone has the right to vote exactly as they see fit. That is what elections are for. The main thing is not to abstain from voting altogether, not to remain silent, indifferent, or completely withdrawn from life. Indifference is the enemy of a free democratic society, as is the loss of hope for the future and mere noise. The rule of law is not sustained by laws alone, but also by trust – the knowledge that the rules apply to everyone and that people are treated fairly. Let us not allow ourselves to be turned against each other – here, in our corner of the world, with our people. There should be as few people as possible who feel – perhaps justifiably – so bad that they are ready to destroy things. We need to trust each other and build the future.
Good people! If you want peace, prepare for... you know. Peace must be maintained. Everyone can contribute to this. The first step: maintain peace of mind. There is too much fear of war in the air. When I come from a discussion about the actual security situation, assessed based on facts, my mind is always much calmer than when reading deliberate fearmongering. I know very well that politics or business is behind it. But still. Yes, the world around us is unpredictable and dangerous. Of course it is. I understand the concern, and I am concerned myself. A global crisis of trust – also true.
Ukraine must be supported in every conceivable way so that the war of aggression against Ukraine ends and a lasting, just peace arrives. So that war criminals are punished and the aggressor pays for the damages. It must be convincingly demonstrated worldwide that international law, a rules-based world order, and the protection of human rights are beneficial to the majority of countries and to all people.
Estonia has been diligently built stronger. The Defence Forces, the Defence League, the Women's Home Defence. The entire broad national defence. Dedicated neighbors in the Baltic and Nordic countries. Poland. All our allies in Europe and NATO. This is all our security. Please: let us not allow fear or hopelessness into our hearts. Fear paralyzes or incites foolishness. We must act wisely. And everyone has the opportunity to do so. I dare to affirm that the future is not dark or predetermined – we are building it ourselves. In times of turmoil, one must see one's great opportunity and skillfully seize it.
Dear listeners, we need more humor and levity. And spiritual fortitude. Culture cannot be considered something that comes after everything else. Culture sustains and carries, consoles, broadens, warns, cleanses the dark corners of the human soul, and helps us become better. Let's not miss out on domestic cultural events. Let's make them inviting and accessible to children and young people; and to those who are short on money or have difficulty moving. Let's value our writers, filmmakers and theater creators, artists, designers, museums – both new and heritage.
Let us always be interested in the way of life and culture of other nations as well. And let us be visible ourselves: exhibitions by Estonian artists around the world, our magnificent orchestras and choirs, theater performances, novels, medals in sports competitions. Scientific research and the inventions that have reached production, collaborative projects. Bold and trustworthy entrepreneurship. Technology, start-up, and deep-tech entrepreneurship, and of course, the defense industry.
But not only that! Nowadays, it is a great achievement if an entrepreneur can produce something special and very well, at a reasonable price and in an environmentally friendly way, and also deliver the products on time. Not just here in Estonia, but all over the world. Estonia's trump card is education. We know this ourselves, and so does the entire educated world. But let's strive harder to ensure that all children in Estonia have a good education and broad opportunities. This should not depend on whether a child studies in a small rural school or in the capital city's districts, whether they live with their parents, in a foster family, or in a children's home, or whether they are still learning the Estonian language. Estonia's future depends on the good education of all Estonia's children.
The leap in artificial intelligence in schools, initiated by President Alar Karis, deserves recognition and continuation. The future belongs to those who know how to use AI wisely while remaining free and skilled as human beings. This new leap must be aimed as far as possible. And always in a way that AI doesn't become 'Ouch!'. Technology must not make us forget that humans must also be able to cope on their own. Excessive dependence on technology and electricity is dangerous for everyone, everywhere. A storm or a thief is enough to land us in big trouble. Let us remain steadfast.
Estonia's Minister of Justice and Digital Affairs, Liisa Pakosta, is leading a global discussion to establish worldwide regulation for artificial intelligence. It is precisely Estonia that must take the lead. We have long experience as a digital state and a complex history. We are able to understand other nations and countries around the world, and perhaps they understand us too. The digital divide does not only run and deepen within societies, sometimes causing great poverty, pain, and resentment. It is running ever more dangerously across the world as well. Therefore, it is necessary to agree that AI must be accessible to the smaller and poorer as well. And that artificial intelligence must serve humanity, not the other way around.
For the protection of the Estonian language and culture, and of all small nations and cultures, it is necessary that they are well and correctly represented in artificial intelligence models. We are in a situation where armies of bots serving the interests of an aggressor state are teaching artificial intelligence to lie. And this lie will ultimately harm everyone. Countries that wish to remain independent and sovereign should be vitally interested in combating hostile propaganda.
The President of the Republic cannot and must not replace the popularly elected Riigikogu, nor the government or the court. The separation and balance of powers is a great value. The President has a significant role in this balancing formula. The date for the National Defence Council, as stipulated in the Constitution, has already been set. The saying 'hard in training, easy in battle' I would further develop to say that if the training is especially tough, there will be no battle. Our goal, after all, is peace.
Against a lack of ideas and homogenization, we could start right here at home with bold thoughts and dreaming. The President's Think Tank is one place for this. Searching, thinking, debating, and humor together bring out the best in people – from academics to schoolchildren. This is how new ideas are born. The President can recognize and support all who work to ensure that families have a place to live and raise children, that the birth of a child does not lead to financial hardship, and that those who want to build a home in the countryside can also get a loan.
Let a child- and family-friendly Estonia become a theme for the upcoming and all elections. Not by cornering or putting anyone on the defensive, but by cheerfully showing how things can be done very well. It's possible that we also need a 'Tiger Leap' for mental health. Yes, of course, we need more psychologists and psychiatrists, and we need to notice and account for individual differences. But we also need to get rid of unnecessary tensions that break people. Excessive, destructive competitiveness, pulling each other down, noise, bullying, injustice, loneliness, great fear and worry, hopelessness – these are not inevitable phenomena of life. Perhaps we dare to free ourselves from them. I will do my best so that we dare. Because why be unhappy and lose when it's possible to be happy and win?
The President can make more audible what is expected and hoped for in Voru and Viru counties, in Mehikoorma and Häädemeeste, on Saaremaa and Hiiumaa, in Paide and Põltsamaa, in all the places where the local community works hard to prevent life from moving away, for farms to flourish, for tourism and business in general to develop, so that there is a point in making an effort. We can only obtain the money needed to maintain our free Estonian state with a strong and adaptable economy.
Therefore, let's set people free! There is no need for a total comfort that makes people lazy and helpless. There is no need for commands, prohibitions, unnecessary bureaucracy, or supervisors everywhere that stifle creativity and entrepreneurship – the head of state can also serve as a reminder of this. If necessary, in the form of a veto.
I will take the time to meet people from different walks of life in different parts of Estonia. To listen to them, to empathize with them, to try to understand. And then to pass the word on. You will see me and my colleagues in gardens, factories, barns, corporate brainstorming corners, schools, nursing homes, village squares, hospitals, city streets, and other places where daily life happens. I'm afraid I won't make it to formal ceremonies as often as I should, so I ask for your understanding in advance. I hope to be in constant communication
with the members of the Riigikogu, the Prime Minister and ministers, the heads of constitutional institutions – understanding and respecting their roles. Here, too, what matters is trust, upholding each other's dignity, and working together for the future of Estonia, for the good of all the people here.
I have said it repeatedly and I will say it again: all previous heads of state have been in the right place at the right time, making Estonia better and greater. Thank you very much! Thank you, President Alar Karis! I would like to separately thank Mrs. Sirje Karis here. Her work for Ukrainian children alone deserves the highest recognition.
Continuing the work of my predecessors, I feel great reverence and responsibility. Dear people of Estonia! If we trust each other, value freedom and responsibility and a clear message, dare to be good people, trust in life, believe in Estonia, and maintain a hopeful outlook, then all good things are possible. Long live Estonia!

Ukraine’s Strikes on Yandex Data Centers, Explained
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
13:56:31 UTC
22:56:31 KST

A wave of attacks against the Russian internet giant Yandex has sent shockwaves across the country in recent days and caused major disruptions to daily life.
Yandex, often referred to as the “Russia’s Google,” provides a range of digital services used by millions of Russians every day. Russian-language media reported widespread outages across the company’s products over the weekend, with people unable to access certain websites and applications.
The attacks, which Kyiv says are a retaliation for Russia’s strikes against similar targets, represent a new phase in Ukraine’s air campaign against Russia. Ukraine has increasingly sought to undermine Russia’s economy by striking infrastructure vital to some of its largest businesses in recent months, but this is the first time that targeting their data centers has become part of that strategy.
What happened?
On Oct. 9, Yandex, Russia’s largest technology company, announced that two of its data centers had been struck by drones, one in the city of Sasovo southeast of Moscow and the other in the Kaluga region southwest of the capital. A third facility in the suburbs of Vladimir east of Moscow would be hit before the weekend was through.
Serious damage was reported at all three locations. In a statement posted on Friday, Yandex said that operations at its Sasovo facility were “completely halted” while part of the infrastructure in Kaluga was “disabled.” The Vladimir facility, meanwhile, was taken completely offline on Sunday, according to the company.
“Yandex teams are working around the clock to ensure our services remain operational and to help those affected by the incident,” the company said after the two initial strikes. “This is our top priority right now, but unfortunately, it’s not easy.”
The effects of the attacks were not limited to the data centers they targeted. Nine people were injured in the Kaluga region, while about 1,600 customers were left without electricity in the Vladimir region, the heads of each region said. Neither explicitly mentioned the Yandex facilities.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Oct. 8 that the attacks were retaliation for Russia’s own strikes against its data centers. Indeed, last month, Moscow struck such facilities in the Kyiv region, causing temporary internet outages for roughly 100,000 households.
Moscow claimed that the data centers it struck were used by Ukrainian military intelligence bodies.
What is Yandex?
To understand the impact these attacks are having on regular Russians’ lives, consider what would happen if Google suddenly went offline.
Gone would be access to the company’s flagship internet browser, but also to its many other essential services: maps, payment, email and its virtual workspace, to name a few.
Like Google, Yandex is a company whose tendrils have stretched to nearly every corner of the Russian technology market since its founding in the 1990s. However, in Russia, its monopoly over digital services is arguably even larger.
While apps like Yandex Maps and Yandex Pay might be expected offerings of Russia’s largest technology company for people in the West, something like the widely used taxi and food delivery app Yandex Go rolls the function of Uber and DoorDash into one. In Russia, they’re all managed by the same company.
What’s more, Yandex offers a cloud computing service that provides digital infrastructure for some of Russia’s largest companies. According to the Yandex Cloud website, the platform has more than 64,000 customers.
How disruptive are the attacks?
As with any other major player in the technology industry, data centers form the backbone of all of these operations.
Understandably, after some of them were hit, people quickly began flagging issues. Russian-language media reported over the weekend that many Yandex apps had gone down temporarily but had been restored. Others were still experiencing interruptions or complete outages on Monday.
Yandex itself urged some users to switch to alternative platforms during the outages. Taxi drivers told the exiled outlet Vyorstka that they received a notification from Yandex advising them to switch to Google Maps or Waze while the company was fixing its servers.
Separately, the websites of other companies that use Yandex’s cloud services were reportedly impacted, including grocery giant Magnit, fast-food chain Vkusno i Tochka and household appliance retailer M.Video, the Kommersant newspaper reported, citing publicly available outage data.
Yandex’s operations outside of Russia also appear to have been affected. According to The Times of Central Asia, users in Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan have reported difficulties accessing the company’s apps. Similar outages were noted in the Armenian capital Yerevan, forcing users to book their taxis with a local competitor, which was in turn strained by the surge in traffic.
Particularly disruptive for Russians was the attacks’ effect on digital financial services. Yandex is so integrated into everyday payments that when its digital wallet application, Yandex Pay, went down, it warranted its own explanation from company leadership.
“All your money is safe,” Dima Pirogov, CEO of Yandex’s FinTech Division, said in a statement posted to the company’s social media platforms on Sunday. “The money itself isn’t stored in the data center. That’s where the servers that power our services are located.”
“We can’t yet give you a precise timeline for restoration,” Pirogov added, “but we promise: we won’t stop until the service is restored.”
How are officials reacting?
President Vladimir Putin has so far not commented on the attacks. That’s not unusual — Putin is rarely the first one to telegraph the Kremlin’s reaction to such developments.
Some hints have emerged, however, that the Kremlin is taking the situation seriously.
On Monday, Digital Development Minister Maksut Shadayev told a State Duma committee that his office was working with the Defense Ministry on measures to protect data centers, a sign that officials are worried about the effect of further attacks.
“The scale of the attacks — which we were all monitoring in real time — was unprecedented,” Shadayev said, adding that “the entire industry is now helping to resolve” the chaos they caused.
As two major questions vex Yandex — how to restore service completely and how to repair damaged infrastructure — the company could be grappling with the fallout from the attacks for a while.
According to a source who spoke to Kommersant, delivering replacement equipment to the damaged facilities could take as long as six months.
A Message from The Moscow Times:
Dear readers,
We are facing unprecedented challenges. Russia's Prosecutor General's Office has designated The Moscow Times as an "undesirable" organization, criminalizing our work and putting our staff at risk of prosecution. This follows our earlier unjust labeling as a "foreign agent."
These actions are direct attempts to silence independent journalism in Russia. The authorities claim our work "discredits the decisions of the Russian leadership." We see things differently: we strive to provide accurate, unbiased reporting on Russia.
We, the journalists of The Moscow Times, refuse to be silenced. But to continue our work, we need your help.
Your support, no matter how small, makes a world of difference. If you can, please support us monthly starting from just $2. It's quick to set up, and every contribution makes a significant impact.
By supporting The Moscow Times, you're defending open, independent journalism in the face of repression. Thank you for standing with us.
Remind me later.

Danish-Lithuanian drone manufacturer Monopulse raises over €2 million  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
13:56:30 UTC
22:56:30 KST

Unmanned aerial vehicle manufacturer MNP Technologijos, operating under the Monopulse brand, has raised over €2 million from investors in Lithuania and abroad. The investment will be used to expand production capacity, support research and development, and accelerate the company’s entry into the Scandinavian and other international markets.
“We operate in a dynamic defence technology sector where technologies are evolving rapidly and customers demand secure manufacturing and resilient supply chains. This investment will enable us to scale our production capacity while ensuring that our customers receive our products quickly and on schedule,” says Justas Poderys, PhD founder and CEO of Monopulse.
The lead investor in the round is early-stage venture capital fund CoInvest Capital. According to Viktorija Trimbel, managing director of the fund, Monopulse is already successfully operating in NATO markets, with its products being integrated into air defence and critical infrastructure protection systems.
“We invest first and foremost in teams, and the Monopulse team brings together a rare combination of deep engineering expertise and a strong understanding of what the military needs today. The company’s products also have clear civilian applications, so we believe that within the next few years, Monopulse could become an integral part of Europe’s defence supply chain – a company that allies turn to not because it is Lithuanian, but because it is the best,” says V. Trimbel.
Monopulse is currently pursuing strategic expansion into the Scandinavian market, while the new investment will enable the company to accelerate its entry into additional markets, including Germany, France and the Netherlands.
A further €560,000 was invested in Monopulse by business angel syndicate NGL Ventures together with 68 individual business angels. This is the largest syndicate in NGL Ventures’ history, driven by two years of successful cooperation with the company.
“What convinced us most was Monopulse’s commercial progress and the team’s ability to deploy capital effectively. Last year, the company more than tripled its revenue while raising a relatively small amount of external capital. Its technology is no longer just a prototype: the Falcon drones developed by Monopulse are already being used by the armed forces of several NATO countries. More importantly, the team continues to develop new products and has a growing pipeline of orders,” says Justinas Pašys, founder and CEO of NGL Ventures.
Other investors participating in the round include a group of angels from the Lithuanian Business Angel Network (LitBAN) and Plug and Play Ventures, an international venture capital firm and innovation platform headquartered in Silicon Valley, United States.
Monopulse develops and manufactures Falcon MK3S unmanned aircraft designed for surveillance and reconnaissance missions. The aircraft belong to NATO Class I (Mini) category and are equipped with multiple cameras, including night vision capabilities. Advanced communication systems ensure that operators can maintain control of the aircraft even in the event of GPS signal interference. The company is also developing the HydroHex unmanned platform, which can not only fly but also operate on the surface of the water.
Critical components used in Monopulse products are manufactured exclusively in countries friendly to Lithuania, ensuring the security and resilience of the company’s supply chain. Monopulse designs and manufactures all major components in-house, from the camera to the flight control computer.

Endover remains the turnover leader in Tallinn’s growing new-build market in 2026  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
13:56:27 UTC
22:56:27 KST

According to Citify statistics, Tallinn’s new-build market has been 7% more active over the first three quarters of this year than last year. Endover leads the developers in sales turnover and sees a growing trend in the capital of people moving from private houses into large apartments.
In terms of turnover, Endover is the leader of Tallinn’s new-build market over the nine-month period: turnover from new sales reached €35.8 million, and the average price per square metre sold by the company exceeded €6,000. Among Endover’s clients, the average apartment purchase was over €400,000.
Across the market as a whole, the average price per square metre has risen by 6% year on year and the average transaction value by as much as 11%, showing that buyers are choosing larger and more expensive homes than before. Comparing districts, 232 new-build sales worth €86 million were made in Põhja-Tallinn this year, at an average price of €5,518 per square metre. In Kesklinn, 220 homes were sold for a total of €89 million, at an average price of €5,955 per square metre.
Sales have picked up particularly strongly in the Volta Quarter in Põhja-Tallinn, which has been Tallinn’s most popular new development for the fourth year running. Volta SKAI, the area’s only new high-rise, which has just reached its full height, has brought extra-large apartments of more than 150 square metres to the market.
Buyers are trading private houses for spacious apartments
According to Annika Saar, Head of Sales at Endover, more and more buyers are moving from a private house to an apartment and looking for distinctive solutions designed as a complete living environment, where everything needed for daily life is close at hand, the home quarter is green and private, the building offers added value such as a rooftop terrace or storage for sports equipment, and the apartment is spacious with a functional layout. “In new developments that meet today’s expectations, buyers are confident enough to join the purchase process as early as the initial construction phase, so that, together with the developer and the architect, they can shape a solution that matches their own vision,” Saar said.
Over the past year, the market for apartments costing a million euros or more has grown along with other segments. The largest percentage jump in the entire market, 300%, has been in transactions above €1.5 million. Apartment deals above €2.5 million, meanwhile, are an entirely new segment in Estonian statistics. The largest known new-build transactions on the Tallinn market in 2025 and 2026 were apartment purchases in the Volta SKAI development worth €2.5 million and almost €4 million respectively.
Investors remain active
Today, homebuyers make up 70% of Endover’s client base and real estate investors 30%. For the latter, both long-term placement of funds and yield-driven investments are on the agenda. “Our homebuyers today prefer larger, three-room apartments in a modern environment. Investors are heading in a similar direction: what matters to them is an area with potential and the quality of the development.”
According to Saar, the company forecasts a steady rise in the price per square metre going forward. Based on these forecasts and sales volumes to date, it makes perfect sense for the company to build apartments at today’s construction prices with future buyers in mind as well.
Endover will soon be bringing a new project to the market in the heart of the city, aimed at both investors and homebuyers. Work is also continuing on the next developments in the Volta Quarter, where a new phase of the Volta HUB building, with commercial space and apartments, is getting under way.
Endover is an Estonian real estate developer with more than 25 years of experience, creating value for the urban space and building comprehensive residential and business environments. The company’s portfolio includes 70 buildings and 2,840 apartments with a total area of 368,000 m².

Karis: The wisdom of the nation is to adapt to every situation, hardship, and crisis  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
13:56:26 UTC
22:56:26 KST

TALLINN - President Alar Karis delivered a speech in the Riigikogu on Monday at the inauguration of Ülle Madise as president, in which he noted that the wisdom of the Estonian people is to adapt in every situation, hardship, and crisis. BNS is publishing the speech in full.
Five years ago, right here in the Riigikogu, I promised to protect the Constitution, the internal and external peace written in its preamble, and to listen and observe patiently. I spoke of a nation that copes. A nation that is not afraid of encountering the unknown.
There have been unexpectedly many of these encounters in recent years. The pandemic, war, inflation, the climate and energy crisis. And finally, the aggressive development of new technology, of artificial intelligence.
Not one of these challenges began in Estonia; the crises have come to us from further away. And as a small country, we are even more affected by them compared to larger ones.
We have had to learn to know these unknowns and, when necessary, change our thinking and behavior. But we have adapted and managed.
What is the president's role in this multitude of crises?
The president's job is to notice. To know how to listen. To unite instead of divide. To seek balance. To preserve diversity. To stand for internal and external peace. At least, that is how I understand this office.
It is easy to talk with friends, but one must also communicate with those whose understanding differs from our own. It is simple to read from talking points, but one must think and act for oneself, based on local circumstances.
It is impressive and memorable to be bold and combative in words, but what is important is achieving results. It is pleasant to listen to the sound of one's own voice, but that is not how one becomes wise.
While in maintaining external peace we can also rely on soft diplomacy and on our friends and allies - especially those closest to us, the Nordic and Baltic countries - in maintaining internal peace, we have no one to rely on but ourselves.
Internal peace begins with trust and cohesion. With the state's attitude. With understandable laws. With avoiding over-regulation. With the responsibility of the lawmaker, the ability to think not only of their votes but of the broader impact of the law. Of the combined effect of laws.
Colliding with ever-new crises, the daily squabbles between politicians, and the constant need for attention and the attention economy characteristic of a fleeting society have heated up the social temperature - the ability to read critically and, if necessary, to disagree has diminished.
Soon we will have election debates that focus on highlighting the opposition between participants. Afterwards, experts will assess who managed to put the other down more skillfully.
But what might be the impact on the activities of our elected bodies if we started to reward cooperation more, valuing the effective passes that lead to the "goals" alongside the goals themselves?
Our discussion culture needs culture. Otherwise, society's mental health will suffer, and self-censorship characteristic of an era of silence will emerge.
Dear friends, I have been asked many times, especially in the last week, what good things I will take with me from these five years?
I have answered that I take with me a firm conviction, the knowledge of the Estonian people's ability to cope. The skill to adapt to hardships and crises. It is precisely in the ability to manage in any situation that the wisdom of the Estonian people lies. This is our cleverness, our substance, our guarantee of survival.
The joy and knowledge of a free country, an excellent living environment, a good education, and a safe home outweigh the difficulties and make us act and decide every day. I also wish for greater courage in decision-making for politicians and officials than before. Otherwise, things will not move forward, and problems will accumulate.
An aging and shrinking Estonia, and Europe as a whole, needs new moves. Bold decisions, smart solutions, the courage to take risks. To change decisions when necessary. To listen to and trust the younger generation.
The advantage of a small country is the ability to be flexible. Renewing education and the economy will give Estonia additional momentum. Implementing new technologies, increasing productivity, expanding in foreign markets, and using the advantages and experiences of Estonia as a digital nation.
In short, focusing on the brain economy, whether it be real or artificial.
Alongside security, artificial intelligence has become one of the most central topics in the world. There are three options - to ignore, to ban, or to adapt.
I do not believe in bans. It is not possible to limit development, but it must be guided, a balance must be found. To offer a safe environment, to make technology work for the benefit of people.
Artificial intelligence has arrived as a great unknown, and Estonia is setting an example of how to cope with it. An idea born at a meeting with unicorns in Kadriorg has today, with the support of schools and the Ministry of Education and Research, grown into a nationwide educational reform that solidifies Estonia's position as a digital nation, attracts attention and interest, and opens doors for us even in the most remote corners.
And most importantly - it gives young people a future-proof education.
I will continue to engage with artificial intelligence from an educational perspective - as the patron of TI-Hüpe and as a member of the UN's global "AI for Good" commission.
As president, I will continue to stand for curiosity and knowledge-based approaches, for diversity and distinctiveness, for internal and external peace, and for the preservation of freedoms and balance.
I thank my advisers, the head and staff of the Office of the President, and all the people with whom, through common work and harmony, the last five years were made possible.
And, of course, my wife Sirje, without whom none of this would have been possible and who took the lead in helping Ukrainian children and advocating for the mental health of young people.
Dear President-elect Ülle Madise, the office of the Head of State of Estonia is a great honor and an even greater responsibility.
I wish you the skill to pay attention, to notice, to ask the right questions, and to find time for contemplation as well.
But especially - to remain yourself. Not to be afraid of encountering the unknown. Strength, wisdom, and a steady mind in holding this office.
I thank you!

Given our geographical proximity to Russia, its ongoing war and its active support for Ukraine, our region understands and feels these threats acutely. This also means we have a responsibility to help shape Europe's security architecture, not individually, but together and in solidarity," Sinkevicius said.
Lithuania will hold the presidency of the Council of the European Union in the first half of 2027, while Norway will take over the chairmanship of the Nordic-Baltic Eight (NB8) next year.

Ivar Vendelin opens DAO, a new Asian buffet restaurant, at Ülemiste Centre  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
13:56:23 UTC
22:56:23 KST

In early November, Estonia’s first Asian buffet restaurant, DAO, opens its doors at Ülemiste Centre, offering more than 100 dishes from a range of Asian cuisines for one fixed price. The restaurant is led by versatile entrepreneur Ivar Vendelin, who aims to expand into the other Baltic states as well.
The Asian buffet restaurant DAO will open on the second floor of Ülemiste Centre near Apollo Kino, occupying more than 800 m². The concept takes its cue from the grand buffet restaurants of Las Vegas, where a wide choice of food goes hand in hand with luxurious interiors and a complete dining experience.
According to DAO’s sole owner Ivar Vendelin, the aim in creating the new concept was to take the best features of buffet restaurants and move the experience a step beyond the usual buffet. “Asian cuisine is incredibly broad, and that is exactly what we want to show with DAO. Usually, a guest picks one cuisine in a restaurant and sticks to a single dish, but here they can try sushi, Indian curry, Korean flavours, wok dishes and teppanyaki over the course of one evening – all of Asia on one plate at once. We want to offer a Las Vegas-style buffet experience at a price that lets people come to DAO regularly, not just on special occasions,” said the experienced restaurateur.
In this way, DAO brings a Las Vegas-inspired concept to Estonian diners in a more affordable format: for one fixed price, guests can freely choose and sample dozens of different Asian dishes on an all-you-can-eat basis. The menu of more than 100 dishes ranges from Japanese, Chinese and Korean cuisine to the flavours of India, Thailand and Vietnam and dishes from Southeast Asia. There is sushi and sashimi, dim sum, curries, naan, wok dishes and much more, all rounded off by a wide selection of desserts and a chocolate fountain.
The kitchen is staffed by chefs specialising in Asian cuisine, and some dishes are prepared right in front of guests. In the Live Wok area, everyone can put together their own dish, and in the evenings and at weekends it is joined by Live Teppanyaki, where chefs grill each guest’s chosen ingredients to order. At lunchtime, DAO offers a more compact selection at a lunch price, while in the evenings and at weekends the buffet expands with more special dishes and premium ingredients.
According to Guido Pärnits, Director of Ülemiste Center, DAO complements the centre’s restaurant and entertainment offering with a concept the market is clearly asking for. “People increasingly expect a shopping mall to give them reasons to come beyond their usual shopping trip, and food, entertainment and time spent together play an ever greater part in that. DAO is an excellent addition to the centre because it creates a compelling evening destination next to Apollo Kino and complements Ülemiste’s already strong restaurant line-up with a clearly distinctive concept,” said the director of center.
Time spent with loved ones guided the design of the restaurant: a carefully considered interior, open kitchen areas and a separate bar create a space where people come not only to eat but also to linger.
DAO’s CEO Kristi Saluste also stresses that the restaurant has to work equally well for a weekday lunch and for a longer evening visit. “At lunchtime, you can eat quickly and easily at DAO, while in the evening you can slow down and enjoy the whole experience: trying different dishes, watching teppanyaki and wok dishes being prepared and discovering new flavours with friends. Drinks from the cocktail bar and a relaxed atmosphere complete the experience. We want people to come to DAO to spend the evening, not just to eat,” said Saluste.
The Ülemiste restaurant is DAO’s first step: the concept was designed from the outset with expansion into other markets in mind. The company’s ambition is to grow DAO into a restaurant chain present both in Estonia and in the other Baltic states.
DAO’s first restaurant opens its doors on the second floor of Ülemiste Centre in early November 2026, right next to Apollo Kino.

VILNIUS - A deal between US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin on diesel exports weakens the West's position, although it is not the worst development of the past two years, Lithuanian Foreign Minister Kestutis Budrys said.
"This latest episode is not the worst we have seen in nearly two years. Trump announced on Friday that he had reached an agreement with Putin on supplying large quantities of diesel in exchange for a temporary easing of US sanctions. The announcement drew criticism from Ukraine, the European Union and some US lawmakers. Budrys said US decisions could be influenced not only by efforts to end the war but also by domestic political factors, including high energy prices.
The minister also warned that one of Europe's biggest challenges next year would be securing funding for Ukraine. He said bilateral support from European Union member states was currently at its lowest level since 2022, even as Ukraine's defence needs were growing and infrastructure destruction continued.
Budrys stressed that Lithuania would honour its commitments to Ukraine and said the European Union's financial support scheme should not prompt other countries to reduce their bilateral aid. However, he noted that maintaining European countries' attention and support would be difficult.
Asked about the potential impact of the agreement on diesel prices and the entry of Russian diesel into the European Union market, Budrys said he did not expect a significant effect on prices or the bloc's position. He stressed that Lithuania would seek to ensure the agreement did not undermine the European Union's sanctions policy.

Hurricane Simon crawls along Mexico's Pacific coast, bringing floods and evacuations
MANZANILLO, Mexico, Oct 12 - Hurricane Simon crept northwest just off Mexico's Pacific coast early on Monday, lashing western states with dangerous winds, heavy rain and flooding that put riverside communities on alert for possible evacuations.
The US National Hurricane Center said Simon was about 50 miles (80 km) west-southwest of Cabo Corrientes in Jalisco state at 5 a.m. local time (1200 GMT), packing maximum sustained winds of 115 mph (185 kph), making it a Category 3 hurricane.
The hurricane was moving northwest at just 2 mph (4 kph) and was expected to continue along that track before turning northeast and moving inland across west-central Mexico around midweek.
Authorities said that Simon could bring life-threatening flooding and mudslides to parts of the Pacific coast and nearby mountains.
The hurricane is forecast to dump an additional 2 to 4 inches (5 to 10 cm) of rain across coastal areas of southwest and west-central Mexico, with isolated amounts of 6 to 8 inches (15 to 20 cm) in parts of Jalisco and Sinaloa. The National Hurricane Center said isolated storm totals could reach 30 inches (76 cm) in parts of Michoacan, Colima and Jalisco.
In the town of Cihuatlan, in Jalisco near the border with Colima, rising water levels in the Marabasco River prompted patrols by the Mexican Army, Civil Protection officials and the Red Cross. Floodwater inundated streets and low-lying areas of the town overnight.
In the port city of Manzanillo, in Colima state, residents waded through flooded homes and streets as navy personnel helped remove water.
"Everything got flooded," said resident Maria Elena Vazquez from inside her home, pants rolled up as the water came up to her ankles.
The National Hurricane Center said that a dangerous storm surge is expected near and east of where Simon approaches the coast, accompanied by large destructive waves. Swells from the hurricane are also forecast to create life-threatening surf and rip current conditions along southwestern and west-central Mexico over the next few days.
Simon had weakened from a stronger Category 4 system, but forecasters said it is likely to remain a hurricane through midweek before rapidly losing strength after moving inland over Mexico's mountainous terrain. REUTERS

UN refugee chief stresses need for protection, warns against making displacement permanent
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
13:54:48 UTC
22:54:48 KST

Beyza Binnur Donmez
12 October 2026•Update: 12 October 2026
The UN High Commissioner for Refugees warned Monday that protecting people forced to flee is essential, but displacement must not become permanent, as prolonged conflicts and shrinking humanitarian resources deepen the global refugee crisis.
Addressing the UNHCR Executive Committee in Geneva, Barham Salih said more than 117 million people have been forcibly displaced worldwide by conflict, violence, persecution, and other threats.
"We must protect people when they are forced to flee. But we cannot accept indefinite displacement as their future," he said.
Salih warned that conflicts are producing displacement faster than they can be resolved, leaving millions trapped in prolonged crises.
He stressed that humanitarian assistance alone cannot provide lasting solutions, calling for greater investment in conflict prevention, diplomacy, and opportunities for refugees to rebuild their lives.
"Success must also mean people recovering agency: being able to work, to learn, to support their families, and to make the choices about their future," he said. "We must measure success not only by the lives we save, but by the lives people are able to rebuild, and the lasting solutions they can find."
Turning to education, Salih said 5.8 million refugee children remain out of school, highlighting persistent barriers to educational opportunities.
He announced plans to launch the "Aiming Higher" initiative, aimed at expanding refugee students' access to university degrees and other higher education qualifications through cooperation with governments, universities, and the private sector.
Meanwhile, the UNHCR faces a severe funding crisis, having secured only $3 billion, or 35%, of its $8.5 billion requirements for 2026 as of Oct. 9, according to the agency's chief.
The agency's workforce has also fallen from nearly 20,000 to under 12,000 since 2024, with nearly 8,000 employees leaving amid major restructuring.
Salih warned that shrinking resources are threatening essential protection services, stressing that efficiency measures cannot compensate indefinitely for declining funding.
"Protection has a floor. Below it, the system does not simply become smaller. The protection we can provide begins to fail," he said.

Cyber-attack similar to OpenAI Medicare breach seems likely in UK, says minister
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
13:52:55 UTC
22:52:55 KST

An AI-driven cyber-attack similar to the OpenAI breach of Australia’s healthcare system is likely, “if not inevitable”, in the UK, according to a senior minister.
Kanishka Narayan, the UK AI minister, indicated that the British government’s own cyber defences would be bypassed by a technology that has developed highly sophisticated skills in cybersecurity.
In a speech Narayan said an incident in June when an OpenAI agent – a computer program acting autonomously – infiltrated Medicare, Australia’s universal healthcare system, could be repeated in the UK.
“It concerns me,” he said. “It seems likely, if not inevitable, that our own cyber defences will be breached.”
Narayan said the agent’s task was “benign” as it searched for information about public spending on medicines, but it nonetheless went after data that it was not authorised to have.
“The Australian government has said that no personal medical records are known to have been accessed, and there is no evidence of wider compromise, but the incident should concern us,” he said.
Speaking at a science and tech hub at Imperial College London, Narayan said the security minister, Dan Jarvis, would lead a government programme to strengthen against cyber-attacks, including from AI. The government will also consider using the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill as a vehicle for introducing AI safety regulations, including making it mandatory to report AI safety incidents.
Narayan spoke before a parliamentary hearing on AI safety on Tuesday into the issue. Senior figures from OpenAI and Anthropic will be among those giving evidence to MPs on the business, innovation, science and trade committee. They will also be joined by the head of the UK’s AI Security Institute, Henry de Zoete.
Narayan confirmed that the institute would gain access to advanced AI models before they were released, after the White House had reportedly placed restrictions on their availability.
“I can confirm that AI scientists at the AI Security Institute are now conducting rigorous evaluations of the latest generations of models, including [Google’s] Gemini … to identify risks early to test robust safeguards to help keep people safe,” he said.
The minister added that leading AI companies must “listen” to warnings of safety risks posed by their technology – and not release models if they carried a serious threat.
“And to the companies developing the world’s most powerful AI systems, my message is: listen when your scientists warn of severe dangers; investigate unexpected behaviours; and if you can’t adequately control the risks, do not release the system,” he said. “I want the labs to be honest.”
Narayan said the UK would “play its part” in coordinating an international response to AI safety by making the technology a “central focus” of Britain’s G20 presidency next year.
“We know that these challenges cannot be addressed by a single country alone, but by virtue of our capability, by virtue of the foundations of our trust, Britain will play its part,” he said.

Two NSC MPs join exodus as Keijzer triggers conference walkout
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Two former MPs for New Social Contract have resigned in protest at the party’s decision to invite right-wing independent MP Mona Keijzer to a weekend conference.
Harm Holman, NSC’s former agriculture spokesman, and Ilse Saris, who covered social affairs, said they no longer felt at home in a party that was drifting towards right-wing populism.
Saturday’s general meeting in Breda ended in chaos when the party’s entire management board resigned following a mass walkout when Keijzer stepped up onto the stage. Acting chairman Ronald de Bruin said the situation had become “untenable” after around half the delegates left the room.
Keijzer had been invited to discuss her hardline conservative movement, Project 2029, which she launched after breaking from the farmers’ party BBB earlier this year.
Holman told TV late night news show Nieuwsuur: “NSC was a reasonable centre party in terms of its policies, but it has becoming a populist party that is moving further to the right. I don’t feel at home there.”
Saris said in a parting note: “In my eyes the party has completely departed from what NSC stood for.”
Een walk-out bij het NSC-congres het moment dat @MonaKeijzer het woord neemt. Vooraf was er al veel consternatie over Keijzer als gastspreker. Het was voor @DirkGotink reden om uit de partij te stappen. Nu loopt de helft de zaal uit https://t.co/4PD2YoYwfn
— Nouschka van der Meijden (@NouschkavdM) October 10, 2026
The decision by NSC’s management board to invite Keijzer as a guest speaker prompted its last elected parliamentarian, MEP Dirk Gotink, to resign his membership.
Gotink, 45, said in a post on LinkedIn that seeking closer ties with Keijzer was “incomprehensible”, despite the NSC leadership insisting that there was no agreement to work with her.
Voters return to CDA
NSC won 20 seats in the November 2023 election, just three months after being founded by Omtzigt, who recruited many of his candidates from his old party, the Christian Democrats (CDA).
But the party’s support collapsed soon after Omtzigt joined the right-wing coalition with Geert Wilders’ far-right PVV, the right-wing liberal VVD and the BBB the following year.
Wilders blamed NSC for blocking his plans to introduce the “harshest immigration policy ever”, while Omtzigt resigned first as party leader and then as an MP, citing the toll on his health and family life.
Many of NSC’s voters reverted to the CDA at the election last October, while NSC itself was wiped out. Holman, 69, also said at the weekend that he had rejoined the Christian Democrats.
