Imagined threat: How Europe learned to manufacture enemies from Israel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
13:30:36 UTC
22:30:36 KST

The rhetoric of “existential threat” has become the dominant currency of political legitimacy in both Israel and Europe. In Israel, this rhetoric is deeply entrenched—a well-documented doctrine of “permanent war” that frames every adversary as an existential danger requiring eradication rather than negotiation or a possible settlement. In recent years, Europe appeared to have adopted the same Israeli playbook, with leaders warning of an imminent Russian attack on NATO territory despite their own intelligence agencies admitting they see no evidence of such a threat. This is not paranoia; it is a calculated rhetoric, deliberately cultivated by warmongering politicians who benefit from sustaining a permanent threat – real or imagined – whether in Israel, Europe, or anywhere else.
The most striking recent exposure of this manufactured threat came not from Moscow, but from a NATO member state on the front line. On 30th September 2026, Lithuanian Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius stated plainly after meeting NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte in Brussels: “Is there any proof, real proof intelligence services are providing, something on the table, that Russia is getting ready for something? And there is actually none.” If any country had reason to sound the alarm, it would be Lithuania due to its bordering of the Russian territory. Yet its prime minister explicitly warned against exaggeration, stating: “You can’t exaggerate and say, Oh, something is happening in the upcoming months or weeks.” When a leader of a frontline state with Russia is publicly dismissing the narrative of an imminent Russian attack, the question becomes unavoidable: who benefits from insisting otherwise?
Israel’s playbook: The doctrine of permanent war and victimhood
Israel’s use of the existential threat narrative is not a reaction to genuine peril but a deliberate strategy. To justify its open-ended military occupation, aggressive and expansionist agenda, Israeli leaders for decades played the victimhood card that it is being under constant existential threats, invoking the Holocaust and the spectre of annihilation.
Imagine how this playbook is blatantly applied, Israeli leaders, after committing a genocide and almost totally destroying Gaza, still say about dangers and threats coming from Gaza.
In both southern Syria and Lebanon, Israel occupies vast areas of both countries while still pretending to be under the threat and danger.
Israeli Army Chief of Staff Eyal Zamir has framed the current confrontation as a “decisive battle” against existential threats that emerged after 7th October, opening the door to continuous fighting that will not stop until the “imagined threat” to the security establishment disappears. David Barnea, while in power as Mossad chief, similarly re-proposed the goal of “overthrowing the Iranian regime” as an existential imperative.
This doctrine serves multiple functions. Domestically, it suppresses any discussion of political alternatives or peaceful settlements, and allows to move ahead with its expansionist agenda in the region, making war the only option on the table.
Externally, it exploits Europe’s guilt over the Holocaust to extract unconditional support for such policies, with Netanyahu claiming Israel is defending “Western civilisation” against “evil regimes.”
The result is a permanent rhetoric that legitimises aggression as self-defence and portrays Israel as a victim.
Europe follows: The Russian threat that isn’t
Over the past years, it became clearer that Europe adopted this same tactic toward Russia. In mid-September, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk told parliament that intelligence assessments suggest Russia may be preparing a drone or missile attack on NATO territory in the near future. However, he did not identify the intelligence services behind his assessment, according news reports. French President Emmanuel Macron backed Tusk’s assessment, calling the warnings “sound and well documented,” and convened an emergency meeting in Paris to discuss “the threat.”
Yet the evidence for this imminent threat is strikingly thin. A senior EU official, speaking anonymously, stated in August 2026 that “European intelligence services generally do not currently see the risk of a Russian attack on European countries, and this assessment has not changed.” The official added that regarding potential threats to NATO members, “we see nothing indicating that anything is currently being prepared.” Estonian Foreign Ministry Secretary General Jonatan Vseviov went further, criticizing what he called “panic on social media.” These official denials are not isolated remarks; they reveal a systematic effort by certain European circles to cultivate a state of enmity with Russia and to keep the narrative of an imagined threat alive on the table—not because the threat is real, but because it serves their political agenda.
Russian President Vladimir Putin has repeatedly denied any intention to attack Europe. “I want to emphasise once again: we are not preparing any military action against Europe, we have no such plans. Most importantly, there is no reason to do so.” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov also dismissed the warnings as “alarmist stories” that “of course have nothing to do with reality.”
The function of manufactured threats
Why would European leaders manufacture a threat that their own intelligence services say does not exist? The answer lies in the same functions the tactic serves in Israel, which is to advance a political agenda over any other one, domestic control, military budgets, and justification of aggressive policies.
Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico warned in September 2026 that some Western politicians are trying to provoke a direct NATO-Russia conflict after their strategy of defeating Moscow via Ukraine failed, calling it a “deadly danger.” The logic is clear: when military and political strategies fail, a new threat must be invented to justify continued militarisation and the suppression of any opposition.
Europe’s adoption of Israel’s playbook is not merely an imitation; it is a shared strategy of governance through permanent emergency. Both Israel and Europe have found that an imagined enemy is more useful than a real one. A real enemy can be negotiated with, contained, or defeated. An imagined enemy is eternal, requiring eternal vigilance, eternal militarisation, and eternal obedience.
The danger of this approach is not just that it manufactures war. It also manufactures the conditions for the erosion of democracy. When every critic becomes a potential traitor and every question becomes a security threat, the space for genuine political debate collapses. The playbook that Israel perfected in its treatment of Palestinians — dehumanisation, permanent emergency, and the criminalisation of dissent — is now being applied to Europe’s relationship with Russia. A stark example on this imitation was documented in early October when Belgian Defense Minister Theo Francken publicly claimed that Russian drones had been detected over Belgian military barracks, presenting it as proof of Russia’s hostile intentions. However, the Belgian public broadcaster VRT investigated and found that the drones never existed. The report revealed that Francken had invented the threats to obtain additional budget funds for his ministry.
While a genuine conflict and dispute do exist between Europe and Russia, Moscow has consistently called for dialogue to resolve their differences. It did so in the context of the war in Ukraine, only to find that Zelensky was provoked – or perhaps even ordered – to reject a negotiated settlement and to continue his endless war with Russia. This serves the interests of some European circles and leaders who persist in portraying an imagined Russian threat, revealing themselves as warmongers as their Israeli counterparts; more committed to prolonging the conflict than to seeking its settlement.

Education ministry wants schools to teach more local dialects
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
13:30:00 UTC
22:30:00 KST

Education ministry wants schools to teach more local dialects
The Ministry of Education wants to make it easier to study regional varieties of Estonian in schools. Students would be able to replace their second foreign language classes with lessons in a regional variety of Estonian.
According to the Ministry of Education, regional varieties of Estonian are currently taught in around 15 to 20 general education schools in Estonia, most of them small rural schools, with just a couple of lessons a week.
However, a draft regulation has now been completed that would significantly expand opportunities to study regional varieties of Estonian starting next school year. Under the proposal, parents would have the right to request such instruction from a school if at least 10 children want to learn their local language variety. Parents at schools that already offer such instruction would not need to submit new requests.
Under the proposal, local language and culture could be studied as an elective. It would also give regional varieties of Estonian equal status with foreign languages in the curriculum, allowing students to study them more extensively as their second foreign language. The specific conditions would be established after the legislation is adopted.
Minister of Education Kristina Kallas told ERR that the change is necessary because children whose native language is Russian or Ukrainian, for example, already have the right to request two hours of instruction a week in their native language, while children who speak Võru, Setu or Mulgi at home do not have the same right.
"In the interests of children's linguistic development and the development of Estonian culture, we need to ensure equal rights so that Setu, Võru and other regional language varieties have similar rights within the education system," Kallas said.
The explanatory memorandum accompanying the draft legislation states that the change was initiated primarily by speakers of South Estonian regional varieties as the protection afforded to regional varieties of Estonian under the Language Act has proved insufficient. The proposed legislation would send a clear message to society that teaching regional varieties of Estonian and local culture is valued and protected through education.
The ministry also noted that demographic changes have led to a decline in the number of small schools, with children increasingly attending larger schools in regional centers. At these schools, instruction in regional language varieties tends to get lost among other interests and activities, making it difficult for those who want to study them to have their needs recognized.
The change would therefore give parents the right to request instruction in a regional variety of Estonian without having to reach agreements that take into account the interests of all parents at the school.
Principal supports the initiative
Jaak Israel, principal of August Kitzberg High School in Viljandi County, said the initiative is worthwhile.
"Everything helps enrich our understanding of language. After all, people need to learn the basics somewhere, including where the Estonian language originated and how it developed," he said.
The school offers an elective course in Mulgi language and culture at the upper secondary level and has also applied for funding under a support program launched by the Ministry of Education this year to help schools teach local language varieties. The application round is still underway, but Israel said the school hopes to use the funding to introduce Mulgi language instruction in the lower grades, replacing one Estonian language lesson a week.
Regarding the Mulgi language elective offered at the upper secondary level, Israel said three students are currently enrolled, although enrollment has been higher in the past. In one year, however, the school ran the course with just a single student.
Kaare Lill, principal of Võru City Center School, said Võru language instruction has only a very limited presence at her school. It is offered as part of extracurricular activities for younger students, with parents able to choose one activity lesson per week from a wide range of options. A child might therefore study Võru for one trimester, robotics for another and something related to art for the third.
Regarding families' interest, Lill noted that if grandparents have not spoken Võru at home and parents themselves have not grown up in a Võru-speaking environment, they may question the point of learning it. More aware parents, however, want their children to have the opportunity. Enrollment in the Võru language club tends to be modest rather than filling up quickly.
Lill therefore believes the proposed change is both necessary and positive in helping keep the Võru language alive, although exactly how it will be implemented remains unclear.
"We may run into some difficulties because we don't have enough teachers who feel confident and have the skills to pass on the Võru language and use it in their lessons. Teachers often come to schools from all over Estonia and they don't have that background," she said.
The principal of August Kitzberg High School in Viljandi County, however, believes finding teachers will not be a problem at his school. Israel said they have an Estonian language teacher who has completed relevant courses and he welcomed the idea of offering Mulgi as a second foreign language.
Israel believes that greater coverage of the issue could also increase parental interest, adding that there is certainly already a group of families interested in the opportunity. However, the change would also need to be accompanied by adequate funding.
Schools to receive support for teaching dialects
According to Kristina Kallas, the change concerns the possibility of teaching regional varieties of Estonian in basic schools. Although upper secondary schools would not be subject to the same requirement, they would still have the option of offering such instruction, as they do with other foreign languages.
"We know that Setomaa High School, for example, already offers Setu language instruction. But this is limited to regions where these language varieties are spoken. Foreign language instruction can be offered uniformly across Estonia, while the teaching of regional language varieties is limited to the areas where they are used," Kallas explained.
To help ensure there are enough teachers, a support program for teaching regional varieties of Estonian is available to fund the publication of textbooks and the development of teaching materials.
Under the draft legislation, responsibility for coordinating the teaching of regional varieties of Estonian and supporting schools would be transferred to the Institute of the Estonian Language, so that individual schools would not have to deal separately with issues such as teaching materials and teacher training.
Instruction in regional varieties of Estonian should not increase students' workloads. However, if a school has no room in its existing timetable, it would be allowed to increase the maximum permitted weekly workload for students by one lesson.
The change would primarily affect schools in the historical areas where the Võru, Setu, Mulgi, Tartu, Saare, Kihnu, Muhu, Hiiu, Kodavere, Kuusalu, Lüganuse and Jõhvi varieties of Estonian are spoken. There are approximately 155 basic schools in these regions.
The requirement would apply only to schools located in areas where distinct regional varieties of Estonian have historically developed.
According to the latest census, 23 percent of people aged 65 and older speak a regional variety of Estonian, compared with just 3 percent of children aged 14 and younger. In total, approximately 160,000 people in Estonia speak a regional variety of the language.
The Ministry of Education has sent the draft amendments to the Basic Schools and Upper Secondary Schools Act to stakeholders for feedback. Under the current plan, the changes would take effect as early as next school year.

‘The Sixty-Year Mission’ Brings the Legacy of ‘Star Trek’ to a New Generation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
13:30:00 UTC
22:30:00 KST

William Shatner wasn’t sure if the audience would approve of his new documentary or not.
When the 95-year-old star took the stage at the Regal Times Square theater for the New York premiere of The Sixty-Year Mission: How Star Trek Changed Television and the World he said “maybe you’ll like it, maybe you won’t.” But, the Captain Kirk actor declared, “you’re going to see a lovely film made by people who cared.”
Focusing on the original Star Trek series, which ran from 1966 to 1969, The Sixty-Year Mission is written and directed by Mark A. Altman, creator of the Inglorious Treksperts podcast. The documentary, which screened during New York Comic Con and hit select theaters this weekend, explores the show’s cultural impact and legacy, and also demonstrates how much it was a product of the political climate of the era in which it was made.
“I think audiences are pleasantly surprised that Sixty-Year Mission shows how the ‘60s shaped Star Trek,” Altman explains. For the film, Altman interviewed dozens of prominent fans and stars, from Shatner and Simon Pegg to Star Trek: The Next Generation stars Jonathan Frakes and Brent Spiner. The president’s niece—and Trek fan—Mary L. Trump praises the show’s pioneering representation, specifically Nichelle Nichols’ Lieutenant Uhura. George Takei, who played Sulu, gives a harrowing account of his time in an internment camp for Japanese Americans during World War II. Others discuss how characters like Spock became heroes for queer fans.
As has been well-documented, these considerations were important for Gene Roddenberry, the show’s creator, who died in 1991. He was a WWII veteran with a progressive bent despite years spent in traditionally conservative spaces like the US Army and the Los Angeles Police Department. Altman insists that “Captain Kirk was ‘JFK: Space Captain,’” and that President Kennedy’s idea of a New Frontier was the final frontier that Trek sought to explore.
Shatner, however, didn’t initially see the show that way at all. “I didn't think in those terms when they offered me the role,” says Shatner, who served as executive producer on Sixty-Year Mission. “I thought, ‘I got a regular paid job.’ Only later did the magic of Star Trek happen.”
Part of that magic, Shatner adds, is how “Star Trek had an effect on people’s lives.” Those people come from many backgrounds, and the show remained accessible because of the very special tension that existed within its politics, Altman explains. “Roddenberry was liberal on social issues but hard-nosed on defense, and that is absolutely what Star Trek is,” he says. “We need our phasers to defeat the Klingons, but we believe in a diverse crew.”
Karim Diané, who plays Jay-Den Kraag on Star Trek: Starfleet Academy, notes that as the person playing the first openly gay Klingon character in the franchise, he’s playing someone who means a lot to viewers. “I wish I could release the DMs because the love I've gotten is overwhelming,” Diané says.
Trek even had a point of view on AI that feels incredibly relevant in 2026 as Trump and Silicon Valley leaders talk about a new era of “superintelligence.” The franchise’s most recognizable AI—the android Data from Next Generation—was an ideal version of the technology. In that series Data consistently struggled to be understood, as both smarter than humans and incapable of emotional intelligence. One episode, “The Measure of a Man,” even addressed whether Data was his own being or merely property.
For Spiner, who played Data, AI’s modern incarnation is far from the thoughtful machine he portrayed. “If only AI could be what Data was: responsible, truly concerned about humanity, considering what serves humans best as opposed to what serves profit best,” he says.

Ukraine expects the EU to open new clusters on October 13 following the law on national minorities

Andrii Sybiha said that the EU could open clusters 2 and 3 on Ukraine’s accession on October 13 following the adoption of the law on the rights of national minorities.
Ukraine expects two negotiation clusters on EU accession to be opened as early as Tuesday, October 13, following Parliament's adoption of the law on national minorities sought by Hungary. This was stated by Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha after meeting with Hungarian Foreign Minister Anita Orbán and thanking the "Hungarian side for its constructive approach," UNN writes.
Details
"Today in Luxembourg, on the sidelines of the meeting of the EU Foreign Affairs Council, I had a very substantive meeting with my Hungarian counterpart, Anita Orbán. We discussed the most pressing issues on our bilateral and European agendas, exchanged views, and agreed on the next steps. We congratulated each other on the successful implementation of our bilateral agreements," Sybiha wrote.

"Today, the Ukrainian Parliament adopted amendments to education legislation to ensure the rights of European national minorities in Ukraine in this area, in line with the EU's best practices. This was done in accordance with Ukraine's commitments under Cluster 1. Therefore, we are fulfilling them," the Ukrainian minister stated.
Ukraine expects two negotiation clusters to be opened as early as tomorrow, October 13.
"Tomorrow, we expect the EU to officially decide to open Cluster 2, 'Internal Market,' and Cluster 3, 'Competitiveness and Inclusive Growth.' I thanked the Hungarian side for its constructive position on this issue," Sybiha noted.
"I will never tire of repeating this: there is no better way to guarantee the rights and security of Hungary's national minority in Ukraine than to bring Ukraine into the EU as soon as possible. Likewise, there is no better way to bring peace closer to Europe than Ukraine's accession to the EU," he continued.

"We also discussed the agenda of the upcoming European Council meeting and EU decisions aimed at stopping the aggressor, forcing it to change its calculations of terror, and bringing it to the negotiating table to achieve lasting peace," the minister said.
"The Ukrainian-Hungarian dialogue is growing stronger, based on mutual respect, good-neighborly relations, and a shared European future in the interests of our peoples," Sybiha emphasized.
Context
On October 12, the Verkhovna Rada adopted in its entirety a bill on ensuring the educational rights of the indigenous peoples of Ukraine and persons belonging to the national minorities (communities) of Ukraine. This is one of Ukraine's steps on the path to EU accession.
Previously, on October 7, EU ambassadors paved the way for the launch of accession negotiations with Ukraine and Moldova concerning the single market and competitiveness. Budapest lifted its veto on the negotiations. Hungary had blocked this step since the summer, demanding that Ukraine adopt legislation concerning the educational rights of national minorities.
Now another EU enlargement "Super Tuesday" is expected on October 13. The European Union plans to hold a series of intergovernmental conferences to advance accession negotiations, including with Ukraine. Approval of the two clusters is expected following the vote in the Verkhovna Rada on national minorities.

The Mystery of Kyrgyzstan’s Newly Launched Satellite(s)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
13:29:00 UTC
22:29:00 KST

On October 1, Kyrgyzstan reportedly joined Central Asia’s other spacefaring nations, successfully launching a domestically designed and produced nanosatellite aboard a SpaceX rocket from Vandenberg Space Force Base in California
According to Kyrgyzstan’s government, the unnamed, loaf-of-bread-sized spacecraft weighs 5 kilograms, cost around $130,0000, was equipped with high-resolution cameras, and was — nearly exclusively — the product of domestic innovation.
The satellite was assembled by two local companies, Kyrgyz Asman and Kyrgyz Electronics, Bishkek stated. The latter company’s director Ilya Cherny did admit that the technology behind the satellite was largely Russian, but pointed out that the team behind its production consisted of 10 homegrown engineers.
The government also said the satellite would help advance Kyrgyzstan’s top agricultural, environmental, and strategic priorities over its purported 15-year lifespan.
In a statement published on September 24, the country’s Ministry of Water Resources, Agriculture and Processing Industry stated the satellite’s data would track crop conditions, detect early signs of drought, and monitor glaciers.
Speaking from California on launch day, Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov said that the country had previously had to pay to obtain this kind of data from other countries, no matter whether it was “information on 100 hectares, 1,000 hectares, or the weather.”
Japarov suggested that the satellite would allow “every square meter” of Kyrgyzstan’s land to be studied to determine its potential arability, while touting the launch as an achievement in national self-sufficiency.
“We did not have our own satellite before… now we will no longer be dependent on [other countries],” Japarov added. “We will control it ourselves 100 percent from Bishkek.”
Cosmically Large Scandal
At first glance, the story of Kyrgyzstan’s satellite launch seemed like a genuine achievement. The country had joined Kazakhstan, Turkmenistan, and – as of this August – Uzbekistan in the ranks of Central Asia’s spacefarers, largely thanks to its own ingenuity.
The success had been extensively covered in domestic, regional, and international media. And then came a confusing development.
On October 2, the day after launch, news reports began to include a previously unmentioned detail: the satellite was a joint effort between Kyrgyzstan and the United Arab Emirates.
Three days later, a Kyrgyz news site published a notice that Kyrgyzstan had established a new space monitoring center to receive, process, and utilize data transmitted from the newly launched Altair satellite.
This was striking for two reasons. First, the name “Altair” had been missing from earlier government press releases. Second – and more importantly – it said the monitoring center would be “provided” data coming from the “UAE-operated” satellite by a body called the Abu Dhabi Maritime Academy.
Suddenly, Japarov’s claims that Kyrgyzstan would be “no longer dependent” on other countries began to ring hollow.
Not only had Russian technology supposedly been used to design the satellite, but the UAE was apparently going to operate the craft, with Kyrgyzstan merely receiving “access” to its data.
It also didn’t help that Gulf-focused news sites were calling Altair the “first satellite developed and built by UAE engineers,” without even mentioning Bishkek’s involvement in the project.
What, then, had happened on October 1? Had Kyrgyzstan really launched a satellite of its own making? If so, in what ways were other countries involved? And if the craft launched from California was primarily an Emirati initiative, would Bishkek walk back its claims of national self-sufficiency?
A Second Satellite?
So far, none of the above questions have been definitively answered. And the matter, described by one prominent regional commentator as a “scandal of cosmic proportions,” has prompted a growing number of increasingly conspiratorial explanations.
Local news outlet Kaktus Media, for example, suggested that two satellites were likely launched on October 1, one developed by the UAE and one with Russian assistance. (It also noted that Kyrgyzstan’s first satellite initiative, launched in 2019 by a team of all-female engineers, seemed not to be involved, having been wound down previously with no details about the project’s completion.)
Tandyr Media, meanwhile, an independent media outlet known for its popular YouTube channel, drew attention in its video covering the launch to a series of Threads posts by an individual named Dima Balakirev, who claimed to have been personally involved in the satellite project’s development.
In his post, Balakirev appeared to depict himself standing next to a different — much larger — satellite than had been shown in the government’s earlier press releases. Incidentally, the photo also clearly showed a line of text reading “Made in UAE” on one side of the satellite.
According to Balakirev, the spacecraft was a joint project with the UAE, entirely funded “by grants and the Abu Dhabi government,” and was an Earth Remote Sensing satellite – that is, likely the satellite that Japarov was referring to when he was talking about Kyrgyzstan’s newfound capacity to survey itself from above. (Subsequent reporting from government-affiliated sources mentioning the Altair satellite likewise suggested that its data would be used in agricultural planning, water resource management, and environmental monitoring.)
Notably, when questioned by Threads users citing the government’s original (smaller) size specifications, Balakirev insisted that national news outlets had confused two different projects:
“The first is a satellite for Kyrgyzstan, which was assembled in Abu Dhabi. This is a joint project with the UAE, and the Emirates are covering the entire cost. The second is a satellite being built by the team at Kyrgyz Electronics. This is a separate project with its own objectives. The figure of 5 kg and 10–12 million soms [$114,350 – $137,200] refers specifically to this one.”
Although Balakirev’s exact title and position are unknown, as Tandyr Media pointed out, the self-described “entrepreneur and techie” appeared to have been present in California alongside Japarov, and shared Instagram stories from the event.
Bishkek, Do We Have a Problem?
Given all that, as Tandyr host Dmitriy Lozhnikov himself concluded, what is left now is a substantially muddied picture.
According to one possible version of events, Kyrgyzstan did launch its smaller, unnamed bread-loaf-sized satellite, whose function is not entirely clear, on October 1. On the same day, meanwhile, the larger, UAE-designed Altair satellite also launched from California – data from which Bishkek has confirmed it is now paying to access.
In another plausible version, proposed by emigre political scientist Aidarbek Raev, the Kyrgyz-designed nanosatellite might not have been launched at all, which would mean that reports of Kyrgyzstan’s national technological achievements have been greatly exaggerated.
The government, meanwhile, has commented little on the affair since the satellite’s supposed launch day. But in any case, it appears the country’s leadership has further cosmic ambitions.
“If there is stability and peace in our country and Central Asia, in the next five to ten years, depending on our readiness, the day will come when we launch a [telecommunications] satellite as well,” Japarov said on October 1.

Nearly half of female footballers consider early retirement over financial, mental health concerns: Report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
13:28:38 UTC
22:28:38 KST

Halis Sünnetci
12 October 2026•Update: 12 October 2026
Nearly half of professional female footballers are considering leaving the game early, citing financial difficulties and mental health concerns, according to a FIFPRO report released Monday.
The 2026 Global Employment Report, based on surveys and interviews with around 800 players worldwide, found that 49% were considering ending their careers prematurely.
Among those players, 59% cited financial reasons, while 46% pointed to psychological stress.
Despite growing revenues in women’s football, the report warned that improvements in pay and working conditions remain uneven across countries and leagues.
Average inflation-adjusted monthly club wages have tripled since 2017 to $2,601, but the median remains at $1,669, reflecting significant pay disparities.
“The professionalisation of women’s football is accelerating in some parts of the world and, as our report highlights, revenues are increasing, however, the progress and benefits are not evenly distributed among players across the world,” said FIFPRO Director of Women’s Football Alex Culvin.
“Away from the best resourced clubs, there is a recurring theme of precarity and fragile conditions,” Culvin added.
Beyond financial insecurity, the study found that 57% of players had experienced mental health difficulties, with half of those affected receiving no support from their clubs.
Employment protections also remained limited, with only 56% of surveyed players holding contracts, 47% reporting insufficient club staffing and just 13% receiving pensions.
Regional disparities were particularly pronounced, as average salaries in 10 Eastern European countries remained below national minimum wage levels despite significant increases in markets such as the US and Mexico.
In response to the findings, FIFPRO called for enforceable minimum employment standards covering salaries, facilities, staffing and healthcare, alongside mandatory psychological support.

Italian Companies on a Trade Mission to the Philippines

Ten Italian companies from the transportation, energy, water, and irrigation sectors participated in a trade mission to the Philippines, organized by the ICE Agency in collaboration with the Italian Embassy. The delegation also included SACE, SIMEST, and Cassa Depositi e Prestiti (CDP).
                                    
The mission aimed to facilitate the entry and consolidation of Italian companies in the infrastructure sector and to strengthen bilateral economic cooperation. Particular attention was given to the “Luzon Economic Corridor,” a project in which Italy is participating and which aims to promote strategic investments in infrastructure, energy, digital connectivity, and advanced manufacturing.
                                    
The first day took place at the Asian Development Bank (ADB), where the delegation met with Vice President Roberta Casali and Executive Director Ivan Faiella, who represents the group of countries that includes Italy. The program included presentations on how to collaborate with the Bank and individual meetings with experts from various sectors of intervention.
                                    
The following day, the companies were received at the Department of Finance by Minister Frederick D. Go. The meetings explored the Luzon Economic Corridor project and investment opportunities in the Philippine market.
                                    
The mission concluded with meetings between Italian companies and 23 Philippine firms. CDP, SIMEST, and SACE also outlined the Italian public financial instruments designed to support the internationalization and commercial presence of companies in the country.
                                    
The initiative followed Italy’s participation in the Asian Development Bank’s “Business Opportunity Fair” last September, as part of its growth diplomacy efforts.

François Picard is pleased to welcome Sandrine Ageorges-Skinner, author, advocate against the death penalty and member of the association "Ensemble contre la peine de mort": Together Against the Death Penalty. She asserts that capital punishment is “really a political agenda, especially in electoral times.”
Ageorges-Skinner examines how electoral pressures, judicial shortcomings and medical ethics shape capital punishment in the United States. Most SAS personnel ‘refusing to answer’ questions from Afghanistan inquiry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
13:27:38 UTC
22:27:38 KST

Most SAS personnel approached by an inquiry into alleged extrajudicial killings in Afghanistan have refused to answer any questions, the judge leading the proceedings has said.
Lord Justice Haddon-Cave is investigating allegations of more than 50 summary killings by UK special forces soldiers as well as claims of an alleged cover-up of illegal activity and inadequate investigations by the Royal Military Police.
In a public hearing, Haddon-Cave said a number of rule 9 requests – written notices asking for information – had been sent to SAS operators who were linked to the deliberate detention operations (DDOs) at the centre of allegations.
“The inquiry has identified numerous SAS personnel from whom it wishes to hear direct evidence as to the DDOs in question and has issued rule 9 requests for information to each of them,” he said.
“A high proportion have indicated their intention to rely on their privilege against self-incrimination and have refused to answer any questions asked by the inquiry.”
Ministers announced the statutory judge-led inquiry after allegations that 54 Afghans were killed in suspicious circumstances by one SAS unit in Helmand province between 2010 and 2011, and accusations that these amounted to war crimes.
A high court case brought by the law firm Leigh Day on behalf of one man, Saifullah, alleged that his father, two brothers and a cousin were killed during an SAS raid on a compound in southern Afghanistan in February 2011.
The inquiry is tasked with determining whether investigations conducted by the Royal Military Police were carried out properly and effectively, and whether there is credible information that “numerous” extrajudicial killings were carried out by British armed forces between 2010 and 2013. The judge said the three-year period “sufficiently captures the allegations currently being made”.
The inquiry will also seek to determine whether the circumstances of the alleged killings were covered up at any stage and what lessons could be learned.
During Monday’s hearing, Haddon-Cave revealed the inquiry had obtained about 10,000 high-resolution photos, taken in the course of the DDOs, which do not appear to have formed part of Royal Military Police inquiries.
He said the inquiry was seeking evidence from Afghan families whose loved ones died during the detention operations, adding that the inquiry had heard “extensive” witness evidence regarding concerns and complaints raised by both UK special forces personnel and other individuals about the manner in which the SAS were conducting detention operations in Afghanistan during the period in question.
Last week, during a high court hearing, the Ministry of Defence identified material that suggested UK special forces personnel deployed on some operations being considered by the inquiry may have committed serious offences under the Armed Forces Act 2006.
The open hearings will continue throughout October and November.
Separately, ministers announced a package of amendments to the Northern Ireland Troubles bill, intended to raise the bar before former soldiers can be prosecuted in cases dating back to the Troubles between 1969 and 1998, in an attempt to meet concerns raised by veterans groups.
In future, prosecutions will have to be approved by the attorney general, and any evidence has to be “new and compelling” as well as essential to the case before veterans are called to court. Legislation would also emphasise there is no equivalence between soldiers and terrorists.

Peace in the Middle East? Kurdish PKK leader discusses regional ‘third world war’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
13:27:16 UTC
22:27:16 KST

The Middle East is changing and is at a crossroads. It is also in the midst of a “Third World War,” Kurdistan Workers' Party (PKK) Murat Karayilan said in an interview published on October 12. “This war is in essence a global war. A Third World War; however, these make it into a regional war. War between Shias and Sunnis. War between Iran and the Arab Gulf States. This comes from a supremacist plan and mentality. A supremacist mentality, regarding how to design the region, how to control it, and how to govern it. It is such a plan,” he told Kamal Chomani of the The Amargi news outlet. This interview spotlights Kurdish issues and the region. It comes at a unique time, as the PKK moves toward disarmament.
Kamal Chomani, a PhD student at the University of Leipzig in Germany, published an important, exclusive interview with Murat Karayilan, a co-founder of the Kurdistan Workers' Party and its current key leader. The interview is for the Amargi news outlet, which described itself as “an independent news and analysis platform covering the Middle East and North Africa.”
Chomani notes in the introduction to his interview, posted on X, that “I spent ten days in the PKK headquarters and caves before finally reaching Murat Karayilan, for this exclusive interview with The Amargi.” He noted, “We begin with the wars reshaping the Middle East and then break down the peace process, in which Mr. Karayilan clearly calls on the Turkish state to end policies of denial and annihilation, and on Kurds to abandon rebellion and work toward establishing a democratic state.” He also noted that the PKK leader has not spoken to an external media outlet for 12 years.
The interview comes at a crucial time for the region, as many states are at a crossroads and Kurdish politics is as well. The PKK, since its founding in 1978, has been one of the key Kurdish movements in the region. The other major Kurdish movement is primarily linked to parties and groups associated with the Kurdistan Democratic Party. The PKK’s main role has been in Turkey, where there was a long conflict with the Turkish government costing thousands of lives. The most recent round of that war restarted in 2015. The PKK also has had branches and influence in Syria, Iran, and Iraq among Kurds. In Syria the main group was the YPG, and in Iran it is PJAK.
As the PKK and the Turkish government have appeared to move toward a peace deal that will see the PKK dissolved and disarmed in Turkey, and in other areas, there are a lot of questions about what comes next. The interview may provide a window into this and appears to show how the PKK wants to get its message out today. The party is often opaque and complex to analyze because of the devotion of its members, many of whom join when they are young.
PKK leader discusses regional changes and the movement's future strategy
In the hour-long interview, which is on YouTube and also translated to English from Kurdish by the Amargi, the PKK leader discusses the current changes in the region. Although this part of the interview is the shortest, it is also the most interesting for our purposes. The PKK's internal ideology and choices, and how it views Turkey today or its concepts of democratic confederalism may be important, but it is the pragmatic choices made by the PKK these days that matter the most.
Karayilan discusses the recent changes in the region. He is asked about how the wars caused by the Hamas October 7 attack have changed the region, and also how changes in Syria, Libya, Iraq, and other places are shaping the region. The interview took place after US forces left Iraq on September 30. It also took place more than eight months after the US left Syria and after the US-backed Syrian Democratic Forces agreed to a deal to integrate with the Syrian government. The SDF’s largest armed component was the YPG, which is linked to the PKK.
PKK leader says global powers are competing for dominance in the Middle East
“The Third World War emerged over time. It differs from the First and Second World Wars in its methods. It’s not a single event; it emerged over time, spread, and continues to this day. It’s a global war among capitalist forces competing for hegemony. It’s a conflict between forces seeking global dominance. You’ve mentioned the Middle East, but there is also the Ukraine-Russia conflict, and Ukraine is supported by NATO states,” the PKK leader says. “The Third World War continues with various methods. The primary objective is to establish dominance in the Middle East. The global capitalist actors led by the US are afraid of China.”
This is an important point. The ideology and worldview that Karayilan mentions views the current conflict as a global war that is between “capitalist forces” fighting for dominance. This is not just between NATO backing Ukraine and the Russian invasion. This is also about the Middle East. He also mentions AI, new technology, and the struggle for control of rare earth elements needed for solar panels and chips. As such, he suggests that one goal of the US and the West is to weaken Russia and block China’s ambitions.
“They’re trying to build a line from Egypt to Kazakhstan to stop China’s advance. This isn't stated openly, but it is the core objective. Energy sources are very important to capitalist forces. Rare earth minerals are also used to produce chips and solar panels. Then there is uranium, as an important energy source,” he says. The conflict has spread, not just to Iran but also to the Gulf and Yemen.
The PKK leader stresses that today war is not a solution. War does not serve the interests of the people. He argues that his movement offers a third way to support democracy. He stresses this when discussing Turkey and the region today. He also stresses how US allies, such as Greece, Turkey, and Israel, do not all agree on strategy, or may even be against each other. Greece and Israel are closely aligned today.
“Tensions exist between the US and NATO partners – they are not all united. So, Iran, on one side, wants to represent the Shia line, but then you’ve got Turkey and Israel as two other sides. There are also conflicts between them. It is true that two days ago the US Secretary of State Marco Rubio stated that they do not allow contradictions between their allies to escalate into war. He was referring to the conflict between Greece and Turkey.”
PKK disarmament raises questions over Turkey's political future
The challenge for the PKK today is that while it has this regional outlook, it continues to stress the need for greater democracy in Turkey. It wants its leader Abdullah Ocalan, who has been in prison for decades, released. The PKK calls Ocalan “Apo,” and Karayilan speaks about how he must administer disarmament. This creates challenges ahead. So far, Ankara has appeared flexible; however, questions remain about what happens next. Will the ruling party use the deal with the PKK to divide the opposition or get votes from Kurds? The AKP has received Kurdish votes in the past, and they need them if they want to stay in power after around two decades of rule.
The interview also delved into the details of the current issues in northern Iraq where the PKK has bases. Turkey has sent forces into the Kurdistan Region of northern Iraq because of this. “We pulled our forces out. They were hidden, but we got them out, some using vehicles, some on the roads. So we pulled out our forces. This year they say ‘Metina too.’ They are next door to each other – Zap and Metina. So they tell us you must pull out from Metina too. We say, ‘Why? Why just us taking steps?,’” Karayilan says. “Finally, after a lot of dialogue and internal discussions, we took the decision to also pull out of Metina. Two days ago. Today is the October 10. So on the 8th, our final forces pulled out of the Metina tunnels. Since then, we have had no one in Metina.” What this shows is how the PKK is not just focused on large ideas about its version of democracy and what it sees as a struggle for world order in the region, but also on its bases and operations that continue to be sticking points in peace with Ankara. Chomani’s interview offers a rare look at the PKK’s current views and helps shed light on what may come next in the region.

Ülle Madise: Attempts to reeducate people have delivered a setback to trust
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
13:27:00 UTC
22:27:00 KST

Ülle Madise: Attempts to reeducate people have delivered a setback to trust
The attempts of the past decade to remake people, to prescribe how they should live, think, feel or speak have inevitably undermined mutual trust. We have learned that lesson. Now we must rebuild trust, Ülle Madise said in her first speech as president.
On September 2, I spoke about how Estonia's greatest treasure is its people. And so it is. We must do everything possible to ensure that there are many people to carry on the Estonian language and culture. To make Estonia the best place to raise children and grow old, to invent and create, to pursue science and do business. To ensure that our children are among the smartest, most well-balanced and happiest in the world. And that the joy of living does not fade later in life, amid the responsibilities of work and family or because of age or health.
Pristine nature, rustling forests. The sea, lakes and rivers. Birds and animals. Plants, mushrooms and bees. Fish and dragonflies. Just one generation from now, the natural world here will be an even greater wonder than it is today. If only we know how to preserve it. Estonia is already one of the most pleasant places in the world to live. Mosquitoes, puddles, good and bad skiing weather included.
Everyone here in Estonia must be able to feel that they themselves, as well as their lives, work and creations, are valuable. That there is plenty of room for all of us, different as we are. With our own interests, views, lifestyles, tastes and native languages.
High culture and pop culture, alternative culture and the underground, the whole colorful spectrum. Rehearsing for the Song and Dance Celebration does not interfere with hip-hop or a midnight rave and vice versa! Estonia is free, exciting, vibrant, evolving and diverse.
Can we preserve such an Estonia and continue building it? I believe that depends on trust, hope for the future and courage.
Perhaps we do not notice it every day or have forgotten, but in most parts of Estonia, kindness, honest work, common sense and helping one another are still held in high regard. A neighbor helps pull a car out of the snow, an elderly person shivering at a bus stop is offered a ride and gets where they need to go, someone else's children get a ride home from practice along with one's own, fresh cucumbers and tomatoes are hung on a neighbor's door handle or apples are left out for anyone to take. Let us notice these things, appreciate them and do our part.
Unfortunately, in my work as chancellor of justice, I saw far too often how someone gives their best, dedicates themselves to helping others, but does not receive the same consideration in return. Yet they could. They should.
Take, for example, a mother who, through circumstances beyond her control, is raising a child alone, working, studying for a profession that society badly needs and volunteering wherever she can. Yet when she herself needs help, she all too often encounters bureaucratic obstruction and cold arrogance in seeking support.
My colleagues and I at the Office of the Chancellor of Justice always stood against soulless bureaucratic procedures wherever we encountered them. What is the point of a system in which officials can shrug their shoulders and coldly declare that "clients did not receive the service," rather than recognize that a child and their mother were left without help?
Fortunately, there are people who find solutions. But do we know how to recognize and appreciate them for it?
Take a police officer who saves the life of a child speeding along on a battery-powered scooter, only to hear the parent respond with ... I will not even repeat it. How can anyone believe that a highly trained officer leaves their family to go to work in the evening simply to harass law-abiding people?
Or a teacher who cares deeply about their students, looks for opportunities to help them spread their wings, comes home in the evening, opens their computer — and there it is! No, not messages of gratitude.
We need much more trust and warm appreciation. Doctors, journalists, police officers, teachers, farmers — each of us, in our respective professions, is a trained specialist doing our best. And trust really must be earned. By genuinely doing our best. All of us, in our lives and work.
The attempts of the past decade to remake people, to prescribe how they should live, think, feel or speak have inevitably undermined mutual trust. We have learned that lesson. Now we must rebuild trust.
For people who have experienced occupation, ideological propaganda of any kind provokes contempt, which can drive even the best of people to write or do things they would otherwise never even consider. And to vote against everything simply for the sake of it. Eventually, resentment translates into election results.
Everyone has the right to vote exactly as they see fit. That is what elections are for. What matters most is that people do not stop voting altogether, that they do not fall silent, become indifferent or withdraw from life entirely.
Indifference is an enemy of a free democratic society, as are the loss of hope for the future and sheer noise. The rule of law rests not only on legislation but also on trust and the knowledge that the rules apply to everyone and that people are treated fairly. Let us not allow ourselves to be turned against one another here in our own corner of the world, among our own people. There should be as few people as possible who feel so bad — perhaps with good reason — that they are prepared to tear things down, because we need to build the future.
If you want peace, prepare for ... you know the rest. Peace must be preserved. Everyone can play a part in that.
The first step is to maintain peace of mind. There is far too much fear of war in the air. Whenever I come away from a discussion of the actual security situation, assessed on the basis of facts, I feel much calmer than I do after reading deliberate fearmongering. Of course, I know that politics or business interests lie behind it. But still.
Yes, the world around us is unpredictable and dangerous. Of course it is. I understand the concern and I worry too. A global crisis of trust? That is true as well. Ukraine must be supported in every conceivable way so that the war of aggression against it ends and a lasting, just peace is achieved. So that war criminals are punished and the aggressor pays for the damage. We must convincingly demonstrate around the world that international law, a rules-based international order and the protection of human rights benefit most countries and all people.
Estonia has worked diligently to make itself stronger. The Estonian Defense Forces, the Estonian Defense League, the Women's Voluntary Defense Organization. Our entire system of comprehensive national defense. Our committed neighbors in the Baltic and Nordic countries. Poland. All our allies in Europe and NATO. All of this is what makes us secure.
Please, let us not allow fear or hopelessness into our hearts. Fear paralyzes us or drives us to do foolish things. We must act wisely. And everyone has an opportunity to do so. I dare to assure you that the future is neither bleak nor predetermined. We are building it ourselves. In times of uncertainty, we must recognize the great opportunities before us and make skillful use of them.
We also need more humor and lightness in general. And something to sustain our spirits.
Culture cannot be treated as something that comes after everything else. Culture sustains and supports us, comforts us, broadens our horizons, warns us, cleanses the dark corners of the human soul and helps us become better people. Let us not miss out on cultural events close to home. Let us make them inviting and accessible to children and young people, as well as to those who have little money or difficulty getting around.
Let us appreciate our writers, filmmakers, theater professionals, artists, designers and museums — both new creations and our heritage. Let us always take an interest in how other peoples live and in their cultures. When I am abroad, I try to visit a museum or church, even if only briefly.
And let us make ourselves visible: exhibitions by Estonian artists around the world, our magnificent orchestras and choirs, theatrical performances, novels, medals won at sporting competitions — all of it matters. So do scientific research and inventions that make their way into production, as well as collaborative projects. Bold and trustworthy entrepreneurship. Technology companies, startups, agricultural businesses and the defense industry, of course. But not only those!
These days, it is a major achievement when an entrepreneur can produce something distinctive and of very high quality, at a reasonable price and in an environmentally responsible way and deliver the products on time. Not just here in Estonia, but anywhere in the world.
Estonia's trump card is education. We know it ourselves and so does the entire educated world, but we must work harder to ensure that every child in Estonia receives a good education and has ample opportunities. This must not depend on whether a child attends a small rural school or one in Tallinn's residential districts, whether they live with their parents, a foster family or in a children's home or whether they are still learning Estonian. Estonia's future depends on a good education for all its children.
The AI Leap initiative in schools, launched under the leadership of President Alar Karis, deserves recognition and continuation. The future belongs to those who know how to use artificial intelligence wisely while remaining free and capable as human beings. The leap that has begun must aim as far as possible. And always in such a way that AI does not become an "ow!"
Technology must not make us forget that people also need to be able to manage on their own. Excessive dependence on technology and electricity is dangerous for everyone, everywhere. All it takes is a storm or a thief to land us in serious trouble. Let us remain resilient.
Estonia's Minister of Justice and Digital Affairs Liisa Pakosta is leading an international discussion on establishing regulations for artificial intelligence. Estonia is exactly the country that should be taking the lead. We have extensive experience as a digital state and a complicated history. We know how to understand other peoples and countries around the world and perhaps they can understand us as well.
The digital divide does not exist or deepen only within societies, where in some places it is causing ever greater poverty, suffering and resentment with each passing year or even month. That is why we need an agreement that artificial intelligence must also be accessible to smaller and poorer countries and that AI must serve humanity, not the other way around.
To protect the Estonian language and culture, and all small nations and cultures, we must ensure that they are properly and accurately represented in artificial intelligence models.
Armies of bots serving the interests of an aggressor state are vigorously spreading falsehoods and teaching artificial intelligence to lie and ultimately those lies will harm everyone. Countries that wish to remain sovereign and independent should have a vital interest in combating hostile propaganda.
The president cannot and must not take the place of the popularly elected Riigikogu, the government or the courts. The separation and balance of powers is of great value. The president has an important role in maintaining that balance.
The date for a meeting of the National Defense Council, as provided for in the Constitution, has already been set. I would take the saying "Train hard, fight easy" a step further: If the training is exceptionally rigorous, there will be no battle at all. And that, after all, is our goal.
We could begin combating a lack of ideas and growing uniformity here at home by encouraging bold thinking and dreaming. The president's think tank is one place for that. Thinking together, debating and sharing humor bring out the best in people, from academics to schoolchildren. That is how new ideas are born.
The president can recognize and support everyone working to ensure that families have places to live and raise children, that the birth of a child does not lead to financial hardship and that someone who wants to build a home in the countryside can also obtain a loan. Let making Estonia a child- and family-friendly country become an issue in the upcoming elections and every election thereafter. Not by backing anyone into a corner or putting them on the defensive, but by cheerfully showing how well things can be done.
Perhaps we also need a Tiger Leap in mental health. Yes, of course we need more psychologists and psychiatrists, greater recognition of individual differences and more consideration for them. But we also need to eliminate unnecessary pressures that are breaking more and more people.
Excessive and destructive competitiveness, pulling one another down, noise, harassment, injustice, loneliness, overwhelming fear and anxiety and hopelessness are not inevitable features of life. I will do my best to help us find the courage. Because why be unhappy and lose when it is possible to be happy and win?
The president can help make the voices of people heard more clearly — what troubles them, what they expect and what they hope for — in Võrumaa and Virumaa, Mehikoorma and Häädemeeste, Saaremaa and Hiiumaa, Paide and Põltsamaa and everywhere that local communities are working hard to keep life from moving away, to ensure that farms flourish, that tourism and business in general develop and that it remains worthwhile for successive generations to make an effort.
The money needed to sustain our free Estonian state can come only from a strong and adaptable economy. So let us give entrepreneurs the freedom to act. We do not need all-encompassing convenience that makes people lazy and helpless. We do not need orders, prohibitions, unnecessary bureaucracy or overseers everywhere, stifling creativity and initiative. The head of state can remind people of that, too. In the form of a veto, if necessary.
I will take time to meet people from different walks of life in different parts of Estonia. To listen to them, share their concerns and joys and try to understand. And then to carry their message forward. My colleagues and I will be seen in gardens, factories, barns, company brainstorming spaces, schools, nursing homes, village squares, hospitals, city streets and other places where everyday life unfolds. I am afraid I will not be able to attend ceremonial events as often as I should and I ask for your understanding.
I hope to maintain regular contact with members of the Riigikogu, the prime minister and ministers and the heads of constitutional institutions, understanding and respecting their respective roles. Here, too, trust, respect for one another's dignity and working together for Estonia's future and the benefit of everyone living here are what matter.
I have said repeatedly and I will say it again: All our previous heads of state have been the right people in the right place at the right time and have made Estonia better and greater. Thank you very much! Thank you, President Alar Karis. I would also like to thank Mrs. Sirje Karis in particular. Her work for Ukrainian children alone deserves the highest recognition.
As I continue the work of my predecessors, I feel a profound sense of humility and responsibility.
If we trust one another, value freedom, responsibility and clear communication, have the courage to be good people, trust in life, believe in Estonia and maintain a hopeful outlook, all good things are possible.
Long live Estonia!
--
Editor: Marcus Turovski

Comedian Giorgio Bracardi dies at 93
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
15:26:57 CEST
22:26:57 KST

Comedian Giorgio Bracardo, best known
for his appearances on mid-80s cult late-night variety show
Quelli della Notte, has died at the age of 93, his family said
Monday.
                                    
Bracaro, who was also a musician and singer, was famous for
characters such as the "Nicaraguan vulture" Scarpantibus and the
pushy journalist Max Vinella from the radio show Alto
Gradimento.
                                    
He had been staying at a care home in Fiano Romano near Rome
after breaking his femur last spring.
                                    
Born in Rome on May 3, 1933, Bracardi grew up in the world of
show business.
                                    
His father was one of the first managers of Rome's Salone
Margherita theater; his mother, Edvige, was a soprano, and his
father, Glauco, was a tenor.
                                    
All five of their children received a musical education and
learned to play an instrument.
                                    
Giorgio was a pianist who later became a composer, even
participating in the Sanremo Festival as a songwriter. However,
Bracardi rose to great popularity with Alto Gradimento, the
radio program he co-created with Renzo Arbore, Gianni
Boncompagni, and Mario Marenco.
                                    
He later made the leap to television with Arbore in the 1985
show Quelli della notte, and also appeared on Pronto, chi
gioca?, hosted by Enrica Bonaccorti and Giancarlo Magalli.
                                    
In 1989, he hosted and starred in Chiappala chiappala on Rai 2.
                                    
In 1995, he moved to Mediaset to join Striscia la Notizia,
playing Lucio Smentisco, a fictional spokesperson for Silvio
Berlusconi.
                                    
In 2001, he was a featured performer on Marco Giusti's Rai 2
program Stracult.
                                    
Bracardi also provided the voice for the character Cattivik in
the animated series broadcast by Mediaset in 2008.

Iran spread anti-Israel, US disinformation to global media through fake journalists, OpenAI says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
13:26:38 UTC
22:26:38 KST

Iran used artificial intelligence to generate social media comments, create at least seven fake journalist personas, and pitch long-form articles to global media outlets as part of a covert influence operation, OpenAI confirmed in an announcement released on Thursday.
OpenAI said it had disrupted two influence operations, one originating in Russia and the other in Iran, that abused its technology to create “false front entities” to promote their narratives about the Russia-Ukraine and US/Israel-Iran wars. The company said both campaigns used “questionable or outright deceitful methodologies to exaggerate the operators’ effectiveness.”
Although influence operations predate the advancement of AI, OpenAI acknowledged that the technology has made them easier to conduct. It noted that Iran's fake journalists closely resembled “Alice Donovan,” a fictitious journalist created as part of a Russian influence campaign in 2017.
OpenAI rated the Iranian campaign a four on its six-point Influence Operation scale, with one representing the lowest level and six the highest. The rating reflected the campaign's success in placing content in mainstream media outlets. Referring to the 30 covert operations it had uncovered over the previous two and a half years, the company said such campaigns aim to get social media posts and other content published by legitimate media outlets to expand their reach and impact.
AI used to disseminate false information through fake authors
Beyond helping operators place content before wider audiences, OpenAI said AI enabled malicious actors to conduct operations with greater scale, efficiency, linguistic fluency, and editorial ability.
According to OpenAI, a cluster of ChatGPT accounts originating in Iran was used to generate content in both Persian and English. The actors reportedly accessed ChatGPT through a VPN and used the model to improve long-form articles and editorial pitches published under fabricated bylines.
The fake bylines belonged to Ervin B. Hoskins, Noah Lamington, Sophia Gonzalez, Michael Harrison, Ericka Feusier, Jenny Williams, and Alice Johnson. All were presented as Western journalists focusing on international politics, the Middle East, human rights, or conflict.
The Jerusalem Post located an article by “Noah Lamington” published in International Policy Digest that sought to portray political insecurity in Israel. The article was headlined “The Knesset Revolt Netanyahu Couldn’t Prevent.”
An article by “Sophia Gonzalez” was also found in the News Register under the headline “Sophia Gonzalez: When diplomacy becomes another weapon of war.” Meanwhile, “Ericka Feusier” appeared to have published extensively on insecurity in Iraq and American unemployment on websites including Eurasia Review, Common Dreams, and the IA Forum.
The articles focused primarily on the US-Iran war, while a smaller proportion of the generated comments addressed US domestic politics. OpenAI identified nearly 100 articles produced by the operation that appeared in syndicated publications and small and medium-sized media outlets around the world.
The earliest article identified by OpenAI was published in July 2025, while the latest appeared in October 2026. The volume of content increased following the outbreak of the US-Iran conflict.
Online outlets shared the AI articles to millions of social media followers
One online outlet that published articles from the influence campaign had nearly two million Facebook followers, approximately 355,000 followers on X/Twitter, and more than 544,000 on Instagram as of August 2026.
Several of the fictitious journalists also maintained social media accounts on X, Facebook, Instagram, or Threads. However, further investigation found that the accounts were operated from within Iran or elsewhere in West Asia.
Despite the campaign's success in placing articles in media outlets, OpenAI noted that none of the generated social media comments attracted substantial engagement.
In July, for example, the campaign produced several X posts claiming that the US was preparing a “large-scale assault” on Iran, followed by a burst of comments posted within a 10-to-13-minute window. Some comments included screenshots of articles generated as part of the campaign, promoting them in an apparent attempt to make the content appear popular.
Based on the operation's overall activity, OpenAI suggested that those behind it were likely commercial actors running a for-hire influence campaign.

Israel, Kurdistan, and the hopes for a strong political alliance - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
13:26:35 UTC
22:26:35 KST

As the Kurdish journalist and researcher Suzan Quitaz put it recently: “Standing with Jewish people in the face of antisemitism is the opposite of being racist.
“It is about standing up against hatred, discrimination, and violence toward people because of their religion or ethnicity. It is standing up against one of the oldest and strongest forms of racism: antisemitism.”
In a twisted way, the closer Kurds and Jews get, and the more visible that becomes, the more people start seeing Kurds as another kind of Jew. Not in a way that changes those people’s attitude toward Kurds, because we were alone in our struggle anyway, but in how they frame the Kurdish political struggle.
Those same people, on the global Left and on the libertarian American Right alike, were always antisemitic, and always on the side of Ankara and Tehran in the name of anti-Americanism (which they veil with the term anti-imperialism).
They stand with Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan’s Ankara and the mullahs’ Tehran; they sided with Saddam’s Baghdad and Assad’s Damascus, and never with the Kurds.
Now they cannot openly side with Ankara or Tehran, but they can present themselves as against American interventionism, against the Gaza genocide.
With Kurds, they have a difficulty: they cannot frame Kurds as imperialist interventionists or Gaza genociders.
In an interview, the American right-wing commentator Tucker Carlson called the Kurds “the most brutal people” he had ever met.
This is the opposite of the truth of Kurdish armed struggles: with exceptions, which the Kurdish movements themselves apologized for and corrected, Kurdish armed struggle has never become uncontrolled violence.
The Kurdish struggle has always taken its legitimacy from its demands for recognition, equality, and self-rule.
On the other side, Saddam Hussein’s Anfal campaign of 1988 murdered (or disappeared) between 50,000 and 182,000 Kurdish civilians.
In September 1979, two weeks after Khomeini declared holy war on the Kurds, Revolutionary Guards entered the unarmed village of Qarna and slaughtered dozens of civilians, children and the elderly among them.
In March 2004, when Kurdish spectators were attacked at a football match in Qamishli, former Syrian president Bashar al-Assad’s security forces opened fire on the Kurdish crowd, and some 30 people were killed in the days that followed.
And Turkey, having successfully labeled Kurdish fighters terrorists, respected none of the rights that any human law would otherwise have protected.
There is a historical connection between treating Kurds this way and antisemitism in its various forms. Charles Dickens hardly needed to name the villain of Oliver Twist; “the Jew” was good enough to describe him.
Hitler and his allies all over Europe needed nothing other than anti-Jewish rhetoric to mass-murder Jews.
Together, we can be a strong alliance
The same can be seen in how people handle suffering in the Middle East. The same people who defend the right of Palestinians to go to their homes never mention the hundreds of thousands of Jews who had to leave Yemen, Iraq, or Syria.
They never mention the depopulation of Kurds in Turkey, Syria, or Iraq in the same way. Antisemitism is not seeing what Jews suffer, and the same formula applies to Kurds today.
This gives the Kurds, my people, the chance to review how they see the world. People do not take sides because of their “beliefs”. Not even the most educated, those we sometimes admire. The litmus paper is our own struggle.
How can they side with Ankara, Moscow, or Tehran, but not with us?
If Israel is so bad, if US interventionism is so bad, how come we benefit from their actions in our region?
The no-fly zone of 1991. The air support at Kobani in 2014. Israel’s public backing of the 2017 independence referendum, when no other state would give it.
Not that American support has ever been more than tactical, but we have lived the fact that these interventions saved our lives and our habitat.
Israel’s rising rhetoric may also be what the moment requires of Israel, in answer to Turkey’s adversarial politics in the region. But it also shows that Kurds have enough argument to build their own representative political organs and to build on those.
These are perfect times, in my opinion. We Kurds are learning what realpolitik is about. Not pity but power struggle.
And there is one way to win: make allies, become stronger, and instead of begging for pity, make your point in a way that forces them to choose sides.
Israel has legitimacy because it is a sovereign country. Kurds have legitimacy because we are imprisoned by outsiders on our own ancestral lands, denied our identity.
Let’s raise our flags together. It means working together in the diaspora.
Jews have the advantage of having been settled in these communities for centuries. Kurds have the advantage of both numbers and an unshakeable legitimacy to live sovereign on our ancestral land.
Combined, this forms one of the strongest aligned diaspora coalitions. We both offer something, and we both benefit. It is a loop that feeds itself and grows stronger.
Let them choose to be on the wrong side. By standing together, we break their perverted “non-legitimacy and oppression” rhetoric.
The writer, based in Vancouver, is a commentator on Kurdish affairs, Kurdistan, and international politics.
