All is quiet on the elections front: Where have all the screaming headlines gone? - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
13:26:30 UTC
22:26:30 KST

Tracking the electioneering vagaries of the parties in the run-up to the October 27 polling day for the 26th Knesset is not an easy task.
With all the latest possibilities available to publicize party messages, whether touting your own platform or attacking your opponent, there are many pictures, clips, memes, speeches, and interviews.
On the other hand, every election campaign has its quiet side. Or even a silent side. Some things are avoided or even suppressed.
Prime Minister Benyamin Netanyahu will probably not refer to the term “responsibility” in his campaign. On the other hand, I am not sure there is anything National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir will not say.
As for Netanyahu’s opposition leaders, issues are being avoided. The media is also muting its references to those issues, if not ignoring them, since they do not help the cause.
One example is the renewed sessions of the Netanyahu trials. In the past month, one witness, former MK Eitan Cabel, basically undermined Case 2000. In it, Netanyahu is charged with criminal corruption for allegedly exchanging favors with Yediot Aharonot.
His testimony also affected Case 4000, the Bezeq-Walla affair. Prosecutors alleged that Netanyahu traded state regulatory benefits for favorable media coverage.
In June 2023, the three judges told the parties they saw “difficulties” in proving the bribery offense and suggested that the prosecution consider withdrawing that count. In June 2026, they repeated their earlier assessment and made clear it had not changed.
A tantalizing media spin-off resulting from that trial was the revelation that in November 2015, prominent journalist Ben Caspit, a foe of Netanyahu, met with police investigator Eran Kamin.
Irregularly, Caspit urged Kamin to open Netanyahu’s baggage at the airport, and that of his wife, as evidence of embezzlement would be found. That development is absent from mainstream media coverage.
There is quiet regarding why the investigation into former military advocate-general Yifat Tomer-Yerushalmi, a second example, has stalled with no prosecution entered.
Now dismissed from service but still receiving financial benefits, she perpetrated the illegal disclosure of the Sde Teiman security-camera video to Channel 12. The person who edited it so maliciously is still unknown. Afterward, she also misled the High Court and other officials about the source of the leak.
The most senior IDF officer in the army’s justice corps is suspected of obstruction of justice, fraud, breach of trust, and abuse of office, too. Since last February, the case has gone nowhere, and we still do not know whether Attorney-General Gali Baharav-Miara or people in her office were involved.
A third matter that has gone very quiet is Qatargate with its overlapping Bild classified-document leak connection. That was highly publicized even as a matter of national treachery.
It also seems to be meriting the quiet treatment, and the media is not relating to the matter. High-profile figures close to Netanyahu were presented to the public as arch criminals.
These included Yonatan Urich, Netanyahu’s close media adviser; Eli Feldstein, a former Prime Minister’s Office spokesman; Srulik Einhorn, long-time Likud campaign strategist; and even Tzachi Braverman, Netanyahu’s chief of staff and current ambassador-designate to the United Kingdom.
Why is there quiet?
With all those figures, why is there quiet? Could it be that there really isn’t anything to make noise over?
One possible reason is that the former Mossad chief David Barnea said in April 2026 that he had not identified damage to Israeli national security or to the hostage negotiations resulting from Qatargate.
The 2024 unauthorized transfer of a highly classified Israeli intelligence document to the German newspaper Bild by some of those same Netanyahu advisors is also under the radar.
We are still waiting for the full report on Brig.-Gen. (res.) Oren Solomon’s internal inquiry into the IDF’s actions and failures during October and his accusation that senior military leadership tried to suppress his critical findings.
To remind us, that article (printed in Israel Hayom with the censor’s approval, incidentally) indicated that Yahya Sinwar and Hamas were deliberately preventing a hostage agreement, including by using the hostages to pressure Israel.
The anti-Bibists fulminated, and the media loudly accused the Netanyahu clique of manipulating public opinion.
However, with now-former White House coordinator for the Middle East Brett McGurk’s admission that “the idea that Hamas just was ready to release all the hostages is complete bulls***,” the Bild leak is in its proper proportion.
McGurk said Israel repeatedly agreed to proposals while Hamas resisted.
In other words, the extremely loud campaign in Hostage Square that the government was preventing any deal was unsupported by the facts.
Actually, now the tables are turned, and the role of the Kaplan Camp in the Hamas decision to go ahead with its invasion plans should be highlighted. Did their activities encourage the idea that Israeli society was imploding? Why is the media silent?
There is quiet because the public relations principle is: if an item serves your goal, quash it and ignore it. Don’t even mention it.
This is true especially if it turns out your own source goes on television to contradict and disavow the fairytale you spread.
Of course, there are two more weeks in the campaign, and I am not a prophet; nor do I suggest any one side is unblemished.
I think it fair that the public be reminded that the many media storms we have experienced over the last few years have either been proven wrong or led nowhere.
If the media goes silent on a hot story and lets it peter out, that may be a sign that something was wrong in the first place, or that the media is supporting one of the sides.
The writer is a researcher, analyst, and commentator on political, cultural, and media issues.

Israel demolishes 80 homes in Palestinian village in Negev, displaces around 400 people
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
13:25:48 UTC
22:25:48 KST

Abdel Raouf Arnaout, Lina Altawell
12 October 2026•Update: 12 October 2026
Israeli authorities demolished around 80 homes in the Palestinian village of Al-Dhahiya in the Negev region of southern Israel on Monday, displacing around 400 people, amid accusations that extremist National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir is using home demolitions as part of his election campaign.
Israel’s public broadcaster KAN said teams from the Israel Land Authority, accompanied by reinforced police forces under Ben-Gvir’s ministry, demolished around 80 homes on claims that they had been “built without permits” in Al-Dhahiya, an unrecognized village north of the city of Rahat.
The demolition came after the Beersheba District Court on Sunday rejected a petition seeking to postpone the demolitions, the broadcaster said, adding that around 400 people had been living in the homes.
In recent weeks, Ben-Gvir has publicly highlighted the demolition of hundreds of homes belonging to Palestinian citizens of Israel, or Israeli Arabs, over alleged construction without permits.
Last Tuesday, Ben-Gvir took part in the demolition of a five-story building housing 70 Palestinians in the At-Tur neighborhood of occupied East Jerusalem, an action the Jerusalem Governorate described as the “electoral exploitation of Jerusalem at the expense of Palestinians.”
The Joint List, an alliance of three Arab parties, denounced the home demolitions as “a blatant assault on the most basic human and national rights of our people.”
“The demolitions were a continuation of the successive Israeli governments’ policies of demolition, uprooting and displacement against residents of Arab villages in the Negev,” the alliance said.
Hassan al-Nasasra, deputy mayor of Rahat, also denounced the demolitions.
“The demolitions are not an implementation of the law in any way, but merely election propaganda for the racist Ben-Gvir and his group,” he said in a statement.
KAN also reported that United Arab List leader Mansour Abbas sent an urgent letter to Attorney General Gali Baharav-Miara demanding an immediate freeze on home demolition orders until the elections are over and a new government is formed.
Israel’s general elections are scheduled for Oct. 27.
Abbas warned against using home demolitions for “political and electoral purposes,” saying Ben-Gvir had publicly boasted about participating in demolitions “in a way that undermines the integrity of the election and the neutrality of law enforcement agencies.”
“Residents of unrecognized villages in the Negev are unable to obtain building permits because of a lack of planning for which the state bears responsibility,” he said, calling for a complete halt to demolitions of inhabited homes in such villages.
Dozens of Palestinian villages in the Negev are not recognized by Israeli authorities, which consider their homes unauthorized and do not connect them to water, electricity or road networks or provide schools, clinics and other basic services.
Last year, the daily Yedioth Ahronoth reported that demolition orders in the region had risen by as much as 400% since the beginning of that year, drawing fire from Israeli rights organizations, which described the campaign as “discriminatory” and specifically targeting the Bedouin community.
Palestinian Bedouins in the Negev are Arab tribes that have lived in the area for centuries and were there before the establishment of Israel in 1948.
Israel was established in 1948 on lands captured by Zionist armed groups, before occupying the remaining Palestinian territories in 1967, including the West Bank, Gaza Strip and East Jerusalem.

Saudi Arabia faces new missile and drone fire after major attacks on airports
RIYADH, Oct 12 - Saudi Arabia said it was facing a new barrage of incoming fire on Monday and that Riyadh airport would remain shut for now, days after Saturday's deadly missile strike on a departure terminal that was claimed by Yemen's Iran-allied Houthis.
Incoming drones and missiles were reported by the Saudi-led coalition backing government forces in Yemen, though there was no immediate news of whether they were intercepted.
The Houthis have been attacking Saudi airports and oil facilities since last week as part of a rapidly escalating conflict that has spilled over from the wider regional conflagration between the United States and Iran.
Those attacks have shut down parts of Saudi airspace, suspending operations at Riyadh airport, and largely emptying the skies over the capital even as the city hosts a major energy conference.
Saudi Arabia now faces a nightmare predicament, having re-entered Yemen's civil war to push the Houthis from the vital Bab el-Mandeb Strait oil route and stop the group making further gains after its sudden advances in September.
With the Yemeni forces Riyadh supports having made some gains against the Houthis around Bab el-Mandeb but still on the back foot on other fronts, Yemeni military sources said, any pressure on the Houthis could take time to pay off.
Saudi Arabia's long-time regional rival Iran offered to mediate between its Houthi allies and the kingdom. "We have repeatedly expressed our readiness to help facilitate dialogue between the parties," foreign ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said on Monday.
Meanwhile, despite intensified Saudi airstrikes against the group, including what Yemeni television said were hits on al-Jawf province on Monday, the Houthis show no sign of letting up their own barrage of attacks on Saudi infrastructure.
The group has repeatedly threatened to target airports and airspace, as well as Saudi oil installations that provide the engine for the kingdom's economy and its ambitious development plans.
UAE CALLS FOR JOINT GULF ACTION
Saudi Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman said at Monday's conference that the kingdom would stay focused on bringing in investment as part of its wider economic development goals.
"The development of our energy system and industrial capability continues," he said.
Saudi Arabia's neighbour the United Arab Emirates on Monday called for a revival of joint Gulf action on security and defence in response to the attacks. UAE presidential adviser Anwar Gargash said the targeting of Saudi Arabia undermined the security of all Gulf states and added that the neglect of collective Gulf security had "emboldened others" to overreach against regional states.
Saudi Arabia and the UAE had been partners in the Yemen conflict for years, but they backed different forces within the Yemeni military coalition supporting the government and fell out last winter.
US President Donald Trump said on Saturday that Washington was considering joining Saudi Arabia in strikes on the Houthis, but there has been no sign yet of any US action. REUTERS

Four men have gone on trial in Warsaw accused of being part of a criminal group that carried out a series of arson attacks in Poland and Lithuania on Russian orders.
The accused – three Ukrainians and one Belarusian – can be named only as Oleksandr H., Stepan K., Vitalii K. and Pavlo T. under Polish privacy law and their trial is taking place behind closed doors for security reasons.
Polish prosecutors say that they were part of an organised group tasked with “committing acts of sabotage and terrorism” on behalf of Russia’s foreign intelligence service in April and May 2024.
Those included a fire that burned down Warsaw’s largest shopping centre, Marywilska 44; another at a store in Warsaw belonging to home improvement chain OBI; and a third at an IKEA store in Vilnius. They also allegedly planned an arson attack on an IKEA store in the Latvian capital of Riga.

Kazakhstan eyes semiconductor manufacturing with Belgian scientists
Kazakhstan is weighing a joint research center with Belgium's KU Leuven, where scientists would pool expertise and develop technologies to process critical minerals and manufacture finished goods, Qazinform News Agency reports.
Zhumabay Bakenov, a Professor at Nazarbayev University and Founding Director General of the Institute of New Materials and Energy Technologies, announced this on the sidelines of the Belgium-Kazakhstan Critical Minerals Seminar.
The seminar findings are to be presented to the King and Queen of Belgium at a roundtable on October 13.
"We have the technologies, but I think it's fair to say they are outdated. KU Leuven is especially known for its processes in enrichment, hydrometallurgy, and pyrometallurgy. Renowned scientists in this field work there. I believe cooperation between Kazakhstan and Belgium, especially through KU Leuven, is very promising. One of our goals is to create joint centers for critical materials in Kazakhstan," the professor said.
At such centers, Kazakh and Belgian specialists would work together to develop technologies for mining, enrichment, and processing of critical minerals.
Kazakh students will also have the opportunity to learn from Belgian specialists under dual-degree programs.
"At these centers, we will work alongside Belgian specialists. Our students will be able to study in Belgium. We also plan to discuss dual-degree programs, under which Kazakh and Belgian students will study together and earn degrees from two universities. As for research and establishing joint centers, we want to move very quickly. If our Belgian colleagues are ready, we are ready to sign agreements, create the centers and finance them jointly," Zhumabay Bakenov said.
The professor also named the products Kazakhstan hopes to manufacture, partly through cooperation with Belgian scientists.
"We want our raw materials to be extracted, enriched, processed and brought to a finished product in Kazakhstan. For instance, we want to manufacture superconductors, semiconductors, catalysts and magnets based on what we have," the professor explained.
Notably, Kazakhstan already exports molybdenum ore and titanium to Belgium.
Earlier, President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev and King Philippe of the Belgians adopted a joint statement outlining key areas of bilateral cooperation.

EXPLAINED: Trump’s Threat to Halt Intelligence, Arms to Ukraine – 5 Things to Know
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
13:24:47 UTC
22:24:47 KST

Over the weekend reports surfaced that the US was considering cutting off American intelligence feeds and arms sales to Ukraine. Kyiv Post broke that down into five things to know.
1. Did the Americans really threaten to cut Ukraine off from all US weaponry and military intelligence?
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
It looks that way. During Saturday talks in Miami between US and Ukrainian delegations on a possible halt to the Russo-Ukrainian War, members of the US delegation said Washington wants Ukraine to stop attacking Russian oil refineries, and if Kyiv refuses, then the US could suspend arms shipments to Ukraine and intelligence sharing with Ukraine’s military.
The threats reportedly were also made in calls on Saturday and Sunday from the State Department, Pentagon, and other US officials to Ukrainian leaders and European capitals. The Financial Times first reported the threats, citing European officials involved in the calls. Reuters and other outlets confirmed the FT account. Axios reported New York real estate mogul Steve Witkoff and Trump son-in-law Jared Kushner as heads of the US delegation in Miami made the threats directly to Kyrylo Budanov, head of Ukraine’s Office of the President and former head of Ukraine’s military intelligence. The Ukrainian delegation quit the planned talks one day early.
According to Western media reports Witkoff and Kushner warned the Budanov team that if Ukraine did not stop attacking Russian oil refineries then the US would consider halting all arms deliveries to Ukraine under the Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List (PURL), a mechanism by which Ukraine’s allies purchase US weapons for Ukraine at a 10 percent markup ordered by Trump. At the same time, reportedly, the US might cut off intelligence collected by the US on Russian military targets and activities, including real-time intelligence feeds.
EU Targets Russian Missiles and Drones in Biggest Sanctions Expansion Since 2022
The United States shut down practically all US arms donations and direct financial support to Ukraine in February 2025 and since then has not reinstated it. Since then, the Trump administration, according to Ukrainian sources, has cut off US military intelligence feeds at least once, for approximately a week in March 2025.
On Sunday, Budanov and the rest of the Ukrainian delegation walked out of the talks, cutting the negotiations short by a day.
2. What would a cut off of US intelligence feeds mean for Ukraine?
The key capacity Ukraine would lose is the earliest warning possible of Russian ballistic missile launches.
President Zelensky and other Ukrainian officials have said that, without that intelligence, Ukraine’s ability to respond to Russian missile strikes would be seriously weakened because alternate means of detecting Russian aircraft and missiles – primarily by Ukrainian and NATO-operated systems – are far less extensive and networked than the Americans’.
Most analysts say a Russian ballistic missile launch in western Russia is detected almost instantaneously by the US, giving residents of Kyiv three to five minutes to take cover before the missile impacts, thanks to US intelligence sharing. Without that warning targeted Ukrainians would have less than half that time, and possibly no time at all, to take cover.
Beyond missile early-warning for Ukraine, the US world-wide satellite and intelligence collection network is a possible gold mine of intelligence on Russia thanks to unique US capacities like super-computing power enabling interception and decoding of adversary communications and electronic emissions. In addition, hundreds of state-of-the-art imagery satellites give the US and its friends, at least theoretically, the ability to inspect every square centimeter of the planet thanks to satellites passing overhead.
For Ukraine, US collection of Russian radar data is especially important because US air war weapons like fighter jets and anti-aircraft missiles are regularly updated with changes in those radars detected by worldwide US electronic eavesdropping, and Ukraine uses both those weapons to defend itself against Russian air attacks.
Another unique US advantage Ukraine might lose is the giant analytical manpower and computer capacity of the CIA and NSA, which covertly suck in data through a worldwide collection effort and turn it into hard intelligence. For Ukraine this might mean not knowing Russian military plans, movements of units or key officers, or the precise location of major Russian weapons systems like warships, combat aircraft and ballistic missile launchers.
A key qualification is, of course, that no intelligence collection effort is perfect. Sometimes the US intelligence community gets it wrong, and like any big state bureaucracy the American intelligence community is fallible. So loss of US analytical capacity is not the same as loss of 100 percent accurate analysis.
3. What would a cut off of US arms and weapons assistance mean for Ukraine?
One of the most damaging effects of a cut off would be the loss of access to US military GPS networks which, in turn, would render “partially-dumb” US weapons operated by Ukraine that use GPS for precision guidance. The most important GPS-dependent weapons used by Ukraine are ATACMS missiles and GMLRS guided rockets fired by the HIMARS/M270 launch system.
Ukraine uses the system most often to hit high-value, fleeting targets, such as meetings at Russian military headquarters or heavy mobile anti-aircraft systems. Almost as important and similarly effective have been guided bomb kits called JDAMS, which, if the GPS works, allow a pilot to select a single point with five meter accuracy on a bridge or bunker line or a bomb strike.
The last time the Americans cut off GPS feeds to Ukraine, in March 2025, these systems effectively became “dumb” and only as accurate as unguided munitions. It is worth noting that Ukraine’s last confirmed ATACMS launch was in February 2026, so it’s possible a US cut off of ATACMS-specific guidance data to Ukraine is irrelevant, because Ukraine has shot off all its ATACMS and the US isn’t sending any more.
In terms of actual weaponry, by far the most important US weapon operated by Ukraine right now is the Patriot air defense system firing an interceptor missile called the PAC-3 MSE, which is the only weapon in Ukraine’s military that can, in practical terms, intercept a Russian ballistic missile. A July statement by Ukraine’s Defense Ministry said that 95 percent of Ukraine’s purchase from the US under PURL, are Patriot-system associated.
Besides Patriot-associated purchases needed to protect Ukrainian civilians and infrastructure from otherwise unstoppable Russian ballistic missiles, a US cut-off of arms sales could gradually make Ukraine’s 1990s-era F-16 fighter jet fleet unflyable because the jet and its spare parts and systems upgrades ultimately are from the American manufacturer Lockheed Martin. Ukrainian air defenses would suffer because the guided missiles fired by Ukraine’s aging F-16s – the long-range AIM-120 AMRAAM and the short-range AIM-9 Sidewinder – are both manufactured by the US company Raytheon.
Major US ground weapons operated by Ukraine, most visibly the M1A1 Abrams tank, the M3 Bradley Infantry Fighting Vehicle, and the M109 Paladin artillery system, similar to the F-16 would over time become more and more difficult for Ukraine to operate were the US to embargo arms sales, because parts needed for maintenance would be cut off.
4. If the Americans cut off intelligence feeds does Ukraine have other ways of getting information about Russia?
With the critical exception of ballistic missile early warning sufficient to let Ukrainians take shelter when the Russians launch a weapon at a city, the answer to that question is “yes.”
Most obviously, Ukraine has been at war with Russia since 2014 and Ukraine’s own spy and electronic eavesdropping networks have years of experience collecting war-critical information about Russia. Ukraine has the additional advantages of a population with millions of native Russian-speakers with millions more relatives in Russia, and a national security apparatus intimately familiar with Russian intelligence practices.
Lost US intelligence on Russia collected by satellites, to some extent, is compensated by Ukrainian agents on the ground. Most analysts say Ukrainian spy networks are probably best-developed in territory recently invaded by Russia, where the population is mostly hostile to the Kremlin.
European states with robust national intelligence efforts or just focusing largely on Russia – predominantly France but firmly including Britain, Finland, Poland, Sweden and the Baltic states – actively assist Ukraine with data collection. France’s CSO (Composante Spatiale Optique) military reconnaissance satellites provide high-resolution images of Russian bases, troop deployments and military infrastructure with resolution reportedly similar to the US’s, with the qualification that CSO passes a camera over a possible target once or twice a day, while a US satellite overpass can take place several times an hour.
The explosion of commercial satellite imagery, purchased by Ukraine or its allies, also helps fill in gaps left by US collection which, although capable, can be distracted away from Russia to other White House priorities like Iran, China, potential illegal migrants in Mexico or drug runners in the Caribbean or east Pacific. Among the commercial networks regularly feeding imagery into Ukrainian intelligence production are Finland’s ICEYE synthetic-aperture radar network, the US’s Maxar, Planet Labs, and BlackSky networks, and Canada’s RADARSAT-2 network.
A final intelligence collection effort that the Americans seem to have little ability to undermine is the NATO-led air defense operation along the Baltics, Poland, Romania and the Black and Baltic Seas that focuses on spotting Russian aircraft, drone and missile launches as early as possible, using ground- and air-based radars operating 24/7. NATO also regularly flies reconnaissance missions sometimes as close as a 100 km from Russian-occupied Crimea and Russia’s Black Sea coast, using electronic emission-sniffing spy planes, most often based in Crete, Romania, Turkey or Great Britain.
By doctrine the flights would search for precise locations of Russian air defense systems and military units so NATO could be prepared in case of war.
Russian officials and milbloggers have long accused NATO of sharing the intelligence with the Ukrainians, a charge NATO has steadfastly denied. In January 2026 President Emmanuel Macron told reporters France was providing about two-thirds of Ukraine’s intelligence needs. The Ukrainians say they have their own means of finding Russian targets.
5. If the Americans cut off arms supplies, does Ukraine have alternatives?
With exception of Patriot and Patriot-related equipment, the answer to that is not just “yes, in the future” but “yes, already.”
The most visible shift in Ukrainian arms needs has been tied to the revolution in ground warfare making drones the dominant weapons system on the ground battlefield and, parallel with that, legacy systems like tanks, infantry fighting vehicles and artillery less critical for fighting a war. Almost all members of the Ukrainian military, from private to general, will say that what Ukraine needs is more short-range tactical drones. However, compared to Ukrainian-made drones, American tactical drones are primitive and manufactured in scant quantities.
The situation is similar for Ukrainian air defense where, besides Patriot missiles to take on the Russian ballistic missiles, the Ukrainians need means of stopping recently developed Russian jet-powered drones. American anti-aircraft missiles are capable of engaging drones like that, but they cost more than the Russian drone. Meanwhile, Ukraine is fielding its own interceptor drones which have the benefit of having been tested not in laboratories and firing ranges, but in actual war against actual Russian weapons.
Germany has also already contributed in a big way to bulk up Ukrainian air defenses with donations of Cold War-era Gepard anti-aircraft cannon that have turned out to be ideal for blowing up Russian drones, an upgraded version of the Gepard, called the Skynex, and 11 IRIS-T SLM air defense systems whose advanced missiles have proved the most effective ground-based air defense system the Ukrainians have. A 12th system is reportedly en route to Ukraine by the end of the year.
Longer-term, France and Sweden have promised and begun pilot training for deliveries respectively of the fully modern Rafale and Gripen fighter jets for Ukraine’s air force, with the first aircraft planned to arrive in Ukraine in 2027.
In late September representatives from Lockheed Martin, the manufacturer of the competing US fighter jet, the F-16, were in Kyiv discussing with the Defense Ministry possible upgrades to Ukraine’s aging F-16 fleet, which without upgrades, compared to the incoming French and Swedish aircraft, would be obsolete. The Ukrainians said they would think about it.

Super El Nino could make 2026 record hottest year
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
13:23:55 UTC
22:23:55 KST

Breadcrumb
Super El Nino could make 2026 record hottest year: climate monitor
An intensifying El Nino pattern set an all-time temperature high in a key Pacific zone in September and could help make this year the hottest globally on record, the director of the EU's climate monitor said Monday.
Global forecasters have been warning for months that this El Nino would likely become the strongest ever observed and the latest record has tumbled even before the episode's expected peak later this year.
The warming phase of a natural climate cycle, El Nino temporarily raises sea temperatures in the tropical Pacific, triggering changes in weather that can increase the risk of drought and flooding, and exacerbate man-made global warming.
The Copernicus Climate Change Service said sea surface temperatures in a tell-tale El Nino monitoring region of the Pacific, known as Nino3.4, had reached an "all-time high" of 29.70C last month.
This exceeded the peak temperatures of previously strong El Nino events of 1982/1983, 1997/1998 and 2015/2016, the EU monitor said.
This year's El Nino, which emerged in June, is "very exceptional" but it is too early to say whether it is the strongest ever observed, Copernicus director Carlo Buontempo told AFP.
As climate change raises ocean temperatures, it can make recent El Nino events appear stronger than past ones, complicating historical comparisons.
Copernicus said it had adopted a new index, which accounts for the warming of tropical oceans, that suggested the current event is not yet stronger than past ones.
"It's a very large event even in that metric," Buontempo said. "This very large event today is happening in a much warmer climate."
Not all forecasters use the same scale to interpret El Nino.
On Friday, Japan's weather agency said that El Nino conditions had reached their "strongest intensity on record".
Record ocean temperatures
As El Nino gathers strength, global average sea surface temperatures hit a record 21.05C for September, topping the previous high of 20.92C for the same month in 2023, according to Copernicus.
Experts have warned that this El Nino, combined with human-induced climate change, could make 2027 the hottest year on record as heat stored in the Pacific is released into the atmosphere.
The weather phenomenon, which typically occurs every two to seven years and lasts around nine to 12 months, can drive world temperatures higher the year after its peak.
But Buontempo said even 2026 could wind up a record breaker as this El Nino builds toward its peak.
"If we follow the the pattern we have seen in the past, we may have a record-breaking 2026, followed by a record-breaking 2027," he told AFP.
After a record-breaking August, the world experienced its second hottest September ever observed, with surface air temperatures averaging 16.27C, the EU service said.
September was 1.63C hotter than the pre-industrial average, a period defined as 1850-1900. It was the second consecutive month that temperature rises exceeded 1.5C.
Buontempo said temperatures would probably remain 1.5C above normal into early next year
The last El Nino event helped make 2024 the hottest year on record after a series of months of temperatures exceeding 1.5C, he said.
But while El Nino plays a role, "the ultimate cause of the rise and the exceedance of 1.5C are anthropogenic emissions of greenhouse gases," Buontempo said.
Nations agreed at the 2015 UN climate talks in Paris to keep global warming "well below" 2C above pre-industrial levels, while pursuing efforts to limit it to 1.5C, in order to limit the effects of climate change.
But the United Nations declared in September that the long-term 1.5C target would be missed in a matter of years.
Scientists say it is crucial to reduce greenhouse gas emissions from fossil fuels to limit the period of "overshoot" above 1.5C and bring temperatures back down as quickly as possible.

Riot police and drone crews in a “peacekeeping” drill

Russia sent motorized rifle, reconnaissance, electronic warfare, and drone units from its Central Military District, the CSTO said. Russia, this year’s chair, prioritized peacekeeping readiness and the joint biological protection and medical unit, a bloc general said.

Pressure on Belarus’s neighbors
In Latvia, armed, masked escorts from Belarus tried to force migrants across this month, the military said, and raiders stole border cameras hours later. Lithuania posted up to 100 soldiers on its border with Russia’s Kaliningrad, and in September NATO’s Italian jets downed a drone that crossed in from Belarus. On 9 October, Minsk summoned Ukraine’s envoy over an alleged drone strike on a Belarusian truck in Russia, and Kyiv rejected the “absurd accusations” of “an accomplice in the crime of aggression against Ukraine.”
Belarus keeps its army on alert
In September, Belarusian armor drilled near the Suwałki Gap, NATO’s land link to the Baltic states, and Lukashenka said the whole army would be checked, up to mobilization. On 12 October, he ordered a snap check of a 6th Separate Guards Mechanized Brigade battalion, state news agency BelTA reported. European spy agencies also warn of more Russian assassination plots against defense executives.
Ukraine’s intelligence still rates the threat from Belarus as low, but each new contingent, missile unit, and airborne brigade there widens what Kyiv and NATO’s eastern flank must watch.

Germany’s labour minister and co-leader of the centre-left Social Democrats (SPD), Bärbel Bas, has quit both posts, citing the death of her stepdaughter and subsequent political attacks against her, in a stinging blow to the fragile coalition government.
“After my stepdaughter’s death, I realised that I need time to come to terms with my grief,” Bas said in a statement posted on Facebook, without giving further details.
Explaining her departure from frontline politics, Bas explicitly blamed public broadsides against her as she grappled with the family tragedy, “unfortunately also from among the ranks of the coalition partner [Friedrich Merz’s conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU)]”.
She said the attacks “continued to intensify during this difficult time for me personally”.
Some CDU lawmakers had criticised Bas’s absences during a crunch phase of an economic reform drive seen as crucial to the teetering government’s survival, although it was widely known she had experienced a death in her immediate family.
Bas’s co-leader at the SPD, Lars Klingbeil, who is also Merz’s vice-chancellor and finance minister, expressed regret at her departure and criticised the sniping against her while she was mourning as “indecent”.
Klingbeil cancelled a planned trip to India to deal with the fallout from Bas’s resignation, and complained about a degradation of the national political discourse.
“We are competitors, and we need a culture of debate. But we also need a culture of mutual respect,” Klingbeil told reporters.
Merz, who has been fighting for his political survival after three disastrous state elections for his CDU last month, thanked Bas for “cooperation based on trust” in government and offered his condolences.
“As a father and grandfather, I can only imagine how deeply felt this loss is for you. I wish you and your family strength,” he wrote on X.
Alice Weidel, co-leader of the far-right Alternative für Deutschland, also gave Bas her sympathies but said her angry words towards the CDU demonstrated that Merz’s coalition government “is at its end”. She added: “We need a fresh start for Germany.”
The AfD, Germany’s biggest opposition party, is leading national opinion polls at about 30% after a strong showing in September’s regional elections, which also resulted in gains for the hard left.
Bas, who will remain an MP for Duisburg in the former Ruhr mining region, is a former president of the Bundestag lower house of parliament and one of the most experienced members of the SPD.
Her ministry oversees large parts of Germany’s costly social welfare system, which Merz has targeted for cuts.
While a representative of the party’s left wing, Bas was widely seen as a constructive team player able to bridge the kind of implacable policy disputes that have plagued Merz’s government since its inception in May 2025.
Her absence will now be keenly felt.
The coalition is deeply divided over plans to revive the sputtering economy, the EU’s largest, with Merz spearheading a pro-business savings drive and the SPD insisting on maintaining protections of workers’ rights and benefits.
The pension system is in particularly urgent need of reform as German society rapidly ages but plans to gradually lift the retirement age have met with angry resistance.
Approval ratings for Merz and his government have plunged over the course of the year, with voters fearing further deindustrialisation in the face of Chinese competition and steep rises in the cost of living.
Merz, a former corporate lawyer, is often perceived as haughty and out of touch, compounding his administration’s woes and giving rise to calls to replace him at the helm.
He has vowed to stay in office and fight for his policy agenda, saying it was the only way to beat back the “poison of authoritarianism” with extremists on the march.
The next general election is due in 2029 but five more state polls loom next year.
One of Merz’s cabinet ministers, Karin Prien, sounded the alarm last week, publicly calling for a change of course in the CDU away from Merz’s harsher stances and rhetoric.
“We bit our tongues for two or three years but that’s no longer an option,” the family affairs minister told Reuters ahead of a weekend party leadership meeting, referring to its centrist wing. “The ‘pure CDU’ approach (pursued by Merz) has failed.”

Reform has accused Labour of having "totally lost control" of the UK's borders, whilst Labour says small boat crossing figures have continued to come down in recent years.
Reform UK leader Nigel Farage has vowed to end the United Kingdom's asylum system for up to five years if the hard-right party gets into power.
Speaking at a press conference in Kent in southeastern England on Monday, Farage renewed his criticism of the government's handling of small boat crossings from mainland Europe as he outlined Reform's stance on those seeking asylum in Britain.
"We will end the asylum system for up to five years," Farage told the audience. "Why are we going to do that? Because we are in the most terrible mess as a country. We literally have no idea who is here, and we frankly can’t afford to take the risk."
"We want to get back to being a normal country," he continued. "A country that puts national security at the top of the agenda; a country that does everything it can to protect its own citizens; and a country that detains and deports people that come illegally."
He also reiterated Reform's pledge to end all small boat crossings within the first 100 days of government.
The next general election is not due to be held until 2029.
Small boat crossings by people looking to claim asylum in the UK have become an increasingly prominent and polarising topic in British politics.
Reform has accused Labour of having "totally lost control" of the UK's borders, whilst Labour says crossing figures have continued to come down in recent years - a line Farage has dubbed as "extraordinary."
Home Office figures show 1,066 migrants arrived in the UK on 15 boats since 5 October.
Late last month, a spokesperson for the department said the government had "made progress tackling the small boats."
"Crossings are down significantly, and we have just recorded the lowest number of summer arrivals since 2020," they said, adding that they "must go further" with countermeasures.
Data released by the Home Office in August showed asylum applications hit a peak of 109,662 in the year ending September 2025 but have since fallen - although they remain above levels seen between 2003 and 2022.
Brexit
In his speech, Farage also made sure to reference the UK's divisive 2016 Brexit vote to leave the European Union, which has once again been making headlines following British Prime Minister Andy Burnham's suggestion that rejoining the bloc was an option for the country.
"One of the biggest reasons for voting Brexit was seeing the madness of what was happening in Europe and saying, 'we don't want that to happen here,'" Farage said as he hit out at European immigration policy. "We need to get back control of our borders."
"Sadly, that hope has been completely betrayed by both Conservative and now a Labour government," he added.
Burnham has repeatedly signalled his intention to move the UK closer to Europe since taking office in July and recently said reentering the EU was one of a number of options moving forward.
The PM told an audience at the Labour Party's annual conference in Liverpool last month that Brexit had "done more harm than good" and that the UK needed a clear strategy on its long-term relationship with the EU.
Reform has ridden a wave of popularity spurred on by its anti-immigration stance, but its momentum has been knocked slightly in recent months amid a series of donations scandals involving Farage.

Spreading the flow: cruise tourism helps Europe protect local identity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
13:21:28 UTC
22:21:28 KST

Today's travellers want more than a photo. They want a story to tell. They want to immerse themselves in the life of places they visit, however fleeting their stay.
When cruise travellers step ashore, they are increasingly looking to connect with a place in a tangible and personal way. From cycling and snorkelling to walking tours to wine tasting, they want to pursue activities that help them to experience the authentic traditions and local culture that give a destination its unique identity.
Across Europe, tourism leaders and local communities are considering how destinations can protect their identity, safeguard the natural environment, ensure that tourism creates local value, and respond to growing visitor demand. As the EU develops its vision for sustainable tourism, understanding the importance of well-planned tourism is key to answering this question.
Take diversification, for example. Encouraging people to visit less well-known places can help to ease pressure on busier sites. Greece offers a compelling example. This is a country that draws visitors from all over the world to enjoy its historical wonders, and stunning coastlines and islands. At the same time, we see growing potential in some of its less famous islands. Since we added the island of Syros to our itineraries, our guests have praised its authenticity and cultural heritage, brought to life through the insight and knowledge of local guides.
Greece is not the only country to offer such potential. Europe is home to countless destinations with unique identities and rich heritage, many of which lie off the beaten track. This winter, for example, we will continue our collaboration with local authorities in the Canary Islands to bring our guests further inland to the villages of Garachico, Betancuria, Teguise and Tejeda. Local traditions, craftsmanship, and gastronomy remain central to everyday life in these villages, where visitors enjoy more meaningful experiences while also creating local value.
The key lesson is that these new itineraries were the result of extensive cooperation. Opening new places in the right way does not happen overnight and requires planning and strong local partnerships. These examples also show a link between the growing demand for more personal, authentic experiences and the need to achieve more balanced tourism flows.
Tourism management means understanding a destination’s vision, its capacity, and the infrastructure needed to support it. That means looking beyond the port to the roads, public transport, walking routes, cycling options, and visitor information. The city of Dubrovnik’s “Respect the City” programme, for example, features visitor management measures including digital data and street signage to recommend the best times to visit popular attractions and help people move through the historic old town more easily.
In fact, when people travel can be just as important as where they travel. Many remarkable destinations have just as much to offer in spring, autumn, or winter as they do at the height of summer. As travellers increasingly spread their trips across the year, there is an opportunity to support local economies beyond the traditional peak season. Off-peak cruise travel is a growing trend, and Europe is seeing the highest increase in share of cruise passengers sailing during off-peak months. This enables destinations to reduce dependence on seasonal peaks and build greater long-term resilience. As travel patterns evolve, policy should help destinations adapt to longer tourism seasons, supporting the infrastructure, services and workforce needed to welcome visitors throughout the year.
With careful planning, collaboration and the right systems in place, cruise tourism can provide a steady and controlled flow of guests. Cruise operators plan itineraries up to two years in advance, which gives destinations time to anticipate demand and manage capacity. The island of Mykonos in Greece shows how this works in practice. The implementation of a digital berthing system has shown how cruise traffic can be monitored and managed, helping support a more balanced distribution of visitors.
As Europe shapes its future tourism strategy, policy should be directed towards helping destinations to manage tourism more effectively.
This includes targeted investment in infrastructure. Better connectivity between transport networks, destinations and visitor experiences helps spread tourism benefits more widely while reducing pressure on the most visited places. Investment should also support development of data tools to support visitor flow management, while clear information at terminals with maps, suggested routes and links to public transport can help travellers discover a region in a more balanced way.
There should be greater support for destination management plans that bring together local authorities, transport providers, and tourism businesses around a shared vision for tourism development. Adopting a holistic approach towards coastal and island tourism, considering cruise, ferries and other forms of maritime travel, would help avoid bottlenecks and shape visitor flows in line with local priorities.
When visitors can explore throughout the year, discover lesser-known places and engage with local culture, tourism can deliver lasting benefits beyond the places that are most visited. With investment in long-term planning and collaboration between destinations and tourism partners, visitors can be welcomed in ways that support local value while preserving what makes each place special.
By Gianni Onorato, CEO MSC Cruises

President Volodymyr Zelensky told the Financial Times in an interview published on Oct. 3 that Beijing was helping Moscow build Rassvet, Russia’s version of SpaceX’s Starlink.
“We know that China works on satellites, works on the possibility of helping Russia with a system similar to Starlink,” he said, adding that “they are getting closer, and they are passing it on to Russia.”
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
What is the threat from Rassvet?
The system is being built by Moscow’s “Bureau 1440” and is designed to operate at an orbit height of around 800 kilometers (500 miles). It will include laser links between satellites and a ground based 5G network.
Following initial launches in July and August, milbloggers said the system was suffering from widescale technical difficulties. In September, Bureau 1440 said it was working on improved systems which Intellinews said was likely being done using Chinese assistance.
Zelensky said that Rassvet could be operational by early 2027, warning US President Donald Trump several times. Most recently, during September’s UN General Assembly in New York, Zelensky called for sanctions to be imposed on Russian and Chinese companies involved in its development.
Intellinews also reported that the satellite system could be part of the military technical cooperation as part of the “CRINK alliance” – an informal grouping between China, Russia, Iran, and North Korea. According to them, CRINK is an attempt to keep ahead of Western weapons systems development.
Ukraine’s TENCORE Bundles 4 Ground Drones in Single AI-Powered Ecosystem
The report suggested that such cooperation could see the fusion between Moscow’s missiles, drones, and other materials with China’s electronics capability.
In January 2023, Yury Borisov, then head of Roscosmos, said Russia had agreed to buy electronic components for rocket and space technology from China after Western sanctions prevented the import of critical supplies, saying that electronics was Russia’s “Achilles’ heel,” as per Interfax.
According to Reuters on Oct. 1, Denys Sienik, deputy chief of mission at the Ukrainian embassy in Washington, said that Russia was rapidly expanding the Rassvet satellite network, aiming to start operations in 2027, which would pose grave risks to Ukraine.
“They will be able to target Ukrainian targets in real time anywhere on our territory,” Sienik said.
Rassvet has currently deployed a relatively small number of satellites compared with the thousands that make up the Starlink constellation. Its capabilities over Ukraine were erratic as connectivity was dependent on the satellite being overhead. Its aim was to establish sufficient numbers that would allow continuous coverage of Russia’s military communications.
Satellite communications are critical
The war in Ukraine has shown that reliable satellite communications are an indispensable component of modern warfare to support command networks, reconnaissance, logistics, and operation of unmanned weapons systems.
Starlink has provided connectivity in areas where conventional communications infrastructure has been destroyed or disrupted – a facility of which was deprived in February 2026 when Elon Musk implemented a “whitelist” system that deactivated terminals not registered and verified by Ukrainian authorities.
The US has also limited Ukrainian access to Starlink for deep strikes into Russia. Meanwhile, China’s defense sector is said to be developing countermeasures to Starlink that could include laser weapons in order to attack and destroy satellites.
Previously on X, Anton Gerashchenko said that 2027 could see Rassvet move from experimental to fully operational, adding that the threat could extend to factories, airfields, ports, and energy sites in Europe where air defense systems would be unable to repel against Russian long-range drone swarms.

Neural network training system boosts Russian forces’ autonomy — expert
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
13:19:27 UTC
22:19:27 KST

MOSCOW, October 12. /TASS/. The introduction of a new system for training military-grade neural networks will, in the long term, make the Russian Armed Forces more autonomous, Alexander Stepanov, a military expert at the Institute of Law and National Security of the Russian Presidential Academy of National Economy and Public Administration (RANEPA), told TASS.
"This platform serves as a universal integrator for virtually the entire data stream generated by the combat use of various types of unmanned systems, which enables comprehensive training of neural networks, the establishment of unified standards and approaches for the operation of such systems, and their centralized development and deep learning. In doing so, we are laying the groundwork for seamless, end-to-end platforms for deploying various types of strike-reconnaissance drones, integrating them into a unified digital ecosystem, and ensuring maximum efficiency and coordination in their use. In this sense – beyond reconnaissance analytics and target designation – we are addressing the task of enhancing the autonomy of our army of the future, with an eye toward the deployment of autonomous robotic systems," the expert said.
According to him, the neural network training system could eventually be used to develop sixth-generation aircraft. "The platform’s scope will extend beyond the atmosphere to include aerospace, facilitating the training of next-generation systems designed to operate in low-Earth orbit and perform tasks such as anti-satellite operations. We are talking about sixth-generation systems – including hypersonic ones – capable of securing our airspace and, if necessary, neutralizing adversary spacecraft carrying various types of weaponry," Stepanov added.
On October 12, the Russian Defense Ministry announced that its specialists created a service that provides developers of unmanned systems with access to live recording data of drones’ combat deployment for the training of military-purpose neural networks. The new service provides developers of unmanned systems with access to a specialized repository containing prepared video footage of the results of the use of FPV drones and other copter drones and fixed-wing unmanned aerial vehicles.
In addition, the ministry’s specialists have created a unified data recognition classifier for machine learning AI systems, which allows developers to work with the database efficiently, in a structured manner, and according to a unified plan. The results of the work conducted by developers of military-purpose unmanned systems are uploaded back to the service, where the information is checked for completeness and compliance with the classifier format, enabling the Defense Ministry to use this dataset to create and train its neural networks.

Haaretz investigation reveals starvation, beatings and inhumane conditions in Israeli prisons
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
13:18:04 UTC
22:18:04 KST

Five Palestinian former detainees have reported starvation, beatings and inadequate medical care in Israeli prisons, according to a Haaretz investigation published on 8th October.
The investigation, by journalists Hagar Shezaf and Nir Hasson, was based on testimonies from five Palestinians released over the past 18 months. Their accounts describe conditions that they say have affected thousands of Palestinian prisoners since the war on the Gaza Strip began.
The testimonies covered Megiddo, Nafha and Ketziot prisons, as well as Ofer and Damon prisons and a military detention centre in Huwwara.
According to the investigation, the five former detainees said they had lost between 15 and 50 per cent of their body weight during detention. They also described physical assaults, collective punishment, repeated humiliation, widespread scabies infections and delays in receiving medical treatment.
They estimated that conditions for detainees from the Gaza Strip could be even harsher.
Among those who spoke to the newspaper was Palestinian journalist Ali Samoudi, 59, who said he had lost about half his body weight during a year in administrative detention. He was released without being formally charged, according to the investigation.
Samoudi described what he said were assaults inside the prisons, as well as shortages of food and medical care. He also reported suffering from several health problems after his release.
Israeli authorities said when they arrested him that they suspected him of transferring money to the Palestinian Islamic Jihad movement, an allegation he denied, according to Haaretz.
The investigation also included the testimony of journalist Samer Khweira, who said he had seen detainees suffering from malnutrition and scabies so severely that they struggled to move. He said he had also caught scabies during his detention.
Khweira added that he still did not know why he had been arrested. He was released without standing trial, according to the report.

Israel weighs sweeping budget cuts before election to salvage failed $1 billion Apache deal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
13:17:34 UTC
22:17:34 KST

Israel's Finance Ministry is preparing to seek parliamentary approval for emergency across-the-board cuts to government spending just two weeks before the October 27 election, in an unusual move aimed at securing urgent defense funding that could help revive a failed $1 billion deal to purchase 12 Apache attack helicopters from the United States.
The ministry is expected to request a special session of the Knesset, Israel's parliament, to approve cuts affecting all government ministries without exception. However, the proposal remains subject to a decision by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, with officials considering reductions totaling between 1 billion and 3 billion shekels.
One possibility being examined is redirecting funds from civilian ministries to rescue the Apache helicopter deal, which collapsed in recent days after Israel failed to sign the purchase agreement and transfer the required funding before the final deadline.
The deal fell through despite three extensions granted by U.S. aerospace manufacturer Boeing, as the Finance and Defense ministries remained at odds over funding equivalent to nearly 1 billion shekels.
The final deadline expired on October 7. With no signed contract or payment from Israel, Boeing informed Israeli officials that the helicopters would be offered to other customers waiting to purchase them.
The state budget currently contains no allocation for the helicopters, meaning that emergency spending cuts would be required if officials determine that the deal can still be salvaged.
The planned purchase, estimated at approximately $1 billion, had been in preparation for more than a year before collapsing amid the unresolved budget dispute.
The Finance Ministry is now awaiting Netanyahu's decision on the scope of the proposed cuts, as well as legal authorization to pursue such a measure so close to a national election.
"We are now waiting for the prime minister's approval and legal authorization to carry out cuts across all government ministries just days before the election," a senior Finance Ministry official said.
Two major questions remain unresolved: whether the Knesset can approve an across-the-board spending reduction so close to the election, and whether the government can secure a parliamentary majority to support it.
It also remains unclear whether the proposed cuts would cover only an initial payment required to revive the helicopter purchase or the full cost of the deal, estimated at approximately $1 billion.
Political opposition could complicate the effort. Several ministers have recently warned that their departments have already exhausted their capacity to absorb further reductions without affecting essential public services.
"We have reached a point where further cuts to our ministry's budget would seriously harm citizens," ministers have said.
That resistance could make securing approval particularly difficult, especially among ministers whose positions on party lists leave them unlikely to return to the Knesset after the election.
The government must now determine whether it can secure both the funding and parliamentary support needed to revive the Apache purchase, after the missed deadline put Israel's planned acquisition of the helicopters in jeopardy.

Australia’s Billionaire Problem and the ‘Corruption of the Democratic Process’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
13:17:00 UTC
22:17:00 KST

Mining magnate Gina Rinehart and close associates have reportedly gifted over AU$3 million to the One Nation Party in the last financial year, in cash and even an entire aircraft. “Reportedly,” as none of this has to be declared publicly until February 2027.
Clive Palmer splurged over AU$260 million on electioneering at the last three national polls, and then some. The land of the “fair go” has never been as egalitarian as it thinks. As long as billionaires dress down and speak rough, they can speak with a loud hailer and burn money to inflate their interests.
Yet even before the billionaires, Australia had a money-in-electoral-politics problem.
The two parties of government, Labor and Liberal, have been running business “forums” or “networks” and charging over AU$100,000 for membership, permitting access to front-benchers at regular gatherings. The electoral commission even held, bafflingly, that these sums were not disclosable “gifts,” because they bought something of value. That is the very form of privileged access that most citizens believe corrupts the democratic process.
Current national laws are laissez-faire, by world standards. Disclosure, as noted, is rooted in an untimely model from the paper-and-pen era of the 1980s. And it only applies to “gifts” over AU$17,300 per annum. Unlike the majority of states, there have been no caps on donations – aside from recent bans on “foreign source” donations, inspired by fears of Chinese influence. Nor have there been caps on national electioneering spending.
Hence the Rinehart, Palmer, and party network examples have all been lawful. And parties at the national level have long enjoyed public funding – “clean money,” but it has been extra cream rather than compensation for any limits.
That legal permissiveness is set to change, from sometime next year. For the first time, party and lobby group electioneering at national elections will be capped. So too will donations. Disclosure of donations will be at a lower level, and closer to “real time.” The change has been a long time coming.
The new laws – around 250 pages, including transitional rules – were the result of protracted negotiations across 2024. They passed in early 2025 with support from the Coalition. One upside of this is that buy-in, from both major parties, means the principles underlying caps and transparency are accepted for the foreseeable future.
This doesn’t mean the laws are ideal. The Greens support the principles, but (rightly) decry that the caps are too generous. The headline cap prevents donations of more than AU$50,000 to one political entity. But that obscures the ability to donate that amount to each division of a nationally organized party, several of its candidates and even a couple of sympathetic lobby groups. The effective cap is more like AU$1.6 million per annum.
The spending cap will be AU$90 million for a national party. That’s roughly at the Palmer level, which in his hands was both a record and a turnoff for voters. Within that total cap, there is a limit of AU$800,000 per targeted, marginal seat campaign. The “Teal” independents say that all the caps need redrafting, alleging unfairness to them. Party candidates benefit from the nationwide spending of their party, promoting its brand, policies, and leadership. Also, parties can fund that wider campaign with multiple donations from a single source, something independents cannot. There is a legitimate concern that rules shouldn’t artificially shield established parties, at a time when party politics is realigning.
Lobby groups will face an AU$11.25 million “electioneering” cap. So sugar daddies of the Teals will be able to do background electioneering supporting them. Interest groups will also still be able to mount unlimited single interest campaigns, providing they just promote their policy interests rather than boosting or attacking parties or candidates.
All-in-all, the new laws are better than nothing, if far from ideal. First, the limits are exceedingly generous. No one wants parties to be starved of resources. Party democracy beats billionaires directly campaigning – like Bloomberg and Musk in the U.S. party machines, however derided, have an ongoing interest in their long-term reputation. Channeling donations through parties, in the Australian way, insulates against corruption. It is far easier to buy a self-interested individual politician, as U.S. experience also shows.
The new laws will dampen the ability of incumbent and business friendly parties to rely on mega-donations, from corporations or unions, into their campaign budgets. In return, the regime will ramp up public funding to AU$5 per vote – or AU$10 per elector given we have House and Senate votes. In addition, mimicking state practice, parties (and independent MPs) will get a second flow of subsidies. In the form of “administrative” assistance, paid at a metric based on the number of Commonwealth MPs they have.
Second, the new laws are unduly complex. Admittedly, regulating the flow of money is hard. There are waterbed effects. So, to mix metaphors, regulation engages in a cat-and-mouse game. But these laws numb my brain, and I’ve spent 30 years studying the area. Parties, especially small or new ones, rely on volunteers at ground level. Not all can afford legal advice. The electoral commission will do well to focus not on missteps by small fry, but on lurks by the well-to-do and well-advised.
Finally, why is there a two-year delay for the new restraints and obligations to come into effect? The official explanation is that the commission needs time to gear up the new disclosure portal and educate itself and others as to the new complexities. One doesn’t have to be too cynical, though, to suspect another motive. Seeing Rinehart shower big money on One Nation – and its explosion in the polls – the major parties want time to catch up, to fill their election coffers ahead of a late 2027 or early 2028 poll. As St. Augustine quipped, “Lord make me chaste; just not yet.”
One thing to watch for is unintended effects. Will big money just reappear in other guises? Palmer, capped in what he can give to his own party, may just run more oblique campaigns directly through a corporate vehicle. Unions and business groups too may campaign more nakedly to help Labor and the Coalition. Astro-turfed groups may appear to strain the law.
Ultimately, there is no perfect regime of regulating money in electoral politics. Integrity values, the ideals of political equality and liberty, and the pragmatic need for fair party resourcing, have to be accommodated. Being part of a cat-and-mouse game, the new laws will inevitably be revisited by the end of the decade.

France Enters Sixth-Generation Fighter Race Solo, Unveils “Super Rafale” Plans
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
13:14:10 UTC
22:14:10 KST

- Category
- World
France Enters Sixth-Generation Fighter Race Solo, Unveils “Super Rafale” Plans
France is moving ahead with its own sixth-generation fighter jet after the collapse of its joint aviation project with Germany, while preparing an advanced “Super Rafale” equipped with artificial intelligence, upgraded engines, and next-generation weapons.
French Air and Space Force Chief of Staff General Jérôme Bellanger outlined plans to accelerate the country’s independent fighter development program and modernize its existing combat aircraft fleet, according to French newspaper Les Echos on October 11.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The move follows the breakdown of the Franco-German Future Combat Air System (FCAS) program, which was intended to produce a next-generation European fighter. France is now pursuing its own aircraft, designated ACF (Avion de Combat du Futur), replacing the previously planned New Generation Fighter (NGF) concept.
Development of the ACF is expected to enter a phase leading to a flying prototype in 2027, with work on an operational version scheduled to begin in 2029. Meanwhile, France plans to officially launch development of the Rafale F5, known as the “Super Rafale,” in December 2026.
The upgraded fighter will feature a new engine, advanced sensors, artificial intelligence, and a high-speed missile designed for France’s airborne nuclear deterrent. It will also serve as a technological foundation for the future sixth-generation aircraft.
France prepares AI-powered fighter and drone operations
France is also developing technology that will allow fighter jets to operate alongside unmanned aircraft.
Under the HypAIRion program, two Mirage 2000 fighters have been converted into flying laboratories to test artificial intelligence systems. The initiative aims to conduct its first coordinated flight involving a Rafale and an accompanying drone in 2028.
According to Les Echos, Dassault Aviation has already tested two AI algorithms aboard a Rafale and simulated a firing engagement involving a Harmattan AI drone.
The technology is intended to improve threat detection, targeting, and coordination between crewed aircraft and drones, allowing them to operate together against enemy air defenses.
France plans 60 more fighter jets by 2035
France also intends to expand its fighter fleet from approximately 170 aircraft to at least 230 by 2035—an increase of more than 35%.
Bellanger said the existing fleet is already being operated at a rate more than 15% above normal utilization levels, reflecting growing demands on French airpower.
The French Air and Space Force is also establishing two new squadrons at Cazaux Air Base. One will operate reconnaissance and strike drones, while the other will focus on high-altitude threats, including ballistic missiles and surveillance balloons.
According to Les Echos, France’s proposed 2027 defense budget includes up to €3 billion in procurement authorizations for the Rafale F5 program and another €2.7 billion for the ACF fighter. Both programs remain dependent on parliamentary budget approval.
The modernization effort comes as European air forces adapt to threats highlighted by Russia’s war against Ukraine, including the widespread use of attack drones and missiles.
The Franco-German Future Combat Air System (FCAS) had previously faced repeated delays due to conflicting national priorities and disagreements over industrial cooperation. Similar challenges affected the joint Main Ground Combat System (MGCS) tank project, raising broader concerns about the future of Franco-German defense cooperation.

Ukraine Struck Yandex Data Centers, Russian Bots Went Silent—Now Questions Are Mounting
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
13:14:05 UTC
22:14:05 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine Struck Yandex Data Centers, Russian Bots Went Silent—Now Questions Are Mounting
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy stated on October 12 that Russian bot activity on social media had declined following Ukrainian drone strikes on Yandex data centers.
Speaking at the Warsaw Security Forum in Poland, Zelenskyy highlighted Russia's extensive network of social media bots, which he described as a tool for destabilizing online discussions.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Zelenskyy noted that "everyone noticed" a reduction in Russian bot activity after Ukrainian drones struck data centers operated by Yandex, Russia's largest internet technology company, according to BBC News Ukrainian.
The president's remarks followed reports of a sharp decline in automated internet traffic originating from Yandex's network, although the available data does not establish whether Russian propaganda operations were affected.
According to an October 12 analysis by The Deep Dive, Cloudflare Radar data showed that automated HTTP requests from Yandex’s AS13238 network fell sharply after October 8 and approached zero on October 11.
At 02:00 UTC on October 11, automated requests stood at just 0.3% of the chart's maximum, compared with 88.2% at the same hour a week earlier. Cloudflare classified 99.6% of HTTP requests to HTML content from the network during the seven-day period as automated.
An HTTP request is a message sent by a browser, application, or automated program to a web server to retrieve information or perform an action. Automated requests can originate from search engine crawlers, monitoring systems, and other software, not necessarily social media bots.
Cloudflare Radar tracks this traffic using network identifiers called Autonomous System Numbers (ASNs). Yandex's AS13238 identifies part of the company's internet infrastructure, allowing researchers to measure requests originating from that network.
The reported decline from 88.2% to 0.3% represents a change in traffic relative to the chart's maximum, not a reduction in the number of social media accounts. Similarly, the 99.6% figure indicates the proportion of requests classified as automated, rather than the share associated with propaganda.
German technology publication t3n also documented the decline, reporting that bot traffic fell to approximately 0.4% of the previous week’s level before recovering to around 20% by the evening of October 11.
These measurements show a sharp reduction in automated network activity, but cannot establish whether Russian propaganda bots disappeared or whether damaged infrastructure stopped generating ordinary automated traffic.
The disruptions followed three reported drone strikes on Yandex facilities in Russia. A data center in Sasovo, Ryazan region, was struck overnight on October 8, followed by an attack on a facility in Kaluga on October 9.
On October 11, another strike forced a Yandex data center in the Vladimir region to shut down, according to the company. The disruptions affected Yandex services and applications operated by businesses relying on its cloud infrastructure.
The decline in automated traffic also prompted speculation about possible links between Russian digital infrastructure and online political activity in Europe, particularly involving Germany's Alternative for Germany (AfD) party.
Czech Member of the European Parliament Tomáš Zdechovský drew attention to claims that online activity supporting AfD had declined after the strikes. The Ukrainian publication The Page highlighted his October 11 remarks questioning whether disruptions to Russian infrastructure had affected the party's online support.
Ukraine's campaign against Yandex infrastructure also exposed the vulnerability of Russia's wider internet segment.
On the afternoon of October 8, hours after a fire broke out at the Sasovo facility, banks, retailers, mobile operators, transportation services, and major news websites suffered outages, with the most serious disruptions in Moscow and St. Petersburg.
The Sasovo site reportedly housed two of Yandex's three supercomputers. It shares an industrial site with the Sasta machine-tool plant, which was also struck overnight and is reportedly linked to supply chains supporting Russia's Iskander ballistic missile production.
