Time to tell US raider Saba Capital to get lost – again | Nils Pratley
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
13:14:04 UTC
22:14:04 KST

Here we go again: another episode in the Saba saga, the story of a New York hedge fund causing havoc in the UK investment trust sector by taking big stakes in funds and then demanding change, often in only vague terms.
The best that can be said about Saba Capital (and it’s not much) is that its belligerent boss, Boaz Weinstein, has disturbed the complacency that used to infect corners of the UK investment trust world, meaning companies that invest in other companies. It is now harder for a board to do nothing if the share price sits at a wide discount to the value of the underlying assets for long periods.
Too often, though, Saba’s assaults look self-interested, short-termist or damaging for UK investors. The attack on Baillie Gifford US Growth Trust, a FTSE 250 constituent usually known by its USA ticker, is all three.
Regular shareholders in USA have roundly told Saba to get lost twice in the past 18 months but they will have to do so again if they value what they own, which they should. The US raider, sitting on a near-30% stake, wants to install three of its nominees on the board via a vote at next week’s annual meeting.
On a long view, USA’s performance has been excellent: an annualised return of 16.7% since launch in 2018, beating the S&P 500 over the period and within the top 10% of all UK investment companies. The only reason an opening, of a sort, has appeared for Saba is because the 16.7%-a-year returns haven’t happened in a straight line. The pop in AI valuations in late-2022 means USA’s five-year statistics are less impressive.
But volatility is what investors accept when they buy into a strategy of backing high-growth US companies for the long-term. The portfolio is stuffed with stakes in big names in the AI world – Anthropic, Databricks, OpenAI, SpaceX and Stripe – that were acquired when the companies were smaller and sometimes still privately owned. A little bit of biodiversity in the UK investment landscape will be lost if USA falls under Saba’s control.
What would a Saba-dominated board do? It’s hard to say definitively because this is all Saba says: “If our nominees are elected, we would urge them to offer all USA shareholders a 100% cash exit at or near NAV [net asset value] – providing a long-overdue liquidity event.”
The absurdity of that proposal lies in the fact that the board of USA says it has already offered Saba what it supposedly wants – a chance to get out at a price nearly equivalent to the value of the assets. But the US hedge fund declined.
The suspicion is that Saba’s nominees could try to appoint Saba itself as manager, or wrap USA into a Saba-managed vehicle. And, note, Saba’s main funds in the US now trade on far wider discounts to asset value than USA’s relatively modest 3%.
Since Saba hasn’t spelled out much, all one can say is that its nominees cannot possibly be regarded as independent. One is a Saba employee; the other two are serial picks in Weinstein’s various campaigns.
Here is broker Investec’s assessment: “Saba offers no credible plan. Shareholders are being asked to give its nominees potential board control on the strength of a conditional, non-binding liquidity proposal, with no roadmap for the future manager, strategy or governance: vote first, then find out later what you’ve voted for.”
The choice, then, is between a known strategy that has been successful, with a few bumps, or a mystery ride under Saba’s tame directors. The analysis should not be hard: shareholders should stick with the existing board. Independence matters.
Here’s the tricky bit, however. Saba’s near-30% holding, plus 7.7% in the hands of assumed sympathiser Sessa Capital, means USA shareholders need to act. “Not voting is a vote for Saba,” says broker Panmure Liberum. “Support the board, or suffer the consequences,” warns Investec. Sound advice.
The annual meeting is on 23 October but, for anybody holding via an investment platform, the effective voting deadline can be as soon as this Wednesday. Those platforms – looking at Hargreaves Lansdown, AJ Bell and Interactive Investor – should be warning clients of deadlines right now. Preferably in red for danger.

Malaysia will raise the worsening transboundary haze crisis at an upcoming ASEAN foreign ministers’ meeting, seeking stronger regional mechanisms to tackle pollution from forest fires in neighboring Indonesia, Foreign Minister Mohamad Hasan said Monday.
The issue will be discussed ahead of the 49th ASEAN Summit in Manila next month, Malaysian state news agency Bernama reported.
Mohamad said existing ASEAN disaster management mechanisms did not adequately address transboundary haze.
“We already have an ASEAN mechanism for natural disasters, but haze is not included or classified as a natural disaster,” he told reporters in Sepang.
Indonesia has deployed about 60,000 personnel to fight the fires, but thick smoke has severely restricted aerial firefighting operations, Mohamad said.
He said Indonesian officials had informed him that 34 airplanes and 34 helicopters were unable to operate because of poor visibility.
Firefighting efforts have also been hampered by the remote locations of burning areas, limited water supplies and persistent underground peat fires.
Mohamad said cloud-seeding operations were currently impossible because suitable rain-bearing clouds were unavailable.
He acknowledged Indonesia's efforts to contain the fires but urged more effective action, citing the impact on Malaysian communities.
Transboundary haze caused by forest and peatland fires has repeatedly affected Southeast Asia, particularly Malaysia, Singapore and Indonesia, raising concerns about public health and regional environmental cooperation.

Americans Hall and Woodford win economics Nobel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
13:13:25 UTC
22:13:25 KST

Portraits of Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford are displayed on a screen after they were announced as this year’s Nobel economics prize laureates. (AP Photo)
American economists Robert Hall and Michael Woodford were awarded the Nobel economics prize on Oct. 12 for their work on how monetary and fiscal policy can help stabilise fluctuations in the economy.
“The laureates’ work has provided us with a stable theoretical foundation for the models that are now used by central banks and governments around the world,” the jury at the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences said in a statement.
“With them, we are better equipped to deal with shocks in the economy, such as energy crises or sudden changes in how much households consume,” John Hassler, chair of the prize committee, said in the statement.
During the oil crises in the 1970s, the existing Keynesian models long used to determine when and how measures should be implemented to tackle recessions or other economic fluctuations no longer worked.
That prompted Hall and Woodford to develop new tools for understanding which policy responses could be the most effective.
“Rather than basing the models on statistical links between macroeconomic variables, such as inflation, production and consumption, they chose to build them on a microeconomic foundation,” the academy jury said.
The economics prize is the only Nobel not among the original five created. It was created instead through a donation from the Swedish central bank in 1968.
Like the other Nobels, the economics prize consists of a diploma, a gold medal and a $1.2 million cheque.
The laureates will receive their prizes at formal ceremonies on Dec. 10, the anniversary of the death in 1896 of scientist Alfred Nobel, who created the prizes in his will.

South Korea decided on October 8 to recall Ambassador Park Ki-chang from Ukraine. It’s Seoul’s first ambassador recall since 2008, when South Korea withdrew its envoy from Japan over a territorial claim to the Dokdo islets.
The decision came 15 days after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy disclosed the transfer of two captured North Korean soldiers to South Korea in a speech to the United Nations General Assembly. Seoul says the two governments had agreed to keep the transfer confidential. However, Kyiv first denied any such agreement before its Foreign Ministry attributed the dispute to differing interpretations.
The two soldiers at the center of the dispute were captured in January 2025 in the Kursk region of Russia. North Korea had sent troops there to support the Russian invasion of Ukraine. The captured soldiers arrived in South Korea in mid-September after saying they wished to settle there.
Zelenskyy’s public announcement of their arrival drew a response from South Korean President Lee Jae-myung on September 24 in a post on the social platform X. He called the disclosure deeply regrettable. Lee also cited the problems that disclosure could cause.
Kyiv rejected that account the next day. Dmytro Lytvyn, a communications adviser to Zelenskyy, denied that any confidentiality agreement existed.
The South Korean presidential office voiced strong regret over the disclosure and Ukraine’s denial on September 27. It demanded an official explanation and apology. It also signaled that additional measures were under consideration. Seong Ghi-hong, senior presidential secretary for public relations, said that Ukraine’s had sought the secrecy itself. He added that Kyiv had cited possible criticism at home for giving up a chance to swap the soldiers for Ukrainian prisoners held by Russia.
The next day, First Vice Foreign Minister Park Yoon-joo summoned Andrii Vieshkin, who is Ukraine’s acting ambassador in Seoul. The vice minister repeated the demands to him.
Still, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha described the dispute on October 1 as a diplomatic misunderstanding. Sybiha did not offer the public apology that Seoul had demanded.
In a post on X the next day, Lee wrote that Ukraine had made the South Korean head of state a “liar” by denying the agreement. He also warned of further measures unless Kyiv publicly apologized.
Lee also broadened his criticism to remarks by Kyrylo Budanov, head of the Ukrainian presidential office. Budanov had warned in an interview on September 27 that tension along the inter-Korean border was rising by the day. Days earlier, suspected North Korean mines had exploded inside the Demilitarized Zone between the two Koreas and wounded three South Korean soldiers. So Lee accused Kyiv of speaking of an imminent clash between the two Koreas as if wishing for war.
On October 6, Foreign Minister Cho Hyun told lawmakers that a message from Ukraine had included words of apology. However, he said it fell somewhat short of the expectations of Seoul.
Kyiv characterized the message differently. Foreign Ministry spokesperson Heorhii Tykhyi said on October 7 that Ukraine had expressed regret over the public criticism between the two countries. The spokesperson also attributed the dispute to differing interpretations of the confidentiality arrangement.
A separate dispute surfaced in the same week. Vladyslav Vlasiuk, the presidential commissioner of Ukraine for sanctions policy, said on October 6 that fuel shipments from South Korean ports had helped Russia offset refinery losses caused by Ukrainian strikes. The South Korean presidential office rejected the claim on October 7.
In the announcement recalling Ambassador Park the next day, the South’s Foreign Ministry said it hoped to settle pending issues through continued consultations with Ukraine.
The Foreign Ministry of Ukraine responded that diplomacy should prevail over emotions. Tykhyi added that diplomatic efforts were underway through private channels.
Park returned home on October 10.
Seoul had good reasons to want the transfer kept quiet. According to Seoul, the families of the two men remain in North Korea, where they could face reprisals over their relatives’ decision to defect.
The National Intelligence Service also told lawmakers on September 30 that the disclosure appeared aimed at building public support in South Korea for arms supplies to Ukraine. Seoul has supported Ukraine with financial and humanitarian aid but not with lethal weapons, even after North Korea began sending tens of thousands of soldiers to fight for Russia.
If Ukraine’s government was hoping to bolster its image with South Koreans, it badly miscalculated. Instead, Kyiv has lost the trust of Seoul, and the harm cannot be repaired in private. Because the disclosure was public, a message passed between ministers cannot solve the problem.
Meanwhile another Ukrainian official opened a second dispute. Vlasiuk raised the fuel claim on October 6 while Seoul was still waiting for an apology. The South Korean government says petroleum products are not on its list of controlled exports. Whatever the merits, the claim muddied a dispute that Kyiv had started. The fuel question belongs in a separate channel on sanctions compliance.
With that question set aside, Seoul has demanded three things. Kyiv should acknowledge that a confidentiality agreement existed. The Ukrainian government should offer an official, public apology. And Kyiv should commit to steps that prevent a recurrence.
Park may return to Kyiv only after Ukraine does all three.

Can South Korea and Ukraine resolve their diplomatic spat over North Korean POWs?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
13:10:00 UTC
22:10:00 KST

Can South Korea and Ukraine resolve their diplomatic spat?
October 12, 2026
South Korea's ambassador to Kyiv returned to Seoul on Saturday, his recall the latest in a series of tit-for-tat actions that have severely strained bilateral ties.
The sudden deterioration in their relationship can be traced back to September 23, when Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told the United Nations General Assembly in New York that Ukraine had transferred two captured North Korean soldiers to South Korea.
The soldiers had been captured by Ukrainian forces in the Russian Kursk region in January 2025 as they fought alongside Russian troops.
The South Korean government immediately expressed its anger at Zelenskyy's revelation, insisting that the two governments had reached an agreement to keep the transfer of the two men in mid-September a secret.
Kyiv hit back, by saying that no confidentiality agreement had been in place, to which South Korea accused Ukraine of effectively lying and demanded an official explanation and an apology.
Ukraine has attempted to smooth over what it has called a "diplomatic understanding," but stopped short of the public apology that was expected in Seoul.
Then, reports emerged last week that a close adviser to Zelenskyy had said that more than 176,000 tons of diesel and other energy products were shipped to Russia from South Korean ports in July and August of this year, which would be a breach of international sanctions.
The office of president Lee Jae Myung in Seoul denied the accusation, and two days later recalled its ambassador to Kyiv.
What is behind Seoul's need for secrecy?
There are several reasons why South Korea wanted to keep the POW transfer secret, Erwin Tan, a professor of international politics at Hankuk University, told DW.
"The first was that revealing that the POWs had been repatriated to South Korea would result in Pyongyang retaliating against the families of the men for surrendering," Tan said.
"Seoul also wanted to maintain a channel for communication with Pyongyang," Tan said. "This is a major consideration for the left-leaning wing of Korean politics, which includes President Lee and has historically favored seeking rapprochement with the North."
Kim Sang-woo, a former politician with the left-leaning South Korean Congress for New Politics and now a member of the board of the Kim Dae-jung Peace Foundation, agrees that the South Korean government wanted to avoid "friction" with the North.
But Kim pointed out that it was always very likely that both Moscow and Pyongyang would find out about the transfer sooner or later and that Lee was being criticized in some quarters at home for appearing weak.
"There is criticism that Lee's administration is effectively appeasing the North, that it has become too soft, and that is a very worrisome situation," Kim said. Yet he admits to being surprised at how quickly the issue escalated.
"I think Lee was very angry that he was publicly being accused of lying about the agreement and it rapidly grew into a very messy confrontation," he said.
Has Zelenskyy's approach backfired?
While it is unclear why Zelenskyy used his high-profile UN speech to announce the repatriation of the two POWs, Kim believes it may have been a calculated move to win more support from Seoul.
Kyiv could have carried out a prisoner swap with the Russians and won the freedom of some of its own men in return.
But, Kim pointed out, Ukraine instead chose to accede to Seoul's request in the hope that South Korea would respond with additional financial and possibly even military support. That move appears to have backfired.
Professor Tan anticipates that the two governments will continue to "vent steam" over the issue.
"Given the high profile nature of the mutual accusations, both sides will probably engage in a mutual blame game for the immediate future, but I doubt that it will turn into a long-term case of mutual acrimony," he said.
"I anticipate that after the furor has died down and the press is looking for the next new story, both sides will quietly resume contact on the basis of mutual pragmatism."

French supermarkets suffer refrigerator shutdown after ‘unprecedented’ cyberattack
- French supermarket chains were hit by an “unprecedented” cyberattack that remotely defrosted refrigerators in hundreds of stores, spoiling fresh and frozen food.
- E. Leclerc, Intermarche and Cooperative U confirmed damage, while Paris prosecutors opened an investigation into the large-scale attack and related fire outbreaks.
- Officials said the attack exposed food security risks and showed the danger of connected industrial equipment, with teams working to restore systems and prevent wider spread.
AI generated
PARIS – Major French supermarket chains on Oct 12 said they had been hit by a cyberattack that caused their refrigerators to defrost in hundreds of stores, forcing spoilt food to be thrown away and raising concerns about food security.
Top retailers E. Leclerc, Intermarche and Cooperative U confirmed to AFP they had been hit by the cyberattack that Cooperative U’s chief executive described as “unprecedented”.
“Food security requires more attention at all levels,” said the EU’s food and agriculture commissioner Christophe Hansen on X, condemning the attack and saying such “exploitation of food” was now a “reality”.
At least 300 shops of Intermarche or its Netto brand were targeted, along with over 100 Cooperative U outlets, and several E. Leclerc stores, the retailers told AFP in separate statements.
Paris prosecutors confirmed the attack, which reportedly also hit other major chains, and also indicated it had prompted outbreaks of fire.
BFM TV said hackers “managed to remotely trigger the forced defrosting of the refrigeration systems in numerous stores”.
Those branches that were affected will have to “throw away all of the products” that are fresh and frozen, Intermarche told AFP.
Specialist French retail sector news website Je Bosse en Grande Distribution said other retail giants Carrefour Market and Monoprix were affected but the companies have yet to confirm this.
E. Leclerc confirmed to AFP “that a cyberattack affected one of its refrigeration equipment suppliers”, resulting in “repercussions on the operation of refrigeration systems in several stores”.
According to a source close to the issue, the refrigeration control systems from Danish manufacturer Danfoss were targeted.
Danfoss told AFP in a statement that most of the affected equipment were “legacy” products which “no longer receive software or security updates”.
It said its AK-SM800 and AK-SC355 fridge regulator systems were notably affected, with a version of the former using “outdated firmware”.
It added that it had long advised supermarkets to update from those models. Danfoss gave no figures of how many systems were affected.
‘Unprecedented’
A person close to French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said France’s cybersecurity agency had already identified “a vulnerability in software supplied by a Danish company and has contacted the vendor”.
“It is liaising with its European counterparts, as other countries may be affected,” and is seeking “to identify other French companies involved in order to alert them” and “prevent the spread”, the source added.
The chief executive of Cooperative U, Dominique Schelcher, described the attack as “unprecedented” and confirmed the cyberattack had affected refrigeration systems since night-time on Oct 11.
“Targeting equipment essential to the preservation of fresh products and to the food supply of the French people is extremely serious and is unprecedented. It is unacceptable,” he wrote on X.
He added that the company’s teams are “fully mobilised” to restore the situation as quickly as possible.
“An investigation will be necessary to shed full light on this attack,” he added.
The office of the Paris prosecutor confirmed to AFP that an investigation has been opened into “the large-scale cyberattack affecting the refrigerators of several major food retail chains across France”.
The probe will help “identify the victims and establish the link with the damage they reported in terms of foodstuff losses and the outbreak of fires”, the prosecutor’s office said.
Intermarche condemned the food waste and financial losses resulting from the attack, without providing figures, and warned there could be issues with insurance policies which do not “cover this type” of in-store incident.
BFM TV said temperatures were “altered remotely, resulting in the destruction of stocks of fresh and frozen products”.
‘A level of sophistication’
The incident comes against the background of growing concern over the potential havoc that can be caused in Europe in all sectors by cyberattacks by malicious actors.
President Emmanuel Macron, a strong supporter of Ukraine in its fight against the Russian invasion, in September ordered measures to protect France’s critical infrastructure from Russian “hybrid attacks”.
Industrial equipment such as refrigeration units, long isolated from the internet, are now connected via sensors or remote monitoring systems, Antoine Hautin of cybersecurity consultancy Almond told AFP.
By likely affecting hundreds of units simultaneously, the attack demonstrated “a certain level of sophistication”, he added. AFP

Shin Bet's answer to 7 October failures is an 'Islam school'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
13:09:23 UTC
22:09:23 KST

Breadcrumb
Shin Bet's answer to 7 October intelligence failures is to 'study Islam', not Israeli occupation
Israel's domestic intelligence agency, Shin Bet, is planning to establish a school of Islamic studies following its failure to anticipate the Hamas-led attacks on 7 October 2023, focusing on religious ideology rather than the decades of Israeli occupation, dispossession and violence that shaped the emergence of Hamas and other Palestinian factions.
The initiative, reported by the Israeli news website Walla, raises questions about Israel's attempts to explain its intelligence failures by a lack of understanding of Islam, rather than examining the political realities that gave rise to Hamas and the institutional failures that allowed the attack to take place.
The project is being spearheaded by Shin Bet chief David Zini and will provide specialised education on Islam, its different schools of thought and Palestinian society to intelligence personnel working across various departments.
The school will operate alongside Shin Bet's existing Arabic-language training programme, which also provides instruction to some Israeli military personnel.
According to Walla, the project will involve academics, researchers, specialist institutions and current and former senior intelligence officials, with its curriculum tailored to the operational challenges facing the agency.
The initiative follows internal investigations into Israel's intelligence failures preceding 7 October, when Palestinian fighters breached the Gaza perimeter and attacked Israeli military positions and communities.
Despite possessing extensive intelligence about Hamas's preparations, Israeli security agencies failed to anticipate the scale and timing of the assault.
Walla reported that one conclusion drawn by Israel's intelligence establishment was that officials lacked sufficient understanding of Islam, Palestinian culture and Hamas's ideological foundations, particularly in Gaza.
Investigators reportedly identified shortcomings in their understanding of the movement's development following the release of Hamas leader Yahya Sinwar from Israeli prison in 2011, as well as the continuing influence of the organisation's founder, Sheikh Ahmed Yassin.
Sheikh Yassin was assassinated in an Israeli airstrike in 2004, while Sinwar was killed by Israeli forces in Gaza in October 2024.
A senior Israeli intelligence official told Walla: "We did not realise the extent to which Hamas hates Israel, how unwilling it is to accept any compromise, or how strong and prepared it was before 7 October, even though the warning signs were clearly visible."
However, framing Hamas primarily through its religious ideology risks reducing a movement rooted in the Palestinian experience of occupation to a question of Islamic beliefs.
Hamas was established in 1987 during the First Palestinian intifada uprising against Israeli occupation, nearly two decades after Israel occupied the West Bank, East Jerusalem and Gaza in 1967.
Although the movement emerged from the Palestinian branch of the Muslim Brotherhood and draws on Islamist ideology, its formation and development were closely related to the Palestinian struggle against Israeli military rule, territorial dispossession and the denial of national self-determination.
Hamas has previously offered Israel a long-term truce if it withdraws from the entirety of the West Bank and Gaza, while signalling its acceptance of a Palestinian state only on those territories.
Its political and armed activities have arguably been shaped by continued occupation, repeated Israeli military offensives, the blockade of Gaza and the failure of successive political efforts to secure Palestinian statehood.
Treating Islam as the central explanation for Hamas's actions therefore risks confusing the movement's ideological identity with the political and historical conditions that produced it.
The focus on Islam also comes amid the Netanyahu government's growing cultivation of far-right political movements in Europe, including parties and figures associated with Islamophobia and hostility towards Muslim immigration.
Israeli officials, particularly Diaspora Affairs Minister Amichai Chikli, have increasingly sought alliances with European nationalist parties around a shared opposition to alleged "radical Islam". The outreach has included France's National Rally, Spain's Vox and Austria's Freedom Party, as Israeli leaders increasingly portray the country as a defender of Western civilisation against an alleged Islamist threat.
Hamas's 7 October assault on Israel took place in a year when Israeli violence in the West Bank and East Jerusalem had already killed more Palestinians in any full year since the UN began recording fatalities in 2005.
Israeli military raids, particularly in Jenin and Nablus, had intensified, while illegal settlement expansion and settler attacks placed growing pressure on Palestinian communities.
In Gaza, Israel had launched another major military offensive in May 2023, carrying out hundreds of airstrikes. The escalation left 33 Palestinians dead, including at least 12 civilians, according to the UN, and damaged thousands of homes.
These developments came against the backdrop of Israel's blockade of Gaza, imposed in 2007, which had devastated the territory's economy and severely restricted the movement of its population.
Just a day before the 7 October attack, The New Arab reported that 2023 had already become the deadliest year for Palestinian children in the occupied West Bank, with Israeli forces killing 47 children since January, surpassing the 45 killed throughout 2022.
Tensions had also intensified at the Al-Aqsa Mosque compound in occupied East Jerusalem, while the prospect of Saudi-Israeli normalisation threatened to further marginalise the Palestinian national question.
Israel's occupation overlooked in 7 October reckoning
Hamas named its operation "Al-Aqsa Flood", citing Israeli actions at the holy site, the blockade, Palestinian prisoners and the occupation among its stated grievances.
The focus on religion risks obscuring a more immediate explanation for Israel's failure to anticipate the attack, as its intelligence agencies had already possessed detailed warnings about Hamas's plans.
Israeli investigations into the 7 October attack have exposed failures that went far beyond a lack of cultural or religious understanding.
Israeli intelligence reportedly possessed detailed information about Hamas's plans, including a document outlining an assault remarkably similar to the one eventually carried out, but senior officials dismissed the scenario as unrealistic.
In September 2026, an investigation published by Haaretz revealed that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had also reportedly received a direct warning from UAE President Mohammed bin Zayed around 10 days before the attack that Hamas was preparing a major offensive.
According to the report, Netanyahu reassured the Emirati leader that Israel was prepared for any scenario but failed to pass the warning to senior Israeli security officials. An Emirati source subsequently confirmed the reported conversation to The Times of Israel, although Netanyahu's office denied it had taken place, calling the allegations an "absolute lie".
Warnings from Israeli surveillance personnel stationed near Gaza were also reportedly ignored, raising questions about institutional complacency and the failure to act on intelligence already available, rather than simply a lack of understanding of Hamas's ideology.
Despite these revelations, three years after the attack, Israel has still not established an independent state commission of inquiry into the political, military and intelligence failures surrounding 7 October, amid opposition from Netanyahu and disputes over how such an investigation should be conducted.

UN rapporteur joins weekly hunger strike over Iran's execution surge and protest crackdown

2026-10-12

Gina Romero Rodríguez, the United Nations Special Rapporteur on Freedom of Peaceful Assembly and of Association (FoAA), is to join a weekly hunger strike on Tuesday to protest the Islamic Republic’s ongoing human rights violations and use of the death penalty to suppress dissent, she announced on X/Twitter on Monday.
Though Rodriguez did not respond to a request for comment from The Jerusalem Post, in a video statement on social media, she confirmed that she would be joining the longstanding weekly “no-execution Tuesday hunger strike” against both the use of the death penalty and the continued denial of the right to free assembly in Iran.
“The death penalty is being used against people for exercising the rights of freedom of assembly, association, and expression, as well as their political rights,” she said, recalling how in January the Islamic regime’s security forces brutally murdered tens of thousands of protesters and have since continued to execute those detained in connection with the demonstrations.
While human rights groups have said upward of 30,000 were killed, Iran’s internet blackout and continued suppression efforts have prevented international groups from reaching an exact figure on those killed. Rodriguez also noted that at least 46 political prisoners and protesters have been executed since March 19.
“This is the highest concentration of political executions in Iran in nearly 40 years. Protesters have been unlawfully detained, and their cases have been riddled with procedural unfairness and underlying gross human rights violations, including torture, enforced disappearances, sexual violence, coerced confessions, and denial of access to lawyers of their choosing,” she said.
“The execution and planned executions of young people, including students and athletes, show how protests and peaceful political associations are being turned into capital offenses and used to stifle dissent.”
Rodgriguez urges international community to join hunger strike
Urging the international community to join her in the hunger strike, she said she wanted to express solidarity with the protesters killed in Iran, including Alireza Sepahi, 24; Alireza Raisi, 21; Siavash Jamshidi Kheirabadi [age unknown]; Ali Hemmati, 21; and Majid Nik-Andish, 25; as well as 26-year-old law graduate Mehdi Khanaki.
Rodriguez also hoped to draw international attention to the cases of former boxing champion Mohammad Javad Vafaie Sani, 30, 18-year-old Shervin Bagherian, and brothers Hamidreza and Abdolreza Fathi [ages unknown], all of whom are on death row.
Sani, whose request for a retrial was rejected in December last year, was arrested in 2020 for taking part in nationwide democracy protests in 2019 and for allegedly supporting the opposition group the People’s Mojahedin Organization of Iran.
Bagherian was sentenced to death on the charge of moharebeh (“enmity against God”) in connection with the Alikhani Square case, in which dozens were arrested over clashes with security forces in Tehran during the January protests. He turned 18 only days before he was arrested at his home and tortured into confessing on state television.
Corruption on earth, enmity against God
The Fathi brothers were sentenced by the Shiraz Revolutionary court to death on charges of “corruption on earth” over allegations of involvement in the death of a Basij member and damage to public property. According to Hengaw, both brothers were tortured into confessing, leaving one of them with a broken arm.
According to a report released by the Human Rights Activists News Agency (HRANA) on Friday, at least 2,003 people were executed in Iran between October 10, 2025, and October 8, 2026, including at least four juvenile offenders. During the same period, at least 230 additional people were sentenced to death.
The majority of the documented executions, 95%, were carried out without any announcement from authorities. Nine of the executions were carried out in public.
HRANA’s documentation found that 57.56% of those executed had been convicted of murder and 36.25% of drug-related offenses. Political and security-related charges of moharebeh or baghi (“armed rebellion”) accounted for 2.4% of executions, while 1.1% involved other or unknown charges.
A further 0.9% were executed on security-related charges, including espionage, assassination, or bombing; 0.8% for rape; 0.8% for non-political moharebeh; and 0.15% for corruption on Earth.
Of 69 people executed on political and security-related charges over the past year, 35 were killed in connection with the January 2026 protests.

14-year-old shoots principal and teacher at French school after bringing shotgun in guitar case
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
13:07:36 UTC
22:07:36 KST

A 14-year-old boy opened fire Monday morning at a school in Aubagne, near Marseille in southern France, lightly wounding the principal and a teacher. The teenager arrived at the middle school armed with a shotgun that was reportedly concealed inside a guitar case and fired several shots at staff members. The principal was wounded in his thighs and the teacher was also struck in the thigh, but neither suffered life-threatening injuries. A staff member overpowered and disarmed the teenager, who was subsequently arrested by police. His motive remains unclear.
The shooting occurred at Joseph Lakanal college, which has approximately 700 students. According to local media reports, the teenager entered the school carrying a 12-gauge shotgun concealed in a guitar case.
Jacques Witkowski, a government official who arrived at the scene, told AFP that "the suspect, for reasons that remain unknown, fired at the principal, who was struck in the thighs by a spray of shotgun pellets."
"He then fired a second shot at a teacher, who was struck by a pellet in her thigh, and fired a third shot in a hallway before a staff member overpowered him," Witkowski said.
The 53-year-old principal and 37-year-old teacher received medical treatment and were taken to hospitals in the area. Authorities said neither suffered life-threatening injuries and no students were hurt.
The person who stopped the gunman was a school staff member responsible for extracurricular activities. According to reports, he rushed at the teenager, overpowered him and took away his weapon before police arrived. The teenager was arrested and taken in for questioning.
The shooting sparked panic at the school, with many students calling their parents after hearing gunfire and witnessing disturbing scenes. Worried parents rushed to the school to pick up their children, and many remained outside into the afternoon as police and emergency responders worked at the scene.
Maryline, the mother of a student at the school, told AFP about the phone call she received from her daughter shortly after the shooting.
"She called me in a panic. She said there was blood everywhere and that it was an attack. I left work and tried to calm her down. When I arrived, I was told the boy had been arrested," she said.
Local authorities established an emergency response center at the school and arranged psychological support for students and staff who witnessed the incident. Security forces cordoned off the area, and the municipality urged residents to stay away from the school to allow emergency crews to work without interference.
Police are investigating what prompted the teenager to open fire, how he obtained the shotgun and how he managed to bring it into the school.
According to Witkowski, the suspect is a ninth-grade student who had not previously come to the attention of authorities for criminal activity or extremism.
"He is a student at the school, in ninth grade, with no known history of criminal behavior or radicalization," the official said.
He stressed that investigators had yet to determine what motivated the teenager to shoot at school staff.
Aubagne Mayor Jean-Pierre Squillari said the suspect had been described as a quiet teenager. He added that the boy's father had recently requested a meeting with teaching staff, although it was unclear whether that request had any connection to the shooting.
The incident came amid a wave of protests by high school students in France over issues including the state of the education system and learning conditions. Some demonstrations have involved clashes with police and incidents of violence, but authorities were quick to clarify that there was no indication of a connection between the protests and the Aubagne shooting.
"The middle school was not affected by the high school student protest movement," local police said.
French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu instructed Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez and Education Minister Édouard Geffray to visit the scene. Sabrina Roubache, the minister responsible for education and vocational training, was also expected to visit the school.
The education minister condemned the attack, saying it reflected the spread of violence in French society, and called for a collective effort to combat the problem.
Knife attacks more common at French schools
School shootings are relatively rare in France, but numerous knife attacks have occurred at educational institutions in recent years.
In April, a high school student was seriously wounded in a stabbing in Ancenis, western France. Two months earlier, in February, a 14-year-old student stabbed an art teacher at a school in Sanary-sur-Mer in southern France, leaving her seriously injured. According to authorities, the teenager stabbed the teacher several times during class in front of other students.
In September 2025, a former student entered a horticultural high school in Antibes, southern France, and stabbed a teacher and a student.
In June 2025, a particularly serious attack occurred in Nogent, eastern France, when a 14-year-old student stabbed a 31-year-old school staff member to death during a police inspection of students' bags at the school entrance. The killing shocked the country and prompted calls for tighter controls to prevent weapons from being brought into educational institutions.
Two months earlier, in April 2025, a knife-wielding high school student killed a 15-year-old girl and wounded three other people at a school in Nantes, western France.
The attack reignited public debate in France over the safety of students and teachers, violence among young people and the need to strengthen security measures at schools.

The state is suing a former IDF company commander for more than NIS one million to recover benefits paid and expected to be paid following sexual offenses he committed against soldiers under his command, the prosecution announced Monday.
The lawsuit, filed on behalf of the Defense Ministry in Nazareth Magistrate’s Court, seeks to hold former captain Ofir Menachem financially responsible for the public cost of the harm he caused. Menachem was convicted after pleading guilty to offenses involving two female subordinates, sentenced to imprisonment and demoted to private. Prosecutors described the civil claim as the first of its kind.
In the lawsuit, the state argues that Menachem’s position as a commander placed him under a heightened duty to protect his subordinates and uphold their trust. Instead, prosecutors say, he used his rank and authority to exploit them, breaching both his obligations toward the subordinate women and public trust in the IDF.
The military appeals judgment describes how Menachem mixed sexual advances with discussions about the soldiers’ service and requests for leave.
According to the judgment, one soldier approached Menachem in May 2022 seeking permission for regular evenings at home because of personal circumstances. During their conversation, he made sexual comments and asked questions of a sexual nature. The soldier felt obliged to participate in the conversation so that he would approve her requests, the judgment recounts.
Former IDF commander exploited authority over female subordinates
Menachem subsequently invited her to his room and repeatedly approached her about meeting with him. She put him off with excuses and feared how he would treat her as her commander if she rejected him. The judgment also describes him telling the two women that they were competing for the same position.
The original indictment was filed in September 2023. Following mediation, Menachem pleaded guilty to an amended indictment in July 2024. His convictions included sexual offenses involving exploitation of authority in military service, sexual harassment through abuse of that authority, and conduct unbecoming.
In February 2025, the military court sentenced him to 22 months in prison, imposed suspended prison terms, demoted him to private, and ordered him to pay the victims a total of NIS 38,000 in compensation.
Military appeals court reduces former IDF commander's prison sentence to 18 months
A military appeals court reduced his prison sentence to 18 months in May 2025. In explaining the reduction, the judges cited the need for gradual increases in sentencing severity and his guilty plea, which spared the women from testifying to establish his guilt. The remaining penalties were unchanged.
The civil claim draws on the criminal findings. The state argues that it may exercise the injured woman’s right to seek compensation to recover the benefits it has paid and expects to pay because of Menachem’s conduct. Any money recovered through this lawsuit would return to the public treasury.

Opponents deem proposed Swiss arms export rules ‘immoral’, ‘anti-Ukraine’

“With this new law, Switzerland is completely relinquishing control over its arms exports,” the coalition opposing the new law told reporters in the capital Bern. The alliance comprises some 28 parties and organisations, including those on the left and the Evangelical People’s Party, as well as NGO Caritas, the Group for a Switzerland without an Army (GSsA), Justitia et Pax, and the Commission of the Swiss Bishops’ Conference.
The relaxation of the War Material Act will once again allow direct exports, even to countries embroiled in civil war. “For 36 countries, including the United States and Argentina – both governed by authoritarian leaders who flout democracy and human rights – the criteria for the export of military equipment will be completely abolished. A blank cheque for [Donald] Trump, [Javier] Milei and their ilk”, writes the alliance in a joint statement.
More
Swiss to vote on loosening arms-export restrictions
‘Not up to arms lobby to decide’
This new law reduces political safeguards and increases the weight of discretionary decisions, argued Alicia Giraudel of Amnesty International. According to her, “this vote is not just about arms exports […] it is about Switzerland’s credibility when it claims to defend human rights, the rule of law and international law”.
If voters approve the bill, the Swiss government will be allowed to waive the authorisation criteria relating to the export of military equipment. The grounds cited are vague “exceptional circumstances” and “Switzerland’s interests”, says parliamentarian Fabian Molina of the left-wing Social Democrats.
And anyone who buys weapons in Switzerland will be able to transfer them to any other country. Switzerland is the only country in Europe to adopt this practice, he added.
Swiss weapons could therefore very easily end up in Sudan or Israel and be used in Gaza. Decisions on arms exports do not merely have security and economic policy implications; they also have direct repercussions on the civilian population, on forced displacement and on refugee flows, said Martina Weber, a member of the Caritas executive board.
Ukraine, however, is excluded from this relaxation of the rules. The alliance sees this exception as a way of appeasing the right-wing Swiss People’s Party and arms manufacturers.

“Especially as the arms industry does not need this law, as it is, unfortunately, doing very well,” said Mazzone. Arms sales skyrocketed in 2025, with nearly CHF1-billion ($1.2 billion) worth of military equipment exported and orders totalling nearly CHF3 billion, the Geneva-based activist said.

====================================================================================================

Lebanon’s only church-bell maker on keeping a 300-year family tradition alive
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
13:06:45 UTC
22:06:45 KST

The story of Lebanon’s last remaining church-bell maker begins with a rifle. In the 18th century, Youssef Gabriel, a local metalworker, was secretly making and equipping Arab revolutionaries with rifles to assist their revolt against the Ottoman empire, which controlled Lebanon at the time.
Then, one day, a Russian engineer came to the Lebanese town of Beit Chabab to make a church bell. Gabriel, intrigued, shadowed the man and picked up the process on sight.
Or, another story goes, the Maronite patriarch at the time, frustrated by the Ottoman empire blocking the import of church bells to Mount Lebanon, tasked Gabriel with making a bell. After several attempts he succeeded and decided to give up making arms, converting his gunsmithery into Lebanon’s first church-bell foundry.
Where the stories converge is that the village, impressed with Gabriel’s handywork, rechristened him Youssef Naffah – naffah meaning useful or successful in Arabic.
Three centuries later, the Naffah family is still making church bells in Beit Chabab. Once one of 10 bell foundries owned by the family, the workshop operated by the master bell-maker Naffah Naffah and his two sons is the last remaining production centre for church bells in Lebanon. It is also the sole source of church bells for much of the Middle East and even Lebanese diaspora communities in Europe, Australia and the US.
Naffah, 57, said: “We have to pass it down to our kids, it’s been 300 years. I didn’t have any choice. My own father, he would come to the workshop when he could barely even walk.”
The foundry sits under his home on the edge of a hill overlooking the red tiled roofs of Beit Chabab and the Lebanese coast that stretches beneath it. The picturesque town, in the Mount Lebanon range about a 30-minute drive from Beirut, offers an escape from the city’s chaos and a refuge from the violence of the country’s last two wars.
The ceiling and walls of the foundry are blackened from decades of smoke that has belched from the furnace, and the floors are cluttered with bells in various stages of construction.
Outside are mounds of white clay mixed with goat hair, each layer drying before the next is applied. The final product forms the interior mould that the molten metal is poured around. Inside the workshop, modern tools mix with the ancient, a hydraulic press sitting next to a well-worn anvil placed on top of a tree stump.
Each bell takes about two months to make. It takes about 40 days to make the interior mould and another month to create the outer mould, with crosses, decoration and the workshop’s signature imprinted on the white clay as it hardens.
The third and final stage is the quickest: a foundry is heated using burning wood, and a mixture of copper and tin is placed inside to be melted down over 24 hours. When the metal is ready, it is poured over the bell mould, hardening within three minutes.
The workshop produces about 25 bells a year, about 20 of which go to churches in Lebanon. The cost of the bell depends mostly on the size, with every 100kg (220lbs) costing $8,000 (£6,000). A medium-size bell that is ready in the foundry and weighs about a tonne costs about $80,000.
“I hate giving the bells away, it always makes me upset, like I’m giving away a child,” said Naffah. He pointed to a mould being worked on, imprints of crosses on its clay interior. “Look at this bell, it’s the work of my two hands. I’ve poured my heart and soul into it.”
Each bell bears the names of those who worked on it. One bell ready to be installed has the name of Naffah, his son Charbel and the patron who commissioned it. Other bells in the shop for repairs – one from 1910, another from 1932 – bear the names of Naffah’s grandfathers.
The family maps Lebanon by its churches, finding evidence of their ancestors up and down the small Mediterranean country. The earliest surviving bell that bears their name is in the town of Qalaat Sahyoun and was forged in 1725.
The ringing of the bells is part of daily life in the villages that wind through Lebanon’s mountains and dot its sprawling coast; on a Sunday morning, the sound mingles with the chirping of the birds.
During the Hezbollah-Israel war in Lebanon, which reignited in March, the Christian villages of south Lebanon were cut off from the rest of the country. Israel’s ground invasion, which bulldozed dozens of villages in south Lebanon, mostly spared the Christian villages, but it left them isolated.
The church was a crucial source of comfort for the besieged Christians. It organised the distribution and transfer of aid in and out of towns and across frontlines when necessary.
Naffah, Charbel and his other son Youssef are determined to preserve this Lebanese tradition and their place within it. Charbel will succeed his father as the master of the family workshop, and Youssef helps when he is not busy with his studies at medical school.
Youssef said if Charbel ever decided he no longer wanted to make bells, he would leave medical school and take his place as master of the foundry.
“We have six churches in the village [Beit Chabab]. If all of the bells played at the same time, I could distinguish between each one from their sound alone,” he said, surveying the village from the edge of the foundry. 
“Traditions are important to us. We are living and breathing tradition here in this workshop.”

Deloitte helped Abramovich conceal $10B in assets, evade taxes: Report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12

22:04:55 KST

Halis Sunnetci
12 October 2026•Update: 12 October 2026
Deloitte Cyprus helped Russian oligarch Roman Abramovich conceal at least $10 billion in assets and allegedly evade millions in taxes through falsified documents, according to an investigation published Monday.
The joint investigation by the BBC, The Bureau of Investigative Journalism (TBIJ), The Guardian and the Organized Crime and Corruption Reporting Project (OCCRP) uncovered more than 1,000 backdated records involving over 100 companies between 1999 and 2013, including documents used to support misleading financial accounts.
In one case, backdated paperwork made more than $10 billion in assets held by Cyprus-based Electus Investments appear to belong to a company with the same name in the British Virgin Islands, keeping the holdings outside public disclosure requirements.
In another case, financial accounts approved by Deloitte omitted $672 million in luxury properties, superyachts and private jets belonging to Abramovich's company Amiscan Investments, according to the investigation.
Investigators also uncovered an alleged tax evasion scheme involving about $2 billion held by Kravin Investments. Backdated documents made the funds appear to belong to another offshore company, potentially allowing Kravin Investments to avoid millions in taxes on interest income.
Abramovich's lawyers denied that he concealed assets, evaded taxes or knowingly participated in improper backdating, saying he legitimately relied on professional advisers.
Deloitte Cyprus said it “acts in compliance with applicable laws” and could not comment on specific correspondence dating back more than 20 years.
The investigation found no evidence of involvement by Deloitte entities outside Cyprus.
Abramovich, the former owner of Chelsea Football Club, was sanctioned by the UK following the war in Ukraine in 2022 over his alleged ties to President Vladimir Putin.

An emergency worker at the site of a Russian attack in Kyiv's Darnytskyi District on Oct. 12, 2026. (Chris Occhicone / The Kyiv Independent)
Russia launched yet another drone attack against Kyiv on Oct. 12, hitting multiple districts of Ukraine's capital and injuring at least three people, city authorities said.
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko first said at 11:32 a.m. local time that air defenses were operating in the city. Three people, including an elderly woman, were injured as a result of Russian drone attacks, he added.

Her father was injured but survived. Neighbors helped her to get him out. "It's nothing short of a miracle that Dad didn't die today," Sheremet said.

Kyiv resident Yana Mohal, 25, woke up to a "horrible and loud" sound in Darnytskyi District, she told the Kyiv Independent. She went outside to see whether she could help Sheremet's father, an "elderly man with a dog," who was trapped in a damaged house.

Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels have claimed responsibility for the attacks, which have raised questions over the robustness of Saudi Arabia's defense capabilities despite its huge military spending.
The fatalities come as the kingdom hosts major corporate conferences, including the World Petroleum Congress, the International Energy Forum Ministerial Meeting and the Future Investment Initiative.
Airlines canceled hundreds of flights scheduled for the coming days, and about 100 flights were forced to divert to other airports, according to Flightradar24. The Federal Aviation Administration warned U.S. carriers of potential risks of flying over and around Saudi Arabia.
Delta Air Lines is scheduled to debut a nonstop flight from Atlanta to Riyadh on Oct. 23, but a spokeswoman said the carrier hasn't made a decision yet on whether to postpone the new route.
U.S. President Donald Trump said Sunday that the U.S. "may" join Saudi Arabia in its retaliation against the Houthis.
Iran's foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi. said Sunday that he had told Saudi Minister of Foreign Affairs Prince Faisal bin Farhan Al Saud by phone that Tehran was willing to take steps to start dialogue between Saudi Arabia and Yemen, where the Houthis are based.
Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmail Baghaei meanwhile said Iran was still reviewing a U.S. response to its proposal for reopening the Strait of Hormuz and would reply through its intermediaries, Reuters reported.

World's largest accounting firm allegedly helped conceal Abramovich's income
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
13:01:08 UTC
22:01:08 KST

Deloitte, the world's largest provider of accounting and audit services, may have helped conceal the income of Russian billionaire Roman Abramovich, thereby enabling the businessman to avoid paying taxes, reports BBC.
Financial statements approved by Deloitte's Cyprus branch reveal that the accounting records of Abramovich's company omitted yachts, mansions, and private jets worth 672 million dollars. Furthermore, Deloitte allegedly recommended a scheme to evade a substantial tax bill through the falsification of documents.
Andrew Mitchell, a barrister and expert in financial services law, stated that evidence obtained by BBC Panorama points to a scheme that constitutes blatant tax evasion and could hardly be more brazen.
Meanwhile, Abramovich's lawyers stated that he denies evading taxes or concealing his income. The billionaire's lawyers stated that Panorama possesses no evidence indicating that Abramovich knew about, authorized, or directed the falsification of any documents, adding that it was legitimate to rely on the advice of professionals.
Deloitte’s Cyprus branch stated that it acted in accordance with the law.
For nearly two decades, Abramovich was the most prominent Russian oligarch in the UK, where he purchased Chelsea Football Club in 2003 and served as its primary financier during the club's most successful period. Following Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Abramovich was placed on the British government's sanctions list and sold the club.
Abramovich is reportedly residing in Turkey, which has not imposed sanctions on him. Assets worth 5.4 billion pounds belonging to Abramovich have been frozen in Jersey, and an investigation has been ongoing for four years. The oligarch's lawyers told the BBC that he denies the allegations raised in Jersey, claiming they are politically motivated.
A BBC investigation has uncovered evidence regarding the management of Abramovich's business empire, raising serious questions about the integrity of some of his professional advisors. The evidence was found in leaked information comprising thousands of documents related to the oligarch's finances and the operations of offshore companies managed from Cyprus between 1995 and 2002.
In 2022, BBC Panorama reported on how Abramovich amassed his wealth through a corrupt deal involving the purchase of a Russian state-owned oil company in the 1990s, which he later sold back for a profit of several billion.
 Abramovich has previously stated that the corruption allegations are false. The profits from the sale of the oil company flowed into a network of offshore entities managed by the Cyprus-registered firm MeritServus. This entity, in turn, belonged to Deloitte—now one of the "Big Four" firms dominating the international accounting sector—until 2005. Even after MeritServus spun off, the two companies continued to collaborate closely on managing Abramovich’s wealth.
Leaked documents from MeritServus reveal some of the methods employed. The first example dates back to 2006, when Cyprus enacted a law requiring the disclosure of corporate financial statements. The new legislation threatened to expose the secrets surrounding Abramovich’s wealth. Deloitte had prepared the 2003 financial statements for Abramovich’s company, Amiscan Investments, but they had not yet been finalized; these statements included luxury assets valued at 672 million dollars. To keep these assets secret, Abramovich’s associates and MeritServus decided to rewrite history and devised a plan to circumvent the new law. The assets were transferred to Amiscan Investments’ parent company in the British Virgin Islands—where they could be concealed—and the transaction was backdated to make it appear as though it had taken place in 2003. Deloitte reviewed backdated documents and determined they were sufficient to remove the relevant assets from Amiscan Investments' accounts. 
Consequently, when Deloitte approved the 2003 financial statements in 2006, houses, aircraft, and yachts vanished with a single signature, leaving Abramovich’s company with assets valued at just 75,000 dollars.
 Deloitte approved the statements even though leaked documents clearly indicate the firm knew they were misleading.
Lord Prem Nath Sikka, a professor of accounting at the University of Sheffield, stated that this constituted a breach of statutory obligations and described the misdating of transactions as quite scandalous.
Panorama also uncovered evidence that backdated documents were used to avoid paying taxes. Another of Abramovich’s Cyprus-based companies, Kravin Investments, was involved in the scheme. In 2003, it held nearly 2 billion dollars in its account. Since this sum generated significant interest income, Abramovich’s company should have paid profit tax; however, his associates had a different idea. In an email sent in August 2005, MeritServus wrote to Abramovich’s Russian partners stating that a plan had been devised following a meeting with Deloitte. If the partners agreed to it, the financial statements and accounting records for 2003 and 2004 would need to be altered. MeritServus informed Abramovich’s partners in Russia that the 2005 report for Kravin Investments would state that the company had generated no profit from the deposited funds. A month later, the Russian partners replied that they agreed to the plan.
MeritServus created a series of backdated documents that misleadingly indicated Kravin Investments was merely managing and investing funds on behalf of its parent company in the Virgin Islands. 
This created the impression that Kravin Investments held no assets of its own and, consequently, was not liable for taxes.
Lawyer Mitchell told Panorama that the lesson to be drawn from these cases is that there are professionals willing to bend and break the rules of their profession—and thereby violate the law—and that seemingly nothing can stop them when it comes to the preparation of documents. 
Vladimir Milov—who served as Russia’s deputy energy minister when Abramovich amassed his fortune and is now a harsh critic of the Russian government—said that for every corrupt oligarch from Russia, the Middle East, or Africa, there is an army of Western financial and legal service providers ready to launder any reputation for a fee and help the oligarchs appear respectable.

====================================================================================================

Two Kremlin campaigns and one miscalculation
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
16:01:04 EEST
22:01:04 KST

Ihor Petrenko, Doctor of Political Sciences, expert of the United Ukraine Analytical Center
Over the past two weeks, Russia has launched two campaigns that are usually discussed separately. One is unfolding in Washington, the other in the skies over Ukrainian cities. Put them together, and a common design becomes visible: to obtain, by going around the negotiating table, what Moscow cannot obtain at it.
The First Campaign: Making Money Without Waiting for Peace
In late September, Putin’s special envoy Kirill Dmitriev held meetings in the U.S. with Trump’s envoys, and then with representatives of the Treasury Department and the Department of Energy. And on October 3, The New York Times reported that a deal on Lukoil’s foreign assets, which the company itself had valued at roughly $20 billion, had been added to the talks on ending the war. According to the newspaper, Putin personally raised the issue at a meeting with Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner on September 5, and the possible buyers include investor Todd Boehly and two Middle Eastern groups that have had business ties to Kushner or the Witkoff family. The deal has not been approved, and the White House has not commented on it.
The Kremlin’s logic here is not about oil. The value of these assets rises the moment sanctions are lifted from them. Consequently, alongside the negotiators there appear people with a financial stake in precisely what Moscow is seeking: sanctions relief before peace, not after it. In parallel, according to The Atlantic, Trump’s envoy John Coale proposed partially easing sanctions in exchange for the release of political prisoners; the idea is at an early stage, but it is already on the table. Putin does not hide his calculation, either. At the Valdai forum on October 1, he called a mutual halt to strikes on energy infrastructure pointless, because sanctions would keep Russian exports from recovering anyway. In other words, in exchange for an energy ceasefire, Moscow wants not reciprocal quiet, but sanctions relief. That same day, Trump linked the rise in diesel prices to strikes on Russian oil refineries – an argument the Kremlin need only pick up.
The Second Campaign: Making the City Unlivable
From October 1 to 4, Russian drones struck Kyiv’s Southern and Northern bridges. A bridge like that cannot be destroyed by a drone, and Moscow knows it. The goal is different – to split the city into two banks every day. In an interview with Reuters, President Zelensky called this a “new doctrine”: strikes on logistics, roads, schools, and hospitals to force people to leave the capital. He also warned that Ukraine would respond with strikes on Russian oil refineries, but not on civilian targets.
An intercepted Russian plan, which the NYT wrote about, envisages up to a thousand missiles, drones, and aerial bombs to cut electricity and heat supply to Kyiv, Kharkiv, and Odesa by 90% and to knock out the water supply. The newspaper was unable to independently verify the document’s authenticity, but the events of the week do not contradict it. On October 3, the Russian Foreign Ministry warned foreign nationals and diplomats against staying in Ukraine.
There is no military objective in these strikes. There are three political ones: to raise the price of an energy ceasefire ahead of a possible meeting in Abu Dhabi, to create a new wave of refugees for Europe, and, most importantly, to turn Ukrainians’ fatigue into a demand on their own government to agree to peace at any price.
Where the Calculation Doesn’t Add Up
Both campaigns rest on the same assumption: a person who is dissatisfied with the government is ready to give up. Sociology says otherwise. According to a KIIS poll conducted August 21 – September 10, 77% of Ukrainians believe that resistance must continue even if Russia leaves cities without electricity, heat, and water. Twelve percent are ready to accept Russia’s demands. Among those who do not trust the president, 65% support resistance. Kyiv is the most telling case: the capital has a negative trust balance toward the president and, at the same time, the highest readiness in the country to hold out – 83%. The city that is most critical of the government is the most resolute in refusing to surrender.
Distrust of the government and readiness to capitulate are different feelings. The Russian operation is built on the premise that they are one and the same.
That said, the reserve of resilience is not unlimited. The share of those ready to endure the war for as long as it takes fell to 48% in April and recovered to 61% by the end of the summer. And all these data were collected before the start of the heating season. It is precisely this gap that Moscow is working with: on September 26, the Center for Countering Disinformation reported a social media campaign calling on people to take to the streets and demand peace agreements, an end to mobilization, and elections, with the organizers being passed off as supposed Ukrainian servicemen.
The easiest way to tell such an operation apart from a genuine protest is by its demand. When people in Odesa last December and in Kamianske in January blocked roads over prolonged power outages, they demanded that the electricity be restored. No one demanded negotiations with Moscow. A genuine protest asks for light, not for peace. One can err here in two directions, and the second mistake is more dangerous: to label people without electricity a “PSYOP” is to do the Kremlin’s work for it.
What This Means for Ukraine
Three concrete things follow from this.
First. An energy ceasefire can only be reciprocal: refinery strikes in exchange for strikes on the power grid, with no linkage to sanctions. Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha has already stated that Kyiv is ready for an energy ceasefire and a Black Sea ceasefire only in combination. Putin himself has estimated the losses from strikes on refineries at roughly 1% of GDP. That is the price of the lever, and it is not handed over for a promise.
Second. On sanctions, work not only with the White House but also with Congress and Europe. The Graham law, which allows tariffs of up to 100% on buyers of Russian energy, was signed on September 18 and has still not been applied even once, even though the Senate passed it by a vote of 86 to 11. And on October 29, the sanctions exemptions that permit certain Lukoil transactions expire. That is the nearest date by which it will become clear which way Washington is moving. If the assets are sold, there is one demand: the money goes into a blocked account until the end of the war.
Third. In winter, trust rests on predictability and results. People can endure an outage schedule, but they cannot endure uncertainty and unfairness, so a government official must come out to those who have blocked a road on the same day. And results are what Friedrich Merz brought to Kyiv on October 4: a package of more than €1.3 billion, including for the joint production of interceptors for jet-powered Shaheds, as well as generators and transformers.
The Kremlin is counting on the cold to do for it what the army could not. So far, the numbers suggest that it is mistaken. This winter’s task is to keep it that way.
