====================================================================================================

Gijs de Best urges shared enforcement to curb illicit trade
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
13:00:49 UTC
22:00:49 KST

One route, many borders: the case for a joined-up fight against illicit trade
Gijs de Best, President of South Asia, Indochina, CIS and Middle East and Africa at Philip Morris International (PMI), on why tackling illicit trade requires countries to share intelligence, align policy and make sure the rules can be enforced.
A smuggler does not stop at a border because the rules have changed. Criminal networks move products and money across jurisdictions. The authorities trying to disrupt them are often still operating within national boundaries.
For Gijs de Best, that mismatch is at the heart of the challenge. He oversees a region of fast-growing markets. Before taking on the role in January 2026, he led PMI's business in the Philippines.
His argument is straightforward: if criminal networks operate across borders, governments need to do the same. That means sharing intelligence, coordinating enforcement and thinking about the risk of illicit trade when policies are designed.
The cost of illicit trade
Lost government revenue is one of the most immediate consequences.
"Illicit trade significantly deteriorates governmental revenues," de Best says. "If you take governmental revenue, every additional dollar earned can be reinvested in health care, in education and infrastructure."
Recent figures illustrate the scale of the issue in Europe. A KPMG study commissioned by PMI and published in June 2026 estimated that 55.3 billion illicit cigarettes were consumed across 38 European countries in 2025. It put the resulting loss in government revenue at around €22.4 billion. Illicit cigarettes accounted for more than one in ten cigarettes consumed in the EU, the first time that has happened since 2014.
The impact goes beyond tax receipts. Illicit markets also put pressure on legitimate businesses and, de Best argues, create risks for consumers.
"Illicit trade undermines legitimate businesses and weakens political institutions," he says. There is a product safety issue too. Illicit products "don't have quality standards. They don't follow safety protocols, they don't follow product standards," he says. "So they impose a risk on consumers using these products."
A problem well beyond Europe
Illicit trade can sometimes be framed as a problem concentrated in wealthier Western economies. De Best sees a different picture.
"That illicit trade is purely an issue in the Western world is often a misconception," he says. "Emerging markets are facing the exact same, if not worse, and they need the funding."
Southeast Asia offers a clear example. PMI estimates that governments across ASEAN lose around $4 billion a year in cigarette excise revenue, with another $2 billion lost to illegal vaping products.
The company has called for greater sharing of customs data between ASEAN member states, including in real time, and has warned that disruption to legitimate supply chains can create opportunities for illegal operators. The issue has particular relevance this year, with the Philippines holding the ASEAN chair.
For de Best, that makes the involvement of emerging markets in international discussions particularly important.
"It's so important they make their voices heard," he says.
Regulation is only as strong as its enforcement
Better regulation can help, but rules on paper are only part of the answer.
"Good regulation without enforcement only impacts the legitimate businesses because they follow the regulation," de Best says. Criminal operators, by definition, do not.
That means policymakers need to think about enforcement from the moment they design regulation. Who will enforce the rules? What resources will they need? Can the measures be implemented in practice? And will they ultimately make consumers safer?
These questions matter because poorly designed measures can increase the compliance burden on legitimate businesses without changing the behaviour of criminal operators.
Building illicit trade into policymaking
For de Best, the answer is to consider illicit trade much earlier in the policy process.
"Combating illicit trade should be an integral part of policymaking," he says.
That approach could bring benefits beyond recovering lost revenue. If governments can reduce the space in which criminal networks operate, they can also help protect legitimate businesses and consumers.
"If done successfully, it will reduce the crime rate and will significantly increase governmental revenues," de Best says.
The challenge is making that cooperation work in practice. Countries need to share intelligence and develop regulation that takes account of consumer protection, enforceability and product standards.
"Only then it will work."
A smuggler's route already crosses borders without asking permission. The response can cross them too, if governments share what they know and write rules they can enforce.

====================================================================================================

Patience with life’s small annoyances is linked to lower anxiety, but it doesn’t buffer spiritual struggles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
13:00:34 UTC
22:00:34 KST

A recent study reveals that while religious and spiritual struggles are linked to higher anxiety in college students, developing patience for daily annoyances can predict a reduction in general anxiety over time. The research, published in Psychology of Religion and Spirituality, suggests that patience improves mental health independently rather than shielding students from the specific stress of existential doubts.
Religion and spirituality often provide a sense of meaning and social support. Yet these belief systems are not uniformly beneficial for psychological well-being. Many people experience profound tensions, doubts, and negative emotions related to their faith. Psychologists refer to these experiences as religious and spiritual struggles.
These struggles can take many forms. They might involve anger toward a divine figure, conflicts with members of a religious community, or deep concerns about moral failures. Previous research links these faith-based tensions to higher anxiety and depressive symptoms. The college years are a particularly common time for these struggles to emerge, as emerging adults frequently question inherited beliefs and explore new frameworks of meaning.
Laura Upenieks, a sociologist at Baylor University, and her colleagues wanted to understand which psychological traits might help people navigate these difficulties. They focused on the virtue of patience. In psychological terms, patience is an active coping skill that involves emotional regulation and the ability to endure hardship without acting impulsively.
The researchers looked at three distinct types of patience. Interpersonal patience involves managing frustration with other people. Life hardship patience reflects the capacity to endure major life difficulties. Daily hassles patience is the ability to tolerate everyday irritations, such as waiting in a long line or sitting in heavy traffic.
The research team suspected that patience might protect individuals from the anxiety associated with spiritual turmoil. They theorized that a patient person might have the emotional stability to process deep existential questions without becoming overwhelmed by fear or stress.
To test this, the researchers examined data from 274 undergraduate students attending a large Christian university in the southern United States. They tracked the students across their college careers. The students completed surveys during their first semester and again during their senior year.
The surveys asked students to rate how often they experienced struggles related to religion or spirituality over the past year. The students also completed a questionnaire designed to measure their generalized anxiety symptoms over the past week. A separate section of the survey measured their levels across the three different types of patience.
The researchers used a technique called latent change score modeling. This statistical approach allowed them to evaluate the starting baseline levels of each trait while simultaneously tracking how those traits evolved and influenced one another over the four-year period. By separating the initial states from the changes over time, the researchers could better isolate the direction of the associations.
At the beginning of college, students who reported more frequent spiritual struggles also reported higher levels of anxiety. This pattern held true over time. Students whose spiritual struggles increased over the four years were likely to experience an increase in their anxiety symptoms as well.
The researchers then looked at whether patience acted as a buffer against this anxiety. They expected that highly patient students would be less affected by the stress of spiritual doubts. The data did not support this hypothesis. The statistical interaction between patience and spiritual struggles was not statistically significant. Patience did not change the trajectory of how spiritual struggles fueled anxiety.
Spiritual struggles often challenge the core belief system that a person uses to understand the world. Because these struggles strike at the foundation of how someone finds meaning, emotional endurance alone is likely not enough to eliminate the resulting distress. The anxiety generated by a crisis of identity or a fear of divine abandonment might simply bypass the regulatory mechanisms of patience.
However, patience still operated as an independent predictor of mental health. During their first semester, students with high levels of interpersonal patience and life hardship patience exhibited lower initial levels of anxiety. Being able to endure major setbacks and tolerate difficult people provided a distinct mental health benefit from the start.
When looking at changes over the four-year period, a different pattern emerged. Changes in interpersonal and life hardship patience did not predict changes in anxiety. Instead, students who developed more daily hassles patience over time showed a notable decrease in anxiety symptoms by their senior year.
This suggests that learning to tolerate everyday annoyances might relieve a general accumulation of stress. Preventing minor irritations from escalating could create the emotional space needed for better overall mental health. Patience seems to set a baseline of emotional stability, even if it does not solve the specific existential crises associated with religious doubt.
The study has a few methodological limitations. The sample consisted entirely of students at a religiously affiliated university. The experiences of these students might not reflect the experiences of individuals at secular institutions or the broader public. The shared religious environment on campus could make spiritual struggles more visible and prominent, as theological commitments are heavily integrated into the academic and social life of the school.
Additionally, the researchers measured religious and spiritual struggles using a single survey question. This broad approach captures the general frequency of distress, but it cannot differentiate between specific types of issues. A person arguing with their pastor might experience a very different type of anxiety than someone secretly doubting the existence of a deity.
The study also relied on self-reported data, which can introduce bias if participants answer in ways they think are socially desirable. The analytical models used in the study are highly complex for a sample of 274 individuals. Replicating the analysis with larger and more diverse populations would help verify the results.
Future research could explore behavioral interventions based on these findings. Training people to manage their reactions to minor daily inconveniences might offer an accessible way to lower generalized anxiety. At the same time, addressing the root causes of spiritual struggles may require entirely different support systems, such as community conversations or pastoral care.
The study, “Religious/Spiritual Struggles, Patience, and Anxiety: A Longitudinal Examination of Virtue and Vulnerability,” was authored by Laura Upenieks, Hiroki Matsuo, Kevin D. Dougherty, Perry L. Glanzer, and Sarah A. Schnitker.

Will schools switch to remote learning if there are water outages in Kyiv? Education officials have answered
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
16:00:26 EEST
22:00:26 KST

Will schools switch to remote learning if there are water outages in Kyiv? Education officials have answered
Kyiv • UNN
Kyiv schools will operate in person only under safe and sanitary conditions. In the event of prolonged outages of electricity or water, classes will be moved online.
Kyiv’s education officials explained whether the capital’s schools will switch to remote learning because of water and power outages, and also spoke about organizing in-person education and what else parents should know — read the details in the UNN article.
Details
The Kyiv City State Administration’s Department of Education and Science explained how education will be organized in Kyiv schools during prolonged power outages, water supply disruptions and other challenges caused by the war. The working format of each institution will depend on the security situation, technical capabilities and ability to ensure proper conditions for children and staff.
If there is no electricity at the school
Where technically possible, schools will use alternative power and lighting sources, including generators, inverters and charging stations. If the lighting is insufficient for written assignments, teachers may conduct lessons orally until the necessary conditions are restored.
If a school cannot ensure proper conditions for children to stay there, students will be transferred to remote learning until the necessary conditions are restored.
If there is no water supply
The school may operate in person only if sanitary requirements are met. If this is impossible because of a lack of water, in-person learning will be suspended and the educational process will be organized remotely until the situation improves.
How in-person learning is organized
When security conditions are favorable, lessons are held on school premises. In the event of an air raid alert, students and teachers move to designated rooms in the shelter.
The city also continues to use the “educational migration” mechanism — organizing classes in available premises of other educational institutions, including both schools and kindergartens, if they meet the necessary requirements.
Kyiv is preparing reserves of water and food in case of emergencies07.09.26, 11:53 • 28743 views
How remote learning takes place
Both children who are in Kyiv and those who have temporarily left the capital study remotely. When necessary, students join online classes from specially equipped workstations in school shelters.
If, because of wartime circumstances, a teacher cannot safely get to the school, they conduct remote online lessons from a safe location with the approval of the school administration.
If a school is damaged, experiences a prolonged power outage, water supply disruptions or another emergency caused by the war, the entire institution may temporarily switch to a remote format until the situation improves. The school administration will inform parents about such changes through designated communication channels.
What parents need to know
If an air raid alert is announced during a remote lesson, the class is suspended so that the teacher and students can move to a safe place.
After the teacher and students move to a safe place, the online lesson continues or the next lesson according to the schedule begins online.
Parents are advised to check the electronic diary and monitor school messages about the learning format, schedule changes and the child’s attendance. At the beginning of the lesson, the teacher records the students’ attendance, and if a child has not joined the lesson, the parents receive a corresponding notification.
The learning format may change depending on the security situation, the consequences of shelling, the availability of electricity, water and heating, and the ability to ensure that children can stay safely at school. The main principle remains unchanged: the educational process continues to the extent permitted by the conditions at the particular institution.

Agios Efstratios: the first Greek island to get all its electricity from renewables
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
13:00:18 UTC
22:00:18 KST

In ten months, the small island of Agios Efstratios has gone from relying entirely on fossil fuels to producing more than 90% of its electricity from renewable sources. Thanks to an EU-funded project, this volcanic island is now self-sufficient with green energy.
The Greek island of Agios Efstratios, colloquially known as Ai Stratis, is betting big on renewable energy. Located in the north-eastern Aegean Sea, this small volcanic island with just 250 residents literally runs on the sun and wind. Previously, the island depended entirely on fossil fuels; now it produces 91% of its electricity from renewables, thus avoiding the emission of about a thousand tonnes of CO₂ into the atmosphere each year, thanks to the European Union-funded Ai Stratis – Green Island project.
According to Dimitrios Kardomateas, Chairman and CEO of the Centre for Renewable Energy Sources and Savings (CRES):
The project relies on a hybrid system consisting of a 900-kW wind turbine, a 225-kW solar farm, a battery system for electricity storage, and automated, real-time energy management—the crown jewel of the project.
Surplus renewable energy is used for heating
Manolis Klados, Project Manager at GEK TERNA Group, explains that “any excess energy is being stored in the battery. And the battery also releases power when there is a shortage on the production of the renewables. And during winter, any surplus from the renewable energy production is being utilised to produce thermal energy. This is stored in this four hot water storage tank of a total volume of 500 cubic metres.”
Green energy from renewable sources is distributed to the island’s residents using the existing electrical grid. As for heating, the independence from fuel oil is a relief for Charalambos Makris, a local resident and manager of two guesthouses. According to Makris, since the project was launched, “There is no need to operate a boiler inside the house, there is no noise at all when the heating is running, and it is very economical.”
Zoi Vlastou, Deputy Mayor for Citizen Services, highlights the importance of the Ai Stratis – Green Island pilot project as a model for other Greek islands and for the country more broadly: https://x.com/goizlyon/status/2105998565247963462?s=20
The total budget for Ai Stratis – Green Island amounts to 7.23 million euros, of which 85% has been financed by the Cohesion Policy of the European Union and the remaining 15% by Greek national funds.
To get this pioneering project off the ground, the team had to overcome numerous challenges, such as the transport, assembly, transfer, and installation of the wind turbine, measuring 77 metres tall and weighing close to 30 tonnes, now located at the island’s highest point. But the biggest challenge was changing Greek energy standards, according to Panagiotis Zorlos, Project Manager at CRES: “Because it's a pilot project, the regulatory framework was very general and not specifically concentrated to such a system which has a lot of particularities.”
Ai Stratis is at the forefront of Europe’s green energy transition. Other Greek islands such as Tilos, Ikaria, and Astypalea are following its example.

Stolen Renoir paintings found behind wall in France, says prosecutor
PARIS – Two paintings by impressionist master Pierre-Auguste Renoir, stolen from a museum in southern France and later discovered hidden behind a wall, have sustained slight damage, prosecutors said on Oct 12.
In September, thieves broke into the museum in Cagnes-sur-Mer and escaped with two works by Renoir, abandoning two others as they fled.
The value of all four paintings had been estimated at €9 million (S$12.9 million).
On Oct 9, the authorities announced that the two outstanding stolen works had been found.
They were a portrait titled Portrait of Madame Colonna Romano and a depiction of a woman at a well called Young Woman at the Well.
Speaking to reporters in Paris, Marseille prosecutor Nicolas Bessone said the paintings were recovered on Oct 8 during a search of a home in the southern town of Clermont-l’Herault.
The discovery of the stolen works followed the arrest of six people, including a woman, on Oct 7, said Bessone.
“The paintings were hidden behind a solid cinderblock wall. They were completely undetectable,” Bessone said.
“It was through interrogation work that investigators were able to get the receiver of the stolen goods to admit that he had indeed taken possession of the paintings.”
A 29-year-old man seen as the main suspect was charged at the weekend after DNA evidence linked him to the theft.
The two paintings were “in relatively good condition”, although “the two works showed signs of damage,” Bessone said, speaking alongside the head of France’s national judicial police, Christian Sainte.
The frame of Young Woman at the Well was slightly damaged, while “the canvas of Portrait of Madame Colonna Romano had a tear,” Bessone said.
The tear was located “on the dress” in the portrait, the prosecutor said, adding that both paintings “will require restoration work”.
Latest heist
Culture Minister Catherine Pegard praised “the efficiency and determination of all those who made this outcome possible”.
“Their commitment made it possible to recover these works in record time,” the culture ministry said.
A spate of heists at French museums – including at the Louvre – has highlighted inadequate security in some cases and led to questions about whether criminal gangs see them as soft targets.
Crown jewels valued at around US$100 million were stolen in broad daylight from the Louvre in Paris in 2025.
While the four suspected Louvre robbers were arrested, the jewels they are accused of grabbing in the seven-minute heist have still not been found. AFP

Google Fitbit Edge: Specs, Features, Price, Release Date
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
13:00:00 UTC
22:00:00 KST

Google’s screenless Fitbit Air made a splash, but it’s been three years since the company updated its display-equipped Charge 6. That older tracker is showing its age, lacking newer automatic workout detection, deeper health metrics, and an IP68 rating. That's where the new Fitbit Edge comes in.
Announced on Monday, it is the successor fitness tracker fans with a screen preference have been waiting for. It sits in a sweet spot at $180—not as costly as a Google Pixel Watch but offering a similar experience in a slimmer, pill-shaped design. And unlike the Pixel Watch, it's compatible with Android and iPhones via the Google Health app. Preorders are available now, and it goes on sale on October 27.
The Fixable Fitbit
The Edge has a user-replaceable battery, a Fitbit first, aligning with Google’s efforts to make its Pixel Watch more repairable. (Likely also due to new battery regulations set to take effect next year in the European Union.) Repair options will vary by region and availability.
If you find the Pixel Watch’s round face too bulky, the Edge's capsule-shaped alternative might suit smaller wrists better. If the Charge 6’s 1.04-inch display was too small, the Edge upgrades it to a larger 1.34-inch screen. The difference is noticeable, and that extra real estate could make a real impact when glancing at your metrics mid-workout.
The Edge borrows a few more attributes from the Pixel Watch, including an altimeter that uses atmospheric pressure to measure elevation changes. That means it can record elevation gain and loss during outdoor activities, track floors climbed, and add more context to your outdoor stats. It also has a far-field skin temperature sensor, replacing the standard device temperature sensor found in other Fitbits. By bringing some of the Pixel Watch’s more advanced hardware to a fitness-first wearable, Google is giving the Edge a compelling middle-ground position in its lineup at a Fitbit-friendly price.
The Edge inherits the Fitbit Air’s improvements while restoring several Charge 6 features the screenless tracker lacks, including built-in GPS and electrical sensors that work with the electrocardiogram (ECG) app. You can also control music playback on a connected Bluetooth device, as you could with the Charge 6, and Google Maps turn-by-turn directions will arrive later this year.
Google also announced more advanced automatic activity tracking for the Edge, using Gemini Intelligence to identify up to 100 workout types. It can track more than 50 exercise modes, up from 40 on its predecessor. Google will also roll out these features to the Pixel Watch 5 and Air. If they work as promised, it means users won't have to log every activity manually.
With a Google Health Premium subscription, the Edge can track blood pressure trends without manual calibration and insulin resistance trends without requiring a blood draw. Google first announced these capabilities alongside the Pixel Watch 5's debut, but they only became available at the end of September. They’re also available on the Air, keeping Google’s screenless tracker up to date as its lineup expands.
The seven-day battery life remains unchanged, but it’s one of the Edge’s biggest advantages over the Pixel Watch. Like the Air, it takes about 90 minutes to fully charge, which is half an hour less than the Charge 6.
One odd omission is a near-field communication (NFC) sensor, which means the Edge doesn’t support contactless payments through Google Wallet. That’s a downgrade from the Charge 6 and a strange function to lose on a fitness tracker that Google is pitching as a step up from its basic Fitbits.
Dressed for Every Occasion
The Edge introduces new digital and analog clock faces, and the Canyon band color returns from the Pixel Watch 5, alongside five other band styles (Active Band, Active Sport Band, Performance Loop Band, Magnet Band, and Metal Links Band). The Stephen Curry collaboration ($220), which also appeared with the Fitbit Air and Pixel Watch 5, is back in the same brown-orange color.
Alongside the Edge, Google is also giving the screenless Fitbit Air a visual upgrade with a new Metal Mesh band. It’s an even dressier strap than the polyurethane Elevated Modern Band. The Air may have initially been designed to disappear on your wrist, but the new band makes it a statement accessory.
If you’re all in on the screenless Fitbit Air, the Edge won’t change your mind. But if you’re not ready to give up a display, the Edge might be a compelling and affordable alternative for both iPhone and Android users. Stay tuned for our review.

The Armed Forces of Ukraine have introduced a unified form for orders on servicemen’s injuries — what will change
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
15:59:50 EEST
21:59:50 KST

The Armed Forces of Ukraine have introduced a unified form for orders on servicemen’s injuries — what will change
Kyiv • UNN
Commanders of the Armed Forces of Ukraine will document injuries using a unified form within five days. This is intended to speed up the issuance of certificates, Military Medical Commission conclusions, and payments.
The Ministry of Defence of Ukraine, together with the Commander-in-Chief and the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, has introduced a single template for an order by a military unit commander concerning the receipt of an injury or trauma. The Ministry of Defence of Ukraine reported this, UNN writes.
Details
The document is intended to standardize the recording of the circumstances of an injury and help avoid delays in issuing the necessary certificates and assigning payments.
The relevant amendments were made to the Instruction on Records Management in the Armed Forces of Ukraine, approved by Order No. 40 of the Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces of Ukraine dated January 31, 2024.
Previously, the Instruction did not contain an approved template for such an order, so military units prepared the documents using different approaches, sometimes with delays. This could slow down the receipt of a certificate on the circumstances of the injury and payments, while incomplete information could complicate establishing the connection between the injury and the defense of the Motherland during the military medical commission examination.
From now on, commanders will have a single template containing a list of the necessary information and a clear deadline for issuing the order. This should help record the circumstances of an injury fully and in a timely manner so that service members can receive the payments they are entitled to and accurate conclusions from the military medical commission
The document provides for recording the main circumstances in which the injury was sustained. In particular, it will specify:
-  the date and place of the incident; 
-  the service member’s position and the tasks they were performing; 
-  the circumstances in which the injury was sustained; 
-  information about the provision of medical assistance and evacuation; 
-  information about witnesses and documents confirming the circumstances of the incident. 
On the basis of the order, a certificate on the circumstances of the injury will be issued, which is necessary for further medical review and processing of payments.
Deadlines for issuing the order and the procedure for receiving the certificate
The commander of the military unit must issue the order within five days of the incident or of receiving information about it.
If several service members were injured as a result of the same incident, their circumstances may be recorded in a single order—separately for each person.
The certificate will be transmitted electronically through the electronic document management system (SEDO). If this is not technically possible or the service member submits a corresponding application, they will be issued a paper copy.
The document will be used when the military medical commission reviews the circumstances of the injury, in particular to establish its connection with the defense of the Motherland, as well as when processing the payments due.
The Ministry of Defence expects that the single order template and the specified deadline for its issuance will make the procedure for documenting injuries more organized and help service members receive the necessary documents in a timely manner.

China's first batch of national parks delivers notable ecological progress
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
20:59:15 CST
21:59:15 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 12 (Xinhua) -- China's first batch of national parks has achieved substantial results since the official designation of five such parks in 2021, the National Forestry and Grassland Administration said on Monday.
Over the past five years, a national park system with Chinese characteristics has taken basic shape, the quality of natural ecosystems in key areas has continued to improve, and populations of flagship species have grown steadily, according to the administration.
In 2021, China established its first national parks: the Sanjiangyuan National Park, the Giant Panda National Park, the Northeast China Tiger and Leopard National Park, the Hainan Tropical Rainforest National Park and the Wuyishan National Park.
The five national parks cover a total area of 230,000 square kilometers and incorporate more than 120 nature reserves of various types and levels.
By implementing a series of measures like habitat restoration, ecological corridor connectivity, and regulation of human activities, the five national parks have delivered notable ecological successes over the past five years.
For instance, as "the water tower of China," the Sanjiangyuan National Park has significantly enhanced its water conservation capacity, channeling an average of 80 billion cubic meters of high-quality water downstream annually. The Giant Panda National Park has opened up 13 ecological corridors linking isolated wild giant panda populations, greatly improving habitat connectivity.
In terms of flagship species protection, the Tibetan antelope population in the Sanjiangyuan National Park has recovered to more than 70,000. In the Northeast China Tiger and Leopard National Park, the number of wild Amur tigers has increased from 27 to 72, and that of wild Amur leopards from 42 to 115.
Meanwhile, national park construction has coordinated ecological protection with livelihood improvement. Nearly 50,000 local residents have been hired as ecological rangers, earning annual wages of 12,000 yuan (around 1,782 U.S. dollars) to 21,000 yuan per person.
China has also implemented the national park law and revised regulations on nature reserves, marking a new stage of law-based and standardized development for the nature reserve system with national parks as the main body.
During the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030), China will continue to promote high-quality national park development and establish new national parks in an orderly manner, the administration added. ■

Across China: Fishing tourism on the rise in historic south China port
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
20:59:12 CST
21:59:12 KST

HAIKOU, Oct. 12 (Xinhua) -- A fishing boat laden with tourists and angling gear eased away from the port in Tanmen Township of the city of Qionghai, south China's Hainan Province, setting off on a leisurely sea-angling trip.
Standing by the rail with his wife and son, a tourist surnamed Cheng from southwest China's Yunnan Province took in the coastal scenery.
"It's my first time fishing at sea, and I'm looking forward to seeing what we'll catch," he said.
The sea angling trip was part of an activity launched in Tanmen during the recent National Day holiday, inviting visitors to spend a day as a fisherman in Tanmen. Tourists boarded boats and cast their lines under the guidance of local fishermen. Many said the experience had given them a real taste of life at sea.
At nightfall, as the boats returned to shore, the seafood street along Fugang Road in Tanmen came alive, with seafood dining offering another way for visitors to experience local fishing culture. After dinner, some tourists settled in for the night at one of more than a dozen traditional fishermen's homestays in nearby Paigang Village.
From sea-angling trips to seafood dinners and fishermen's homestays, Tanmen is seeking to connect different parts of the visitor experience and encourage tourists to spend more time and money in the town.
During the National Day holiday earlier this month, Tanmen received about 89,600 tourist visits and generated approximately 3.08 million yuan (around 457,564 U.S. dollars) in tourism revenue, according to local statistics.
Behind these experiences lies a broader effort to diversify the economy of a town long shaped by fishing. Tanmen, notably, has preserved much of its traditional fishing-village landscape, while generations of seafaring experience, port infrastructure and maritime heritage have laid the foundation for the development of recreational fisheries.
In recent years, Tanmen has explored new business models combining leisure activities, fishermen's homestays, seafood sales and educational tours.
Yang Liguo, from Beijing, is one of those working in Tanmen's recreational fishing sector.
"My work gave me a deep affection for the sea. On a random sea-angling trip in Hainan, I began thinking about having my own recreational fishing boat," Yang said.
In 2025, Yang invested more than 3 million yuan to convert a 205-tonne wooden fishing boat into a recreational sea-angling vessel, which retains an all-wood structure. Its cabin preserves traditional maritime tools, including a compass and old fishing nets, while modern rescue equipment has been installed.
For Yang, the appeal of Tanmen extends beyond its fishing grounds. The town's maritime culture, passed down through generations, was another major reason he chose to operate there.
"We invite veteran local captains aboard to share stories about Tanmen fishermen's voyages, allowing visitors to experience the history of the Maritime Silk Road and the culture of Geng Lu Bu, traditional handwritten sailing-route manuals used by local fishermen," he said.
Since the vessel began operating in May 2025, it has hosted educational tours involving over 2,500 participants, Yang noted.
According to official statistics, Qionghai's recreational fishery output value reached 284 million yuan last year. From January through August 2026, meanwhile, Tanmen received 1.33 million tourist visits and generated tourism revenue of 47.8 million yuan.
The government also plans to develop Tanmen into a recreational fishing hub, upgrade its recreational fishing pier, improve supporting facilities such as tourism service complexes, and provide more tourism products in sightseeing, cultural experiences, accommodation and science education.
Li Zhi, Party chief of Tanmen Township, recently inspected the renovation of Tanmen's central fishing port. The town has also taken the port renovation as an opportunity to develop facilities for recreational fishing.
"The first phase has been completed, and work on the second phase is underway. The port upgrade is intended to serve traditional fishing as well as the emerging recreational fishing sector," Li said.
The upgraded port is set to include a 310-meter pier dedicated to recreational fishing, with capacity for up to 19 recreational fishing boats, as well as a beach, an observation lighthouse and a seafood market.
"Both traditional fishing and recreational fishing need to develop well. That is how local people can improve their livelihoods and fishermen can enjoy better lives," Li said. ■

Cyprus closer than ever to joining Schengen but political hurdles relating to the Green Line and British Sovereign Base Areas remain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
12:59:00 UTC
21:59:00 KST

Cyprus: Green Line complicates island's Schengen ambitions
October 12, 2026
Cyprus is closer than ever to joining the Schengen Area.
Together with Ireland, Cyprus is currently the only member of the European Union not to be part of Europe's border-free travel zone.
After years of preparations and the implementation of 120 technical recommendations, Nicosia received a positive assessment from the European Commission in July, confirming its technical readiness.
The recommendations, issued as part of EU evaluations dating back to 2021, covered areas including border controls, visa policy, access to European security databases and police cooperation. Their implementation required technological upgrades as well as legislative and administrative reforms.
On October 1, Cyprus's Deputy Minister for Migration and International Protection, Nicholas Ioannides, confirmed that "all recommendations made by the European Commission are now considered to have been implemented."
According to Ioannides, Cyprus is technically ready to join Schengen, with the next step being to secure the necessary political agreement.
Austria, the Netherlands express reservations
However, a positive technical assessment alone is not enough for Cyprus to join the Schengen Area.
Accession requires a unanimous decision by the EU Council following consultation with the European Parliament.
According to information obtained by DW, Austria and the Netherlands have already informally expressed reservations over security concerns linked to the Green Line, which divides the island of Cyprus, and the special status of the British Sovereign Base Areas.
Although neither country has officially threatened to veto Cyprus's accession, their reservations carry particular weight.
Both Austria and the Netherlands have previously raised objections to the expansion of the Schengen Area to Bulgaria and Romania.
What is the Green Line?
Perhaps the most significant obstacle is the Green Line, the approximately 180-kilometer-long (112 miles) ceasefire line that has divided Cyprus since Turkey's military intervention in 1974.
It separates the areas controlled by the internationally recognized Republic of Cyprus from the Turkish-controlled northern part of the island.
The buffer zone is monitored by the United Nations Peacekeeping Force in Cyprus (UNFICYP), while the Green Line itself is not an internationally recognized state border.
Crossings between the two sides take place at nine designated crossing points and are governed by a special EU regulation.
This unique arrangement poses a challenge to Schengen membership, as the Republic of Cyprus does not exercise effective control along the entire length of the line. At the same time, Nicosia rejects any arrangement that could turn the Green Line into an external border, either legally or even symbolically.
"The issue raised by some Schengen countries is that the Republic of Cyprus does not control the entire Green Line. It may control the crossing points, but there are also open stretches of land," Dr. Nasia Hadjigeorgiou, associate professor of Transitional Justice and Human Rights at the School of Law of UCLan Cyprus, told DW.
"For it to be considered to have full control, something would have to change. Either the Cyprus problem would have to be resolved, or a strictly controlled physical border would have to be established. There is no other way," said Hadjigeorgiou.
Why are the British Sovereign Base Areas an issue?
Another obstacle to Cyprus's Schengen ambitions is the presence of the British Sovereign Base Areas of Akrotiri and Dhekelia, which remained under UK sovereignty when Cyprus gained independence in 1960.
Together, the two areas cover 254 square kilometers (98 square miles), almost 3% of the island, and remain British sovereign territory.
The main complication concerns the Dhekelia base area, which borders both the territory controlled by the Republic of Cyprus and the self-declared Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus, which is not internationally recognized.
Two crossing points, at Pergamos and Strovilia, are located in this area, where checks are carried out by British authorities. The UK is no longer a member of the European Union.
Dr. Nasia Hadjigeorgiou explains the difficulties arising from this unusual arrangement: "This is problematic because the area in question is controlled on one side by the authorities in the occupied north and on the other by the British Sovereign Base Areas."
"As a result, the United Kingdom would be controlling who enters and leaves the Schengen Area. This is an unusual situation, since it is normally the Schengen member states themselves that decide who can enter and leave the area," she said.
According to information obtained by DW, Nicosia and the British Sovereign Base Areas have already begun discussions on upgrading border control procedures at Pergamos and Strovilia to bring them into line with EU requirements.
Political negotiations with EU countries
In the meantime, Nicosia has stepped up its diplomatic efforts to secure the necessary consensus.
Deputy Minister for Migration Nicholas Ioannides held bilateral meetings with his counterparts from Austria, the Netherlands and Finland on October 1 on the sidelines of the EU Justice and Home Affairs Council meeting in Luxembourg. Cyprus's accession to Schengen was among the issues discussed.
Cyprus also secured significant political backing on October 7 during the summit of the nine Mediterranean EU member states (MED9) in Croatia.
In their joint declaration, the leaders welcomed the European Commission's positive assessment and called for the timely completion of Cyprus's accession process.
Nevertheless, diplomatic sources speaking to DW on condition of anonymity cautioned that despite the positive signals, Cyprus's entry into the Schengen Area should by no means be taken for granted.
The same sources consider it highly likely that the EU may choose to wait for the outcome of the ongoing efforts to resolve the Cyprus problem before making a decision that could create additional political and practical complications.

Estonia's bailiffs afraid for their safety, expect state to act
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
12:57:00 UTC
21:57:00 KST

Estonia's bailiffs afraid for their safety, expect state to act
Threats against bailiffs have become more frequent in Estonia. The Chamber of Bailiffs and Trustees in Bankruptcy calls for action from policymakers and the police.
There have been cases in Estonia in which bailiffs' property has suffered varying degrees of damage. The incidents do not always involve physical attacks, with bailiffs frequently facing insults, threats and humiliation. The situation has worsened in recent years, said Arvi Pink, a board member of the Chamber of Bailiffs and Trustees in Bankruptcy.
"The question here is how the state can assert its authority in such a situation. These 35 bailiffs are an integral part of our state governed by the rule of law," Pink said.
Pink added that while law enforcement agencies respond to physical violence, they tend not to respond to threats and intimidation.
"Is the attitude that this simply comes with the job and should be considered normal or is it actually unacceptable? Our position is that it is unacceptable," Pink stressed. He also gave an example.
"A mother of two receives a photo of knives and brass knuckles from a debtor who works as a butcher, along with a message saying, 'I intend to use these on you!' When we contacted law enforcement, the response was that this comes with our job, that it does not constitute a real threat and so on."
Police recommend reporting all threats, regardless of the circumstances. If there is an immediate danger, a police patrol should be called to the scene. In the case of a written threat, it should be documented and forwarded to the police who will then decide what action to take, explained Anders Allandi, head of the investigation unit at the Ida-Harju Police Station.
"If the elements of a criminal offense are present, we will initiate criminal proceedings. However, when it comes to threats, it is very important for an independent third party to assess the situation objectively and determine how credible the threat is and whether there is reason to believe it will actually be carried out. A bailiff's work is inherently somewhat confrontational: When an ordinary person faces debt collection proceedings, it creates tension and they may often make emotional statements that they do not necessarily mean," Allandi said.
In its appeal, the chamber also noted that bailiffs today face so-called sovereign citizens who believe that the government and other institutions constitute a "malicious elite" conspiring against citizens. As a result, sovereign citizens believe they are not obliged to comply with laws, regulations or court rulings. The Chamber of Bailiffs and Trustees in Bankruptcy stressed that this issue must be addressed and limits must be set.
"Bailiffs exercise public authority, which is state authority. If people are allowed to treat bailiffs the way they are sometimes treated today, debtors and citizens more broadly will come to believe that such behavior is acceptable. This, in turn, undermines the very foundations of the rule of law and, ultimately, our entire state," Pink said.
The Chamber of Bailiffs and Trustees in Bankruptcy has also proposed a meeting with the minister of justice and digital affairs to discuss ways to prevent or mitigate dangerous situations. The meeting has yet to take place, but Minister Liisa-Ly Pakosta said in a written response that she is willing to discuss possible next steps.
--

Відео: Федоров

Philippe stood ready to defeat Le Pen. Now his allies are doubting his chances.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
12:53:59 UTC
21:53:59 KST

PARIS — Edouard Philippe was once seen as the only man capable of defeating Marine Le Pen in next year’s French presidential election. But his lackluster campaign as the country’s voice of reason is putting his allies on edge — and some of them are starting to wonder if he has what it takes.
The former center-right prime minister promised a “massive” campaign platform that would fix France, put its finances back on track and restore the country’s standing in the world. And while Philippe has upped his campaign tempo in recent weeks, his proposals tend to fall flat.
POLITICO spoke to six members of Philippe’s political family, some of them campaign team members, who shared doubts about his strategy and chances of success. Some were granted anonymity to speak candidly about internal matters.
Advertisement
“It’s unbelievable how nothing is making an impact,” a campaign official told POLITICO ahead of Philippe’s decision to announce his plans for a flagship pensions reform. “I can’t stop thinking about it.”
Philippe is still the best-placed mainstream candidate to challenge far-right Le Pen, who commands a substantial lead in the polls. But his poll ratings have stalled over the past year, and he is now locked in a tight race with far-left candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon to clinch a second place which would qualify him for the runoff. MEP Raphaël Glucksmann, who trails the duo in most surveys, could see a boost for his campaign after scoring a decisive victory in the recent center-left primary.
FRANCE NATIONAL PARLIAMENT POLL OF POLLS: ÉDOUARD PHILIPPE AS THE CENTRIST CANDIDATE
Philippe is facing a pileup of problems: He has yet to unite the center behind him, remains burdened by a decade of centrist rule and is struggling to gain traction among voters with his pitch as the plain-speaking pragmatist fighting populism.
“Philippe is the most honest guy I know,” said an ally, “but he needs to unite and find a project that rallies people around him.”
Meanwhile, Le Pen and Mélenchon are dominating headlines with political one-upmanship and at times inflammatory proposals. The two populists locked horns last week over school protests, with Le Pen accusing Mélenchon of fueling the violence, and the far left positioning themselves as the protectors of France’s youth against police violence.
“The risk is great” that Le Pen and Mélenchon will squeeze him out of the race, Philippe’s ally added.
Advertisement
Stale marriage
Philippe, who left his position as prime minister under President Emmanuel Macron in 2020, has been planning his bid to succeed him for years. But things haven’t quite gone to plan on the campaign trail, where he has faced upsets and distractions.
When Philippe recently announced his unpopular proposal to push back the retirement age to 65, it was supposed to be a make-or-break moment in his campaign. Instead, it went almost unnoticed.
First, he was forced to delay his flagship announcement because Macron decided to address the nation about Russian threats and spiraling fuel costs. When he finally got round to it, it was overshadowed by antisemitism allegations against National Rally leader Jordan Bardella.
Ultimately, his 20-minute speech detailing his pensions plans on YouTube garnered only 70,000 views.
A day later, Mélenchon livestreamed a two-hour Q&A session with students from HEC, one of France’s top business schools. It got 550,000 views.
But according to Philippe’s campaign spokesperson Arnaud Péricard, the battle will be won in the long run.
Advertisement
“We’re not firing an arrow and then running away … Voters shouldn’t be underestimated; they can understand why our pensions system needs fixing,” he said. “But we aren’t mere accountants … We want a return of a powerful France that can lead on energy, industry; that’s why we need to balance our books.”
But a mix of economic realism and European ambition sounds all too familiar after a decade of Macron’s presidency — and even insiders know there’s little appetite for it. “There’s no desire for the centrist bloc. It’s a bit like marriage after 10 years,” said the same ally quoted above.
But for Philippe, a pro-European who was one of Macron’s coalition partners, there’s not much else he can offer.
“It’s difficult for the moderates: They know what state the country is in. They understand interest rates, debt and deficits,” said OpinionWay pollster Bruno Jeanbart. “They have to campaign as if things will get better, but it’s going to be difficult. We’ll have to work longer, accept more social spending, less benefits. There is no good news.”
Cornered
The silver lining for Philippe is that while he’s not doing too well, his immediate rivals aren’t doing any better. Conservative leader Bruno Retailleau is stuck on single-digit polling figures, while centrist Gabriel Attal, leader of Macron’s Renaissance party, has relentlessly campaigned throughout the summer but is still lagging behind and looks increasingly isolated.
Party insiders are confident Philippe will prevail, but admit the drawn-out centrist battle is dragging their champion down.
Advertisement
“We are at a bit of a standstill, and letting ourselves get boxed into a duel with Attal,” complained a senior official from Philippe’s Horizons party.
When Philippe and Attal announced their education proposals simultaneously last month, “people didn’t notice our proposals, they just saw the squabbling with Gabriel Attal,” the official added.
A member of Philippe’s campaign team said there was “little bandwidth” to make an impact because there were “too many” centrist candidates. “Maybe we’ll have to wait before addressing some campaign topics,” the official said.
In the coming weeks, Philippe’s team hopes to drain Attal’s support among lawmakers and local representatives, according to two allies, and force him to throw in the towel.
But that’s unlikely to provide Philippe with a much-needed boost, said a centrist senator, as enthusiasm is flatlining at the local level too. “There’s no real movement anywhere,” the senator said. “And the French aren’t really listening.”
Pauline de Saint Remy and Elisa Bertholomey contributed reporting.

Israeli soldiers say ordered to drop heavy bombs on inhabited Gaza buildings without evacuation: Report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
12:52:52 UTC
21:52:52 KST

Four Israeli military intelligence soldiers acknowledged they received instructions to use “heavy bombs” against inhabited buildings in the Gaza Strip without evacuating residents first, in strikes that killed and injured hundreds of Palestinians, according to a media report on Monday.
The soldiers gave their accounts to the Israeli newspaper Haaretz, as Israel continues its genocide in Gaza, which began in October 2023.
The Israeli army has repeatedly claimed that it warns civilians in Gaza to evacuate before strikes, a practice Israeli officials, including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, have frequently boasted.
However, soldiers' testimonies contradict these claims, as they revealed a complete change in open-fire regulations since the start of the war on Gaza, where approximately 2.4 million Palestinians live.
One intelligence soldier, identified only as A, who was tasked with tracking Hamas commanders in Gaza, said: “We knew almost nothing about Hamas and its military wing at the field level.
“In October 2023, we started almost from scratch to identify where their members and operatives were,” he said.
He added that the criteria for defining a target were quickly loosened, alongside “a sharp change in the concept of proportionality and the use of heavy weapons” and a significant easing of the policy governing the killing of civilians considered “collateral damage.”
Expanded targeting policy
Haaretz said the testimonies of the four soldiers portrayed “a fundamentally different concept of warfare, in which even relatively minor targets could be considered sufficient justification for attacks to harm civilians.”
The newspaper said the large number of civilians classified by the military as “collateral damage” was not simply the result of failures or mistaken identification, but stemmed from a policy of expanding the use of firepower “to the maximum extent.”
Haaretz said similar accounts had been presented during the three years of the war and that efforts to compensate for the intelligence failures of Oct. 7, 2023, “contributed to unprecedented tolerance for civilian casualties.”
The newspaper cited an Oct. 31, 2023 Israeli airstrike on a large residential complex in the Jabalia refugee camp in northern Gaza as one example. The stated target was Ibrahim Biari, a Hamas battalion commander in Jabalia.
“We knew Biari was underground, beneath large buildings, but we did not know beneath which building,” said a soldier identified only as D.
“So they chose buildings that were still inhabited and decided to destroy all the buildings above the tunnel where he was located. We did not carry out an evacuation because it was important to kill him without allowing him to escape,” he said.
Soldier A, who said he took part in the mission, said members of the targeting cell understood that the number of civilians likely to be harmed “was extremely high.”
“In the military intelligence estimates of potential collateral damage, there was talk of 250 to 300 people, so the decision was passed up for direct approval by the chief of staff,” he said.
“After the strike, as time passed, we understood that the number of dead was around 250,” he added, referring to Palestinian civilians.
“I remember being shocked when several densely populated buildings were flattened, killing hundreds, in order to kill a battalion commander who only a few weeks earlier would not even have been considered a target,” he said.
Responding to the Jabalia massacre, the Israeli army claimed that the strike had been “replanned several times to reduce harm to civilians,” saying the expected number of civilian casualties “was not in the hundreds.”
The army claimed that after the strike, “the damage was found to have exceeded its initial assessment.”
Civilian bloodshed
Nadav Weiman, executive director of Breaking the Silence, a left-wing Israeli organization, denounced the army’s conduct in Gaza.
“We cannot allow the killing of 300 civilians to assassinate a battalion commander,” he said. “Nor can we kill 20 civilians to kill every Hamas truck driver and then claim publicly that we did everything possible to prevent harm to innocent people.
“It is time for those who issued these orders to take responsibility instead of trying to get rid of the soldiers who courageously decided to tell the public the truth,” Weiman said.
In November 2024, the International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants for Netanyahu and former Defense Minister Yoav Gallant over war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza.
The International Court of Justice, the UN’s principal judicial organ, is also hearing a case brought by South Africa and joined by several countries accusing Israel of genocide against Palestinians in Gaza.
Haaretz said another case described by the soldiers involved the Oct. 13, 2023 targeting of Hamas commander Ali Qadi.
According to the newspaper, an intelligence soldier in the Gaza Division had warned that Qadi “was behaving unusually,” but the division’s intelligence officer disregarded the warning.
“A few days after the war began, Qadi became a target and was subjected to heavy fire,” soldier A said.
“He was in the house with his family, and they decided to kill him. The army quickly announced that he had been killed, but in reality Qadi was the only person who survived the attack. Everyone who was killed had no connection to the target,” he said.
Without evacuation
Another soldier, identified as B, who served in a drone unit, said that after the war began, the division was authorized to operate under expanded parameters, meaning attacks expected to injure up to 20 noncombatants “did not require approval from a senior official outside the targeting cell.”
A third soldier, identified as C, who served in military intelligence, said that several months after the ground offensive began on Oct. 27, 2023, his unit was asked to prepare an entry zone into Gaza City for a maneuvering division.
He said several high-rise buildings in the area were considered a threat to Israeli troops and that an intelligence assessment estimated that about 25% of residents were still inside their homes.
“When we tried to ask how many residents remained and whether that was reasonable, we were told that those residents were targets for the forces on the ground. I could not understand or believe that we were talking about such numbers,” he said.
He added that the forces planning to enter the area could have waited considerably longer before approving the attack.
“So in the early stages we attacked without a full evacuation. Defending the soldiers was given priority, which is understandable, but the numbers (of civilian casualties) kept growing and became unreasonable,” he said.
The Israeli army has killed more than 74,300 Palestinians and injured over 175,400 others in a brutal war since October 2023 that has left the entire enclave in ruins.

Erdoğan says access to safe food is matter of national security
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
12:52:29 UTC
21:52:29 KST

President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan sent a video message to the opening ceremony of World Food Forum.
President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan has said access to safe food is a fundamental component of national security, calling for greater efforts to combat food waste and ensure a sustainable future for coming generations.
“We cannot speak of peace, tranquility or prosperity in a world where we witness millions struggling to survive without even dry bread on the one hand, while food waste continues to increase on the other,” Erdoğan said in a video message sent to the opening ceremony of the World Food Forum.
The president said Türkiye was contributing to efforts to leave a livable world for future generations, particularly in areas such as climate change, environmental protection and food security.
“Acting on this premise, we view access to safe food not merely as a matter of supply, but as a fundamental element of our national security, and we are taking steps accordingly,” he said.
“According to global reports, the largest share of food waste — 60 percent — occurs in households, that is, at the consumer stage... Around 1.5 billion tons of food produced worldwide is lost or wasted each year.”
Erdoğan also called for support for Türkiye’s candidate, Mehdi Eker, in the election for director-general of the United Nations Food and Agriculture Organization.
A veterinarian and agricultural economist by training, Eker served as Türkiye’s minister of food, agriculture and livestock from 2005 to 2015. He was elected to parliament in 2002, 2007, 2011 and 2018.

Use Russian assets to curb voter backlash over funding Ukraine, Kyiv says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
12:52:26 UTC
21:52:26 KST

Ukraine's Minister of Foreign Affairs, Andrii Sybiha attends a meeting with Panama's Foreign Minister, Javier Martinez-Acha (out of frame), at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs in Panama City on March 13, 2026. | Martin Bernetti/AFP via Getty Images
BRUSSELS — The EU should use frozen Russian assets to fund Kyiv’s defense, Ukraine’s Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said, adding that doing so would counter claims from the far right and far left that Europe is footing the bill for the war.
Using the assets would reassure “skeptical audiences across Europe” ahead of a year of major elections, Sybiha said, in a nod to votes in countries including France and Italy in 2027. In France, presidential frontrunner Marine Le Pen has vowed to end financial aid to Kyiv; in Italy, Roberto Vannacci is challenging Giorgia Meloni from the right and opposes continued support for the war-torn country.
Advertisement
The G7 immobilized roughly €300 billion in Russian central bank reserves in 2022, including about €210 billion in the EU — most of which are held at Belgian financial depository Euroclear. Belgium, backed by Italy, rejected an EU proposal late last year to use these assets to back a loan for Ukraine, citing legal and financial risks and fears of Russian retaliation.
The push gained fresh momentum over the summer, when Sweden, the Netherlands, Poland and Spain urged the European Commission to reopen talks and explore ways to overcome Belgium’s objections. But Belgium again shot the idea down.
Sybiha sought to address the Belgian concerns, saying Ukraine’s finance ministry had proposed placing the assets under collective EU control, making the decision to use them and any liability a shared responsibility.
“Belgium’s exposure is a reason to share the risk, not to do nothing,” Sybiha said.
Sybiha also rejected concerns that using the reserves would undermine the euro or weaken Europe’s leverage in future peace talks. The euro’s credibility, he wrote, “rests on Europe’s ability to defend order and principles.” And the leverage provided by the frozen assets “is not in holding the money — it is in spending it.”
He dismissed the risk of Russian retaliation against Western companies, saying Moscow had already seized control of European business assets, including Nestlé, Auchan and Metro. “Keeping the assets immobilized did not deter it,” he wrote.
Russia plans to spend a record €180 billion on its military in 2027, more than 40% above its 2026 spending, Sybiha said. He called on EU leaders to act this fall, warning that a delay would prolong the war and raise the cost of defending Ukraine.
