‘This deal doesn’t help’: Europe slams Trump’s plan to buy Russian diesel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
12:52:02 UTC
21:52:02 KST

European governments rebuked U.S. President Donald Trump’s plan to import hundreds of thousands of tons of Russian diesel, and vowed to keep isolating Moscow and supporting Ukraine as it heads into a brutal wartime winter.
Trump said over the weekend he would import 300,000 tons of Russian diesel, weeks ahead of U.S. midterm elections in which the Republicans are polling badly and in which energy prices and cost-of-living concerns are expected to play a major role.
“This deal doesn't help neither the price of oil products nor the unity of the transatlantic community,” Lithuanian Foreign Minister Kęstutis Budrys said at a gathering of the bloc’s foreign ministers on Monday morning, adding “it is not the European way.”
Irish Foreign Minister Helen McEntee called Trump’s announcement of a deal with Moscow “concerning,” while German Minister of State for Europe Gunther Krichbaum said every dollar spent on Russian energy funded the purchase of weapons used against Kyiv.
The EU’s top diplomat, Kaja Kallas, reminded Washington that “Russia has started this war. We should not forget this.”
On Monday, Zelenskyy suggested that Washington had other motives for pursuing an energy agreement with Moscow, arguing that the Russian fuel involved would make little difference to global supplies.
Speaking at the Warsaw Security Forum, Zelenskyy said proposed Russian diesel deliveries were insignificant compared with global monthly consumption of roughly 120 million tons.
"I don't think that this will have a tangible impact," Zelenskyy said. "I believe that there are different rationales behind this decision."
Advertisement
Zelenskyy also suggested Washington should consider an alternative arrangement with Kyiv. "Why doesn't America then conclude a diesel deal with Ukraine?" he asked. "Let's propose a diesel deal with Ukraine."
He also revealed that Kyiv had not been informed beforehand of Trump's announcement that he had secured an energy ceasefire. "No, we did not know about that," Zelenskyy said. "We've learned that from the media as well."
On their way into their meeting, the EU's foreign ministers remained united in their insistence that increasing pressure on Moscow was the only way forward.
“Obviously our position has not changed — pressure on Russia, sanctions, support to Ukraine, Russia’s isolation is the way to peace,” Latvian Foreign Minister Baiba Braže said.
The British Foreign Office’s minister of state Stephen Doughty said London was “not planning to follow suit with” purchasing Russian energy and would ratchet up “economic pressure” on Moscow.
“Pressure, pressure, pressure on Russia,” Lithuania’s Budrys said.
Advertisement
What ceasefire?
Trump’s claim that Ukraine and Russia had agreed to an “energy ceasefire” drew confusion from Kyiv and its allies over the weekend, with Zelenskyy saying the truce and its terms were “news” to him but that he would support it nonetheless — provided Moscow followed suit.
Just hours after Trump’s announcement, however, Russian bombs fell on Ukrainian power plants, causing widespread blackouts.
Kyiv is bracing for its fifth winter since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022, which Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said last month could prove “tragically critical” for Ukraine due to Russia’s near-constant strikes on infrastructure.
At the opening session of the Warsaw Security Forum on Monday, Tusk slammed "anyone who is trying to introduce any symmetries, who suggests it is Ukraine responsible for the war," saying doing so "gives a valuable present, gift, to the aggressor, to Putin."
Kallas said any ceasefire shouldn’t “only apply to the refineries, where Ukraine has one and Russia has plenty,” adding that would “definitely [be] in the benefit of the Russians.”
She also called on Washington to join Brussels and London in imposing harsh sanctions on Russia. “Of course the U.S. is our biggest ally,” she said, “but our message is clear: If we want to end this war, the only way we can do this is putting more pressure on Russia.”
Advertisement
Ukraine’s financial needs are set to come up at a meeting of European heads of state and government on Thursday in Brussels. The IMF estimated that Kyiv will face a financing gap of $30 billion to $35 billion next year.
"Ukraine will be front and center at this week's European Council," European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said in a statement Sunday night after a phone call with Zelenskyy, adding the war was entering a "new, grimmer phase."
Zoya Sheftalovich contributed reporting from Brussels. Nick Vinocur contributed reporting from Warsaw.

====================================================================================================

Ukraine’s Summer of Adaptation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
12:51:02 UTC
21:51:02 KST

Throughout the spring and summer of 2026, Russia tried to encircle Ukraine’s “fortress belt” in the Donetsk region. One group was to advance from the Lyman area in the north, another from Dobropillya in the southwest, and the two were meant to meet near Barvinkove in the Kharkiv region. Moscow hoped to isolate Sloviansk and Kramatorsk without a frontal assault on either city, but by autumn the northern half of that plan had collapsed.
It collapsed north of Lyman. There the 3rd Army Corps under Brig. Gen. Andriy Biletsky ran Operation Vivaldi for months in near silence; Kyiv acknowledged it only on September 15. Ukrainian officials have since given figures of between roughly 140 and 176 square kilometers (54 and 68 square miles) retaken.
The Washington-based think tank Institute for the Study of War (ISW), which counts only geolocated gains, gives a lower number, but notes that part of the advance was probably made earlier and not reported. In its assessment, Vivaldi broke the northern arm of the Russian pincer and cost Moscow both ground around Lyman and a central element of its campaign plan, including the approach to Sloviansk from the northeast.
The operation is not over. Biletsky has said that Operation Vivaldi, like its namesake’s best-known concertos, has four seasons. ISW believes the third is now underway.
Moscow’s own figures bear little relation to independent counts. At the OSCE, the United Kingdom dismissed Russia’s claim to have taken more than 670 square kilometers (259 square miles) in September. By ISW’s count, Russia ended that month with a net loss of about 81 square kilometers (31 square miles).
Russia Suffers 50,000 Casualties in 1 Month – NATO
In other sectors, Russian pressure continued without an operational result. Russian units attacked daily on the Pokrovsk and Kostyantynivka axes, yet the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS), another Washington think tank, measured their progress in tens of meters per day. The Zaporizhzhia front stayed largely stable, and the northern and Kupiansk sectors served mostly to pin Ukrainian forces in place.
One plan, several chains of command
What made Vivaldi work was less any single weapon than the way different structures were combined. The 3rd Army Corps planned and led the operation, using drones, ground robots and mechanized assaults under one headquarters. Attached to the corps were the 66th Mechanized Brigade, a tank group from the 8th Regiment of the Special Operations Forces, the 10th “DOZOR” mobile border detachment and Artan, a special unit of Ukraine’s defense intelligence (HUR), which fought in one of the operation’s phases. Army, special operations, border guard and intelligence units answer to different chains of command, yet here they worked to a single plan, and commanders on the ground credit the motivation of their troops for holding it together.
On the Zaporizhzhia axis, Artan, led by Col. Viktor Torkotiuk (call sign “Titan”), had been attacking Russian positions long before Vivaldi was made public. The unit reported offensive actions near Stepnohirsk as early as February, and in mid-May, together with neighboring units, it cleared key parts of the settlement. According to HUR, Russia sent VDV reconnaissance troops, considered elite, to retake Stepnohirsk in late May. Artan let them come closer and caught them in an ambush. The Russians refused an offer to surrender and opened fire; the group was destroyed without Ukrainian losses. Holding Stepnohirsk keeps Russian artillery and drone crews further from the city of Zaporizhzhia.
Artan’s ground robots did a large part of the carrying. According to the unit, over the summer they covered about 4,258 kilometers (2,646 miles) on the front line, delivered more than 41 tons of supplies to forward positions, transported captured Russian soldiers and pulled 45 Ukrainian servicemen out from under fire. Torkotiuk describes the purpose plainly: “Technology is transforming the combat capabilities of frontline units. Innovative logistics frees up capacity and forces for active operations and offensive actions.”
The most telling figure, though, is the split among the evacuated. Only 10 were Artan’s own; the other 35 came from neighboring units. A robot fleet run by one unit was serving the whole sector, and that is the model robotic logistics will need if it is to grow beyond individual brigades.
Strikes in depth
At the same time, Ukraine stepped up its campaign against Russian logistics and fuel. Drone units of the Unmanned Systems Forces, commanded by Robert “Madyar” Brovdi, and of the Special Operations Forces put the land corridor to Crimea under fire. Brovdi said that from June 7 Russia’s “Vostok” group officially banned military cargo traffic on the R-280 highway through Mariupol, Berdiansk and Melitopol to Simferopol. Ukrainian long-range drones hit the Omsk refinery, Russia’s largest, some 2,500 kilometers (1,553 miles) from Ukraine, in July and again in October. On Oct. 9, they reached the refinery in Ukhta in the Komi Republic.
Manpower
Ukrainian and Western estimates of Russian losses are close. CSIS puts them at 30,000 to 34,000 killed, wounded or missing per month in 2026, while Russia recruits about 27,000 people a month.
Oleh Ivashchenko, head of HUR, told The Times that Russian generals have asked Putin to mobilize 800,000 people after the September State Duma elections. Daily recruitment, he said, stands at about 1,000 to 1,200, occasionally rising above 1,500.
Limits of the Ukrainian model
None of this makes Ukraine’s position comfortable. Drones and robots save infantry, but they do not replace it, and the army still lacks the people to rotate units out of the line as often as it should. Ground robots come in many models from many manufacturers, which speeds up innovation but complicates training, spare parts and repair, and Russian drones and electronic warfare already hunt them. Ukraine builds most of its long-range strike drones itself, yet it still depends on partners for air defense missiles, satellite intelligence and much of the money behind its own production lines.
Risks: the front and Washington
Russia is likely to resume pressure on the Pokrovsk and Kostyantynivka axes this autumn, relying on infantry infiltration rather than armored thrusts. A breakthrough looks unlikely at present force levels, but constant attrition will test Ukrainian manpower further. Russia will also continue its winter strikes on Ukraine’s power grid, one of the few tools it has that can affect Ukrainian society quickly.
Washington has become the bigger uncertainty. In mid-September President Donald Trump announced that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to stop striking each other’s energy facilities, although neither side had signed anything. The Financial Times reported that Putin did not want a truce before winter, expecting attacks on Ukraine’s grid to force concessions from Kyiv. Zelensky said Ukraine would stop its strikes if partners could guarantee that Russia did the same. The Kremlin welcomed the idea, asked for sanctions to be lifted and kept hitting Ukrainian power plants.
On Oct. 9, Trump announced a deal with Putin to buy Russian diesel, starting with more than 300,000 tons and rising to several million. The Associated Press described it as a stunning reversal of years of American pressure on Moscow. Only weeks earlier Trump had signed a sanctions law that directs his administration to penalize the main buyers of Russian oil and gas. With this deal, the United States becomes a buyer of Russian fuel itself. Zelensky called it “a weak decision by strong partners.” Two days later the Financial Times reported that Washington had threatened to halt purchases of American weapons for Ukraine under PURL unless Kyiv stopped striking Russian refineries.
So Ukraine is being asked to drop the one form of pressure that is visibly hurting Russia’s war economy, while Russia keeps its winter campaign against Ukrainian energy and gains a new buyer for its fuel. Whatever the intent in Washington, the Kremlin is likely to conclude that high fuel prices in an American election year can win it relief its troops could not win at the front.
Europe would pay for that conclusion too. Oil revenue pays for Russia’s army, and each month of relief gives Moscow more time to rebuild forces that European governments already plan against on NATO’s eastern flank. If pressure on Washington works for Russia in Ukraine, Moscow has every reason to try it against European capitals next.
What NATO should take from Ukraine
Allied militaries follow this war closely, yet most of what Ukraine has learned this year exists in the habits of its commanders, engineers and units rather than in written doctrine.
The 3rd Army Corps achieved operational surprise on a battlefield watched by thousands of drones and satellites, because deception and information discipline were planned as carefully as fires. Artan’s figures put a number on something allied logisticians have so far mostly modelled: ground robots carrying a real share of frontline supply and casualty evacuation, across unit boundaries, so that infantry can be used for fighting. Further back, the campaign against the R-280 and Russian refineries has been fought largely with Ukrainian-made drones, cheap enough to use in quantity and able to reach targets 2,500 kilometers away.
NATO armies have rehearsed much of this in exercises. Ukrainian units have done it for months against the army the alliance is preparing to deter. If allied planners keep those units at arm’s length and treat Ukraine as a source of reports rather than a partner in force design, they will learn the same lessons later and pay more for them.
What is at stake this winter is whether Russia can win through pressure on Washington what it failed to win at Lyman. If Ukraine’s deep strikes are traded for cheaper diesel while Russian missiles keep hitting Ukrainian power plants, Moscow gains an operational advantage without taking a single village.
Russia still has more men and more artillery, and this summer it could not make them count. Whether that remains true now depends on Ukraine’s partners: on whether they leave it the means to strike deep, and whether they treat what Ukraine has built as part of Europe’s own defense.

Federal agents searched Representative Ilhan Omar’s home Monday morning as part of a criminal investigation, according to the department of justice and reports in the Associated Press and Fox News.
In a social media post later on Monday, Omar criticized the raid as an attempt by the Trump administration “to target politcal enemies and weaponize law enforcement”.
A video posted by Fox showed what appeared to be law enforcement in HSI jackets at what Fox News said was Omar’s Washington DC residence.
“Today in the Washington DC, area, Homeland Security Investigations executed a judicially authorized search warrant secured by the Department of Justice. This enforcement action is part of an ongoing federal criminal investigation,” a DoJ spokesperson told the Guardian.
It was unclear what the nature of the warrant was. Omar’s office did not respond to a request for comment, and the White House and department of homeland security referred comment to DoJ. Citing two unnamed sources “close to the investigation,” Fox News reported that the search was related to a criminal fraud investigation concerning Omar’s immigration paperwork, which her late father filled out when she was a child.
Donald Trump and key allies have accused Omar of fraud related to her family’s immigration history, fantasizing openly about denaturalizing her and expelling her from the country.
The congresswoman has consistently denied the accusations, though Trump has repeatedly made them national news with gratuitous attacks against Omar, who along with Representative Rashida Tlaib became the United States’s first Muslim congresswoman in 2019.
But even amid a presidency known for political and legal retribution against his critics, the search of Omar’s DC home just three weeks before a crucial midterm election day will surely lead to new accusations that Trump was using the government for his own political ends.
Administration officials, and the president himself, have long hinted at a federal investigation into Omar. “Let’s see what happens,” Trump said at a rally on Saturday after attacking Omar by name, adding that Vice-President JD Vance “and our people are looking at it very strongly”.
It was just the latest in months of talk about investigating Omar. Trump in December accused her of having “married her brother” and said she “should be thrown the hell out of our country”, a reference to a years-old but unsubstantiated claim that Omar sought to help her ex-husband – who they allege is really her brother – obtain immigration papers via a sham marriage.
Days later, his “border czar” Tom Homan said: “We’re pulling the records now,” referring to Omar, and said a fraud investigator in Homeland Security Investigations, the ICE division that historically has been tasked with investigative work, would look into the matter.
In March , Vance told rightwing media personality Benny Johnson: “We actually think that Ilhan Omar definitely committed immigration fraud” and that he had recently spoken to top Trump aide Stephen Miller about “what the remedies are”. Homeland security secretary Markwayne Mullin told Johnson last month that there was an ongoing investigation and “something’s going to happen”.
“We know that she married her brother to try to bring him into the United States,” Mullin said. “We know he lives now in London. We feel that there may be more to this, the whole family migration, and possibly some illegal activity for them to come to the United States to begin with. But all of us, we’re investigating.”
Soon after, Homan said he could not “comment on an ongoing criminal investigation.
“We’ll let HSI, Homeland Security Investigations continue to do their investigation,” he added.
Omar’s social media post after the raid on Monday said: “I’m OK. Make no mistake: this is an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement.”
The congresswoman also said Trump had spent years targeting her “with baseless lies and smear campaigns”.
“This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation.”
Omar has for years denied unsubstantiated rumors from Trump and others about herself and her family, including the accusation that her ex-husband, Ahmed Nur Said Elmi, is in fact her brother, and that the marriage was part of an effort to earn him immigration status. Marriage fraud is a felony, though it has a five-year statute of limitations. Omar and Elmi formally divorced in 2017 after separating in a religious divorce years earlier.
The New York Post last month also quoted an unnamed “top immigration official” who said “the Trump administration could initiate a denaturalization process” against Omar if there is sufficient evidence that she or her father lied on immigration applications. The story noted accusations that Omar was older than her recorded age of 17 when she was naturalized, which could be relevant because she received citizenship via her parents. The report also raised questions about Omar’s father, who reportedly claimed to be an educator, though his obituary later described a military career.
As the most prominent Somali-American in the United States, Omar has faced years of racist attacks from the president and his supporters.
At his rally Saturday, Trump said of Somalia: “All they have is crime and squalor” and suggested that “our” US constitution did not belong to Omar. Two days earlier, he had written that Minnesota “is being taken over by Somali Immigrants”, even though the vast majority of Somali-Americans in the state are US citizens.
“The Somalians should not be allowed to get away with what they are doing,” Trump wrote, urging supporters in the state to “fight back!”
Somali-Americans, especially, have borne relentless insult from the White House in Trump’s second term. In December, the president referred to them as “garbage” who “come from hell, and they complain, and do nothing but bitch”.
“Let them go back to where they came from and fix it,” he added.

One-way traffic on IJssel river lifted but “drought is not over”
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
The highways agency Rijkswaterstaat has lifted restrictions on the IJssel river that forced ships carrying freight from Arnhem to Zutphen to take a 300km detour.
A one-way system was imposed on September 24 after the river level dropped as a result of the summer drought both in the Netherlands and further upstream in Germany and Switzerland.
The agency said it was able to allow ships to travel in both directions now that the water level has risen to 1.45m above its baseline, but it warned that the drought period is “not over”.
Koninklijke Binnnenvaart Nederland, which represents inland waterway users, said the ending of the restriction was welcome, but shipping operators were still having to contend with limitations such as transporting lighter loads.
“The problems are not over. Low water is still having a big impact on inland shipping,” a spokesman said.

Fiji Criticized in U.S. Trafficking Report Over Failure to Tackle Grace Road Cult
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
12:48:00 UTC
21:48:00 KST

Reported by
Fiji has been granted a one-year reprieve from a potential downgrade that could lead to U.S. aid cuts, amid concerns over its efforts to combat human trafficking, including its response to the Korean doomsday sect the Grace Road Group, according to a U.S. State Department report released last week.
This year’s Trafficking in Persons (TIP) report kept Fiji on its “Tier 2 Watchlist” of countries that do not fully meet the State Department’s minimum standards for combating human trafficking, noting that the Pacific island nation had failed to secure a trafficking conviction for three years running.
“Official complicity and corruption undermined anti-trafficking efforts and allowed traffickers to operate with impunity” in Fiji, the Oct. 8 report found.
However, the State Department granted Fiji a one-year waiver sparing it from being automatically downgraded to Tier 3, a designation that would have put it alongside countries including Iran and Afghanistan and could result in restrictions on U.S. non-humanitarian assistance.
Fiji, a country of just under a million people, has been on the Tier 2 Watchlist since 2024, but last year’s TIP report was the first to single out Grace Road.
Previous OCCRP reporting has revealed how Grace Road has become one of Fiji’s largest conglomerates, with businesses including supermarkets, beauty salons, and restaurants. The group has built ties with members of the country’s elite, despite consistent allegations that members are beaten and subjected to slave-like work conditions. The group’s leader, Shin Ok-joo, is currently imprisoned in Korea and other leading group members in Fiji are wanted by Korean law enforcement.
“Foreign nationals, including from the Republic of Korea and the United States, who are members of a religious organization, the Grace Road Group, experience conditions indicative of human trafficking,” this year’s TIP report said. “Victims associated with the organization have reported being forced to work excessive hours with no rest days, physical violence, passport confiscation, extortion, and unpaid wages.”
While the report said that Fijian police continue to investigate trafficking allegations involving members of the Grace Road Group, it also said that the government “continued to inadequately respond to INTERPOL red notices for leaders of the organization associated with related allegations, leading to further concerns of official complicity.”
“Despite public reporting on suspected forced labor in this organization since at least 2018, the government has never prosecuted or convicted any offenders associated with the allegations,” the report said.
Earlier this year, two American women who escaped Grace Road told OCCRP that they were ready to return to Fiji to testify against the group.
Grace Road Group denied the allegations in the TIP report, saying in a statement that they were “not findings by any Fiji court and should not be reported as established facts.”
“Grace Road Group’s businesses in Fiji are lawful commercial operations,” it said.
The TIP report also noted other alleged trafficking operations in Fiji.
“Traffickers exploit foreign victims, including from Thailand and China, as well as Fijian women and children in sex trafficking, using commercial sex establishments, hotels, private homes, massage parlors, websites and cell phone applications to facilitate the exploitation of sex trafficking victims,” it said.
A nation on the Watchlist that has failed to improve after two years normally would be relegated to Tier 3. However, Fiji was given a one-time waiver because it had “devoted sufficient resources to a written plan that, if implemented, would constitute significant efforts to meet the minimum standards, the report said.
The waiver gives Fiji until next year to make clear progress or be downgraded.

Uniform tax rules for aircraft leasing should help resolve existing disputes — Katamadze
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
15:47:46 EEST
21:47:46 KST

Uniform tax rules for aircraft leasing should help resolve existing disputes — Katamadze
Kyiv • UNN
The Ministry of Finance has an instrument in the form of a tax consultation for the possible resolution of disputes over the taxation of aircraft leasing for previous years.
When preparing a general tax consultation on the taxation of aircraft leasing, the Ministry of Finance of Ukraine should take into account not only future transactions, but also create conditions for resolving existing disputes between airlines and law enforcement agencies. This will make it possible to establish a unified approach to the taxation of lease payments for aircraft. Hryhol Katamadze, president of the Association of Taxpayers of Ukraine, expressed this opinion in an exclusive comment to UNN.
Details
The Ministry of Finance now has an opportunity to take an important step toward business — to use the instrument of a general tax consultation not only to determine the rules for taxing aircraft leasing in the future, but also to consider situations that arose earlier. Within the scope of its powers, the Ministry of Finance can establish in the consultation a clear approach to applying tax rules to transactions from previous years that have already become the subject of disputes. The tax system should be predictable: companies must understand the rules under which they operate and be able to plan their activities. After all, if the state seeks to create favorable conditions for doing business, it must not only establish rules but also help eliminate legal uncertainty where it has already led to conflicts between businesses and government agencies. This concerns not only the aviation industry but also a general principle: tax rules should be clear, consistent, and the same for everyone
How disputes over aircraft leasing arose
The issue of taxing lease payments by Ukrainian airlines to nonresidents became the subject of a dispute after the Economic Security Bureau began interpreting such payments as royalties in 2024. This approach served as grounds for opening criminal proceedings against at least five airlines.
Representatives of the aviation industry dispute this interpretation and point to the need for a unified approach to applying the Tax Code of Ukraine and international treaties on the avoidance of double taxation.
What instrument does the Ministry of Finance have?
To resolve the situation, businesses appealed to the Ministry of Finance. The ministry confirmed that it is working on the issue of taxing lease and rental payments for aircraft made to nonresidents. After receiving and analyzing practical cases involving airlines, the Ministry of Finance plans to prepare a draft general tax consultation.
According to Hryhol Katamadze, when preparing this document, it is important to consider the application of the relevant rules to transactions that have already become the subject of a dispute.
In this situation, the Ministry of Finance has an instrument that allows it not only to clarify the rules for taxing aircraft leasing in the future, but also to clearly define in a general tax consultation its approach to transactions from previous years that have already become the subject of disputes. Disputes over aircraft leasing did not arise today — they concern transactions from previous years and have already had specific consequences for businesses. Therefore, within the scope of its powers, the Ministry of Finance should clearly explain the application of tax rules to such transactions, including with regard to the legislation and international treaties in force at the time the payments were made. This will help establish a legal basis for considering existing disputes
A general tax consultation does not mean the automatic termination of criminal proceedings; rather, it is an instrument through which the Ministry of Finance explains the practical application of tax legislation in situations where its provisions allow for ambiguous interpretation. Its possible impact on existing disputes will depend on the content of the explanations, the circumstances of specific cases, and the legal mechanisms that may be applied.
Therefore, when preparing the consultation, it is important to take into account practical examples from airlines, the positions of businesses, and the specific features of international treaties on the avoidance of double taxation. This will make it possible to formulate a consistent position for the state, create a basis for the legal settlement of disputes that have already arisen, and reduce the risk of similar conflicts recurring in the future.

Nobel Prize for economics awarded to Hall and Woodford for work on ‘smoothing’ crises
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
12:47:15 UTC
21:47:15 KST

Two US economists have won the 2026 Nobel economics prize for their work developing models that help central bankers and finance ministers to stabilise their countries, avoiding long recessions and runaway inflation.
Robert Hall of Stanford University, California, and Michael Woodford of Columbia University, New York, were recognised for developing the “microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilisation”, giving policymakers better tools to smooth out the peaks and troughs of their economies.
The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences said it was recognising the pair for generating “a paradigm shift in stabilisation policy”, awarding them the prize worth a combined $1.2m (£900,000).
“New Keynesian models, a result of their research, allow us to explain and quantify how stabilisation policy affects business cycles and are now used by central banks and finance ministries around the world,” the academy said.
These models improved on John Maynard Keynes’s stabilisation models, which struggled to handle the impact of the oil shock in the 1970s, when countries suffered high inflation, weak growth and high unemployment at the same time.
Hall and Woodford demonstrated how traditional models could be reconstructed, based on how individual households and businesses collectively affect an economy through their actions.
Hall’s work was based on forward-looking consumer behaviour rather than the more mechanical rules of thumb used by Keynes, which linked key variables such as inflation, unemployment and gross domestic product (GDP).
Woodford built on this work to create the New Keynesian model, a full macroeconomic stabilisation framework that is the main tool for policymakers now.
This model was used after the 2008 financial crisis by policymakers as they steered the global economy away from the risk of a second great depression.
“The laureates’ work has provided us with a stable theoretical foundation for the models that are now used by central banks and governments around the world. With them, we are better equipped to deal with shocks in the economy, such as energy crises or sudden changes in how much households consume,” John Hassler, the chair of the committee for the economics prize, said.
Hall and Woodford’s work also led to the development of forward guidance, where central bankers communicate where they expect interest rates to be in the future. That became an important tool after the 2008 financial crisis, and the Covid pandemic, when interest rates were cut to record lows.
Forward guidance has had its critics, though – the current chair of the US Federal Reserve, Kevin Warsh, has argued it should only have a “limited and circumscribed” role in normal times, to avoid “creating ambiguity in the name of clarity”.
And in 2014, the then Bank of England governor, Mark Carney, was labelled an “unreliable boyfriend” for dropping hints over interest rate rises that never came to pass.
Woodford said he was “elated”. “It’s a tremendous honour. It’s a surprise but I’m feeling very good about it,” he told reporters in Stockholm by phone after receiving the news.
The Columbia University president, Jennifer L Mnookin, said: “I offer my deepest congratulations to Michael Woodford on this tremendous honour.
“What a tribute to his groundbreaking work alongside Robert E Hall that has fundamentally reshaped the theoretical foundations of stabilisation policy and provided us with the tools to navigate economic upturns and downturns more effectively.”
Hall is also known for coining the idea that US economists can be divided into freshwater and saltwater varieties.
The fresh water group, who tend to be based at inland universities located near the Great Lakes, such as the University of Chicago, believe in free markets, neoclassical price theory, rational expectations and monetarism.
Salt water economists, though, cluster at coastal universities, such as Harvard, MIT, UC Berkeley, Yale, Princeton, UCLA and Columbia. They tend to be Keynesians and New Keynesians, believing that governments and central banks can affect demand in their economies.
The economics Nobel prize is not one of the five created by Alfred Nobel. Instead, it was invented by Sweden’s central bank, and is known as the Sveriges Riksbank prize in economic sciences in memory of Alfred Nobel.

====================================================================================================

Can Turkey and Pakistan defend Saudi Arabia from the Houthis?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
12:46:37 UTC
21:46:37 KST

Breadcrumb
Can Turkey and Pakistan defend Saudi Arabia from the Houthis?
Turkey and Pakistan's promise of rapid military support for Saudi Arabia faces a more urgent test after weekend attacks on Riyadh’s international airport killed 12 people and forced its closure.
Turning that commitment into effective protection will depend on what its partners can spare, how their forces operate alongside Saudi units and how far Ankara and Islamabad are willing to enter the conflict.
At an emergency meeting in Riyadh on 5 October, the three countries pledged to implement their collective defence commitments and rapidly deploy agreed forces and capabilities to Saudi Arabia, subject to their national legislation.
The decision marked a significant step for the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement they signed in August, but left troop numbers, equipment, missions, and deployment schedules publicly unspecified.
Their contributions also begin from different positions. Pakistan already has an established military presence in the kingdom and has reportedly supplied weapons and advisers to Yemeni government forces.
Turkey is considering additional defensive assistance while explicitly ruling out offensive operations abroad under the pact.
The immediate test is whether these commitments can address Saudi vulnerabilities quickly enough to matter - and whether protecting the kingdom can remain separate from supporting its campaign in Yemen.
What Riyadh needs
Saudi Arabia’s requirement extends beyond additional troops. In September, drones struck the East-West Pipeline south of Medina, causing injuries and damage and prompting a precautionary shutdown of the route carrying crude to Red Sea export terminals.
Riyadh said the drones originated in Iraq, but no group claimed responsibility, and the Islamic Resistance in Iraq denied involvement. Earlier attacks on Eastern Province oil facilities had already raised concerns about Iran-aligned Iraqi factions, adding a northern threat to the Houthi challenge from Yemen.
The aviation threat escalated sharply over the weekend. An attack on King Khalid International Airport on 10 October killed 12 people and wounded more than 300, including Saudi and foreign nationals. On 11 October, the Saudi-led coalition said another projectile struck Terminal 4, causing a fire, while air defences intercepted a cruise missile nearby.
The airport remained closed that day. Neither weekend attack had been claimed at the time of reporting. The Houthis nevertheless renewed their warning against using Saudi airports and airspace, exempting Mecca and Medina.
The attacks followed earlier strikes that killed three Saudis, including a Saudia pilot, and a Sudanese national at Riyadh airport. Sustained protection of civilian infrastructure has become an immediate requirement.
“Saudi Arabia is primarily seeking to strengthen its air defences against Houthi drone strikes targeting critical infrastructure,” Sebastian Sons, an expert on Saudi Arabia, told The New Arab.
Sons expects Turkey to contribute equipment and technological expertise, while Pakistan could expand cooperation in training, capacity-building, and troop deployments. The potential division of labour reflects different strengths, although the governments have not publicly detailed their respective assignments.
For Riyadh, successful protection has economic as well as military consequences. Attacks on energy infrastructure and airports threaten business activity and complicate efforts to present the kingdom as a secure investment destination.
The WPC Energy Congress was still going ahead in Riyadh on 11 October, Saudi authorities said, despite the airport closure. Reinforcing defences could help Saudi Arabia sustain support for its Yemeni partners while reducing exposure at home.
The military campaign is also continuing. On 10 October, the Giants Brigades said they had repelled a Houthi attack north of Dhubab Airport near the Bab el-Mandeb, alongside Saudi-led airstrikes on Houthi reinforcements.
The coalition said it was working to dismantle the group’s ballistic missile network. Neither statement establishes that the Houthis’ ability to strike Saudi territory has been eliminated.
Turkey's available capabilities
Ankara’s contribution could initially draw on technical relationships already in place. According to reports, technical teams, air-defence systems, and electronic warfare equipment have been present in Saudi Arabia since last year. Turkish officials described plans for additional personnel and equipment, with further deployments dependent on parliamentary action.
Barın Kayaoğlu, a Turkish independent analyst and consultant, said the available options would depend on Saudi requirements. ASELSAN’s Korkut, an anti-aircraft gun system designed to intercept threats at close range, is one candidate.
“Some of those systems could be transferred over to the Kingdom,” he told The New Arab. Gun-based defences could help protect Saudi facilities against drones without relying solely on more expensive missile interceptors.
In early October, ASELSAN announced a $125 million export contract for weapon and electronic warfare systems. Saudi interest makes the Kingdom a possible buyer, although the announcement names neither the customer nor the delivery schedule. Ukraine is another potential destination, as Kyiv had received a small number of Korkut systems earlier this year for use against Russian attacks.
Kayaoğlu also identified MKE’s Tolga short-range air-defence system, as well as ASELSAN’s Gürz, which combines guns and missiles on a mobile platform like the Russian Pantsir-S1. For wider coverage, he suggested “the ALP-class radars and perhaps even the Hisar short-to-medium range air defence systems”.
The former would help detect and track threats, while the latter would provide interception beyond the reach of close-range guns. Such systems could reinforce lower defensive layers. Kayaoğlu cautioned that the longer-range Siper is not known to have anti-ballistic-missile capabilities.
Saudi interest in Turkish air defence also predates the current crisis. Around SAHA Expo 2026 in Istanbul, reports described Saudi interest in ASELSAN’s Korkut for low-altitude threats, proposed Kalkan surveillance radars linked to mobile command-and-control shelters, and a Roketsan proposal for six Hisar-O batteries to protect oil facilities and airbase corridors.
Availability also depends on personnel. “Some of it will relate to what and who can be spared to go to KSA,” Kayaoğlu told The New Arab. “Active-duty personnel are harder to spare; contractors or company personnel are much easier.”
Company technicians or recently retired personnel could support equipment sooner than a larger military contingent could undertake an operational mission. Still, in Kayaoğlu’s view, “showing the political commitment to a Mecca Pact partner is even more important than what and who is being sent”.
Kayaoğlu said a deployment of serving troops would require parliamentary approval, separately from ratification of the Mecca Pact. Existing bilateral agreements reportedly permit some technical assistance, while the unpublished pact’s implications for future authorisations remain unclear.
Ankara has drawn a public boundary around its involvement. Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said on 8 October that military delegations were assessing Saudi needs, particularly air defence, electronic warfare, and technical support, while ruling out sending Turkish troops abroad to conduct attacks under the agreement.
“Unless the Houthis decide to target Turkish civilian vessels transiting the Red Sea and the Bab el-Mandeb, I do not see Ankara getting involved in Yemen’s civil war and opening a new front with Iran,” Kayaoğlu said.
The maritime domain could nevertheless offer scope for limited involvement. Surveillance, escort, intelligence-sharing and coalition coordination could support Red Sea security while maintaining a boundary between defensive assistance and offensive operations in Yemen.
Pakistan's head start - and its limits
Pakistan’s longstanding military relationship with Saudi Arabia gives it a different starting point. Reuters reported in May that Islamabad had deployed about 8,000 troops under the 2025 Strategic Mutual Defence Agreement, alongside a squadron of JF-17 light jet fighters, two squadrons of drones and a Chinese-made HQ-9 air-defence system. Sources told the agency that Pakistani personnel operated the equipment, financed by Saudi Arabia.
This gives Islamabad an existing air-combat, unmanned and ground-based air-defence presence, adding to those already stationed in the kingdom under earlier agreements. Reportedly, the pact could eventually allow for up to 80,000 Pakistani troops to support Saudi border security if required.
“Pakistan’s existing military presence gives it an established framework for cooperation, easing coordination and potentially allowing it to provide certain capabilities more quickly,” John Calabrese, a senior fellow at the Middle East Institute, told The New Arab.
“But an existing presence does not automatically translate into the capacity, much less the political authorisation, for a substantially larger deployment.”
Pakistan’s involvement reportedly extends to support for forces inside Yemen. In early October, Reuters reported four cargo-plane deliveries to Aden in September containing air-defence systems, light artillery, drones and counter-drone systems. A Pakistani official also said military advisers were working alongside Saudi counterparts supporting Yemeni troops.
The publicly reported categories do not establish models, quantities, readiness or the advisers’ precise duties. But assistance to Yemeni forces raises a question that a deployment confined to Saudi territorial defence does not: whether Islamabad’s contribution facilitates operations inside Yemen.
“I think the distinction could become blurred very quickly,” Calabrese said. Pakistan may describe its mission as protecting Saudi territory and infrastructure, he explained, while support to Yemeni forces risks drawing it into the conflict itself.
Domestic decision-making has also changed since 2015, when Pakistan’s parliament voted to remain neutral in the Saudi-led intervention while pledging to defend the kingdom. Reuters reported on 8 October that the latest commitment to rapid deployment had proceeded without a parliamentary vote. That political contrast does not, by itself, establish how quickly further units could become operational.
Islamabad must also preserve relations with neighbouring Iran, its diplomatic channels and capacity to manage its own security challenges. Calabrese expects those considerations to discourage an open-ended commitment, even as Pakistan seeks to demonstrate solidarity with Riyadh.
What rapid support can change
Across both contributions, speed depends on more than transporting equipment. Operators, maintenance, ammunition, communications and arrangements for coordinating engagements must be available. Protection of selected facilities may be achievable before a wider network is established, but the announced pledge gives no public basis for assigning a firm timetable.
For Saudi Arabia, additional support could improve protection and coordination without delivering a decisive battlefield outcome. “However, even with increased external support, a decisive military victory over the Houthis remains unlikely,” Sons said.
That makes the partnership’s political effect important alongside its operational contribution. “Beyond their practical value, Turkish and Pakistani support carries symbolic weight, allowing Riyadh to demonstrate regional unity and solidarity with non-Arab partners,” he added.
Sons sees these relationships as part of Saudi strategic diversification, complementing its ties with Washington. The kingdom, he said, will continue seeking greater US engagement against the Houthis. That possibility became more explicit over the weekend: on 10 October, Trump said the United States was considering joining Saudi strikes. This remained a possibility rather than an announced intervention.
The first measure of success will therefore be whether additional systems and personnel assume defined defensive missions and reduce Saudi exposure to attacks.
How much further the partnership changes the war will depend on its partners’ willingness to sustain that support - and whether their efforts to limit involvement survive the demands of an expanding conflict.
Francesco Salesio Schiavi is an Italian specialist in the Middle East. His focus lies in the security architecture of the Levant and the Gulf, with a particular emphasis on Iraq, Iran, and the Arab Peninsula, as well as military and diplomatic interventions by international actors

Ukraine’s TENCORE Bundles 4 Ground Drones in Single AI-Powered Ecosystem
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
12:46:10 UTC
21:46:10 KST

TENCORE, a Ukrainian developer of unmanned ground vehicles (UGVs), launched what it calls the country’s first comprehensive ecosystem of ground robots, combining four platforms for frontline logistics, amphibious operations and emergency response under a single architecture, the company wrote.
The company said the ecosystem is meant to replace what it described as an ad hoc “technological zoo” of disparate UGVs that military units have had to assemble from dozens of developers.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
According to TENCORE, that patchwork has led to fragmented logistics, a heavy maintenance burden, redundant crew training and communication incompatibilities.
TENCORE develops UGVs for military and dual-use applications. The company said it has delivered over 4,000 robotic platforms to the Armed Forces of Ukraine (AFU) and deployed them across more than 50 combat brigades since the start of Russia’s 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
                                                                                                                                                                         A TOR 4×4 wheeled unmanned ground vehicle (UGV) developed by Ukrainian arms maker TENCORE, equipped with run-flat tires and an open cargo bed for tactical logistics, stands in a studio shot released with TENCORE’s ecosystem launch. (Photo courtesy of TENCORE)                             
Europe: Assemble, Decide, Engage!
The ecosystem rests on four platform classes.
- TerMIT is the flagship tracked UGV, with a modular design that adapts for frontline logistics, medical evacuation, engineering missions and remote weapon stations.
- TOR is a high-mobility 4×4 wheeled vehicle with run-flat tires, intended for tactical logistics and cargo transport in high-threat environments.
- MAT1LDA, developed by NODRICS, is an 8×8 amphibious wheeled all-terrain vehicle built to cross water obstacles and complex off-road terrain.
- TRAX UTILITY is a dual-use emergency response platform designed for civil protection and specialized units.
                                                                                                                                                                         Five of TENCORE’s unmanned ground vehicles, including tracked and wheeled platforms configured for cargo transport and weapons payloads, stand side by side in a studio shot released with the company’s ecosystem launch. (Photo courtesy of TENCORE)                             
TENCORE’s top management said the company’s ground robots are “[taking] the risks instead of people” on the frone lines.
“Time is a luxury reserved for companies born outside of wartime. Our experience is forged in harsh reality, driving us beyond standalone products. We are building a new architecture of security – in Ukraine, Europe, and globally,” the management was quoted as saying in the press release.
“We build so that machines take the risks instead of people, and we open our doors to every developer ready to shape the future of defense technology with us,” it added.
                                                                                                                                                                         A TerMIT tracked unmanned ground vehicle (UGV), fitted with a rocket launcher, sits on a black eight-wheeled platform in a studio shot released with TENCORE’s ecosystem launch. (Photo courtesy of TENCORE)                             
As part of the ecosystem, TENCORE also developed AI KIT – a hardware and software module that lets UGVs switch to autonomous mode and continue their mission route or return to base during a complete loss of signal under electronic warfare.
The launch also doubles as an invitation to Ukrainian and international defense tech engineers, startups and hardware developers. TENCORE offered what it called an acceleration pathway to integrate custom innovations onto serial, battle-tested, and certified platforms.
The company cited production capacity of over 500 units per month and compliance with ISO 9001:2015 and AQAP 2110:2016 quality standards that are NATO-eligible.

EU foreign ministers have approved over 1,600 new sanctions listings targeting Russia’s military-industrial complex, with more than half linked to the production chain for ballistic missiles, EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said.
“This is the single largest expansion of our sanctions list since Russia started its war,” Kallas wrote on X.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The 22nd sanctions package covers 1,646 entities and individuals, according to The Moscow Times. With the new listings, nearly 4,650 entities and individuals are now under EU sanctions over Russia’s war against Ukraine.
The measures target people and companies involved in missile development, testing, and manufacturing, as well as the production of fuel, engines, and specialized materials used in missile systems.
“More than half are connected to the production chain for ballistic missiles,” Kallas said.
Reuters reported that the blacklist also includes manufacturers of specialized textiles, synthetic fibers, and carbon fibers used in weapons production.
The package further targets drone manufacturers and shipyards that service submarines, while 77 individuals are being sanctioned for participating in State Duma elections held in Russian-occupied Ukrainian territories.
The EU has also added seven North Korean entities and individuals accused of helping Russia’s war effort, amid growing concern over military cooperation between Moscow and Pyongyang.

“We are making it significantly harder, slower and more expensive for Russia to produce the weapons it uses to kill Ukrainians.”

Ukraine passes minority rights law, paving way for breakthrough in EU accession talks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
12:42:59 UTC
21:42:59 KST

Ukraine’s parliament passed a minority rights law, easing a years-long dispute with Hungary. Diplomats expect Budapest to approve two more EU accession clusters on Tuesday, and Prime Minister Péter Magyar could meet President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Brussels on Thursday.
Ukraine’s parliament passed a law strengthening minority rights on Monday, easing years of tensions with Hungary and paving the way for Kyiv to advance its EU accession talks.
The legislation, approved by 266 of the 450 deputies in the Verkhovna Rada, strengthens protections for the use of minority languages in schools and at cultural events.
The rights of the roughly 100,000 ethnic Hungarians living in Ukraine’s Transcarpathia region have strained relations between Budapest and Kyiv for years. The previous Hungarian government, led by former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán, had blocked progress in Ukraine’s EU accession talks since 2023 over the dispute.
In June, new Prime Minister Péter Magyar agreed an 11-point action plan with Ukraine and lifted Hungary’s veto on opening the first two negotiating clusters. However, Budapest made further progress conditional on Kyiv formally adopting the minority rights legislation.
Following Monday’s vote, diplomats expect Hungary to approve the opening of two additional clusters, covering the internal market and competitiveness, at an intergovernmental conference on Tuesday.
The breakthrough could also pave the way for the first bilateral meeting between Magyar and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
Magyar said over the weekend that the two leaders could meet at the European Council summit in Brussels on Thursday. An earlier meeting had been put on hold after Magyar made the talks conditional on progress over minority rights.
Relations between Hungary and Ukraine deteriorated sharply under Orbán, whose government repeatedly clashed with Kyiv and obstructed its EU membership bid. Orbán also ran a fiercely anti-Ukraine election campaign, portraying Kyiv as a threat to European security.
After his landslide election victory in April, Magyar, who took office in May, promised a more pragmatic approach towards Ukraine.
But tensions resurfaced in September when he clashed with Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha over Hungary’s participation in Zelenskyy’s Carpathian summit, aimed at boosting development in the region.
Magyar criticised Ukraine for listing Hungary as a participant without his approval, while Sybiha accused him of echoing Orbán’s rhetoric.

'Gods would be aghast': SC seeks balance between faith and public health in firecracker debate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
12:42:49 UTC
21:42:49 KST

NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Monday stressed the need to balance religious sentiments with public health concerns while considering restrictions on firecrackers in Delhi-NCR. It said a greater public awareness and voluntary adoption of less polluting practices could offer a way forward.A bench comprising Chief Justice of India Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana said it was not inclined to hurt religious sentiments but emphasised that citizens should be encouraged to celebrate festivals in ways that minimise air and noise pollution."We will not hurt religious sentiments but at the same time, people should themselves come forward and opt for it. The whole exercise should involve a balancing approach," the Chief Justice said, according to news agency PTI.The bench was hearing suo motu proceedings concerning air pollution in the National Capital Region, covering issues including firecrackers, stubble burning and solid waste management.During the hearing, Justice Bagchi questioned the religious basis for bursting firecrackers, asking, "What is religious about bursting crackers?"Senior advocate Aparajita Singh, who is assisting the bench as amicus curiae, highlighted the health risks associated with air pollution, particularly for children, elderly people and those with existing health vulnerabilities.
"Gods would be aghast if they knew that children were suffering and getting sick in their name," Singh said, responding to arguments linking firecrackers with religious practices, PTI reported.She also flagged difficulties in enforcing restrictions on the duration of firecracker use, arguing that limits on the number of hours allowed would have little impact without effective implementation.
"It sounds really nice in court, that it is only two hours or one hour. But the court also knows that it is not implemented. It is impossible for police officers to be on every street all the time," Singh said.The amicus suggested referring the issue to the Commission for Air Quality Management (CAQM), the statutory body responsible for air quality management in the region, so that it could examine the available material and associated medical concerns.The bench, however, cautioned against issuing directions that might be difficult to implement on the ground."We have to be extremely careful in passing an order unless we are in a position to make it manageable and enforceable," the Chief Justice said, adding that restrictive directions were often perceived as coercive.

Ukrainian defence tech company Phantom Defense acquires anti-drone net developer, unveils counter-UAV system – photos, videos
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
15:42:00 EEST
21:42:00 KST

Ukrainian defence tech company Phantom Defense acquires anti-drone net developer, unveils counter-UAV system – photos, videos
Ukrainian defence tech company Phantom Defense has acquired Karakurt, which develops nets designed to ensnare drones, bringing its team on board. The company has also unveiled its new Manhal counter-UAV system.
Source: Phantom Defense in a comment to Ukrainska Pravda
Details: Phantom Defense has signed an agreement to acquire Karakurt in full and integrate its technologies into its own ecosystem.
"The integration of net-based UAV interception technologies into the Phantom Defense ecosystem will enhance protection for frontline units and infrastructure against a range of unmanned threats," the company noted.
The Karakurt system uses a special launcher module to fire a net on an incoming drone. The net tangles around its propellers, preventing them from spinning freely and bringing the drone down.
Phantom Defense says Karakurt's nets can bring down enemy drones without blowing them up, leaving the aircraft intact for Ukrainian defence forces to examine or potentially put to use.
According to the company, drone nets are also cheaper to produce and maintain than anti-aircraft missile and artillery systems, allowing them to be deployed widely among units along the line of contact.
The use of drone nets also helps minimise the risk of collateral damage caused by explosions and debris. The company says this makes the technology suitable for defending critical infrastructure and civilian facilities against various drone threats.
Karakurt systems come in several variants, tailored to different drone types and operating conditions. The M3, M4 and A4 models, compatible with DJI Mavic, Matrice and Autel platforms, fire nets downwards to intercept enemy drones lying in wait on rooftops or on the ground.
The FPV and LS variants, meanwhile, are designed for FPV drones and specialised platforms. Their nets are launched forwards, and a built-in mechanism holds the intercepted drone in place. The systems are intended to tackle fast-moving targets.
According to Phantom Defense, Ukrainian military personnel have used more than 50,000 Karakurt kits in the past six months. The company says it has received more than 5,000 video recordings confirming successful interceptions as part of a programme in which it replaces used components free of charge.
Phantom Defense reports that a single State Border Guard Service crew has taken down more than 500 Russian drones using anti-drone nets in just six months.
"The integration of Karakurt into our ecosystem will help address the demand for affordable, effective close-range drone interception systems among military units," said a representative of Phantom Defense.
A Russian drone being intercepted using the Karakurt drone net. Video: Phantom Defense
Under the agreement, Phantom Defense also unveiled Manhal, a close-range drone interception system designed to protect military equipment, fixed positions and unmanned ground vehicles from enemy drones.
Manhal combines artificial intelligence with daylight and thermal imaging cameras to detect aerial threats and recognise targets automatically. According to its developer, the system can launch a net within one second of detecting a target. The net ensnares the drone, bringing its flight to an end.
A Russian drone being intercepted using the Karakurt drone net. Video: Phantom Defense
Each Manhal system is equipped with six net launchers and can intercept drones at distances of 5-15 metres. Its built-in battery provides at least eight hours of autonomous operation. The system can also run on an additional battery module or draw power from the combat vehicle's electrical system.
Background: Ukrainska Pravda previously wrote that the Blade interceptor drone from Phantom Defense has passed the Ministry of Defence's codification process. It is designed to intercept fixed-wing drones and can reach speeds of up to 310 km/h.

German firms outline new infrastructure and green energy plans in Baku
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
12:41:18 UTC
21:41:18 KST

German industrial giants, including Siemens Energy, are exploring opportunities to support Azerbaijan's green energy transition, as the country aims to handle 30 million tonnes of transit cargo by 2030.
German energy and infrastructure heavyweights are exploring new opportunities in Azerbaijan. Their plans cover both gas supplies and renewable energy, at a time when Europe seeks to reduce its dependence on Russian fossil fuels.
Speaking at the German-Azerbaijani Connectivity Conference 2026, which was hosted by the German-Azerbaijani Chamber of Commerce (AHK Azerbaijan) in Baku, European corporate leaders outlined concrete investment plans ranging from fossil fuels to renewable energy networks along the Middle Corridor.
The gathering brought together more than 250 participants, including over 35 guests from Germany and Azerbaijani policymakers.
A new pillar of economic cooperation
Nargis Wieck, Executive Director of AHK Azerbaijan, stressed the need to build on strong bilateral trade ties to encourage concrete investments.
Wieck told Euronews that one of the key questions was how to “deepen our economic cooperation through concrete projects”.
She also said that part of the chamber’s role involves “helping German companies become part of Azerbaijan’s economic ecosystem, and Azerbaijani companies integrate more closely into German and European value chains”.
German Ambassador Dirk Lölke noted that after President Ilham Aliyev’s recent visit to Berlin, regional connectivity could become the "second pillar" of bilateral economic relations, alongside energy cooperation.
Accelerating the green energy transition
On the energy front, Siemens Energy said it was ready to provide critical technology and expertise for Azerbaijan’s renewable energy sector and the planned Caspian-Black Sea-Europe Green Energy Corridor.
Frederik Doye, Senior Vice President for Europe at Siemens Energy, emphasised that Azerbaijan’s vast offshore wind potential positions the country as a vital energy link connecting Europe, the South Caucasus, and Central Asia.
Azerbaijan plans to develop 8 GW of wind and solar projects by 2032, according to Deputy Minister of Energy Elnur Soltanov.
He said that the priority was to develop the partnership in a number of areas, including "renewable energy, energy connectivity, energy efficiency and the broader energy transition".
"Our goal is to connect this potential to European markets through several complementary routes - the Caspian-Black Sea-Europe Green Energy Corridor, the Central Asia-Azerbaijan Corridor, and westward links to Türkiye and Europe via Georgia and Nakhchivan," he added.
Beyond generation, German technology providers are setting their sights on power grid modernisation, battery energy storage systems (BESS), and electric vehicle charging infrastructure.
Julia Egel, Head of Stakeholder Engagement at AHK Azerbaijan, noted that German firms are perfectly positioned to support Azerbaijan's mandate to boost renewable power generation. The country's stated target is to increase the share of renewables in its installed electricity generation capacity to 30% by 2030.
Egel also announced an upcoming trade mission of German energy companies to Azerbaijan, with plans for targeted business-to-business meetings and potential German pavilions at next year's Baku Energy Week.
Securing gas supplies
Alongside renewable energy projects, German companies are looking to secure gas supplies. German gas importer VNG AG said it was interested in a long-term supply agreement with the State Oil Company of Azerbaijan (SOCAR) lasting 15 to 20 years.
The firm aims to significantly boost current import volumes to stabilise European markets in the short term before transitioning to fully decarbonised systems. The company also said it was interested in working more closely with SOCAR on biomethane, renewable energy, hydrogen and decarbonised fuels.
Separately, German wind turbine manufacturer Enercon is exploring the possibility of setting up local production in Azerbaijan using German financing and technology.
"We are currently exploring investment opportunities in Azerbaijan and how we, as a wind turbine manufacturer, can become active here," company representative Tayfun Bayraktar said on the sidelines of the conference.
While the company has not yet received a formal proposal, Bayraktar noted that successful talks could eventually lead to a local manufacturing facility with export potential.
He added that the size of any investment would depend on demand, with a single 7 MW wind turbine currently costing around €7 million to €8 million.
Digitalising the Middle Corridor
Beyond energy, the conference also focused on logistics and digital infrastructure.
As Azerbaijan pushes to expand its role along the Middle Corridor, the German business community is stepping up its logistical support. Azerbaijan expects total transit cargo passing through the country to reach 30 million tonnes by 2030.
Deputy Minister of Economy Samad Bashirli presented the Alat Free Economic Zone as a platform for German manufacturers to establish export-oriented production, citing the country's stable macroeconomic environment.
Deputy Minister of Digital Development and Transport Rashad Hasanov emphasised Azerbaijan's ambition to become a regional base for global tech firms.
He underlined the importance of digitalisation in improving the Middle Corridor's efficiency and strengthening Azerbaijan’s role as a bridge between Europe and Asia.

Microsoft president says washing machines, milk face more safety rules than AI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
12:38:21 UTC
21:38:21 KST

Halis Sunnetci
12 October 2026•Update: 12 October 2026
Microsoft President Brad Smith warned that artificial intelligence is subject to weaker safety rules than everyday household products, calling for stronger safeguards, including emergency shutdown mechanisms and mandatory incident reporting.
"Right now, your washing machine is subject to more safety rules than AI. Every carton of milk that you see in the grocery store is subject to safety rules and inspection," Smith told the BBC's Big Boss Interview podcast, which was released Sunday.
Describing AI as both a "tool and a weapon," Smith said technology companies need emergency mechanisms, often known as "kill switches," to pause or slow AI systems if they escape human control.
He also called for laws requiring companies to report incidents involving AI systems that behave dangerously and notify those affected.
Smith proposed independent government evaluations of new AI technologies to assess potential risks.
"We know how to do this for other products," Smith said. "We should build on that knowledge and think about how to apply it to AI."
His remarks come amid debate over whether the development and deployment of advanced AI should be slowed until stronger safeguards are in place.
"When you look at AI agents that have escaped human control, when you look at models that are so powerful that they're putting the world's cybersecurity at risk. I would say: The moment has arrived," Smith said.

EU aims to replace US-provided strategic military enablers: Defense commissioner
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
12:38:16 UTC
21:38:16 KST

Melike Pala
12 October 2026•Update: 12 October 2026
The EU must develop its own strategic military capabilities to replace key assets currently provided by the US, particularly if Washington shifts resources toward the Indo-Pacific, European Commissioner for Defense and Space Andrius Kubilius said Monday.
Speaking at the Warsaw Security Forum 2026, Kubilius stressed that Europe must be prepared to assume greater responsibility for its own security and ensure it can deter potential threats on multiple fronts.
"If Americans really, because of that development, will shift their resources into the Indo-Pacific, we need to be ready to replace what we call strategic enablers, what Americans now are providing to Europe," he said.
He identified space capabilities as one of the key areas in which Europe needs to strengthen its strategic autonomy, highlighting the development of the EU's IRIS² secure satellite communications system.
Kubilius said the bloc hopes to begin the first operations of IRIS² in 2029, describing it as a European equivalent of Starlink that will provide secure satellite communications using advanced technologies, including quantum technologies.
However, he acknowledged that Europe faces significant challenges in developing the capabilities needed to build and deploy such systems independently, particularly in the area of launch vehicles.
"Our big challenge really is also to have capabilities to build those systems using our launching systems, because that is where we are quite heavily behind," he said, identifying the development of European launch capabilities as a priority.
Beyond developing strategic enablers, Kubilius highlighted the need to address structural weaknesses in Europe's fragmented defense industry.
He said the EU is working to overcome fragmentation and develop a more integrated defense market, including through projects covering drone defense, the eastern flank, anti-ballistic and anti-missile systems, air defense, maritime security, and a space shield.
Kubilius framed these efforts as part of a broader transformation needed to prepare Europe for what he called "NATO 3.0" and "Europe 3.0."
