====================================================================================================

The China-EU Trade Truce Buys Time
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
12:37:00 UTC
21:37:00 KST

Like last month’s summit between the U.S. and Chinese presidents, the China-EU Trade and Investment Consultations in Beijing were primarily about stabilization rather than a breakthrough. EU Trade Commissioner Maros Sefcovic and Chinese Commerce Minister Wang Wentao closed a handful of agreements and confirmed that neither side wants a trade war. However, the structural issues remain unresolved. What both sides gained is time.
For the European Union, the choice is increasingly difficult: secure real concessions from Beijing to address structural trade imbalances or deploy stronger unilateral measures to protect its industrial base. Compounding this dilemma is Europe’s risk of becoming an adjustment variable in the China-U.S. strategic competition, absorbing diverted Chinese exports when tensions escalate while losing market opportunities and negotiating leverage when Washington and Beijing strike bilateral deals. Washington holds the technology lever, while Beijing controls critical minerals and key nodes of global supply chains. Europe depends on both.
The most concrete outcome of the talks concerns the automotive sector. Under a preliminary deal, Chinese exports of hybrid and plug-in hybrid vehicles to the EU could be curbed more than half against projected levels over the next four years. The stakes are high. In 2025, the EU imported more than 1 million Chinese-made cars, worth $15.5 billion (13.7 billion euros) and up 30 percent in volume on 2024. Hybrids tell the story best: 659 Chinese hybrids sold in the EU in 2022, versus more than 160,000 in the first seven months of 2026, plus almost 218,000 plug-in hybrids.
Chinese brands now hold almost 12 percent of Europe’s new-car market, up from 1 percent five years ago, and roughly a third of plug-in hybrid sales. In the United States, Chinese cars are absent. Washington has effectively shut Chinese electric vehicles out of its market through 100 percent tariffs, while Europe remains far more exposed to Chinese automotive imports. The U.S., a market of 16.2 million new vehicles, bought fewer than 90,000 China-made vehicles in 2024, almost all of them Western brands built in China.
The rapid expansion of Chinese carmakers has intensified competitive pressures on European manufacturers, particularly in Germany and France, which had pushed for tougher trade measures. The proposed 50 percent reduction in Chinese hybrid exports is a step forward, but it is measured against projected growth, not current volumes.
China’s hybrid expansion accelerated after the EU imposed tariffs on Chinese battery-electric vehicles in 2024. Manufacturers shifted toward hybrids, which were exempt from those duties. While Washington imposed steep barriers to Chinese electric vehicles, Brussels left a significant loophole. The hybrid cars deal is therefore less a breakthrough than an attempt to correct a weakness in Europe’s trade policy.
As for whether the deal will work, much will depend on enforcement. Effective restrictions could give European automakers time to adjust. Weak implementation would allow Chinese exports to expand further, forcing Brussels to consider tougher measures and risking retaliation that could disrupt supply chains and investment on both sides. Meanwhile, Chinese automakers are increasingly moving from exports to manufacturing inside Europe. The strategic question is no longer simply how many Chinese cars are imported in the European market, but where industrial value is created, who controls the technology, and where the jobs are located.
The second result concerns market access and trade rebalancing. Brussels and Beijing agreed to cut tariffs on a range of EU products to the most-favored-nation (MFN) rates set under WTO rules. The goods covered, from car parts to olive oil and footwear, account for nearly $4.7 billion in exports. If implemented, the measure would save European exporters at least $260 million in duties.
Set against the trade figures, however, it is a small gain. In her State of the Union speech, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen called the EU’s deficit with China “unsustainable.” It now runs at more than 1 billion euros a day. The goods deficit rose from 306 billion euros in 2024 to 360 billion euros in 2025 and could reach 400 billion euros ($470 billion) this year, according to Eurostat.
The United States, meanwhile, moved in the opposite direction. In 2025, its goods deficit with China fell by almost a third to $202 billion, the lowest in two decades, as imports from China dropped 30 percent. China’s share of U.S. imports fell to about 9 percent, the lowest since it joined the WTO in 2001. The EU’s goods deficit with China is now twice America’s. What Washington kept out with tariffs, Europe increasingly absorbs.
Sefcovic defended the new deal with China as the result of an intense negotiation, noting that Washington had needed far more rounds to get its own deal. But he warned against complacency.
The third result concerns critical raw materials, above all rare earths and permanent magnets. This is where Europe depends on China most – 98 percent of EU demand for rare earth magnets is met by Chinese imports. Beijing will ease export licensing for European companies through a green channel. That matters for carmakers, renewables, and defense. But Beijing keeps control of the licenses, and with it the power to turn supplies on and off.
Washington got more. At the Busan summit in October 2025, the United States secured a one-year suspension of China’s new export restrictions and general licenses for its companies. The White House summit in September 2026 extended that suspension until January 10, 2027. Brussels obtained faster procedures for licenses that remain individual and revocable. Washington negotiated with tariffs and semiconductor controls on the table. Europe only trade-defense tools it has yet to use.
The industrial strategies differ as well. The United States has stepped up directly, with the Pentagon taking a stake in MP Materials and Washington forging minerals deals with Australia and Japan. Europe is relying on the Critical Raw Materials Act and RESourceEU, a sound framework but slower and less funded. Faster licenses make Europe’s supplies more predictable, but they do not make it less dependent.
That’s not to say Europe has no leverage. Four days before the talks, France and Germany jointly called for stronger trade defense instruments against Chinese overcapacity, subsidies, and market distortions. Beijing got the message. In response, official Beijing urged Paris and Berlin not to push the EU toward protectionist tools. Germany’s position carried the most weight. The European Commission went to Beijing with more leverage than before.
EU leaders will discuss the deal at the European Council on October 15–16. They will find a difficult balance in it. The hybrid agreement limits Chinese exports that hurt European carmakers. The rare earth agreement eases Chinese exports that the same carmakers rely on. Europe wants fewer of some Chinese goods and a steady supply of others, and on both counts the decision rests with Beijing. The recent truce calms the relationship but leaves the imbalances in place.
What Europe does with the next few months will matter more than the deal itself. If it invests in competitiveness, innovation and economic security, it can negotiate from strength next time. If it doesn’t, it will remain the adjustment variable in a rivalry it does not control.

Written by Dron, read by Astafieva and Proidakov — what is known about the 2026 Radio Dictation of National Unity
Kyiv • UNN
The text of the 27th Radio Dictation was written by veteran Artur Dron. On October 27, the readers will be Artur Proidakov and Dasha Astafieva.
This year, the author of the text for the Radio Dictation of National Unity – 2026 is writer and veteran of the Russian-Ukrainian war Artur Dron, while the readers are Ukrainian language and literature teacher Artur Proidakov and public figure and volunteer Dasha Astafieva. This was announced live on Ukrainian Radio by Yuliia Sheludko, coordinator of the Radio Dictation and producer at Ukrainian Radio, reports UNN.
Details
The 27th Radio Dictation of National Unity will be broadcast across Ukraine and around the world on October 27, Ukrainian Writing and Language Day.
Artur Dron is a Ukrainian writer, author of the poetry collection "We Were Here" (2023), the prose book "Hemingway Knows Nothing" (2025), and the new book "St. Panteleimon's Hospital," which is currently in print. In March 2022, Dron joined the Armed Forces of Ukraine and served as part of the 125th Separate Territorial Defense Brigade. He took part in combat operations in Donetsk, Kharkiv, and Zaporizhzhia regions. In October 2024, he suffered a serious injury and was demobilized. His books focus on military service, the memory of fallen heroes, and his personal experience of living with the reality of war.
The Radio Dictation unites us every year. Through my text, I want to show how language unites everyone, working separately with each person. I want people to write the Radio Dictation and feel how we use the same words while each thinking about something personal
The voice of the Radio Dictation of National Unity will be Ukrainian-language advocate and the first teacher in the history of Ukraine to be named among the top ten teachers in the world in the 2023 Global Teacher Prize, Artur Proidakov. The reader is also the author of the book "Who Does It Like That!? How to Teach a Child to Learn" and executive director of the educational foundation "MriiDii."
It is a great honor and an incredible responsibility for me to read the Radio Dictation. As a Ukrainian language and literature teacher, I realize that the Radio Dictation stopped being merely a test of literacy long ago. It is that solemn moment when thousands of Ukrainians in different cities and countries simultaneously write one text in Ukrainian. And it is another opportunity to record an important fact: language truly unites us
This year, the text of the nationwide dictation will also be read in the voice of Dasha Astafieva — a public figure who, since the beginning of the full-scale invasion, has shifted her activities toward volunteering and supporting the Armed Forces of Ukraine. Today, Dasha is the founder of the UnderBooks reading app, which promotes Ukrainian literature.
For me, this event is yet another proof that dreams come true! Thank you for choosing us, and thank you for believing in us. Ukrainians must dream, unite, stand together, and win. The Radio Dictation of National Unity is a unique tradition that every conscious Ukrainian should honor. Let's write together!
We would like to add
Last year, the Radio Dictation of National Unity was read live by theater and film actress Nataliia Sumska, while the text was written by writer and translator Yevheniia Kuznietsova. Her text, "We Have to Live!" became an impetus for popularizing dialect words and increased interest in old and long-forgotten words.
A duet reading of the Radio Dictation is something new for our audience and for us ourselves. It is a certain experiment with which we hope to meet the expectations of listeners who are drawn to a prominent media personality, as well as those who were waiting for a teacher-reader. Life moves quickly, so we wanted to introduce innovations. The duet is one of them. We recognize the risks, but from the perspective of the project's dramaturgy, it is original and interesting

Nobel economics prize awarded to Robert Hall and Michael ⁠Woodford
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
12:35:08 UTC
21:35:08 KST

Nobel economics prize awarded to Robert Hall and Michael Woodford
The Swedish academy says the academics’ models are ‘now used by central banks and governments around the world’.
The 2026 Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences has been awarded to US academics Robert Hall and Michael Woodford for their work on how monetary and fiscal policy can help stabilise fluctuations in the economy, according to the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences.
The winners of the prestigious award, formally known as the Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel and the final prize to be given out this year, were announced on Monday.
The two laureates developed new macroeconomic models that improve people’s ability to implement effective stabilisation policies, enabling fiscal and monetary policy measures that can reduce damaging swings in the economy.
“The laureates’ work has provided us with a stable theoretical foundation for the models that are now used by central banks and governments around the world,” John Hassler, chair of the Committee for the Prize in Economic Sciences, said in a statement.
“With them, we are better equipped to deal with shocks in the economy, such as energy crises or sudden changes in how much households consume.”
During the oil crises in the 1970s, the existing Keynesian models used to determine when and how measures should be implemented to tackle recessions or other economic fluctuations stopped working. Hall and Woodford then developed new tools to understand what policy responses could be the most effective.
“Rather than basing the models on statistical links between macroeconomic variables, such as inflation, production and consumption, they chose to build them on a microeconomic foundation,” the academy said. “This encompasses an understanding of how the total mass of individual households and businesses affect the economy through their actions.”
The economics prize, first awarded in 1969, is not part of the five original awards created in the 1895 will of industrialist and dynamite inventor Alfred Nobel, but was instead established by Sweden’s central bank.
The majority of previous laureates have been from the United States. Only three women have ever won, most recently Claudia Goldin in 2023 for her work on how gender has affected pay and employment over time in the US.
Last year’s winners – Joel Mokyr, Philippe Aghion and Peter Howitt – won for their work on “creative destruction” and how new technology and production methods can boost growth and living standards.
Like the other Nobel awards, the economics prize consists of a diploma, a gold medal, and a $1.2m cheque.
The Nobel prizes for medicine, physics, chemistry, literature and peace were announced last week, with South African jurist Navi Pillay and Canadian writer Anne Carson among the winners.

HAIKOU /China/, October 12. /TASS/. The southern Chinese province of Hainan welcomed over 4.75 million tourists during the National Day holiday, also known as "Golden Week," Hainan Ribao reported.
According to the newspaper, the Hainan Province Department of Tourism, Culture, Radio, Television, and Sports announced that the region experienced a 13.1% year-over-year increase in tourist traffic on October 1-7. Official estimates show that during the seven-day period, vacationers spent more than 6.87 billion yuan (about one billion dollars - TASS) on the island, which is a 14.7% increase compared to the same period in 2025.
Hainan Ribao pointed out that 32,900 foreign tourists visited Hainan during the Golden Week. This figure is 18.4% higher than last year and 88.6% higher than during the same period in 2024.
Despite the increase in local market activity, the number of daily complaints received from tourists in the province decreased by 22.7% year-over-year during the reporting period. According to the authorities, this indicates an improvement in service quality and public safety, as well as the effectiveness of measures to eliminate various risks and prevent emergencies. Data from local law enforcement agencies show that no major accidents occurred in Hainan over the weekend.
In addition to beach vacations, which have traditionally been very popular, tourists showed great interest in cultural and entertainment events, including performances by artistic groups, visits to local villages, and educational programs for children and their parents. Vacationers also actively visited Hainan’s museums, which welcomed more than 236,000 visitors during the week. In addition, there was a boom in trips to sites associated with historical events from the revolutionary years.
Meanwhile, local tour operators have noted an increase in tourists traveling to Hainan and exploring destinations in the province’s central region, not only to coastal areas. As a result, hotel occupancy rates were high not only in the resort city of Sanya and the provincial capital of Haikou, but also in smaller towns. Traffic on the island's orbital highway increased by 10.5% compared to the same period in 2025, surpassing 4.39 million people.

‘Let’s Sign a Diesel Deal’: Zelensky Challenges Trump
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
12:34:20 UTC
21:34:20 KST

President Volodymyr Zelensky has proposed signing a Ukrainian “diesel deal” with US President Donald Trump, arguing that Kyiv – not Moscow – can help determine whether Russian refineries operate and fuel shipments leave the country.
Speaking by video link at the Warsaw Security Forum on Monday, Oct. 12, Zelensky questioned the stated economic justification for Washington’s agreement to allow Russian diesel onto US and global markets.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“If there are such deals, then why doesn’t America conclude a ‘diesel deal’ with Ukraine?” Zelensky said in remarks later published on his Telegram channel.
“Let Ukraine offer a ‘diesel deal.’ We influence whether these ships sail or not, whether these refineries work or not.”
On Friday, Trump announced an agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin allowing Russian diesel exports despite Western sanctions imposed over Moscow’s invasion of Ukraine.
Ukraine offers reciprocal energy arrangement
Zelensky said Ukraine would suspend strikes against Russia’s oil and diesel infrastructure if Washington could guarantee that Moscow would stop attacking Ukraine’s electricity system.
“Electricity is important to us,” he said. “If we can be guaranteed protection for our electrical system, we will not respond against Russian diesel infrastructure.”
Ukraine’s power grid is connected to the European network, Zelensky noted, meaning that an undamaged Ukrainian energy system could also supply cheaper electricity to European countries experiencing shortages.
Berlin Opposes Wartime Elections in Ukraine
“So yes, let’s sign an appropriate ‘diesel deal’ with the president of the United States,” he said.
Trump announced on Sunday that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an immediate “energy ceasefire,” but provided no terms, timetable or monitoring mechanism.
Zelensky said Kyiv learned about the supposed agreement from the media and had not received confirmation that Moscow had accepted it.
Ukraine refrained from striking Russian refineries overnight, according to Zelensky, while Russia continued attacking Ukrainian power facilities, including a thermal power plant in Kharkiv.
Kyiv remains prepared to observe an energy ceasefire if Russia does the same and accepts enforceable guarantees, Zelensky said.
Zelensky disputes effect on diesel prices
Zelensky argued that the volumes Russia could put on the market would be too small to meaningfully change global prices.
He estimated that Russia could export between 300,000 and 500,000 metric tons of diesel per month, compared with global monthly consumption of approximately 120 million tons.
“What impact could that have? I think none,” he said.
In a separate part of his remarks, Zelensky estimated Russia’s overall influence on the global diesel market at 2.2%. He did not specify the source or methodology behind that figure.
Energy analysts have similarly questioned whether Trump’s announced Russian supplies would meaningfully reduce prices. The initial shipment of 300,000 tons represents only a small fraction of global consumption and would take time to reach buyers.
Zelensky said the current energy crisis originated primarily in the Middle East rather than from Ukrainian strikes against Russian refineries.
“If Putin is not given opportunities, then his influence in other areas will also be negligible,” he said.
Russian blockade risks global food crisis
Zelensky also warned that international attention to diesel prices was overshadowing a potentially larger crisis caused by Russia’s disruption of Black Sea shipping.
According to Zelensky, countries could begin experiencing the effects of an agricultural crisis within one or two months as Ukrainian grain exports remain blocked.
“There will not be enough food for countries on the African continent, some Asian countries and the Middle East,” he said. “Russia is now blocking the sea.”
Disrupted Black Sea shipping has already pushed wheat prices to three-year highs, reduced exports and forced major buyers to seek more expensive supplies elsewhere.
Russia has also rejected proposals to revive a Black Sea grain arrangement that would restore large-scale Ukrainian agricultural exports.
“We do not see any signals from Russia that they want the war to end. We do not see even elementary steps toward de-escalation,” Zelensky said.
He said the US was less directly exposed to this threat and was therefore concentrating primarily on energy prices.
“This is another challenge. This is hunger, and it could affect many countries,” he said. “We can stop many different crises before they begin.”

European allies publicly back Zelensky after Trump says Ukraine needs a new president
Europe’s largest countries rallied behind Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky after U.S. President Donald Trump said Ukraine needs a new leader.
German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said that Germany remains on the side of Ukraine and its government and “fully support the President as he carries out his difficult duties.”
British Defense Secretary Wes Streeting said: “We stand with President Zelensky.” He stressed that London would like to see “strong Western unity in resolve and support for Ukraine” and said he considered it his duty to help bring that about.
French President Emmanuel Macron also said that Paris “will continue to stand by Ukraine and President Zelensky.”
On Saturday, Trump said Zelensky “could’ve made many deals and for some reason he never does,” and said he believed it was “time for Ukraine to get a new President.”
In response, Zelensky said he’s ready to hold new presidential elections without waiting for the war to end, though he said that would require a 60-day ceasefire. He said he would accept whatever choice the Ukrainian people make. “If President Trump really wants to have some changes in — during elections, I also shared it with his team. So please tell Putin, give us two months, 60 days off. Total ceasefire, 60 days, and we will organize elections,” Zelensky said.
The rift between Trump and Zelensky became public amid Trump’s demands that Kyiv stop striking Russian oil refineries and a deal between Moscow and Washington to ease U.S. sanctions on Russian diesel exports.
On Sunday, Trump announced that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an energy ceasefire, though what exactly this meant was unclear. Zelensky first said Trump’s statement came as news to him, but later said Ukraine’s Armed Forces “had received all the relevant orders,” without specifying what he meant.
This morning, Zelensky said that Russian drones struck a power plant in Kharkiv immediately after Trump’s statement. He said he was confident that “Putin does not read Truth Social, and his Shaheds drones follow a different set of instructions.” Zelensky warned that Ukraine would respond to Russian strikes.
“This winter, if Russia does not agree to an energy ceasefire, we will respond. That is why yesterday the American president’s post drew real interest and real hope that the energy ceasefire could actually work. We in Ukraine immediately supported this idea,” Zelensky added.
Moscow did not officially comment on Trump’s remarks about the ceasefire. Regarding Trump’s comments about replacing the Ukrainian president, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said:
Trump said he believes it’s time for a new president. Why? Because the president of Ukraine needs to make very responsible and very difficult decisions to stop this war. Either Zelensky takes on that responsibility, shows that political will, or he doesn’t. So far, he hasn’t.
Regarding the 60-day ceasefire to hold elections, Peskov said he believed Ukraine’s president needed that time not for elections, but “to regroup, heal wounds, and continue the war.” He did not rule out that Putin “would be prepared to order that no strikes be carried out against Ukraine on election day, specifically on election day.”

Taiwan’s Nanya Technology sees DRAM prices rising in Q4
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
12:31:46 UTC
21:31:46 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Nanya Technology expects DRAM prices and its gross margin to rise further in Q4 as severe supply shortages persist, company President Li Pei-ying (李培瑛) said Monday.
At an online investor conference, the company reported Q3 revenue of NT$133.649 billion (US$4.19 billion), up 61.9% from the previous quarter, as the average selling price of DRAM rose more than 60%, per CNA. Sales volume fell 4% to 6% as inventory was largely depleted.
Gross margin rose 6.2 percentage points from Q2 to 85.7%, while net profit totaled NT$87.627 billion, or NT$25.40 per share. Net profit for the first nine months reached NT$163.877 billion, with earnings per share of NT$49.28.
Li said the expiration of long-term contracts at the end of June and the adoption of new prices in July drove the sharp increase in Q3 gross margin, per Liberty Times. With DRAM still in short supply, prices are expected to rise further in Q4, potentially lifting gross margin again, though increases will vary by product.
Growing AI use is driving demand for higher-capacity, higher-bandwidth, and customized memory, Li said. AI infrastructure, including servers, networking, storage, and system management, accounts for more than 20% of revenue, a share expected to grow. Strong DDR4 demand, meanwhile, means the company plans to keep DDR5 at around 10% of revenue in the short term.
Equipment installation at Nanya Technology’s new 5A fab is scheduled to begin in Q1 2027, with monthly capacity targeted at 30,000 wafers by the end of 2028 and 50,000 by the end of 2030. Li said customer validation of the 1C process is expected to begin in early 2027, while development of newer processes remains on schedule.

Taiwan secures first breeding cattle export market in Philippines
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
12:31:21 UTC
21:31:21 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Philippines has approved imports of breeding cattle from Taiwan, opening the country’s first overseas market for the animals after two years of negotiations, the agriculture ministry said Monday.
CNA reported that the Animal and Plant Health Inspection Agency received confirmation of the approval on Friday through Taiwan’s representative office in the Philippines. Breeding cattle can now be exported if they meet Philippine import and quarantine requirements.
Taiwan applied for export approval in 2024, and Philippine officials visited that November to inspect cattle farms. In May 2025, the Philippines approved Meigui Farm in Tainan and Hesheng Farm in Changhua County as eligible exporters.
However, exports could not begin until both sides agreed on quarantine rules and animal health certificate requirements. Further talks, supported by Taiwan’s representative office in the Philippines, led to final approval ahead of the National Day holiday, per Liberty Times.
The agency said the agreement marks a milestone for the domestic livestock industry, which already exports breeding pigs, per CTS News. It is the first time Taiwan has gained approval to export breeding cattle.
The deal allows the two approved farms to enter the Philippine market and creates new business opportunities for local cattle breeders. It also marks a step toward expanding Taiwan’s livestock exports beyond its existing markets, per CTEE.
The agency said it would continue working with agricultural and veterinary research institutes to maintain animal health and meet export standards. It also plans to seek access to more overseas markets to strengthen the livestock industry’s competitiveness.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Ocean Affairs Council said Thursday that National Kaohsiung University of Science and Technology has developed shotcrete reinforced with recycled ocean waste to protect coastal slopes, according to a press release.
The council subsidized the university’s development of structural fibers made from discarded fishing nets and plastic bottles. Mixed directly into shotcrete, the fibers replace steel wire mesh, which is vulnerable to rust in coastal environments. The university also used sensors to monitor changes in the slopes.
NKUST Civil Engineering Professor Chen Sung-ching (陳松靖) led the project to protect the country’s fragile southern badlands coastline. The team turned recycled fishing nets and bottles into structural fibers mixed with green shotcrete to replace rusting steel wire mesh.
Shotcrete uses compressed air to spray concrete onto surfaces. The high velocity helps the concrete adhere to the target area.
The council said the university extracted threads from fishing nets and pressed them into thick, structural-grade fibers mixed with concrete as a building material. It added that the material is safer and easier to deploy than steel wire mesh and can reinforce slopes against earthquakes or rockslides.
The council said each cubic meter of shotcrete uses 6 to 10 kilograms of ocean waste while reducing carbon emissions by 27 kilograms. It estimates that the material could protect coastal slopes for more than 12 years and reduce lifecycle maintenance costs by more than 20%.
The team also sprayed sensors onto the slopes with the shotcrete. The sensors use a wide-area connection to relay slope data around the clock.

Did Ukrainian strikes on Yandex data centres cause Russian bot activity to plummet?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
12:31:09 UTC
21:31:09 KST

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said social media had become less hostile following Kyiv's strikes on Russian technology giant Yandex's data centres, as web users report plummeting bot activity.
Ukrainian strikes on Russian technology giant Yandex's data centres have been followed by a dramatic decline in automated online activity, raising questions about whether the attacks may also have disrupted Moscow's influence operations abroad.
The sudden drop fuelled speculation in Europe and the United States about just how much of the political debate on social media might have been driven by Russian bots.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy weighed in on Monday, saying social media platforms had become noticeably less hostile.
"When we started responding to Russia's operation against our data centres and when our strikes reached Yandex data centres, it suddenly became a little easier to breathe on many social media platforms," Zelenskyy said addressing the Warsaw Security Forum.
"A lot of people, a lot of people noticed it, and there was less hate, less division and fewer provocations because there were fewer bots."
"And it's pretty clear where those bots were coming from," he added.
"If they disappeared when Yandex went offline, this proves again and again that Europe is not the source of the problems."
"Europe is not the one making everything more difficult," he said.
Three data centres targeted
Three data centres operated by Yandex, often described as Russia's equivalent of Google, were hit by Ukrainian drone strikes over the past few days.
The facilities were located in Sasovo, in the Ryazan region, the Kaluga region, south-west of Moscow and the Vladimir region, east of the Russian capital, where the latest strike was reported on Sunday.
The attacks damaged the company's infrastructure and disrupted services. Yandex confirmed that operations at its Vladimir facility had been suspended following a drone strike.
"Following a drone attack, the infrastructure of the Vladimir data centre was damaged," the company said in a statement published on Telegram.
"Operations at the data centre have been completely suspended. The remaining infrastructure resources are unstable and the platform is down."
According to an analysis of Cloudflare Radar data, automated traffic originating from Yandex's network fell by approximately 94% on Sunday compared with its average levels in the second half of September.
However, the figures also include legitimate automated traffic, such as search-engine crawlers, and do not establish whether Kremlin-linked social media bots were affected.
Political repercussions across Europe and the US
In Germany, claims of a sharp decline in online activity surrounding the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) circulated widely following the attacks, although no independently verified figures have emerged.
Czech MEP Tomáš Zdechovský questioned the apparent coincidence between the disruption and the reported decline in activity around the party.
"If confirmed, this is telling: Russian data centres get hit, and online activity around AfD suddenly plummets," he wrote on X.
Similar claims emerged in Britain, where online activity associated with Reform UK was also reported to have declined following the attacks.
In the United States, social media users reported fewer apparently automated pro-conservative responses on X, the platform owned by Elon Musk.
The speculation has attracted attention from prominent political figures and commentators, including Laura Loomer, a right-wing activist and supporter of Donald Trump, Russian opposition figure and former world chess champion Garry Kasparov, and Michael McFaul, the former US ambassador to Russia.
The debate comes just weeks before the US congressional midterm elections in early November, amid longstanding concerns about foreign interference and the influence of automated accounts on political discourse.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — KMT Legislator Lee Yen-hsiu (李彥秀) defended her remarks on drug policy Monday after protesters demanded an apology outside her Taipei constituency office over her comments about social workers.
CNA reported that the Taipei Social Workers Union accused Lee of misrepresenting social workers’ role in addiction treatment. The union said her comments could stigmatize vulnerable groups and undermine public health efforts to reduce drug-related harm.
The dispute began after Lee warned that public spaces used for exercise and community activities could become places where social workers distribute drugs or medication to people with addiction. She questioned the risks such arrangements could pose to neighborhood safety.

She argued that addiction treatment should follow existing medical procedures, including methadone treatment administered under professional supervision at health care facilities.
Lee also said she respects social workers and recognizes the pressures they face, including long hours, heavy workloads, and poor working conditions. She maintained that their professional role and rights should not become tools for political attacks.
DPP Spokesperson Wu Cheng (吳崢) accused Lee of refusing to acknowledge the harm caused by her comments. He also criticized Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安) for defending Lee and called on both politicians to apologize to social workers, per Liberty Times.

Kurdish PKK militants quit some camps in north Iraq, Turkish sources say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
12:30:43 UTC
21:30:43 KST

Kurdish PKK militants quit some camps in north Iraq, Turkish sources say
ANKARA, Oct 12 - Militants from the outlawed Kurdistan Workers Party (PKK) have withdrawn from four camps in northern Iraq in the first step of an intended disbandment, Turkish security sources said on Monday.
Turkey's parliament in August passed a law to set out parameters for the PKK's dissolution as part of a peace process hoped to end a decades-old conflict that has killed tens of thousands and ravaged the mainly Kurdish southeast.
The legislation provides protections for many former militants who have not committed specific crimes and facilitates the suspension of sentences for some convicted of PKK membership, paving the way for their reintegration into society.
The security sources said the PKK had from last Thursday withdrawn from the Hebat, Yajk, Sabri and Sason camps in the Baze district of Iraq's Metina region in evidence that the peace process was pressing ahead.
Once it ceased all activities, PKK members could join social integration programmes in education, economic and other areas as part of the legal framework for disbandment, the sources added.
The peace process between Turkey, which has NATO's second-largest army, and the PKK began in late 2024, but came to a near standstill earlier this year due to the Iran war and concerns about regional instability.
There was no immediate comment from Iraq or the PKK on the withdrawals.
The PKK is designated a terrorist organisation by Turkey, the United States and the European Union. It launched its insurgency in 1984 and initially sought an independent Kurdish state in southeast Turkey, but later refocused on seeking autonomy and Kurdish political rights.
Last month, Turkey agreed to gradually hand over a military camp for its forces in northern Iraq to the Baghdad government, as part of a recalibration of security threats amid the peace process. REUTERS

Denying 'respite' to Kiev
Vladimir Zelensky has not earned a break in fighting: "I do not think he has earned a respite."
Russia will not be taken in by his promises: "I do not think we will ever again be had by assurances and promises. President [of Russia Vladimir Putin] has made this very clear. We continue to achieve the objectives of the special military operation. They are well known to everyone. We have never changed them, unlike Zelensky and his European masters, who keep zigzagging and changing course. Therefore, we have nothing to justify ourselves for to anyone."
Middle East
Russia believes that the Israeli army is violating international law and fueling tensions in Lebanon: "In light of Israel’s ongoing actions in Lebanon, we reaffirmed the Russian Federation’s principled position in support of the sovereignty, unity and territorial integrity of the Lebanese Republic. And, of course, we stand by our assessment that the use of force by the IDF, the Israeli army, grossly violates international law and fuels further tensions and escalation in Lebanon."
Russia welcomes the launch of US-mediated direct dialogue between Israel and Lebanon: "We welcomed the launch of direct dialogue between Israel and Lebanon mediated by the United States. We stressed the need for an immediate ceasefire, as civilians are suffering, and the need to steer the conflict toward a political and diplomatic settlement, including to ensure the comprehensive implementation of the long-standing United Nations Security Council Resolution 1701, which sets out all the necessary obligations of the parties. Had this resolution been implemented, the problems Lebanon and Israel are facing today would have been resolved long ago."
"Russia actively supports Lebanon and the Lebanese side in discussions at the United Nations Security Council. The next opportunity will come before the end of this year, when the mandate of the United Nations Interim Force in Lebanon is due to be discussed. These forces have played a very important role in preventing escalation from becoming completely destabilizing, because they are unable to prevent escalation altogether; they simply lack the physical capacity to do so."
Russia sees opportunities to advance an agenda for resolving all problems in the Middle East: "We very much hope that, both in our contacts with the Lebanese and in our contacts with the Israelis, which we maintain, we will be able to make progress. We have always said that we are interested in ensuring Israel’s security in the context of a full settlement of its relations with its Arab neighbors and a comprehensive resolution of all problems in the Middle East on the basis of United Nations Security Council resolutions, which, of course, also implies the creation of a Palestinian state. We see opportunities to advance such an agenda. However, this requires our Israeli colleagues to share the understanding that a solution acceptable to all is necessary, and we are persistently urging them to do so."
Relations with Lebanon
Russia appreciates Lebanon’s understanding of the root causes of the conflict in Ukraine: "We appreciate the understanding that the Lebanese side consistently demonstrates regarding Russia’s actions and the root causes of this conflict."
During the talks, Russia and Lebanon reaffirmed their "mutual commitment to further expanding political dialogue and strengthening partnership ties in various fields."
Moscow hopes Lebanese Foreign Minister Youssef Rajji will attend the seventh session of the Russian-Arab Cooperation Forum: "We hope my Lebanese counterpart will take part in the upcoming seventh session of the Russian-Arab Cooperation Forum at the level of foreign ministers, which is scheduled to be held in Moscow before the end of the year."
Russia and Lebanon have agreed to resume the work of the intergovernmental commission on trade, economic, scientific and technical cooperation as soon as possible: "To this end, we agreed to resume the work of the intergovernmental commission on trade, economic, scientific and technical cooperation, which has not met since 2018, as soon as possible."

Some 13 wounded in explosion of unknown ordnance near Lebanese border
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
12:30:20 UTC
21:30:20 KST

A 14-year-old boy was killed, and 24 others were injured, some seriously, in an explosion involving an unexploded Hezbollah cluster munition between Kibbutz Manara and Kibbutz Yiftah in northern Israel on Monday, according to the IDF, with the military declaring the incident a mass-casualty event.
Students and staff members from the ORT Ma'alot Yeshiva High School were among the victims, according to a statement by the local municipality. Haifa's Rambam Health Care Campus said it admitted three teenagers and one adult to the trauma unit after evacuating them from the scene, while Safed's Ziv Medical Center is treating 14 injured victims in total. Galilee Medical Center is treating an additional six victims, one of whom sustained serious injuries.
The municipality noted that the students were in the area on an annual field trip, with the Israel Fire and Rescue Authority saying that a preliminary investigation showed evidence that one of the students put the Hezbollah cluster munition into his bag, which later detonated. According to MDA, two of those seriously injured were 14 years of age, with eight of those moderately injured being children, as well as 12 of those with minor injuries.
IDF, rescue helicopters, bomb disposal teams, MDA paramedics respond
Northern District police officers and bomb disposal experts responded to the incident, as well as IDF and Hatzalah helicopters, and Magen David Adom paramedics. Israel Police Commissioner Daniel Levi and Northern District Commander Meir Eliyahu also arrived on scene to assess the situation, with the commissioner later noting that the field trip "received approval from the relevant authorities" to the best of his knowledge.
Levi added that he is considering scaling back field trips to the area in the near future "to re-examine whether allowing children to go out (on such trips) puts them at risk." N12 News later reported on Monday that Education Minister Yoav Kisch is expected to announce the move, which would take effect on Tuesday.
An MDA medical technician at the scene of the explosion said he witnessed children holding and assisting their injured friends when he arrived.
"Everyone tried to help their friends as best they could," he said. "Some even applied tourniquets to their friends to stop the bleeding."
MDA paramedics described the chaos on scene, with one noting the variety of injury degrees among the victims.
"There was a great deal of commotion and shouting at the scene," he recalled. "We found several casualties with varying degrees of injury lying on the access path from the main road, while others were walking around the area."
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, other officials respond to explosion
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was briefed on the incident and is holding continuous situational assessments, according to the Prime Minister's Office (PMO).
The Education Ministry also responded, saying that it is working "in cooperation with the security forces... to provide answers to the students, the education staff, and their families."
"We ask that everyone act responsibly and avoid spreading unverified information, while the details of the event are still being clarified," the ministry added.
Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot said in an X/Twitter post that his "heart is with the family of the deceased, the injured, and their families," saying that he is praying "together with all Israeli citizens for the swift recovery of the injured."
An operations center staffed by social workers and psychologists has been set up in the area "to provide care for the students," Ma'alot Mayor Moti Ben-David told Army Radio later on Monday. A bus was sent to collect any non-injured students at the scene.
An additional site to treat victims suffering from shock was set up at Zive Medical Center, including a dedicated team for the treatment of children and teenagers, according to the Health Ministry.
Beterem CEO: Parents should speak to children about danger of unexploded ordnance
Orly Silvinger, CEO of Beterem, an Israeli child safety organization, said the incident calls attention to the danger unexploded ordnance poses to children and that parents must teach them not to touch, or even go near, suspicious objects.
"To a child, unexploded ordnance may look like an intriguing, harmless object, but it can be deadly," she emphasized. "Parents, do not assume 'it won't happen to us.' Make it clear to children of all ages, including teenagers, that if they see a suspicious object, they must not approach, touch, or try to move it. They should move away, tell an adult immediately, and call 100 to report it to the police. A simple, clear conversation with children can save lives."
According to data compiled by the organization, three children were killed, and 10 were wounded in incidents involving landmines, explosives, or unexploded ordnance between 2016 and 2026.
Meit Asher Regional Council head Moshe Davidovitz reiterated the call for Israeli citizens to be "vigilant on trips," asking them not to approach unexploded ordnance and to report any sightings to authorities.

US launches immigration raid of Democratic congresswoman Ilhan Omar's home
Unknown

Democratic lawmaker and Trump critic Ilhan Omar’s home raided in immigration fraud probe
- US authorities raided Democrat Ilhan Omar’s Washington-area home at dawn on Oct 12 in an ongoing immigration fraud probe.
- The case centres on immigration paperwork filled out by Omar’s late father when she was a child, according to Fox News Digital sources and a Justice Department spokesman.
- The raid came before the Nov 3 midterm elections, as Trump kept attacking Omar and other Muslim lawmakers, drawing criticism for anti-immigrant and anti-Muslim rhetoric.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – Federal officials conducted a predawn raid on Oct 12 on the Washington-area home of Democratic Representative Ilhan Omar of Minnesota, an outspoken critic of Donald Trump who has been the target of political insults by the Republican president, as part of an ongoing investigation.
A person familiar with the investigation said it is related to alleged immigration fraud, and part of the probe concerns the Somali-born lawmaker’s immigration paperwork, which was filled out by her late father when she was a child.
“Today in the Washington, D.C. area, Homeland Security Investigations executed a judicially authorised search warrant secured by the Department of Justice. This enforcement action is part of an ongoing federal investigation,” a department spokesman said in an e-mail.
Homeland Security Investigations is part of US Immigration and Customs Enforcement, or ICE.
Tom Homan, the Trump administration’s border czar, told Fox Business Network that the Justice Department is leading the investigation with the Department of Homeland Security. Homan declined to get into the specifics of an ongoing criminal investigation.
The raid came a little more than three weeks before the Nov 3 midterm elections, when President Donald Trump’s Republicans will be trying to defend their thin majorities in the US Congress.
Omar, a prominent progressive who is running for re-election, represents a safe Democratic district. She was re-elected in 2024 by a margin of 50 percentage points.
Minnesota Democrats condemned the raid.
“Americans see this for what it is,” Minnesota governor Tim Walz, a Democrat, wrote on social media. “President Trump is abusing his power to go after political opponents weeks before an election.”
Justice Department policy bars federal prosecutors and agents from timing any action to affect the outcome of any election or benefiting a candidate or political party. The department has historically avoided taking investigative steps against political candidates within about 60 days of an election.
During Trump’s second term in office, the Justice Department has investigated and brought charges against a range of his perceived political enemies.
It has charged former FBI Director James Comey, New York state Attorney-General Letitia James and Trump’s former national security adviser turned critic John Bolton.
It also has investigated Democratic lawmakers who urged the US military not to follow illegal orders, Democratic Senator Adam Schiff and Federal Reserve officials Jerome Powell and Lisa Cook.
The case against James and one of two brought against Comey were thrown out by a federal judge. Bolton pleaded guilty and is scheduled to be sentenced later in October. Grand juries and federal judges have stymied several other probes.
Omar, who has been a frequent target of Trump’s political insults, called his focus on her an “unhealthy and creepy obsession”. He has also cast the Somali American community as a threat to Minnesota in a burst of anti-Somali and anti-Muslim rhetoric.
Last week, he called Democratic candidate for US Senate from Michigan Abdul El-Sayed, who is Muslim, a “RADICAL Extremist” and “Terrorist Sympathizer”, while offering support for the Republican candidate, Mike Rogers.
Civil rights advocates have criticised his rhetoric towards minorities and immigrants, including when he previously called Somalis “garbage”.
In February, he said Omar and Democratic Representative Rashida Tlaib of Michigan, who is also Muslim, should be “institutionalised” and sent back to “where they came from”.
Both lawmakers criticised Trump during his State of the Union address as he touted his administration’s hard-line immigration crackdown and its immigration enforcement actions.
Omar has repeatedly said she and her family have faced death threats, which she attributes to “hateful political rhetoric”, especially from Trump.
In September, a Minnesota man who squirted vinegar on Omar was sentenced to one year and two months in prison after pleading guilty to assaulting a federal official.
Anthony James Kazmierczak admitted to attacking Omar because he disagreed with her progressive political views. REUTERS

Prominent Iranian Human Rights Lawyer Arrested
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
12:30:10 UTC
21:30:10 KST

A prominent human rights lawyer and activist has been arrested in Iran, sources close to him told RFE/RL’s Radio Farda.
Amirsalar Davoodi was arrested in court in the central city of Isfahan on October 11 while defending a client, said the sources who spoke on condition of anonymity for security reasons.
The charges against him are unknown, and it is unclear where he is being held.
Davoodi’s arrest comes amid an intensifying crackdown on dissent in the Islamic republic, where the authorities have jailed lawyers, activists, journalists, and intellectuals.
The growing clampdown coincided with the mass protests against Iran’s clerical rulers in January and the ongoing war with the United States and Israel that began in late February.
Mass Protests
Davoodi represents several people who have been arrested for their roles in the nationwide protests.
Among them is Mahshad Keshani, a protester and the fiance of Alireza Sepahi, a demonstrator who was executed on October 4.
Before Sepahi’s hanging, Davoodi held a wedding ceremony in absentia for the couple. Davoodi also labelled his client’s execution “unfair” and challenged the head of Iran’s judiciary to a live TV debate.
Sepahi is among the five people who have been convicted and executed for their alleged role in the killing of four Iranian special forces members in Isfahan on January 8.
Seven other defendants are also at risk of execution over the case. The families of many of the defendants say they have been tortured in prison and forced to confess to charges they deny.
Several of them have been charged with moharebeh, or "waging war against God," aiding and abetting moharebeh, destruction of public property amounting to moharebeh, assembly and collusion, and propaganda against the Islamic republic.
Iran has witnessed a surge in executions of what human rights groups consider political prisoners -- from demonstrators to alleged members of banned groups and those convicted of spying -- since the start of the war with the United States and Israel on February 28.
Davoodi, who has a history of representing political prisoner cases, has been repeatedly arrested and jailed.
In 2019, he was sentenced to 30 years in prison, which was reduced to 15 years on appeal. After serving over two years in prison, he was released on bail.
In 2023, Davoodi was awarded the Ludovic Trarieux International Human Rights Prize, one of the world's oldest and most prestigious international human rights award given to a lawyer by their peers.

Trump thinks Ukraine needs a new president. Who could replace Zelenskyy?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
12:30:09 UTC
21:30:09 KST

Trump thinks Ukraine needs a new president. Who could replace Zelenskyy?
Popular former general Zaluzhnyi leads potential challengers, alongside intelligence chief Budanov and reformer Fedorov.
Kyiv, Ukraine – The White House wants Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy gone.
“I think it’s time for Ukraine to get a new president,” United States President Donald Trump told reporters on Saturday, claiming that Zelenskyy’s months-long strikes on Russian refineries had hurt global diesel supplies.
But Trump’s wish is not Ukraine’s command.
Even though Zelenskyy’s five-year presidential term expired in 2024, Ukraine’s constitution and martial law grant him a wartime extension. Many Ukrainians want their political establishment to be renewed, but are reluctant to see a presidential vote before the four-and-a-half year war is over.
In response to Trump’s remarks, Zelenskyy proposed holding a vote if Russian President Vladimir Putin guaranteed a 60-day ceasefire.
However, if the elections are held in the near future, who could compete with Zelenskyy?
“If the elections are held fast, one of the former military [commanders] is Zelenskyy’s most probable rival,” Kyiv-based analyst Igar Tyshkevych told Al Jazeera.
Meanwhile, old political heavyweights such as former President Viktor Poroshenko, who lost the 2019 presidential vote to Zelenskyy, and former Prime Minister Yulia Tymoshenko, who is being investigated for corruption, do not stand a chance, he said.
Valerii Zaluzhnyi: ‘Most probable alternative’
Ukraine’s former top general and current ambassador to the United Kingdom tops the lists of Zelenskyy’s rivals.
“At least since 2023, and especially since 2024, after his resignation, the most probable alternative to Zelenskyy, his most dangerous competitor who can defeat him in the election is Valerii Zaluzhnyi,” Volodymyr Fesenko, head of the Kyiv-based Penta think tank, told Al Jazeera.
Almost two-thirds of Ukrainians – 64 percent – trust him, according to an October 8 poll by the Rating Group, a Kyiv-based pollster, and only 25 percent “distrust” him.
This trust is rooted in his 2022 military triumphs.
After defending Kyiv in the early weeks of Russia’s 2022 full-scale invasion, Zaluzhnyi led counteroffensives that returned 40 percent of Russian-controlled territory to Ukraine.
He was fired in 2023 after a long-anticipated summer counteroffensive yielded no results.
Zaluzhnyi remains a man of mystery when it comes to the most pressing postwar matters.
Burly and imposing, the 53-year-old is deliberately taciturn, leaving the public guessing about his views on Ukraine’s economic restoration, crippling demographic crisis or push to join the European Union.
He does not take part in talk shows, barely talks to journalists and occasionally publishes opinion pieces with detailed analyses of war-related problems and general statements about securing lasting peace and security guarantees from Ukraine’s Western partners.
Zelenskyy’s second chance?
The former comedian was elected in 2019 with 73 percent of the vote, the highest result in Ukraine’s post-Soviet history.
Despite a string of corruption scandals in his inner circle, the 48-year-old is popular enough to take another swing at a presidency.
More than half of Ukrainians – 53 percent – trust him, although 40 percent do not, according to the Rating Group’s poll.
However, Trump’s renewed animosity may benefit Zelenskyy again.
After his February 2025 row with Trump in the Oval Office, Zelenskyy’s approval ratings hit a wartime high of 67 percent.
However, Zelenskyy may have ruined his own chances with his appointment policies.
“He came to power under the slogans of resetting the power, of picking the most competent, not the most trusted” ministers or advisers, analyst Tyshkevych said.
Kyrylo Budanov: Trusted by more than half of Ukrainians
Lt. Gen. Kyrylo Budanov is the second most popular and charismatic military leader who has a shot at becoming Ukraine’s president.
The 40-year-old former top military intelligence officer was appointed head of Zelenskyy’s administration in January.
Budanov led daring operations against Russia, including a raid on Russian-annexed Crimea in 2016 to plant explosives at a military airfield.
In 2020, Zelenskyy appointed him head of the defence ministry’s intelligence directorate (GUR), which became an aggressive, tech-driven special forces service.
The GUR’s sea drone attacks damaged Russia’s Black Sea Fleet, forcing it to retreat from annexed Crimea to the Russian port of Novorossiysk.
Budanov is trusted by 53 percent of Ukrainians and mistrusted by 31 percent, according to the Rating Group’s poll.
Mykhailo Fedorov: Young, popular, daring
At 35, Fedorov is the youngest person on the list of potential presidents. He rose to fame after Zelenskyy appointed him minister of digital transformation in 2019, and managed to radically simplify bureaucratic procedures in the corruption-plagued nation. His ministry launched Diia, a smartphone app that lets users access more than 100 government services online.
In January, Zelenskyy appointed Fedorov, who had zero military background, as defence minister in charge of logistics, budgets, reforms, anticorruption measures and deals to secure multibillion-dollar Western aid or loans.
Fedorov cracked down on corruption schemes by making procurement of new weaponry, food and medical supplies more transparent.
He radically boosted the number of drones that paralysed Russia’s supply routes, destroyed arms and fuel depots, oil refineries and air defence systems.
He also increased the number of ground robots to supply food and ammunition and rescue wounded soldiers.
But the reforms angered Oleksandr Syrsky, the actual commander-in-chief, who reportedly pushed for Fedorov’s dismissal in July.
Fedorov’s supporters rallied throughout Ukraine for weeks, while his approval ratings soared from 35 percent in June to 65 percent in July, according to the Rating Group’s polls.
However, in August he made an unpopular move saying Ukraine should hold a presidential vote, and his current approval stands at 38 percent.
Yevhenii Khmara: Ukraine’s unknown defence minister
The top five list ends with Yevhenii Khmara, a general who replaced Fedorov as defence minister.
A relative unknown until his appointment in July, he is trusted by 29 percent of Ukrainians and distrusted by 16 percent.
He was a career intelligence official with a low public profile, but another 43 percent of those polled did not know who he was, according to the survey.
Low hopes for a foreign minister and an ex-president
Numbers six and seven on the list are Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha, a career diplomat who secured crucial support from Turkiye and Poland, and ex-president Poroshenko.
Both are trusted by 24 percent of Ukrainians.
But Poroshenko, who came to power in 2014 on an anti-corruption ticket but got involved in a graft scandal with overpriced spare parts for military equipment, holds a low popularity rating – 70 percent of those polled distrust him.

Record art auction spares Estonian Artists' Association from property sales
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
12:29:00 UTC
21:29:00 KST

Record art auction spares Estonian Artists' Association from property sales
The Estonian Artists' Association (EKL) says its record €2.3 million fundraiser art auction will spare the union from having to sell some property after a €700,000 fraud loss.
EKL president Maarin Ektermann told ETV's "Terevisioon" Monday morning that the three-day weekend auction raised nearly three times the amount they lost to fraud this spring, giving the organization more options for recovering financially.
Of the 162 works offered from its historic collection and donated by artists, only three went unsold. Starting bids ranged from €100 to €40,000, to make the auction accessible to a broad audience, though some prices climbed as much as 13-fold.
Several works also fetched six-figure sums, including a record €205,000 for Jaan Elken's painting "Juhikabiin" — the highest ever for a work by a living Estonian artist.
"When we started working on this over the summer, it was one of our plans for getting out of our [financial] crisis," Ektermann said. Thanks to the successful auction, the union can certainly leave some of its planned real estate unsold.
"The rest we can provide more details on at the extraordinary general meeting in mid-November," she added.
Even so, Ektermann said the EKL has no intention of becoming a regular player in the art auction market.
"After the financial fraud, we quickly decided not to ask the state for help; we wanted to try to manage on our own," she explained. "Our art collection was one of the assets we had to sell."
The union president hopes the fundraiser auction sparks greater interest in buying and owning art, including among those who previously saw them as elitist or felt art auctions weren't for them.
The EKL will first pay artists their agreed shares — 5 percent for works from its collection and 15 percent for newly donated works — and review the auction's operating costs.
After repaying its loans and restoring its financial stability, the union will draw up recommendations for its council on how best to use the remaining funds to support Estonian art, in line with the EKL's statutes.
Ektermann said she hopes to outline some priorities at the meeting next month.
Gallery owner: They know what they're paying for
Commenting on the recent auction's record-setting Elken sale, Haus Gallery owner Piia Ausman said the price reflected the rarity of works from the artist's hyperrealist period — and competition between informed buyers.
"I don't know who took part in the bidding, but I can only assume anyone willing to pay up to €100,000 for a work in today's Estonian art market — and in this case more than €200,000 — knows what they're paying for," Ausman said. "Even the artist himself no longer has any works from that period."
She also credited the auction's extensive media attention, which was amplified by the major union fraud loss behind it.
"This has been an extraordinary auction," Ausman said. "It has generated a huge amount of publicity itself, with the €700,000 fraud scandal playing a major role in that. All these factors came together to make the auction a phenomenon in its own right."
The gallery owner said the auction could have a lasting impact beyond the proceeds, including by prompting the EKL to improve its management and public profile.
She also hopes the union will invest in making its historic art collection more accessible online, potentially including information about the works' market value.
"You could say this has been one of the most profitable losses in Estonian society," Ausman added.

Germany paying diplomatic price for double standards on Gaza, experts warn
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
12:28:47 UTC
21:28:47 KST

Germany’s approach to Israel’s war in Gaza is undermining its credibility as a defender of human rights and weakening its diplomatic influence, a former ambassador and a foreign policy expert warn.
They say Berlin’s support for the Netanyahu administration has raised doubts about its commitment to international law, with consequences for its standing at the United Nations and its relations with countries in the EU and beyond.
Martin Kobler, a former German ambassador, told Anadolu that Germany’s failure to win a UN Security Council seat in June was “a major foreign policy disaster.”
The UN General Assembly on June 3 elected the non-permanent members of the UN Security Council for 2027–28. In the contest for the two Western seats, Portugal received 134 votes and Austria 131. Germany, with 104, came third and lost.
It marked the first time Germany lost a bid for a non-permanent UN Security Council seat, according to diplomats.
The German government has blamed a late campaign and accused Russia of lobbying against a German seat.
Kobler, however, said the main reason was that countries withheld their votes because they saw hypocrisy in Berlin’s dealings with Israel.
“It was the double standard. In particular when it comes to a comparison between what we say in Ukraine and other conflicts like Gaza,” he said, referring to Berlin’s selective defense of international law – demanding accountability for Russia’s actions in Ukraine while shielding Israel from similar scrutiny over Gaza.
Kobler said doubts about Germany’s consistency in defending international law had also affected its standing elsewhere at the UN.
“In the past, we had a good credibility record,” he said.
He pointed to Berlin’s positions on the Syria conflict, war in Ukraine and Myanmar, where Germany intervened at the International Court of Justice and argued that those responsible for the genocide against the Rohingya had to be held accountable.
“We advocated a broad interpretation of genocide, but switched to a narrow interpretation only a week after the South Africa case against Israel began,” he said, referring to Berlin’s change of stance once the ICJ began examining South Africa’s case accusing Israel of committing genocide in Gaza.
Germany has condemned Russia’s war in Ukraine as a breach of international law and has championed EU sanctions on Moscow.
On Gaza, the same government has been reluctant to name violations, has continued arms sales to Israel and has blocked EU moves to increase pressure on Netanyahu’s coalition.
Niels Annen, Germany’s candidate to lead the UN refugee agency, was also passed over in December 2025 when Secretary-General Antonio Guterres nominated former Iraqi President Barham Salih instead. The General Assembly then elected Salih by consensus.
“It is a whole series that shows us that we are losing credibility in this respect and this has consequences,” Kobler said.
Chancellor Friedrich Merz, a staunch ally of Israel, has repeatedly cited the country’s historical responsibility – shaped by the crimes of the Nazi era and the Holocaust – to help ensure Israel’s security.
He has rejected calls for a total arms embargo on Israel and blocked proposed EU measures, including sanctions and suspension of the EU-Israel trade agreement.
In 2025, Merz criticized the International Criminal Court’s arrest warrant for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and promised to find ways to welcome Netanyahu in Berlin.
“Fundamentally, an Israeli prime minister must be able to travel to Germany,” he said. “He is a democratically elected prime minister of the only democracy in the entire region.”
Kobler sharply criticized Merz for rejecting the authority of the International Criminal Court and for promising to welcome Netanyahu in Berlin.
“This is something I deeply deplore because the international criminal court system is a legacy of our own history,” he said, referring to the post-war system of international justice that grew out of the trials of Nazi leaders.
“One cannot say that this international criminal court system is just for dictators, so to say just for African dictators, but not for democratically elected prime ministers,” he said.
“It is also there for democratically elected prime ministers. And this double standard is something which – in particular, in the global south – has not gone unnoticed.”
Kobler warned that the German government’s current policy is not only undermining its own international credibility but also risks weakening the institutions that uphold international law, the very institutions Berlin says it wants to protect.
He stressed that Germany’s historical responsibility requires it to speak up as a true friend of Israel, to pursue more active diplomacy and to warn that the current course is not in Israel’s own security interests.
Polls conducted over the past year show substantial public opposition to aspects of Berlin’s Israel policy.
Voters are taking an increasingly critical stance toward Berlin’s Israel policy, with a clear majority rejecting military support for Israel and calling for stronger pressure on Netanyahu’s government.
In a recent Forsa poll, 58% of Germans said Berlin should apply greater pressure on Netanyahu’s coalition over its policies in Gaza and the West Bank.
Another survey released by the Koerber Foundation last November found that 82% opposed Germany’s military support for Israel. Sixty percent rejected the idea that the Holocaust gives Germany a special responsibility for Israel.
A separate YouGov survey from September 2025 found that 62% of Germans believe Israel’s military campaign in Gaza amounted to genocide.
Philip Holzapfel, a former adviser to EU foreign policy chief Josep Borrell and now a nonresident senior fellow at the Barcelona Centre for International Affairs, said growing public and political pressure on the Merz government had so far produced only limited change.
Berlin briefly and partly suspended arms exports that could be used in Gaza in August 2025, then lifted that restriction in November after a ceasefire and returned to case-by-case review. Approvals rose once the curb was removed.
Preliminary Economy Ministry figures show military export approvals for Israel worth €799 million ($896 million) from January through June. Israel ranked sixth among destinations, and the half-year total was already about four times the full-year figure for 2025.
“If there are reasons to suspect that there's a risk that arms could be used in war crimes, or could disturb the peace and security of the region, then they cannot be authorized,” Holzapfel said, citing the Arms Trade Treaty, a pact Germany championed, and domestic law that restricts sales into conflict zones when serious violations are a risk.
Holzapfel questioned how Berlin could ensure that arms supplied to Israel would not be used in the fighting.
“We're talking about ammunition, we're talking about spare parts for Merkava tanks, we're talking about things that obviously are used in whatever conflict. So I think that the legal situation is quite clear there,” he said.
Germany also faces a case brought by Nicaragua at the International Court of Justice over alleged breaches of its obligations concerning Gaza, including through arms supplies to Israel. The court held hearings on Germany’s preliminary objections in September.
Holzapfel also criticized the Merz government for blocking coordinated European measures that could raise pressure on Israel. Berlin has stalled efforts inside the EU to suspend parts of the EU-Israel association agreement and to impose sanctions on right-wing Israeli ministers. Ireland, France, Spain and Slovenia have acted alone, including with entry bans.
“Germany is currently the member state within the EU that carries the brunt of responsibility for EU inaction. There’s absolutely no doubt about it,” he said.
He added that the EU could in fact play a significant role in pressuring the Israeli government to end human rights violations, return to diplomacy, pursue a political solution and allow more humanitarian aid into Gaza.
“The European Union has immense leverage by virtue of its size, of its economy, of the historic ties to Israel and to the Middle East,” Holzapfel said. “We have a very close relationship and the leverage is there. It just needs to be used, also in the interest of Israel.”
If Berlin keeps blocking, he said, Germany’s diplomatic losses will likely continue, above all with governments in the Global South and in Arab and Muslim countries.
That unease could surface again in the days ahead, Holzapfel warned, as Germany seeks a three-year seat on the UN Human Rights Council for 2027-29, with the vote set for this week.
Germany and Ireland are the only candidates for the two Western European and Others seats. Berlin, therefore, faces a lower hurdle than in the Security Council race – though it still needs 97 of 193 votes in a secret ballot.
The math favors Germany this time, but Holzapfel said a win is far from certain. Even a successful bid with limited support could indicate continuing discontent with Berlin’s policy, he added.
“I can imagine that the effect we saw in the UN General Assembly vote in June will most probably also be visible there,” he said. “How it will end is hard to predict – whether by another fiasco or whether Germany manages to win – but I’m almost certain that there will be a visible effect of these dynamics.”

On the possibility of an 'energy truce'

- Russia wants lasting peace in Ukraine and is ready to do everything necessary to achieve it: "The Kremlin has said repeatedly, and President [of Russia Vladimir] Putin has said so as well, along with officials at other levels: we want lasting peace, not a ceasefire, and we are ready to do everything possible to achieve it."
On a settlement in Ukraine
- Europe clearly does not belong to the "peace camp" seeking a settlement to the Ukrainian conflict; instead, it is part of the "war camp" that is doing everything it can to prolong the crisis: "The Europeans clearly do not belong to the ‘peace camp,’ which seeks a path to a peaceful settlement [of the conflict in Ukraine]. - Moscow welcomes the work of American negotiators on a peaceful settlement in Ukraine: "We are much more impressed by the efforts of American negotiators. We are grateful to them for pursuing those efforts."
- Russia is not seeking a split between the United States and Europe over the Ukraine conflict but a solution that could help pave the way toward a peaceful settlement: "We aren’t seeking a split here but we are looking for really effective measures and responsible solutions that will enable us to reach a peaceful settlement."

Israeli producer had access to data harvested by Poland using Pegasus spyware, say prosecutors
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
12:27:25 UTC
21:27:25 KST

Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!
Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.
Data harvested from mobile phones by the Polish authorities using Pegasus spyware were transmitted outside Poland and were accessible to the tool’s Israeli producer, Polish prosecutors have revealed as part of an investigation into the use of Pegasus under the former government.
Prime Minister Donald Tusk says that the case is “one of the biggest scandals in Polish history since the fall of communism”, and that it is “beyond any doubt” that the Israeli firm behind Pegasus, NSO Group, cooperates with Israeli intelligence.
Tego o Pegasusie jeszcze nie słyszeliście. pic.twitter.com/etvhTE9EWa
— Donald Tusk (@donaldtusk) October 12, 2026
Pegasus is a powerful and controversial tool that allows the extraction of large amounts of data from mobile phones without users’ knowledge. A number of countries have been found to have used it to spy on opposition figures.
In 2017, Poland, under the government of the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) party, purchased Pegasus from NSO. The spyware was subsequently used against hundreds of targets, including a number of PiS’s political opponents.
Among them was the head of the 2019 election campaign of Tusk’s centrist Civic Coalition (KO) party (which was then known as Civic Platform, PO). Last year, Tusk revealed that his own wife and daughter had been among those caught up in the surveillance.
PiS, however, has insisted that Pegasus was a necessary tool to fight crime and ensure national security. It says the spyware was only used with court approval against targets legitimately suspected of wrongdoing.
After a coalition led by Tusk took power from PiS in December 2023, it launched investigations into the use of Pegasus under the former government.
Today, the National Prosecutor’s Office released its latest findings, based on analysis by experts at the forensic research office of Poland’s Internal Security Agency (ABW).
The experts confirmed that Pegasus allowed the harvesting of emails, instant messaging and text messages; the content of telephone conversations, both via mobile networks and internet calls; browsing histories, calendars and contact lists; photos, videos and other files; and location data.
“Additionally, Pegasus allowed the use of the device’s built-in microphone and cameras to record audio and video in real time and take screenshots,” reports the National Prosecutor’s Office.
