— Waldemar Żurek (@w_zurek) October 12, 2026
The ABW experts also highlighted serious concerns over management and security of the harvested data, noting that Poland’s Central Anti-Corruption Bureau (CBA), which was responsible for using the spyware, “did not have full control over the Pegasus system”.
“The CBA did not have passwords to access some accounts with administrative privileges and some system components remained under the control of the manufacturer [NSO],” wrote the prosecutor’s office. “The server module responsible for infecting mobile devices remained under the manufacturer’s exclusive control.”
Data transmitted through the Pegasus system travelled outside Polish territory, through “servers located in various parts of the world”, in a network managed by NSO and “beyond the CBA’s control”, found the experts.
Meanwhile, NSO “had technical access to materials from operational surveillance”, although prosecutors say that the experts “did not determine whether the manufacturer actually obtained access to materials from specific operations”.

In a video commenting on the latest findings, Tusk said that the investigation into Pegasus was “coming to a head”. He called it “one of the biggest scandals in Polish history after the fall of communism”.
The former PIS authorities signed a contract for a spyware system “over which they de facto had no control, because control remained in the hands of Israel and an Israeli company…whose cooperation with Israeli intelligence is, of course, beyond doubt”, said the prime minister.
“They paid money for a system that de facto transferred all possible data on Polish citizens, Polish opposition leaders and Polish independent prosecutors…to the Israeli side,” he added. “This is no longer [just] a scandal…We’re talking about a crime against the state.”
Two former heads of Polish security agencies have been charged over the use of Pegasus spyware under the former PiS government.

Later on Monday, a separate parliamentary committee set up by the ruling coalition to investigate the use of Pegasus also revealed unclassified sections of a report on its findings.
In addition to the information released by prosecutors, the commission also said that the CBA had never obtained the required IT security accreditation for Pegasus, meaning that it was used without meeting requirements for protecting classified information.
The commission’s chairwoman, Magdalena Sroka, also said that courts granting authorisation for the use of Pegasus were not informed of its full capabilities, such as the ability to access the entire contents of phones, reports broadcaster RMF.

Legal proceedings are already underway against a number of former officials in relation to Pegasus. In February, prosecutors charged the former heads of the AWB and Military Counterintelligence Service (SKW) with abuse of power for approving the use of Pegasus despite being aware of legal shortcomings.
Previously, the former head of the CBA was charged with the same offence, while one of his deputies was charged with unlawfully disclosing material from surveillance of Roman Giertych, an MP from Tusk’s KO party who has also worked as a lawyer for Tusk and his family.

12 teens wounded after unexploded shell explodes near Israel's northern border
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
12:26:05 UTC
21:26:05 KST

One Israeli was killed and 24 others were wounded in an explosion caused by a previously unexploded ordnance on Monday near Israel's border with Lebanon during a high school field trip, emergency services reported.
The wounded at the scene near Kibbutz Yiftach include seventh- to ninth-grade students and staff members from ORT Ma'alot's religious high school. A preliminary police investigation found that one of the students had put the unexploded ordnance in his bag, after which it detonated.
The police and Education Ministry are considering suspending school trips to northern Israel in the coming days following the explosion. Additional school trips to the area are scheduled for Tuesday, but the ministry has yet to decide whether they will proceed as planned or be canceled until inspections of the area are completed.
Two teenagers were seriously wounded, two adults and eight teenagers were moderately wounded, and another 12 teenagers sustained light injuries, according to Magen David Adom.
The IDF said an initial inquiry indicated that the explosion was likely caused by a Hezbollah cluster bomb that had remained in the area and detonated. The military added that the incident was still under investigation.
The Israeli army is investigating whether the trip received the required approvals before it was authorized to take place. At all sites and along all routes opened to the general public, the IDF is required to inspect the area and clear any unexploded ordnance beforehand.
The IDF said that its forces were at the scene to provide assistance and that Air Force helicopters were on their way. It added that the circumstances of the incident were being investigated.
A source in the Education Ministry said the trip had received the required approvals. The ministry has yet to officially confirm this and is checking whether the route taken by the students was the one approved by its situation room. The mayor of Ma'alot-Tarshiha, the town where the wounded students' school is located, also said the trip had been approved by the ministry.
During the war that began in February, Iran and Hezbollah fired cluster missiles and rockets on several documented occasions at the Ramim Ridge and the area around Metula. Such munitions leave behind large numbers of unexploded bomblets. The bomblets from Iranian cluster munitions were relatively large, while those left behind by Hezbollah rockets were smaller.
Mayor Moti Ben David said unexploded ordnance had been a constant concern since the start of the war, and that the municipality was trying to determine how it exploded.
During the war, Iran and Hezbollah fired cluster rockets on several documented occasions toward the Ramim ridge and the area around Metula in northern Israel. Cluster munitions leave behind large numbers of unexploded submunitions. While the bomblets released by Iranian cluster munitions were relatively large, those released by rockets were smaller.
The use of cluster munitions poses significant challenges for rescue and recovery forces, as many unexploded submunitions are left behind. These can remain in the field for months or even years and may detonate if touched.
The high rate of unexploded submunitions is one of the main reasons for an international convention banning cluster munitions. Neither Iran nor Israel is a signatory to the convention.
In August, six foreign workers were wounded in an unexploded ordnance blast in an agricultural area near Metula in northern Israel. Three of the workers, two seriously wounded and one moderately wounded, were taken by helicopter to a hospital in Haifa, and the others were transferred to a hospital in Safed, medical sources said.
During the period when northern Israel's civilian security squads were called up for reserve duty, one of their roles was to search the area for as many unexploded ordnance items as possible to prevent casualties.
However, locating unexploded ordnance in open areas is more difficult because, unlike built-up areas, fewer eyewitnesses can report them. "It's easier to locate ordnance that exploded, even if the blast itself wasn't captured on cameras or seen by people, because you can identify vegetation or even trees that were burned in the immediate vicinity of the impact," a security source told Haaretz. According to the source, "if a piece of ordnance did not explode, it's much harder to locate, especially if it's a very small bomblet."

EU Hits Russia With Nearly 1,600 New Sanctions Listings in Largest Expansion Since Full-Scale Invasion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
12:24:37 UTC
21:24:37 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
EU Hits Russia With Nearly 1,600 New Sanctions Listings in Largest Expansion Since Full-Scale Invasion
European Union foreign ministers have approved nearly 1,600 new sanctions listings targeting Russia’s military-industrial complex, marking the largest expansion of the bloc’s sanctions list since the beginning of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Kaja Kallas announced the decision on X on October , emphasizing that more than half of the newly approved listings are connected to Russia’s ballistic missile production supply chain.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“EU Foreign Ministers just adopted nearly 1,600 new sanctions listings targeting Russia’s military-industrial complex. This is the single largest expansion of our sanctions list since Russia started its war.,” Kallas wrote.
She also stressed that the decision demonstrates continued European unity in efforts to restrict Russia’s ability to manufacture weapons used in its war against Ukraine.
“More than half are connected to the production chain for ballistic missiles. We are making it significantly harder, slower and more expensive for Russia to produce the weapons it uses to kill Ukrainians,” Kallas stated.
According to earlier reporting by Euronews, the new measures will target 743 individuals and 826 organizations accused of supporting Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
The sanctions list will also include 77 Russian lawmakers who ran in September State Duma elections held in temporarily occupied Ukrainian territories.
The latest expansion follows discussions over the scope of the EU’s proposed 22nd sanctions package, including concerns about the potential impact of certain restrictions on European industries.
In one such case, the EU removed a Russian company and an individual associated with it from the proposed package at Estonia’s request. The company supplies strategically important rare-earth materials to an Estonian processing facility.

The attacks marked one of the most significant disruptions to Saudi aviation in years, adding to pressures on an industry already grappling with conflict across the Middle East.

The disruption has forced airlines across Europe and Asia to suspend services, while the Federal Aviation Administration advised US carriers on Sunday to exercise caution when flying to or over Saudi Arabia.

Russia Loses More Than 50,000 Troops in September, Including Up to 28,000 Killed, NATO Says
Russian forces suffered more than 50,000 casualties in Ukraine during September 2026, including as many as 28,000 soldiers killed, according to estimates provided by a senior NATO military official.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Bloomberg on October 11, the NATO official, speaking on condition of anonymity, estimated Ukrainian casualties during the same period at approximately 5,000 personnel. If accurate, the figures indicate that Russian losses were more than ten times higher than those sustained by Ukrainian forces.
The official attributed Russia’s high casualty figures partly to its continued use of infantry assaults against heavily defended Ukrainian positions. Russian troops have been advancing through areas described as “kill zones,” where Ukrainian forces employ attack drones, land mines, artillery, and other defensive systems.
Despite the reported losses, Russian forces have continued offensive operations in an effort to capture additional Ukrainian territory.
Bloomberg reported that Ukraine has simultaneously intensified strikes against Russian infrastructure, including oil refineries and data centers, while Ukrainian ground forces have recaptured more than 125 square kilometers of territory.
The Kremlin has not released official figures for its military losses, and the NATO estimates have not been independently verified.
Earlier, Ukraine’s General Staff reported that Russian forces suffered 46,230 personnel losses in September, the highest monthly figure recorded in 2026. The total surpassed 42,860 losses in July and 42,020 in August, reflecting a continued increase in Russian casualties throughout the year.

Ukrainian Phoenix Drones Destroy 3 Russian Grad Launchers, 2 Tanks and Artillery Systems in One Week

- Category

Ukrainian Phoenix Drones Destroy 3 Russian Grad Launchers, 2 Tanks and Artillery Systems in One Week
Ukraine destroyed three Russian BM-21 Grad multiple rocket launchers, two tanks, several artillery systems, and an armored vehicle across the Lyman, Toretsk, and Dobropillia directions during a week of combat operations, Ukraine’s Phoenix unmanned systems unit reported on October 11.
The unit reported that its drone operators destroyed a Typhoon-VDV protected armored vehicle and a BM-21 Grad system on the Lyman direction while the launcher was moving toward a combat mission.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
On the Toretsk direction, Phoenix reported destroying another fully loaded Grad launcher, along with two D-30 howitzers, a Giatsint-B artillery gun, and two tanks.
The unit also stated that Russian infantry attempted to shelter from Ukrainian drones and shoot them down with improvised means, but did not disclose casualty figures.
On the Dobropillia direction, Phoenix operators destroyed a third Grad launcher that Russian forces had attempted to conceal.
The unit also reported detecting Russian troops using so-called anti-thermal camouflage cloaks intended to reduce visibility to thermal imaging systems. Phoenix stated that the camouflage failed to prevent its drones from detecting and striking Russian personnel.
The BM-21 Grad is a Soviet-designed 122 mm multiple launch rocket system used to deliver salvos against area targets. The Typhoon-VDV is a Russian protected armored vehicle developed for airborne forces and designed to transport personnel while providing increased protection against mines and small-arms fire, the unit wrote.
Days earlier, Ukrainian Combat Hawks strike drones destroyed a Russian BM-21 Grad launcher and disabled a 152 mm Msta-B howitzer. The 25th Separate Sicheslav Air Assault Brigade reported that the Grad was destroyed together with its crew and ammunition.

Ukraine Lures Russian Elite Special Forces Into Deadly Ambush, Wipes Out Two Groups
Ukrainian military intelligence operatives neutralized two groups of Russian special forces during a counter-sabotage operation in the Zaporizhzhia direction, capturing one Russian soldier after identifying the units’ movements and setting up an ambush.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence Directorate (HUR) on October 11, the operation was carried out by members of its Timur Special Unit against personnel from Russia’s 10th Separate Guards Special Purpose Brigade, a formation affiliated with Russian military intelligence.
Ukrainian intelligence officers identified the composition of both Russian groups and tracked their movement routes using intelligence gathered from human sources, including individuals within Russian forces, alongside technical reconnaissance capabilities.
Based on this information, Ukrainian operatives positioned themselves along the identified routes and organized an ambush. Once the Russian personnel entered the targeted area, Ukrainian forces opened fire and subsequently conducted a clearing operation.
HUR confirmed that one Russian special forces soldier was taken prisoner. The agency did not specify how many Russian personnel were killed or wounded during this particular engagement.
The targeted 10th Separate Guards Special Purpose Brigade is a regular Russian military intelligence formation whose personnel previously participated in Russia’s wars against Georgia and Ukraine, as well as Moscow’s military intervention in Syria.
According to Ukrainian intelligence, members of the brigade had already been documented operating in temporarily occupied Ukrainian territories in 2014 and 2015, during the early stages of Russia’s military aggression against Ukraine.
HUR also provided broader figures for the Timur Special Unit’s operations in the Zaporizhzhia direction. According to the agency, Ukrainian intelligence personnel have inflicted 448 irreversible Russian personnel losses and captured another 85 Russian soldiers over the course of the operation.
Earlier, in March 2026, Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence reported that fighters from its Khymera unit, had cleared Russian infantry positions in the Zaporizhzhia direction. At the time, the unit had reportedly inflicted more than 300 Russian casualties, including killed and wounded personnel, and captured 39 soldiers during defensive operations in the area.

Russia Strips FSB Patrol Boats of Coast Guard Markings and Adds Anti-Drone Armor in the Baltic
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
12:23:48 UTC
21:23:48 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russia Strips FSB Patrol Boats of Coast Guard Markings and Adds Anti-Drone Armor in the Baltic
Russia has begun modifying patrol boats operated by the FSB Border Guard’s Coast Guard for missions in the Baltic Sea, giving at least one Project 12200 Sobol vessel dark camouflage, according to images published by OSINT researcher Spectre Crouton on October 11.
The vessel had previously carried a dark-blue hull, white superstructure, Coast Guard identification stripes, and a visible hull number. In the newer images, those markings are gone, and the entire boat has been repainted in a dark geometric camouflage pattern and fitted with additional protection against drones.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Metal grilles have been installed above the bridge and superstructure, apparently intended to provide protection against FPV drones and munitions dropped from above, according to Militarnyi.
Similar improvised anti-drone structures have become increasingly common on military vehicles and ships as low-cost UAVs become a growing threat to exposed equipment.
Additional equipment is also visible toward the stern, including an inflatable boat, suggesting the vessel may be receiving a broader package of modifications for more demanding operational tasks in the Baltic.
Project 12200 Sobol patrol boats were developed by the Almaz Central Marine Design Bureau in St. Petersburg in the early 2000s. Their original role centers on border protection, coastal patrols, and anti-smuggling missions rather than frontline naval combat.
The Sobol displaces about 57.5 tons, measures roughly 30.3 meters in length and 5.8 meters in beam, and can reach speeds of approximately 47 to 50 knots. The vessel is operated by a crew of six, giving it a relatively small footprint and high speed for coastal interception and patrol work.
Earlier, Russian Defense Minister Andrei Belousov awarded the commander of the Baltic Fleet corvette Soobrazitelny after the Russian warship fired signal flares toward a Danish military helicopter in international waters near Gedser, Denmark.

Abramovich Aides Backdated Documents to Hide Assets and Avoid Taxes, Report Says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
12:23:42 UTC
21:23:42 KST

Aides to Russian billionaire Roman Abramovich, including employees of accounting firm Deloitte Cyprus, allegedly backdated more than 1,000 documents to conceal assets and help his businesses avoid taxes, according to an investigation published Monday.
The Guardian and the Bureau of Investigative Journalism examined corporate records from the Cyprus Confidential leak, a collection of more than 500,000 documents that includes internal correspondence.
The investigation describes an alleged scheme spanning at least 1999 to 2013, in which documents for more than 100 companies linked to Abramovich were backdated, sometimes by as much as five years. Deloitte Cyprus signed off on financial statements based on those records, the report said.
Abramovich and his longtime aide Eugene Tenenbaum deny wrongdoing.
The investigation identified Tenenbaum and Demetris Ioannides, the former chairman of Deloitte Cyprus, as central figures in the alleged arrangements. Ioannides later founded Meritservus, which served as Abramovich’s main financial adviser for nearly two decades.
One case involved Kravin Investments, a Cyprus-registered company that received about $3 billion from the sale of shares in Russian oil producer Sibneft in May 2003 and retained roughly $2 billion.
The money generated interest that should have been subject to tax in Cyprus, according to the investigation.
In correspondence from 2005, Ioannides said Kravin’s financial statements for 2003 and 2004 needed to be amended. Documents were subsequently produced showing that Kravin was merely holding the money on behalf of Kelvedon Worldwide, a company registered in the British Virgin Islands.
Those documents were dated 2003 despite having been created at least two years later, the investigation said. The arrangement removed the $2 billion from Kravin’s balance sheet, along with the associated tax liability.
Another case concerned the transfer of $98 million out of Cyprus-based companies holding Sibneft shares in 2000.
Backdated consultancy agreements purported to show that an intermediary had earned the money by advising on share purchases and would pass 99.9% of it to Abramovich as an agency commission, the report said. The share transactions had taken place a year earlier.
The leaked records included 50 promissory notes, with repayment applications bearing Abramovich’s signature.
The journalists also examined records relating to about $650 million in property and luxury assets, including the Fyning Hill estate in England’s West Sussex, a London penthouse, a French chateau, aircraft, helicopters, yachts and cars.
Those assets disappeared from the accounts of Cyprus-based Amiscan Investments after documents were produced suggesting they had been transferred to another company in early 2003, according to the investigation.
The report also raised questions about evidence presented during a 2008 legal dispute involving Abramovich and his former Sibneft-Yugra business partner, Shalva Chigirinsky.
Tenenbaum told the High Court of England and Wales that he had not known the details of the disputed transactions before spring 2004. The leaked correspondence, however, indicated that he had approved agreements in 2003, including the transfer of Sibneft-Yugra shares to an Abramovich-owned company, the investigation said.
Some documents submitted to support Abramovich’s position also appeared to have been backdated, according to the report. The court ultimately declined to hear the merits of Chigirinsky’s claim, which exceeded $5 billion.
Deloitte Cyprus said it complied with applicable laws and could no longer access the decades-old correspondence.

How diesel became the new geopolitical battleground, and what it means for the world
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
12:22:54 UTC
21:22:54 KST

Access to diesel, the fuel that powers global economic activity, has become the latest geopolitical battleground amid two raging wars, setting off a domino effect across nations and hitting the Global South hardest.
Diesel prices are going through the roof in most of the world. Even in the US, which retains the capacity to subsidise retail consumers as the world’s richest country, the diesel price has gone up 70 percent since it attacked Iran on February 28.
But the diesel crisis is far worse in the Global South, where poorer countries lack emergency stockpiles or massive cash reserves to protect consumers from an existential threat to basic food supply chains, transport, and critical infrastructure.
Some countries, like the Philippines, have declared national energy emergencies, while others, such as Sri Lanka, have rationed fuel supplies. In some African countries, fuel prices have surged by up to 150 percent.
In Pakistan, the government has adopted a daily price revision mechanism for diesel, which is now 40 percent more expensive than it was at the start of the US-Israeli war against Iran.
Analysts point out that unlike previous price shocks driven mainly by crude constraints, the current upswing in diesel prices is partly due to a deficit in refinery capacity.
Drone and missile attacks by Iran and its allies have targeted large crude processing plants in Kuwait, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, and Bahrain.
Russian refineries have also come under a spate of attacks by Ukraine in what is being described as the ‘energy war’; Russian refineries are now operating at 60 percent of capacity.
The price of diesel has increased more than the price of petrol — used mostly by passenger cars — for two main reasons. One, diesel supplies were already tighter than those of gasoline, even before the start of the Iran war.
And two, refineries in the Gulf countries that came under fire produced more diesel than petrol. No other countries had the idle capacity that could be tapped immediately to make up for the production loss.
As a result, millions of barrels of Middle Eastern and Russian diesel have disappeared from the global market.
To counter the shortage, the US has struck a deal with Russia to buy diesel, even though heavy sanctions otherwise restrict Moscow's ability to sell energy worldwide.
Separately, US President Donald Trump announced an “energy ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine on October 11, even though Ukrainian leader Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he was still waiting to see the deal's details.
Resource nationalism rears its head
Analysts say the global diesel crisis has unleashed a wave of ‘resource nationalism’ in which top producers limit supplies, driving global ‘crack spreads’, or refining margins, to historic highs.
Last month, Moscow extended a strict ban on diesel exports through the summer and autumn, stating shipments would not fully return until Western sanctions were lifted.
Likewise, Beijing temporarily paused fuel exports to prioritise its domestic inventory.
Before striking a diesel import deal with Russia, the US aggressively pressured European allies to release strategic reserves or face a US diesel export ban, setting off a global alarm.
Baris Alpaslan, an economist and chief adviser at IC Holding – a Turkish conglomerate with energy production and distribution businesses – makes a distinction between resource sovereignty and resource nationalism.
“I think we need to distinguish between the legitimate exercise of resource sovereignty and the broader consequences of resource nationalism,” he tells TRT World.
Protecting domestic supply is a real duty, particularly during a major crisis, he says.
But the problem arises when many countries do it all at once.
“(Export bans) may shift part of the economic cost of a geopolitical crisis onto countries that had little or no role in causing it, particularly poorer, fuel-importing economies in Africa, Asia and Latin America,” he says.
Higher diesel prices quickly feed into transport costs, food prices, and broader inflation, he says.
“The frustration in the Global South is understandable. Many of these countries are price takers in global energy markets, with limited fiscal capacity to cushion their populations against external price shocks,” he says.
The collective result can be a deeper global shortage, with the poorest and most import-dependent economies often bearing a disproportionate share of the cost, he says.
New battle lines
Yasar Sari, director of the Haydar Aliyev Centre for Eurasian Studies at Ibn Haldun University, tells TRT World that access to diesel is already pushing countries to “form alliances around fuel supplies, rather than ideology”.
He points to India’s import dependence – more than 80 percent of its crude requirement – and the strain of balancing outside diplomacy with negotiations inside BRICS, a group of emerging economies mostly from the Global South.
The May BRICS summit produced no joint statement and referred only to “differing views among some members” of the bloc, which includes both Iran and the UAE as full members.
The absence of a joint statement indicated that energy security issues are eroding regional cohesion, he notes.
China’s heavy inventories, estimated to be 1.49 billion barrels and described as mostly crude, still give Beijing leverage to hold product at home, he adds.
European countries hold the largest emergency diesel reserves, with France and Germany together accounting for more than a third of the EU’s strategic stocks, he says.
American public stocks provide a regional cushion at best, not a global store, he notes.
This is the reason the US has pressed France and Germany to draw those stocks down, with restrictions on US diesel exports held out as leverage ahead of the US midterms planned for the first week of November.
Sari refers to the 1973 Arab oil embargo, when producers from the Gulf cut supply to states that had backed Israel.
But he highlights the difference between then and now: “(Fuel) weaponisation is less about producers withholding supply and more about importers hoarding it – a reverse embargo in which vulnerable nations scramble to secure what remains,” he says.
According to Alpaslan, energy access is increasingly becoming a source of geopolitical leverage.
A government short of diesel for farms, freight or power may be more receptive to a supplier that can offer reliable deliveries or favourable financing, he says.
His concern is that energy insecurity can narrow the foreign-policy choices available to poorer countries.
“The real test is whether access to essential fuel remains governed primarily by reliable trade and commercial considerations, or increasingly becomes an instrument of political pressure,” he says.
Survival beyond wars
Sari says China and South Korea can shield home markets and limit exports. Indonesia, the Philippines, Bangladesh and Ethiopia cannot.
“Fuel access isn’t causing a clean geopolitical split, but it is accelerating fragmentation, with each nation’s survival strategy shaped by its reserves and ability to pay,” he says.
How long can that be managed?
Sari says the window to manage the crisis without triggering catastrophic damage to the global economy is narrow – likely measured in weeks, not months.
Even a political settlement would not quickly restore normalcy, he notes.
He describes the G7’s 100-million-barrel release as a gesture that only buys time.
Ending both wars today will end the war premium almost at once, he says.
“But physical supply recovery would take months to years because of damaged refineries, disrupted shipping, and structural changes in trade flows,” he says.

Basel Zoo welcomes gorilla newborn months after fatal incidents
A new gorilla baby was born last September at Basel Zoo. The father is the dominant male, Yeba, who fatally injured a newborn gorilla and another young male in the group last July.
Makala, an 11-year-old female, gave birth to her first baby on September 24, which happened to be World Gorilla Day, the Basel Zoo announced on Monday. The baby is a male named Xola. Its birth comes after a difficult period for the group of Western lowland gorillas living at the Swiss zoo.
Last July, the 14-year-old dominant male, Yeba, bit his first baby – born just a few days earlier – during a fight with the mother, the 37-year-old female Joas. Shortly before this tragedy, the 11-year-old male Mobali had to be euthanised after being bitten on the genitals by Yeba.
+ Baby gorilla bitten to death by father at Basel Zoo
Following these two fatal incidents, the zoo had stated that it was monitoring the group dynamics and consulting with experts. It had stepped up its vigilance in anticipation of the expected birth of the new baby.
Breastfeeding
The female Makala is caring attentively for her newborn and carries her snugly against her. Over the coming months, Xola will remain close to her mother, who breastfeeds her regularly. Gorilla mothers breastfeed their young for three to four years.
So far, social interactions within the gorilla group have been going smoothly, the zoo reports. For the time being, the mother is keeping her distance from the other members of the group and retreats to a quiet spot when their curiosity gets the better of them.
+ Swiss conservationists want Basel zoo gorilla breeding to stop
The female Qaziba (aged 7) is showing a keen interest in the baby, which she expresses through cautious approaches and gentle caresses. These interactions are important for young females and will stand them in good stead later on when they raise their own young.
Western lowland gorillas are classified as “critically endangered” on the IUCN Red List. Their population continues to decline due to hunting and the destruction of their natural habitat.

Anduril bets on mass-produced missile interceptors
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
12:18:58 UTC
21:18:58 KST

- Anduril unveiled Steelfin, a family of two-stage surface-to-air interceptors aimed at cruise, ballistic and hypersonic missiles, with flight tests planned next year.
- The company plans to build several thousand a year and says Steelfin will fit existing launchers including Patriot, Mk 41 and Typhon.
Anduril Industries has unveiled Steelfin, a family of surface-to-air interceptor missiles designed to shoot down cruise, ballistic and hypersonic missiles at a fraction of the cost of today’s interceptors, with flight tests set to begin next year.
The company announced Steelfin on Oct. 12, the first day of the Association of the U.S. Army’s annual meeting in Washington. Anduril says it plans to build on the order of several thousand Steelfin missiles a year in the short term. It did not give a unit price, name a customer or say which U.S. service is backing the program, saying only that it has been developing Steelfin for years while investing alongside multiple customers. The company has completed ballistic testing with representative air vehicles but has not yet flown a Steelfin missile.
The first stage is a solid rocket booster that can be swapped for different motors depending on how far and how fast the missile needs to fly, and how tightly it must pack into a launcher. The second stage is a common “terminal interceptor” that carries the airframe, electronics, software and flight controls shared across the family, with open interfaces so Anduril can drop in different seekers and mission systems without redesigning the missile.
Anduril says the approach lets it build versions for every layer of air and missile defense, from short-range point defense of a single site to upper-tier ballistic missile defense, while aiming for a fraction of the cost of current interceptors in each class. The company did not say what those benchmark costs are, but a single Patriot PAC-3 MSE interceptor costs about $4 million, and the Missile Defense Agency is pursuing a separate low-cost interceptor effort with a target price below $750,000 per round.
Because the variants share parts, Anduril says they can run down the same production line with the same tooling and workers, letting it shift output to whichever version is in demand. The company also says the common interfaces let it buy commercial components and use multiple suppliers.
Steelfin is designed to fire from launchers the U.S. military already fields, including the M903A2 launcher used by the Patriot air defense system, the U.S. Navy’s Mk 41 Vertical Launch System aboard cruisers and destroyers, the U.S. Army’s Typhon mid-range missile launcher, and newer containerized launchers. Anduril says it will work with existing fire control systems such as the U.S. Navy’s Aegis and the U.S. Army’s Integrated Battle Command System, known as IBCS, rather than requiring a new command network.
The launch comes as U.S. air defense stocks have been drawn down by combat in the Middle East. This month alone, Raytheon received contracts worth up to $6.3 billion for SM-3 Block IB interceptors and up to $24.4 billion for SM-6 missiles to replenish U.S. Navy inventories. Anduril already makes smaller counter-drone interceptors such as Roadrunner and Anvil, but Steelfin is its first family aimed at cruise and ballistic missiles.

The Verkhovna Rada is set to raise the threshold for large-scale privatization — what is envisaged
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
15:17:53 EEST
21:17:53 KST

The Verkhovna Rada is set to raise the threshold for large-scale privatization — what is envisaged
Kyiv • UNN
Parliament supported a bill on changes to the privatization of state property. Buyers will pay 5% for the preparation of assets, but no more than 1,000 minimum wages.
The Verkhovna Rada adopted as a basis a bill providing for amendments to the privatization of state property. In particular, buyers of state assets will pay fees for the preparation of documentation, while the value threshold for large-scale privatization will also be increased to UAH 1 billion. UNN reports this with reference to a parliamentary session.
Details
Bill No. 16011 "On Amendments to Certain Laws of Ukraine Regarding Increasing the Efficiency of State Property Privatization" was adopted in the first reading and as a basis by 244 MPs.
According to the document, large-scale privatization assets will include state- or municipally owned assets whose value, according to financial statements, exceeded UAH 1 billion in the last reporting year.
Previously, this amount was UAH 250 million.
The document also provides for the creation of an authorized legal entity that will be 100% state-owned, fall under the management of the State Property Fund of Ukraine, and be designated by the Cabinet of Ministers upon the submission of the SPFU.
The entity will be able to prepare technical documentation, register property rights, conduct audits, restore primary documents, and handle the marketing and presentation of assets to potential buyers. It is also proposed to allow its employees to be involved in performing the duties of managers of enterprises being prepared for privatization.
A fee of 5% of the sale price is proposed for preparing state property for privatization. At the same time, its upper limit will be capped at an amount equivalent to 1,000 minimum wages as of January 1 of the respective year. Currently, this amounts to UAH 8 million 647 thousand.
It should be noted that this bill is important for receiving the next tranche from the World Bank.
To remind you
In October, the State Property Fund of Ukraine will put four large assets up for privatization auctions, including state-owned enterprises and confiscated sanctioned assets.

Battery-electric car market share hits 20.7% in EU
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
12:15:16 UTC
21:15:16 KST

Gokhan Ergocun
12 October 2026•Update: 12 October 2026
In the first half of 2026, battery-electric cars captured a 20.7% share of the EU market, which rose from 15.6% a year earlier, according to the European Automobile Manufacturers' Association (ACEA).
Hybrid-electric car registrations took 37.3% of the market to remain the top choice for EU consumers.
The combined market share of petrol and diesel cars dropped to 29.7%, down from 37.8% in the previous year.
Electrically-chargeable vans reached a 13.2% market share, which increased from 9.5% in the first half of 2025.
Registrations for electrically chargeable trucks grew 47.7% to secure 4.8% of the market.
Electric bus registrations surged 56.8% to reach 27.7% of the overall market.
Meanwhile, global new car registrations dropped 4.9% to 35.7 million units in the first six months of 2026.
Weaker domestic demand in China, which fell 23.2%, primarily drove this global decline.
Regional performance remained uneven across global markets.
EU new car registrations grew 5.7% to reach nearly 5.9 million units.
Global car production fell 1% to 37.6 million units during the six-month period.
The EU auto trade surplus narrowed 34.2% to €28.7 billion as imports rose and exports fell.
Imports from China surged 70.5% in value to €10.5 billion.
EU exports to key destinations weakened, particularly the US and Türkiye.
The US and UK combined still represented 48% of the total EU car export value.

Remediable Service Statement Delivery Update
Update on Advocate General for Scotland v Milroy
The Ministry of Defence (MOD) can confirm that it has been granted permission to appeal in the case of Advocate General for Scotland v Milroy.
The appeal will now proceed through the next stage of the legal process. As the matter remains before the courts, it would not be appropriate to comment in detail.
Further updates will be provided in due course.
Mr Milroy originally made a claim against MOD in June 2020 on the grounds that the way in which MOD calculates the attendance-based pay divisor for Volunteer Reservists and the failure to provide access to an occupational pension for reserve service before 1 April 2015 amounted to less favourable treatment of part-time workers.
In April 2023 the Employment Tribunal heard the case. The judgment of the Employment Tribunal was in favour of the claimant.
MOD subsequently appealed the judgment and that appeal was heard in December 2025 at the Employment Appeal Tribunal. In January 2026, the Employment Appeal Tribunal dismissed MOD’s appeal and upheld the Employment Tribunal’s findings.
Following the judgement MOD submitted a request for leave to appeal directly to the Employment Appeal Tribunal. This was refused by the judge of the Employment Appeal Tribunal in February 2026.
An application for leave to appeal was subsequently submitted to the Inner House, Court of Session, which was heard at an oral hearing on 8 October 2026. MOD can confirm that it has received permission to appeal following the oral hearing.
Early Leavers – Pension Rights Notice
A world class pension scheme for your military service
When a member of the armed forces reaches their retirement age, they receive one of the most generous pensions available in the UK. This fairly reflects the unique sacrifice they have provided their country throughout their career.
All members of the armed forces are automatically enrolled into the Armed Forces Pension Scheme. Unlike all other public schemes, members pay 0% in contributions each month. The scheme is unfunded and paid from the public purse.

Transfers in and out of the schemes
If you have built up pension benefits elsewhere before joining the armed forces you have the option to transfer in the value of your other benefits to receive a service credit in your Armed Forces Pension Scheme.
Before you apply to DBS Veterans UK for a transfer in, you need to obtain details of the amount of your transfer value from your previous pension scheme, and then an estimate from DBS Veterans UK of the additional pension that this will buy. If you decide to go ahead with the transfer, you should make your application to DBS Veterans UK in writing.
You must be serving in the armed forces to be eligible to transfer in and once you have committed yourself to a transfer from your previous pension scheme, you cannot change your mind and you will have given up forever your rights and those of your dependants under the previous schemes.
Transfers into AFPS 15 must be completed within one year of joining the scheme. For members who remain solely in AFPS 75 and AFPS 05 who may still make transfers in from a non-public service scheme. AFSP 75 the transfer in must be made before your 54 birthday and in AFPS 05 the transfer in must be made before the beginning of your final year of service before your pension is due.
If you leave without receiving immediate pension benefits (including leaving with an Early Departure Payment (EDP) under AFPS 15 or AFPS 05) you have the option to transfer the value of your deferred pension benefits to other defined benefit schemes. A pension in payment cannot be transferred.
However, the government has prevented transfers from unfunded public service defined benefit schemes (such as the AFPS to funded defined contribution schemes in UK or abroad. The Pension Schemes Act 2015 and the Taxation of Pensions Act 2014 made this rule. Application for pension transfers should be made to:
DBS Veterans UK Pensions Division

Resettlement Grant
Resettlement Grants assist those leaving the regular armed forces to resettle into civilian life after completing a substantial period of service. A Resettlement Grant is not a pension.
It is a tax-free lump sum paid to regular service personnel, who, at the time they leave the services, are not eligible for Early Departure Payment benefits, an Immediate Pension or ill health award (or any other immediate pension benefits) and they meet Resettlement Grant qualification criteria, which are:
- AFPS 2015 and AFPS 2005: all personnel need to have 12 years’ relevant service (from date of entry)
- AFPS 1975: Officers to have at least 2 years’ Commissioned service and have 9 relevant years of reckonable service from age 21
- AFPS 1975: other ranks to have 12 relevant years of reckonable service from age 18.
The value of the Resettlement Grant at April 2025 is:
- AFPS 2005 and AFPS 2015: £14,059
- AFPS 1975: £20,397 (Officer) and £14,058 (Other Rank)
Please see the latest tri-service codes published each year on gov.uk.
The Resettlement Grant is increased each year at the same rate as armed forces pensionable pay.
Only 1 resettlement grant is awarded, for those who have service in more than one scheme. If personnel are re-employed after leaving they may have to re-pay some or all of the grant. See the re-employment booklet for more details.

Israel's advancing 'Yellow Line' displaces more Palestinians
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
12:14:49 UTC
21:14:49 KST

Breadcrumb
Israel's advancing 'Yellow Line' is pushing more Palestinian families towards the sea
On Sunday morning, under heavy gunfire, dozens of Palestinian families in Gaza City's Shuja'iyya neighbourhood were forced to flee as Israeli forces moved yellow concrete blocks towards their tents without warning.
Mahmoud Obeid, a 42-year-old father of four, told The New Arab that he woke up that morning and saw Israel's yellow-painted cement blocks that designated where the so-called "Yellow Line" was had advanced to within a short distance of his family's tent.
"We woke up to find the yellow blocks right next to our tents in the Shuja'iyya neighbourhood," he described.
Forced to flee, Obeid spent the night with a family with whom he had no previous ties. His wife and children remained in their tent, waiting for him to find alternative shelter before they head out as well.
"I don't know where to take my family," he added. "Once again, I am heading into the unknown. There is nowhere left to pitch my tent, and the western areas of Gaza City are overcrowded with displaced people."
The advance of the so-called "Yellow Line" is further shrinking the already limited space available to Gaza's displaced population.
Um Mohammed Owaida, a resident of Shuja'iyya, told TNA that she no longer knew how to protect her children from repeated displacement after being forced to gather the family's belongings in haste.
"Just when we think we've found a place to stay, something happens that forces us to leave again. We have no home to return to and nowhere else to go. Our only thoughts are how to protect our children and where we can find space to pitch our tent," she described.
She fears that Israel will push forward concrete blocks even further, leaving her family with fewer options.
"The western areas are packed with displaced people. Even if we found a small spot, we wouldn't know how long we could stay before being forced to leave once more," she added.
Official Palestinian estimates indicate that Israel controls approximately 70 per cent of the Gaza Strip, which covers around 365 square kilometres, forcibly concentrating more than two million Palestinians to an ever-shrinking area, much of it already overwhelmed by destruction.
Some residents in Gaza describe this process as akin to pressing a syringe, with them inside it: as pressure increases at one end, its contents are forced towards the other.
As the space available in eastern Gaza narrows, more families are pushed westward, where tents stand crowded together and opportunities to find shelter continue to diminish. The question is no longer simply where many will go to, but whether anywhere remains to stay.
Repeated displacement is particularly difficult for elderly people, the sick and children, who struggle to endure the physical and psychological toll of moving from one place to another.
Um Abed al-Batniji, an elderly Palestinian woman, told TNA that she was exhausted by the prospect of having to leave her current shelter yet again.
"We no longer have the strength to leave every time," she remarked. "We are elderly; we cannot walk long distances or carry our belongings. All we want is a place to lay our heads and feel somewhat safe, yet we do not know if we will remain there until the next morning."
"We have come to fear sleep, not knowing what might happen when we wake up. We dread finding ourselves forced to gather what little we own and flee again, with no idea where we might go next," she added.
"The advance of the line and the movement of yellow concrete blocks into new areas are raising concerns about the shrinking space available to Palestinians and the displacement of more families towards overcrowded western areas," Gaza-based political analyst Ahed Ferwana said to TNA.
The analyst stressed that these developments suggests Israel seeks to impose "a new reality on the ground", further restricting Palestinian movement and determining where Palestinians can live, in addition to Israel's continued violations of the ceasefire agreement, as part of its overall policy of genocide.
According to Gaza's Government Media Office, 5,474 Israeli violations had been recorded since the agreement took effect last year, and Israel has killed at least 1,488 Palestinians and wounded another 5,280 during this period.

Ukraine expects two EU negotiating clusters to open on 13 October, foreign minister says after talks with Hungary
Following talks with Hungarian Foreign Minister Anita Orbán in Luxembourg, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha has said he expects that the EU will make a formal decision to open two negotiating clusters in Ukraine's accession negotiations on 13 October.
Source: European Pravda, citing Sybiha on X (Twitter)
Details: Sybiha noted that he and Orbán "discussed the most pressing issues on our bilateral and European agendas, compared notes and agreed on the next steps" and "congratulated each other on the successful fulfilment of our bilateral agreements".
He recalled that "the Ukrainian parliament has adopted amendments to education legislation to ensure the rights of European national minorities in Ukraine in this area, in line with EU best practices".
"Tomorrow, we expect the EU to officially decide to open Cluster 2, 'Internal Market', and Cluster 3, 'Competitiveness and Inclusive Growth'. I thanked the Hungarian side for its constructive position on this matter," Sybiha said.
He also briefed his Hungarian counterpart on "Russia's intensification of attacks on Ukraine's capital and other peaceful cities".
The ministers also discussed the agenda for the upcoming European Council meeting and the EU's decisions aimed at "stopping the aggressor, forcing it to change its calculus of terror, and bringing it to the negotiating table to achieve a lasting peace".
"Ukrainian-Hungarian dialogue is growing stronger, based on mutual respect, good-neighbourliness, and a shared European future in the interests of our peoples," Sybiha concluded.
Background:
- On Monday, Ukraine's parliament passed amendments to the law on education in a bid to secure Hungary's agreement to the opening of the second and third negotiating clusters in Ukraine's EU accession negotiations.
- The EU Committee of Permanent Representatives (Coreper) is ready to approve the EU's common negotiating positions on the opening of the second and third accession negotiating clusters with Ukraine on Monday 12 October following the adoption of the amendments on minority education rights by the Verkhovna Rada.

The ministry said peace and stability in the Middle East were crucial to the international community, including Japan, particularly for energy security.

Indonesia on Monday also expressed concern over escalating fighting in Yemen, Houthi attacks on Saudi airports, rising civilian casualties and worsening humanitarian conditions in Yemen.

Gaza families protest Israeli torture of Palestinian prisoners
Families of Palestinian prisoners held in Israeli jails staged a protest in Gaza City on Monday demanding an end to escalating Israeli abuses, including beatings, torture and medical neglect.
The demonstration, attended by representatives of Palestinian political factions and national and Islamic organisations, called for urgent international intervention to protect more than 9,500 Palestinian prisoners held in Israeli jails.
Organised by the Prisoners Committee of the National and Islamic Forces and the Higher Committee of Families of Prisoners from the Gaza Strip, the protest was held outside the headquarters of the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) in western Gaza City.
The demonstration formed part of a weekly gathering held every Monday in solidarity with Palestinian prisoners.
Protesters carried Palestinian flags, photographs of detainees and banners demanding an end to physical and psychological abuse, as well as protection for prisoners under international law.
Jamil Ashour, a member of the political bureau of the Palestinian Arab Front, said the protest aimed to amplify the voices of Palestinian prisoners and reaffirm that their rights could not be extinguished with time.
Speaking on behalf of the Prisoners Committee of the National and Islamic Forces, Ashour described the conditions endured by prisoners in Israeli jails, including physical beatings, daily torture and systematic deprivation of basic rights.
He warned that Israeli authorities were disregarding international laws and conventions protecting prisoners and called on Palestinian organisations to intensify efforts to highlight their suffering.
Ashour also urged international human rights organisations to document Israeli abuses and hold those responsible accountable.
He called on the ICRC to visit Palestinian prisoners, assess their detention conditions and ensure they have access to adequate food and medical care.
"The Palestinian people, despite all the sacrifices, will remain steadfast and committed to their national rights until the occupation ends," he stressed.
Azza Mansour, the wife of Palestinian prisoner Ahmad Mansour, also addressed the demonstration on behalf of the Higher National Committee of Families of Prisoners from the Gaza Strip.
She said Palestinian prisoners were facing a campaign of abuse, including repeated assaults, severe beatings and surprise raids on their cells by Israeli prison authorities.
"There are sick prisoners who are denied their most basic right to medical treatment, prisoners held in solitary confinement, female prisoners subjected to constant humiliation, and children who are being tortured," she said.
Mansour condemned international silence over the physical and psychological abuse of Palestinian detainees.
"Silence is no longer an option. Our prisoners are not numbers, but fathers, mothers and children who have the right to freedom and human dignity," she added.
She urged the ICRC and other international organisations to intervene, ensure regular visits to Palestinian prisoners and demand an end to beatings, torture, medical neglect and other forms of mistreatment.
The demonstration comes amid growing concerns over conditions in Israeli prisons, with Palestinian prisoners and rights organisations reporting an escalation in abuse, torture and deaths in custody since October 2023.

Famine risk grows in 'many' parts of Sudan amid conflict, drought, funding shortages: IPC

Beyza Binnur Donmez
12 October 2026•Update: 12 October 2026
Famine risk is growing in "many" conflict-affected areas of Sudan as severe El Nino-induced drought, displacement, and humanitarian funding shortages worsen food insecurity, a global food security monitor warned Monday.
The Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC) said new evidence indicates rapidly deteriorating conditions across Greater Darfur and Greater Kordofan, with "increased risk of famine," as well as "alarming levels of acute food insecurity and malnutrition" in several localities.
In two displacement camps in South Darfur, global acute malnutrition rates reached 38% and 30.8%, exceeding the 20% famine threshold for the weight-for-height measure.
The IPC alert said that "alarmingly, this is occurring alongside severe hunger and elevated mortality levels."
In Nyala, South Darfur, severe acute malnutrition among children accessing nutrition services more than doubled from 5.2% to 11.4% between January and August.
The IPC warned that severe drought, compounded by ongoing fighting, threatens agricultural production, with poor vegetation growth affecting at least half of croplands in several states.
Meanwhile, Sudan's humanitarian response plan faces a 57% funding gap, severely limiting lifesaving assistance.
The IPC called for immediate humanitarian access, especially in North and West Kordofan, and increased funding.
"Without this, catastrophic food insecurity, acute malnutrition, and excess mortality will likely intensify, placing countless lives at risk," it warned.

Iran continued its drone attacks on Kurdish Iranian opposition groups on Monday. Iran has struck the Kurdistan Region of Northern Iraq, according to reports in local Kurdish media and a statement from the Democratic Party of Iranian Kurdistan (KDPI). The party said that “at 12:01, a drone struck the Azadi camp in Koya.” This occurred in the middle of the day, just after noon. Images online showed a drone flying through the sky.
Koya is located between Erbil, the capital of the Kurdistan Region, and Sulaymaniyah, on the border with Iran. Koya has long been an area where Kurdish Iranian dissident groups have camps and housing for their members who have fled the Islamic Republic over the last decades.
Rudaw media in the Kurdistan Region of Northern Iraq added that “two drones struck a camp belonging to the Iranian Kurdish opposition group, Kurdistan Democratic Party of Iran, in Erbil province’s Koya district on Monday, causing material damage but no casualties, a senior party official and a security source told Rudaw English, as Kurdish political leaders gathered in Erbil for a regional forum.”
Iran continues to show that it will attack Kurdish groups.
American forces left Iraq on September 30. Many Kurdish leaders expressed concern that this could leave their region in northern Iraq vulnerable. They lack air defenses, and Baghdad has denied them the ones they need for protection. Iraq in general does not have proper air defenses, a result of years of misrule and Baghdad’s inability to acquire relevant defensive capabilities.
Iran carries out over 1,000 strikes in Kurdistan region
Iran has carried out more than 1,000 drone and missile attacks on the Kurdistan Region, many of them targeting Kurdish opposition groups. The Islamic regime’s goal is to threaten and intimidate these groups and terrorize the region. It doesn’t want the groups rising up in the Kurdish regions of western Iran.
Rudaw noted that the KDPI camp “had been evacuated before the attack and no one remained at the site.”
A security source also confirmed to Rudaw English a second drone attack on the same site,” KDPI said. “This is the 175th time the Islamic Republic has attacked the Democratic Party of Iranian Kurdistan.”
Meanwhile, KDPI spokesperson Khalid Azizi told Rudaw that the group was not sending its forces into Iraq. KDPI appears to be messaging in order to reduce tensions.
An Iranian diplomat recently appeared to threaten the Kurdistan Region. The KRG government in Erbil has long sought to balance its relations with Iran while also having some of the Kurdish opposition groups present.
“We have discussed this with both the Iraqi government and the Kurdistan Regional Government [KRG]. We have decided and pledged that we will not turn Iraqi Kurdistan or Iraq into a rear front,” Khalid Azizi, the KDPI spokesperson, told Rudaw’s Hiwa Jamal on Monday.
Rudaw noted that “Azizi said the party saw no need to deploy armed units into Iranian Kurdistan, arguing that Kurdish opposition groups and their supporters inside Iran were already engaged in a civil struggle.”
Suicide drones utilized by IRGC
The Hana Human Rights group, which focuses on human rights violations in Iranian Kurdistan, described the drone attack as targeting the housing complex of families of the KDPI. “According to information received by the Hana Human Rights Organization, Iranian Islamic Republic suicide drones that had flown from Piranshahr toward the Kurdistan Region of Iraq targeted one of the camps housing the families of members of the Democratic Party of Iranian Kurdistan in Koysinjaq [Koya].”
The new attack comes days after KDPI issued a statement on Friday responding to comments by Consul General of Iran Faramarz Asadi, who accused Kurdish opposition parties of forming an alliance under pressure from foreign powers. The KDPI defended the Alliance of Political Forces of Iranian Kurdistan, which was launched in February and brings together several Iranian Kurdish opposition groups.
The alliance was a “political decision aimed at cooperation and coordination to achieve the legitimate aspirations of the Kurdish nation in its own homeland. It is not evidence supporting the accusations Tehran has leveled against them,” the KDPI said.
Iran has called the Kurdish groups “terrorists.” Only hours after Asadi made his comments, two explosive-laden drones targeted a base belonging to the Khabat Organization of Iranian Kurdistan near Erbil.

The next generation of Israeli entrepreneurs is in defense tech - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
12:11:08 UTC
21:11:08 KST

For decades, Israel's technology story has been defined by its ability to turn military experience into commercial innovation. Cybersecurity is perhaps the clearest example. Young Israelis left elite military units with technological expertise, identified problems that extended far beyond the battlefield, and built companies that became global leaders.
Today, we are witnessing the beginning of another shift. Some of Israel's most ambitious entrepreneurs are no longer looking only to cybersecurity, enterprise software, or consumer technology for their next venture. Increasingly, they are choosing defense tech.
This is not simply a consequence of October 7, nor is it a temporary response to war. It reflects a broader transformation in the global technology industry and in how the next generation of Israeli entrepreneurs thinks about the problems worth solving.
From cyber to the battlefield
Five or 10 years ago, launching a defense start-up was far from an obvious choice for an Israeli entrepreneur. Defense markets were considered difficult to enter. Procurement cycles were long, customers were governments, regulation was complex, and venture capital investors often preferred the scalability and speed of software businesses. Many talented engineers and military veterans naturally gravitated toward cybersecurity, cloud computing, and enterprise software instead.
That calculation is changing.
The wars in Ukraine and the Middle East have exposed new technological needs at extraordinary speed. At the same time, rising geopolitical tensions have pushed governments across Europe, the United States, and elsewhere to rethink defense spending and technological preparedness.
The result is a market that looks very different from the one entrepreneurs faced only a few years ago.
But perhaps the most important change is not the amount of capital entering the sector. It is the people entering it. We are seeing entrepreneurs and early employees who combine operational military experience with backgrounds in artificial intelligence, cloud computing, software, and other areas that historically sat outside the traditional defense industry. We are also seeing experienced executives from Israel's defense companies who have spent years managing complex technological programs choose to build their own companies. This combination is particularly powerful.
Israel's unique advantage
Defense technology is different from conventional software. Understanding the technology is not enough. Founders need to understand how a product will actually be used under operational conditions, how military customers think, and what problems genuinely need to be solved.
Israel has an unusually deep pool of people with exactly that experience.
At the same time, it has one of the world's most mature start-up ecosystems. Engineers and entrepreneurs who understand AI, cloud infrastructure, and software can work alongside people who have spent years dealing with operational challenges in the field.
The convergence of these two worlds is difficult to replicate elsewhere.
Because it is already influencing the technologies being developed. Autonomous systems, counter-drone technologies, advanced sensing, cutting-edge artificial intelligence, and new forms of maritime and aerial defense are increasingly being approached with the speed and mindset of the technology industry rather than solely through traditional defense development cycles.
That distinction matters. The technological requirements of modern warfare are evolving too quickly for innovation to take years.
The start-up model enters defense
The traditional defense industry will remain essential. Building complex military platforms at scale requires enormous engineering, manufacturing, and integration capabilities.
Start-ups serve a different role.
They can focus on a single problem, experiment quickly, take technological risks, and adapt their products as operational needs evolve. The most interesting question, therefore, is not whether start-ups will replace traditional defense companies. They will not.
The question is what becomes possible when start-up speed is combined with the capabilities of established defense industries and the needs of military customers.
This is also why international collaboration will become increasingly important. No Israeli defense tech start-up should be built with Israel as its only market.
The challenges these companies are addressing are global. European countries are increasing defense investment, the United States is looking for ways to accelerate defense innovation, and militaries around the world are confronting many of the same challenges.
For Israeli entrepreneurs, the opportunity is therefore significantly larger than the domestic market. Building relationships with international investors, defense companies, governments, and military customers early will be critical to creating the next generation of global companies.
A new generation of Israeli technology companies
Israel has reinvented its technology ecosystem before.
The country's cybersecurity industry did not become a global powerhouse overnight. It emerged because a unique concentration of talent, experience, capital, and market demand came together at the right moment.
Defense tech may now be approaching a similar moment. There is capital entering the sector. There is global demand. Technological breakthroughs in AI, autonomy, robotics, and sensing are changing what is possible. Most importantly, a generation of Israeli entrepreneurs increasingly sees defense not as an old industry, but as one of the most consequential technological challenges of their careers.
For many of them, the motivation also differs from previous startup cycles. Recent events have made the problems they are trying to solve tangible and immediate. Building technology that protects soldiers, civilians and critical infrastructure is no longer an abstract market opportunity.
That sense of purpose should not be underestimated.
The next great Israeli technology company may still be a cybersecurity company, a fintech platform or an enterprise software business. Israel will continue to produce all of them.
But when we look at where some of the country's most ambitious engineers, experienced executives and returning entrepreneurs are choosing to spend the next decade of their lives, a new direction is becoming increasingly difficult to ignore.
The next generation of Israeli entrepreneurship is already taking shape. A significant part of it will be built in defense tech.
The author is a founding partner of Kinetica Ventures and an experienced investor in defense tech and cybersecurity, with a background spanning venture capital and the US Department of Defense.

European Union foreign ministers agreed on Monday to establish a new support mission in Lebanon aimed at advising and training the country's military and internal security forces.

The mandate of the UN Interim Force in Lebanon is set to expire at the end of 2026, when it is expected to begin a year-long drawdown and withdrawal.

He also warned against individuals seeking to “exploit divisions” and “turn people against members of the Fatah movement.”
To counter these efforts, he said that Fatah members should refrain from criticizing their leader, “even if you believe that he does not possess all the qualities a leader should have,” arguing that unity was essential to strengthening the movement.
“The road ahead of you is difficult. You must always understand that you are being targeted,” Shahab told Fatah members.
“There is a saying in popular culture: when the arrows are directed at you, know that you are on the right path… God has protected [Fatah]. And why has God protected us? Because of the blood of the martyrs and the souls of those who sacrificed their lives. Their presence and their sacrifices continue to protect the Fatah movement.”

Hall and Woodford win Nobel Prize in economics
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Hall and Woodford win Nobel Prize in economics
American economists Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford have won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences for research that helped improve policies to stabilise economies, reports a Qazinform News Agency correspondent.
The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences announced the award on October 12, recognizing their contributions to the foundations of macroeconomic stabilization.
Their work connects the decisions of households and businesses with developments across the wider economy. The researchers developed models that strengthened understanding of how governments and central banks can respond to economic fluctuations.
Such models help policymakers assess how changes in interest rates, public spending and taxation affect consumption, investment and economic activity. They provide a framework for designing measures to limit damaging swings in output and employment.
The award recognizes the importance of understanding individual economic behavior when shaping policies intended to support stability.
Formally known as the Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel, the economics prize was established in 1968 to mark the Swedish central bank’s 300th anniversary.

Alar Karis: Ingenuity what makes Estonians who they are and guarantees survival
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12

Alar Karis: Ingenuity what makes Estonians who they are and guarantees survival
In his farewell speech to the Riigikogu, Estonia's outgoing President Alar Karis emphasized the country's resilience in the face of successive crises, called for greater trust and cooperation in politics and urged bold decisions to address future challenges.
Five years ago, in this very spot here in the Riigikogu, I pledged to uphold the Constitution, to defend the internal and external peace enshrined in its preamble and to listen and observe with patience. I spoke about a nation of people who cope, who are not afraid to face the unknown.
This we have had to do a surprisingly large number of times in recent years: the pandemic, war, inflation, the climate and energy crises and the aggressive development of new technology in the form of artificial intelligence.
None of these challenges originated here in Estonia, but have reached us from further afield. And, as a small nation, we are affected by them even more than larger countries.
We have had to familiarize ourselves with these unknowns and, where needed, change the way we think and behave. In so doing, we have adapted and managed to cope.
What is the role of the head of state in the midst of these crises?
It is their job to be observant, to know how to listen, to unite rather than to divide, to strike a balance, to maintain diversity, to champion peace at home and abroad. At least, this is how I have understand my role.
It is easy to talk to friends, but you must also speak with those whose views differ from your own. It is easy to reel off talking points, but you have to think and act for yourself, taking local circumstances into account.
It may be memorable and impressive to be outspoken, even combative in your words, but it is achieving results that matters. And while it can be nice to hear the sound of your own voice, it doesn't make you any smarter.
In maintaining peace abroad, we can rely not just on soft diplomacy, but also on our friends and allies — particularly those closest to us, our Nordic and Baltic neighbors. But when it comes to maintaining peace at home, we have no one to rely on but ourselves.
That internal peace begins with trust and a sense of belonging, with the attitude taken by the state, with comprehensible laws, with efforts to avoid over-regulation, with the responsibility of lawmakers and their consideration not just for those who vote for them, but also for the wider impact of those laws and the interplay of them.
Constant grappling with new crises, petty squabbling among politicians and the never-ending need for attention characteristic of instant gratification culture and the attention economy have fired up society — and, in the process, undermined its ability to think critically and, where necessary, to hold a dissenting view.
Election debates will soon be upon us which seek to highlight the differences between the candidates, with experts then assessing who was best at putting the others in their place.
But what impact might it have on the performance of our elected officials if, instead, we were to reward teamwork and recognize the passes that led to goals as well as the goals themselves?
Our culture of debate needs culture. If it is starved of it, then society's mental health will suffer and the self-censorship characteristic of this silent era will take hold.
I have been asked many times, especially in the last week, what I will be taking away from my five years in office.
My answer has been the same each time: a firm conviction, in fact the certainty, that the people of Estonia have it in them to cope, to adapt to crises and difficulties. It is precisely in our ability to deal with any situation that the wisdom of our nation lies. It is our ingenuity, that which makes us who we are and that which guarantees our survival.
The knowledge, indeed the joy, that we live in a free country that offers such quality of life, including a good education and a safe place to live, outweighs all difficulties and drives us to press ahead in our day-to-day lives and make important decisions. Therein I would like to see politicians and officials showing more mettle in their decision-making. If they don't, then things simply won't get done and problems will pile up.
Estonia, like the rest of Europe, is both aging and shrinking and needs new approaches: bold decisions, clever solutions, the courage to take risks and, where necessary, to rethink decisions, listening to and trusting the younger generation.
One benefit of being a small country is the ability to be flexible. The modernization of education and the economy is boosting Estonia: the introduction of new technologies, enhanced productivity, expansion into foreign markets and utilizing our advantages and experience as a digital nation. All of which can be summarized as focusing on the intelligence economy, be it human or artificial.
Alongside security, AI has become a core issue around the world. We have three options in regard to it: ignore, outlaw or adapt.
I don't believe in bans. There is no restricting development. Instead, it must be guided and a balance struck. We must provide a safe environment and put technology to work for the benefit of people.
AI has arrived as a great unknown and Estonia is setting an example of how to deal with it. With the support of schools and the Ministry of Education and Research, an idea born from a meeting with unicorns in Kadriorg has grown into a nationwide educational reform that cements Estonia's status as a digital nation, attracting both attention and interest and opening even the farthest-flung doors to us.
Most importantly, it provides youngsters with an education that will prepare them for the future.
I will continue to work on AI from an educational perspective after my time in office, as both a patron of AI Leap and a member of the UN's global 'AI for Good' commission.
And as a former president, I shall continue to champion curiosity and a knowledge-based approach, diversity and uniqueness, internal and external peace and the preservation of balance and freedoms.
I would like to thank my advisers, the director and staff of the Office of the President and all those I have worked with who, in sharing my values and vision, have helped make the past five years possible.
I also thank, of course, my wife Sirje, without whom none of this would have been possible and who took the lead in assisting Ukrainian children and speaking out on young people's mental health.
President-elect Madise,
The office of head of state of Estonia is a great honor, but an even greater responsibility.
May you have the ability to observe, to notice, to ask the right questions and to find the time to think about things as well.
More than anything else, however, may you remain ever true to yourself and unafraid of encountering the unknown. I wish you strength, wisdom and resolve in carrying out your role.
--
Editor: Marcus Turovski
