CSTO holds two joint military exercises in Belarus with over 1,500 personnel
The Collective Security Treaty Organization (CSTO) began two joint exercises in Belarus on Sunday: Indestructible Brotherhood-2026 and Barrier-2026, Xinhua reported.
The opening ceremony of the command-post exercise involving the CSTO Collective Peacekeeping Forces were held at Victory Square in the Belarusian city of Vitebsk. Contingents from Belarus, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Russia and Tajikistan assembled in the square, and participants laid flowers at memorials honoring Soviet liberators, partisans and underground fighters in the region.
The ceremony was attended by Major General Vladimir Bely, Belarusian chief of the General Staff of the Armed Forces and first deputy defense minister, Lieutenant General Ruslan Shpekbaev, deputy chief of the CSTO Joint Staff, and Colonel Alexander Ilyukevich, commander of Belarus' Special Operations Forces of the Belarusian Armed Forces.
In his remarks, Bely warned of a shifting global security landscape and stressed the need to strengthen regional cooperation within the CSTO to counter growing threats.
He pointed to Western policies and actions that he said were increasing regional security risks and underscored the importance of effective joint training.
Separately, the 8th Radiological, Chemical and Biological Protection Brigade in the Minsk region held the opening ceremony of a special exercise under Barrier-2026, focusing on joint radiological, chemical and biological protection and medical support within the CSTO framework.
The exercises involve not only armed forces but also personnel from internal affairs agencies, police, internal troops and emergency services. Indestructible Brotherhood-2026 will focus on peacekeeping operations, while Barrier-2026 will simulate responses to biological threats.
The two exercises will be held at the Losvido and Starodorozhsky training grounds, respectively.
More than 1,500 servicemen and over 300 units of military and special equipment will participate in the exercises, including approximately 80 unmanned aerial vehicles.
The CSTO comprises six member states: Armenia, Belarus, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Russia, and Tajikistan.
Earlier, it was reported that on the sidelines of the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly, the Minister of Foreign Affairs of Kazakhstan, Mukhtar Tileuberdi, participated in a working meeting of the foreign ministers of the CSTO member states.

Pakistani physics gold medalist’s death sparks fraud investigation over fake US scholarship
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
12:10:52 UTC
21:10:52 KST

[ISLAMABAD] The death of a 24-year-old Pakistani physics gold medalist who dreamed of becoming a scientist has sparked a national outcry and prompted a federal investigation into an alleged education consultancy fraud that cost her family millions of rupees.
For more stories from The Media Line go to themedialine.org
Laiba Ejaz, from Sargodha in Pakistan’s Punjab province, was found dead on Friday, October 9, at a weekly market in Islamabad’s G-10 sector. Police said her body was found hanging from a tree, with a traditional scarf tied around her neck.
Investigators are examining allegations that two suspects defrauded Ejaz and her family of 9.3 million Pakistani rupees (around $34,000) by promising to secure her admission to Harvard University, along with a scholarship and a US visa. The suspects allegedly supplied forged admission letters, scholarship documents, and payment receipts.
Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif ordered a thorough investigation, describing Ejaz’s death as “extremely tragic” and instructing Islamabad Police to arrest those responsible and ensure “exemplary punishment,” according to a statement from the Prime Minister’s Office.
Following his directive, Pakistani Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi and State for Interior Minister Talal Chaudhry visited the bereaved family on Saturday. Islamabad Police and the Federal Investigation Agency (FIA) launched investigations into the circumstances surrounding her death and the alleged fraud.
According to preliminary findings obtained by The Media Line, 2.9 million rupees were transferred through Ejaz’s bank account, while the remainder was paid in cash. Investigators believe the alleged deception caused severe psychological distress before her death.
Ejaz had earned a gold medal in physics from the International Islamic University Islamabad and hoped to continue her education in the United States before pursuing a scientific career.
Her family said she had been searching for an overseas education consultant when she met Muhammad Nauman, who claimed he could arrange her university admission, scholarship, and visa.
After receiving payments from the family, Nauman allegedly produced a forged Harvard admission letter. According to officials, the document was rejected when Ejaz appeared for a visa interview at the US Embassy in Islamabad.
Her family said she became increasingly distressed as questions emerged about the authenticity of the documents and the whereabouts of the money.
The financial sacrifice behind her academic ambitions was considerable.
Her father, Ejaz, has sold milk and yogurt on the streets of Islamabad since 1994. Although he did not complete primary school, he was determined that his four daughters would receive an education through the master’s degree level.
Laiba, the youngest of his seven children, hoped to follow her eldest sister, who received a scholarship to study in China and now works as a translator for a major Chinese company in Lahore.
To finance Laiba’s plans, her father sold a plot of land he had purchased to build a family home. Her mother pawned her jewelry to help meet the consultant’s financial demands, according to relatives.
The family said Ejaz had previously been offered a scholarship to study in Saudi Arabia through her university but declined because she was determined to pursue higher education in the United States.
On Saturday, the FIA registered a criminal case against Nauman and an alleged female accomplice, Fatima Sarwar, following a complaint filed by Ejaz’s maternal uncle, Amjad Ur Rehman.
A copy of the first information report (FIR) obtained by The Media Line alleges that the pair, acting with other individuals, deceived the family through the fraudulent scholarship and visa arrangement. In Pakistan, an FIR is a formal police record of an alleged crime that sets the criminal investigation in motion.
Law enforcement sources told The Media Line that Nauman was arrested during a late-night raid in Islamabad’s H-13 sector, where he had reportedly been staying in a rented room to avoid detection.
Investigators reportedly recovered material from his mobile phone suggesting possible involvement in other online fraud schemes and the blackmail of women. Those allegations remain under investigation.
Sources also alleged that Nauman had previously been dismissed from his position with the Anti-Corruption Department in Quetta over accusations of fraudulent activities.
Case is impersonation scam, says FIA director
FIA Director Gen. Usman Anwar characterized the case as an impersonation scam rather than a conventional education consultancy fraud. He said the alleged female accomplice had falsely presented herself as Nauman’s contact in the United States.
Rehman, a lawyer and the complainant in the case, told The Media Line that Nauman had claimed to have access to scholarship and financial sponsorship documents through a woman named Aiza, purportedly based in the United States.
Believing those assurances, the family proceeded with the application process. However, as Nauman’s conduct became increasingly suspicious, relatives began checking the authenticity of the documents.
Rehman said the family contacted Harvard University directly and made inquiries through its own contacts at the US Embassy in Islamabad. Neither institution could verify the documents supplied to Ejaz, he said.
Zaid bin Afzal, Ejaz’s brother-in-law, told The Media Line that Nauman had repeatedly postponed her visa interview. On three or four occasions, he allegedly contacted her the night before a scheduled appointment to inform her that it had been canceled.
During his final conversation with Ejaz, Nauman reportedly claimed that another interview had been scheduled for October 12 and demanded payment of the remaining 2.2 million rupees before that date.
By then, Afzal said, Ejaz had discovered the alleged deception and was deeply distressed.
On October 9, she left home without informing her family where she was going. Before leaving, she had been online with her elder sister, Afzal’s wife, while her laptop remained at home.
Afzal said Ejaz contacted him shortly before her death and pleaded with him not to reveal the alleged fraud to her father.
“Don’t tell my father about the fraud committed against me; otherwise, he will die,” she said, according to Afzal.
He said Ejaz had concealed Nauman’s final demand for money from other family members.
Afzal later went to the market in Islamabad’s G-10 sector, where he said he discovered her body. He alerted police, who removed the body and transported it to a hospital.
The case has renewed concerns about fraudulent consultants targeting Pakistani families seeking educational opportunities abroad.
FIA has previously investigated similar cases
Pakistan’s FIA has investigated several cases involving forged university admission letters, scholarship documents, visas, and other paperwork used to exploit prospective students and their families.
In a separate recent investigation, the agency’s Anti-Corruption Circle raided education consultancy and courier offices in Islamabad and arrested 22 people, including six officials from the Pakistani Foreign Affairs Ministry.
The suspects allegedly produced or used counterfeit apostille stickers, forged stamps, and fraudulent documents while charging substantial fees for expedited services and paying bribes to facilitate the process. Authorities said the counterfeit authentication stickers had circulated across Pakistan, potentially causing financial losses to the national treasury.
Media reports have also alleged that unofficial channels collected approximately 12 billion rupees ($43 million) over one year to process roughly 800,000 documents, raising further questions about oversight of document authentication and overseas application services.
Bilal Ranjha, an education consultant based in Lahore, told The Media Line that many young Pakistanis seeking opportunities at Western universities turn to questionable intermediaries in the hope of bypassing standard admission requirements.
He said the desire for shortcuts had created opportunities for fraudulent and unqualified consultants to charge exorbitant fees for forged documents and promises they could not fulfill.
Ranjha estimated that 90% of young people who seek such shortcuts resort to falsified paperwork, although he did not provide supporting data for that estimate.
He also alleged that some individuals involved in fraudulent operations had connections to embassy employees, either through direct employment or personal contacts. The allegations were not independently verified.
Ranjha emphasized that legitimate applicants seeking admission to universities in the United States and Europe can use established procedures without relying on questionable intermediaries. Universities generally communicate admission decisions and send official documents directly to applicants, he said, allowing students to verify offers through recognized institutional channels.
Naheed Khan, an Islamabad-based youth rights activist, told The Media Line that Ejaz’s death should be understood in the context of Pakistan’s wider economic and institutional difficulties rather than viewed solely as the alleged misconduct of one consultant.
Khan said poverty, unemployment, and limited opportunities at home were putting increasing pressure on young Pakistanis, many of whom see overseas education and employment as a path toward financial security and a better future.
She called for stronger enforcement of existing laws, more effective regulation of overseas education consultants, and public policies aimed at protecting students and their families from exploitation.
Khan also questioned whether the institutions responsible for overseeing education consultancy services were providing adequate safeguards for young people pursuing opportunities abroad.

Kazakhstan grants citizenship to nearly 11,000 since January
10,965 people obtained Kazakhstan citizenship between January and September 2026, Qazinform News Agency reports.
In the first nine months of 2026, Kazakhstan granted citizenship to 10,965 people. 3,335, or 30.4%, were minors.
The majority of new citizens were kandas — ethnic Kazakhs returning to their historic homeland. Over the period, 8,769 kandas received citizenship, accounting for 80% of the total.
Another 1,088 people (9.9%) obtained citizenship under a simplified procedure under an agreement between Belarus, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, and Russia.
Under the Convention on the Nationality of Married Women, 796 people (7.3%) received Kazakhstan citizenship. Another 305 people (2.8%) acquired citizenship by presidential decree, and seven more were granted it as ethnic Kazakhs studying at universities in Kazakhstan.
The largest number of new citizens was registered in the Almaty region — 3,276 people, or nearly 30% of the national total.
Rounding out the top five were Astana (1,038), the Zhetisu region (1,036), Almaty (861), and the Zhambyl region (684).
Notably, 8 out of every 10 people granted Kazakhstan citizenship over the nine months were kandas. Nearly a third of new citizens were children under 18.
Qazinform previously reported that Kazakhstan is home to forty-four residents who have turned 100.

What we know about Pope Leo XIV's upcoming operation to remove lung nodule
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
12:10:48 UTC
21:10:48 KST

The Vatican press office has said doctors expect the pope's recovery to take around a week. That would make it possible for him to leave for his visit to Latin America as planned on 6 November.
Pope Leo XIV has said he will have an operation to remove a lump on his lung this week, the first time a pope has made a personal medical announcement of this kind.
The 71-year-old is otherwise healthy and is known for his love of sport.
Here is what we know.
When will the operation take place?
The pope said the operation was planned "in the coming days" and the Vatican press office said it would be at the beginning of the week, without giving a date.
Italian media have speculated that the operation could be on Tuesday, although the pope is due to preside over a Mass in St Peter's Basilica on Wednesday morning with Church leaders from around the world and there have so far been no announced changes in his schedule.
The Vatican press office has said doctors expect the pope's recovery to take around a week. That would make it possible for him to leave for his visit to Latin America as planned on 6 November.
The 11-day trip will take him to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru, a country close to the pope's heart as he worked there as a missionary for two decades and took on Peruvian citizenship.
What is a pulmonary nodule?
A pulmonary nodule is a small growth of tissue in the lung. Most are benign, meaning they are non-cancerous. But a small percentage can be an early stage of lung cancer.
Most small nodules cause no symptoms and are only discovered during checks for other health issues.
Larger nodules can cause shortness of breath, chest pain and persistent coughing, sometimes with blood.
The operation is normally carried out under general anaesthetic with the patient breathing through a tube.
Where will the operation take place?
The operation is expected to take place at Rome's Gemelli hospital, where popes are usually treated.
Pope Leo XIV's predecessor Francis spent weeks there for treatment before his death last year.
John Paul II, head of the Church from 1978 until his death in 2005, was treated nine times at Gemelli, Rome's largest hospital, and spent a total of 153 days there.
He quipped that the hospital was like "Vatican number three."
The Vatican ultimately created a top-floor apartment at the hospital site, accessed by a long corridor guarded by Italian and Vatican police.
Besides the pope's room, the suite reportedly includes a meeting room for medical staff, a kitchen, bathroom and rest areas.
There is also a small chapel.

Iraq targets lingering ISIS pockets with airstrikes, operations in security vacuum after US pullout
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
12:10:46 UTC
21:10:46 KST

In the wake of the US withdrawal from Iraq on September 30, the Iraqi government has increased airstrikes and operations against the Islamic State to avoid ISIS seizing the opportunity to try to mount a comeback. ISIS, though, has been considerably weakened and generally only consists of scattered cells in very rural areas. Iraq appears to be trying to send a message that it will not allow ISIS to exploit the situation.
ISIS rose in Iraq in 2014 during a time of sectarian tension and chaos. The United States had left Iraq in 2011. Under Prime Minister Nouri al-Maliki, it was not a strong state. Maliki, who was very pro-Iran, was seen as an abusive prime minister by Iraqi Sunnis. The large Arab cities resented his rule. When ISIS appeared as an alternative, sweeping into Iraq from Syria, many backed it in places such as Mosul, Ramadi, and Fallujah.
ISIS was able to defeat two Iraqi army divisions and take most of the equipment from the depots of the units. That move gave it a lot of strength.
Today, ISIS no longer has such strength or any of the influence that gave it power in the past. It consists of aging fighters or a few young recruits and it is scattered in various areas.
However, it has pockets that have never been defeated. One is in the Hamrin Mountains and areas near the Hawija district. Some of these cells have connections further north in the area of Mount Qarachogh, where ISIS has exploited the vacuum in power between the Kurdistan Regional Government and the Iraqi federal forces.
F-16 Airstrikes destroy ISIS elements in Iraqi territory
On Sunday, Iraq’s Security Media Cell, which posts official statements on the Iraqi security forces, said that it had carried out strikes against ISIS.
It said that “based on intensive field monitoring to track terrorist elements, and relying on precise and confirmed intelligence provided by the Military Intelligence Directorate, and in joint coordination with the Aerial Reconnaissance and Surveillance Center in the Office of the Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces, F-16 aircraft carried out two airstrikes targeting a hideout belonging to remnants of ISIS elements in the Nareen area within the Diyala Operations Command sector, resulting in its complete destruction.” The statement didn’t name Islamic State, but it was clear it was the target.
Iraq is worried about ISIS activity west of Kirkuk. It sent Brig.- Gen. Abdul Amir Al-Shammari, director of the Office of the Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces, to chair a meeting with the Deputy Chief of Staff of the Army for Operations and the Commander of Kirkuk Operations.
“The director of the office listened to a detailed briefing from the commanders regarding the plans for the deployment of units and their openness within the sector of responsibility of the Kirkuk Operations Command,” Iraq’s Security Media Cell said.
“The meeting witnessed in-depth discussions regarding the enhancement of security measures and the securing of borders and villages within the sector, and the attendees concluded with a number of important recommendations that emphasized the importance of intensifying intelligence efforts and coordinating efforts among the various security units to ensure security stability and protect citizens in the province.”
Further reports discussed the threat of ISIS in Iraq.
Shafaq News noted that “ISIS militants struck the same village in Kirkuk’s Hawija district twice in less than 24 hours, and both times they went after the cameras. The attacks disabled thermal imaging equipment that Iraqi forces use to watch open farmland and valleys at night. They have also renewed attention on stretches of northern Iraq that local commanders concede are not fully covered.”
Iraqi, Kurdish forces fighting ISIS for decades
It also noted how Hawija, west of Kirkuk, has been an ISIS hotbed for years.
During the war on ISIS, there was a line of hills overlooking the valley near Hawija. The Kurdish Peshmerga held this line at the time. During most of the war the Peshmerga looked down on the ISIS-held areas in the desert around Hawija. It remained an Islamic State holdout until October 2017, when the Iraqi federal government finally conquered it.
Shafaq said that “on the evening of October 5, militants attacked a position held by the 3rd Battalion of the Federal Police’s 9th Brigade in al-Bargliya, in Hawija’s al-Danadish sector. One officer was killed, four were wounded, and several thermal cameras at the site were destroyed.”
Meanwhile, Arab Weekly noted that “Iraqi security forces carried out an airborne assault on six suspected Islamic State hideouts in Kirkuk province on Monday, highlighting Baghdad’s continuing campaign to eliminate the group’s remaining cells nearly nine years after declaring victory over the militants.”
Iraq’s Joint Operations Command said they had sent forces by helicopter into Zghaitun.
Rudaw, a Kurdish media outlet, wrote that “Iraqi F-16 fighter jets carried out two airstrikes targeting an alleged Islamic State (ISIS) hideout in Diyala province late Sunday, destroying the site as concerns grow over the group’s movements in areas where security gaps persist between Iraqi forces and Kurdish Peshmerga.”
Meanwhile, in nearby Kirkuk, there is a meeting taking place as candidates seek out the office of governor. According to Shafaq, several Turkmen candidates are running.
In another development, Shafaq noted, “Iraqi Oil Minister Basim Mohammed Khudair is heading to Saudi Arabia to prepare for Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi’s upcoming visit, with discussions expected to focus on reviving a long-idle oil pipeline linking Iraq to the Saudi Red Sea port of Yanbu, a government source told Shafaq News on Monday.”
The pipeline stretches from the Zubair oilfield in Iraq’s southern Basra province to Yanbu and was built in the 1980s.
“Operations ceased in 1990, following Iraq’s invasion of Kuwait, while Saudi Arabia repurposed sections on its territory in 2001 to connect with its East-West pipeline, which provides an alternative export route bypassing the Strait of Hormuz,” Shafaq noted.

NBU, IFC sign agreement on digital finance in Ukraine
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
15:10:44 EEST
21:10:44 KST

The National Bank of Ukraine (NBU) and the International Finance Corporation (IFC), a World Bank Group member, in partnership with Switzerland’s State Secretariat for Economic Affairs (SECO), signed an agreement on developing digital finance, financial innovation, cashless payments, digital resilience and financial literacy on the sidelines of the IMF and World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok on Monday, according to an Interfax-Ukraine correspondent.
“We will improve the regulatory sandbox, develop open banking and work on creating an Innovation Hub. Our task is to shape an environment in which new financial solutions move faster from idea to practical use, and financial services become more accessible,” NBU Governor Andrei Pyshnyy said on Facebook.
The agreement aims to develop instant cashless payments and strengthen the digital resilience of financial institutions to ensure the continuity of financial services, provided Ukraine’s payment infrastructure meets best international practice, he said.
“The project will run until 2029. We have a sufficient horizon to turn international expertise into concrete solutions for the Ukrainian financial market,” Pyshnyy said.
The IFC board of directors approved the advisory project ‘Digital Finance Future Ukraine’ in May this year, and it has an estimated total budget of $2.83 million aimed at developing digital financial services and attracting private capital, the IFC said on its website.
The project involves cooperation not only with authorities but also with financial institutions, fintech companies and venture and private capital market participants.
The IFC said the project has three components. The first aligns Ukrainian legislation and the regulatory environment for digital financial services with EU standards. The second modernizes financial infrastructure and attracts private capital to the fintech sector, including through open banking, venture capital and direct investment. The third promotes cooperation, innovation and regional integration of the fintech market and gives its participants tools and knowledge to spread digital financial services and expand access to capital.

Russia’s deadly strikes on the Ukrainian population Russia Ukraine Conflicts Statement On : October 09th 2026 France utterly condemns Russia’s strikes against Ukrainian civilians and infrastructure in the past few days. 2026-10-12

21:10:35 KST

The IDF is investigating allegations that commanders in the Combat Engineering Corps' 603rd Battalion and the 7th Brigade failed to follow operational procedures during an accident in Lebanon last Thursday that killed Capt. Eliav Haim Tzapalamus, 21, from Haifa.
Tzapalamus's family said Sunday morning that their son might have been saved had military procedures been followed.
According to the family, only one Humvee was sent on the mission, despite operational orders requiring at least two vehicles to travel together in Lebanese territory.
The family claims that after the Humvee overturned, Tzapalamus remained trapped beneath it for approximately 20 to 30 minutes. The other soldiers, who were injured in the accident, were unable to call for help because the radio communication system had stopped working.
The soldiers also struggled to turn the overturned vehicle upright, which the family believes contributed to Tzapalamus's death.
His relatives maintain that a second vehicle could have allowed the soldiers to summon help sooner, right the Humvee more quickly, and provide lifesaving medical treatment.
The IDF's Northern Command is investigating the circumstances of the accident, including whether the force complied with operational orders governing vehicle movements in Lebanon.
IDF examines what caused Humvee to overturn
Maariv has learned that the Humvee was heading toward Israeli territory to transport soldiers when the accident occurred.
The vehicle overturned on a road near the Litani River in the eastern sector of southern Lebanon.
Although the road is paved in the area where the accident occurred, the route presents several driving challenges, including steep descents, winding sections, sharp inclines, and stretches of damaged or unpaved road.
The IDF is examining what caused the Humvee to overturn, particularly given that the vehicle is designed to maintain strong traction on both paved roads and rough terrain.
Preliminary findings suggest that the driver had undergone the required training and was experienced in operating the vehicle.
Investigators also believe the Humvee was traveling at a reasonable speed, although they are examining whether it was moving too quickly for the road conditions along the section where the accident occurred.
Investigators are also examining whether a rock on the road caused the driver to lose control, leading the Humvee to overturn onto its right side.
Three other IDF soldiers were lightly wounded in the accident. They were evacuated to a hospital for medical treatment, and their families were notified.
In a separate incident earlier that day, two soldiers were lightly wounded following the improper use of ammunition.
Katz pays tribute to fallen officer
Defense Minister Israel Katz paid tribute to Tzapalamus following his death.
"At this difficult time, my heart is with the family of the late Capt. Eliav Haim Tzapalamus, a combat officer in the 7th Brigade, who fell during operational activity in southern Lebanon," Katz said. "On behalf of the entire defense establishment, I share in the family's profound grief and offer strength to his commanders and comrades."
"I wish a speedy and full recovery to the soldiers wounded in this difficult incident. May his memory be blessed."
The IDF offered its condolences and support to Tzapalamus' family.
"The IDF shares in the sorrow of the bereaved family and the wounded and will continue to support them," it said. "The matter is under investigation and has not yet been presented to the bereaved family. Once the investigation is concluded, its findings will be presented to the family with full transparency."

EU adopts record sanctions on Russia's defense industry
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
15:09:34 EEST
21:09:34 KST

The European Union has adopted its biggest-ever sanctions package against Russia over its war on Ukraine, listing almost 1,600 individuals and entities linked to the Russian military-industrial complex, the EU Council said.
"In response to Russia's continued and increasingly large-scale aggression against Ukraine, and in particular its recent brutal military campaign aimed at deliberately destroying civilian infrastructure and causing severe suffering to the civilian population, the EU Council today adopted additional restrictive measures against 1,569 individuals and entities linked to the Russian military-industrial complex. The list includes 826 Russian companies and 743 executives of these enterprises," it said.
The council said this is the largest package of sanctions listings adopted at one time in the EU's history. The total number of individuals and entities under sanctions within the regime supporting Ukraine's territorial integrity has reached almost 4,600.
"Today the EU decided to impose the largest sanctions package since 2022. Almost 1,600 sanctions listings target the Russian military-industrial complex. More than half of them concern the production chain of the ballistic missiles that Russia uses every day to kill Ukrainian civilians. The bombing of bridges in Kyiv, grain ships and the National Academy of Sciences are not the actions of a country that wants peace. Now is not the time to ease pressure on Moscow, but to increase it," EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Kaja Kallas said.
The council said the package specifically targets mid-tier suppliers, which form the 'core' of Russia's military industry, generating annual turnover of at least EUR 20 billion and employing more than 250,000 people.
The listed companies supply key components for some of Russia's most advanced weapons systems, including missiles, drones and aircraft. These components include electronics, including semiconductors, microchips and computers; communications equipment, including radars, antennas and receivers; aviation, satellite and missile systems; explosives and ammunition; and optical and navigation systems, it said.
The council said the listings were adopted under the EU framework of restrictive measures against actions that undermine or threaten the territorial integrity, sovereignty and independence of Ukraine. Those listed under this sanctions regime are subject to an asset freeze, and making funds or economic resources available to them or for their benefit, directly or indirectly, is prohibited. Listed individuals are also subject to a travel ban to the EU, it said.

Far right surges as crises threaten Sanchez: Could Vox lead Spain?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
12:08:19 UTC
21:08:19 KST

Vox rises as Sanchez battles political turmoil: Could Spain swing right?
Snap vote could bring the conservatives and far right to power as polls show falling support for Sanchez, one of Europe’s last leftist leaders.
Madrid, Spain – “What I really hate about [Prime Minister Pedro] Sanchez is how keen he is to allow more migrants into our country,” said Alberto Munoz, who wears the red and gold wristband of Vox party supporters.
The 24-year-old computer programmer from Barcelona is among a growing group of young Spanish people who are attracted to the far-right, anti-immigration party.
Eight years ago, Vox was a tiny party on the fringes of Spanish politics. But polls suggested it is getting closer to power as Spain heads to snap elections on November 29.
To reach a parliamentary majority, 176 seats are needed. According to a recent survey by the leading centre-left newspaper El Pais, the conservative People’s Party (PP) and Vox – whose support is predicted to double from the last elections in 2023 – would secure 198 seats. If the PP forms a coalition with Vox, it would be the first time the hard right would return to power in Spain since the death of Francisco Franco in 1975.
In the most recent elections in 2023, the PP won the most votes but not enough to lead on its own, and it did not enter a coalition with Vox. Sanchez of the Socialist Workers’ Party instead formed a government with the help of the Catalan nationalist party, Together for Catalonia.
Since then, the PP has formed four regional governments with Vox, and the parties share power in about 100 councils. A coalition between them now would likely see Sanchez defeated.
“There is hope for Spain with these elections. We will fight for victory and to convince Spaniards we are worth voting for,” Jose Antonio Fuster, national spokesman for Vox, told Al Jazeera. “But the PP cannot make the same mistakes as 2023 and must not start dividing up ministries until we have won.”
Sanchez’s party is predicted to win 112 seats in November, down from 121 three years ago.
If the Socialists lose, it would spell the end of one of the last left-wing governments left in Europe after advances for the far right in France, Germany, Italy, Austria and Finland as populism sweeps Europe.
Steven Forti, an expert in the far right who lectures in contemporary history at the Autonomous University of Barcelona, said, like other far-right parties in Europe and Latin America, Vox distances itself from the Franco dictatorship.
Santiago Abascal, the Vox leader, once told the Spanish parliament that Sanchez’s government was the “worst for the past 80 years” – implying the Franco dictatorship was better.
“It is dog whistle politics – you do not make an explicit reference to the dictatorship. Vox is like other far-right parties in that respect,” Forti told Al Jazeera.
“Young people are attracted to Vox by a feeling of rebellion against the established parties, nationhood and antimigrant feeling. If the polls are right, they will be in power with the PP, but what matters is what ministries they control.”
Vox is the only party that has substantially increased its support. A survey for RTVE, the state broadcaster, projected that the far-right party would increase its seats in parliament from 33 to 65 while it indicated the PP’s support had not risen and all left-wing parties had lost support.
Antonio Alonso, a lecturer in international relations at the University CEU San Pablo in Madrid, said right-wing parties were more stable than their badly divided opponents.
“What is key is that the far left is split into so many different groups and it will be hard to mobilise them as one front together. Meanwhile, the right with the PP and Vox is more unified,” he told Al Jazeera.
Alberto Nunez Feijoo, the PP leader, plans to play on voters’ anger over corruption scandals that have hit Sanchez.
“This is an election between corruption and decency, between decline and prosperity, between a government that aspires only to survive and a country that is thinking about its future,” he told reporters after Sanchez announced the snap elections.
He also pledged to build 200,000 homes each year and cut taxes.
Fired up by a housing crisis that has seen tens of thousands of people protest across Spain, Sanchez called the vote in an audacious gamble to rally support and confound the polls.
It was the eviction of 87-year-old Maria del Carmen Abascal from her Madrid home, a flat she had lived in for seven decades, which inflamed public opinion and prompted activists to camp out in central Madrid and other cities. Known across Spain as Maricarmen, she died this month after the protests.
When two government bills designed to protect people like Abascal were defeated in parliament, it prompted huge demonstrations, and Sanchez decided to capitalise on this tide of anger and call the elections.
Observers said Sanchez hopes the strength of feeling over the housing crisis might eclipse anger over corruption scandals involving members of his family, the perceived mishandling of the Ceuta migration crisis and an amnesty for Catalan separatists who led a failed independence bid in 2017.
The two defeated housing measures to protect tenants from eviction were later passed by the acting government.
“They protect the most vulnerable and, in some way, begin to bring order to what is currently a deeply dysfunctional market that does not operate according to the logic of supply and demand because of rampant speculation,” Sanchez told reporters.
However, even though Sanchez is renowned as a clever political operator, this gamble may not be enough. Even before Sanchez’s announcement of the elections, the Socialists had trailed in almost every opinion poll for months with most voters saying they would back the PP and Vox.

Hungarian Ad Agency Got Millions From Firm Owned by Orban’s Billionaire Friend
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
12:07:00 UTC
21:07:00 KST

Just a few years after launching in 2020, Megafon Digital Incubator Center had become one of Hungary’s most influential political advertising agencies, mainly running social media campaigns in support of the ruling party and its leader, Viktor Orbán.
But Megafon appears to have lost its sense of purpose since Orbán was swept from power in national elections this past April. Four months after that stunning loss, its website was taken offline.
Now, internal documents from a firm called V-Híd Zrt reveal the source of much of Megafon’s income. Around $12 million in donations came from that company, which is owned by Lőrinc Mészáros, Orbán’s childhood friend.
Mészáros became fabulously wealthy during Orbán’s 16 years in power, building a business empire spanning sectors from construction to banking and energy. Mészáros’ companies won seven percent of all public procurement contracts — together worth about $2 billion — between 2018 and 2020 alone, according to Transparency International.
József Péter Martin, executive director of Transparency International’s Hungarian chapter, said the relationship between Megafon and Mészáros illustrates how Orbán and his Fidesz party relied on affluent elites and friendly media — and how those allies benefited in turn.
“It’s a vicious cycle,” Martin told OCCRP’s member center, Direkt36.
“Mészáros’s company wins the public procurement contract and gets rich as a result. He uses that money to fund a private company that works to keep Fidesz in power by spreading propaganda,” he said.
Research groups like the Rule of Law Lab at New York University have documented in detail how Orbán and Fidesz co-opted the media to maintain power.
Public broadcasters became government mouthpieces, while there was a “consolidation of private outlets under allied ownership,” the Rule of Law Lab said in a report early this year. Eventually, the report noted, Mészáros “became Hungary’s largest media owner.”
Mészáros did not own Megafon, but his company’s money was key to its operations, according to the documents obtained by Direkt36. They show that payments from V-Híd amounted to one third of Megafon’s total revenue from 2022 to 2024. The funding grew year-by-year, accounting for more than half of Megafon’s entire income in 2024.
The payments from V-Híd were referenced in the documents as “donations.”
Neither V-Híd nor Megafon responded to requests for comment. Mészáros did not respond to requests for comment.
Communications included among the documents show a cordial relationship between the two companies. In one February 2023 exchange, Megafon’s founder, István Kovács, wrote to V-Híd to express gratitude for the donations his company had received — and to say the company was open to more funding.
“On behalf of the entire Megafon team, I would like to once again thank you for your previous support,” Kovács wrote in an email.
A week later, a V-Híd executive issued an internal order: “Please transfer the 500 million to Megafon now!”
That amount — worth about $1.4 million at the time — was sent by V-Híd the same day, according to a transfer receipt included in the documents. In July 2023, V-Híd made another transfer of about $1 million.
Funds from V-Híd helped Megafon pump out a steady stream of pro-Fidesz messages on social media. These included videos posted before the 2024 municipal elections accusing the opposition of trying to drag Hungary into war by supporting Ukraine in its fight against Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022.
Megafon kept campaigning in the run-up to the vote this year, organizing an event featuring Orbán, and posting pro-Fidesz messages on social media.
But the advertising agency’s fortunes were about to change.
After winning elections in April, Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar pledged to stop state advertising being funneled into pro-Fidesz media — including almost 500 outlets that had been consolidated as part of the Central European Press and Media Foundation (KESMA).
Some outlets reportedly stopped publishing and others downsized, including Mediaworks, which was owned by Mészáros and folded into KESMA. Mediaworks announced in mid-June that it would undertake a restructuring process that would involve “changes in staff numbers.”
Megafon appears to have suffered a similar fate. A document from a company that provides Hungarian business intelligence and commercial registry data shows that the Megafon had 72 employees in April. By August, the company was down to three staff members, and its website was taken offline.

Southeast Asia Has a Serious Drug Problem
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
12:07:00 UTC
21:07:00 KST

Southeast Asia is awash in meth.
In June 2025, anti-drug police in Thailand descended on a small tourist boat moored at a pier in Rayong, a seaside town south of Bangkok. Aboard the ship, inside plastic bags disguised as corn flour packages, they found an alarming cargo: 2.4 metric tons of crystal methamphetamine. This one shipment, bound for overseas markets, was bigger than the entire annual total of meth seizures that Thailand made in 2016. An official from the Department of Special Investigation later told the press that the shipment was worth an estimated $9.15 million – and would sell for ten times that once it hit foreign shores.
Thailand’s meth bust was just the tip of the iceberg. Just a few weeks before that, authorities in Indonesia seized a cargo ship near Batam Island, just south of Singapore. On board they found a similar haul: 2.1 tons of crystal meth. It was the largest drug confiscation in Indonesia’s history.
There were more mega-seizures in late 2025 and early 2026. In September 2025, authorities in Yangon confiscated 1.8 metric tons of crystal meth and 4 million methamphetamine tablets, which authorities said were set to be smuggled to Malaysia. In February 2026, Malaysia confiscated 76 sacks of crystal meth, totaling around 1.5 tons, from two vessels off the east coast of peninsular Malaysia. Two months after that, Thai authorities confiscated 2 metric tons hidden in a pickup truck en route to a port in eastern Thailand.
According to experts, all of these meth shipments originated in the Golden Triangle, the rugged region where Thailand’s borders converge with those of Myanmar and Laos. For decades the Golden Triangle has been associated with narcotics – initially heroin, synthesized from the poppies that grow well in the region’s cool upland climate.
But over the past decade, the Southeast Asian drug trade has shifted decisively toward synthetic drugs – particularly methamphetamine. These are cheaper to make, easier to transport, and not dependent on the weather for a good harvest.
Southeast Asia’s drug labs are now pumping out unprecedented amounts of meth. According to the U.N. Office on Drugs and Crime – or UNODC – regional seizures of methamphetamine hit a new record of 349 tons in 2025, up from 236 tons the year before. In 2015, regional seizures captured just 65 tons. And these drugs are being sold all around the world.
The UNODC says that last year, Southeast Asia accounted for around 94 percent of all the methamphetamine seizures in the entire world. The UN agency reported an “immense volume of methamphetamine trafficked through land-based and maritime routes.”
Everybody knows that drug seizures represent only a small fraction of the total amount of drugs being trafficked through the region. Southeast Asia is facing down the biggest drug crisis in its history.

MOSCOW, October 12. /TASS/. A research team featuring two institutes of the Russian Academy of Sciences and the Moscow Institute of Physics and Technology (MIPT) completed a large-scale study of a complex natural phenomenon in the northern seas: very powerful internal waves in the Kara Gate Strait. The scientists linked this phenomenon to sea tides, press service of the Russian Ministry of Science and Higher Education said.

"The waves are strong enough to shift water layers vertically by almost 30 meters. Their combination helps explain why the waves appear regularly in different parts of the strait and how they spread in different directions."
Seawater is heterogeneous: lighter, warmer or desalinated waters may lie above denser ones, the scientists continued. Boundaries between such layers can swing the sea surface. This is how internal waves arise. The emerging waves may be tens of meters, while at the same time the surface may remain almost calm. When destroyed, these waves enhance the water mixing and participate in the transfer of heat and nutrients between the depth and surface layers.
One of the areas where internal waves are particularly common is the Kara Gate Strait between Novaya Zemlya and the Vaygach Island. Here, strong tidal currents pass over a complex underwater terrain: shallow hills are next to deep troughs. Previously, specialists associated the origin of short internal waves in the strait with the internal tide transformation - a slow oscillation of water layers caused by tidal forces. However, satellite images have shown a more complex picture: numerous groups of waves were diverging in different directions.
During the MIPT Floating University Expedition of the Russian Ministry of Science and Higher Education on board the Dalniye Zelentsy scientific research vessel in July 2023, scientists measured the water temperature and salinity at different depths. By using frequent measurements, scientists could trace the rapid displacement of water layers. Over eight hours of observations, they recorded more than 30 wave-like vibrations, some of which reached almost 30 meters.
The off-board data was compared with satellite images and tidal currents calculations, taking into account the updated bottom relief. The satellite images have shown traces of internal waves: the currents associated with them change the small ripples on the sea surface, creating specific stripes. The joint analysis helped to connect the observed waves with conditions of their origin. Having compared off-board measurements, satellite imagery, and calculations of tidal currents, the researchers identified three mechanisms for the formation of such waves.
Wave formation mechanisms
The first mechanism operates when the current passes over an underwater elevation. The water rises and falls, disturbing boundaries between layers of different densities. Conditions are especially favorable when the flow velocity is close to the internal wave's propagation velocity. When the current changes, the developed disturbances may separate from the obstacle to go further in the form of groups of short waves. In the strait's some shallow areas, a suitable regime may occur up to four times a day, the researchers said.
The second mechanism is related to the internal tide. Its extended wave gradually changes shape, becomes steeper and generates a sequence of shorter waves. Observations have shown that both mechanisms can operate in the same area, and their contribution varies during a tidal cycle. Results of data comparison indicate that during high tides, the role of the internal tide transformation increases, and when they weaken, grows the role of wave formation in the stream above the bottom.
Researchers associate the third mechanism with the sea front - the boundary between waters with different properties. Tidal currents move this boundary across the strait. According to observations, its position has changed by about two to three kilometers within less than a day. The authors suggest that such movements are capable of generating separate groups of internal waves. This explanation is consistent with satellite images in which waves are propagating from the frontal zone into different directions.
The scientists noted separately the role of tide's daily component. The calculations have shown that the associated currents in the Kara Gate can be comparable in speed to the currents of the main semi-diurnal tide. Therefore, in understanding the origin of waves, it is important to take into account the combination of tides with different periods.
Water masses and sea ice
"Hydrological conditions in the Kara Gate are changing constantly: the current may be strengthening or weakening, and the water masses boundaries are shifting. This affects the formation of internal waves, the mixing of different layers, and even the sea ice. In winter, when practically the entire Arctic is ice-trapped, intense currents along with the tide can completely destroy sea ice: we can often see this on satellite images, but it is very complicated to get to those places in winter," said Ilya Kopyshov of the Marine Polar Research Laboratory at the Marine Hydrophysical Institute of the Russian Academy of Sciences, the study's first author.
The obtained results help in tracing how the tide energy transforms into short internal waves, and further on it may be spent on mixing the water. This is necessary for a more accurate description of heat exchange in the Arctic seas to refine climate models. According to the authors, a similar combination of mechanisms may operate in other Arctic straits with strong tides and pronounced separation of water into layers.
The analysis of the internal waves' formation mechanisms was supported by a grant from the Russian Science Foundation. The work featured specialists of the Moscow Institute of Physics and Technology, the Marine Hydrophysical Institute of the Russian Academy of Sciences (Sevastopol), and the Shirshov Institute of Oceanology of the Russian Academy of Sciences. The results are published in the Journal of Geophysical Research: Oceans.

Rada passes law on worker safety, health to EU standards
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
15:05:09 EEST
21:05:09 KST

The Verkhovna Rada has passed a law on a new system of workplace safety and health built on European approaches to managing occupational risks.
A total of 246 MPs voted for bill No. 10147 on workplace safety and health as a whole at a plenary session on Monday.
The new system is based on the principles of risk assessment, control and management, which are the basis for similar systems in developed countries in Europe and worldwide, the bill's explanatory note says.
The consistent hierarchy of these principles is set out in Council Directive 89/391/EEC and includes risk prevention and assessment, elimination of sources of risk, and adapting work to the worker, especially in designing workplaces and choosing production equipment and working methods, it says.
The change in the system's principles also means a change in the object of state policy, from the current 'occupational safety' or 'labor protection' to the European 'worker safety,' it says. The key task of the policy should be to set requirements not for the process of organizing safety but for its results, namely full elimination or minimization of risks to workers' lives and health.
Following the European example, the law introduces a system of minimum workplace safety and health requirements and requires employers to assess regularly the risks that may arise at a specific workplace and to develop and implement measures to minimize or eliminate them.
The document also provides for mandatory liability insurance for expert organizations when they sign contracts for services in workplace safety and health.

What to know about Pope Leo XIV's upcoming lung surgery
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
12:04:37 UTC
21:04:37 KST

Pope Leo XIV is to undergo surgery this week to remove a lung nodule — a small growth of dense tissue inside the lung. Here is what to know about the procedure.
Pope Leo XIV is scheduled to have an operation in the "coming days" to remove “a localised nodule” in his lung that was “detected at a very early stage.” It is the first medical event of his 17-month papacy and the first time a pope has made a personal medical announcement of this kind.
Speaking on Sunday during his weekly address in St Peter's Square, the 71-year-old pontiff said doctors found the nodule during “recent checkups” and believed intervention was best option.
“I have decided to undergo surgery to have it removed," he said.
What is a pulmonary nodule?
Pulmonary nodules are round areas in the lung where the tissue is abnormally dense. They are usually non-cancerous; most small ones cause no symptoms and are discovered only during checks for other health issues.
However, a small percentage can signal an early-stage lung cancer. The risk is higher in older people, smokers and those with a family history of the disease.
If the nodule is cancerous and removed at an early stage, the prognosis is “excellent,” and surgery alone may be sufficient treatment, Stephen Liu, a lung cancer expert at Georgetown’s Lombardi Comprehensive Cancer Center, told the Associated Press.
How common are they and what causes them?
Lung nodules are very common and appear in roughly one-third to one-half of all chest CT scans or X-rays. Diagnoses are increasing as medical imaging technology and routine scans become more widespread.
Pulmonary nodules fall into two main categories: cancerous (malignant) and non-cancerous (benign).
Benign nodules, the most common type, can result from lung infections, such as pneumonia, or from inflammation. Malignant ones are caused by lung cancer or by cancer that has spread elsewhere in the body.
How is the surgery and the recovery?
The operation to remove a nodule is normally carried out under general anaesthetic, with the patient breathing through a tube.
The Vatican said the pontiff will undergo surgery early this week and is expected to remain in the hospital for about a week afterwards to recover.
The pope will be treated at Rome’s Agostino Gemelli Polyclinic, a private non-profit Catholic teaching hospital. The facility has a special apartment set up for pontiffs, which includes a meeting room for medical staff, a kitchen, a bathroom, rest areas and a small chapel.
Pope Leo’s immediate predecessor, Pope Francis, was treated there during a long illness, prompted by a respiratory crisis before his death in April 2025.
Who is in charge while the Pope is in surgery?
The Vatican has no specific rules governing who takes over if a pontiff becomes totally incapacitated. Even while unconscious during surgery, Pope Leo remains pope and retains his authority.
Pope Francis remained in charge throughout his lengthy hospitalisations, as did St John Paul II before him. Both made appointments and issued laws and statements from the hospital.
Medical advances and popes’ longer lifespans, however, have highlighted this gap in church law and prompted calls for the Vatican to prepare for a pope becoming too ill or incapacitated to govern.

The organisations said these disruptions could increase the risk of disease outbreaks, particularly in densely populated areas hosting residents and displaced families.

- Greece says six Turkish drones made eight air traffic infringements and five violations of Greek national airspace over the Aegean on Oct. 10.
- Greek forces intercepted the drones, which flew over the northeastern, central and southeastern Aegean, the general staff said.
Six Turkish military drones flew into Greek-claimed airspace over the Aegean Sea on Oct. 10, Greece’s Hellenic National Defense General Staff said, the latest in a run of near-daily incidents this month.
The Greek military recorded eight infringements of air traffic rules inside the Athens Flight Information Region and five violations of Greek national airspace by the drones. The flights took place over the northeastern, central and southeastern Aegean. Greek forces detected, identified and intercepted the drones in line with international rules and standard procedure, the general staff said. It did not say which Turkish drone types were involved, how long they stayed in the area or what aircraft Greece used to intercept them.
An infringement means a Turkish military aircraft entered the Athens Flight Information Region, the area where Greece manages air traffic, without filing a flight plan with Greek controllers. A violation means the aircraft crossed into what Greece considers its national airspace, which it sets at 10 nautical miles (about 18.5 km) from its coastline. Turkey recognizes only 6 nautical miles, matching the width of Greek territorial waters, and does not accept that its military flights need to file plans with Athens. Ankara regards the flights as taking place in international airspace.
The Oct. 10 incidents followed several similar days. On Oct. 6, the general staff reported seven Turkish aircraft over the Aegean, including two armed F-16 fighters, a CN-235 maritime patrol plane and four drones, which together logged 10 infringements and 15 violations. On Oct. 8, five Turkish drones and an ATR-72 maritime patrol aircraft recorded five violations and seven infringements.
The flights came days after U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio visited Athens, where he described Greece as a key strategic partner of the United States and NATO ally. Greece and Turkey are both NATO members but have long disputed airspace limits, maritime boundaries and the demilitarization of Greek islands near the Turkish coast. Mock dogfights between Greek and Turkish fighters were common for years before the two governments improved ties in 2023, and in recent years Turkish drones have made up a growing share of the recorded incidents.

====================================================================================================

One essential ingredient for AI safety? Democracy | Matthew Botvinick
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
12:00:54 UTC
21:00:54 KST

AI safety is having a moment. After years as a topic for techies and futurists, the potential risks from artificial intelligence systems – from cyberattacks to hyper-persuasion to rogue behavior – are suddenly under discussion both in the corridors of power and around kitchen tables.
In fact, the conversation now reaches beyond classical safety concerns, getting into AI’s impact on economic life and the environment, as well as possible responses, from alignment research to government regulation.
This expanding public discussion is coming none too soon, as recent news about AI security breaches makes clear. However, something important is still missing. For all its vibrancy, the public debate has not yet focused on one of the most important requirements for AI safety: constitutional democracy.
To see why democracy matters for AI safety, imagine that we have already built a powerful AI system that is “safe” in all the now-familiar senses: it cannot escape human control, cannot launch cyberattacks or make bioweapons, and cannot power killer robots. Now picture that system in two different political contexts, one democratic, the other authoritarian.
Placed inside a healthy democracy – a constitutional republic, with free and fair elections, protected civil liberties, and robust rule of law – AI could bring massive benefits, advancing science and medicine, expanding education and bolstering economic prosperity. Under the right conditions, AI could strengthen democracy itself, helping citizens make their voices heard, improving policymaking and making government services more efficient and accountable.
Now consider the authoritarian scenario. Here, everything flips. AI becomes a tool for government surveillance and censorship, for propaganda and for political suppression and entrenchment. No imagination is required to conjure this scenario. It is already playing out in China, Russia, Iran, Venezuela, several Gulf states and elsewhere.
Placing these two scenarios side by side reveals an elemental truth: there can be no such thing as safe AI unless we secure the future of constitutional democracy and the rule of law. It doesn’t matter how “safe” your AI is if you live under authoritarian rule; you will not be safe. In short, AI safety requires political freedom.
Once this fact sinks in, it becomes clear that we must reverse the retreat of democracy that has occurred around the world over the past two decades, including, here at home, the steady erosion of constitutional checks under administrations of both parties.
Of course, preserving democracy has always been a worthwhile goal. With the AI era looming, it has become an urgent one.
To complicate matters, AI itself will put new pressure on democratic institutions. As AI starts to affect jobs, the resulting economic insecurity may create openings for demagogues of every stripe.
By creating national security crises – cyberattacks, for example – AI will multiply opportunities for governments to invoke emergency powers, powers that, once claimed, are rarely relinquished. And as AI is integrated into executive-branch functions, traditional checks and balances may be disturbed, and the risk of political surveillance will grow.
In the longer term, if AI replaces a majority of jobs – an outcome that economists such as Daniel Susskind and Anton Korinek are concerned about – ordinary citizens will face a serious risk of losing their leverage over those who govern them. To see why, we need only look at present-day petrostates, where governments that do not depend on taxing their citizens’ work often disregard those same citizens’ rights.
A solid first step toward countering these risks would be to update our legal codes, setting limits on executive power by reforming emergency and surveillance law, and ensuring due process by narrowing the circumstances in which the state secrets privilege may be invoked.
In the US, this would mean, for example, revisiting the National Emergencies Act and International Emergency Economic Powers Act, and closing the “data broker” loophole in intelligence work. As executive agencies begin to leverage AI, we should also furnish Congress and the courts with equally powerful AI tools, so that their oversight can keep pace.
The principle here is not new. As James Madison wrote, “Ambition must be made to counteract ambition,” only here in a digital setting.
Longer-term, to avoid widespread political disempowerment, we will need to renew our traditions of self-government, involving citizens more directly in policymaking and government oversight. If we play our cards right, AI itself may help, making information easier to access and helping citizens reason together – town halls for a digital age.
Buttressing political freedom in these ways would be important in its own right. Today, however, it is also a form of AI safety work.
Who is best positioned to drive the needed reforms? Policymakers, civic organizations and ordinary citizens must all participate.
But there is another key player: the AI industry. While the major AI labs are willing to weigh in on specific policy issues, most have recently gone quiet on the topic of democracy itself.
Over the past year, a number of AI-industry leaders have justifiably stressed the need to equip military and intelligence agencies with AI, so that democracies can compete abroad. But the same leaders have been conspicuously absent from the debate over the health of democracy at home.
The tech sector was not always so reserved. In 2013, Apple, Google, Microsoft, Facebook, Twitter, Yahoo, LinkedIn and AOL joined forces to publish an open letter to the president and Congress, stating that government surveillance methods had “tipped too far in favor of the state and away from the rights of the individual – rights that are enshrined in our constitution”.
In 2018, Microsoft publicly asked Congress to limit government use of facial recognition technology, writing: “We must ensure that the year 2024 doesn’t look like a page from the novel 1984.” And as recently as 2021, companies including Alphabet, Amazon, Apple, Facebook, IBM, Microsoft and Twitter published an open letter opposing proposed changes to state voting laws, declaring: “We stand for democracy.”
More recently, however, many tech companies have fallen silent. This is understandable. These companies answer to their investors, and in the current environment, speaking out can put shareholder value at risk.
That, however, should not be the end of the story. The leading AI labs all describe AI safety as core to their mission. If they mean what they say, then – for the reasons I’ve highlighted – they bear a duty to stand up for basic constitutional principles, despite the commercial risks.
Journalists, researchers and ordinary citizens can help them recognize that duty by insistently pointing out the connection between safety and freedom.
It is good that people outside the AI industry are suddenly talking about AI safety. AI will affect everyone, and everyone should be involved in shaping how it is built and used.
But we need to make political freedom a centerpiece of the discussion. We need to build public awareness that AI safety fundamentally depends on democracy. Only by bearing this point firmly in mind can we avoid the dangers of AI and reap its potentially immense benefits.
- Matthew Botvinick is the author of the forthcoming book AI and Political Freedom and a senior fellow at Yale Law School. He has held multiple research positions in the AI industry, including at Google DeepMind and currently Anthropic, but writes here exclusively in his Yale role

Gurdeep Loyal’s quick and easy recipe for Turkish lamb and hot pepper paccheri | Quick and easy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
12:00:54 UTC
21:00:54 KST

Biber salçası is a Turkish paste made from concentrated cooked red peppers and salt. It comes in two varieties: acı (spicy) and tatlı (sweet). The hotter version adds a deep, umami heat to cumin-spiced lamb in this pasta recipe, which in Turkey is known as markana. Traditionally, markana is served with garlicky yoghurt and a generous drizzle of chilli butter enlivened with pul biber and sumac. With flavours this loud, it’s best to use a large pasta shape such as paccheri, because its cavernous middles can hold satisfying morsels of the filling.
Turkish lamb and hot pepper paccheri
Prep 10 min
Cook 25 min
Serves 4
1 tbsp olive oil
1 large red onion, peeled and diced
Fine salt 
500g lamb mince
2 tsp cumin seeds, crushed
6 garlic cloves, peeled and crushed
4 tbsp acı biber salçası (hot Turkish pepper paste)
3 tbsp tomato puree
1 tsp dried mint
Sugar
400g paccheri 
200g natural yoghurt
Finely grated zest and juice of 1 large unwaxed lemon
50g unsalted butter
1 tsp pul biber or chilli flakes
1 tsp sumac
15g fresh dill, leaves finely chopped
Pour the olive oil into a wide, deep frying pan, then add the onion and a quarter-teaspoon of salt, and saute for four minutes. Add the lamb mince, cumin and four of the crushed garlic cloves, and cook for six to seven minutes, until the meat is just beginning to brown.
Add the hot pepper paste, tomato puree, dried mint, a teaspoon of fine salt and a generous pinch of sugar, and cook for two minutes. Pour in 250ml water, turn down the heat to medium-low and simmer gently for 10 minutes.
Meanwhile, cook the pasta in salted boiling water according to the packet instructions, then drain.
In a small bowl, mix the yoghurt with the remaining two crushed garlic cloves and the lemon zest.
Melt the butter in a small frying pan and cook for three to four minutes, until it just begins to tint brown. Stir in the pul biber and sumac, then take off the heat.
Stir most of the lemon juice and most of the dill into the lamb sauce, then add the drained pasta and mix well to coat. Swirl over the garlic yoghurt, followed by the sumac butter, garnish with more dill and another squeeze of lemon, and serve straight from the pan.

Kuwait has bought an air defence system built in Britain under a £370 million contract that will create a hundred jobs in the United Kingdom, according to the Ministry of Defence.
The contract with MARSS Systems Limited, an EOS company, covers skilled engineering and manufacturing roles, and the work will expand the company’s British offices with production based in Bristol.
MARSS will provide and integrate the system for Kuwait, bringing together jammers, radars and interceptors with its NiDAR platform, an AI-enabled command and control centre, to improve the country’s ability to detect, deter and defeat airborne threats.
The deal forms part of Taskforce Sabre, the British effort that brings government and industry together to help Gulf states secure systems and weapons quickly, and it follows Iranian missile and drone attacks in the region.
Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry Luke Pollard said: “This deal is a clear demonstration of the UK delivering on its promise to support our regional partners.

Johannes Pinl, chief executive of MARSS, said: “Countering drones and aerial threats is not about any single system, it is about an intelligent, layered architecture that detects, decides and defeats within seconds, and MARSS has built exactly that.
“Through 2027, MARSS will integrate the sensors and effectors that protect Kuwait’s people, critical infrastructure and national assets, backed by British engineering and new skilled jobs here in the UK.”
Britain has already supported Kuwait with Rapid Sentry, a ground-based air defence missile system, and the Royal Air Force’s ORCUS counter-drone system is operating in the country, helping personnel detect drones early and act on what they find.
The Ministry of Defence describes the latest contract as building on that existing support and cementing Britain’s role as a defence partner to Kuwait and the wider Gulf region.
