When women share a husband, physical fights between co-wives are common across cultures
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
12:00:33 UTC
21:00:33 KST

A cross-cultural analysis of ethnographic records suggests that when women share a husband in polygynous marriages, physical fights between co-wives are common. Physical aggression was documented in most of the 19 cultures examined, providing evidence that women’s competition can include direct confrontation when the stakes are high, in contrast to the prevailing view that female rivalry is mostly indirect. The research was published in Evolution and Human Behavior.
What drives competition among women? Evolutionary theories have suggested that women avoid physical fights to protect their survival and the lives of their children, relying instead on indirect social tactics. For example, a theory called the “staying alive” hypothesis, proposed by psychologist Anne Campbell in a 1999 paper, suggested that natural selection favored risk-averse strategies in women because physical injury could severely harm the survival chances of their highly dependent infants.
Building on this idea, a 2013 review summarized the prevailing scientific view that women primarily compete for mates through indirect aggression, such as gossip and social exclusion, rather than physical fights. This aligns with a study covered by PsyPost in 2023, which found that women reported more envy toward well-off same-sex peers than men did and were more likely to engage in indirect competition such as gossip and spreading rumors.
However, anthropological surveys of polygynous marriages, in which a man has more than one wife at the same time, indicate a different pattern. When high-stakes resources and partners are on the line, direct physical conflict between women appears common. For instance, a 2005 cross-cultural study of polygynous societies found that co-wives routinely experience intense jealousy and often resort to verbal and physical violence when competing for their shared husband.
Maryanne L. Fisher of Saint Mary’s University in Canada set out to examine this dynamic systematically. She notes that much of the evidence for indirect competition comes from laboratory and survey studies of young women in Western countries competing over low or hypothetical stakes with rivals they did not know. In Fisher’s reading, the staying alive hypothesis was always conditional: women weigh the costs of physical risk more heavily than men, but direct aggression should become more likely when the payoff is high enough. She used co-wife arrangements as a test case, since co-wives compete repeatedly, over years, for resources that bear on their reproductive success and their children’s survival.
To explore how co-wives compete, Fisher analyzed ethnographic records, which are detailed written accounts by anthropologists and other observers who studied or lived among particular communities. The records came from the eHRAF World Cultures database, a comprehensive collection of cultural texts. She examined records from 19 distinct cultures spanning five major world regions (Africa, the Middle East, North America, South America, and Oceania), ranging from hunter-gatherer groups to intensive agricultural communities. Fisher coded the historical and cultural texts using a four-part system focused on the causes of co-wife competition, the modes of competition used, how conflicts were resolved, and what strategies were used to prevent disputes in the first place.
Fisher searched the database for records combining polygamy and wives with terms such as aggression, violent, and fight, and kept only records that directly described competition or conflict between co-wives. Three cultures turned up in the search but were excluded because their records described peaceful relations or no conflict between co-wives. Each remaining culture was coded for whether a given behavior was documented at all, so the percentages below reflect the share of cultures where a behavior appeared in the records, not how often it occurred. A second, independent coder applied the same scheme, and the two refined their definitions until they fully agreed.
The analysis indicates that competition for the husband’s sexual and emotional attention was the primary cause of conflict, documented in 14 of the 19 cultures (73.7 percent). This included jealousy over sleeping arrangements, fear of being replaced, and competition for general affection. Competition over material resources, such as food, garden plots, livestock, and unequal distribution of resources to children, was the second most frequent cause, present in 7 of the 19 cultures (36.8 percent). Status competition, such as rivalry over who is senior wife, was a third cause, identified in 5 cultures (26.3 percent).
When looking at how women competed, direct physical aggression was the most frequently documented method. Fisher found explicit accounts of physical fighting in 12 of the 19 cultures (63.2 percent). This low-level direct combat included behaviors like hitting, biting, hair-pulling, and occasionally the use of objects like sticks or paddles, though a few accounts were more severe, including one in which a woman was knocked senseless and others describing fights that caused injury. Verbal aggression, such as face-to-face shouting matches, direct insults, and arguments, was documented in 10 cultures (52.6 percent).
Covert hostility, where women maintained an icy or deliberately hostile atmosphere without open fighting, appeared in 6 cultures (31.6 percent). Less common strategies included the use of supernatural means, such as curses or food pollution rituals, which were noted in 4 cultures (21.1 percent). Gossip and social exclusion, often considered classic indirect tactics, appeared in only 2 cultures. In a few cultures, competition took the form of property destruction, such as tearing a rival’s belongings or deliberately ruining her prepared food.
Because indirect tactics were split into many separate categories, Fisher also grouped them into a single category for a fairer comparison. Combined indirect aggression appeared in 9 to 11 of the 19 cultures (47 to 58 percent), depending on how broadly it was defined, compared with 12 cultures for physical aggression. Direct confrontation of any kind, physical or verbal, was documented in 14 cultures (73.7 percent).
The findings suggest that physical confrontation is a common element of co-wife rivalry, occurring alongside indirect strategies rather than replacing them.
The study also looked at how disputes between co-wives were handled. The most common resolutions, each documented in 9 of the 19 cultures (47.4 percent), were the husband intervening to arbitrate or separate the wives and the permanent dissolution of the relationship, such as a wife fleeing or being expelled. Less frequently, conflicts were arbitrated by community members, such as in-laws or neighbors, which happened in 8 cultures (42.1 percent). Only rarely were co-wives documented resolving a conflict through quiet negotiation among themselves.
Many societies also had arrangements that kept co-wives apart or reduced friction between them. The most common preventative measure was the spatial separation of wives, documented in 11 cultures (57.9 percent). This involved housing wives in separate dwellings, assigning them different cooking fires, or even placing them in completely different settlements, which Fisher interprets as a way of managing co-wife conflict.
Another common preventative strategy, found in 7 cultures (36.8 percent), was a cultural preference for marrying sisters, known as sororal polygyny. Ethnographic records often stated that men preferred sisters as co-wives because they tended to fight less than unrelated women. Evolutionary theory suggests that individuals are less likely to harm close genetic relatives because they share many of the same genes, meaning a sister’s reproductive success indirectly benefits the other sister. Fisher argues that the cross-cultural prevalence of this arrangement suggests societies implicitly recognize the volatility of non-kin co-wives and organize households to deter anticipated conflict.
“This study provides a valuable cross-cultural perspective by reviewing 19 different cultures, challenging the lab-based view that women’s competition is always indirect,” said Farid Pazhoohi, an interdisciplinary psychologist and researcher at the University of Plymouth who was not involved in the research.
Pazhoohi noted that the results should be viewed in their specific context. “[W]hile readers might mistakenly interpret this as proof that women are universally violent, the findings instead point to a flexible strategy where women use direct aggression when the stakes are high enough to outweigh the risks,” he told PsyPost.
As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind. The study relied on a sample of 19 cultures, which limits how broadly the prevalence estimates can be generalized. Fisher also notes that the contrast with laboratory studies is suggestive rather than a direct test, since those studies differ from ethnographic records in their populations and methods. The sample was uneven as well: 13 of the 19 cultures were in the Americas, while Africa was represented by a single culture.
Pazhoohi also pointed out limitations in the study’s design. “Because it relies on second-hand ethnographic records, observational secondary data is inherently less informative for pinning down strict causal relationships. While we can spot broad patterns, we cannot isolate direct cause-and-effect or rule out hidden confounders,” he said, referring to other factors that could explain the pattern.
“Furthermore, reducing complex cultural behaviors down to summary percentages and binary metrics (such as noting whether a behavior is simply present or absent) can conceal individual variations and local context,” Pazhoohi added. “Historical field notes are prone to reporting biases, meaning dramatic physical fights are much easier for ethnographers to record than covert hostility or quieter tensions.”
Fisher acknowledges this issue as well, noting that her search terms were geared toward overt conflict, so the prevalence of indirect tactics should be read as a minimum. The data also captured whether conflict occurred but not its intensity or duration. Future longitudinal research could show how verbal disputes escalate into physical fights and when these conflicts are successfully interrupted.
The study, “The battle of the brides: Co-wife competition and aggression across 19 cultures,” was authored by Maryanne L. Fisher.

UK Greens boycott The Telegraph over 'racist, antisemitic' caricature of Zack Polanski, Mothin Ali
The UK Green Party has announced it will be refusing engagement with The Telegraph over a "racist and antisemitic" cartoon depicting party leader Zack Polanski and Deputy Leader Mothin Ali.
The party has demanded an apology and immediate action from the right-wing paper, which published the caricature on Saturday.
The cartoon depicts Ali dressed in visibly Muslim garb and wearing a Palestine badge and one saying "Zionism is racism", sitting at a table preparing to eat the severed head of Polanski. Titled "Eat your Greens", the cartoon also shows Polanski, who is of Jewish heritage, with exaggerated facial features.
“The depictions of Zack and Mothin are instantly recognisable as racist and antisemitic, and we will always challenge this kind of behaviour wherever we see it," a spokesperson for the Green Party said in a statement shared with The New Arab.
"The Telegraph has previously called out other papers for giving space to similar tropes, so we insist it practices what it preaches and acts immediately to address the harm it has caused. Until this is resolved and the paper is once again acting in line with accepted editorial standards, we refuse to support its journalism."
In a separate statement shared with The New Arab, Ali said: “This racist cartoon turns me into a stand-in for all Muslim Green Party members, portraying us through two classic tropes: as a violent menace that will decapitate others and as a subversive force seeking to devour the party from within.
“The same cartoon gives Zack a hooked nose he doesn’t have, purely because he’s Jewish. It's the second time the Telegraph has used that crude antisemitic trope, and our party is refusing to engage with its journalists until we get an apology.
“The Telegraph is pushing Islamophobia and antisemitism to try and divide our movement, but it won’t work. Zack, myself and our entire party are united in support of Palestinians and against the racist drivel the Telegraph spouts.”
Muslim Greens and Jewish Greens also issued a joint statement on Sunday slamming the cartoon, saying that the depiction of Polanski "evoke[d] troubling historical antisemitic caricatures".
"The depiction of a Muslim political figure as menacing, violent and grotesque, alongside imagery reminiscent of antisemitic caricatures of a Jewish political leader, raises serious concerns about Islamophobia, antisemitism and anti-Palestinian racism," it added.
The cartoon's publication comes amid sustained media scrutiny of the Greens' recent adoption of the "Zionism is racism" motion at their recent party conference -- a stance which The Telegraph has been critical of in its coverage.
Questions also hang over Polanski's leadership of the Greens after his failure to win the Holborn and St Pancras by-election last week, despite securing a record number of votes for his Party in the London Labour stronghold.
However, this is not the first time that The Telegraph has been accused of anti-semitic depictions of the Green leader.
A cartoon published in May, also by the paper's chief political cartoonist Patrick Blower, showed Polanski similarly with exaggerated facial features.
The cartoon even drew criticism from pro-Israel "media monitoring" group CAMERA, which described the cartoon as showing Polanski with a  "gratuitously elongated nose, and hair which resembles a kippah", adding that "his facial expression conveys an ugly, sinister, scheming quality that evinces the “Happy Merchant” caricature (aka, Jew Face)".

UN aid operation underway in Nepal following fresh floods
The United Nations has rushed to assist Nepal following new flash floods in the central Gorkha district on Sunday that swept away homes and bridges just weeks after catastrophic flooding in the north.
At least five people are missing and 95 have been rescued, according to the authorities. Hundreds are affected.
It is believed the disaster was caused by a landslide that blocked the Budhi Gandaki River.
‘We stand with Nepal’
“Our hearts are with every family affected by the Budhi Gandaki floods,” the UN Country Team said on social media. “We stand with Nepal.”
The UN is supporting the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA) in getting food to those who lost their homes.
The World Food Programme (WFP) said on Sunday that three trucks carrying ready-to-eat food and relief supplies were on the way to help meet the immediate needs of affected communities.
Food security at risk
The “devastating” floods have damaged key roads, crops and livestock, threatening local food security, the UN Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) said in a post on social media.
The UN Country Team said FAO drones and satellite imagery by the UN humanitarian affairs office OCHA are being used to “map damage in places roads can’t reach.”
Families in need
The raging flood waters disrupted essential services that children and families rely on, including water supply, education and healthcare. Displaced families now require safe shelter, clean drinking water, child protection and psychosocial support
UN children’s agency UNICEF is supporting rapid assessments to identify impacts and to determine priorities for the immediate response.
UNICEF also has stocks of emergency supplies pre-positioned and ready for deployment, including hygiene kits, water treatment supplies, dignity kits, winter clothing, education materials and psychosocial support services.
Communities in Nepal are still reeling from the impact of flooding in late August that was triggered by a glacier collapse in the Himalayas. At least 1,400 people were killed and more than 5,000 are still missing.

‘Efficiency has limits’: UNHCR chief warns refugee protection is buckling under cuts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

‘Efficiency has limits’: UNHCR chief warns refugee protection is buckling under cuts
The money is running out faster than needs are growing: with 117 million men, women and children now forced from their homes, the UN refugee agency (UNHCR) has received just $3 billion of the $8.5 billion it needs this year – and its chief, Barham Salih, warns that the global support system for asylum-seekers risks buckling.
Protection at risk
UNHCR was created after the Second World War with the pledge that people fleeing persecution should be protected and not sent back to places where they might be in danger. Today, that pledge is under strain as deep funding cuts take effect.
In his first keynote address to UNHCR’s Executive Committee meeting in Geneva on Monday, Mr. Salih stressed that the world’s most vulnerable are going without the help they need.
“There is…a difference between doing more with less and being asked to do the impossible,” he said, while also highlighting the “exceptionally difficult year” at the agency, marked by the departure of 8,000 staff since 2024.
Cost of cuts in Sudan, Chad and beyond
He added: “In Sudan, insufficient funding threatens specialised medical care, legal assistance and psychological support for more than 50,000 survivors of conflict-related sexual violence. In Chad, services for thousands of unaccompanied and separated children and children with specific protection needs are at risk.”
In Ethiopia, meanwhile, refugee registration has been halted for tens of thousands of people arriving from South Sudan and Eritrea, while hundreds of thousands more are awaiting verification and integration into the national identification system.
Worldwide crisis
Conflicts are uprooting people faster than governments and aid agencies can help them.
So far in 2026, UNHCR has responded to 22 emergencies in 18 countries, from Yemen to the Horn of Africa and from Sudan to the Sahel.
Despite growing humanitarian needs, the agency has received less than one third of its funding requirement for this year.
Mr. Salih warned that countries that have hosted refugees for decades are frustrated at the lack of international solidarity, while refugees themselves are increasingly afraid for their safety, amid deep cuts to assistance.
The result is that women and girls are more exposed to violence and exploitation, children are losing years of education and persons with disabilities face protection barriers, the High Commissioner said, in an appeal for greater support.
“Efficiency has limits. There comes a point when greater efficiency cannot compensate for fewer resources. When funding falls below that point, the consequences are not abstract, they are borne by people who depend on it,” he insisted.
Inhumane treatment
At the end of last month, Mr. Salih – a former Kurdish politician and President of Iraq – told the Security Council that the situation for refugees today was “genuinely, truly, inhumane”.
Speaking in Geneva, the UNHCR chief highlighted an initiative launched earlier this year that aims to halve the number of refugees living in protracted displacement and depending on humanitarian assistance by 2035.
Nearly 14.5 million refugees in low and middle-income countries currently rely on aid to meet their basic requirements, he said.
“We cannot claim success simply because assistance has been reduced or responsibility has been transferred to host countries,” he added.
“Success is measured by whether people’s lives have genuinely improved and whether they have become self-reliant and active contributors to their communities. For those who still require humanitarian support, our responsibility remains.”
Mr. Salih urged solidarity and empathy with asylum-seekers, whose long-standing plight and hardship remains unresolved around the world. “When we speak about refugees and displacement, we should do so with humility,” he said.
“None of us knows who may be forced to flee tomorrow, or who may be called upon to offer refuge.”

Azerbaijan’s school hijab ban: What’s behind it, and what’s next?

Azerbaijan’s school hijab ban: What’s behind it, and what’s next?
Protests have broken out as some schools begin preventing students and teachers from attending classes.
An Azerbaijan government decision to indirectly prohibit students and staff from wearing the hijab in schools has sparked protests.
The amendment approved last month stopped short of explicitly banning the Muslim headscarf but barred clothing in schools that the government said violates the “principle of secularism”.
The decision has sparked protests as some schools began preventing students and teachers from attending classes.
Teacher Zahra Hasanova told Al Jazeera that she was informed she could no longer wear the hijab at school. “To be honest, I am a little emotional. I am hurt,” she said. “[The hijab] is a personal choice, and if one day I want to take it off, that should be my choice too.”
How has the ban played out?
The state-run Azerbaijani Press Agency (APA) said the amendment to the Descriptions of Uniforms for Students of State General Education Institutions aimed to ensure a unified dress code that reflects the country’s “secular principle”.
About 96 percent of Azerbaijan’s population identifies as Muslim. Its constitution defines the country as secular while also guaranteeing religious freedom.
The APA added that clothes that reflect the “history, culture, and national and moral values of the Azerbaijani people” may be worn for celebrations pending approval by the Pedagogical Council, which operates under the Ministry of Science and Education.
Such clothing ensures that teachers reflect “professional standards” and will have positive effects on the “school’s public reputation”, it said.
Have protests taken place?
The measure has sparked protests and a social media campaign in Azerbaijan. Videos circulated showing students hugging their teachers and crying as they were turned away from schools.
Local media outlets reported that students in at least two schools in Azerbaijan boycotted classes in protest against the restrictions.
Imprisoned journalist Polad Aslanov, who is serving a 113-year prison sentence after being convicted of high treason in 2020, launched a hunger strike over the new requirements.
“Despite being in prison, I am raising my voice against the trampling of our constitutional rights by employing the only means of struggle available to me – a hunger strike!” Aslanov wrote in a message posted on Facebook by his wife, Gulmira Aslanova.
Reports of internet blackouts have not been confirmed by data from watchdogs, including Open Observatory of Network Interference and NetBlocks.
Have other countries reacted?
A social media campaign followed by protests also spread to Turkiye. Some have drawn parallels between the developments in Azerbaijan and Turkiye’s “post-modern coup” in 1997 when women wearing headscarves were banned from attending university classes and dismissed from their civil service jobs or were forced to resign.
Demonstrators last week gathered outside Azerbaijan’s consulate in Istanbul to protest the restrictions affecting Muslim women, calling on authorities in Baku to reconsider the decision.
Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev issued a veiled criticism of Turkiye, a strong ally of Azerbaijan, for the protests. In a speech at his New Azerbaijan Party congress, Aliyev warned not to “interfere with our lifestyle” without directly mentioning Turkiye.
Authorities in Ankara did not officially respond to Aliyev’s comment. Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, however, mentioned in his September 23 address at the United Nations General Assembly that Muslim women were facing increasing discrimination.

Is a “Hardwired Pause” of AI Possible?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
11:55:59 UTC
20:55:59 KST

Various parties concerned about the risks that artificial intelligence (AI) pose to humanity have called for a pause in its development. But such a call faces a difficult collective action problem.
Can it be solved?
I have been skeptical (and suggested an alternate type of approach to AI safety here). But a new report argues that a pause is indeed possible.
Drafted by the Working Group on AI Pause Feasibility, an interdisciplinary group led by statistician William Fithian and philosopher Wesley H. Holliday (both of Berkeley), the report‘s focus is:
a scenario in which world leaders would prefer pausing to not pausing if they could be confident that others were also pausing or that defections from a pause would be detected within a reasonable timeframe. In such a pause-willing scenario, is a pause for at least a decade feasible?
Their answer is that a “hardwired pause” is feasible. What is a hardwired pause?
A hardwired pause would stop the production of training-capable AI chips, which are needed to develop more powerful AI models. Over time a hardwired pause would also phase out most or all of the pre-pause stock of such chips. It would replace them with inference-only AI chips, which are capable of fast, energy-efficient AI inference on approved models but are not practically useful for training new frontier AI models, even if stolen or seized, due to the way the chips are constructed.
Such a pause is feasible, they argue, mainly because of two sets of facts. The first concerns chip production:
The supply chain for AI chips is highly concentrated with several chokepoints, bolstering governments’ abilities to enforce rules on the production of such chips. In addition, bypassing existing supply chains is extraordinarily difficult.
The second concerns the demands of training new models:
Because training new models requires large numbers of training-capable chips, the feasibility of verification is an inherently quantitative question: while it is next to impossible to detect an evader who is using a single computer to train a small AI model, it is far easier to detect an evader who is training a frontier-scale AI model using hundreds of thousands or millions of chips... To research and train a new model that would significantly advance the frontier after a hardwired pause, absent an unforeseen methodological breakthrough, an evader would need to marshal a significant fraction of the world’s total computing capacity for months or years at a time.
The above quotes are from the executive summary of the report. The full report is here, and a press release from Berkeley about it is here.
Discussion welcome.
(via Wesley Holliday)

Chinese-owned rental cars recorded Norwegian military drill
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
11:55:48 UTC
20:55:48 KST

- Chinese-owned rental cars used in a Norwegian Home Guard exercise stored video of soldiers, their movements and codes entered at military gates, a participating officer said.
- The recordings were deleted afterward, but it is not known whether the data stayed only on the cars; Volvo Cars denies any security risk.
Rental cars used by Norway’s Home Guard during a large exercise in September recorded video of soldiers, their routes and the codes they typed into military gates, according to a soldier who took part, Norwegian business daily Dagens Næringsliv reported.
The cars were rented by the Norwegian Armed Forces from Hertz in Norway, which belongs to Volvo Cars and, through Volvo, to China’s Geely group. At least two of them were electric cars from Deepal, a brand of Chinese automaker Changan, according to Norwegian media. Soldiers discovered during Exercise Hovedstad, or “Capital,” that the vehicles had a recording function no one had asked for or told them about. The unit kept using the cars for the rest of the exercise because few other vehicles were available.
Lt. Fredrik Blanck, who took part in the exercise, told the newspaper that the stored video showed who got in and out of the cars, where they drove, who they picked up and how long they stayed at different locations. He said the recordings also captured the access codes soldiers entered to open military gates and doors, and that it was unclear whether the data stayed in the car or went anywhere else. Two other unnamed sources confirmed the account to Dagens Næringsliv, and newspaper VG said a separate source told it the recordings were raised during the exercise.
The recordings were deleted from the cars after the exercise, according to Norwegian media, but it is not known whether the data was stored only on the vehicles. Volvo Cars rejected the idea that Chinese ownership poses a security risk and said no data can be shared with Geely without a legal basis. The Norwegian Armed Forces had not publicly explained why the cars were rented or whether it will review the use of such vehicles.
Exercise Hovedstad ran from Sept. 14 to 18 and was the Home Guard’s largest exercise of the year. About 5,000 soldiers from the Oslo and Akershus Home Guard District trained across the capital region, including around the parliament and government buildings. Part of the exercise focused on protecting Oslo Airport, Gardermoen, in wartime. The Home Guard is Norway’s territorial defense force, made up mostly of reservists who guard key infrastructure at home.
Modern cars carry cameras for parking, driver monitoring and dashcam-style recording, along with GPS and internet connections that can send data back to the manufacturer. That has raised concerns about Chinese-made vehicles in several Western countries. In Norway, Oslo’s public transport operator Ruter said last year that tests found the Chinese bus maker Yutong had remote access to the software of electric buses it had supplied, which in theory could allow them to be stopped.
It is not clear whether the Deepal cars were set to record by default, whether the video was ever uploaded, or whether the Norwegian Armed Forces will bar Chinese-owned or Chinese-built vehicles from future exercises.

Israel has reportedly introduced restrictions barring foreign airline pilots and cabin crew who hold citizenship in countries without diplomatic relations with Israel from serving on flights entering its airspace, with United Airlines and Air France reportedly adjusting their crew assignments in response.
The new security measures come after the attempted hijacking of a Flydubai flight to Tel Aviv last month by an Omani co-pilot. The incident raised concerns about Israel's screening of foreign flight crews and prompted Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to order a review of aviation security.
On Thursday, Israel's Kan public broadcaster reported that the Transportation Ministry's Aviation Security Operations Center had issued a series of new and updated directives following the Flydubai incident. According to Kan, the guidelines bar pilots and flight attendants who hold citizenship in countries that lack diplomatic relations with Israel, including dual nationals.
"The airline is exclusively responsible for ensuring that all flight crew members do not hold citizenship, or are not dual nationals, of countries that do not have official diplomatic relations with the State of Israel," the directive reportedly says.
On Saturday, Live and Let's Fly, an aviation blog, reported that United Airlines had notified its pilots and flight attendants of the new policy, asking affected crew members scheduled to fly to Tel Aviv to contact the airline's scheduling department.
"Our teams will work with you to make any necessary scheduling adjustments," the airline told employees, according to an internal memo that the blog did not publish.
The same day, French investigative website Mediapart reported that Air France had issued a similar memo to its pilots and flight attendants, informing them of the new restrictions and their implications for crew scheduling.
Both outlets published lists of countries whose nationals are barred from serving on flights entering Israeli airspace. The lists include Saudi Arabia, Iran, Malaysia, Venezuela and Pakistan, as well as Oman, the home country of the Flydubai co-pilot involved in the attempted hijacking.
Live and Let's Fly reported that the restrictions apply to nationals of 29 countries, while Mediapart listed 31, adding Nicaragua and Colombia.
Business Insider Africa reported on Monday, citing the United Airlines memo, that ten African countries are also included: Algeria, Comoros, Djibouti, Libya, Mali, Mauritania, Niger, Somalia, Sudan and Tunisia.
Both Nicaragua and Colombia severed diplomatic ties with Israel in recent years over the war in Gaza. However, Colombia's new president has pledged to strengthen ties, and Bogota's embassy in Jerusalem is expected to officially open later this week.
Netanyahu ordered a review of security procedures for foreign civil aviation four days after the Flydubai incident. He instructed National Security Council chief Shmuel Ben Ezra to appoint an examiner to conduct a thorough review of aviation security. Haaretz previously reported that the National Security Council had warned of shortcomings in the Transportation Ministry's screening of foreign flights.
Haaretz has contacted both United Airlines and Air France for comment.
On September 30, Flydubai Flight 1073 was traveling from Dubai to Tel Aviv when its Omani co-pilot, later identified as Hamam al-Hammami, attacked the captain in an attempt to seize control of the aircraft. Despite his injuries, the captain, Indian national Smit Machchhar, managed to open the cockpit door, allowing passengers and crew members to intervene. Two other pilots and several Israeli passengers subdued al-Hammami, and the plane landed safely in Saudi Arabia.
Last Friday, the United Arab Emirates' attorney general confirmed earlier reports that al-Hammami, inspired by the September 11 attacks, had planned to crash the plane into Ben-Gurion Airport, Israel's largest airport, according to state-run news agency WAM.

Love blooms on a hostile colony world in
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
11:55:02 UTC
20:55:02 KST

One of science fiction’s oldest themes is its insistence that the future isn’t inevitable. Few contemporary authors embody that idea more than Becky Chambers, whose stories imagine alternative futures—not through grand revolutions or galaxy-spanning battles but through ordinary people trying to care for one another.
As a defining voice of the “hopepunk” genre, Chambers has built a reputation for science fiction that prizes empathy as much as imagination. Her latest novel, As You Wake, Break the Shell, brings us to the hostile, unpredictable world of Fortune, where acid rain falls and billowing volcanoes shroud the horizon. The story follows a reclusive botanist and a spacefaring pilot across alternating timelines as they search for connection and purpose, attempting to navigate a life where Fortune has never favored the bold.
We caught up with Chambers to discuss a toxic planet’s world-building, scientific accuracy in storytelling and the motivational merits of unrelenting spite.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
[An edited transcript of the interview follows.]
This story spends a lot of time on a colony planet with a poisonous atmosphere. What does designing an ecosystem teach you about designing a civilization?
Everything. It’s really important for me to start with what the environmental conditions are because that’s going to affect everything from what we’re eating, what we’re building houses out of, what kind of clothes we have—and all of those things, in turn, affect culture. There is so much about our values, our personalities, that are actually molded by the physical environments we exist in, both natural and constructed.
Starting from [the questions] “what do we have” and “what do we not have” is really important for me. Suppose someone’s eating a sandwich. What’s in the sandwich? It’s a throwaway line that seems like it doesn’t matter, but it’s actually really important to say whether or not there’s lettuce in this sandwich, because that does communicate a lot of information about how this world works.
For this book, I had a really big table of crops [to reference], what are we growing, how are we growing it, what’s available and what’s not?
Those are details I spend a lot of time sussing out before I really get into the thick of drafting the story.
What specific ideas inspired the scientific foundation for this story?
Botany is the big one. I have always had an appreciation for plants but not any actual sort of technical knowledge about what it is that I’m looking at. So I did a lot of research for this book into how plants work, and specifically into seeds, which is a topic I have become fascinated by the more I learn about it. Seeds are a big part of this book, as are plants and the way they communicate with each other.
How does scientific accuracy influence your storytelling? Do you often find yourself molding the plot to fit the science, or vice versa?
I look at science as partially a foundation but more of a tool that I use to color the world that I’m in. I want it to feel tangible and possible, but I’m very willing to take some liberties here and there for the sake of getting the feeling across.
I tend to think of what I’m doing as more like impressionism than photorealism. If you think of something like Monet’s Water Lilies, for example, it doesn’t look like a real pond, right? But it feels like a real pond. And I often use a similar approach with my work. I am not necessarily painting you a picture of the cosmos as it actually exists, but what I’m trying to communicate is the sense of wonder and awe that I feel when I’m experiencing those things in the real world. So it’s a matter of getting the emotional quality of discovery across, and sometimes that does mean taking shortcuts.
With As You Wake Break the Shell, I kept it within the realm of “with sufficient technology, this could be possible.” Is it probable? Probably not. There are a lot of things that I gloss over because they’re not things that everyday people outside of science would know about or understand. We know [in the reality of the story] that there are giant space-dwelling creatures out there. We don’t need to know how it is that they evolved or what kind of world it is that they came from. Those are questions that interest me as a person who is into real science, but they don’t serve the story.
This book has a knack for taking the unknown and making it feel familiar while making the familiar feel unknown, simply by showing it from a new perspective—for instance, that of an enormous, cargo-toting space behemoth. How do you get into the headspace of examining humanity from the outside?
It’s a highly technical process that involves me sitting in my armchair and just staring at the ceiling and thinking about what it would be like to have a body other than mine, and just sort of deconstructing everything that makes me down to the raw components and trying to figure out what it is that’s necessary and what’s not.
I take a lot of inspiration from the natural world. I have a really keen interest in invertebrate life and in deep-sea life, and I have a real interest in animal intelligence that exists in nonmammalian creatures.
What would it mean to communicate through color? What would it mean to communicate through pheromones? What does the world feel like if you don’t have a sense of sight like we do? I just love taking any one of those traits and then expanding it to make something that we would recognize as a person, regardless of whether they physically look like us or not. How does that make you think about yourself? How does that make you think about existence?
As You Wake, Break the Shell is a love story as much as a space story. What did pairing those genres let you explore that you couldn’t do with either one on their own?
It allowed me the freedom to not segment any of the things I was thinking of into separate boxes. This was a really personal book for me in that I’m writing about everything I care about in this one. I’m writing about the natural world, I’m writing about society, and I am also writing about love, romantic love, and these are all things that are extremely important to me in my everyday life.
We have a bazillion stories about “and then they lived happily ever after,” but I actually want to see what that looks like because it’s never that simple.I feel that the most interesting parts of a relationship are what happens “after,” and so that was what drove a large part of my decision to have [the book] be a split timeline, where it’s very clear from the jump that they’re going to be together a long time and we’re going to see all these different stages in what makes them them, because I do think that that’s an area that is underexplored.
You’ve said before that you write the stories that you need to hear. What did you need to hear from this book?
I wanted to see a relationship that matched my own. Queer representation in media is better than ever in a lot of ways, and yet it’s still very rare to see anybody over their 20s.
By the time we started getting more stories about coming of age or people falling in love when they’re young, I was already too old for those stories. I was feeling a real frustration in not finding love stories that spoke to me where I am now in my life. It was one of those things of, “I guess I’ll just have to write it myself.”
Your work has been described as “wholesome,” “thoughtful” and “heartwarming.” How much of your inspiration and motivation actually comes from spite?
[Maniacal cackling] So much! I’m so happy you asked this question because so many people come at it from, like, “How do you maintain hope? How do you maintain the sense of coziness?” And the answer is that I am so pissed off all the time about everything. And honestly, so much of it does come from a place of looking at so many of the directions we are headed in the real world, so many of the decisions we are making about technology, about the environment, about how we organize ourselves as a society, feeling the crushing, overwhelming despair that I know we all feel and then just flipping that off and saying, “I’m sorry, I don’t accept that this is all there is and that it has to be like this.”

Anduril Unveils Steelfin Missile as a Low-Cost Alternative to the PAC-3, With Plans to Produce Several Thousand Missiles Per Year

20:54:06 KST

Anduril Industries has presented the Steelfin family of anti-aircraft interceptor missiles, which it positions as a low-cost alternative to the PAC-3 missiles used in the Patriot air defense system.
The War Zone reported this.
The developer aims to ensure the new missiles are compatible with existing air defense infrastructure.
According to the media, the Steelfin missiles are being developed to launch from the M903A2 launcher used for the PAC-3 family of interceptor missiles.
Anduril spokesperson Steve Milano told The War Zone that the Steelfin configuration, designed to perform PAC-3 missions, will provide about 80% of PAC-3’s capabilities at less than half the cost of a PAC-3 missile.
The company also plans to ramp up production to several thousand interceptors per year, using a common production line for different missile versions.
The modular design will allow for the replacement of engines, warheads, and other components depending on the mission. The missiles will feature a two-stage design. The first stage will be a booster that determines range and flight characteristics, while the second stage will be the interceptor itself.
The company is developing the Steelfin family to intercept cruise and ballistic missiles, as well as hypersonic targets. Anduril is also exploring integrating the missiles with the Mk 41 ship-based vertical launch system and the Typhon ground-based system.
According to Anduril representative Steve Milano, a more powerful Steelfin configuration will be able to perform the tasks of the THAAD missile defense system at a significantly lower cost.
The company has already conducted ballistic tests of prototype models and plans to begin flight tests of various configurations in 2027.
Militarnyi previously reported that the American company Lockheed Martin had developed a new PAC-3 Edge interceptor missile for the Patriot air defense system. It is designed to counter hypersonic and other modern missile threats.

Ukraine: Zelenskyy accuses Russia of ceasefire violations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
11:54:00 UTC
20:54:00 KST

Ukraine reports Russian strikes despite Trump 'ceasefire'
October 12, 2026
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Monday said Russia carried out strikes, despite US President Donald Trump claiming a "ceasefire" had been agreed over the weekend.
Trump announced unilaterally on social media on Sunday evening that "both parties" had agreed to an "energy ceasefire" which was "effective immediately."
There was no immediate confirmation from Moscow and Zelenskyy told the news site Axios within minutes of Trump's claim that the ceasefire was "news for me."
Ukrainian energy facility attacked
On Monday morning, Zelenskyy told the annual Warsaw Security Forum that there had been "Russian violations of the energy ceasefire announced President Trump" overnight, while the mayor of the northeastern city of Kharkiv reporting at least 12 injuries in attacks on energy facilities.
"It was clear that [Russian President Vladimir] Putin does not read Truth Social," Zelenskyy said, referring to Trump's social media platform.
"If Russia wants us to stop our long-range strikes against its oil refineries and oil exports, then it must stop its strikes against our energy system and critical infrastructure and stop killing our people," he said via video link, adding that he learned about the apparent ceasefire through the media.
Zelenskyy: Ukraine 'will respond' if no ceasefire
Zelenskyy expressed readiness in principle to back an agreement to refrain from attacks on energy infrastructure, but said such a ceasefire must be backed up by security guarantees.
"This ceasefire, it can work, and it can become a major step toward ending the war if the Americans truly step in now and make sure Russians respect it," he said.
"We are waiting for the of the conditions between the Americans and Russians, and we are waiting to see one specific step the Americans are ready to take.
"If Russia does not agree to an energy ceasefire, we will respond."
EU: No sign of Russia sticking to ceasefire
The European Union's foreign affairs chief Kaja Kallas said on Monday at a meeting of EU foreign ministers in Luxembourg that the bloc would "welcome the energy ceasefire if it holds" but added: "We haven't yet seen that Russia will also stick to it."
French President Emmanuel Macron also insisted that a "real ceasefire" be "respected by both sides" but said: "I have not noted, over the last 48 hours, any energy ceasefire coming from the Russian side."
The Russian government said on Monday that President Putin would only consider a ceasefire for a single day in the event that Ukraine intended to hold a presidential election.
The Kremlin earlier rejected a 60-day election ceasefire idea proposed by President Zelenskyy.
"I do not think he deserves a respite," said Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov.

'Unprecedented' cyberattack targets refrigeration units at hundreds of French supermarkets
Hundreds of French supermarket chains were targeted overnight Sunday to Monday in a cyberattack that affected the refrigerators of up to 200 Intermarché stores and almost 100 Coopérative U locations, according to the retailers. Carrefour said that 80 of its supermarkets had also been hit.
Major French supermarket chains Intermarché, Coopérative U and Carrefour were hit by a cyberattack that caused their refrigerators to defrost, the two retailers told AFP on Monday.
Some 150-200 Intermarché shops were targeted in the attack, along with almost 100 Coopérative U outlets, they said.
Paris prosecutors confirmed the attack, which reportedly also hit other major chains, and also indicated it had prompted fire outbreaks.
The chief executive of Cooperative U, Dominique Schelcher, described the attack as "unprecedented" and confirmed the cyberattack had affected refrigeration systems since Sunday night.
"Targeting equipment essential to the preservation of fresh products and to the food supply of the French people is extremely serious and is unprecedented. It is unacceptable," he wrote on X.
Carrefour said 80 of its supermarkets had been hit but that the vast majority of its 6,000 stores had not been affected.
Read moreCombating foreign digital interference: ‘France is among the top three in Europe’
BFM TV said France's largest supermarket chain E. Leclerc was also affected, with hackers "managing to remotely trigger the forced defrosting of the refrigeration systems in numerous stores". Contacted by AFP, E. Leclerc did not immediately confirm the information.
Those branches that were affected will have to "throw away all of the products" that are fresh and frozen, Intermarché told AFP.
Specialist French retail sector news website jebosseengrandedistribution.fr said other retail giants Carrefour Market and Monoprix were affected, but the companies have yet to confirm this.
'Unprecedented'
The chief executive of Coopérative U, Dominique Schelcher, described the attack as "unprecedented" and confirmed the cyberattack had affected refrigeration systems since Sunday night.
"Targeting equipment essential to the preservation of fresh products and to the food supply of the French people is extremely serious and is unprecedented. It is unacceptable," he wrote on X.
He added that the company's teams are "fully mobilised" to restore the situation as quickly as possible.
"An investigation will be necessary to shed full light on this attack," he added.
Read moreTax hack: What we know about the cyberattacks on French government agencies
The office of the Paris prosecutor confirmed to AFP that an investigation has been opened into "the large-scale cyberattack affecting the refrigerators of several major food retail chains across France".
The probe will help "identify the victims and establish the link with the damage they reported in terms of foodstuff losses and the outbreak of fires", the prosecutor's office said.
Intermarché condemned the food waste and financial losses resulting from the attack, without providing figures, and warned there could be issues with insurance policies which do not "cover this type" of in-store incident.
BFM TV said temperatures were "altered remotely, resulting in the destruction of stocks of fresh and frozen products".
Read moreMacron orders plan to protect France's critical infrastructure against 'Russian hybrid attacks'
The incident comes against the background of growing concern over the potential havoc that can be caused in Europe in all sectors by cyberattacks by malicious actors.
President Emmanuel Macron, a strong supporter of Ukraine in its fight against the Russian invasion, last month ordered measures to protect France's critical infrastructure from Russian "hybrid attacks".

Turkish security sources have announced that the PKK has evacuated four residential areas in northern Iraq in line with the implementation of the “terror-free Türkiye” project.
The sources reported that the area evacuated on Oct. 8 by the PKK was the Baze region near Metina in northern Iraq.
“This development is a clear indication that the terror-free Türkiye project is advancing with determination,” the sources said.
Launched in late 2024, Türkiye’s anti-terror bid stipulates the full disarmament and dissolution of the PKK, ending decades-old terrorism that claimed the lives of more than 40,000 people.
The process was further strengthened and matured after the Turkish parliament overwhelmingly voted in favor of a comprehensive framework law that tackles political and social aspects of the terror-free Türkiye bid.
In case all the weapons are laid down and the disarmament process is completed, the framework law will take effect and postpone legal procedures against certain members of the terror group for five to 10 years.
The sources recalled the importance of the implementation of this process for the future of Türkiye and informed that it is being run in a committed way and without giving concessions.
Citing the framework law, security sources emphasized that future stages of the initiative will intensify efforts to reintegrate PKK members into society.
They added that holistic programs in education, economics, and other key fields are being developed to support this transition and firmly solidify domestic peace and stability.
The sources said the ultimate goal of the “terror-free Türkiye” process is to “create an environment where all the different segments of the society will live together, in peace and stability across every corner of Türkiye, rooted in the foundation of Turkish-Kurdish brotherhood.”

Sassari who became trapped in the Gorropeddu cave in Urzulei.
                                    
Rescuers, who have been working since Sunday afternoon and
throughout the night, cleared the cave entrance and stabilized
the access walls this morning to prevent further collapses; they
have now reached the narrow passage where the young caver—alive
and conscious—has been trapped for 20 hours following a rockfall
that caught him by surprise while he was exploring the cave.
                                    
The teams on site (48 members of the Sardinia Alpine and
Speleological Rescue Corps, alongside 30 firefighters
specializing in USAR-M, SAF, and TAS operations, with support
from the Dorgali Civil Protection) cleared boulders from the
entrance and are now proceeding with the delicate manual removal
of material obstructing the passage where the caver remains
trapped beneath the debris.
                                    
The operation is taking place in an extremely confined space—a
work area of approximately 1.5 by 1.5 meters—characterized by
highly unstable conditions.
                                    
As they excavate and remove material, rescuers must stabilize
the walls by installing retaining boards to prevent further
collapses and allow for safer progress.
                                    
A helicopter is expected to arrive shortly, carrying additional
materials and equipment needed to secure the site, with the aim
of enabling rescuers to reach the man and remove the earth and
stones pinning him down.

11:50:10 UTC
20:50:10 KST

Russia could carry out increasingly dangerous operations on NATO territory within the coming months, including sabotage attacks and strikes against weapons depots supplying Ukraine, the head of the Czech Republic's intelligence service warned Monday.
Michal Koudelka, director general of the Czech Security Information Service, told a parliamentary security conference that Moscow appeared to be adopting a strategy of "escalation for de-escalation," potentially taking greater risks to pressure Western countries supporting Ukraine.
"This could involve sabotage attacks on the territory of a NATO member state against a facility connected to aid for Ukraine, a drone or missile attack on a weapons depot intended for Ukraine, or, in an extreme case, even a limited military action against one of the neighbouring member states of the Alliance," Koudelka said.
However, he emphasized that the most extreme scenario, a direct Russian military operation against a NATO member state, was not an immediate threat.
"Russia has all its forces concentrated in Ukraine," he explained.
Koudelka said his agency had no specific intelligence indicating an imminent direct threat to the Czech Republic but was closely monitoring Russian activities targeting the country and its NATO allies.
According to the intelligence chief, Moscow's hybrid operations, which can include sabotage, cyberattacks and other disruptive activities, are designed to undermine cohesion within NATO and weaken the alliance's collective response to Russia's war in Ukraine.
His assessment comes amid growing concerns over the possibility that Russia could expand its confrontation with Western countries beyond Ukraine without launching a full-scale military attack against NATO.
Russian President Vladimir Putin said earlier this month that Moscow had no plans to attack any European country and wanted peaceful coexistence with its neighbors.
Russia has also repeatedly denied allegations that it is responsible for sabotage operations or other forms of hybrid warfare targeting European countries.

Saudi Arabia further suspends flights after latest deadly Houthi attack on airport

20:49:34 KST

Saudi Arabia has been forced to suspend all flights to and from its main international airport in Riyadh until next Saturday after a further round of Houthi missile attacks caused more damage and left one person dead. Some airlines, including Gulf Air and Bahrain Air, had already said they were cancelling flights until next Saaturday. More missiles were fired at Saudi Arabian cities by the Houthis on Monday, Saudi Arabian’s military spokesperson said.
The Gulf nation announced it was suspending flights from Riyadh, its second busiest airport, after Houthi missiles killed 13 people on Saturday and left more than 300 injured. Saudi state TV broadcast CCTV footage that showed passengers deluged in smoke and falling masonry as they queued at the airport terminal to board a plane just as the Houthi missile struck.
The country has pressed ahead with the 25th WPC Energy Conference in Riyadh, hoping to project an image of normality. But some senior oil executives did not attend or appeared virtually.
The Saudi energy minister, Abdulaziz bin Salman, told the conference that “fear has no place in the Saudi lexicon”, emphasising that the resilience of the kingdom’s energy system and the determination of its people to confront crises. Amin Nasser, the president and chief executive of Aramco, said Saudi Arabia had invested deeply in protecting its supplies, but “no nation, even one as capable and confident as ours, can safeguard them alone.”
He added: “Markets can diversify suppliers. They cannot diversify geography […] when energy infrastructure in this region is targeted, the consequences reach economies everywhere.”
An urgent review is under way as to how Houthi missiles are repeatedly penetrating badly stretched Saudi air defences. Schoolchildren and some office workers were advised to work from home. The Houthis have also targeted the city of Khamis Mushait, and the King Fahd international airport in Dammam.
Interceptor missiles are needed to protect government buildings, oil facilities and infrastructure hubs across a wide geographic area. The Houthis have vowed to attack Saudi airports across the country.
Houthi attacks since last month have targeted fuel tanks at Riyadh airport and its affiliated warehouses, destroying a parked Airbus A320 passenger plane and damaging at least five other aircraft.
The crown prince, Mohammed bin Salman, has not been seen in public since Tuesday last week, reflecting the pressure he is under to find a way out from a war that has intermittently dogged his leadership since 2014. Saudi Arabia badly needs stability to continue the slow diversification of its economy from oil dependence, but has not found a way to restore it in Yemen.
Inside Yemen, fighting continued in and around Taiz, the third city, and the most populous governorate, with Saudi planes mounting eight separate strikes on any assembly of Houthi forces. As many as 60 fighters died on Sunday from both sides.
The governor of Taiz, Nabil Shamsan, on Sunday issued an urgent call to lift the Houthi siege and warned a shortage of medicines meant the city would soon run out of emergency surgical and intensive care services.
Overall the Houthis claimed the Saudis had mounted 124 raids on Sunday. The Saudis are seeking to locate Abdul-Malik al-Houthi, the reclusive leader of the Houthis, with rumours of his assassination repeatedly circulating, but Saudi Arabia does not seem to have contemporary intelligence on his precise whereabouts either in the capital Sana’a or in its stronghold of Saada.
On the diplomatic front, Abbas Araghchi, the Iranian foreign minister, spoke to the Saudi foreign minister, Faisal bin Farhan, on Sunday to see if there was a way in which Iran could act as a mediator between the Saudis and the Houthis, a group that Iran has trained and armed. Mohammed al-Bukhaiti, a member of the Houthi Political Bureau claimed Saudi Arabia accepted the mediation offered by Iran and proposed first a one-month truce, and then a two week truce, but the Houthis had rejected both offers.
He said “the battle this time is not like its predecessors; the arena is no longer the same arena, and the cards have changed. Therefore, a comprehensive settlement must be put in place between Riyadh and Sana’a, the Houthi capital because every day that passes in this battle will expand its scope and deepen its losses, and the settlement that is possible today may become difficult or impossible tomorrow”.
A meeting of the UN security council in New York on Tuesday is expected to debate a resolution calling the Houthis a foreign terrorist organisation.
The exiled leader of the Southern Transitional Council (STC), Aidarous al-Zubaidi, called for southern forces to fight on all fronts, and not just to defend the borders of the former South Yemen, in a move that is likely to be welcomed by Saudi Arabia as it supports the week-old call by the UN-recognised government to drive the Houthis out of the whole of Yemen, rather than just from the southern governorates.
The STC has a vision of an independent South Yemen that would recreate the separate state that existed between 1967 and 1990. The reunification of Yemen at the end of the cold war proved fragile and many southerners nurse longstanding grievances about the distribution of resources in the unified state.
The STC’s authority has been challenged by Abd al-Rahman al-Mahrami, the Salafist leader who commands the powerful Southern Giants Brigades.
Despite Araghchi’s efforts to reach out to the Saudis, Mohsen Rezaei, the more hardline secretary of Iran’s supreme national security council, claimed Iran was hitting five or six small vessels in the strait of Hormuz every night, explaining the vessels were being used by the Emirati military to move oil through the strait to larger tankers, thus breaching the blockade that Iran is seeking to maintain to push up oil prices and weaken Donald Trump.
Esmail Baghaei, the Iranian foreign ministry spokesperson, said Trump’s treatment of Volodymyr Zelenskyy, including his call for the Ukrainian president to stand aside showed the risks in dealing with Trump. He said: “Being an enemy of America can be dangerous, but being a friend of America is deadly. You can see for yourself what America’s friendship and enmity with its allies is like.”

Telecommunications operator Telia Finland has announced restructuring negotiations that could result in the elimination of 355 positions as part of a wider reorganisation affecting approximately 900 jobs across its Nordic and Baltic operations.
The company said on Monday, 12 October, that around 2,050 positions in Finland would fall within the scope of the negotiations, which are expected to last six weeks.
Add Helsinki Times as a preferred source on Google (opens Google in a new tab)
The proposed restructuring forms part of parent company Telia Company's plans to simplify its organisation, reduce overlapping functions and transfer more decision-making responsibilities to national subsidiaries.
Although the changes could eliminate 355 positions in Finland, Telia expects to create approximately 75 new roles in the country. Another 50 positions are expected to transfer from the parent company to Telia Finland.
The restructuring aims to bring operational responsibilities closer to customers and individual markets, allowing national businesses to respond to changing demand without relying as heavily on centralised group functions.
"Our goal is for Telia to be known for quality, security and an excellent customer experience," Telia Finland chief executive Holger Haljand said in a company statement.
"Customer expectations are changing, and we want to ensure our ability to respond to them faster than before," he added.
At group level, Telia aims to achieve annual gross savings of approximately one billion Swedish kronor, equivalent to more than €89 million, through the proposed organisational changes.
The company expects to eliminate around 900 positions across its operations while transferring approximately 220 roles from central group functions to national subsidiaries.
Telia operates telecommunications businesses across the Nordic and Baltic countries. The restructuring would give its national units greater responsibility for operations and business development.
The company said its Finnish operations would receive additional responsibilities as part of the changes, requiring adjustments to existing organisational structures and working practices.
Telia has not specified which departments or locations in Finland would face the proposed reductions.

Lebanese Prime Minister Nawaf Salam on Monday vowed that authorities would deal firmly with all illegal weapons, days after security forces seized a truck carrying explosives suspected of belonging to Hezbollah.
A judicial official had told AFP that authorities on Thursday detained two suspected members of the Iran-backed group at a security checkpoint in Dahr al-Baidar, near a road linking Lebanon with Syria, as they headed to Beirut.
They were allegedly transporting half a tonne of explosives, 250 kilogrammes (551 pounds) of TNT and 250 kilogrammes of C4, the official said.
Salam on X confirmed that "it has become known that a few days ago a truck was stopped" in Dahr al-Baidar "carrying hundreds of kilogrammes of explosive materials" including C4.
"We will not be lenient in following up and expanding the investigation in order to identify all those involved in this criminal operation, and those behind them," he said.
"We will deal with weapons outside the legal framework will the required firmness," he added, whether regarding their possession, transportation or use.
Salam also said that he understood "Lebanese worries" over the C4, particularly as it "has been used in a number of political assassinations" in Lebanon's history.
Disarmament efforts face major hurdles
Hezbollah until recently was the most influential political and military force in Lebanon, enjoying key support from Iran and ousted regime leader ruler Bashar al Assad.
The group has been accused of carrying out assassinations of political figures who opposed Damascus, particularly between 2005 and 2008.
A UN-backed court in 2020 sentenced a fugitive Hezbollah member for the 2005 assassination of former Lebanese prime minister Rafic Hariri, with the court subsequently sentencing two more Hezbollah members in absentia.
Lebanese authorities last year committed to disarming Hezbollah, after hostilities between Israel and Hezbollah erupted in 2023 and culminated in all-out war the following year, decimating the group's leadership.
The 2024 toppling of Assad also severed the group's key weapons supply line from Iran, and Syria's new authorities regularly say they have seized weapons headed for Lebanon.
However, Hezbollah this year drew Lebanon into the US-Israeli war on Iran with rocket fire at Israel, which responded with air strikes and a ground invasion.
The cash-strapped Lebanese army faces enormous challenges in carrying out its mission of disarming Hezbollah and deploying in south Lebanon, including under an Israel-Lebanon framework reached in June this year.

Miriam González launches new party to take on Spain’s big two in snap election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
11:47:59 UTC
20:47:59 KST

Lawyer Miriam González is entering politics with new party Democracia21. She is married to British politician Nick Clegg, former UK deputy prime minister, and says she wants to "regenerate Spanish politics".
Miriam González presented Democracia21 in Madrid over the weekend, the new political party with which she hopes to break away from Spain's traditional parties and appeal to centrist voters, with the aim of "reinvigorating Spanish democracy".
Spain has a new name in the electoral race for 29 November: Miriam González Durántez announced on 10 October her candidacy for the general election at the head of Democracia21 (d21), a newly created party that will make its debut only in Madrid and Barcelona, with plans to expand across the country in future contests at the ballot box.
Who is Miriam González?
Born in 1968 in Olmedo (Valladolid), she is the daughter of two teachers and studied in Belgium thanks to a scholarship. She is a lawyer specialising in international trade, and her public profile grew over many years in the United Kingdom, where she lived with her husband Nick Clegg, Liberal Democrat leader and deputy prime minister between 2010 and 2015 in the coalition government led by David Cameron.
González is also the founder of the charity Inspiring Girls. In Spain she led the civic platform España Mejor, which became the seed that grew into a move into party politics.
At the launch she justified her decision as a personal commitment, saying she felt "a monumental debt" to the country for the opportunities she received as the granddaughter of farmers. Clegg attended the event, along with former Union Progress and Democracy party figures such as Rafael Calduch, Fernando Maura and Beatriz Becerra.
Will it be a successor to Ciudadanos?
The comparison with the centrist Ciudadanos or Citizens Party, arises almost automatically; however, González sidesteps it. According to reports, she avoids choosing between centre-left, centre or centre-right, and insists she does not want to rebuild any previous party. Before founding Democracia21 she described herself as "liberal in the British sense".
Her project is presented as cross-cutting and focused on institutional regeneration. So although Democracia21 hopes to attract moderate voters tired of the two major blocs, any parallel with Ciudadanos should be treated as political analysis rather than as something the candidate herself claims.
Housing is centrepiece of Democracia21's programme
The housing crisis, the main concern for Spaniards, sits at the core of her manifesto. She proposes a national plan to build new neighbourhoods, under cross-party agreements that would provide legal certainty for ten years.
She proposes scrapping all housing-related taxes for people under 35. She is also urging Pedro Sánchez and Alberto Núñez Feijóo to negotiate with Brussels over €10 billion in unspent Next Generation European funds, to create a sovereign fund for protected and affordable housing.
Immigration based on control and integration
On migration, González describes it as an asset for Spain, but argues that the state must decide the conditions of entry and exit.
Her most quoted line after the presentation of Democracia21 was that xenophobic discourse must be banished, while at the same time deciding who enters, how and when.
Institutional regeneration as a flagship policy
Her most forceful axis is the clean-up of institutions. She proposes cutting the number of political advisers by 90%, professionalising the civil service on merit and ability, and changing the General Council of the Judiciary.
She adds that the Public Prosecutor's Office should be accountable to Parliament, that there should be courts specialised in corruption, the abolition of special legal privileges and cuts to subsidies for parties and foundations.
She also wants parliamentarians to meet their voters "at least every two weeks", following the British model. In education, she advocates more flexible degree programmes and more work placements; in the economy, she calls for fewer barriers to entrepreneurship.
A test in Madrid and Barcelona
Democracia21 is starting from scratch and will only stand in the constituencies of Madrid and Barcelona, which limits its ceiling of representation. Her aim is to win over those who, in her words, are tired of voting "while holding their nose" because of the stench of polarisation and tension that has marked political discourse in recent years.
Whether or not it manages to become a real alternative will depend on whether its message of regeneration, housing and consensus catches on in a campaign lasting less than two months.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky on Oct. 12 reiterated his readiness to adhere to the energy truce — provided that Russia follows suit.
Ukraine will halt its strikes against Russian refineries only if Moscow ceases its attacks against the Ukrainian power grid, Zelensky said on Oct. 12, signaling that a refinery-only truce makes little sense for a country with a single, badly damaged refinery.

AI boom could widen income inequality, Labor MP warns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
11:45:08 UTC
20:45:08 KST

AI boom could widen income inequality, with only a handful of 'toll collectors' benefiting
In short:
Labor MP Andrew Leigh says artificial intelligence (AI) could see wage gaps shrink but he is concerned overall income inequality could rise.
He warns that a handful of AI companies could end up being the main economic beneficiaries.
What's next?
This week a Senate committee looking into AI guardrails will table their interim findings to the government.
If a handful of artificial intelligence (AI) companies become "toll collectors" for the rest of the economy, overall income inequality could rise even as wage gaps shrink, an MP is warning.
The assistant minister for productivity, competition, charities and treasury, Andrew Leigh, will make a case for whether AI increases inequality, during a speech to JPMorgan AI Conference tomorrow.
In an advance excerpt of his speech, Mr Leigh will argue that the biggest gains from AI may flow to those who own the technology, rather than those who use it.
"If a handful of AI companies become toll collectors for the rest of the economy, overall income inequality could rise even as wage gaps shrink," he will say.
Mr Leigh will make the link that while AI makes a junior worker more productive, it could reduce the number of junior workers a firm needs.
He will say the employment scoreboard currently reads: some concerning signals for young Americans, much less movement in Denmark, and Australian entry-level outcomes that remain solid.
It is possible that the US is atypical, or that effects there are driven primarily by the shift towards working from home. But it is also possible that the US is experiencing the impact of AI a year or two earlier than the rest of the advanced world.
He will argue if the junior accountant catches up with the senior accountant, the wage premium attached to education and experience falls and wage inequality could decline.
"Yet total income inequality could still rise. The reason is ownership," Mr Leigh will outline.
"It is quite possible for the first to become more equal while the second becomes more unequal. That could occur if pay packets equalise but the economy tilts in favour of capital."
He will highlight that AI can be a huge driver of productivity and economic benefit for Australia, but first people have to be able to trust that the technology is working for them, and not the other way around.
As assistant minister for competition, he says he is now "thinking hard about the effects of market structure".
He argues if every bank, law firm, retailer and manufacturer relies on a small number of upstream AI systems, then the model provider begins to resemble a toll road sitting across a growing share of the economy.
"The economic question is the size of the toll."
Mr Leigh will warn that a business may achieve a productivity improvement, yet retain only part of it if suppliers possess pricing power and competitors quickly copy the innovation.
Conversely, an AI provider with market power may collect rents across downstream industries.
Therefore the risk of AI on inequality is not primarily through its effect on the wage distribution but on who gets hired, who owns the productive assets, and how much of the surplus is captured by firms with market power.
"AI could narrow the gap between the novice and the expert, but at the same time, it could widen the gap between people who earn mainly from their work and people who earn heavily from owning productive capital."
Mr Leigh will state that AI will boost productivity but distributing the benefits fairly is the real challenge.
"Our government will apply the enduring values of fairness to make AI work for Australians."
Bipartisan agreement on AI guardrails within reach
The Joint Select Committee on Artificial Intelligence will this week table their interim findings to the government on AI guardrails.
Chair and Labor MP Jo Briskey joined Afternoon Briefing with the committee's deputy chair and Liberal senator Jonno Duniam to reveal they had come to an agreement about the direction the country should take on AI.
The committee was established to examine the opportunities and risks of AI, and the barriers to adopting the technology.
The federal government is trying to break a months-long gridlock over reforms to copyright laws, as AI companies seek to train their technology on creative content.
Ms Briskey said she sees a pathway to a bipartisan deal that will ensure creatives remain in control of their work.
"That's the key principle for us when negotiating the outcome, but as the study said, we have to get it right for Australia's interest and AI working for us, not the other way around," Ms Briskey said.
Senator Duniam said there needs to be a recognition of Australia's sovereignty and right for people who own copyright to be recompensed for the work they produce.
"I believe there is an opportunity for us to build our own sovereignty under our laws on our terms, our benefit," he said.
