Vicious circle of lacking experience leaving young people out of work in Estonia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
11:45:00 UTC
20:45:00 KST

Vicious circle of lacking experience leaving young people out of work in Estonia
A recent study suggests that employers could help address the problem by offering paid internships, while schools and families could begin guiding young people's career choices at an earlier age.
"In the past, the concern was more that young people were dropping out of university because they had already found jobs. Now they have completed higher or vocational education, but they can't find work. What has changed?" said Liina Maria Lepik, executive director of research and consultancy firm Center for Anthropology (AK). Rising youth unemployment is also reflected in national statistics: The unemployment rate among young people stood at 22.8 percent in the first quarter of 2026 and 22.4 percent in the second quarter. "When the overall unemployment rate is 7 percent, but youth unemployment is 22 percent, something is seriously wrong," Lepik said.
Seeking to better understand the reasons behind high youth unemployment and the barriers young people face when entering the labor market, AK teamed up with consulting firm Miltton to investigate the issue. Their qualitative study was based on 13 in-depth interviews with young people in Estonia ages 19 to 26 from a range of backgrounds. The researchers also included an autoethnographic account of one AK intern's experience looking for work.
During the interviews, participants were asked to describe their experiences applying for jobs and how these affected their daily lives and self-esteem. They were also asked to discuss factors that helped or hindered their job searches and the compromises they were willing to make to find employment. "The main problem is that employers demand work experience before young people have had a chance to gain any," said Miltton psychologist Eva Maria Kangro.
A problem for all stakeholders
According to the study's authors, young people in Estonia have found themselves caught in a vicious cycle when trying to enter the labor market. They pursue higher education and eagerly apply for various jobs during or after their studies. After receiving brief rejections, they submit more and more applications, while employers, overwhelmed by the flood of resumes, become increasingly less responsive. "Young people themselves describe this vicious cycle as being expected to have relevant work experience when applying for their first job, but no one is willing to give them the opportunity to gain it," Lepik said.
There is no single party to blame for the situation. According to Lepik, the vicious cycle has emerged through the combined actions of young people themselves, employers, the education system and the government and breaking it will likewise require efforts from all sides. Kangro said another contributing factor is that artificial intelligence is already replacing some entry-level jobs. "It would be easy to blame AI right away, but the problem is more systemic: There is a gap between education and working life," she said.
The study found that Estonia's higher education system and the education system more broadly is slow to respond to changes in society. By the time an OSKA report identifies which jobs are needed in the labor market, the corresponding curriculum updates, commissioned by the Ministry of Education and Research, reach universities several years later. "Ultimately, by the time a young person graduates, the education they chose to pursue may already be outdated and no longer needed in the labor market," Lepik said.
This is particularly painful in fields previously promoted as careers of the future. For years, the prevailing message was that people working in IT would always be able to find jobs, but the rise of AI has now eliminated entry-level positions in that very sector. "There have also been political shifts in the meantime. Now, young people graduating with degrees in sustainability and materials technology say their future has either already passed them by or has yet to arrive," Lepik added.
Employers are increasingly placing greater value on a diverse set of skills than on a university degree. "The ability to adapt quickly and be comfortable with technology is important. What matters now are entirely different skills from those universities have been equipping us with for decades," Lepik said.
Connections matter, but the work must be a good fit
The study also found that young people's socioeconomic backgrounds have a significant impact on how they begin their working lives. For example, only young people whose families can afford to support them can take on unpaid internships. "One young person who participated in our study even made the rather sad comment, 'I feel that if I were from Tallinn, I would have a much more successful life.' This highlights regional inequality," Lepik said.
Even more important than where young people come from are the personal connections they and their families have. Some participants admitted they saw no point in submitting their resumes because they believed no one would read them without the right connections. "Connections and networks matter a great deal. On the other hand, experience shows that when young people take the initiative and contact employers they are interested in directly, they do manage to find jobs that way," Kangro said.
During the interviews, young people were also asked about their expectations of jobs and employers. The findings showed that they increasingly prefer working environments that foster intrinsic motivation. "Young people don't just come to work to do a job. They want to do meaningful work in an environment that supports their development. When that kind of environment is in place, young people are extremely dedicated and willing to put in even more effort than required," Kangro said.
According to Lepik, young people often avoid sectors that conflict with their values. "For example, industries that harm people or the environment, and for some, the defense industry as well," she said. Young people also do not want work to come at a significant cost to their personal lives, involve long hours of overtime or expose them to a toxic workplace. "Perhaps we're the ones who should be learning from young people that this isn't a normal working environment. Maybe young people are wiser now, but the labor market doesn't yet know how to recognize that," Lepik reflected.
'Get in touch when you need me'
In light of the study's findings, the authors have issued recommendations for all parties involved in the vicious cycle of youth unemployment. As a psychologist, Kangro believes the first step should be to offer parents training on how to help young people shape their futures. "Parents have considerable power to encourage their children to explore different opportunities. The idea shouldn't be to choose a particular field because it will pay off, but rather to give children opportunities to try out different skills from an early age," she explained.
Parents can also support their children in gaining early work experience, whether through volunteering, youth work camps, farm work or extracurricular activities. Where possible, the researchers recommend that parents take their children to work to shadow them and introduce them to their professions.
"Education needs to respond more quickly and we probably need to start improving the reputation of vocational education," Lepik continued. She said that while higher education is fashionable and vocational education is still looked down on in some circles, the labor market actually needs people with vocational skills. "Vocational and applied higher education should be presented as positive choices, not as alternatives for those who couldn't get in elsewhere," Kangro agreed.
General education schools could introduce career planning earlier rather than leaving it until the final year of upper secondary school and organize more job-shadowing days and company visits. "Universities and vocational schools could also strengthen their ties with employers by providing practical experience throughout students' education and building a strong network of internship opportunities," Kangro recommended. This would require closer cooperation between universities and professional associations.
The researchers also suggest that the government consider tax incentives for internships undertaken during university studies. "University students already have health insurance coverage and when they take up internships during their studies, it makes a considerable difference to employers if payroll taxes are 33 percent lower," Lepik explained.
The research team also believes employers should give young people fresh out of school a chance, even when choosing from a large pool of applicants, whether through trial assignments or practical assessments. "A motivated young person learns quickly and soon becomes an indispensable employee. Right now, young people aren't even being given the chance to prove themselves," Lepik said. It is also important for employers to offer longer, paid internships, as these help reduce economic inequality when entering the labor market.
For young people who lack connections, the researchers recommend actively building them. Volunteering, joining school or university student organizations and taking the initiative can all help. "If there's an employer you admire, it's worth approaching them even if you don't have anything specific to offer at the moment. Tell them, 'I admire what you do, your work is important and if you ever need me, please get in touch,'" Lepik advised.
The study's report is available on the Center for Anthropology's website.
--

He also highlighted that UNESCO’s fundamental vision is to build lasting peace in the minds of women and men through education, culture, science, communication, and dialogue.
Hence, UNESCO and its national commissions bear a great responsibility for fostering regional peace, Fartousi noted.
Underscoring the unparalleled role of national commissions in aligning UNESCO’s global priorities with national realities and capacities, the official said strengthening national cooperation with UNESCO and its National Commissions is among the top priorities of the Iranian National Commission.
The Traditional Meeting of UNESCO National Commissions was opened by UNESCO Director-General Khaled El-Enany and Assistant Director-General for Africa Priority and External Relations Lidia Brito.
The discussions centered on reaffirming the role of National Commissions as a bridge between UNESCO and Member States, enhancing intersectoral cooperation, and increasing field office synergy.
Iran urges UNESCO to help restore scientific infrastructure damaged in war
On October 1, the head of the National Committee for Management of Social Transformations (MOST) called for UNESCO to play an effective role in safeguarding knowledge, ensuring uninterrupted access to learning, and rebuilding academic centers damaged during the US-Israeli imposed war against the country.
Highlighting the destructive impact of conflicts on educational institutions and human capacities, Seyyed Ziae Hashemi said the international community needs to pay close attention to these outcomes, IRNA reported.
The official made the remarks while addressing the extraordinary session of the Intergovernmental Council of MOST Program, which took place at UNESCO headquarters on October 1 in Paris; the official and the Secretary General of Iran’s National Commission for UNESCO attended the session online.
Referring to the impacts of the US-Israeli war against Iran, and the damage inflicted on certain educational and scientific institutions, cultural heritage and civilian infrastructures, he called for UNESCO to utilize its capacities for rebuilding scientific and educational capacities, strengthening international cooperation, and supporting sustainable development.
“International responses must be tailored to the specific circumstances of each crisis, while simultaneously placing the fundamental principles of protecting human lives, safeguarding knowledge, and ensuring the continuity of learning at the heart of these efforts,” he added.
“The catastrophic dimensions of war in Gaza have inflicted irreparable damage on civilians, educational centers, cultural and scientific activities; the international bodies have to make it clear what they can do within the frameworks of BRIDGES and MOST to protect knowledge, sustain education and research,” he added.
The restoration of the right to education for Afghan girls and women was another issue raised by the official.

Access to knowledge, equal learning opportunities, and universal participation in research are fundamental rights in human society.

The Intergovernmental Council (IGC) of the MOST Program was established by UNESCO Member States in 1994. It is composed of 35 Member States elected by the General Conference, whose representatives meet every two years to guide and oversee the planning and implementation of the MOST Program. The IGC defines the MOST Program’s broad priorities, reviews its activities and achievements, and helps strengthen the link between social and human sciences research and public policy.
Through its work, the IGC provides a platform for Member States to exchange on contemporary social transformations and to promote more inclusive, evidence-based policies aligned with national priorities.

Recsuers said Monday it is a race
against time to save a 31-year-old Sardinian potholer who has
been trapped in a cave on the island since a rockslide on
Sunday.
                                    
Rescue operations are continuing apace for the caver from
Sassari who became trapped in the Gorropeddu cave in Urzulei.
                                    
Rescuers, who have been working since Sunday afternoon and
throughout the night, cleared the cave entrance and stabilized
the access walls this morning to prevent further collapses; they
have now reached the narrow passage where the young caver—alive
and conscious—has been trapped for 20 hours following a rockfall
that caught him by surprise while he was exploring the cave.
                                    
The teams on site (48 members of the Sardinia Alpine and
Speleological Rescue Corps, alongside 30 firefighters
specializing in USAR-M, SAF, and TAS operations, with support
from the Dorgali Civil Protection) cleared boulders from the
entrance and are now proceeding with the delicate manual removal
of material obstructing the passage where the caver remains
trapped beneath the debris.
                                    
The operation is taking place in an extremely confined space—a
work area of approximately 1.5 by 1.5 meters—characterized by
highly unstable conditions.
                                    
As they excavate and remove material, rescuers must stabilize
the walls by installing retaining boards to prevent further
collapses and allow for safer progress.
                                    
A helicopter is expected to arrive shortly, carrying additional
materials and equipment needed to secure the site, with the aim
of enabling rescuers to reach the man and remove the earth and
stones pinning him down.

Interior Minister Mustafa Çiftçi (AA File Photo)
Türkiye has pledged to step up efforts to tackle Turkish criminal gangs operating across Europe, with Interior Minister Mustafa Çiftçi announcing plans to visit Germany and Italy for talks with his counterparts on cooperation in combating organized crime and securing the return of fugitives.
Çiftçi has embarked on a series of visits to countries where members of Turkish criminal networks are believed to have sought refuge to evade legal proceedings at home.
Since taking office in February, he has visited neighboring Georgia and Bulgaria before traveling to Greece last week, where he met with Greek Minister for Citizen Protection Michalis Chrisochoidis and Minister for Migration and Asylum Thanos Plevris.
Speaking to local broadcaster KonTV over the weekend, Çiftçi vowed to intensify the crackdown on organized crime, warning fugitives against assuming they could evade justice by fleeing abroad.
He said his upcoming visits to Germany and Italy would help strengthen cooperation to track down and repatriate suspects wanted in Türkiye.
Turkish gang leader Barış Boyun was arrested in Italy in May 2024 during a joint operation and is currently held at L’Aquila prison under the 41-bis regime, a stringent detention system that severely restricts contact with the outside world.
Italy has rejected Türkiye’s requests concerning Boyun’s extradition and asylum.
In Germany, meanwhile, numerous members of Turkish criminal gangs, specifically Daltons, are known to operate.
Türkiye has increasingly focused on so-called “next-generation gangs,” which have expanded their activities in recent years.
Unlike traditional Turkish mafia groups, these networks frequently recruit minors and teenagers to carry out crimes ranging from extortion to murder. They also use social media to publicize their activities, glorify criminal behavior and attract new recruits.
“As of the end of September, we had conducted 1,741 operations targeting 625 criminal organizations as part of our campaign against next-generation gangs. The total reflects repeated operations against certain groups. These efforts resulted in 8,170 people being arrested and remanded in custody,” Çiftçi said.
He stressed that the groups operate beyond Türkiye’s borders, with members often fleeing overseas when they come under pressure from law enforcement.
“Next-generation criminal organizations do not confine their activities to Türkiye. When they get into trouble, their members immediately flee abroad. I visited Bulgaria in recent months to address this issue, followed by Georgia, where I met with the interior minister. On Thursday [Oct. 8], I was in Greece, holding separate talks with the ministers responsible for citizen protection and migration and asylum,” he said.
Çiftçi said the meetings focused on security cooperation, the activities of emerging criminal networks and the countries in which their members seek shelter.
Türkiye secured the extradition of 736 people from abroad during the first nine months of the year, according to Çiftçi. He said the individuals had committed crimes in Türkiye before fleeing overseas in an attempt to escape prosecution.
“We will increase that number through our upcoming visits and continued security diplomacy. We will pursue every one of them and bring them back to Türkiye,” he added.

German industry expects Russian sabotage against the country’s companies to persist and take more forms, the deputy head of the Federation of German Industries (BDI) told Handelsblatt. His warning follows alarms from Germany’s intelligence services, which describe the country as a main target of Russia’s covert campaign in Europe.
Russia keeps striking Ukrainian cities and power plants every day while trying to weaken the European support that keeps Ukraine fighting. Germany is home to arms makers producing with and for Ukraine, so pressure on its companies targets the supply behind Ukraine’s defense.
Industry expects attacks to last and change form
The warning came from Holger Lösch, the BDI’s deputy managing director.
“German industry is preparing for the threat to persist and for attack methods to become more varied,” he told Handelsblatt. “Companies don’t end up in the crosshairs by chance,” he added.
Russian influence and sabotage operations are no longer an abstract scenario, and companies, critical infrastructure, and defense supply chains are already among their targets, Lösch said. Companies now receive more threat warnings, and their cooperation with the authorities has improved significantly, he noted. “What is still missing are joint procedures to quickly derive concrete measures from warnings,” Lösch said, calling the protection of the economy a cornerstone of national security.
German intelligence describes a Russian shadow war
The warning comes a week after a public hearing of the intelligence oversight panel of the Bundestag, Germany’s parliament, on 5 October. There, Martin Jäger, head of Germany’s Federal Intelligence Service (BND), said Russia was waging a shadow war against Germany. “Germany has become a main obstacle to Russian hegemonic power projection in Europe and thus a target of Russian action,” Jäger said. “The danger of attacks against targets in Germany remains real and present,” he warned.
Sinan Selen, head of the Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution (BfV), Germany’s domestic intelligence agency, told the same hearing that Russia was showing a readiness for sabotage and killings.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said on 1 October that Germany was preparing for further hybrid attacks, “including serious ones,” and would respond “quickly and very clearly,” as it did after the drone attack at Leipzig airport.
Drone bombs, arson, and paid saboteurs on German soil
In August, a drone carrying Semtex explosives hit the wing of a Ukrainian An-124 cargo plane at Leipzig/Halle Airport but did not explode. Germany blamed Russia on 1 September, and German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said Germany was not at war with Russia but was a “target of war.”
German authorities suspect Russian intelligence of commissioning an arson attack near two Munich defense firms, and a confidential Federal Criminal Police Office (BKA) assessment counted more than 165 suspected sabotage cases in Germany between January and August. The same assessment recorded 747 suspicious drone incidents involving 1,068 drones over critical infrastructure, military sites, and defense companies.
The throwaway agents Moscow sent after a Bavarian drone boss arming Ukraine—and how Germany stopped them
Germany’s Military Counterintelligence Service (MAD) warns that the threat from low-level agents, locals paid small sums for one-off jobs such as arson or photographing military sites, has increased significantly. European intelligence agencies also report that Russia is increasingly targeting defense company executives, including at smaller drone makers, and the BfV has advised some German firms to hire close protection.
As long as Germany keeps backing Ukraine, Russian pressure on its companies is unlikely to ease, and the gap between warnings and action that industry flagged leaves smaller firms, with fewer resources for security, the most exposed.

UN official: Environmental protection must be integral to post-war recovery
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
11:41:43 UTC
20:41:43 KST

UN official: Environmental protection must be integral to post-war recovery
TEHRAN – UN Resident Coordinator in Iran Christine Weigand has stressed the far-reaching and long-term environmental consequences of war, saying environmental protection must be incorporated into both emergency response measures and long-term recovery plans, as protecting the environment ultimately means safeguarding human health, livelihoods and the future.
Weigand made the remarks in Tehran on Sunday at a conference on the environmental consequences of war and human rights.
Referring to the loss of human lives, the displacement of families and the destruction of homes and infrastructure, she said the environment and valuable ecosystems were also among the victims of war, warning that the damage inflicted on them could persist for generations.
Conflicts and environmental degradation, she noted, reinforce one another, deepening human suffering, undermining livelihoods and food security, and making reconstruction and the achievement of sustainable development more difficult.
Weigand also referred to the United Nations’ designation of November 6 as the International Day for Preventing the Exploitation of the Environment in War and Armed Conflict in 2001. She noted that contaminated water resources, damaged agricultural land and degraded ecosystems have consequences that extend far beyond the immediate destruction caused by war, undermining communities’ ability to rebuild their lives.
Citing examples of environmental damage in the conflicts in Gaza and Ukraine, the UN official addressed the consequences of attacks on oil facilities and water infrastructure in Iran. She said attacks on oil facilities had released smoke containing hazardous substances into Tehran’s atmosphere, while damage to a desalination facility on Qeshm Island had reportedly disrupted water supplies to more than 25 villages.
Weigand also warned of the possibility of oil pollution reaching the mangrove forests on Qeshm Island, emphasizing that such contamination could threaten sensitive coastal ecosystems along the Persian Gulf.
Recalling her own experience of air pollution in Tehran following the attacks on oil facilities, she said that, for millions of people, the issue was not merely an environmental concern but one that directly affected the air they breathed every day.
The UN Resident Coordinator cautioned that the disappearance of visible smoke does not necessarily mean the danger has passed. Burning oil can release hazardous compounds, she explained, and the resulting pollution can contaminate soil and water, affect agricultural produce and threaten human health. These consequences may persist long after a conflict ends, with children and future generations particularly vulnerable.
Emphasizing that investment in environmental protection is an investment in people and their future, Weigand said healthy ecosystems sustain community livelihoods, provide clean water and safe food, and strengthen societies’ resilience to crises. Conversely, the degradation of these systems increases vulnerability and makes recovery more difficult.
She identified evidence-based assessments, stronger national environmental management capacities, cooperation among different sectors and national and international institutions, and investment in climate change adaptation as essential measures for protecting and restoring the environment in conflict-affected countries.
Weigand also highlighted the longstanding cooperation between the UN Country Team in Iran and national partners in areas including climate resilience, sustainable water resource management, biodiversity conservation and pollution reduction. She reaffirmed the UN’s commitment to continuing this cooperation and its readiness to support national efforts to address emerging environmental needs.
Concluding her remarks, the UN official stressed that commitment to protecting and restoring nature must remain unwavering in the face of global environmental challenges.
“Our shared responsibility is to protect what remains, restore what has been damaged, and invest in building a more sustainable and peaceful future for all,” she said.

Mustafa Prize laureate donates award money to support young scientists
TEHRAN – Turkish Professor Mehmet Toner, a 2025 laureate of the Mustafa Prize, has pledged his share of the prize money to support the development of the Rasul Medal and provide research grants for young scientists.
Toner was named one of three laureates of the Mustafa Prize in 2025. Under the prize’s regulations, the $500,000 cash award was divided among the three recipients.
The biomedical engineering scientist has now pledged his share of the award to jointly support young scientists through the Rasul Medal and fund research grants for early-career researchers.
Before Toner, Professors Ugur Sahin, Omid Farokhzad, and Wahab Mirrokni, laureates of the Mustafa Prize in 2019, 2023, and 2025, respectively, had also donated their prize money to establish and sustain the Rasul (PBUH) Medal.
Born in 1958, Toner is a professor of biomedical engineering at Harvard Medical School. He received the sixth Mustafa Prize in 2025 for developing nanomicrofluidic systems. The technology isolates circulating tumor cells from the bloodstream, enabling earlier disease detection, monitoring of treatment progress, and the development of more precise therapies.
The Rasul Medal is presented alongside the Mustafa Prize to young scientists from the Islamic world under the age of 40.
The initial list of nominees for the second edition of the Rasul Medal, has been finalized.
The shortlist comprises four nominees in engineering sciences, four in mathematics, four in computer science, eight in biological and medical sciences, two in chemistry, and two in physics. The award ceremony for the final winners is scheduled to be held in December.
The initial list considered for the Rasul Medal included more than 100,000 candidates across seven scientific fields. The biological and medical sciences category accounted for 55,878 candidates, followed by 4,675 in physics, 7,897 in chemistry, 1,965 in mathematics, 5,589 in computer science, and 26,377 in engineering sciences. In addition, 14 candidates in the field of nanotechnology met the required criteria to be included in the initial list.
In order to appreciate prominent scientists and provide the ground for scientific cooperation and development worldwide, the Mustafa Prize was established in 2012 as a symbol of scientific excellence at the international level.
The Mustafa Prize, a top science and technology award, is granted biennially to the top researchers and scientists of the Islamic world in three categories: “Life and Medical Science and Technology”, “Information and Communication Science and Technology”, and “Basic and Engineering Sciences”.
The Prize is granted to works deemed to have improved human life, have made tangible and cutting-edge innovations on the boundaries of science, or have presented new scientific methodology.
One of the objectives of the Mustafa Prize Foundation is to establish a scientific network. The goal is not merely to introduce the prize laureates, but also to connect scientists, enabling them to be identified while creating an environment conducive to synergy, collaboration and mutual scientific exchange.

September was world's second warmest on record as temperatures exceeded 1.5°C
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
14:39:17 EEST
20:39:17 KST

September 2026 was the world's second warmest September on record, with global temperatures reaching 1.63°C above pre-industrial levels for the second consecutive month, according to data released on Monday by the EU's Copernicus Climate Change Service.
The global average temperature reached 16.27°C, exceeding the 1991–2020 September average by 0.82°C. Only September 2023 was warmer, by 0.11°C.
Add Helsinki Times as a preferred source on Google (opens Google in a new tab)
The findings mark the first time since November 2025 that global temperatures have exceeded the 1.5°C threshold for two consecutive months. Scientists expect the current period of elevated temperatures, which began in August, to continue into 2027 as El Niño conditions strengthen.
"September was the second warmest on record globally, with exceptionally high temperatures experienced again across parts of Europe after an extreme summer," said Carlo Buontempo, director of the Copernicus Climate Change Service.
He warned that crossing the Paris Agreement's long-term warming threshold was approaching, although individual months above 1.5°C do not constitute a breach of the agreement's long-term target.
The Finnish Meteorological Institute said repeated monthly exceedances indicate that long-term global warming is approaching the same level.
"Current estimates suggest that the 1.5-degree threshold will be reached more permanently towards the end of this decade," researcher Mika Rantanen said.
Europe recorded its third warmest September, with an average temperature of 16.26°C, or 1.54°C above the 1991–2020 average.
Western Europe experienced its joint warmest September, matching the 2023 record at 2.51°C above average. The region had already recorded its warmest summer.
Finland also experienced warmer-than-average conditions, with temperatures across much of the country exceeding the 1991–2020 average by between 1°C and 1.5°C, according to the Finnish Meteorological Institute.
The prolonged warmth coincided with drought across western, central and parts of eastern Europe. River flows reached record September lows in sections of the Rhine, Danube, Vistula and Garonne-Dordogne, disrupting shipping, agriculture and water supplies.
Dry conditions intensified across parts of Spain, Portugal, France, Italy, the western Balkans and Greece. Rainfall towards the end of September brought some relief but also caused flooding in parts of France and Spain.
Ocean temperatures reached a September record. The average sea surface temperature outside the polar regions climbed to 21.05°C, surpassing the previous record of 20.92°C set in 2023.
In the tropical Pacific, temperatures in the Niño 3.4 monitoring region reached 29.70°C, exceeding previous peaks associated with major El Niño events.
Copernicus reported that Antarctic sea ice reached its third-lowest winter maximum in the satellite record. September's monthly extent stood approximately 6% below average.
Arctic sea ice reached its annual summer minimum, ranking 14th lowest in the satellite record, while its monthly extent was approximately 10% below average.

2026-10-12
11:39:01 UTC
20:39:01 KST

African power at the UN: Will the continent get the veto?
At the 81st session of the UN General Assembly in September, appeals for Africa to gain two permanent seats on the UN Security Council (UNSC) grew louder, with leaders from Asia, Latin America, and Africa advocating for systemic equality.
Demands for fair representation have become Africa’s most persistent diplomatic priority at the United Nations since the African Union adopted the Ezulwini Consensus in 2005. At the September sitting, Kenyan President William Ruto reminded delegates that the equality proclaimed in the General Assembly ends at the Security Council doors.
Ruto argued that Africa’s 54 countries comprise almost a quarter of the UN’s membership, and its people represent about one-fifth of humanity. Nevertheless, the continent still has no permanent Security Council seat.
“That imbalance might have reflected the world of 1945; it does not reflect the world of today. Reform must lead to equitable and permanent representation for Africa, with all the prerogatives and privileges of permanent Council membership,” Ruto told the session.
Ghana President John Dramani Mahama said Africa’s exclusion from permanent membership of the Security Council was “fundamentally unacceptable in the 21st century,” calling for permanent representation with full rights and veto powers.
“Security Council reform is not a favor to Africa; it is an imperative for the legitimacy, credibility, and survival of the United Nations,” Mahama said.
Outgoing UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres observed that the Security Council, designed in the aftermath of World War II, must be reformed to reflect today’s world with the legitimacy and effectiveness that today’s challenges demand.
“When the UN was founded, most of Africa was still under colonial rule. Today, Africa still has no permanent representation on the Council. A 21st-century Security Council without permanent African seats is unjust and indefensible. This must change,” Guterres said.
“Not just fill seats but bring meaningful change”
But even as calls for Africa to get a permanent UNSC seat grew bolder, experts on the continent say something needs to be put right first. Faisal Roble, a Horn of Africa political analyst based in Arusha, Tanzania, says Africa’s grievance is legitimate, but diplomacy alone cannot fix it.
Roble says Africa must be well-represented in rooms where decisions about its future are made because the current arrangement befits neither the continent nor the United Nations’ legitimacy.
“Africa is asking to help govern global security while at the same time it is home to several places providing a setting for some of the world’s gravest security failures. The continent must show it has capability by first putting its house in order,” Roble told RT.
Roble observes that support for Africa’s demand for equal power on the Security Council exists beyond the continent. Still, leaders must show the continent “will not just fill seats but bring meaningful change to the critical UN institution.”
“The argument should now move beyond Africa having 54 countries and more than 1.5 billion people to what the continent brings to the table. The current five permanent members have both military and financial power, and Africa must then bring something unique and different,” Roble said.
Roble argues that for Africa to succeed, it must move “beyond mere diplomatic rhetoric” and strategize on how to overcome structural obstacles to pushing through an amendment to the UN Charter that will grant the continent two permanent seats on the UNSC.
“Africa can get the required two-thirds support from member states to push through the amendment, but it must strategize on how such an amendment can get ratification by all five permanent members because here is where the real obstacle is,” he notes.
“Homegrown solutions that can fix the continent’s problems”
Dr. Jalale Getachew Birru, a security and peace analyst at Armed Conflict Location & Event Data (ACLED), says it will be impossible for Africa to secure a permanent seat with veto powers at the UNSC if the continent cannot prove that it can end its own wars.
“Africa has continuously relied on the big brothers in solving every economic, social and political problem at home. The continent has unending conflicts, and this portrays it as poorly placed to help manage the world’s security concerns,” Dr. Birru told RT.
According to the expert, permanent UNSC membership carries responsibility for international peace and security. If Africa cannot handle its own conflicts, it will find it harder to persuade skeptical capitals like Washington and London that the continent deserves equal powers on the council.
“To a great extent, the majority of decisions made at the UNSC affect Africa, and it is for this reason that the continent must have a voice at the table, but our leaders must demonstrate to the whole world that they have homegrown solutions that can fix the continent’s problems without waiting for support and direction from the West,” the expert said.
Dr. Birru argues that Africa’s leverage in its quest for a permanent UNSC seat is to “show that African institutions and solutions work.”
“Africa must take more responsibility for its own security”
Mesenbet Assefa, Senior Fellow at the HORN Institute, explains that having a functional AU Peace and Security Council will strengthen Africa’s quest to gain power at the UNSC.
He says the AU must stop responding selectively to crises on the continent, especially those perpetuated by sitting heads of state, and that African governments need to show they can carry out the responsibilities they are asking to share.
“It will be ironic for Africa to get a permanent seat and veto powers at the UNSC when the AU peace and security council is dysfunctional. Africa must take more responsibility for its own security by funding mechanisms that curb the flow of arms and illicit minerals that sustain the unending crises on the continent,” said Assefa.
He added, “Africa must take a prominent and leading role in ending the current conflicts in Sudan, DR Congo, Ethiopia, South Sudan, and the Sahel.”
At the same time, Assefa notes that Africa must arrive at the negotiating table with a settled proposal on which of its members will serve as permanent members of the UNSC.
“With support from Russia, China and France, Africa might succeed in pushing for two permanent seats on the UNSC, but there will be trouble on the allocation of the seats, and this will complicate the whole process. The continent’s quest will be deflected the moment they start arguing over who sits where,” Assefa told RT.
The Security Council has primary responsibility for maintaining international peace and security. It has five permanent and ten non-permanent members elected for two-year terms.
Each member of the council has one vote. The five permanent members – China, France, the Russian Federation, the United Kingdom, and the United States – have veto powers which they can use to overrule any decision made.

Israel's war on Nobel Laureate Navi Pillay is a war on international law itself
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
11:36:40 UTC
20:36:40 KST

The announcement that South African human rights lawyer Navi Pillay won the Nobel Peace Prize apparently knocked off balance the Israeli Foreign Ministry's social media staffer.
"If there were an award for lies, hatred, and blood libels, Navi Pillay wouldn't just be a contender. She'd be a frontrunner," the ministry wrote on the day the prize was awarded. It added: "Now that the Nobel commission has rewarded the biggest lie of the 21st century, Joseph Goebbels is certainly applauding from hell."
Israel's ambassador to the United Nations, Danny Danon, also raised the dead when he wrote that Menachem Begin, Henry Kissinger and Martin Luther King were turning in their graves.
These reactions reflect the chasm that has opened in the last decade between Israel on one side and UN agencies and the mainstream of international law on the other. The relationship with Pillay, which has mostly seen downturns since 2011, is a mainstay of this chasm that will largely shape Israel's relations with the world in the coming decades.
Pillay went from a state visit to Israel in 2011 to severe criticism of the occupation and Israeli human rights violations in the West Bank. Heading a UN commission of inquiry, she went from lambasting Hamas' crimes on October 7 to harsh reports on suspected Israeli war crimes in Gaza, even concluding that Israel's actions amounted to genocide.
In her reports, Israelis can find not only detailed documentation of crimes by both sides but also evidence and conclusions on Israel's failure to protect its citizens. To some extent, Pillay also entered the vacuum created by the government's refusal to form a state commission of inquiry.
Pillay, 85, has served as an anti-apartheid activist, the UN human rights commissioner, the first non-white woman justice on South Africa's Supreme Court, and a member of the tribunal that prosecuted the perpetrators of the Rwandan genocide. So her opinion can't be easily dismissed. The detailed reports she heads are packed with facts and legal analyses.
In 2011, when she served as UN human rights commissioner, she was the last person in that office to visit Israel. She met with senior officials at the time including President Shimon Peres and Supreme Court President Dorit Beinisch. She even visited Yad Vashem.
Such a trip has now become unimaginable, after Israel's radicalization and distancing from the UN and international law. All commissioners after Pillay have been boycotted by Israel, which ceased cooperation with the UN Human Rights Council.
In 2021, the council held a special session following the events of May that year – an air war between Israel and Gaza and Jewish-Arab violence in Israel. The council appointed an independent commission of inquiry for the region and put Pillay at its helm. With some justification, Israel argued that the commission enjoyed a broad mandate compared to similar UN committees. Its brief included not only the West Bank and East Jerusalem but also Israel itself and even the right to investigate the "roots of the conflict."
The commission's mandate also does not require periodic renewal but renews automatically. All told, the wide mandate and Pillay's stature made her reports crucial in shaping the international legal discourse on Israel.
In October 2022, the commission recommended that the UN General Assembly request an advisory opinion from the International Court of Justice in The Hague on the legality of the occupation. The opinion handed down two years later was unequivocal: Israel violates international law and its control of the West Bank is illegal. The opinion, approved by the General Assembly, became a milestone in how the international community views Israel and the occupation. For example, recent decisions by European countries to boycott products from the settlements are largely based on this decision.
In May 2023, the commission published a report on civil society in Israel and the parts of the West Bank governed by the Palestinian Authority. The report was highly critical of both sides, addressing Israel's restrictions on journalists and rights activists, as well as infringements on freedom of expression and restrictions on civil society organizations and journalists in PA territory and Hamas-ruled Gaza.
Later that year, the commission began investigating the events of October 7. Its basic rule was that an event was verified when there was supporting information from at least "two independent and reliable sources." In cases of sexual violence or torture, where verification of testimony can be particularly difficult, a single reliable primary source or consistency with a pattern of similar events may suffice.
On this basis, the commission published two reports in June 2024. The first dealt with the events of October 7, and the wide mandate it received three years earlier allowed it to address Hamas crimes' in Israel.
The report on October 7 spans 59 pages and includes close analyses of the main sites including kibbutzim, army bases, Zikim Beach and Sderot. In fact, in the absence of a state commission of inquiry, the UN report is a broader and more detailed document than any published by the Israeli government on the events of October 7. (The Israeli army has published detailed investigations into most of the major events, but Israelis have still not received a comprehensive report on what happened in the Gaza border communities.)
The commission determined that Hamas committed a long list of war crimes including murder, abductions, torture, beheadings, the desecration of bodies, the burning of bodies and sexual violence. But according to the panel, the Israeli authorities failed to protect the citizens, security forces were not deployed quickly enough, and the activation of the so-called Hannibal Directive, which allows "all means" to prevent the capturing of soldiers – caused the deaths of at least 14 civilians.
Lacking a state commission of inquiry's conclusions, Israelis can at least be content that a commission headed by a Nobel Peace Prize laureate determined that the authorities abandoned the citizens. Immediately after this report was published, a second document addressed Israel's response to Hamas' attack and included harsh criticism of the bombings and harm to innocent civilians in Gaza.
As evidence mounted of possible war crimes by Israel, Pillay's reports became increasingly harsh. Throughout 2024 and 2025, she published reports on systematic sexual violence against Palestinian detainees and civilians and the destruction of Gaza's healthcare system. In September 2025, the commission published its most scathing report, declaring that Israel had committed genocide.
The commission determined that the Israeli army and other security forces committed four out of five acts considered genocide under the 1948 UN Genocide Convention: killing members of a group, causing serious bodily or mental harm, deliberately inflicting conditions of life designed to physically destroy the group in whole or in part, and imposing measures intended to prevent births in the group. The fifth act, of which Israel was not accused, is "forcibly transferring children of the group to another group."
"It is clear there is an intent to destroy the Palestinians in Gaza through acts that meet the criteria set forth in the Genocide Convention. The responsibility for these atrocity crimes lies with Israeli authorities at the highest echelons who have orchestrated a genocidal campaign for almost two years now with the specific intent to destroy the Palestinian group in Gaza," Pillay said. The report joined numerous others by rights groups and petitions by legal scholars.
Due to Pillay's standing and the commission's meticulous investigation, the panel has special status in the world of international law. Israel, of course, angrily rejected the report and berated its authors and conclusions. But the chasm that has opened between Israel and the doyens of international law can no longer be bridged.
International law doesn't behave like domestic law. It is heavily influenced by the political balance of power, and the backing of the Trump administration has so far allowed Israel to keep ignoring it. The wheels of international justice grind even slower than the judges in Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's corruption trial.
But they do grind, and, as Pillay's reports show, the chasm that has opened between Israel and international norms will shape Israel's image for the foreseeable future.

NATO commander Grynkewich warns Russia attack would be 'utterly futile'
WARSAW, Oct 12 - NATO's top commander bluntly warned Russia on Monday that his forces would destroy "anything and everything" involved in any attack if Moscow was "foolish enough" to launch an assault on alliance territory.
Outlining his "theory of victory" at a security conference in Warsaw, U.S. Air Force General Alexus Grynkewich said NATO was a defensive alliance but it would block, blunt and break any attack against any of its members to ensure the assault proved "utterly futile".
Grynkewich, NATO's Supreme Allied Commander Europe, made his remarks at a time of rising tension between European nations and Russia.
European governments have accused Moscow of stepping up a campaign of sabotage, drone incursions and cyberattacks against them and Russia warned last month it would use nuclear weapons if NATO attempted to cut off its exclave of Kaliningrad.
In his speech to the Warsaw Security Forum, Grynkewich did not mention by Russia name but his message was clearly directed at Moscow. NATO's 2022 Strategic Concept describes Russia as the most significant threat to the alliance's security.
"If someone is foolish enough to attack us, we will fight," he said. "We will stop the attack and deny them the ability to achieve their objectives, whatever those might be. We will, in short, ensure any attack, against any ally, proves utterly futile."
Grynkewich issued a clear message to Moscow that, if necessary, this would involve massive retaliation, striking far beyond the forces in the area under attack.
"Should the adversary choose to press the attack or commit his reserves, we will break the warfighting system engaged against us," he said.
"This includes not just the attacking force itself, but anything and everything that supports, sustains, and controls that force." REUTERS

BIG stacks floating terraces above green public space in tirana

BIG stacks floating terraces above green public space in tirana
a translucent facade, slender columns, and an open ground plane shape a proposal that brings public space, community facilities, and the surrounding landscape into a single architectural framework.
BIG raises cloud-like building above public park in albania
Bjarke Ingels Group (BIG) wins the Fountain Plaza Tirana international design competition with a proposal that raises the building above a park-like public realm in Tirana, Albania. The project combines elevated building volumes, a translucent facade, and a network of slender columns to create an architecture that remains open to the landscape. BIG approaches the site as a continuous public environment, integrating an open-access library, community facilities, and a covered public auditorium with the surrounding greenery.
The proposal rests on the idea that the building and landscape should operate as one. A dense field of slender, cane-like columns lifts the structure above ground level, leaving space for public activity and allowing pedestrians to move through the footprint. The jury particularly praised this permeability, describing the scheme as one of the most generous park experiences among the competition entries.
The upper floors are set back to bring natural light into the covered auditorium and make room for planting. Vegetation and public spaces extend beneath and around the building, while the structure provides shade and shelter. Its translucent facade contrasts with the slender supporting columns, giving the building a light, layered appearance.
Fountain Plaza Tirana connects public space, water, and urban life
An open-access library and integrated community facilities are intended to make the ground level an active social destination rather than a residual space beneath a large building. The covered auditorium adds another public program, creating an area for collective gatherings within the elevated structure. This emphasis on shared space also informs the relationship of the project with its wider urban context. According to the jury, BIG’s proposal considers the possibility of pedestrianizing the adjacent traffic road and extending the park toward the neighboring area. These moves suggest an approach that reaches beyond the immediate footprint of the building, treating the competition as an opportunity to reconsider how pedestrians, green space, and surrounding infrastructure might connect. The jury highlighted the integration of the adjacent canal as an active component of the team’s design, linking the waterway to the environmental and microclimatic conditions of the site.

Iran to expand nuclear technology applications in healthcare
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
11:34:49 UTC
20:34:49 KST

Iran to expand nuclear technology applications in healthcare
TEHRAN – The Ministry of Health and the Atomic Energy Organization of Iran (AEOI) have signed a memorandum of understanding to expand the application of nuclear technology in the healthcare sector.
Health Minister Mohammad-Reza Zafarqandi and AEOI chief Mohammad Eslami signed the agreement, which primarily aims to control Aedes mosquito populations and combat dengue, chikungunya, and Zika viruses through the sterile insect technique (SIT), IRNA reported.
The initiative is an environmentally friendly pest control method; male mosquitoes are mass-reared and sterilized using irradiation. The release of sterilized male insects significantly declines the insect population.
Accordingly, both parties will utilize the scientific, research, and technological capacities of the country to launch a center for Aedes aegypti mass-rearing, and conduct pilot and field studies to evaluate the effectiveness of the technology.
The AEOI will help supply gamma or X-ray irradiation equipment, train personnel, provide specialists in the fields of irradiation and dosimetry, and guarantee the performance and maintenance of the delivered equipment.
Mosquitoes only need a small amount of water to lay eggs. Bowls, cups, fountains, tires, barrels, vases, and any other container storing water make a great nursery.
Dengue is a viral infection transmitted to humans through the bite of infected mosquitoes. The disease is transmitted through the bite of Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus mosquitoes. These mosquitoes also transmit the Zika and Chikungunya viruses, making them a significant threat to public health.
Dengue disease has different infectious phases, including the fever phase, critical phase, and recovery phase.
Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus have been recorded in the country. Aedes aegypti is a more invasive mosquito that is more common in Iran. Due to the physiology of this mosquito, people in contaminated areas are told to wear clothes that cover most parts of their bodies for the first two hours of the morning and two hours before evening.
Transmission occurs two days before symptoms and two days after the fever. The disease can spread from mosquitoes to humans, from humans to mosquitoes, and from humans to humans through blood transfusion, organ transplant, and mother to child in pregnancy.
The lifespan of Aedes mosquitoes is between one and 4 weeks; they take blood meals every 1 – 2 hours, accounting for 40 to 50 meals throughout their lifespan.
About 40 to 80 percent of patients with dengue have mild or no symptoms. By adhering to sanitation practices, dengue fever cases can be reduced by 70 percent.
Aedes aegypti was first reported in Hormozgan province in 2019. Now, the mosquito is found in Hormozgan, Sistan-Baluchestan (Chabahar and Konarak), Bushehr, and Fars provinces.
The other species, Aedes albopictus, has been observed in the northern and northwestern provinces, including Gilan, Mazandaran, Ardabil, East Azerbaijan, and Zanjan.
According to the World Health Organization (WHO), about half of the world’s population is now at risk of dengue, with an estimated 100–400 million infections occurring each year.
Prevention and control of dengue rely on vector control. There is no specific treatment for dengue/severe dengue, and early detection and access to proper medical care greatly lower fatality rates of severe dengue.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan’s machinery exports reached NT$109.24 billion (US$3.44 billion) in September, up 35.8% from a year earlier and extending their year-on-year growth streak to 20 months, the Taiwan Association of Machinery Industry (TAMI) said Monday.

TAMI warned that conflict in the Middle East continues to affect energy and raw material prices, while geopolitical tensions and export controls on high-tech goods and rare earths could disrupt global supply chains, per RTI. As the machinery industry relies heavily on overseas markets, longer lead times and difficulties sourcing key components could affect orders and exports, it said.
The machine tool sector remained weaker, with exports totaling NT$5.32 billion in September, down 1.8% from a year earlier, according to the Taiwan Machine Tool and Accessory Builders’ Association, per CNA. Exports in the first nine months fell 1.9% to NT$47.42 billion, while imports rose 15.8% to NT$15.83 billion.
The association said the sector showed diverging trends, as exports of key components rose 13.1% in the first three quarters despite declining finished-machine shipments. Component exports to Italy, India, and Vietnam grew, while demand for machine tools was strong in India, Vietnam, and Malaysia.
TAMI said the weaker Japanese yen and South Korean won continued to weigh on the competitiveness of machine tools. The US was the largest destination for machinery exports in the first nine months, accounting for 26%, followed by China at 21.1% and Singapore at 7.6%.

Ukraine Reveals Russia’s Kinzhal Missile Secrets—From Nuclear Warheads to 22 Unsanctioned Manufacturers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
11:31:32 UTC
20:31:32 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine Reveals Russia’s Kinzhal Missile Secrets—From Nuclear Warheads to 22 Unsanctioned Manufacturers
Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence Directorate (HUR) has revealed new details about Russia’s Kh-47M2 Kinzhal aeroballistic missile, identifying 58 Russian companies involved in its production, 22 of which remain outside international sanctions.
The findings were published on HUR’s War&Sanctions portal, alongside an interactive 3D model of the missile, detailed information about its components, and a list of Russian enterprises involved in its manufacturing.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Ukrainian intelligence, the Kinzhal, officially designated 9-S-7760, is a single-stage, solid-fuel missile with an integrated warhead. Approximately 90% of its components are shared with the 9M723 ballistic missile used in Russia’s Iskander-M operational-tactical missile system.
Despite these similarities, the Kinzhal has several distinguishing features, including a tail aerodynamic fairing that separates after engine ignition and a radar seeker that Russia describes as capable of operating in all weather conditions.
HUR noted that while an active radar seeker has been proposed for the Iskander missile, its use in strikes against Ukraine has not been documented. The Kinzhal also features an active electronic jamming system alongside its S-200 decoy deployment system.
Ukrainian intelligence identified two types of warheads currently used in the Kinzhal: a penetrating high-explosive warhead and a specialized nuclear warhead. The penetrating version has a thick metal casing designed to breach reinforced concrete and other fortified structures.
Russia is also reportedly developing a new modification equipped with a high-explosive fragmentation warhead. According to HUR, this development could be linked to problems with the missile’s guidance accuracy, as penetrating warheads require greater precision to effectively strike hardened targets.
These reported limitations have also coincided with a shift in Russia’s missile production priorities. HUR said Moscow significantly reduced its state defense orders for Kinzhal missiles in 2026, redirecting manufacturing capacity, components, and raw materials toward producing 9M723 Iskander-M ballistic missiles.
Another factor behind this shift is the limited availability of aircraft capable of carrying Kinzhal missiles. These include modified MiG-31I interceptor aircraft and their predecessors, the MiG-31K, neither of which is currently being produced by Russia’s aviation industry.
HUR said it plans to release a separate list of Russian companies responsible for modernizing and maintaining these aircraft.
Beyond the missile’s technical characteristics, Ukrainian intelligence also highlighted gaps in international sanctions targeting Russia’s defense industry.
Of the 58 Russian enterprises identified as participants in Kinzhal production, 22 have not been sanctioned by any country in the international sanctions coalition.
“Despite certain shortcomings, Russia continues its efforts to modernize its Kinzhal missiles. To counter the aggressor’s plans, it is necessary to coordinate sanctions against all companies involved in their production and strengthen controls over technologies actively used by the Russian Federation,” HUR added.
The disclosure comes amid Ukrainian efforts to target Russian facilities associated with the production of missile systems, including the Kinzhal. Satellite imagery previously revealed significant damage to Russia’s Volgogradpromproekt chemical plant, a facility linked to the production of Iskander, Kinzhal, and Kalibr missiles, following a Ukrainian strike involving an FP-5 Flamingo cruise missile.

‘Energy ceasefire’: What’s behind Trump’s love-hate ties to Russian oil?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
11:30:54 UTC
20:30:54 KST

‘Energy ceasefire’: What’s behind Trump’s love-hate ties to Russian oil?
Trump’s energy truce sparks criticism over aiding Russia’s war finances amid diesel shortages and rising consumer costs.
US President Donald Trump has announced an immediate “energy ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine, days after easing sanctions on Russian fuel to tackle soaring domestic and global fuel prices.
The energy truce, announced on Sunday, marks another shift in Washington’s approach to Russian energy, as the Iran-US war and recent Ukrainian strikes on Russian energy facilities disrupted global oil supplies and pushed up fuel prices. Trump has even asked Ukraine not to attack Russian oil facilities, as Moscow remains a major exporter of diesel.
The spike in diesel prices in recent weeks has particularly put pressure on Trump’s Republican Party ahead of November’s midterm elections. Surveys show Americans hold the Trump administration responsible for the soaring fuel prices amid the unpopular US war on Iran.
“Attacks on refineries and energy facilities have taken capacity out of an already stretched global fuel market, pushing up costs for transport, agriculture and businesses, with the pain ultimately passed on to consumers,” Susannah Streeter, chief investment strategist at Wealth Club, told Al Jazeera, referring to the mutual attacks on energy sites by Ukraine and Russia.
“A genuine ceasefire could help protect supplies and ease some of that pressure, particularly as winter approaches.”
However, she warned it was too early to call it a “diplomatic breakthrough”, citing Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s statement that the energy truce came as a surprise to him.
Trump’s decisions have drawn criticism from US politicians and European allies, who warn that allowing Russian fuel back into global markets could provide Moscow with new revenue to finance its war in Ukraine. In March, the Trump administration gave a sanctions waiver to Russian seaborne oil.
So, why has Trump repeatedly changed his position on Russian energy, and what is behind his latest decisions?
What is the ‘energy ceasefire’ Trump announced?
On Sunday, Trump said Russia and Ukraine had agreed to immediately stop attacking each other’s energy infrastructure.
“Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!” he wrote on Truth Social, without providing further details.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he was not aware of the energy truce, saying the deal was “news to me” but welcomed the announcement nonetheless.
However, he said Russian drones continued targeting Ukrainian energy facilities, including a power plant in Kharkiv, after Trump’s statement.
“We are waiting for the details of the conditions between the Americans and Russians, and we are waiting to see one specific step the Americans are ready to take,” Zelenskyy said on Monday during a video address to a security conference in Warsaw.
“This energy ceasefire, it can work, and it can become a major step towards ending the war if the Americans truly step in now and make sure Russians respect it.”
Ukraine has repeatedly targeted Russian oil refineries, arguing that energy revenues help fund Moscow’s war. Russia, meanwhile, has attacked Ukraine’s electricity and heating infrastructure throughout the four-year conflict.
Academic Alexey Muriaev has urged caution over Trump’s announcement, questioning whether an agreement has actually been reached, and if so, what it entails.
“Is it about suspending attacks on oil refineries? And if that’s the case, then the situation would be inadequate, because Ukraine’s oil refineries have already been taken out by Russia’s strikes beforehand,” Muraviev, senior research fellow in Defence and Strategic Studies at Edith Cowan University, told Al Jazeera.
“So, in this sense, it would mean effectively Ukraine suspending unilateral action against Russia’s oil refinery facilities.”
Muriaev also linked the announcement to Trump’s diesel agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin, suggesting it may be a signal to Zelenskyy.
“Attacking Russian oil refinery capability would probably be interpreted by Washington as an attack on US economic interests,” he said, referring to the agreement on diesel exports through April 2027.
What’s the state of global oil prices?
The ongoing conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine have continued to keep global oil markets under pressure.
On Monday, Brent crude, the international benchmark, fell to about $103.04 a barrel following Trump’s ceasefire announcement and Russian diesel deal, while US West Texas Intermediate crude traded at about $90.96.
However, prices remain elevated because of the US-Israel war on Iran, which began on February 28, and disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz, a key waterway through which one-fifth of the world’s oil supplies flow.
Recent attacks on Saudi oil installations and airports by Yemen’s Houthis and the fighting around the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandeb Strait have put further pressure on oil prices.
Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries have compounded diesel shortages, affecting a fuel essential for the agriculture and trucking industries.
The crisis prompted the Group of Seven nations last week to agree to release 100 million barrels of emergency oil and diesel reserves. The G7 decision came after pressure from Trump.
How has the Trump administration zig-zagged between punishing and embracing Russian energy?
Washington’s approach to Russian energy has shifted repeatedly since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
Under President Joe Biden, the US banned Russian oil and energy imports in March 2022, seeking to cut off revenue used to finance Moscow’s war.
But Washington simultaneously supported a G7 price cap on Russian oil, designed to restrict Moscow’s earnings without removing too much supply from global markets.
Moreover, the Biden administration also accepted India’s continued purchases of Russian crude to prevent global prices from rising.
After returning to power last year, Trump initially intensified pressure on Moscow. In August 2025, his administration imposed additional tariffs on Indian goods over New Delhi’s purchases of Russian oil.
Two months later, Washington sanctioned Russian energy giants Rosneft and Lukoil, accusing Moscow of failing to seriously pursue peace negotiations to end the war in Ukraine.
However, Washington’s approach took a dramatic turn this year. On March 5, Washington issued a 30-day waiver allowing India to buy Russian oil stranded at sea, as disruptions to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz amid US attacks on Iran threatened global supplies.
A week later, the Trump administration expanded the exemption, allowing countries worldwide to buy sanctioned Russian oil and petroleum products already loaded onto tankers, with the waiver lasting until April 11.
In September, Trump urged Ukraine to stop attacking Russian refineries, blaming the strikes for global diesel shortages.
On October 9, he announced an agreement with Russian President Putin for Moscow to release more than 300,000 tonnes of diesel immediately, with another 1.5 million tonnes to follow.
Why has Trump changed his position on Russian oil frequently?
Trump’s shifting public position on Russian energy reflects ongoing, and often competing, political and economic pressures.
“Trump is caught between his geopolitical ambitions and the domestic political consequences of expensive energy,” Susannah Streeter of Wealth Club, told Al Jazeera.
She said Washington was trying to pressure Moscow over its war in Ukraine while simultaneously allowing Russian fuel sales that could generate additional revenue for the Kremlin.
“The shift may deliver a short-term political gain if supplies increase and prices ease, but it could come at a longer-term diplomatic cost,” she said, adding that the benefits appeared limited while the Middle East war continued.
US diesel prices reached a record $6.52 per gallon in September, placing Trump under pressure ahead of the November 3 midterm elections.
However, according to academic Muriev, the US president’s public rhetoric should be distinguished from his administration’s actions.
“I don’t really see inconsistency in Trump’s approach because, apart from his public rhetoric, apart from his frequent media posting, there’s been a more steady approach on behalf of his administration,” he told Al Jazeera.
He pointed to discussions between Russian and American officials in August and September, suggesting that negotiations over the latest diesel agreement may have begun well before Trump’s announcement last Friday.
Muriev suggested the timing of the announcement could be politically motivated, allowing Trump to claim a victory on energy prices before the midterms.
Moreover, Moscow also has an interest in helping Trump retain political influence because his administration appears more willing to negotiate with Russia than former President Biden was. Trump has been relatively more accepting of the Russian position on the Ukraine war and has even blamed Zelenskyy for failing to end the war.
“For Putin, it’s not just about scoring immediate economic benefit, but also achieving longer-term political and strategic goals,” Muriev said, referring to other issues such as Iran, cybersecurity, space cooperation and nuclear arms control.
The energy crisis has also created contrasting consequences for American businesses.
While higher oil prices can boost revenues for US energy producers, they increase operating costs for businesses dependent on fuel.
Susannah Streeter said cheaper diesel could provide relief to trucking companies, farmers and manufacturers, although the additional Russian supplies were unlikely to make a significant difference while disruptions in the Middle East continued.
She also warned that frequent changes to sanctions could create uncertainty for companies making long-term investment and supply-chain decisions.
“If sanctions are relaxed, reimposed or changed at short notice, companies face greater uncertainty over sourcing, compliance and the risk of being caught on the wrong side of a policy reversal,” she said.

We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Ukrainian Defense Minister Yevhenii Khmara, speaking at a briefing attended by a UNITED24 Media correspondent, domestic jet engine production has become one of the country’s most critical defense-industrial priorities.

More powerful engines are intended for medium-range and long-range attack drones, as well as cruise missiles capable of striking targets deep inside Russian territory.
The push comes as Russia increasingly deploys faster jet-powered attack drones, creating new challenges for Ukrainian air defenses and increasing demand for interceptors capable of catching high-speed targets.
