Giants Brigades lead southern Yemen fightback against the Houthis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
11:30:30 UTC
20:30:30 KST

Giants Brigades lead southern Yemen fightback against the Houthis
Yemen’s Southern Giants Brigades have emerged as one of the leading forces against the Houthis.
On October 5, groups linked to the former Southern Transitional Council (STC), including the powerful Southern Giants Brigades, and troops of the internationally recognised government of Yemen, launched a major offensive against the Houthis near the strategically important Bab al-Mandeb strait.
It was part of a nationwide military campaign aimed at driving the Houthis, an armed group also known as Ansar Allah or Supporters of God, out of territories under their control, including the vital coastline region seized by the Iran-linked group in September.
By Monday afternoon, the pro-government force, led by the Giants Brigade, said they had managed to cut off the main road linking the Red Sea port city of Mocha with the Bab al-Mandeb, a vital waterway for energy supplies.
This effectively gave the anti-Houthi forces one of their first major military gains in years and followed an announcement by Rashid al-Alimi, chairman of Yemen’s Presidential Leadership Council (PLC), of a major offensive against the Iran-backed group. It also highlighted the effectiveness of anti-Houthi forces – which include units with contrasting political goals – when working together.
This has seen STC-affiliated groups, some of whom seek independence for the south, ally with pro-government national forces against the Houthis.
The collaboration between these two factions follows a high-profile conflict in southern Yemen in January, when Saudi-aligned Yemeni government forces defeated the United Arab Emirates-backed STC, resulting in the relative centralisation of anti-Houthi forces.
Among the leading formations in the recent government offensive led by this alliance are the Giants Brigades, which have their roots in the southern separatist movement.
The force is commanded by Abd al-Rahman Abu Zaraa al-Muharrami, a Salafi who studied at the ultraconservative Dammaj religious school in the northern governorate of Saada.
Formed largely by Salafi fighters during the battle against the Houthis in the southern city of Aden in the first half of 2015, the Giants Brigades have become one of Yemen’s most formidable military forces during the war.
The brigades, believed to have been armed, trained and funded by the UAE, rose to prominence in 2017, leading an offensive that captured large swaths of Yemen’s western coast from the Houthis. The advance was eventually halted on the outskirts of the Red Sea port city of Hodeidah following the United Nations-brokered Stockholm Agreement in late 2018.
In January 2022, the Giants Brigades achieved another major victory against the Houthis, seizing three districts in the southern governorate of Shabwa and advancing deeper into neighbouring Marib. Their offensive came to a halt after the Houthis launched an attack on Abu Dhabi on January 17, 2022.
Al-Muharrami had no known military background before the war, which began with the Houthis’ capture of Sanaa in September 2014, and the group has largely stayed out of infighting between anti-Houthi forces.
He joined Yemen’s eight-member PLC in April 2022, around the time his forces adopted the name Southern Giants Brigades, signalling their growing southern political identity. The formation later joined the STC, further strengthening the brigades’ ties with the southern separatist movement.
When STC forces collapsed following the Yemeni government offensive in January, al-Muharrami flew to Riyadh and voiced support for the Saudi-led initiative to unify southern forces.
The Giants Brigades’ involvement in the war against the Houthis is now seen as a test of its political allegiance, with some observers arguing that it remains fundamentally a separatist force.
Some believe that the Giants Brigades’ previous advances against the Houthis into Hodeidah suggest that the group does not necessarily have a separatist agenda.
They have also pointed to the group’s spearheading of the latest military offensive against the Houthis beyond southern Yemen, where many former STC units have remained confined, as another sign of its stronger commitment to national unity.
Fathi bin Lazraq, editor of the Aden Al-Ghad newspaper and an outspoken critic of southern separatists, believes that the Giants Brigades would be willing to fight the Houthis anywhere in Yemen.
“These forces are part of the contingent that has been fighting the Houthis since 2015, having been formed in Yemen following the collapse of the Yemeni army,” he told Al Jazeera. “They engage the Houthis from military, political, civil and religious standpoints.”
Bin Lazraq described the Giants Brigades as a powerful fighting force and pointed to their previous operations in northern areas, including Hodeidah and Marib. He also believes that the word “Southern” in their name did not necessarily mean they supported secession or would refuse to fight beyond the borders of the formerly independent South Yemen state.
But unlike Homeland Shield Forces, which were established by PLC head al-Alimi in January 2023 and placed under his direct command, making their allegiance to the internationally recognised government clear, the Giants Brigades operate in a more grey area.
“They do not fight as ‘Southern forces’ per se, but rather as part of the legitimate government forces backed by the [Saudi-led] coalition,” bin Lazraq said. “While they operate under the banner of southern forces, they do not claim to be separatist, or anything of the sort, given that they have fought in Hodeidah and Marib.”
The Giants Brigades, and even more hardline separatist STC-affiliated forces, had come to recognise the dangers posed by the Houthis and the need to ally with government forces to fight the group.
“Everyone believes that the Houthis pose a threat: if we do not go to them, they will come to us. The Giants Brigades and other forces are all united in a single battle to confront the Houthis,” he said.
But accusations that the Giants Brigades have southern separatist aspirations are also not unwarranted. The group’s current offensive is focused on areas within the borders of the former South Yemen entity, including the Bab al-Mandeb strait.
Some of their fighters taking part in the offensive around Bab al-Mandeb have raised the former South Yemen flag, and embedded journalists have also shared footage showing soldiers expressing southern separatist sentiments.
STC President Aidarous al-Zubaidi, who has not appeared publicly since the defeat of his forces in January, weighed into the debate by offering condolences for fighters killed in the offensive, describing them as martyrs, and criticising what he says is others taking credit for victories by southern forces.
“The South will not allow the victories of its armed forces to be stolen under slogans that do not reflect its reality,” al-Zubaidi said on X.
Anwar al-Tamimi, a spokesperson for the STC, told Al Jazeera that the participation of southern forces in the campaign was focused on capturing and securing the Bab al-Mandeb and surrounding areas, which separatists consider part of the state they seek to restore.
“The participation of southern forces is aimed at protecting and securing the south’s borders, a principle deeply rooted in southern military doctrine and central to the southern cause. Bab al-Mandeb falls within the territory of the former People’s Democratic Republic of Yemen,” he said.
Al-Tamimi did not rule out the possibility of southern forces advancing deeper into northern Yemen to secure their gains and borders, following similar military operations in the north.
The Giants Brigades remained loyal to the southern independence movement despite their participation in the wider anti-Houthi offensive.
“The Giants Brigades are southern brigades driven by a southern combat ethos, alongside elements of Salafist ideas,” al-Tamimi told Al Jazeera.
“This serves to reinforce the southern national project rather than bypass it. The Giants Brigades are a southern force; they carry the flag and banner of the south, and there is no issue with that. They are part of the southern armed forces – and a very active part at that.”

Swiss churches adopt ten guidelines on use of AI
Unknown

Swiss churches adopt ten guidelines on use of AI
A handful of Christian churches and organisations in Switzerland have adopted ten "commandments" or guidelines for dealing with artificial intelligence. In their view, technological possibilities should be assessed in terms of their benefit to human well-being.
Under the title “Humanity in the Digital Age”, five churches and organisations published ten ethical principles on Monday for dealing with artificial intelligence (AI). These principles combine the Christian view of humanity with the specific challenges posed by AI, the group said in a joint statement.
The AI guidelines were drawn up by the Evangelical Reformed Church of Switzerland (EKS), the Swiss Bishops’ Conference, the umbrella organisation Freikirchen.ch, the Christian Catholic Church of Switzerland and the Swiss Evangelical Alliance. It is encouraging that the five churches and organisations are speaking out jointly on AI, said EKS President Rita Famos in a press release.
More
Revelation or cliché? AI-Jesus appears in Lucerne church
AI is changing the way we learn, work and interact with one another. The principles, such as “truth requires scrutiny and transparency”, provide guidance for church institutions, congregations and organisations.
According to Charles Morerod, president of the Swiss Bishops’ Conference, the new guidelines are intended to combine theological questions with the practical use of AI tools. For Frank Bangerter, Bishop of the Christian Catholic Church of Switzerland, AI must not merely benefit those who already hold power.
“Technological progress is only good if it serves everyone,” said Bangerter. The guidelines should deliberately focus on those who would otherwise be left behind, he added.
Back in May, Pope Leo XIV had called for strict international guidelines on the use of AI in his first encyclical. The head of the world’s 1.4 billion Catholics warned of the numerous dangers that this revolutionary new technology poses to human coexistence. In the treatise, which runs to more than 100 pages and is entitled “Magnifica Humanitas”, the Pope also highlights the opportunities offered by these new technologies.

US threatens to cut intel sharing, arms shipments to Ukraine in push to protect Russian oil refineries, sources confirm

US threatens to cut intel sharing, arms shipments to Ukraine to protect Russian oil refineries, sources confirm
The Kyiv Independent has learned that the Trump administration threatened senior Ukrainian military and government officials in a push to protect Russian oil refineries.
Two Ukrainian officials said their U.S. counterparts had made clear that Washington would hold Kyiv responsible if Russian energy infrastructure were struck during the recently announced ceasefire.
"They called all the top military officials with threats," one Ukrainian official told the Kyiv Independent. "They're telling everyone that they're going to turn off both the intelligence sharing and PURL."
The threats come after a confusing 48 hours during which U.S. President Donald Trump announced a controversial "deal" with Russian President Vladimir Putin to import Russian diesel, followed by repeated demands that Ukraine replace Volodymyr Zelensky as president, followed by Trump announcing a unilateral "energy ceasefire" between Russia and Ukraine, which blindsided both Moscow and Kyiv.
Multiple senior Ukrainian officials told the Kyiv Independent that Kyiv had not been informed in advance of Trump's Oct. 11 ceasefire announcement. After the announcement, Ukrainian officials reportedly came under pressure to abide by the ceasefire and refrain from striking Russian oil refineries.
Russia continued to attack Ukrainian energy infrastructure, with the Kharkiv thermal power plant being hit just hours after Trump's announcement.
According to another official, President's Office Deputy Head Pavlo Palisa, in charge of military affairs, and Mykhailo Drapatyi, commander-in-chief of the Ukrainian Armed Forces, had received calls from the American side.
PURL — which stands for "Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List" — is a Europe-led initiative that aims to provide Ukraine with critical U.S. weaponry, financed primarily by NATO members. In the first year of the initiative, $6.7 billion worth of weaponry was provided through the scheme.
Although direct U.S. military aid has been suspended since Trump's inauguration, intelligence sharing has continued.
Speaking to the Russian news agency TASS, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov declined to comment on the reported energy truce but said Russia was "ready to do everything possible" to achieve "long-term peace."
Nonetheless, the Ukrainian president signaled Kyiv's willingness to abide by the terms of the ceasefire, while adding they would need more information about the exact proposal.
Ukrainians remain skeptical that the one-sided energy ceasefire will hold.
"Immediately after (Trump's ceasefire) post, Russia launched a targeted strike on a power plant in Kharkiv, causing further damage to our energy system," Zelensky said during an event attended by Kyiv Independent journalists at the Warsaw Security Forum.
"It was clear that Putin does not read TruthSocial."
"We agreed to an energy ceasefire. The American team knows very well what this means for us. We do not have major oil reserves, large oil export capacity, or dozens of oil refineries," Zelensky said.
He repeated Ukraine's willingness to agree to a mutual energy ceasefire, but reiterated it would have to include energy infrastructure, not just refineries, as Ukraine does not have any functional oil refining infrastructure.
"In Ukraine, we have just one oil refinery. And it was badly damaged by Russian strikes long, long ago. So importing oil products is simply our reality," Zelensky said.
"And that is why our offer is honest and clear. We are ready to respect an energy ceasefire if Russia is ready to do the same. We agree if they agree," he continued.
"And we have already shown that we mean it. Last night, Russian oil refineries were not burned. But at midnight, a Russian jet-powered Shahed struck a gas production facility in Ukraine."
Editor's note: An earlier version of this story incorrectly stated that Deputy Head of the President's Office Pavlo Palisa had confirmed the information to the Financial Times.

How Trump’s Policies Are Testing Farmers’ Loyalty Ahead of Midterms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
11:28:27 UTC
20:28:27 KST

Rising diesel and fertilizer costs, coupled with President Donald Trump’s shifting tariff policies, have made it harder for Oklahoma farmer Brent Rendel to plan future crops. Over the past few months, he says, the political mood among fellow farmers—traditionally some of the President’s most reliable supporters—has begun to shift.
“From my discussions with other farmers, there is a higher level of dissatisfaction with what's going on with the [Trump] Administration,” says Rendel. “You didn't used to really see that, but now we're seeing it and hearing it.”
That dissatisfaction could pose a political problem for Trump and Republicans ahead of the pivotal midterm elections. Trump won 69% of the rural vote in 2024, but an AP-KFF poll, conducted in August, found that 57% of rural voters disapprove of Trump’s handling of the economy. Among rural Republican voters, around one-quarter (27%) disapproved of his handling of the economy—and that group was "substantially less likely" than those who approved to say they were certain to vote in November.
Three-quarters of rural voters described the cost of living in their communities as “fair” or “poor.” A Reuters/Ipsos poll, conducted in June, had already put Trump's approval rating among rural Americans dropped at a new low of 50%, with just 31% approving of his handling of economic issues.
The findings come as Democrats poll competitively in some traditionally Republican states such as Texas, Iowa, and Kansas. Democratic leaders are also addressing farmers' economic frustrations in their policy proposals. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer and Sen. Amy Klobuchar, ranking member of the Senate Agriculture Committee, last month unveiled a bill intended to lay the groundwork for “America’s first-ever fertilizer reserve.” American farmers are “getting crushed from all sides by this Administration,” Schumer said as he introduced the Strategic Fertilizer Reserve Act with endorsements from the National Farmers Union and New York Farm Bureau.
Farmers and agricultural experts interviewed by TIME described four overlapping pressures: Trump’s expansion of low-tariff beef imports, rising fertilizer and diesel costs stemming from a global energy crisis triggered by the Iran war, and tariffs that have increased some production costs while provoking retaliation against American exports.
The impact has been felt by consumers, who have seen a steady climb in grocery prices. In one September AP-NORC poll, 64% of Americans said Trump has “gone too far” on imposing new tariffs on other countries. Trump’s latest tariff row with Canada has prompted further economic concern, particularly in rural states such as Montana, which listed Canada as its largest export market in 2025.
In response, White House spokesperson Olivia Wales told TIME that Trump “has repeatedly affirmed his support for America’s great farmers and ranchers.”
She added: “While the President has been clear about temporary disruptions as a result of the conflict in Iran, the Administration continues to implement the proven Trump agenda of tax cuts, deregulation, and energy abundance to keep America on a solid economic trajectory.”
Trump campaigned on promises to keep the U.S. out of foreign wars and focus on prosperity at home.
The farmers who spoke to TIME say the economic consequences of his policies are now reaching their day-to-day operations.
Beef imports
The average price of ground beef in the U.S. has risen sharply since the end of 2020. It climbed from $5.58 per pound in August 2024 to $6.92 in August 2026, according to U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics data. Shrinking cattle herd sizes, drought and strong demand have all contributed to the increases. At the start of this year, the U.S. cattle inventory hit a 75-year low.
The price surge has created a political challenge for Trump.
“A major part of [Trump’s] campaign to households around the U.S. two years ago, was the fact that they could keep inflation low,” says Joe Glauber, a research fellow at the International Food Policy Research Institute, noting that many rural Americans and farmers are concerned that this hasn’t materialized.
Trump’s 90-day scheme to suspend tariffs on 300,000 metric tons of imported foreign beef to ease the strain on grocery bills went into effect on Sept. 1. The stated intention was for the imported beef to be sold at 25% lower than market price.
But the American Farm Bureau Federation (AFBF), an agriculture lobbying group, has urged Trump to reverse course, citing its own analysis that found the increased imports have not lowered prices for consumers. The AFBF tracked daily prices of 80% lean ground beef at 41 grocery stores in 22 states, starting the day after the proclamation went into effect. In 30 of those 41 stores, ground beef prices cost relatively the same on Sep. 23 as they did on Sep. 2.
Incumbent Texas Commissioner for Agriculture Sid Miller, an eighth-generation farmer and rancher, says farmers have felt the effects of the fallout of the beef import scheme.
“I haven't talked to one rancher that's not upset about it,” says Miller. “Just the packers and the processors are reaping the benefits, not the consumer or the cattle rancher. Calves that are going to market now are bringing $300-500 a head less.”
Derrell Peel, a professor of agricultural economics at Oklahoma State University who specializes in livestock and cattle markets, says ground beef has become the “poster child for higher food prices,” making it a focus of the political debate.
“Cattle producers increasingly feel that Trump is willing to throw them under the bus to try to get lower beef prices before the election,” Peel tells TIME. “None of the political actions have had any significant impact on beef prices and there is no quick solution to high beef prices.”
In Florida, Kansas, Kentucky, Missouri, Montana, Nebraska, North Dakota, Oklahoma, South Dakota, and Texas—10 major beef-producing states—Trump has seen a decline in approval rating, according to Civiqs polling data collected between Aug. 21-Sep. 21.
“For Republicans, as a rule, our strongest voting bloc is the rural areas of the United States,” says Miller.
“I think we're going to lose some statewide races in Texas because of multiple things,” he adds, listing tariffs, diesel fuel costs, and fertilizer prices as other key concerns. “It's like death from 1000 cuts.”
Recent ICE raids targeting meatpacking plants across Kansas, Oklahoma, and Texas are also causing concern and placing further strain on the U.S. beef supply chain.
“ICE [recently] raided workers from packing plants in Kansas, shutting the packing plants down,” says Miller. “That lowers prices for the cattlemen because the cattle back up, they can't get processed, and it raises prices for the consumer, because there's less beef on the market.”
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin on Sept. 25 disputed the nature of the raids and said “ICE is not conducting worksite operations in Kansas.” Industry groups said worker absences nevertheless forced some plants to close temporarily.
Fertilizer
Steve Sheffels, a wheat farmer who serves as president of the Montana Grain Growers Association, says that around 40% of his expenses go towards buying fertilizer. He says that outlook could become “dire” if prices continue to rise.
Rising fertilizer costs, combined with extreme weather in Montana over the past year, has led Sheffels to conclude that “we are not able to produce our crops and make money doing it.”
Sheffels highlights a specific example of how his costs have risen since the onset of the Iran war.
“We just got done seeding this fall, and the cost of starter fertilizer, which has a lot of potassium in it, was just under $1,000 a ton,” he says. “Last year, it was $600 a ton.”
The rise of fertilizer costs is a major concern as crops such as corn and wheat heavily rely on nitrogen fertilizer. Natural gas is key in the production of nitrogen-based fertilizers, including urea and anhydrous ammonia. Exports of liquified natural gas from Gulf countries have been severely disrupted by the war and shipping disruptions have continued.
The shipping of natural gas exports via the Strait of Hormuz “remained effectively suspended” through August, according to data published last month, while other fertilizer product exports “remained sporadic and subdued” across the month.
In April, 94% of farmers responding to a Farmer & Rancher Policy Sentiment survey said the Iran war had impacted their business by raising fertilizer costs, energy costs, or both. While the survey came amid a sharp spike in fertilizer prices across April to June, concerns remain.
The price of anhydrous ammonia was up 9.3% as of late September compared to late February, before the onset of the war. The price of urea is up 7.9% for the same period, according to data from analytics company DTN.
Diesel fuel
In the U.S., the price of diesel hit record highs last month, sitting at a national average of over $6.52 per gallon on Sept. 22, according to the American Automobile Association.
Trump signed an Executive Order last week to waive the off-road requirement for a specific type of tax-free diesel fuel primarily used by the agriculture industry. Temporarily allowing highway use of red-dyed diesel “will put money directly back in the pockets of American farmers, truckers, and workers,” the White House said. While it may help lessen the costs associated with the transportation of harvested goods, Rendel says it “won’t be the solution for our farm economy woes.”
Days later, the President also announced that Russia had agreed to supply over 300,000 tons of diesel fuel to the American and global marketplace.
Prior to these efforts, Trump floated the possibility of a diesel export ban. But he ruled out the idea on Oct. 2 as the G7 group of nations committed to a co-ordinated release of 100 million barrels of diesel alongside other reserves through the International Energy Agency (IEA), in an effort to stabilise world energy markets.
In the meantime, farmers continue to grapple with increased prices.
“Diesel directly affects farm production costs for field operations, planting, harvesting, and for shipping both inputs and outputs,” says Peel. “The impact [when prices are increased] is very immediate.”
In the August AP/KFF poll, 67% of rural voters said they were “very or somewhat” worried about gasoline or other transportation costs.
Rendel is already feeling the impact. Last month, he explains, he had diesel delivered to his farm that cost him over $5 a gallon.
“I know in a lot of the world, that's probably not ridiculous, but for farm diesel, which is subjected to a lower tax rate in the U.S., that is ridiculous,” he says. “Anytime it goes over $4, it gets painful, and now we're already over five.”
“Fuel is a real strong pain point for everyone. As long as the war is going on, there's really not going to be any significant relief available,” he adds.
Crop farmers in particular rely on heavy, diesel-fueled machinery to sow and harvest.
“If fertilizer prices rise, which they have risen over the past year or so, you can really look at your soil fertility and make decisions that can save you some money. When seed prices go up, you can shop around and maybe find less expensive seed or reduce your seeding rates,” Rendel says. “But fuel's not that way. My combine, when I'm harvesting soybeans, uses about 200 gallons of fuel per day, and that doesn't change.”
Diesel is also essential for transporting goods once they are harvested. “I’ve got to deliver the grain to the buyer. The fuel is a very inflexible expense,” Rendel says, citing a lack of alternatives.
Sheffels is feeling the impact of transport costs as a result of diesel fuel prices, too. “We're having to pay more to get our grain moved around in the short term,” he says. “In the long term, it's going to have a huge [financial] impact because of the distances.”
The renewed trade war with Canada has added to concerns for farmers in the U.S., after negotiations between the two countries collapsed in August. Canada’s retaliatory tariffs on U.S. goods took effect last month, with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney matching the levies imposed by the Trump Administration. Canada's counter tariffs apply to products covering $27.6 billion in imports from the U.S., focusing on sectors such as steel, dairy, appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper, among other products.
“The U.S. and Canadian economies are highly integrated,” says Peel. “There are no winners in trade wars in general and especially in this one with so many components that will be impacted.”
Overall, tariffs on key production inputs have imposed roughly $2.6 billion in additional costs on crop farmers from February 2025 through July 2026, according to data from the Association of Equipment Manufacturers.
Following Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit to the White House in late September, Beijing agreed to drop tariffs on various U.S. agricultural products. However, soybeans were excluded from the list, and will remain subjected to 10% tariffs, offering little relief to farmers like Rendel.
Soybeans remained the top U.S. agricultural export to China in 2025, even as shipments fell by roughly three-quarters between 2024 and 2025 amid Trump’s implementation of wide ranging tariffs on Beijing.
For farmers already facing higher diesel and fertilizer costs, shrinking export markets create pressure at both ends of the supply chain. “You're hitting people at both levels, at the input level, and then look at the prices they get for their commodity if they're not able to export it,” says Glauber, from the International Food Policy Research Institute.
Sheffels says the repeated policy shifts are disruptive for farmers across America.
“The level of uncertainty that we've had to live with is completely unacceptable,” he says. “It's impossible to make investment decisions when you don't know what the rules are going to be five minutes from now, let alone in six months.”
With the midterms fast approaching, the question for Republicans is whether that frustration will change how some farmers vote—or whether they vote at all.

Rise in poverty is ‘a wake-up call for the world’, UN development chief says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
11:28:07 UTC
20:28:07 KST

Rise in poverty is ‘a wake-up call for the world’, UN development chief says
The number of people living in “multidimensional” poverty has risen for the first time in 15 years, reaching 1.2 billion, as families struggle to meet their basic needs.
The finding comes in the 2026 update of the global Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI) published by the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) and Oxford University, which measures overlapping hardship across health, education and standard of living.
The 1.2 billion figure represents 51.5 million more people than in the 2025 update. Of this number, more than half are children – 617 million – and 83 per cent live in rural areas.
‘This is unacceptable’
“The rise in poverty should be a wake-up call for the world,” said UNDP Administrator Alexander De Croo.
“Behind these figures are 1.2 billion people facing hardships that reinforce one another: hunger, missed schooling and a lack of clean water or electricity. This is unacceptable.”
The index was developed in 2010 to measure poverty beyond what people earn.
Overlapping deprivations
It examines 10 indicators of health, education and standard of living, such as nutrition and child mortality, years of schooling, and access to electricity, drinking water and sanitation.
A person is considered “multidimensionally poor” if they are deprived in one-third or more of the indicators.
Sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia account for the overwhelming majority of deprivations across every indicator.
Mixed picture, fragile success
The 2026 update – which covers 108 countries, representing some 78 per cent of the global population – reveals that the increase in poverty is partly due to population growth outpacing efforts to improve living standards.
In 95 countries where no new survey data was available, updated population estimates increased the number of people counted as poor by nearly 16 million.
The remainder of the increase comes from 13 countries where data was gathered, reflecting the genuine change in poverty incidence and the associated demographic change, as well as differences in indicator coverage.
The updated surveys also revealed a mixed picture on the ground. Five of these countries – Egypt, Nepal, Tajikistan, Angola and Zambia – have reduced the share of people living in multidimensional poverty, however population growth outpaced poverty reduction in both Angola and Zambia, meaning that the total number of people living in poverty still increased.
Meanwhile, Nigeria provides an example of how fragile progress in tackling poverty can be. Although the country made significant reductions in multidimensional poverty in the 2010s, both the poverty rate and the number of people struggling to make ends meet have increased.
‘Progress is possible’
The international community has pledged to reduce the proportion of people living in poverty by at least half before the end of this decade, in line with the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).
The authors of the 2026 MPI update believe that this target is achievable.
“We know progress is possible,” Mr. De Croo insisted. “Countries that have tackled these challenges together, rather than in isolation, have shown what determined action can achieve.”
UNDP reported that 33 countries have halved their MPI value in fewer than 15 years, including six in sub-Saharan Africa. In Eswatini, the share of people living in multidimensional poverty has fallen from nearly 39 per cent to eight per cent.
Meanwhile, China recorded the fastest reduction among countries with available data by halving its MPI value from 9.5 per cent to 4.2 per cent in just four years (2010-2014).
The shows that many countries continue to make progress, with some reducing poverty rapidly and at scale, underscoring both the urgency of renewed action and the possibility of success, the agency said.

Accuracy Problems: Russia Developing New Kinzhal Missile Warhead
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
11:27:44 UTC
20:27:44 KST

Russia is developing a new version of its air-launched Kinzhal ballistic missile with a high-explosive fragmentation warhead, potentially in response to problems with its accuracy, Ukraine’s military intelligence agency (HUR) said.
On Monday, Oct. 12, HUR disclosed the assessment alongside an interactive 3D model of the missile and information about its components and manufacturers published on its War & Sanctions website.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The Kinzhal, designated 9-S-7760 and widely known as the Kh-47M2, currently has two warhead configurations: a penetrating high-explosive warhead designed to breach reinforced structures and a nuclear warhead. Its published specifications list a warhead weight of 450 kilograms (992 pounds).
The proposed modification would add a high-explosive fragmentation warhead, which causes damage through both blast and fragments.
HUR said the development could be directly linked to guidance problems, noting that precision is particularly important for a penetrating warhead intended to strike hardened targets.
Russia significantly reduced its state defense orders for Kinzhal missiles in 2026, redirecting manufacturing capacity, components, and raw materials toward the ground-launched 9M723 Iskander-M ballistic missile, HUR said.
The agency attributed that shift to the Kinzhal’s accuracy problems and limitations affecting the aircraft used to launch it.
Kinzhal missiles are carried by modified MiG-31I and MiG-31K interceptor aircraft. HUR said those aircraft have a limited remaining service life and are no longer manufactured by Russia’s aviation industry.
Russia Needs Just 5 Drones to Test NATO, Kuleba Says
The Kinzhal is a single-stage, solid-fuel missile, with an integrated warhead. According to HUR, about 90% of its components are common to the Iskander-M’s 9M723 missile.
Key differences include a tail fairing that separates after the engine starts, a radar seeker described by Russia as capable of operating in all weather, and an active jamming system alongside equipment that releases decoys.
HUR’s online model identifies components including the missile’s radar seeker, navigation equipment, solid-fuel engine, and penetrating warhead, as well as the companies involved in their manufacture.

A blow to Putin’s digital empire: what the loss of Yandex data centers will mean
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12

A blow to Putin’s digital empire: what the loss of Yandex data centers will mean
Kyiv • UNN
Following the FP-1 attacks, three of Yandex’s supercomputers stopped working, causing disruptions to services and risks for thousands of companies. Experts predict mounting pressure on Russia’s economy and digital infrastructure.
Ukrainian strikes on the data centers of Russia’s "Yandex" may have consequences far more serious than temporary disruptions to the search engine, taxi, or other popular services. The stability of companies using cloud infrastructure, as well as certain digital tools used by the Russian war machine, has been jeopardized. UNN, together with experts, examined how significant the consequences of the strikes on "Yandex" will be for russia.
Three of "Yandex’s" supercomputers have stopped working: what is known about the strikes
Ukrainian long-range FP-1 drones attacked the data centers of the Russian company "Yandex", which housed powerful computing systems used, in particular, to develop artificial intelligence technologies.
On the night of October 8, the Defense Forces of Ukraine struck a data center in Sasovo (Ryazan region), where two of the company’s three supercomputers, "Chervonenkis" and "Lyapunov," were located; on October 9, a large data center in the Kaluga region was attacked; and on the night of October 11, the third "Yandex" supercomputer, "Galushkin," in the city of Vladimir was hit.
According to investigations by Russian opposition media, dictator vladimir putin may own a stake in "Yandex" through his proxies. Thus, the company is under the control of the kremlin.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy explained that the strikes on Russia’s digital infrastructure were a response to similar Russian attacks on Ukrainian data centers.
What consequences are already being felt by Russians
Launched in 2000, "Yandex" has long since evolved into an entire ecosystem combining taxi, delivery, mapping, online commerce, data storage, cloud computing, and artificial intelligence services, and even has its own payment system. For example, Yandex Cloud is a platform for hosting information systems, processing data, and managing business processes.
After the Ukrainian strikes, all three of the company "Yandex’s" major supercomputers stopped working. Russians are reporting disruptions to "Yandex.Go," "Yandex.Pay," "Yandex.Music," "Kinopoisk," "Yandex.Eats," "Yandex.Lavka," and "Home with Alice" on social media.
Users are reporting problems ordering taxis, having food delivered, paying for purchases, using electronic maps, and watching films. The real-time movement of public transport has stopped being displayed on "Yandex.Maps," and the electric scooter rental service is not working.
Moreover, platforms such as those operated by "Yandex" may host companies and systems involved in transmitting television content. Therefore, disruptions to the operation of this infrastructure could potentially affect not only internet services but also the delivery of signals to some television channels.
According to IT expert Oleksandr Hlushchenko, the destruction or serious damage of a data center causes a certain segment of digital infrastructure to go offline, and specific services operating on that site begin to degrade. At the same time, Hlushchenko notes that Russian infrastructure was not prepared for a full-scale war and systematic strikes on such facilities. At the same time, he says, the kremlin has long been conditioning Russians to accept that the internet may disappear.
They shut down mobile internet, test so-called white lists, and constantly increase the number of banned resources and services. Therefore, if an average Russian’s "Yandex.Food" is not working, they may not even be surprised: their mobile internet is not working either. In this sense, the kremlin is effectively preparing the population for digital restrictions
A welcome bonus following the strikes on data centers in russia was a decline in the activity of Russian bots on social media, recorded not only in Ukraine but also in Europe, particularly in Poland. According to social media users, the number of posts inciting hostility between Ukrainians and Poles decreased significantly there.
Thousands of Russian companies under threat
Large data centers power many digital systems, and disruption to their operations would have a chain reaction for businesses, Russian state institutions, and even the military machine. According to local media reports, the outage affecting Yandex has already been felt by companies in Russia, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Uzbekistan, Belarus, and Armenia.
If the operation of such infrastructure is disrupted, the consequences can extend far beyond the technology company itself. These are major economic losses
Oleksandr Hlushchenko draws attention to one of the main vulnerabilities of Russia’s digital system. Unlike Ukraine’s, Russia’s IT infrastructure is centralized.
First, two can play this game. Second, Russia’s telecommunications infrastructure is physically much larger than Ukraine’s, because Russia is a large country with enormous distances. Therefore, its data centers and communications channels are located in different regions. At the same time, the Russian internet segment, particularly in terms of data hosting and the provision of digital services, is largely centralized and monopolized. And finally, Russian companies do not always have somewhere to quickly move their data and computing capacity
According to experts, even the availability of backup capacity does not guarantee uninterrupted operation after strikes on major data centers. Transferring the load to other locations can cause delays, overloads, and degraded service performance. There is also a risk of information loss if clients have not created backups.
If Yandex has backups of its own data at other sites, it can restore them. But if a client stored its data in only one location and did not make backups, the consequences could be much more serious. In that case, some of the information could be lost forever
It is important that even the temporary unavailability of digital resources can cost businesses money due to halted operations, disrupted logistics, and the need to restore infrastructure.
The economic impact of the strikes on Yandex
Economic expert Ihor Harbaruk suggests viewing attacks on data centers in the context of a strategy to weaken the Russian economy.
I would describe this strategy as a strategy of a thousand jabs. You cannot kill a person with one jab, but when there are a thousand of them, their cumulative effect can be entirely different. The same applies to war: a single strike on an oil refinery, logistics facility, or data center will not necessarily lead to a strategic turning point. But when such strikes accumulate, they create systemic pressure on the enemy’s economy and infrastructure
According to him, it is currently difficult to assess the specific losses from any particular strike on facilities in Russia.
However, the general logic is clear: when the operation of major digital platforms is disrupted, this potentially affects trade, logistics, and the services sector. Similar dependencies exist for other major companies, including Wildberries and Ozon. And that means taxes—and, accordingly, money for the war
The actual financial losses will depend on the cost of the damaged equipment, the duration of the downtime, restoration expenses, and possible customer attrition. Modern data centers require servers, graphics accelerators, cooling systems, power supply systems, and high-speed network components. In the case of supercomputers, the requirements are even higher. According to experts, alternative import channels, such as China, may only partially compensate for the shortage and do not guarantee the rapid acquisition of equipment.
If companies using Yandex services have to spend additionally on backups, data migration, and the purchase of servers, this will increase operating costs and may affect tax revenues to the Russian budget.
Cybersecurity specialist Kostiantyn Korsun does not rule out problems in the banking system in the event of large-scale and prolonged disruptions to Yandex’s operation.
In a certain scenario, such disruptions could also affect economically important systems, including banking services. If people began to face widespread inability to use financial services, this could heighten public anxiety and negatively affect economic activity. However, speaking of an inevitable banking or economy-wide collapse solely on the basis of strikes on data centers would be premature
Will the Russian army be affected by the loss of Yandex supercomputers?
Military expert Oleksandr Kovalenko notes that for the military, the ability to navigate terrain, obtain information about topography and landscape, determine the elevations of various objects, and analyze the characteristics of an area is particularly important. Russians use all this data when planning and carrying out military tasks.
The Russian army is largely dependent on civilian digital infrastructure, and in this context, Yandex plays an important role. The company is one of the key providers of digital services and software tools in Russia, which can be used by both government agencies and the military. This involves a wide range of tasks – from record-keeping and data processing to cartography, navigation, geolocation, and computing resources. Above all, these are geodata, cloud computing, and navigation technologies
For example, the Russian military uses Yandex Maps to obtain cartographic information. Kovalenko recalled that some Russian units had even publicly demonstrated their use of the service, and in 2025 the Russian military prosecutor’s office went to court seeking restrictions on servicemen’s publication of materials revealing the use of Yandex Maps.
The Russians use Yandex Cloud to work with large volumes of information, conduct analysis, and develop software solutions. According to Kovalenko, if such tools are involved in military projects, they could potentially support various processes – from processing intelligence data to operating artificial intelligence systems.
Let us imagine a situation: a servicemember has information about the terrain, topographical features, the location of certain objects, and the movement of the enemy. They need to process this data, compare it, and make a decision. Various digital tools, mapping services, and computing systems may be used for this. If artificial intelligence is involved in such a process, it also requires appropriate computing capacity. That is why I view strikes on data centers not only as economic or social pressure on Russia, but also as an issue that could potentially have military significance
Cybersecurity specialist Kostiantyn Korsun adds that a significant part of the Russian war machine’s activities related to data processing, the operation of websites and servers, and other digital processes depends on ordinary internet infrastructure. At the same time, encryption, traffic anonymization, and other protective measures are used.
As for the direct impact of strikes on data centers on the situation at the front, it will most likely be significantly smaller than we would like. I would even say that this impact could be minimal. Certain consequences are possible for rear headquarters located far from the line of contact and actively using the regular internet for their work. But the situation directly on the front line is different
This is because the Russians have virtually no internet connection on the front line, so the use of services such as Yandex Maps is limited.
But this does not mean that such strikes are entirely pointless. Their potential effect should be considered more broadly – in the context of the economy, digital infrastructure, and the dependence of Russian businesses on major technology platforms
Can the strikes increase pressure on the Kremlin?
Experts interviewed by UNN agree that Ukrainian strikes on Russian facilities have a cumulative effect and will gradually weaken Russia’s economy and its technological capabilities.
This does not mean that a single strike will automatically cause a logistical collapse. But if such losses become systematic, their cumulative effect may be much more tangible. This is precisely the point of gradually weakening the key nodes of the Russian economy
Clearly, the more of Russia’s critically important technological facilities are put out of operation and the more difficult they are to restore, the more costly the war against Ukraine becomes for the Russian economy.

Which airlines have cancelled Saudi flights amid Houthi attacks?
Major international airlines have suspended flights to Saudi Arabia following escalating Houthi attacks and threats against airports across the kingdom, leaving passengers facing cancellations, delays and diversions.
The disruption follows a series of attacks on Riyadh's main airport over the weekend that killed at least 12 people and injured more than 300, forcing authorities to temporarily close King Khalid International Airport.
The Houthis have warned that Saudi airports remain potential targets, raising concerns about further disruption to international air travel.
Some airlines have suspended services until mid-October, while others have extended cancellations until the end of the month.
Here's what to know about the flight cancellations, affected airports and travel warnings.
Which airlines have suspended flights to Saudi Arabia?
Several major international airlines have suspended flights to Riyadh, while others have cancelled selected services to Jeddah and Dammam.
According to Reuters, Lufthansa Group has suspended flights to Riyadh until 16 October, while Air France-KLM has halted services to the Saudi capital until the end of the month.
Other airlines have announced the following cancellations:
- Flydubai: All flights to and from Riyadh cancelled through 14 October.
- Air India: Riyadh services suspended until 15 October.
- Air India Express: Riyadh flights suspended until 14 October.
- SriLankan Airlines: Riyadh services suspended until 18 October.
- Etihad Airways: Selected flights between Abu Dhabi and Riyadh, Jeddah and Dammam cancelled between 11 and 13 October.
- Emirates: Flights between Dubai and Riyadh, Jeddah and Dammam affected by cancellations on Monday, 12 October.
- Air Arabia: Cancellations and schedule changes affecting Saudi routes.
- Qatar Airways and Kuwait Airways: Riyadh flights cancelled.
- Gulf Air: Flight cancelled to and from Riyadh until 17 October.
- Delta Air Lines: Delayed the inaugural flight that was set to launch between Atlanta and Riyadh on 23 October until March 2027, citing "evolving developments in the region".
The cancellations do not amount to a complete suspension of international flights to Saudi Arabia, with several airports continuing to operate despite significant disruption.
Are Saudi Arabia's airports still open?
Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport has been the worst affected following the weekend's deadly attacks.
Saudi authorities extended a notice to air missions (NOTAM) closing the airport until midnight local time on Saturday, 17 October.
Flight-tracking platform Flightradar24 ranked Riyadh's airport as the world's most disrupted airport on Monday.
Elsewhere, airports remain operational but are experiencing delays and cancellations.
Jeddah: King Abdulaziz International Airport remains open, although flights have faced significant disruption. Flightradar24 ranked it the world's second-most disrupted airport on Monday, after Riyadh.
Dammam: King Fahd International Airport is continuing operations despite delays. It has also received flights diverted from Riyadh.
Medina: Air traffic was continuing around Prince Mohammad bin Abdulaziz International Airport on Monday, according to live flight-tracking data.
Despite the disruption, aircraft are continuing to use Saudi airspace, according to flight-tracking data collected on Monday.
Why are Saudi airports being targeted?
The flight cancellations follow an escalation in attacks by Yemen's Houthis against Saudi Arabia, including the deadly strikes on Riyadh's airport over the weekend.
On Sunday, Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree renewed the group's warning against using Saudi airports, describing them as "potential targets and sites for operations by our forces".
He urged airlines, airport employees and passengers to take the warning seriously.
The Houthis have, however, said that the holy cities of Mecca and Medina are exempt from their threats.
The warnings have raised concerns about the safety of civilian aviation and the possibility of further disruption if attacks continue.

Which countries have issued travel warnings for Saudi Arabia?
Several countries have updated their travel advice amid the escalating attacks, warning citizens about security risks and disruption to flights.
Australia and New Zealand issued warnings on Monday urging travellers to avoid Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport and reconsider travel through other Saudi airports.
The warnings follow similar advisories from the UK, US, Canada, Japan and South Korea.
The UK's Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office advises against all but essential travel to several parts of Saudi Arabia, including Riyadh, Aseer, Najran and Jizan provinces.
On Sunday, it added Jeddah and Dammam to the areas covered by that advice.
British authorities also advise against all travel within 10 kilometres of the border with Yemen.
Meanwhile, the US Embassy in Riyadh has advised American citizens to reconsider travel to Saudi Arabia as a whole, citing threats linked to the Houthis and continuing security concerns surrounding the US-Israeli war with Iran.

Sybiha to EU: this week must be week of strength, mobilization — peace through strength, not concessions
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
14:25:48 EEST
20:25:48 KST

Minister of Foreign Affairs of Ukraine Andriy Sybiha states that he will tell his counterparts – foreign ministers of EU member states – that following "strange steps" in recent days, this week must become a week of strength, and peace must be achieved through strength, not concessions.
He said this to journalists in Luxembourg on Monday upon arriving at the EU Foreign Affairs Council meeting.
"After certain strange steps taken in recent days, Europe must show firmness and act decisively. This must become a week of strength – let me emphasize once again: a week of strength and mobilization of our diplomatic efforts. We need peace achieved through strength, not concessions," Sybiha stated.
The Ukrainian minister did not directly mention U.S. President Donald Trump's statements regarding the so-called "energy truce" and the necessity of holding elections in Ukraine, but these particular remarks by the American leader have recently become the subject of discussion in international politics regarding Russia's war against Ukraine.
Sybiha emphasized that President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy is "a strong leader who knows how to overcome challenges with dignity."
"My message to European colleagues today is simple: the era of dependency is over, Europe must take its future into its own hands, speak with one voice, and restore peace. Stop Putin in Ukraine – he is already at your doorstep," he urged.
According to the Foreign Minister of Ukraine, for Europe right now "it is a matter of leverage and tools: how to pressure Russia, how to raise the price for it to continue this war." In this context, he pointed to Russian assets frozen in the EU.
"Europe can no longer remain inactive regarding frozen Russian assets. The power of influence lies not in simply holding these funds, but in using them for defense. Russia must pay, not European taxpayers," Sybiha said.
He noted that there are reservations on this issue, and the Ukrainian side is ready to discuss them in terms of "shared responsibility, rather than a burden that falls solely on Belgium." As another tool of pressure on Russia, the Ukrainian minister named sanctions and isolation – "no stages or stadiums for Russian war propaganda."
Sybiha also stressed the need for Ukraine to protect its skies and energy infrastructure.
"We are ready for an energy truce. We are ready for any format of mutual agreements. For anything that is not a unilateral step. Yesterday statements were made [by Trump], but just hours after them Russia attacked our energy facilities... No one should believe Putin's words. Instead, one should look at his actions," the Foreign Minister of Ukraine pointed out, referring to known acts.
Speaking about the prospects of Ukraine's EU membership, he expressed conviction that the time has come to open the next negotiating clusters.
He also intends to inform colleagues about what Ukrainian soldiers need right now, as well as the state of play regarding peace efforts.
"Russia is betting on winter. Europe must bet on Ukraine. Every air defense system, every interceptor missile saves lives. Russia understands only the language of strength. The stronger the pressure on the aggressor, the closer Ukraine's security will be – and therefore, Europe's security," Sybiha stated.
He also reported that the Ukrainian side intends to propose sanctions against 10 more Russian oligarchs, while describing the recent removal of two from the EU list as a mistake.
"And I hope that one of the most powerful packages – the 22nd sanctions package – will be adopted as soon as possible," Sybiha added.

EU imposes sanctions over Russian State Duma "elections" in occupied territories of Ukraine
The Council of the EU has added 77 individuals to its sanctions list in connection with the illegal "elections" to the Russian State Duma in the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine.
Source: press service for the Council of the EU, as reported by European Pravda
Details: The Council has decided to adopt restrictive measures against 77 individuals who were involved in the illegal sham "elections" for the Russian State Duma, held in September 2026 in the territories of Ukraine that Russia has temporarily and illegally occupied.
The European Union has unequivocally condemned the organisation of these so-called "elections" in the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine, which breaches Ukrainian and international law, including the UN Charter, and undermines Ukraine's independence, sovereignty and territorial integrity.
The listings agreed today include 74 candidates who stood for election for various parties in the so-called "Donetsk People's Republic", the so-called "Luhansk People's Republic" and Zaporizhzhia and Kherson oblasts, as well as the so-called "Republic of Crimea and the City of Sevastopol". By running in the Russian State Duma "elections" these individuals actively contributed to efforts to legitimise Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine and to support Russia's illegal occupation of territories of Ukraine.
For the same reasons, the Council has imposed restrictive measures on three members of the Central Election Commission of the Russian Federation for organising the sham elections.
Those listed today are subject to a travel ban that prohibits them from entering or transiting through EU territories, and to an asset freeze. Additionally, EU citizens and companies are forbidden from making funds, financial assets or economic resources available to them.
The relevant legal acts have been published in the Official Journal of the European Union.
Background:
- On 12 October, EU foreign ministers approved the expansion of sanctions lists to include nearly 1,600 new names.
- On 12 October, the EU Foreign Affairs Council is also due to discuss the possibility of restricting the movement of Russian diplomats between EU member states, potentially including a complete ban on travelling outside the country in which they are accredited.
- The EU has also been discussing since the summer restrictions on issuing visas to people who fought in Ukraine on Russia's side. The EU's 21st sanctions package introduced a mechanism for banning visas for Russian military personnel, but the ban itself has not yet taken effect.

Russia Suffers 50,000 Casualties in 1 Month – NATO
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
11:20:39 UTC
20:20:39 KST

Russia suffered more than 50,000 military casualties in Ukraine during September, including as many as 28,000 troops killed, according to an assessment by a senior NATO military official.
The figure covers both killed and wounded personnel and represents one of Russia’s heaviest months of the war, Bloomberg reported on Sunday, Oct. 11.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The unnamed official, who discussed the assessment on condition of anonymity, estimated that Ukrainian forces suffered approximately 5,000 casualties over the same period.
That would put Russia’s total monthly losses at roughly 10 times Ukraine’s. Neither estimate could be independently verified, and Ukrainian authorities rarely disclose comprehensive figures for their own military casualties.
Russian troops sent into “kill zones”
The NATO official attributed Russia’s heavy losses partly to its continued attempts to advance through heavily defended Ukrainian positions.
Russian commanders have been sending troops into what the official described as “kill zones” covered by armed drones, landmines, artillery, and other defensive systems.
Despite the cost in personnel, Moscow continues offensive operations along several sections of the front.
At the same time, Ukrainian forces have intensified long-range strikes against Russian oil refineries, data centers, and other facilities supporting Moscow’s war effort. Ukrainian ground operations have also reportedly returned more than 125 square kilometers (48 square miles) of territory to Kyiv’s control.
Russia Needs Just 5 Drones to Test NATO, Kuleba Says
The NATO assessment broadly corresponds with figures released by Ukraine’s General Staff, which estimated that Russia lost 46,230 personnel in September. The Ukrainian military did not specify how many were killed and how many were wounded.
Russia’s total losses near 1.55 million
By Wednesday, Oct. 7, Ukraine’s military estimated that Russia’s total personnel losses since the beginning of the full-scale invasion had reached nearly 1.55 million.
That figure also combines troops killed and wounded and has not been independently confirmed.
Russia does not publish comprehensive information about military casualties or recruitment. Moscow’s last detailed official death toll was released during the early months of the invasion and is widely considered outdated.
Estimates from Ukraine, NATO, and Western intelligence agencies vary because they use different sources and methodologies, while distinguishing between deaths, injuries, and troops who later return to service remains difficult.
War places growing pressure on Moscow
The rising casualties come as the Kremlin spends heavily to recruit personnel and sustain offensive operations.
Russia’s defense expenditure is expected to approach 17 trillion rubles, or approximately $199 billion, in 2026 – around 40% higher than the government’s original plan announced at the end of 2025, according to Bloomberg.
German Federal Intelligence Service Chief Martin Jäger said last week that President Vladimir Putin’s war had created a situation in which ending the invasion without paying a domestic political price was becoming increasingly difficult.
The Kremlin has continued relying on large enlistment bonuses, regional recruitment campaigns, and pressure on vulnerable groups to replace battlefield losses while avoiding another publicly declared nationwide mobilization.

UN refugee agency's funding shortfall is impacting refugees worldwide, its chief says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
11:20:19 UTC
20:20:19 KST

Asked to ‘do the impossible’: UN refugee chief warns aid cuts threaten vital lifelines
- UNHCR chief Barham Salih warned that deep funding cuts are forcing painful global aid reductions. The agency has only US$3 billion (S$3.8 billion), or 35%, of the US$8.5 billion it needs for 2026.
- UNHCR has cut staff from 20,000 in 2024 to just under 12,000. Salih said “protection has a floor”, and warned the crisis is already harming refugees and partners.
- Aid cuts are threatening key work in Chad, Ethiopia and the Americas. The Americas face a 32% budget cut in 2027, while displaced people there may rise to 24.5 million.
AI generated
GENEVA – Deep funding shortfalls are forcing the UN refugee agency (UNCHR) to make painful cuts across its humanitarian operations worldwide, and there are limits to how much restructuring can offset shrinking donor support, its chief warned on Oct 12.
UNHCR has secured only US$3 billion (S$3.8 billion), or 35%, of the US$8.5 billion in funding it requires for 2026, High Commissioner Barham Salih told the agency’s executive committee at a meeting in Geneva.
The shortfall follows aid cuts by countries, including the United States under President Donald Trump, at a time of record global displacement.
Funding for 2026 remains uncertain although the expected figure of around US$2.68 billion could improve after a UNHCR donor pledging conference in December, Salih said.
UNHCR has launched one of its largest restructurings in its history because of the budget squeeze, with Salih saying its workforce has been reduced since 2024 from 20,000 employees to just under 12,000.
“Protection has a floor. Below it, the system does not simply become smaller. The protection we can provide begins to fail,” he said.
Salih cautioned that restructuring could not compensate indefinitely for lower funding, and that the funding crisis is already having tangible consequences for refugees and humanitarian partners.
“There is a difference between doing more with less and being asked to do the impossible,” he said.
UNHCR is seeking to preserve frontline operations by cutting jobs at its Geneva headquarters and worldwide regional offices, with 88% of staff remaining outside headquarters, Salih said.
About 95% of the staff doing protection work, such as registering refugees and providing legal assistance, and helping refugees find longer-term solutions, such as returning home safely, have been retained in field locations, he said.
He cited several examples of programmes under threat.
In Chad, he said, insufficient funding risks disrupting specialised medical care and legal assistance for more than 50,000 survivors of conflict-related sexual violence who fled neighbouring Sudan.
In Ethiopia, refugee registration has been suspended for tens of thousands of refugees from South Sudan and Eritrea, he said.
Colombia has raised concerns on behalf of Latin American countries that their region is being disproportionately impacted.
The Americas, which include the US, Canada, Latin America and the Caribbean, face a budget reduction of 32% in 2027 compared to 2026, or about US$485 million – the largest budget reduction of any region – while the number of forcibly displaced and stateless people in the Americas is projected to increase by 4% to about 24.5 million people in 2027, Salih said. REUTERS

Russia Weighs Drone Defenses for Data Centers After ‘Unprecedented’ Yandex Attacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
11:20:19 UTC
20:20:19 KST

Russia is working on measures to protect data centers from drone attacks after a series of “unprecedented” strikes on tech giant Yandex’s facilities, Digital Development Minister Maksut Shadayev said Monday.
“Yandex faced an unprecedented attack. The Digital Development Ministry, together with the Defense Ministry, is working on the issue of protecting these facilities,” Shadayev told a State Duma committee, according to Interfax.
He did not specify what protective measures were under consideration.
His comments follow drone attacks on three Yandex data centers in four days that have caused server outages that triggered service disruptions for users. The strikes hit facilities in the Ryazan, Kaluga and Vladimir regions between Thursday and Sunday.
The disruptions affected Yandex’s ride-hailing, food delivery and payment services, as well as companies that rely on Yandex Cloud, including online retailer Wildberries and fast-food chain Vkusno i Tochka.
Industry analysts told the Kommersant newspaper that replacing damaged server equipment could take up to six months.
Shadayev said backup systems and the distribution of computing capacity across multiple sites had helped services continue operating despite the scale of the attacks, adding that companies across the industry were helping address the disruptions.
Russian IT companies and mobile operators had begun buying mobile data centers even before this month’s attacks, the BBC’s Russian service reported. The outlet linked one supplier to a senior Federal Security Service (FSB) officer.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has described the targeted attacks as retaliation to Russia’s recent missile strikes against Ukrainian server facilities in Kyiv.
Russia has conducted a strike campaign against Ukrainian data centers and telecommunications infrastructure over the past month, including targets in central Kyiv.
Last month, the exiled news outlet Novaya Gazeta Europe reported that a large stake in Yandex was controlled by people linked to Bank Rossiya and President Vladimir Putin’s inner circle following the sale of the company’s Russian business in 2024.

Russia’s Main Tank Factory Now a ‘Repairer’ Not ‘Manufacturer’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
11:19:01 UTC
20:19:01 KST

The pro-Russian milblogger Andrei Tarasenko who discusses all things armor related on his Btvt.info Telegram channel expressed disgust at the current state of Russia’s main tank manufacturer. As it celebrated the 90th anniversary of its founding on Sunday, Oct. 11, the Uralvagonzavod (UVZ) tank factory located in Nizhny Tagil, which received congratulations from President Vladimir Putin, Tarasenko asked: “What has this plant… that has taken over all of Russia’s tank production, become?”
He lamented the fact that since the closure of the Kirov Spetsmash tank plant in 2017 UVZ was now the only major tank manufacturer left, and its capability had run down ever since. “Previously, they focused on quantity, sacrificing quality. Now, they can’t even deliver the required quantity,” he writes.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Battle losses outweigh new production
Recent media reports seem to support Btvt.info’s cries from the heart. Several social media sites, including that of Jakub Janovsky, posted images of battle-damaged Russian tanks, identified by bloggers as T-90Ms, loaded onto flatbed train wagons which they said were on their way to the UVZ factory for repair.
Janovsky, a lead analyst with the Oryx project – which documents equipment losses in the war in Ukraine from open sources, said it is likely that tanks subjected to factory repair are being portrayed in some areas as “new production.”
Telegraph Columnist Calls Trump’s Russia Diesel Deal ‘Catastrophic’
Tarasenko argues that repairs used to be the responsibility of the network of “BTRZ” military armored repair plants, but there has been a deterioration in capability of these facilities due to a combination of financial and commercial reasons.
“Where did the production capacity go? Was it sold to India and Iran? Who knows? The plant [UVZ], which should be assembling new tanks, is now dismantling old ones – this grand scheme is driven by the fact that this process costs the same or even more than to build a new tank.”
New versus repaired – the distinction matters
The United 24 website, in an article published on Oct. 8, says that analysts have asserted that some T-90Ms leaving declared as new builds by UVZ were actually refurbished hulls from older T-90 variants, which casts doubt on its announcement earlier last week that it had delivered another batch of T-90M and upgraded T-72B3M tanks fitted with the Arena-M active counter drone system Russia had demonstrated during the Tsentr-2026 maneuvers.
Janovsky argues that the distinction matters. The recycling of battle-damaged vehicles rather than genuinely newly manufactured tanks prevents analysts from accurately assessing the progress of the war.
This is much more than just a numbers game: it could drive decisions by Ukraine’s partners on the levels of financial and military support they offer.
