Thales to open what could be Japan’s first foreign-run defence maintenance base
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
11:18:07 UTC
20:18:07 KST

The facility could be the first in Japan set up by a foreign defence company to maintain military equipment and support its operation, according to Nikkei.
French defence company Thales SA will establish a maintenance and operational support base in Japan for military equipment, Nikkei reported on Monday, but neither an opening date nor a location has been revealed.
Chairman and chief executive Patrice Caine told the Nikkei business daily that the base "will mark a milestone toward Thales's long-term engagement in Japan".
The facility could be the first in Japan set up by a foreign defence company to maintain military equipment and support its operation, the newspaper reported.
The new maintenance base will check the condition of military equipment and diagnose faults, according to Nikkei. Initially, it will focus on equipment for the Maritime Self-Defence Force, with plans to extend its work to the Ground and Air Self-Defence Forces.
Caine cited technologies such as radar and sonar as possible areas for cooperation with Japan, saying that he hoped to "provide support in areas where Thales has an advantage in terms of performance".
The facility’s work could also extend to civilian equipment in the future, the newspaper said.
The report comes as Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi continues to increase defence spending amid concerns over China's rapid military expansion and North Korea’s weapons programmes.
Alongside its maintenance plans, Thales is also expanding local production. It will transfer technology for its 2R2M heavy mortar system to Japan Steel Works, which will begin producing it in Japan in 2027, according to Nikkei.
Thales has been supplying Mitsubishi Heavy Industries with sonar for underwater vehicles used by Japan’s Maritime Self-Defence Force to detect mines.
Thales has operated in Japan since 1970, with activities spanning defence, aerospace and digital security.
The company's share price in Paris was up by about 1.5% around midday on Monday.

====================================================================================================

Ukraine’s FM: Russia’s war budget makes the case for using frozen assets now
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
11:18:05 UTC
20:18:05 KST

Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha speaks during a briefing marking Ukrainian Defence Industry Day in Kyiv, on April 13, 2026. | Tetiana Dzhafarova/AFP via Getty Images
Andrii Sybiha is Ukraine’s minister of foreign affairs
Europe can no longer remain immobilized on Russian assets. Now is the time to use them for Ukraine’s defense and recovery.
This decision, which is long overdue, would be a game changer that could shift the balance in Ukraine’s favor — particularly if taken alongside strong sanctions pressure. But to achieve this, we have to be faster and more decisive than Russia.
Advertisement
According to the latest reports, Russia plans to spend a record €180 billion on its military in 2027 — more than 40% above its 2026 defense allocation. And that is only part of the picture. The country’s draft federal budget allocates a combined €669 billion to defense and security for the 2027–2029 period.
These figures make clear Russia wants war. Moscow is increasing the pressure, intensifying its terror against Ukrainian civilians and raising the cost of defense for both Ukraine and Europe. But as the cost of war grows, it should grow faster for the aggressor.
The higher the price for Moscow, the sooner peace will be restored. Half-hearted pressure on Russia and half-measures in support of Ukraine will only prolong conflict and increase the overall price tag. Decisive steps can bring it to a close.
Local residents stand amid the rubble of a five-storey residential building following a Russian attack that killed seven people, including three children, in Zaporizhzhia on October 10, 2026. | Daria Nazarova/AFP via Getty Images
At the end of August, Sweden, the Netherlands, Spain and Poland addressed the European Commission, urging renewed discussion on the full use of immobilized Russian assets. We are grateful to them. But it is now time to turn this discussion into a legal process: launch a permanent platform, engage experts and develop the decision.
Europe has taken the hardest step already. In 2022, the G7 immobilized some €300 billion in Russian central bank reserves, roughly €210 billion of them in the EU. In 2024, the G7 borrowed $50 billion for Ukraine against the future windfall profits on those reserves. And in December 2025, the bloc made the immobilization open-ended.
What remains undecided is the only step that matters: using the assets themselves.
Advertisement
Every argument for and against this has been heard, and the debate now revolves around its scope and how to mitigate associated risks.
The prevailing view is that the decision to use these assets must not expose any single country to disproportionate risk — above all Belgium, where most of the assets sit at Euroclear. We agree. To that end, Ukraine’s Finance Ministry proposed a clear plan to the European Commission: placing the assets under collective EU control, so that the decision to use them — and the liability for doing so — is European, not Belgian.
An outside view of the headquarters of the Euroclear Group financial institute in Brussels, April 9, 2025. | Nicolas Maeterlinck/Belga Mag/AFP via Getty Images
Belgium’s exposure is a reason to share the risk, not to do nothing.
Another common argument is that any decision must cover immobilized assets in every jurisdiction, not only those at Euroclear. Again, we agree — with one caveat: This can be done but on parallel tracks. Europe should not make its own decision contingent on protracted global coordination when its security is in peril.
Skeptics raise four objections of principle against the full use of these assets: that using them breaks the rule of law, that it undermines the euro as a reserve currency, that it gives away leverage in peace talks, and that Russia would retaliate by seizing Western assets.
Let’s take these arguments in turn.
Advertisement
On rule of law: Under the International Law Commission’s 2001 Articles on State Responsibility, a state that commits an internationally wrongful act owes full reparations, and injured states may take countermeasures to induce compliance. And in November 2022, the U.N. General Assembly recognized that Russia must bear the legal consequences of its aggression, including reparations.
The same articles also require countermeasures to be reversible, and Ukraine’s position honors that: The legal title stays in an EU-governed vehicle, Ukraine receives financing rather than ownership, and the arrangement unwinds the day Russia pays what it owes.
On the euro: This has already been tested. When the reserves were immobilized in February 2022, the euro’s share of global reserves did not move. Reserve holders understood then what they understand now — that this principle applies to a state waging a war of aggression in breach of the U.N. Charter, not to anyone else. Moreover, the euro’s credibility as a reserve currency rests on Europe’s ability to defend order and principles.
Members of the General Assembly vote on a draft resolution during a special session in the General Assembly Hall at United Nations Headquarters on November 14, 2022 in New York City. | Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images
On leverage: These assets have been immobilized for more than four years and have not moved Moscow any closer to peace. A country budgeting €669 billion for a war of aggression is not bargaining for its reserves. What deters Russia is Ukraine’s capacity to keep fighting — and that is precisely what a European solution on these assets would fund. The leverage is not in holding the money, it is in spending it.
Finally, on seizing Western assets in Russia: Putin has been doing this since 2022. This September alone, Moscow took control of the Russian businesses of Nestlé, Auchan, Leroy Merlin, FM Logistic and Metro, following Danone and Carlsberg. That is why, as early as March 2022, we urged companies to leave. The confiscation of European property has already happened — and keeping the assets immobilized did not deter this.
Let us be clear about what we are not proposing. We are not proposing outright confiscation — the legal title will not transfer. We are not proposing a Belgian decision — the risk will be shared at the EU level. And we are not proposing a precedent for anyone else. The conditions — a war of aggression condemned by the U.N. General Assembly — are met by only one state.
Advertisement
Russia must be the one to pay for the damage it has caused and continues to cause, not European taxpayers.
We should be sending the right signal to Moscow: That it will not outlast our resolve.
We should be sending the right signal to skeptical audiences across Europe ahead of a major election year: That the rising cost of Ukraine’s defense will be covered at the expense of Russia.
Last but not least, we should be sending the right signal to the Ukrainian people: that they are not alone in confronting the aggressor.
The full use of Russian assets would bring tangible and immediate results, strengthening Ukraine on the frontline and bringing peace closer. After four years, Europe should no longer be immobilized on major decisions. It needs political will, collective commitment and a solid legal formula.
We urge EU leaders to make this vital decision without delay. And we look forward to the European bravery in taking this critical step.

2026 Nobel Prize in Economics goes to Robert E. Hall, Michael Woodford
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
19:17:13 CST
20:17:13 KST

STOCKHOLM, Oct. 12 (Xinhua) -- The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences announced Monday that the 2026 Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel has been awarded to Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford for "microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilization."
The academy said the laureates have developed macroeconomic models that have significantly improved the ability to implement effective stabilization policies. Based on these models, well-timed fiscal and monetary policy measures can help smooth economic fluctuations.
"The laureates' work has provided us with a stable theoretical foundation for the models that are now used by central banks and governments around the world. With them, we are better equipped to deal with shocks in the economy, such as energy crises or sudden changes in how much households consume," said John Hassler, chair of the Committee for the Prize in Economic Sciences.
Both laureates were born in the United States. Hall is a professor at Stanford University, while Woodford is affiliated with Columbia University. ■

Interview: Chinese automakers gain greater visibility in European market, says Paris Motor Show director
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
19:16:56 CST
20:16:56 KST

PARIS, Oct. 12 (Xinhua) -- Chinese automakers are becoming more visible in the European market, with their product offerings becoming more structured and their technological level continuing to improve, said Serge Gachot, director of the Paris Motor Show.
In a recent interview with Xinhua ahead of the 2026 Paris Motor Show, Gachot said the biennial event would bring together more than 60 automakers and over 100 exhibitors from Europe, America and Asia, with Chinese automakers having a more visible presence than at the previous edition.
"The content of the automobile itself is evolving," Gachot said, adding that electrification, software, artificial intelligence, connectivity and automated driving are playing an increasingly important role.
"The Paris Motor Show thus showcases an automobile that is no longer limited to the powertrain and the vehicle itself, but increasingly integrates various technologies and new uses," he said.
Speaking about Chinese automakers, Gachot said their product offerings had become more structured. "They no longer come only with competitively priced electric vehicles, but with broader ranges, mainstream and high-end positioning, and greater attention to design, onboard technologies and the digital experience," he said.
Gachot also noted that the technological level of Chinese automakers had continued to improve, particularly in batteries, driving range, connectivity and driver-assistance systems. "This evolution is driving a growing commercial presence of Chinese automakers in Europe," he said.
On the localization of Chinese automakers in Europe, Gachot said Chinese automakers are also beginning to localize part of their activities in Europe, including production, research and distribution, adding that it would strengthen their integration into the European automotive industry.
"By investing in production, research or local supply chains, they become directly involved in this ecosystem," he said.
He said such localization would strengthen competition, while cooperation would also increase.
"Intelligent driving is a good illustration: it requires combining automotive expertise, software, sensors, data and artificial intelligence. No single player necessarily masters the entire chain alone," he noted.
On the European market for electrified vehicles, Gachot said the transition was already well underway.
"In France, electric vehicles represented 30 percent of new car sales as of the end of August 2026, compared with 20 percent for the whole of 2025. In Germany, they reached 26 percent, compared with 19 percent a year earlier," he said.
The price remains a key factor in consumers' choice of a vehicle, Gachot said, but it needs to be considered alongside the cost of use, driving range, ease of charging and available infrastructure, as well as comfort, digital features and the software experience, which are playing an increasingly important role.
Gachot also recalled his visit to Auto China 2026 in Beijing in April, which left a strong impression on him.
He said the automobile was also being redesigned around the passenger experience, with new formats, including SUV-style multi-purpose vehicles, placing greater emphasis on space, comfort and connectivity.
"As the car takes on an increasing share of driving, value is also shifting toward what people can do inside: relax, work, communicate or entertain themselves," he said.
"We are witnessing not only the rapid progress of an industry, but also an evolution in the very conception of the automobile." ■

SUVA, Oct. 12 (Xinhua) -- Plastic waste found at every coastal stop during Fiji's Paddle for Hope campaign has highlighted growing concerns over the country's waste management system and the long-term sustainability of its coastal environments, the Pacific Recycling Foundation said.
Amitesh Deo, founder of the foundation, said the findings underscored persistent shortcomings in waste management and the need for coordinated efforts to protect coastal areas that are vital to Fiji's tourism industry, reported Fiji Broadcasting Corporation on Monday.
As a major tourism destination in the South Pacific, Fiji relies heavily on its natural attractions, including pristine beaches and marine ecosystems, to draw international visitors.
Plastic pollution threatens these environmental assets, potentially undermining the country's tourism appeal while placing additional pressure on local communities and conservation efforts.
Deo said tackling the problem required a comprehensive approach covering waste collection, recycling, processing and the tracking of discarded materials to determine their final destinations.
Public awareness campaigns alone would not be enough to curb pollution without accessible recycling services, reliable waste collection and adequate processing facilities, he added.
Deo also called for greater support for established recycling programs and grassroots initiatives, stressing the importance of incorporating informal waste collectors and community-based recyclers into national waste management strategies.
Without urgent and coordinated action, plastic pollution could intensify across Fiji and the wider Pacific over the next 10 to 20 years, Deo warned, making it increasingly difficult to protect coastal ecosystems and sustain tourism-related economic activities. ■

China-EU consensus on vehicle trade averts escalation of trade frictions: commerce ministry
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
19:16:24 CST
20:16:24 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 12 (Xinhua) -- The consensus reached between China and the European Union (EU) on hybrid and electric vehicle trade has helped prevent an escalation of trade frictions, a spokesperson for China's Ministry of Commerce said on Monday.
The spokesperson made the remarks in response to speculation by some foreign media outlets over details of the trade arrangements, particularly those concerning hybrid vehicles, following the latest meeting of the China-EU trade and investment consultation mechanism in Beijing.
The spokesperson said China and the EU had engaged in sustained dialogue under the mechanism and reached consensus on a number of outcomes, helping maintain a stable and balanced relationship between these two key trading partners.
Guided by the principles of mutual respect and equal consultation, the two sides held intensive talks on hybrid and electric vehicle trade, addressing economic and trade differences and each other's concerns in a balanced manner, the spokesperson noted.
Regarding hybrid vehicles, the two sides emphasized and confirmed three basic principles: respect for facts, non-discrimination and compliance with World Trade Organization (WTO) rules.
Citing Eurostat data, the spokesperson said the EU imported 107,000 hybrid vehicles from China in 2024 and 302,000 in 2025.
Building on the 2025 level, the two sides reached an arrangement allowing for further increases, ensuring room for Chinese enterprises to maintain exports and achieve steady growth while taking into account the legitimate concerns of industries on both sides based on actual conditions, the spokesperson said.
Under the principle of non-discrimination, no measures will specifically target Chinese products, let alone discriminate against Chinese enterprises. The quota allocated to China will be no lower than that granted by the EU to any other source of imports, according to the spokesperson.
The two sides also confirmed that the trade arrangement should comply with WTO rules. China reserves all its rights under the WTO framework, including the right to resort to dispute settlement and seek trade compensation, the spokesperson said.
Regarding electric vehicles, the spokesperson said China and the EU achieved a "soft landing" in the EU's anti-subsidy case in January this year, with the bloc issuing a general guidance document on price undertakings. The EU will continue to advance relevant procedures concerning price undertakings by companies involved in the case, as well as other review procedures, the spokesperson added.
The spokesperson stressed that the consensus, reached on the basis of reciprocity and mutual benefit, has effectively safeguarded the interests of Chinese enterprises, prevented an escalation of China-EU trade frictions, and provided a stable, predictable and sustainable environment for bilateral trade and investment, contributing to the stable, balanced and sound development of China-EU economic and trade relations. ■

====================================================================================================

Britain&#8217;s Jerusalem mission stays open, but its work with Palestinians is in doubt
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
11:16:07 UTC
20:16:07 KST

On 8 October, 2026, Israel’s foreign minister, Gideon Sa’ar, announced that the British Consulate General in Jerusalem “ceases operations today”. Overnight, workers had taken down the plaque reading “British Consulate General” from the building in Sheikh Jarrah, Reuters reported. In a statement that day, Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband renamed it the “UK Mission, Jerusalem”, described it as “independent, operational” and said it would continue its services and its work with the Palestinian people.
The two governments are describing the same agreement. Sa’ar says 20 of the post’s 27 diplomats, the consul general among them, will leave, and that the seven who remain will do “very limited” work. The British statement gives no figures; it says a number of staff and families have been temporarily withdrawn. Britain has now agreed to the immediate reduction, while saying it does not accept that Israel has the legal right to close the consulate.
The dispute began on 8 September, when Miliband announced in the Commons a ban on imports from Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, which Britain regards as illegal. He promised immediate sanctions on extremist settlers who had supported or incited violence, and said legislation for a wider sanctions regime could take up to nine months. He accused settlers of ethnic cleansing, and Sa’ar dismissed the accusation as a lie.
Eleven other countries, including France and Canada, backed action against settlement trade. The same day, Sa’ar ordered the consulate closed within 30 days, expelled British officials from Ramallah and from the US-led coordination centre for Gaza, halted British training of Palestinian Authority security forces and barred 12 British figures, 11 of them MPs, from entering Israel.
Britain has not withdrawn its announced settlement measures, and Miliband says it “stands steadfast” behind them. It has suspended retaliation rather than renouncing it. The Foreign Office says the building will stay open following discussions with the Israeli government, and that Britain will not take reciprocal action “while such discussions are underway and credible”. It describes the staff withdrawals as temporary and promises to “build back up our presence” in the coming months, without giving a date.
READ: UK removes signage from East Jerusalem consulate as Israeli closure deadline expires
According to the Financial Times, British government figures said London had decided that it was not right to retaliate during Israel’s election campaign, which ends with polling on 27 October. The same report says UK officials defended the deal by pointing out that Israel’s original threat was to close the consulate altogether, and that keeping a presence in Jerusalem would make it easier to build back up.
Israel’s leverage lay in the diplomatic status of the consulate’s staff. The post’s origins date to 1838, and it has been a consulate general since the British Mandate ended in 1948. Like the handful of other states with such posts, Britain never asked Jordan or Israel for an exequatur, the formal permission a host state grants a foreign consul, because asking would have implied accepting their sovereignty over the city. The post reported to London rather than to the embassy in Tel Aviv. It conducted Britain’s political relations with the Palestinian leadership, carried out its development work in the West Bank and Gaza, and gave consular help to British nationals there.
In Britain’s legal view, the consulate never needed Israel’s consent to exist. Its staff needed Israel’s paperwork to work. The closure order threatened to strip their Israeli accreditation within 30 days. Dominic Grieve, a former attorney general, argued in a paper for the Britain Palestine Project that the closure was “an unlawful assertion of Israeli sovereignty over occupied East Jerusalem”. The Palestinian foreign ministry made a similar argument in 2021, when Israel opposed Washington reopening its own Jerusalem consulate: East Jerusalem, it said, “is an inseparable part of the occupied Palestinian territory”, and Israel, as the occupying power, had no right to veto the decision.
In the House of Lords, Foreign Office minister Lord Wood acknowledged that Lord Hannay’s legal objection might have merit, but said Israel could prevent the consulate from operating. When the closure was ordered, Alon Liel, a former director-general of Israel’s foreign ministry, said: “The Israeli reaction is not against Britain. It’s against Palestine.”
The announcements leave unclear what restrictions the remaining diplomats will face when travelling or meeting Palestinian officials, and they give no account of the locally employed staff who work alongside them.
Britain recognised the State of Palestine on 21 September, 2025. Two months later, the Scottish National Party MP Brendan O’Hara asked whether the consul general would present credentials to the Palestinian president as ambassador, and the Foreign Office replied that the post’s future status would be determined “in due course”. Turning a Jerusalem consulate into an embassy to Palestine would itself be a statement about the city’s final status, which Britain says is still to be determined. The consulate’s ambiguity was useful because it left that question open while the work continued.
On 5 January, 2026, Palestine upgraded its London mission to an embassy, headed by Husam Zomlot. Britain’s side of the relationship depends on permissions from a third state: Israel accredits Britain’s diplomats in Jerusalem and controls the occupied territory in which they work.
Israel has used similar restrictions against other countries. After Spain announced its decision to recognise Palestine in May 2024, Israel ordered its Jerusalem consulate to stop providing consular services to Palestinians in the West Bank. Norway and Ireland faced retaliation for recognition. In September 2026, Israel announced it would revoke the accreditation of Dutch diplomats in the West Bank after the Netherlands began enforcing sanctions on settlement goods.
The American case differs: in 2019, the Trump administration merged its own Jerusalem consulate into its new embassy by choice, whereas Israel imposed the restrictions on European diplomatic missions. With Spain, the Netherlands and now Britain, Israel has used the same instrument: restricting the diplomats through whom a government deals with Palestinians. France and Sweden, which also joined the British measures, keep consulates in Jerusalem that deal with the Palestinian Authority, and so have a direct interest in whether the British arrangement becomes a precedent.
Miliband should explain which functions the reduced mission can still perform and how he intends to restore its staff. He should also say what Britain will do if Israel prevents diplomats from returning or obstructs their work with Palestinians.

====================================================================================================

French MPs push exit tax on crypto above €800,000 and fines for undeclared wallets
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
11:15:32 UTC
20:15:32 KST

French MPs want wealthy crypto investors who leave the country to pay tax on their paper gains, under an amendment backed in committee last week alongside fines of up to €10,000 for undeclared self-custody wallets, though every measure must be voted on again.
Moving abroad from France could soon cost the richest holders of digital assets more, as lawmakers seek to bring Bitcoin and other crypto into a levy already paid by relocating equity investors.
On Thursday, the National Assembly’s finance committee, the cross-party panel that vets budget bills before the full lower house debates them, voted to extend France’s exit tax to crypto-assets from 1 January 2027.
The current levy taxes unrealised gains when people who have lived in France for at least six of the past ten years move abroad with shares and other securities cumulatively worth more than €800,000.
The amendment would apply the same threshold to a household’s crypto, including tokens on foreign platforms or in self-custody wallets that owners control directly.
As with shares, payment would be deferred for moves within the EU and to some other countries, and the tax is cancelled if the assets are kept for two to five years.
The amendment does not set a rate or mention social charges, which make up 18.6 points of the 31.4% levied on departing shareholders’ gains, leaving unclear what crypto holders would pay.
Its sponsors, Communist MP Nicolas Sansu and 16 left-wing colleagues, argue that crypto escapes a levy applied to securities of equal value, inviting tax avoidance.
Wallets, stablecoins and other measures
The committee also backed a plan by centrist MP Charles de Courson to make taxpayers declare self-custody wallets worth a combined €100,000 or more at year-end, or face fines of up to €10,000. Currently, only crypto accounts abroad must be reported.
Citing a parliamentary inquiry that flagged crypto as a fraud risk, its backers say French investors made an estimated €3.5 billion in crypto gains in 2021 but declared only €400 million in holdings.
France’s Court of Audit has said that figure was in fact declared gains.
Crypto advocates warn such a data register could leak and endanger holders, amid a wave of crypto-linked kidnappings in France.
Police counted more than 40 crypto-linked kidnappings in France between January and mid-April, after about 30 in all of 2025.
In one of the best-known cases, kidnappers seized David Balland, co-founder of French crypto wallet maker Ledger, and his partner in January 2025, cutting off one of his fingers to press a crypto ransom demand before police freed them.
A second Sansu amendment, which also sets no rate, would make swapping crypto for stablecoins, tokens pegged to a currency such as the US dollar, taxable from 2027 under the existing 31.4% flat tax on crypto gains.
Tax is currently only due on cashing out or spending crypto.
MPs also voted to let investors offset crypto losses against gains for ten years and to raise a planned fine for ignoring tax authority requests for documents from €10,000 to €50,000 per request. The government’s bill applies it to financial institutions, crypto firms and online platforms.
The committee rejected a broader wealth tax including crypto and a bid by centre-right MP Paul Midy to make up to €1,000 a year of crypto payments tax-free.
What happens next
On Friday, the committee voted down the revenue part of the government’s 2027 budget bill, which covers taxes, by 31 votes to 3.
France’s constitution requires the full Assembly to debate the government’s original budget, with committee changes normally put to MPs as amendments.
With the revenue part rejected, none carry over, so the crypto amendments must be re-tabled from Tuesday.
MPs vote again on the revenue part on 20 October and the whole bill on 17 November, before the Senate takes over. Last year, they threw out the revenue part by 404 votes to 1, wiping out their changes.
The French Parliament has until 10 December to pass the budget, after which the government can enact it by ordinance.
With France’s 10-year borrowing costs briefly topping 5% this month for the first time since 2002 and parties eyeing next spring’s presidential election, the minority government faces an uphill battle to pass the budget.

UK's Farage pledges to suspend asylum claims for up to five years
LONDON, Oct 12 - Nigel Farage, leader of the populist Reform UK party, announced on Monday he would ban anyone being granted asylum for up to five years if his party wins the next national election as part of a crackdown on immigration to Britain.
Farage, a leading figure in the Brexit campaign, said the roughly 90,000 pending asylum applications would be declared void, new claims would be automatically rejected, and failed applicants would be returned either to their home countries or a safe third country.
Speaking on the south coast of England, Farage said he could impose tariffs, visa bans or airspace restrictions on countries refusing to accept the return of asylum seekers.

Reform UK was leading in the opinion polls until this summer, but a combination of ongoing police and parliamentary investigations into how the party is funded plus Andy Burnham taking over as Labour prime minister has pushed the party into second place. Reform UK denies breaking electoral law.
The next election is due in 2029. Immigration remains the top issue for British voters, according to the polls, driven in part by frustration over successive governments' failure to stop tens of thousands of asylum seekers arriving in boats from mainland Europe.
In the year ending in June, Britain received 85,891 asylum applicants, a 21% decrease compared to the same period a year earlier. Individuals from Pakistan, Eritrea, Iran, Sudan and Afghanistan made up the largest number of applicants.
Reform said on Monday it would scrap all legal routes for asylum resettlement, but exempt Ukrainians who fled to Britain after Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022.
Refugee charities have said Farage's deportation plans would mean sending asylum seekers back to countries, such as Afghanistan or Iran, where they could face persecution, torture and death. REUTERS

How Apple Puts Indigenous Languages on the iPhone Keyboard
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
11:15:00 UTC
20:15:00 KST

Chuck Hoskin Jr. fondly recalls watching a room full of Cherokee immersion students crowd around a screen to watch How to Train Your Dragon. Except Hiccup and Astrid weren't speaking English—the protagonists were speaking Cherokee, dubbed by voices from the local community.
“They're hearing it in our mother tongue—that didn't happen a generation ago,” Hoskin Jr., principal chief of the Cherokee Nation, tells WIRED. “We're a long way, thankfully, from rote classroom instruction and memorization to a world where kids can see the sort of creativity that sparks imagination and helps every kid become more articulate and literate.”
The Cherokee Nation has around 1,500 active speakers left, and most are over 70. Hoskin Jr. says the community is rapidly losing that generation, which is why it has spent time training up second-language learners. It even has a baby immersion program, hoping their first words are Cherokee.
“The foes we’ve had historically are the so-called Age of Discovery, colonization, the displacement of our people economically and geographically, boarding schools,” he says. “But it's nothing compared to the mathematics we’re up against now. Which is why we’re filled with this urgency every day to do all we can to find partners that can help us accelerate what we want to do.”
One of those accelerants is Apple. The Cherokee Nation has long collaborated with the iPhone maker, and Cherokee was the first Native American language included in iOS in 2010. Today, Apple says its iOS keyboard supports more than 200 languages and language variants, with a handful added last year in iOS 26, like Haitian Creole and Nez Perce. In iOS 27, it expanded support for Indigenous languages to include other Native American languages like Blackfoot, Comanche, and Northern East Cree.
The goal is to meet young people where they already spend much of their waking hours: phone screens. Hoskin Jr. says that to revitalize and save a language, it has to become accessible. Apple says the effort isn't as simple as translating words. It’s a multi-year endeavor that requires deep research, and the company leans on community members for their expertise.
But the process doesn’t start in Cupertino. It actually begins with Unicode. You may have heard of the name—it’s the organization that approves and standardizes the new emoji that appear on your smartphone every year. It also handles time zone localization, currency names, imperial versus metric, and so on.
Before you can type or read a character on a smartphone screen, it needs to exist as a recognized character in the Unicode Standard. “Everything does start with Unicode in terms of a language, but it actually starts with characters and scripts,” says Unicode CEO Toral Cowieson. “We now have more than 157,000 characters that are included.”
Cowieson calls Unicode a kind of digital Switzerland—a neutral consortium where rivals like Apple, Microsoft, and Google sit at the same table as linguists and volunteer contributors. (Cowieson told WIRED earlier this year that Unicode had only four full-time employees.) Proposing a language, verifying it, and then encoding the character set can take three to five years.
After a script is encoded, platforms like Apple and Google need to add font support. Without this step, a character could appear as an empty box—often called “tofu.” Next is orthography: a set of rules and systems for writing a language. Often, languages have a well-defined orthography, but when it’s not standardized, communities use ad hoc replacements because historically available keyboards don't support it.
Take the glottal stop—the speech sound made in the throat between the syllables when you say, “uh-oh.” Some languages have distinct characters for glottal stops, but as some keyboards don’t support them, many indigenous cultures use alternatives, like a question mark, to represent the sound. That's when Apple connects with the community to figure out the best way to represent the sounds in digital text.
That brings us to the keyboard layout. When a community already has an established physical keyboard layout—like Osage—Apple adapts it directly to the software keyboard. Some cultures prefer the QWERTY layouts people are already familiar with.
Other languages need more custom approaches. For example, Nez Perce, or Nimipuutímt, does not use capital letters. Rather than having the Shift key toggle traditional uppercase letters, Apple repurposed it to reveal an accented secondary layer, so users don’t have to hold down individual keys to see those characters, which can slow typing. In the Cherokee language, each character mostly represents a consonant combined with a vowel sound, a form known as syllabary. Apple added adaptive vowel keys on the bottom row, so when a user types a consonant, these keys change to show the vowel combinations they can make.
That’s a newer change to the Cherokee keyboard—one Apple approached the community about, meaning building a keyboard for a language isn’t a one-and-done project.
But digitizing an indigenous culture’s language hasn't always been harmless. Genner Llanes-Ortiz, a Maya scholar and researcher at Bishop's University, studies how Indigenous people use digital technologies to reclaim language heritage. He recalls how Māori speakers rejected proposals to sell their language to tech companies.
“There’s a historical memory about the ways of dispossession that Indigenous peoples have experienced in the world,” Llanes-Ortiz says. “Māori working in their own revitalization efforts have been very firm in protecting access and storage of their linguistic materials because they have been exploited. They have experienced extraction of knowledge in the past.”
Language sovereignty and data ownership are top of mind, according to Chirasree Mandal, an Apple software engineer. “We don’t own anything, and we make it very clear that we are not trying to silo any data that we gain from this process,” she says. “It’s about making sure that the best choice for representing someone’s language is being made on our platform so they feel good using it.”
For its part, a Google spokesperson tells WIRED it has a long history of bringing lesser-known and Indigenous languages to its platforms so people can communicate, pointing to collaborations to integrate languages like Manx and Māori. Google also says it’s exploring how generative AI can simplify the coding and research required for new languages, but “successful integrations require direct participation from native speakers” for the keyboard to meet the community’s needs.
Hoskin Jr. says that writing in syllabary is seen as a badge of honor for young Cherokee speakers. People type their names in Cherokee on Facebook—that’s empowering. But he sees that progress as vulnerable to broader political rhetoric in the US that pushes a monolithic, English-speaking America, which he says bypasses several chapters, including Native American history.
“The greatest enemy we have right now for saving the Cherokee language is the passage of time and the fragility of human life,” Hoskin Jr. says. “Time is precious to everyone, but particularly precious to us in this mission.”

Mort à la révolution! Why UK film loves a failed rebellion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
11:14:33 UTC
20:14:33 KST

The British are perverse. We fetishise our failures, even if they are essentially tangential to a national narrative that should be about imperial conquest, slavery and being unremittingly unpleasant to foreigners. We tell and retell, for instance, the story of Captain Scott even though he died in Antarctica in 1912 after losing the race to reach the south pole first to the unacceptably Norwegian Roald Amundsen. Similarly, Christopher Nolan’s 2017 film Dunkirk typified the British tendency to snatch national glory from the jaws of defeat. And then there was the tragicomic disaster of the Charge of the Light Brigade during the 1853-56 Crimean war in which our boys raced to putatively glorious if stupid deaths. It’s as if, for us British, pointless sacrifice and embracing failure are what heroism means. And our cinema has colluded with this perversity.
But there is an exception to this national veneration of failure. Britain has been reluctant to embrace its revolutionary defeats. There is, for instance, no film dealing with the Chartist movement’s 19th-century struggle for universal suffrage. Even more strikingly yet, it is only now, in 2026, that a film has been made about the calamitous 1381 Peasants’ Revolt, even though it is a pivotal event in British history. Paul Greengrass’s The Uprising, starring Andrew Garfield as a – let’s just get this over with – revolting peasant, joins a mere handful of other movies, including Kevin Brownlow and Andrew Mollo’s 1975 Winstanley, Bill Douglas’s 1986 Comrades and Mike Leigh’s 2018 Peterloo, that dare depict how radical collective action was crushed by a ruthless state.
For Stephanie Barczewski, author of Heroic Failure and the British, our fetishisation of glorious disaster is a corollary of the 19th-century British private school ethos of stoic duty and crypto-S&M suffering culled from an ancient Roman exemplar. Revolutionary failure doesn’t fit this template; hence, one might suppose, its absence from our cinema.
The Uprising, however, for all its flaws and missteps, is a bold attempt to correct a national wrong by depicting a collective uprising devoid of heroism. Greengrass tries to make sense of how a mass movement of riff-raff from the rough ends of Kent and Essex arose, and how its momentum was compromised of factionalism and conflicting aims. It shows how, ultimately, the revolutionary leaders were duped by the boy king Richard II, leaving the rebels winding up to be either slaughtered en masse in London’s Smithfield or skulking defeated back to their homes to work harder to pay the poll tax whose unfairness they had risen up against in the first place.
It is an important – if belated, improbable and commercially dubious – addition to our national story.
In contrast, other countries have been more fortunate in their revolutionary heritage and as a result their national cinemas teem with examples of successful uprisings. From the advent of cinema, for instance, Americans have incessantly revelled in making movies about their war of independence – including silent features such as 1917’s The Spirit of 76 and DW Griffith’s America (1924), not to mention Bugs Bunny in Friz Freleng’s delightful period romp of a cartoon Bunker Hill Bunny (1950). The French have been making cinematic homages to their 1789 revolution going back the 1913 biopic Robespierre.
In Russia, Grigori Aleksandrov and Sergei Eisenstein’s October, in 1928, typified how the Bolshevik revolution’s success against the odds made Russian spirit what it is. Movies such as Neil Jordan’s Liam Neeson-fronted biopic Michael Collins (1996) and The Wind That Shakes the Barley (2006), set during the Irish war of independence and starring Cillian Murphy, depicted the triumphs and tragedies of Ireland’s revolutionary heritage – even if the latter had an English director in the shape of Ken Loach.
But it isn’t just the deeply classist notion of what failures count as heroic that has made British cinema reluctant to embrace our failed revolutionary heritage. It is the result of how our culture has been reverse-colonised by Hollywood, with historical narratives only deemed filmable if they fit into American movie industry’s tropes. Whenever Hollywood deigns to make a movie about British history, it includes Downton-style upstairs-downstairs hokum, those crazy sexed-up murderous Tudors and, of course, that cod-historical franchise that never stops giving, Robin Hood.
Equally, it is axiomatic in Hollywood that political struggles are always about one thing – a very American notion of freedom, individual freedom from presumed oppression. That’s why Mel Gibson’s 1995 Braveheart was possible: even though William Wallace’s struggles against the English ended in failure with his execution at Smithfield (not far from where Wat Tyler was murdered by Richard II’s lackeys), the biopic involved the classic Hollywood trope of the little guy fighting for freedom. Any other political goal (tax reform, wealth redistribution, solidarity, fraternity) scarcely makes a dent in the Hollywood narrative juggernaut.
And that’s what makes Greengrass’s The Uprising problematic. Compromised by Hollywood values, it is conflicted about representing a failed political revolution as what it was – a collective struggle. It depicts the Peasants’ Revolt in the frame of one fictional man, Garfield’s Ploughman. Conceived by Greengrass as a representative everyman, Ploughman – with a disregard for historical truth that should make the film’s historical adviser Dan Jones wince – pops up Zelig-like to parlay with the king, catch the king’s mother’s eye, rally the rebels, scythe down the bad guys, as if he were a real-life historical figure. The collective struggle becomes individualised drama, betraying the positioning of the apostrophe – what happened in 1381 was the Peasants’ Revolt not the Peasant’s Revolt.
Worse yet, the film includes a very silly coda in which, a year after the defeat of the revolt, Ploughman and a rump of rebels have retreated to the English greenwood to form an outlaw band of unmerry men. The corollary of this coda is to make the Peasants’ Revolt a kind of origin story for the legend of Robin Hood, even though that is nonsense: the folkloric rebel operated – if at all – about 200 years earlier. The whole idea may seem ridiculous, but the US distributors for The Uprising, Focus Features, leaned into this barmy interpretation by changing the film’s title to The Uprising: The Rise of Robin Hood earlier this year, suggesting that it would show events “that helped inspire the legend of Robin Hood”. Sensible Guardian readers will know of course that Robin Hood was a supporter of Richard I and foe of King John both of whom ruled England almost exactly two centuries earlier.
Such absurdities are a great shame since Greengrass’s – worthwhile – intention was to make a film about the Peasants’ Revolt that resonates topically for our age. A collapse in trust of our rulers, a seemingly endless cost of living crisis, widening inequality, political discourse dominated by lies and nonsense: 2026 is more like 1381 than we realise.
It’s worth pointing out that there has been one successful military revolution in British history, namely the English civil war. Cinema of course has been a failure at depicting it: there was Ken Hughes’s wildly inaccurate 1970 drama Cromwell starring Richard Harris and Alec Guinness and Mike Barker’s 2003 To Kill a King with Tim Roth and Dougray Scott. But our most enduring and successful revolution was scarcely cinematic: the so-called Glorious Revolution of 1688-89 in which the Catholic King James II was replaced by his Protestant daughter Mary II and her Dutch husband William III of Orange was hailed by Bertrand Russell as “the most moderate and successful of all revolutions. Its aims were modest, but they were exactly achieved.” Yawn! Who wants to see that movie?
Perhaps the greatest film about British revolutionary failure was the aforementioned Winstanley, about a group of proto-communists called the Diggers who settled common land on St Georges’s Hill outside Weybridge, Surrey during the English civil war. They hoped to create a utopia devoid of private property and for a few weeks lived self-sufficiently until they were violently evicted by the local gentry. To clinch the point that the Diggers’ experiment was a failure, just go on to property website Rightmove. There you can find a “stunning and elegant” £25m mansion on Cavendish Road, St George’s Hill with “fairway views, seven individually themed bathrooms, two staff apartments, and a leisure complex” and 1.5 acres of carefully landscaped gardens. Not what their leader Gerrard Winstanley wanted at all. He wrote: “Was the Earth made to preserve a few covetous, proud men to live at ease, and for them to bag and barn up the treasures of the Earth from others, that these may beg or starve in a fruitful land; or was it made to preserve all her children?” Our radical history, so often absent from our national cinema, has been built over in a field in Surrey for real estate scarcely any of us can afford. A very British coup if ever there was one.

As drones reshape warfare, Lithuania brings them into the classroom
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
11:14:18 UTC
20:14:18 KST

In Lithuania, children learn to build and programme drones at school. Similar projects exist in Germany. But what can pupils learn from these unmanned systems?
Focused faces, the buzz of propellers and drones weaving through an obstacle course in a school hall.
At the "Sietuvus" Progymnasium in Vilnius, drones have become part of everyday school life, with children aged six to 14 attending so-called "drone classes."
Alongside maths, Lithuanian and physical education, pupils learn to build and programme their own drones.
What may seem an unusual addition to the curriculum comes at a time when drones are increasingly associated with warfare and security threats.
Recent incidents, including an attempted drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport, have highlighted the potential risks posed by the technology.
Drones have also become a defining feature of modern warfare in the war in Ukraine, as well as the US-Israeli war against Iran.
But the drone classes at Sietuvos Progymnasium have little to do with the conflicts dominating the headlines.
"It's not just about flying drones," said Vytautas Mitala, Vilnius's deputy mayor. Flying is only one part of the programme, he explained.
More important are learning to programme and build drones, as well as understanding maps and the physics behind how they work.
Drones as a regular part of the curriculum
The programme aims to teach pupils STEAM skills – science, technology, engineering, arts and mathematics – and give them a broader understanding of technology, rather than simply showing them how to fly drones.
Mitala believes the combination of practical experience and technical knowledge could open up career opportunities for young people in the future.
The programme is designed for pupils from around Year 5, when they are about 11. In Lithuania, 70% of teaching time is devoted to the compulsory curriculum, leaving teachers free to decide how to use the remaining 30%.
Programming is introduced much earlier, in Year 1, meaning pupils already have some basic technical knowledge by the time they begin building drones.
For Mitala, the earlier children are introduced to these subjects, the better.
"You should introduce younger children to these fields, show them what is possible and spark their curiosity," he said. The programme builds on subjects already taught in schools, but it has yet to be adopted across the city.
So far, only a handful of state schools in Vilnius are ready to incorporate drone education into their regular curriculum. Others draw on elements of the programme in lessons or offer drone activities as after-school clubs.
Investment in Lithuania's future
Mitala stressed that the drone classes were not about militarisation, but about helping children understand a technology that is becoming increasingly important.
For Lithuania, however, there is also an economic incentive. The main motivation for introducing drones into schools is the country’s ambition to develop its industries and tap into new economic opportunities, the deputy mayor said.
Vilnius wants to strengthen its position in fields such as biotechnology and establish a foothold in semiconductor manufacturing. Both sectors require technical skills that, Mitala argued, need to be taught from an early age.
The aim, then, is not simply to teach children to fly drones, but to spark their interest in programming, construction, robotics and the technology behind them. Companies have told Mitala that introducing pupils to technical subjects only in their final year of school is "already a little too late."
Children need to encounter these fields earlier if they are to develop an interest in them, he said. In the longer term, drone education is intended to reach more schools in Vilnius and become a permanent part of the curriculum. A programme spanning grades one to 12 is planned.
Pupils compete in drone races
Euronews visited a drone class during a press trip organised by the Baltic office of Germany's Friedrich Naumann Foundation. The lesson began like any other, in a classroom.
Equipped with computers, a 3D printer and an array of drones, the classroom is where pupils learn what needs to be checked before a drone takes off.
"Before take-off, the surroundings and the device must be checked, the battery must be inserted correctly, the flight area must be free of obstacles and the drone may only be launched with the teacher’s permission," the instructions read.
Once the safety rules have been explained, the pupils move to a hall, where an obstacle course awaits them. A series of hoops, boxes and instructions tests their skills as they compete to guide their drones through the course in the shortest time. The competition is not confined to "Sietuvus" Progymnasium.
During the last school year, 33 schools from across Vilnius were invited to take part in the so-called "drone games" at the school.
Matas and Kasparas, both 14, came second in the most recent competition. Matas told Euronews that he had started the drone course three years ago. He would not describe it as easy: it had taken him that long to reach his current level of skill. His next goal is to learn to control a larger drone, which he said is more difficult "because of the movements."
Do drone classes only exist in Lithuania?
The Baltic states are often regarded as European pioneers in digitalisation. Drone classes are one example of how technology is being introduced in schools, and the idea is by no means limited to Lithuania.
In Germany, too, pupils can learn to build, programme and fly drones. At Dortmund's Geschwister-Scholl comprehensive school, eighth-graders took part in a project called "Aircraft of the Future," developing their own drones from the initial planning and computer-aided design to 3D printing and programming.
At Limes Grammar School in Welzheim, about 40km east of Stuttgart, pupils in grades eight to 12 learn to programme and control so-called indoor drones, as well as coordinate the flight paths of several drones at once – a technique known as drone swarming.
The club also explores the technology behind the aircraft, including their design, sensors and flight stabilisation. Pupils put their skills to use in their own film projects, recording school events from the air before editing the footage themselves.
For such projects to become more than isolated initiatives, funding is also a key consideration.
Programmable drones equipped with sensors share important features with robots and can therefore be used in robotics and STEM education – science, technology, engineering and mathematics – in schools, according to a statement sent to Euronews by Germany's Federal Ministry for Education, Family Affairs, Senior Citizens, Women and Youth.
Their purchase and use must, however, serve a specific educational purpose and comply with the requirements of the DigitalPakt Schule, as well as the rules of the individual federal states.
The DigitalPakt Schule is a funding programme run by the federal and state governments to support the digitalisation of schools, including through investment in technical equipment and digital learning materials.
Programmable drones may also qualify for funding, provided they are used for educational purposes and meet the relevant criteria.
More broadly, STEM projects in Germany receive support from a range of sources, including the federal government, the Länder, municipalities, businesses and foundations.
The education ministry said, however, that it did not have a complete overview of all the programmes available.

UK PM accuses Russia of Brexit meddling (VIDEO)
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham claims that Russia “clearly” interfered in the 2016 Brexit referendum which led to Britain leaving the EU, without providing evidence to back up the rehashed allegations.
Speaking on ‘The Rest is Politics’ podcast on Sunday, the prime minister said he sought answers about Russia’s alleged involvement after taking office this summer.
“I asked the question coming to Downing Street: Well, was there interference in the 2016 referendum from Russia? I’ve had the clear answer that yes, there was.”
Burnham did not identify who provided the assessment, what evidence supports it, or whether any alleged interference affected the result. Defending the timing of his unsubstantiated claim – ten years after Brexit – Burnham argued that voters need to understand that some political movements were “instigated via our enemies, namely Russia.”
Britain voted to leave the EU in the June 23, 2016 referendum, with 51.89% backing Leave against 48.11% for Remain, with 72.2% turnout. The vote was driven largely by demands to reclaim sovereignty, control immigration, cut EU regulations and budget contributions, and pursue independent trade deals, amid widespread dissatisfaction with the political establishment.
Allegations of Russian interference through media activity and bots allegedly boosting pro-Leave sentiment have surfaced before, but Burnham is the first sitting prime minister to publicly make the claim. Previous governments denied that Russia influenced the vote, citing “no evidence of successful interference” or any impact on the result.
Russia has dismissed the allegations as baseless speculation and part of a pattern of Western accusations. Moscow has not yet commented on Burnham’s claims.
Russian interference?
Western governments have repeatedly pointed the finger at Russia over elections and political developments, including recent contests in Germany, France, Moldova, and Georgia. On the podcast, Burnham recalled a conversation with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, whose CDU was defeated by the right-wing Alternative for Germany (AfD) in three major state elections in recent weeks. According to Burnham, Merz also raised the issue of Russian involvement, citing the AfD’s alleged ties to Moscow.
Russia firmly rejects the allegations of political interference. Officials maintain that Russia respects the sovereignty of other states and does not interfere in their internal affairs, describing the accusations as part of domestic political struggles and anti-Russia campaigns.
Russia, meanwhile, has accused the West of meddling abroad. Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said earlier this year that Western governments interfere through color revolutions, military force, and “electoral neocolonialism” – using politically biased election monitoring, media campaigns, and external pressure to influence other countries’ political processes and challenge unfavorable results.
Russia has accused Britain of interference in the Ukraine conflict, citing extensive weapons deliveries, military training, and intelligence support for Kiev, as well as former Prime Minister Boris Johnson’s alleged role in derailing the 2022 peace talks. Moscow argues that London’s actions make it a de facto party to the conflict and obstruct peace efforts. Lavrov said in August that British involvement in missile strikes on Russia gave the country grounds to regard the UK as a party to the conflict, “with all ensuing consequences.”
Brexit reversal looming?
Burnham’s decision to revisit alleged ‘Russian interference’ comes as his government considers closer ties with Brussels. At the Labour Party’s annual conference last month, he argued that Brexit has done “more harm than good,” and suggested that rejoining the EU could feature in the party’s next election manifesto, opening the door to reversing the vote.
Economic assessments have generally found that Brexit has hurt Britain’s economy, which has experienced weak growth since leaving the EU. Recent estimates suggest that GDP is 6% to 8% lower than it would have been had the country remained.
A YouGov poll last month suggests that 59% of Britons support rejoining the EU, with 32% opposed. However, support for closer ties without rejoining the EU, single market, or customs union is higher, at 73%.
Critics of reversing Brexit, including Reform UK leader Nigel Farage, argue that rejoining the EU would force Britain to surrender control over immigration, regulation, and trade policy while taking on new financial obligations.
Commenting on Burnham’s allegations of Russia meddling in an interview with The Guardian on Monday, Farage called the prime minister “a liar,” dismissing the claims as part of a longstanding “Russia hoax.”
“The prime minister is a liar. Yes, a liar... There was no Russian interference. And the Russia hoax has run all the way through this,” he said, citing previous denials under Boris Johnson and Foreign Office minister Stephen Doughty’s assertion that any attempted meddling failed.

Cuba denies involvement with island-bound fuel shipments seized by US
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
11:10:33 UTC
20:10:33 KST

Cuba denies involvement with island-bound fuel shipments seized by US
HAVANA, Oct 12 - Cuba's top energy official denied any link between the nation's communist-run government and shipments of Cuba-bound biodiesel seized in September by US authorities, rejecting US claims that the island nation was involved in those deals.
The US said last week that it had seized 90 separate shipments of biodiesel worth nearly $3 million under contracts involving a sanctioned Cuban state energy trader known as ENETEC, part of a crackdown on what the US alleges are illegal shipments of fuel to the island.
Cuban Minister of Energy and Mines Vicente de la O Levy said he had no knowledge of any of the shipments intercepted by the US Department of Homeland Security.
"We can assure you that there was no contract of any kind with ENETEC S.A.," de la O Levy told Reuters in an exclusive interview at his Havana office. "No Cuban state-owned company has managed to secure a fuel contract, whether for small or large quantities."
The oil blockade imposed by the US — initiated following the detention of Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro in January — have vastly worsened Cuba's existing energy crisis. Fuel, water and electricity shortages, combined with soaring prices, have brought the island to the brink of a humanitarian crisis.
The US has since early this year allowed fuel exporters to ship gasoline and diesel to the island's nascent private sector but prohibits any such shipments to Cuba's government. Imports of fuel from US companies have soared in recent months but remain a fraction of what the island's economy needs, de la O Levy said.
“I would venture to say that the amount entering the country doesn't even cover 3% of its fuel needs,” he said.
Cuba and the United Nations have called US efforts to limit fuel shipments to Cuba "illegal" and contrary to international law.
The US has openly said it is seeking to topple Cuba's government.
COBALT AND NICKEL
De la O Levy said that the island government intends to remain in the business of nickel and cobalt mining, but that significant barriers remain to restarting production due to stiffened US sanctions.
Cuba is a top global producer of cobalt, according to the US Geological Survey, and has significant reserves of nickel, both essential in the production of batteries and automobiles.
Canada's Sherritt International Corp has for more than 30 years participated in a joint venture with the Cuban government at Cuba's largest mine, at Moa, but announced earlier this year that it would suspend operations due to US sanctions.
The Canadian mining company later said it had signed a non-binding agreement in May with Gillon Capital LLC, a Dallas-based development firm, to sell a stake in its Cuban mining business. Gillon's vice chairman is Ray Washburne, a longtime backer of US President Donald Trump.
De la O Levy said any purchase involving the joint venture would involve shares in the Canadian company, not a direct acquisition of the joint venture with the Cuban government.
"We have always made it clear that what the US company would be buying are shares in Sherritt, not in the joint venture," he stated. "The Canadian company is publicly traded, and any investor has the right to buy its shares."
Cuba said it would be willing to continue operating under the joint venture's existing rules should a deal be inked.
“But any restart would require discussions on how to supply fuel and spare parts, as well as how to handle payments for exports and production inputs,” de la O Levy said. “If the intention is to resume nickel production, all those issues would need to be resolved.”
Neither Sherritt nor Gillon immediately responded to a request for comment on the minister's statements.
RENEWABLE ENERGY
De la O Levy said Cuba was pushing ahead with its planned transition to renewable energy.
He said 144 solar farms with a combined capacity of 1,418 megawatts have been installed over the past several years, assuring baseline daytime production of electricity despite the US fuel blockade.
The island's domestic crude oil production remains stable, he said, but is almost entirely allocated to thermoelectric power plants.
Around 40% of Cuba's electricity comes from domestic oil.
Electric transport has also expanded, with the country now boasting over a million motorcycles and tricycles, while renewable energy sources have been installed at all of the country's small health clinics, maternity homes, nursing homes and funeral homes, he said.
"We are moving forward with our solutions little by little, though not as fast as we would like," the official stated. REUTERS

MOT: Cancer treatment delays in Finland lead to poorer outcomes than in Nordics
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
14:08:06 EEST
20:08:06 KST

Yle's investigative programme MOT has found that Finland lacks comprehensive national data on cancer treatment delays. This comes despite earlier findings that patients in Finland have poorer survival outcomes than those in other Nordic countries for several types of cancer.
Treatment delays are also examined in MOT's recent documentary, Slowly Towards Cancer Treatment (Hitaasti syöpähoitoon).
Unlike other Nordic countries, Finland does not have a national cancer quality registry to collect hospital data on treatment outcomes and help identify delays and differences in care.
Funding for its development has also been cut from next year’s budget.
Instead, researchers must study delays in individual types of cancer. An ongoing study coordinated by Outi Kuittinen, professor of oncology at the University of Eastern Finland, is examining delays in lung cancer treatment in Kuopio, Tampere, Turku and Rovaniemi.
MOT was the first to receive the unpublished results. In terms of lung cancer, the study found that the average time from the onset of symptoms to treatment in Finland is approximately five months — or 155 days.
More than 50 days of that average delay is attributed to the patient, 41 days to primary healthcare and 58 days to specialised healthcare.
The corresponding total delay is 107 days in Sweden and 67 days in Denmark, according to MOT.
The reasons for the delays have not been fully investigated. However, cancer organisations have found that some people put off seeking medical help because of financial concerns or fear of a diagnosis.
"I believe that all doctors who treat cancer see that the diagnostic path is too slow," Kuittinen says.
Delays can occur when patients struggle to get appointments, healthcare professionals fail to recognise symptoms or general practitioners make diagnostic errors. In specialised healthcare, waiting for imaging, reports, and sample collection can add further time.
Kuittinen says better training for primary care doctors and faster access to scans could help. She also advocates a fast-track system for people suspected of having cancer.
Patient cases highlight delays
Heidi Rintahaka was 39 when she was diagnosed with an aggressive form of triple-negative breast cancer. Her first drug treatments at Helsinki University Hospital (HUS) began six weeks after her initial symptoms. During that time, the tumour grew from three centimetres to eight.
"It seemed pretty unbelievable, but it never occurred to me to demand anything," Rintahaka says.
About six months after her most recent surgery, she noticed suspicious redness on her chest six. A public health centre took a skin biopsy, but she ended up waiting nearly a month for the results. In the meantime, she sought care at a private cancer hospital, where results were available within days.
The health centre eventually told her that its sample had shown no cancer. An hour or two later, a doctor at the private hospital called to say cancer had been found in the sample taken there.
"A completely incomprehensible situation. An obvious medical error," she says.
MOT found that the biopsy at the health centre had been taken incorrectly.
Cancer strategy lacks funding
Finland adopted its first national cancer strategy in November 2025, following work by more than 200 experts. However, its implementation has progressed slowly.
A roadmap developed by oncologists and the Ministry of Social Affairs and Health estimates that implementating the strategy would require 140 million euros in funding.
The ministry declined to publish the roadmap under its own name, saying this could incorrectly suggest that funding had already been secured.
Tuula Helander, the biotechnology and pharmaceuticals director at the health ministry, was involved in developing the strategy and roadmap. She said securing funding for the strategy’s proposed measures would ultimately depend on political decisions.
"Many important areas and issues are competing for the same money, and the decision on how to allocate the money is political," she stated in a response forwarded by the ministry’s communications team.
Next year's state budget allocates no funding to improving cancer treatment outcomes. It also cuts 400,000 euros earmarked for developing a national cancer quality registry. Professor Kuittinen is critical of the decision.
"That's ridiculous, because treating one patient with aggressive lymphoma easily costs 400,000 euros," Kuittinen says.
Cancer experts argue that investing in the strategy could ultimately save both money and lives.
In Denmark, a public quality register has helped improve treatment outcomes for lymphoma and lung cancer.
Minister of Social Affairs and Health Wille Rydman (Finns) acknowledges that cancer is a major societal issue, but says many other diseases also require attention.
Young women face diagnostic challenges
Breast cancer diagnoses can also be delayed in younger women, partly because the disease is less common in this age group and dense breast tissue can make tumours harder to detect, says Päivi Auvinen, chief physician at Kuopio University Hospital’s cancer centre.
Julia, 32, was initially diagnosed with benign breast tumours. Eight months later, she was diagnosed with cancer that had grown considerably and spread to lymph nodes in her armpit.
She had repeatedly tried to obtain another appointment but was unsuccessful because her earlier tumours had been classified as benign.
Kuittinen criticises the extension of Finland's treatment guarantee from two weeks to three months, arguing that patients whose symptoms are incorrectly assessed as non-urgent may wait too long.
"Three months is a disaster for many cancers if that one phone conversation leads to the wrong category," she says.
