Why boarding schools must do more to tackle child-on-child sexual abuse
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
11:06:14 UTC
20:06:14 KST

Benji* was in his early teens when a fellow pupil at one of the country’s most prestigious independent schools began a series of sexual assaults against him that went on for years.
He had previously been happy at school, where he excelled at sport. Then one night he woke in his dormitory to find the other boy’s hand on his penis. “I just froze,” said Benji.
The boy threatened to beat him up if he reported what had happened, and the abuse began to accelerate. He would forcibly masturbate Benji three or four times a week. From there he began to force Benji to engage in fellatio every two to three days.
“It slowly got worse and worse,” said Benji. “He said he would beat the shit out of me. He claimed he had taken pictures of me when I was sleeping. He said he would put them up around the school and make this rumour up that I was gay.”
Awareness and safeguarding have improved significantly in UK boarding schools after decades of shameful revelations about sexual abuse, but experts say children who live and learn in institutions away from their parents will always be more vulnerable.
In the past, the focus has been on the appalling experiences of pupils who have been sexually abused by their teachers. Today, attention has also turned to the sexual violence perpetrated by one pupil on another – in boarding schools, as in other schools.
Earlier this month, a Guardian investigation uncovered the horrifying scale of child-on-child sexual abuse in schools, with at least 1,700 sexual offences against under-13s, including multiple rapes, reported to police every year.
It was not until more than a decade later that Benji felt able to disclose what he had suffered. “I was not in a place where I wanted to let out what happened to me. I was massively ashamed.” He abused alcohol and drugs and tried to kill himself. “I would do anything to blank it out. I was angry with the world.”
After leaving school, he went abroad where he began to do seasonal work. “Until I was 26, I was running away from the darkness. I did not want to deal with it. I didn’t want to have to think or relive it.”
After spiralling downwards, Benji finally told his mother. Horrified, she contacted the school. The police became involved, there was a trial and in September 2021 the perpetrator, Christopher Brewer, was convicted of 12 offences against Benji and one other pupil.
Jailing Brewer for three years, the recorder of Bristol, Judge Peter Blair, said Brewer had “ruined” Benji’s life. “He felt a complete sense of powerlessness. This was not a very long way away from sex slave.”
“I look back on that court case and that’s the proudest moment of my life,” Benji told the Guardian. “It’s the only time in my life when I’ve felt powerful. I had to do this for myself so I could move on, and could slowly become happier.”
Following the criminal case, Benji pursued a civil negligence claim against the school. The school denied liability, and a compensation settlement was finally agreed. Now he feels compelled to speak up to support others.
“If I can make a change to someone who is dealing with a similar situation, if I could change someone’s life for the better, it would make everything that happened worth it.”
Andrew Lord, a partner in the abuse claims team at Leigh Day, represented Benji in his civil action. “I have advised several families whose children have been impacted by abuse in boarding schools, and a great number describe still feeling the impact many years later.
“It is no longer credible for any school to plead ignorance on the shocking prevalence of sexual violence among pupils, nor is it acceptable to not have an immediate plan to investigate and mitigate these potential harms.
“There has been a growing awareness of these issues for several years, and the idiosyncrasies of a boarding school setting can create additional flashpoints of concern. Schools ought to be aware and prepared for when a disclosure of abuse occurs.”
Richard Scorer, who is head of abuse law at Slater & Gordon, said from his experience a “disproportionate” number of civil claims over child-on-child sexual abuse involve boarding schools. “Because, obviously, children are there more of the time and in circumstances where they might be dressing or undressing.
“They’re living not just a school life, but their private lives as well. So there’s probably a bit more coming from boarding schools in terms of what we see.” Wealthier families may also be more likely to seek legal redress.
Sam*, also represented by Lord, was a pupil at another renowned boarding school when an older student from a nearby dormitory got into his bed and sexually abused him. There were other incidents.
Sam did not report the abuse immediately. He felt too embarrassed, and in the months that followed, he lived in a state of terror. “I could hear his door open. I was frozen in fear.”
Eventually, Sam confided in a fellow pupil; it was reported to the housemaster, and he was asked to give a written statement. Yet, much to Sam’s alarm, in the days after disclosure, the boy was allowed to stay in the dormitory opposite.
The incident was finally reported to the police by Sam’s family, but there were no charges. “Ultimately I think the school did not want any bad press,” said Sam. But the abuse had a devastating and lasting impact on Sam.
Though he managed to secure a place at university, he had a “terrible” time. He hid in his room and left without completing his degree. “I think the assault and the aftermath did really change me.
“What I really feel I lost was confidence. I lost confidence in the school, which was in a position of care and responsibility. And I lost my own self-confidence to do anything.” Sam brought a civil action against the school, claiming negligence and safeguarding failures. The school denied liability and a settlement was reached.
Gabrielle Shaw, chief executive of the National Association for People Abused in Childhood (Napac), said awareness and safeguarding have improved, and there is greater recognition that children can be sexually abused by other children.
“But policies alone do not keep children safe. Boarding schools have an especially high duty of care because children live as well as learn there and may be separated from trusted adults outside the institution.
“Every pupil needs a safe route to speak out and a response that takes them seriously, protects and supports them, and acts appropriately. Crucially, it must be without reputation or institutional interests taking precedence.
“Children in boarding schools are not inevitably vulnerable to abuse. The real test is whether they trust adults enough to tell them, and what those adults do next.”
Robin Fletcher, chief executive of the Boarding Schools’ Association (BSA), said safeguarding young people is the top priority of every boarding school. “Over the past decade, BSA has worked to strengthen schools’ ability to recognise and respond to abuse through specialist training, conferences and safeguarding guidance.
“That work addresses child-on-child abuse as well as abuse by adults, helping staff identify concerns and respond appropriately rather than waiting for a child to make a disclosure.
“Any safeguarding incident reinforces the need for strong processes, training, support and a culture where abuse and abusers have no place in any school.”
* Some names have been changed

The company is part of Volvo Cars’ corporate structure. China’s Zhejiang Geely Holding Group is Volvo Cars’ majority owner.
In 2024, the Norwegian Armed Forces’ logistics organization signed nationwide framework agreements with two suppliers for vehicle rentals: First Rent A Car Norway AS and RAC Norway AS. The maximum combined value of the contracts is NOK 350 million.
First Rent A Car’s link to the Chinese automotive group runs through Volvo Cars. An official European Commission decision on the acquisition of First Rent A Car states that Volvo Cars gained full control of the company, while Zhejiang Geely Holding Group controlled Volvo.
As of 2026, Geely remains Volvo Cars’ majority owner. Geely Sweden Holdings owns about 78.65% of Volvo Cars’ shares, and the China-based Zhejiang Geely Holding Group ultimately owns it.
The military’s use of modern civilian vehicles also raises separate security concerns. In its Risiko 2025 assessment, Norway’s National Security Authority warned that a modern car can contain more than 200 electronic sensors.
If external actors gain access to such data, they could use it for surveillance, tracking movements, or intelligence-gathering.
In its National Threat Assessment 2026, Norway’s counterintelligence service, the Police Security Service, stated that Chinese intelligence and security agencies had expanded their capacity to conduct operations in Norway, including in cyberspace and through human intelligence sources.
In May, a Chinese national was arrested in Norway on suspicion of complicity in espionage. The suspected target may have been the Andøya spaceport, which is strategically important to the country.
In August 2025, the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) banned Chinese-made vehicles from entering military bases. The restrictions were introduced as a precautionary measure to reduce the risk of sensitive information being collected on military premises.
In November 2025, the IDF began removing Chinese-made official vehicles from officers’ use over information-security concerns.
The collection of information through civilian electronic devices is also a concern for other NATO countries. In April, the German Armed Forces (Bundeswehr) restricted the use of personal smartphones, tablets, and smartwatches when handling classified information due to the threat of espionage by Russia and China.

AI fuelling growth while putting Asia’s young workers at risk, IMF meeting hears
AI investment is propping up global growth amid energy shocks, but leaders at the IMF summit warn of a job tsunami threatening Asia’s youth
4-MIN READ4-MIN
 Listen
Aidan Jonesin Bangkok
An investment surge into artificial intelligence may be helping prop up a global economy battered by energy supply shocks, but the technology’s potential to cull jobs requires swift mitigation if Asia’s youth are to secure a place in the future workforce, delegates were warned at the IMF–World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok on Monday.
Soaring energy prices, persistent inflation and mounting debt framed the opening of the week-long summit, which was last hosted in the Thai capital in 1991.
Unusually, the US has not sent its Treasury Secretary to attend the gathering, despite triggering the energy crunch following its war against Iran, taken alongside Israel, in February.
Since then, oil prices have oscillated around US$100 a barrel thanks to the partial closure of the Strait of Hormuz, driving up inflation and forcing governments to drain reserves or borrow heavily to cushion consumers from high costs.

Saudi energy minister says global energy security faces ‘real test’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
11:04:05 UTC
20:04:05 KST

Lina Altawell and Mohammad Sio
12 October 2026•Update: 12 October 2026
Global energy security is facing a “real test” amid escalating tensions in the region, Saudi Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman warned Monday, stressing that the Kingdom has prepared plans to safeguard supplies before crises emerge.
“Global energy today faces a real test, and we have put plans in place to preserve energy security before crises occur,” Prince Abdulaziz said during the 25th WPC Energy Congress in Riyadh.
He made the remarks in his speech at the official inauguration of the four-day congress, which opened Sunday. Saudi Arabia is hosting the event for the first time.
The minister said Saudi Arabia intends to remain a key pillar of global energy security while pursuing its long-term energy strategy.
“Our eyes are focused on what would deliver us into the future -- the future of our sons and daughters and their sons and daughters,” he said in his speech, as cited by a ministry statement.
Riyadh had become a center for discussions on energy security, Prince Abdulaziz said, stressing that Saudi energy policy would continue to focus on long-term objectives rather than short-term pressures.
He said Saudi Arabia will overcome the challenges it faces and continue pursuing its long-term plans and commitments.
“Recent developments in the region and the Kingdom have reinforced that energy security cannot be taken for granted, particularly as supply routes come under pressure and infrastructure is targeted,” he said.
Saudi Arabia has invested for decades in infrastructure, spare capacity, storage, alternative export routes, technology, domestic supply chains and human capabilities, he said.
“Resilience must be built before crises occur,” the minister said.
He added that localization should not be viewed only as an economic objective, but also as “a strategic capability that supports business continuity and recovery when international supply chains are disrupted.”
Prince Abdulaziz said energy-system resilience is measured not only by spare production capacity, pipelines and power-generation capacity, but also “by the ability to maintain, repair, reroute, substitute, recover and continue delivering supplies under pressure.”
He said Saudi Arabia’s ability to withstand disruptions and recover contributes to the reliability of international energy supplies and reinforces its role “as a trusted partner in the global economy.”
“There can be no energy future for all without energy security for all,” he said, stressing that energy security and the transformation of the energy sector should advance together.
The congress, held under the theme “Pathways to an Energy Future for All,” runs from Oct. 11-15 in Riyadh.
More than 25,000 participants are expected to attend, including over 100 ministers and nearly 500 CEOs from 80 countries, according to figures provided by the Saudi Energy Ministry.
The event is held amid escalating hostilities between Saudi Arabia and Houthis in Yemen, with airports and other civilian and energy facilities targeted in recent days.
Shipping through the Strait of Hormuz has also faced disruptions following restrictions Iran imposed on vessel transit in April 2026, after the US and Israel launched a war against Iran in February that year.

Global steel demand expected to remain flat in 2026, rebound in 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
11:01:17 UTC
20:01:17 KST

Gokhan Ergocun
12 October 2026•Update: 12 October 2026
Global steel demand is projected to remain virtually unchanged in 2026 before returning to growth in 2027, according to the Short Range Outlook report released by the World Steel Association on Monday.
The association forecast world steel demand to remain flat at 1.72 billion metric tons in 2026, while expected to grow 1.7% in 2027 to reach 1.75 billion metric tons.
Speaking on the outlook, Alfonso Hidalgo de Calcerrada, chair of the worldsteel economics committee, said the anticipated recovery is proving slower and more gradual than previously expected.
Demand outside China is forecast to grow 1.5% in 2026 and accelerate to 4% in 2027.
Chinese steel demand is expected to contract 2% in 2026 due to the ongoing property investment downturn and weak infrastructure spending.
The association projected China's demand contraction to narrow to 1% in 2027 as real estate declines slow down.
Steel demand in developing economies excluding China is forecast to expand 1.9% in 2026 and 5.1% in 2027.
India remains the fastest-growing major steel market, with demand expected to expand 7.9% to 172.4 million metric tons in 2026 and 8% to 186.2 million metric tons in 2027.
Steel demand in the Gulf Cooperation Council region is projected to drop about 11% in 2026 due to regional conflicts deferring project starts, before rebounding 11.3% in 2027.
ASEAN-5 demand is set to grow 5.2% in 2026 and 3.2% in 2027, led by strong construction activity in Vietnam.
Developed world steel demand is forecast to grow 1% in 2026 and 2.2% in 2027 following stabilization in 2025.
US steel demand is projected to rise 2% in 2026 and 1.5% in 2027, supported by data centers and energy infrastructure investments.
EU apparent steel use is expected to drop 0.3% in 2026 before rebounding 3.1% in 2027.
Japanese steel demand is set to grow 0.9% in 2026 and 1.7% in 2027, while South Korean demand is expected to rise 1.8% in 2026 and 1.3% in 2027.

Zelensky: Ukraine will respond if Russia rejects energy truce
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
11:01:00 UTC
20:01:00 KST

Zelensky: Ukraine will respond if Russia rejects energy truce
President Volodymyr Zelensky ade this statement in a video address to the Warsaw Security Forum, according to a Ukrinform correspondent.
“Putin doesn’t read Truth Social, and his ‘Shaheds’ follow a different set of instructions. But these posts affect the lives of millions of people, which makes this very important, first and foremost in Ukraine,” the President said.
He explained that Russia is trying to use yet another winter against Ukraine by destroying the country’s energy infrastructure on a daily basis.
“But this also applies to Russia—not only its oil refineries, those oil refineries that Putin shamelessly tries to present to the world as a solution, claiming that this can somehow resolve the problem of disruptions in the global oil supply caused by the crisis in the Strait of Hormuz and the war in the Middle East,” Zelensky emphasized.
He stated that if Russia does not agree to an energy truce, Ukraine will respond.
“Yesterday’s post by the U.S. president sparked genuine interest and real hope that an energy truce could actually work,” he said, adding that Ukraine immediately supported this idea, just as it had done previously when Kyiv itself proposed a similar energy truce.
“We have agreed to an energy truce. The U.S. side knows very well what this means for us. We do not have large oil reserves, significant export capacity, or dozens of oil refineries. We import large quantities of diesel fuel and other petroleum products,” Zelensky stated, adding that Ukraine is grateful to its European partners for these supplies, singling out Poland and Norway in particular.
“The main issue for us is electricity. Russia launched a campaign of strikes against our power generation facilities and power grids years ago. And every winter, including this one, the Russians try to make these strikes even more intense. We experience power outages every day,” the President said.
He added that in response, Ukraine is striking at Russia’s oil sector, for which gasoline shortages and oil refineries ablaze are “painful.”
“But these are not the volumes that could be lost due to a crisis in the Strait of Hormuz,” the President emphasized. “If Russia wants us to stop targeting its oil refining and oil exports, it must stop striking our power grid and critical infrastructure, and stop killing our people,” Zelensky stated, noting that during his talks with world leaders, he had heard words of support in this regard.
Explaining that Ukraine has only one oil refinery, he stated that it had long since been severely damaged by Russian strikes, so importing petroleum products is a new reality for Ukraine.
“Therefore, our proposal is honest and clear. We are ready to respect an energy ceasefire if Russia is ready to do the same. We agree if they agree,” Zelensky said, adding that Ukraine is already sending the appropriate signals.
“Last night, Russian oil refineries were not on fire, but at the same time, Russian jet drones struck a gas production facility in Ukraine and a regular gas station,” Zelensky noted. “Thus, there have already been violations of the energy ceasefire announced by the U.S. president on Russia’s part.”
He added that throughout the day, even more Russian drones have continued to attack Ukraine, including the country’s capital. “We shot down many of them; otherwise, there would have been even more damage to our energy infrastructure. At the moment, Putin’s response to Trump is Russian attacks,” the President emphasized.
According to him, Ukraine is awaiting details of the conversation between the U.S. and Russian sides, as well as the steps the U.S. is prepared to take.
“This energy ceasefire could work and become a major step toward ending the war if the Americans truly do everything to ensure that the Russians respect the energy ceasefire,” Zelensky concluded.
He addressed the American side, noting that they would watch this speech on Monday morning, U.S. time: “We are grateful to America and support the idea of an energy truce, but Russia must also show that it agrees to the energy truce. And if the U.S. side requires it, we are ready to provide our own guarantees so that they can be certain we can be trusted.”
According to him, it is important that both Ukraine and the U.S. view this situation in the same way and set priorities correctly.
“No one in Europe is a source of destabilization or war. No one in Europe rejects peace or wants to wage an endless war,” the president emphasized, noting that Europeans seek the warmest possible relations with the U.S.
“Everyone in Europe wants this, except Russia,” Zelensky stated.
As reported, U.S. President Donald Trump stated on October 11 that an energy ceasefire in the war between Russia and Ukraine would allegedly take effect on Sunday and called on the parties not to violate it.
President Zelensky said he was unaware of such an agreement, but confirmed Ukraine’s readiness for a ceasefire if Russia also stops its attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure.
The Armed Forces of Ukraine received the relevant orders following U.S. President Donald Trump’s statement regarding the energy ceasefire.

Fraternities are the most likely place for US campus rapes. Should they be shut down?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
11:00:53 UTC
20:00:53 KST

Daniel R Schwarz, an 85-year-old English literature emeritus professor, still works at Cornell University after 59 years because he loves teaching and “watching young people grow”, he said.
Most of his students, he also said, have not been part of fraternities at Cornell in Ithaca, New York, where seven men allegedly gang-raped a woman in 2024.
The incident, which has sparked national outrage, and other alleged wrongdoings at fraternities have prompted Schwarz and others to call for the abolition of “Greek life” at US colleges. In recent months, fraternities across the US have been implicated in multiple hazing cases; in Pennsylvania, one fraternity was even exposed as being at the center of a drug-dealing network.
But even with a long history of scandal, critics of Greek life – so-called because of the letters of the Greek alphabet that make up most fraternity and sorority names – are uncertain that schools in the US will close them. At many colleges, they are a fixture of campus life, help students form friendships and can make institutions more attractive to high schoolers, a particular concern for university leaders as they grapple with a declining birth rate.
In short, they argue, if students wish to pledge allegiance to fraternities and sororities, colleges won’t stop them.
“All the Greek alumni would have pitchforks, and it would be a whole debacle rather than kind of letting this play out in the press and then just going back to business,” said Lucy Taylor, a University of Maryland graduate and the creator of the podcast Snapped about the sordid history of fraternities and sororities.
In 1825 at Union College in Schenectady, New York, five seniors feeling “an aching void” after the dissolution of a military company at the school formed a secret society for “literary and social purposes”, according to The Company He Keeps: A History of White College Fraternities. It became Kappa Alpha Society, the country’s first social fraternity.
Such groups opened at colleges across the country, and joining them became a rite of passage for some students. Comedy film classics like Animal House and Old School celebrated the shenanigans that occur at frat parties. Fraternities and sororities were also created at historically Black colleges, where they are often a vital part of campus life, providing crucial social support and post-college networks.
But there has also always been a darker side to the organizations. The first hazing incidents were reported in the 1870s, and the first death at a fraternity house occurred in 1873 during an initiation at Cornell, according to a report, Fraternities in North America, in the Ebsco database.
From 1838 to 2025, there has been an average of two hazing deaths reported annually, according to Hazinginfo.org, which tracks such incidents.
This year, an 18-year-old at Northern Arizona University died from alcohol poisoning after he and three other Delta Tau Delta pledges passed around two bottles of vodka to ensure they vomited, the Associated Press reported. The fraternity’s national organization closed the chapter, and a 20-year-old pleaded guilty to felony hazing.
Hazing has been an issue at Black fraternities, too. In 2025, at Southern University in Louisiana, a 20-year-old student died after allegedly being punched four times in the chest as part of a hazing ritual. The alleged perpetrator was charged with manslaughter and criminal hazing.
At Penn State, 14 people were arrested in August for running a cocaine-trafficking ring out of two fraternities in which hazing allegedly played a role.
In addition to abusing pledges, fraternity members have long been accused of encouraging women to drink so that they can take advantage of them. In a 2019 survey from the Association of American Universities, a quarter of undergraduate women reported experiencing nonconsensual sexual conduct. The setting where it was most likely to occur was a fraternity.
In August, the University of Tennessee issued a safety notice to students after three reports of sexual assault, two of which included suspected drugging at fraternities, according to WBIR. In April at the University of Arkansas, a 19-year-old allegedly raped a woman at his fraternity, Kappa Sigma, months after another woman received a temporary order of protection against him, KNWA reported.
At Cornell, the school suspended fraternity parties and social events in 2022 after reports that over the course of a weekend, one student was sexually assaulted and at least four others were drugged at residences affiliated with fraternities.
Then, in 2024, the event allegedly occurred that has prompted a national reckoning with Greek culture: a 20-year-old female student, known as Jane Doe, said later that she had been drugged and raped by seven members of the Chi Phi fraternity.
Despite concerns over toxic behavior at fraternities and sororities, students still join because they want community and friends, said Jennifer Freyd, professor emeritus of psychology at the University of Oregon, who has studied sexual assault on college campuses.
A member of a different Cornell fraternity said he joined because he had a large friend group in high school but had not found the same connections on campus.
“When I met the people in my fraternity, I felt that these were people that I felt would not only just be my friend, but be a support system,” including by giving career advice and connecting him with alumni, said the student, who asked not to be named for fear of being doxed.
Students also join because family or friends encourage them and convey that the organizations “bring them power and status”, Freyd said.
But to achieve that, some students often must engage in hazing rituals.
During initiation rites, students “engage in humiliation, and there is a tradition in fraternities of objectifying women’s bodies and in sororities of complying with fraternities”, Freyd said.
In September, police arrested two fraternity leaders at the University of Wisconsin-Madison after partially clothed pledges were discovered in the basement of the frat house covered in food, condiments and other liquids.
Sorority leaders can also contribute to the unhealthy environment.
New York magazine recently reported on the “Ozempidemic” at colleges. Students are taking GLP-1 drugs to get skinny enough to “get into the sisterhood of their dreams”.
“The drug is new but the pressure isn’t. Sororities have always ranked women by how they look,” said Taylor, the podcast creator.
She joined Alpha Phi as a freshman and was initially “feeling validated and excited about all my new friends”, she said.
But after she posted a photo on social media of herself in a bikini, a fellow member commented, “SNAP”, which stood for “So Not Alpha Phi”, Taylor explained.
A student then sent an email urging members to “keep the booties tucked away” and to use “SNAP if you think you see something that might not be the best image for our chapter”.
Even after taking it down, Taylor felt ostracized from other members.
While she was shamed for the photo, she also felt as though she were living in a “rape culture”.
She said members were told not to leave a fraternity before midnight because “we don’t want to seem rude”.
“It was just normal if someone didn’t remember hooking up with someone from the night before. Blacking out was totally normal,” said Taylor.
She alleges she was raped by a fraternity member. She left the sorority after seven months.
“The Greek system, in my judgment, supports alcoholism, sexual harassment, bullying under the guise of hazing, groupthink and, of course, the objectification of women,” said Schwarz, whose students have confided in him about sexual harassment.
The Guardian asked the North American Interfraternity Conference, a trade association of fraternities, about the benefits of Greek life and concerns that fraternities are incubators of sexual assault.
Hillary Brewer, the organization’s chief communications officer, did not respond to a question about whether sexual misconduct is pervasive at fraternities but stated in an email that they “are an accelerator for success in college and beyond. They create lifelong connections to the campus, community and friends.”
Asked whether the alleged gang-rape at Cornell was indicative of a larger problem, she stated: “Any fraternity man who commits or is complicit in sexual assault should be held accountable to the fullest extent of the law. The men involved in the incident at Cornell were immediately expelled from the fraternity and the chapter was disbanded. We will continue to call for necessary personal accountability when members neglect their fraternal obligations.”
Despite concerns about Greek life, Schwarz said, university leaders haven’t stopped it out of fear that alumni will stop donating money.
Colleges must grapple with the fact that their customer base will likely shrink because people are having less children. The United States is projected to experience a 13% decline in high school graduates from 2025 to 2041, according to the Western Interstate Commission for Higher Education.
Michael Kotlikoff, Cornell’s president, said that the school would take “a serious look at the role of fraternities and sororities in campus life”, but officials are not considering ending Greek life, the Associated Press reported.
On Wednesday, the Ithaca Common Council voted to stop issuing permits to Cornell student groups, including fraternities, WSYR reported.
The Cornell fraternity member interviewed by the Guardian said the administration’s response to the alleged gang-rape was “incredibly frustrating”. Two students were expelled and a third who graduated was barred from campus. Four others were given lighter punishments – including two suspensions – but allowed to remain at the school.
Fraternities who “have too many people at an event, at a party, they get a far greater punishment than what seems to have happened to” the Chi Phi members, he said.
He does not think the school should force fraternities to close.
“When you get rid of Greek life, you get rid of some of the most passionate people that cared about the school, right? And so why would someone like that donate to the school if the school is eliminating something that was a key part of their time at Cornell?” he said.
Schools like Bowdoin College, Middlebury College and Swarthmore College have, however, shut down Greek life and survived. This week, the University of Arizona dean initiated an “interim activities suspension” at its fraternities, the New York Times reported.
“The alleged behaviors range from physical assault, drugs and alcohol, hazing and creating unsafe environments for our students,” the dean stated in a letter to fraternities and sororities. “Some cases are also under criminal investigation.”
Freyd used to think Greek life could be reformed but changed her mind because leaders must “overcome the generations of tradition that are misogynist and bonding over humiliation. That is enormous work.”
She thinks colleges should eliminate Greek life.
“The colleges and universities that make change in this domain, it’s going to be hard, and it will take courage,” Freyd said. “But it will really be worth it.”

Step toward EU accession: Verkhovna Rada adopted a law on education in the languages of national minorities
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
14:00:48 EEST
20:00:48 KST

Step toward EU accession: Verkhovna Rada adopted a law on education in the languages of national minorities
Kyiv • UNN
On October 12, the Verkhovna Rada adopted Law No. 16119 on education in the native language for national minorities and Indigenous peoples with 266 votes. The law brings Ukraine closer to the EU.
On October 12, the Verkhovna Rada adopted in its entirety a bill on ensuring the educational rights of indigenous peoples of Ukraine and persons belonging to the national minorities (communities) of Ukraine. This is one of Ukraine’s steps on the path to joining the EU. The parliament reported this, UNN writes.
Details
"Education in the languages of national minorities and indigenous peoples of Ukraine. The Verkhovna Rada adopted the relevant law (No. 16119). It was supported by 266 members of parliament," the statement said.
The document guarantees children from national minorities and indigenous peoples of Ukraine whose languages are official EU languages the right to receive education in their native language alongside the state language.
"In particular, the initiative provides for the possibility of granting schools the status of a national minority institution if more than half of the children there study in the respective language. The bill is one of Ukraine’s steps on the path to joining the EU," the Verkhovna Rada said.
"Bill No. 16119 on the educational rights of national minorities has been adopted: 273 in the first reading, 266 in its entirety. An instruction is immediately issued to the chair of the Verkhovna Rada to sign it urgently and submit it to the President for signature," MP Yaroslav Zhelezniak clarified on social media.
Currently, according to the document’s record, the bill is "being prepared for signature."
Background
On October 7, EU ambassadors opened the way for the start of negotiations with Ukraine and Moldova within the accession process on the single market and competitiveness. Budapest lifted its veto on the negotiations. Hungary had been blocking this step since the summer, demanding that Ukraine adopt legislation concerning the educational rights of national minorities.

Smaller firms still having issues getting into defence
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
12:00:44 BST
20:00:44 KST

Companies trying to break new ground in defence still find it very difficult to get into the government market, a former senior Royal Air Force officer who now advises across the industry told the Apex Europe conference in London on Wednesday.
Air Vice-Marshal (Retired) Gary Waterfall, senior defence advisor at Clarion Defence and Security, speaks into DSEI UK and also runs a portfolio business of around ten companies, none of which he would describe as being on the front line in the way some of his fellow panellists are.
He placed himself deliberately outside the part of the market that is currently getting all the attention, and did it with some relish. “I’m very much sat in the rear echelon, from primes through SMEs into small businesses, all of which are trying to get a worthwhile foothold in the market without having maybe the lure of the sexy dish of the day, very much in that drone environment, yet with a lot to contribute,” he said.
Recent work with a private equity company has sharpened the point for him, and he said the gap between the rhetoric about private investment and what actually happens is wide. “Defence talks about intended growth. Let’s go out, let’s get some private investment in to actually get the gears moving and working,” he said. “The reality is, when you’re trying to break new ground, it’s very difficult to get into government and defence in terms of marketplace. So I see that from an investor perspective. I also see that across all of the SMEs that I’m working with.”
His second argument was that defence companies have more to learn from outside the sector than they generally admit, and he reached for motorsport to make it. “Formula One technology is a real classic, where they raced last weekend, they’re racing next weekend, and they’re going to win, and they’re iterating through rapid cycles the whole time,” he said. “I’m involved with one of those companies, and it’s fascinating to watch them outstrip the pace of defence thinking, as they’re always thirsty for information.”
He also asked the panel to look further ahead than the current reaction cycle. “What we’ve heard is a lot of reacting to what the threat’s doing, and then iterating away. But let’s think beyond that. Let’s think beyond to where we might be going with degrees of certainty, the further out you go, and look at how you best advocate your technologies to meet that threat,” he said.
In Ukraine the loop is closed and innovation is happening in contact, he said, and companies there are doing an extraordinary job of it. The harder question is what firms outside that fight are doing to make themselves better at innovating, and his answer was that defence-based companies still have a great deal to learn.
Air Vice-Marshal Waterfall retired from the Royal Air Force before moving into advisory and investment work, which gives him a view of the industry from both the customer and the supplier sides. The panel was chaired by Lieutenant General (Retired) Stuart Skeates, chairman of Apex Europe.

Brain injury triggers unexpected hormone release in progenitor cells
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
11:00:27 UTC
20:00:27 KST

Following a brain injury, specific progenitor cells produce a neuropeptide to prevent their neighboring cells from maturing too quickly, a process that aids in tissue repair. This regulatory mechanism also guides myelin formation in the developing and adult brain under healthy conditions. The findings were published in the journal Cell Reports.
The central nervous system relies on myelin, an insulating layer that forms around nerves. This protective sheath allows electrical impulses to transmit quickly and efficiently along nerve networks. Oligodendrocytes are the specialized cells responsible for producing this vital myelin.
When the brain is injured or developing, it needs to generate new oligodendrocytes. These mature cells arise from oligodendrocyte progenitor cells, which migrate to where they are needed and transform into their final, myelin-producing state. This maturation process requires strict regulation to ensure the cells survive and function properly.
Neuropeptides are small protein-like molecules that brain cells use to communicate. Unlike classical neurotransmitters that cross tiny gaps between two specific cells, neuropeptides are released in large amounts and wash over a broader area. This localized broadcasting process is known as volume transmission.
Corticotropin-releasing hormone is one of the most heavily studied neuropeptides in biology. It is primarily known for coordinating the body’s response to stress by interacting with its main cellular receptor, CRHR1. Researchers Clemens Ries, Jan M. Deussing, and their colleagues at the Max Planck Institute of Psychiatry sought to understand how this hormone might act outside of traditional stress pathways.
The research team used genetically modified mice that produce a fluorescent red marker whenever a cell expresses the corticotropin-releasing hormone. In a small study involving brain injuries like tiny stab wounds, the researchers tracked the cellular response. They observed that cells producing the hormone aggregated around the injury sites, with the first such cells detectable as early as twelve hours after injury.
By applying specific chemical stains to the brain tissue, they identified these glowing cells. The cells were not neurons, as one might normally expect for this specific hormone, but rather oligodendrocyte progenitor cells. This marked an early and unusual secretory response by these progenitor cells to physical brain trauma.
To understand the ultimate fate of these specific progenitor cells, the researchers tracked them for over four months. They found that these cells multiplied heavily in the days immediately following the initial injury. Over the following weeks, they reliably transformed into mature oligodendrocytes.
These newly formed oligodendrocytes successfully integrated into the healing brain tissue. They extended their physical processes to form myelin sheaths around local nerve fibers. Once established, the cells survived for the entire duration of the four-month observation period.
Because neuropeptides operate by binding to specific receptors, the team searched for cells in the injury area equipped with the CRHR1 receptor. Using a different strain of genetically modified mice, they highlighted the receptor’s exact location. They discovered a completely separate group of oligodendrocyte progenitor cells expressing this receptor.
This finding established a potential communication network in the damaged tissue. One group of progenitor cells was releasing the hormone in response to injury, while a distinct neighboring group was equipped to receive that signal. The researchers then designed experiments to see what information the signal carried.
The researchers tested what happens when this communication is disrupted. They bred mice lacking the ability to produce the hormone in progenitor cells, as well as mice completely lacking the CRHR1 receptor. After inducing brain injuries, they compared these altered mice to regular mice.
In the altered mice, the progenitor cells equipped with the receptor matured into myelin-producing cells much faster than normal. Under typical conditions, the hormone acts as a brake, forcing the cells to delay their maturation. Removing the signal removed the brake.
While maturing faster might sound beneficial for wound healing, it proved detrimental in cases of larger brain injuries. The rapid maturation led to a noticeable drop in the number of oligodendrocytes that survived long-term. The researchers suspect that the injured environment contains high levels of oxidative stress.
The hormone-induced delay likely helps the cells wait for these harsh conditions to subside before completing their vulnerable final transformation. Moving beyond injury models, the team investigated whether this signaling network operates in healthy, uninjured brains. They counted the receptor-equipped progenitor cells in mice at various ages.
The team noted that these specific progenitor cells naturally increase in number as the mice grow into adulthood. To test the network’s role in healthy development, they examined postnatal mice lacking the CRHR1 receptor. In these young mice, oligodendrocytes formed earlier than usual in the brain’s white matter.
This confirmed that the hormone system also prevents premature cellular maturation during normal brain development. The researchers then evaluated how this early developmental shift affected the adult brain’s physical structure. They analyzed the brains of adult mice lacking the receptor using magnetic resonance imaging.
The researchers utilized a specialized imaging technique that detects the density of myelin by measuring how protons interact with surrounding macromolecules. The imaging revealed that mice lacking the receptor possessed a higher overall myelin content across multiple brain regions, including the corpus callosum. To see the microscopic details, the team employed electron microscopy.
Using the electron microscope, they measured the mathematical relationship between the radius of the inner nerve axon and the radius of the entire myelinated fiber. A lower ratio indicates a thicker myelin sheath relative to the nerve size. The microscopic analysis showed a structural shift in how myelin was distributed across the nerve fibers.
Smaller nerve fibers received thicker myelin sheaths than usual. In contrast, the myelin sheaths on larger nerve fibers were unusually thin. This suggests the hormone network helps ensure myelin is distributed in the correct proportions based on nerve fiber size.
Readers should exercise caution when interpreting these results in the context of psychological stress. While corticotropin-releasing hormone is heavily involved in emotional stress responses, this study focuses strictly on localized tissue signaling after physical trauma or during baseline cellular development. The results do not imply that psychological stress directly alters myelin through this specific pathway.
The study features limitations regarding the genetic models used in the experiments. The primary mouse model lacking the receptor had it deleted globally, meaning the receptor was missing in neurons as well as progenitor cells. This systemic absence could indirectly influence the behavior of the brain’s glial cells.
Future investigations will need to use genetic models that delete the receptor exclusively in oligodendrocyte progenitor cells. Additional studies could also explore how this hormone network responds to diseases that actively destroy myelin.
The study, “Neuropeptide CRH prevents premature differentiation of OPCs following CNS injury and in early postnatal development,” was authored by Clemens Ries, Tibor Stark, Benoit Boulat, Torben Ruhwedel, Jan Philipp Delling, Antonio Miralles Infante, Julia T. von Poblotzki, Alessandro Ulivi, Iven-Alex von Mücke-Heim, Simon Chang, Kenji Sakimura, Keiichi Itoi, Dennis B. Nestvogel, Alessio Attardo, Michael Czisch, Klaus-Armin Nave, Wiebke Möbius, Leda Dimou, and Jan M. Deussing.

Feds Got Warrants to Use Fake Cell Towers to Hunt Down Don Lemon’s Producer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
11:00:00 UTC
20:00:00 KST

US law enforcement agents obtained authorization to use a controversial surveillance device capable of intercepting cell phone signals to find and arrest a 21-year-old college student who helped produce journalist Don Lemon’s coverage of an anti-ICE protest, court filings show.
The former student, Jerome Richardson, who has since graduated from Temple University, is among 39 people charged with conspiring to violate worshippers’ civil rights and interfering with religious worship at Cities Church in St. Paul, Minnesota, in January. Protesters said they targeted the church’s January 18 service because one of its pastors, David Easterwood, also led ICE’s St. Paul field office. Those charged include journalists Georgia Fort and Lemon, a former CNN host, who say they were there to cover the demonstration.
Twelve days after the protest, judges in two states began signing warrants authorizing agents to use so-called cell-site simulators, commonly known as Stingrays or IMSI catchers, to target Richardson’s phone: one in Minnesota on January 30 and another in Pennsylvania the next day. The purpose, his lawyers wrote in a motion seeking to exclude the tracking evidence, was “locating and arresting him.”
Agents also applied for cell-site simulator warrants targeting the phones of Fort and Jamael Lundy, then a Minnesota State Senate candidate. They separately sought pen register orders, which can log the numbers a phone contacts, for Fort and a number WIRED traced to Lemon. It's unclear whether a judge approved any of those applications.
The records reviewed by WIRED do not establish whether investigators actually deployed a cell-site simulator to locate Richardson or whether judges approved the applications targeting Fort and Lundy. In a July letter filed in court, Fort’s lawyers said prosecutors “did not know” whether the surveillance applications had been authorized or had yielded evidence.
Cell-site simulators impersonate cell phone towers to locate a target’s phone. In doing so, they can also collect identifying information from any nearby cellular device, including those belonging to people who aren’t suspected of a crime. That indiscriminate collection has made the devices controversial among privacy advocates, who describe them as dragnet surveillance tools.
The use of cell-site simulators has long been shrouded in secrecy. FBI records released in 2023 showed that police borrowing its simulators had to agree to keep details of their use secret, even in court. Privacy advocates have long warned that the devices could be turned against protesters and journalists.
“Using an advanced surveillance capability such as a cell-site simulator against members of the free press for reporting stories that are unfavorable to the president is an appalling attack on the First Amendment,” says Cooper Quintin, senior staff technologist at the Electronic Frontier Foundation, a tech-focused civil liberties nonprofit. Quintin has spent years researching the devices and developing tools to help people detect them. Using EFF’s detection software, WIRED found evidence suggesting a cell-site simulator was deployed near the 2024 Democratic National Convention in Chicago, though who operated it and for what purpose remain unknown.
Attorneys for Lemon, Lundy, and Fort did not respond to requests for comment. Richardson’s attorneys declined to comment on the record.
The previously unreported warrants are a product of a campaign of contentious investigative tactics waged by federal agents in pursuit of people connected to the protest at Cities Church. According to court records, the Department of Homeland Security demanded journalists’ telephone and YouTube records under a customs authority that requires no prior judicial approval. Agents also sought records identifying everyone who had purchased a particular beanie at REI in the Minneapolis–St. Paul area over a period of more than two years. Defense attorneys have identified 92 customs summonses and are challenging the government’s authority to issue them.
The cell-site simulator warrants raise serious questions about both the accuracy of the information investigators presented to judges in their effort to obtain authorization for surveillance tool’s use, as well as why they sought such intrusive tracking to find Richardson in the first place.
The affidavits supporting the applications to track Richardson claimed video showed Fort, Lemon, Richardson, and others “chanting with agitators.” Prosecutors have since conceded that Lemon and Fort did not chant. According to her lawyers, the government acknowledged that the false claim appeared in at least 15 warrant affidavits.
DHS policy says cell-site simulators are deployed only “in the fraction of cases in which the capability is best suited to achieve specific public safety objectives,” but it’s unclear what specific public safety reason justified its use in this case. Investigators obtained a second simulator warrant to locate Richardson, then a senior at Temple University, two days before he walked up to a federal courthouse in Philadelphia and voluntarily surrendered. He was released on bond that afternoon.
The Justice Department responded to WIRED’s request for comment by writing in an email that the department “speaks through its court filings.” DHS declined to discuss ongoing investigations or investigative methods and referred questions to the US Attorney’s Office for the District of Minnesota, which did not respond to a request for comment.
The warrant was signed January 31, the same day Richardson posted a YouTube video saying he expected to enter federal custody “in the coming days,” suggesting he had no intention of fleeing. It is unclear whether the warrant preceded the video, leaving questions about why investigators sought such an intrusive tool to find someone who was publicly anticipating his arrest and whom prosecutors agreed to release the day he surrendered.
While Richardson’s suppression motion asks to suppress evidence obtained from the phone tracking, it does not specify whether agents used a simulator or obtained evidence through either.
A former federal prosecutor who spent a decade working on counterterrorism cases says using a simulator to locate someone is not necessarily unusual. But based on the court records they reviewed about Richardson’s case, they called the government's tactics aggressive: “I don’t understand why it would be at all necessary.” They spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak on the record
Richardson, a St. Paul native, had led an NAACP chapter at 16 and served as executive director of Minnesota Teen Activists, according to his fundraiser’s organizer. He described his work for Lemon as handling logistics and connecting him with local contacts. He drove the journalist to Cities Church, where Lemon livestreamed the demonstration and interviewed protesters and churchgoers. Prosecutors allege Richardson joined chants and obstructed congregants.
In his video, Richardson defended his role. “I was proud to support his work,” he said of Lemon. “This is the price of being unapologetic about humanity and love of Christ.”
The government’s initial effort to obtain arrest warrants met resistance from judges. A magistrate judge refused five of eight warrants, and after an appeals court rejected the Justice Department's bid to override that decision, the department withdrew its request. In a filing with the appeals court, the chief judge wrote that two of the five “were not protestors at all; instead, they were a journalist and his producer” and that there was “no evidence that those two engaged in any criminal behavior.” Prosecutors later secured a grand jury indictment on January 29.
The way the government chose to arrest some defendants has also drawn objections from defense lawyers. Lemon’s attorneys say in court filings that prosecutors rejected their offer to arrange his surrender; agents instead arrested him shortly before midnight at a Beverly Hills hotel while he was covering the Grammy Awards. Fort’s lawyers say agents arrested her at home rather than allowing her to turn herself in.

Rada passes law on national minority educational rights required to open EU negotiating clusters
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
13:59:38 EEST
19:59:38 KST

The Verkhovna Rada passed as a whole the law 'On Amendments to Certain Laws of Ukraine on Ensuring the Educational Rights of Indigenous Peoples of Ukraine and Persons Belonging to National Minorities (Communities) of Ukraine' (bill No. 16119), designed to unblock the opening of two negotiating clusters on Ukraine's EU accession by lifting Hungary's veto.
A total of 266 MPs voted for it at a plenary session on Monday, according to an Interfax-Ukraine correspondent.
By faction and group, the votes were: Servant of the People 177, European Solidarity 16, Batkivshchyna 11, Holos 6, Platform for Life and Peace 11, Restoration of Ukraine 11, For the Future 9, Trust 15 and non-affiliated MPs 10, the correspondent said.
Rada Speaker Ruslan Stefanchuk signed the law immediately after the vote, and it will be sent at once to President Volodymyr Zelenskyy for signing.
The law formalizes the right of children from national minorities and indigenous peoples of Ukraine to study in their native language alongside the state language, not instead of it.
"The Ukrainian language remains a guaranteed part of education for every child. No provision of the bill narrows the sphere of the state language; on the contrary, it preserves guarantees of its study, free command and use in the educational process ... It is important that the additional rights provided by the bill apply exclusively to languages that are official languages of the European Union and to languages of indigenous peoples of Ukraine, and do not apply to Russian," the Education and Science Ministry said earlier.
For example, if a school has a class taught in Hungarian, its pupils will be able to use the language of the EU country, alongside Ukrainian, not only in lessons but also in communication with teachers and other participants in the educational process.
The document also formalizes the concept of a general secondary school with the status of a national minority (community) institution. To qualify, at least 50% plus one of a school's pupils must study in the minority language. The ministry estimates that 149 schools, about 1.2% of all general secondary schools in Ukraine, will be entitled to claim the status.
Separately, regardless of status, any school with at least one class or group taught in a minority language has the right to duplicate signs, education documents (at parents' request) and official documentation in the minority language for that class.
Schools that receive the status under the law must keep at least 20% of pupils studying in the minority language to retain it. If the share falls below 20%, the right to the status ends, subject to agreement with the ministry.
The law also lets parents initiate an expansion of the list of subjects taught in Ukrainian. If a child studies in a class or group taught in the language of an indigenous people or a national minority that is an official EU language, the number of subjects taught in Ukrainian may be increased. Expanding the list requires the written support of at least two-thirds of the parents of the class.
The law requires that reorganization or liquidation of municipal schools with the status of 'national minority/indigenous people school' be agreed with the ministry. The founder must also guarantee pupils the chance to continue studying, at parents' request, at a school with the corresponding status in the same community. The ministry estimates that this provision could affect at most 141 municipal schools in Zakarpattia, Chernivtsi, Odesa and Lviv regions.
The law also clarifies how the requirement for a state certificate in Ukrainian applies to heads of private schools that have a class or group taught in the language of a national minority or indigenous people. It applies only to heads who already hold the post when the law takes effect. They are exempt from the obligation to confirm their command of the state language with a certificate while in that post, though the obligation to know and use the state language remains. The ministry said the provision has limited scope and covers the heads of 29 institutions nationwide.
Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar reacted earlier to the submission of the bill to the Rada, saying he expects the rights of the Hungarian national minority in Ukraine to be fully ensured in practice.
Deputy Prime Minister for European and Euro-Atlantic Integration Vsevolod Chentsov said earlier that clusters 2 and 3 ('Internal Market' and 'Competitiveness and Inclusive Growth') of Ukraine's EU accession talks could be opened on October 13 if the Rada passed the law on national minorities' educational rights the day before.
Hungarian Foreign Minister Anita Orban confirmed on October 12 that the Ukrainian parliament's passage of the law would allow the next clusters for Ukraine to be opened at an intergovernmental conference scheduled for October 13.

Lettuce engineered to produce meat proteins
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
10:59:28 UTC
19:59:28 KST

Perhaps you enjoy a burger in a lettuce wrap once in a while—but what if greens were also crucial to the patty? That’s the ultimate promise of new research showing lettuce can be engineered to produce myoglobin, a protein found in meat.
Myoglobin (and its better-known relative hemoglobin) contains the compound heme, the red pigment in blood. Adding heme can give plant-based meat alternatives a meaty flavor and the ability to “bleed.” For example, Impossible Foods uses a compound called leghemoglobin (a heme protein derived from soybeans) to flavor its meat alternatives. But using myoglobin, which is found in animal tissue, could lead to vegetarian products that not only look and bleed like red meat but smell more like it, too.
In the study, published in Frontiers in Plant Science, the researchers describe how they got lettuce and tobacco plants to produce myoglobin for the first time, says lead author Alexia Groff, who worked on the project as a Ph.D. student at Imperial College London. The team engineered the plants’ photosynthesizing chloroplasts—the cell structures that typically turn sunlight into food—to make them do the job.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
In previous attempts to make myoglobin using nonanimal sources such as yeast, the protein-production directions were placed in the nucleus’s genome, but Groff and her colleagues found that adding them to the chloroplast genome instead could yield more of it—perhaps producing myoglobin even more efficiently than animals do.
Right now yeast fermentation is the standard method of producing heme (as leghemoglobin), but the sterile environment and industrial equipment necessary for manufacturing can be pricey. Plants are much easier to grow. “Row-crop protein production would likely be faster than fermentation-derived production,” says Adam Leman, a principal scientist at the Good Food Institute, who was not involved in the study. “If existing crop-processing equipment can be used, costs for isolating and purifying a myoglobin-rich fraction could be quite low.”
Lettuce is especially promising: the medium itself is edible, meaning lettuce-produced myoglobin could move more easily through the regulatory steps that can slow down the path from laboratory to market. A more streamlined process could also mean less money spent in production—and far less energy use.
The meat industry is a voracious energy consumer: 60 percent of agricultural energy use comes from farming and transporting animal products. Making meat substitutes less resource-intensive is a step toward more sustainable food systems—even if it means making meat proteins in a vegetable.
“In science, there were things that we used to think were impossible that now are an everyday occurrence,” Groff says. “I’m very excited for what the future of this sector is going to look like.”

Light-controlled cells, multimessenger astronomy and lessons from an old turtle on aging
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
10:59:16 UTC
19:59:16 KST

Rachel Feltman: Happy Monday, listeners! For Scientific American’s Science Quickly, I’m Rachel Feltman. You’re listening to our weekly science news roundup.
Some of the biggest stories in science last week were the announcement of the Nobel Prize awards in Chemistry, Physics, and Physiology or Medicine. So we’re going to focus on those groundbreaking research topics today—with a fun little animal story at the end to send us off, of course.
Let’s start with the prize for physiology or medicine, which was announced last Monday. This year’s award went to Karl Deisseroth at Stanford University, Peter Hegemann at Humboldt University of Berlin, and Georg Nagel at the University of Wurzburg in Germany. They were recognized for their discoveries around light-gated ion channels and optogenetics.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Optogenetics allows scientists to switch individual brain cells on and off. Because neurons use electrical signals to communicate with one another, scientists realized almost a century ago that they could use electrical stimulation to activate brain cells. Optogenetics combines this idea with genetic engineering to allow for more targeted, less invasive, safer cell stimulation than used to be possible. After genetically modifying neurons to make proteins that react to light, researchers can control those cells with a flash of light instead of an electrode.
Hegemann and Nagel contributed to the field by studying a single-celled alga that swims toward light, which they found had to do with a particular protein that opened up pores in the cell membrane when exposed to light. Deisseroth took those findings and applied them to experiments in living mammals.
We spoke to him about his win last week. Here he is explaining the impact of his discovery:
Karl Deisseroth: You know, once you know what matters for function, you can ask: How can dysfunction be addressed? You know, are there cells that cause dysfunction? Are there cells that can counteract dysfunction in a precise way? And what we're doing now is—and many others as well—is we're seeing: how can we leverage this precision to find new treatments, new medications, new neuromodulator approaches that build on this foundation of causality?
You know, this brings an opportunity that might help me communicate more with the public and to share the excitement of science, how discovery happens, how unlikely things get nurtured and that it takes time and it takes risk but that the outcome can be amazing if we’re willing to take the time and the risk.
Feltman: Last Tuesday saw Francis Halzen from the University of Wisconsin–Madison secure a rare solo award in Physics for the discovery of high-energy neutrinos of extraterrestrial origin. Here to tell us more about his contributions to the field is Joseph Howlett, a senior reporter at Scientific American and our resident physics expert. Tell us about those neutrinos, Joe!
Joseph Howlett: So neutrinos are my personal favorite fundamental particle. Of the 17 that we know about, the neutrinos are the ones we know the least. And that's why they've netted five times the Nobel Prize in Physics now.
The main thing that makes neutrinos different from other particles is that they pass through regular matter almost all the time without interacting. So there's neutrinos coming from space, from faraway black holes where super violent things are happening, like supernova and accretion, and these send out these very high-energy neutrinos. They make it all the way to Earth, but almost all the time they pass right through. We never notice that they're here. They're actually passing through us all the time. Neutrinos from the sun go right through our bodies without interacting.
It's really hard to build a detector that can catch a neutrino. And Halzen had this super ambitious idea to do so at the South Pole. He spearheaded the IceCube Neutrino Observatory. They chose Antarctica because it's a place with a lot of ice, and ice is great because when a neutrino interacts with ice, the light shines right through. It can go right through the ice like it's not there, all the way to whatever cameras you've buried inside.
So that was Halzen's great idea was that the Earth built this natural detector for us, right? All we have to do is put the cameras there to capture the light. So they bored these mile-deep holes with hot water jets and then lowered these strings of expensive cameras into each of them.
They span like a cubic kilometer of ice. And when a neutrino passes through that ice, usually it goes right through, but very rarely it will interact with one of the water molecules and produce a shower of light. And because the cameras are there, they can capture that light and say where that neutrino came from and how much energy it has.
So for the first time, we're able to see these neutrinos from these very, very faraway galaxies.
And actually, IceCube was the first experiment to see neutrinos from outer space, from outside of our solar system with this super high energy. So we've learned a lot about the universe thanks to this one experiment. It's also heralded this new era that astronomers call multimessenger astronomy. Basically, we've been looking at the sky with telescopes for hundreds of years, right? Measuring the light from faraway galaxies, from stars, X-rays even from black holes. But neutrinos are a whole new thing. They're not light. We're able to see the universe through a different lens. And when you combine this with the light measurements from all the telescopes in space and across the world, and you combine them additionally with gravitational wave detectors, which are another new technology that's won a Nobel Prize recently, now we have these three lenses that together can look at the same faraway objects and teach us all kinds of new things about them.
The thing about the multimessenger era is that it's just beginning. IceCube's only been operating for 16 years, and it's got a lot of life left to live, so we're gonna continue to learn all kinds of new things about the universe thanks to neutrinos, especially combined with these other experiments measuring light and gravitational waves.
Feltman: Thanks for breaking that down for us, Joe.
Last but not least is the Nobel Prize in Chemistry, which this year honored Henri Kagan of Paris-Sud University and Kenso Soai of the Tokyo University of Science for their pioneering research on autocatalysis in asymmetric organic synthesis. Try saying that one five times fast!
Many molecules come in two versions that are mirror images of each other. They can’t be superimposed over one another, the same way you couldn’t lay your right and left hands on top of each other and get them to line up. That’s called chirality, which happens to be one of my favorite words. When chemists create chiral molecules in the lab, they typically end up with equal amounts of each version. But that's not ideal, because the proteins in your cells—and in the natural world in general—are made from only one of those mirror images. Kagan and Soai figured out how to create just one of those mirror images at a time.
We’ll wrap up today’s news roundup with a story about a very, very old tortoise. The oldest tortoise, in fact. And not just the oldest tortoise, but the oldest terrestrial animal known to man. His name? Jonathan.
Giant tortoises are known generally for their long lifespans, but at around 190 years old, Jonathan is at least a century older than seems to be standard for his kind. And yeah, he is definitely that old. Photographs have confirmed that he was fully mature when he was brought to the island of Saint Helena in 1882, which means he had to have been at least 50 at the time.
A study published last week in Science Advances aims to explain how Jonathan is still alive and kicking all these years later. Genetic analysis of the tortoise compared with four of his peers apparently revealed mutations associated with DNA repair, cancer, telomere maintenance, mitochondrial health, insulin regulation, and other pathways associated with aging.
The researchers also took a look at the methylation of Jonathan’s genome. Methylation is when a small chemical tag gets added to DNA, which generally serves to turn a gene off. One sign of aging is a process called methylation entropy, which is where random patterns of methylation start to become more common. In other words, your body gets worse at targeting the right genes to switch off, which makes it more likely that some important protein won’t get made the way it’s supposed to.
In Johnathan’s genome, methylation entropy was unusually low in gene regions associated with mitochondrial function, RNA processing, and genome repair. That could give scientists some clues about what genes to target if they want to increase lifespan for other animals.
Speaking of longevity: We’ll be back on Wednesday to talk about why there’s so much shoddy science in this very buzzy field of research.
Science Quickly is produced by me, Rachel Feltman, along with Fonda Mwangi, Allison Rodgers and Jeff DelViscio. This episode was edited by Alex Sugiura. Marielle Issa and Aaron Shattuck fact-check our show. Our theme music was composed by Dominic Smith. Subscribe to Scientific American for more up-to-date and in-depth science news.
For Scientific American, this is Rachel Feltman. Have a great week!
