Jaak Prozes: Supporting Finno-Ugric peoples a matter of identity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
10:59:00 UTC
19:59:00 KST

Jaak Prozes: Supporting Finno-Ugric peoples a matter of identity
Our 25 million linguistic relatives need support. Supporting Finno-Ugric peoples is a matter of our national security and identity, Jaak Prozes writes in an overview originally published in Sirp magazine.
The past few years have been turbulent for cooperation among Finno-Ugric peoples, with various events and organizations promoting such cooperation ceasing to exist or scaling back their activities one after another.
In the Russian Federation, the prevailing view is that there is neither the money nor any real need to continue developing cooperation among Finno-Ugric peoples in its previous form as this draws Russia's Finno-Ugric peoples away from the richness of the Russian language and culture. Even when Finno-Ugric cooperation is discussed there, it is invariably in the context of the unity of the Russian Federation's ethnic groups and its imperialist policies, which leave no room for contacts with Estonians, Finns or Hungarians. It is as though we do not exist and it is clear that such cooperation is regarded as hostile to the Russian Federation.
At the same time, events involving Finno-Ugric peoples do still take place in Russia. Unfortunately, however, all major Finno-Ugric gatherings there are accompanied by the militaristic, propagandistic beating of war drums demanding blood. Shed blood, blood, blood, dear Finno-Ugric peoples! Defend and liberate the land and die because that is precisely what Russia needs right now!
Of course, no one in Russia talks about the rights of Finno-Ugric peoples, the root causes of their languages becoming endangered or their current situation as ethnic groups. Attempts to raise these issues, whether at home or in international organizations, are punishable. As a result, several Finno-Ugric activists are being held in pretrial detention or even in penal colonies, while still more have received suspended sentences or fines. Some protesters and dissidents, meanwhile, have left the country.
We're not small together
How should we Estonians — the Republic of Estonia — act now? What opportunities do we have to support Finno-Ugric peoples and do we even want to support them? Let me explain what I mean by support. I certainly believe it is essential to continue organizing a wide range of events that promote cooperation among Finno-Ugric peoples and raise awareness of them. This should take place at the academic level, but especially in the fields of culture and education. It is extremely important to foster a sense of unity among Finno-Ugric peoples — small nations — and to create a perception that we are equals and that our national achievements are valued.
One important occasion for fostering this sense of unity is the celebration of Kindred Peoples' Day, which should be a natural part of the calendar, particularly in our educational institutions. Unfortunately, this is not the case because for some reason the Finno-Ugric issue is seen as something separate, peripheral, something concerning Finns or other Finno-Ugric peoples. What is forgotten is that this is our own concern, that we ourselves are a Finno-Ugric people and that our language, Estonian, is a Finno-Ugric language.
Supporting Finno-Ugric peoples is therefore, in fact, supporting ourselves and our national identity. Of course, it also means supporting Finno-Ugric peoples without states of their own, valuing their languages and cultures and keeping them in our thoughts amid their current, indescribably difficult circumstances. Thinking about them is certainly the least Estonians can do, but even the smallest initiative that raises awareness of Finno-Ugric peoples and thereby of ourselves is of great national value.
On the one hand, this allows us to see Estonians as part of something larger — after all, we have nearly 25 million linguistic relatives, which is no small number. On the other hand, thinking this way also brings us to a deeper cultural value that underpins our identity — consider, for example, the works of Kaljo Põllu and Veljo Tormis or the films of Lennart Meri.
Only three Finno-Ugric peoples — Estonians, Finns and Hungarians — have states of their own and in the current circumstances, this is particularly significant. We belong to both the European Union and NATO, but our peoples are also connected by even closer ties that encompass almost every aspect of life. Even so, it seems that we need an even stronger sense of unity that would allow us to consolidate these closely related peoples more effectively. To bring us together so closely that we would be almost one. Estonia, for example, has numerous cooperation and friendship agreements with Finland and local governments and schools in our kindred countries also maintain contacts to some extent. However, this cooperation is haphazard and, from what I have observed, a far cry from what was happening in the early 1990s.
Why is that? It is worth reflecting on, especially in these difficult times, when alongside national security we should also be talking about the security of our national identity. Should we not make a determined effort to strengthen our ties through more frequent exchanges, at least during Kindred Peoples' Day celebrations, but ideally, of course, throughout the year? After all, we are kindred peoples regardless of the season.
Kindred People's Program must continue
There is another level of support that particularly concerns me. This is the level of the Estonian state — our national policy and, I would say, our moral responsibility. It is true that the very existence of the Estonian state supports Finno-Ugric peoples, but the state also provides funding to the Fenno-Ugria Foundation whose statutory mission is to develop cooperation among Uralic peoples and support the development of their culture, education and research. At Fenno-Ugria's initiative and by a decision of the Estonian government, the Kindred Peoples' Program was established in 1998.
Over more than 25 years, this program, now officially referred to as a support measure, has funded nearly 1,000 projects. Educational projects have accounted for the largest share, enabling hundreds of students from Finno-Ugric peoples to study at Estonian universities. The program has also supported the development of academic research in Finno-Ugric languages and the publication of translated literature and works of fiction.
The Kindred Peoples' Program became an important source of support for writers producing literature in Finno-Ugric languages who often had to hear Russian government officials tell them there was no money to publish their books. The program's efforts to recognize cultural figures and community leaders among Finno-Ugric peoples have also been highly valued as it presents several awards that encourage the work of Finno-Ugric activists.
Unfortunately, we recently received news that the Kindred Peoples' Program, administered by the Ministry of Education and Research, may be discontinued because Russia launched its war against Ukraine and Estonia has ended cooperation with Finno-Ugric peoples living in Russia. In other words, supporting Finno-Ugric peoples no longer has a place in our country's policies — or so the ministry officials administering the Kindred Peoples' Program seem to be saying.
This suggests that we have forgotten that Finno-Ugric peoples without states of their own form our cultural and linguistic hinterland. If they disappear, we might as well start asking today who will be next. The current situation is such that the survival and development of the languages and cultures of Russia's Finno-Ugric peoples are almost impossible without outside assistance. Who else should help them if not Estonia, Finland and Hungary?
As Estonian President Lennart Meri said during the Kindred Peoples' Day celebrations in 1993: "Estonia, Hungary and Finland are the only Finno-Ugric peoples to have established independent states of their own. We must clearly recognize our obligations toward our linguistic relatives. President Toomas Hendrik Ilves has also spoken about Estonia's responsibility toward small stateless peoples, their cultures and their distinct identities.
We now appear to be entering an era that could be characterized as an age of great-power ambitions, threatening those who are weaker and smaller. Smaller countries that stop supporting small stateless peoples and their own kindred peoples thereby undermine their own fundamental national values and their linguistic and cultural roots.
There is another interesting aspect to consider: Russia's reaction. The news that the Republic of Estonia may stop supporting Finno-Ugric peoples is probably music to the ears of Russian government officials. Applause rings out in the Kremlin — you did it, and you did it to yourselves!
Support for Finno-Ugric peoples has long been a thorn in the side of Russian officials. One example is the reaction of Sergei Naryshkin, the former speaker of the Russian State Duma, to Udmurt linguist and poet Aleksei Arzamazov. When Arzamazov praised Estonia's Kindred Peoples' Program for supporting the publication of literature in Udmurt, something Russia itself was not doing sufficiently, Naryshkin responded that Estonia was supporting the Udmurts not with its own money but with American funds and that the purpose of this support was to divide Russian society and exert external pressure on Russia.
Where do we go from here? The Kindred Peoples' support measure (program) must certainly continue operating in Estonia because this is a matter of our national security, national identity and values. By supporting Finno-Ugric peoples, we are helping ourselves.
--
Editor: Marcus Turovski

A unique shape, a 3D einstein tile, has been discovered
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
10:58:54 UTC
19:58:54 KST

It may look like a child’s Lego creation, but it’s a mathematical marvel. Researchers have just discovered a three-dimensional “einstein” tile—a special shape with unique capabilities.
The finding follows a major announcement from 2023, when a new hat-shaped tile called an “einstein” rocked the popular mathematics world. David Smith, an amateur mathematician, discovered that shape. In an article later published in Combinatorial Theory, he and three other researchers—Joseph Samuel Myers, Craig Kaplan and Chaim Goodman-Strauss—proved that “the hat” was the first known example of a two-dimensional aperiodic monotile, also called an “einstein” (ein Stein roughly translates to “one shape” in German). In other words, the hat is a shape that can infinitely tile, or cover, a 2D surface without ever creating a repeating pattern. These building-block hats can be placed next to one another to create bigger and bigger shapes that also look like the hat. But each individual hat will be situated in a nonrepeating pattern that continues to change no matter how large the overall tiling is.
Now a researcher has taken this concept into the third dimension with a 3D shape dubbed the Chair44 monotile. Chair44 can infinitely tile a three-dimensional space by covering it without gaps or overlapping shapes. Moreover, that tiling is aperiodic, meaning that the pattern is never repeated. The finding was announced by Ioannis Tsiokos, director of Automorph, which he describes as an AI research lab.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
“I’m not a mathematician myself,” says Tsiokos, who is the sole human author of the preprint announcing Chair44. Tsiokos says he used Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5.1 artificial intelligence model to write the paper and the OpenAI model ChatGPT-6 Astra to search for a 3D monotile, including to verify that the Chair44 monotile met the criteria for an einstein.
Chair44 isn’t exactly the first example of such a monotile in three dimensions, according to Kaplan, a computer scientist whose research focuses on the intersection of mathematics and art. “For decades, we’ve known of an aperiodic monotile in 3D: a shape known as the Schmitt-Conway-Danzer biprism,” Kaplan says. That biprism, however—a kind of convex polyhedron—“obeys the letter of the law of aperiodicity but not the spirit,” making it weakly aperiodic, he notes. The Chair44 discovery, on the other hand, fulfills a decades-long quest to find a strong example.
“I’m pleased that we have the solution to what was, until recently, a nagging open problem in tiling theory,” Kaplan says. “We can also hope that this discovery will generate renewed excitement in the mathematics of tilings and encourage more young people to play around with geometry.”
Propagating the Chair
To understand the geometric intuition behind the Chair44 shape, Tsiokos says, imagine a large cube composed of eight tiny cubes that are joined together. Next, remove just one cube. “Now you have a seven-cube chair,” he says.
The next goal on this journey is to create a bigger “chair” shape. That larger shape can be constructed by connecting four of these smaller chairs. To create a full tiling, just repeat this process over and over again, ad infinitum.
As you build bigger and bigger chairs, however, you must arrange the smaller chairs in a nonrepeating pattern so that the resulting tiling will be aperiodic.
“The trick” to ensuring an aperiodic tiling “is that you need to grow the chair in such a way that the behavior of the chair grows with it,” Tsiokos says. “To have this iterative, recursive building of chairs” requires making sure “that there are some sort of key locks between the chairs so that they form bigger and bigger chairs” that are made from a nonrepeating tiling pattern.
Experts Respond
When the hat monotile was discovered, it was so lauded that five researchers organized a two-day Hatfest celebration at the University of Oxford. Time will tell if Chair44 inspires its own celebration. For now, the reception to the finding has been mixed, largely because of Tsiokos’s significant use of generative AI in the proof.
“There was a lot of human work that went into what went into Astra to do this,” Tsiokos says.
Chaim Goodman-Strauss, one of the mathematicians behind the hat proof and an outreach mathematician at the National Museum of Mathematics, wrote a preprint reacting to the Chair44 results. In it, he described Tsiokos’s paper as having “hallmarks of an LLM-driven research paper,” including “so much irrelevant puff to push through.” Goodman-Strauss is one of at least two researchers who have now presented their own human-written proofs demonstrating that Chair44 is an aperiodic monotile.
Tiling problems have been “a big part of my career,” Goodman-Strauss says. He has studied the shape that Tsiokos calls Chair44 for more than 30 years, he says, and is used to calling it “the L.”
To explain how tiling with the shape works, Goodman-Strauss begins with an L-shaped building block. “You can make a bigger version of it out of eight little copies,” he says. “The problem is, that shape can also do all kinds of other crazy stuff,” he says. But because you can build a tiling from increasingly larger L shapes made up of smaller ones that are organized without repeating a pattern, each tile exists within what he calls “a supertile” that’s arranged in a unique configuration out of the smaller tiles.
Hence, Chair44 or the L is an aperiodic monotile in 3D.
Felix Flicker, a theoretical physicist at the University of Bristol in England, was one of Hatfest’s organizers. “I know a lot of mathematicians are unhappy with how the tile was discovered,” Flicker says. “The positive take is that we have a new important result.” The announcement comes after a summer in which AI models have repeatedly conquered many of math’s longstanding open challenges, including one of the seven Millennium Prize Problems. “The risk is that our jobs get reduced to sifting through AI slop in search of nuggets of gold,” Flicker says.
Flicker also wrote a Chair44 preprint, which he says aims to “provide the first human-written, human-readable, and therefore referee-able and defensible proof that Chair44 is a strongly aperiodic monotile.” (Even Flicker noted in his paper that he used Claude for coding and discussions in his study.)
Tsiokos’s Chair44 paper “is just the first example of something that we’re going to be encountering a lot of” in terms of generative AI usage, Goodman-Strauss says. “One of the big lessons here in the age of LLMs is that we should remember all the [math] questions we asked before that were difficult to deal with.” Perhaps some of those problems can now be solved through the use of LLMs as a mathematician’s tool—although those technologies aren’t a substitute for human reasoning, he notes.
The use of generative AI to find new potential math research results isn’t going away. “It’s just that we have got to come to terms with what’s expected in terms of communication” of those results, Goodman-Strauss says.

citroën revives the iconic 2 CV as a compact electric concept with a roll-up fabric roof
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

citroën revives the iconic 2 CV as a compact electric concept with a roll-up fabric roof
unveiled at the 2026 paris motor show, citroën's 2 cv concept reinterprets the 1948 classic as a compact electric car measuring just 3.76 metres.
CITROËN 2 CV CONCEPT REIMAGINES THE 1948 CLASSIC
At the 2026 Paris Motor Show, Citroën is bringing the 2 CV back to the drawing board — and this time, it runs on electricity. The 2 CV Concept revisits the French manufacturer’s most recognisable small car, first unveiled at the same event in 1948, with an emphasis on lightness, affordability and everyday practicality. Rather than simply reproducing a familiar silhouette, Citroën is exploring the ingredients for a new electric model that it plans to introduce by 2028, preserving the original’s philosophy of making mobility accessible without sacrificing personality.
At just 3.76 metres long, the concept is actually shorter than its predecessor, a rather unusual achievement in an automotive industry accustomed to making everything bigger. Its silhouette retains the original’s rounded proportions, vertical windscreen and flowing roofline, while introducing a more contemporary expression. Circular LED headlights appear to float beside the sculpted bonnet, 18-inch steel wheels reinterpret the classic design, and the bright Infra Red bodywork shifts between orange, yellow and red tones depending on the light. The manually retractable fabric roof is another familiar touch, bringing the original’s open-air character into the electric era.
PLAYFUL TECHNOLOGY SHAPE THE ELECTRIC CAR INTERIOR
Inside, the Citroën 2 CV Concept takes a similarly unconventional approach. A cylindrical structure replaces the traditional dashboard, bringing together a single-spoke steering wheel, simplified controls and an eight-inch square touchscreen featuring comic-book-inspired graphics by Belgian illustrator Jean-Luc Delvaux. Essential driving information appears through the Smart Vision display, positioned within the driver’s field of vision. The cabin also combines yellow tartan upholstery with beige details inspired by the Bakelite components of earlier models, creating an interior that feels deliberately cheerful rather than technologically intimidating.
Practicality comes with a few surprises. The front bench seat can be removed and used outdoors during a picnic, while a detachable Radioën unit doubles as a portable speaker. Instead of a central console, passengers get a removable storage basket made from wood and bio-based plastic using 3D printing, and flexible fabric straps replace conventional door handles. Above, the roll-up fabric roof opens the cabin to daylight, while a string of lights suspended from the headlining introduces an unexpected festive touch. Apparently, even a short drive deserves a little atmosphere.
CITROËN’S ELECTRIC 2 CV LOOKS TO SIMPLICITY FOR THE ROAD AHEAD
Some of the smallest details carry the strongest references to the original. The accelerator and brake pedals feature illustrations of a hare and a tortoise, while the door compartments are designed to accommodate eggs, recalling the famously practical specifications of the first 2 CV. Numbers printed on the windscreen mark 1948, the original launch; 1990, the end of production; and 2026, the concept’s debut. Even the horn and start-up sound echo those of the historic model. These playful gestures turn automotive heritage into something that can be experienced rather than simply admired.
Beyond nostalgia, Citroën is proposing a different approach to affordable electric mobility. The future European-built production model is targeting a starting price of around €15,000, while the concept’s engineering aims for a weight close to one tonne, reduced manufacturing complexity and easier repairs through independently replaceable bumpers. A collaboration with Michelin also explores digital tyre-monitoring technology that uses vehicle data instead of dedicated tyre sensors. ‘Reinventing the 2 CV isn’t about replicating a car from the past,’ says Citroën CEO Xavier Chardon. Whether the eventual production car can retain this same balance of simplicity, ingenuity and character remains the more interesting question.

designer: Citroën Design Team
brand: Citroën | @citroen
Location: Paris, France (2026 Paris Motor Show)

2026 Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences: how Hall and Woodford’s research helps overcome unemployment and crises
Kyiv • UNN
Robert Hall and Michael Woodford were honored for their research into the microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilization. Their work explains unemployment, inflation, and the impact of monetary policy.
On Monday, October 12, the names of the laureates of the 2026 Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences became known.
They were American economists Robert Ernest Hall and Michael Dean Woodford. The men were awarded the prize for research that helped explain how the decisions of individuals, businesses and financial institutions affect the economy as a whole and how states can counter crises.
UNN has compiled all the interesting information about this year's triumphants and how their scientific achievements could change the global economy.
It should be noted that this is the final award of this year's Nobel Week, during which researchers in the fields of medicine, physics and chemistry, as well as the laureates of the prizes in literature and peace, have already been honored. This year, the monetary award was increased to 12 million Swedish kronor.
Who was tipped to win the Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences
This year's forecasts by international media and analysts featured researchers of the labor market, behavioral economics and monetary policy. One of them was American economist David Autor, known for his work on the impact of automation, technology and global trade on employment and wages. Colin Camerer and George Loewenstein were also mentioned; they study how psychological factors influence people's economic decisions. Other possible contenders included Michael Woodford, whose work focuses on monetary policy and inflation expectations.
Why Hall and Woodford were awarded the prize
They received the prestigious award with the citation "for the microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilization."
The scientific work of Robert Ernest Hall and Michael Dean Woodford focuses on the relationship between the behavior of individual market participants and the overall state of the economy. In particular, it concerns the mechanisms behind the formation of prices, employment, consumption, inflation expectations and the impact of interest rates on economic activity.
The main idea of this area of research is that understanding inflation, unemployment or an economic downturn requires more than analyzing nationwide indicators alone. It is also necessary to take into account how households make decisions about spending, how businesses set prices and wages, and how investors assess future risks. This approach makes it possible to create economic models that explain the causes of crises and help assess the consequences of decisions by central banks and governments.
Who is Robert Ernest Hall
Robert Ernest Hall is an American economist and emeritus professor at Stanford University. His research covers macroeconomics, the labor market, unemployment, consumption and economic fluctuations.
One important area of his work was the study of the causes of rising unemployment during recessions. In particular, Hall examined why it becomes more difficult for people to find jobs during an economic downturn and why employment recovery can take considerably longer than the economic crisis itself.
In his work, the economist showed that the increase in unemployment during recessions is largely associated with a reduction in employment opportunities, rather than solely with an increase in the number of layoffs. His scientific insights became important for developing government employment policy, forecasting economic recovery and assessing the consequences of crises for workers and employers.
What Michael Dean Woodford is known for
Michael Dean Woodford is an American economist and professor at Columbia University, known for his research on monetary policy, inflation and the mechanisms through which central banks influence the economy. One of his best-known works is the book Interest and Prices: Foundations of a Theory of Monetary Policy, published in 2003.
Woodford paid particular attention to how citizens' and businesses' expectations regarding future prices and interest rates influence economic decisions already today. His research helped explain why the effectiveness of monetary policy depends not only on the actual raising or lowering of rates, but also on how clearly the central bank communicates its future actions.
For example, expectations of higher borrowing costs may prompt businesses to postpone investment and consumers to reconsider major purchases even before the policy rate changes. This mechanism is important for managing inflation and maintaining financial stability.
Why the research of this year’s Nobel laureates is important for the economy
Research into the microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilization helps explain how economic policy affects people’s daily lives. When a central bank raises its policy rate, this may lead to higher borrowing costs, reduced consumer spending, and slower investment. At the same time, such a step can curb inflationary pressures. However, the outcome depends on many factors: people’s expectations, businesses’ behavior, conditions in the labor market, and confidence in financial institutions.
Economic models that take these factors into account are used to analyze the consequences of monetary decisions, assess the risks of recession, and choose economic stabilization measures.
For Ukraine, these approaches also have practical significance, particularly when analyzing inflation, currency expectations, lending, and the recovery of economic activity amid the war.
At the same time, economic models do not guarantee accurate forecasts of crises, since the behavior of market participants may change under the influence of unforeseen circumstances.
How much money will the winners receive in 2026?
In 2026, the monetary award for each Nobel Prize will amount to 12 million Swedish kronor. Compared with last year, the sum has been increased by one million kronor. The Nobel Foundation explained the decision by its desire to preserve the value of the award. The increase took place in the year marking the 125th anniversary of the first Nobel Prize ceremony.
If several researchers receive the prize, they will divide the funds in accordance with the organizers’ decision. Along with the monetary award, laureates receive a medal and a diploma.
Why the Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences has a special status
The official name of the award is the Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel. Unlike the five traditional Nobel Prizes, it was not provided for in the inventor’s will. It was established by Sweden’s central bank in 1968, and the first laureates were honored in 1969.
Through 2025, inclusive, the prize in economic sciences had been awarded 57 times, and 99 scholars had become laureates. In 2025, the prize was awarded to Joel Mokyr, Philippe Aghion, and Peter Howitt for explaining economic growth through innovation. In 2024, the award went to Daron Acemoglu, Simon Johnson, and James Robinson for research into the influence of social institutions on countries’ prosperity. In 2023, the laureate was Claudia Goldin, who studied the position of women in the labor market. And in 2022, Ben Bernanke, Douglas Diamond, and Philip Dybvig were honored for their work on banks and financial crises.
The award is presented for research that helps us better understand economic growth, financial crises, labor markets, and the behavior of companies and individuals.
Reminder
Earlier, UNN reported that Canadian writer Anne Carson had become the 2026 Nobel laureate in literature. She was honored for her innovative dialogue with the classical tradition.

Norway's data protection authority has fined Microsoft-owned advertising technology company Xandr 92 million Norwegian kroner ($9.6 million) for illegally sharing sensitive personal data, the authority announced Monday.

Tyeb Mehta’s ‘Rickshaw Puller’ fetches record Rs 69.1 crore at Volte Una auction
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
10:54:08 UTC
19:54:08 KST

Tushar Jiwarajka, Founder of Volte Una, with the Tyeb painting.
For much of his life, artist Tyeb Mehta lived in a cramped one-room Bombay apartment that doubled as a studio by day and a bedroom at night.It was only in the 1990s that he and his wife Sakina could afford to move into a two-bedroom apartment in Lokhandwala. Today, his paintings command staggering sums. The latest is Rickshaw Puller, which sold for Rs 69.1 crore at Volte Una’s inaugural auction, setting a world auction record for the artist.The sale surpassed the previous record of Rs 61.8 crore, set by Trussed Bull in April 2025, and makes Rickshaw Puller the fourth-most expensive Indian work of art ever sold at auction.Painted in 2002, during the final decade of Mehta’s career, the acrylic on canvas depicts the rickshaw puller, a figure he returned to in his later work. The painting attracted multiple bidders in the final minutes before the auction closed.
The record is particularly striking for an artist known for his exacting standards, who routinely destroyed works he considered unworthy. It also marks a significant debut for Volte Una, a new auction house built around an unusual premise: selling one major work at a time rather than offering multiple lots in a single sale.The single-lot format is designed to give collectors time to engage closely with each artwork before bidding, with an emphasis on privacy and discretion.“We are thrilled that we were able to respect Tyeb Mehta’s painting by exposing it to the most serious and discreet collectors globally in private settings,” said Tushar Jiwarajka, Founder of Volte Una. “And we have introduced a business model that allows the traditional buyer’s premium to be significantly reduced, putting that money back in the pockets of consignors and successful bidders.”Volte Una’s next auction, scheduled for the end of November, will feature a work by M F Husain from the renowned Herwitz Collection.

French student protesters mull fresh demos to maintain momentum
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
10:54:00 UTC
19:54:00 KST

French high school students Monday were planning a new stage of their campaign for improved conditions and launch wave of demonstrations to maintain momentum.
The new protests, scheduled for Tuesday, could be a turning point in the movement, launched in mid-September, which the government hopes is already winding down.
On Friday, the government noted a dramatic drop in the number of blockades and meetings outside the country's lycees, where students – most between 15 and 18 – complete their high school education.
More than 96% were opening Friday, said the Education Ministry.
The authorities are all the more keen to see the student protests end given that online activists have called for demonstrations next Saturday to protest the cost of living.
For President Emmanuel Macron's administration, that brings back troubling memories of the grassroots Yellow Vest movement.
Their protests, launched in 2018 over a planned fuel tax rise, saw massive demonstrations and clashes between police and protesters that shook the presidency during Macron's first term in office.
The government is still counting the cost of the high school protests.
A government source told journalists last week that the cost for damage caused by the demonstrations was "at least 30 million euros."
On Friday, the justice ministry said more than 6,800 people had been detained since the demonstrations started, 86% of them minors.
After clashes between some protesters and riot police left some students severely injured, sparking criticism of police tactics, the government suspended the use of stun grenades that cost one student his hand.
Police are investigating 18 alleged cases of misconduct within their ranks.
Last week, the government came up with concrete proposals to try to address the students' demands.
Education Minister Edouard Geffray announced late Thursday that some 3,000 substitute teachers would be deployed in the coming days to replace absent staff at the 114 worst-affected high schools.
Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu Sunday promised to make changes to the planned budget 2027 to respond to some demands set out in an online platform the government set up to gather students' views.
The student organizations behind the protests are yet to be convinced, however.
The Union of High School students described the initial announcements last week as "crumbs." They are maintaining their demand for an extra 10 million euros to be invested in the country's lycees.
France's 10,000 medical students, however, are beginning to express concern at the effect any continued school blockades could have on exams starting Monday that help determine their eventual speciality.
They do not want to see the students' action disrupt such a crucial stage of their education.
Last Thursday's student demonstrations mobilized tens of thousands of people across France: 71,500 according to Interior Ministry figures.
Nearly 256,000 took part in last Tuesday's day of action.
And one poll, carried out by Ipsos-BVA and published Sunday, said 54% of respondents backed the high school student protests.
They had the most sympathy with student complaints about the excessive size of classes and with the need to renovate the country's crumbling schools.

“Many Dutch adults can only swim one stroke”
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
10:53:17 UTC
19:53:17 KST

“Many Dutch adults can only swim one stroke”
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Former junior Romanian swimming champion Vlad Pațurcă moved to the Netherlands alone at the age of 21. Since then he’s founded his own swimming school in Amsterdam-Noord, where he now coaches hundreds of people. He idolises former Dutch Olympic swimming champions and dreams of one day building a squad of competitive swimmers.
How did you end up in the Netherlands?
I was a competitive swimmer in Romania, a freestyle sprinter, and swam for the youth national team. In 2021 I visited the Netherlands for the first time. The first city I saw wasn’t Amsterdam but Assen, in the north, and I fell for the Dutch way of life straight away: the quiet, the order, the way everything seemed designed for people. After that I didn’t want to be anywhere else.
I moved here at 21, with little work experience and no idea how Dutch law or business worked, and started coaching at a large adult swim club. In my first months there I saw how many adults wanted lessons. In 2024 I opened my own swim school, Win and Swim, in Amsterdam-Noord.
I paid for the first pool lane out of my own pocket and started with five or six swimmers. Since then we’ve taught more than 300 adults.
How do you describe yourself – an expat, lovepat, immigrant, international?
An international. The Netherlands is home now. Many of the people I teach are internationals too, often adults learning to swim from scratch.
How long do you plan to stay?
For good. I’ve built my business here and the plan is to grow it: more hours and new locations in Amsterdam first, then children’s lessons and other Dutch cities.
My dream is a performance squad, where I train competitive swimmers. Besides the swim school, I help companies with AI solutions.
Do you speak Dutch and how did you learn?
Not yet, and that’s a real challenge when you run a business. So far I’ve run Win and Swim almost entirely in English, and I’m learning Dutch now so I can take the business further.
In my first years here I did A1 through a free government course while I was living in Almere. After I moved to Amsterdam I wanted to continue with A2, but the free places go first to newcomers who need the lessons to integrate, for example to find work. I was already working and settled here, so I wasn’t in that group.
What’s your favourite Dutch thing?
My favourite thing is that things just work. When I opened my company, I entered my details online at the KVK chamber of commerce, went in the next day to sign and that was it: the company was open.
In Romania I’d have been running from one office to another, printing and signing papers. Here, sorting something out at the bank or the council is just as easy.
How Dutch have you become?
Dutch enough to appreciate the directness. People had told me the Dutch are cold. They’re not cold, just very direct, and at first that felt harsh. Now I value that nobody beats around the bush and nobody makes promises they don’t keep.
Which three Dutch people (dead or alive) would you most like to meet?
Pieter van den Hoogenband, Inge de Bruijn and Maarten van der Weijden. The first two are freestyle sprint legends, and sprint freestyle was my event. Van der Weijden came back from leukaemia to win Olympic open-water gold in 2008.
What’s your top tourist tip?
In summer, swim outdoors, but only at an official swimming spot (zwemlocatie), where the water quality is checked. Het Twiske, just north of Amsterdam-Noord, is a good one. And get on a bike. Here people of every age and every job cycle every day, and it’s the best way to see the country.
Tell us something surprising you’ve found out about the Netherlands.
Almost everyone here learned to swim as a child: around 94% of Dutch youngsters hold at least one swimming diploma. You’d expect a country of strong swimmers, but the reality is more nuanced. Many Dutch adults can only swim one stroke, breaststroke with the head out of the water.
The system teaches survival rather than swimming as a sport, which makes sense in a country full of canals. As a result, many Dutch adults come back to lessons later to learn freestyle and the other strokes.
If you had just 24 hours left in the Netherlands, what would you do?
Spend the day on my bike, out of the city, and end it with one last swim.
Vlad was speaking with Louis Gore-Langton

Trump’s NATO envoy calls for moving military forces east as US reviews troops in Europe
Matthew Whitaker called for an overhaul of NATO’s bases and military infrastructure to move forces eastward as America reviews its troop presence in Europe.
Matthew Whitaker, permanent representative of the United States to NATO, speaks at the Reagan Library on January 14, 2026 in Simi Valley. | Mario Tama/Getty Images
WARSAW — NATO must modernize its military infrastructure to move forces and equipment from Western to Eastern Europe “where we would expect any future conflict,” U.S. Ambassador to NATO Matthew Whitaker said Monday.
Speaking on a panel at the Warsaw Security Forum, Whitaker’s comments came as Washington reviews its military presence on the continent — with the ambassador saying that Europe ranks fourth among Washington’s strategic priorities, behind homeland security, the Western Hemisphere and the Pacific.
He pointed to outdated military bases, fuel supply chains and agreements governing the stationing of American troops in Europe as areas requiring attention under the ongoing U.S. force posture and basing review.
Advertisement
He emphasized the importance of military mobility and “moving things from the west to the east,” citing discussions with EU Defense Commissioner Andrius Kubilius. European officials warn that Russia could be ready to attack a NATO country by the end of the decade.
Whitaker did not announce any decisions to relocate or withdraw American forces. He nevertheless made clear that Washington is reassessing its global commitments to avoid spreading its military resources too thin.
“Superpowers and great global powers have mostly had challenges when they get overextended,” Whitaker said, adding that U.S. President Donald Trump wants allies to become “capable and not dependent.”
“The United States isn’t stepping back. We’re just asking you to step forward,” he said.
Whitaker also criticized countries that are falling short of their defense-spending commitments.
He said he had recently delivered a “very strong message” to political leaders in Czechia. The country’s defense spending for this year is approximately 1.8% of GDP, falling short of NATO’s current 2% benchmark.
Advertisement
European governments must continue strengthening their armed forces, he argued, warning that the continent still lacks many of the capabilities it needs to defend itself.
Kubilius, meanwhile, stressed the need to reduce Europe’s military dependence on Washington, highlighting EU efforts to develop its own drone defenses, satellite communications and surveillance capabilities.
Polish presidential adviser Marcin Przydacz, also on the panel, urged Western European allies to accelerate defense spending while emphasizing that NATO, rather than the EU, must remain responsible for Europe’s collective defense.

Ukraine's parliament passes minority schools bill to appease Hungary, advance EU talks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
10:51:29 UTC
19:51:29 KST

Ukraine's parliament passes minority schools bill to appease Hungary, advance EU talks
Editor's note: The story has been updated with the latest details.
The parliament on Oct. 12 passed a bill reinforcing the educational rights of Ukraine's national minorities, a step that Hungary demanded before allowing Kyiv's EU talks to move forward.
The vote paves the way for the EU to formally open two more accession clusters with Ukraine and Moldova at a meeting in Luxembourg on Oct. 13.
The bill passed with the support of 266 lawmakers, according to lawmaker Yaroslav Zhelezniak. It still requires a presidential signature to become law.
The law would give Ukraine's Hungarian-speaking community and other EU-language national minorities more room to use their language in education. Roughly 80,000 ethnic Hungarians live in Ukraine's westernmost Zakarpattia Oblast.
According to the new legislation, schools where more than 50% of pupils study in the relevant minority language may be granted special status, and the head or deputy head of such a school must be proficient in that language, among other measures outlined in the bill.
"We welcome today’s important step by the Ukrainian Parliament on minority education rights. A positive result of months of joint work and constructive dialogue," Hungary's Foreign Minister Anita Orban said on X.
"Thank you to our Ukrainian partners. Let's keep this momentum going!" Orban added after the vote, as she met her Ukrainian counterpart, Andrii Sybiha, on the sidelines of an EU foreign ministers' meeting in Luxembourg on Oct. 12.
The bill covers official EU languages but not Russian, reflecting Kyiv's ongoing push to remove Russian from official and public spaces and counter decades of Moscow-imposed Russification.
Fresh momentum for EU talks
Hungary's Kremlin-friendly former Prime Minister Viktor Orban spent years blocking Ukraine's EU accession talks, claiming Kyiv failed to protect the rights of its Hungarian minority.
The victory of Peter Magyar's pro-European Tisza party in the Hungarian parliamentary elections in April provided new impetus to resolve the issue.
In early summer, Kyiv and Budapest announced an agreement on the educational, linguistic, and cultural rights of Ukraine's Hungarian minority.
Hungary then lifted its veto on Kyiv's EU accession talks, allowing the launch of clusters one and six — lists of reforms focused on democratic institutions and the rule of law, and on external relations, respectively — in June and July.
The agreement also allowed Moldova's accession talks to move forward, as the EU has politically linked the membership bids of Kyiv and Chisinau.
But Budapest later blocked the launch of additional clusters until Kyiv begins implementing changes under the agreement, starting with educational rights.
Ukraine expects that the passage of the law will help unblock two more clusters, addressing internal market and competitiveness — a step that was preliminarily cleared by EU envoys on Oct. 7.
"I will never tire of repeating: there is no better way to guarantee the rights and security of the Hungarian national minority in Ukraine than to ensure Ukraine's accession to the EU as soon as possible," Sybiha said.
While meeting his Hungarian counterpart in Luxembourg, Ukraine's chief diplomat "thanked the Hungarian side for its constructive position" on accession talks.
Ambassadors of the 27 EU countries must now decide whether to open the next clusters at a meeting of permanent representatives later on Oct. 12.
A European diplomat told the Kyiv Independent that unless Budapest raises any new concerns regarding the vote, it is broadly expected that the envoys will reach a consensus.
This will clear the way for the formal opening of the clusters at the Intergovernmental Conference on Oct. 13.

No public funds for bank liquidations, says VP Yılmaz
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
10:51:09 UTC
19:51:09 KST

Vice President Cevdet Yılmaz spoke on a live broadcast by Anadolu Agency, Oct. 12, 2026. (AA Photo)
Investigations into the troubled funds are continuing, Vice President Cevdet Yılmaz has said, adding that no public money will be used in the liquidations of those funds.
“Investigations are continuing regarding people who obtained very high returns or unfair gains through illegal transactions,” Yılmaz said on Oct. 12 during a live broadcast by Anadolu Agency.
Addressing the process following the return of unlawful gains, Yılmaz said legal responsibilities would remain in force.
“If there has been an unlawful transaction, responsibilities do not disappear,” he said.
Yılmaz said authorities moved quickly to prevent the incident from spreading to the broader fund market and damaging the overall financial system.
“The problematic funds were, in a sense, placed under quarantine. Measures were imposed on seven companies and 131 funds under them,” he said.
He added that a judicial process is underway.
“Many people are currently under arrest, in custody or under investigation, and many have given statements. Asset freezes have been imposed and travel bans have been introduced,” Yılmaz said.
According to Yilmaz, the Fund Coordination Board established during the process has held four meetings and adopted key principles.
He also said the State Supervisory Council had launched a broad-based field investigation involving around 15 inspectors and auditors covering all relevant institutions.
“Independent financial authorities and all of these institutions will be examined and investigated. Administrative shortcomings and individual responsibilities will be revealed through this process,” he said.
“There are seven companies and 131 problematic funds. These funds account for 4.6 percent of all funds and 7.7 percent of the total fund portfolio. More than 455,000 investors are involved in these funds,” he said.
He noted that three of the seven companies had accepted ordinary liquidation procedures and were liquidated as of Oct. 8.
“Payments have been made to nearly 44,000 citizens, and 17 funds have consequently exited the system,” Yilmaz said.
He added that more than 2,000 investors were involved in closed-end funds managed by the three entities undergoing ordinary liquidation, and that those funds would be liquidated according to their own structures and characteristics.
Yilmaz stressed that neither ordinary nor extraordinary liquidation would involve the use of public resources.
“There will be no use of public funds in either ordinary or extraordinary liquidation,” he said.
Explaining the reason, Yilmaz said the state does not provide guarantees for capital markets and investment funds.
“There is no state guarantee in fund markets or capital markets. In the banking system there is a state guarantee up to a certain amount, but such a guarantee does not exist in capital markets,” he said.

carsten höller’s goggles turn the world upside down to challenge perception
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
10:50:54 UTC
19:50:54 KST

carsten höller’s goggles turn the world upside down to challenge perception
inspired by a 19th-century psychology experiment, the wearable artwork turns familiar surroundings into an unsettling test of perception and movement.
carsten höller’s goggles disrupt our sense of orientation
‘The dream is the confusion machine I didn’t have to build,’ Carsten Höller told designboom in our interview back in April, describing his fascination with experiences that interrupt our usual sense of control. For the artist, dreams represent an extraordinary disruption of reality when the mind generates an environment that feels entirely convincing, even as perception becomes unstable and voluntary movement disappears. Höller explores a related uncertainty through his installations, from slides that induce physical vertigo to rotating beds and wearable devices that interfere with how we experience our surroundings.
Höller’s Upside-Down Goggles, first presented in 1994, invert the wearer’s field of vision, making familiar surroundings appear upside down. Simple gestures, such as walking through a room or reaching for an object, suddenly require a different kind of attention. The space may remain the same but moving through it is no longer intuitive.
seeing the world upside-down
Back to the 1890s, American psychologist George M. Stratton wanted to understand how we perceive the world as upright when the image projected onto the retina is inverted. To investigate, he constructed an optical apparatus that reversed his visual field, allowing him to observe how his perception and movements responded to this unfamiliar arrangement. In his first experiment, published in 1896, Stratton wore the apparatus for 21.5 hours over three days. He followed this with a longer investigation in 1897, wearing it for 87 hours over eight days.
As he moved around his garden and through the surrounding village, he recorded the difficulties of coordinating his movements with what he saw. Spatial relationships became unfamiliar, forcing him to rethink how what he could perceive through his sight related to his bodily experience. Stratton’s observations helped establish visual adaptation as a subject of psychological research. His experiment suggested that perception involves more than the passive reception of images and is shaped by the relationship between sight, movement, and experience.
an experiment in perception
Höller describes noticing a slight shift in perception after only five minutes of wearing the goggles. The experience changes considerably when the subject wearing the pair begins to move. Forms seem to slide into one another, while objects appear unexpectedly close or far away. The visual inversion is only part of the effect, as movement alters the apparent relationships between things and makes the surrounding space harder to read.
These observations bring the work back to the relationship between vision and physical experience. We rarely have to think about how we judge a distance, reach for a glass, or step around a chair. Such actions depend on an ongoing coordination between what we see and how we move. The goggles interrupt that coordination, turning familiar gestures into uncertain ones. There is also a difference between adapting to an unfamiliar image and feeling at ease within the world it presents.
Stratton’s experiments explore the changes that could occur over extended periods of inverted vision. Höller’s observations, by contrast, begin with minutes of wearing the device, when perception may start to shift but movement remains unfamiliar. The wearer must act within a world that looks recognizable in its details but no longer behaves as expected. Höller’s goggles make the act of navigating an ordinary space feel newly uncertain. What usually passes unnoticed, the coordination of sight, distance, and movement, becomes the central experience of the work.

Ukrainian strikes hit a site housing Russian troops in Khrustalnyi, a city in Russian-occupied Luhansk Oblast, overnight on 12 October, according to local reports. Satellite fire data recorded blazes at a former motor depot there, in an area Russia once used as a logistics base for its offensive in the region.
Russia keeps attacking in Ukraine’s Donetsk Oblast and strikes Ukrainian cities and power plants every day. Its offensive depends on troops, ammunition, and fuel moved through occupied Ukraine, so strikes there reach the supply chain behind the front.
Fires at a former motor depot in occupied Khrustalnyi
Ukrainian forces launched heavy strikes around Khrustalnyi in eastern Ukraine overnight, the Ukrainian monitoring channel Exilenova+ reported. It counted three separate fires and one large blaze, and said local residents reported a hit on a site where Russian troops were based. Ukraine’s military had not officially commented on the strike by the publication time of this article on 12 October.
NASA’s Fire Information for Resource Management System (FIRMS), which tracks active fires by satellite, shows blazes at a former motor transport enterprise and an industrial zone in Khrustalnyi, Ukrainian military outlet Militarnyi reported. Three fire hotspots appeared there at 01:10 and spread by 02:07, the outlet said.
Ukraine also hit the site on 16 June 2022, striking an ammunition depot there, and local residents then heard secondary detonations, Militarnyi said. The site served as an important logistics base for Russia’s 2nd Army Corps in its offensive on Sievierodonetsk and Lysychansk, two cities in Luhansk Oblast, the outlet added.
Explosions at a Crimean airfield Russia used to launch drones overnight
Drones attacked occupied Crimea from the evening of 11 October into the night, and Russian air defenses, including mobile fire groups, fired across the peninsula, Krym.Realii, Radio Liberty’s Crimea service, reported. Explosions sounded in Simferopol, Feodosiia, and Yevpatoriia, among other places, the Crimean monitoring Telegram channel Crimean Wind said, according to the outlet.
Subscribers told the channel about a series of explosions and a glow at Russia’s Hvardiiske military airfield in Simferopol district as air defenses fired. Krym.Realii said neither Ukraine’s nor Russia’s military had commented and that it could not verify the reports independently.
Ukraine says it struck a Bastion in Crimea, the launcher Russia pairs Zircon and Oniks missiles on
Overnight, Russia also launched attack drones at Ukraine from several directions, including Hvardiiske in occupied Crimea, Ukraine’s Air Force reported.
Ukraine’s General Staff said in August that a 3 August strike on the Hvardiiske airfield destroyed nine aviation fuel tanks and damaged two aircraft hangars.
Ukraine keeps hitting Russian rear areas in occupied territory
On 10 and 11 October alone, the General Staff reported hitting a Russian repair base and supply depots in occupied Luhansk Oblast, along with Russian troop concentrations near Lysychansk and two other towns there.
Ukraine has also kept up its campaign of so-called middle strikes, drone attacks on Russian supply lines in occupied territory beyond the front. French mapper Clément Molin counted 770 confirmed drone hits on Russian trucks in September, up from 630 in August, with the strikes concentrated on supply routes running through occupied southern Ukraine into Crimea.
Strikes on troop sites and airfields far behind the front leave Russia fewer safe places in occupied territory to house troops and launch drones, adding to the battlefield losses Ukraine’s drones already inflict.

Balkan temperatures swing as heavy rain heads for Greece
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
10:48:26 UTC
19:48:26 KST

Temperatures fluctuated dramatically in the Balkans last week, with unusually large differences between daytime highs and overnight lows – known as the diurnal range.
An area of high pressure over the region brought prolonged sunshine during the day, while clear skies at night allowed temperatures to drop rapidly as heat escaped into the atmosphere without cloud cover to slow the cooling.
In Kosanica, Montenegro, the average maximum temperature in October is 15C (59F), while the average minimum is 4C. However, on 4 and 5 October the difference between daytime highs and overnight lows reached 30C, more than double the October average.
Elsewhere in Europe, high pressure will build across the north and west over the coming week, pushing an area of low pressure southwards towards the Mediterranean. The low-pressure system will deepen as it crosses the Adriatic and Ionian seas before moving eastwards into the Aegean Sea by the middle of the week.
Spells of heavy rain and strong winds are expected to sweep across Greece as a result. Forecast models suggest widespread rainfall of 50-150mm, with the highest totals expected around the island of Skiathos.
Towards the end of the week, the system will continue eastwards, bringing showers to parts of Crete, which was hit by severe flooding a week earlier. Those storms swept some cars and trees into the sea.
Meanwhile, Hurricane Simon, a category 4 storm, is moving close to Mexico’s Pacific coast, near the state of Jalisco. It is the latest of 21 named storms in the Pacific this season, 11 of which have reached hurricane strength.
At the time of writing, Simon has a central pressure of 933mb and maximum sustained winds of nearly 150mph (241km/h). However, the hurricane is expected to weaken rapidly if its core moves onshore, cutting it off from the warm ocean waters that fuel it.
Heavy rainfall is affecting south-western Mexico, where totals could reach 300-400mm across a wide area, rising to 400-500mm in the wettest locations.

France calls for preparation of new EU sanctions package against Russia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
10:47:42 UTC
19:47:42 KST

Seyma Erkul Dayanc
12 October 2026•Update: 12 October 2026
France has called for the preparation of a new package of EU sanctions against Russia in the coming weeks, French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said Monday, as the bloc seeks to maintain pressure on Moscow over its war in Ukraine.
“We want all this to continue. That is why we are calling for the preparation, in the coming weeks, of a 22nd package of sanctions,” Barrot said ahead of an EU Foreign Affairs Council meeting in Luxembourg.
He said the latest package included 1,600 new listings targeting Russian individuals and entities linked to the country's military-industrial complex, bringing the total number of EU designations since the start of the war from 3,000 to 4,600.
Barrot described the measures as part of the EU's continuing pressure on Moscow.
“These are measures that contribute to increasing the cost Vladimir Putin pays for this colonial and imperialist war, which must absolutely stop,” he said.
He argued that EU sanctions had deprived Russia of resources it could otherwise have used to finance its military campaign.
“Have the sanctions worked? Yes, they have deprived Vladimir Putin's Russia of the equivalent of €500 billion ($580 billion) in resources that would otherwise have been poured into this war,” Barrot said, describing the amount as equivalent to more than three years of military spending.
He added that the EU's sanctions would remain in force despite other countries' engagement with Moscow.
“Our sanctions apply and will continue to apply,” he said.
Barrot said the EU would continue to put pressure on Russia's so-called shadow fleet, which Moscow uses to circumvent sanctions.
“We will continue to exert pressure on the shadow fleet,” he said, announcing that France would host an international conference on the issue in Paris this autumn.
US sanctions against ICC
Barrot also strongly condemned US sanctions against the International Criminal Court (ICC), which could take effect within six months.
“We want dialogue to begin, particularly between the European Union and the United States, so that the latter can reverse these decisions,” he said.
“If that fails, we stand ready to activate the Blocking Statute,” he added, referring to an EU mechanism designed to protect European companies and institutions from certain foreign sanctions.
Barrot described the ICC as a “pillar of the architecture of international law” and said the court needed to be able to function properly.
Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia
Barrot also condemned Houthi attacks on Riyadh airport in Saudi Arabia, which he said caused numerous casualties, including a French national who was seriously injured.
“Our teams on the ground, at embassies and consulates, are in close contact with her family and relatives to ensure that they have everything they need,” he said.
“These attacks must stop, because they pose dangers to the region and, more broadly, to the world that we cannot accept,” he added.

Russia’s Ministry of Defense has developed a specialized service that gives drone developers access to data on the combat use of drones.

Drone strike kills dozens near Sudan displacement camp – rights group
The death toll from a drone strike blamed on Sudan’s paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) near a camp for displaced people in Blue Nile state has risen to 41, according to a local rights group.
On Friday, the Emergency Lawyers group reported the revised death toll, accusing the RSF of targeting civilians. Local authorities have put the number of fatalities at 32, with another 43 people injured, according to Al Jazeera Arabic. The attack took place also on Friday in the Abu Shandi area, near the Ethiopian border.
The RSF-allied Sudan Founding Alliance (TASIS) has denied responsibility for the attack, instead accusing Egypt of carrying it out. In a statement reported by the Sudan Times on Saturday, coalition spokesman Ahmed Tugud Lisan claimed that an Egyptian drone had been launched from a police facility in Wad al-Mahi with the involvement of Egyptian specialists. The allegations against Egypt have not been independently verified.
The rights organization Shahid Evidence has called for an independent international investigation into the incident, including an examination of the drone’s type, flight path, and launch location. The group said responsibility should be established through physical and digital evidence, as well as witness testimony.
Separately, at least 72 gold miners were killed in an airstrike near Sudan’s border with Egypt on Saturday, according to Emergency Lawyers. The organization accused the Egyptian Air Force of carrying out the attack, but the allegation has not been independently verified. Egypt has not officially commented on the incident. The Sudan Tribune reported that survivors put the death toll at more than 200, although the figure remains unconfirmed.
The attacks come amid an ongoing civil war between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the RSF, which erupted in April 2023. According to UN estimates, 33.7 million people in Sudan need humanitarian assistance, while more than 8.5 million remain internally displaced.
Sudan descended into chaos in April 2023 when fighting erupted between the national army, the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF), and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF). The conflict followed months of tension between their commanders, Abdel Fattah al-Burhan and Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, known as Hemedti, over a planned transition to civilian rule. What began in the capital, Khartoum, as a power struggle has devastated the country, killing tens of thousands, displacing millions, and pushing parts of Sudan into famine.
Regional and international peace efforts, including African Union mediation and Saudi-US talks in Jeddah, have repeatedly stalled. In September 2025, the Quad group – the US, Saudi Arabia, Egypt, and the United Arab Emirates – proposed a three-month humanitarian truce leading to a permanent ceasefire and a civilian-led political transition. Burhan rejected a subsequent US-led proposal that November, arguing it would dismantle state security institutions while leaving the RSF in place. The paramilitaries said they accepted the truce.
The UAE’s involvement has deepened mistrust of mediation. Sudan’s army-backed government severed diplomatic ties with Abu Dhabi in May 2025, accusing it of supporting the RSF. The UAE denies supplying weapons to the paramilitaries. Relations with Washington deteriorated further in September 2026 after the US questioned both factions’ legitimacy. Sudan rejected the remarks and called for peace efforts free from foreign dictates.
Meanwhile, rival administrations have entrenched Sudan’s divisions. Burhan’s government returned to Khartoum in January 2026 after the army recaptured the capital, having operated from Port Sudan during the fighting. In July 2025, the RSF-aligned TASIS coalition announced a rival government based in Nyala, Darfur, with Dagalo heading its governing council. The UN Security Council and African Union rejected the move.
Several RSF commanders have defected to the Sudanese Army since 2024. Most recently, Lieutenant Colonel Mohamed Azraq al-Fanjari reportedly switched sides with around 300 fighters and 30 military vehicles on Thursday.

IMF chief warns AI could disrupt jobs, widen Asia's economic divide
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
10:44:34 UTC
19:44:34 KST

Artificial intelligence could help offset the economic drag from Asia's ageing populations, but the technology also threatens to disrupt jobs and widen the gap between advanced and developing economies unless governments act quickly to prepare workers, the International Monetary Fund head said on Monday.
IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva described AI as a “slow-moving tsunami” at the IMF and World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok, warning that it would have profound consequences for jobs, growth, education and even how governments generate revenue through taxation, given the expected shift from labour to capital.
The IMF estimates that AI could lead to 40 percent of jobs being augmented, downgraded or eliminated, over time, she said. An initial study showed that 10 percent of jobs in the US already required AI skills.
While routine, repetitive jobs were shrinking, low-paying jobs were increasing in two lower-paying sectors, construction and data centres.
"It is a transformative technology. It so completely changes how we work, how we live," she said, noting that an AI assistant now gave her a 30-second message about her schedule each day.
The US, China and India are the most important producers in the AI supply chain, but many of the firms building the needed infrastructure are in Asia, Georgieva said, referencing Thailand, host of this year's annual meetings.
Who gains from AI?
“We cannot imagine today what the world of work will look like five years from now,” Georgieva said, urging policymakers to study the changes and act on the lessons they provide.
The stakes are particularly high in Asia, where ageing populations are expected to shrink the workforce in major economies. China, Japan and South Korea could lose nearly a quarter of their working-age populations by 2050, according to findings presented in an IMF book on the region's economic challenges and opportunities.
AI-driven productivity gains could more than offset some of that demographic pressure. The IMF estimates that AI could lift growth in advanced Asian economies by between 0.5 and 1 percentage point.
But the benefits are unlikely to be evenly distributed.
Krishna Srinivasan, director of the IMF's Asia and Pacific department, said advanced economies were more exposed to AI but better positioned to capture its gains, while emerging markets faced a greater risk of falling behind.
“What matters is whether AI augments workers or automates jobs,” Srinivasan said, adding that reforms to improve skills and productivity could accelerate adoption in emerging economies by a decade or more.
AI impact on entry-level jobs
World Bank President Ajay Banga, who has made jobs a central focus of his presidency, said the development bank was focused on leveraging "small AI", which is not dependent on large language models, to generate enormous productivity gains for farmers, healthcare systems, educators and others in emerging markets.
Singapore's President Tharman Shanmugaratnam, speaking at the same event, said governments should address how AI was reducing job opportunities for graduates.
"There is a particular problem that we have to address very soon ... and that is that, the first rung in employment, your first job upon graduation, is now seeing less demand," he said.
He said the world should also guard against AI resulting in a "new divergence" in growth and job creation between developing and advanced economies.
"AI is going to widen the divergence if we are too passive about it," he said. "So we've got to do everything we can to first use AI to create good jobs and to create jobs that can be done well by human beings, can allow them to ride up a career ladder despite AI."

A principal and a teacher were shot and wounded at a middle school in Aubagne, southern France, on Monday, officials said.
“A student is suspected of being responsible,” Education Minister Edouard Geffray said in a post on US social media company X.
He added that he was heading to the Lakanal middle school with Interior Minister Laurent Nunez and Sabrina Roubache, a lawmaker representing the Bouches-du-Rhone department.
The principal, 53, was shot in the right hip, while a 37-year-old teacher was wounded in the thigh, French broadcaster BFMTV reported.

Macron decries ‘spread of unbridled violence’
The Marseille prosecutor’s office opened an investigation into attempted murder, prosecutor Nicolas Bessone said in a statement.
Bessone said the student fired once or twice in a first-floor common area shortly after 9 am (0700GMT), injuring the principal and teacher, who were both in the corridor.
Both were hit in the lower limbs and taken to hospital, with neither injury considered life-threatening.
The student then went to the second floor and again fired twice, the prosecutor said.
One shot was fired toward the floor in front of a teacher, while the other was fired inside an occupied classroom, hitting the blackboard.
No students were injured, said Aubagne Mayor Jean-Pierre Squillari.
The shooting was unrelated to high school protests taking place in France, according to local reports. The school had not been affected by closures elsewhere.

U.S. Army takes delivery of first Korean-built wheeled howitzer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
10:42:19 UTC
19:42:19 KST

- The U.S. Army received its first Hanwha-built Mobile Tactical Cannon prototype, a wheeled K9-based howitzer meant to replace the towed M777.
- The deal covers six prototypes with options for 12 more, worth up to about $263 million, with fielding targeted by 2031.
The U.S. Army has received its first Mobile Tactical Cannon, a wheeled 155 mm howitzer built by Hanwha Defense USA that the service is testing as a replacement for the towed M777, less than a year after it first asked industry for proposals.
Brig. Gen. Robert “RJ” Mikesh Jr., the Army’s portfolio management executive for offensive fires, told reporters on Oct. 8 ahead of the Association of the U.S. Army’s annual meeting that the cannon had been on display at an “Army Modernization Day” on Capitol Hill earlier this month, Military Times reported.
“We’re excited to have that and get ready to test it,” said Mikesh. “And get that soldier feedback, that we think is so important.”
The Army picked Hanwha in August under an Other Transaction Authority agreement, a faster contracting route for prototypes. The four-year deal is worth about $100.3 million to start and up to roughly $263 million if all options are used. It calls for six prototypes to be delivered quickly, with options for 12 more, for testing and experiments with soldiers. Hanwha beat a crowded field that included BAE Systems, General Dynamics Land Systems, American Rheinmetall, a Leonardo DRS and KNDS team, and an Elbit Systems of America, Anduril and Oshkosh team.
The Mobile Tactical Cannon is Hanwha’s K9 Mobile Howitzer, an eight-wheeled version of the tracked K9 that has served with the South Korean Army since 1999. K9 variants are now used by about 10 other countries, and Hanwha says more than 2,500 have been fielded worldwide. The company is building an integration and test site in Opelika, Alabama, to develop and deliver the howitzers in the United States.
“What enabled that was this close partnership under the PAE construct and trying new and novel ways of contracting,” said Mikesh. “In this case, we were not going after a clean-sheet design; we were looking for mature and available technologies. We opened our aperture for companies around the world, knowing that they’d have to onshore production within two years. That howitzer is now on contract.”
The new gun is meant to give units more range and protection than the M777, a lightweight towed howitzer the Army has used since 2005 that must be hitched to a truck and set up by its crew. The M777 can hit targets out to about 24 km (15 miles) with standard rounds and about 40 km (25 miles) with the Excalibur guided shell. The K9’s longer 52-caliber barrel can reach more than 60 km (37 miles), and a self-propelled gun can fire and move before counter-battery fire arrives.
The Army plans to field the cannon first to Stryker brigade combat teams, then to Mobile and Infantry brigade combat teams. It also wants to use the prototypes in its 155mm Artillery Propulsion Modernization project, which is testing new propellants, charges and ignition systems to hit targets out to 70 km (43 miles). In late August the Army issued a separate solicitation for a tracked version of the Mobile Tactical Cannon, which Hanwha has said it will also pursue.
Army leaders want a ready version of the Mobile Tactical Cannon fielded by 2031.

Volodymyr Zelenskyy has vowed to respond to Russia’s continuing attacks on the Ukrainian power grid as European leaders rally around Kyiv amid a feud with Donald Trump over Ukraine’s strikes on oil refineries.
Speaking to a gathering of European security officials in Warsaw on Monday, the Ukrainian president said Kyiv would retaliate if strikes on its power grid continued: “If Russia does not agree to an energy ceasefire this winter, we will respond.”
On Sunday, Trump announced an “energy ceasefire” between Kyiv and Moscow that Zelenskyy said neither side had agreed to. On Monday, Zelenskyy said he was “surprised” by the post, which went online while Kyiv was being attacked by Russian Shahed drones.

The Kremlin refused to say on Monday whether it agreed with Trump’s Truth Social post, which claimed a ceasefire was “effective immediately”. It also rejected Zelenskyy’s proposal that Russia stop bombing for 60 days so Ukraine could hold a presidential election. Moscow wanted an overall peace deal first, it said, which, for the Kremlin, means Kyiv’s capitulation.
The fast-moving row between Washington and Kyiv began on Friday when Trump announced he was lifting sanctions on Russian diesel exports. He said the move would reduce global and domestic fuel prices before next month’s US midterm elections.
Both Republican and Democratic politicians have criticised the move, pointing out that the deal violates a US law that blocks Russian energy imports. On Monday Trump defended it. “I made the right choice for the American People – ALWAYS, AMERICA FIRST!” he wrote in a social media post.

An equally irate Trump said Zelenskyy should “damn well stop” hitting Russian refineries. Ukraine needed a “new leader”, he said on Saturday.
Ukraine has said it is ready to negotiate an energy ceasefire that would take the pressure off its electricity grid before the winter. European leaders have voiced support for Kyiv in its dispute with Washington, saying Russia was responsible for the continuing strikes on energy infrastructure in both countries.
“We welcome the energy ceasefire when it holds,” the EU foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, said at a meeting of European foreign ministers on Monday. “We haven’t yet seen that also Russia will stick to it.”
Ministers from the Baltic states criticised a US decision to lift sanctions on imports of Russian diesel, which had been blocked as part of punishment for Putin launching the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
“This deal doesn’t help, neither the crisis of the oil products, nor the unity within the transatlantic community when it concerns Russia,” said Lithuania’s foreign minister, Keʂtutis Budrys. “And it is not the European way. Our way is to increase pressure because we already see how it works.”
Russia has increased its attacks on Ukrainian infrastructure, using jet-powered drones and ballistic missiles ahead of the cold winter months, leading to blackouts and water shortages far earlier in the season than has been usual during the war.
Trump’s proposal was for both sides to halt strikes on oil refineries but Kallas said that deal favoured Russia, which has far more refineries.

The Kyiv Independent newspaper said Ukraine’s commander in chief, Mykhailo Drapatyi, had received a call from the US telling him to stop bombing. “They called all the top military officials with threats,” a Ukrainian official told the newspaper.

“No one should be misled,” he said, adding that Russia “never adheres to any agreements unless forced to do so”.
He urged Ukraine’s military to ignore Trump and “ramp up” their attacks on Russian oil and gas complexes. “Clearly, this is having a very significant effect. Otherwise, you wouldn’t be hearing all this pressure from the Kremlin on the White House demanding that it stop. Of course, it is having a huge impact.”
