Co-care scheme may help prevent 9% of stroke, heart failure cases in next decade
Over 200,000 Hongkongers in co-care scheme as of January, with 40 per cent of those screened diagnosed with diabetes, hypertension or pre-diabetes
About 9 per cent of stroke and heart failure cases may be prevented in Hong Kong over the next decade through a government co-care scheme, according to a university projection.
Launched in 2023, the Chronic Disease Co-care Scheme has enrolled more than 200,000 residents as of January. Originally a pilot scheme, it was regularised in March, with about 40 per cent of those who completed screening diagnosed with diabetes, hypertension or pre-diabetes.
“The co-care scheme effectively enables individuals who have not yet been diagnosed … to receive early management from a multidisciplinary team to comprehensively control cardiovascular risks,” said William Wong Chi-wai, clinical professor and chairman of the University of Hong Kong’s (HKU) department of family medicine and primary care.

Jetten condemns planned US sanctions against ICC, urges dialogue
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Dutch prime minister Rob Jetten has condemned the United States’ decision to impose sanctions on the International Criminal Court in The Hague and said the Netherlands would defend the institution “brick by brick”.
In a joint press conference with Antonio Costa, president of the European Council, Jetten said the announcement by Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Friday was “deeply regrettable”. He went on: “We’re very much disappointed by this escalation and condemn the announced sanctions.”
Jetten said the next six months would be a “crucial” time after the Trump administration delayed the onset of the measures to allow “time for states parties to demonstrate meaningful progress on diplomatic and legal resolutions that address fundamental US concerns regarding the ICC.”
Rubio said the court was a threat to American servicemen who faced being prosecuted for their actions during overseas missions, even though the United States is not a member.
The US has also attacked the decision to serve arrest warrants on Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former defence minister Yoav Gallant.
“We will ban transactions with this rogue court, cutting off their resources and crippling its ability to operate,” he said.
Nobel Prize
The announcement came hours after South African jurist Navi Pillay, who has served as a judge at both the ICC and the International Court of Justice in The Hague, was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize.
Jetten called for “open dialogue” with the US over the next six months “to prevent the sanctions being implemented in April”, but he added: “At the same time we are preparing for a more difficult situation.”
He would not say if the Netherlands, as the host of the ICC, would ask the European Union to activate its blocking statute, ordering EU-based businesses not to comply with the sanctions, but he said: “We will do everything to protect the ICC.”
The sanctions will cut the court off from any US company or organisation, including providers of financial and technology services. They are the first measures to be announced against the institution rather than individual staff members.
The Trump administration has so far sanctioned 13 judges and officials at the ICC, including the court’s president, Tomoko Akane, and senior prosecutor Abdoulaye Saye, preventing them from travelling to the US or using banking services.

Changhua County targets illegal farm wastewater with smart monitoring
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
10:40:49 UTC
19:40:49 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Changhua County is using smart monitoring technology and legal measures to tackle years of pollution in the Dongluo River, a waterway affected by illegal wastewater discharges.
Business Today reported that the river, often called Changhua’s “mother river,” has long been polluted by wastewater from livestock farms and households, as well as illegally dumped garbage. The county is home to 595 livestock farms and is a major supplier of milk, eggs and meat in Taiwan.
Livestock wastewater is a major source of pollution, but illegal discharges are difficult to catch. Some operators release untreated wastewater at night or during off-peak hours, making it harder for authorities to collect evidence and issue fines.
To address the problem, the Changhua County Environmental Protection Bureau introduced what it calls Taiwan’s first data-driven smart water monitoring network. The system tracks water conditions and helps officials identify possible pollution incidents.
In 2022, the bureau worked with the Changhua District Prosecutors Office to investigate illegal wastewater discharges involving 19 livestock farms. The case led authorities to combine legal enforcement with measures to prevent further pollution.
Prosecutors agreed to defer prosecution if the operators invested in a livestock wastewater treatment center. The arrangement allowed the farms to avoid immediate prosecution while requiring them to help fund improvements to wastewater treatment.
Changhua County Environmental Protection Bureau Director Chiang Pei-ken (江培根) said wastewater pollution remains a major challenge for the county. The monitoring network and cooperation with prosecutors aim to improve river conditions while allowing the livestock industry to continue operating.
The initiative goes beyond fines by requiring polluters to contribute to long-term wastewater treatment. It also gives authorities additional tools to detect illegal discharges and prevent further damage to the river.

139 people dead, including 15 children, after migrant boat capsizes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
10:39:22 UTC
19:39:22 KST

139 people dead, including 15 children, after migrant boat capsizes off Africa: "Overwhelmed with all the bodies"
At least 139 people, including children, have died after a boat carrying more than 300 migrants capsized off the coast of Djibouti in east Africa, the International Organization for Migration said Sunday.
"This is a devastating loss of life. Our thoughts are with the survivors and the families who have lost loved ones or remain without news of their relatives," Alexandre Coissac, IOM chief of mission in Djibouti, said in a statement.
That number only includes those buried by authorities in Djibouti. Others have been buried by the migrants themselves, but they won't be added to the official count until authorities can verify the bodies, Coissac told the AP via the phone.
"What is terrible is that they were buried with no names, in a common grave, like in a war situation," Coissac said. "They all have a mother, a father, and we may never learn what happened."
Coissac said the migrants boarded the ship in the evening of Oct. 8 and that it sank very soon after, close to the shore, "mainly because it was overcrowded."
"The local authorities did their best," Coissac said, "but they were overwhelmed with all the bodies that kept coming at once towards the shore."
The IOM said among the bodies recovered were nine girls and six boys. More than 80 people survived the shipwreck, all Ethiopian nationals. IOM released video of the aftermath of the wreck, showing the capsized vessel and victims' clothes on the shore.
He said authorities were bringing the surviving migrants to the IOM rescue center in Obock where they receive medical assistance after swallowing sea water, and psychological support.
"They're all in a state of shock," said Coissac, who visited the area of the shipwreck Saturday. "I tried to talk to some of them but it's very difficult."
Some of the migrants in the IOM center are already aware that their family members died during the shipwreck. Others were given access to phones to call loved ones back home to notify them they are alive.
At least 84 people remained missing in one of the deadliest shipwrecks yet on the popular but perilous crossing from the Horn of Africa to the Arabian Peninsula, where many migrants seek work in rich Gulf nations.
The boat was traveling from Djibouti to Yemen when it capsized on Thursday night or Friday morning, according to the IOM. More than 80 people survived, all of them Ethiopian nationals, it said.
The Geneva-based U.N. migration agency said the vessel had 305 people on board and warned that the death toll could still rise.
Personal items likely belonging to the migrants, including shoes, were seen on a beach in a video shared by IOM. Rescue work continued as fears grew for the missing.
Tens of thousands of migrants from the Horn of Africa travel every year through Djibouti and across the Bab el-Mandeb Strait toward Gulf countries in search of safety and economic opportunities, the IOM said in its statement.
That movement has continued despite newly escalating fighting in Yemen, on the other side of the strait.
"This is a devastating loss of life," said Coissac. "This tragedy is a stark reminder of the dangers faced by migrants along this migration corridor as they seek economic opportunities."
In recent weeks, at least 2,000 Yemenis have received aid in Djibouti as the fighting has escalated in Yemen between the Saudi-backed, internationally recognized government and Iranian-backed Houthi rebels.
That's the opposite direction from the movement of the migrants who died in the shipwreck and the typical migration patterns of recent years: The tens of thousands who cross from eastern Africa toward Yemen each year have typically been looking for work in places like Saudi Arabia.
More than 900 migrants died or went missing along the route last year, according to IOM's Missing Migrants Project, while the number undertaking the journey increased by 18%.
Earlier this year, IOM said 53 people were dead or missing after a boat capsized in the Mediterranean Sea off the Libyan coast. Only two survivors were rescued.
"No one gets into a boat like that unless they believe there is no other safe way," IOM Director-General Amy Pope said. "We cannot keep treating these deaths as normal. Safe and legal pathways save lives. I am asking governments and donors to act before the next boat goes down."

Russia would not need to deploy hundreds of thousands of additional troops to test NATO’s resolve – just a handful of drones targeting critical infrastructure could be enough, Ukraine’s former Foreign Minister Dmytro Kuleba said, as he accused Russian President Vladimir Putin of preparing for a broader confrontation with Europe.
In an interview with the Axel Springer Global Reporters Network, Kuleba, who served as Ukraine’s foreign minister from 2020-24, said Russia’s growing anti-European propaganda and preparations for further conflict indicated that Moscow was escalating its pressure on European countries.

“Anti-European hysteria is being fueled in Russia, which I interpret as the preparation for a broader conflict with the rest of Europe,” Kuleba said. “We [Ukrainians] don’t have to drag you – Putin will drag you into the war.”
Kuleba said he did not expect Russia to launch a full-scale ground offensive beyond Ukraine.
Instead, he said that Moscow could target NATO countries with drones and missiles in an attempt to expose weaknesses in their security systems and test the alliance’s unity.
“The truth is that Russia does not need 400,000 more people to wage that war. It needs five drones,” he said.

Europe: Assemble, Decide, Engage!

Kuleba says Putin is not seeking peace

“He’s not looking for a solution, for a pause, and there will be no moment when he will start looking for it,” Kuleba said.
He contrasted Europe’s preference for solutions that benefit both sides with what he described as Putin’s zero-sum worldview, in which one side must win and the other must lose.
“For him, a solution that benefits both sides is not the best option. For him, the world works on the principle of victory and defeat,” Kuleba said.

“The bombing of cities is a direct consequence of Russia’s failure to defeat Ukraine on the battlefield,” he added.
He argued that the attacks were intended not only to disrupt daily life in Ukraine but also to weaken the resolve of its international partners to continue supporting Kyiv.
“They don’t just want to turn out the lights in Ukraine. They want to paralyze the country,” Kuleba said.
He described the worst-case scenario as the collapse of essential urban systems, including electricity, water and drainage services.
Despite the risks, Kuleba said he believed Ukraine could endure the coming winter because of its size, mobility and ability to adapt to changing conditions.
“I believe Ukraine is too large, too mobile, and too adaptable. That’s why I think we’ll get through this winter,” he said, while warning that “the price will be much higher than last year.”

Ukraine Hits 8 Russian Ballistic Missile Launchers, Forcing Moscow to Alter Planned Attacks
Ukraine has struck eight Russian ballistic missile launchers since the beginning of September, destroying three and damaging five others. The attacks have already forced Russian forces to cancel or alter planned missile strikes against Ukrainian cities, disrupting Moscow’s ability to carry out ballistic attacks.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to a UNITED24 Media correspondent, Ukrainian Defense Minister Yevhenii Khmara revealed the results during a briefing with journalists on October 10, describing the strikes as part of Ukraine’s strategy to counter Russia’s ballistic missile threat by targeting launch systems before they can fire.
The targeted weapons included Russia’s Iskander ballistic missile systems and S-400 launchers adapted to strike ground targets.
“During September and early October, the Defense Forces struck eight launchers used for ballistic attacks. Three were destroyed and five damaged,” Khmara said.
He emphasized that the operations had already produced operational results, forcing Russian troops to abandon or revise some scheduled missile attacks.
The strikes come as Ukraine faces a persistent shortage of interceptor missiles capable of countering Russian ballistic weapons.
According to figures shared during the briefing, Russia launched 76 ballistic missiles against Ukraine in September alone, some of which were intercepted. Khmara warned that existing and anticipated interceptor deliveries remain insufficient to fully protect Ukrainian cities from such attacks.
Ukraine is therefore prioritizing faster deliveries of Patriot interceptor missiles, particularly PAC-3 and PAC-2 GEM-T, while working with international partners to identify available stockpiles.
“We need dozens and hundreds of missiles, not single deliveries,” Khmara stressed, calling for accelerated transfers rather than waiting for lengthy procurement contracts. Meanwhile, Ukrainian forces are increasingly targeting the launchers themselves as an alternative way to reduce Russia’s missile threat.
Earlier, on October 8, Ukrainian forces struck the Sasta machine-tool plant in Russia’s Ryazan region, reportedly linked to the production of components for Iskander ballistic missile systems. The facility supplies specialized manufacturing equipment to Russia’s defense industry, including enterprises involved in missile production.

Over 700 researchers attend computer science conference at BGU, celebrating 'golden age' of tech
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
10:38:33 UTC
19:38:33 KST

More than 700 computer science professionals and students attended the national computer science conference on Thursday to discuss the field's future amid the changes brought about by artificial intelligence.
Organized by the Ben-Gurion University of the Negev's Stein Faculty of Computer and Information Science, the conference also marked the faculty's one-year anniversary, established in 2025.
The conference also featured the launch of the Israeli Computer Science Association, which aims to establish a national framework for Israel's academic and professional computer science community.
The association seeks to strengthen ties between institutions, promote conferences and community initiatives, and develop position papers on issues affecting the future of computer science in Israel.
For its first two years, the association will be managed by Ben-Gurion University. Its leadership is then expected to rotate among Israeli universities.
The conference also featured the presentation of the association's first awards for outstanding research achievements.
The awards committee, chaired by Prof. Yuval Filmus, selected four recipients, including Dr. Haggai Maron of the Technion-Israel Institute of Technology, Dr. Oded Padon of the Weizmann Institute of Science, Dr. Yuval Dagan of Tel Aviv University, and Dr. Liat Peterfreund of the Hebrew University of Jerusalem.
Mobileye CEO Prof. Amnon Shashua also attended the conference and delivered a guest lecture on the development of machine intelligence and its impact on scientists, researchers, and experts.
AI doesn't make computers obsolete, Israeli expert says
"Artificial intelligence does not make computer science obsolete. It is ushering in the golden age of the field," said Prof. Shakhar Smorodinsky, head of the Institute for the Theory of Computing at Ben-Gurion University's Stein Faculty of Computer and Information Science and chairman of the Israeli Computer Science Association.
"Writing code is only one part of computer science. As AI tools become better at writing code, the ability to define problems, develop algorithms, design systems, verify correctness and safety, and understand the limitations of the models themselves becomes increasingly important," Smorodinsky said.
"It is precisely in the age of artificial intelligence that Israel needs greater scientific depth, not less."
Smorodinsky also emphasized the need to establish a shared framework for Israel's computer science community.
"The establishment of the association provides Israel's computer science community with a shared framework for cooperation and for expressing a professional voice on issues relating to research, teaching, and national policy. We want to connect researchers from all institutions, identify shared needs, and promote initiatives that the entire community can benefit from," he said.
"We believe that the new association and the conference we established will strengthen the modern understanding of computer science as a broad, diverse, and dynamic field, and we intend to make this event a tradition," said Prof. Ariel Felner, conference organizer and deputy dean of Ben-Gurion University's Faculty of Computer and Information Science.

Three Yandex Data Centers Hit in Four Days—Now All of Its Supercomputers May Be Down
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
10:38:02 UTC
19:38:02 KST

- Category
- Defense Tech
Three Yandex Data Centers Hit in Four Days—Now All of Its Supercomputers May Be Down
A series of Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian data centers may have knocked all three of Yandex’s supercomputers offline, potentially taking out half of the six largest supercomputing systems operating in Russia, Russian technology outlet T-Invariant reported on October 11.
The first strike came overnight on October 8 against Yandex’s Sasovo data center in Russia’s Ryazan region. The facility, operating since 2014, hosts two of the company’s three supercomputers—Chervonenkis, with a peak performance of 29.42 petaflops, and Lyapunov, rated at 20.03 petaflops.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Chervonenkis is Yandex’s most powerful machine and had been Russia’s strongest newly built supercomputer of the past 15 years. When it entered service in 2021, it ranked 19th in the global TOP500 list. It has since fallen into the second hundred as sanctions and limited access to advanced hardware made infrastructure upgrades increasingly difficult.
A second strike followed on October 9 against Yandex’s data center in Kaluga, located in the Grabtsevo industrial park. Yandex describes the site as its largest data center and one of the biggest such facilities in Russia. Two days later, on October 11, another strike hit the company’s Vladimir data center, home to its third supercomputer, Galushkin, which has a peak performance of 20.64 petaflops.
According to T-Invariant, all three Yandex supercomputers are now out of service. Experts interviewed by the outlet said the attacks may have caused enormous damage to Russia’s high-performance computing infrastructure, particularly because the facilities were built long before physical protection against drone strikes became a serious consideration.
“Yandex built its centers and supercomputers in peacetime and for peacetime. All development focused on normal human life; nobody imagined drones would hit the roof. Earthquakes and other natural disasters are not expected in the Ryazan and Vladimir regions, so nobody thought about investing in physical protection for the buildings,” one supercomputing expert told the outlet.
Yandex built the systems primarily to train neural networks and handle large-scale machine-learning workloads. All three rely on AMD EPYC processors and NVIDIA A100 accelerators connected through high-speed InfiniBand networking—hardware that Russian companies have found increasingly difficult to obtain in large quantities.
One expert argued that restoring systems of this scale could prove far more difficult than simply repairing a damaged building.
“It will not be possible to restore supercomputers of this level. And it is not even about the availability of money. The main problem is not even sanctions, but the shortage of chips and other components: there is a huge queue for them around the world. However, the costs of gray and black imports are also very high,” the specialist said.
T-Invariant noted that Russia’s remaining major supercomputing capacity is concentrated around Moscow. Sberbank’s Christofari and Christofari Neo are located in Skolkovo, an area considered relatively well protected by air defenses, while MTS operates its GROM supercomputer in Lytkarino. Yandex also maintains other data centers in Mytishchi and Ivanteyevka in the Moscow region.
Previously, Russia’s internet segment suffered widespread outages hours after a retaliatory Ukrainian drone strike hit a Yandex data center in the Ryazan region.

Russia has used attacks on energy facilities in order to deny Ukrainian civilians power, heat and running water during the war, hoping to wear down public resistance to Moscow's full-scale invasion. Ukrainian officials describe the strategy as "weaponizing winter," and fear Russia could ramp up such attacks as cold weather approaches.

"We haven't yet seen that also Russia will stick to it," EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said at a meeting of the bloc's foreign ministers in Luxembourg.
"Personally, I would also welcome that the cease-fire would include people not being killed, not only energy," she added.
Ukrainian and European officials reacted with dismay to Trump's diesel deal with Putin, saying it will help fund Russia's war effort.

Russia's Yandex will need six months to replace drone-damaged equipment
The Russian company Yandex will need at least six months to replace the damaged infrastructure of three data centres that came under drone attacks between 8 and 11 October.
Source: Russian media outlet The Insider
Details: Yandex will have to procure new equipment through multiple sources, including abroad, to offset the losses more quickly.
Obtaining a significant volume of server equipment before the end of 2026 is virtually impossible, IT market participants commented to the Russian publication Kommersant. They expect that increased demand from cloud providers will lead to an additional rise in server prices as early as the fourth quarter.
Yandex acknowledged that it cannot yet state a timeline for the repair of the infrastructure.
Market participants also expect prices for server equipment and cloud services to increase due to a deficit in computing capacity and the costs associated with protecting against new attacks.
The Insider discovered that certain Yandex Cloud services have already grown in price by more than 16.6% following two tariff hikes in 2025-2026.
Other data centre operators have begun procuring anti-drone protective equipment. Some are already modernising protection systems for external engineering infrastructure. These costs will subsequently be reflected in the price of cloud services for customers.
The specific estimates for the future tariff increases operators have not yet provided.
The previous price increase occurred on 1 May 2025, affecting the majority of cloud services. At that time, the company raised tariffs by 8%, also due to the rising cost of equipment and other expenses.
By comparing the data published by the company over two years, The Insider calculated that the cumulative tariff increase for individual cloud services reached 16.6%.
As of 12 October, Yandex has still failed to restore normal operation of its cloud platform following three drone attacks.
Yandex Cloud is still operating in emergency mode, with engineers working around the clock to restore the infrastructure. Clients continue to be advised to use alternative sites for data hosting and backup.
The company also warned of delays in technical support operations due to a high volume of inquiries. Meanwhile, Yandex provided no new details regarding the availability of individual cloud services.
Disruptions continue to affect users of a number of services as well. In particular, Yandex Pay clients complain about being unable to transfer or withdraw money, while taxi drivers and couriers are unable to withdraw their earnings. Some buyers have encountered difficulties when attempting to request refunds for concert tickets via Intickets, as confirmation codes fail to arrive at Yandex Mail.
Background:
- On 8 October a fire broke out at the Sasta plant in Sasovo, Russia's Ryazan Oblast, where a data centre operated by Yandex DC is located and which is important to Russia's defence industry. Telegram channels have reported an attack on the plant.

Ukraine’s Zelenskyy accuses Russia of violating Trump’s ‘energy ceasefire’
The European Union also announced that it officially added almost 1,600 new sanctions on Russia’s military industrial complex.
Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has accused Russia of violating the “energy ceasefire” that United States President Donald Trump unilaterally announced at the weekend and promised to respond if the attacks continue.
Speaking at the Warsaw Security Forum via video link on Monday, the Ukrainian leader urged the US to step in to ensure that Moscow abides by the truce in the four-and-a-half-year Russia-Ukraine war, noting that there have already been “Russian violations of the energy ceasefire announced by President Trump”.
Zelenskyy said Ukraine was “horribly surprised” that despite Trump’s announcement, Russia struck several energy facilities, including a power plant in Kharkiv.
“We are waiting for the details of the conditions between the Americans and Russians, and we are waiting to see what specific steps the Americans are ready to take,” he said.
“This energy ceasefire, it can work, and it can become a major step toward ending the war if the Americans truly step in now and make sure Russians respect it … If Russia does not agree to an energy ceasefire, we will respond,” Zelenskyy told the Warsaw Security Forum.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said talks for a possible “energy ceasefire” were ongoing, but rejected Zelenskyy’s proposal for a 60-day truce to allow elections to take place.
“In the Kremlin, both President Putin and officials at other levels have repeatedly stated we do not want a ceasefire,” Peskov said. “We want long-term peace and are prepared to do everything possible to achieve it.”
Trump’s announcement on Sunday that the two countries had agreed to an “energy ceasefire” caused confusion. It came two days after Trump declared a temporary easing of US sanctions on Russian diesel, prompting outrage from European allies and Kyiv, who said it would only embolden Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Both Ukraine and Russia have been launching mutual attacks on each other’s energy infrastructure for months, adding to upward pressure on global energy prices that have risen amid the US-Israel war on Iran.
Zelenskyy initially denied any knowledge of the agreement and said it was “news to him”, according to Axios.
Trump has previously taken to his Truth Social account to announce truces or other arrangements before either Kyiv or Moscow confirmed them.
“An energy ceasefire and other steps to reduce escalation and guarantee security are truly needed here in reality, not just on Truth Social,” Zelenskyy added.
European leaders expressed encouragement at the proposed ceasefire, but agreed with Zelenskyy that it had not taken effect.
“I have not noted, over the last 48 hours, any energy ceasefire coming from the Russian side,” French President Emmanuel Macron told reporters at a Paris auto show.
At the Warsaw Security Forum, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said that “Russia is not interested in a ceasefire, de-escalation, or peace … that is why I will go to Brussels to urge all European partners to consider increasing sanctions.”
In Brussels, the European Union announced that it has officially added almost 1,600 new sanctions on Russia’s military-industrial complex, including individuals and entities involved in the war, in a bid to maintain pressure on Moscow.
“This is the single largest expansion of our sanctions list since Russia started its war,” EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas wrote online. “Europe is again showing a united front … We are making it significantly harder, slower and more expensive for Russia to produce the weapons it uses to kill Ukrainians.”
Meanwhile, Russia attacked Ukrainian gas production facilities belonging to its state oil and gas company Naftogaz in the Kharkiv region overnight, which caused a fire, the company said on Monday.
“The attack damaged critical equipment. Our employees are doing everything possible to repair the damage as quickly as possible and prevent risks to the stable operation of the energy system,” Naftogaz acting CEO Sergii Fedorenko wrote on Telegram.
A day earlier, Zelenskyy had said that Ukraine was ready to halt attacks on Russian oil refineries if Moscow ceased its own attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure.

Swiss section of Great St. Bernard tunnel to get 1,000 solar panels
The company that runs the Great St. Bernard tunnel has decided to expand its use of renewable energy. It is set to install 7,000 square metres of solar panels. These are currently being installed on the approach road leading to the tunnel, on the Swiss side.
A thousand panels, tilted at 60 degrees, will be gradually installed between late 2026 and 2027. Some 3,000 square metres will be operational by the end of this year, with the remainder (4,000 square metres) to be ready over the course of next year. A trial phase took place between 2022 and 2025. In total, the system will generate 450 MWh per year, equivalent to half the tunnel’s energy requirements.
‘A winter supplement’
“We have a large flat roof area,” Baptiste Cavin, maintenance and projects engineer at Tunnel du Grand-St-Bernard SA, told news agency Keystone-SDA. “This solar farm will provide a welcome winter supplement to our current generation. The electricity requirements (lighting, electromechanical systems, ventilation) of our facilities are, in fact, considerable.”
More
Swiss Alpine solar farms struggle to deliver on their promise
The company already generates renewable electricity via a hydroelectric power station located inside the tunnel, powered by a small dam built on the Great St. Bernard Pass road.
A region renowned for its sunshine
The total cost of the works is around CHF2 million ($2.4 million). These are being carried out by the company’s own staff. The project is therefore fully carried out by the company and has no connection with utility company Romande Energie’s floating solar park in the Alps, at Lac des Toules, which is not far from the future installation, situated at an altitude of 1,900 metres.

The region is considered suitable for the installation of solar panels, given the high cumulative sunshine levels recorded in the elevated parts of the municipality of Bourg-St-Pierre over many years.

How Jantar Mantar became Delhi's designated protest site and what changes now
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
10:34:39 UTC
19:34:39 KST

Jantar Mantar’s changing role in Delhi’s history of dissent.
NEW DELHI: Jantar Mantar, one of Delhi's best-known protest venues, has lost its status as a designated site for demonstrations. On October 12, Delhi Police de-notified the site and named three alternatives: Ramlila Ground, Burari Ground and CBD Ground in East Delhi.The decision follows recommendations from a committee constituted by the ministry of home affairs (MHA) to examine alternative venues for protests and demonstrations.
For several decades, Jantar Mantar has been synonymous with protests in the national capital, a place where farmers, students, workers and political organisations have gathered to raise their demands. More recently, it became the centre of youth-led protests over the NEET paper leak, with demonstrators demanding reforms to the examination system and the resignation of then Union education minister Dharmendra Pradhan.
Jantar Mantar’s legacy: A landmark site of dissent faces a shift
However, Delhi's address for protests has not always been Jantar Mantar. Before it emerged as a prominent hub for demonstrations, the sprawling lawns around India Gate and the Boat Club, close to Parliament and the government's principal offices, were among the capital's most important spaces for political mobilisation.The latest decision marks another chapter in the history of how authorities have regulated where citizens can assemble to make their voices heard.
Before Jantar Mantar, there was Boat Club
For decades after Independence, the Boat Club lawns near India Gate were an important venue for political rallies.The lawns near modern-day Central Vista gave demonstrators proximity to Parliament, the government's principal offices and other institutions at the centre of national power.The scale of the gatherings, however, also presented challenges for the authorities.One of the defining episodes came in 1988, when farmer leader Mahendra Singh Tikait led a massive agitation in Delhi. Farmers gathered at the Boat Club and surrounding lawns to press their demands, bringing a large mobilisation into the heart of the capital.The episode became a turning point in the debate over whether such prominent public spaces should remain open to large demonstrations.Authorities increasingly sought to regulate gatherings in central Delhi, citing concerns around security, traffic and public order.READ ALSO: SC permits Congress delegation to file petition within premises as Rahul leads INDIA bloc march
When Rajpath became a protest ground
In 'India After Gandhi: The History of the World's Largest Democracy', historian Ramachandra Guha recounts how the lawns along present-day Kartavya Path, formerly Rajpath and known as Kingsway during British rule, became a prominent site of political dissent in the early 1990s.The book recalls tents occupied by people from different parts of the country, representing causes ranging from demands for a separate state and better prices for agricultural produce to recognition for regional languages.Other groups included industrial workers, Tibetan refugees seeking Indian citizenship and Hindu religious organisations campaigning on cow slaughter.The lawns near the country's most prominent government buildings in Lutyens' Delhi became a temporary home for movements that wanted their demands to be seen and heard.But the encampments did not last. Guha writes that the tents were dismantled in the early 1990s, with the government concerned about the impression created by visible demonstrations near the ceremonial heart of the capital.Protesters subsequently regrouped near Jantar Mantar, where they remained visible to people passing through the busy commercial district.The restrictions on gatherings around Boat Club and Rajpath helped set the stage for Jantar Mantar's emergence as a prominent location for demonstrations.Live Updates: Delhi SIR Protest: Crowd swells as police stop Rahul, INDIA bloc leaders marching towards SC
How Jantar Mantar became Delhi's protest address
Built by Maharaja Sawai Jai Singh II in the 18th century, Delhi's Jantar Mantar is an open-air astronomical observatory designed to track celestial movements.Over time, the area around the historic site evolved into a major hub for protest movements, offering demonstrators a prominent public platform while remaining easier to manage than larger, more central locations.Located close to busy Connaught Place and within reach of Parliament and government offices, it allowed demonstrators to bring their demands into public view without occupying the expansive lawns around India Gate.The site hosted protests involving workers, farmers, civil society groups and citizens campaigning on a range of social and political issues.Its prominence grew further during the anti-corruption movement led by social activist Anna Hazare in 2011, when demonstrations demanding a stronger Lokpal mechanism brought corruption and accountability to the centre of national political debate.As the movement grew, Ramlila Maidan became the venue for larger gatherings and Hazare's prolonged fast. The two locations demonstrated how different sites in Delhi could accommodate protests of different scales.The significance of Jantar Mantar was not simply a matter of geography. It became an established public address for people seeking to draw the attention of political leaders, government officials and the media to their grievances.Over the years, Jantar Mantar has witnessed protests on a range of issues, from Anna Hazare's campaign for a Lokpal Bill and the 2017 Tamil Nadu farmers' agitation to demonstrations against the Citizenship (Amendment) Act and the wrestlers' protests against Brij Bhushan Sharan Singh in 2023.More recently, it became the centre of demonstrations by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) over the NEET paper leak and demands for the resignation of then Union education minister Dharmendra Pradhan.However, its status as a designated protest venue did not mean that demonstrations could take place without restrictions. Police permissions, public-order measures and court directions continued to determine how the site could be used.ALSO READ: 'Resign': Congress Keralam unit to 'dear' CJI Surya Kant, draws BJP fire
When the right to protest reached the Supreme Court
In October 2017, the National Green Tribunal (NGT) ordered an end to protests at Jantar Mantar following complaints about noise, sanitation and disruption to residents.The restrictions were subsequently challenged before the Supreme Court.In its July 23, 2018, judgment in Mazdoor Kisan Shakti Sangathan v Union of India, the Supreme Court examined restrictions on protests at Jantar Mantar and the Boat Club, including the effects of demonstrations on residents and public spaces.The court recognised peaceful assembly and protest as fundamental rights under Articles 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(b) of the Constitution. At the same time, it acknowledged that the exercise of these rights could be regulated to protect public order and the interests of other citizens.ALSO READ: FIR against Kejriwal, AAP leaders for 'chaos' at Bangla Sahib during CEC protestThe judgment addressed the competing claims of demonstrators and residents, making clear that one group's rights could not simply extinguish those of another.It called for a balance between the right to protest and the need to prevent unreasonable disruption.The constitutional basis for that balance is set out in Article 19. Article 19(1)(b) guarantees citizens the right to assemble peacefully and without arms, while Article 19(3) permits reasonable restrictions in the interests of the sovereignty and integrity of India or public order.
The latest decision comes amid protests by opposition parties and the youth-led CJP against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over alleged electoral irregularities and the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.The proposed CJP protest on October 10 was met with extensive security arrangements, detentions and restrictions on movement in parts of Delhi.Under the new arrangement, Jantar Mantar will no longer be a designated protest venue. Ramlila Ground, Burari Ground and CBD Ground in East Delhi have been identified as alternatives.Delhi Police has said a detailed and revised standard operating procedure for demonstrations at these three venues will be issued separately.The decision changes where organisers can hold demonstrations under the designated-venue system. However, de-notification should not be confused with a blanket prohibition on all peaceful assembly, which remains subject to constitutional protections and lawful restrictions.
Why the location of a protest matters
The significance of the decision extends beyond the physical relocation of demonstrations. The location of a protest affects its visibility, the ease with which people can reach it and its proximity to the institutions being addressed.A venue in central Delhi offers demonstrators a different kind of access and public visibility from a ground farther away from the corridors of power.For organisers, the choice of location can therefore be an important part of how a protest communicates its message.
Among the newly designated venues, Burari Ground and CBD Ground in East Delhi are farther from the central government district than Jantar Mantar.At the same time, large demonstrations in central Delhi can create challenges for traffic management, security and the daily movement of residents.The October 10 protests, for instance, were accompanied by extensive security arrangements and disruptions to movement across parts of the city.The latest decision once again brings into focus a question that has shaped Delhi's protest history for decades: how to balance the right to peaceful demonstrations with security, public order and the functioning of the national capital.

The projected shortfall in tax revenues to the state budget for 2026, estimated at UAH 70 billion, is the result of objective challenges, including the destruction of businesses, logistics infrastructure and the metallurgical industry, as well as port blockades, rather than a hole in the budget, Finance Minister Serhiy Marchenko said.
"It is difficult to expect businesses that have been destroyed to pay taxes at the levels that were planned. But that does not mean we are not taking steps to restore the situation," Ukrainian Finance Minister Serhiy Marchenko said during the government question hour at a meeting of the Verkhovna Rada on Monday.
According to him, the government has substantially increased domestic borrowing beyond the planned amount to cover the tax revenue shortfall this year.
"I think the situation is manageable. The only thing we cannot control is the fulfillment of our international commitments," the minister added.

External financing needs were estimated at approximately $50 billion, but international assistance inflows were insufficient: $2.4 billion was received in January 2026, $1.5 billion in February, $1.7 billion in March, $1.3 billion in April, $500 million in May, and $11.3 billion from the European Union in June. From January through September, the state budget's general fund had already received nearly UAH 50 billion less in revenue than planned, including shortfalls of UAH 32 billion in August and September.
Marchenko said that, according to data for the first eight months of 2026, the economy recorded zero growth in gross domestic product (GDP), while inflation was accelerating under the influence of increased spending and supply disruptions. Consumer prices rose by 1.2% in September, and annual inflation accelerated to 10%.
As previously reported, Ukrainian Prime Minister Serhiy Koretsky estimated state budget tax revenue losses resulting from attacks on businesses at UAH 70 billion. However, he noted that this estimate reflected the situation as of September.
Later, in an interview with Interfax-Ukraine, Roksolana Pidlasa, head of the Verkhovna Rada Committee on Budget Issues, noted that the state budget's total revenue shortfall for the year could exceed UAH 70 billion. According to her, the general fund had received UAH 49.5 billion less than planned over the first nine months. The shortfall in domestic and import VAT alone exceeded $1.5 billion, although this was partially offset by overperformance in personal income tax and corporate income tax revenues.

AlterMe Review: Fitness Built Around My DNA
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
10:34:00 UTC
19:34:00 KST

Easy-to-follow workouts based on my DNA and readiness score. Variety of chill yoga or breathwork sessions plus more intense strength, dance, and cardio workouts. The app tracks nutrition and sleep and analyzes meals.
TIRED
Workouts are short—ranging from five to 40 minutes. DNA results are interesting, but there’s no quick fix to fitness. Premium price.
When I was asked to review AlterMe’s fitness system that claims to use DNA and biometric data to create a personalized fitness, nutrition, and recovery program, I was intrigued. I’ve used some of the best fitness trackers before, but have never tried a system that combines DNA testing, personalized workouts, nutrition insight, and its own smart wearable all within a single ecosystem.
I’m someone who needs constant fitness motivation to stay on track. Rather than push myself through strenuous weights and cardio, I prefer feel-good Pilates and an ice bath at my local David Lloyd gym. But in an effort to step out of my comfort zone and try something a little more challenging, I decided to give AlterMe a go.
I’ve used numerous fitness apps over the years, such as Bala and Freeletics, but not one that suggests specific fitness workouts based on my DNA testing results. AlterMe combines guidance across exercise, nutrition, sleep, and recovery, going beyond simply reporting on your DNA and biometric data to suggest small, manageable actions to drive behavioral change over time.
There’s no denying that it comes at a premium price, but having workouts and nutrition guidance in one place helped me build better habits—even if the DNA insights weren’t particularly revelatory.
Getting Set Up
Photograph: Emily Peck
AlterMe’s all-in-one health and fitness program is built around a DNA test and a smart ring that measures data and provides insights and workouts in the app. It’s convenient, but this is an expensive offering. The entry-level AlterMe Essential plan is $1,299, and the AlterMe Advanced plan is $1,899. Both offer biometric tracking, nutrition insights, and fitness workouts accessible from the app, but the Advanced plan gives you a more in-depth DNA analysis and lifetime membership as opposed to the Essential’s three-year membership.
Upon signing up and answering questions on my weight-loss goals, height, weight, and general fitness levels, I was sent both a DNA cheek-swab kit and a ring sizing kit. I emailed AlterMe to confirm my ring size and sent the DNA swab back in the mail. Within two weeks, I received my AlterMe smart ring and had booked in a date to talk over my Fitness and Wellness Genetic report with an AlterMe representative. I’ve been diving in and out of the app and following the fitness workouts for over six months now.
A Tailored Fitness and Wellness Genetic Report
AlterMe app via Emily Peck
Research into genetic influence on athletic performance is still developing, and AlterMe acknowledges that its genetic findings reported through DNA testing have not been clinically validated. However, the company conducts its own research to produce a personalized Fitness and Wellness Genetic Report. It says it uses “a rigorous genetic interpretation process that adheres to strict scientific standards” with “scientific integrity” and “robust research.” AlterMe also states that saliva samples are processed in the US in a CLIA- and CAP-certified lab that meets local regulations.
With this in mind, I approached the DNA test report with equal measures of skepticism and intrigue, as should anyone curious to get more insight into their health and well-being.
The report claimed to use my DNA to reveal how my body responds to different types of exercise, nutrition, recovery, and stress. It suggested types of exercise to suit me and how I could approach training and recovery. Strength training, for example, was identified as the best fit for my genetic profile, while my genetic response to carbohydrates was rated as “lower than average.”
Perhaps not surprisingly, the report told me that I’m “externally motivated to exercise,” suggesting I may not naturally enjoy physical activity just for the sake of it. That certainly felt familiar.
Representatives at AlterMe explained how these assessments are determined: “Our assessment looks at markers associated with several traits, including how body composition changed during exercise interventions. For cardio-related body composition response, the markers in our scientific review are ADRB2 rs1042713 and LPL rs328. For resistance training, the model draws on a set of obesity and body composition markers, including variants near FTO, GNPDA2, NEGR1, and SLC39A8.”
So far, everything was sounding on point. But despite the personalized insights, I hadn’t discovered anything particularly groundbreaking.
Smart Ring Bling
Photograph: Emily Peck
AlterMe has its own smart ring wearable, designed to provide health insights and work alongside the app. The ring uses PPG sensors to monitor metrics such as heart rate and blood oxygen, alongside a temperature sensor and an accelerometer to track activity. It then uses data including my HRV, resting heart rate, sleep, and recent activity load to turn the raw measurements into a “Readiness score” from 0 to 100, before suggesting a workout tailored to my current state and my DNA insight.
This type of health tracking is similar to what you get with Oura's Ring 5 offering. The key difference is that AlterMe is a more closed ecosystem, combining its wearable data with its own genetic insights to generate an AI-powered workout plan every day based on my biometrics.
Oura, meanwhile, provides detailed sleep, activity, readiness, and broader health insights as well as guided fitness content within its app and integration with services such as Apple Health. Its primary focus, however, remains tracking and interpreting your health and activity data, whereas AlterMe puts more emphasis on the personalized workouts it prescribes.
The ring has a titanium outer frame and comes in either a gold finish, silver, or Stealth black. My gold finish has picked up some scuff marks over the couple of months I’ve been wearing it. While the gold finish looks good, I found the ring quite bulky—and thicker than the sleek Oura Ring 5—which means it sometimes gets in the way when I’m lifting weights.
Tailored Workouts Depending on ‘Readiness’ Score
Within the stats section of the app, I was able to view my daily calorie burn, step count, distance covered, sleep duration, and readiness score—all data the ring was providing. The app then provides a daily workout to follow. The workouts can be as low-key or as challenging as I want, depending on how I am feeling. I could choose from stretch, strength, cardio, yoga, or combat-style sessions, so there’s no excuse to skip a workout. As AlterMe representatives told me, the biometric data collected can help make a recommendation, but it can’t capture every detail about how I feel—soreness, illness, stress, injury, or demands of the day may change what feels right, for example—which is why you get the option to choose your level.
“Giving you a choice is also an intentional part of the AlterMe experience,” say AlterMe representatives. “Without choice, it’s hard for you to stay consistent. We want to offer useful guidance while leaving you in control of your effort. Your choice adds context and makes the plan easier to fit into real life.”
On the days I had poor sleep the night before, the app recommended a lighter workout or recovery session—the 15-minute breathwork session has become a particular favorite. On the days I’d slept well, I was tasked with a more strenuous session depending on my current level, from beginner to level 6.
While the workouts are easy to access and follow, I found them short—20 minutes was the average workout time, with 40 minutes being the longest session I tried. But it is possible to stack the workouts if you want to push yourself further. There’s also a way to track activities such as a run or group workout outside the guided library of workouts.
I trust that the app was recommending workouts to suit my health stats and genetic traits, and I mostly felt good when following them. But there were some days when I was feeling terrible due to poor sleep, and the app was telling me that my readiness score was high, which left me feeling a little confused. But I dutifully obliged with the suggested workout—even if I did opt for a shorter 20-minute session. On the days I had forgotten to wear my ring to bed the night before, the app would ask me to self-score from 1 to 10 on how I was feeling before a workout was suggested.
AI Nutrition Coach and Body Scanning
Exercise is just one piece of the fitness puzzle, and one of the pros of the AlterMe app is that it has a nutrition tracker. Rather than having it provide a single diet plan, I like the way the app can generate meal and snack ideas by referencing my DNA to keep me hitting my macro targets. You can generate a recipe and then log it if you decide to make it. Simply by clicking “generate recipe” I could get breakfast, lunch, dinner, and snack ideas in under 20 seconds. The recipes are pretty enticing too—Zesty Lemon Herb Grilled Chicken Qith Roasted Green Beans and Quinoa was one I tried. But I found the snack ideas most helpful, as I’m always thinking about snacks—Roasted Edamame With Smoked Paprika and Sea Salt is a particular favorite.
In the Nutrition tab of the app, I could access personalized calorie and nutrition guidance based on my DNA results, weight, BMI, activity level, and weight-loss goals. My DNA report suggested I have an average response to protein and a low response to carbs and fats. I like how easy it is to log food in the Nutrition tab in the app and instantly see whether I’d hit my protein, fat, and carb macro goals. I often forgot to track everything I ate, but on the days I remembered to do so, I found it easy to track my calorie intake and meals.
AlterMe app via Emily Peck
The app also has a 3D/body composition scanning feature to analyze body shape and provide stats on things like BMI, estimated body-fat percentage, and lean mass.
You do need to put in your height and weight when you sign up, but this feature adds more. As AlterMe told me, BMI is calculated from height and weight, but the scan provides a much fuller view by creating a standardized 3D model and estimating body-fat percentage, lean mass, body shape, and body part circumferences. Repeated scans help show whether and where the body is changing, giving members a clearer way to compare their progress with their goals. You need to use your phone camera to capture a picture of your body shape, but turning as it takes photos. I found this feature a little intrusive, as I didn’t really want to take photos of myself to put on the app. But if this doesn’t bother you, I think this is a compelling extra.
Is the AlterMe App Worth It?
There are numerous workout apps and wearables that can track your health data, but this personalized program that combines DNA testing, a smart ring wearable, and on-demand workouts in one ecosystem is a unique offering. It’s convenient, but pricey, and it's important to note that while the DNA testing can be insightful, it hasn’t been clinically validated. There are also understandable privacy concerns around handing over DNA data, although AlterMe notes on its site that it destroys samples after testing and extracted DNA is retained for just 45 days for quality assurance.
My journey with AlterMe has generally been positive, but it hasn’t altered me. It has made me more aware of what I eat and made me feel physically stronger due to the regularity of my training sessions. I like wearing the ring and having an app that suggests an optimum workout based on my biometrics. Having a tailored workout to follow has made me feel good—particularly on the days that I haven’t felt like training. When I feel stuck in the gym and not sure which exercises to do, I take out the app and simply follow a workout. It makes me feel like I have a personal trainer in my pocket, ready to bark orders at me whenever I need a little push. I think if you’re willing to follow the workouts and track your nutrition, AlterMe can be a helpful tool for building positive habits and improving fitness. You could, alternatively, use the money and invest in a good personal trainer—whatever you decide, it’s always nice to have options.

How China and the EU pressed pause on trade war – and what it took to get there
EU officials spoke of a ‘paradigm shift’ in wake of surprise trade deal, saying the ‘nature of the rebalancing exercise has changed’
Weeks of high-wire negotiations between China and the EU culminated in a surprise trade deal that will, among other measures, impose strict quotas on Chinese hybrid car exports to the bloc and slash Chinese tariffs on a variety of European goods.
The deal, unveiled on Friday, takes some of the heat out of searing bilateral trade tensions and temporarily averts the prospect of a bruising trade war.
Beijing agreed not to retaliate against Brussels’ move to curb imports of Chinese hybrid cars, which will see shipments capped at 350,000 units per year, rising at 6 per cent annually. This will leave exports at less than half the 800,000 vehicles the EU has projected will be shipped in 2026.
Asked on Monday how Beijing grew to accept the concessions – after Chinese officials spent weeks rejecting the prospect of voluntarily limiting auto shipments – Brussels framed its position with a time-worn business maxim: “The customer is always right.”

South Korea tests drone wingman concept with FA-50 light fighter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
10:33:31 UTC
19:33:31 KST

- KAI flew its FA-50 light combat aircraft in formation with its AAP jet drone for 20 minutes on Oct. 8, holding 9 to 30 meters apart.
- KAI plans further tests with the FA-50 pilot controlling the drone in flight and multi-drone formations flown by an AI pilot.
Korea Aerospace Industries has flown its FA-50 light combat aircraft in formation with a jet-powered drone for the first time, a test the company says is the first real manned-unmanned formation flight in South Korea.
The flight took place on Oct. 8 over the sea south of Goheung, in South Jeolla Province, KAI said on Oct. 12. The FA-50 and the company’s Adaptable Aerial Platform, or AAP, flew side by side for 20 minutes at about 2,100 meters (7,000 feet), holding a distance of 9 to 30 meters (30 to 100 feet) between them. They flew at 360 km/h (224 mph), a speed KAI chose for stability and safety. KAI did not say whether the drone was flying autonomously, under remote control or with input from the FA-50 pilot during the test.
The AAP is a small jet drone weighing about 150 kg (330 pounds), 3.1 meters (10 feet) long with a 2.2-meter (7-foot) wingspan, and a top speed of 790 km/h (490 mph), according to KAI. The company has developed it with its own money since 2024, and the drone first flew in October 2025. KAI is training it with an artificial intelligence pilot the company calls KAILOT.
KAI designed the AAP to fly ahead of crewed fighters into heavily defended areas and carry out reconnaissance, electronic jamming, decoy and strike missions. This kind of pairing, known as manned-unmanned teaming, lets a pilot send cheaper drones into the most dangerous part of a mission.
KAI said it will gradually raise the drone’s speed toward its maximum and widen its operating range. Next, it plans tests in which the FA-50 pilot controls the AAP’s mission in flight, and formation flights with several drones flown by the AI pilot. The company says the work will feed into a future South Korean unmanned combat aircraft.
KAI laid out a three-phase plan for the effort in 2024. The second phase, running from 2025 to 2028, is meant to end with a demonstration of an FA-50 controlling up to four drones at once. The third phase, through 2037, would move the technology to a two-seat version of the KF-21 fighter.
The FA-50 is a supersonic light fighter developed from KAI’s T-50 trainer. Beyond South Korea, it is flown or on order in Poland, the Philippines, Malaysia, Indonesia, Iraq and Thailand, and KAI has said it hopes existing operators will add drone-teaming capabilities to their jets. KAI showed a scale model of an FA-50 flying with AAP drones at the World Defense Show in Riyadh in February.

Eritrea seeks UN action against Ethiopia over war threat

Eritrea seeks UN action against Ethiopia over war threat
Eritrea has asked the UN Security Council to take deterrent measures against Ethiopia, accusing its neighbor of using allegations of invasion by Eritrean forces to justify a war aimed at securing sovereign access to the Red Sea.
The appeal follows Ethiopia’s notification to the Security Council last week that Eritrean forces, including mechanized units, had advanced up to 60 km inside the northern Tigray region. Foreign Minister Gedion Timothewos sought international support for Ethiopia’s right to self-defense, demanded the immediate withdrawal of the troops, and called for the UN to unequivocally condemn the alleged incursion.
Eritrean Information Minister Yemane Gebremeskel rejected the accusations on Friday, calling them “audacity and duplicity in their most extreme forms.”
In a letter published on Saturday, Eritrean Foreign Minister Osman Saleh rejected Addis Ababa’s claim that it was acting in self-defense as “deceitful attempts to rationalize its brazen acts of war against a sovereign UN member State.” He warned that a confrontation would devastate both countries and destabilize the region.
“Eritrea requests the UN Security Council to forcefully condemn Ethiopia’s deplorable declaration of war against Eritrea … and take the requisite deterrent measures against it in accordance with Chapter VII of the UN Charter,” Saleh wrote. Those provisions allow sanctions and military action.
The confrontation comes amid renewed fighting in northern Ethiopia after the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) formed an alliance with six other armed groups last month to overthrow the federal government. TPLF forces seized airports in Mekelle, Tigray’s regional capital, and the cities of Axum and Shire. Federal troops and allied fighters retook Mekelle on October 4 following the TPLF’s withdrawal.
At least 52 civilians were killed around Alamata in southern Tigray in late September, the BBC reported, citing hospital sources. More than 720 wounded people had been admitted to hospitals in Korem, Alamata, and Shire by September 25, according to Doctors Without Borders.
Ethiopia accuses Eritrea of supporting the armed groups, which Asmara denies. Ethiopian troops and allied fighters entered Adigrat near the Eritrean border on Saturday, Reuters reported. US-based conflict monitor ACLED reported multiple suspected Ethiopian drone strikes targeting Eritrean troops and ammunition in the area on Wednesday and Thursday.
The violence has sparked fears of a return to full-blown war in the East African country, which has struggled to maintain stability since a peace deal in November 2022 ended a brutal two-year conflict in Tigray. Eritrean troops fought alongside Ethiopia’s federal army during the 2020–2022 Tigray war, but relations have since soured over Addis Ababa’s maritime ambitions. On October 1, Asmara severed diplomatic ties after Ethiopia expelled ten Eritrean diplomats and closed its embassy in Eritrea.
Ethiopia became landlocked when Eritrea gained independence in 1993. Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed calls sea access an existential issue and says it should be secured through peaceful dialogue, while Asmara sees his government’s ambitions as a threat to its sovereignty.

EXPLAINED: Trump’s Energy Truce in Ukraine – Fourth Time’s the Charm?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
10:31:24 UTC
19:31:24 KST

On Sunday, US President Donald Trump claimed Kyiv and Moscow had agreed to an energy truce.
The surprise announcement followed his equally surprising Friday announcement of a diesel deal with Russia, in which Moscow would supply millions of tons of diesel to the world market, before he lambasted Kyiv for attacking Russia’s refineries and called for President Volodymyr Zelensky’s removal.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Kyiv has maintained that it would only agree to a bilateral energy truce, under which Russia would stop attacking Ukraine’s energy grid in exchange for Kyiv halting strikes on Russian refineries as, despite Trump’s Sunday announcement, Ukraine’s power plants have continued to come under Russian attacks on Monday morning.
But the latest proposal, according to Axios, covers only refineries, of which Ukraine has just one compared with Russia’s dozens, which inevitably favor Moscow.
Fourth time’s the charm?
The Sunday announcement marked the fourth major US attempt to boast of an energy truce since Trump returned to office in January 2025.
The previous announcement was recent, on Sept. 14, when Trump similarly declared an energy truce on his Truth Social platform.
“Ukraine has agreed not to hit Russian Energy targets. Russia has agreed to do so, likewise,” Trump wrote.
Zelensky, without saying Kyiv had agreed, said it supported the idea if the truce was bilateral and enforced. Moscow, meanwhile, called it a “very good idea” without elaborating, and Trump’s declared truce fizzled out as Ukraine’s energy grid continued to be pounded and Russia’s refineries continued to be set ablaze.
Trying to Make Sense of Trump’s Ukraine Policy
Premature announcements aside, why has an energy truce never materialized?
Below is an overview of the previous attempts, originally published on Sept. 15, 2026, but with slight revisions, outlining when and where everything went wrong.
Trump’s previous attempts on energy truce
The early 2026 attempt was short-lived, while the most serious attempt yielded a 30-day truce proposal in March 2025.
In March 2025, everyone ostensibly agreed to a 30-day energy truce soon after Trump’s return to office – only not the same version.
These differing interpretations allowed both sides to accuse the other of violations and use them to justify retaliatory strikes, while the lack of a monitoring mechanism also dampened the proposal’s effectiveness.
In short, US officials said Washington had reached separate agreements with Ukraine and Russia to “develop measures for implementing” a ceasefire, but the duration and list of facilities differed for each.
From the Russian side, it listed March 18 as the start date – despite the official talks in Saudi Arabia starting on March 23 – and omitted facilities that Kyiv said were included in its version.
In a statement to European Pravda at the time, Ukraine’s Ministry of Energy said Russia’s list did not include its oil and gas production facilities, contrary to Kyiv’s agreement with the US. The exact list of facilities Kyiv presented was unclear.
And violations soon took place – on March 28, Russia struck gas production facilities in Ukraine’s Central Poltava region. The same day, Russia accused Ukraine of firing US-made HIMARS missiles at the Sudzha gas metering station in the Kursk region bordering Ukraine, a claim that Kyiv dismissed as a Russian “false flag.”
In other words, no ceasefire.
Another attempt at an energy truce took place in early 2026 and lasted a few days.
In late January, Trump said he had appealed to Russian leader Vladimir Putin to stop strikes on Kyiv and Ukrainian energy infrastructure to facilitate peace talks. Moscow confirmed the request and said it would last until Feb. 1, while Kyiv said there was no deal yet, but it would reciprocate nonetheless.
On Feb. 2, Russia resumed strikes on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure, leaving locals in the Kharkiv, Sumy, Dnipropetrovsk, and Cherkasy regions without power.
Why might Ukraine and Russia want an energy truce?
Ukraine is concerned about a difficult winter, while Russia is facing an unprecedented fuel crisis.
For Ukraine, energy infrastructure – including power stations, substations and gas storage facilities – was hit hard by Russian attacks in previous winters. Repairs are costly and time-consuming, and with the country facing a budget crunch, any further Russian strikes would put additional pressure on a battered system.
For Russia, meanwhile, Ukrainian strikes on oil infrastructure have hit export revenues and severely cut domestic fuel supplies, raising concerns about public discontent. A recent think tank report suggested that Russia’s overall exports and revenues dropped by 7% and 8% respectively, with extra spending needed to import gasoline and diesel to keep the country running.
But at the same time, both Kyiv and Moscow also expect each other to break this winter, with top officials and commanders calling the season a win-or-break moment in the war, casting doubt on whether an energy truce can hold.

Pupil shoots and wounds teachers with hunting rifle in southern France
PARIS – A French middle school pupil shot and wounded a headteacher and a female staff member with a hunting rifle at a school near Marseille on Oct 12, causing panic as children ran for cover, the local mayor and a student said.
A supervisor at Joseph Lakanal college disarmed the 14-year-old before police arrived, Aubagne mayor Jean-Pierre Squillari told reporters.
Both victims were hospitalised but neither suffered life-threatening injuries, he added.
There was no immediate indication that the shooting was linked to a three-week wave of protests, some violent, that have rocked high schools across the country.
French President Emmanuel Macron condemned those incidents of violence on Oct 12.
He also said on X he stood in full support and solidarity with the injured, the students and their parents after the Oct 12 shooting.
“I salute the composure and exemplary response of the educational team, which made it possible to avoid the worst,” he said.
BFM TV said the 14-year-old student had entered the school with the rifle hidden in a guitar case. He was later detained by police.
“It’s a kid who goes to that school. He entered with a rifle, the investigation will determine how, and fired twice in a corridor towards the principal and a teacher,” Squillari said.
‘We were panicking, we ran’
One student told Reuters that her maths teacher had played down the bang of the first gunshot blast as noise from nearby construction works. A subsequent blast was followed by an alarm and classes emptied into the corridors.
“We were panicking, we ran,” the student said.
“There were two ways out: one passage to the sports hall and one passage to go outside. Survival instinct took over and I ran towards the outside.”
Far-right leader Marine Le Pen, the frontrunner in the race to replace Macron next spring, said the government was losing control of security in schools.
“Schools, which should be sanctuaries, are now places where people risk their lives. Insecurity has entered the school. Many pupils and teachers go there with a knot in their stomach.”
Macron’s education and interior ministers are due to travel to the college later in the day.
Eddy Sid, a spokesperson for the SGP-FO police union, told BFM TV there was no apparent link between the shooting and high school protests against understaffing and lack of funding for schools.
There had been no blockades at the Joseph Lakanal college, he added. REUTERS

Belarus Tests Upgraded Konkurs with Laser Guidance and Remote Launch
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
10:30:02 UTC
19:30:02 KST

The State Authority for Military Industry of the Republic of Belarus has successfully completed live-fire tests of an upgraded 9M113 Konkurs anti-tank guided missile.
The agency announced this on October 8.
During the modernization, specialists replaced the original electronic units with modern ones and installed a laser receiver in place of the missile’s wire-guidance coil.
The missile remained controllable throughout its flight over a range of at least 5 km.
In addition, the upgraded system allows the operator to launch missiles remotely.
According to the Belarusian agency, these modifications have increased the missile’s operational range and improved guidance accuracy.
Despite the demonstration, the upgraded missile’s technical specifications have not been disclosed.
Militarnyi previously reported that Belarus’s defense industry had unveiled an automated control and guidance system for the BM-21 Grad and BM-27 Uragan multiple-launch rocket systems.
The 9M113 Konkurs is a Soviet anti-tank guided missile developed to engage armored vehicles. It entered service with the Soviet Army in 1974.
The missile uses a semi-automatic guidance system. The operator keeps the sight on the target, while the control system tracks the missile’s flight and sends commands to correct its trajectory.
In the baseline version, commands are transmitted via a wire that unwinds during flight. This system does not rely on a radio link and requires the operator to track the target until impact.
The baseline 9M113 missile has a shaped-charge warhead and a range of up to 4 km when launched from a combat vehicle. The upgraded 9M113M Konkurs-M variant features a tandem shaped-charge warhead designed to engage armored vehicles equipped with reactive armor.

A New Anti-Aging Drug Looks to Turn Back the Clock on Skin Age
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
10:30:00 UTC
19:30:00 KST

A wave of biotech companies is looking to prove that it’s possible to slow down the aging process. Mountain View, California–based Rubedo Life Sciences is starting with the most outwardly visible sign: the skin.
The company’s experimental treatment is showing early promise that it may be able to reduce the appearance of aging, according to data the company presented at the Aging Research and Drug Discovery meeting in Boston earlier this month.
In a small clinical trial, Rubedo tested its topical cream on 11 people with atopic dermatitis, an inflammatory skin condition and the most common type of eczema. The drug targets a mechanism of cellular senescence, a biological state in which damaged or stressed cells permanently stop dividing but do not die. These senescent or “zombie” cells accumulate as people age and can release substances that contribute to inflammation and tissue damage, which contributes to disease.
After four weeks of using the cream, participants lowered the biological age of their skin by about two years, on average. That estimate was based on an aging “clock” designed by a different company, Mitra Bio, which performed an independent analysis on participants’ skin samples. One person in the trial had a reduction of more than 11 years in skin age. Separately, Rubedo found that its treatment was tied to a reduction in inflammation-related markers and a 10 percent increase in a type of collagen associated with skin elasticity and structure.
Biological or epigenetic age is an estimate of how well a person is aging compared to their calendar age. Aging clocks like Mitra’s attempt to calculate this number by looking at patterns of methylations, chemical modifications to DNA that regulate how genes function and can change over time. That metric doesn’t necessarily prove that the body or a particular organ or tissue has become functionally younger, though.
“Our idea is to find ways to change the trajectory of how we age,” says Marco Quarta, Rubedo’s cofounder and chief scientific officer. “Aging is complex. There are many mechanisms, but cellular senescence is one of them.”
Senescent cells are also involved in normal biological processes, such as wound healing and tumor suppression, but their accumulation over time is associated with many age-related conditions. Getting rid of them is one of the leading strategies that anti-aging and longevity companies are pursuing.
Rubedo’s approach aims to clear out senescent cells by targeting a protein known as GPX4, a gatekeeper for cell survival. By transiently turning off GPX4, the drug is designed to make senescent cells more susceptible to ferroptosis, a regulated form of cell death, while reviving stressed, non-senescent cells nearby.
In a separate study, researchers looked at the drug’s effect on actinic keratosis, a skin condition caused by sun damage and produces rough, scaly skin patches and can sometimes progress to skin cancer. In a trial of 18 people, the cream led to a 46 percent reduction in total lesions after a month of use.
Rubedo is studying the same drug for psoriasis and skin with sun damage. Soon, the company will add androgenetic alopecia, a type of hereditary hair loss, to the list. CEO Frederick Beddingfield, previously the chief medical officer at Allergan, where he launched Botox, sees potential in a lower-potency, over-the-counter version for general skin aging, which would compete with retinol. The company is also formulating the drug into a pill to study whether it can be used to treat metabolic conditions associated with aging.
“It's great to see them doing this work,” says Eric Verdin, president and CEO of the Buck Institute for Research on Aging, which has developed several aging clocks. “I would probably be a little circumspect about what these clocks really measure, because right now, there are a proliferation of them.”
Plus, the results that patients will care about is how their skin actually looks and feels, not a result from a biological aging test.
And senescence is just one piece of the aging puzzle, says Anthony Rossi, a dermatologist at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center. “Some senescent cells are good because they turn things off, like cancer progression.”
He says the science is novel but the work is still very early-stage, and it will be interesting to see how it affects biological aging in people with healthy skin, not just those with certain skin conditions. “The best anti-aging routine right now is sleep, a good diet, and exercise,” he says. For now, at least.
