Americans Hall and Woodford win Nobel Prize in economics for stabilisation models
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
10:29:53 UTC
19:29:53 KST

The economics prize is the only Nobel not among the original five created in the will of Swedish scientist Alfred Nobel, who died in 1896.
American economists Robert Hall and Michael Woodford were awarded the Nobel economics prize on Monday for their work on how monetary and fiscal policy can help stabilise fluctuations in the economy.
"The laureates' work has provided us with a stable theoretical foundation for the models that are now used by central banks and governments around the world," the jury at the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences said in a statement.
"With them, we are better equipped to deal with shocks in the economy, such as energy crises or sudden changes in how much households consume," John Hassler, chair of the prize committee, said in the statement.
During the oil crises in the 1970s, the existing Keynesian models long used to determine when and how measures should be implemented to tackle recessions or other economic fluctuations no longer worked.
That prompted Hall and Woodford to develop new tools for understanding which policy responses could be the most effective.
"Rather than basing the models on statistical links between macroeconomic variables, such as inflation, production and consumption, they chose to build them on a microeconomic foundation," the academy jury said.
"This encompasses an understanding for how the total mass of individual households and businesses affect the economy through their actions."
The economics prize is the only Nobel not among the original five created in the will of Swedish scientist Alfred Nobel, who died in 1896.
It was created instead through a donation from the Swedish central bank in 1968, leading detractors to dub it "a false Nobel."
But like the Nobels in chemistry and physics, the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences chooses the winner and follows the same selection process.
Last year, the award went to American-Israeli Joel Mokyr, France's Philippe Aghion and Canada's Peter Howitt for research into how technology drives and affects growth.
Like the other Nobels, the economics prize consists of a diploma, a gold medal and a $1.2 million (€1 million) cheque.
The laureates will receive their prizes at formal ceremonies on 10 December, the anniversary of the death in 1896 of scientist Alfred Nobel, who created the prizes in his will.

Valkyrie ‘fighter drone’ makes first flight in Europe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
10:27:07 UTC
19:27:07 KST

- Airbus and Kratos completed the first European flight of the U740 Valkyrie, with a rocket-assisted takeoff and speeds up to Mach 0.8.
- The companies aim to deliver a combat-ready drone wingman to Germany by 2029, but no order has been placed.
Airbus and Kratos have flown the Valkyrie uncrewed combat aircraft in Europe for the first time, a step toward offering Germany a drone wingman for its Eurofighters by 2029.
The flight, announced on Oct. 12, took place at a test site in northern Europe that the companies did not name. Airbus Defence and Space CEO Mike Schoellhorn told Reuters it happened on Sept. 29. The aircraft, which Airbus calls the U740 Valkyrie, took off without a runway using a rocket booster, flew at several altitudes and speeds up to Mach 0.8, and had its mission changed in flight. The companies said all test objectives were met.
This first flight did not yet carry Airbus’ own mission system, called MARS. Airbus plans to install it for later, more complex tests. MARS is the software and hardware that lets the aircraft fly missions on its own and coordinate groups of drones, with a human kept “on the loop” to approve critical decisions. Airbus pitches it as a European “brain” that gives Germany and other buyers full control of the software, data and mission hardware rather than depending on the U.S. maker.
“In an increasingly complex and contested threat environment, air forces require affordable combat mass,” said Mike Schoellhorn, CEO of Airbus Defence and Space. “By pairing Kratos’ proven airframe as a ‘program of record’ with Airbus’ sovereign European mission system, we are able to offer a robust, sovereign, affordable, and combat-ready CCA system by the end of the decade.”
The Valkyrie is based on Kratos’ XQ-58, which has been flying in the United States since 2019. The European version is 9.1 meters (30 feet) long with an 8.2-meter (27-foot) wingspan and weighs about 3 metric tons (6,600 pounds) at takeoff. Airbus says it has a range of more than 5,000 km (3,100 miles), a ceiling of 45,000 feet (13,700 meters), an internal weapons bay and pylons under the wings. It can be launched from a rail without a runway or take off and land conventionally.
“First flights typically include plenty of learning opportunities, but with the maturity of the Valkyrie system and the well-integrated Airbus and Kratos team, this flight was an amazing success,” said Eric DeMarco, president and CEO of Kratos.
Airbus and Kratos announced their partnership in July 2025, aiming to give the German Air Force an operational collaborative combat aircraft, or CCA, by 2029. Earlier this year, Airbus said it was preparing the first two Valkyries for flight testing in Germany. Schoellhorn told Reuters the company expects to test the drone teamed with Eurofighters in 2027. In the United States, the U.S. Marine Corps has picked the Valkyrie as the basis for its first operational collaborative combat aircraft.

Iran deaf athletics team exceed expectations: chief
TEHRAN - Iran Deaf Sports Federation President Masoud Farahani has praised the national deaf athletics team’s performance at the Asian Championships in Penang, Malaysia, saying the team achieved the best possible results at minimal cost.
Iran’s national deaf athletics team secured 12 medals — five gold, three silver and four bronze — to finish runners-up at the Asian Championships in Penang, Malaysia. The result highlights the immense potential of Iran’s deaf athletes and their ability to compete with the continent’s best.
“First and foremost, I would like to congratulate the great Iranian nation, the country’s deaf community, our champion athletes, their dedicated families and hard-working coaches on this valuable achievement,” Farahani said.
“The message behind this success is clear: hearing impairment is never a limitation on ability, talent or determination. Through hard work, discipline, self-belief and perseverance, our athletes have demonstrated that, given equal opportunities and adequate facilities, they can proudly raise Iran’s flag on the international stage,” he added.
“These medals represent more than sporting success. They are a source of hope and confidence, promoting social inclusion and participation for millions of people with disabilities and their families.,” Farahani added.
“In the women’s events, Iran fielded two athletes in the 10,000m and 5,000m races, as well as one competitor in the discus throw. Fortunately, discus thrower Elaheh Golmohammadi captured the gold medal. However, Sima Abdollahi and Zahra Chehreh Alam had to compete in events outside their specialist disciplines. The women’s 5,000m and 10,000m races were cancelled before the competition began because the number of entrants failed to meet the minimum requirement. As a result, the two athletes were unable to compete in their preferred events and did not win medals in the disciplines they entered,” the president stated.
“I had not predicted that we would finish as runners-up. I expected us to place somewhere between third and fourth,” Farahani said.
“Several sports were contested at these championships, but we competed only in athletics and still managed to finish second overall. We won the most medals and achieved the best possible result with the least expenditure.”
He added that sending the team to the competition had been challenging amid the prevailing circumstances in Iran, including the country’s recent involvement in war and fluctuations in foreign exchange rates. Despite these financial and logistical difficulties, the delegation made the trip and returned with an outstanding result.
“Our focus is not simply on winning a handful of medals at a single competition. Our goal is to establish a sustainable pathway for talent identification, athlete development, improving coaches’ expertise and strengthening our presence at Asian and world-level competitions,” he said.
“We must make greater use of the potential across our provinces, improve training facilities and ensure that talented deaf athletes have opportunities to progress, regardless of where they live or their families’ financial circumstances.
“To sustain these results, we must also strengthen specialist support, medical care, sports nutrition and regular training camps.”
The Iranian federation’s president said the team’s performance was an encouraging sign of what could be achieved through determination and efficient use of resources, while stressing that continued investment in athlete development would be essential to maintaining Iran’s competitiveness on the continental and global stages.

Taiwan aims to raise pilot retirement age to 58 as new F-16V jets arrive
Addressing fatigue concerns, chief of staff says the island’s air force has moved away from scrambling fighters to shadowing PLA aircraft
The proposed retention scheme comes as the island’s air force prepares to form operational squadrons around 66 new F-16V Block 70 fighters ordered from the United States, adding pressure to an already stretched pool of experienced pilots.
Under the plan, pilots could serve until they turn 58 – up from about 48 for lieutenant colonels and 52 for colonels – extending their current service limits of 26 and 30 years, respectively.
The air force would also create 72 additional posts for highly qualified lieutenant colonel and colonel pilots who have served at least 14 years, allowing them to retain their rank and focus on flying rather than command or administrative duties.
Defence Minister Wellington Koo Li-hsiung said on Monday that the arrangement was designed to keep experienced pilots in uniform when many faced a choice between remaining in the military and pursuing longer, potentially more lucrative careers with commercial airlines.

====================================================================================================

Spain's housing crisis is testing the limits of Europe's welfare state
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
10:23:03 UTC
19:23:03 KST

When 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal was carried from her Madrid home on a stretcher last month, images of her eviction spread across Spain and turned a long-running housing crisis into a political revolt.
Abascal had lived in the apartment for more than seven decades.
After the property changed hands, she could not afford the sharply increased rent and was eventually removed from the home, despite repeated efforts by tenant activists to stop the eviction.
She died in hospital last week, two weeks after being evicted. Her lawyer did not disclose a cause of death. But her story has become a symbol of a contradiction at the heart of Spain's housing crisis.
Housing is recognised as a right under Spain's constitution, yet the country has one of the smallest social housing stocks in the European Union, at just 1.7 percent.
This figure is nowhere near enough, according to political analyst Klaus Jurgens.
“We can argue that Spain’s social welfare model has become a rather capitalist one, in which access to housing as a social right is severely restricted, particularly during economic crises when people struggle to make ends meet,” Jurgens tells TRT World.
This is not the right direction, especially under a left-leaning government, Jurgens argues.
“Spain seems to have overlooked the importance of housing, perhaps because it considered itself a welfare state where everything was going well. But it neglects the fact that people also need a roof over their heads and the private market is not the solution.”
Some 73 percent of Spaniards own their homes, but more than half of people aged 18 to 34 now live with their parents or depend on them financially.
House prices rose at three times the rate of wages last year.
A right on paper, a market in practice
Spain's shortage is severe. The country's central bank estimates a deficit of around 750,000 homes, potentially reaching one million by 2028.
But the problem isn't just the number of homes. Construction has failed to keep pace with demand in the cities where people need housing, while planning remains fragmented between the central government, regions and municipalities.
Short-term rentals and rising demand in urban centres have added further pressure.
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez's Socialist government attempted to intervene directly. Its housing package included stronger protections against evictions, measures to limit rent pressures and restrictions affecting corporate purchases of property.
Parliament rejected the package after right-wing lawmakers and the Catalan party Junts opposed it, arguing that tighter regulation would further restrict supply.
Three days later, Sanchez announced that he would dissolve parliament and call a snap general election for November 29, following the defeat of two government housing decrees by the People's Party (PP), Vox and Junts.
Jurgens argues that even if the snap election brings the opposition to power, making social housing a priority would not offer an immediate solution.
“How long will that take? You cannot build tens of thousands of homes in a week. Even under the most optimistic assumptions, increasing the current 1.7 percent share would take between two and four years.”
For Jurgens, the political fallout from the housing crisis reflects a broader revolt against the establishment, fuelled by dissatisfaction with living standards and social conditions.
“We have the migration issue in enclaves such as Ceuta, dissatisfaction with social conditions and, sometimes, it takes just one issue to trigger a wider revolt,” Jurgens says.
“Sanchez has a reputation for coming back from political setbacks. Whoever wins the next election will have to contend with widespread public discontent,” he adds.
A broader European problem
Spain's crisis reflects a wider European failure to guarantee secure housing, although the pressures vary across countries.
In Greece, almost 29 percent of the population lived in households spending more than 40 percent of their disposable income on housing in 2024, the highest share in the EU.
Ireland's rents have more than doubled since 2010, leaving thousands reliant on emergency accommodation.
Even Germany, with its larger social housing sector, is not immune, as households spent an average of 25 percent of their disposable income on housing in 2024.
Jurgens argues that Spain’s housing crisis reflects the broader European crisis, warning that dissatisfaction with living standards and purchasing power is fuelling support for fringe parties.
“Look at Germany and the far right AfD, or the UK and Nigel Farage’s Reform UK. When people are dissatisfied with their purchasing power, they tend to vote for parties on the political fringes,” Jurgens says.
“This is a very dangerous situation in many European countries,” he adds.
“In Vienna, 43 percent of the housing stock is social housing. In Germany, the figure is just 3.3 percent, while in the United Kingdom it stands at 17 percent. Even when comparing Germany’s 3.3 percent with Spain’s 1.7 percent, we must acknowledge that Germany’s figure is also insufficient.”
Housing insecurity and the rise of the far-right
The problem across Europe extends beyond affordability to the risk of losing a stable home altogether.
Eurostat data for 2023 found that 4.9 percent of people aged 16 and older across the EU had experienced housing difficulties at some point in their lives, including staying temporarily with friends or relatives, using emergency accommodation or sleeping in a public space.
The share rose to 8.5 percent among people at risk of poverty or social exclusion, compared with 3.9 percent among those not at risk.
Greek-administered Southern Cyprus recorded the highest rate at 11.2 percent, followed by Finland at 10.8 percent, while Denmark, France and Sweden each recorded rates above 9 percent.
The consequences are also closely tied to escaping poverty. Across the EU, financial hardship accounted for 25.9 percent of reported housing difficulties, while finding a job was the most common route out of them, cited by 26.5 percent of people who had overcome such difficulties.
Moving into social or subsidised private housing accounted for another 20.4 percent. That many people rely on employment to regain stable housing, while one in five overcome the problem through subsidised accommodation, highlights the limits of leaving housing security to individual purchasing power.
Spain's exceptionally small social housing stock makes that contradiction particularly visible, but the European figures suggest the underlying challenge is shared across very different welfare systems.
“Look at the eastern German states, where the AfD is currently so strong. People don't vote for fringe parties because they want to stage a revolution. They want to express their dissatisfaction,” Jurgens says.
“The vast majority of these voters are neither far-right nor far-left. They are simply disgruntled.”
“If there is political will, it is possible to build a social housing system that provides genuine social welfare without bankrupting government finances. It can be funded through the national budget,” Jurgens says.
“This brings us back to public dissatisfaction. Investing in defence is necessary, unfortunately, but if that spending becomes disproportionate to the needs of people who cannot afford a roof over their heads, something is wrong with society and with the social welfare model across Europe,” he adds.

On the Macao side, police plan to expand eligibility for iris recognition clearance and add more automated lanes to keep travelers moving. ■

Xinhua Headlines: Extended holiday boosts Chinese travel demand across Europe
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
18:21:11 CST
19:21:11 KST

* According to Trip.com Group data, 62 percent of Europe-bound flight bookings from Sept. 25 to Oct. 7 were for departures before Sept. 30. The average stay in Europe increased from 14.8 days in 2025 to 16.1 days.
* Tour guide Zhang Hongbo in Barcelona has noticed that Chinese visitors are increasingly willing to spend on quality restaurants, attentive service and admission to historic buildings they might once have viewed only from outside.
* Aviation consultancy CAPA said in an April analysis that capacity between China and Western Europe had surpassed 2019 levels, driven by Chinese airlines.
WARSAW, Oct. 12 (Xinhua) -- For Chinese tourist Zou Yini and her friends, some of the greatest pleasures of their National Day holiday in Europe came from strolling through Barcelona's neighborhoods, browsing shops, and sampling local cuisine.
After visiting France, the three continued to the Spanish city, where they spent several days exploring its culture and relishing its laid-back atmosphere.
In China, this year's travel window combined two holidays separated by three days: the Mid-Autumn Festival from Sept. 25 to 27, and the National Day holiday from Oct. 1 to 7, giving ambitious travelers a possible 13-day getaway.
The extended travel period fueled greater demand for long-haul trips to Europe, with some countries welcoming more visitors than last year and new opportunities for businesses across the continent.
LONGER HOLIDAYS, WIDER HORIZONS
For European tourism businesses, this year's holiday travel season began before Oct. 1, the first day of China's seven-day National Day holiday or Golden Week, as Chinese visitors set off earlier and stayed longer.
According to Trip.com Group data, 62 percent of Europe-bound flight bookings from Sept. 25 to Oct. 7 were for departures before Sept. 30. The average stay in Europe increased from 14.8 days in 2025 to 16.1 days.
The longer holiday period brought fresh business opportunities. In Italy, hotel bookings by Chinese travelers more than doubled year on year during the period, while flight bookings rose more than 40 percent, according to Italy's tourism industry federation Federturismo, citing Trip.com Group data.
Interest also extended to destinations in Italy such as Bolzano, Sorrento and the Dolomites, giving travelers opportunities to combine visits to major cities with mountain scenery and regional attractions.
France saw a similar demand. Citing Trip.com data, Tourism publication L'Echo touristique reported in September that hotel bookings in France by Chinese mainland travelers from Oct. 1 to 7, also known as the Golden Week, increased 129 percent year on year.
Paris remained the main draw, with bookings up 132 percent, but the 15 most-booked destinations outside the capital posted average growth of 123 percent. They included Chamonix, Lyon, Strasbourg, Marseille, Bordeaux and Nice.
Demand was also strong for organized tours. Shanghai-based Spring Tour said its Golden Week packages covering Spain and Portugal, the Balkans, Northern Europe and Greece had sold out by mid-August.
A representative of the Association of Chinese Tour Guides in Hungary said seven-day tours linking Hungary, the Czech Republic, Slovakia and Austria sold out by late August.
BEYOND LANDMARKS
The changing pattern of Chinese travel is also reflected in how visitors spend their time and money.
In Paris, Chinese tourist Zhang Wen visited the Louvre, but another experience offered a different perspective on the city: a musical walk through Montmartre.
Singer and guide Anne-Sophie Guerrier brought the neighborhood's musical history to life through songs and stories at the former homes and performance venues of French singers, and provided a Chinese-language guidebook for Chinese visitors.
"The combination of live performances, stories and the neighborhood's historic atmosphere made the experience lively, romantic and memorable," Zhang said. "It offered me a different way to discover the culture and history of Paris."
Tour guide Zhang Hongbo in Barcelona has noticed that Chinese visitors are increasingly willing to spend on quality restaurants, attentive service and admission to historic buildings they might once have viewed only from outside.
"Now a lot of people want to know more about Spanish culture: how people live, how they have fun, how they eat," he said.
In Switzerland, Chinese visitors are seeking a different kind of experience.
A Shanghai tourist surnamed Zhao spent several days exploring the mountains in the Jungfrau region. Immersing himself in nature mattered more than simply visiting a long list of attractions.
Tourism providers are adapting to these changing preferences. Oliver Hammel, CEO of Jungfrau Railways, said large Chinese tour groups had increasingly given way to smaller groups since the pandemic, while independent travel had also grown. Many independent visitors now use travel passes to explore multiple attractions across the region.
In the Balkans, tour operator Yang Xiaoliang said his company served 329 Chinese visitors in 64 groups during the National Day holiday, with an average of about five travelers per group. Families and friends made up a significant share of customers choosing eight- to 10-day itineraries.
The company's packages combine transport and accommodation with optional experiences such as wine tasting, boat trips, local dining and cultural activities, allowing travelers to tailor their spending to their interests.
FACTORS BEHIND TRAVEL BOOM
The most immediate factor behind the surge in long-haul travel was more time off than usual this year, making trips involving long flights and multiple destinations more feasible.
Gu Sui, general manager of China Southern Airlines' Spain office, said taking extra days off around public holidays had spread departures over a longer period, easing congestion during the traditional peak travel period.
Longer stays also allow travelers to spread the cost of intercontinental travel over more days of sightseeing and leisure, making distant destinations more worthwhile.
Improved air connectivity was another factor.
Aviation consultancy CAPA said in an April analysis that capacity between China and Western Europe had surpassed 2019 levels, driven by Chinese airlines.
As of early October, about 85 weekly nonstop passenger flights connected Germany with destinations on the Chinese mainland, with Frankfurt accounting for roughly two-thirds of the total.
This year's new services and increased frequencies included Air China's Frankfurt-Beijing Daxing route and China Southern's Guangzhou-Urumqi-Frankfurt service, as well as more frequent flights between Frankfurt and Shanghai.
In Croatia, Air China's new Beijing-Bucharest-Zagreb service opened another gateway for Chinese visitors.
Zagreb recorded a 7 percent year-on-year increase in Chinese arrivals and an 8 percent rise in their overnight stays in September, according to Martina Bienenfeld, director of the Zagreb Tourist Board.
"This is a very promising start, especially considering that only a few weeks have passed since the new route was established," she said.
European destinations are also working to turn improved connectivity into deeper engagement with Chinese visitors. One example is the "More than 88 hours in Madrid" campaign, which encourages extended stays in the Spanish capital.
The Polish Tourism Organisation's 2026 action plan includes updating a WeChat-based guide for independent travelers with interactive maps and attraction information, as well as pilot training and certification programs to help hotels, restaurants and attractions better serve Chinese guests.
The Zagreb Tourist Board maintains a presence in Beijing and Shanghai. It recently promoted the Croatian capital's year-round events and cuisine in Beijing.
Zagreb is also showcasing an art installation at the Shanghai International Light Festival through mid-October, as the two cities mark 46 years of sister-city ties.
"All these activities, combined with the new air link, are vital components of our long-term strategy to position Zagreb in the Chinese market," said Bienenfeld.

US economists Hall, Woodford win 2026 Nobel Prize in Economics
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
10:19:07 UTC
19:19:07 KST

Gokhan Ergocun
12 October 2026•Update: 12 October 2026
US economists Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford were awarded the 2026 Nobel Prize in Economics "for microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilization."
The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences announced the winners of the 2026 Nobel Prize in Economics during a news conference.
Hall and Woodford demonstrated how to reconstruct economic models to revitalize stabilization policies.
Their approach focuses on building models on microeconomic foundations rather than relying on statistical links between macroeconomic variables like inflation, production and consumption.
This method provides a deeper understanding of how the combined actions of individual households and businesses affect the overall economy.
Born in the US state of California in 1943, Hall continues his work as an economics professor at Stanford University.
Woodford, born in the US state of Massachusetts in 1955, serves as an economics professor at Columbia University.

X-Bow to build boosters for U.S. Army’s cheap cruise missile
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
10:18:41 UTC
19:18:41 KST

- Leidos selected X-Bow Systems to develop and produce booster motors for the U.S. Army’s Low-Cost Containerized Munition, with full-rate production planned in 2027.
- Leidos’ agreement covers an initial 3,000 missiles; the value of X-Bow’s deal and the number of motors were not disclosed.
Leidos has picked X-Bow Systems, a New Mexico rocket motor maker, to develop and build the booster motors for the U.S. Army’s Low-Cost Containerized Munition, a ground-launched cruise missile the Pentagon wants to buy in large numbers.
X-Bow announced the selection on Oct. 12 at the Association of the U.S. Army’s annual meeting in Washington. Under the agreement, the company will design the motor, run qualification tests and static test fires, and then move to full-rate production in 2027. Neither company disclosed the value of the deal or how many motors X-Bow will build.
The booster is the solid rocket motor that pushes a missile out of its launch container and up to flying speed in the first seconds after launch. Solid rocket motors have become one of the main bottlenecks in U.S. missile production, with most of the work long concentrated among a handful of large suppliers.
“Modern conflict is decided by how many rounds you can put downrange, not how exquisite each one is,” said X-Bow founder and CEO Jason Hundley.
The Department of War launched the Low-Cost Containerized Munition program in May, signing framework agreements with Leidos, Anduril, CoAspire and Zone 5 Technologies as part of its “Arsenal of Freedom” effort to field precision weapons in volume. Leidos said its agreement covers an initial 3,000 missiles. The Pentagon has laid out plans to buy roughly 10,000 low-cost cruise missiles over three years across the program.
Leidos’ design builds on its AGM-190A Small Cruise Missile, known as Black Arrow, which was developed for launch from aircraft. The company says its containerized version is about twice the size of the AGM-190A, carries more fuel for longer range, and uses a modular airframe and open architecture so it can be upgraded quickly. It will be ground-launched at first, with possible ship- and air-launched versions later. Production is planned at Leidos facilities in Huntsville, Alabama, and McEwen, Tennessee.
X-Bow, based in Albuquerque, builds solid rocket motors using its own additive manufacturing process for the propellant. The company said the Leidos award is the sixth new propulsion program it has won in 2026, across the U.S. Navy, U.S. Army and the Missile Defense Agency, and that it recently completed its first major production contract with more than 2,100 rocket motors delivered. In July, the Missile Defense Agency awarded X-Bow about $11 million to develop a solid rocket motor for a low-cost interceptor, and the company has also worked on motors for the U.S. Navy’s Standard Missile family.

Nearly half of foreign TV series on Russian streaming service have been censored,Mediazona reports
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
10:15:53 UTC
19:15:53 KST

Nearly half of foreign TV series on Russian streaming service have been censored,Mediazona reports
Nearly half of the foreign television series available on the streaming service Amediateka have been censored, according to the independent Russian news outlet Mediazona, which examined 472 series, comparing the original versions with their Russian adaptations frame by frame.
Mediazona found 75 hours of censored scenes across 200 of the series it reviewed. More than half of that total — 44 hours — involved LGBTQ+ topics. The second-largest category, 12 hours, involved political content: mentions of Vladimir Putin, references to the war in Ukraine, and real or fictional episodes from the history of Russia or the USSR. Scenes involving incest, pedophilia, drugs, and “non-traditional” sex were also frequently cut.
Beyond outright scene removal, Amediateka often “softens” words and concepts in translation. When a character’s homosexuality comes up, for example, the line “he’s gay” becomes “he’s different.”
According to Mediazona, partner studios produce translations for Amediateka following a specific set of guidelines that outline translation requirements. Amediateka then reviews the translated, corrected, and dubbed content and makes additional edits.
Amediateka is the official Russian distributor of series from studios such as HBO, Showtime, AMC, and Warner Bros. Other major streaming services, including Okko and “Kinopoisk,” use Amediateka’s translations for these series.
Mediazona reports that Amediateka has been cited for its content at least six times: four citations for incorrect age ratings, and two under the law on “propaganda of nontraditional relationships.”

Far-Right Election Groups Are Now Targeting Nursing Homes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
10:15:00 UTC
19:15:00 KST

With just weeks to go until the midterms, election denial groups have found a new target: nursing homes.
The groups, led by the right-wing Election Integrity Network, have claimed without evidence that left-wing organizations are perpetrating voter fraud inside nursing homes, care homes, and assisted-living facilities. The network is now recruiting their followers to contact and question those facilities.
“These left-wing groups go into the nursing homes, and they go into the group homes, and they basically steal the votes of these most vulnerable,” Cleta Mitchell, the Election Integrity Network’s founder, said in a recent appearance on Steve Bannon’s War Room show.
As evidence, Mitchell referenced a case in Wisconsin from 2020 in which a sheriff alleged that eight residents in a care home had their votes filled out for them. The Wisconsin Election Commission rejected the claims. Mitchell told Bannon the case could have cost president Donald Trump the 2020 election, though that wouldn’t be possible: Trump lost Wisconsin in 2020 by over 20,000 votes.
Mitchell’s group has been urging followers to download a toolkit from the Election Integrity Network website and email and call nursing homes in their area. The group has also created multiple images for followers to share on social media which reinforce the idea of widespread voter fraud at nursing homes.
In one campaign, the network shared a series of posts that mapped residential care facilities in competitive congressional districts in states including Arizona, California, New Hampshire, Pennsylvania, and Virginia. The posts identified “vulnerable residents” who “may become targets for political predators seeking easy access to ballots.”
Mitchell and the Election Integrity Network did not respond to requests for comment.
The effort is part of a much broader push by election deniers to undermine trust in the midterms. And just like the claims of noncitizen voting and widespread mail-in voter fraud, they have been supercharged by the Trump administration.
In July, the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) issued a memo that removed previous guidance on how staff at nursing homes could help residents to vote, such as assisting with mail-in voting or transporting residents to polling locations. The new memo replaced that guidance with threats of prosecution if staff “engage in inappropriate coercion or other violations of residents’ rights.”
The memo also claimed that the agency has “become aware of several allegations of instances in which resident rights were unlawfully violated.” However, the examples cited in the memo did not lead to any proven cases of voter fraud. CMS did not respond to a request for comment.
In August, senators led by Elizabeth Warren and Alex Padilla slammed the changes, writing in a letter to CMS that rather than protecting the country’s 2 million nursing home residents, the new rules would disenfranchise them.
“CMS issued a memo that appears to be an attempt to intimidate nursing home staff from assisting residents in the voting process,” the senators wrote in the letter, addressed to CMS administrator Mehmet Oz (who himself has flip-flopped on whether the 2020 election was rigged).
But now, with less than a month to go before the midterms, groups like the Election Integrity Network—which has close ties to the White House—are pushing the narrative that nursing homes are a hive of vote rigging activity.
Another election denial group, the New York–based Project Civicia, has launched a similar campaign, entitled “Adopt a Care Facility.” The group told WIRED that it could not share how many people were taking part in the campaign but repeated the claims made by CMS about voter fraud in Wisconsin, in addition to other allegations.
“We do not presume wrongdoing by a facility because its residents need voting assistance,” Kim Hermance, cofounder and president of Project Civica, tells WIRED. “There are other public cases of forged absentee applications and similar problems. Separately, in our own review of New York records, we noticed people over 85 who appeared to register and vote for the first time shortly before an election. That is not illegal by itself, but it raised a basic question about how facilities handle the process.”

D66 wants children heard without parents’ consent in abuse cases
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
10:13:06 UTC
19:13:06 KST

D66 wants children heard without parents’ consent in abuse cases
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Children who show serious signs of abuse would be interviewed quickly, and without their parents’ consent if necessary, under a draft bill published by coalition party D66 on Monday.
The proposal, by MPs Marijke Synhaeve and Hanneke van der Werf, has been put online so organisations can respond before it goes to parliament, broadcaster NOS reported. “What we want,” Synhaeve said, “is for children to be better heard, seen and helped.”
Currently, care workers can normally only contact a child if the parents or guardians agree. Exceptions are possible under strict conditions, but they are complicated and rarely used. Recent serious abuse cases have led leaders to consider altering policies.
Under what the MPs call the “child first act”, a specialist team would have to hear the child within 48 hours when there are signs of a criminal offence.
The team would include medical, youth care, safety and justice experts, and would draw up a plan covering protection, support and, if needed, prosecution.
The approach is based on the Barnahus model, Icelandic for “children’s house”, which is already used in many other countries.
Missed signals
D66 first announced the plan in June, citing two cases in which children’s calls for help went unanswered. The foster parents of a 10-year-old girl in Vlaardingen were jailed for 8 years last November for abuse that left her permanently disabled.
Government inspectors found that the girl had made several efforts to get help but was ignored.
In May, two women in the Groningen town of Stadskanaal were arrested on suspicion of severely abusing a 6-year-old girl and a 7-year-old boy. In both cases, signals from the children or people around them were not properly followed up, NOS said.
A majority of MPs backed similar ideas during a recent debate on domestic violence, news agency ANP reported in June. Far-right JA21 MP Ingrid Coenradie also put forward the same idea in that debate.
Synhaeve said she does not expect the bill to create a lot of extra work or lead to more children being taken into care. She said it would instead improve cooperation between agencies.

Estonian politicians call for changes to president's role and election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
10:12:00 UTC
19:12:00 KST

Estonian politicians call for changes to president's role and election
As Ülle Madise takes office as Estonia's next president, politicians are debating changes to the presidency itself, from its powers to how the head of state is elected.
Madise attended an ecumenical harvest service at Tallinn's St. Mary's Cathedral (Toomkirik) on Sunday, continuing a tradition that has evolved over the years. Estonia's first three presidents following the restoration of independence attended thanksgiving services on their inauguration days.
While Kersti Kaljulaid declined, Alar Karis and now President-elect Ülle Madise have taken part in ecumenical services bringing together representatives of the country's various churches.
Beyond such ceremonial traditions, politicians say the presidency itself may need a rethink, including the powers the office holds and how the head of state is elected.
Kristjan Järvan (Isamaa), a deputy mayor of Tallinn, pointed to the head of state's exclusive authority in Estonia to declare martial law.
"If that one person is missing or unable to make a decision, no other mechanism exists for declaring martial law," he said.
MP and former justice minister Madis Timpson (Reform) said the President of the Republic Election Act should be amended so that if the Riigikogu fails to elect a president, the electoral college would make the final choice rather than sending the process back to the Riigikogu.
The candidate to receive the most votes in the electoral college would simply win, he explained, adding that "this is one thing that does not reflect well on Estonia as a country."
Direct elections
Conservative People's Party of Estonia (EKRE) MP Anti Poolamets, meanwhile, argued that direct elections would give the president greater authority.
"An honor guard won't save the president; we need to focus on substance," he said, calling for greater independence in foreign policy as well.
"Give the president more freedom to think independently on foreign policy, rather than treating them like the Foreign Ministry's lapdog who gets kicked out of Kadriorg the moment they express an opinion," Poolamets added.
MP and Social Democratic Party (SDE) chair Lauri Läänemets disagreed, warning that direct elections would likely produce a party politician rather than a nonpartisan head of state.
"Under the current Constitution, a nonpartisan president who provides oversight and sees the bigger picture is much better than a politician elected by the people," he explained.
Ülle Madise will be sworn in at the Riigikogu on Monday at 3 p.m.

Kremlin rejects Ukrainian leader's idea of a 60-day ceasefire, says it wants an overall peace deal
MOSCOW, Oct 12 - The Kremlin on Monday rejected a 60-day ceasefire idea proposed by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy to allow his country to hold presidential elections, saying it wanted an overall peace deal instead.
"Please tell Putin, give us two months, 60 days of total ceasefire, 60 days, and we will organise elections," Zelenskiy told ABC's "This Week" on Sunday.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters on Monday that Russia wanted a long-term peace deal rather than a temporary ceasefire.

Russia has long pressed Ukraine to hold elections and says that its failure to do so makes Zelenskiy an illegitimate leader. Elections in wartime are prohibited by Ukrainian law. REUTERS

Bardella antisemitism dispute tests French far right's decade-long makeover
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
10:10:22 UTC
19:10:22 KST

Bardella antisemitism dispute tests French far right's decade-long makeover
PARIS, Oct 12 - Joseph Martin saw his hopes of becoming a far-right National Rally (RN) lawmaker derailed in 2024 after journalists unearthed a seemingly antisemitic post.
It was RN president Jordan Bardella who initially withdrew support for Martin's candidacy, seeking to show zero tolerance for antisemitism as the party tried to convince voters it had shed its toxic past and was ready for top office.
So as the RN closes ranks around Bardella while he grapples with his own accusations of antisemitism – which he denies – Martin said the RN chief should be held to the same standard and step aside while the claims are investigated.
"He judged me, condemned me and excluded me from the RN," said Martin, who was eventually cleared to run after the RN agreed his post was not antisemitic. However, he lost and saw his subsequent application to represent the party in future votes rejected, essentially ending his political career.
The discrepancy between how the RN handled accusations against the two men - one the rising star of the party and the other a little-known regional candidate - raises questions about one of its most fundamental claims: that it has decisively broken with the antisemitism that marked parts of its history.
"There's been packaging, cosmetics and strategy, but the ideas persist," said Sciences-Po university political scientist Gilles Ivaldi.
BARDELLA STANDS HIS GROUND
Bardella has denied the allegations by investigative outlet Mediapart, which published purported antisemitic and conspiratorial comments he made in chats as a teenager, calling them "crude fakes" and saying he would file defamation lawsuits.
Still, the scandal represents the gravest threat yet to the 31-year-old's rapid political ascent, while also posing a headache for RN presidential candidate Marine Le Pen as she seeks to win the presidency after three failed attempts.
Le Pen, who leads polls ahead of next year's vote, has led a decade-long rebrand of the RN, while Bardella has visited Israel to show the party is free of the antisemitism for which its founder, Marine's father Jean-Marie Le Pen, was convicted.
"This affair shines a harsh light on what the National Rally really is," said Socialist lawmaker Guillaume Garot. However, he also acknowledged the controversy was competing for attention with a long list of voter concerns, from high school protests and a weak economy to geopolitics.
ALLEGATIONS MAY HURT LE PEN IN RUN-OFF VOTE
The RN has rallied to Bardella's defence, while also playing down the scandal. "I think it has absolutely no impact on the ground whatsoever," Le Pen aide Renaud Labaye told Reuters.
Some 74% of the French believe the messages are problematic if true, according to an IFOP poll for LCI TV, but only 21% say their opinion of Bardella has deteriorated.
Bardella struck a defiant tone when challenged by a Mediapart journalist at a press conference last week.
"Your little operation doesn't seem to be cutting through," he said. "You'd have loved to see me on my knees, but you clearly don't know me very well."
Ivaldi said the RN's most loyal voters were unlikely to abandon the party as their priorities were purchasing power, energy prices, immigration and crime. But the scandal could hurt Le Pen in a run-off, when victory would depend on attracting conservative voters beyond the RN's traditional base.
"If there is an impact, it is more likely to be among second-round voters, particularly those who pay closer attention to the RN's ideological profile," he said.
INTERNAL TENSIONS
The controversy comes at a delicate moment in the relationship between Le Pen and her protege Bardella, who had been the party's de facto presidential candidate until a Paris appeals court cleared her to run in a shock July ruling.
Bardella had increasingly asserted his independence in the run-up to that verdict, and party officials said frictions have since grown, including over the RN's rapprochement with Le Pen's niece, Marion Maréchal, an anti-abortion firebrand and potential Bardella rival.
RN Senator Joshua Hochart played down the tensions but said Bardella was willing to make his disagreement known.
"Bardella isn't just Marine Le Pen's protégé. His views count and he's right to say when something isn't working," he said.
Although Le Pen has backed Bardella over the antisemitism claims, political rivals and analysts say he has been weakened.
"The case complicates Marine Le Pen's campaign," Ivaldi said. "He is no longer the major asset he was for her."
And in a party with a long history of sidelining ambitious politicians from outside the Le Pen clan, Bardella's future remains uncertain, Ivaldi said.
Eric Zemmour, a former presidential candidate from the extreme-right Reconquest party, was blunt about Bardella's diminished status.
"Jordan Bardella is in the process of being marginalized from the heart of the RN," he said on RTL radio on Monday, predicting he would now never become Le Pen's prime minister. "It's finished all that." REUTERS

EU deal with China limits imports of hybrid electric vehicles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
10:10:13 UTC
19:10:13 KST

The EU is to limit the number of hybrid electric vehicles imported from China to 350,000 cars a year, the European Commission has confirmed.
Imports have been soaring in the past two years; about 800,000 battery and plug-in hybrids are likely to be sold this year.
The EU expects that the quota, which will come into force in December, will halve China’s market share, which now stands at 6% in a landmark four-year agreement made in Beijing last week.
The annual limit on imports of hybrids will be taken under the World Trade Organization safeguard measures, which mean it can be implemented swiftly without the type of investigations needed in anti-dumping measures.
Any cars imported above the quota level will not be subject to tariffs, but will remain blocked in customs at docks in Europe.
Chinese vehicles assembled within the EU, such as those made in Hungary or, in future, Spain, will not be subject to the quota, officials have confirmed, but EU companies making cars in China will.
China’s exports of hybrids to the EU tripled to €6.7bn (£5.7bn) in the first half of this year, from €2.2bn a year earlier, according to Chinese customs data.
As part of the deal, China has also agreed to drop some tariffs on auto parts and cut duties by half on footwear, olive oil and ice-cream from the EU.
Officials stressed that the quota is fully supported by China, and further dialogue on cars and other imports including chemicals, renewable energy and furniture is continuing.
“We will continue the dialogue on some products … this is by no means the end of the story,” an official said.
Last month, the EU called for feedback on a new rule that could oblige companies to diversify their supply chains while the“Made in Europe” legislation would do the same in public procurement.
On Thursday, EU leaders will discuss a French-German proposal for a “kill switch” or new instrument that would allow Brussels to block access to the single market for certain goods in the event of any harmful development, such as a ban on rare earths crucial for the tech and automotive industries.
The deal on hybrid EVs comes amid mounting concern over the £1bn-a-day trade deficit the EU is now running with China.
Up until recently, the EU’s strategy for tackling what it says is an “unsustainable” trade imbalance has been to seek to increase exports to China.
Sources said there has been “a paradigm shift” with concerns of deindustrialisation and job losses in the industrial heartlands forcing a renewed focus on curbing imports rather than increasing exports.
“We are closely surveilling, our imports. We know what’s coming in. We know where there’s a surge, and we know what hits the hardest in terms of our deindustrialisation,” said an official.
Andrew Small, the director of the Asia programme at the European Council for Foreign Relations, said China was likely to “suck the EU into drawn-out negotiations” on other sectors but the mood had changed in the EU.
“I think if China had offered a deal like this earlier in the year, say in spring, it would have been much easier to take the heat out. My sense is that things have now moved somewhat too far politically,” he said.

Lithuania says Trump-Putin diesel deal weakens Western position on Russia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
10:10:00 UTC
19:10:00 KST

Lithuanian Foreign Minister Kęstutis Budrys said Monday that a deal between US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin on diesel supplies weakens the West’s position on Russia, although he described it as less serious than other developments over the past two years.
“This latest episode is not the worst we have seen in nearly two years. But it is certainly regrettable, as it does not help achieve a coordinated sanctions policy toward Russia between Europe and the United States, and slightly weakens our position as the West,” Budrys told journalists in Luxembourg ahead of a meeting of the European Union’s Foreign Affairs Council.
Budrys said Washington had repeatedly made decisions without closely coordinating with Europe, despite the effectiveness of joint action.
“Whenever we coordinated, we saw how effective it was, but that did not always happen,” he said, adding that the latest development was not entirely new.
However, Budrys stressed that the agreement should not change the EU’s sanctions policy.
“The European Union has imposed restrictions on imports of oil products into the bloc, and we will not change our position, as we believe this is one of the more effective measures to restrict financial flows to the Russian war machine,” he said.
Trump announced Friday that he had reached an agreement with Putin on supplying large quantities of diesel in exchange for a temporary easing of US sanctions. The announcement drew criticism from Ukraine, the EU and some US lawmakers.
Budrys said Washington’s decisions could be influenced by domestic politics, including high energy prices, as well as efforts to end the war in Ukraine.
The Lithuanian minister also warned that securing funding for Ukraine would be one of Europe’s biggest challenges next year. Bilateral support from EU member states is currently at its lowest level since 2022, he said, even as Ukraine’s defence needs increase and Russian attacks continue to destroy infrastructure.
Budrys said Lithuania would honour its commitments to Ukraine and urged other EU countries not to reduce their bilateral aid because of the bloc’s financial support scheme. He acknowledged, however, that maintaining European countries’ attention and support would be difficult.
Asked whether the agreement could affect diesel prices or lead to Russian diesel entering the EU market, Budrys said he expected no significant impact. Lithuania would work to ensure the deal did not undermine the bloc’s sanctions policy, he added.
Trust in US ‘has not wavered’
Meanwhile, Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius said Monday that Lithuania continued to trust the US.
“Lithuania’s trust has not wavered. We still think and firmly believe that America is our strategic partner,” he said during a visit to Warsaw. “Of course, politicians are often active, but this does not mean their statements or tweets fundamentally change bilateral relations. We welcome American initiatives to seek and find ways to achieve lasting peace, and any initiatives in this area are welcome. It is important that these initiatives actually work, as President Zelensky also said today.”
Parliament Speaker Juozas Olekas, meanwhile, stressed that any agreements must be consistent with Ukraine’s interests and international law. He said an energy ceasefire would be an important step but must not involve unilateral concessions to Russia.
Olekas also said Lithuania would not recognise Ukrainian territories seized by Russia and supported Ukraine’s right to determine its own domestic, foreign and security policies.

Exclusive: Finland pushes to all but eliminate Russian travel in EU
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
10:09:23 UTC
19:09:23 KST

LUXEMBOURG — Finland's Foreign Minister Elina Valtonen has made five requests to the EU that would drastically curtail Russian citizens' ability to travel into and around the bloc, in a letter dated Oct. 12 and seen by the Kyiv Independent.
"The Kremlin must see that continued aggression will deepen its isolation. I ask you to take these proposals forward as an urgent priority," writes Valtonen, as EU foreign ministers meet in Luxembourg.
The first demand is to "stop issuing Schengen visas to Russian nationals for non-essential travel, including tourism." Finland has placed national restrictions since 2022, she said, but several countries — notably France, Spain, and Italy — have opposed attempts to ban Russian tourist visas.
Valtonen writes that she would support a German proposal "for visas with limited territorial validity," but only as an interim measure.
Second, Valtonen calls for a binding visa ban as a sanctions measure against Russian President Vladimir Putin's inner circle and any people or entities sanctioned by the EU.
And third, Finland wants to refuse visas to "Russian athletes and sports team members with close ties to the Russian government."
The reentry of Russian athletes at world sporting events has caused considerable anger in EU political circles, and the EU's Sports Commissioner, Glenn Micallef, is attending the Oct. 12 foreign ministers' meeting — for the first time — to discuss what actions can be taken.
Valtonen also reissued the call for a visa ban on Russian ex-combatants from entering the EU, which was previously proposed in the EU's 21st sanctions package from July, but was watered down as countries could not agree on the mechanism for enforcement.
The ex-combatants ban was also mentioned ahead of the foreign ministers' meeting by Valtonen's Estonian counterpart, Margus Tsahkna, who warned of the risk their entry to the EU represents, with "many of them supported by the Russian secret services."
And finally, Finland has asked the European Commission "to submit a robust amendment to the visa code," that would "enable the (European) Union to impose binding visa restrictions swiftly and consistently when its political or security relations with a third country deteriorate severely."
The European Commission is expected to propose a new visa law in January that will take a much tougher approach toward countries that threaten the EU, such as Russia.

The World Skate Games 2026 are being held in Asunción, Paraguay, from October 2 till 18. Bringing together more than 8,000 participants from 91 countries, the event serves as an official world championship for roller sports and skateboarding.
Athletes are competing across 14 disciplines, including inline speed skating, artistic roller skating, skateboarding, inline freestyle, downhill skating, inline hockey, rink hockey, and skate cross.
The World Skate Games provide athletes with an opportunity to compete for official world championship titles, represent their national teams, and showcase the results of years of training and international competition.
Akylbekov's historic bronze medal marks a major milestone for Kazakhstan's roller sports, highlighting the country's growing potential on the international stage and drawing attention to a new generation of promising athletes.

Kazakhstan ranks among world’s top 50 largest economies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

19:07:41 KST

Kazakhstan ranks among world’s top 50 largest economies
Kazakhstan has entered the world’s top 50 largest economies, securing the 48th spot in the global ranking after a record economic performance in 2025, Qazinform News Agency reports.
The period from 2019 to 2026 has marked a major transformation in Kazakhstan’s public administration and social structure. A key institutional milestone was the adoption of a new Constitution following a nationwide referendum on March 15, 2026, providing a solid economic foundation for political reforms.
In 2025, Kazakhstan’s gross domestic product (GDP) reached 159.6 trillion tenge, recording real growth of 6.5%. As a result, the country improved its position in the World Bank’s global ranking, moving up from 55th to 48th place and securing its position among the world’s 50 largest economies.
The country’s macroeconomic resilience has also been supported by increased investment. Annual investment in fixed capital rose from 12.6 trillion to 23.5 trillion tenge, while cumulative foreign direct investment (FDI) inflows exceeded $162 billion from 2019 through the first quarter of 2026.
Under the Government’s new 2026-2028 Macroeconomic Stabilization Programme, Kazakhstan aims to maintain annual economic growth of at least 5% and reduce inflation to 5-7% by 2028.
Earlier, it was reported that Kazakhstan ranked 34th among 100 countries in World Population Review’s 2026 list of the world’s most powerful nations.

Russia continued attacking Ukraine's energy infrastructure after US President Donald Trump announced an immediate ceasefire covering energy facilities, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Monday, raising questions about whether Moscow had agreed to the arrangement.

Add Helsinki Times as a preferred source on Google (opens Google in a new tab)
He also confirmed attacks on energy facilities in Kyiv and other regions.
"Immediately after the post, Russia launched a targeted strike on a power plant in Kharkiv, causing further damage to our energy system," Zelenskyy told the conference.
"It's clear Putin doesn't read Truth Social," he added, referring to the platform where Trump announced the agreement.
Trump claimed on Sunday that Russia and Ukraine had accepted an immediate halt to attacks on each other's energy infrastructure.
"Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!" he wrote.
Zelenskyy said Ukrainian officials learnt about the announcement through media reports rather than diplomatic channels. The Kremlin had not publicly confirmed its participation by Monday morning.
Despite the confusion, Zelenskyy said Ukraine would honour an agreement covering energy infrastructure if Russia followed the same terms.
"We are ready to respect an energy ceasefire if Russia is ready to do the same. We agree, if they agree," he said.
The Ukrainian president insisted that any arrangement must protect electricity generation, transmission networks and gas facilities rather than focus exclusively on oil refineries.
Ukraine has one refinery, in Kremenchuk, which Russian attacks have damaged. Russia operates a network of refineries that Ukrainian drones have targeted to disrupt fuel supplies and reduce Moscow's energy revenues.
"If Russia wants us to stop our long-range strikes against its oil refineries and oil exports, then Russia must stop its strikes against our energy system and critical infrastructure, and stop killing our people," Zelenskyy said.
According to Axios, an unnamed White House official said Trump's announcement concerned oil refineries, with a wider agreement covering electricity infrastructure potentially following later.
Ukrainian authorities reported further attacks overnight. Kharkiv's CHP-5 power plant came under fire on Sunday, while strikes damaged electricity networks in Izyum and energy and railway facilities in the Zhytomyr region.
A missile attack on a grocery store near Kharkiv killed three people and injured at least 22, including two children, according to regional governor Oleh Syniehubov.
Zelenskyy said Russia had carried out more than 200 strikes against Ukrainian electricity facilities during the preceding week, alongside 17 attacks on oil and gas infrastructure.
European officials questioned the ceasefire announcement.
"We welcome the energy ceasefire when it holds. We haven't yet seen that also Russia will stick to it," EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said ahead of a meeting of foreign ministers.
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk called for further sanctions against Moscow and said Russia's continued attacks demonstrated its response to ceasefire proposals.
The dispute follows Trump's decision on Friday to ease restrictions on Russian diesel exports under an agreement intended to increase fuel supplies.
Zelenskyy criticised the arrangement, arguing that additional energy revenue would help finance Russia's war.
The Financial Times, citing unnamed European officials, reported that Washington had threatened to restrict intelligence sharing and weapons procurement arrangements unless Kyiv stopped attacking Russian refineries.
Trump also called for Ukraine to elect a new president. Zelenskyy responded that elections required a full ceasefire, citing martial law and the difficulty of allowing frontline troops to vote.
He said a 60-day halt to fighting would provide an opportunity to prepare elections and address the legislative obstacles.
Ukraine has suspended national elections under martial law since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022.

⁠US economists Robert ⁠Hall, Michael Woodford win 2026 Nobel economics prize
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
10:05:56 UTC
19:05:56 KST

US economists Robert Hall, Michael Woodford win 2026 Nobel economics prize
The two Americans have been honoured for their work on ‘smoothing out economic peaks and troughs’
American-born economists Robert Hall and Michael Woodford have won the 2026 Nobel economics prize for their work on how monetary and fiscal policy can help stabilise fluctuations in the economy.
Hall, 83, is affiliated with Stanford University in California, and Woodford, 70, with Columbia University in New York.
The announcement was made in Sweden’s capital Stockholm, with the winners honoured “for microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilisation”.
One of their key insights is that economies can only be kept on an even keel by taking into account the millions of decisions made at a micro-level by households and businesses, rather than by using top-down theories of how economies work.

Trump to campaign in Ohio, Alaska with Republicans facing tight races

Trump to campaign in Ohio, Alaska with Republicans facing tight races
WASHINGTON, Oct 12 - With little more than three weeks to go until Election Day, President Donald Trump will make a new campaign swing this week through normally friendly territory where some Republican candidates are facing tough fights.
Trump's latest foray will take him to Ohio, Alaska, Arizona and Montana, all states he won in 2024, as polls show Republicans at risk as they try to hang on to control of the US Congress for the president's last two years in office.
Trump, facing political headwinds due to high gasoline prices and his war in Iran, has largely stuck to friendly turf during his 32-day sprint to the November 3 elections.
By the end of the week, Trump will have campaigned in 11 states in two weeks. This includes two stops each in Texas and Ohio, as well as a Tuesday rally in Alaska. These are all states where Republicans are hoping to hang on in competitive US Senate races.
Trump told reporters on Saturday night after a trip to Clarksville, Tennessee, that he was stopping in friendly areas to thank voters in states that backed him in the past. But he said he would also campaign in more contested areas.
"I want to give some recognition to places that have just backed me automatically, like Tennessee, and I'll be going to Ohio, which backed me, but we have very close races," he said.
In Youngstown, Ohio, on Monday, Trump will rally for Republican Senator Jon Husted, who is locked in a close race with Democrat Sherrod Brown. In Alaska, Republican Senator Dan Sullivan is in a close contest with Democrat Mary Peltola.
Larry Sabato, director of the Center for Politics at the University of Virginia, said Trump's travel appears to have strategic objectives.
"His staff is putting him in places where he's likely to be able to draw a friendly crowd to the rally," Sabato said. "And these candidates he's campaigning for might well win."
Trump's presence in competitive areas is also energizing his opponents. “This is my very first protest,” 59-year-old Democratic voter Marilyn Makiewicz said in an interview outside Trump’s recent rally in Vandalia, Ohio. “I think he is doing these rallies because he's worried about the election.”
White House officials said the stops on Trump's campaign swings are geared toward drawing the president's most loyal supporters to get out and vote. Trump has repeatedly urged his followers to "pretend I'm on the ballot."
"Some of them may not show up for a candidate unless Trump gives them a reason,” one of the officials said of Trump's base of supporters. REUTERS

“Ordinary Ukrainians will pay for cheaper global diesel prices with their lives,” he wrote.
Trump announced the agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin on Friday. Under its terms, Russia is expected to immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel to US and global markets, followed by another 500,000 tons in November, and 1 million tons more afterwards.
The US Treasury Department issued a waiver permitting Russian diesel sales and imports despite sanctions imposed over Moscow’s war.
“Sell-out of the Ukrainian cause”
Coughlin described the agreement as a “massive sell-out of the Ukrainian cause,” arguing that the new export revenue could help Russia finance further attacks.
He also criticized Trump for blaming Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries for surging US diesel prices. The primary cause of higher fuel costs is the US-led war against Iran rather than Ukraine’s attacks on Russian energy infrastructure, Coughlin argued.
Trump is facing political pressure over energy prices ahead of the November midterm elections. He has demanded that Ukraine stop striking Russian refineries and warned President Volodymyr Zelensky that he had “better damn well stop” if Kyiv wanted continued Western support.
Trying to Make Sense of Trump’s Ukraine Policy
The US president also urged Ukrainians to elect a new leader who could reach an agreement with Moscow.
Coughlin argued that Trump’s approach reflected not only concerns about fuel prices but also his long-running hostility toward Zelensky, dating back to Trump’s first presidential term.
The columnist predicted that the diesel agreement would damage Trump’s reputation more than Zelensky’s, particularly if the Russian supplies failed to lower prices before the election.
Deal faces bipartisan backlash
Republicans fighting in the midterm elections have turned on Donald Trump over his diesel deal with Putin.
Two republicans have spoken out, with another incumbent in a key state, describing the deal as a “grave error.”
Other Republicans have also rounded on the US president, suggesting his attempts to assuage energy price concerns may already be backfiring.
Zelensky condemned the agreement, accusing Washington of demonstrating weakness and warning that renewed Russian revenue would lead to more attacks and deaths in Ukraine.
Trump subsequently announced an immediate “energy ceasefire” between Ukraine and Russia, claiming that both sides had agreed to halt strikes on energy infrastructure.
Kyiv said it was prepared to comply if Moscow reciprocated but had not received clear details of the arrangement. Russia continued striking Ukrainian power facilities after Trump’s announcement, while the Kremlin did not immediately confirm that it had accepted the truce.

‘Critical moment’: World leaders urged to course correct on nature protection ahead of COP17 summit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
10:02:10 UTC
19:02:10 KST

Game-changing global nature pact still has potential – but nations need to speed up progress, conservationists urge.
Governments are falling short on their commitments to protect the plants, animals and ecosystems that sustain life on Earth ahead of this month's UN biodiversity summit.
The so-called COP17 summit in the Armenian capital, Yerevan, will be a reckoning for the nearly 200 nations that joined the landmark Paris Agreement for Nature in 2022 but have been slow to act on its objectives.
It set 23 targets for halting and reversing nature loss by 2030, including reducing pollution, protecting threatened species and conserving 30 per cent of the world's land and oceans.
But the world is off-track to meet these goals, according to a draft review by the United Nations Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD), which oversees the biennial international negotiations on protecting the natural world.
"COP17 comes at a critical moment," says An Lambrechts from Greenpeace International.
"The most important outcome from Yerevan must therefore be a clear course correction. Governments need to move beyond restating promises and agree on concrete actions."
Astrid Schomaker, executive director of the UN biodiversity convention, says that progress was being made and the 2030 goals were "still reachable – but only with significant change being made".
This includes reducing incentives for politically sensitive industries like agriculture and fossil fuel production, areas where governments have made very little headway to date.
"Do I think we're moving in the right direction? Yes, but way too slowly," Schomaker says.
Around 10 heads of state are expected in Yerevan for a leaders' summit on Friday (16 October) to start proceedings "and tell the negotiators to be ambitious and constructive" when talks formally begin on 19 October, she says.
What's holding progress on nature conservation back?
The nature summit comes weeks before the annual international climate negotiations (COP31) in neighbouring Türkiye, and is the first time nations have taken stock of progress since the biodiversity pact was adopted.
Drawing on national reports and other inputs, a "global review" of collective improvements and pitfalls is being finalised.
A draft scorecard published in July painted a mixed picture of progress.
Some countries have taken strides toward the '30x30' conservation goal (protecting 30 per cent of Earth's land and waters by 2030), said Campaign for Nature in a September analysis.
But taken together, government pledges would cover only 27 per cent of land and inland waters by the end of this decade if enacted in full. For oceans, the figure would be just 12 per cent.
Money is a major barrier to the success of the biodiversity goals and an expected source of tension at COP17.
Nations are lagging behind a pledge to raise $200 billion (€179b) a year for biodiversity by 2030 from public and private sources, including $30 billion (€27b) a year in international finance for developing countries.
Wealthy countries are under pressure to fill the gap but face their own budget challenges, making the issue politically fraught.
The United States, which is not a party to the biodiversity convention, is not involved in the talks.
"The more time you spend talking about funding, the less you talk about objectives," a French government official told news agency AFP.
Decision makers must 'unite in fight' for survival of life on Earth
Attention at the Yerevan summit is expected to focus on how the private sector can make up the shortfall.
Under scrutiny will be the lacklustre performance of the Cali Fund, a milestone UN initiative launched in February 2025.
The fund aimed to raise $1 billion (€894m) a year from corporations for conservation in developing countries but so far has attracted just $6,000 (€5,363).
"Everyone was hoping... this would be a game changer. And we continue to believe that it absolutely has the potential," although corporate engagement had been "slower" than anticipated, says Schomaker.
Subsidy reform has also proved to be a roadblock, with barely any movement toward the 2030 goal of reducing nature-harmful incentives by $500 billion (€447b) a year.
For every dollar invested in protecting or restoring nature, about $30 (€27) still goes into activities that degrade it, according to UN figures.
In October, more than 130 businesses and financial institutions – including Nestle and H&M Group – called on governments to reform incentives, citing $2.6 trillion (€2.3t) in annual public spending "that rewards practices depleting the soils, water and ecosystems".
Guido Broekhoven from nature conservation organisation WWF International says that repurposing subsidies must be "a matter of priority" at COP17.
"At a time when geopolitical tensions are putting multilateral cooperation under pressure, it's even more important to show the world that our decision-makers can still be united in the fight for the survival of life on Earth," Greenpeace's Lambrechts says.

"Germany cannot be a second- or third-rate player when it comes to developing services and capabilities; we must remain at the forefront, given the challenges we face," Dobrindt said.
Created after World War Two, when memories of Nazi rule were still fresh, the German services have traditionally been more constrained than those of allies such as France, Britain or the US. REUTERS

Africa’s cultural landmarks: tombs of Buganda kings
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
10:01:00 UTC
19:01:00 KST

Kasubi Hill, in Kampala, the capital of Uganda, is the resting place of four kings of Buganda – a centuries-old monarchy still central to the lives of the Baganda people. Their tombs are built from vegetal materials that demand constant upkeep and leave the structures vulnerable, as became clear in March 2010 when a fire destroyed much of the tomb complex. Directed by the Ethiopian-American filmmaker Sosena Solomon, and featuring the prime minister of the Buganda Kingdom and the architects and artisans involved in the restoration, the film documents both the careful work of reconstruction and the tombs’ indispensable role in Baganda society. In doing so, Solomon’s film captures how these grand structures embody the spirituality and values of the Baganda people.
The film is part of the short documentary series Africa’s Cultural Landmarks, produced by the Metropolitan Museum of Art in collaboration with the World Monuments Fund.

EU announces cap on Chinese hybrid car imports
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
10:00:56 UTC
19:00:56 KST

The European Union will cap imports of hybrid vehicles from China to 350,000 a year, a senior EU official said on Monday after Brussels and Beijing agreed to moderate their entry to the bloc.
"This will cut by more than half the current exports to the EU, which we estimate are likely to reach up to 800,000 units in 2026," the official said.
The cap will apply from 2027 for a period of four years, rising by six percent annually from the second year onwards.
The EU will use its safeguard measure, which allows the bloc to limit imports to stop the flood of a certain product to Europe.
The subject of hybrid vehicles is sensitive because these models have become one of the main routes through which Chinese manufacturers enter the EU market.
The EU in 2024 set hefty additional tariffs on Chinese electric cars, alleging they benefit from unfair state subsidies.
Beijing and Brussels agreed to "moderate" China's exports of hybrids and plug-in hybrids to the EU last week, but details of the plan were not immediately made public.
The Commerce Ministry in Beijing said on Monday that Europe imported 302,000 hybrid vehicles in 2025 and that last week's deal would be based on such levels.
According to Chinese customs data, such exports to the EU tripled to US$7.5 billion in the first half of this year from US$2.5 billion a year earlier.
The ministry said in a statement the talks were part of efforts to balance broader economic and trade concerns.
The consensus "strongly safeguards the practical interests of Chinese enterprises, avoids escalation of China-EU trade frictions, and provides both sides with a stable, predictable, and sustainable trade and investment environment," it added.
Both sides agreed that the export quota on hybrid vehicles for China would not be lower than quotas allocated to other import sources and that EU measures must not specifically target its products or discriminate against its firms.
Both also agreed on an upward adjustment of hybrid vehicle exports from 2025 figures to ensure opportunities and stable growth for Chinese enterprises, the ministry added in its statement.
"The two sides reached a rising arrangement based on 2025, ensuring export space and stable growth for Chinese enterprises," the ministry said.
The agreement was struck on Friday after European trade commissioner Maros Sefcovic held two days of talks in Beijing to avert a damaging trade war.
The export deal will be on the agenda of a meeting of EU leaders on Thursday, during which they will explore what next steps Europe should take. (AFP & Reuters)
