‘This deal doesn’t help’: Europe slams Trump’s plan to buy Russian diesel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
09:51:50 UTC
18:51:50 KST

European governments rebuked U.S. President Donald Trump’s plan to import hundreds of thousands of tons of Russian diesel, and vowed to keep isolating Moscow and supporting Ukraine as it heads into a brutal wartime winter.
Trump said over the weekend he would import 300,000 tons of Russian diesel, weeks ahead of U.S. midterm elections in which the Republicans are polling badly and in which energy prices and cost-of-living concerns are expected to play a major role.
“This deal doesn't help neither the price of oil products nor the unity of the transatlantic community,” Lithuanian Foreign Minister Kęstutis Budrys said at a gathering of the bloc’s foreign ministers on Monday morning, adding “it is not the European way.”
Irish Foreign Minister Helen McEntee called Trump’s announcement of a deal with Moscow “concerning,” while German Minister of State for Europe Gunther Krichbaum said every dollar spent on Russian energy funded the purchase of weapons used against Kyiv.
The EU’s top diplomat, Kaja Kallas, reminded Washington that “Russia has started this war. We should not forget this.”
On Monday, Zelenskyy suggested that Washington had other motives for pursuing an energy agreement with Moscow, arguing that the Russian fuel involved would make little difference to global supplies.
Speaking at the Warsaw Security Forum, Zelenskyy said proposed Russian diesel deliveries were insignificant compared with global monthly consumption of roughly 120 million tons.
"I don't think that this will have a tangible impact," Zelenskyy said. "I believe that there are different rationales behind this decision."
Advertisement
Zelenskyy also suggested Washington should consider an alternative arrangement with Kyiv. "Why doesn't America then conclude a diesel deal with Ukraine?" he asked. "Let's propose a diesel deal with Ukraine."
He also revealed that Kyiv had not been informed beforehand of Trump's announcement that he had secured an energy ceasefire. "No, we did not know about that," Zelenskyy said. "We've learned that from the media as well."
On their way into their meeting, the EU's foreign ministers remained united in their insistence that increasing pressure on Moscow was the only way forward.
“Obviously our position has not changed — pressure on Russia, sanctions, support to Ukraine, Russia’s isolation is the way to peace,” Latvian Foreign Minister Baiba Braže said.
The British Foreign Office’s minister of state Stephen Doughty said London was “not planning to follow suit with” purchasing Russian energy and would ratchet up “economic pressure” on Moscow.
“Pressure, pressure, pressure on Russia,” Lithuania’s Budrys said.
Advertisement
What ceasefire?
Trump’s claim that Ukraine and Russia had agreed to an “energy ceasefire” drew confusion from Kyiv and its allies over the weekend, with Zelenskyy saying the truce and its terms were “news” to him but that he would support it nonetheless — provided Moscow followed suit.
Just hours after Trump’s announcement, however, Russian bombs fell on Ukrainian power plants, causing widespread blackouts.
Kyiv is bracing for its fifth winter since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022, which Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said last month could prove “tragically critical” for Ukraine due to Russia’s near-constant strikes on infrastructure.
At the opening session of the Warsaw Security Forum on Monday, Tusk slammed "anyone who is trying to introduce any symmetries, who suggests it is Ukraine responsible for the war," saying doing so "gives a valuable present, gift, to the aggressor, to Putin."
Kallas said any ceasefire shouldn’t “only apply to the refineries, where Ukraine has one and Russia has plenty,” adding that would “definitely [be] in the benefit of the Russians.”
She also called on Washington to join Brussels and London in imposing harsh sanctions on Russia. “Of course the U.S. is our biggest ally,” she said, “but our message is clear: If we want to end this war, the only way we can do this is putting more pressure on Russia.”

Ukraine’s financial needs are set to come up at a meeting of European heads of state and government on Thursday in Brussels. The IMF estimated that Kyiv will face a financing gap of $30 billion to $35 billion next year.
"Ukraine will be front and center at this week's European Council," European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said in a statement Sunday night after a phone call with Zelenskyy, adding the war was entering a "new, grimmer phase."

Recently, Tumanska's family also lost her grandson, who was defending Ukraine from the Russians.
Source: Zaporizhzhia School No. 23 on Facebook
Details: Bronislava Tumanska taught mathematics and held the title of master teacher. In memories shared by her colleagues, she was a mentor to schoolchildren and students, holding great authority among fellow educators.
The school recalls that Bronislava taught children not just to solve problems but to think, overcome difficulties, believe in their own strength and be decent human beings. Children respected her and parents valued her.
Back in 1969, Bronislava was one of those involved in the opening of the school.
Quote from Zaporizhzhia School No. 23: "Bronislava Andriivna was among those who opened this educational institution, laid its traditions and created the good name of the school, which became a second home for many generations of pupils.
She left her mark not only in the history of the school but also in the hearts of hundreds of students to whom she gave her knowledge, emotional warmth, and a piece of her own heart."
Details: A former student of Bronislava Tumanska, a serviceman who goes under the alias "Mozart", told Ukrainska Pravda.Zhyttia (Life) that the teacher was a very charismatic person.
Quote from "Mozart": "For more than 50 years, she instilled a love of mathematics in children. She taught me at the music college. Incredibly energetic, very humane and with a kind heart.
I think all her students clearly remember her favourite phrase 'don't poke the bear' whenever anyone annoyed her."
Details: Another former student of Bronislava, Anastasiia Sukhyna, told UP that all students adored the maths teacher.
Quote from Anastasiia: "Bronislava Andriivna taught us mathematics at the Platon Maiboroda Zaporizhzhia Music College. For me, she will forever remain in my memory as a very charismatic, active, cheerful and joyful woman.
She always supported us before performances on stage. She became an integral part of my memories of the music college, of those interesting and rich years of study. I will always remember her with warmth and immense respect."

"I had the happiness of studying under Bronislava Andriivna for several years at the music college, and I remembered her for the rest of my life! I will always remember her charisma and strong character!" noted student Alla.

Always stylish, beautifully dressed, dignified, in high heels, with appropriate make-up and beautiful jewellery. That is how she is in the photograph, and that is how I will remember her for the rest of my life. It hurts so much that I haven't been able to recover for days. Her whole life she grieved for her daughter, who passed away far too early due to illness. Then she lost her grandson, who defended Ukraine. And so many worthy people she taught into the world."
Background: On 10 October, 23 people were killed, including two students from local schools – first-grader Yelyzaveta Skorochyshyna and eighth-grader Anna Mur-Zak, as a result of the Russian attack on Zaporizhzhia.

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
09:46:18 UTC
18:46:18 KST

Serhat Tutak and Emir Yildirim
12 October 2026•Update: 12 October 2026
Turkish Trade Minister Omer Bolat is heading to Brussels on Tuesday for a two-day visit to discuss economic and trade agreements with the EU.
During the minister’s visit to the Belgian capital, the third meeting of the Türkiye-EU High-Level Trade Dialogue will be held, co-chaired by Bolat and Maros Sefcovic, the EU commissioner for trade and economic security.
Ongoing Customs Union disputes, green and digital transitions, and a review of the EU’s Industrial Accelerator Act proposal will be discussed.
The meeting will also involve consultations on public procurement, digital trade and trade defense instruments.
The Türkiye-EU Business Roundtable meeting will also be co-chaired by the two officials to discuss operational and cross-border e-commerce challenges, as well as steps to improve investment predictability.
Bolat will also attend the Türkiye-EU Business Summit, organized in cooperation with the Foreign Economic Relations Board and the European Business Summit, to discuss cooperation opportunities in trade and investment, alongside talks on energy, security, industrial policies and economic resilience.
The minister will take part in the Türkiye-Belgium High-Level Roundtable meeting organized in collaboration with the Foreign Economic Relations Board and the Federation of Belgian Enterprises.
This platform will deepen existing cooperation and explore new investment opportunities following the Belgian economic mission’s visit to Türkiye in May, led by Queen Mathilde of Belgium.
A separate session organized alongside the Automotive Exporters’ Association and the European Reform Center will specifically scrutinize the regulatory impacts of the draft Industrial Accelerator Act.
Bolat will also meet with Teresa Ribera, the European Commission’s senior vice president for a clean, fair and competitive transition.
This meeting will center on the EU’s emerging competitiveness agenda and new industrial policies impacting existing EU-Türkiye economic integration.
During meetings with members of the European Parliament, Bolat’s main agenda item for his visit to Belgium will be the draft Industrial Accelerator Act.
The minister is expected to push for inclusive industrial regulations respecting established supply chains, urging policymakers to implement trade defense instruments that protect the shared value chains cemented by the longstanding Türkiye-EU Customs Union.

Fire that damaged cables under railway bridge is suspected arson
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Police are investigating a fire under a railway bridge in Rotterdam that led to trains being cancelled over the weekend as a suspected act of sabotage.
The door to a technical area in Rotterdam-Delfshaven was forced open and a fire was started that damaged around 35 cables, 15 of which were destroyed, network operator ProRail said.
All trains between Rotterdam Centraal and Delft Campus were suspended until 9.15pm on Sunday as engineers worked to repair the damage.
The stretch of line is one of the busiest in the Netherlands, carrying long-distance trains from Amsterdam to Zeeland and Limburg via Holland Spoor station.
A police spokesman told Dutch News: “We have secured camera footage and we are examining it. Forensic investigators are also studying possible leads.”
Junior infrastructure minister Annet Bertram said she was shocked by the incident. “I find it appalling and worrying that this appears to be arson and a deliberate act,” she told NOS.
Schiphol disruption
In a separate incident, trains to Schiphol airport were disrupted for several hours by problems with an overhead power line, but ProRail has ruled out arson as a cause.
More than 20 sprinter trains between Amsterdam and Hoofddorp were cancelled between 1.30pm and 9pm as engineers worked to repair the fault at Riekerpolder. “It is an intersection, which means trains are not running in a large area,” a spokesman said on Sunday.
International services were also affected, with trains to Brussels starting and ending in Rotterdam.

Russia is plotting to assassinate defense industry executives in Europe, Western intelligence agencies warn, FT reports
Western intelligence services have warned the heads of European defense companies that Russia is stepping up efforts to physically eliminate them, the Financial Times reported, citing five sources it spoke with.
The Kremlin has ordered an expansion of sabotage and “hybrid” operations in Europe to “fatally weaken support for Kyiv,” the FT’s sources said. Assassination attempts on civilians in Europe are becoming an increasingly prominent part of those plans, the newspaper wrote.
FT sources said Moscow is targeting CEOs and other senior executives at defense companies, as well as leaders of smaller firms, particularly those that produce drones or drone components.
In response, companies have increased personal security for senior executives. Germany’s domestic intelligence agency, the BfV, has stepped up its work with employees and management at German defense companies, including recommending they hire private security details.
Russian military intelligence is believed to be responsible for planning and carrying out the sabotage. FT sources said the GRU has recently adapted its methods: its operatives now work more closely with organized crime groups, rely on cross-border agent networks, and split reconnaissance, logistics, planning, and execution across different cells or individuals rather than relying on lone agents recruited online.
Even so, one FT source said the actions of Russian agents “were still amateurish” in many cases and are easy to thwart.
One intelligence official who spoke with the journalists believes Russia’s main goal “is still psychological.” “Just by making people feel they might be a target, they are having their effect. They want individuals to think twice before doing business with Ukraine,” the official said.
In summer 2024, it was reported that Russia had been planning the assassination of Armin Papperger, the head of the German arms company Rheinmetall, which, among other things, produces artillery shells and military equipment for Ukraine. Later, NATO confirmed that it had known about these plans — as well as other instances of sabotage and subversion that Russia is believed to be behind.

18:43:00 KST

Iran continues to review a U.S. response to its proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and will reply through intermediaries once the review is complete, Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said Monday.
Baghaei also told a press conference that Iran continues to exchange messages via intermediaries, without elaborating. Qatar and Pakistan, among others, have acted as mediators in efforts to end the war that began with U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran on Feb. 28.
"The exchange of messages between Iran and the U.S. through mediators continues," Baghaei said.
"We are reviewing the Americans’ proposals for negotiations. Iran’s preconditions must be observed for any negotiations," he added.
After a June interim cease-fire crumbled and on-off strikes resumed, Iran presented its proposal in mid-September and later confirmed receipt of a U.S. response.
However, the process has since stalled, with Iran’s security chief saying Sunday that Washington’s response did not sufficiently address Tehran’s seven conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz and returning to negotiations.
A central point of disagreement has been Washington’s insistence on addressing Iran's nuclear program from the outset.
Tehran says negotiations should initially focus on reopening the Strait of Hormuz, which before the war carried about a fifth of the global trade in oil and liquefied natural gas (LNG) and restoring security in the waterway.
Baqhaei added that Russia also continues to play a "constructive" role regarding Iran’s nuclear file, pointing to Moscow’s involvement in the 2015 nuclear agreement.
He said Iranian and Russian relations are based on mutual trust and that Tehran welcomes supportive efforts by friendly countries, but stressed that, "technically and precisely," mediation between Iran and the U.S. remains in the hands of countries such as Pakistan and Qatar.
Turning to the Strait of Hormuz, Baqhaei said developments there were a direct consequence of U.S. and Israeli attacks on Iran and rejected suggestions that Tehran’s actions were intended to create negotiating leverage.
"What we have seen in the Strait of Hormuz since Feb. 28 was the direct result of the U.S. and the Israeli regime's attack on Iran," he said.
"With the current U.S. approach, security will not return," he added.
Baqhaei rejected U.S. assertions that Iran had lost its leverage, saying such claims did not correspond with realities on the ground.
"They can say Iran has lost its leverage, but we are doing our work," he said, arguing that energy markets were not responding to Washington’s assertions.
Baqhaei also said that Iran was "deeply concerned" by escalating attacks between Yemen's Tehran-backed Houthis and Saudi Arabia, after 14 people died in two days of strikes on Riyadh's airport.
"We are deeply concerned about the developments taking place in the Arabian Peninsula," he said, adding that Tehran was ready "to help facilitate dialogue between the parties."
A Houthi strike on Riyadh's international airport on Sunday killed one person and wounded 11 others, a day after 13 died in the deadliest strike on Saudi soil in more than a decade.
"We absolutely do not want hostilities and war to continue between two Islamic countries," Baqhaei said, urging the parties to resolve the situation "through dialogue and engagement."
The Houthis are part of the Iran-backed "Axis of Resistance," a network of groups opposed to Israel that also includes Lebanon's Hezbollah and Iraqi Shiite armed groups.

Ukraine Tests New Bars Interceptors Against Russia’s 800 Km/h Jet Drones—and Scores Five-for-Five
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
09:42:23 UTC
18:42:23 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine Tests New Bars Interceptors Against Russia’s 800 Km/h Jet Drones—and Scores Five-for-Five
Ukraine is expanding its air defense capabilities to counter Russia’s increasingly sophisticated aerial threats, including jet-powered drones capable of reaching speeds of up to 800 kilometers per hour.
During a meeting with journalists on October 10, Ukrainian Defense Minister Yevhenii Khmara outlined the multilayered structure of Ukraine’s air defense network, according to a UNITED24 Media correspondent.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
He explained that the system includes surface-to-air missile systems, man-portable air defense systems (MANPADS), gun turrets, electronic warfare equipment, and specialized units operating interceptor drones.
According to the minister, the Defense Ministry is simultaneously working to secure additional interceptor drones, fighter aircraft and their ammunition, anti-aircraft missile and artillery systems, gun turrets, electronic warfare equipment, and other defensive technologies.
Khmara emphasized the importance of anticipating future threats and maintaining sufficient reserves of weapons and equipment to ensure Ukraine can respond to emerging Russian capabilities.
“We also know what technologies Russia is developing, including jet-powered drones capable of reaching speeds of 800 kilometers per hour. We are working to find countermeasures against the next generation of threats. Manufacturers and the defense industry have been tasked with developing proposals and prototypes,” Khmara said.
While acknowledging that Russian jet-powered drones remain a significant challenge, the minister highlighted recent successes in using interceptor drones against these faster aerial targets.
According to Khmara, one Ukrainian unit achieved a perfect interception rate during a combat operation involving five Bars interceptor drones.
“During a combat operation, one unit used five Bars interceptors to destroy five aerial targets. That is a 100% success rate. This experience is now being studied and scaled up, with additional specialists and units joining the effort,” he said.
The Defense Ministry is now examining how to expand the use of these systems across additional units, drawing on the operational experience gained during successful interceptions.
Beyond interceptor drones, Ukraine has also recorded successful engagements against jet-powered unmanned aerial vehicles using large-caliber gun turrets.
Khmara said Ukraine already operates hundreds of these systems, with efforts underway to increase their deployment and develop longer-range versions.
At the same time, conventional air defense systems continue to play an important role in countering Russian aerial threats.
“At the same time, surface-to-air missile systems and MANPADS are also demonstrating their effectiveness. We are focused on procuring both the systems themselves and the missiles for them, and we are discussing this with partners in various countries,” the minister added.
Ukraine is also preparing to introduce additional technologies specifically designed to counter high-speed Russian drones.
Speaking earlier, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the country expected to begin using several types of small anti-aircraft missiles against jet-powered drones in the second half of October, although the systems had not yet been deployed operationally.
“There are several types of them. We will obviously see the results this month. Toward the end, in the second half of this month, we expect to see the results. Suspected Drone Explodes in Moldova Despite No Recorded Airspace Violation
A drone carrying a warhead crashed into a tree in a forest in central Moldova on the night of October 10, prompting a response from military and explosives specialists.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Police later confirmed that the explosive component had been safely neutralized, while national air surveillance systems reportedly failed to detect any unauthorized entry into the country’s airspace.
According to NewsMaker on October 11, Moldova’s Defense Ministry and national police reported the incident near the village of Geamăna in the Anenii Noi district, where residents of nearby communities reported hearing an explosion. No injuries were reported.
In a subsequent update, Moldovan police confirmed that the drone had struck a tree approximately 13 meters above the ground, about 100 meters from a road.
Specialists from the police explosives unit successfully neutralized the drone’s warhead, eliminating the risk of an uncontrolled explosion.
Investigators also recovered damaged fragments of the aircraft scattered across the forest floor. Additional forensic examinations are planned to establish the drone’s origin and determine the circumstances of the incident.
Police received the initial report at approximately 10:20 pm on October 10, after which military personnel, explosives specialists, and emergency responders were dispatched to the area.
Despite the incident, Moldova’s Defense Ministry stated that national air surveillance systems had not recorded any unauthorized flights during the relevant period.
Authorities have not identified the drone’s origin or confirmed its model. Residents were advised to avoid the crash site and refrain from touching suspicious debris.
The incident comes amid repeated airspace violations involving drones and missiles since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of neighboring Ukraine in February 2022.
The incident follows a similar case on September 30, when a Russian Geran-4 drone equipped with a turbojet engine entered Moldovan airspace before crashing into trees and exploding near a road in the Orhei district. Investigators recovered drone fragments, including engine components and parts marked “Geran-4,” while authorities temporarily restricted airspace during the incident.

French centre left must wage ‘existential battle’ to prevent far right winning presidency
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
09:41:59 UTC
18:41:59 KST

The European lawmaker Raphaël Glucksmann has urged the French centre left to wage an “existential battle” to prevent Marine Le Pen’s far right winning the 2027 presidential election after he was chosen as the social democrat candidate for the presidency.
“We’ve got to rid our hearts of the spirit of defeat,” Glucksmann, the founder of the small party Place Publique, said on Monday morning after his decisive win in a centre-left primary race held by the Socialist party.
In his first interview since being designated a presidential candidate on Sunday night, Glucksmann told France Inter radio that the country was living in a “historic moment”, with the far right at the gates of power. He said the 2027 presidential election campaign would be brutal and “like no other we have ever experienced”. He said it would be unbearable to have a centre left “that doesn’t believe in victory”, adding that he could restore a “pride in social democracy”.
At present the centre left sits substantially behind the far right in the polls and also trails the radical left politician Jean-Luc Mélenchon, who is polling high but with whom Glucksmann refuses to work.
Glucksmann, 46, an essayist and intellectual who argues he is very different to career politicians, is staunchly pro-Europe and pro-Ukraine. His candidacy marks the first time the Socialist party will not have its own presidential candidate since the party was founded in 1969. The party suffered two crushing defeats in the last two presidential elections.
Glucksmann has been a member of the European parliament since 2019. He strikes a more reformist and centrist tone than the Socialist party, but has cooperated with it in the past, presenting joint electoral lists. He has made no secret of his presidential ambitions but needed the Socialist party machine behind him for his campaign.
Glucksman is polling at between 9% and 14%, well behind the frontrunner, Le Pen. He also trails the centre-right contender Édouard Philippe, who served as prime minister under Emmanuel Macron.
Crucially, he is also behind Mélenchon, whose party, La France Insoumise, boycotted the Socialist primary and has presented itself as the biggest force in a divided left.
Glucksmann is tasked with regaining centre-left voters who jumped ship to support Macron, though his critics on the left accuse him of being too centrist. He said the French president, who is standing down next spring, “wasted 10 years” failing to act on the climate emergency.
Glucksmann is known for being a campaigner on international issues. He took part in documentary work to raise awareness of the aftermath of genocide in Rwanda and is a former adviser to the anti-Moscow former Georgian president Mikheil Saakashvili.
Glucksmann, who has been accused by opponents of being too much of a Paris intellectual, said he “lost sleep at night” worrying about how the social-democratic left had lost the working class in France. He said the centre left needed to regain “a form of radicality that we lost” and the focus of this would be environmental policy.
He told the daily Libération he made no apology for being an intellectual and would use his background to “better explain the moment we’re living in” rather than relying on “slogans”.
Glucksmann’s partner, Léa Salamé, is the star presenter of the French public broadcaster’s flagship evening news programme. She has stepped down from presenting the news while he runs for president.

Pope Leo sticks to busy schedule before surgery to remove lung nodule
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
09:40:52 UTC
18:40:52 KST

Pope Leo to be hospitalised on Tuesday ahead of surgery, Vatican says
VATICAN CITY, Oct 12 - Pope Leo will go into hospital on Tuesday before surgery to remove a small growth found on one of his lungs, the Vatican said, as the pontiff kept up a busy schedule on Monday, holding seven previously planned meetings in the morning.
Leo, 71, said on Sunday that the growth, a small nodule, had been found on a recent check-up, was "well-contained" and had been spotted early.
The nodule was found during a routine health check, the Vatican press office told journalists earlier on Monday, before confirming that the pope is expected to be hospitalised late on Tuesday morning, ahead of his surgery.
It did not say when the actual operation would take place.
A regular advisory on the pope's daily schedule, issued at noon (1000 GMT) on Monday, said he met that morning with visiting bishops from Argentina, Nicaragua and the United States, among others.
In a meeting at the Vatican with members of a Rome-based charity group on Monday, the pope spoke in a strong, clear voice, thanking them for their work.
COMPLICATION RATE FOR NODULE REMOVAL LOW
Leo, elected pope by the world's cardinals in May 2025, is relatively young for a Church leader. He enjoys sports, including tennis, and is not known to be a smoker or to have had health issues previously.
The Vatican has said the pope's recovery is expected to take about a week.
A nodule on the lung is a small, localised lesion that can be benign. The American Thoracic Society says fewer than 5% of lung nodules overall prove cancerous, although risk rises with age, size, and other factors such as smoking.
Dr. Federico Venuto, chief of thoracic surgery at Rome's Policlinico Umberto I hospital, said surgeries to remove lung nodules are usually minimally invasive, and can sometimes involve use of a thin camera tube called a thoracoscope.
"The complication rate is extremely low," he told Reuters.
POPE'S TRANSPARENCY ABOUT HEALTH UNUSUAL
Leo's decision to discuss his upcoming surgery publicly on Sunday marked a contrast with his predecessor, the late Pope Francis, who died in April 2025 at age 88.
Francis was hospitalised several times as he grew frail in his later years and did not usually announce his hospital visits in advance, sometimes sparking a media frenzy over his health.
Canadian Cardinal Gérald Lacroix said on Monday that he was grateful for Leo's transparency.
"I really appreciated yesterday ... (that) he himself said, 'This is what's going on,' very transparent, and asked for prayers," said Lacroix. "I like that."
Leo, the leader of the 1.4-billion-member Church, had several public appointments on his calendar for this week, including a Mass in St. Peter's Square on Wednesday morning.
The Vatican said the Mass would now be led by Filipino Cardinal Luis Tagle, a Vatican official whom Leo last week approved as the dean of the Church's college of cardinals, in the first selection of an Asian cleric to the elite role.
In the event of a papal death or resignation, the dean of the cardinals is responsible for organizing the secret conclave to elect his successor.
The pope is the final earthly authority for the world's Catholics and does not have a deputy who steps in when he is sick. When a pope is incapacitated, the business of the Vatican's vast bureaucracy carries on as usual, holding off on any decisions that require papal approval. REUTERS

EU sanctions nearly 1,600 people linked to Russia's military industry
EU foreign ministers have approved sanctions against nearly 1,600 people linked to Russia's military industry, more than half of whom are involved in ballistic missile production, EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas has said.
Source: European Pravda, citing a post by Kallas on X (Twitter)
Details: Kallas said that EU foreign ministers on Monday 12 Monday approved the addition of nearly 1,600 new names to the EU's sanctions lists. She said the measures target Russia's military industry.
More than half of those sanctioned are linked to the ballistic missile production chain, she added.
"This is the single largest expansion of our sanctions list since Russia started its war," she said.
"We are making it significantly harder, slower and more expensive for Russia to produce the weapons it uses to kill Ukrainians," Kallas noted.
Background:
- On 12 October, the EU Council is also due to discuss the possibility of restricting the movement of Russian diplomats between EU member states, potentially including a complete ban on travelling outside the country in which they are accredited.
- The EU has also been discussing since the summer restrictions on issuing visas to people who fought in Ukraine on Russia's side. The EU's 21st sanctions package introduced a mechanism for banning visas for Russian military personnel, but the ban itself has not yet taken effect.

RIYADH – Saudi Arabia dealt with new drone and cruise missile attacks on Oct 12, posing fresh security threats to the kingdom following the weekend’s deadly strikes on its capital’s airport.
“We have detected and are monitoring a threat involving drones and cruise missiles against the kingdom and the threat is being dealt with,” the state-run Saudi Press Agency reported. It cited defence ministry spokesman Turki al-Maliki on behalf of a Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis.
The Saudi authorities extended on Oct 12 a suspension of operations at the King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, where two separate attacks over the weekend killed at least 14 people and wounded more than 300, many critically. King Fahd International Airport in Dammam was targeted separately.
The skies over Riyadh were virtually empty on Oct 12.
The airport in Riyadh cancelled 99.7% of all scheduled flights on Oct 11, according to aviation analytics firm Cirium. As the violence stretched into Oct 12, Saudi-led forces in Yemen vowed a “decisive” response.
Against that backdrop, Energy Minister Abdulaziz bin Salman, one of the most senior Saudi officials to speak publicly in the wake of the strikes, sought to project resilience, telling oil industry executives that the kingdom remained committed to providing energy security.
“There is no way that somebody will break our back. We are like a phoenix. We come out of the ashes all the time and every time,” Prince Abdulaziz said at an energy event on Oct 11.
At the World Petroleum Congress (WPC) on Oct 12, he called for a serious response to events of recent weeks, while noting that Saudi Arabia should remain focused on economic diversification and investment. The gathering itself has been disrupted by the hostilities, with some executives who had been scheduled to attend, including the chief executives of BP and Shell, withdrawing.
The Houthi attacks over the weekend marked a sharp escalation in the Yemen war, where Saudi Arabia has long supported the internationally recognised government.
On Oct 11, a strike hit Riyadh’s international airport, killing one person, just hours after another Houthi-claimed attack on the site killed 13 people and left hundreds of others wounded, forcing operations there to be suspended.
The attacks on Saudi Arabia, a regional powerhouse and the world’s top oil exporter which has poured billions of dollars into its military, were the deadliest to hit the kingdom in a decade.
‘Full-fledged war crime’
Although Saudi Arabia has poured billions into its military, Houthi attacks continue to slip through.
“Saudi air defences have been able to intercept some Houthi missile and drone attacks, but Saudi Arabia is so large that it’s simply impossible for them to consistently defend themselves,” said Thomas Juneau, security analyst at Ottawa University.
Houthi media reported two Saudi strikes in Yemen’s Houthi-controlled Sanaa governorate on Oct 11.
A spokesman for the Houthi-run health ministry said on X that one of the strikes killed a civilian and wounded five others.
The Oct 10 attack on Riyadh drew condemnation from the United Nations and leaders around the world, including US President Donald Trump, who said he was considering joining Saudi strikes against the Houthis.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, whose country does not have diplomatic relations with Saudi Arabia, also denounced the “horrific terrorist attack”.

Why CJI declined to meet Rahul Gandhi, Kharge amid protests against Gyanesh Kumar
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
09:32:33 UTC
18:32:33 KST

CJI Suryakant, Rahul Gandhi and Mallikarjun Kharge
NEW DELHI: Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant had declined a request from Lok Sabha leader of opposition Rahul Gandhi and Rajya Sabha leader of opposition Mallikarjun Kharge for a meeting to discuss issues arising from the ongoing protests in Delhi.He said the matters are already pending before the Supreme Court and discussing them administratively would violate the principle of separation of powers.
In a letter dated October 11, the CJI advised the two Opposition leaders to approach the Supreme Court through the judicial process instead of submitting a memorandum on the administrative side. He also assured them that any petition filed on the issues would be heard at the earliest possible opportunity in accordance with the law.The request concerned allegations of irregularities involving the Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) and the Election Commission of India, alleged arbitrary arrests of students, the closure of metro stations and the cancellation of trains amid protests in the national capital.READ ALSO: How Jantar Mantar became Delhi's designated protest site and what changes nowExplaining his decision, CJI Surya Kant said the issues raised by Gandhi and Kharge were “already sub judice before the Supreme Court of India.”“Therefore, convening a meeting to discuss pending cases would wholly contravene the principle of Separation of Powers, an intrinsic facet of the basic structure doctrine of the Constitution of India, and would be incompatible with the established ethics and judicial propriety,” the CJI said.
He also clarified that the Supreme Court did not have administrative powers to address the concerns raised in their letter, but could examine them through its judicial jurisdiction.“However, in the exercise of our jurisdiction under Article 32 of our Constitution, along with other plenary powers, including that of judicial review, we are duty-bound to consider on the judicial side the gravamen of issues affecting the citizens of India,” he said.The CJI reiterated the Supreme Court’s commitment to protecting citizens’ fundamental rights and said they could seek their enforcement through the legal process.“Supreme Court of India reiterates its commitment to preserve and protect the Fundamental Rights of every citizen of India and they are entitled to seek enforcement of such rights at all hours through the procedure known in law. It would thus be more appropriate on your part to invoke the judicial powers of the Supreme Court of India, instead of submitting a memorandum on the administrative side,” he said.Pointing to the court’s schedule, CJI Surya Kant said matters involving similar issues were listed for hearing on Tuesday, October 13, 2026. He invited the Opposition leaders to file a petition on Monday, either physically or through the court’s e-filing facility.“If so advised, you may submit your petition on Monday, either physically at the Supreme Court of India, between 10:30 A.M. and 04:30 P.M., or alternatively, by utilising the e-filing option, which permits filing at any time and on any day. You have my assurance that any such petition shall be heard at the earliest possible opportunity, in accordance with the law,” he said.Gandhi and Kharge had sought an appointment with the CJI amid Opposition protests demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over allegations of electoral irregularities, including what Congress has described as “vote chori”.
Kharge said in a social media post on Sunday that the Opposition would continue its fight and that he and Gandhi had written to the CJI seeking a meeting.“We will continue our fight. Tomorrow, we are also going to meet CJI. I have written a letter, and Rahul Gandhi has also written a letter. We have scheduled a meeting between 4-5pm, during which we will apprise him of the situation... Chaos is being created in the country by home minister and PM, and everywhere an undeclared emergency is imposed,” Kharge said.The CJI’s response leaves the Opposition leaders free to pursue their concerns through a formal petition, with the court indicating that related matters could be taken up through judicial proceedings.

Trump turns to Russian diesel ahead of midterms, but analysts see little price relief
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
09:31:22 UTC
18:31:22 KST

U.S. President Donald Trump's latest geopolitical dealmaking effort to ease a diesel supply crunch ahead of November's midterm elections is unlikely to make a dent in prices, according to analysts.
Trump's declaration of an "energy ceasefire" between Russia and Ukraine on Sunday surprised policymakers across the world — not least in Kyiv — and prompted oil prices to fall on Monday, despite Russia striking a power plant shortly after the announcement. Oil later rose.
The president's declaration comes after he announced a deal for Russia to release 300,000 metric tons to the U.S. and global markets immediately, followed by another 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons after that. Moscow will then deliver another 3 million tons of diesel based on the condition of Russia's refineries, Trump said.
Trump has sought to tame inflation ahead of the congressional midterms in November, when his Republican Party is at risk of losing both houses.
According to the Pew Research Center, 84% of registered voters say the economy is "very important" to their vote.
Diesel prices hit a record high average of $6.5276 a gallon in late September, according to AAA, as the wars in Ukraine and the Middle East took their toll on supply.
"Trump is exploring all avenues to bring down diesel prices before the mid-terms," Mohit Kumar, chief European economist at Jefferies, said in a note on Monday.
"The deal with Russia has drawn opposition both from within the US and from European leaders, as it would be bypassing the Russian sanctions in place," he added.
"While more supply of diesel would ... ease some pressure on diesel prices, the volumes agreed are unlikely to make a substantial difference."
Russia's 'mystery' diesel supply
The U.S. Treasury has issued a temporary license easing sanctions on Russian diesel to facilitate the deal Trump announced Friday.
Lombard Odier analysts said in a Monday note that the agreement, in addition to Chinese plans to resume refined-fuel exports, are "potentially significant because diesel shortages have amplified the inflationary consequences of disrupted energy supply, particularly through transportation, agriculture and industrial production."
But they cautioned that "announced shipments are not equivalent to delivered supply," and "neither agreement immediately restores damaged infrastructure or normalizes maritime transportation."
Neil Atkinson, former head of the Oil Division at the International Energy Agency, was less optimistic, telling CNBC in a note: "Where the volumes to supply the Trump deal come from is a mystery, unless it comes from domestic supply, which will cripple the Russian economy."
Atkinson noted that the G7 recently authorized the release of 50 million barrels of oil products, mainly diesel, but "it has made almost zero difference to the underlying diesel market tightness" due to lack of clarity over how much will be released, or when and where.
"The same will be true of the new US/Russian deal to allow exports from Russia," he said. "Even if the initial 300 kt (about 70 kb/d over a month) were available tomorrow it would have little impact.
"The lack of impact is because the US uses 3.7 million barrels a day of diesel. The world uses 29 million barrels a day of diesel. The US is sitting on 105 million barrels of commercial diesel stocks," Atkinson added.
"Pre-war, the Middle East Gulf exported nearly 1 million barrels a day of diesel. This is still largely lost due to damage to refineries and the difficulty of exporting products by ship."
Deal to 'fail economically' — and embolden Putin
In a Monday note to clients, analysts at Singapore's Quantum Strategy outlined a particularly pessimistic outcome.
"We expect this deal to fail economically. We remain long distillates and crude. We remain short US assets," they wrote.
"We expect Putin to read the deal as an open invitation to escalate his gray-zone warfare in Europe to a much higher level. The effects would be negative for the Euro and for EU sovereign debt, as European powers scramble to ensure their defense."

Ukraine's deputy culture minister: Culture a key component in resistance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
09:30:00 UTC
18:30:00 KST

Ukraine's deputy culture minister: Culture a key component in resistance
Ukrainian culture is at the heart of the war because Russia is seeking to destroy Ukrainian identity and claim Ukraine's cultural heritage as its own, Ukrainian Deputy Culture Minister Ivan Verbytskyi told ERR.
When a country is fighting for its survival, culture may seem like something that can wait. At the same time, culture is at the center of the battlefield. The Kremlin is trying to destroy Ukrainian identity, while Ukrainians are defending it. How do you see the relationship between war and culture?
As you rightly said, culture is at the heart of this war because the reason the war began was not territory or people, but Ukrainian identity, our right to be ourselves, with our own culture and history.
They claim that Ukraine, Ukrainian culture and Ukrainian history do not exist. They want to destroy them or claim them as Russian. Culture is always a target of attack. At the same time, we are defending our culture.
Culture is also important as a source of resilience. It is not so much about what you do, but who you are. When your identity is attacked, you defend yourself, your country and your culture. Culture is important here because it is how our identity is formed and developed within society.
Culture is at the heart of the war. It is a matter of national security because culture can be used as a weapon. We see this with Russia, which uses social media, films, exhibitions, museums and various cultural spheres to influence other societies and peoples, spreading its narratives to wider audiences. That is why culture is extremely important.
I also want to thank the Estonian people and government for standing with us in defending Ukrainian culture. You support us in other areas of the war as well, but particularly when it comes to culture.
Hundreds of cultural heritage sites in Ukraine have been damaged by Russia.
How are you protecting or restoring these sites? What resources do you have?
Our main goal is to protect and preserve as much as possible. This means evacuating museum collections from war zones. They are at risk because museums and cultural treasures are being targeted for destruction. We are trying to evacuate as much as possible from the front lines.
Another important issue is damaged and destroyed sites. When buildings have been damaged, our first step is to stabilize and preserve them. It is important to prevent further deterioration from wind, rain or snow.
Our priority is to salvage as much as possible from damaged buildings, but also to document everything and digitize inventories of cultural objects. Otherwise, the Russians will claim that everything belongs to them.
We are also creating 3D models of buildings. In several cases, this is already the only way to preserve a record of a building so that it can eventually be restored.
For example, at the Kyiv-Pechersk Lavra, one of Kyiv's most important cultural monuments, which also has a long history of destruction, we created several 3D models over the past few years.
Now that the cathedral was damaged in a Russian attack on June 15, with its roof almost completely destroyed, we have a 3D model that will allow us to restore and rebuild the building and show it to the world again.
You said that culture is part of resilience. To what extent are you consciously using it to mobilize society?
We are not using it that way. Society is doing it on its own. For example, it is difficult to get tickets to theaters or concert halls in Kyiv because people want to maintain their connection to culture.
Culture has a healing effect. This is extremely important during a crisis when there is so much stress. People need something to lean on and culture provides that safe environment. It offers a safe space in which to reflect on what is happening around them.
One visible aspect of cultural policy is the shaping of public spaces and the removal of monuments. Ukraine has taken down numerous monuments to Soviet leaders, but also monuments to writers such as Alexander Pushkin and Mikhail Bulgakov. Could you explain some of the background? Where do you draw the line in deciding which monuments to remove, and why?
Culture is part of politics. Every artistic gesture is also political. We ask ourselves why there are countries and places where monuments to Pushkin stand, while elsewhere there are none.
Strangely enough, the dividing line coincides with the borders of the former Soviet Union. It was not because people loved Pushkin so much. There was no enormous following for Russian literature. It was a symbol of imperialism, a way for Russia to try to turn these places into Russian spaces. Into the "Russian world," as they called it.
They used culture, religion and other means to achieve this. They used them as weapons to gradually, subtly, though sometimes not so subtly, exert power and make these places their own.
Today, it is difficult for Ukrainians to appreciate such literature or art amid the aggression and suffering we experience every day. For Ukrainians who witness death, tension and pain every day, it is unbearable to see these monuments and symbols in their surroundings.
That is why it is important to create a psychologically safe environment where people can live in peace and do not have to see things that bring back painful memories. Symbols of the very culture being used to kill us.
Another issue is Russian and Belarusian athletes who are increasingly returning to international competition. What do you think of this development? How should other athletes, including Estonian athletes, behave toward them or interact with them?
We know that Estonia has a very good policy on this issue. Thank you very much for that.
From our perspective, there are several dimensions to this issue. The first is the human dimension.
When Russian athletes meet Ukrainian athletes at a competition, those Ukrainian athletes may have lost relatives or siblings in Russian attacks. They may have had to sit in bomb shelters instead of training in sports halls.
It is not safe for them to be alongside Russian athletes, some of whom are members of the Russian military or military sports clubs. Some have received medals and awards from the Russian Defense Ministry.
For the Russian Defense Ministry, sport is part of its power. It is one of the ways Russia demonstrates its strength to the world. They use these opportunities to display Russian influence, including the Russian flag.
A national flag does not represent only sport or culture. It is also political.
This is not a political symbol we can share. For us, it is a political symbol of our suffering, of the deaths of Ukrainians. It is unbearable for us to treat this as something normal, because going to kill your neighbor is not normal.
What do you think Ukraine will look like after the war?
I hope we will be able to rebuild on the foundations of what we have today. That means a flourishing culture and a desire to be ourselves and live normal lives.
And with the support and solidarity we have received from around the world, especially here in Estonia, I hope that when the war finally ends, we will have tremendous creative potential to build a better world together and live in peace, solidarity and mutual support.
We would like to invite everyone to Ukraine after the war to see and experience it for themselves and so that we can thank everyone who is standing by our side today.
--

Zelensky Accuses Russia of Breaking Energy Ceasefire as Kremlin Says Talks Ongoing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
09:30:00 UTC
18:30:00 KST

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky accused Russia on Monday of violating an “energy ceasefire” announced by U.S. President Donald Trump, urging Washington to ensure Moscow abides by the agreement as the Kremlin said contacts over a possible truce were ongoing.
Russia attacked gas production facilities belonging to Ukraine’s state oil and gas company Naftogaz in the Kharkiv region overnight, causing a fire and damaging critical equipment, the company said Monday.
Ukrainian drone attacks, meanwhile, appeared to spare Russian oil refineries overnight after Trump made the surprise announcement that the ceasefire had taken immediate effect.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters Monday that contacts over a possible energy ceasefire were continuing. He declined to say whether it would apply only to oil refineries, saying further information would be released in due course.
“There were Russian violations of the energy ceasefire announced by President Trump,” Zelensky told a security conference in Warsaw via video link.
Zelensky said he had learned about the agreement through the media and was awaiting details of the terms discussed by Washington and Moscow.
“This energy ceasefire, it can work, and it can become a major step toward ending the war if the Americans truly step in now and make sure Russians respect it,” he said.
The Kremlin has not formally confirmed that it agreed to a ceasefire. Sources close to the Russian government told Bloomberg that Moscow remained skeptical that Washington could deliver a binding agreement on terms favorable to Russia.
Naftogaz acting CEO Sergii Fedorenko said employees were working to repair the damage from the overnight attack.
“Our employees are doing everything possible to repair the damage as quickly as possible and prevent risks to the stable operation of the energy system,” he said on Telegram.
Zelensky also said in his nightly video address Sunday that Russian forces had struck a combined heat and power plant in Kharkiv, Ukraine’s second-largest city, that evening. A Ukrainian official said the attack took place after Trump’s ceasefire announcement.
“The Armed Forces of Ukraine have received all the appropriate orders,” Zelensky said in the address.
Russia’s Defense Ministry said air defenses intercepted 151 Ukrainian drones over 10 Russian regions and annexed Crimea overnight. Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said 37 drones were destroyed as they approached the capital between Sunday evening and Monday morning.
Local authorities and independent media reported no new strikes on Russian oil refineries, which Ukraine has repeatedly targeted in recent months.
Russian attacks on other targets continued Monday. The Defense Ministry said its forces struck a cargo vessel carrying military supplies near the Ukrainian port of Odesa. Local officials said Russian shelling and air attacks injured at least 12 people in Kharkiv that morning.
In Russia’s southern Rostov region, firefighters continued battling a blaze at the Novoshakhtinsk oil refinery following a drone attack Saturday, the exiled news outlet Astra reported.
Authorities in the southwestern Belgorod region said one civilian was killed and three others were injured Sunday evening.
Separately, Peskov rejected Zelensky’s proposal for a 60-day ceasefire to allow Ukraine to hold presidential elections, saying Moscow wanted an overall peace deal instead.
“Please tell Putin, give us two months, 60 days of total ceasefire, 60 days, and we will organize elections,” Zelensky told ABC’s “This Week” on Sunday.
Peskov said Putin and other Russian officials had repeatedly stated that they did not want a temporary ceasefire and were prepared to work toward long-term peace.
Russia has long pressed Ukraine to hold elections and says that its failure to do so makes Zelensky an illegitimate leader. Elections in wartime are prohibited by Ukrainian law.
Reuters contributed reporting.

'We have one refinery' — Zelensky says energy ceasefire must cover power grid, not just oil
Ukraine will halt its strikes against Russian refineries only if Moscow ceases its attacks against the Ukrainian power grid, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Oct. 12, signaling that a refinery-only truce makes little sense for a country with a single, badly damaged refinery.
"In Ukraine, we have just one oil refinery. And it was badly damaged by Russian strikes long, long ago," Zelensky said in a video address to the Warsaw Security Forum.
The news comes shortly after U.S. President Donald Trump claimed on his Truth Social platform that both Kyiv and Moscow agreed to an energy truce — an announcement that took Ukrainian officials by surprise.
The Ukrainian president confirmed that Kyiv learned of the supposed truce only from media reports, but reiterated his readiness to adhere to it — provided that Russia follows suit.
"We are ready to respect an energy ceasefire if Russia is ready to do the same," Zelensky added in his speech, noting that Ukraine did not attack any Russian refineries overnight, while Moscow struck a Ukrainian gas production facility.
Russian forces also struck a power plant in Kharkiv on Oct. 11 shortly after Trump's announcement, and the Kremlin has not confirmed adherence to any truce.
"It was clear that (Russian President Vladimir) Putin does not read Truth Social, and his 'Shahed' drones follow a different set of instructions," Zelensky remarked. "But this post is actually about something that affects the lives of millions of people — and that makes it very important."
Adding to the confusion, an undisclosed White House official told Axios that Trump's announcement concerns only oil refineries and that a broader ceasefire covering the energy grid could come next.
Russia is one of the world's largest oil refiners, boasting a wide network of refineries whose production helps fund Moscow's war machine in Ukraine.
Ukraine effectively has only one oil refinery, in Kremenchuk in central Poltava Oblast, which has faced heavy attacks since the start of Russia's all-out invasion.
While Ukrainian drones have been targeting Russian refineries throughout the war to undercut the Kremlin's wartime revenues, Moscow has been attacking the Ukrainian energy grid and other critical infrastructure sites, leading to large-scale outages of electricity, water, and heat.
Ukrainian officials warn that Russia is preparing another massive campaign against energy infrastructure this winter.
"This winter, if Russia does not agree to an energy ceasefire, we will respond," Zelensky warned.
The last few days saw Trump ramp up pressure on Kyiv, demanding that Ukraine halt attacks on Russian refineries and suggesting that the Ukrainian people replace Zelensky if they want an end to the war.
Trump also announced a deal to buy Russian diesel and blamed Ukrainian attacks for the global diesel supply crisis, despite evidence that the U.S. war against Iran is the primary cause of the current shortage.
Kyiv's European allies have already expressed skepticism about the alleged energy truce.
"We haven't yet seen that also Russia will stick to it," said Kaja Kallas, the EU's chief diplomat. "Of course, personally, I would also welcome that the ceasefire would include people not being killed."
Belgian Foreign Minister Maxime Prevot said that while the announcement is a "good thing... the Russians have continued to attack energy infrastructures at the gates of winter in Ukraine, especially in Kharkiv, and so things must be followed up effectively."

The EU has extended the sanctions mechanism concerning the use of chemical weapons until 2031
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
12:28:33 EEST
18:28:33 KST

The EU has extended the sanctions mechanism concerning the use of chemical weapons until 2031
Kyiv • UNN
The Council of the EU has extended the sanctions regime against chemical weapons until October 30, 2031. The restrictions cover 31 individuals and 6 organizations.
The Council of the EU has decided to extend for five years, until 30 October 2031, the sanctions regime against the proliferation and use of chemical weapons. This was reported by the press service of the Council of the EU, UNN writes.
This is the first time the sanctions regime has been extended for such a long period. The Council also decided to extend for one year, until 30 October 2027, the individual sanctions under this regime
Overall, the restrictive measures apply to 31 individuals and six entities. They are subject to an asset freeze, and the provision of funds or economic resources, directly or indirectly, to or for the benefit of these individuals and entities is prohibited. In addition, individuals included on the sanctions list are subject to a ban on entering the EU.
The purpose of the sanctions regime is to contribute to the EU’s efforts to counter the proliferation and use of chemical weapons, as well as to support the implementation of the Convention on the Prohibition of the Development, Production, Stockpiling and Use of Chemical Weapons and on Their Destruction (CWC).
Background
On 22 March 2018, the European Council reaffirmed that the use of chemical weapons, including the use of any toxic chemicals as weapons under any circumstances, is wholly unacceptable, must be systematically and resolutely condemned, and poses a threat to the security of us all.
On 15 October 2018, the Council of the EU adopted the legal framework for introducing restrictive measures against the proliferation and use of chemical weapons. The EU is closely monitoring developments in this area and may decide at any time to extend the sanctions and amend the list of individuals and entities to which they apply.
On 3 July 2026, the Council of the EU decided to additionally impose restrictive measures on six Russian nationals involved in the development of chemical weapons, including epibatidine.

Maps show how Israel’s ‘Yellow Line’ keeps squeezing Palestinians in Gaza
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
09:27:12 UTC
18:27:12 KST

Maps show how Israel’s ‘Yellow Line’ keeps squeezing Palestinians in Gaza
A year into a ‘ceasefire’, Israel restricts access to 65 percent of Gaza and crams 2.1 million people into the rest.
Israel has expanded its military occupation in the Gaza Strip in violation of a United States-brokered ‘ceasefire’, forcing Palestinians into an ever-smaller share of the besieged territory, devastated by Israel’s ongoing genocidal war.
Nearly two-thirds of Gaza is now under Israeli military control or subject to access restrictions.
The original ‘Yellow Line’, established under US President Donald Trump’s 20-point plan to end the war, marked the area to which Israeli forces initially withdrew. They were expected to make further withdrawals gradually, but instead, they have seized more territory.
On Sunday, Israeli forces moved yellow concrete blocks dozens of metres west in Shujayea, a neighbourhood in southeastern Gaza City, forcing Palestinian families to flee and bringing more of the neighbourhood under Israeli military control.
“It’s not simply about where the ‘Yellow Line’ is today but where it can move next,” Al Jazeera’s Ibrahim al-Khalili said, reporting from Gaza City. “For families who have been repeatedly displaced in the past three years, the situation remains dire, and they have to make the impossible decision of where they can go.”
More than 90 percent of Gaza’s 2.1 million population has been forcibly displaced by Israel’s war, launched on October 7, 2023, after Hamas-led attacks on southern Israel.
Using maps, Al Jazeera shows how much of Gaza Israel has grabbed since the ‘ceasefire’.
Gaza before the war
Before the war, Palestinians were spread across the Gaza Strip, a 365sq km (141sq-mile) territory roughly 41km (25 miles) long and from 6km to 12km (4 to 7 miles) wide.
That made it one of the most densely populated places on Earth with about 6,000 people per square kilometre, similar to Nairobi or London. Each person had, on average, about 160sq metres (1,722sq ft) of land.
Even then, not all of Gaza’s land was accessible. Israel enforced a buffer zone along the fence with Israel, and Palestinians who approached it risked being shot. In 2010, the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) estimated that the restricted area covered 17 percent of Gaza’s land and 35 percent of its farmland.
Gaza has been under an Israeli land, air and sea blockade since 2007.
Gaza at the ‘ceasefire’
Under the first phase of the “ceasefire”, Israeli forces were to withdraw to the “Yellow Line” within 24 hours, after which a 72-hour period began for the handover of Israeli captives held in Gaza. Trump first published a map of the line on his Truth Social platform.
The line left Israel in control of 53 percent of the Strip, mostly farmland and border areas in the east, and confined Palestinians to the remaining 47 percent, about 172sq km (66sq miles).
By October 2025, two years of war had killed more than 67,000 Palestinians, and tens of thousands more had left the territory, reducing Gaza’s population to about 2.1 million.
Pushed into less than half of Gaza’s territory under the “ceasefire”, its density doubled to about 12,000 people per square kilometre, comparable to New York City. Each person was left with about 82sq metres (883sq ft).
Gaza today
Since the “ceasefire”, Israeli forces have repeatedly moved the yellow concrete blocks marking the “Yellow Line” farther west, sometimes overnight, expanding the areas under their control. Satellite imagery has also documented continued demolitions in areas held by Israeli forces.
The research group Forensic Architecture estimated that Israel controlled 58 percent of Gaza by December. In March, the Israeli military sent aid agencies maps of a new “orange line”, a restricted zone beyond the “Yellow Line” where humanitarian movements must be coordinated with the army.
According to OCHA, restrictions now cover 65 percent of Gaza. Israel itself said it controls about 70 percent of the territory, a UN official told the Security Council in June.
That leaves 2.1 million people in about 35 percent of the Strip, roughly 128sq km (49sq miles). The population density has nearly tripled since before the war to about 16,000 people per square kilometre, close to central Tokyo.
Each person now has about 61sq metres (657sq ft) of land for everything: shelter, roads, schools, hospitals and farmland.
Unlike Tokyo, Gaza has little space left to house its people. The UN Satellite Centre, UNOSAT, found 82 percent of structures in the Strip are damaged or destroyed. The UN Food and Agriculture Organization says only 3 percent of Gaza’s cropland is both undamaged and accessible.
OCHA says the remaining 35 percent of Gaza is “already overcrowded” and access restrictions are a key obstacle as aid groups try to relocate families before the rainy season. More than 950,000 people live in displacement sites at risk of flooding, according to the UN, most of them in tents and makeshift shelters, as seen in the satellite image below.
Approaching the ‘Yellow Line” can be deadly. Israel treats areas beyond it as a free-fire zone, and Palestinians who come near it have been shot. Nearly 1,500 people have been killed across Gaza since the ceasefire was announced.

Russia struck a gas production facility in the Kharkiv region; hostilities have caused power outages in three regions
Kyiv • UNN
A drone strike caused a fire at a gas production facility; critical equipment was damaged, and there were no casualties. There are power outages in three regions.
Russia attacked a gas production facility in the Kharkiv region, causing a fire at the site, the Naftogaz Group reported on October 12. Due to damage to energy equipment resulting from hostilities, as of the morning of October 12 there were new power outages in three regions, the Ministry of Energy and NPC Ukrenergo reported. This was reported by UNN.
Gas production
Overnight, Russia attacked the Naftogaz Group’s gas production infrastructure in the Kharkiv region. The strike by a jet drone caused a fire
As Naftogaz stated, "the company’s employees were in a shelter during the shelling. No one was injured"
"The attack damaged critical equipment. Our employees are doing everything possible to eliminate the consequences of the strike as quickly as possible and prevent risks to the stable operation of the energy system", - acting Chairman of the Naftogaz Management Board Serhii Fedorenko said.
"Currently, Group specialists are working to eliminate the emergency situation and repair the damage at the facility", the statement said.
What is happening with the energy system
There are also consequences of the hostilities for the energy system, the Ministry of Energy reported.
"Due to the hostilities, some consumers in the Donetsk, Zaporizhzhia and Kharkiv regions remain temporarily without electricity", the Ministry of Energy reported on October 12.
Where the security situation permits, crews are already working to restore power. Energy workers are doing everything possible to return electricity to Ukrainians’ homes as quickly as possible, the ministry said.
Bad weather also caused interruptions in power supply.
"Due to bad weather, 63 settlements in the Ternopil, Zhytomyr and Khmelnytskyi regions remain without electricity. Repair crews are working to restore power", the ministry reported.
Outage schedules
"As a result of grid restrictions caused by previous Russian attacks, hourly outage schedules and capacity limitation schedules for industry and businesses are being implemented today in a number of regions of Ukraine. This is a necessary step that helps prevent grid overloads and protect the system from large-scale accidents", the Ministry of Energy reported.
"To prevent overloads of equipment damaged by previous Russian shelling, capacity limitation schedules for industry and hourly outage schedules (up to 1.5 rounds) for all categories of consumers are being implemented today in some regions from 06:00 until the end of the day", NPC Ukrenergo clarified.
The Ministry of Energy emphasized, however, that "operational information about the consequences of attacks and the condition of the energy system is published exclusively on official resources, without unnecessary detail. Please use only verified sources and do not disseminate materials that could help the enemy".
Consumption
According to Ukrenergo, electricity consumption has increased. Today, October 12, as of 09:30, it was 1.7% higher than at the same time on the previous working day—Friday, October 9. The reasons for the changes are the smaller scale of the restrictions applied, as well as cloudy weather and rain in some regions, which reduces the efficiency of household solar power plants and consequently increases the amount of electricity consumed from the grid. Yesterday, October 11, the daily consumption peak was recorded in the evening. It was 1.9% higher than the peak recorded on the previous Sunday—October 4.
"Please limit the use of high-powered electrical appliances from 17:00 to 22:00", Ukrenergo urged.

BEIJING, Oct. 12 (Xinhua) -- China is intensifying its crackdown on food safety crimes and tightening oversight of online food sales and other emerging business models, according to a new guideline.
The guideline, issued by the Commission for Political and Legal Affairs of the Communist Party of China Central Committee, calls for tougher penalties for serious offenses and closer coordination between food safety regulators and criminal justice authorities.
A commission representative said on Monday that China's food safety situation remained generally stable, but authorities faced new challenges as food safety crimes became more sophisticated, increasingly exploited online platforms and spanned multiple stages of the supply chain.
The guideline identifies meat products, school meals, health foods, vegetables and fruit as top enforcement priorities. It also calls for tighter scrutiny of food production, online sales, catering services and imports.
To improve coordination between administrative enforcement and criminal proceedings, the guideline calls for clearer procedures for referring suspected criminal cases and better information sharing between agencies.
China also plans to expedite revisions to the food safety law to clarify the regulatory responsibilities of businesses involved in fresh food e-commerce, food delivery and livestream sales.
The guideline also calls for authorities to update lists of banned additives as investigations identify new illegal substances.
It further urges authorities to address food safety risks uncovered in individual cases and strengthen oversight across the supply chain. ■

Economic Watch: China rolls out "token factories" to drive AI economy
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
17:25:49 CST
18:25:49 KST

This photo provided by iSoftStone Information Technology (Group) Co., Ltd. shows a scene inside a token factory at the Beijing Economic-Technological Development Area in Beijing, capital of China, Sept. 21, 2026. (Xinhua)
BEIJING, Oct. 12 (Xinhua) -- As AI applications gain momentum, China is accelerating the rollout of "token factories" in a bid to build an economic order suited to the AI era.
Every time a user prompts an AI model to generate code, images or video, tokens are consumed behind the scenes. In March, China adopted "ciyuan" as the official Chinese term for "token," giving its AI services a standard unit for measuring, settling and tracking usage -- similar to how electricity is measured in kilowatt-hours.
In late September, Beijing unveiled an action plan to accelerate the development of the token economy for 2026-2028. "This is the first provincial-level policy in China specifically dedicated to the token economy," said Zhang Jinrui, an official with the Beijing Municipal Bureau of Economy and Information Technology.
"With the rollout of Beijing's new policy, tokens are no longer just a technical term associated with large models. The token economy has officially entered a stage of industrial application and institutional development," said Liu Yong, president of the Beijing-based Zhongguancun Internet Finance Institute.
The Beijing action plan calls for building world-class token factories and establishing tiered evaluation standards, with throughput capacity, time to first token, PUE (power usage effectiveness) and cache hit rate as core metrics, to ensure the large-scale supply of high-quality tokens.
A token factory can be thought of as the AI era's equivalent of a power plant. It integrates electricity, chips, data and models to directly produce tokens. Unlike traditional data centers that only rent out computing cards, customers no longer need to deploy models or optimize inference themselves -- they simply pay for the tokens they use.
In the Beijing Economic-Technological Development Area, the Chinese capital's first token factory is now in operation, with a daily capacity of up to 1.4 trillion tokens in its first phase.
The plan also designates token distribution platforms as part of the city's new infrastructure layout, exploring market-based pricing and circulation mechanisms for tokens, so that tokens can truly be measured and traded as an economic factor.
On the application side, the new policy encourages the development of general-purpose and industry-specific AI agents, bringing token capabilities into sectors such as industry, research and government affairs.
Chen Guangming, an official with the Beijing Municipal Bureau of Economy and Information Technology, said token consumption is currently growing fastest in AI-generated content and programming, and more vertical industries will become potential growth drivers for token consumption in the future.
"In the internet era, competition was all about traffic and user attention. In the AI era, the logic has shifted -- what matters now is the quality and efficiency of outputting effective tokens," Liu said, adding that the shift from a traffic economy -- one built on user visits and attention -- to a token economy represents a new trend in China's economic development.
Data from China's National Data Administration shows that by June, the country's average daily token calls had surpassed 500 trillion. "More than half of those calls were made in Beijing," Zhang said, noting that the city has so far registered 242 large models for public use.
Beijing's early push is aimed not merely at building a series of token factories, but at exploring institutional rules suited to the token economy, making the city a testing ground for the industry's development, according to local authorities.
Elsewhere, localities across China are developing token economies tailored to their own strengths, as part of efforts to implement the State Council's guidelines on the "AI Plus" initiative. The guidelines aim to build a systematic support framework for AI covering models, data, computing power, applications, open-source development, talent, policies and regulations, and security.
In May, north China's Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region, drawing on its green computing resources, launched a token trading platform integrating model calls, token matching and transaction settlement. Nanning, capital of south China's Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region, is exploring new models such as cross-border data compliance and remote model inference delivery, helping domestic computing power and large-model capabilities reach ASEAN markets as standardized token services. East China's Anhui Province, meanwhile, encourages banks to offer "token loans" as a financial tool for the token economy.
Industry observers generally agree that the global token economy remains in its early stage but holds vast potential. A research report by CICC, a Chinese investment bank, sees "token factories" as one of the fastest-growing and most commercially promising business models for large-model developers in the near term. JPMorgan predicts that China's AI inference token consumption will grow about 370-fold between 2025 and 2030.
China's three major telecom operators rolled out token packages in May for individual users as well as government and enterprise clients, bringing token commercialization further into reach for individual consumers.
Li Lingran, an engineer at an internet company in Beijing, says using large AI models at work has become as essential as water. He now spends more than 200 yuan (about 30 U.S. dollars) a month on tokens, even more than his traditional mobile phone bill. "This is a shift you can't ignore," he said. ■
This photo provided by iSoftStone Information Technology (Group) Co., Ltd. shows a scene inside a token factory at the Beijing Economic-Technological Development Area in Beijing, capital of China, Sept. 21, 2026. (Xinhua)
