SYDNEY, Oct. 12 (Xinhua) -- An estimated 456,000 people in the Australian state of Western Australia, including almost 99,000 children, are living in poverty in 2026 as rising housing costs and inadequate household incomes deepen financial hardship, according to a new report.
The 2026 Poverty Snapshot, released by the Bankwest Curtin Economics Center, found that 15.1 percent of the state's population lived in poverty, up from 11.8 percent in 2021. The number has increased by about 145,000, or 47 percent, over five years, according to a statement released Monday by Australia's Curtin University.
The report estimated that around 180,000 Western Australians were living in deep poverty, while more than 650,000 had incomes below 60 percent of the national median after housing costs.
The state capital Perth's median weekly rent reached 720 Australian dollars (about 502 U.S. dollars) in June 2026, having more than doubled since June 2020. More than one in four private renters in the state were living in poverty, the report found.
Children faced particularly severe hardship, with almost half of those living in poverty in deep poverty, compared with about one in four in 2021. Children in poverty faced an average household income shortfall of 224 Australian dollars a week.
The report called for expanded social and affordable housing, stronger support for households experiencing rental stress and measures to ensure incomes keep pace with living costs. ■

4. Vallecas protest understandable but counterproductive

Some supporters blame club president Raul Martin Presa for the problems and fear he wants to move Rayo away from its traditional home.
Their anger is understandable, given the importance of Vallecas to the club's identity, but disrupting matches risks making the situation worse.
Rayo could face a stadium closure of between one and three matches, according to reports, potentially depriving the team of home support just as it has returned to its own ground. ■

In September, Russian forces lost more than 50,000 personnel in fighting in Ukraine, including up to 28,000 killed.

Ukrainian losses over the same period are estimated at around 5,000 personnel.

In July, Russian occupation forces suffered 42,860 confirmed personnel losses.
President Volodymyr Zelensky clarified in his address that 30,272 of those Russian troops were hit by drones.
BBC and Mediazona journalists have identified 258,989 Russian military personnel eliminated in the war against Ukraine.
Researchers estimate that these figures may account for 45% to 65% of the actual death toll, as the Russian authorities do not publish official casualty statistics.

China's NEV share of new car sales hits record 61.6 pct in September
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
17:25:17 CST
18:25:17 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 12 (Xinhua) -- New energy vehicles (NEVs) accounted for a record 61.6 percent of China's monthly new car sales in September, marking the third consecutive month above the 60 percent threshold, while the cumulative share for the first three quarters rose to 53.6 percent, industry data showed on Monday.
In the first three quarters of 2026, NEV output and sales reached 12.483 million and 12.472 million units, respectively, both up by more than 10 percent year on year, according to the China Association of Automobile Manufacturers (CAAM).
Overall auto output and sales in September stood at 2.99 million and 2.956 million units, respectively, up 11.4 percent and 9 percent month on month.
NEV output and sales for the month reached 1.814 million and 1.823 million units, up 12.2 percent and 13.6 percent year on year, respectively.
In the first three quarters, auto output and sales totaled 23.246 million and 23.271 million units, edging down slightly year on year.
Vehicle exports maintained rapid growth. In September, China exported 1.053 million vehicles, up 61.4 percent year on year, including 571,000 NEVs, more than double the figure a year earlier, the data showed. NEVs accounted for more than half of total vehicle exports for the fourth consecutive month.
During the January-September period, auto exports totaled 8.205 million units, including over 4 million NEVs, more than double the level a year earlier.
"Despite a complex and severe external environment, exports have continued to grow rapidly, demonstrating strong resilience, while domestic new growth drivers are being steadily unleashed and the share of NEV sales is rising steadily," said Chen Shihua, deputy secretary-general of CAAM.
Looking ahead to the fourth quarter, the industry is expected to maintain steady operation, Chen said. ■

China Focus: China's school autumn breaks take shape as cities roll out local plans
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
17:25:16 CST
18:25:16 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 12 (Xinhua) -- China is turning a national policy initiative for school spring and autumn breaks into local arrangements, as cities across the country announce autumn holidays for students.
The breaks are designed to enrich students' social experiences and promote their all-round development. They also give families more time for leisure and can help spread tourism spending more evenly throughout the year.
In the latest example, the education bureau of Shenzhen, in south China's Guangdong Province, said on Oct. 9 that all schools providing compulsory education in the city, including private schools, would have a four-day autumn break from Nov. 17 to 20, 2026, and a two-day spring break on April 1-2, 2027. Kindergartens may follow the same arrangement, while high schools can set their own schedules based on their circumstances. The city said it would not require make-up school days after either break.
Local arrangements vary. In Sichuan Province in southwest China, Chengdu will let districts and schools schedule a three-day autumn break over the last three days of the second week of November, linked to the weekend. Zigong has fixed its break for Nov. 16-18, creating a five-day break with the preceding weekend.
In Fuzhou, in the eastern province of Fujian, different districts and county-level areas have different dates. Ningbo, in east China's Zhejiang Province, will schedule its break for Nov. 25-27. Guizhou Province in southwest China has issued guidance setting the autumn break at three days in general, with mid-November as the suggested time.
The moves come about seven months after China's 2026 government work report called for introducing spring and autumn breaks for primary and secondary school students in areas where conditions permit, along with a system of staggered paid leave.
Beyond providing students a break from classroom routines, the new arrangements could also encourage families to travel during less busy periods, potentially benefiting tourism and related businesses.
An earlier pilot in Sichuan provided an indication of the possible impact on tourism. During a five-day autumn break in November 2025, ticket bookings for scenic spots in the province more than quadrupled from the same period a year earlier, while bookings for flights departing Chengdu rose 22 percent from the previous week, local media reported.
While social media users generally welcomed the introduction of spring and autumn breaks, some raised practical questions. One user from Guangdong asked who would care for primary school children when parents were working.
Local authorities are working to address childcare needs. Measures in local guidance include school-provided care, study camps and group activities for students whose parents cannot take leave.
In Altay, in northwest China's Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region, the three-day "snow break" scheduled for Dec. 16-18 will be combined with the following weekend to create a five-day holiday.
Authorities there plan to organize activities using local winter resources, including ice-and-snow study trips, winter sports and cultural experiences. Schools will reduce written homework and encourage practical assignments related to winter sports and local ice-and-snow culture. Free school-provided care will be available during the break for students who cannot join study trips.
The arrangements show how school holidays can be adapted to local conditions to extend learning beyond the classroom while giving families more flexibility.
Making the breaks work for families also requires coordination between school calendars and workplace arrangements. Lu Ming, a national political advisor and a professor of economics at Shanghai Jiao Tong University, said in March that employers should allow greater flexibility during school breaks so parents could adjust shifts or take leave to spend time with their children. Where parents cannot take time off, he said, schools and community organizations could organize activities with government support.
In China, autumn school breaks are tailored to local conditions rather than set under a uniform national system. Their longer-term success will depend not only on school calendars but also on parents' access to leave and the availability of school-provided or community-based care for children whose parents cannot take time off. ■

Number of schoolkids in Switzerland set to drop by 2035
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
09:25:00 UTC
18:25:00 KST

Number of schoolkids in Switzerland set to drop by 2035
According to government estimates, the number of university students is set to rise by more than 20% over the next nine years. From 2029 to 2035, the number of primary school pupils is expected to fall as a result of the decline in the birth rate.
Depending on the level of education, primary and tertiary student numbers in Switzerland are set to develop very differently up to 2035. This is evident from the education scenarios for 2026 to 2035 published on Monday by the Federal Statistical Office (FSO). The FSO emphasises that the results are subject to uncertainty due to unclear birth and immigration figures.
At primary level, the number of pupils has risen sharply in recent years. However, since 2022, birth rates have been falling, which is why the number of primary school pupils is expected to peak between 2027 and 2028, and then fall by 8% by 2035, according to the FSO’s forecast. A decline is expected at lower secondary level from 2033 onwards.
More
Why the Swiss school system is so successful
The FSO forecasts moderate growth for lower secondary education, with a 10% increase in basic vocational training and a 12% rise in general education programmes. An increase of 17%, to 41,300 students, at higher technical colleges is also expected in higher vocational education.
At universities, universities of applied sciences and teacher training colleges, federal authorities anticipate 305,000 students at Bachelor’s and Master’s levels by 2035. This represents an increase of 21% compared with 2026. The main reasons are population growth and the rise in the number of international students.
This surge in university enrolment comes at a time when young graduates are finding it increasingly difficult to enter the job market. According to the University Graduates Survey, conducted by the Federal Statistical Office in August, unemployment among graduates rose noticeably between 2023 and 2025. The only exception to this trend is teacher training colleges.

Ex-director who oversaw Grenfell cost-cutting leaves council housing role after backlash
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
09:24:59 UTC
18:24:59 KST

A housing director who oversaw cost cutting at Grenfell Tower before the fatal fire has left a £150,000-a-year senior council housing role after a backlash from bereaved families and survivors.
Laura Johnson was the director of housing at the Royal Borough of Kensington and Chelsea (RBKC) at the time of the 2017 Grenfell fire which killed 72 people, and was criticised in the subsequent inquiry for her role in budget-cutting decisions prior to the blaze.
It was found that she pushed for a new contractor to carry out the tower’s renovation works on a lower budget, which ultimately meant metal cladding was swapped for combustible plastic-filled panels to save money.
In August, she was appointed the director of development and property at the Barnet Group, which manages the borough’s 13,000 council homes, on a salary of £157,078, a move described by bereaved families and survivors as “outrageous and disrespectful”.
In a letter to Joe Powell, the Labour MP for Kensington and Bayswater where Grenfell Tower stood, the company confirmed that Johnson was “no longer employed by The Barnet Group”.
Eamon McGoldrick, the chair of the board, said in the letter: “We fully recognise the depth of feeling surrounding the Grenfell Tower tragedy and its continuing impact on bereaved families, survivors, residents and the wider community.
“We also fully acknowledge legitimate public interest concerning governance of senior appointments.”
He said he could not go into specific details about Johnson’s situation and it is not clear exactly what led to Johnson’s job being terminated.
It is understood that Angela Rayner, the housing secretary, wrote to the Barnet Group last month asking for further information about Johnson’s appointment and on what basis it was made.
A spokesperson for Grenfell United, which represents survivors and bereaved families, welcomed the news and said it was a “scandal” Johnson had been given the role.
“More than nine years after Grenfell, it should not take bereaved families and survivors campaigning for a housing organisation to take the inquiry’s findings seriously,” they said.
“But this does not end with Johnson. Others whose conduct was singled out by the Grenfell Tower public inquiry continue to hold positions of authority, have responsibility for health and safety, and draw large salaries.
“The inquiry’s findings are there for everyone to read, yet those criticised continue their careers as though nothing has happened. It is an outrage that such damning findings have done nothing to stop them being entrusted with public safety.”
Powell said: “It’s totally inappropriate for any individual criticised by the inquiry to continue to work in housing, particularly while criminal investigations are ongoing. It’s right that Laura Johnson is no longer in such a position.
“The Grenfell Tower inquiry was clear about the failings of the RBKC and senior individuals involved in the management of their housing, including the tower.”
Last month, a Barnet Group spokesperson insisted Johnson was the “strongest candidate” for the role in a competitive field, and that it had considered her “professional experience, subsequent performance, references, qualifications and overall suitability for the role”.
A Barnet Group spokesperson said: “We can confirm that Laura Johnson is no longer employed by The Barnet Group.
“In common with any employer, we owe obligations of confidentiality to those working for us, applying for, or being considered for any role at any level. For that reason, it would be inappropriate for us to comment further.”
Last month the Metropolitan police said it had asked prosecutors to consider charges including manslaughter and fraud against 54 individuals, and 20 companies and organisations, in relation to the Grenfell fire.
The Crown Prosecution Service said charging decisions would be made before the 10th anniversary of the disaster on 14 June 2027.

‘We still love you’: NATO envoy seeks to reassure Europe over US military pullback
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
09:24:57 UTC
18:24:57 KST

US Ambassador to NATO, Matthew Whitaker, has enthused that there is no “love” lost between Washington and Brussels amid a more Europeanised NATO.
US Ambassador to NATO Matthew Whitaker told European Commissioner for Defence Andrius Kubilius that Washington remains committed to Europe’s defence, amid an ongoing US military review withdrawing thousands of troops and key strategic assets from the continent.
“We still love you,” Whitaker said at the Warsaw Security Forum on Monday in the Polish capital.
“I keep telling our European allies… the United States isn't stepping back.”
His remarks came during a panel on NATO 3.0 — a US-backed model that calls for Europe to take the lead with its conventional defences as American forces draw down from the continent and shift their attention elsewhere.
Kubilius said NATO 3.0 did not mean the United States was saying, “We don’t love you anymore, Europeans, so you should do your own job”. Rather, he argued, Europe needed to develop the capabilities to deter aggression on its own territory.
“Europe needs to take responsibility in our hands,” he said.
Kubilius has previously estimated that replacing US strategic military assets could cost Europe up to €500 billion. Experts have also suggested that Europe could need 300,000 additional troops to defend itself against Russia in a scenario in which Washington continues to withdraw its military support.
Since Donald Trump returned to the White House, Washington has sought to redirect military resources towards other regions, including the Indo-Pacific, to counter China’s growing influence.
The Pentagon’s review of US military deployments in Europe is expected to conclude by December, with its findings to be presented to US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth. The assessment could pave the way for further reductions in America’s military presence on the continent.
However, separate force reductions are already under way. In May, for example, the Pentagon ordered the withdrawal of approximately 5,000 troops from Germany and cancelled a planned deployment of a long-range fires battalion.
Whitaker said he did not want to “preview” further measures under the review because “it is not ready”, but argued that Washington’s push for a more European NATO was “working”.
“The proof is in where we're sitting today, here in Poland, spending 4.7% on core defence and leading really the alliance to a stronger, more capable military,” he said.
Allies agreed to raise their core defence spending target from 2% to 3.5% of gross domestic product (GDP) by 2035 at the 2025 NATO summit in The Hague, alongside a further 1.5% for broader security and defence spending.
"That is what the United States is expecting from all of its allies," Whitaker said of the overall 5% defence spending target.
Poland is among NATO’s highest spenders on core defence as a share of GDP, according to the alliance’s latest estimates.
The effort to increase defence spending also comes as the European Union seeks to strengthen its military capabilities by 2030, amid warnings from European intelligence agencies that Russia could pose a more direct threat to NATO in the coming years.
But the rearmament drive is facing significant hurdles. A leaked version of the European Defence Agency's landmark report — aiming to assess the progress — reveals major capability gaps, most notably in drone defences and maritime warfare.

Utrecht weighs tougher measures on landlords after lack of fines
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
09:24:40 UTC
18:24:40 KST

Utrecht weighs tougher measures on landlords after lack of fines
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Utrecht fined only 1 landlord last year despite receiving almost 200 complaints for breaking rules designed to protect tenants. The city is now considering a tougher approach modelled on Rotterdam, which issued 25 penalties in the second half of the year alone.
The figures were reported by regional broadcaster RTV Utrecht. Rotterdam received 667 complaints in 2025, and its fines ranged from €1,000 to tens of thousands per offence.
The threat of a fine is often enough to resolve a dispute since many renters are too scared to even report illegal or abusive practice for fear of losing their homes amid the housing crisis, but the city showed that when tenants did make reports, rents fell an average of €350 for private tenants.
Under the “good landlord law”, which came into force in 2023, landlords cannot discriminate against or intimidate tenants. Deposits are capped at 2 months’ basic rent, and service charges may only cover actual costs.
Unlike Rotterdam, Utrecht gives landlords a warning before handing down a penalty. It says it wants to avoid having fines overturned in court for being too heavy.
Research published by the Federation of Private-Sector Tenants (FHCS) in December last year found that Utrecht lacked the resources to look for abuses itself and relied entirely on complaints from tenants. Only around half of those complaints were taken further, usually because of a lack of evidence.
Fines are also rare in other big cities. In The Hague, around 600 complaints in two and a half years led to dozens of penalty orders but only 3 fines, which are being contested, according to the FHCS.
Amsterdam’s public list of sanctions showed only 1 fine, for intimidating tenants, which could still be challenged. Last October, the city warned a landlord who would only rent to working Dutch women that he faced a fine of up to €10,000.
Utrecht has not yet decided whether to follow Rotterdam’s lead, but believes fines could deter landlords and prevent repeat offences. It aims to introduce a rental permit in 2028, so that rents can be checked before a home is let.
The city also plans to do more to inform tenants about their rights and its complaints hotline. Every council is required by law to run a hotline for complaints about landlords.

Investigations implicate Deloitte, one of the world’s largest accounting firms, in alleged tax-evasion schemes involving Russian billionaire Roman Abramovich’s Cyprus companies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
16:17:20 UTC
01:17:20 KST

Investigations implicate Deloitte, one of the world’s largest accounting firms, in alleged tax-evasion schemes involving Russian billionaire Roman Abramovich’s Cyprus companies
Deloitte, one of the world’s largest consulting and auditing firms, helped falsify documents to conceal Russian billionaire Roman Abramovich’s wealth and enable him to evade taxes, according to a joint investigation by the BBC and the Bureau of Investigative Journalism (TBIJ). The Guardian published a separate report on the same case.
The investigations draw on leaked documents and emails from MeritServus, a Cyprus-based corporate services provider previously reported to have managed Abramovich’s businesses. One episode dates to 2006, when Cyprus passed a law requiring companies to publish their financial statements. At the time, Abramovich’s assets were held by the Cypriot company Amiscan Investments. Its balance sheet listed $672 million in assets: a mansion in the English county of West Sussex, an apartment in London, an estate in southern France, helicopters, private jets, and yachts, including the 115-meter (377-foot) Pelorus. Abramovich reportedly owned all these assets at the time.
Abramovich’s aides and MeritServus decided to transfer the assets to Amiscan’s parent company in the British Virgin Islands, where companies did not have to disclose their financial statements. According to the investigation, they backdated the paperwork to make it appear that the transfer had taken place in 2003.
Deloitte’s Cyprus office reviewed the documents and deemed them sufficient to remove the assets from Amiscan’s financial statements, leaving it with just $75,000 in assets. The Guardian reported that emails in the leaked files show Deloitte Cyprus employees took part in discussions about this scheme to make the assets “disappear.” Deloitte signed off on Amiscan’s financial statements with the valuable assets removed.
Another episode described in the investigations involves the Cypriot company Kravin Investments. In May 2003, its accounts held about $2 billion that Abramovich had received from selling assets in Russia. Some of the money was lent to other companies. All these funds should have been subject to tax in Cyprus. But documents show that Abramovich’s advisers soon began devising a plan to “eliminate” tax liabilities that could be “very large.”
They decided to alter Kravin’s financial statements and accounting records for 2003 and 2004 retroactively. The documents made it appear that Kravin did not own the funds but merely managed them on behalf of its parent company in the British Virgin Islands. This allowed the advisers to claim that the Cypriot company had no taxable income.
Citing the leaked correspondence, the BBC reported that Abramovich’s advisers devised the tax evasion plan after meeting with Deloitte representatives.
Another scheme concerns Electus Investments, a Cypriot company linked to Abramovich. Its accounts held $10 billion. Leaked emails show that in 2006, MeritServus proposed backdating documents to make it appear that a company with the same name in the British Virgin Islands had owned these assets since 2003. As a result, when the Cypriot company’s financial statements became public, its accounts showed just $145,000.
Abramovich’s lawyers denied any wrongdoing and said he had relied on advice from his advisers and Deloitte’s Cyprus office. Deloitte Cyprus said it had always complied with local law. It said it could not comment on the specific allegations because the documents and correspondence cited by the journalists concerned events from 20 years ago and were “no longer accessible.”

Zelenskyy says Russia ignored Trump's 'energy ceasefire' and kept attacking Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
09:22:38 UTC
18:22:38 KST

Zelenskyy addressed the Warsaw Security Forum in one of his first reactions to renewed turmoil with Washington, following Trump's surprise energy ceasefire announcement and controversial diesel deal with Russia.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy accused Russia on Monday of violating an energy ceasefire announced by Donald Trump, saying Kyiv had not even been consulted about the purported agreement and had only learned of it through the media.
"We did not know about that. We've learned that from the media as well, that the president of the United States has secured an energy ceasefire," Zelenskyy said.
Speaking at the Warsaw Security Forum, Zelenskyy questioned whether Moscow had agreed to the proposal at all, saying he had seen neither a public endorsement from Russia nor any let-up in its attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure.
"We have not seen that they support this ceasefire anywhere," he said, pointing to continued Russian strikes on Ukrainian energy facilities.
Large parts of Kyiv were without electricity and water when Trump made his announcement, as repair crews struggled to restore power following Russian strikes. Shortly afterwards, Russia launched another targeted attack on a power plant in Kharkiv, Zelenskyy said.
"It was clear that Putin does not read Truth Social," he remarked, referring to Trump's social media platform.
Zelenskyy also accused Russia of striking a Ukrainian gas production facility and a petrol station overnight, while Ukraine had refrained from attacking Russian oil refineries.
Despite the continued attacks, he said Kyiv remained willing to observe a reciprocal halt to strikes on energy infrastructure.
"We are ready to respect an energy ceasefire if Russia is ready to do the same. We agree if they agree," he said.
Zelenskyy offered to sign formal guarantees if Washington considered them necessary, but stressed that the US would have to secure Moscow's compliance.
Trump-Putin diesel deal sparks backlash
Zelenskyy's remarks followed several days of mounting tensions with Washington, beginning on Friday when Trump announced a deal with Vladimir Putin to supply Russian diesel to US and global markets, in an attempt to bring down soaring fuel prices ahead of November's US midterm elections.
The US Treasury subsequently issued a six-month licence easing sanctions on Russian diesel already loaded onto tankers, allowing deliveries until April 2027 — a sharp reversal of Washington's efforts to restrict Moscow's energy revenues.
The move drew criticism from European leaders and US lawmakers, including a bipartisan group of senators who urged Trump to reverse course, warning that the deal could provide Moscow with fresh revenues to finance its war against Ukraine.
Trump, meanwhile, blamed Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries for rising fuel prices and demanded that Zelenskyy halt them. On Saturday, he went further, suggesting Ukraine needed a new president and accusing its wartime leader of obstructing efforts to end the war.
On Sunday, Trump announced on Truth Social that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an immediate energy ceasefire, although neither side had publicly confirmed an agreement.
It was not the first such declaration. A similar announcement in September failed to halt the strikes.
Against this backdrop, Zelenskyy used his Warsaw address to make a pointed appeal for Washington to change course.
"We need American pressure on Russia, not sanctions relief, not concessions, but real pressure," he said.
He argued that Ukraine's strikes on Russian oil refineries and exports were a response to Moscow's sustained campaign against Ukrainian energy infrastructure, and that both sides would have to halt such attacks for a ceasefire to work.
Zelenskyy offers elections if Trump secures 60-day ceasefire
Responding to Trump's renewed pressure to hold presidential elections, Zelenskyy said voting remained impossible under current security conditions, with Russian attacks now taking place around the clock.
"From a security standpoint, that's completely impossible. We have attacks day and night," he said.
He also pointed to the logistical challenges of organising a vote for more than a million Ukrainian military personnel, including those serving on the front line.
Nevertheless, Zelenskyy signalled that he was prepared to seek changes to Ukraine's legal framework if Washington could secure a comprehensive ceasefire with Moscow.
"If there is a ceasefire and if the Americans reach such an agreement with the Russians, I'm ready to engage with our Parliament and find difficult solutions," he said.
He suggested this could involve changes to legislation and even the constitution, although constitutional amendments are prohibited under martial law.
Zelenskyy then turned Trump's own diplomatic engagement with Moscow into a challenge to the US president, arguing that Washington should be able to use its influence over Putin to secure a complete halt to hostilities.
"And if we have at least a 60 day full ceasefire, then I'll be ready to work on holding elections," he said.
Zelenskyy warns of Russian hybrid attacks
Beyond the dispute with Washington, Zelenskyy warned that Ukrainian intelligence had uncovered further Russian plans to destabilise European countries.
"Our intelligence services know that Russia is planning many, many aggressive hybrid operations against Europe, against different countries, against your countries," he told the forum.
"There is no such thing as a small act of destabilisation," he added, urging European governments to remain vigilant and united.
Zelenskyy also appealed for continued military assistance, including ammunition for Ukraine's F-16 fighter jets, air-defence interceptors and funding for domestic weapons and drone production.
He called for closer defence-industrial cooperation with Poland, arguing that joint production and technological partnerships could strengthen both countries' security.
The Ukrainian president also urged European leaders to prevent further delays in Ukraine's EU accession negotiations, saying progress was essential not only politically but also for the morale of Ukrainians living through another winter of war.
"Please do not allow any pauses in Ukraine's European integration," he said.
Zelenskyy said Kyiv expected to open two negotiating clusters and wanted another two opened by the end of the year.
"Our people need to feel that despite all the difficulties, Ukraine's European future is close," he said.
He concluded by urging European leaders to ensure Washington understood that an energy ceasefire, de-escalation and credible security guarantees were urgently needed in practice, rather than simply being announced on social media.
"In reality, not just on Truth Social," he said.

Accused of raping two girls, Louisiana man set to become police chief after opponent quits
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
09:21:35 UTC
18:21:35 KST

Christopher Paul, 48, who was arrested last month on suspicion of raping two 13-year-old girls nearly 20 years ago, is poised to become police chief of the small Louisiana town of Elizabeth, despite facing two criminal charges of second-degree rape. With his only opponent having withdrawn from the race, Paul is now the sole candidate for the position, and Louisiana law does not prevent him from taking office while the charges remain unresolved.
The extraordinary situation has sparked criticism in Elizabeth, a town of approximately 400 residents. Local officials are already considering changing how the police chief is selected, as the prospect grows that a man awaiting trial on serious sexual assault charges could soon be responsible for enforcing the law.
Paul, a Republican, registered as a candidate for police chief on August 6. About a month later, he was arrested over allegations that he raped two girls, both 13 at the time, in 2005 and 2006. He faces two counts of second-degree rape and was released on $60,000 bail.
According to Allen Parish Sheriff Doug Hebert, the investigation began in early August after police received a complaint concerning alleged assaults dating back approximately two decades. Detectives interviewed the complainants and additional witnesses before obtaining an arrest warrant. Paul surrendered to authorities on September 8 and was taken into custody.
Paul initially faced another candidate, Zachary LaCaze, who intended to run as an independent in the November 3 election. However, LaCaze announced on September 23 that he was withdrawing after discovering that his federal government employment prevented him from continuing his campaign.
LaCaze works at the Fort Polk military installation and said he was initially told he could run for office provided he did not identify himself with a political party. He later learned that because his opponent was running as a Republican, his candidacy was subject to restrictions under the federal Hatch Act, which limits certain political activities by government employees.
Faced with a choice between keeping his job and continuing his campaign for police chief, LaCaze decided to withdraw.
Speaking to local television station KPLC, LaCaze acknowledged the consequences of his decision.
"I have a lot of concerns if it happens, but it's out of my hands," he said when asked about the possibility that his withdrawal would effectively hand Paul the position.
LaCaze withdrew after the official deadline for new candidates had passed, leaving Paul without an opponent and positioning him to take office without a contested election.
According to Louisiana election authorities, LaCaze's name may still appear on ballots because of the late withdrawal, but notices will be posted at polling locations explaining that the race has been canceled following his departure.
Mayor: ‘We have no authority to change the ballots’
The unusual circumstances have left local officials facing a legal dilemma. Under Louisiana law, a felony conviction can disqualify someone from holding public office, but pending criminal charges alone do not prevent a candidate from running or serving.
Unless Paul is convicted of an offense that would make him ineligible, he remains legally entitled to assume the position. The new police chief's term is scheduled to begin January 1, 2027.
Elizabeth Mayor Mandy Leo Green issued a statement to residents amid the controversy, stressing that neither she nor the town council has the authority to remove Paul from the race.
"Charges are allegations, not a conviction," she emphasized.
"The candidate in question has been arrested and charged, but has not been convicted of any crime. Under the law, anyone accused of a crime is presumed innocent until proven guilty in a court of law. This is an important part of our justice system."
Green added that the local administration and town council cannot alter the ballots despite concerns surrounding the election. She invited residents to attend a council meeting scheduled for Monday, October 12, to express their views.
Meanwhile, the Youth Peace & Justice Foundation, an American organization dedicated to preventing violence against children, has called on Paul to voluntarily withdraw his candidacy until the criminal proceedings against him are resolved.
Paul declined to comment on the allegations when approached by local media but made clear that he intends to remain in the race.
In response to the situation, the Elizabeth town council has approved a special ballot measure for December 12, allowing residents to decide whether to change the process for selecting their police chief.
Under the proposal, the position would no longer be filled through direct elections. Instead, the police chief would be appointed with the approval of the town council.
According to council documents, the vote will take place about a month after the November election in which Paul is expected to be declared the winner, and less than three weeks before the new police chief's term begins.
It remains unclear when the proposed change would take effect if approved and whether it could have any impact on Paul's anticipated term. The official documents also do not explicitly state whether the decision to hold the vote was prompted by the criminal case.
Residents have another possible option under Louisiana law: a recall procedure aimed at removing an elected official from office.
In a community the size of Elizabeth, initiating such a process would require signatures from 40% of eligible voters, according to state rules.
For now, with only weeks remaining before the November election, the small Louisiana town faces an extraordinary prospect: its next police chief, the person responsible for enforcing the law, could be a man awaiting the outcome of two serious charges involving the alleged rape of underage girls.

Iran says it will reply to US response on Hormuz proposal once review over
DUBAI, Oct 12 - Iran is still reviewing a US response to its proposal regarding the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and will reply to Washington via intermediaries when the review is over, foreign ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said on Monday.
Baghaei also told a press conference that Iran continues to exchange messages via intermediaries, without elaborating. Qatar and Pakistan, among others, have acted as mediators in efforts to end the war that began with US and Israeli strikes on Iran on February 28.
After a June interim ceasefire crumbled and on-off strikes resumed, Iran presented its proposal in mid-September and later confirmed receipt of a US response. But the process has since stalled, with Iran’s security chief saying on Sunday that Washington’s response did not sufficiently address Tehran’s seven conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz and returning to negotiations.
A central point of disagreement has been Washington’s insistence on addressing Iran's nuclear programme from the outset. Tehran says negotiations should initially focus on reopening the Strait of Hormuz, which before the war carried about a fifth of the global trade in oil and liquefied natural gas (LNG), and restoring security in the waterway.
Regarding the escalating conflict between Saudi Arabia and Yemen's Houthis, an Iranian ally, Baghaei reiterated Tehran's openness to help resolve the crisis through dialogue.

NATO 'intentionally ambiguous' on what could trigger Article 5 — commander
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
09:17:34 UTC
18:17:34 KST

BRUSSELS, October 12. /TASS/. NATO deliberately preserves uncertainty about what could lead to invoking Article 5 of the North Atlantic Treaty, which provides for collective defense in case of an attack on a member state, NATO’s Supreme Allied Commander Europe General Alexus Grynkewich said.
"We are intentionally ambiguous about what would cause Article 5 to be triggered," he told Poland’s TVP World in an interview.
According to Grynkewich, the alliance could also invoke "other articles" if needed, including Article 4, which calls for consultations within the NATO Council if a member state believes its security is under threat.
The general pointed out that Article 4 had been invoked "zero times" even during the Cold War. "Allies consulted and dealt with the issue without any formal mechanism. And I think that that’s a model of just staying calm, carrying on and working our way through this," he added.
Earlier, Bloomberg reported that "NATO’s top military commander is working on a strategy for achieving a quick victory against a Russian attack on its eastern flank, with a particular focus on integrating new defense technologies like drones and AI into traditional power." The document, called "Theory of Victory," will be presented by Grynkewich on October 12. Sources told Bloomberg that the goal is to clarify how the alliance would handle a possible incursion into NATO territory. Grynkewich’s spokesman declined to discuss details of the plan, emphasizing that the alliance was "purely defensive."
According to the Bloomberg report, if NATO was attacked, "it would block an incursion with a mix of land forces and other assets from NATO’s Eastern Flank Deterrence Initiative, a concept relying on low-cost drones, minimally crewed systems and AI-enabled targeting." "After gaining freedom of maneuver, it would seek to destroy enemy command and control" with the goal of defeating enemy forces "quickly and overwhelmingly," the news agency added.

Airbus Valkyrie combat drone completes first European flight
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
10:15:58 BST
18:15:58 KST

Airbus and Kratos have completed the first European flight of the U740 Valkyrie uncrewed combat aircraft, with the demonstrator reaching Mach 0.8 during a test campaign intended to support development of a European Collaborative Combat Aircraft capability by 2029, according to Airbus.
The flight took place at a test facility in northern Europe on 29 September and included a rocket-assisted launch, manoeuvres at several altitudes and speeds, and changes to a pre-planned route while the aircraft was airborne. Airbus said all objectives for the first flight were achieved.
Speaking during a media briefing on the programme, Hendrik Zippel, Airbus Head of CCA Collaboration and Development, described the flight as “picture-perfect” and said preparations began at 6am before the aircraft was moved from its hangar to the launch position.
The Valkyrie took off at around 10.30am using rocket boosters, which separated after approximately two seconds. Zippel said the aircraft initially flew a diamond-shaped pattern before entering a longer racetrack profile used to test different flight conditions.
“We then entered into a longer racetrack pattern where we flew at several flight levels, 10,000, 20,000, 30,000 feet, with several acceleration and deceleration phases,” he said.
“We went up to 0.8 Mach, and also tried out the reconfiguration of a pre-planned route, and all of this went very successfully.”
The flight also tested the procedures required to recover the aircraft at the end of the mission, with Airbus saying the vehicle came down inside the planned recovery area. Zippel said the actual landing point was substantially inside the boundary established before the test.
The aircraft flown in September is based on Kratos’ Valkyrie platform, which Airbus intends to combine with its own Multi-platform Autonomous Reconfigurable and Secure mission system, known as MARS.
Airbus describes MARS as the mission-system layer that will provide control over mission applications, software, data and hardware, while adding autonomous functions and the ability to coordinate multiple aircraft. The company says a human will remain within the command hierarchy for critical decisions.
The next flight-test campaign is planned for the middle of 2027 and is expected to include the first increment of the MARS mission system integrated into the aircraft.
Zippel said: “After flight test is before the flight test. The next flight tests are planned mid of next year. We plan to then have already integrated into the birds, into the aircrafts, the first increment of our MARS mission system.”
Airbus is aiming to offer the resulting system as a Collaborative Combat Aircraft that could operate autonomously or under the direction of crewed fighters, including the Eurofighter.
According to an Airbus news update, Mike Schoellhorn, CEO of Airbus Defence and Space, said: “In an increasingly complex and contested threat environment, air forces require affordable combat mass.”
He added: “By pairing Kratos’ proven airframe as a ‘program of record’ with Airbus’ sovereign European mission system, we are able to offer a robust, sovereign, affordable, and combat-ready CCA system by the end of the decade.”
Airbus says the U740 Valkyrie is 9.1 metres long with a wingspan of 8.2 metres and has a maximum take-off weight of approximately three tonnes. The aircraft has an internal weapons bay as well as external payload stations beneath the wings, while the company quotes a range exceeding 5,000 kilometres and a service ceiling of 45,000 feet.
The aircraft can use rocket-assisted launch equipment rather than depending on a conventional runway, although Airbus says runway take-off and landing remain available as an alternative. The company sees that flexibility as a way of dispersing uncrewed combat aircraft away from established airbases.
Eric DeMarco, President and CEO of Kratos, said: “First flights typically include plenty of learning opportunities, but with the maturity of the Valkyrie system and the well-integrated Airbus and Kratos team, this flight was an amazing success.”
Airbus and Kratos are now moving towards more complex flight testing in which the European mission system will begin to be introduced into the aircraft, with the companies continuing to target a combat-ready CCA capability by 2029.

IEA urges additional diesel releases ahead of key meeting
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
09:15:42 UTC
18:15:42 KST

Tightening global diesel markets prompted the International Energy Agency to call on its members to accelerate previously agreed releases from strategic oil reserves, prioritising diesel. The IEA also asked member states to assess "whether additional diesel releases are necessary".
Ahead of the International Energy Agency's (IEA) governing board meeting this Thursday, its executive director Fatih Birol has written to member governments calling for further action as global diesel markets face tight supplies.
Birol suggested that members that have not yet released all the oil they pledged in March, when the IEA agreed to release 400 million barrels, should speed up their remaining releases, prioritising diesel. Some countries have already released more than they initially pledged.
All members were also asked to assess whether additional diesel releases are necessary and, if so, explain how much they could release and when.
The governing board will review these efforts at its meeting on 15 October.
“As we did in March, I believe we can once again demonstrate the IEA’s capacity to act together in support of energy security and economic stability,” Birol said in the statement published on Sunday.
The G7 previously announced plans to release up to 100 million barrels of oil to curb soaring energy prices. However, an internal document seen by Euronews showed that these volumes would fulfil outstanding March commitments, rather than add to the original 400-million-barrel pledge.
"Of its 400 million barrels, 326 million have been released. Because some members over-delivered, the 100 million barrels in the G7 statement can be covered within the existing action if everyone fulfils their commitments," the document states.
Diesel prices have been soaring amid global fuel shortages. The Iran war disrupted crude oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz, while damage to refineries has also restricted fuel supplies.
According to Kpler, crude oil and condensate exports from the Middle East Gulf, excluding Iran, returned to pre-war levels in September. However, much of that oil now travels through alternative routes or is transferred between tankers offshore.
The IEA statement comes two days after US President Donald Trump announced a diesel supply deal with Russia. Washington temporarily eased sanctions on Russian diesel, allowing its sale and delivery, including imports into the US, until 7 April 2027.
Moscow said it was ready to supply oil and petroleum products to the US and global markets following a telephone conversation between Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin.
"I am convinced this will have a positive impact on the entire global economy," Putin said, according to the Russian statement.
European sanctions remain in place, but additional Russian supply to the global market could help lower diesel prices. The impact will depend on how much fuel Russia can deliver, with damage to its refineries limiting production.
Brent crude, the international oil benchmark, remained above $100 a barrel on Monday morning. European diesel futures fell about 3% to around $1,437 a tonne.

In pictures: Gaza's olive harvest shrinks as war damage, Israeli access restrictions hit farmers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
09:12:34 UTC
18:12:34 KST

Palestinian farmers in Gaza are facing a difficult olive harvest this year as production declines, large areas of agricultural land remain damaged and many groves are inaccessible because they lie in areas controlled by the Israeli army or beyond the so-called “yellow line.”
On accessible farmland, farmers continue picking olives and separating them from leaves and branches despite shortages of fertiliser, irrigation water and agricultural supplies, as well as higher labour, transportation and pressing costs.
The pressures have left many families unable to store their usual annual supplies of olive oil and olives.
On July 13, Gaza’s agriculture ministry estimated losses to the sector from Israel’s genocidal war, which began on October 8, 2023, at more than $3 billion, including $1.49 billion in direct damage and $1.59 billion in indirect losses.
Kamel Baraka, a farmer from Deir al Balah in central Gaza, said olive tree yields had fallen significantly.
“A tree that produced around 100 kilograms (220.4 pounds) of olives before the war now produces no more than 20 (44 pounds) to 30 kilograms (66 pounds),” Baraka told Anadolu.
That represents a decline of around 70 percent to 80 percent, he added.
“A season that once provided an important source of income for farmers, traders and workers now barely meets the needs of some families because of current conditions and shortages of essential agricultural supplies,” Baraka said.
“Olive cultivation requires constant care, fertiliser, irrigation and other inputs that have become increasingly difficult to obtain,” he added.
Massive damage
Damage to farmland and restrictions on access have also directly reduced the harvest.
“Large areas of olive groves in eastern parts of central Gaza lie in zones farmers cannot reach, particularly east of Salah al-Din Street and around the ‘yellow line,’” Baraka said.
The “yellow line” is a notional line inside Gaza to which the Israeli army withdrew under the first phase of US President Donald Trump’s plan to end the war, under which a ceasefire deal took effect on October 10, 2025. It separates areas in eastern Gaza that remain under Israeli army control from areas west of the line where Palestinians are allowed to move.
“Farmers in Deir al-Balah, Bureij and Maghazi face difficulty reaching agricultural land that had been a major source of olive production,” Baraka said.
He said available farmland west of Salah al-Din Street is insufficient to meet residents’ needs for olive oil and olives.
Before the war, preparations for the harvest began about a month in advance, with farmers arranging workers and preparing equipment for picking and transport, while families stored olives and oil for the year ahead.
Those preparations have declined as production falls and costs rise, with some farmers now collecting only enough olives for household consumption and limited quantities for sale.
Costs triple
Farmers are also struggling with sharply higher transportation and pressing costs, as well as shortages of containers needed to store olive oil.
“The cost of pressing olives has risen to around three times what it was before the war,” Baraka said, adding that the increase has placed further pressure on farmers whose incomes have already fallen because of lower production.
“Before the war, olive press owners often transported harvests from farms to pressing facilities, while farmers now struggle to find transportation even for small quantities,” he added.
Higher costs for pumping water and irrigating trees, combined with shortages of fertiliser, labour and storage containers, have made preserving the harvest and storing oil increasingly difficult, particularly for families that depend on farming for their food needs.
“The olive season, once an opportunity for farmers to improve their livelihoods and secure food supplies for the year, has become an exhausting season that provides many of them with only a fraction of what they need,” Baraka said.
Since Israel’s genocidal war began on October 8, 2023, Gaza’s agricultural sector has sustained widespread damage, according to the agriculture ministry.
The ministry said 158,909 dunams (39,267 acres) of agricultural land have been damaged out of a total 182,247 dunams (45,033 acres), or around 87 percent, sharply reducing crop production and the capacity to provide food.
The genocidal war also has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians and injured over 175,000 others, according to Palestinian figures, also destroying about 90 percent of the besieged enclave's infrastructure.

OMA adapts historic houston coffee plant into music and arts academy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
09:11:28 UTC
18:11:28 KST

OMA adapts historic houston coffee plant into music and arts academy
inspired by montessori principles, the adaptive reuse project organizes classrooms, libraries, and performance spaces into a connected learning environment, giving new life to an industrial landmark.
OMA reimagines a Houston coffee plant as a school
OMA transforms Houston’s historic 1930s J.A. Folger & Co. coffee plant into the Frank Liu Jr. Academy for Music and Arts (FLAMA), a tuition-free public charter school designed around music, creative learning, and community. Led by OMA partner Jason Long and project architect Salome Nikuradze, the 6,050-square-meter project sits along Houston’s Buffalo Bayou East corridor, across from the future Turkey Bend development. Now under construction, the school combines the adaptive reuse of an industrial building with a spatial approach that treats education as a collective cultural experience.
FLAMA organizes learning around shared spaces
The architects at OMA organize FLAMA across three stories, arranging its programs according to the developmental stages of its students, with younger children occupying the lower levels and older students moving upward. Drawing on Montessori principles, the design supports independence, openness, and collaborative learning through a series of shared spaces that OMA calls ‘neighborhoods.’
Each floor is organized around two central gathering areas, or ‘cymbals,’ with classrooms, practice rooms, and academic programs arranged around them. Rather than treating circulation as a means of moving between enclosed classrooms, the design makes shared space an integral part of the educational experience. These commons accommodate informal gatherings, independent study, project work, and performances, allowing everyday activities to overlap.
music shapes the architecture
At ground level of FLAMA, the youngest students share an intimate common area for play, movement, and drum circles, reflecting the Montessori emphasis on physical development. Nearby, students in grades one and two gather around a larger open space, where a sculptural staircase curves like a French horn and provides a setting for informal performances. On the upper floors, the shared spaces shift toward reading, collaboration, and more focused study. Students in grades three through five use an open library with flexible furniture that accommodates group projects and after-school activities.
Above, a second library commons serves grades six through eight, with more concentrated areas for independent work. The two libraries connect through an opening in the floor shaped like the letter ‘f.’ The form references the forte symbol in musical notation, the f-shaped sound holes found on string instruments, and the academy’s own name. Beyond its visual reference, the opening establishes a connection between floors that allows light and sound to pass between the two learning environments. At the center of the school, a double-height cafetorium brings students together for lunch, assemblies, and performances. A large circular opening and curved auditorium staircase recall the body of a banjo, transforming a space for daily meals into a setting for collective gathering and musical expression.
bringing daylight into an industrial structure
One of the main challenges in turning the former coffee plant into a school is bringing natural light into the building. OMA places classrooms along the exterior walls to give them access to daylight, while new circular skylights bring light into the central shared spaces. The team also preserves elements of the building’s industrial past. The original windows along the street facades are restored and upgraded to meet current energy standards. Inside, a landscaped courtyard introduces a more playful approach, with colorful geometric window divisions that give the historic building a new identity. The courtyard connects the industrial history of the building with its new role as a school.
project info:
 name: Frank Liu Jr. Academy for Music and Arts (FLAMA)
architect: OMA New York | @omanewyork
location: Houston, Texas, United States
area: 6,050 sqm (65,120 sq ft)
 partner: Jason Long
project architect: Salome Nikuradze
client: Lovett Commercial
architect of record: RDLR Architects
landscape architect: SWA Group
structural engineer: IMEG
MEP: DBR Engineering
acoustics: Salas O’Brien

US Asian ally tests Russian trade route to Europe
