18:06:31 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — ProLogium Technology is expanding into AI data centers and aviation as weak EV demand and high costs slow the commercialization of all-solid-state batteries, Nikkei Asia reported Sunday.
ProLogium CEO Yang Ssu-nan (楊思枏) said non-automotive uses are expected to account for 40% of the company’s production capacity by 2032. The company began mass-producing automotive batteries in Taiwan in 2024 and plans to invest NT$185.75 billion (US$5.82 billion) in a French factory, potentially raising its annual global capacity to 14 GWh by 2032.
The company sees data centers as a key market, with generative AI driving demand for emergency power supplies, per CommonWealth Magazine. It believes its batteries’ high output and lower fire risk make them suitable for use near servers and aims to begin sales for these applications around 2028.
ProLogium is also developing batteries for aviation, per Nikkei Asia. In June, it began research with Dutch electric aircraft startup Elysian Aircraft on batteries for planes with a range of about 1,000 kilometers, while partnerships in unmanned aviation could lead to deployment around 2027. Yang said non-automotive applications generally command higher prices.
The move comes amid intensifying competition in the EV battery market. US EV sales have fallen since the Trump administration ended purchase subsidies in September last year, while Chinese manufacturers, which hold about 70% of the global battery market, have expanded output and improved conventional lithium-ion technology.
The average price of lithium-ion batteries fell 40% per kilowatt-hour from 2020 to 2025, according to the International Energy Agency. Automakers are also adopting cheaper batteries that use fewer rare metals, while solid-state alternatives remain costly because of expensive electrolytes and the investment needed for production facilities.
Other manufacturers are pursuing non-automotive markets as well. US-based QuantumScape, a partner of Volkswagen and Honda Motor, announced plans to diversify this year and established business units for data centers, aviation, and defense over the summer.
Japanese automakers continue to target solid-state batteries for EVs. Toyota Motor is working with Idemitsu Kosan and Sumitomo Metal Mining toward commercialization in 2027 or 2028, while Nissan Motor aims to develop mass-production technology in fiscal 2028.
Nagoya University visiting professor Sato Noboru said solid-state batteries are unlikely to exceed 10% market share until electrolyte costs fall and other technical improvements are made, per Nikkei Asia. He expects widespread adoption no earlier than 2035.

Taiwan health minister opposes legalizing marijuana
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
09:06:23 UTC
18:06:23 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Health Minister Shih Chung-liang (石崇良) said Monday that he opposes legalizing marijuana and that the health ministry will not introduce community drug supply programs, CNA reported.
Shih said the health ministry supports measures to reduce the health risks of drug use but opposes programs that provide drugs directly to users. Some legislators had suggested reviewing overseas approaches, including supervised injection facilities in Canada, to assess whether they could work in Taiwan.
UDN reported that Taiwan introduced harm reduction programs in 2005 after HIV infections rose among people who shared needles. The measures include providing clean needles to prevent infections and methadone treatment to help people manage drug dependence.
The programs now operate across all 22 cities and counties, with 163 drug treatment facilities nationwide. Many offer methadone therapy as part of addiction treatment.
Shih also distinguished between illegal drugs and medicines. He said some controlled substances have medical uses but require strict oversight because of the risks of misuse and addiction, per Liberty Times.
On drug testing in schools, Shih said screening students at higher risk could help detect drug use early. However, inaccurate results could lead to students being wrongly identified as drug users or cases going undetected.
He said testing must be accompanied by counseling, referrals, and follow-up care. Schools must also protect students’ rights and avoid stigmatizing those who test positive.

Taiwan police warn of rise in scam calls using North American dialing code
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
09:06:08 UTC
18:06:08 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Calls displaying numbers with North America’s +1 dialing code are on the rise in Taiwan, with scammers impersonating the 165 anti-fraud hotline or telecommunications providers, the Criminal Investigation Bureau (CIB) said Monday.
An analysis of Whoscall’s database and CIB intelligence identified nearly 200,000 calls from suspicious +1 numbers in August and September, according to a press release.
Whoscall is a mobile app developed by Taiwanese cybersecurity firm Gogolook that identifies unknown callers and filters fraudulent messages. The company said scammers have been switching between different dialing codes every two to three weeks to evade detection.
In August alone, Gogolook identified about 260,000 scam calls beginning with +422, accounting for 55.8% of calls displaying overseas numbers.
The International Telecommunication Union has not assigned +422 as a country calling code. Scammers can make calls appear to come from such numbers by altering the caller ID.
Calls beginning with +1800 and +1953 picked up in September, with more than 20,000 recorded from each prefix.
The analysis also found that scammers impersonated government agencies, including the National Communications Commission and Financial Supervisory Commission, to obtain personal information.
The CIB urged the public to heed the warnings in Mandarin and Taiwanese played before international calls: “This is an international call. Beware of scams.”
Taiwanese government agencies and the 165 anti-fraud hotline will never call from numbers beginning with “+,” the bureau added.

Taichung Suncake Culture Festival to take place Oct 17
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
09:06:04 UTC
18:06:04 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taichung City Government Economic Development Bureau Director Chang Feng-yuan (張峯源) announced Monday that the 2026 Taichung Suncake Culture Festival will take place at Wenxin Forest Park on Saturday.
Chang said the 21st festival will bring together more than 80 pastry makers and souvenir brands at the park, offering discounted products and coupons, per CNA. He said the festival has expanded beyond traditional pastries to include other foods and merchandise that represent the city.
Chang added that the 2027 festival would expand further, bringing together neighboring municipalities and major cities around the world.
Suncakes, one of Taichung’s most iconic treats, date back to the Qing dynasty and Japanese colonial era, per Liberty Times. Local history researcher Lin Liang-che (林良哲) suggested that the pastry originated from flaky butter pastries that were made smaller after customers complained about their size.
A suncake pastry chef said the pastry was initially known as maltose cake, per TVBS. Tai Yang Tang, a pastry shop on Ziyou Road, became so well known for its maltose cakes that people began referring to the pastry by the shop’s name. Tai yang means “sun” in Mandarin.
Other local legends offer different explanations for the name. Some say the pastry was used as an offering to the gods during a solar eclipse, while others attribute its invention to a pastry apprentice seeking to win the favor of his master’s daughter. Another theory holds that the red stamp in the center of the cake resembles the sun.
Pastry chef Wei Ching-hai (魏清海) is credited with refining the suncake into its modern form, with local legends identifying him as its inventor. Wei’s pastry shop, Chuan An Tang, has since been converted into the Taiwan Museum of Suncake, which showcases the pastry’s history and offers hands-on suncake-making courses, per Mirror Media.
The National Museum of Taiwan History featured a suncake in a 2019 exhibition on Taiwan’s social movements, per ETtoday. After then Deputy Secretary-General of the Cabinet Hsiao Chia-chi (蕭家淇) complained that Sunflower Movement protesters had allegedly eaten his suncake, protesters began buying suncakes in bulk in response.

Cute cats and street fighters: The best things to do, hear, see or watch in Europe this week
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
09:05:18 UTC
18:05:18 KST

Fontaines D.C. bring synths and psychedelia with their latest album 'Dopamine Chamber' while a new exhibition near Paris explores all things cute. Here's what to look out for this week.
What makes you feel better during the colder months? If the answer includes cats, spooky TV, 90s video games or more cats, we've got good news.
The Louvre-Lens in France has become an explosion of pastel pink cuteness for its latest exhibition, which celebrates all things wide-eyed, fluffy and glittery. It's ideal for families and the perfect antidote to any October gloom.
Meanwhile, Irish rockers Fontaines D.C. have created a sonic mood board for their fifth studio album 'Dopamine Chamber', which swirls with synths, psychedelia and the sudden urge to disappear on a dance floor.
For those looking to embrace Halloween's approach, look no further than the new Friday the 13th TV adaptation, Crystal Lake. But if campy kung fu and martial arts are more your thing? Street Fighter, based on the legendary arcade game franchise, is about to "hadoken" onto the big screen.
Keep scrolling to find out more about what's coming up this week.
Exhibitions and events
So Cute! The Art of Happiness
When: Until 18 January 2027
Where: Louvre-Lens (Lens, France)
In a world that can often feel overwhelmingly scary, we've never needed the calming reprieve of cuteness more. From sculptures of chubby babies to pastel plushes and Internet cats, the Louvre-Lens explores the many manifestations of mignon throughout history in this joyful new exhibition. There are nearly 300 works in total, including Egyptian animal figures, renaissance portraits, trendy toys and bedazzled reinterpretations of masterpieces — all displayed within an adorable-maxxed space of pastel pink walls and cat-eared archways. It not only asks visitors to reflect on the happiness such aesthetics give us, but also their use for rebellion — and manipulation. Anyone that owns cute cats can certainly attest to the latter!
Ruth Asawa: Retrospective
When: 18 October 2026 - 10 January 2027
Where: Fondation Beyeler (Riehen, Switzerland)
Japanese American artist Ruth Asawa remains a pioneer within the world of abstract art, best-known for her intricate wire sculptures that captured the geometry of organic matter. However, her career was so much more than just these — incorporating everything from figurative drawings to life casts and even outdoor fountains. This diversity is captured at the Fondation Beyeler's retrospective; a comprehensive exploration of Asawa's ability to transform materials into reality-bending marvels that still inspire profound contemplations. Find out more here.
Bonus highlight: One not to be missed for photography enthusiasts and historians: ‘Light and Magic: The Birth of Art Photography’ opens at Tate Modern in London from 14 October 2026 until 21 February 2027.
Movies
Street Fighter
Where: Cinemas
When: 16 October
It's Showtime! After two rival martial artists are recruited for a World Warrior Tournament, so begins a collision course with violent criminals, inner-demons — and each other. Based on the legendary 90s video game series of the same name, it's the latest in a long line of previous adaptations that have spanned everything from live-action features to anime web series. For fans and wannabe warriors this is an ideal outing that packs all the (rising dragon) punches while not taking itself too seriously.
Bonus highlight: Russian-language thriller Minotaur (which is also France's choice for the 2027 Oscars) is out at French cinemas from 14 October, with a staggered release across the rest of Europe to follow in November.
TV series
Crystal Lake
Where: SKY/NOW
When: 19 October
Dim the lights, burrow under a blanket and prepare to enter Camp Crystal Lake. Set in the summer of 1972, shortly after a young Jason Voorhees drowned, this new prequel show unravels the events that took place eight years before the first Friday the 13th film. Linda Cardellini (Freaks and Geeks, Scooby-Doo, DTF St. Louis) stars as Jason's mother, Pamela, whose grief unleashes dark secrets from her past — and fuels a slow descent into madness. Much like Mike Flanagan's recent Carrie adaptation, the episodic format allows for a deeper origin story that explores the psychology behind one of horror's most legendary villains.
Bonus highlight: Sylvester Stallone returns for season four of crime series Tulsa King, out on 16 October on Paramount+.
Music
Fontaines D.C. - Dopamine Chamber
When: 16 October
More than two years since the release of 2024's Romance (one of our favourite albums that year), Irish post-punk band Fontaines D.C. have returned with Dopamine Chamber — a mood board of synth-driven sounds that explore societal issues. Bonus highlights: Two other notable albums this week include 'Cookie Happened' by Eels and 'No Bad Memories' by The Avalanches — both out on the 16 October. Find out more about them in our fall album previews list.

The second missile was launched at 9:36 a.m. It reached an altitude of approximately 70 km and traveled more than 910 km.

The previous ballistic missile launch took place on October 30, 2026. At the time, North Korea launched a missile toward the Sea of Japan, which Pyongyang described as a “strategic intermediate-range missile.”
According to North Korean officials, the missile can change its trajectory at low altitudes and supports at least four selectable flight modes, depending on the target and mission.
North Korea also conducted a ballistic missile launch on September 20, 2026.
The missile was launched at 3:00 p.m. Japan time. Japanese estimates say it reached a maximum altitude of about 60 km and traveled about 440 km. The missile landed in the Sea of Japan, outside Japan’s exclusive economic zone.
North Korea later officially confirmed the test and released photographs of the missile. According to North Korean officials, the military tested a new variant of the Hwasong-11Ma-1 ballistic missile equipped with a hypersonic glide vehicle warhead.

Russia's foreign trade surplus up 16.4% in January-August to $102.9 bln
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
09:04:25 UTC
18:04:25 KST

MOSCOW, October 12. /TASS/. Russia’s foreign trade surplus increased by 16.4% in January-August 2026 year-on-year to $102.9 bln, according to figures released by the Federal Customs Service.
Exports gained $37.8 bln in the reporting period to $304.2 bln, while imports grew by $23.3 bln to $201.3 bln. Consequently, Russia’s trade turnover went up by 13.75% in January-August 2026 year-on-year to $505.5 bln.
Exports from Russia to European countries fell by 1.03% to $38.6 bln, while imports rose by 8.26% to $49.8 bln, according to the service. That said, Russia’s exports to Asian countries increased by 19.08% to $244 bln, while imports from those countries added 16.29% to $137.8 bln.
Russian exports to African countries edged up by 0.72% to $14 bln, while imports rose by 6.67% to $3.2 bln.
Exports to countries of North and South America lost 10.59% to $7.6 bln, while imports from those countries were flat at $10.4 bln.
Mineral products accounted for the largest share of Russia's exports in the period, reaching $170.6 bln (up 14.5%), followed by metals and metal products (up 22.2% to $55.6 bln), and agricultural products (up 20.17% to $28.6 bln).
Machinery, equipment, and vehicles were Russia's largest import item, which increased by 15.21% from January to August, reaching $97.7 bln, followed by chemical products (up 10.86% to $39.8 bln), and agricultural products (up 4.68% to $29.1 bln).

Nice compact size for smaller hands or reading on the go. Aluminum back makes the e-reader heavier, but not so heavy it's uncomfortable. Colors are beautiful. Double the storage of the plastic version. Compatible with new Kindle Click remote. Aluminum is ad-free (plastic version can be ad-free if you pay extra).
TIRED
Expensive for the least amount of features in a Kindle. No warm light, and no auto-adjusting light like you'll get on the aluminum version of other Kindles. Not compatible with Kindle Page Turn Cover.
The Kindle Aluminum has no right to be this beautiful.
Amazon announced a new Kindle lineup at the start of the month, with new versions of the Kindle, Kindle Paperwhite, and Kindle Colorsoft. The base Kindle is the first one available, with both a plastic version and an aluminum version. It's simply named the Kindle Aluminum, while the aluminum versions of the Paperwhite and Colorsoft are now the new Signature Editions with extra features (like wireless charging, an auto-adjusting front light, and a couple AI features).
The Kindle Aluminum only offers the AI features compared to the Signature Editions, while also including a different body, 32 GB of storage, and no lock screen ads. It's not really enough to validate the price change, yet still I find myself loving it.
Notably, it comes in two colors, Seaglass Green and Alpine Sky. The latter is currently sitting just a few inches away from me as I write this, glinting in the sunlight. It's the shade of blue I had hoped the MacBooks would be when Apple released its Sky Blue color in 2025, and every single reader friend I've shown it to has said they want it for the color alone. Even my editor, who strongly prefers physical books (which is hilarious given that she edits my ever-growing list of e-reader reviews, including this one), said just looking at my photos made her want one.
It's a smart move on Amazon's part. There's little reason to upgrade your Kindle if you already have one, but most generations only came in black. The last generation just had one color for the Kindle and one for the Paperwhite. Now, with the base Kindle, you have two colors of the plastic version (the classic black and Ube purple) and the aforementioned green or blue aluminum—these options could have plenty of existing Kindle owners champing at the bit to upgrade.
But it's hard to say it's worth it just for the color, since you could always buy a case instead. It's not a bad device, and there are some improvements—just not enough to justify the price tag.
New Body, Same System
The 12th-generation Kindle still has the same 6-inch screen, but the device's overall form factor has changed. The screen is flush with the rest of the body now, rather than sitting indented, and the new Kindle body is actually a quarter of an inch shorter than the 2024 Kindle's. That sounds like a small increment (and it is!), but having both devices side-by-side, it was easy to spot. The new Kindle also felt like it fit better in my palm, perhaps due to the smoother aluminum backing.
It's also heavier, thanks to the backing. Amazon says the Kindle Aluminum is 5.7 ounces, while the plastic 2026 Kindle is 4.9 ounces. (The 2024 plastic Kindle is 5.56 ounces.) Despite the tiny difference in weight between the 2024 Kindle and the new aluminum version, the aluminum felt palpably heavier to me—almost as if felt like my hand was putting more effort into holding it up. I double-checked on my kitchen scale, and it really is only a 0.2-ounce difference. I had my husband try both models, and he agreed that the aluminum felt heavier and was surprised at how small the difference really was. I think the smaller frame makes the weight sit a little differently.
Opening the 2026 Kindle Aluminum sends you to the same interface as any other Kindle. You'll have a homepage and your library page, and the same set of menus by tapping the right-hand corner dots or swiping down from the top of the page. I did find that while the page-turn speed seemed nearly identical, the new Kindle opened up books much faster than the 2024 Kindle. On the latter, I always had to wait a handful of seconds for my latest Kindle Unlimited read to open (I'll own up to it currently being Verity, my first and very likely last Colleen Hoover book), but the 2026 Kindle near-instantly opened it each time.
The other difference turned out to be the front lights. While neither model has a warm-color front light, the Kindle Aluminum's light tone seemed a touch warmer than the bright-blue tinge of the 2024 Kindle. It was still too blue to comfortably read in dark mode before bed, but side by side, I could see an improvement. It's hard to tell in my photo below, but I know I'm not hallucinating after seeing multiple similar photos already uploaded to the Kindle's Amazon reviews.
Colorful Cost
Ultimately, you don't need this Kindle if you already have one, and $190 is a steep price to pay for a model that doesn't even have a warm option for the front light. The real draw here remains the color body, and Amazon has done a good job with this. My TikTok feed is full of e-reader fans talking about the Ube shade, while the shine of the Alpine Sky is one I would've been eyeing had I not ended up reviewing it. I also like that the aluminum body really does feel like an upgrade when I hold it in my hands.
Amazon might be trying to take a page from Apple's playbook for the iPhone, encouraging you to upgrade your Kindle every two years for the new colors, the way superfans update their smartphones. While Kindle has a much lower cost of entry, that's because a smartphone comes with many more features and upgrades. The Kindle will always have one use: as an e-reader that shows you books. Unlike the second- to third-gen Kindle Scribe update, Kindle isn't providing a new homepage experience, though you will get two of the AI-powered features the Scribes have (Story So Far, to recap where you left off in a story, and Ask This Book—coming soon, to ask about a story). You aren't even getting the auto-adjusting light that aluminum versions of the Paperwhite and Colorsoft will have.
It's a good gift for Christmas for someone who already has everything, or an excuse to finally upgrade your own Kindle if it's starting to lag. But you might also want to wait and see if the Paperwhite or Colorsoft Signature Editions are the way to go instead, especially since only those two models will be compatible with the new Kindle Page Turn Cover ($80) that will give you on-device page-turn buttons. Neither the 2026 Kindle Aluminum nor the plastic version will be compatible with this accessory, making it even harder to justify upgrading, but they will at least work with the Kindle Click remote ($35).
Again, this isn't a bad Kindle. The faster book openings and slightly warmer (though still not actually warm) front light, and double the storage make it a legitimate upgrade to the 2024 model. If you don't already have a Kindle, it's not a bad choice if you want to get one of the prettiest models available. It's up to you if that's worth spending almost $200 on.
You'll likely be just as happy with the plastic Ube version and spend between $20 and $40 less, depending on whether you want ads or not (though it does have half the storage of the aluminum model, at 16 GB). Still, this is a much higher price than these basic Kindles used to be available for. Hopefully we will see these Kindles on sale for Black Friday, but I wouldn't hold my breath for any good sales this year.

WARSAW – A mass deployment of police to Polish schools has helped calm tensions, Prime Minister Donald Tusk said on Oct 12, after three recent stabbing attacks in four days sparked fears of copycat violence.
The authorities have dismissed rumours that the attacks were linked to an online challenge or organised group.
However, the government says the glorification of violence online is harming young people and it is fast-tracking legislation to make it easier to remove harmful content.
“Our actions and probably the passage of time have led to a significant reduction in online tension and risky situations,” Tusk told a crisis meeting.
“We will continue as long as we observe situations that give cause for concern,” he said.
Police launched the mass security operation late last week after rumours spread online of a planned “Bloody Friday” wave of knife attacks following violence at schools on Oct 7 and 8.
Interior Minister Marcin Kierwinski said around 20,000 police officers were deployed to schools on Monday, equivalent to roughly one-fifth of the national force.
Dozens of arrests
The operation has led to 135 arrests, authorities said, as police cracked down on threats and online posts linked to the unrest.
Police Commander-in-Chief Marek Boron said the offenders were mainly young people inspired by last week’s attacks trying to get attention with online pranks, while others were inspired by computer games or Nazi subcultures.
In one incident, police said a boy created a model of his school in the Roblox game and simulated attacks on students. He was found to possess a firearm, ammunition and knives.
On Oct 12, prosecutors in the south-eastern city of Lublin said police detained a 21-year-old Ukrainian citizen on suspicion of planning to “murder a stranger using a knife, driven by racial hatred” as part of “Bloody Friday”.
The latest stabbing occurred on Oct 10, when three people were injured at a further education college in Warsaw.
It followed an attack on Oct 8 in Leszczydol-Nowiny, north-east of the capital, where a 15-year-old former pupil wearing a helmet-mounted camera killed a school caretaker and wounded two teachers.
On Oct 7, a 19-year-old injured 10 people, including himself, at a school in Ostroleka, north of the capital.
‘Grim trend of violence’
Tusk on Oct 11 condemned what he called a “grim trend of violence” fuelled by the glorification of extremist ideologies and violent criminals online.
Digital Affairs Minister Krzysztof Gawkowski said the authorities were monitoring online activity around the clock and had detected increased activity by Russian bots linked to the security situation.

Marham runway repairs done three weeks ahead of plan
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
10:00:29 BST
18:00:29 KST

Resurfacing work at RAF Marham has been completed in five weeks against an eight-week programme, and Lightning Force operations ran from a taxiway while all three runways were out of use, according to the Defence Infrastructure Organisation.
The £3.5 million project covered 28,000 square metres of the runway intersection, last resurfaced in 2018, and dealt with deterioration below the surface as well, with just over 4,000 square metres of underlying pavement needing repair before the new surface could go down. A further 675 square metres was resurfaced on Runway 05.
Because the work sat at the intersection, every runway was unavailable at once. Contractor movements were coordinated with air traffic control and the airfield manager so the taxiway could carry Lightning Force flying with as little disruption as possible.
Tim Fenton, the organisation’s project delivery manager, said: “Completing these essential repairs is an important investment in the resilience of RAF Marham’s airfield infrastructure. By working closely with the Station and our delivery partners, we were able to tackle the immediate deterioration while also taking the opportunity to address additional requirements as part of the same programme of work. This has reduced the need for future intervention and helped ensure the airfield can continue to support Lightning Force operations.”
Flight Lieutenant Steve Southward of RAF Central Region said the scope had been extended through collaboration between the station, the organisation, VIVO and Air Infrastructure to take in further repairs while contractors were already on site.
VIVO carried out the work with sub-contractor Allied and four specialist sub-contractors. Alongside the £3.5 million spent, the team recorded a £3.8 million saving by adopting an approach that removed the need for an on-site concrete batching plant.
Marham is the main operating base for the F-35B Lightning force and home to 617 Squadron and 207 Squadron, the operational conversion unit for the type.
Infrastructure of this kind has been a persistent weak point across the estate, and the Ministry of Defence has acknowledged a substantial maintenance backlog across its airfields and accommodation.

Kremlin agrees with Trump on need for Ukraine leadership change
Ukraine needs a new leader with the political will to end the conflict with Russia, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has said. His comments came after US President Donald Trump stepped up pressure on Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky, whose presidential term expired more than two years ago, to hold new elections.
Speaking to RIA Novosti on Monday, Peskov said Trump believes it is high time for Ukraine to elect a new leader because “Ukraine’s president must make very responsible and very difficult decisions to stop this war.”
“Either Zelensky takes on this responsibility and shows such political will, or he does not,” Peskov continued, adding that he has so far failed to do so.
Asked whether Russia wants a particular Ukrainian leader, Peskov replied: “What matters to us is that someone in the Kiev regime demonstrates the political will to recognize the realities on the ground and move toward a peaceful settlement.”
The comments come after Trump suggested on Saturday that it is time for Ukraine to get “a new president,” accusing Zelensky of repeatedly rejecting opportunities for peace. He added that he believes Russia wants an agreement and Zelensky does not.
Zelensky’s presidential term expired in May 2024, but he has since refused to hold new elections, citing martial law. Moscow has since declared him illegitimate, while suggesting that his questionable status is a major obstacle to signing a binding peace agreement. Former Defense Minister Mikhail Fedorov argued that Zelensky fears a new election due to potential competition from former army chief Valery Zaluzhny. Fedorov is also viewed as a potential candidate.
An unnamed White House official told Axios that “Trump is really mad” at Zelensky over the attacks on Russian oil refineries. A Financial Times report claimed that the Trump administration threatened to suspend intelligence sharing and block US weapons sales through the NATO-coordinated PURL procurement mechanism unless the Ukrainian strikes stop.
On Sunday, Trump announced that Russia and Ukraine had reached an energy ceasefire. Zelensky replied that the announcement was “news for me,” but expressed readiness to stop attacking Russian refineries if the country stops its strikes on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure. Russia has yet to comment.
Zelensky has also argued that elections in Ukraine can only be organized if Russia agrees to a 60-day ceasefire.
Moscow has opposed the idea of a temporary ceasefire, arguing that it would only serve to allow Kiev time to rebuild its battered forces and receive more weapons from the West.
The US pressure intensified after Trump’s phone call on Friday with Russian President Vladimir Putin, after which the sides reached a major deal on diesel exports to the US to alleviate the global fuel shortage.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
08:59:00 UTC

Ukraine simplifies logging procedures for defense and fortification works in border regions
This was reported by the Ministry of Agrarian Policy and Food, according to Ukrinform.
“Given the changing operational situation, defense forces must be able to establish the necessary defensive lines and engineering structures as quickly as possible. Therefore, our task is to eliminate unnecessary procedural delays where they concern national security and defense, while ensuring clear rules for carrying out such work,” emphasized Minister of Agrarian Policy and Food Taras Vysotskyi.
In particular, the plan calls for shortening the processing time for documents required to issue a logging permit for logging operations in the border zone.
“If the work is necessary for the construction, development, and maintenance of engineering and technical structures, fortifications, fences, border markers, clearings, and related infrastructure, the decision to issue a logging permit will be made within two business days of receiving the application,” the ministry explained.
In addition, provisions have been made for emergency logging in the event of a change in the operational situation. Defense force units will be able to cut down and remove trees and shrubs to create defensive lines, natural barriers, and obstacles to enemy movement without obtaining a logging permit and, if necessary, without prior inspections by commissions in areas of active combat operations and in territories designated by a decision of the regional defense council located along Ukraine’s state border with the Russian Federation and the Republic of Belarus.
“The implementation of this resolution will allow for the necessary work to be carried out more expeditiously in areas where the security situation requires it, particularly in border regions,” the Ministry of Agrarian Policy emphasized.
As previously reported, the procedure for logging for defense purposes and the construction of fortifications in Ukraine has been simplified as much as possible and is regulated by Cabinet of Ministers Resolution No. 454 of April 23, 2024 (with the latest amendments and updates to the rules for timber harvesting). It is designed so that military units can quickly obtain materials and erect defensive structures without unnecessary bureaucracy.

Nationwide strike disrupts public transport, services across Belgium

Melike Pala
12 October 2026•Update: 12 October 2026
Public services across Belgium faced disruptions on Monday as workers affiliated with the trade union ACOD staged a nationwide strike against government policies, planned budget cuts and measures affecting public sector employees.
The strike affected public transportation, broadcasting, education, postal services and waste collection, with the extent of disruptions varying across the country, according to Belga news agency.
Belgium's national railway operator SNCB (NMBS) said seven out of 10 Intercity trains were operating under an alternative timetable, while only half of local trains were running.
Most peak-hour trains, which normally provide additional services during morning and evening rush hours, were cancelled.
In Flanders region, public transport operator De Lijn reported that around 40% of its buses and trams were not operating, with approximately 61% of services running across the region.
In Wallonia region, transport operator TEC warned of disruptions across its entire network, while Brussels public transport operator STIB said service interruptions could not be ruled out.
Disruptions were also expected in schools, as the ACOD Education union filed a strike notice, particularly affecting institutions within the Flemish GO! education network.
Public broadcasters VRT and RTBF also experienced significant disruptions following the strike call.
The strike could also affect postal deliveries and household waste collection.
Postal operator Bpost anticipated disruptions comparable to those experienced during the previous Friday's industrial action.
Waste collection services were also expected to face interruptions in several municipalities, particularly in the Brussels-Capital Region.
Brussels-Cleanliness warned that it could take several days for waste collection operations to return to normal.
The strike was called by ACOD, the socialist public sector trade union, as part of wider opposition to government budget proposals and planned spending cuts.

EU leaders face budget showdown as Germany leads revolt over spending plans
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
08:57:36 UTC
17:57:36 KST

An Irish compromise proposal for the EU’s long-term budget has drawn fire from the net-paying countries over its size and its focus on cutting ‘modern’ priorities. The Commission and MEPs have countered, warning of the risks of a less ambitious, more rigid budget.
EU leaders are heading for a bruising battle over the bloc’s next long-term budget this week, after a German-led coalition of net contributors rejected the latest compromise proposal as insufficient.
On Saturday, the Irish presidency of the EU Council proposed cutting €141 billion from the overall budget, bringing it to €1.622 trillion in 2025 prices for the seven-year period from 2028 to 2034.
But Berlin and its allies insist the cuts do not go far enough, while other member states and EU institutions have criticised the proposal for lacking ambition.
“We are still far from an agreement. The size of the new proposal is not a basis for agreement. The EU budget must be affordable for those who bear the brunt of financing it,” German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said in a statement.
“Everyone must contribute to the necessary adjustments, because prioritising and modernising EU spending is a task for us all,” he added.
Germany and its allies object not only to the overall size of the budget but also to how the cuts are distributed, with emerging priorities such as competitiveness and defence bearing the brunt.
“Defence, research and new technologies are being hit disproportionately hard. Europe needs to strengthen itself in these areas. Savings need to be found in a balanced way across the entire budget,” Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo said in a statement.
The Irish proposal concentrates the deepest cuts on programmes favoured by the so-called “frugals”, who prefer to call themselves “modernisers”. Competitiveness funding would fall by 13% and global cooperation by 17%.
By contrast, traditional policies such as agriculture and cohesion are largely spared, with a mere 3% reduction. They are backed by the “Friends of Cohesion”, a group of 17 southern and eastern European countries including Italy and Romania.
It is not the first time the frugals’ own priorities have borne the brunt. In June, the then Cypriot presidency proposed cutting the European Competitiveness Fund and the Global Europe programme by almost 4%.
“There is an urgent need to strengthen the link between the political realities of the European leaders and the negotiations on the MFF [Multiannual Financial Framework],” an EU diplomat told Euronews.
“The Netherlands cannot accept this proposal. At this rate, there will be no deal by the end of the year,” warned Dutch Finance Minister Eelco Heinen.
Sweden’s Minister for EU Affairs Jessica Rosencrantz likewise called the proposal “unreasonable,” adding that “we are therefore nowhere near an agreement.”
The frugals are not alone in their disappointment. The Friends of Cohesion welcomed with a sigh of relief that funding for their farmers and poorest regions was spared significant cuts. But they also say the next budget looks unambitious given the challenges facing the bloc.
Excluding the repayment of NextGenerationEU, the post-pandemic recovery instrument, the budget would amount to a mere 1.02% of EU gross national income. According to leading MEPs, that is a 10% cut to the current budget in real terms.
“The choice before us is not between a cheap and an expensive Europe. It is between an underfunded Europe at the mercy of the next crisis, and a properly funded Europe that can tackle challenges and respond to Europeans’ needs,” said MEP Carla Tavares (Portugal/S&D).
In a joint statement on Monday, the leaders of the four main pro-EU groups in the European Parliament - European People’s Party, Socialists and Democrats, Renew Europe and Greens/EFA - rejected the Irish compromise text, saying it cannot serve as a basis for an agreement with the Parliament.
Meanwhile, the Commission’s Director-General for Budget, Stéphanie Riso, told EU ambassadors on Sunday that she had severe concerns, not only about the lack of ambition but also because the proposal risked making the EU much more rigid.
She singled out the cuts to Brussels ' public administration, largely supported by the member states, and the EU Facility, an instrument meant to give the budget room to react to shocks, which the Irish proposal drastically cuts by 40%.
"We are also concerned by the substantial reduction in the flexibility of the budget, including cuts to instruments designed to respond to unforeseen needs and crises. Flexibility is essential if the EU budget is to remain effective and able to react to change over the next seven years," Commission spokesperson Balazs Ujvari said on Monday.
The long-term budget will be discussed at the European Council summit on Thursday and Friday, when EU leaders are expected to provide political direction to break the deadlock.
“We are hearing more of the same arguments. We are getting to a point where we need leaders to advance the discussion,” a second EU diplomat told Euronews.
This article was updated with additional information.
Jorge Liboreiro contributed to the reporting.

Gaza olive harvest battered by war as production plunges, farmland becomes inaccessible
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
08:57:20 UTC
17:57:20 KST

Palestinian farmers in Gaza are facing a difficult olive harvest this year as production declines, large areas of agricultural land remain damaged and many groves are inaccessible because they lie in areas controlled by the Israeli army or beyond the so-called “yellow line,” Anadolu reports.
On accessible farmland, farmers continue picking olives and separating them from leaves and branches despite shortages of fertilizer, irrigation water and agricultural supplies, as well as higher labor, transportation and pressing costs.
The pressures have left many families unable to store their usual annual supplies of olive oil and olives.
On July 13, Gaza’s Agriculture Ministry estimated losses to the agricultural sector from Israel’s genocidal war, which began on Oct. 8, 2023, at more than $3 billion, including $1.49 billion in direct damage and $1.59 billion in indirect losses.
Kamel Baraka, a farmer from Deir al-Balah in central Gaza, said olive tree yields had fallen significantly.
“A tree that produced around 100 kilograms (220.4 pounds) of olives before the war now produces no more than 20 (44 pounds) to 30 kilograms (66 pounds),” Baraka told Anadolu.
That represents a decline of around 70% to 80%, he added.
“A season that once provided an important source of income for farmers, traders and workers now barely meets the needs of some families because of current conditions and shortages of essential agricultural supplies,” Baraka said.
“Olive cultivation requires constant care, fertilizer, irrigation and other inputs that have become increasingly difficult to obtain,” he added.
-Massive damage
Damage to farmland and restrictions on access have also directly reduced the harvest.
“Large areas of olive groves in eastern parts of central Gaza lie in zones farmers cannot reach, particularly east of Salah al-Din Street and around the ‘yellow line,’” Baraka said.
The “yellow line” is a notional line inside the Gaza Strip to which the Israeli army withdrew under the first phase of US President Donald Trump’s plan to end the war, under which a ceasefire took effect on Oct. 10, 2025. It separates areas in eastern Gaza that remain under Israeli army control from areas west of the line where Palestinians are allowed to move.
“Farmers in Deir al-Balah, Bureij and Maghazi face difficulty reaching agricultural land that had been a major source of olive production,” Baraka said.
He said available farmland west of Salah al-Din Street is insufficient to meet residents’ needs for olive oil and olives.
Before the war, preparations for the harvest began about a month in advance, with farmers arranging workers and preparing equipment for picking and transport, while families stored olives and oil for the year ahead.
Those preparations have declined as production falls and costs rise, with some farmers now collecting only enough olives for household consumption and limited quantities for sale.
-Costs triple
Farmers are also struggling with sharply higher transportation and pressing costs, as well as shortages of containers needed to store olive oil.
“The cost of pressing olives has risen to around three times what it was before the war,” Baraka said, adding that the increase has placed further pressure on farmers whose incomes have already fallen because of lower production.
“Before the war, olive press owners often transported harvests from farms to pressing facilities, while farmers now struggle to find transportation even for small quantities,” he added.
Higher costs for pumping water and irrigating trees, combined with shortages of fertilizer, labor and storage containers, have made preserving the harvest and storing oil increasingly difficult, particularly for families that depend on farming for their food needs.
“The olive season, once an opportunity for farmers to improve their livelihoods and secure food supplies for the year, has become an exhausting season that provides many of them with only a fraction of what they need,” Baraka said.
Since Israel’s genocidal war began on Oct. 8, 2023, Gaza’s agricultural sector has sustained widespread damage, according to the Agriculture Ministry.
The ministry said 158,909 dunams (39,267 acres) of agricultural land have been damaged out of a total 182,247 dunams (45,033 acres), or around 87%, sharply reducing crop production and the capacity to provide food.
The war also has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians and injured over 175,000 others, according to Palestinian figures, also destroying about 90% of the enclave’s infrastructure.

Wind power could save Türkiye $4 Billion a Year in gas imports, Industry group says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
08:56:45 UTC
17:56:45 KST

(AP Photo)
Türkiye’s current wind power capacity could help the country save nearly $4 billion annually in natural gas imports, according to İbrahim Erden, chairman of the Turkish Wind Energy Association (TÜREB).
Erden said that every 1,000 megawatts of installed wind power capacity reduces natural gas imports by about $250 million per year based on current energy prices.
“Türkiye’s wind power capacity, which exceeds 16 gigawatts, provides the opportunity to save nearly $4 billion annually in natural gas imports at current energy prices,” he said.
Erden noted that renewable energy sources have accounted for more than 40 percent of Türkiye’s electricity generation in recent years, with the share exceeding 60 percent in the first eight months of this year.
He also said global wind power installations increased by 165,000 megawatts last year, of which 2,000 megawatts were added in Türkiye.
Recalling that Türkiye raised its combined wind and solar installed capacity target for 2035 to 120 gigawatts in 2024, Erden said TÜREB aims for wind power to account for 48 gigawatts of that total.
According to Erden, Türkiye needs to add around 8,000 megawatts of new wind and solar capacity annually to reach the 120-gigawatt target by 2035.
He added that if the country’s wind power capacity reaches the 48-gigawatt level targeted by TÜREB, electricity generation from wind would roughly triple, and the reduction in natural gas imports could reach approximately $10 billion to $12 billion per year under current price and production assumptions.

Delhi braces for more protests against election chief amid crackdown
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
08:55:46 UTC
17:55:46 KST

Indian opposition defies lockdown, marches to demand election chief sacking
Opposition parties joined by student groups have petitioned the Supreme Court, seeking the election chief’s ouster.
New Delhi, India — India’s main opposition leader Rahul Gandhi led dozens of members of parliament and thousands of other protesters in a tense march to the Supreme Court on Monday, submitting a petition demanding the resignation of the country’s election chief even as tens of thousands of police officers shadowed them, stopping them from physically reaching the court.
Congress Party leader Gandhi was joined by his sister, Priyanka, who is also a member of parliament, and other prominent leaders on top of a truck that slowly made its way through a sea of supporters towards the court.
The police had set up a series of barricades to stop them from reaching the Supreme Court. But some Congress Party supporters crossed the first set of barricades after climbing over them. As they approached the second barricade, police officials tried to push back, and clashes appeared imminent.
But Congress leaders then announced that Gandhi and others had managed to submit their petition to the court, even if not physically, and their truck turned around.
Yet leaders from the Congress, other opposition parties and the Gen Z-led “Cockroach” protest movement have signalled that they are still deciding their next steps — their demand for Election Commission chief Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation unchanged. The Cockroach Janta Party movement had forced out Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan in July.
Rahul Gandhi, heir to India’s most influential political dynasty, is seeking to turn a summer youth uprising into a broader challenge to Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s decade-long dominance of Indian politics, putting the Hindu nationalist government under growing pressure.
In a press briefing on Monday, Gandhi said the Modi government had put the capital city “in jail”. More than 30,000 police officers were deployed on New Delhi’s streets.
‘No constraints on Modi’
India’s Election Commission, a supposedly autonomous body tasked with overseeing the world’s largest electorate, has been criticised after revelations that its chief, Kumar, frequently overruled concerns raised by the other two election commissioners about the integrity of changes to the voter database.
For months, India’s opposition parties have argued that the election commission is compromised, sabotaging elections at the behest of Modi’s Hindu majoritarian Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) for its electoral benefit. The BJP denies the allegations.
Since June last year, the commission has been revising and updating statewide voter lists. It has since removed more than 130 million names, which critics say has disproportionately deprived minorities and other vulnerable groups in India of the right to vote.
Gandhi has called for the chief election commissioner to be tried for treason. “We will not spare you,” he said, referring to Kumar, at his Monday press briefing.
Opposition politicians allege that protest rallies by leaders including Gandhi have been met with violent and brutal force, as seen in videos showing them being detained.
“[The protesters] came with love in their hearts, not hatred or anger,” Gandhi said, referring to a protest on Saturday. “They were beaten, both by cops and BJP goons.”
“Narendra Modi … cannot silence India’s voice. These cowards cannot intimidate us. They will have to step aside,” he wrote on X, calling on people from all walks of life to join the protest on Monday.
Analysts say circumstances this time around are starkly different from the summer protests, when CJP-led demonstrators demanded the resignation of then-Education Minister Pradhan.
Asim Ali, a political analyst in New Delhi, told Al Jazeera that the mobilisation of the wider opposition would not stop, but the Modi government was unlikely to back down.
“The crackdown this time on students is making it apparent that it would be tougher for young protesters this time, and students can’t get beaten up and dragged violently daily,” he said. “Going forward, the opposition parties stand to be the front face of the protests, and they need to lead from the front.”
Since 1975, when then-Prime Minister Indira Gandhi imposed a state of national emergency suspending civil liberties, “India saw more civil politics grow into mainstream, where opposition parties were allowed space,” Ali said.
He added that after five decades, “those democratic gains have vanished – and there are no constraints on this government by independent institutions.”
Rasheed Kidwai, a political analyst, said he has seen New Delhi at the centre of “several big opposition political rallies, held in areas near the parliament, hosting hundreds of thousands of people”, when the police did not interfere, unlike the crackdowns this year.
Kidwai said that the violent detention of members of parliament, in particular, was worrying.
“We are seeing a big change from when politicians were more tolerant of dissent,” he noted.
Cat-and-mouse chases
With an unprecedented security deployment in central New Delhi designed to prevent protests, youth leaders are turning to new tactics.
Neha Bora, the president of the All India Students’ Association (AISA), a left-wing group affiliated with the Communist Party of India, has often tricked Delhi police in order to stage protests in recent days.
Bora, a post-doctoral student of theatre, came to national prominence for her fiery speeches in the July protests, becoming a leading face of the Gen Z movement challenging Modi’s Hindu nationalist politics.
Aditi Thakur, a 23-year-old student in the capital, has turned on notifications for all of Bora’s posts on social media. “A call to protest can come anytime, anywhere,” she told Al Jazeera.
Bora does not reveal when or where she is going to stage a protest until just 30 minutes before, to avoid detentions by the police. Her supporters are alerted via social media to join her at a given location in the capital.
On Sunday, she picked a congested street near central Delhi — and was able to jump several barricades to reach the heavily secured Parliament Street, before being chased down and dragged into a police van.
Even Thakur couldn’t catch her, she told Al Jazeera, laughing. “These are guerrilla times, but peacefully. If the government cracks down on us, we also need to adapt,” she said. “It is a fun cat-and-mouse chase every day. I’m hooked on it.”
The Gandhi-led Congress is also adopting similar measures, holding flash rallies at unannounced venues, then running away from police.
The mood is changing
A defining feature of the July protests – a watershed moment for wrestling concessions from the government – was Gen Z’s humour in the face of police brutality.
Now, protesters are prepared for a more serious confrontation, even if demonstrations remain peaceful, say analysts.
“We are seeing that humour changing more into anger this time,” Asim Ali said.
The biggest challenge for the government is disruption in central New Delhi, which, Ali said, the government cannot allow on a daily basis. The area is home to most federal government offices, as well as being a major business hub.
Protesters know that too, and that gives them leverage.
“We are seeing this movement grow into a bigger anti-government, anti-Modi movement,” Ali said.

Ukraine Feeds 3 Million Schoolchildren for Free Despite Russian Attacks and Blackouts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12

17:55:02 KST

- Category
- Life in Ukraine
Ukraine Feeds 3 Million Schoolchildren for Free Despite Russian Attacks and Blackouts
Ukraine is fighting to protect not only its territory, but also the future of a generation growing up under Russian attacks. In exclusive interviews with UNITED24 Media, Ukraine’s education minister and the UN World Food Programme’s country director explain how school nutrition reform is supporting families, transforming education, and restoring a sense of normalcy for children.
Air raid sirens and power outages have become part of everyday school life in Ukraine, but even in frontline regions, children continue receiving hot meals. At School No. 7 in Romny, Sumy region, around 350 lunches are prepared daily, with meals served in shelters when air raid alerts interrupt classes.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The school is one example of Ukraine’s nationwide effort to provide free, nutritious food to approximately three million children despite Russia’s ongoing invasion.
According to Ukraine’s Ministry of Education and Science on September 21, the government expanded its free school meals program on September 1, 2026, to cover students in grades 1–11 (12) attending municipal schools in person or through blended learning.
The initiative is part of a broader school nutrition reform launched in 2020 at the initiative of Ukraine’s First Lady, Olena Zelenska.
During a visit to Romny School No. 7, Ukrainian Minister of Education and Science Andrii Butenko and UN World Food Programme (WFP) Country Director Richard Ragan examined how the program operates in a region facing continued Russian attacks.
The school has 738 enrolled students and operates through a combination of in-person and remote learning. With WFP support, its kitchen received five pieces of modern equipment, including a combi steam oven, electric stove, dishwasher, cooking boiler, and vegetable cutter.
A diesel generator was also provided to help the kitchen continue operating during electricity outages caused by Russian attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure.
Beyond free lunches—how Ukraine is changing school nutrition
Speaking exclusively to UNITED24 Media, Butenko explained that the reform goes far beyond simply providing children with free food.
“This is also support for families because the child will definitely be fed at school,” the minister said, pointing to the challenges parents face during frequent air raid alerts and power outages.
He emphasized that the initiative is also intended to change children’s eating habits by introducing healthier, more balanced meals.
“This reform involves changing eating habits. It won’t happen tomorrow, or even the day after,” Butenko told UNITED24 Media. According to the minister, recent surveys indicate that more than 80% of both parents and children are satisfied with the school meals program.
The reform has also introduced stricter nutritional standards, including reduced salt content and carefully balanced seasoning. For WFP, maintaining school meals during wartime is not only about nutrition but also about helping children continue their education.
“Having hot meals at school brings kids to school. It’s important to invest in their nutrition, so it enhances their ability to learn,” Ragan told UNITED24 Media. “It’s not easy to do a program like this, and you’re fighting a war at the same time,” he added.
Ragan said he was particularly impressed by the coordination between teachers, parents, kitchen staff, and school administrators, who continue working despite the constant threat of Russian attacks. He also praised the quality of the meals after personally trying the food prepared at the school. “It’s a lot better than the food I had when I was at school,” he said.
Feeding children on the frontlines as Russia’s war continues
The effort extends far beyond Romny. With WFP assistance, 298 Ukrainian school kitchen modernization projects have received support, including 100 in the Sumy region alone.
For the 2026–2027 academic year, WFP plans to support approximately 200,000 children across 1,800 schools in eight frontline regions: Chernihiv, Sumy, Kharkiv, Dnipropetrovsk, Odesa, Mykolaiv, Kherson, and Zaporizhzhia.
More than 1,000 school cooks have already begun training in preparing healthy, balanced meals and operating modern kitchen equipment, with another 220 expected to join practical training sessions in October.
The Ukrainian government has allocated nearly UAH 14.4 billion ($345 million) in 2026 for state subsidies to local budgets supporting free school meals. The program combines government funding, local resources, and international assistance to modernize kitchens and maintain food services.
However, significant challenges remain. Across the eight frontline regions, approximately 2,400 school kitchens still require modernization, while 388 educational institutions lack kitchen facilities altogether.
The importance of protecting Ukrainian children extends far beyond education and nutrition. As of September 25, Russia’s full-scale invasion had killed 744 Ukrainian children, while another 2,363 remained missing, according to Ukrainian Ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets.
Despite these difficulties, Ragan believes Ukraine’s determination to keep children learning and eating properly during wartime is an important investment in the country’s future.
“The fact that Ukraine is really focused on this during a time of war is fundamentally important,” he told UNITED24 Media.

Russia Launches Manhunt for Europe’s Top Defense Executives, FT Reports
Russia is reportedly targeting senior executives and key employees of European defense companies for assassination, as Moscow expands covert operations aimed at intimidating arms manufacturers and disrupting military support for Ukraine.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to the Financial Times on October 11, intelligence officials from five European countries warned that Russian intelligence agencies are increasingly targeting personnel at both major defense manufacturers and smaller companies, particularly those producing drones and military equipment for Ukraine.
European intelligence services have already identified and disrupted several suspected Russian operations, including cases involving surveillance of potential targets near their homes and workplaces.

Germany’s domestic intelligence agency, the Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution (BfV), has increased its engagement with defense companies in response to the threat. Executives and employees have been advised to strengthen security arrangements, including hiring private protection.
BfV President Sinan Selen has warned German lawmakers that Russia is deliberately planning violent attacks against individuals, with organized criminal groups playing an increasingly prominent role in such operations.
Several defense industry executives told the Financial Times that they had increased personal security over the past six months following warnings from intelligence services. Others have introduced additional protective measures when traveling internationally.
The growing security requirements are also creating financial challenges for defense manufacturers. Smaller companies and startups face potentially significant expenses associated with protecting employees, facilities, and sensitive operations.
According to the FT, one defense company relocated its production operations to another part of Western Europe because of threats attributed to Russia.
European intelligence officials believe the reported assassination plots are intended not only to eliminate specific individuals but also to intimidate the wider defense industry.
By making executives and employees fear becoming targets, Moscow reportedly hopes to discourage European manufacturers from supplying weapons, drones, and military technologies to Ukraine.
The Financial Times also reported that some suspected Russian operatives have demonstrated limited operational capabilities, allowing European security services to detect surveillance activities and prevent planned attacks.
The reported threats follow an earlier Russian plot to assassinate Armin Papperger, CEO of German defense manufacturer Rheinmetall. In January 2025, NATO confirmed that US and German intelligence agencies had thwarted the assassination plan, which was reportedly part of a broader campaign targeting European defense industry leaders supplying Ukraine.

What do emergency and governor rule in Pakistan’s Khyber Pakhtunkhwa mean?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
08:54:25 UTC
17:54:25 KST

What do emergency and governor rule in Pakistan’s Khyber Pakhtunkhwa mean?
Pakistan has taken control of a province governed by Imran Khan’s PTI. Here is what the move means and what happens next.
Islamabad, Pakistan – The federal government has taken direct control of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (KP), the northwestern province governed by jailed former Prime Minister Imran Khan’s Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party until now.
President Asif Ali Zardari signed a proclamation on Sunday, on the advice of Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, imposing a state of emergency and declaring that the provincial government could no longer function in accordance with the Constitution, the legal basis for governor’s rule. On Monday, Minister of State for Interior Talal Chaudhry said the province’s chief minister, Sohail Afridi, was detained.
“The fundamental grounds for imposition of emergency are law and order, fight against terrorism, and to save innocent people from the dreadful consequences of terrorist activities,” Law Minister Azam Nazeer Tarar said at a news conference in Islamabad on Sunday, alongside Information Minister Ataullah Tarar, Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi and other officials.
PTI, which has governed the province since 2013, has rejected the move. It came after talks collapsed between the federal government and the PTI over a planned march to Islamabad demanding the party leader’s release.
Here is what the two measures mean, who now runs the province and how long the arrangement could last.
Who runs Khyber Pakhtunkhwa now?
Under the government’s decision, Governor Faisal Karim Kundi will take over the functions of the provincial government. Kundi belongs to the Pakistan Peoples Party (PPP), an ally of Sharif’s government.
Parliament — where Sharif’s Pakistan Muslim League (Nawaz), the PPP and their other allies hold a majority — takes over the powers of the provincial assembly, where PTI has a majority. The chief minister, ministers, advisers, special assistants and advocate general “shall forthwith cease to hold office”, the proclamation says.
Hassan Abdullah Niazi, a Lahore-based lawyer and adjunct faculty member at the Lahore University of Management Sciences (LUMS), offered a different interpretation.
“However, this does not mean that the KP Assembly or its elected chief minister have been permanently removed. It is more akin to thinking they are dysfunctional until the emergency is lifted, at which point they must be restored,” he told Al Jazeera.
An 11-member advisory council will assist Kundi. The army, already deployed in the province, is expected to assist him and his team in maintaining law and order.
A separate federal order has established a secretariat for 12 “designated districts”, most of them in the former tribal areas along the Afghan border. It will be headed by an additional chief secretary, whose orders will carry the same legal effect as those of the provincial government.
“No province has been divided anywhere. It is only that these are the war-hit districts where more funding and more focus will be needed at this time, and for that this has been set apart,” Naqvi said at Sunday’s news conference.
The order also states that the constitutional provision requiring the judiciary to be separated from the executive “shall not apply” to the designated districts.
“The constitutional provision that mandates the separation of the judiciary from the executive has been suspended, allowing executive officers to perform judicial functions,” Rida Hosain, a Lahore-based constitutional lawyer, told Al Jazeera.
Why did the government invoke both measures?
Article 232 of Pakistan’s Constitution allows the president to declare an emergency when security is threatened by an “internal disturbance beyond the power of a provincial government to control”.
Article 234 applies when a governor reports that a province cannot be governed in accordance with the Constitution.
The proclamation cites “terrorist” attacks of “unprecedented level of violent intensity” and says the provincial government “has failed to demonstrate the ownership, will and intent to adequately deal with the menace of terrorism”.
According to the Pakistan Institute for Conflict and Security Studies (PICSS), an Islamabad-based independent think tank, armed men carried out at least 1,066 attacks in the country in 2025, up from 908 in 2024.
The number rose sharply in 2026 as PICSS recorded 1,232 attacks nationwide in the first nine months – the majority of which occurred in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Balochistan province in the southwest.
“But this situation was so grave and exceptional that the requirements in both provisions, the conditions that demand them, were such that both provisions were exercised,” Tarar said.
Information Minister Ataullah Tarar went further, accusing the provincial government of links to armed groups.
“This was the carefully considered view, from start to finish, of all cabinet members that the PTI government in KP is hand in glove with the terrorists,” he said, without providing evidence.
Naqvi said the government had dozens of pieces of evidence against the provincial government. None has been made public.
PTI chairman Gohar Ali Khan questioned why the measures were applied across the province if the security concerns were concentrated in specific districts.
“If there is terrorism and an emergency is needed in 12 districts, then why is governor’s rule across the whole province?” he said at a news conference in Islamabad after the government’s briefing.
Taimur Jhagra, a PTI leader and former provincial finance minister, rejected the government’s allegations.
“Of course the provincial government was fighting terrorism. We own the fight against terrorism individually and collectively. If the issue was terrorism, then Balochistan should have had a state of emergency before KP,” he told Al Jazeera.
What has happened since Sunday?
PTI says Afridi, the chief minister until Sunday, and other party leaders are under arrest.
“We know the CM, the provincial president, Junaid Akbar, the speaker, Babar Swati, and some other leaders have been detained. The government has not revealed where they are,” Jhagra said.
Naqvi had also indicated on Sunday that PTI figures could be detained.
“Definitely, them or whoever else is needed for law and order, to maintain it, we will take into protective custody. But those among them who are wanted will be arrested, and everyone else will be released as soon as law and order improves,” Naqvi said.
Tarar, relaying Naqvi’s position at the same news conference, said some PTI figures had already been taken into preventive custody.
PTI says several provincial ministers and lawmakers were detained even before Sunday.
Internet monitor NetBlocks reported late on Sunday that network data showed a major disruption to connectivity in parts of the province.
District administrations closed schools and colleges in Peshawar, Mardan, Swabi and Nowshera on Monday.
Meanwhile, in Punjab province, Imran Khan’s sisters Aleema Khan, Uzma Khan and Noreen Niazi have been held in custody since September 20-21, under a public order law that allows preventive detention for 30 days.
How long can the measures last?
Provinces have been placed under governor’s rule at least eight times since 1949. Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, then known as the North West Frontier Province, faced it in 1975 and 1994.
Because Zardari acted without a resolution from the provincial assembly, the Constitution requires both houses of Parliament to approve the emergency within 10 days, by October 21.
Sessions of the National Assembly and the Senate have been called for Tuesday.
The emergency must also be placed before a joint parliamentary sitting within 30 days. It lapses after two months unless approved by the joint sitting.
Once approved, however, the Constitution sets no fixed end date. The emergency remains in force until it is revoked or a majority of the total membership of both houses votes against it.
Governor’s rule under Article 234 has a separate limit. Parliament can extend it in two-month increments, for a maximum of six months in total.
“The emergency provisions allow the executive to suspend certain fundamental rights, and there is no fixed time limit for how long an emergency can continue, allowing for prolonged federal control,” Hosain said.
Gohar said PTI would challenge the measures in the courts and the assemblies.
“We have not formally called off the long march at all. Our struggle, as I told you, will absolutely continue,” he said.

What is ‘pilgra-merch’? The travel trend turning souvenirs into trip inspiration
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
08:53:04 UTC
17:53:04 KST

Tourists are showing off how well-travelled they are through destination-specific grocery tote bags or branded hotel caps.
Long gone are the days when your souvenirs were limited to whatever you could hastily grab from the airport gift store before rushing to your gate.
Nowadays, buying something you can only get in that specific destination has become a key part of the travel experience, at least according to Skyscanner’s latest travel trends report.
Dubbed “pilgra-merch”, the trend is the latest iteration of the millennial phrase “pics, or it didn’t happen”, says fashion psychologist Shakaila Forbes-Bell.
“Fashion brands have been leaning into this trend by providing more sensation-seeking style experiences from mystery bags to pop-ups, all of which you have to be ‘tapped in’ to know about,” she said.
“This community-driven aspect is key to creating a coveted pilgra-merch item. When a bag, a tote, or a mug becomes sought after, it’s often positioned as something only a ‘real traveller’ would know about. This positioning taps into our ingrained desire to belong and fear of being othered, which ultimately heightens the item’s desirability.”
Some 23% of travellers have made a trip in the past year to buy something they couldn’t purchase online, with 28% of Gen Z saying they are most proud to buy a limited-edition grocery tote, while 22% of Millennials are showing off their branded robes or caps from luxury hotels.
Where to embrace the ‘pilgra-merch’ trend
Skyscanner’s trends report focused on two ‘pilgra-merch’ examples – the Trader Joe’s tote bag, and Ritz Paris’ merchandise – but we think you can do better than that.
If you want supermarket merch that not everybody has, Family Mart in Japan has you covered. Last month, the chain released 47 different pairs of socks to represent the country’s prefectures.
Exclusively available in Family Mart stores within the prefecture in question, you’ll be able to flex on people about all the under-the-radar places you’ve visited.
While the “pilgra-merch” trend is more about instantly recognisable items that show off how well-travelled you are, we think buying a unique item you’ll use everyday that isn’t necessarily branded is a much better use of your cash.
With autumn finally upon us, it’s time to start thinking about upgrading your wardrobe – so why not head to one of the Handknitting Association of Iceland’s stores to pick out 100% wool, locally-made jumpers and cardigans?
Alternatively, if you’re all sorted for jumpers, you could head to Riga, where SENĀ KLĒTS sells mittens knitted in traditional Latvian designs which are filled with symbolism.
For when the weather warms up again, there are several places on the continent where you can get custom-made sandals, the most famous of which is probably Melissinos Sandals in Athens.

The second missile was launched at approximately 9:36 a.m. It reached a maximum altitude of about 70 km and traveled more than 910 km.
The Japanese government relayed the relevant information to aircraft and vessels in the vicinity. As of this moment, no reports of damage or other consequences have been received.
