Israeli president warns election tensions could deepen divisions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
08:51:32 UTC
17:51:32 KST

Sahin Demir
12 October 2026•Update: 12 October 2026
Israel’s President Isaac Herzog warned Monday that tensions surrounding the upcoming parliamentary elections could deepen divisions in Israeli society.
In an interview with Israeli daily Yedioth Ahronoth, Herzog said election periods naturally carry risks of greater polarization.
“We are in an election period, and naturally such a period is dangerous because it could lead to some kind of radicalization that could tear us apart even further,” he said.
Asked whether he feared that one side might refuse to accept the election results, Herzog said: “I believe everyone will accept the election results.”
He urged Israelis to vote and stressed that political competition should not further divide society.
“Elections are not a civil war. Elections are the way to clarify issues, make decisions and understand that the day after, we continue together,” Herzog said.
He pledged to work to prevent Israel from being forced into another election if the Oct. 27 vote fails to produce a stable governing coalition.
“I am doing everything to ensure that Israel has a stable government,” he said. “I will do absolutely everything I can to prevent repeat elections.”
Herzog said Israel faces major national challenges and should avoid returning to repeated elections and prolonged political deadlock.
Asked whether he would seek to promote a unity government if the election produces a stalemate, Herzog declined to endorse any particular coalition.
“It would not be right for me to say, two weeks before the elections, what kind of government should be formed,” he said.
Herzog also said he was working closely with the Central Elections Committee over possible attempts to interfere with the vote.
He said he recently brought representatives of major technology companies together with committee chairman Justice Noam Sohlberg and his team to discuss possible scenarios, including attempts to disrupt the elections from inside or outside Israel.
 
‘Moral stain’
Herzog also addressed violence in the occupied West Bank, describing occupier attacks against Palestinians as unacceptable and saying authorities should consider using administrative detention in some cases against those responsible.
He said violence in the occupied territory was a “moral stain,” adding that innocent Palestinians should not be attacked.
Herzog also addressed Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s ongoing corruption trial, saying the case should be brought to an end through a plea agreement.
He said he had offered to mediate between the sides at the President’s Residence, but Netanyahu had not responded, adding that the offer remained open.
Netanyahu has been on trial since May 2020 on charges of bribery, fraud and breach of trust in three corruption cases. He denies wrongdoing and has repeatedly described the charges as politically motivated.
His testimony in the cases concluded in June after 98 court hearings spanning around 18 months.
In November 2025, Netanyahu formally requested a presidential pardon from Herzog in connection with the corruption charges.
The Oct. 27 election will determine the composition of Israel’s 120-seat Knesset, where at least 61 seats are generally needed to form a governing majority.
Netanyahu, whose current government took office in late 2022, is seeking another term, while opposition parties are attempting to secure enough parliamentary support to form an alternative government.
Recent opinion polls have shown a closely divided political landscape, with neither Netanyahu’s bloc nor his opponents consistently securing a clear governing majority.
Israel has experienced prolonged political instability in recent years, holding five parliamentary elections between 2019 and 2022 after repeated difficulties in forming or maintaining governing coalitions.
The upcoming election also comes amid continuing political disputes over accountability for the events of 2023 and calls for an official investigation into the failures surrounding them.

Hiiumaa residents can no longer give birth on the island
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
08:51:00 UTC
17:51:00 KST

Hiiumaa residents can no longer give birth on the island
Women on Hiiumaa haven't been able to to give birth on their home island since July. However, no clear arrangements have been made for transporting expectant mothers to the mainland and back or covering the associated costs.
Kärolyn Kivistik, who lives in Kärdla, is expecting her fifth child on November 8 and her hospital bag is already packed. This time, however, packing it was more complicated than before.
Kivistik said that in the past, her husband had been able to quickly bring her anything she needed. "Now I have to think everything through carefully because I'll be in the city and there won't be any way for someone to bring me things I've left at home," she explained.
Since Hiiumaa Hospital stopped providing maternity services on July 1, Kivistik will have to travel to the mainland to give birth and she does not want to make the journey while in labor. As a mother of a large family, she wants to stay home as long as possible, but she will likely have to head to the capital a week before her due date.
"These children like to be born at night," Kivistik said, adding that ferries do not operate at night, making it difficult to wait for labor to begin on Hiiumaa.
The family has budgeted nearly €1,000 in additional expenses, as renting an apartment near a Tallinn maternity hospital alone costs almost €500. But what bothers her even more than the extra expense is the uncertainty surrounding the arrangements.
Staff shortage to blame
In fact, Hiiumaa Hospital has all the facilities needed to provide maternity services. What it lacks is staff. A pediatrician retired on July 1, there was no gynecologist available on four days in September and in October the hospital will have to manage for about a week without an anesthesiologist. Yet all of these specialists are essential to ensuring that childbirth is as safe as possible.
On Monday, a proposed plan outlining what the journey to give birth might look like was presented to the board of the hospital in Kärdla. According to Hiiumaa Hospital Director Riina Tamm, these are still only preliminary recommendations and do not address the main concern: how expectant mothers will get to the mainland and back and who will cover the costs.
"Where will she stay in Tallinn? Who will pay for her accommodation? She travels to Tallinn, gives birth, but how does she get back? Who will bring her home? Does she have to make her own way back? Should the municipality arrange it or should the hospital? And again, who pays for it all?" Tamm asked. She acknowledged that these are important questions that must be resolved before such a change can be implemented.
As a midwife, Tamm has helped deliver hundreds of babies on Hiiumaa, but she now admits frankly that she would no longer want her own loved ones to give birth on the island. Complications during childbirth can become critical within minutes and the hospital is not equipped to handle such emergencies. This is also why women with high-risk pregnancies have been sent to the mainland for years. But what awaits women on Hiiumaa who do not want to travel to the mainland ahead of time to await labor?
"If everything goes smoothly — the woman arrives, we have an ambulance available and a ferry is just about to depart from Hiiumaa — the patient can reach the Women's Clinic at East Tallinn Central Hospital in three hours and 45 minutes. The ferries are already operating on their winter schedule, with three hours between departures," Tamm explained.
Transport by helicopter would take two hours to reach the hospital, but only if weather conditions permit flying, a helicopter is available and its allotted flight hours have not been exhausted.
A problem of regional policy
Tamm believes this is not just a problem for the small Hiiumaa Hospital or Hiiumaa Municipality. "This is actually a regional policy issue," she added.
In Tamm's view, the state has failed to do its job. The possibility of closing maternity units was first discussed back in 1998, yet the decision on whether to close them has ultimately been left to individual hospitals.
Vivian Arusaar, head of midwifery at East Tallinn Central Hospital, said women who have already gone into labor will not be turned away, but the hospital cannot offer extended accommodation. However, if maternity services continue to be concentrated in larger centers, a solution will have to be found.
Arusaar suggested that the Estonian Health Insurance Fund could be given the option of funding hotel-style accommodation at hospitals. "It is common elsewhere in the world for people to travel hundreds of kilometers to receive healthcare and many large hospitals of regional importance actually have patient hotels," she explained.
According to Heli Paluste, a healthcare network expert at the Ministry of Social Affairs, the decision to close a maternity unit rests with the hospital's board, not the ministry, because hospitals operate autonomously. To ensure high-quality maternity care, a hospital should handle at least 300 births a year, a threshold met only by hospitals in Tallinn, Tartu and Pärnu.
Paluste did not rule out similar decisions being made in the near future. Time will tell whether this happens and which counties might be affected.
Hospital boards in charge of decisions to close wards
Hospital board leaders met at the ministry on Friday where, according to Paluste, it was again emphasized that decisions on any potential maternity unit closures would remain the responsibility of hospital boards.
Where maternity services have been discontinued at Estonia's general hospitals, it has been due to declining birth numbers. The closures have been driven either by financial considerations or staff shortages.
Paluste said patient hotels had been discussed before, but funding them would come at the expense of already scarce healthcare resources. The ministry believes that providing financial assistance to expectant mothers facing economic hardship should be the responsibility of local governments.

Yunus Turk and Emir Yildirim
12 October 2026•Update: 12 October 2026
Türkiye’s flag carrier Turkish Airlines will resume flights between Istanbul and Minsk, making it easier for businesspeople from both countries to visit each other, the chair of the Türkiye-Belarus Business Council within the Foreign Economic Relations Board (DEIK) told Anadolu.
Fatih Isik stated that the resumption of flights will pave the way for exploring new opportunities in the auto supply industry, machinery, energy equipment, and production technologies.
He noted that Belarusian industrial infrastructure and Türkiye’s production and export capacity can work together for potential joint production and access to third-country markets, but international sanctions on financing, payment systems, and logistics stand in the way of developing economic relations.
He stated that Turkish businesses need to further diversify their products and sectors to increase trade between the two countries, particularly Turkish exports to Belarus.
He mentioned that Belarus boasts a strong production infrastructure in engines and engine components, electric buses and other public transport vehicles, machinery and equipment, iron and steel, chemicals and petrochemicals, and lumber and forest products.
“We aim to establish a balanced trade structure that gathers the production capabilities of the two countries in a complementary way,” he said.
“Turkish firms can supply Belarusian manufacturers of automobiles, heavy vehicles, and machinery, while we also see cooperation potential in the energy, machinery and spare parts, production equipment, construction, and building material sectors,” he added.
Isik stated that the council prioritizes options for joint production in Belarus and jointly entering third-country markets, taking cooperation beyond product sales.
The council discussed the more effective use of alternative rail routes alongside existing routes with Belarusian authorities to facilitate commercial activities.
“The options we’re evaluating include Turkish public banks opening Belarusian branches and developing financing and payment channels for products not subject to sanctions,” he said.
The two sides also talked about new production investments in the Mogilev Free Economic Zone, such as offers regarding special lease terms of around $1.50 per square meter, which would allow Turkish investors to engage in production under a long-term lease model.
“Talks are underway for price quotes, procurement, and commercial contacts, and we deem these meetings in Minsk and Mogilev as a part of a process to follow up on concrete investments, joint production, and trade projects, as we aim to boost Türkiye’s exports to Belarus and reach a bilateral trade volume of $3-4 billion, up from the $2 billion figure currently,” he added.

The Marché Couvert des Enfants Rouges in the Marais district has existed since 1615 and draws its name from the red outfits that orphans wore at a hospital near the market until 1772.
A fire has destroyed the French capital's oldest covered food market, a popular street food venue named after red-clad orphans, authorities said on Monday.
The Marché Couvert des Enfants Rouges in the Marais district has existed since 1615 and draws its name from the red outfits that orphans wore at a hospital near the market until 1772.
Food & Wine ranked it fifth worldwide for street food this year, after other eating spots in London, Bangkok, the French city of Lyon and Mexico City.
"The market was completely destroyed" overnight from Sunday to Monday, Lieutenant Colonel Pierre de Bouvier told reporters on site in the early hours of the morning.
"Nothing remains of the covered market," he said, adding that it's metal structure had "partially collapsed" inside.
The mayor of the central Paris district, Ariel Weil, said he was relieved the fire was under control and would not spread further.
"The worst has been avoided," he said. "No neighbouring buildings have been affected."

EU passes sanctions against Russia's illegal election in occupied Ukrainian territories

Unknown Publisher

EU passes sanctions against Russia's illegal election in occupied Ukrainian territories
LUXEMBOURG — EU foreign ministers unanimously approved 77 new sanctions listings on Oct. 12, targeting people who ran in and helped set up Russia's September sham election on illegally occupied Ukrainian territory, the Irish EU Presidency confirmed for the Kyiv Independent.
Russia held its State Duma elections from Sept. 18 to 20, while voting in occupied Ukrainian territories began in late August.
Of the 77 sanctioned individuals, 74 ran as candidates, while the remaining three were newly elected members of Russia's electoral commission. Most election organizers and 24 candidates were already subject to EU sanctions.
Ukraine already sanctioned over 40 people involved in those elections on Sept. 26, and the EU had previously passed election-related sanctions after Moscow banned the only remaining anti-war party, Yabloko (Apple), from competing.
The Russian State Duma elections were the first elections for Russia's lower house of parliament to be held in the occupied Ukrainian territories after Russia had issued Russian passports en masse to Ukrainians there, requiring them to renounce their Ukrainian citizenship.
However, the State Duma elections were not the first Russian-organized votes held in the occupied territories.
In September 2022, Russian occupation authorities held sham referendums in the occupied parts of Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia, and Kherson oblasts.
Russia organized so-called regional elections in the occupied territories in 2023 and held presidential elections there in 2024, in which Russian President Vladimir Putin was again declared the winner.
Also on Oct. 12, the EU passed almost 1,600 sanctions listings targeting Russia's military-industrial complex.

Hunger grips Gaza, with more than 1.4 million people acutely short of food as aid remains insufficient to meet basic needs.

More than a year after a “ceasefire” between Hamas and Israel was supposed to open the way for food into the devastated enclave, hunger still defines daily life for many Palestinians in the Gaza Strip.
Without the kitchen run by humanitarian groups, al-Masri says, her family will have “nothing at all”. Here’s what Trump’s latest U-turn really means for Russia and Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
08:46:26 UTC
17:46:26 KST

Here’s what Trump’s latest U-turn really means for Russia and Ukraine
The latest turn in Russia-US relations has shocked Kiev, outraged the EU, provoked discontent among a considerable number of politicians in the US, and left many observers around the world perplexed.
The Trump administration’s sudden decision to suspend sanctions on Russian diesel supplies appears to contradict its recent actions, including the adoption of tough new sanctions legislation intended to increase pressure on Moscow, and while some attribute the reversal to US President Donald Trump’s unpredictability, others see the beginnings of a new policy, or evidence of a fundamental change in the administration’s approach to Ukraine.
To understand what’s happening, however, we must look beyond the peculiarities of the US president’s public behavior. Trump’s extravagance, which frequently borders on the absurd, often conceals a relatively clear set of objectives, but whether those objectives are sensible is another question.
The most likely explanation for his latest reversal lies in domestic American politics, as the congressional midterm elections are less than a month away, and the Republican Party faces difficult prospects. Trump maintains an air of indifference, but losing control of both houses of Congress would condemn him to two years of political confrontation and considerable frustration.
He probably understands that there’s little prospect of fundamentally improving the economic situation, particularly consumer prices, before voters go to the polls, so for now, the emphasis is on psychological impact.
Russia isn’t the first country Washington has approached about increasing fuel supplies to international markets, and the more agreements Trump can announce, the more opportunities he has to proclaim that the White House is working tirelessly to protect ordinary Americans from rising prices.
The expectation, presumably, is that voters will forget how much of the present difficulty stems from Trump’s own actions in the Persian Gulf.
We shall soon discover whether this approach works, but there’s nothing particularly irrational about it, and Trump is pursuing a deliberate political objective. The fact that his latest decision contradicts previous statements doesn’t trouble him because he’s long operated on the assumption that words have value at the moment they’re spoken, but impose few obligations thereafter.
What does this mean for Russia, beyond the welcome prospect of additional budget revenues?
Colleagues from the Vatfor project have identified an important development, in that for the first time since the beginning of the conflict, the US president has made a significant decision regarding Russia without making Ukraine the determining consideration.
Until now, the Ukrainian question has been inseparable from virtually every aspect of Washington’s policy towards Moscow, but this time, not only has it been set aside, the decision directly contradicts Kiev’s interests at a particularly difficult moment.
Hence the indignation of the Ukrainian leadership, as from its perspective, the Americans have behaved unfairly.
There are probably several reasons for this change, but the principal one appears to be Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky’s unwillingness to accommodate Washington’s demands that Ukraine stop attacking Russian energy infrastructure.
The strikes have become one of Kiev’s principal instruments of warfare, and American requests to curtail them have largely gone unanswered.
Trump, meanwhile, has become fixated on Russian oil supplies as a means of addressing rising fuel prices, and their importance shouldn’t be exaggerated, even if additional Russian supplies alone are unlikely to transform the global market. Nevertheless, Trump has evidently decided that Zelensky bears responsibility for aggravating the situation.
Once the US president reaches this conclusion, persuading him otherwise becomes extremely difficult. Therefore, for the moment, Kiev’s objections have simply been disregarded.
The more consequential question concerns American intelligence assistance, because to stop, or at least substantially reduce, Ukrainian attacks on Russian targets, Washington would have to restrict the intelligence it provides to Kiev, and much of this information amounts, in practical terms, to targeting assistance.
Trump already demonstrated willingness to use this instrument when around a year and a half ago, he temporarily suspended intelligence cooperation for several days to put pressure on the Ukrainian leadership.
A longer interruption would be a different matter and it would represent a genuine change in Washington’s approach to the conflict, effectively distancing the US from its Ukrainian partner, but whether Trump is prepared to take this step is uncertain.
There is, after all, an extensive informal coalition interested in maintaining the present course, and it includes the US defense industry, increasingly influential technology companies, European governments, and their political allies in Washington.
Trump encountered these forces during his previous attempt to advance his preferred settlement following the Anchorage summit, and that initiative ultimately produced little, so it remains to be seen whether the present effort will fare any better.
If Washington proves unwilling to exert sustained pressure on Kiev, the latest initiative could gradually lose momentum, and this is especially likely after the congressional elections, when the immediate political value of announcing presidential achievements will diminish.
The decisive question, therefore, is whether the US leadership can compel its partners to move in the direction it considers necessary, and if it can, an opportunity for further negotiations on a settlement could emerge.
There’s also a second conclusion which is particularly important for Russia, because Washington’s latest actions offer a glimpse of how Russia-US relations could develop after the military phase of the conflict ends.
The enormous collection of sanctions imposed on Russia is unlikely to disappear, and removing them would be exceptionally difficult, both procedurally and politically, given too many restrictions have become embedded in law and institutional practice.
Instead, the sanctions will probably remain formally in place, while decisions about their enforcement are taken according to circumstances; thus, when a particular restriction conflicts with US interests, Washington could suspend its application, but when the circumstances change, it can be restored.
In other words, sanctions will become instruments to be activated or deactivated according to immediate political and economic requirements, rather than permanent expressions of an immutable policy, and this is an important distinction between the American and European approaches.
The Americans generally display a greater degree of pragmatism as they are perfectly capable of proclaiming principles with great conviction, abandoning them when circumstances demand it, and returning to the same principles when doing so becomes convenient. European governments, by contrast, have increasingly bound themselves to political commitments from which retreat is both institutionally complicated and publicly embarrassing.
For Moscow, understanding this difference will be essential when constructing its future relationship with Washington now that the confrontation over Ukraine has reached a stage at which its consequences extend far beyond the immediate military and territorial questions.
Whatever the eventual outcome, it will help determine the structure of future political relations between Russia and the various components of the Western world, and while that structure is already beginning to emerge, its geometry remains unsettled, and the lines are still moving.

Russia’s Apophis mission to help shed light on asteroid’s origin — Moscow University
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
08:45:18 UTC
17:45:18 KST

MOSCOW, October 12. /TASS/. Russia’s mission to the asteroid Apophis, which is being prepared by Moscow State University, could provide fundamentally new information about its origin and evolution, Vladislav Osedlo, deputy director for research at the university’s Skobeltsyn Institute of Nuclear Physics, told TASS.
The asteroid will pass 32,000 kilometers from Earth’s surface on April 13, 2029. The space object poses no threat, but its approach will create unique conditions for researchers to study it. In Russia, Lomonosov Moscow State University has initiated a mission to Apophis. In an earlier conversation with TASS, Moscow State University Rector Viktor Sadovnichy highlighted its importance for predicting larger-scale asteroid threats. Researchers at the Institute of Nuclear Physics are currently working on the technical parameters of a spacecraft and its flight to the asteroid.
"One [of the devices planned for installation on board] is a gamma spectrometer. Gamma rays emitted by a substance can help researchers remotely determine its elemental composition and obtain completely new information about the origin and evolution of the asteroid’s material," the researcher told TASS on the sidelines of the Science 0+ international festival held in Moscow over the weekend.
He noted that Apophis’ approach to Earth would constitute a unique physical experiment conducted by nature itself. Researchers are particularly looking forward to obtaining important data on the effects of Earth’s gravitational field on the asteroid and its surface.
Discovered in 2004, Apophis is about 350 meters in diameter. NASA’s OSIRIS-APEX and the European Space Agency’s RAMSES missions are scheduled to observe the asteroid.
Science 0+ festival
The Science 0+ festival is one of the key events of Russia’s Decade of Science and Technology, announced by President Vladimir Putin. The festival has been taking place in Russia and abroad since 2006 at the initiative of Moscow State University Rector Viktor Sadovnichy.
Over 10,000 events were held at 300 venues across Moscow on October 9-11. Before the end of the year, festival activities will also take place in Belarus, China, Serbia, India and some other countries as part of BRICS Science Week 0+. TASS is the general information partner of the Science 0+ festival.

Osteoporosis in Switzerland going undiagnosed and untreated

Osteoporosis in Switzerland going undiagnosed and untreated
According to the Swiss Rheumatism League, osteoporosis – a rheumatic bone disease – often goes undiagnosed and inadequately treated in Switzerland. According to the International Osteoporosis Foundation (IOF), around 684,000 women affected by the condition in this country do not receive any treatment.
The Rheumatism League notes, on the occasion of World Rheumatism Day on Monday, that the extent of the shortfall in care for men is not yet known. The Rheumatism League now aims to raise awareness of healthy bones through its first national osteoporosis campaign and to encourage people to address their bone health at an early stage using the new osteoporosis risk check.
According to the league, from the age of 50 onwards, one in two women and one in five men will suffer a bone fracture due to osteoporosis at some point in their lives. The condition often develops over many years without causing any symptoms.
More
Does tracking your health data make you healthier?
The Rheumatism League notes that even after a bone fracture, a targeted assessment is often not carried out. This gap in care leads to preventable fractures.
In Switzerland, there has so far been a lack of widespread public awareness. The campaign, with slogans such as “No world is cushioned enough for brittle bones” or “No world is soft enough for brittle bones”, focuses on everyday life rather than medical imagery. The call to assess bone health at an early stage is intended to encourage people to address their own bone health and potential risk factors sooner.

Penny Wong urges Palestinian Authority to hold elections 'without delay'
In short:
Penny Wong has urged the Palestinian Authority to hold elections after they were postponed.
The Opposition and pro-Israel groups have called on the government to hold Palestine "accountable" after statehood recognition.
What's next?
The Palestinian Authority says general elections will be held in September 2027.
Foreign Minister Penny Wong has labelled the Palestinian Authority's (PA) decision to postpone general elections as "deeply disappointing", as the Coalition accused Labor of "prematurely" recognising Palestinian statehood.
President Mahmoud Abbas on Saturday postponed what would have been the first Palestinian elections in 20 years, scheduled for November, until September 2027, citing changed conditions.
"We call on the Palestinian Authority to ensure elections take place without delay," Ms Wong said.
"Credible elections are an important element of the Palestinian Authority's commitment to the international community on reform, democratic renewal and accountable governance.
"Continuing to delay elections undermines the prospects of a two-state solution."
The Executive Committee of the Palestine Liberation Organization (PLO) cited ongoing Israeli attacks in the occupied West Bank, continued strikes on Gaza, and Israel's refusal to allow election materials or international observers to enter Gaza as key factors for the delay.
"These conditions prevent the establishment of an appropriate environment for elections and undermine guarantees for the safety of voters, candidates and electoral workers," the PLO said in a statement.
Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar on X accused the Palestinian Authority of "once again deceiving the international community".
"[Mr Abbas's] attempt to drag Israel into this, falsely claiming that Israel imposed obstacles to holding elections, is yet another ridiculous lie designed to evade responsibility and accountability," Mr Sa'ar wrote.
Israeli outlet, the Jerusalem Post, has separately reported Israel's elections, scheduled for October 27, could be postponed if Israel returned to war with Iran within the next three weeks.
Pro-Israel group demands PA accountability
Australia last year joined 156 other UN member states in recognising Palestinian statehood, with "clear requirements" set out by the international community.
At the time of the decision, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said Mr Abbas gave "direct undertakings to Australia" including commitments to hold democratic elections.
Australia/Israel & Jewish Affairs Council (AIJAC) executive director Colin Rubenstein has called on the government "to hold the PA accountable for breaking yet another key commitment underpinning Australia's recognition of a Palestinian state".
"Recognition of Palestinian statehood by Australia, however premature and counterproductive it was, should not remain a blank cheque.
"The Albanese government must explain what consequences will follow for the PA's repeated refusal to abide by the very commitments upon which recognition was based."
Coalition blasts 'premature' recognition
Shadow Foreign Minister Ted O'Brien on Monday joined AIJAC in calling on the prime minister to "explain" what actions the government would take if elections were not held next year.
"The promise of democratic elections gave Labor's premature recognition of Palestine a veneer of legitimacy, and now that veneer has been stripped away," Mr O'Brien said.
"The Australian government should be pressing for that decision to be reversed."
France's government has urged the Palestinian Authority to reverse its election delay, which the French foreign ministry said would "deprive the Palestinian people of their right to democratically express themselves" for the first time in two decades.
Ms Wong has not gone that far.
"We look forward to the Palestinian Authority making progress on the commitments it has made to Australia and the international community, so that next steps like diplomatic relations and the opening of embassies can proceed," she said.

France Launches Development of Its Own 6th-Generation Fighter and ‘Super Rafale’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
08:40:06 UTC
17:40:06 KST

After withdrawing from the joint Franco-German FCAS fighter program, France is launching its own project to develop a next-generation fighter and modernize its air force.
Chief of Staff of the French Air and Space Force Jérôme Bellanger made the statement, Les Echos reports.
France has definitively parted ways with Germany and is accelerating the development of its own aircraft, designated ACF (Avion de combat du futur).
The new fighter jet will replace the NGF (New Generation Fighter) concept and succeed the Rafale F4 aircraft.
Meanwhile, in December, France’s Ministry of the Armed Forces and Veterans Affairs is expected to officially launch the development phase of the ‘Super Rafale’ fighter F5 version.
This version will feature new engines, artificial intelligence, electro-optical systems, and a hypersonic missile for nuclear deterrence.
The development phase for the ACF prototype is scheduled to begin in 2027, with creation of the production variant set to start in 2029.
To integrate combat AI, the French Air and Space Force is launching the HypAIRion project, which converts two Mirage 2000 aircraft into flying laboratories.
The project’s main goal is to conduct the first joint flight of a Rafale fighter in tandem with a guided wingman drone in 2028.
France plans to expand its fighter jet fleet to at least 230 aircraft by 2035, up from the current 170.
The Air Force is also establishing two new squadrons at Cazaux Air Base, one specializing in reconnaissance and strike drones.
The second squadron will focus on high-altitude threats, including ballistic missiles and reconnaissance balloons.

France urges Palestinian authorities to reverse decision to delay legislative elections
France regrets Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas' decision to postpone legislative elections and a presidential poll, a foreign ministry spokesperson said on Sunday, urging him to reconsider.
Abbas on Saturday postponed legislative elections due next month until 11 September 2027, and called a presidential poll for the same date, blaming Israel and the security situation in the Palestinian territories for the delay.
"France is calling on the Palestinian authorities to reverse their decision and to organise parliamentary and presidential elections throughout Palestine as soon as possible," the French foreign ministry spokesperson said in a statement.
For months, there had been serious doubts that the Palestinian Authority vote would go ahead in late November.
The Palestinians have not held legislative or presidential elections since 2005-06, after which Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas' rival, Hamas, seized control of Gaza, ousting his loyalists.
The decree said Israeli military attacks, settlement expansion, settler violence and movement restrictions in the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, along with Israel's continued withholding of Palestinian tax revenues, created challenges to preparing for and holding elections on the previous date.
In Gaza, the decree pointed to "exceptional security and humanitarian conditions", the incomplete withdrawal of Israeli forces, the lack of progress in reconstruction and the failure to implement arrangements for deploying international stabilisation forces and police.
Israeli restrictions on access for election commission staff and international observers to Gaza and East Jerusalem also complicated preparations, the decree said.
The decision to postpone followed a resolution by the Palestine Liberation Organisation's executive committee and consultations with Palestinian factions and political forces. It also aimed to allow time for a comprehensive Palestinian national dialogue to strengthen unity and address challenges facing the electoral process.

Corruption watchdog abandons Bruce Lehrmann submarine secrets probe
In short:
The NACC has abandoned a probe into ex-political staffer Bruce Lehrmann, who was accused of taking classified material from his former boss's office.
The 31-year-old sued the special minister of state and the then-head of the NACC, who he accused of abusing their power.
Those proceedings are ongoing.
Bruce Lehrmann is no longer under investigation for allegedly using secrets about French submarines for his own ends.
The ex-political staffer got the reprieve on Monday after a letter from the National Anti-Corruption Commission (NACC) informed him it had abandoned the probe.
The notification ends part of a saga that began with officials raiding the 31-year-old's home in June 2024 over allegations he swiped secret documents from the office of former defence minister Linda Reynolds five years earlier.
The sweep, conducted under an operation dubbed "Ivanhoe", included seizing a blue moleskin diary, which the government claimed contained eight pages of classified security information.
"The former commissioner decided to take no further action concerning the investigation in Operation Ivanhoe," the corruption watchdog's letter reads.
Mr Lehrmann then sued Special Minister of State Don Farrell and then-NACC commissioner Paul Brereton, saying the raids were an abuse of the watchdog's power.
He also alleges he was unlawfully forced to give evidence at two secret hearings in October 2024 in Hobart, where he resides, and described the agency's investigation as driven by "frivolous, James Bond-like allegations".
His legal skirmishes with Mr Farrell and Mr Brereton are ongoing.
"The NACC has been a colossal waste of taxpayer money," Mr Lehrmann said in response to the watchdog's letter on Monday.
"Over two years the former commissioner used his powers to personally advance a conspiracy that I was a spy and traitor to the nation, selling defence secrets to foreign countries.
"The NACC needs to be abolished and replaced with nothing."
Mr Lehrmann was accused of foraging for the classified information on the French submarines days after he allegedly raped his colleague Brittany Higgins in then-senator Reynolds's parliament house office, in March 2019.
The rape allegations were found to be proven, on the balance of probabilities, by Federal Court Justice Michael Lee in 2024.
That finding was upheld twice by the Full Federal Court and the High Court.
Mr Lehrmann has denied the sexual assault claims, which remain untested in a criminal court.
The ex-Liberal staffer remains party to a second anti-corruption investigation, Operation Greenough, into whether federal police misused information during their probe into Ms Higgins's alleged sexual assault.

Trump faces growing criticism over plan to import diesel from Russia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
08:37:50 UTC
17:37:50 KST

Amid the ongoing conflict involving Iran—which is affecting international fuel prices—US President Donald Trump has faced mounting criticism regarding a plan to import diesel fuel from Russia, the BBC reports.
On the 9th of Otober, Trump announced that Russian dictator Vladimir Putin had agreed to immediately make 300,000 tons of diesel available to the US and international markets, with the possibility of further shipments to follow. This announcement came despite the fact that, just weeks earlier, the US had signed legislation imposing new sanctions and tariffs on countries importing Russian oil and natural gas. Trump's proposal has also drawn criticism from various Republican and Democratic politicians, who argue that such a deal violates US law.
The US President stated that Russia could supply an additional 500,000 tons of diesel in November, followed by another million tons of fuel. This could later be supplemented by a further three million tons of diesel—to be delivered over a short period—depending on the capacity of Russian oil refineries. In a post on Truth Social, Trump stated that his top priority is lower prices, particularly for America's great farmers, ranchers, and truck drivers.
Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak confirmed Trump's remarks to the state news agency TASS, stating that export volumes could reach three million tons per month in the near future.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has described the deal as a gift to Putin, equating it to an investment in a war that needs to end.
It is reported that the US Treasury will suspend sanctions on Russian diesel exports until the 7th of April, while other assets will remain frozen.
On the 11th of October, a group of seven senators (three Democrats and four Republicans) stated that the deal violates US law and urged Trump to abandon it. They argued that the US should not provide financial benefits to Putin while Russia continues to kill Ukrainian civilians. The senators added that Congress had explicitly banned the import of Russian energy resources in 2022 to prevent US money from funding Russian aggression in Ukraine. Trump’s Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Fox News that the deal would be carried out within the framework of the law to lower fuel prices, and that any member of Congress claiming otherwise was mistaken.
Fuel prices on the international market have risen significantly since the US and Israel began a war against Iran in late February, and Tehran responded by effectively closing the Strait of Hormuz, through which approximately 20% of the world's energy supplies are transported. 
With the midterm elections approaching, the rise in prices has become a key issue in the US. 
The midterm elections, scheduled for the 3rd of November, will determine whether Republicans retain control of the US Congress. Polls indicate that a large number of Americans are dissatisfied with Trump’s economic performance and do not support the war in Iran. Meanwhile, Trump is seeking ways to sway public opinion in favor of the Republicans.
The impact of the war with Iran is being felt particularly acutely in US agricultural states, where the machinery used relies primarily on diesel fuel. Analysts have questioned Russia's ability to supply diesel of adequate quality and whether the supplied quantities will actually help lower prices. Approximately 3.6 million barrels of diesel fuel are consumed daily in the US, and even if Russia delivers 300,000 tons of fuel in October, that would amount to only half of the daily consumption.
Trump's idea has also faced criticism in other countries. Several international leaders have condemned it, including Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and British Defence Secretary Wes Streeting.
Meanwhile, on the 11th of October, the US President announced that Russia and Ukraine had agreed on an energy truce. The Ukrainian President welcomed the move, whereas Moscow has not issued any public comments.

The Trump-Putin diesel deal has been badly received by EU foreign ministers, who say it undermines transatlantic unity at a time when Russia intensifies its attacks on Ukraine.
The European Union will continue to apply sanctions on Russia despite the diesel deal struck by United States President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin over the weekend, foreign ministers said on Monday.
The deal, as announced by Trump on social media, envisages that Moscow will release 300,000 tonnes of diesel to the US and global markets immediately, with an additional 500,000 tonnes in November and one million more after that.
To facilitate the arrangement, Washington issued a broad sanctions waiver for Russian diesel until April 2027, raising concerns in Ukraine and among its allies.
"The US is our biggest ally, but our message is clear: if we want to end this war, the only way we can do this is (by) putting more pressure on Russia," High Representative Kaja Kallas said on Monday morning as foreign ministers gathered in Luxembourg.
"Russia has started this war. We should not forget about this."
Kallas urged the White House to enforce the bill promoted by Senator Lindsey Graham that envisions far-reaching sanctions and tariffs on Moscow. But the law, approved in the wake of Graham's sudden death, leaves the decision to the president's discretion.
"If they would enact the Graham bill, we could really put the pressure so that Russia will finish this war," Kallas said.
Ireland's Foreign Minister Helen McEntee said the Trump-Putin diesel deal was "concerning" but insisted the bloc would continue its yearslong strategy.
The EU adopted on Monday its largest-ever addition to its sanctions list, targeting more than 1,600 people and entitiesaccused of propping up Russia's war. More than half of them are connected to ballistic missile production.
"What we need to do is refocus and redouble our efforts in keeping pressure on Russia," McEntee said upon arrival.
"Our priority has to be to maintain that pressure, but also to maintain our channels with the US, because this is not going to be achievable without the support of the US."
Her Swedish counterpart, Maria Malmer Stenergard, criticised the diesel deal and encouraged her European peers to tap into the immobilised Russian assets to ramp up their military and financial support for Ukraine.

"EU countries, regardless of what happens with the US, must stay calm and carry on and increase support by using the frozen assets and increase the pressure on Russia."
Her Lithuanian counterpart, Kęstutis Budrys, was also highly critical, saying the diesel deal "doesn't help, neither the prices of the oil products nor the unity within the transatlantic community".
"It is not the European way," Budrys told reporters.

Estonia's Margus Tsahkna linked the agreement to the "domestic situation" in the US ahead of next month's midterm elections, where Trump's Republicans trail the Democrats, and predicted its material impact would be limited.
Trump has struggled to contain the backlash against his war on Iran, which is widely seen as the main reason behind the pronounced rise in fuel prices.
Tsahkna also said the energy ceasefire suddenly announced by Trump on Sunday was "not working", pointing to Russia's relentless airstrikes on Ukraine.
The truce is reportedly designed to cover oil refineries as a first step, which would make it heavily lopsided. Ukraine has just one plant while Russia has 32 major ones.
Kyiv has systematically hit Moscow's oil industry to cripple its war chest and gain leverage. But the strikes have angered Trump, leading to his deal with Putin.
"Energy is extremely important because the winter is going to be cold," Kallas said.
"It is important that it does not only apply to the refineries, where Ukraine has one, and Russia has plenty. It is definitely (to) the benefit of the Russians."

Lithuania to use Norwegian aid for prison upgrades
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
08:37:00 UTC
17:37:00 KST

Lithuania plans to invest most of €36 million in Norwegian funding over five years to modernise prison infrastructure in Vilnius and Kaunas, while the remaining money will go toward improving prison operations and probation services, the Justice Ministry said.
An agreement on the Justice program is expected to be signed in December, with implementation scheduled to begin in early 2027 and continue through 2030-31.
The ministry said €25.4 million would be allocated to prison infrastructure. The funding will be used to equip 160 cell-type detention places at Vilnius prison and 50 at Kaunas prison, as well as upgrade 41 prison security and supervision posts.
Another €8.2 million will go toward improving prison operations, including training staff in a holistic security model and modern working methods at prisons in Panevėžys, Marijampolė and Kaunas.
The plans also include introducing advanced electronic monitoring to track the movement of convicts and psychoactive substances, and upgrading the penal system’s information system.
Probation services will receive €2.4 million to develop a pilot reintegration centre based on a “one-stop shop” model, introduce digital alerts to warn crime victims when people who harmed them are nearby, and provide electronic monitoring equipment capable of detecting psychoactive substances. The funding will also support staff training.
The program envisages new resocialisation programs for vulnerable groups of convicts and greater involvement by nongovernmental organisations.
Deputy Justice Minister Martynas Dobrovolskis said particular attention would be paid to staff skills, resocialisation, probation effectiveness and modern technology.
“Our goal is to create a safer, more modern system that promotes human integration into society,” he said in a ministry statement.
Lithuania will implement the program in cooperation with the Norwegian Correctional Service Directorate. The two countries have worked together for years to modernise the penal system, strengthen rehabilitation and reduce reoffending.
Justice Minister Rita Tamašunienė discussed progress in these areas with her Norwegian counterpart, Astri Aas-Hansen, last week.
Last December, then-Finance Minister Kristupas Vaitiekūnas signed memorandums covering €118 million in funding allocated to Lithuania by Norway, Iceland and Liechtenstein. At the time, €54 million was earmarked for civil protection programs and €55.7 million for justice programs.
The three donor countries use the funding to reduce economic and social disparities and strengthen bilateral relations with 15 EU countries in Central and Southeastern Europe and the Baltic states.

Ukrainian Refinery Strikes Pause After Trump Ceasefire Announcement
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
08:36:44 UTC
17:36:44 KST

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky accused Russia on Monday of violating an “energy ceasefire” announced by U.S. President Donald Trump, urging Washington to ensure Moscow abides by the agreement as the Kremlin said contacts over a possible truce were ongoing.
Russia attacked gas production facilities belonging to Ukraine’s state oil and gas company Naftogaz in the Kharkiv region overnight, causing a fire and damaging critical equipment, the company said Monday.
Ukrainian drone attacks, meanwhile, appeared to spare Russian oil refineries overnight after Trump made the surprise announcement that the ceasefire had taken immediate effect.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters Monday that contacts over a possible energy ceasefire were continuing. He declined to say whether it would apply only to oil refineries, saying further information would be released in due course.
“There were Russian violations of the energy ceasefire announced by President Trump,” Zelensky told a security conference in Warsaw via video link.
Zelensky said he had learned about the agreement through the media and was awaiting details of the terms discussed by Washington and Moscow.
“This energy ceasefire, it can work, and it can become a major step toward ending the war if the Americans truly step in now and make sure Russians respect it,” he said.
The Kremlin has not formally confirmed that it agreed to a ceasefire. Sources close to the Russian government told Bloomberg that Moscow remained skeptical that Washington could deliver a binding agreement on terms favorable to Russia.
Naftogaz acting CEO Sergii Fedorenko said employees were working to repair the damage from the overnight attack.
“Our employees are doing everything possible to repair the damage as quickly as possible and prevent risks to the stable operation of the energy system,” he said on Telegram.
Zelensky also said in his nightly video address Sunday that Russian forces had struck a combined heat and power plant in Kharkiv, Ukraine’s second-largest city, that evening. A Ukrainian official said the attack took place after Trump’s ceasefire announcement.
“The Armed Forces of Ukraine have received all the appropriate orders,” Zelensky said in the address.
Russia’s Defense Ministry said air defenses intercepted 151 Ukrainian drones over 10 Russian regions and annexed Crimea overnight. Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said 37 drones were destroyed as they approached the capital between Sunday evening and Monday morning.
Local authorities and independent media reported no new strikes on Russian oil refineries, which Ukraine has repeatedly targeted in recent months.
Russian attacks on other targets continued Monday. The Defense Ministry said its forces struck a cargo vessel carrying military supplies near the Ukrainian port of Odesa. Local officials said Russian shelling and air attacks injured at least 12 people in Kharkiv that morning.
In Russia’s southern Rostov region, firefighters continued battling a blaze at the Novoshakhtinsk oil refinery following a drone attack Saturday, the exiled news outlet Astra reported.
Authorities in the southwestern Belgorod region said one civilian was killed and three others were injured Sunday evening.
Separately, Peskov rejected Zelensky’s proposal for a 60-day ceasefire to allow Ukraine to hold presidential elections, saying Moscow wanted an overall peace deal instead.
“Please tell Putin, give us two months, 60 days of total ceasefire, 60 days, and we will organize elections,” Zelensky told ABC’s “This Week” on Sunday.
Peskov said Putin and other Russian officials had repeatedly stated that they did not want a temporary ceasefire and were prepared to work toward long-term peace.
Russia has long pressed Ukraine to hold elections and says that its failure to do so makes Zelensky an illegitimate leader. Elections in wartime are prohibited by Ukrainian law.
Reuters contributed reporting.

President Herzog speaking to a delegation of French Jewish leaders: 'Blaming Jews has become, once again, the default mode in Europe'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
08:35:30 UTC
17:35:30 KST

'Blaming Jews has become the default mode,' President Herzog addresses a delegation of French Jewish leaders
Herzog said boycotts and sanctions harm the Palestinians first and absolve Hamas leadership of responsibility
"What we are seeing in Europe today is that blaming the Jews has become, once again, the default mode, the easiest solution, a cathartic and satisfying disguise for the anger and disappointment over Europe’s own failings and fears." This is what Israeli President Isaac Herzog said to a visiting delegation of the Consistoire, the central religious institution of French Jewry.
The delegation of community leaders and public officials from across France was led by Consistoire President Élie Korchia and included the Chief Rabbi of France Haïm Korsia.
Herzog began by acknowledging how the community was feeling. "I know that it has not been an easy time to be a Jew in the world. It certainly has not been an easy time to be a Jew in France," he said. He then described what that has meant for Jewish communities, alluding to the antisemitism in Europe during the 20th century which led to the Holocaust.
"In a Europe that not so long ago turned on its Jews and on itself, today Israel is demonized, while its Jewish communities contract in fear, forced, once again, into a defensive posture between two identities, and denied, once again, simple, safe belonging."
Herzog drew a line between criticism and what he sees now. "Disagreeing with Israel on its strategy or on its political venue is legitimate debate," Herzog said. "But that is not what's going on in Europe and in France. What we are seeing in Europe today is pure scapegoating."
The President called the blanket rejection of Israel and attempts to isolate it "a grave error."
Suggested articles
On boycotts and sanctions, Herzog was blunt. "Calling for boycotts and sanctions is not simply morally wrong. It reflects a deep alienation from Europe's own intellectual inheritance while speaking to the darkest shadows of its past." He said, adding, "Boycotts and sanctions harm, first and foremost, the Palestinians, robbing them of jobs and income. At the same time, they absolve corrupt Hamas leadership of any responsibility for their rabid antisemitism or for their crimes against their own people."
Herzog closed on a hopeful note about the two countries. "I would like to see Israeli and French entrepreneurs and scientists, artists and teachers, investors, and companies doing far more together," he said. "I believe in this with my whole heart."

Short on interceptors, Ukraine goes after the launchers: eight Russian ballistic systems hit, three destroyed since September, a minister says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
08:35:00 UTC
17:35:00 KST

Ukraine has been striking the launchers Russia uses to fire ballistic missiles at its cities, Ukrainian Defense Minister Yevhenii Khmara told journalists. He said the strikes have already disrupted some Russian attack plans, but supplies of anti-ballistic interceptors still fall short of the threat.
Russia strikes Ukraine’s cities and power grid with drones and missiles every day as it prepares to leave civilians without power and heat this winter. Ballistic missiles are the part of that barrage Ukraine still struggles to stop, so every launcher put out of action before it fires means fewer missiles to intercept.
Iskander and S-400 launchers hit since September
Ukrainian forces hit eight launchers used for ballistic strikes on Ukraine in September and early October, destroying three and damaging five, Khmara said. They belonged to Russia’s Iskander tactical missile systems and S-400 air defense systems, he added. Such strikes have already forced Russia to cancel or change planned ballistic attacks, the minister said.
The S-400 was designed to shoot down aircraft and missiles, but Russia also uses it to fire ballistic missiles at Ukrainian cities, including Kyiv. In mid-September, Ukraine reported hitting two S-400 launchers near Vygonichi in Russia’s Bryansk Oblast. Russia had used the same systems against Kyiv the night before.
Can’t intercept the missiles? Hit the factories—Ukraine’s other way to stop Russia’s ballistic missiles
On 23 August, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Ukrainian forces had hit an Iskander launcher near the border. He described it as part of a separate operation to hunt nearby launch positions and linked the tactic to low stocks of anti-ballistic missiles.
Strikes on launchers while interceptors stay scarce
Khmara called the launcher strikes Ukraine’s asymmetric response to a ballistic threat that remains critical.
“Existing and potential supplies of missiles for anti-ballistic defense are not enough to fully cover this threat,” he said.
Instead of waiting for large long-term contracts, the Defense Ministry is looking for missiles in partners’ available stocks to speed up transfers, Khmara added. “We need dozens and hundreds of missiles, not one-off deliveries,” he stressed.
Meanwhile, Russia significantly cut its 2026 state orders for Kinzhal air-launched ballistic missiles, Ukraine’s military intelligence said on 12 October. It redirected the production capacity, components, and raw materials to Iskander-M ballistic missiles, the agency added.
Russia’s missile and drone attacks continue
Overnight on 12 October, Russia attacked Ukraine with a Kh-59 guided missile and 121 attack drones, 76 of them jet-powered, Ukraine’s Air Force reported. Air defenses downed or suppressed 89 drones, but strikes hit 15 locations, and the attack was still going on in the morning.
Russia’s new ballistic missile could reach western Ukraine—and it may be tested there within months
In the week to 11 October, Russia hit Ukraine’s power generation and transmission facilities more than 200 times and its gas and oil sites 17 times, Zelenskyy said. Russian attacks that week killed more than 150 people and injured more than 700, he added.
Jet-powered drones are still the main problem for Ukraine’s air defense. It stops more than 90% of slower propeller-driven Shaheds, compared with about 55% for the jet ones.
Ballistic missiles have struck Kyiv repeatedly this autumn. On 24 September, Russian ballistic and hypersonic missiles damaged a maternity hospital in the capital. On 7 October, a Russian missile barrage killed 22 people in Pryluky, Chernihiv Oblast.

The website and app of supermarket chain Albert Heijn in Belgium and the Netherlands are unavailable due to what is described as an “IT incident”, the company reports. Its logistics systems are also down, meaning the chain can no longer deliver groceries ordered online. Rival Delhaize is also affected.
Supermarket chains Albert Heijn and Delhaize hit by IT woes
The problem began on Sunday afternoon. “We took immediate measures to protect our IT environment. Part of this involves the preventative temporary shutdown of a number of systems,” said Albert Heijn.
Customer service and logistics systems have also been temporarily shut down, meaning that groceries ordered online cannot be delivered.
The shops remain open, but last week’s promotional prices are still visible on the electronic labels in the racks. “These are the prices for last week’s promotions, a lower price may therefore be shown on labels in the racks and a higher price at the check-out.”
It is not clear whether any customer data has been leaked. “We are investigating the incident and working to restore our services. Protecting the data of our customers, staff and partners is our top priority,” the company said in a statement.
Impact on Delhaize
Delhaize has also taken immediate steps to protect its IT systems. “All our shops in Belgium and Luxembourg remain open and customers can continue to do their shopping as normal,” Delhaize assures us. The company is doing everything it can to get the systems up and running again as quickly as possible.
For the time being, customers cannot place orders for this week. Due to the IT incident, customer services are temporarily unavailable, although the app and website remain accessible.
“Protecting the data of our customers, staff and partners is our absolute priority. We are currently unable to say when all our systems will be available again,” the company states.

Mohammed Sameai and Lina Altawell
12 October 2026•Update: 12 October 2026
The Yemeni army said Monday it carried out a series of airstrikes on Houthi positions in the southwestern province of Taiz as military escalation continues to rage across the country.
The army’s Taiz Military Axis said in a statement that warplanes bombed Houthi positions in the Al-Arsouma, Al-Maraziqan and 60th Street areas north of Taiz.
Other strikes targeted Jabal al-Mun'im and Tabbat al-Khalwa west of the city, as well as a Houthi military camp in eastern Taiz, it added.
The statement did not provide details on the results of the strikes, and there was no immediate comment from the Houthis.
The attacks came on the eighth day of Operation “Dawn of Yemen”, which Presidential Leadership Council Chairman Rashad al-Alimi said is aimed at restoring state institutions and retaking the capital Sanaa from the Houthis.
The developments are part of a military escalation that began in July, the broadest since a period of relative calm following a truce that began in April 2022.
Yemen has been at war since the Houthis seized Sanaa and several provinces in September 2014, before a Saudi-led coalition intervened in March 2015 in support of the country’s internationally recognized government.

It is important that the "energy truce" apply not only to oil refineries, of which Ukraine has one while Russia has many. This is undoubtedly beneficial to the Russians. ====================================================================================================

EU votes through largest ever Russia sanctions list
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
08:32:03 UTC
17:32:03 KST

LUXEMBOURG — EU foreign ministers voted through almost 1,600 new restrictions targeting Russia's military-industrial complex on Oct. 12, the largest single addition to the sanctions lists ever.
The new listings target industry players ranging from shipyards and aviation companies to electronics manufacturers, armored vehicle repair facilities, and aerospace companies, and were first reported on by the Kyiv Independent on Sept. 21.
"This is the single largest expansion of our sanctions list since Russia started its war," chief EU diplomat Kaja Kallas said, adding that more than half of the listings "are connected to the production chain for ballistic missiles."
"We are making it significantly harder, slower, and more expensive for Russia to produce the weapons it uses to kill Ukrainians."
The new additions take the total number of Russia sanctions passed by the EU from around 3,000 to over 4,500.
The new listings appear to have been compiled using a rather general criterion, namely, their entitlement to subsidies from the Russian government and their designation by the Russian state as part of the military-industrial complex.
EU sanctions entail freezing assets owned by these entities but held within the bloc and banning transactions with sanctioned entities.
It is unclear whether any of these entities did business with EU countries or held assets in the EU.
However, a senior EU official told the Kyiv Independent that the impact of the sanctions on the newly targeted entities' ability to do business with third countries should not be underestimated.
Southeast Asian countries, in particular, the official said, are unwilling to risk hurting relations with the EU by doing business with companies sanctioned by the bloc.
Ultimately, the aim of the sanctions is to hamper and make more expensive the running of Russia's war machine. Anything that complicates its ability to source western components, the EU official explained, is surely a good thing.

Feature: China-Central Asia archaeological cooperation extends exchanges along Silk Road
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
16:31:37 CST
17:31:37 KST

TASHKENT/BISHKEK, Oct. 12 (Xinhua) -- Archaeological finds are being sorted and examined at a laboratory in Bukhara Region, Uzbekistan, and Wang Shujing is working there for the joint study of an ancient burial site along the Silk Road.
The slope of the burial passage, the arrangement of human remains -- thanks to 3D modelling technology -- the original layout of the Gamkhurd I burial site gradually takes shape on the computer screen.
Wang, from the School of Archaeology and Museology of Peking University, is the leader on the Chinese side of a Sino-Uzbek archaeological expedition, which started in August 2025 with the Samarkand Archaeological Institute.
The team's work includes field excavations of the Gamkhurd I burial ground, where the Bukhara oasis and the desert steppe join in Navoi Region.
Based on burial structures and the characteristics of those unearthed, the joint archaeological team tentatively dated the burial ground to between the 2nd century BC and the 2nd century AD -- a period coinciding with major migrations across the Eurasian steppes and intensified interactions among civilizations along the ancient trade route of the Silk Road.
The team incorporates Chinese specialists in natural sciences and modern material analysis techniques, enabling in-depth research work. Djamal Mirzaakhmedov, who heads the Uzbek side, noted that the collaborative study also makes a significant contribution to the study of the history of Uzbek nomadic and agrarian tribes and peoples.
While filling gaps in the study of regional ancient history, the cooperation, evidently, also carries on the legacy of mutual learning among civilizations along the Silk Road.
Similar cooperation is also seen in Kyrgyzstan, in another aspect of archaeology.
At the Ak-Beshim archaeological site in Chui Oblast, known to Chinese people as the ancient city of Suyab, Bai Yushu, a cultural heritage conservation expert from the Dunhuang Academy in Northwest China, is scrutinizing the ruins alongside fellow researchers to identify signs of structural deterioration.
"Currently, this archaeological site is suffering the erosion of wall foundations, flaking, structural cracking, and the formation of erosion gullies," Bai said, noting that without timely, effective interventions, the damage could become irreversible.
Trying to help, Chinese specialists constructed an experimental wall in an open space nearby with similar environmental conditions and soil properties. They replicated ancient construction techniques, and monitored the changes inside and outside the wall to document the progression of structural deterioration.
The specialists are also conducting reinforcement trials on the wall to assess various conservation techniques. Proven methods are expected to be applied more widely at the Ak-Beshim site in efforts to keep its original appearance as faithfully as possible.
Aisin Duishanalieva, an official for the protection of historical and cultural monuments under the Kyrgyz culture ministry, highlighted the modern scientific methods employed by the Chinese specialists, and expressed hope that the cooperation on conservation work will continue.
The staff from the Dunhuang Academy have the experience of doing conservation work on the ruins of the Beiting Ancient City in Northwest China's Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region, which, like Ak-Beshim, is located on the northern side of the Tianshan Mountains and is severely affected by the regional microclimate.
Like in Ak-Beshim, their conservation methods and techniques may also be used elsewhere in Central Asian countries.
The archaeological cooperation between China and Central Asian countries is not only of academic significance, but the joint finds also help revisit the history of development and prosperity along the Silk Road, with traces seen of exchanges, mutual learning among civilizations, as well as their enrichment and advancement. ■

Global vine, wine congress kicks off in northwest China's Ningxia
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
16:31:20 CST
17:31:20 KST

This photo taken on Oct. 12, 2026 shows an exterior view of the venue of the opening ceremony of the 47th World Congress of Vine and Wine in Yinchuan, northwest China's Ningxia Hui Autonomous Region. (Xinhua/Wang Peng)
YINCHUAN, Oct. 12 (Xinhua) -- The 47th World Congress of Vine and Wine opened on Monday in Yinchuan, capital of northwest China's Ningxia Hui Autonomous Region, China's top wine-producing area.
This is the first time the congress, held alongside the 24th General Assembly of the International Organization of Vine and Wine (OIV), has been hosted in Asia since its launch in 1924.
The event has drawn more than 800 participants, including delegates from 51 OIV member states, diplomatic envoys to China from 25 countries, representatives from 47 countries and international organizations, leading experts and scholars in the wine sector from at home and abroad, as well as heads of domestic business associations and leading enterprises.
Themed around building a new landscape for the global vine and wine industry, the congress features an opening ceremony, a seminar on high-quality development of the Chinese vine and wine industry, a sci-tech sub-session, industry visits and a closing ceremony.
Over 400 academic papers from 35 countries will be showcased at the sci-tech sub-session, introducing cutting-edge global wine technologies and helping drive the transformation and upgrading of China's vine and wine industry.
The 6th China (Ningxia) International Wine Culture and Tourism Expo opened alongside the congress, attracting 84 world-renowned wineries and enterprises from distinctive production areas in 16 countries. It has also drawn a total of 146 leading domestic wineries from Ningxia and other core production areas in China.
The eastern foot of Helan Mountain in Ningxia has become China's largest contiguous wine grape production area. This region has 607,000 mu, or about 40,467 hectares, dedicated to wine grape cultivation and development, accounting for nearly 42 percent of China's total.
Ningxia, home to 261 wine enterprises, including 130 wineries, produces 140 million bottles of wine annually.
The local wine industry has also become a driver of tourism. Wineries in Ningxia receive more than 3.7 million tourist visits each year, generating combined benefits of over 50 billion yuan (around 7.4 billion U.S. dollars). ■

India condemns tanker attacks as two sailors go missing
Two Indian sailors are missing after a tanker was attacked off Oman on Sunday. A second tanker was also struck on the same day in the Strait of Hormuz, but the Indian crew on board were unharmed.
New Delhi condemned the strikes on the two commercial vessels. 
The Nicaragua-flagged MT Petro Dolphin was reportedly struck by a drone at Sohar Anchorage on October 11. Nine of the 11 Indian crew members were rescued and are safe, while Oman’s Coast Guard is searching for the other two, Indian Shipping Minister Sarbananda Sonowal said. 
Another tanker, the Marshall Islands-flagged MT Valthera, was hit by an unidentified projectile while passing through the Strait of Hormuz the same day, causing a fire on board. All Indian seafarers aboard the vessel were reported safe. 
India’s embassy in Muscat is coordinating with the Omani authorities and the respective ship management companies to locate the missing sailors and assist the crews, the Indian Foreign Ministry said. “The recurring attacks on commercial shipping in the region are deeply concerning,” the ministry said, warning that they risk further aggravating tensions.
Statement on the attacks on commercial vessels in the Strait of Hormuz region ⬇️ 🔗 https://t.co/SqBo213LvT https://t.co/t4zJMeZSdZ
— Randhir Jaiswal (@MEAIndia) October 11, 2026
New Delhi called for immediate de-escalation through dialogue and diplomacy, stressing that attacks on commercial vessels, seafarers, and civilian infrastructure must stop.
Indian crews have been caught in several recent attacks. On October 9, the Panama-flagged tanker MT Gem No. 2 was struck at Sharjah Anchorage in the United Arab Emirates, but all 22 Indian sailors aboard were reported safe.
Three days earlier, 11 Indian seafarers were among 12 crew members injured when the Panama-flagged tanker MT On Peace was hit by an unidentified projectile off Oman.
Tanker-related security incidents in the Strait of Hormuz have reached their highest weekly level since the Middle East conflict began in February. At least 12 incidents, including attacks, attempted attacks, and harassment, were recorded between September 28 and October 5, Reuters reported, citing maritime security sources.
The risks to Indian nationals have extended beyond commercial shipping. An Indian national died following Saturday’s missile strike on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, while at least ten other Indians were injured.
The airport was struck again on Sunday, killing a Pakistani national, according to Saudi authorities. Yemen’s Houthi movement claimed responsibility for the attacks.

Ushar Danielein Kuala Lumpur
With his reformist credentials battered by coalition compromises and a looming general election, Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim has used his 2027 budget to launch a fresh wave of anti-corruption measures.
But as his government nears its four-year mark, analysts warn that restoring public confidence will require more than additional funding and tighter legislative oversight.
The measures, announced when Anwar presented Malaysia’s 2027 budget on Friday, include 1.1 billion ringgit (US$269 million) to strengthen enforcement agencies, a proposed bill to tighten oversight of government-owned entities and greater transparency in public procurement.
Yet concerns persist over the independence of the Malaysian Anti-Corruption Commission (MACC), while promised reforms – including separating the roles of the attorney general and public prosecutor – remain incomplete.

Lithuania calls on EU to designate Russia's foreign intelligence agency a terrorist organization

Unknown Publisher

Lithuania calls on EU to designate Russia's foreign intelligence agency a terrorist organization
Russia will not stop its hybrid attacks against Europe until the EU shows it is serious, and calls Moscow's foreign military intelligence agency a terrorist organization, Lithuania's Foreign Minister Kestutis Budrys told journalists ahead of an Oct. 12 meeting of EU foreign ministers.
"We have to review GRU, Russia's military intelligence (agency), which in their operations is already acting as a terrorist organization," Budrys said.
"That is why it is for the EU to designate this organization as a terrorist organization and everyone who is related to them," he added.
GRU has been linked to a series of hybrid attacks across Europe: including a recent arson attack in Munich and the Leipzig airport drone attack in August.
And Budrys is particularly familiar with GRU's work, having worked most of his career for Lithuania's State Security Department — the country's civilian intelligence and security agency which assesses and eliminates threats to national security.
"Only when we increase our sanctions, when we show that we are serious, will we deny Russia the possibility to raise havoc in our capitals," Budrys said.
For Budrys, the EU did the opposite in September, when it bowed to pressure from France, Slovakia, and Luxembourg, and delisted two oligarchs.
"When we projected our weakness by delisting two prominent oligarchs from our sanctions, we saw how Russia reacted to it. They escalated, escalated both in Ukraine and now they're escalating in Europe, in our countries," Budrys said.
The EU maintains a terrorist list that includes both individuals and entities and functions similarly to the EU's Russia sanctions.
However, no Russian entity has yet been filed on the EU terrorist list, which only contains Islamists such as Hamas, Islamic State, and the perpetrators of the 9/11 attack against the U.S.

Burnham says 'public will be the boss' in any future decisions about closer relationship with EU
Burnham confirmed that he wanted to open a discussion about the UK’s future relationship with the EU.
If we are serious, if we are serious about promoting growth, controlling immigration, upholding our values and security, it is a conversation we must have.
The status quo is not good enough for Britain.
Worse, it would be a major dereliction of duty to turn away.
We need to take a calm, clear-eyed, rational look at the world as it is today to consider what is best for our country.
Our immediate priority is securing a successful outcome at the summit, and I believe we should then set up a serious dialogue about the different options for our relationship in the long term.
At every stage, the British public will be the boss, and I am clear that public opinion currently supports a pragmatic approach like the one I am suggesting.
Burnham fails to rule out eventually accepting EU freedom of movement after being challenged by Labour and Tory MPs
The Labour MP Jonathan Hinder, who represents Pendle and Clitheroe, asked Burnham to confirm that, as long as he remains PM, “there will be no return to freedom of movement”.
