What we have to look at are the options that are available for the long-term relationship. This country in the next decade needs to know where it’s going.

As I’ve said many times this afternoon, we will honour the manifesto in full, and the red lines are in place.

The honourable gentleman is getting way ahead of himself. There is no proposal for a referendum. There’s no deal on the table. This is just not true. As soon as I became foreign secretary I asked the security services the same question and they replied that there was no evidence of any successful interference in the 2016 referendum, by Russia or any other power.

I’m sure I heard her say at her conference that increasing growth would be the operating principle of any government that she leads.
So how can she justify turning her back on a deal that is potentially on the table now to add billions to the UK economy? How can they justify turning their back on farmers and the food industry?
And referring to her attack on his negotiating tactics, Burnham added sarcastically: “Because the Tories were so good, weren’t they, at negotiating deals with our with our partners?”

Europe: Assemble, Decide, Engage!
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
08:28:19 UTC
17:28:19 KST

Caught between two wars, Europe cannot afford to drift and keep saying it isn’t in either of them. And the alarm bells are ringing louder than ever as of October 2026:
- Both Russia and Iran are escalating their military pressure and posture because they see a divided West without a clear strategy or end-state – only attempts at containment.
- Donald Trump has lifted sanctions on Russian diesel sales, throwing Putin a lifeline at Ukraine’s expense, while threatening to withhold US military intelligence if Ukraine does not stop striking Russian oil infrastructure.
Let’s set aside the fact that Trump’s diesel move is unlikely to achieve his primary goal of lowering US fuel prices, but experts expect the impact to be minimal. So, let’s focus on what Europe can do.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Short-term fuel politics
European governments opposed Trump’s war on Iran from the outset. In retrospect, however, leaving the US to act alone was not in Europe’s interests. Trump may not have consulted European governments before launching the campaign, but that should not have prevented Europe from seeking a role in shaping the conflict’s course and consequences.
The transactional nature of Trump’s foreign policy
Many find this approach appalling as it appears to lack the ideas and values that should underpin a political program. Yet, the reality of international politics is that it is transactional.
Even when states share certain values, their interactions follow a basic equation: we want you to do this, and in exchange, we offer you that. The incentives may take the form of carrots, but they can just as easily be replaced by sticks when cooperation gives way to coercion.
When Donald Trump adopted this scaffolding as the principle of his foreign policy, Europeans rejected this approach as unprincipled and beneath the standards they set for themselves.
‘A Financial Lifeline’ for Putin: US Senators Say Trump’s Diesel Deal Violates Law
But as Europe is not a hegemon capable of imposing its own rules on the world, shouldn’t it be pragmatic and play the cards it is dealt, using whatever leverage it has to advance its interests?
Europe’s response to the war in Iran was to reject military intervention. Europe announced it was not going to participate and even condemned the US for doing so.
The restraint was seen by Iran, Russia, and Trump
This was yet another sign of European weakness. Why? Because it reflects the same reluctance we have seen in Europe’s response to Russia.
We are not at war with Russia, goes the argument. Never mind that Russia is waging a hybrid war against Europe and a full-scale, brutally kinetic war against Ukraine. Europe, meanwhile, continues to shelter behind the principle that NATO is only a defensive alliance and Europe has not been attacked.
In the case of Iran, the logic is much the same: keep our heads down and hope diplomacy will do the job. But at what cost?
Decades of European diplomatic engagement have failed to stop the Iranian regime from pursuing uranium enrichment to levels necessary for nuclear weapons, supporting armed terrorist groups such as Hamas, and contributing to a regional network of militant organizations that threaten Israel.
Psychology has long recognized that perceived weakness can embolden bullies. And those who stay on the sidelines should not be surprised when they find themselves with no voice and no influence.
Europe has every reason to value diplomacy. But when diplomacy fails to change a regime’s behavior, simply carrying on as before is not a strategy. It is a refusal to confront reality. And it is only attempts at containment.
And when containment has no defined objective, it becomes mere postponement and postponement has a price: giving adversaries time to test limits, adapt, and push further.
The West spent years trying to persuade its adversaries to play by its rules. It failed – never developing a strategy for confronting enemies who had no intention of playing by it.
Strategic failure staring the West in the face
Europe is not as weak as its inactions would suggest. But what could it do? Send troops to Ukraine? To the Strait of Hormuz?
Well it should be prepared to do both and clearly communicate it to Tehran and Moscow. Why? Because both regimes are authoritarian threats to the West.
- Were diplomatic cables to Tehran saying that Europe was ready to support the US in its war, or merely assuring Iran that Europe would not engage in Washington’s war, in other words, that it was hiding behind the US?
- Have diplomatic phone calls to Vladimir Putin ever indicated that Europe is ready to close the sky over Ukraine, or only telegraphing that this war is senseless?
And that is the brutal essence of Europe’s weakness: it does not have a coherent strategy with a clearly defined end goal and a credible deterrent to help achieve it.
To have such a strategy, Europeans must first find courage, assemble, and answer these questions: What kind of Russia does Europe want to live with? What kind of Iran?
Ukraine: Defeat Russia or prevent victory drift?
The West armed Ukraine enough to survive Russia’s invasion, but not enough to change Moscow’s strategic calculations, fearing nuclear escalation and regime collapse. Yet this taught Russia that nuclear threats could prevent its defeat.
The fundamental choice remains: seek accommodation with Moscow or make territorial expansion strategically unviable. Russia’s growing aggression suggests the West cannot pursue both.
Iran: Diplomacy without an end-state
Decades of sanctions, inspections, and diplomacy failed to resolve concerns over Iran’s nuclear program and regional proxies. After Trump withdrew from the 2015 nuclear deal in 2018, European efforts to preserve it ultimately failed, postponing the problem rather than resolving it.
The 2026 war exposed the consequences. Without a coherent strategy, Western divisions widened, giving Iran opportunities to exploit them and escalate the conflict.
Donald Trump set a new course for US foreign policy, but Europe failed to set a course of its own, falling into the wait-and-see mode.
The West’s enemies see its lack of strategy as a green light to act with impunity. A strategy can be built through dialogue. Recently, Denmark and Greenland have shown that talking to the Trump administration is possible and can produce results.
The views expressed in this opinion article are the author’s and not necessarily those of Kyiv Post.

Frankfurt Book Fair: Rights lawyer Sands awarded peace prize
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
08:26:00 UTC

Frankfurt Book Fair: Rights lawyer Sands awarded peace prize
October 12, 2026
The 2026 Frankfurt Book Fair concluded on Sunday with the awarding of the Peace Prize of the German Book Trade to the Franco-British lawyer and author Philippe Sands.
Sands was honored in the presence of German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier as a committed humanist "who, despite growing resistance, fights tirelessly for human rights, justice and mutual understanding."
The jury said that his work was based on a "commitment to the universal rights of every human being, evidenced in his advocacy for victims of war crimes, racism, torture and colonial injustice."
Sands criticizes Germany's 'silence' on Israel
Sands, a professor of law at University College London and human rights lawyer at the International Court of Justice in The Hague, used his acceptance speech to criticize Germany for what he called its "inappropriate silence" regarding Israel and its actions in the Gaza Strip and the West Bank.
Sands said human rights abuses should be clearly named, especially among allies, stating: "It's not antisemitic. It's not anti-Israel. It's the truth."
Sands, himself a descendent of Jews driven out of what is now Lviv in western Ukraine during the German occupation in the Second World War, became known to a broader audience through his 2016 book East West Street: On the Origins of Genocide and Crimes Against Humanity.
The work, which details the lives of two Jewish lawyers, Hersch Lauterpacht and Raphael Lemkin, and the origins of international criminal law, was translated into dozens of languages, including German as Rückkehr nach Lemberg (Return to Lviv) in 2018.
"Germany knows all about ethnic cleansing," Sands said in Frankfurt, referring to criticism leveled at Israel by many states over its treatment of Palestinians.
"So why the silence? Silence is not the way. Not for a family. Not for a community. Not for a country."
Sands also condemned the Hamas attacks of October 7, 2023, as "appalling" and "a monstrous crime against the norms of international law" and acknowledged that Israel, like any state, has a right to defend itself.
"[But] this right is not unlimited and must be practiced within the boundaries of international law."

Ukrainian scam call centers shift their focus to Western countries — expert
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
08:25:44 UTC
17:25:44 KST

MOSCOW, October 12. /TASS/. Ukrainian scam call centers are now targeting Western countries, including Switzerland, Poland, Lithuania, and Latvia, having realized that they can't prey on Russia anymore, retired FSB Major General Alexander Perelygin told reporters.
"A remarkable turn of events has taken place recently. Our law enforcement agencies and special services are taking very active countermeasures, and public awareness campaigns are underway. This has reduced opportunities for fraud in Russia. Meanwhile, the [call centers’] appetites have grown. So how does organized crime respond in this situation? It seeks out new hunting grounds. Western Europe is one such place," the expert noted.
According to him, reports are already appearing in the Swiss press about the challenges local law enforcement agencies are facing in investigating Ukrainian scam call centers on their territory. Poland, Lithuania, and Latvia are facing the same problems. "Moreover, as I understand it, they’ve now set their sights on the US," Perelygin emphasized.
The expert attributed this development to the fact that Western countries have long ignored the problem, believing that Russia overblew the issue. "Now, Westerners are fed up with these call centers as they've begun to cause problems for them," he noted. According to Perelygin, one publication said that Russians now account for only 10-15% of the victims of Ukrainian call centers. "In short, now that this infection has spread to neighboring countries, they should understand that breeding it is foolish, because tomorrow it will be on their doorstep," the expert concluded.

Closure of Riyadh airport extended after deadly Houthi strikes
Oct 12 - Saudi authorities said on Monday they were extending the suspension of operations at the international airport in the capital, Riyadh, after deadly weekend attacks by Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis.
Operations at King Khalid International Airport, Saudi Arabia's second-busiest airport after Jeddah, were suspended to "allow for the completion of procedures to ensure the safety and operational readiness of the airport's facilities", the Saudi civil aviation authority said in a statement.
The airport has been shut since an attack on Saturday that killed 13 people and wounded more than 300, the deadliest in the kingdom in more than a decade. On Sunday, another attack killed one person and injured nearly a dozen others.
The attacks marked one of the most significant disruptions to Saudi aviation in years, adding to pressures on an industry already grappling with conflict across the Middle East.
The airport cancelled 99.7% of all scheduled flights on Sunday, according to aviation analytics firm Cirium. An air traffic tracker from Flightradar24 showed no planes over the city.
The disruption has forced airlines across Europe and Asia to suspend services, while the Federal Aviation Administration advised US carriers on Sunday to exercise caution when flying to or over Saudi Arabia.
Lufthansa Group has cancelled all flights to Riyadh until October 16, while Air France-KLM has extended a previous suspension of services to and from the Saudi capital until the end of the month.
Abu Dhabi’s Etihad Airways was among the airlines that further extended Saudi flight cancellations, affecting around 20 flights to Riyadh, Jeddah and Dammam on Monday and Tuesday.
The escalation with the Houthis has raised concerns over the broader economic impact. Saudi Arabia's real GDP is projected to contract by 3.6% this year, reflecting a combination of factors including lower oil activity.
The attacks have put events scheduled in Riyadh this month under pressure, including the kingdom's flagship investment conference and the WPC Energy Congress, where several top oil executives were dropped from the programme. REUTERS

Where will I notice Monday’s public sector strike?

Following Friday’s day of action, the socialist trade union ACOD is organising another trade union protest against government policy today, 12 October: a strike in the public sector. The impact will be noticeable across various sectors.
The socialist public-sector trade union ACOD is striking today against the underfunding of public services and the threat of further budget cuts.
Disruption is expected in various sectors as a result of the strike.
Rail operator NMBS
3 out of 10 InterCity trains will not be running Belgium’s state-owned rail operator NMBS says. It has drawn up an alternative timetable. The rail strike runs from 10.00 pm Sunday until last trains on Monday.
This means that 7 out of 10 IC trains are running today. In addition, 1 in 2 Local and Suburban trains are running. Few P or commuter trains are running; these are the trains that normally provide extra services during the morning and evening rush hours.
“NMBS advises its passengers to plan their journeys carefully by regularly checking the online journey planner ,” said NMBS spokesperson Dimitri Temmerman.
Flemish local transport company De Lijn
There is also disruption on the De Lijn network today: 4 in 10 De Lijn buses and trams are not running, reports the Flemish transport company.
Across Flanders as a whole, an average of 61 per cent of all buses and trams will be running, but there are differences between the regions.
Like NMBS, De Lijn has drawn up an alternative service based on the staff available.
De Lijn advises passengers to always check its route planner via the website or app before setting off. “Services that are cancelled will not appear in the route planner,” it states. The bus stop and route pages indicate cancelled services with the message ‘not running’.
Brussels local transport company MIVB
The MIVB says all bus and metro lines are operating at a reduced capacity. Some tram lines are also operating.
Passengers can visit the website or use the app for the most up-to-date information. The transport company does, however, expect “significant disruption”.
Education
Disruption extends to schools. Socialist union ACOD Education has given notice of a strike. Traditionally, ACOD has a stronger presence in the GO! official education network.
Flemish public broadcaster VRT
VRT 1 TV will only be showing archive programmes, abridged news bulletins and an episode of VRT NWS Terzake. VRT Canvas, the second channel, will be showing the same content as VRT 1. Ketnet, the channel for youngsters, will only be showing pre-scheduled programmes.
No scheduled programmes will be broadcast on the radio. The radio stations will only be playing music. There is a news bulletin every hour but there is no regional news.
Visual banners and audio messages will be shown regularly on television and radio. In this way, the trade unions are making it clear that a strike is underway.
Other sectors
The strike may also affect household waste collection, which could be disrupted in many towns and municipalities.
For example, Net Brussel is urging residents not to put out their bin bags today. Waste collection may also be disrupted in Ghent, amongst other places.
The strike may also cause disruption in prisons and detention centres, as well as at postal services provider Bpost.

Top oil executives dropped from event schedule after Riyadh attacks
DUBAI, Oct 12 - Several top energy executives were dropped from the schedule of the WPC Energy Congress in Riyadh, as Saudi authorities pressed ahead with the event despite deadly attacks on the capital claimed by Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis.
The chief executives of ExxonMobil, TotalEnergies, Shell, Chevron and BP had all been expected at the event, which began on Sunday, but were no longer on the agenda that conference organisers released early Monday.
“To everyone who travelled to Riyadh, thank you,” said Saudi Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman, who opened Monday’s session of the gathering for energy policy and industry.
“You know this country is safe and that we hold your protection at whole heart…Our gathering here does not mean the risk is gone.”
Prince Abdulaziz said the events of recent weeks were serious and that the kingdom’s response must be “equally serious".
The strikes are a blow to Vision 2030, Saudi Arabia's multi-billion-dollar programme to diversify the economy away from oil, modernise society and position the kingdom as an investment and tourism hub.
Hosting international events is a priority of the programme, which was already facing delays and recalibrations. Prince Abdulaziz said the kingdom must remain focused on the decades ahead and Vision 2030 must continue.
The WPC Energy Congress was originally scheduled for April of this year, but was postponed after the US and Israeli war on Iran began in late February. Saudi Arabia was named host in October 2022, the first time the event, first held in Britain in 1933, has been held in the kingdom.
Chief executives of major energy companies are a regular fixture at WPC Energy events and had been scheduled to speak on stage this week about global oil and gas markets, energy security and the energy transition.
A BP spokesperson said the company had "made every effort to participate" in the conference. "Unfortunately, due to travel disruption we are unable to be there in person. We greatly value our long-standing partnerships across the region."
Shell declined to comment and TotalEnergies, ExxonMobil and Chevron did not immediately respond to Reuters' request for comment.
The WPC Energy Congress is taking place this week at a conference centre some 10 kilometres (6 miles) from Riyadh’s international airport, which has been attacked four times in the last week.
One person was killed and nearly a dozen hurt in a new attack on the airport on Sunday evening, Saudi authorities reported, a day after a strike claimed by Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis killed 13 people and wounded more than 300, the deadliest attack in the kingdom in more than a decade. REUTERS

Estonia's August goods exports rise 3% as imports jump 10%
Estonia's goods exports rose 3 percent on year in August while imports increased 10 percent, widening the trade deficit to €360 million.
August exports totaled about €1.5 billion euros and imports exceeded €1.8 billion euros at current prices, Statistics Estonia reported Monday. Finland, Latvia and Lithuania were Estonia's main foreign trade partners.
Imports of mineral products rose 30 percent year over year, including a 67 percent jump in automotive fuel.
"This was mainly influenced by the rising prices of petroleum on the global market," said Jane Leppmets, a foreign trade statistics analyst at the agency.
Electrical equipment accounted for 15 percent of commodities exports, followed by agricultural and food products at 11 percent.
Exports to Finland, Estonia's largest export market, made up 17 percent of the total, followed by Latvia at 13 percent and Lithuania at 10 percent.
Shipments to Latvia grew the most at 19 percent, mainly due to increased exports of mineral products, including natural gas and electricity.
Imports grew most in value from Lithuania, rising €50 million euros, or 28 percent, as deliveries of mineral products, including automotive fuel, increased.
Lithuania tied with Finland to account for 12 percent of Estonia's imports, while Latvia made up 11 percent.

Drought conditions in Switzerland persist despite rainfall

Drought conditions in Switzerland persist despite rainfall
The autumn rains that fell up until the weekend have only temporarily alleviated the drought, which remains severe in Switzerland. The situation remains tense, according to MeteoSwiss.
After a long spell of mild weather with summer-like temperatures, the northern Alps experienced several wet autumnal days from Thursday onwards. These days unfolded “almost as if from a meteorology textbook”, wrote the Federal Office of Meteorology and Climatology (MeteoSwiss) on its blog on Friday.
Between 20 and 40 millimetres of rainfall were recorded north of the Alps. However, a significant proportion of this water evaporated or ran off due to the dry ground.
In many parts of the country, the rainfall deficit persists. “Over the last 30 days, rainfall amounts have averaged less than 50% of the long-term average,” a MeteoSwiss spokesperson told news agency Keystone-SDA on Sunday. In some places, they reached only 15 to 35% of the normal level.
More
Drought in Switzerland: Europe’s ‘water tower’ runs dry
In the Jura and on the Swiss Plateau, rivers and lakes are still at particularly low levels. Many monitoring stations are recording flow rates so low that, statistically, they occur only once every 10 to 30 years. Historically low levels have even been recorded on the Upper Rhine.
High risk of forest fires
The drought is also having an impact on the risk of forest fires. On the map produced by the Federal Office of the Environment (FOEN), a band indicating a significant risk stretches from cantons Valais to St Gallen. In some parts of Upper Valais, the risk is even classified as “very high”.
More
How drought affects Swiss forests
The situation is unlikely to change much in the medium term. A few drops of rain are expected locally next week, but days are likely to remain generally dry, according to MeteoSwiss. Maximum temperatures of up to 19C are forecast for German-speaking and French-speaking Switzerland.
In the longer term, however, the situation could ease. Over a 90-day period, the rainfall deficit is expected to begin to decrease slowly following a slight increase next week, according to the drought bulletin.

US Marines to deploy missile systems on Japan island near Taiwan for first time
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
08:17:45 UTC
17:17:45 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The US Marine Corps plans to deploy anti-ship and air-defense systems to Japan’s Yonaguni Island, about 110 kilometers from Taiwan, for the first time during a military exercise later this month.
In an article published Saturday by The National Interest, defense analyst Harrison Kass described the planned deployment as part of a “significant transformation in Marine Corps strategy.” The shift emphasizes small, mobile missile units across the Pacific rather than traditional amphibious assault operations.
The deployment is planned for the biennial Keen Sword exercise, scheduled for Oct. 19–29, involving Japan’s Self-Defense Forces and the US military. The Marine Corps plans to bring its Navy-Marine Expeditionary Ship Interdiction System (NMESIS) and Marine Air Defense Integrated System (MADIS) to Yonaguni.
Yonaguni is Japan’s westernmost inhabited island, near maritime routes connecting the East China Sea and the Pacific. In a Taiwan Strait conflict, “the waters near Yonaguni would become one of the most crucial operating areas in the world,” Kass said, adding that anti-ship missiles could “complicate” Chinese naval movements.
Japan established radar and surveillance facilities on Yonaguni in 2016 as regional security concerns grew, per Defense News. During Chinese military exercises around Taiwan in August 2022, a Chinese ballistic missile landed in waters about 80 kilometers from the island.
NMESIS combines an unmanned ground vehicle with a launcher capable of carrying two Naval Strike Missiles, Kass said. The sea-skimming cruise missiles have a publicly reported range of about 185 kilometers, potentially putting waters off northeastern Taiwan within reach from Yonaguni.
MADIS provides short-range air defense using vehicle-mounted sensors and weapons to counter drones, helicopters, and low-flying aircraft. While NMESIS provides anti-ship firepower, MADIS is designed to protect deployed Marines and missile units from aerial threats.
The systems are part of the Marine Corps’ Force Design modernization initiative, which shifts away from some traditional heavy equipment, such as tanks, toward mobile expeditionary units, precision missiles, drones, and reconnaissance capabilities in contested coastal areas.
Japan is also expanding its missile defenses in the southwestern island chain. Japanese Defense Minister Koizumi Shinjiro said in February that Japan plans to deploy a Type 03 surface-to-air missile unit on Yonaguni by 2030.
The Type 03 system has a reported range of about 50 kilometers and can track up to 100 targets simultaneously while engaging as many as 12, per UDN. Koizumi described the planned deployment as a measure to strengthen Japan’s southwestern island defenses.
During this year’s Keen Sword exercise, Japan’s Ground Self-Defense Force is expected to train with its Type 25 anti-ship missile system, which has a reported range of 1,000 kilometers, UDN reported. It will also use the Type 88 anti-ship missile system, which has a range of about 180 kilometers.

Federal agents raid anti-Israel US congresswoman's home amid reported immigration fraud probe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
16:01:27 UTC
01:01:27 KST

Federal agents searched the Washington, D.C., home of Democratic Rep. Ilhan Omar on Monday as part of a federal criminal investigation reportedly involving immigration fraud allegations, in an extraordinary operation targeting one of President Donald Trump's most prominent political critics just three weeks before the US midterm elections.
The early morning search was carried out by agents from Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), the investigative arm of US Immigration and Customs Enforcement. The Justice Department confirmed that agents had executed a search warrant authorized by a judge, but did not publicly specify the nature of the investigation.
The department said the operation was part of an ongoing federal criminal investigation. Fox News reported that investigators were examining immigration documents completed by Omar's late father when she was a child. 
The search has attracted significant attention because Omar, a progressive Democrat representing Minnesota, has long been a target of attacks by Trump and other senior Republicans. Its timing, less than a month before congressional elections, has also raised questions about the Justice Department's longstanding practice of exercising particular caution when conducting politically sensitive investigations close to an election.
CNN described the operation as an unusually aggressive investigative step against a politician actively seeking reelection.
Immigration fraud allegations and claims Omar married her brother
Omar, who was born in Somalia, arrived in the United States at age 12 after her family spent time in a refugee camp in Kenya. She was elected to the House of Representatives in 2018, becoming, alongside Palestinian American Democrat Rashida Tlaib, one of the first two Muslim women elected to Congress.
Since then, she has won reelection three times and is now seeking a fifth term representing Minnesota's 5th Congressional District, which includes Minneapolis.
Republican politicians and conservative commentators have for years raised allegations about Omar's immigration history, including an unsubstantiated claim that she married her brother to help him obtain immigration status or student loans.
Omar married British citizen Ahmed Nur Said Elmi in 2009, and the couple divorced in 2017. She has repeatedly denied that Elmi is her brother, describing the allegations as "disgusting lies."
Republicans have also accused her of tax irregularities and suggested that she entered the United States in 1995 using a false name or different family identity to circumvent delays in refugee applications.
Those allegations have not been established as fact, and the Justice Department has not publicly confirmed whether they are directly connected to Monday's search.
Vance accused Omar of immigration fraud without presenting evidence
In May, Vice President JD Vance publicly accused Omar of immigration fraud, saying that he and Deputy White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller were exploring ways to investigate the Minnesota congresswoman.
"It certainly seems like something fishy is there, but everybody's entitled to equal justice under the laws," Vance said at the time.
He said officials intended to examine the allegations and pursue prosecution if investigators found evidence of criminal wrongdoing.
In a separate interview with conservative podcast host Benny Johnson, Vance made a more categorical accusation, claiming without presenting evidence that Omar had committed immigration fraud against the United States.
Omar's office strongly rejected the accusations.
Her chief of staff, Connor McNutt, accused Vance of deliberately spreading falsehoods to distract attention from the administration's policies and political difficulties.
"This is rich coming from someone who literally said they were willing to 'create stories' to redirect the media," McNutt said.
He described the allegations as a ridiculous lie and an attempt to divert attention from the administration's war with Iran, rising gasoline prices and declining Republican polling numbers.
McNutt also used the phrase "pedophile protection party" in his criticism of Republicans, referring to allegations that the Trump administration had sought to prevent the release of documents connected to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
Trump calls for Omar to be institutionalized
Omar has become one of Trump's most frequent targets, particularly over her progressive political positions, criticism of Israel and outspoken opposition to his immigration policies.
Trump and senior administration officials have also repeatedly criticized Minnesota's large Somali American community, of which Omar is a member.
Earlier this year, the administration launched a major immigration enforcement operation in the region involving ICE agents. Omar and her allies accused Trump of employing anti-Somali and anti-Muslim rhetoric, while the congresswoman described the president's repeated focus on her as a disturbing and unhealthy obsession.
The confrontation intensified in February, when Trump said Omar and Tlaib should be institutionalized and sent back to the places they came from.
The remarks followed criticism of the president by the two lawmakers during his State of the Union address, in which he praised his administration's restrictive immigration policies and enforcement operations.
Omar has repeatedly said that she and her family face death threats, which she attributes to hateful political rhetoric, particularly statements made by Trump.
The security concerns have also been accompanied by physical attacks.
Last month, a Minnesota man was sentenced to 14 months in prison after being convicted of spraying Omar with vinegar during a public appearance.
The attacker, Anthony James Kazmierczak, acknowledged that he targeted the congresswoman because he disagreed with her progressive political views.
An extraordinary raid weeks before US elections
The search comes at a particularly sensitive moment in American politics, with congressional midterm elections scheduled for November 3.
The Justice Department traditionally follows guidelines intended to prevent investigative actions from improperly influencing elections, particularly when candidates for public office are involved.
CNN noted that searching the residence of a sitting member of Congress just weeks before an election is an exceptionally unusual step.
The operation also follows renewed attacks by Trump on other Muslim Democrats who have criticized Israel.
Last week, the president targeted Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic candidate for Michigan's US Senate seat, while endorsing his Republican opponent, Mike Rogers.
Trump described El-Sayed as a radical extremist and a sympathizer of terrorism. El-Sayed has also been an outspoken critic of Israel and has accused it of committing genocide in Gaza.
Omar's criticism of Israel and the 2019 entry ban
Omar has been among the most outspoken critics of Israel in the Democratic Party, taking positions that have repeatedly generated controversy both in Washington and Jerusalem.
Even before the October 7, 2023 Hamas attack and the subsequent war in Gaza, she supported the Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions movement, known as BDS, which campaigns for economic and political pressure on Israel.
She has also compared Israel's treatment of Palestinians to South Africa's former apartheid system and accused Israel of genocide in Gaza.
During her first term in Congress, Omar faced criticism from members of her own party over statements about American support for Israel that many interpreted as antisemitic.
One particularly contentious episode involved her suggestion that American politicians supported Israel because of financial contributions from the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, known as AIPAC.
In 2019, Israel barred Omar and Tlaib from entering the country, a decision that drew criticism even from prominent supporters of Israel within the Democratic Party.
Monday's search now places Omar at the center of another major political confrontation. Federal authorities have confirmed that a criminal investigation is underway, but have not disclosed its precise scope or announced charges against the congresswoman.

Abduction of Palestinians by Israeli occupiers on rise in occupied West Bank: Officials
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
08:17:26 UTC
17:17:26 KST

Ayser Al-Iss and Lina Altawell
12 October 2026•Update: 12 October 2026
Abductions and arbitrary detention of Palestinians by Israeli occupiers have increased across the occupied West Bank, particularly targeting farmers and rural communities, Palestinian officials and rights groups said Monday.
Salah al-Khawaja, director of the Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission’s office in the central West Bank, told Anadolu that such incidents were often accompanied by abuse and violence.
“Palestinians were being detained at makeshift checkpoints or seized during attacks on farmers and rural and Bedouin communities,” he said.
Amir Daoud, the commission’s documentation official, said the repeated attacks make farmers fear for their lives and freedom when accessing their land and could discourage them from reaching their fields.
“The impact of the attacks extends from the victim to the entire village and becomes a means of intimidating residents and weakening their connection to their land,” Daoud said.
The UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) said in May 2025 that it had documented around 36 incidents since October 2023 in which Israeli occupiers, some wearing military uniforms, abducted or detained at least 50 Palestinians, including three children.
Palestinian rights group Al-Haq also said in a Sept. 24 report that documented cases showed an “increasing pattern” of abductions and unlawful arbitrary detentions.
In the latest reported incidents, Israeli occupiers abducted seven Palestinians on Saturday, according to the official Voice of Palestine radio.
The outlet said three abductions were reported in Nahalin west of Bethlehem, three in Qaffin north of Tulkarem and a farmer in Beit Imrin near Nablus, adding that their fate was not immediately known.
Daoud accused the Israeli army of providing protection to occupiers during some incidents, saying the Qaffin attack took place under army protection.
 
Systematic policy
Settlement affairs researcher Jamal Juma said the abductions were part of a “systematic policy” targeting Palestinian presence in Area C, which makes up around 60% of the occupied West Bank and remains under full Israeli control.
Under the 1995 Oslo II Agreement, which was intended as a temporary arrangement, the occupied West Bank was divided into Areas A, B and C.
Area A is under full Palestinian civil and security control, Area B under Palestinian civil and Israeli security control, while Area C remains under full Israeli control and makes up around 60% of the West Bank.
The incidents have drawn particular concern during the olive harvest season, when Palestinian farmers face attacks including beatings, denial of access to fields, theft of crops and damage to trees.
According to the official Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission, more than 26,000 olive trees were cut down or damaged across the West Bank during the first half of 2026.
The olive harvest season began on Sept. 20 with olives intended for pickling, while harvesting varieties used for olive oil production is scheduled to begin on Oct. 15.
Since Israel began its genocide in Gaza in October 2023, attacks by the Israeli army and occupiers against Palestinians and their property have intensified across the occupied West Bank, including East Jerusalem.
The attacks include killings and arrests of Palestinians, the demolition of homes and structures, the burning of mosques and vehicles, bulldozing of agricultural land, preventing farmers from reaching their fields, stealing crops, displacement and illegal settlement expansion.
Palestinians warn that Israel is paving the way through such measures for the formal annexation of the West Bank, in a move that would undermine the possibility of establishing a Palestinian state as envisioned in relevant UN resolutions.

Lithuanian lawmakers propose legal protection against AI voice cloning
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
08:17:00 UTC
17:17:00 KST

Lithuanian lawmakers have proposed amendments to the Civil Code that would establish a legal right to one’s voice, requiring consent for its reproduction, publication or other use, amid growing concerns about artificial intelligence-generated deepfakes.
The proposed protection would cover recordings of a person’s actual voice as well as imitations and artificially generated voices that could be used to identify them.
Exceptions would apply to parody and satire, provided they did not mislead the public about a recording’s authenticity or violate a person’s honour, dignity, professional reputation or privacy.
Conservative lawmaker Vytautas Kernagis, one of the proposal’s authors, said advances in AI made it increasingly difficult to distinguish genuine voices from synthetic ones, creating opportunities for disinformation and fraud.
Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni last week registered the phrase “Io sono Giorgia Meloni” (“I am Giorgia Meloni”) as an EU trademark to protect herself against AI-generated voice imitations.
Lithuanian Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius has no plans to follow her example, saying trademark protection against unauthorised commercial use would not address political deepfakes.
The government said it would assess whether Lithuanian law adequately protects people’s voices and digital likenesses. Sinkevičius’ AI adviser, Linas Eriksonas, said Lithuania should also examine Denmark’s proposal to prohibit the publication of realistic digital replicas of a person’s appearance and voice without consent.
President Gitanas Nausėda also has no plans to introduce special legal measures to protect his voice.
Democratic lawmaker Agnė Širinskienė backed the proposed amendments, saying the need for protection had grown as technology made realistic voice cloning possible.
Conservative lawmaker and opera singer Vytautas Juozapaitis also supported discussing the issue but stressed that malicious deepfakes must be distinguished from creative works.
Parody and artistic expression should remain protected, he said, while deliberately deceptive imitations should be addressed.

September 2026 2nd-warmest on record globally: EU climate service agency
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
08:16:01 UTC
17:16:01 KST

Melike Pala
12 October 2026•Update: 12 October 2026
September 2026 was the second-warmest September on record globally, with average temperatures reaching 1.63C above pre-industrial levels, according to the latest data released by the Copernicus Climate Change Service (C3S) on Monday.
The EU's climate monitoring service said that September marked the second consecutive month this year in which global temperatures exceeded the 1.5C threshold above pre-industrial levels.
The global average surface air temperature stood at 16.27C (61.29F), which was 0.82C above the 1991-2020 average.
Carlo Buontempo, director of the Copernicus Climate Change Service, said September was marked by exceptionally high temperatures across parts of Europe following an extreme summer.
"We are in a new run of months above 1.5C, and with a strong El Nino still intensifying it is likely to last into 2027," Buontempo said.
 
Western Europe records warmest September
Europe experienced its third-warmest September on record, with the average temperature over European land reaching 16.26C (61.27F), or 1.54C above the 1991-2020 average.
Western Europe recorded its joint-warmest September, tying with 2023 at 2.51C above the seasonal average.
The region also experienced widespread dry conditions, particularly across western, central and parts of eastern Europe, with drought conditions intensifying in several areas compared with August.
 
El Nino pushes sea temperatures to record levels
The average sea surface temperature across extra-polar oceans between 60 degrees south and 60 degrees north reached 21.05C (69.89F) in September, the highest level recorded for the month.
Sea surface temperatures remained exceptionally high across much of the tropical Pacific as El Nino conditions strengthened.
Prolonged dry conditions across Europe resulted in exceptionally low river flows, with parts of the Rhine, Danube, Vistula, and Garonne-Dordogne recording their lowest September levels.
Dry conditions intensified or expanded across parts of the Iberian Peninsula, France, Italy, the western Balkans, and Greece.
Outside Europe, below-average precipitation affected parts of North and South America, North Africa, the Horn of Africa, Siberia, Central Asia, Pakistan, China, and southeastern Australia.
 
Antarctic sea ice reaches 3rd-lowest winter maximum
The Antarctic sea ice extent reached its third-lowest annual winter maximum in the satellite record, while the monthly extent was approximately 6% below the September average.
The Arctic's daily sea ice extent reached its annual summer minimum, ranking the 14th lowest in the satellite record.
Monthly Arctic sea ice extent was around 10% below average.

Concessions
The government is still counting the cost of the high school protests.
A government source told journalists last week that the cost for damage caused by the demonstrations was “at least €30 million (S$43 million)”.
On Oct 9, the justice ministry said more than 6,800 people had been detained since the demonstrations started, 86% of them minors.
After clashes between some protesters and riot police left some students severely injured, sparking criticism of police tactics, the government suspended the use of stun grenades that cost one student his hand.
Police are investigating 18 alleged cases of misconduct within their ranks.
Last week, the government came up with concrete proposals to try to address the students’ demands.
Education Minister Edouard Geffray announced late on Oct 8 that some 3,000 substitute teachers would be deployed in the coming days to replace absent staff at the 114 worst-affected high schools.
Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu on Oct 11 promised to make changes to the planned budget 2027 to respond to some demands set out in an online platform the government set up to gather students’ views.
‘Crumbs’
The student organisations behind the protests are yet to be convinced, however.
The Union of High School students described the initial announcements last week as “crumbs”. They are maintaining their demand for an extra €10 million to be invested in the country’s lycees.
France’s 10,000 medical students, however, are beginning to express concern at the effect any continued school blockades could have on exams starting on Oct 12 that help determine their eventual speciality.
They do not want to see the students’ action disrupt such a crucial stage of their education.
The Oct 8 student demonstrations mobilised tens of thousands of people across France: 71,500 according to interior ministry figures.
Nearly 256,000 took part in Oct 6’s day of action.
And one poll, carried out by Ipsos-BVA and published on Oct 11, said 54% of respondents backed the high school student protests.
They had the most sympathy with student complaints about the excessive size of classes and with the need to renovate the country’s crumbling schools. AFP

‘She had a hand in everything’: Kfar Saba mayor's wife at heart of sweeping bribery probe

2026-10-12
08:15:00 UTC
17:15:00 KST

She holds no official position at Kfar Saba City Hall, but investigators suspect Meital Saar, wife of Mayor Rafi Saar, played a central role in an alleged corruption network that steered municipal contracts to businesspeople in exchange for cash bribes. Police sources described her as a "dominant figure" who "had a hand in everything," alleging that businesspeople seeking lucrative city projects approached her directly and paid her bundles of cash.
The allegations emerged Monday as police arrested 17 suspects, including the mayor and his wife, in a sweeping municipal tender-rigging investigation. Rafi Saar has since temporarily suspended himself from office, while employees at City Hall struggle to absorb the revelations. Some remain convinced the mayor will emerge from the investigation unscathed, but police sources have painted a different picture of his wife's influence over municipal affairs.
"He is an elected official, she holds no public office, but she had a hand in everything," sources in the National Fraud Investigations Unit said, describing Meital Saar's alleged involvement in helping businesspeople secure major tenders, from renovations of educational institutions to cleaning services and the placement of food trucks.
One source described the suspected corruption in particularly stark terms. "This was a city that was sold, nothing less than that," he said, adding that there had long been widespread talk suggesting the mayor's wife "held the key to running the city."
Investigators from Lahav 433 remained inside Kfar Saba City Hall on Monday, examining computers and seizing documents in an effort to substantiate the allegations. "It's a complete shock. We never imagined there was anything criminal going on inside this building," one municipal employee told ynet. "I believe he'll get through this easily because he's an honest man."
Some employees who arrived at the municipal building in the city center early Monday morning were surprised to find police investigators already at work.
The investigation is continuing at both City Hall and the municipal economic development company, with detectives collecting documents and examining computer records.
"There are quite a few police officers inside," another municipal employee said. "They're not asking many questions. They're mainly collecting documents and checking computers." During searches at the mayor's home, investigators also found luxury watches and handbags.
Déjà vu at City Hall: ‘Unfortunately, we know the protocol’
For some municipal employees, the investigation has revived uncomfortable memories. Kfar Saba's previous mayor, Yehuda Ben Hamo, was convicted in a corruption case and sentenced to 24 months in prison in April 2022.
"We're all relatively calm here," one employee said. "Unfortunately, most of us were here the last time something like this happened, so we know the protocol."
This time, however, the municipal economic development company is also implicated in the investigation. Employees describe it as an entity operating separately from the municipality. Its CEO, attorney Sagi Chen, was among those arrested on suspicion of offenses involving public corruption, bribery, fraud and breach of trust, money laundering and tax violations.
At the center of the case are Rafi and Meital Saar, who investigators suspect worked together to promote the interests of businesspeople and associates, including individuals with alleged criminal connections, in exchange for cash bribes.
Police conducted searches at approximately 30 locations as the investigation became public. The undercover operation began about a year and a half ago, following dozens of intelligence reports raising suspicions of widespread corruption within the municipality.
According to information collected by investigators, the couple allegedly worked to direct municipal tenders, properties and projects to associates, businesspeople and individuals with financial interests, some of whom are known to police for criminal activity.
In return, investigators suspect Meital Saar received bundles of cash from those individuals, with whom she maintained direct contact.
How the mayor's wife allegedly steered municipal tenders
According to investigators, the suspected scheme revolved around Meital Saar's contacts with businesspeople seeking municipal contracts. Those interested in securing projects allegedly approached the mayor's wife, established quid pro quo arrangements and relied on her assistance to win tenders.
Police suspect that, to conceal preferential treatment of certain businesspeople and the alleged manipulation of tenders, municipal projects were transferred from City Hall to the economic development company.
Investigators believe the couple coordinated with the company's CEO, who allegedly knew in advance which bidder was supposed to win each tender brought before him.
Sources familiar with the investigation said that, in some cases, obstacles were allegedly placed in the way of competing bidders until they were forced to withdraw. The projects were then allegedly awarded to businesspeople whose connections with the couple were suspected of benefiting them.
The allegations cover almost every area of municipal operations, including school renovations, food trucks, the opening of businesses, leisure and entertainment complexes, sports projects, transportation, traffic lights, street lighting and cleaning services.
Another central aspect of the investigation concerns the couple's lifestyle and their allegedly extensive use of cash.
According to National Fraud Investigations Unit sources, Rafi and Meital Saar maintained a lavish lifestyle, paying numerous expenses in cash, including overseas travel, jewelry, clothing and handbags.
"We're not investigating a technical violation involving the use of cash. If that were the issue, we would find a great many offenses of that kind," investigators explained, emphasizing that the transactions were being examined as part of the suspected bribery scheme.
During the police raids, including searches of municipal offices, investigators discovered large quantities of cash, packaged and concealed in locations where detectives had anticipated finding it.
Expensive jewelry, luxury watches and evidence of overseas flights and shopping trips were also found in the couple's possession. During their most recent return to Israel, customs officials at Ben Gurion Airport discovered 20,000 shekels in cash in Meital Saar's possession, and she was questioned at the scene.
The couple also drove expensive, recently purchased vehicles.
A separate line of investigation concerns suspected connections between the mayor, his wife and criminal figures operating in the Sharon region. According to intelligence obtained by police, individuals known to Central District police for criminal activity allegedly assisted Saar during the local election campaign.
Investigators suspect those individuals pressured political candidates running against Saar in an effort to influence the election. Police are examining the nature of the relationships between the alleged criminal figures and the couple, as well as suspicions that those same individuals subsequently exerted pressure on the mayor and his wife.

Breadcrumb
Trump's 'energy ceasefire' sparks confusion as Russia strikes Ukraine
US President Donald Trump sowed confusion on Sunday, announcing an "energy ceasefire" between Ukraine and Russia that sparked astonishment in Kyiv, silence from Moscow and support from Ukraine's Western allies.
But the ceasefire appeared shaky at best as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Russia struck multiple Ukrainian power plants on Sunday, including one in the capital and another in Kharkiv, leading to power outages and outrage.
Trump's announcement came two days after he declared a temporary easing of US sanctions on Russian diesel, prompting outrage by European allies and Kyiv, who said it would only embolden Russian President Vladimir Putin.
"Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine," Trump said early Sunday on Truth Social. "Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!"
Zelensky appeared to express surprise at the announcement, saying he was seeking further details, but added that "Ukraine supports the ceasefire, and it is important that Russia support it as well."
Russia has yet to confirm its agreement.
Zelensky later said that multiple Ukrainian power stations had been hit and that "Ukrainian skies have been infested with Russian 'shaheds' all day," referring to a type of drone originally designed by Iran that is now used extensively by Russia.
Since launching a full-scale invasion of its neighbor in 2022, Russia has systematically hit Ukrainian energy infrastructure, leading to energy and heating shortages—prompting Ukraine to hit back at Russian oil refineries it says fund the war.
More recently, Trump's war in Iran has led to oil shortages and ensuing price spikes, creating major headwinds for his Republican Party ahead of midterm elections early next month.
'Up to our people'
The ceasefire appeared to garner support on Sunday from Ukraine's key western allies, including the UK, France, Canada and the European Commission.
Several leaders called on Russia to uphold the deal.
But that support was in contrast to broad criticism of the US-Russia diesel deal earlier in the week, which has led to mounting tensions between Trump and Zelensky.
Zelensky said the diesel deal was a "weak decision," while several of Ukraine's European allies expressed outrage and pledged to increase pressure on Moscow.
Seven US senators—including four Republicans—released a statement Sunday blasting the diesel deal with Russia, saying it was illegal.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney added to the chorus on Sunday after a call with Zelensky, saying the diesel deal "is in direct opposition to the efforts of Ukraine, Canada and our allies to create peace and stability in Europe."
Asked about the criticism on Saturday, Trump said it was "time for Ukraine to get a new president" who would finally settle the war.
Zelensky pushed back, telling ABC News that "it's up to our society, up to our people to choose one or another leader."
He said that fuel prices were rising because of the US-Israeli war on Iran and the blocked Strait of Hormuz.
"Everybody understands it," he said.
Support for Zelensky
Germany's foreign minister said Sunday that Berlin continued to "fully support" Zelensky.
"Europe needs stability and that means that we are very clearly continuing to stay by the side of Ukraine and its government," Johann Wadephul said in Berlin.
EU chief Ursula von der Leyen also backed the Ukrainian leader "as he leads the fight for his people's freedom."
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham also said his country "strongly supports President Trump's call today for a sustained energy ceasefire to start now."
In Kyiv, several residents expressed concern about Trump's call for Zelensky to be replaced.
"I believe our president is the best, and Americans should think about their own president," said 40-year-old Olesia Goncharuk.
"We Ukrainians decide our own fate and our own freedom, and we are free people," she told AFP.

It also confirmed that the Bulgarian state would continue to assist in the case within the scope of its authority.

Trump, who is not on the ballot but is campaigning to help Republicans keep control of Congress, said last week that he and his campaign would pay for the adverts. The White House later told AFP the post "was not referring to reimbursement."

IMF chief alarmed at ‘slow-moving tsunami’ of AI for jobs, taxes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
08:10:00 UTC
17:10:00 KST

IMF chief alarmed at ‘slow-moving tsunami’ of AI for jobs
- IMF chief Kristalina Georgieva warned AI is a “slow-moving tsunami” for jobs and taxes, and said governments must rethink education and act now.
- She said AI is already cutting demand for routine human work, hurting young job seekers, and may widen inequality as gains stay with a narrow group.
- Georgieva also warned AI could weaken tax revenues, but said it may lift growth by up to one percentage point in advanced Asian economies, which could offset ageing costs.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – The head of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) has warned of the disruptive threat from artificial intelligence to the labour market and taxation, urging policymakers to rethink education and act now to help society adapt.
“It is a slow-moving tsunami, but tsunami nonetheless,” managing director Kristalina Georgieva said on Oct 12 during her first appearance at the annual meetings of the IMF and World Bank in Bangkok.
Speaking at a session on AI’s impact on employment, she said the technology is already hollowing out demand for many human workers by taking over routine, repetitive tasks. At the same time, it is increasing low-paying jobs in sectors like construction, which she said is “not a story to celebrate”.
It is a transformation with far-reaching consequences for public finances, Georgieva said.
The risk is that AI strains government revenues by tilting the economy towards capital and away from labour – traditionally the main source of tax income.
The comments are the latest warning about the potential shock from AI on jobs and the global economy.
Young workers in AI-exposed fields have already seen a slowdown in hiring, leaving new entry-level applicants far more vulnerable. Concern is also growing that the technology will widen inequality, with its gains so far concentrated among a narrow set of workers and economies despite a global investment supercycle.
“We cannot today imagine what exactly the world of work will be five years from now,” she said. “But we can be disciplined and carefully assess what is happening, and then draw lessons, but – most importantly – act on them now.”
Despite the employment headwinds, the technology can ultimately prove a positive for growth overall. The IMF estimates the spread of AI can add up to a percentage point to growth in advanced Asian economies.
Such a growth boost “is a very big deal”, Georgieva said, adding that it will “more than offset” the drag from ageing in rich countries across the region. BLOOMBERG

We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.

Russian Defense Ministry creates service for training military-purpose neutral networks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
08:07:59 UTC
17:07:59 KST

MOSCOW, October 12. /TASS/. A service for training military-grade neural networks has been created under the purview of the Russian Defense Ministry, the ministry reported.
"The Defense Ministry of the Russian Federation has created a service that provides developers of unmanned systems with access to live recording data of drones’ combat deployment for the training of military-purpose neural networks," the ministry stated.
The new service provides developers of unmanned systems with access to a specialized repository containing prepared video footage of the results of the use of FPV drones and other copter drones and fixed-wing unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs).
In addition, the ministry’s specialists have created a unified data recognition classifier for machine learning AI systems, which allows developers to work with the database efficiently, in a structured manner, and according to a unified plan. The results of the work conducted by developers of military-purpose unmanned systems are uploaded back to the service, where the information is checked for completeness and compliance with the classifier format, enabling the Defense Ministry to use this dataset to create and train its neural networks.
"This method helps enhance the resilience and adaptability of the Russian Armed Forces to modern challenges in the field of artificial intelligence," the ministry emphasized.

The commander's move comes as NATO seeks to send Moscow a signal to halt what Western officials call a "hybrid" campaign of sabotage and interference against supporters of Ukraine in Russia's war against Ukraine.
In recent months, fears have grown that the Kremlin is stepping up its actions following high-profile incidents, including the discovery of an explosive-laden drone at a German airport.
"The Supreme Allied Commander's theory of victory is simple: to maintain NATO's advantage, consistent with and based on the alliance's deterrence and defence plans," Colonel Martin O'Donnell, the U.S. general's spokesman, said last week.
"But given the unstable and complex global security situation, we need to create the conditions now to deter aggression and, if necessary, prevail in the event of an attack," O'Donnell said, noting that the theory provides the basis for this.
Grynkewich's presentation is unlikely to reveal many new details of NATO's strategy and is intended both to send a signal to Moscow and reassure members on the alliance's eastern flank.
Western officials say that Moscow's "hybrid attacks" have become more reckless as Kremlin forces have become bogged down in Ukraine, and that they risk causing significant loss of life.
The alliance, whose primary aim is to deter an armed invasion by Russia, is trying to determine how to deal with "grey zone" incidents below the threshold of open conflict.
NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte urged countries to "stay calm, carry on and support Ukraine."
"We must not be naive... about Russia, but they know that we are stronger," Rutte said last month.
But the increase in Russian activity is taking place at a time of potential vulnerability for Europe. Allies are now preparing for a possible reduction in U.S. forces in Europe, as the Pentagon reviews its deployments on the continent. The results of the process are expected to be announced by the end of the year.
Pentagon has begun a review of the US military presence in Europe28.07.26, 16:45 • 4023 views

Siberian hunters declare open season on bears after spate of deadly attacks
- Hunters in Podtesovo, Siberia, are killing bears after deadly attacks. Mikhail Kondakov said locals asked for action after two women were killed while mushroom picking.
- Russia says brown bear numbers have more than doubled to 308,000 in 30 years. Officials are drawing up urgent measures after at least 22 deaths since spring.
- Residents say they live in fear as bears enter homes, parks and gardens. They want the animals controlled, but worry hungry bears may stay active even in winter.
AI generated
PODTESOVO, Russia – A brown bear bounds across the Siberian taiga before two hunters close in on their prey. Three shots ring out and the bear quickly drops dead in the long grass.
Cradling his rifle as he rests his hand on the dead animal’s fur, hunter Mikhail Kondakov says he and others have heeded requests from residents in the nearby settlement of Podtesovo after a fatal bear attack on local women.
“The bear situation in the settlement is very difficult at the moment,” Kondakov told Reuters.
“Bears have increasingly been coming directly into the settlement. This year we had a tragedy – two women who went mushroom picking were killed by a man-eating bear. We decided to start hunting bears because there are so many of them.”
Bear population has spiralled out of control
The problem is nationwide. The Russian government said in September it was drawing up urgent measures to control the population of brown bears that has spiralled out of control in some regions, with at least 22 people killed in attacks since this spring, according to state media.
The population of brown bears has more than doubled in the last three decades to 308,000 according to government data, in part due to shorter and milder winters.
Experts cited in Russian media have said bears have been forced to look further afield for food in 2026 because an early and dry spring meant there was a lack of berries for them to feed on.
People have also been blamed for leaving food waste out in the open where it attracts bears and for ignoring safety rules.
In Krasnoyarsk, the Siberian region where Kondakov is hunting and which is home to nearly 27,000 bears, investigators said in September that they had opened a criminal case into the local environment ministry, accusing it of failing to keep bear numbers under control, negligence which they said had led to the deaths of seven people in that month alone.
In Podtesovo, a settlement of around 3,500 people perched on the right bank of the River Yenisei, a simple wooden cross stands on the grave of Zoya Gubanova along with a colour photograph of the late pensioner.
Gubanova, 67, was killed on Aug 31 in a bear attack while out gathering mushrooms, a popular Russian pastime.
Chatting outside her wooden house, Yulia Markova, a local resident, says the situation has become intolerable.
“We have been living in fear for almost two months now, we cannot even go out for a walk in the evening. People are afraid to let their children go out alone. This is not a cuddly toy, it is not some soft, harmless teddy bear. It is a wild animal. And who knows what its intentions are, what kind of mood it is in when it comes here. Maybe it is simply curious, or maybe it is looking for its next victim,” she said.
Markova said that locals, like bear attack victim Gubanova, had not fully understood the danger posed by bears and that people had initially felt sorry for them because they clearly did not have enough nuts and berries to eat in 2026.
But she said hearts had hardened after the bears started coming into the settlement in large numbers.
“We have never seen an invasion like this before,” said Markova.
Bears coming into parks where children play
Watching her daughter relax at the local playground, pregnant mother Valeriya Efremova said heightened bear activity had changed locals’ lives.
“When the bears started coming out of the forest, we restricted outings as much as possible, even to the park. It was really frightening because bears were even coming into the park where children play. Going out after dark was absolutely out of the question. Even now, although the number of sightings seems to have fallen, at least according to the information we have, you still walk around looking over your shoulder,” she said.
Nikolai Zhilinsky, another local, said people were waiting for the weather to get colder and for the bears to hibernate, but he said people would still be worried even when that happened.
“We are not sure that all of the bears will hibernate. There are too many of them and they are hungry,” he said. He was afraid to go fishing in his boat in case he was attacked by a bear, he added.
Vladimir Vagin, another local, said people feared they could be attacked in their own gardens. He pointed to an area near a raspberry bush in his own garden where he believed a bear had been.
Driving through the settlement after dark, he noted how empty the streets were.
“People don’t go out because they are afraid,” he said. REUTERS

EU should 'hold a mirror to itself' on Russia sanctions before criticizing others — Latvian minister on Trump diesel deal
Editor's note: This article was updated to include comments from Belgian Foreign Minister Maxime Prevot.
LUXEMBOURG — The EU should first consider its own track record on applying sanctions before criticizing others, Latvia's Foreign Minister Baiba Braze said on Oct. 12 when asked to comment on a U.S. deal to buy Russian diesel.
"Let's look at ourselves. The EU first took out two big Russian oligarchs, the biggest ever supporters of (Russian President Vladimir) Putin's regime, from the sanctions," Braze said ahead of a meeting of EU foreign ministers in Luxembourg.
Braze was referring to the Sept. 21 decision to delist Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman from EU sanctions, which was pushed for by Slovakia, Luxembourg, and France.
"Before we criticize the others, obviously we should hold a mirror to the EU itself," Braze said.
The Latvian minister and representatives of other 26 EU countries are expected to vote on two new sanctions packages, one against people who ran in Russia's September election on illegally occupied Ukrainian territory, and another 1,600 listings against Moscow's military-industrial complex — the largest ever single list of new additions.
"Obviously, our position has not changed. Pressure on Russia, sanctions, support to Ukraine. Russia's isolation is the way to peace. We all want peace," Braze said.
Her Lithuanian counterpart, Kestutis Budrys, likewise reiterated his criticism of the EU's previous decision to delist the two oligarchs.
"When we projected our weakness by delisting two prominent oligarchs from our sanctions, we saw how Russia reacted to it. They escalated, both in Ukraine and now in Europe, in our countries," Budrys said.
Belgian Foreign Minister Maxime Prevot also said Belgium regrets the withdrawal of the two names.
"Belgium thinks that, on the contrary, we must intensify them to continue to have an impact," Prevot said.
Belgium, Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania are the only countries known by the Kyiv Independent to have abstained from the vote to delist the two oligarchs, after being among the strongest opponents to the move.
On U.S. President Donald Trump's diesel deal more widely, Estonia's Foreign Minister, Margus Tsahkna, played down the impact.
"I don't think that in real life this diesel deal is actually going to change anything... it is much more connected to the domestic situation in the U.S., with the midterms coming," Tsahkna said.
"We have had this kind of turbulence from President Trump's side to Ukraine before. We need to focus on what we can do, and it is obvious that Europe must do more to support Ukraine," Tsahkna said, echoing his Latvian colleague's position.
Germany's European Affairs Minister Gunther Krichbaum described the Trump deal with Russia as "not our way."
"I would wish that everyone contributes to putting further pressure on Russia... every euro, every dollar that flows from energy purchases here into Putin's cash register helps Russia produce and use new weapons against Ukraine," Krichbaum warned.
And the EU's top diplomat Kaja Kallas called on the U.S. to "put sanctions in place so that we can actually finish this war."
Then, "all these effects of attacks on refineries would not be there, would not be necessary if the war is over," Kallas added.

Fire destroys Paris's oldest covered food market

A fire early on Monday has destroyed the French capital's oldest covered food market, a popular street food venue named after red-clad orphans, authorities said.
The Marché Couvert des Enfants Rouges (Red Children's Market) in the Marais district of Paris, which has existed since 1615, draws its name from the red outfits that orphans wore at a hospital originally located near the site of the market. The market was given its name at the end of the 18th century after the hospital closed in 1772.
The US magazine Food & Wine had ranked it fifth worldwide for street food this year, after other eating spots in London, Bangkok, the French city of Lyon and Mexico City.

The area around the market smelt charred on Monday morning, while a thick layer of firefighting foam covered the pavement in front of one of the market's entrances, an AFP reporter said.
Its main metal gate had survived intact from the blaze.
But beyond the entrance, "the market was completely destroyed", Lieutenant Colonel Pierre de Bouvier told reporters.
"Nothing remains of the covered market," he said, adding that its metal structure had "partially collapsed" inside.
'Heart of Paris'
Authorities said the fire broke out at 3:00am (0100 GMT) but the fire brigade did not receive a call until 4:15am.
Bernard Geliot, a man who lives opposite the market, told AFP he was woken up by the "the noise and the flames" around 4:10am.

Jean-Marc Ferrandery, who managed a cafe inside the market, said he reached a nearby street corner minutes later.
