How India travels: A tale of two wheels and many divides
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
08:02:33 UTC
17:02:33 KST

A quarter-century ago, an advertising campaign presented the two-wheeler as a symbol of “Naye Bharat ki Nayi Tasveer”. But is the India of 2026 still commuting mainly on two-wheelers, has it moved to cars, or are more people walking? The answer depends a great deal on which states people live in, whether they are in a village or a city, and on their gender. All three, in varying degrees, shape how people get around and how much they pay for it.Among some of the extremes featured in India’s National Household Travel Survey, in Puducherry, 92.7% of workers use a two-wheeler as their primary mode. In Nagaland, more than seven in ten walk. West Bengal has the highest published bicycle share, Ladakh stands out for buses, and Sikkim for cars. Conducted from July 2025 to June 2026, the survey covered 4,92,023 households and 18,44,179 people aged six and above.At the national level, the old two-wheeler image still rings true, though the averages hide big regional differences. Among workers who travel at least 1km to work, 42.6% mainly use a two-wheeler, 28.3% walk and 10.7% cycle. The average one-way trip to a fixed workplace takes 25 minutes, and travel costs about ₹785 a month per worker.
India on the move
Rural-urban divide
Between India and Bharat, the numbers shift substantially. In rural India, workers are split almost evenly between two-wheelers at 37.1% and walking at 36.6%.
In cities, the balance tips firmly towards the engine, presumably because of longer distances. Two-wheelers rise to 52.3% and walking falls to 13.5%. Autos, buses and cars all carry a bigger share too.The metro and local-train story is overwhelmingly urban. The survey’s Train/Monorail/Tram category, which includes metro rail and suburban or local trains, carries 5% of urban workers but just 0.4% of rural ones. In urban Maharashtra, home to Mumbai’s suburban railway, the share is 20.7%. It is 16.5% in urban West Bengal and 14.4% in Delhi, known for its metro network.The survey reports Rail separately. That category accounts for just 0.2% of workers nationally, 0.2% in rural India and 0.3% in urban India.
Two Indias, Two Ways to Travel
Students take the bus, workers take the bike
Students and workers commute very differently. In villages, 40.5% of students walk and 18.9% cycle. In cities, buses at 33.7% and autos at 14.4% play a bigger role. Nationally, 37% of students walk, 29.5% take a bus and 15.8% cycle, while only 6.7% use a two-wheeler. Among workers, buses account for just 6.7%, exactly the share two-wheelers have among students.The contrast is sharpest in Kerala, where buses carry 72% of students but 24.9% of workers. Age changes the picture too. Students aged 15 to 29 walk far less than those aged 6 to 14, 22.2% against 47.3%, and cycle more, 21.4% against 11.9%.
Men ride, women walk
Among workers, 47.1% of men use a two-wheeler to get to work. Among women, it is 18.4%. About half of female workers, 50.6%, walk, against 24.1% of men. Women are also much more likely to take the bus, 14% against 5.3%.It would be easy to put this down to rural India, where more people walk. But the divide holds in cities too. There, 57% of male workers use two-wheelers, against 25.8% of women, while women are twice as likely as men to walk, 24% against 11.6%. The bicycle divide is even starker in relative terms. Among workers, 12.3% of men cycle to work but only 1.7% of women do.
The Gender Divide in India’s Commute
Yet among students, the sexes are much closer. Some 17.7% of male students cycle, against 13.4% of female students. Odisha makes the contrast particularly striking. Female students there cycle almost as often as male students, 32.8% against 34%. Among workers, though, the Odisha gap opens up. Some 25.5% of men cycle to work, against 5.8% of women.
Short commutes, steeper city bills
Most work commutes are under half an hour. Some 83.4% of workers travelling to a fixed workplace get there within 30 minutes. Students do even better, with 87.6% reaching school or college within half an hour.However, travelling in cities is much costlier. The average urban trip to work takes 27 minutes, just four more than in villages, but costs ₹1,044 a month against ₹612, about 71% more. Urban students pay about 71% more too, even though their average trip is a shade shorter, 22 minutes against 23 in villages.Even within cities, there are stark differences. Workers in urban West Bengal and urban Delhi spend about the same time getting to work, 36 and 35 minutes on average. But the urban West Bengal worker spends about ₹825 a month, while the urban Delhi worker spends about ₹2,081, roughly two and a half times as much.
Urban West Bengal also has a much bigger long-commute tail. Some 13% need over an hour to commute, against 4.1% across urban India. Hence, lower monthly spending there does not necessarily mean a quicker journey.
City Travel Comes at a Price
The work clock
Across India, 56.5% leave for work between 8am and 10am. In Mizoram and Ladakh, some 97.1% and 95.1% of commuters leave between 8am and 10am.Evenings vary even more. Across India, 31.1% leave work at 6pm or later. In Tamil Nadu it is nearly half, 48.9%, with Gujarat at 45.2% and Delhi at 44.6%. Men are more than twice as likely as women to be leaving that late, 34.1% against 16%.Take work and study out of the picture and far fewer people step out at all. On a given day, 18.7% of people aged six and above travelled at least 1km for some other reason, 23.8% of males and 13.3% of females.They also get there differently. Among men making such trips, 40.1% use a two-wheeler, against 17.6% of women. Among women, 30.4% take an auto or e-rickshaw, against 12.7% of men. For women, autos and e-rickshaws play much the same role that two-wheelers do for men.
For long trips, the bus still rules
In the 28 travel days before the survey, 11.3% of households made an overnight trip of 50km or more that kept a member away from home for more than 24 hours. More than half of these households, 55.8%, used the bus as their primary mode.The separately reported Rail category comes next at 17.7%. Cars account for 15.1% and two-wheelers 8.8%. Another 3.3% fall under Train/Monorail/Tram. Just 0.6% travelled by air.
Few of these trips were about work. Some 70.2% of households making overnight trips travelled for socialising, communication or religious purposes.How far are people travelling? The answer is not provided in the details released so far. The survey collected trip distances, as well as information on licences, household vehicles and bus or rail passes, but none of these appears in the released estimate tables.A quarter-century after the “Naya Bharat” pitch, the two-wheeler still leads the national picture. But the survey shows how much that picture hides, and the big missing piece is how far India travels. At a time when there is demand for metros in every Tier 2 city and road and rail connectivity is better than ever, the full data, when released, will help policymakers make more informed decisions about how to prioritise India’s transport needs.

HMS Dragon went from dry dock to deployment in a week
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12

17:00:18 KST

A Type 45 destroyer sent from maintenance to the eastern Mediterranean in seven days has returned to Portsmouth after 214 days away, having shielded the British bases in Cyprus from drone and missile attack, according to the Royal Navy.
HMS Dragon was in dry dock when she was activated as part of the British response to the conflict in the Middle East, which had brought the sovereign base areas on Cyprus under attack. Working alongside Army and Royal Air Force capabilities, the destroyer formed part of the shield against air attack over the island.
General Sir Gwyn Jenkins, the First Sea Lord and Chief of Naval Staff, said: “HMS Dragon’s seven-month deployment has shown the Royal Navy at its best.
“Deployed at short notice, her crew have protected our bases on the island of Cyprus, safeguarded shipping and worked closely with our allies across the Mediterranean and Middle East. They have operated in some of the world’s most dangerous waters with skill and professionalism. Every member of Dragon’s crew should return home proud. And to the families who supported them throughout, thank you for the sacrifices you have made.”
The ship was later sent east of Suez to provide air defence for a proposed international mission to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, sailing through the Bab el Mandeb Strait at the foot of the Red Sea, where Houthi forces in Yemen have been firing missiles and drones at shipping since 2023. Dragon also ran maritime security patrols in the Indian Ocean and spent a period attached to the French carrier strike group led by FS Charles de Gaulle.
Around 950 friends and family met the ship at Portsmouth Naval Base and along the harbour walls.
Vice Admiral Steve Moorhouse, the Fleet Commander, said: “The resilience, professionalism and fighting spirit of Dragon’s ship’s company throughout the last seven months have been outstanding. In an increasingly uncertain world, we need a warfighting ready Navy that can respond at pace wherever the nation requires. Dragon has shown exactly what that looks like. To the friends, families and loved ones who have supported the ship’s company throughout this challenging deployment, thank you, your contribution has underpinned Dragon’s success.”
Dragon is the third of six Type 45 destroyers, all based at Portsmouth, and the class is the fleet’s first line of defence against aircraft, missiles and drones.

Berlin shopkeeper attacked after displaying posters against antisemitism for Oct. 7 anniversary
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
07:58:51 UTC
16:58:51 KST

A 67-year-old shopkeeper who uses a wheelchair was repeatedly attacked by groups of youths in Berlin's Kreuzberg district after displaying posters opposing antisemitism to mark the third anniversary of the October 7 massacre, Berlin police said on Saturday.
The shopkeeper, Hans-Georg Lindenau, called police to his store on Falckensteinstrasse on Friday evening and reported a series of attacks that began on Wednesday, October 7, according to a police statement.
At approximately 7:20 p.m. on Wednesday, a group of about six youths entered the store, verbally abused Lindenau, and sprayed him with pepper spray.
On Thursday, at around 7 p.m., a group of up to six youths returned to the store and again sprayed him with pepper spray. Lindenau cried out for help, prompting the youths to flee.
However, the suspects returned shortly afterward as Lindenau was preparing to close the shop. According to police, they again sprayed him with pepper spray and beat him. Following the assault, Lindenau complained of pain in his face.
The harassment continued on Friday. Several eyewitnesses told police they saw a group of up to eight youths arrive at the store on electric scooters, punch and kick the entrance door, and then flee. The door was damaged in the incident.
Lindenau runs M99, a store selling literature, posters, and accessories associated with left-wing protest movements.
Speaking to the German newspaper Bild, Lindenau estimated that the attackers were between 10 and 15 years old and said they had asked him whether he was Jewish. He also said that during one of the attacks, the assailants struck him with a starter pistol.
Berlin police said the investigation had been transferred to the State Security Division of the city's criminal police, which is examining a possible antisemitic motive. No arrests were reported.
Over 2,000 antisemitic offenses recorded in Berlin in 2025
The attacks come amid a wave of antisemitism in Berlin since the October 7, 2023, Hamas massacre.
According to Berlin police figures, 2,268 antisemitic offenses were recorded in the city in 2025, an increase of 24.3% compared with the previous year and more than six times the number recorded in 2022.
RIAS, an organization that monitors antisemitic incidents, documented 2,197 incidents in Berlin in 2025, an average of approximately six per day.
Although that represented a decline from the 2,521 incidents recorded in 2024, the figure remained significantly higher than in the years preceding the war.
Last week, ahead of the third anniversary of the massacre, RIAS warned that antisemitism remained widespread in Berlin in 2026.
The organization said Jewish residents were avoiding certain locations and reducing their presence in public spaces because of concerns for their personal safety.

Gaza BoP expects progress after elections, rejects 'Telegraph' conflict-of-interest claims -report

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
07:58:42 UTC
16:58:42 KST

The Gazan Board of Peace expects the "very substantial groundwork" laid for the establishment of post-war governance and reconstruction in the Gaza Strip to transition into full-scale execution after the US midterms, according to a Saturday report by The Telegraph.
Little progress was expected to be made prior to the October 27 Israeli elections and the subsequent midterm elections in the US in early November, the Telegraph reported citing "well-placed" sources.
“It’s not like we’re not moving. There is movement. There’s a lot going on, but maybe nothing that can be seen from the outside as ‘major movement’ before the elections,” a source was quoted as saying.
The report, which was published as an investigation into alleged conflicts of interest within the organization, said that "extensive planning" and "detailed groundwork" have been established over the past six months in preparation for the rebuilding of Gaza.
Board officials insist political obstacles remain the main challenge
The Telegraph report identified overlapping financial interests involving several senior figures in the initiative, including Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, US special envoy Steve Witkoff, and billionaire financier Marc Rowan, raising questions about the relationship between their private business activities and their roles in shaping Gaza's future.
At the center of the investigation is Affinity Partners, the private equity firm founded by Kushner, which has attracted billions of dollars in investments from Gulf sovereign wealth funds, including those associated with Saudi Arabia, Qatar, and the UAE.
According to The Telegraph, Phoenix was the largest institutional shareholder in Smart Shooter, an Israeli defense technology company that recently secured a US military contract worth up to $150 million.
The company manufactures artificial intelligence-assisted rifle sights and other weapons systems, including remotely operated gun platforms and armed drones. Its technology has been used by the IDF during operations in the Gaza Strip.
Despite the concerns raised by the investigation, officials involved in the Board of Peace rejected suggestions that financial interests were influencing its decisions.
Concerns over conflicts of interest were “bull----”, one of the sources told The Telegraph. “We literally have never had a single discussion at any point about business interests.”
Two people familiar with the board's operations told The Telegraph that the principal obstacles to implementing the Gaza plan were political rather than economic.
They said substantial preparations had been completed for a new Palestinian administration, an international stabilization force, and the establishment of a Palestinian police force.
The Telegraph investigation comes as the implementation of Trump's Gaza peace plan remains stalled, despite the ceasefire agreement that entered into effect on October 10, 2025.
Although the initial agreement facilitated the release of the remaining Israeli hostages, Hamas's disarmament, the establishment of new security arrangements, and major reconstruction efforts remain unresolved.
The Board of Peace's implementation roadmap calls for the transfer of Gaza's civilian governance to a Palestinian technocratic administration, alongside security arrangements intended to prevent armed groups from retaining control of the enclave.
A source within the board recently insisted that the organization was continuing to advance its plans, despite limited visible progress ahead of the Israeli election.
Kushner also marked the first anniversary of Trump's peace initiative on Friday, highlighting achievements including the return of the hostages while acknowledging the challenges remaining in Hamas's disarmament.
The latest investigation adds a further issue for the board to address as it attempts to translate months of diplomatic planning into concrete changes on the ground.
While its members maintain that private financial interests have not influenced their diplomatic work, questions surrounding their investments could complicate efforts to establish public confidence in the international body tasked with overseeing Gaza's reconstruction.
Board of Peace: Telegraph publishes 'sensationalization' with little substance
The Board of Peace responded to The Telegraph report. In a statement posted by the organization on X/Twitter, it said the investigation is manufacturing conflict while failing "to identify a single Board of Peace contract, procurement decision, or diplomatic action influenced by the commercial interests it describes. There’s a whole lot of insinuation and very little substance conveniently wrapped into a sensationalized headline."
The statement also pushed back on the report's account of Kushner's private equity firm, Affinity.
"Affinity owns a minority stake in Phoenix, one of Israel's largest publicly traded, highly regulated financial institutions, managing approximately $220 billion across thousands of investments. Through its managed portfolios, Phoenix held shares in a small defense company that later won a *U.S. government* contract, not a Board of Peace contract...There was no Board of Peace involvement, no Board of Peace decision, and zero demonstrated personal benefit."
The Board of Peace statement went on to defend its progress in Gaza.
"Hamas has accepted a disarmament plan, the International Stabilization Force and Gaza’s transitional administration are preparing to deploy, and initial police recruits have been selected. Of course, significant challenges remain, and there is hard work ahead of us, but a year ago none of this architecture existed," the statements read. "These accomplishments would have made for a worthwhile story given the enormous positive consequences for the region."
The statement concluded by saying the bottom line is that the Board of Peace is committed solely to peace. It argued that too many people have become invested in perpetuating conflict - not just terrorists - but also members of an "international architecture" that they claim is invested in continuing a cycle of violence.

Police also arrested 15 others in the public corruption scandal, including the director-general of Kfar Saba's economic development company and several businesspeople. Seven additional suspects were detained for questioning.
Investigators suspect that Saar, other senior officials, and businesspeople were involved in serious corruption offenses, including bribery, fraud, and breach of trust.
According to police, those involved allegedly manipulated public tenders to unlawfully award contracts to local business owners in exchange for benefits and bribes, primarily paid in cash.

Police have arrested or detained 24 suspects in connection with the case so far.
Police investigate alleged involvement of criminal figures
Police suspect that Saar's wife played an unusually prominent role in the bribery scheme and in efforts to ensure certain businesspeople won contracts across various municipal sectors.
Investigators also believe that known criminal figures from central Israel were involved, either directly or indirectly, in the scheme over an extended period.
Police are examining whether these individuals helped secure tender awards and whether they were involved in acts of violence connected to the case.
During the undercover investigation, which lasted more than a year, Lahav 433 investigators used extensive intelligence resources and investigative methods to gather evidence and strengthen their suspicions against those involved.
On Monday morning, as the investigation entered its overt phase, police raided offices, businesses, and suspects' homes, searched premises, and seized money and property.
All suspects were taken to Lahav 433 headquarters for questioning.
Depending on the investigation's progress and findings, police are expected to request extensions of the suspects' detention at the Rishon Lezion Magistrate's Court.
The investigation is being conducted with the involvement of the Economic Department of the State Attorney's Office.

Spain national day military parade: 4,380 troops, 82 aircraft and Dragón armoured vehicles debut
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
07:57:53 UTC
16:57:53 KST

Madrid puts on its finery for the National Day of Spain parade, with general elections looming and tensions high over the housing crisis and migration pressures.
This year's military parade to mark Spain's national day takes place against an unusual political backdrop.
Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez announced last week that an early general election would take place on 29 November and the 2026 parade is being staged with parliament dissolved and the country on the verge of an election campaign.
As is customary, the ceremony is presided over by the Spanish monarchs, King Felipe VI and Queen Letizia, together with their daughters, Princess Leonor and Infanta Sofía.
The route starts next to the Botanical Garden in Madrid, continues along the Paseo del Prado and the Paseo de Recoletos and ends at Plaza de Colón.
More than 4,300 military personnel, 82 aircraft, 183 vehicles and 286 horses will take part.
Joining them are members of Spain's security forces and police and other public bodies, as well as several canine units.
The Dragón, anti-drone systems and a notable absence
The main innovation this year is the debut of three Dragón 8x8 armoured vehicles from the Army, two infantry models and one combat engineer variant, assigned to the King Alfonso XIII 2nd Brigade of the Legion.
Two Marine Corps vehicles equipped with the Aracne anti-drone system and two Asturcón drones from the UME also make their debut, designed for surveillance and tackling forest fires.
They highlight the growing importance of defence against drones, something the war in Ukraine is clearly underlining.
By contrast, no units from Ceuta will parade this year, as the Defence Ministry is keeping them deployed in the enclave because of tensions caused by the illegal entry of thousands of migrants from Morocco in July.
Heroes of the air
The aerial display is the one that draws the most eyes year after year. It will bring together 82 aircraft in 18 formations, led by two F/A-18s from Wing 15, and will include a flypast by the Airbus A330 MRTT escorted by fighter jets, like those that safeguard security beyond our borders, reflecting Spain's commitment to NATO.
Before that, paratroopers will descend along the route: Staff Sergeant Pablo García Matanza will be the lead jumper and Corporal First Class José Antonio Lago will carry the national flag, measuring 24 square metres.
The Spanish Legion is another of the public's favourite moments. This elite force marches at a much faster pace than the rest, around 160 steps per minute compared with 90 for the Regulares units, making it one of the most applauded.
As tradition dictates, the Patrulla Águila will paint the colours of the national flag across the sky, bringing the parade to a close.

Large anti-capitalist protest in Bern causes no major incident
Around 1,000 people took part in an unauthorised demonstration against capitalism and imperialism in the Swiss capital Bern on Sunday. The police, deployed in large numbers, prevented a march through the city centre. There were no major incidents.
The police reached this conclusion on Sunday evening. All roadblocks had been lifted, it announced on X. However, one person had been stopped who felt disturbed by the demonstration and was carrying several knives. They were taken away for further investigation. In addition, the police carried out identity checks and seized materials. There were also incidents of vandalism.
The unidentified organisers had called for a rally to mark the first anniversary of the Gaza demonstration that had escalated. In October 2025, during several hours of violent unrest in the city centre, police officers, demonstrators and bystanders were been injured. There was also extensive damage to property.
More
Thousands join pro-Palestinian protest in Bern amid clashes with police
This time, the organisers had announced that they wanted to avoid a “confrontational demonstration”. They opted for a decentralised approach with several assembly points. The largest crowd gathered in the afternoon at the Rosengarten, a popular meeting place for families and tourists.
Route dictated by the police
From there, the demonstrators marched through the outlying districts towards the Reitschule. They were accompanied by numerous police officers, including some from other cantons. Using loudspeaker announcements, the police made it clear that they would not permit any other route.
A few groups heeded calls on the internet and were out and about elsewhere in the city. The calls mentioned, for example, UBS, the Amthaus and the Raiffeisenbank. However, the cantonal police were also omnipresent in the city centre. Shortly after midday, they had already begun carrying out targeted identity checks, as they reported on the messaging service X.
Against occupations and repression
The rally was generally directed against capitalism and imperialism. The demonstrators called for an end to military occupations and state repression, as well as for the protection of indigenous peoples and the restoration of their historical land rights and rights to self-determination.
More

The procession was characterised by people wearing the keffiyeh – the Palestinian headscarf – and numerous chants of “Free, free Palestine”. Signs bearing the word “Israhell” were also visible, a correspondent for the Keystone-SDA news agency reported.
The violence at the 2025 Gaza demonstration had caused a major political stir. On Sunday, both the cantonal director of security, Philippe Müller, and Alec von Graffenried, the city councillor responsible for the city of Bern, were on site monitoring the events.

Iran rejects that route and demands that all vessels use a northern passage close to its own coastline, seeking permission from its military.

U.S., U.K., Australia, Canada and others condemn Iranian attacks, including "hybrid activities," after air base incident
The foreign ministers of the U.S., the U.K, Australia, Canada and 23 other countries, many in Europe, have released a joint statement condemning hostile activities by Iran on foreign soil.
The statement came on the heels of British Prime Minister Andy Burnham saying a recent security incident at England's RAF Fairford air base, which was until recently home to U.S. long-range bombers, was "almost certainly directed" by Iran's Revolutionary Guard.
The countries said Monday that they "condemn in the strongest terms Iran's use of violent attacks, including the acts of lethal plotting, arson, sabotage, cyber-attacks, and other hybrid activities against us and our partners."
Linking the RAF Fairford incident to other recent attacks in Europe "targeting Jewish communities, Iranian journalists, and U.S. interests," the countries said: "Any attempt by Iran to threaten, silence, intimidate, harass, harm, or coerce people on our territories through proxies or any other means is unacceptable."
"Anyone who conducts hostile activities on behalf of Iran, or any other state, should know that we will take action to identify, investigate, disrupt, and prosecute these acts."
U.K. prime minister says RAF Fairford air base plot "highly likely to have been coordinated in Iran"
The security incident at a British base used by American bombers to strike Iran during the ongoing war was "highly likely to have been coordinated in Iran" by the regime's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Monday.
British police have arrested and then released on bail seven men in connection with the alleged plot. The decision to free the men, whom British police say remain under investigation and monitoring, drew criticism from President Trump, who said in September the incident "might be" linked to Iran.
"I can confirm our assessment that it is highly likely to have been coordinated in Iran, almost certainly directed by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard," Burnham told lawmakers in the U.K. Parliament on Monday.

Saudi Arabia will continue implementing its economic goals and investing in energy infrastructure, industrial capacity and international partnerships despite the challenges presented by the ongoing conflict in the Middle East, Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman said Monday.
Speaking at the World Petroleum Congress in Riyadh, the minister said Saudi Arabia had overcome major challenges throughout its history and would continue to do so, insisting that "fear has no place in the Saudi dictionary."
He said Riyadh's hosting of the international event reflected its position as an "energy security capital," adding that the participation of senior officials and experts from around the world showed international confidence in the kingdom and its ability to ensure the safety of visitors.
He spoke as the Saudi capital's main international airport remained shutdown after a week of strikes by Iran-backed Houthi rebels in neighboring Yemen that killed 20 people.
The minister acknowledged that risks to the global energy system had not disappeared and he said that made international dialogue and cooperation essential to protecting supplies and stabilizing markets.
Bin Salman cited the East-West Crude Oil Pipeline as an example of Saudi long-term strategic planning, saying it provided an alternative route to transport oil amid ongoing impediments in the Persian Gulf and Strait of Hormuz, and that it had helped the kingdom supply global markets during the exceptional circumstances of the war.
He credited state energy giant Saudi Aramco's expertise with helping restore operations quickly when disruptions do occur — which they have on multiple occasions during the U.S.-Iran war. "Criminal prosecutions against lawyers - particularly those handling political, security, and human rights cases - have in recent years become an ongoing pattern," it said.
The arrest was also confirmed by the U.S.-based Human Rights Activists News Agency (HRANA), which said Davoudi's whereabouts were unclear.
Rights groups say Iran has in recent months executed 34 people in connection with the January protests in a bid to intimidate society and prevent further demonstrations. In 2025, the country doubled its use of executions, according to Amnesty International.
BY: CBS/AFP
Saudi capital's airport to remain closed following deadly weekend strikes by Houthis
Saudi Arabia's General Authority of Civil Aviation on Monday extended the temporary closure of King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh after it was struck by Houthi missiles twice over the weekend in attacks that killed 14 people .
GACA said in a statement that it would extend the suspension of all operations at the capital's airport "to complete the necessary procedures to verify the safety of the airport's facilities and their operational readiness, in coordination with the relevant authorities."
The airport has been closed since Saturday, when a Houthi strike killed 13 people, including a U.S. citizen. One more civilian was killed Sunday in a subsequent strike, and attacks last week by the Iran-backed rebel group killed six people.
Iran says U.S. and Israel responsible for Strait of Hormuz disruption
Iranian Foreign Minister Spokesperson Esmail Baghaei blamed the U.S. and Israel on Monday for the ongoing disruption to commercial shipping traffic through the Strait of Hormuz.
During his weekly press briefing, Baghaei noted that before the U.S. and Israel launched joint airstrikes on Iran at the end of February, the Strait of Hormuz was open.
"Everything we are witnessing in the region" was a result of the "actions of the United States and the Israeli regime," including the economic consequences of the disruption to shipping through the strait, Baghaei said.
"If the governments that are concerned about this situation are genuinely serious about their concerns, they should address the party responsible for creating this situation and seize every opportunity to compel the United States to stop its acts of aggression," he said.
Tehran and Washington both claim to have control over the strait, and they are imposing competing blockades in the Persian Gulf and the strait.
President Trump has offered various justifications for launching the war on Iran, but has recently stressed it as a necessary means of ensuring the regime in Tehran cannot build a nuclear weapon.
Houthis step up battle to seize major city of Taiz from Yemen's Saudi-backed government forces
Houthi fighters have ramped up their siege of the Yemeni city of Taiz, where fighting has killed more than 60 people in the past 24 hours, military sources from both sides told the French news agency AFP on Monday.
The Houthis have blocked all exits from the city - a major urban center in Yemen's southwest that, if it falls to the Iranian proxy force would give the Houthis a strategic foothold from which to threaten the de facto Yemeni government capital of Aden, further to the south.
The fighting over the last day alone has killed at least 22 pro-government forces and 40 Houthi fighters, the sources said. The Houthi sources told AFP reinforcements were being sent to the area.
On Sunday, health officials warned of a "humanitarian catastrophe" in Taiz, with medicine, medical equipment and fuel "on the verge of running out."
Taiz is inland from the Red Sea coast and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, where the Houthis captured swathes of territory in a rapid offensive last month.
CBS/AFP
Brent crude oil price creeps back over $105 a barrel despite Trump's Russian diesel announcement
The price of Brent crude oil, the international benchmark, was trading over $105 a barrel early Monday, hitting a two-week high despite President Trump's deeply controversial plan to purchase diesel from Russia.
Mr. Trump said in a social media post on Friday that he'd struck a deal to buy diesel during a phone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin, aiming to tamp down a spike in fuel prices ahead of the Nov. 3 U.S. midterm elections.
But the plan runs counter to U.S. efforts to cut the flow of money Russia gets from oil and gas sales that can be used to pay for its war against Ukraine. A bipartisan group of six U.S. senators called Sunday for the administration to "immediately reverse course" on the plan.
Early Monday, the price of Brent crude edged up about 1% on the day to just over $105 per barrel, while U.S. benchmark crude climbed by a similar amount to just over $92.
CBS/AP
Iran-backed Houthis blame Saudi Arabia for new strikes
Airstrikes targeted two districts in Yemen's Houthi-held capital of Sanaa, the Iran-backed rebel group said Monday, accusing Saudi Arabia of launching the attacks around midnight local time.
A spokesman for Yemen's Houthi-run health ministry said the strikes killed one person and wounded 12 others in Sanaa.
Ministry spokesman Anees al-Asbahi said a strike on a salt factory in Sanaa's Hamadan district killed on eman and wounded eight people. A separate strike on a house wounded a woman and three children, he said.
The rebels' media center said Saudi Arabia carried out the strikes, which came as the Houthis continued to fire missiles and drones at the Saudi capital's primary airport and other infrastructure.
Those attacks have killed at least 20 people at Saudi airports over the last week, including three killed on Oct. 6 and 7 at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh and Abha International Airport; three killed at King Khalid on Oct. 8; 13 people killed by the deadliest single strike on Riyadh's airport Saturday; and one who died in the latest attack on the facility on Sunday.
Saudi Arabian authorities did not immediately confirm their latest strikes in Yemen, but the kingdom has been battling the Iran-backed Houthi rebels for more than a decade in the country.

Iran says it's still reviewing U.S. response to 7-day ceasefire proposal and indirect talks continue
Iran's Foreign Minister spokesperson Esmail Baghaei said Monday that Tehran was still reviewing the U.S. response to a ceasefire proposal Iran put on the table last month, and that the regime continues communicating via mediators.
"I can tell you that the exchange of messages between Iran and the United States through mediators is continuing," Baghaei said, adding that there had "already been considerable discussion of the seven points" in the proposal.
Late last month Iran presented a ceasefire proposal that calls for Tehran to lift its restrictions on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and to resume talks on its nuclear program in seven days if the U.S. lifts its naval blockade of Iranian ports, waives sanctions on Iranian oil sales and observes a ceasefire that includes Lebanon.
President Trump has publicly rejected the Iranian offer, but negotiations have continued between the two sides via mediators.
U.S. embassy in Saudi Arabia urges "extreme caution" in country's airports
The U.S. embassy in Saudi Arabia on Monday urged American citizens to exercise "extreme caution" when using all major airports in the country, following a weekend of strikes that killed a total of 13 people.

U.S. fighter jet strikes, disables commercial vessel in Gulf of Oman, Pentagon says
The U.S. military disabled a Panama-flagged commercial vessel in the Gulf of Oman Saturday by firing on it with a fighter jet, the U.S. military's Central Command said.
According to CENTCOM, the fighter jet fired a "precision munition" at the Ocean Molica, also known as the "Arika Sun," that disabled the "ship's propulsion without harming the crew."
The ship had recently departed an Iranian port. Iran's ports have been under a U.S. blockade since a ceasefire between the two countries collapsed in July.
Four commercial vessels have been disabled by U.S. forces and 135 ships have been turned around since the blockade took effect on July 14, CENTCOM said.
During that period, U.S. forces have also destroyed 10 tankers that are believed to be part of a "shadow fleet" that transports sanctioned Iranian oil and petroleum products, CENTCOM said.
Saudi airport passenger terminal is struck again, a day after 13 were killed
A projectile struck a passenger terminal at the international airport in Riyadh on Sunday, a day after a missile hit the same terminal and killed 13 people, the Saudi-led coalition fighting Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen said. The Houthis claimed responsibility for those attacks and others.
Saudi authorities said one person, described as a Pakistani national, was killed, and 11 were injured in the latest attack on the domestic terminal complex at King Khalid International Airport.
The airport - struck four times in the past five days - has been closed since Saturday's missile attack, which was the deadliest in a Gulf Arab nation since the Iran war began. Over 300 other people were wounded, some critically.
One American citizen was among the victims of Saturday's strike, the U.S. embassy in Riyadh said.

U.S. "may" join Saudi strikes on Houthis, Trump says
President Trump left open the possibility the U.S. will join Saudi Arabia's battle against the Iran-backed Houthis on Saturday.
"We may. We're gonna look at it," Mr. Trump said when asked about the possibility as he left the White House for a campaign rally in Tennessee. "We just found out about the recent attack [on the airport]. So we'll make a decision– we move very quickly."
Mr. Trump was also asked about whether the Houthi strike on Riyadh's airport would change his previously announced decision not to launch any potential strikes on Iran until after the midterms.
"Well, we're gonna take a look," he responded.

EU has not yet seen Russia comply with the energy ceasefire
The European Union welcomes the agreement on an energy ceasefire between Ukraine and Russia, but has yet to see evidence that Moscow is complying with it, and is therefore calling for increased sanctions pressure.
Source: European Pravda, citing remarks made to reporters by Kaja Kallas, High Representative of the EU for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy, before the start of the EU Foreign Affairs Council meeting in Luxembourg on 12 October
Quote from Kallas: "We welcome the energy ceasefire when it holds. We haven't yet seen that also Russia will stick to it. Personally, I would also welcome that the ceasefire would include people not being killed, not only energy."
Details: Kallas emphasised the importance of protecting Ukrainian energy infrastructure ahead of winter and at the same time cautioned against an agreement that would apply only to oil refineries.
"Energy is extremely important because the winter is going to be cold. And so it's important that it doesn't only apply to the refineries, where, you know, Ukraine has one, and Russia has plenty, so that is definitely in the benefit of the Russians," Kallas said.
She also called for continued sanctions pressure on Russia.
Background:
- On 12 October, the foreign ministers of the EU member states are set to approve 1,646 new listings – the largest ever amount of Russia sanctions approved at once.
- On 12 October, the EU Foreign Affairs Council will also discuss the possibility of introducing further restrictions on the movement of Russian diplomats between EU member states, potentially including a complete ban on travel outside the country to which they are accredited.
- On 11 October, Trump claimed that Ukraine and Russia had agreed to an immediate energy ceasefire.
- A White House official told Axios that an "energy ceasefire", as understood by the US president, means that Russia and Ukraine will stop attacks solely on each other's oil refineries.

AI supports global economic growth but may transform 40% of jobs - IMF
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
10:55:58 EEST
16:55:58 KST

AI supports global economic growth but may transform 40% of jobs - IMF
Kyiv • UNN
AI may transform or eliminate 40% of jobs and reduce demand for newcomers. At the same time, it supports global growth at 3%.
Artificial intelligence is supporting global economic growth, but at the same time it could change the nature of 40% of jobs worldwide and reduce demand for entry-level workers. Kristalina Georgieva, Managing Director of the International Monetary Fund, said this during a speech in Bangkok, UNN reports, citing Reuters
Artificial intelligence — you can love it or hate it, but it is already here. It is precisely this shift into a higher gear that allows the global economy to grow at a rate of around 3% — despite the fact that we are being held back by the shock associated with disruptions in energy supplies
Georgieva added that the artificial intelligence investment boom, which has already caused a "demand shock and an investment shock," could accelerate economic growth in developed Asian countries by 0.5–1.0%, and in developing Asian economies by 0.2–0.8%.
At the same time, she said, over time artificial intelligence could result in 40% of jobs being augmented with new functions, devalued or eliminated altogether.
"This is a technology that is fundamentally changing everything. It is completely changing the way we work and live," she said, noting that she now receives a 30-second message every day from an AI assistant about her schedule.
A previous study showed that 10% of jobs in the United States already required artificial intelligence skills.
Although the number of routine jobs is declining, the number of low-paid vacancies is increasing in two low-wage sectors: construction and data center operations.
It is noted that in July, the IMF forecast global economic growth of 3% in 2026. On Tuesday, the Fund will release an updated forecast.

07:55:10 UTC
16:55:10 KST

Russia has lost 1,554,310 troops in Ukraine since the beginning of its full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported on Oct. 12.
The number includes 1,470 casualties that Russian forces suffered over the past day.
According to the report, Russia has also lost 12,410 tanks, 25,527 armored combat vehicles, 162,056 vehicles and fuel tanks, 51,090 artillery systems, 2,209 multiple-launch rocket systems, 1,703 air defense systems, 443 aircraft, 356 helicopters, 2,927 unmanned ground vehicles, 35 ships and boats, and two submarines.
Ukraine's General Staff has not revealed its own losses during the full-scale invasion, citing operational secrecy.
Independent Western think-tank reports agree that the Russian casualties significantly surpass Ukraine's losses, with the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) estimating the ratio to be "roughly 2.5:1 or 2:1."
A January 2026 CSIS report said Ukraine has likely suffered between 500,000 and 600,000 casualties from February 2022 to December 2025, of which between 100,000 and 140,000 are thought to be killed in action.
While Ukrainian officials rarely disclose the figure, President Volodymyr Zelensky told France TV on Feb. 4 that at least 55,000 Ukrainian soldiers have been killed in action since the beginning of the full-scale war, in addition to significant numbers who are missing in action.
The intensity of Russian drone attacks and the fighting has made it extremely difficult for Ukraine to retrieve the bodies of fallen soldiers, which are needed for DNA confirmation.

AI less regulated than milk, Microsoft president says in warning over safety
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
07:52:46 UTC
16:52:46 KST

Artificial intelligence is less regulated than milk and washing machines, the president of Microsoft has said, as the tech industry warns over the safety of AI.
Brad Smith said there should be more safety rules to govern the technology including a legal obligation to a “victim” if their system was breached by rogue AI agents.
He told the BBC: “Right now, your washing machine is subject to more safety rules than AI. Every carton of milk that you see in the grocery store is subject to safety rules and inspection.”
There are growing calls from experts, politicians and regulators for tougher rules to control AI, as well as warnings from Anthropic, Google DeepMind and OpenAI that the pace of the technology’s development should slow.
Smith said AI could be a “tool and a weapon” that should be regulated urgently.
Companies needed “emergency brakes”, also known as “kill switches”, to pause or slow down AI if it grew out of control, he told the BBC.
Microsoft, which operates AI infrastructure and is a shareholder in the ChatGPT owner, OpenAI, is led by chief executive Satya Nadella. On Saturday, Nadella also called for AI models to have an “emergency brake”.
He wrote: “We can’t treat super intelligence as a set of nested black boxes and simply accept or reject its recommendations, answers, and actions.
“We must build contained systems whose behaviour we can observe, limits we can test, and actions we can always contain.”
His and Smith’s comments came as Britain’s AI minister, Kanishka Narayan, prepared to call on firms developing frontier AI to do more to make sure it is safe.
In a speech on Monday, Narayan is expected to say companies building AI models should do more to deal with risk and build better safeguards. He will also say the UK government is preparing to legislate to increase oversight of AI, according to reports.
Experts have said enemy states could also steal unreleased, powerful AI models. Geoffrey Irving, a former chief scientist at the UK’s AI Security Institute, said that AI companies did “not have security that would prevent an adversarial country from stealing the models”.
Meanwhile, cases of rogue AI behaviour continue to come to light. Last week, Anthropic revealed that when it was testing a version of its Claude model, the AI contacted police and falsely claimed it could help solve a murder.

Trying to Make Sense of Trump’s Ukraine Policy
Unknown

Most people were stunned when, ahead of November’s mid-term elections, US President Donald Trump declared that he would allow Russia to sell him diesel in an attempt to reduce the price to consumers in the US, in an obvious attempt to shore up his voter base.
They should not be surprised. This declaration was in line with all other aspects of Trump’s policy towards Russia.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Trump can’t square the circle
Trump has all along blamed Ukraine and President Volodymyr Zelensky for the war, since he could not care less about truth and he supports President Vladimir Putin and Russia.
On three occasions the US has voted with Russia and a dozen rogue states in the United Nations against condemning Moscow for its war of aggression against Ukraine. When Trump became president, he immediately stopped all financial aid and arms to Ukraine. Even more outrageously, he demanded Kyiv should repay for far more than the US had given.
Trump is simply an enemy of Ukraine.
Trump’s problem is that neither the US public nor the republicans in Congress share his love for Putin. He has to tread a careful line, hindering the republicans in Congress from helping Ukraine, while not antagonizing them too directly.
Lindsey Graham’s “Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act.” Was such an “egg of Columbus” [a brilliant, simple, and unexpected solution to a problem that once seemed impossible to solve.]
No less than 86 of 100 senators voted it through, compelling Trump to sign it into law in September. It might have appeared as if the president had to impose severe sanctions on Russia in line with this law, but as with so many US laws it grants the president authority to waive certain sanctions – which I was convinced he would do. The question was only how.
Russia Strikes Ukrainian Power Plants After Trump Announces Energy Truce, Zelensky Says
As so often, Trump attempted to turn the political tables with his decision to allow Russia to export diesel to the US and the world. The obedient US Treasury instantly issued a general license allowing this for half a year, although the US Treasury had prohibited all importation of Russian energy on March 8, 2022, in response to Russia having started its war on Ukraine.
A veiled attempt to circumvent the Graham act
Trump has claimed that this latest measure would reduce US diesel prices, even though the actual volumes involved are tiny in relation to US consumer demand let alone the rest of the world. I believe he has another aim – to see the Graham Act fall by the wayside.
Zelensky reacted by correctly saying that Trump’s new decision was a gift for Putin. It would allow Moscow to finance new military equipment to continue its war. He also said that in taking the deal the Kremlin meant Russia “can keep fighting, to mean they keep dropping bombs on cities.”
Trump has never in any way protested Russia’s terror bombing of Ukraine, its hospitals, schools or residential buildings in any way. He has not even complained when Russia has bombed US-owned civilian enterprises in Ukraine – Cargill, Coca Cola, Pepsi Cola, Flex, Mondelez, etc.
Trump’s deranged reaction
Trump responded to Zelensky with fury. He claimed that Zelensky “wants to make problems for the world” by continuing to authorize attacks on Russian refineries. “He’d better damn well stop,” Trump said, before demanding that Ukraine should “get a new leader who can make a deal.”
His demand that “it’s time for Ukraine to get a new president,” was yet another an anti-democratic statement by Trump. In comparison he continually praises brutal dictators such as Putin, China’s Xi Jingping, North Korea’s Kim Jong Un and Egypt’s Abdel Al-Sissi.
Trump proves US to be an unreliable partner
Trump has broken Western sanctions against Russia in a big way – but he wants to go further in his pro-Putin endeavors. As Trump talked to Putin and eased the sanctions on Russia, his envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner were meeting with a Ukrainian team in Miami. They threatened that the US would stop sharing intelligence with Ukraine unless Ukraine stopped striking Russian oil refineries.
The Ukrainian delegation appears to have ended their meeting after they were informed that Trump had gone behind their backs with his diesel agreement with Putin. But is any intelligence from the pro-Putin Trump administration reliable?
Why would anybody talk to Witkoff and Kushner? Neither is a real public servant. Neither works for the US national interests. They are dealmakers allegedly making hundreds of millions of dollars on dubious business deals in their own interest while posing as government representatives.
On Sept. 5, they met with Putin in the Kremlin. The New York Times reported that Putin offered them and their investment consortium Lukoil’s assets abroad, previously assessed at $22 billion, for a knock down price. The value would rise substantially if the Trump-controlled US Treasury eased sanctions on these assets. It is unclear what Putin wanted in return. Reuters reported that Witkoff and Kushner also discussed purchasing and reviving Nord Stream II for Russian gas deliveries to Europe.
It appears as if the Trump administration, notably Trump himself, Witkoff, and Kushner, have only one interest in Ukraine: to make money. They appear prepared to sell their country to the benefit of Putin while hoping that by ending Western oil and gas sanctions on Russia they will make billions.
The world should unite behind Zelensky
President Zelensky is doing the right thing. He needs to stand up against these crooks, who claim to represent the USA, without unnecessarily provoking them by calling them out for their perfidy.
Meanwhile, he needs to mobilize Ukraine’s true allies and supporters. Europe, Canada and Kyiv’s other friends need to stand up for democracy together with Ukraine.
It is a matter of diplomatic technique how to do this most effectively, but European unity and action are obvious needs.

He made the remarks in his weekly press briefing on Monday, emphasizing, "As long as the United States persists in its blockade and military aggression, security will not return to the strategic Strait of Hormuz."
He seized this opportunity to commemorate the name and memory of famous and outstanding Persian poet Hafez Shirazi, noting that Hafez holds a unique and special place among all poets, especially for Iranians and is considered an inseparable part of Iranian-Islamic culture and civilization.
In response to the recent speech by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Baghaei emphasized that the address should be viewed as part of America’s cognitive warfare against Iran.
Presenting a distorted picture of historical events to justify Washington’s warmongering is both dangerous and an affront to Greek culture and civilization, he emphasized.
"Mr. Rubio has inadvertently acknowledged important realities, including the fact that Iran has endured for millennia. The West as it exists today, in terms of meaning and thought, would not exist had Iranian and Muslim thinkers not served as translators and interpreters of Greek ideas during the dark ages of the Middle Ages. Iranian civilization has consistently established and sustained itself through acts of connection and creation," he underlined.
Addressing Rubio’s advisors with a sarcastic tone, Baghaei noted, “I urge them to present a copy of the * Divan of Hafez * to the US Secretary of State Rubio, so that he may become acquainted with the refinement of Iranian civilization and culture. The United States cannot portray itself as the representative of Western and Greek civilization.”
The Americans and those who drafted Rubio’s speech were aware of these contradictions but deliberately ignored them in order to justify aggression and violence, he said, adding, “Undoubtedly, European countries and those who consider themselves heirs to Western civilization have a duty to clarify their position on this matter.”
In his reaction to Trump’s recent remarks claiming that Iran has lost its leverage in the Strait of Hormuz, he emphasized the gap between American claims and the reality on the battlefield, stating, “What we are witnessing in the Strait of Hormuz today is not an act of leverage by Iran, but rather the result of a direct US attack on our country's territory.”
Noting that Iran has taken necessary measures in accordance with international law and in defense of its national sovereignty, the foreign ministry spokesman reiterated, “As long as the United States persists in its blockade and military aggression, security will not return to this strategic waterway."
Stating that the security of the Strait of Hormuz is of greater importance to Iran than to any other country, Baghaei added, "Through its acts of aggression, the United States has created trouble not only for the region but also for itself and the entire world. This reality must be kept alive in the eyes of global public opinion."
Elsewhere in his remarks, the spokesperson referred to Iran-Russia Cultural Week, describing it as one of the most magnificent joint cultural events between the two nations.
The cultural event was held in four Russian cities and was warmly received by the Russian public and officials as well.
In response to a question regarding Iran's stance on the recent agreement between Russia and the United States concerning diesel fuel, he said, "Each party makes decisions based on its own interests, and we, as the Islamic Republic of Iran, will act based on our own national interests."
Pointing to the contradiction in the American narrative, Baghaei added, “I find it interesting if the Strait of Hormuz issue had indeed been resolved, why was the American side compelled to turn to Russia to purchase oil?"
The foreign ministry spokesman then pointed to the recent telephone conversation between Iran’s Foreign Minister Araghchi and his Saudi counterpart bin Farhan, emphasizing, “It is natural for the media to make their own claims. Iran’s consultations with regional countries are ongoing, and we are deeply concerned about recent developments in the Arabian Peninsula.”
Iran once again declares its readiness to assist in any way with dialogue between the Yemeni and Saudi sides. Continued tension serves only the interests of the Zionist regime in the region, and Iran does not accept the continuation of war between two Islamic nations. The people of Yemen have the right to live a dignified life in an atmosphere free from pressure and tension, he continued.
In response to a question regarding the details of the US response to Iran’s seven-day plan and whether a reply has been conveyed to the mediators, Baghaei stated that exchange of messages through mediators is ongoing. What was raised on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly and is known as Iran’s seven-day plan reflected Iran’s legitimate and legal demands.
Lifting the naval blockade, halting the war on all fronts, releasing Iran's frozen assets, and everything else agreed upon in the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding will be raised as Iran's indisputable rights in any negotiation, he stipulated.
Regarding the recent meeting between the presidents of Iran and Russia and Vladimir Putin’s subsequent phone call with Donald Trump, the foreign ministry spokesperson stated that Iran’s consultations with Russia concerning the nuclear issue are nothing new. Russia played a positive and constructive role in reaching the JCPOA understanding. A relationship based on mutual trust is a valuable asset shared by the two countries, and Iran is committed to preserving and strengthening this bond.
Baghaei emphasized that Pakistan and Qatar continue to play a mediating role between Iran and the United States.
In another part of the press conference, Baghaei pointed to the double standards displayed by regional and European countries regarding the attacks on Yemen and Saudi Arabia, stating this is not the first time Iran has witnessed a dual approach by global powers toward international issues.
Regarding the detention of students in France following the student protest, he stated that Iran has unequivocally condemned this action and made its position clear. Iran also pursued the matter with the French Embassy in Tehran during a meeting convened by the country’s human rights division and conveyed to them its concerns regarding the gross violation of human rights in France.
The French government must address the detention of five to six thousand individuals, the use of violence against students, and the presence of police forces inside classrooms, Baghaei stated.

Financial Times: US threatened to cut off weapons deliveries and intelligence sharing with Ukraine unless Kyiv stopped striking Russian oil refineries
The United States threatened to cut off intelligence sharing with Ukraine and halt the PURL mechanism, through which European countries buy American weapons for Kyiv, unless Ukraine stopped striking Russian oil refineries, sources told the Financial Times.
Calls making these demands came in on Saturday, October 10, and on Sunday, according to the agency’s sources.
“They are calling Kyiv… they are calling everyone [in Europe],” said an official who received a call from a representative of the U.S. Defense Department.
Donald Trump announced on October 11 that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an energy ceasefire. The Kremlin did not officially comment on the situation.

Premier Giorgia Meloni have both reaffirmed Italy's closeness to

on Sunday that he will have surgery on lung nodule in the next
few days.

which also treated his predecessors from John Paul II onwards,
and the Vatican said it should take about a week for him to

peaceful convalescence and a swift, complete recovery".

that of the Italian Government" for the "trial" Leo is facing.

their support and affection," she said.

The time to start bright light therapy is October, expert says
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
10:47:48 EEST
16:47:48 KST

People who suffer from negative symptoms in the autumn and winter should already start using bright light therapy lamps in October, according to research professor Timo Partonen, from health agency THL.
By October, the autumnal equinox has already passed and daylight hours get slightly shorter day by day until the winter solstice December 21 — at least in the Northern Hemisphere.
The increased darkness particularly affects people in Finland, where sunlight can be absent entirely for months in its northernmost areas.
According to Partonen, October is the most typical month for seasonal symptoms to start appearing.
The symptoms can include deteriorated sleep quality, reduced sociability, lowered mood, decreased physical activity as well as sugar cravings, particularly in the afternoon or evening.
Seasonal symptoms often worsen in November and typically disappear on their own only in February.
Spending time near bright light is the primary way to ease seasonal symptoms, Partonen explained.
"When you spend time in bright light regularly in the mornings, symptoms may ease already within the first week," he said.
Some seasonal sufferers use bright light lamps throughout the winter. Partonen recommends first-timers try a bright light lamp — especially if they've noticed symptoms that they don't have in the spring or summer.
Bright light eases seasonal symptoms: it reduces fatigue, improves mood and increases physical activity and sociability. Initially it often eases afternoon and evening sugar cravings.
"That's usually a sign that the bright light is working. If there are other seasonal symptoms alongside the sugar cravings, those too generally start to ease after this," he explained.
Most people suffering from seasonal symptoms get clear relief from bright light, says Partonen. If a bright light lamp doesn't help ease seasonal symptoms or treat their more severe form — Seasonal Affective Disorder — it's worth seeing a doctor.
Using a bright light lamp carries hardly any risks if the lamps are used correctly. However, two things are worth bearing in mind, according to Partonen.
People with eye conditions should check with a doctor, who has diagnosed the condition, that using a bright light lamp as directed is safe.
Using a bright light lamp can also potentially cause overstimulation in people prone to strong mood swings.

Germany news: Söder demands CDU supports of the AfD in Saxony-Anhalt reveal themselves
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
07:46:00 UTC
16:46:00 KST

Merz: Trump Russia diesel deal 'out of question' for Europe
Published October 12, 2026last updated October 12, 2026
What you need to know
- Merz said the order of the day was new EU sanctions on Russia not diesel deals with Russia, saying Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelenskyy 'can rely on Germany'
- Bavarian state premier Markus Söder has accused some conservative bloc members in Saxony-Anhalt of being cowards
- Bärbel Bas, Germany's education minister and the co-chair of the SPD, has resigned amid coalition infighting with Chancellor Merz's CDU
- The winner of Germany's most prestigious literary peace prize has cricized the country's support of the Israeli government
Here are the latest headlines and reports from across Germany on Monday, October 12:
Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add DW as a Preferred Source on Google.
German fighter jets to take part in NATO nuclear drill
Germany is sending three Tornado fighter jets to Italy to take part in NATO's annual nuclear deterrence exercise, Steadfast Noon, which begins on Tuesday.
The aircraft, normally stationed at Büchel air base in western Germany, have been deployed to Aviano Air Base in northern Italy, a German Air Force spokesperson told the DPA news agency.
Several dozen German military personnel will also participate in the exercise, which rehearses NATO's ability to deploy nuclear weapons in the event of a conflict.
No live nuclear weapons will be used. NATO says the exercise is routine, unrelated to current world events and not directed against any particular country.
The alliance has not disclosed details of this year's scenario. Last year's exercise involved around 2,000 personnel and more than 70 aircraft.
Germany participates in NATO's nuclear-sharing arrangements, under which German aircraft could deliver US nuclear weapons in a conflict.
Germany's Merz slams Trump's Russian diesel deal
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has criticized US President Donald Trump's agreement to import Russian diesel, calling for tougher sanctions on Moscow instead.
"We take note of the agreement between the United States and Russia on diesel exports," Merz said in Berlin on Monday. "For Germany and Europe, such a decision is out of the question."
Merz said Russia would only negotiate seriously under pressure and called for further sanctions following Russian attacks on Ukraine's civilian energy infrastructure.
He also questioned Trump's announcement of an immediate halt to Russian and Ukrainian attacks on each other's energy facilities, saying Moscow had responded with massive strikes.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Trump's announcement of the partial ceasefire came as news to him, while the Kremlin has not confirmed that it has taken effect.
Merz reaffirmed Germany's support for Ukraine and said efforts to achieve a just and lasting peace would be discussed at this week's EU summit.
Tennis: Alexander Zverev will be world number 1 for the first time
The long-awaited mathematical confirmation has arrived: Germany's Alexander Zverez will take the top spot in the men's singles tennis rankings at the end of the year.
A shock straight set defeat for Carlos Alcaraz on Monday in Shanghai against unseeded Belgian player Zizou Bergs made Zverev claiming the number 1 ranking innevitable.
Aged 29, Zverev will be the oldest player ever to take over the top spot for the first time in his career.
He said that knowing he'd finish the season at number was a "dream come true," and said he'd concentrate on finishing the season "in style."
It's been a year of breakthroughs for Zverev, whose career to date had long seen him living in the shadows of greats like Roger Federer, Rafael Nadal and Novak Djokovic, and later Jannik Sinner and Carlos Alcaraz.
He won his first two Majors, at the French Open and then the US Open, and was also runner-up to Sinner at Wimbledon.
Sinner has not played since that final because of injury. Coupled with some patchy form from Alcaraz, this opened the door for Zverev to push to overtake them in the annual rankings.
The last — and only — German man to top tennis' world rankings was Boris Becker, who had two brief mid-season stints at number 1 in 1991. He did not finish the year as number 1, though.
Angelique Kerber also spent a combined seven and a half months at women's singles number 1 across three stints between 2016 and 2017, including at the end of the 2016 campaign. Steffi Graf meanwhile dominated the women's rankings for much of the period between 1987 and 1997.
SPD, Greens and Left party begin coalition talks in Mecklenburg-Lower Pomerania
The Social Democrats (SPD) have opened up coalition talks with the Greens and the Left party in Germany's northeastern state of Mecklenburg-Lower Pomerania, sources confirmed to local media.
The three parties have already held exploratory discussions on working together and received permission from party leadership bodies to move forward.
This comes several weeks after the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) came in first in the state election with 38.2% of the vote. However, without an outright majority and no other parties willing to work with them, they were unable to form a government.
Together the SPD, Greens and Left will hold 32 seats in the 71-member state parliament, giving them three more seats than the AfD.
The regional party leaders, including incumbent SPD state premier Manuela Schwesig, are expected to issue a joint statement later today.
The trio faces a tight turnaround to secure a coalition agreement, as the state's new parliament will sit for the first time on October 20, after which there is a four-week deadline to hold an election for premier.
Klingbeil cancels India trip, calls for SPD leadership vote
Vice-Chancellor and Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil has nixed a planned trip to India, saying that the Social Democrats need to hold a new vote for party leadership.
His announcement came shortly after the resignation of his party co-chair Bärbel Bas.
Klingbeil did not say whether he would run again, but confirmed that the rest of the party's top officials agreed the election was necessary.
Wadephul hails EU Russia sanctions
German Foreign Minsiter Johann Wadephul praised an "unprecedented sanctions blow" the European Union has levelled against Moscow.
"We are making it harder for Putin to continue his war of aggression in violation of international law, and his cynical attempt to wear down Ukraine's civilian population through murderous bombing campaigns," Wadephul said in a statement.
On Monday, EU foreign ministers met in Luxembourg to finalize the sanctions package.
It targets some 1,600 individuals and businesses related to Russia's war effort, and another 77 people and groups related to what the EU sees as illegal elections in occupied Ukrainian terrorities.
"We are increasing the pressure until Putin is ready to negotiate seriously about peace in Ukraine," Wadephul said, though he missed the Luxembourg meeting to participate in a CDU party summit in Berlin.
Frankfurt Book fair prize winner criticizes Germany's stance on Israel
Franco-British lawyer and author Philippe Sands accepted the prestigious Peace Price presented every year at the Frankfurt Book Fair, the premiere event of the German publishing industry.
Presdent Frank-Walter Steinmeier praised Sands as a committed humanist "who, despite growing resistance, fights tirelessly for human rights, justice and mutual understanding."
A professor of law at University College London and human rights lawyer at the International Court of Justice in The Hague, Sands used his acceptance speech to criticize Germany's "inappropiate silence" on the Israel's actions in the Gaza Strip and the occupied West Bank.
"It's not antisemitic. It's not anti-Israel. It's the truth," he said of the government's behavior.
You can read more about Sands and his speech here.
Cologne teenager badly injured while 'trainsurfing'
Public broadcaster WDR has said that 14-year-old was badly injured on Sunday night in Cologne after engaging in "trainsurfing," or attempting to ride on the top of a moving train.
The boy is reportedly fighting for his life at a local hospital after being struck by a powerful electrical current moving between the train and the overhead wires that power it. Authorities believe he could have been hit by 15,000 volts.
Trainsurfing is, of course, illegal, and still uncommon. However, authorities are worried that social media videos may encourage young people to attempt the dangerous stunt.
Söder: Those who voted for AfD speaker should show 'backbone'
"Do you want to go somewhere else? Then just say so," Bavarian leader Markus Söder said during an interview with public broadcaster ARD.
As a member of the CSU, the Bavarian sister party of Chancellor Merz's Christian Democrats (CDU), Söder was referencing bloc members in the state of Saxony-Anhalt who are believed to have voted for a member of the far-right in a secret ballot.
Last week, Tobias Rausch of the Alternative for Germany (AfD) — whose chapter in Saxony-Anhalt is classified as right-wing extremist — was elected state parliamentary speaker.
This marked the first time the AfD has seen a member elected to such a position, and the first time in postwar Germany that a right-wing extremist has risen to this rank.
The populist BSW party had declared their intention to support Rausch's nomination alongside the AfD, but his win with 48 votes means that other lawmakers must have voted for him too. It is strongly suspected that these were members of the conservative CDU.
Rausch's election prompted outrage across Germany, including from CDU members who have accused their colleagues of abandoning the so-called "firewall" — the agreement amongst the country's mainstream parties not to support the AfD.
Söder called it "pretty poor form," from the CDU members in Saxony-Anhalt, saying they should "at least have the backbone" to make their decision public.
Labor minister and SPD co-chair Bärbel Bas resigns
Citing "open attacks" by members of senior coalition partners the CDU, Bärbel Bas has stepped down as co-leader of the SPD and as federal labor minister.
She also said a recent death in the family had influenced her decision to resign.
You can read our full report on the latest trial for Chancellor Merz's coalition here.
