Merz: Trump Russia diesel deal 'out of question' for Europe
Published October 12, 2026last updated October 12, 2026
What you need to know
- Merz said the order of the day was new EU sanctions on Russia not diesel deals with Russia, saying Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelenskyy 'can rely on Germany'
- Bavarian state premier Markus Söder has accused some conservative bloc members in Saxony-Anhalt of being cowards
- Bärbel Bas, Germany's education minister and the co-chair of the SPD, has resigned amid coalition infighting with Chancellor Merz's CDU
- The winner of Germany's most prestigious literary peace prize has cricized the country's support of the Israeli government
Here are the latest headlines and reports from across Germany on Monday, October 12:
Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add DW as a Preferred Source on Google.
German fighter jets to take part in NATO nuclear drill
Germany is sending three Tornado fighter jets to Italy to take part in NATO's annual nuclear deterrence exercise, Steadfast Noon, which begins on Tuesday.
The aircraft, normally stationed at Büchel air base in western Germany, have been deployed to Aviano Air Base in northern Italy, a German Air Force spokesperson told the DPA news agency.
Several dozen German military personnel will also participate in the exercise, which rehearses NATO's ability to deploy nuclear weapons in the event of a conflict.
No live nuclear weapons will be used. NATO says the exercise is routine, unrelated to current world events and not directed against any particular country.
The alliance has not disclosed details of this year's scenario. Last year's exercise involved around 2,000 personnel and more than 70 aircraft.
Germany participates in NATO's nuclear-sharing arrangements, under which German aircraft could deliver US nuclear weapons in a conflict.
Germany's Merz slams Trump's Russian diesel deal
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has criticized US President Donald Trump's agreement to import Russian diesel, calling for tougher sanctions on Moscow instead.
"We take note of the agreement between the United States and Russia on diesel exports," Merz said in Berlin on Monday. "For Germany and Europe, such a decision is out of the question."
Merz said Russia would only negotiate seriously under pressure and called for further sanctions following Russian attacks on Ukraine's civilian energy infrastructure.
He also questioned Trump's announcement of an immediate halt to Russian and Ukrainian attacks on each other's energy facilities, saying Moscow had responded with massive strikes.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Trump's announcement of the partial ceasefire came as news to him, while the Kremlin has not confirmed that it has taken effect.
Merz reaffirmed Germany's support for Ukraine and said efforts to achieve a just and lasting peace would be discussed at this week's EU summit.
Tennis: Alexander Zverev will be world number 1 for the first time
The long-awaited mathematical confirmation has arrived: Germany's Alexander Zverez will take the top spot in the men's singles tennis rankings at the end of the year.
A shock straight set defeat for Carlos Alcaraz on Monday in Shanghai against unseeded Belgian player Zizou Bergs made Zverev claiming the number 1 ranking innevitable.
Aged 29, Zverev will be the oldest player ever to take over the top spot for the first time in his career.
He said that knowing he'd finish the season at number was a "dream come true," and said he'd concentrate on finishing the season "in style."
It's been a year of breakthroughs for Zverev, whose career to date had long seen him living in the shadows of greats like Roger Federer, Rafael Nadal and Novak Djokovic, and later Jannik Sinner and Carlos Alcaraz.
He won his first two Majors, at the French Open and then the US Open, and was also runner-up to Sinner at Wimbledon.
Sinner has not played since that final because of injury. Coupled with some patchy form from Alcaraz, this opened the door for Zverev to push to overtake them in the annual rankings.
The last — and only — German man to top tennis' world rankings was Boris Becker, who had two brief mid-season stints at number 1 in 1991. He did not finish the year as number 1, though.
Angelique Kerber also spent a combined seven and a half months at women's singles number 1 across three stints between 2016 and 2017, including at the end of the 2016 campaign. Steffi Graf meanwhile dominated the women's rankings for much of the period between 1987 and 1997.
SPD, Greens and Left party begin coalition talks in Mecklenburg-Lower Pomerania
The Social Democrats (SPD) have opened up coalition talks with the Greens and the Left party in Germany's northeastern state of Mecklenburg-Lower Pomerania, sources confirmed to local media.
The three parties have already held exploratory discussions on working together and received permission from party leadership bodies to move forward.
This comes several weeks after the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) came in first in the state election with 38.2% of the vote. However, without an outright majority and no other parties willing to work with them, they were unable to form a government.
Together the SPD, Greens and Left will hold 32 seats in the 71-member state parliament, giving them three more seats than the AfD.
The regional party leaders, including incumbent SPD state premier Manuela Schwesig, are expected to issue a joint statement later today.
The trio faces a tight turnaround to secure a coalition agreement, as the state's new parliament will sit for the first time on October 20, after which there is a four-week deadline to hold an election for premier.
Klingbeil cancels India trip, calls for SPD leadership vote
Vice-Chancellor and Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil has nixed a planned trip to India, saying that the Social Democrats need to hold a new vote for party leadership.
His announcement came shortly after the resignation of his party co-chair Bärbel Bas.
Klingbeil did not say whether he would run again, but confirmed that the rest of the party's top officials agreed the election was necessary.
Wadephul hails EU Russia sanctions
German Foreign Minsiter Johann Wadephul praised an "unprecedented sanctions blow" the European Union has levelled against Moscow.
"We are making it harder for Putin to continue his war of aggression in violation of international law, and his cynical attempt to wear down Ukraine's civilian population through murderous bombing campaigns," Wadephul said in a statement.
On Monday, EU foreign ministers met in Luxembourg to finalize the sanctions package.
It targets some 1,600 individuals and businesses related to Russia's war effort, and another 77 people and groups related to what the EU sees as illegal elections in occupied Ukrainian terrorities.
"We are increasing the pressure until Putin is ready to negotiate seriously about peace in Ukraine," Wadephul said, though he missed the Luxembourg meeting to participate in a CDU party summit in Berlin.
Frankfurt Book fair prize winner criticizes Germany's stance on Israel
Franco-British lawyer and author Philippe Sands accepted the prestigious Peace Price presented every year at the Frankfurt Book Fair, the premiere event of the German publishing industry.
Presdent Frank-Walter Steinmeier praised Sands as a committed humanist "who, despite growing resistance, fights tirelessly for human rights, justice and mutual understanding."
A professor of law at University College London and human rights lawyer at the International Court of Justice in The Hague, Sands used his acceptance speech to criticize Germany's "inappropiate silence" on the Israel's actions in the Gaza Strip and the occupied West Bank.
"It's not antisemitic. It's not anti-Israel. It's the truth," he said of the government's behavior.
You can read more about Sands and his speech here.
Cologne teenager badly injured while 'trainsurfing'
Public broadcaster WDR has said that 14-year-old was badly injured on Sunday night in Cologne after engaging in "trainsurfing," or attempting to ride on the top of a moving train.
The boy is reportedly fighting for his life at a local hospital after being struck by a powerful electrical current moving between the train and the overhead wires that power it. Authorities believe he could have been hit by 15,000 volts.
Trainsurfing is, of course, illegal, and still uncommon. However, authorities are worried that social media videos may encourage young people to attempt the dangerous stunt.
Söder: Those who voted for AfD speaker should show 'backbone'
"Do you want to go somewhere else? Then just say so," Bavarian leader Markus Söder said during an interview with public broadcaster ARD.
As a member of the CSU, the Bavarian sister party of Chancellor Merz's Christian Democrats (CDU), Söder was referencing bloc members in the state of Saxony-Anhalt who are believed to have voted for a member of the far-right in a secret ballot.
Last week, Tobias Rausch of the Alternative for Germany (AfD) — whose chapter in Saxony-Anhalt is classified as right-wing extremist — was elected state parliamentary speaker.
This marked the first time the AfD has seen a member elected to such a position, and the first time in postwar Germany that a right-wing extremist has risen to this rank.
The populist BSW party had declared their intention to support Rausch's nomination alongside the AfD, but his win with 48 votes means that other lawmakers must have voted for him too. It is strongly suspected that these were members of the conservative CDU.
Rausch's election prompted outrage across Germany, including from CDU members who have accused their colleagues of abandoning the so-called "firewall" — the agreement amongst the country's mainstream parties not to support the AfD.
Söder called it "pretty poor form," from the CDU members in Saxony-Anhalt, saying they should "at least have the backbone" to make their decision public.
Labor minister and SPD co-chair Bärbel Bas resigns
Citing "open attacks" by members of senior coalition partners the CDU, Bärbel Bas has stepped down as co-leader of the SPD and as federal labor minister.
She also said a recent death in the family had influenced her decision to resign.

EU foreign policy chief says Trump's diesel deal must not benefit Moscow
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
07:45:37 UTC
16:45:37 KST

EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas on Monday called on the US to align with the bloc's sanctions policy against Russia, saying coordinated pressure from Washington and European partners could help bring an end to the war in Ukraine.
Speaking to reporters ahead of the EU Foreign Affairs Council meeting in Luxembourg, Kallas said efforts to pressure Moscow would be more effective if the US joined the EU and UK in imposing further sanctions on Russia.
“It would work so much better if our partners from the UK and from the US would be aligned with us,” she said, adding that Washington's adoption of the Graham bill on Russia could significantly strengthen pressure on Moscow.
"We could really put the pressure so that Russia will finish this war," Kallas said.
She said sanctions had deprived Russia of €1 trillion ($1.1 trillion), adding that measures targeting the country's so-called shadow fleet were also making it increasingly difficult for Moscow to fund the war.
On US President Donald Trump's announcement of an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine, Kallas said the EU welcomed the arrangement but had yet to see whether Moscow would comply.
She stressed the ceasefire should extend beyond energy infrastructure to include an "end to the killing of people."
Kallas also questioned the scope of the arrangement, noting that Ukraine had one refinery while Russia had several, and said the ceasefire should not benefit Moscow.
Trump said on Sunday that he had struck a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin during a phone call, under which Moscow would supply more than 4 million tons of diesel to global markets.
The US Treasury Department temporarily waived sanctions on Russian diesel through April 2027 under a general licence. Zelenskyy condemned the agreement, saying "gifts to Putin will not bring peace."
On Trump's call for new elections in Ukraine, Kallas recalled that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy had indicated his readiness to hold elections as soon as possible if a ceasefire were established.

Israel not expected to attack Iran before elections, opposition leader says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12

16:45:20 KST

Abdel Ra’ouf Arnaout and Sahin Demir
12 October 2026•Update: 12 October 2026
Israeli opposition leader Yair Lapid said Monday that intelligence available to him does not indicate that Israel is expected to go to war with Iran before the country’s parliamentary elections on Oct. 27.
Lapid accused Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of using warnings about a possible war with Iran or an attack on Israel as part of his election campaign.
As opposition leader, Lapid receives security and military briefings from Netanyahu, particularly concerning major military operations or the possibility of war.
Speaking to local radio station 103 FM, Lapid criticized Netanyahu’s handling of security threats ahead of the elections.
“The prime minister can dominate the agenda by warning of an imminent terrorist attack or a war with Iran. Whether that is good for Israel is a question voters should ask themselves,” he said.
Israeli media reported that Netanyahu chaired a security meeting Sunday evening to discuss developments concerning Iran.
“Based on the intelligence available to me, no war with Iran is expected before the elections,” Lapid added.
The Oct. 27 elections are widely viewed as a major political test for Netanyahu and opposition parties seeking to form an alternative government.
Recent opinion polls have shown opposition parties ahead of Netanyahu’s bloc, but without a clear parliamentary majority to form a government.
On Sept. 29, Netanyahu warned that Israel’s enemies might attempt attacks ahead of the elections, prompting Lapid to accuse him of spreading fear for political purposes.
Following a security briefing with Netanyahu, Lapid said there was no reason to alarm the public and insisted that the elections should proceed as scheduled.

Iran offers to mediate Saudi-Houthi talks as attacks mount
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
07:45:19 UTC
16:45:19 KST

Breadcrumb
Iran offers to mediate Saudi-Houthi talks amid mounting attacks
Iran has offered to help launch talks between Saudi Arabia and Houthi rebels as increasing attacks on the kingdom and renewed airstrikes on Yemen threaten to deepen the regional conflict.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi made the offer during a phone call with his Saudi counterpart, Prince Faisal bin Farhan, on Sunday evening, according to a statement from Iran's foreign ministry.
Araghchi expressed Tehran's readiness to provide all forms of assistance to facilitate dialogue between Riyadh and the Iran-backed Houthis and support efforts to reach a political settlement.
The two ministers also discussed the latest regional developments, with Araghchi expressing concern over rising tensions and warning that continued reliance on military action would further complicate the situation.
He stressed that the region's crises could not be resolved through military means and urged greater emphasis on political solutions.
Separately, Saudi Arabia's foreign ministry confirmed the call on Sunday, saying the two ministers had discussed the latest regional escalation and efforts to address it.
However, the Saudi statement provided no further details about the diplomatic initiatives discussed or whether any agreements had been reached.
The diplomatic contact came amid intensifying hostilities between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis, including repeated missile and drone attacks targeting Saudi airports.
A recent Houthi attack on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh killed at least 12 people and injured 309 others, while Abha airport in southern Saudi Arabia has also been targeted.
On Sunday evening, the Saudi-led coalition reported another attack on King Khalid International Airport, saying an unidentified projectile struck Terminal 4 and sparked a fire.
Coalition spokesman Turki al-Maliki said on X that emergency crews were working to contain the blaze. He subsequently announced that Saudi air defences had intercepted and destroyed a cruise missile near the airport.
Meanwhile, airstrikes targeted two districts of Yemen's capital, Sanaa, around midnight on Monday, according to the Houthis.
The group's media centre said the strikes hit the Hamdan and Thourah districts and blamed Saudi Arabia for the attacks, although it provided no further details.
The strikes come amid renewed military operations by the Saudi-led coalition and Yemeni government forces against Houthi positions in Sanaa, Taiz and areas surrounding the strategically important Bab al-Mandeb Strait.
The intensifying confrontation coincides with growing threats to maritime security elsewhere in the region.
India's foreign ministry said on Monday that two Indian sailors were missing after a drone struck the commercial tanker MT PETRO DOLPHIN near the Strait of Hormuz on Sunday.
The vessel was carrying 11 Indian crew members when it was attacked.
A second tanker, the Marshall Islands-flagged MT VALTHERA, was also struck by an unidentified projectile, causing a fire on board. All 11 Indian sailors aboard that vessel were reported safe.
India condemned the attacks on commercial shipping, warning that they risked further destabilising an already volatile region.
The latest developments have also prompted calls for greater security cooperation among Gulf states.
Anwar Gargash, a diplomatic adviser to the United Arab Emirates leadership, called on Monday for joint Gulf action to counter attacks by Iran and its allied groups.
He warned that attacks on Saudi Arabia threatened the security of the UAE and other Gulf countries, stressing that their security was indivisible.

Turkish auto production shrinks 6 percent in January-September
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
07:44:28 UTC
16:44:28 KST

Türkiye’s automotive production declined in the first nine months of 2026, while the domestic market also contracted, according to data released by the Automotive Manufacturers Association (OSD).
Total vehicle production fell 5.9 percent year-on-year in the January-September period to 971,159 units, while passenger car output dropped 17 percent to 528,366 units.
During the same period, the overall automotive market shrank 13 percent from a year earlier to 832,521 units. The passenger car market contracted 15.5 percent to 627,977 units.
Imported vehicles continued to dominate the passenger car market, accounting for 65 percent of sales in the first nine months of the year.
However, sales of imported passenger cars fell 23 percent year-on-year, while sales of domestically produced passenger cars increased 2 percent. Imported light commercial vehicle sales declined 9 percent, whereas domestic light commercial vehicle sales rose 11 percent, said OSD.
Despite weaker production and domestic sales, automotive exports increased in value terms. Total automotive exports rose 3 percent year-on-year to $30.5 billion in the January-September period.
Passenger car exports, however, declined 8 percent to $7.8 billion during the same period.
In September alone, total vehicle production increased 5.1 percent year-on-year to 129,571 units, while passenger car production decreased 3.8 percent to 70,197 units.

Meanwhile, "a U.S. deal to purchase some Russian diesel is a drop in the ocean", he added.

Trump also called for Ukraine to "get a new leader" after Volodymyr Zelensky slammed Washington's easing of Russian diesel sanctions, as Trump grapples with high fuel prices weeks before midterm elections in the world's biggest economy.
Saudi Arabia's energy minister acknowledged meanwhile that the kingdom's infrastructure and resilience had been tested following a wave of deadly attacks by Yemen's Houthis.

Also in view this week for markets is the start of the corporate earnings season, with U.S. banking giants JP Morgan, Goldman Sachs and Bank of America due to report.
Tech giants will follow later in October and November, with traders keen to get an idea on the outlook for the AI sector as it invests vast sums despite growing concerns over the technology.

Fuel prices at filling stations on October 12: where fuel has become more expensive
Kyiv • UNN
At Ukrnafta, A-95 Energy gasoline increased in price to UAH 91.90, while gas rose to UAH 44.90. KLO, WOG, OKKO, SOCAR, and UPG did not change their prices.
On October 12, some Ukrainian fuel station networks revised their fuel prices. UNN reports which ones increased their prices and which operators kept them at the previous level.
Details
The most noticeable price changes occurred in the Ukrnafta and BRSM-Nafta networks. At the latter, autogas became 19 kopecks cheaper per liter, while the price of A-95 gasoline and diesel fuel increased by up to UAH 1 per liter.
At Ukrnafta, A-95 Energy gasoline increased by UAH 3 to UAH 91.90 per liter. Autogas also increased in price, now costing UAH 44.90 per liter. At the same time, standard A-95 gasoline and other products remained unchanged.
The KLO, WOG, OKKO, SOCAR, and UPG networks did not change their prices that day.

China Focus: Ancient southern China canal finds new life as living heritage
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
15:39:01 CST
16:39:01 KST

NANNING, Oct. 12 (Xinhua) -- On free mornings, Ai Chenggang gets on his bicycle and rides along the Lingqu Canal, checking for rubbish tangled on the banks and watching out for children playing too close to the water.
Ai, in his 70s, has spent his life in Xing'an County in south China's Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region, where the canal has flowed past homes and fields for more than two millennia.
"This canal is what home means to us," he said.
The waterway Ai tends, quiet and enduring, is drawing crowds of visitors from far and wide this week.
Canal experts and enthusiasts from around the world are gathering in the city of Guilin in Guangxi for the World Canals Conference, which opened on Monday. The Lingqu Canal, about 60 kilometers from downtown Guilin, is a centerpiece of the event.
The conference has brought together representatives from canal cities, research institutions and waterway organizations in more than 20 countries. It is the third time the event has been held in China and the first in Guangxi. Discussions focus on how to preserve historic waterways while maintaining their value for local communities along the banks.
AN ANCIENT LINK
Ai's work as a canal guardian follows a family tradition. He is a descendant of the doujun, canal keepers who once patrolled the banks, repaired embankments and operated water gates to keep boats moving safely.
This role faded when roads and railways replaced the canal as a transport route, and Ai now serves with a volunteer group protecting the waterway.
The 37-kilometer Lingqu Canal was built on the orders of Emperor Qinshihuang of the Qin Dynasty (221 B.C.-207 B.C.), connecting the Xiangjiang and Lijiang rivers and, through them, the Yangtze and Pearl river systems.
Originally built to transport supplies for Qin armies campaigning in Lingnan, it later became a vital trade route linking China's interior with the southern region.
Along with Dujiangyan and the Zhengguo Canal, Lingqu is regarded as one of ancient China's three major hydraulic projects.
No cargo ships travel its waters today, but the canal still irrigates farmland, aids flood control and feeds the Lijiang River flowing through Guilin's famous karst landscape. Locals walk and rest under old trees on its banks, while farmers continue to work nearby fields.
Chen Xinghua, a former deputy director of the Xing'an county museum, has studied Lingqu for decades.
Figurines depicting foreigners, dating to the Han Dynasty (202 B.C.-220 A.D.), have been unearthed near the canal, offering evidence of early cultural exchanges between China's interior and the outside world, he said.
"Lingqu was an important part of the ancient Maritime Silk Road," Chen noted. "Protecting it helps us better understand the past and draw lessons for the present."
In 2018, Lingqu was listed as a World Heritage Irrigation Structure, the first in Guangxi to receive this designation.
KEEPING IT ALIVE
Protecting a canal involves more than restoring old stonework.
Authorities have banned quarrying along the waterway, improved sewage treatment and cleared waste, while regional and local regulations provide legal protection for the site.
Further efforts will focus on preserving the canal's original structures, expanding archaeological research, and using digital technology to make its history more accessible to the public, according to Wu Xiaogang, spokesperson of the Guilin municipal government.
Tourism has grown alongside these efforts.
The 12,000-square-meter Lingqu Museum houses more than 10,000 cultural relics. An immersive theater, meanwhile, takes visitors on a simulated boat ride through different periods of the canal's history, with warships from the Qin Dynasty, passenger boats from the Tang Dynasty (618-907), and merchant vessels from the Ming and Qing dynasties (1368-1911) appearing on a 360-degree screen.
The Lingqu scenic area received more than 1 million tourist visits in 2025, including over 10,000 visits by participants in educational tours, boosting business for local restaurants, hotels and transport operators.
For local residents, protecting the Lingqu Canal and preserving its cultural heritage have become part of everyday life.
Zeng Jinglan, 69, grew up beside the canal. A finger painter whose works have been exhibited around the world, she returned to Xing'an three years ago and opened a studio nearby.
"I grew up drinking water from the canal," she said. "In summer, my friends and I ran along its banks, listened to stories about it and watched my father paint by the water."
Today, the canal's scenery, plants and wildlife inspire her paintings. She hopes her art will help keep its cultural heritage alive for future generations.
More than 2,000 years after Lingqu was built, another canal has opened in Guangxi. The 134.2-kilometer Pinglu Canal, which began operating in September this year, gives southwestern China a shorter waterway route to the sea.
Experts said the two canals underscore the enduring role of waterways in connecting regions, facilitating trade and driving China's development.
Ai still gets on his bicycle and follows the canal his ancestors once guarded. The cargo boats have disappeared. Generations of canal keepers have come and gone. But the water is still flowing.
"As long as the canal is here, our home has a root," Ai said. ■

9th China Now Music Festival concludes in New York
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
15:38:56 CST
16:38:56 KST

NEW YORK, Oct. 12 (Xinhua) -- The ninth China Now Music Festival concluded Sunday at Lincoln Center in New York City with a concert showcasing the resilience and aspirations that connect the American and Chinese peoples.
The symphonic oratorio Men of Iron and the Golden Spike returned to the New York stage after its premiere at the 2019 China Now Music Festival.
Featuring a large orchestra as well as 120 choristers and vocal soloists, the work honors thousands of Chinese laborers who helped build the United States' first transcontinental railroad in the 1860s.
"In this divisive moment in our country, I hope this piece reminds audiences that the United States has always been shaped by diverse ethnic communities, and that the stories of Chinese laborers deserve their rightful place in our shared history," said Zhou Long, Pulitzer-winning composer of the oratorio.
The closing concert also featured the premiere of symphonic suite Chasing the Sky, composed by Chinese composer Li Shaosheng.
The piece blends traditional Chinese instrument suona with a symphony orchestra, reflecting humanity's shared dream of reaching beyond the horizon.
"Symphony, rooted in the West, has continued to evolve, with styles constantly changing. Many outstanding works have emerged from Eastern countries," Li said. "I hope to see more and more Chinese symphonic works performed on stages in the United States."
The festival, which opened on Oct. 2, was co-hosted by the U.S.-China Music Institute of Bard College Conservatory of Music and the Central Conservatory of Music of China.
The annual event, created in 2018, is dedicated to promoting the understanding and appreciation of music from contemporary China through concerts and academic programs. ■

World Insights: Deadly Riyadh airport attack heightens security concerns, risks wider conflict
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
15:38:33 CST
16:38:33 KST

ADEN, Yemen, Oct. 12 (Xinhua) -- A deadly Houthi attack on Riyadh's main international airport has heightened the risk of regional escalation, putting pressure on Saudi Arabia to respond and raising the prospect of deeper involvement by outside powers.
Saturday's attack on a passenger terminal at King Khalid International Airport killed 12 people and injured 309 others, according to Saudi authorities. The Saudi-led coalition vowed a firm response, while U.S. President Donald Trump said Washington "may" join Saudi Arabia in striking the Houthis.
As the confrontation widens, analysts interviewed by Xinhua said the airport attacks are intended to shift the costs of war from Yemen's battlefields onto Saudi Arabia itself. Yet, they warned that a strategy designed to strengthen Houthi leverage could instead harden Riyadh's position, encourage deeper regional involvement and make the escalating conflict increasingly difficult to contain.
PRESSURE BEYOND BATTLEFIELD
"Targeting Riyadh's airport is about more than military damage. It's about undermining confidence, disrupting economic activity, and pressuring Riyadh to reconsider its involvement," Hisham Al-Omeisy, conflict analyst and senior Yemen advisor with the European Institute of Peace, told Xinhua.
He described the approach as "asymmetric warfare": unable to compete conventionally with Saudi Arabia, the Houthis can move pressure beyond Yemen's frontlines and threaten sensitive infrastructure deep inside the kingdom.
Jarrah Mutlaq Al-Qazaa, media adviser at the Kuwait Journalists Association, likewise viewed the airport attacks as part of a broader effort by the Houthis to shift the costs of the conflict onto Saudi Arabia, while emphasizing the wider implications of targeting such a prominent civilian facility.
"The objective goes beyond military retaliation," Al-Qazaa told Xinhua. "It is about raising the costs for Saudi Arabia in terms of national security, economic activity and international image."
He perceived an international airport as not merely a transport hub, but also a symbol of a country's connectivity, security and international standing. The repercussions of an attack, he said, could therefore extend beyond physical damage to flight disruptions, higher aviation insurance costs and broader perceptions of security in the kingdom.
Abdul-Ghani Al-Iryani, a senior researcher at the Sana'a Center for Strategic Studies, told Xinhua that the pressure also serves a broader political objective. He said the Houthis are "seeking to pressure Saudi Arabia to return to a previously negotiated road map" that he described as favorable to the group at the expense of Yemen's internationally recognized government.
Yet, the analysts warned that the same strategy intended to build Houthi leverage could backfire after Saturday's civilian casualties. Al-Qazaa said that mounting civilian casualties could narrow rather than expand Riyadh's room for compromise.
"The higher the civilian toll, the more difficult it becomes for Saudi Arabia to make concessions amid domestic and international political pressure," he said.
Echoing those concerns, Yemeni political analyst Khalil Muthanna al-Omari told Xinhua that attacks on airports "raise the stakes considerably," potentially inviting stronger Saudi retaliation and broader international coordination against the group.
"With each escalation, the room for stepping back becomes narrower," al-Omari said.
DEFENSE CHALLENGE
The strikes have simultaneously exposed a second dimension of the confrontation: the difficulty of completely shielding Saudi Arabia's vast territory from increasingly diverse Houthi missile and drone threats, analysts said.
Ali Bin Hadi, an Aden-based military observer, told Xinhua that "repeated penetrations suggest potential gaps" in the defensive shield, arguing that "years of warfare have given the Houthis time to study Saudi defenses and adapt their methods."
Saudi Arabia's geography compounds the challenge, Bin Hadi said, with airports, cities and oil installations dispersed across a vast area while drones and low-flying cruise missiles can stretch expensive defensive systems.
The mounting pressure on Saudi defenses has also brought the potential roles of Pakistan and Türkiye, Saudi Arabia's security partners under the Mecca Agreement, into sharper focus, raising questions over how far they could become involved should the confrontation widen, according to analysts.
Al-Iryani said the precise scope of commitments under the Mecca Agreement remains unclear, and Bin Hadi cautioned that stronger defenses alone would not resolve the underlying conflict.
The same uncertainty surrounds Washington. Trump's suggestion that the United States could join Saudi strikes has raised the possibility of direct U.S. involvement, but the analysts differed over how readily Washington might cross that threshold.
Bin Hadi sees "little appetite in Washington for another confrontation with the Houthis" after previously seeking to disengage from that front. "Washington may help contain the fire, but it is unlikely to step into it," he said.
Al-Qazaa, however, said continued escalation could alter that calculation. He said the likelihood of direct U.S. military involvement would depend largely on whether Houthi attacks continue to cause heavy casualties, the extent to which Riyadh seeks U.S. participation, and whether Washington sees scope for limited strikes capable of restoring deterrence without drawing it into a prolonged war.
ROAD TO TALKS
Despite the intensifying confrontation, analysts broadly agreed that the path to diplomacy remains open, though they differed over what a viable political settlement would need to achieve.
Bin Hadi said Saudi Arabia "now faces a difficult choice" between a broader military confrontation with potentially heavy costs and renewed efforts at de-escalation, while years of aerial warfare have made the Houthis increasingly resilient to airstrikes.
"A prolonged state of neither full war nor genuine truce will continue to exhaust all sides," he said. "That equation is unlikely to remain sustainable."
Al-Omeisy went further, arguing that even a successful Saudi-Houthi accommodation would address only "one layer of the crisis." He said a viable settlement requires credible security guarantees, a more unified Yemeni government, and a political process that addresses the fundamental question of state authority.
"This is a Yemeni conflict, not simply a Saudi-Houthi dispute," Al-Omeisy said. "Ending Saudi-Houthi hostilities without addressing Yemen's underlying conflict would merely postpone the next war."
The Riyadh attack has therefore sharpened two intertwined questions: whether escalating pressure can produce deterrence without triggering a wider confrontation, and whether any eventual de-escalation can move beyond a Saudi-Houthi understanding toward resolving Yemen's underlying conflict.
As attacks increasingly cross national borders while fighting intensifies inside Yemen, the answers may determine not only the trajectory of the renewed war, but also how far its consequences spread across the Gulf and the wider region. ■

Nearly 1 bln people projected to have osteoarthritis by 2050: report
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
15:38:25 CST
16:38:25 KST

SYDNEY, Oct. 12 (Xinhua) -- Nearly one billion people worldwide are projected to be living with osteoarthritis by 2050, up from about 600 million in 2023, according to a new roadmap released on Monday.
There remains no cure and no drug that can stop or slow the disease, prompting researchers to call for stronger health policies to address the growing global disability burden, according to a statement released Monday by Australia's Curtin University.
The global health policy roadmap published in The Lancet on World Arthritis Day by a Curtin University-led group of international researchers said osteoarthritis remained under-recognized in health policies globally and was often inadequately integrated into healthcare delivery for chronic diseases, and inconsistently and often inappropriately treated and prevented.
The roadmap calls on governments to recognize osteoarthritis as a major chronic disease, improve access to evidence-based care, invest in prevention by addressing excess body weight and joint injuries, and integrate osteoarthritis care with broader chronic disease and rehabilitation services.
"Osteoarthritis faces an image problem -- it's perceived and dismissed in communities as an unavoidable part of aging with limited management options," said the report's lead author Professor Andrew Briggs from Curtin University.
Professor Lyn March, a co-senior author from Australia's Kolling Institute, said the global disability burden attributed to osteoarthritis increased by 65 percent between 1990 and 2023.
Rising obesity rates, population aging and increasing joint injuries are expected to drive further growth in cases in coming decades, the researchers warned. ■

The protests have become one of the most significant political challenges of Modi's third term, drawing together opposition parties, student groups and activists angered by the voter roll revision.

"As for Russia, the significance of the diesel deal can hardly be overstated. First, Russian producers previously exported a much larger quantity of diesel. Second, the domestic market experiences the least deficit specifically in diesel," Shostak said. "Supplies from Russia will almost certainly be performed by companies on various sanctions lists, for whom this will be a good way to test how the US regulator applies exemptions to the rules," he added.

The company, it added, aims to transfer around 220 positions primarily from its central Technology unit to its country-level operations.

EU chief diplomat responds to Trump's call: Ukraine needs ceasefire to hold elections

Source: Kaja Kallas, EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy, ahead of a meeting of the EU Foreign Affairs Council in Luxembourg on 12 October
Details: Kallas stressed that elections in Ukraine could be held once hostilities had ended, while the international community's efforts should currently focus on forcing Russia to stop the war.
"Well, every, almost every constitution has provision that when you have a war going on, then you can't have elections, and I understand that President Zelenskyy has also said that if there would be a ceasefire, then he's willing to have the elections as soon as possible," Kallas said, commenting on US President Donald Trump's call for new elections in Ukraine.
The EU's top diplomat also pointed out that elections inevitably involve political strife within a country, while Ukraine continues to face external aggression.
"Elections are always fighting between different groups inside the country while the attacks are coming from outside, and that's why it is really important to keep the people together while the war is going on," she said.
Kallas emphasised that international efforts should be focused on forcing Russia to end the war.
"If the pressure is put on Russia so that they will stop this war, I'm sure that Ukraine will have elections," she noted.
Background:
- US President Donald Trump said on 10 October that he believed it was time for Ukraine to have a new president.
- In response, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that Ukrainians should decide who their president is and that he was prepared to organise elections if Russia agreed to a full 60-day ceasefire.

One person was killed and 11 others injured in an attack at the airport, the country's civil aviation authority said early Monday.
In an earlier strike on the same airport, 12 people were killed and more than 300 others injured.

Ukrainian defence intelligence discloses details of Russian Kinzhal aeroballistic missile
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
10:31:00 EEST
16:31:00 KST

Ukrainian defence intelligence discloses details of Russian Kinzhal aeroballistic missile
Defence Intelligence of Ukraine (DIU) has posted an interactive 3D model, information on the components and manufacturers involved in the production of the Russian 9-S-7760 aeroballistic missile, better known as the Kh-47M2 Kinzhal.
Source: DIU; War&Sanctions portal
Quote from DIU: "The Kinzhal is a single-stage solid-propellant missile with an integrated warhead. In terms of components, the missile shares 90% of its components with the 9M723 ballistic missile used in the Iskander-M short-range ballistic missile system."
Details: DIU pointed out that the main differences of this missile include the presence of a tail fairing that detaches after engine launch, an active radar seeker (in the Iskander, an active radar seeker currently exists only on paper and its use in strikes against Ukrainian territory has not been recorded), which the Russians calls "all-weather", and an active jamming station, in addition to the S-200 decoy dispensing system.
Quote from DIU: "The Kinzhal has two types of warhead: a penetrating high-explosive warhead in a thick metal casing for breaching floor slabs, concrete and fortified structure; and a special nuclear warhead. The enemy is currently working on a modification with a high-explosive fragmentation warhead. These changes may be directly linked to problems with the missile's guidance accuracy, as high precision is especially vital for a penetrating warhead. It is precisely because of this that the enemy significantly reduced state defence orders for these missiles, redirecting production capacity and supplies of components and raw materials towards the production of 9M723 Iskander-M ballistic missiles."
Details: The intelligence service cited the limited lifespan of carrier platforms – MiG-31I interceptor fighters and their predecessor, the MiG-31K, which the Russian's aviation industry is no longer producing – as the second reason for this reprioritisation.
DIU also published data on 58 Russian companies involved in the production supply chain for the Kh-47M2 Kinzhal aeroballistic missiles. Significantly, 22 of them are still not subject to sanctions from any of the countries in the sanctions coalition.
Quote from DIU: "Despite individual shortcomings, Russia is continuing to work on modernising the Kinzhal. To thwart the aggressor's plans, sanctions against all the companies involved must be synchronised and control over technologies actively used by Russia must be tightened."
Background: DIU previously identified an NVIDIA Jetson Orin computer module in the S-71 Monochrome, a new Russian cruise missile. The use of this component may indicate that artificial intelligence technologies are being implemented in the missile.

How green is Europe's urban public transport? A data-driven reality check
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
07:30:00 UTC
16:30:00 KST

The reality behind Europe's green public transport push
October 12, 2026
An electric plug icon on their windows makes them easy to spot in cities like Brussels and Madrid. Quietly navigating the streets, electric buses have become an increasingly common sight on Europe's streets in recent years.
Michela Le Pira, assistant professor of transportation at Italy's University of Catania, says removing tailpipe emissions — the gases and particles generated when a combustion vehicle is running — might be "the easiest strategy to improve public transport."
Most Europeans live in urban settings, and road transport harms air quality. In 2023, almost 300,000 deaths across the EU were caused by air pollution levels exceeding the World Health Organization's (WHO) recommended thresholds.
Of all fine particulate matter (PM2.5) concentrations in European urban areas, about 14% come from road transport, including public, private and freight transport. Additionally, towns and cities account for nearly a quarter of the European Union's transport greenhouse gas emissions (GHG).
DW and the European Data Journalism Network evaluated more than a decade's worth of data from more than 100 reports and sources on public transit and the emissions it causes, and identified 148 sustainability commitments by local authorities and transport operators in 33 cities across Europe. The analysis focuses on motorized mass transit, leaving out bikes and pedestrians as well as taxis, shared vehicles and e-scooters.
More electric buses, thanks to EU funds
The EU wants to become the first climate-neutral continent by 2050. A key part of that plan is cutting transport-related GHG emissions by 90% from 1990 levels.
As DW's analysis shows, Copenhagen is the only EU capital that has almost electrified its entire bus fleet — its vehicles do not have combustion engines and therefore do not produce tailpipe emissions. In cities like Rome, Lisbon and Nicosia, more than 90% of buses still run on diesel, and metros and trams account for less than 10% of their public transport fleet.
Although cars still dominate European streets, "electric buses are one way to reduce local air pollution," said Martin Baierl, data analyst with Transport & Environment, an advocacy non-profit for clean transport.
EU funds enabled many cities to increase their electric and alternative fuel bus fleets from 2021 on.
Electric buses comprise 20% of the total fleet in EU capitals and selected cities. Their number increased by 55% between 2021 and 2025 — equivalent to 1,234 more such vehicles on the road. The number of diesel-only buses has been declining since then, although they still outnumber those running on alternative fuel.
Slow road to sustainability in some cities
In addition to decarbonizing the bus fleet and helping to reduce air pollution, embracing electric models can help to lower noise and public transport operating costs. All the more so if the city produces its own electricity, explains Baierl. However, the outlay for e-buses is higher than for diesel models. In 20 out of the 31 cities with data to analyze, over 50% of the bus fleet is made up of traditional vehicles.
Brussels, for example, was an early adopter of moving away from traditional diesel-powered buses, switching to hybrids instead. Now the Belgian capital is in the process of electrifying its fleet, but at a slower pace. "It's not easy to know what the right technology will be in the end," Baierl said.
Another example is hydrogen-powered buses, which also produce zero emissions but are more costly to operate than their electric counterparts.
Many cities have not fully committed to zero-emissions despite EU targets
Transportation is the only major sector where greenhouse gas emissions remain above 1990 levels, despite the EU's ambition of a 90% reduction by 2050.
On average, public transport — including buses, trams and metros — is used for more than a quarter of trips in the 10 largest EU capitals, according to recent data from the non-profit group CDP (formerly the Carbon Disclosure Project). In Stockholm, the share is 49%, while in the smaller Slovenian capital of Ljubljana, it's 11%. DW analysis of transport sustainability pledges reveals that only four cities have explicitly committed to achieving zero emissions in buses or all public transport.
Rail transport is climate-friendly, but scarce
Yannis Papadimitriou lives 85 kilometers (about 53 miles) away from Athens, the EU capital with the highest air pollution mortality risk. He travels to work by commuter rail, a means of transport he'd like to see promoted more.
"For me it is a very conscious choice to use electric public transport, especially trains, which are the safest, most environmentally friendly and quickest way of transport."
Though trains, trams and metros run on electricity, there are more buses within city boundaries, and in many urban areas the majority still run on diesel.
Public transport's emissions go beyond the tailpipe
In Northern Europe, 15 kilometers away from Copenhagen, Poul Kattler also used to commute to work. He is now retired and takes the bus more frequently with his grandchildren. Despite Copenhagen having an almost completely fossil-fuel-free public transport system (only one bus runs on biomethane), the metro expansion, which is responding to the city's growth, comes with its own set of concerns.
"The whole construction phase [of the new metro line] is extremely environmentally demanding," Kattler said. If the construction emissions are considered, "the CO2 balance would be very poor for the metro now."
But in the long run, the benefits of a new metro line in reducing CO2 emissions outweigh its construction-related emissions, Le Pira said.
Combustion or exhaust emissions are not the only way transport pollutes the air and the environment. Indirect emissions, like those coming from electricity generation or fuel production, add to transport's CO2 footprint. Brakes and wheels release non-exhaust particle matter when wagons or vehicles slow down.
Since 1992, buses and any vehicle running on fossil fuels in the EU have been subject to stricter emissions standards. Fine particle emissions from buses and heavy-duty vehicles had dropped by 92% in 2022 according to the European Environment Agency. Yet overall road transport non-exhaust emissions from tire wear have increased 58% in two decades, as cars have become heavier.
Shifting from cars to a multimodal transport system
With a few exceptions, EU member states are not close to cutting greenhouse gas transport emissions by 90%, as envisioned by the EU's 2050 target.
Zero-emission public transport is one step toward decarbonizing transport in cities and meeting GHG reduction goals. The next challenge is to get people out of their cars.
"If we talk about sustainable mobility in general and not only clean public transport, the main problem is the model shift from private cars to public transport," Le Pira said.
On average, private automobiles account for more than a third of transport in the largest EU capitals, according to CDP data.
Cheaper ticket prices for groups, like students, and disincentives for car use, such as low-emission zones, are two complementary ways of attracting more passengers while reducing private transport.
In her research work, Le Pira investigates how public transport can be more efficient and appealing for city dwellers, for example, by combining transport modes where people step off their bikes and onto a train. This kind of solution could be particularly relevant for small cities "where cars are still the main transport mode."
According to Baierl, places with good public transport draw people in. "Cities where not everybody has to use a car are just more livable," he said.
Edited by: Gianna-Carina Grün and Sarah Steffen
Fact check: Eva Lopez
DW's data team contributed research to this project.

====================================================================================================

What Drapatyi has brought to the role of commander-in-chief – and what the military thinks
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
10:30:00 EEST
16:30:00 KST

Has the thaw begun? What Drapatyi has brought to the role of commander-in-chief – and what the military thinks
In mid-July 2026, as angry protesters carrying cardboard signs massed outside the President's Office, Volodymyr Zelenskyy spent several days meeting corps and group commanders and deputy commanders.
As Ukrainska Pravda reported at the time, the president asked them about the situation on the front line, problems with supplies, staffing and so on.
He didn't ask what they thought of the then commander-in-chief, Oleksandr Syrskyi, nor did he offer any of them the job. He had already made a decision – one that to a large extent had been forced upon him.
That decision was to appoint Mykhailo Drapatyi.
"Those meetings were probably necessary so the president could see how the transition of military command would play out – whether everything would fall apart if the commander-in-chief were removed. Because Syrskyi had built a system in which everything revolved around him," a high-ranking source in military circles told Ukrainska Pravda.
"Syrskyi eliminated any competition around him. To climb the career ladder, you had to be loyal. Basically, his only potential rivals were Drapatyi and [Lieutenant General Andrii] Hnatov. He sidelined Drapatyi from the command and curtailed his powers at the Joint Forces Command, and he turned Hnatov into an ally," the source added.
A third candidate for the post of commander-in-chief – whom Syrskyi did not "eliminate", because he actually saw him as his successor – was Oleh Apostol, Commander of the Air Assault Forces. But Apostol "did a very clever thing", as one UP source jokingly put it, and ruled himself out of such a fate.
Given that the president did appoint Drapatyi, it can be concluded that all the commanders assured him that the front line would not collapse without Syrskyi.
Meanwhile, Zelenskyy needed to reassure several thousand protesters with cardboard signs as soon as possible that he was listening to them and was prepared to meet one of their demands (though not the most pressing one).
And so, as a result of major political protests in central Kyiv, the Ukrainian military got a new commander-in-chief: 43-year-old Mykhailo Drapatyi. Adored among some sections of the military, Drapatyi has a reputation for treating his troops humanely and is the polar opposite of Syrskyi in the public imagination.
Over the two and a half months that Drapatyi and his team have been in post, they have been virtually absent from the public eye. Surprisingly, this was a deliberate decision by the commander-in-chief himself.
One insider told UP: "They say Drapatyi holds a lot of international meetings, but for now he doesn't want them publicised. He visits the troops – less often than Syrskyi, yes, but he does go – and again, there are barely any communications about that from either the Commander-in-Chief's office or the General Staff. Still, his visits occasionally crop up in posts by brigades and battalions, as happened, for example, with the R.U.G. [an assault regiment within the Khartiia Corps that Drapatyi visited and that later made the visit public – ed.]. That's his approach, his vision. The idea is that when there are results, then we'll talk about them."
Ukrainska Pravda decided to fill this information gap by speaking to around two dozen officers of various ranks and analysing Commander-in-Chief Drapatyi's first steps – as well as providing examples of how those steps are being received within the military.
A rapid and sweeping purge of personnel
In mid-August, one of UP's sources in the defence forces showed us part of a table listing potential appointments by the new commander-in-chief.
Several of the names, including some senior people – corps commanders and deputy commanders – had an abbreviation written next to them that stands for "Transfer to the reserve battalion". In other words, dismiss them from their posts.
This came as something of a surprise to us, since the military doesn't usually make personnel decisions quite so ruthlessly. The fact is that the Ukrainian army really does have a shallow bench, and most senior military posts are short-lived. So anyone who reaches the top of the pyramid tends to avoid making enemies before the moment when the pyramid inevitably turns upside down again.
Drapatyi, however, appears to have chosen a different path.
Firstly, he did indeed transfer several dozen colonels, brigadier generals and other officers to the "reserve battalion".
Drapatyi embarked on a "purge" both within the General Staff – where he wants to retain people with combat experience and the ability to command troops – and across the military, where changes have long been overdue. Among those sent to the reserve battalion were Oleksii Maistrenko, commander of the 11th Corps; Oleksandr Bakulin, commander of the 19th Corps; Andrii Malinovskyi, Commander of Rocket Forces and Artillery; and Oleksandr Nesterenko, Deputy Commander of the Ground Forces.
"Maistrenko found out he'd been dismissed from the media. Right in the middle of a meeting, during a video conference, he asked: 'Is it true that I'm being fired?'" people in one unit told UP several weeks ago.
"There is a reserve battalion for officers, and it's never been filled on anything like the scale we've seen over the past month and a half. Around 15 officers were dismissed from the General Staff's International Cooperation Directorate in a single day and transferred to the reserve battalion," another insider added.
Secondly, Drapatyi "rehabilitated" two officers who had been sidelined from commanding troops under his predecessors – Serhii Sobko and Emil Ishkulov.
In 2024, after a fairly successful stint with the Territorial Defence Forces Command, Sobko was abruptly exiled to the 11th Corps (towards the end of his time there, he publicly criticised micromanagement in the military). Ishkulov was sent to the 7th Air Assault Corps after refusing to take the 80th Brigade into Russia's Kursk Oblast without additional resources.
After taking office, Drapatyi brought Sobko into the General Staff, where he became acting Deputy Chief of the General Staff, and appointed Ishkulov commander of the 11th Corps, which is responsible for the defence of Sloviansk and Kramatorsk.
It remains to be seen whether Oleksandr Shyrshyn, the former battalion commander in the 47th Brigade who criticised the senior command over "idiotic missions in Kursk Oblast", will also be "rehabilitated". Those remarks not only cost him his post but also earned him enemies in one of the assault regiments.
So who has replaced the colonels and brigadier generals Drapatyi dismissed?
It's hard not to notice that a large number of senior positions, particularly in the Ground Forces, have gone to officers from the Air Assault Forces. They include Ishkulov, who now commands the 11th Corps; Valerii Skred, who took over the 19th Corps; and Sviatoslav Zaits, who became Commander of the Ground Forces.
Even the post of Chief of the General Staff went to an Air Assault Forces officer – Ihor Skybiuk.
Asked whether this was Drapatyi's own decision, one well-informed source replied succinctly: "Drapatyi was prepared to work with practically anyone who was suggested to him." Another source, however, cautiously hinted immediately after Skybiuk's appointment that it had been more of a compromise.
"With Syrskyi, he and Hnatov were basically a single unit. If Syrskyi went to the front, Hnatov would handle all the meetings in Kyiv and all the international meetings. It's not like that with Drapatyi and Skybiuk; their relationship is somewhat different," the source told UP.
Asked how much freedom Drapatyi has over personnel decisions, the well-informed source quoted above said that "no one is putting obstacles in his way". However, the fact that some officers are in their posts in an acting capacity rather than having been formally appointed calls that assertion into question, to say the least.
The mass "airdrop" of maroon berets [air assault officers] into senior positions was perceived by some military personnel, journalists and analysts as a concession to the paratrooper wing of the military. The theory was that the political leadership had appointed a commander-in-chief from the Ground Forces, but placated their Air Assault Forces rivals by making their representatives chief of the General Staff and corps and brigade commanders.
Our sources rejected this interpretation, however, insisting that it is purely a matter of professionalism and the aforementioned shallow bench.
"The paratroopers aren't bad. They're good. Who else are you going to choose?" was how a National Guard source summed it up.
Air Assault Forces officers were not the only ones to find the path to promotion opening up after Drapatyi's appointment. Younger brigade commanders have also moved up the ranks. Bohdan Shevchuk, commander of the 141st Brigade, for example, was appointed commander of the 20th Corps. Shevchuk has a rather controversial reputation within the military for his authoritarian leadership style, including from his time serving in the 68th and 59th Brigades. Serhii Shatalov, commander of the 37th Brigade, took over the 30th Marine Corps.
A handful of Drapatyi's colleagues from his previous job at the Joint Forces Command have also been promoted. Yurii Pohribnyi, who headed logistics at the Joint Forces Command, became the new and long-awaited commander of the Logistics Forces.
"Interaction between the Defence Ministry and the General Staff has improved significantly since Karpenko [the previous commander of the Logistics Forces – ed.] was dismissed – it's all lovey-dovey now," a Defence Ministry source told UP. "You can see they're determined to change everything, to sort out fuel [the defence forces have faced a huge fuel shortage in recent months – ed.], repairs and all sorts of other areas where there are major corruption risks."
Some members of the Joint Forces Command team, including communications and digitalisation personnel, also moved to Kyiv with Drapatyi and joined the commander-in-chief's staff.
"He hasn't changed over the past two months," one source who has worked with Drapatyi in various military structures for several years said with a smile. "He still greets everyone and asks how they're doing. He's very considerate."
One question that remains unresolved is the position of Commander of the Air Force – namely whether Anatolii Kryvonozhko, who has frequently come in for criticism, will remain in the job.
Insiders reminded UP that the Air Force has an even shallower bench than, say, the Ground Forces.
Unlike virtually all other branches of the military, which have been significantly replenished by people from civilian life since the full-scale invasion, the Air Force still remains a closed and largely unreformed system because it requires highly specialised knowledge and skills.
Another unanswered question is what will happen to Syrskyi's legacy – the assault regiments.
After his departure, the assault units found themselves in an extremely disadvantageous position: reinforcements were temporarily suspended, some personnel were transferred to other units, the regiments were placed under the operational control of various corps, and even Dmytro Voloshyn, the potential commander of the Joint Assault Forces which have not yet been set up, was sent back to the front.
What Drapatyi sees as a long-overdue response to the disproportionate expansion of the assault units (and, frankly, is common sense) has been met with outright hostility within those units. Among their rank-and-file soldiers, meanwhile, it has created complete uncertainty about what will happen next.
This was particularly true of those units that received no preferential treatment even before Drapatyi's appointment – the 1st and 475th Assault Battalions.
Several unrelated sources told UP that the commanders of these units had approached Drapatyi, emphasising their effectiveness and asking to operate with greater autonomy, but their requests had been turned down.
No final decision has been made on what will happen to the assault regiments or whether a Joint Rapid Response Forces Command will be created at all. For now, they remain temporarily assigned to the corps.
As far as Ukrainska Pravda is aware, the future of the assault units is not currently a top priority.
Meanwhile, commanders of non-assault units have told UP that since Drapatyi took over, they have noticed "a fairer distribution of personnel".
"Previously, all the brigades combined would get 10,000+ people a month, and all the assault units would get the same number. Now that's finally changed," one commander told us.
A thaw in the military command
The first word brigade and corps commanders use to describe Drapatyi's first few months in the job is "freedom".
Drapatyi has chosen a different approach to his predecessor, who would tell some brigade commanders how and where to fight – right down to the coordinates where they were supposed to establish a position. He has embraced decentralised command (mission command), moving away from the micromanagement that Syrskyi had become notorious for.
The сommander-in-сhief no longer commands troops directly, but does so, as the military hierarchy envisages, through the group of forces under the relevant Operational Command.
In civilian terms, it works roughly like this: employees are now given tasks by their line managers, and not the company director over the phone.
Since taking office, Drapatyi has reorganised the system of groups of forces somewhat.
He disbanded the Skhid (East) Group of Forces commanded by Viktor Nikoliuk – presumably because he was dissatisfied with Nikoliuk's performance – and merged Dmytro Voloshyn's Kursk Group of Forces into Mykhailo Shandar's Pivnich (North) Group of Forces.
There are now six groups of forces operating across the entire front.
Four have existed for some time: Pivnich (North), Pivden (South), Zakhid (West) and the Joint Forces Group. Two others were recently created by Drapatyi: Tsentr (Centre), commanded by Andrii Biletskyi, and Azov, commanded by Denys Prokopenko. They were put together on the fly.
It is these newly created groups that will have to fight the latest and particularly challenging battles in Donetsk Oblast – for the Kramatorsk urban area and for Dobropillia.
"The battle for Donbas is the number one priority for both us and them [the Russians – ed.]. We cannot withdraw from there," a senior source stressed in a conversation with UP.
Notwithstanding the critical comments that the sources interviewed for this article made about former commander-in-chief Oleksandr Syrskyi, it is only fair to point out that he handed Drapatyi a front in considerably better shape than the one he himself inherited in 2024.
When Syrskyi took over from Valerii Zaluzhnyi, he had to stop an "avalanche" that was advancing from Avdiivka towards Pokrovsk at tremendous speed. Drapatyi, by contrast, took office with a relatively stable front, with the defence forces even holding the advantage on the battlefield in some areas.
Ukrainska Pravda sources say the corps reform launched by Syrskyi has played a major role in this. Not every corps has managed to develop into a strong formation, but the 3rd Corps, for example, has significantly improved the performance of the relatively weak brigades assigned to it, effectively retraining them in how to fight.
Military personnel joke among themselves that the "division" of Donetsk Oblast between Azov and the 3rd Corps will only intensify the years-long rivalry between the two formations in terms of both their combat record and the creativity of their media campaigns. The thinking is that each will want to deliver the best results.
"This is definitely an effective command decision, and we're already seeing the results," one officer told UP. "The brigades are amazed that someone is actually moving into the second line of defence behind them, that they haven't simply been abandoned."
"I know that both Biletskyi and Redis [Denys Prokopenko – ed.] have been given additional brigades. But just think how enormous the sectors they'll have to cover now will be. I think these groups of forces would be effective if they had no more than two or three brigades each," another commander said, voicing his concerns.
In the context of the reorganisation of the groups of forces and the situation on the battlefield, another front deserves particular attention: Zaporizhzhia.
One little-known fact is that this summer, former Commander-in-Chief Syrskyi pulled the command of the 7th Air Assault Corps away from the Dobropillia front and abruptly sent it to Volyn Oblast to repel a potential offensive from Belarus.
After taking office, Drapatyi reversed this decision and redirected the corps command to Zaporizhzhia (much to the relief of the 7th Corps, since, objectively speaking, there wasn't much for them to do in Volyn). The reason is that the Russians continue to build up forces near Huliaipole with the aim, according to UP information, of making a large sweeping manoeuvre from the town to form an encirclement around the city of Zaporizhzhia itself.
"We spent no more than two weeks in Volyn before coming to Zaporizhzhia," a source in the 7th Corps told UP. "We were tasked with reinforcing the Pivden (South) Group of Forces with another corps. Several brigades have been placed under our command, along with the 225th Assault Regiment. Overall, everything is good. The only issue is that we're here without our own complement of troops – we'd prefer to fight with our own units, because that means better coordination and greater effectiveness."
And the new groups of forces are unlikely to be the last innovation in the military command system.
Several of our sources said that Drapatyi, following the NATO model, wants to return the Joint Forces Command to its original purpose and put it in charge of the entire front.
At present the Joint Forces Command has a relatively small area of responsibility covering parts of Sumy and Kharkiv oblasts.
"The Joint Forces Command is supposed to command the war – that's what it was set up for," one colonel told UP. "Before the full-scale invasion, all exercises were conducted on the basis that the Joint Forces Command controlled all the groups. Then things went a bit off course, and later Syrok [Syrskyi – ed.], in order to undermine Drapatyi, broke up the Dnipro Operational Strategic Group altogether and turned it into a group of forces."
"The General Staff prepares reserves, handles strategic planning and works at the international level. The Joint Forces Command runs combat operations," added one corps chief of staff.
The move away from micromanaging brigades and corps has brought another change: Drapatyi no longer spends several hours every day hearing reports from every commander. This saves the сommander-in-сhief's time and prevents unnecessary dissemination of information.
"Syrskyi used to hear reports from everyone every day and might issue specific instructions on how the situation should develop, including where troops should advance. In other words, his focus was on overseeing the implementation of assigned tasks," one senior military officer told us.
"Drapatyi doesn't do that. It's the group commanders' job. Drapatyi's focus is on strategic and systemic issues.
And when commanders do speak to the сommander-in-сhief, he isn't interested in a standard report on 'what happened'. He wants statistics, an analysis of the problems and potential solutions – in other words, what conditions need to be created so that a particular commander can accomplish their mission. And that's the right approach."
The same officer added that Drapatyi is trying to get all commanders to use the Delta situational awareness system (yes, there are still some groups of forces in the Ukrainian military that don't) and requires them to make practical use of all the digital solutions available.
Changing the system
In its first few months, Drapatyi's team has turned its attention to several matters that may seem insignificant to civilians but are in fact fundamental to the military. These range from the 16 principles of leadership, which set out the framework for what the commander-in-chief expects of soldiers and officers, to the development of a military education reform spearheaded by Serhii Sobko.
However, in our view, another document deserves the most attention.
Two senior sources told UP that Drapatyi's team has drawn up what may be the first "war plan" of its kind. It has been under consideration by the National Security and Defence Council for several weeks.
This is precisely the kind of plan – a strategic vision – that commanders have regularly complained about not having in conversations with UP. How, they ask, can we move forward unless we understand the ultimate objective? If, for example, we want to retake Mariupol, when are we going to do it, and what are we going to do to achieve that?
"We need a grand strategy for the next 30 or so years so that we, as commanders, understand where we are heading," members of one corps command told UP.
The plan is intended to answer two questions: what exactly the Ukrainian military needs to do to preserve Ukraine, and within what timeframe.
Alongside these broader strategic issues, the plan also addresses more practical matters, such as the military's approach to defence. For example, whether it makes any sense to keep soldiers on the front line whose role is essentially to serve as the military's "eyes and ears", with virtually no ability to engage in combat.
***
Drapatyi's first steps as a commander inspire respect and a natural curiosity: will he manage to rebuild the system? If not all of it, then at least a few of its layers – preferably those closest to the foundations.
The relatively stable front line, at least for now, gives him and his team time to make these changes.
Some things, however, certainly cannot wait – such as countering the Russian jet-powered drones that attack cities in the rear every day. The lack of a ready-made technical solution that can be deployed at scale will soon become part of Drapatyi's responsibility as well.
Given the intensity with which the Russians are currently attacking cities in the rear, it is reasonable to assume that over the next six months to a year, the war in the skies will demand significantly more time, effort and money than Ukraine has devoted to it in the past. And that raises the question: can a commander-in-chief who comes from the Ground Forces, and has always commanded the war on the ground, defeat Russia in the skies?
Olha Kyrylenko, Ukrainska Pravda
Translated by Myroslava Zavadska
Edited by Teresa Pearce
