Houthis hit Riyadh airport again day after strike killing dozen
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
07:30:00 UTC
16:30:00 KST

Yemen's Houthi rebels on Sunday night carried out a fresh strike on a passenger terminal at Riyadh's international airport, the Saudi-led coalition said, one day after a missile hit the same terminal and killed 12 people.
Saudi authorities said one person, described as a Pakistani national, was killed, and 11 were injured in the latest attack on the domestic terminal complex at King Khalid International Airport.
The airport – struck four times in the past five days – has been closed since Saturday’s missile attack, which was the deadliest in a Gulf Arab nation since the Iran war began. Over 300 other people were wounded, some critically.
The sharp escalation in the war's new front threatens to draw in greater U.S. military involvement. President Donald Trump has said he is weighing joining the fight against the Houthis. There was no White House comment Sunday.
India’s embassy in Saudi Arabia said one of its citizens died Sunday of injuries sustained in Saturday’s attack, which would bring the toll to 13. Saudi authorities later said King Fahd International Airport in Dammam also was attacked, with few details. The city is on the Persian Gulf near Bahrain and Qatar.
The latest strike in Riyadh came shortly after the Houthis said the airport in the rebel-held Yemeni capital of Sanaa had been struck again, and blamed the Saudis.
On Sunday night the Houthi-run al-Masirah TV channel reported further strikes on Sanaa, blaming Saudi Arabia. Saudi Arabia has not commented on the strikes.
At stake, again, in this escalation are global supplies and prices of oil as well as commercial shipping through a crucial alternative waterway to the Iran-threatened Strait of Hormuz – along with civilians and aviation throughout the region.
There was no sign Sunday that Trump had followed up on plans to speak with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, who has been seeking assistance against the war-hardened rebel group that is currently Iran's most dynamic proxy.
A U.S. intervention could prompt the Houthis to halt shipping through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait at the southern end of the Red Sea off Yemen, further restricting the flow of oil out of the Persian Gulf. The rebels seized key areas along the strait last month.
The Saudi-led coalition, backing forces with Yemen's internationally recognized government, has been trying to seize them back.
The rebels' strikes against Saudi airports, oil infrastructure and military facilities highlight a problem. The kingdom is running low on missile interceptors and has asked France, Britain, Pakistan and Egypt to deploy air defense support to the region, regional officials told The Associated Press last month, with one noting that the U.S. has seen its own stock dwindle during the Iran war.
Some airlines have suspended flights serving Saudi airports and some embassies have cautioned citizens about the risks of using them, after multiple Houthi warnings about the rebels' use of Saudi airspace.
Sunday’s attack occurred as the Saudis hosted a major international energy conference in Riyadh, with other high-profile events including an investment gathering on the horizon.
Saudi Arabia under Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman has sought to open more to the world as a business and tourism destination, but the Houthi attacks threaten those efforts.
"There is no way that somebody will break our back. We are like a phoenix, we come out of the ashes all the time," the Saudi energy minister, Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman Al Saud, told the conference.
He added that the kingdom is also working on pipelines in addition to the East-West one that was attacked and closed for days last month, with no details.
Earlier Sunday, the Houthi-run Health Ministry said a child was killed and six people wounded in a suspected Saudi airstrike on a house in Sanaa.
The ministry also claimed 91 Yemenis have been killed by the Saudi-led coalition in five weeks, 60% of them women and children.
There was no immediate comment from Saudi authorities on the claims, as fighting in Yemen surges after a major military offensive was launched against the Houthis a week ago.
Inside Saudi Arabia, identities emerged for some of those killed in Saturday's attack in Riyadh, including an Egyptian flight attendant and a Syrian widow living in the kingdom.
The government has previously said the dead also include four Saudi citizens, as well as two Bangladeshi nationals, one Palestinian, one American, one Jordanian and one Sudanese national.
Early Monday, Saudi Arabia released videos of the moment of the strike captured by security cameras. They show people, many dressed in the white robes of Mecca-bound pilgrims, standing in line in a busy hall, while others scroll phones in a nearby seating area before a fireball erupts, following by people throwing themselves to the floor and running for safety.
The Houthis until recently had been largely on the Iran war’s sidelines. They have developed their military capabilities in recent years to become one of Tehran’s most powerful allies. Now they're pressuring its regional rival and a key U.S. ally.
Late Sunday, Saudi Arabia and Iran said their foreign ministers had spoken by phone. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said he warned against insisting on a military approach and ignoring a political solution and said Tehran was ready to help start a dialogue between the Saudis and the Houthis.
The Saudis and Houthis began fighting in 2015, when the kingdom entered Yemen’s civil war on behalf of the government. Relative calm after a 2022 cease-fire ended in July when the Houthis resumed attacks, saying the Saudis fired on the Sanaa airport as a plane from Iran was trying to land.
The attack revived anger over the Saudi-led blockade that has largely isolated Houthi-run areas. The rebels declared a blockade on Saudi Arabia.
Now the Saudi-led coalition is providing air support for Yemeni government forces attempting to reverse Houthi territorial gains.
But the rebels' pressure tactics could backfire, said Ahmed Nagi, the International Crisis Group’s senior analyst for Yemen: "Rather than pushing Riyadh to step back, attacks on critical Saudi infrastructure could make the Saudis more determined to continue the campaign."

Truce-violating Israel kills 5 Palestinians in Gaza in 24 hours
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
07:30:00 UTC
16:30:00 KST

An Israeli strike killed at least two people in southern Gaza Monday, health officials said, day after killing three more across the Palestinian enclave.
Two casualties were reported when an Israeli drone hit a group of Palestinians northwest of Rafah, the sources said, as Israel continues to violate a cease-fire in effect since last October.
The drone fired at least one missile at the group near Muawiya Mosque in the al-Mawasi area northwest of the city, according to witnesses.
Separately, Israeli artillery fired shells toward areas northeast of Khan Younis in southern Gaza, locals said.
Israeli naval forces also opened fire and launched shells toward the Gaza City coast in the north, with no injuries reported, they added.
Earlier Sunday, three Palestinians were killed and several others injured Sunday in an Israeli drone strike on a tent in southern Gaza.
A medical source at Nasser Hospital said the bodies of three Palestinians and several wounded people were brought to the facility after the strike near the hospital in the southern al-Buraq area of central Khan Younis.
Witnesses told Anadolu Agency (AA) that an Israeli drone fired at least one missile at the tent, which was being used as a mobile phone charging point.
Also Sunday, a medical source at al-Shifa Hospital said Jihad Iyad al-Ghandour, 6, died of serious wounds sustained Saturday when Israeli soldiers opened fire in the Jabalia refugee camp in northern Gaza.
Separately, Israeli forces expanded the area under their control in eastern Gaza City early Sunday, injuring two Palestinians, including a pregnant woman and forcing dozens of families to flee their homes, according to local Palestinian sources.
The sources told AA that Israeli military vehicles advanced tens of meters beyond their existing positions in the Shujaiya neighborhood overnight from Saturday into Sunday, under cover of heavy gunfire and artillery shelling.
They said the troops were accompanied by armed Palestinian militias cooperating with and supported by the Israeli army, while quadcopter drones provided cover.
Israeli forces fired heavily toward the area stretching from the vegetable market in the east to the Shujaiya intersection on Salah al-Din Street in the west, the sources added.
For about a week, eastern areas of Gaza, particularly the eastern parts of the Tuffah and Shujaiya neighborhoods, have witnessed nighttime demolitions, gunfire, heavy artillery shelling and military vehicle movements near the "yellow line," according to the sources.
The line separates areas occupied by Israeli forces in the east from areas where Palestinians are permitted to remain in the west.
Israeli cease-fire violations have killed 1,488 Palestinians and injured 5,281 as of Sunday, according to the latest figures from Gaza's Health Ministry.
Since the war began in October 2023, more than 74,000 Palestinians have been killed and over 175,000 injured, while around 90% of Gaza's infrastructure has been destroyed, according to the ministry.

The Cultural Life of Colors in Latin American Interiors
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
07:30:00 UTC
16:30:00 KST

A color has a biography. A color can have an origin, but it can also transform. It can move between materials and disciplines, from a local practice into architecture, from something ordinary into something symbolic. It can lose one association and acquire another, or persist without anyone consciously thinking of it as cultural. Its life unfolds through the conditions in which it is produced, used, repeated, and inhabited. As these conditions change, so do the meanings a color can carry.
The interior is a place where these histories converge. A color inside a room can carry traces of a territory, a material practice, a climate or a history of inhabitation. Its presence does not necessarily depend on an intention to represent any of these things.
Color can become part of a place through the continuity of materials and ways of living, acquiring significance beyond the surface on which it appears.

Gaza olive harvest battered by war as production plunges, farmland becomes inaccessible
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12

Gaza olive harvest battered by war as production plunges, farmland becomes inaccessible
'A tree that produced around 100 kilograms (220.4 pounds) of olives before the war now produces no more than 20 (44 pounds) to 30 kilograms (66 pounds),' farmer Kamel Baraka tells Anadolu
Hosni Nedim and Lina Altawell
12 October 2026•Update: 12 October 2026
GAZA CITY, Palestine / ISTANBUL
Gaza Agriculture Ministry estimates agricultural sector losses from war at more than $3B
Palestinian farmers in Gaza are facing a difficult olive harvest this year as production declines, large areas of agricultural land remain damaged and many groves are inaccessible because they lie in areas controlled by the Israeli army or beyond the so-called “yellow line.”
On accessible farmland, farmers continue picking olives and separating them from leaves and branches despite shortages of fertilizer, irrigation water and agricultural supplies, as well as higher labor, transportation and pressing costs.
The pressures have left many families unable to store their usual annual supplies of olive oil and olives.
On July 13, Gaza’s Agriculture Ministry estimated losses to the agricultural sector from Israel’s genocidal war, which began on Oct. 8, 2023, at more than $3 billion, including $1.49 billion in direct damage and $1.59 billion in indirect losses.
Kamel Baraka, a farmer from Deir al-Balah in central Gaza, said olive tree yields had fallen significantly.
“A tree that produced around 100 kilograms (220.4 pounds) of olives before the war now produces no more than 20 (44 pounds) to 30 kilograms (66 pounds),” Baraka told Anadolu.
That represents a decline of around 70% to 80%, he added.
“A season that once provided an important source of income for farmers, traders and workers now barely meets the needs of some families because of current conditions and shortages of essential agricultural supplies,” Baraka said.
“Olive cultivation requires constant care, fertilizer, irrigation and other inputs that have become increasingly difficult to obtain,” he added.
Massive damage
Damage to farmland and restrictions on access have also directly reduced the harvest.
“Large areas of olive groves in eastern parts of central Gaza lie in zones farmers cannot reach, particularly east of Salah al-Din Street and around the ‘yellow line,’” Baraka said.
The “yellow line” is a notional line inside the Gaza Strip to which the Israeli army withdrew under the first phase of US President Donald Trump’s plan to end the war, under which a ceasefire took effect on Oct. 10, 2025. It separates areas in eastern Gaza that remain under Israeli army control from areas west of the line where Palestinians are allowed to move.
“Farmers in Deir al-Balah, Bureij and Maghazi face difficulty reaching agricultural land that had been a major source of olive production,” Baraka said.
He said available farmland west of Salah al-Din Street is insufficient to meet residents’ needs for olive oil and olives.
Before the war, preparations for the harvest began about a month in advance, with farmers arranging workers and preparing equipment for picking and transport, while families stored olives and oil for the year ahead.
Those preparations have declined as production falls and costs rise, with some farmers now collecting only enough olives for household consumption and limited quantities for sale.
Costs triple
Farmers are also struggling with sharply higher transportation and pressing costs, as well as shortages of containers needed to store olive oil.
“The cost of pressing olives has risen to around three times what it was before the war,” Baraka said, adding that the increase has placed further pressure on farmers whose incomes have already fallen because of lower production.
“Before the war, olive press owners often transported harvests from farms to pressing facilities, while farmers now struggle to find transportation even for small quantities,” he added.
Higher costs for pumping water and irrigating trees, combined with shortages of fertilizer, labor and storage containers, have made preserving the harvest and storing oil increasingly difficult, particularly for families that depend on farming for their food needs.
“The olive season, once an opportunity for farmers to improve their livelihoods and secure food supplies for the year, has become an exhausting season that provides many of them with only a fraction of what they need,” Baraka said.
Since Israel’s genocidal war began on Oct. 8, 2023, Gaza’s agricultural sector has sustained widespread damage, according to the Agriculture Ministry.
The ministry said 158,909 dunams (39,267 acres) of agricultural land have been damaged out of a total 182,247 dunams (45,033 acres), or around 87%, sharply reducing crop production and the capacity to provide food.
The war also has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians and injured over 175,000 others, according to Palestinian figures, also destroying about 90% of the enclave's infrastructure.

Russia shelled the railway in the Zhytomyr region - what is the situation with train services
Kyiv • UNN
Railway and energy infrastructure facilities in Korosten district were hit. As of the morning of October 12, more than 30 trains are delayed en route.
Russia has attacked Ukraine’s railway again. In Zhytomyr region, railway and energy infrastructure facilities in Korosten district came under enemy fire. This was reported by Vitalii Bunechko, head of the Zhytomyr Regional Military Administration, on social media on October 12, UNN writes.
Zhytomyr region has once again come under enemy strikes. Since the evening, the enemy has repeatedly shelled the north of Zhytomyr region. Railway and energy infrastructure facilities in Korosten district were hit. As of now, no information about casualties or injuries has been received
The State Emergency Service noted that the enemy had repeatedly shelled the north of Zhytomyr region since the evening, and that "the Russians shelled railway infrastructure facilities in Korosten district."
"The attacks caused fires, which rescuers promptly extinguished. Due to the threat of repeated shelling, SES specialists withdrew to safe locations," the State Emergency Service said, showing the aftermath.
What is happening with train services
As of 10:20 a.m. on October 12, according to Ukrzaliznytsia, 38 long-distance passenger trains are delayed en route. The longest delays—more than 5 hours—are affecting trains 31/32 Zaporizhzhia–Przemyśl and 3/4 Dnipro–Uzhhorod.
Suburban trains have also been affected by the changes.
According to Ukrzaliznytsia, in Zhytomyr region, train No. 6461 Korosten–Zhytomyr is running from Berdychiv-Zhyt. station with a delay of 1 hour 2 minutes. "We are continuing to operate along the route and apologize for the inconvenience. In the event of an increased threat, the train will be stopped. Train service will resume only after the air raid threat has ended," Ukrzaliznytsia stated.
Suburban trains are also delayed in other regions. In particular, as of 9:30 a.m. on October 12, this affected Volyn, Rivne region, Kharkiv region, Dnipropetrovsk region, and Zaporizhzhia.

‘A pack of lies’: Abby Choi’s mother rejects claims Kwong family repaid her debts
Cheung Yin-fa says she gambled up to HK$100,000 at mahjong parlours for ‘entertainment’, but denies debts ever led to debt collectors harassing her family
The mother of slain Hong Kong socialite Abby Choi Tin-fung has denied in court that she was repeatedly in debt because of gambling, calling her former son-in-law’s claim that he had financially supported her “a pack of lies”.
Cheung Yin-fa accused Alex Kwong Kong-chi on Monday of acting unscrupulously by demanding the return of HK$150,000 in shopping expenses she owed him, while failing to repay any of the more than HK$70 million he had received from Choi for investment.

Hungarian FM: adoption of national minority education bill today enables opening of 2 EU clusters for Ukraine Tuesday
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
10:27:15 EEST
16:27:15 KST

Minister of Foreign Affairs of Hungary Anita Orbán hopes that the Verkhovna Rada of Ukraine will adopt the law on education for national minorities today, which would allow the next negotiation clusters for Ukraine's EU accession to be opened at the intergovernmental conference scheduled for October 13.
She made the statement on Monday in Luxembourg upon arriving at the EU Foreign Affairs Council meeting. On Tuesday, also in Luxembourg, the Ukraine–EU intergovernmental conference is expected to take place, where the second and third negotiation clusters could be opened.
"Today, the law on education for national minorities was submitted to the Verkhovna Rada of Ukraine for consideration. This is the result of a bilateral agreement that we agreed upon with the Ukrainian side in May and June. Last week, this bill was approved by the Ukrainian parliament's Committee on Education, and now it is under consideration by the Verkhovna Rada. We expect its adoption today, so I look forward to news from Kyiv," Orbán said.
She recalled that the adoption of this bill was a condition for opening the subsequent negotiation clusters, and in the event of a positive decision, Hungary "can allow the opening of the second and third clusters." "This also brings us a step closer to holding the intergovernmental conference with Ukraine," the Hungarian Foreign Minister stressed.
She also thanked "both Hungarian and Ukrainian experts and politicians whose efforts made this possible." "This aligns with European and Hungarian interests and values," Orbán added.
After that, according to the Hungarian minister, "implementation is an extremely important stage." "We will monitor this both from the Hungarian side and at the level of intergovernmental cooperation. The intergovernmental economic committee will operate, including an education subgroup whose work we have already initiated. This will become one of the first platforms where, together with representatives of national minority organizations in Zakarpattia, we will monitor the implementation of this law," she noted.

If Netanyahu goes, does anything really change for Palestinians?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
07:27:14 UTC
16:27:14 KST

If Netanyahu goes, does anything really change for Palestinians?
Analysts say opposition victory in October 27 polls may bring only marginal change and no fundamental shift on Gaza or West Bank.
Four rival Israeli political movements have agreed to work together in a bid to unseat Israel’s longest serving prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu.
The factions – the Yashar party, the Democrats, the Yisrael Beytenu party and the Together alliance – span different parts of Israel’s political spectrum but say they are united in their goal to “preserve and strengthen Israel as a Jewish and democratic state”.
The opposition grouping is in a close battle with a pro-Netanyahu coalition heading into the October 27 elections, recent polling indicated, although neither side appeared on track to win a parliamentary majority.
The election comes as Israel faces a series of domestic crises that are tearing at its social fabric, including questions over political accountability for alleged corruption and security failures, disputes over ultra-Orthodox military service and efforts to exclude Arab parties from political life. The country also faces growing backlash abroad, including from allies, over its continuing attacks on Gaza and Lebanon as well as settlements, which are illegal under international law, and settler pogroms in the occupied West Bank.
Analysts said the combination makes the upcoming elections among the most consequential in Israel’s history but even an opposition victory may bring only marginal change for Palestinians suffering record levels of settler violence and mass displacement. While the opposition alliance has taken Netanyahu to task personally, there is little daylight between them when it comes to Israel’s foundational policies in Gaza and the West Bank.
“Palestinians should not expect a fundamental change in Israeli policy if the Netanyahu bloc loses power,” said analyst Samer Jaber, a doctoral researcher specialising in political economy at Royal Holloway, University of London.
“The major political blocs share core positions on the Palestinian question, including support for the existing settlement structure, while the state institutions that formulate and implement policy would remain unchanged,” he added.
What is the anti-Netanyahu coalition?
The leaders of the four major Jewish-led opposition movements gathered on September 26 and signed a declaration promising not to attack each other in the run-up to the elections and to collaborate in forming a government after the vote.
In addition to Yair Lapid, who leads the official opposition in Israel’s Knesset, the meeting included Gadi Eisenkot, who heads the Yashar party; Naftali Bennett, who leads the Together alliance, cofounded by Lapid; Avigdor Lieberman, who heads Yisrael Beiteinu; and Yair Golan, who leads the Democrats. The declaration does not set out an official leader although Eisenkot is viewed as the opposition’s most likely candidate for prime minister. In a joint statement, the figures said defeating the current government was their “shared highest objective”.
Of the four opposition parties, Yashar is projected to be the strongest. A recent poll by Israel’s Channel 12 suggested Yashar would win 23 seats in parliament, the most of any party and more than the 21 seats projected for Netanyahu’s Likud.
Trailing is the Together alliance, projected to win 13 seats, followed by Yisrael Beiteinu and the Democrats, each projected to win nine.
That would give the opposition a combined 54 seats in the 120-seat Knesset, seven short of a majority. Netanyahu’s alliance, which includes several ultra-Orthodox and far-right parties, is projected to win 49 seats.
Arab-led parties, representing the Palestinian citizens of Israel, who make up about 20 percent of the population, are projected to win 13 seats, but most leaders of the Jewish-led opposition bloc have ruled out joining forces with them.
Roi Zur, an assistant professor at the University of Essex who leads a research project on Israeli parties’ political ideology and policy, said the anti-Netanyahu coalition has a chance to win if turnout is on its side, noting that several parties that do not “strictly oppose” the prime minister could fall below the 3.25 percent threshold to enter the Knesset, shaking up the balance.
“If these parties waste enough right-wing votes, the opposition might translate their support into power,” Zur told Al Jazeera. “But this might not be enough.”
Even if the opposition alliance manages to find a way to oust Netanyahu, it would likely be weak and incapable – or unwilling – to overhaul Israeli policy in the West Bank and Gaza, analysts said.
“An anti-Netanyahu government will most likely be a very disparate coalition with a very thin majority, if any, in the Knesset. That would make it difficult for such a government to agree on any substantial perceived concessions, such as withdrawing completely from Gaza,” Anders Persson, a political scientist specialising in the Israel-Palestine conflict, told Al Jazeera.
“It would also make it difficult for the international community to meaningfully pressure such a government because there will always be a fear that an anti-Netanyahu government could quickly collapse.”
‘Mostly right-wing’
While their positions vary, most leaders of the anti-Netanyahu alliance have taken hardline positions on Gaza and the West Bank that give Palestinians little reason for optimism.
Yashar’s Eisenkot, a former Israeli military chief, has called the idea of a Palestinian state “delusional”, and he supports “strengthening” Israeli settlements. However, he opposes full Israeli annexation of the West Bank and has said he would dismantle smaller Israeli outposts not approved by the Israeli government. He also opposes the current government’s E1 settlement plan, which in effect would cut the West Bank in two. On Gaza, Eisenkot supports pursuing a United States-backed peace plan but only from a place of “strength” and only after “Hamas’s total disarmament”.
Israeli attacks across Gaza since the start of a “ceasefire” in October last year have killed nearly 1,500 Palestinians, bringing the overall death toll since the start of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza in October 2023 to more than 74,000, according to the enclave’s health officials.
Bennett, a former Likud member who served in multiple Netanyahu-led governments, has described himself as “more right-wing” than Netanyahu and advocated exceptionally draconian policies in Gaza, including once calling for a “shoot-to-kill” policy against Palestinians trying to cross into Israel. Bennett staunchly opposes a Palestinian state and supports settlement expansion although he has criticised Israeli settler pogroms against Palestinians. With respect to the future of Gaza, he wants Israeli forces to stay in the enclave until Hamas is disarmed and proposes that Egypt, rather than Turkiye or Qatar, should play a future security role.
Lieberman’s Yisrael Beytenu party also supports settlement expansion, including the E1 plan. He backs annexing all of Area C of the West Bank – which constitutes 60 percent of the territory and is already under full Israeli control – while transferring control of other parts of the territory to Jordan. On Gaza, his party wants Israel to retain “freedom of action”, cut off water and electricity and eventually transfer governance to “an agreed-upon international entity”.
Golan’s Democrats party is the only one to support a form of two-state solution although it frames it as “responsible separation” that includes the “full demilitarisation” of the Palestinian state and complete Israeli security control of the Jordan Valley and other key areas. His party also supports complete demilitarisation for Gaza and a reconstruction process that involves regional states.
Palestinian lawyer and analyst Diana Buttu said each of the opposition leaders “has supported Israel’s genocide in Gaza” while backing settlements or not believing in full “equality for Palestinians”.
This orientation reflects hardening views within Israeli society itself.
According to a September Pew Research Center poll, only 17 percent of Israeli respondents said peaceful coexistence alongside an independent Palestinian state is possible. And according to an August survey by the Jewish People Policy Institute, 38 percent of Jewish Israeli participants favoured annexing the entire West Bank and more than half supported retaining the settlements as part of any future agreement on a Palestinian state.
‘Lessen the harms’
Nevertheless, some analysts said a new government could roll back or slow down some of the most “controversial and radical steps” of Israel’s current government, which includes far-right settlement proponents Itamar Ben-Gvir, the minister of national security, and Bezalel Smotrich, the minister of finance. Smotrich last month said Israel should “go to war” in the West Bank and repeat what it “did in Gaza”.
Changes enacted by a new government would likely include suspending the E1 settlement project and cracking down “on extremist settler violence/terrorism in the West Bank”, said Dov Waxman, a professor of political science at the University of California, Los Angeles, who specialises in Israeli politics and the Israel-Palestine conflict.
A new government would also be expected to “allow more humanitarian aid to enter Gaza in a more predictable, consistent manner and for reconstruction to finally begin there”, he added.
Ehab Jabareen, a Palestinian political analyst and researcher in Israel, told Al Jazeera that a new government led by Netanyahu’s opponents would likely be “more receptive to US and international pressure”, giving more space for potential reconstruction in Gaza.
But overall, Jabareen said, such a government is unlikely to alter Israel’s overarching “paradigm” towards Palestinians. “I would expect the difference to be less about whether Israel maintains control over the Palestinians and more about how the control is exercised, legitimised and managed,” he said.
Amjad Iraqi, senior analyst for Israel and Palestine at the International Crisis Group, said any “shades of difference” would be meaningful for Palestinians who are currently “suffering nearly uninhibited brutality”.
“We’re at a point of mitigation,” Iraqi told Al Jazeera. “It is about trying to lessen the harms. Palestinians are not in a position to expect any kind of radical shift, but every life saved, every piece of land saved matters a lot for people on the ground.”

Tried to blow up a bus carrying Ukrainian Armed Forces personnel — a student from Kyiv detained in Rivne

Unknown Publisher

Tried to blow up a bus carrying Ukrainian Armed Forces personnel — a student from Kyiv detained in Rivne
Kyiv • UNN
The SBU detained a student from Kyiv who planted explosives under a bus carrying military personnel and installed a camera to monitor it. He faces up to 12 years in prison.
In Rivne, a student from Kyiv suspected of preparing a terrorist attack commissioned by Russian special services was detained. According to the investigation, he planted explosives under a bus carrying Ukrainian Armed Forces personnel and installed a camera to monitor the soldiers boarding the bus. The Security Service of Ukraine reports this, UNN writes.
Details
The investigation established that, to carry out the terrorist attack, the enemy recruited a student from Kyiv who planted a homemade bomb under a bus transporting Ukrainian servicemen.
Opposite the parking lot, the agent installed a telephone camera disguised as a juice carton, with remote access for Russian special service operatives.
With the help of the “video trap,” the Rashists hoped to monitor the servicemen boarding the bus and blow it up while it was en route to its destination
SBU officers uncovered the enemy’s plan in advance, neutralized the explosives, and detained the agent at the city bus station as he hurriedly attempted to leave the regional center for Kyiv after planting the IED, intending to “lay low.”
A smartphone was seized from the detainee, which he used to “report” to the russian federation that the explosives had been planted at the site of the planned terrorist attack.
According to the case materials, the intelligence task was carried out by a student at one of the capital’s universities. He came to the attention of Russian special service operatives while looking for “quick” earnings in Telegram channels on the subject.
After recruiting him, the Rashists “sent” him to Rivne to prepare the bombing of a military vehicle carrying Ukrainian Armed Forces personnel.
Upon arriving in the city, the agent settled in a rented apartment and later received coordinates from his handler in the russian federation for a cache, from which he retrieved a homemade explosive device.
It was established that the explosives had been reinforced with two glass bottles containing a flammable liquid to increase their destructive effect.
Currently, investigators of the Security Service have notified the detainee that he is suspected under Part 2 of Article 15 and Part 2 of Article 258 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine (completed attempt to commit a terrorist act).
The offender is being held in custody without the right to bail. He faces up to 12 years in prison with confiscation of property.

Sourcing Natural Stone from Iran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
07:26:09 UTC
16:26:09 KST

Sourcing natural stone from Iran requires more than competitive pricing. Buyers must assess material quality, verify specifications, confirm availability, and understand export responsibilities before placing an order. This guide explores Iranian natural stone sourcing models, quality assessment, cost evaluation, and export coordination. It also explains how ALPREY, an independent Iranian natural stone sourcing and export partner, works with selected suppliers and manufacturers to identify suitable marble, travertine, onyx, and other natural stone products according to buyers’ requirements. Clear specifications and order-specific confirmation support more transparent and informed purchasing decisions.
Sourcing Natural Stone from Iran: From Quarry Selection and Quality Assessment to Export Coordination
The international natural stone market is shaped by more than visual appeal, color variety, or competitive pricing. For importers, distributors, processors, and project buyers, a successful transaction depends on material quality, reliable supply, transparent specifications, and clear export arrangements. A stone that looks attractive in a photograph or sample may not be available for a commercial order with the same characteristics, dimensions, or delivery conditions.
Iran offers international buyers a diverse range of natural stones, including marble, travertine, onyx, limestone, and granite. Accessing this potential, however, requires an understanding of the supply chain and the selection of a commercial partner suited to the buyer’s needs. The distinction between quarry operators, manufacturers, exporters, and independent sourcing companies can affect pricing, quality control, and accountability throughout a transaction.
Understanding Natural Stone Sourcing Models in Iran
Natural stone sourcing from Iran follows several commercial models. Quarry operators focus on extracting stone blocks, while processing plants turn raw materials into slabs, tiles, and cut-to-size products. Export companies may supply materials manufactured in their own facilities or sourced from other producers for international markets.
Independent sourcing and trading companies also operate in this market. Their role does not necessarily involve direct extraction or manufacturing. Instead, they identify suitable supply sources, match materials with buyers’ specifications, and coordinate commercial and export procedures.
No single model is ideal for every buyer. The right choice depends on product type, order volume, quality-control requirements, specification complexity, and the responsibilities expected from the supplier. Before comparing quotations, buyers should clarify each partner’s role and understand how product information and specifications will be verified.
Stone Quality: Beyond Color and Appearance
Product images are the starting point of a quality assessment, not its conclusion. Natural variations in color, veining, texture, fissures, and other geological characteristics can affect appearance and processing yield. The significance of each feature depends on the stone’s intended application.
For block purchases, relevant information includes length, width, height, approximate weight, visible condition, and actual photographs taken from multiple angles. Industrial buyers should also consider potential losses during cutting and processing when assessing the economics of a purchase. For processed products, thickness, dimensions, surface finish, dimensional tolerances, edge quality, and consistency across the shipment should be defined according to project requirements.
Buyers should distinguish between archival images, representative samples, and photographs of the actual shipment. An image of similar stone does not confirm current availability or prove that a consignment meets the required specifications. For quality-sensitive orders, agreed acceptance criteria and a pre-shipment inspection can help reduce the risk of disputes. Where necessary, independent inspection can be arranged according to the scope and criteria agreed by both parties.
For larger or repeat orders, buyers should also consider whether the agreed reference sample represents the acceptable range of natural variation across the shipment. Where consistency matters, the parties can document the approved sample, inspection method, grading criteria, and procedure for addressing non-conformities before production or loading begins. Recording these points in the purchase order helps establish a shared basis for evaluation and makes later discussions more objective.
How Competitive Pricing Translates into Cost-Effective Purchasing
Export quotations can only be meaningfully compared when they are based on equivalent terms. Price differences may reflect variations in stone grade, dimensions, quality, order quantity, delivery terms, or the costs included in the offer. The lowest initial price does not necessarily represent the lowest overall cost for the buyer.
A thorough evaluation should consider the material price alongside packaging, loading, inland transportation, export formalities, international freight, and potential destination charges. International Commercial Terms, including EXW, FOB, CFR, and CIF, allocate costs and responsibilities between sellers and buyers in different ways. The appropriate term should reflect the actual shipping route and the commercial agreement between the parties.
Transparent pricing means clearly distinguishing confirmed costs from items that remain subject to stock verification, inspection results, documentation, or shipping arrangements. This supports more informed decisions and reduces the risk of unrealistic expectations.
The Role of Export Coordination in the Supply Chain
Sourcing suitable stone is only the beginning. Specifications must match the order, packaging must suit the product and transport method, and responsibilities for documentation, loading, and logistics should be clarified before shipment.
The destination, shipment volume, product format, and transport route can all affect operational planning and final costs. Preparation and delivery timelines should therefore reflect the actual order status and shipping arrangements rather than generic or unverified promises.
For professional buyers, an export partner’s value extends beyond the quotation itself. It also lies in clarifying transaction stages, defining responsibilities, and maintaining communication between purchasing requirements, supply sources, and shipment arrangements.
ALPREY: An Independent Approach to Natural Stone Sourcing and Export from Iran
ALPREY is the international export brand of Arda Tejarat Deniz Co., Ltd., a legally registered Iranian company based in Urmia, West Azerbaijan Province. Its focus is the international sourcing and export of Iranian natural stone, particularly marble, travertine, and onyx.
ALPREY does not own quarries or directly operate extraction or manufacturing facilities. Instead, it works as an independent sourcing and trading partner, cooperating with selected Iranian suppliers and manufacturers to identify materials that match buyers’ specifications and requirements.
Depending on the order, the process may include reviewing the buyer’s inquiry, coordinating with suppliers, checking specifications, assessing quality, preparing export arrangements, and coordinating logistics. Product formats are evaluated against the buyer’s needs and actual supply conditions. These may include natural stone blocks and, where appropriate, processed stone products.
A central principle is distinguishing general product offerings from confirmed availability. Stone type, dimensions, quantity, quality, pricing conditions, and supply feasibility must be assessed for each inquiry and confirmed before the transaction is finalized. This allows proposals to reflect the buyer’s actual requirements and the specific order conditions rather than unverified claims about stock or supply capacity.
This model may suit importers, distributors, processing facilities, and project buyers seeking Iranian natural stone, particularly when coordination between product specifications, suppliers, and export requirements is essential.
How to Submit a More Precise Purchase Inquiry
To obtain a quotation that can be properly evaluated, buyers should specify the stone type, preferred color, product format, dimensions or thickness, quantity, surface finish, destination country, and preferred delivery term. Reference images and project-specific quality requirements can further reduce ambiguity.
Buyers should also ask about current availability, material origin, estimated preparation time, packaging method, inspection options, and the export documentation that can be provided. Precise initial specifications make quotations easier to compare and assess against project requirements.
Conclusion
Successful stone sourcing involves more than selecting attractive material. It requires alignment between technical specifications, quality assessment, commercial transparency, and export planning. By understanding the supplier’s business model, verifying information about the actual consignment, and comparing quotations on an equivalent basis, buyers can make better-informed purchasing decisions.
Within this framework, ALPREY operates as an independent Iranian natural stone sourcing and export partner, focusing on identifying suitable materials and coordinating commercial and export stages. Confirming each order’s specifications and terms before finalization supports a more transparent and professional purchasing process.

Humanitarian crisis deepening amid global conflicts, says ICRC president
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
07:23:57 UTC
16:23:57 KST

Humanitarian crisis deepening amid global conflicts, says ICRC president
Humanitarian aid is in crisis as funding falls, support wanes and respect for international humanitarian law erodes. ICRC President Mirjana Spoljaric explains why protecting civilians in Gaza or Ukraine hinges on political will, and why autonomous weapon systems should be banned.
SRF: During the UN General Assembly High-Level Week in New York in September, you were heavily involved in promoting international humanitarian law and humanitarian aid. Are heads of state and government aware of how many issues are in disarray in this area?
Mirjana Spoljaric: They are certainly aware of the situation. The question is what effect this awareness will have. We need to take it a step further and move towards action.
As soon as we start talking about international humanitarian law, it becomes clear that countries need to adapt their military strategies so the situation on the ground improves. That’s when dialogue becomes difficult, because it’s highly political. Empathy and solidarity have a hard time gaining traction.
SRF: Do certain key parties to conflicts – such as in Ukraine or Gaza – not care about principles like the protection of the civilian population?
M.S.: Every government representative knows just how dire the situation is in Gaza. What is lacking is the political will to actually improve the situation.
Food aid is not enough. What is needed are machines or dual-use goods, but it is forbidden to import them. Pressure must be put on influential states like the US and Israel to lift such sanctions.
What are dual-use goods?
Dual-use goods are products that were originally developed for everyday civilian use or for industry, but which could theoretically also be misused for military purposes, such as the manufacture of weapons or surveillance systems.
Because these goods can pose a security risk, they are subject to strict government checks. Anyone wishing to export them abroad requires official authorisation to do so.
SRF: Do the governments of influential countries still support the Geneva Conventions?
M.S.: Our global initiative to promote international humanitarian law is supported by 118 states. At a summit in Jordan in December, international humanitarian law will be made a political priority. Several heads of state have confirmed that they will travel to Jordan.
SRF: Where do you see the most serious breaches of international humanitarian law?
M.S.: The all-too-flexible interpretation – let’s call it that – of international humanitarian law and wanton destruction are rife. We are witnessing this today in all conflicts.
Millions of people are being displaced and tens of thousands killed, very often as a consequence of violations of international humanitarian law.
SRF: Developments in weapons systems also contravene the Geneva Conventions and we are seeing the resurgence of nuclear weapons and new autonomous weapons systems. What can be done about this?
M.S.: UN Secretary-General António Guterres and I recently reaffirmed our demand to curb autonomous weapon systems. Weapon systems that decide on life and death without human command must be banned.
A growing number of states are seriously concerned about what the future of warfare will look like if artificial intelligence is given free rein.
SRF: We are moving towards a world in which the principle of “law before power” no longer applies, but rather “power before law” in other words, the law of the strongest. What are the consequences for humanitarian aid?
M.S.: The principle of “might before right” undermines economic development, investment in human capital and social progress.
Only within a rules-based legal order can children attend school without fear, young people pursue education or vocational training with confidence, and adults find work that provides a decent living. All of this depends on the rule of law prevailing.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — President Lai Ching-te (賴清德) said Monday that the government will increase support for vocational education to help young people develop skills needed by industry.
Speaking at a meeting with Taiwan’s delegation to the 48th WorldSkills Competition, Lai said skilled workers are essential to economic growth. He pledged to strengthen cooperation among schools, training systems, and businesses to better prepare students for employment.
CNA reported that Taiwan sent 53 competitors to the WorldSkills Competition, which ended in Shanghai on Sept. 27. The team competed in 47 categories and won three gold, three silver, and seven bronze medals, along with 30 medallions for excellence, placing third among 68 teams.

With global supply chains changing and artificial intelligence reshaping industries, Lai said workers need practical skills, creativity, and knowledge across different fields. He stressed that vocational education must adapt to help students meet future job demands.
The government has allocated NT$16 billion (US$505 million) to the second phase of its youth employment program, which runs from 2023 through this year. Lai said the program had helped more than 800,000 young people find jobs as of August, with another phase being planned.
The government is also expanding overseas training opportunities for young people. The labor ministry plans to send young skilled workers to Japan this year, with similar exchanges planned for Germany and Australia.
Lai said these exchanges would allow participants to learn new skills and bring valuable experience back to Taiwan. He also encouraged the WorldSkills competitors to share their knowledge and help improve professional standards.
He said their achievements went beyond winning medals, as international competition had strengthened their confidence and problem-solving abilities. Lai urged them to continue developing their skills and contribute to the country’s industrial growth.

Drones Hit Key Russian Railway Bridge Over Don, Disrupting 25 Trains and Crimea Routes
Drones damaged a major railway bridge across the Don River in Russia’s Rostov-on-Don overnight on October 10, forcing railway authorities to suspend traffic in both directions and disrupting at least 25 passenger trains, including services connected to temporarily occupied Crimea.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Russia’s North Caucasus Railway on October 10, a drone attack damaged the railway drawbridge on the Rostov–Bataysk section, forcing the temporary closure of both tracks. Russian officials acknowledged the damage as a large-scale drone attack swept across the Rostov region.
The disruption initially delayed 14 long-distance passenger trains and two commuter services, with some departures running nearly four hours behind schedule. The number of affected long-distance trains later rose to 25, according to Russia’s Federal Passenger Company.
The delays affected major routes connecting Moscow, St. Petersburg, and other Russian cities with destinations in southern Russia, including Adler, Novorossiysk, Anapa, and Mineralnye Vody. Passengers facing delays exceeding four hours were provided with food and water.
The disruption also reached temporarily occupied Crimea. Russian railway operator Grand Service Express reported delays affecting its Tavria services traveling through the Rostov region, with some trains running up to three and a half hours behind schedule.
The bridge is an important railway crossing over the Don River, connecting Rostov-on-Don with routes extending farther south. Its location makes it a significant transport link between central Russia, the North Caucasus, and routes serving temporarily occupied Crimea.
Russian railway authorities reported that traffic across both tracks resumed at 7:49 a.m. local time. However, the disruption continued to affect schedules throughout the day. By the evening of October 10, 13 passenger trains were still running behind schedule, according to the Federal Passenger Company.
The full extent of the damage remains unclear. While monitoring channels reported possible damage to the bridge’s lifting mechanism, there has been no official confirmation that the mechanism was disabled.
Earlier, on October 6, the Ukrainian partisan movement ATESH reported that Russian authorities were urgently reinforcing key road and railway bridges across the Don River, fearing Ukrainian strikes. The measures reportedly included anti-drone defenses, electronic warfare systems, and preparations for alternative crossings in case critical transport links were damaged.

Ukraine's Defense Forces neutralized 89 Russian targets overnight into Monday; however, impacts of enemy air attack assets were recorded across 15 locations, the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported.
"According to preliminary data, as of 09:00, air defense shot down or suppressed 89 Russian UAVs of the Shahed type (55 of them jet-powered), Gerberas, and other drone types," the statement reads.
In total, overnight into October 12 (from 18:00 on October 11), the enemy attacked with an Kh-59 guided air missile from the airspace over the Black Sea, as well as 121 strike UAVs including Shahed (76 of them jet-powered), Gerbera, Banderol/Dan-T, and Parodiya decoy drones from the directions of Orel, Kursk, Primorsko-Akhtarsk (Russia), occupied Donetsk region, and occupied Crimea (Hvardiyske).
The air attack was repelled by aviation, anti-aircraft missile troops, electronic warfare and unmanned systems units, and mobile fire groups of the Ukrainian Defense Forces.
Meanwhile, impacts of Russian air attack assets were recorded at 15 locations, and falling debris from downed targets was reported at four locations.
The attack remains ongoing, with about ten Russian UAVs currently in Ukrainian airspace, the command added.

‘Most dangerous tech ever invented’: Bill Gates challenges Trump’s AI stance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
07:21:24 UTC
16:21:24 KST

‘Most dangerous tech ever invented’: Bill Gates challenges Trump’s AI stance
Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates has challenged US President Donald Trump’s approach to AI, warning that the government cannot leave the world’s “most dangerous technology” entirely in the hands of the companies that develop it.
Trump signed the White House Accord on Super Intelligence last month alongside representatives of Google, OpenAI, Meta, xAI, Anthropic, and Nvidia, establishing voluntary safety commitments and internal oversight mechanisms.
Speaking to CNN’s State of the Union on Sunday, Gates questioned whether Trump’s agreement with America’s biggest tech companies goes far enough to prevent potentially catastrophic abuses.
“The idea that for the most dangerous technology humans ever invented, that that’s the final word, that just the companies themselves are the only check that society has,” Gates said, warning that “it’s clear we’re not doing enough.”
He argued that government agencies must take a more active role, comparing AI to aviation and medicine, where the authorities enforce safety standards. “The government so far is pretty much a bystander to something that’s going on in private companies.”
Gates identified cyberattacks as the most immediate danger and warned that criminals could exploit AI models stripped of safeguards against hacking and bioterrorism. “When you have bad people, no safeguards, and then the latest models, that’s where over the next year... we are going to have a lot of negative surprises,” he said.
His warnings follow a series of incidents involving AI agents acting beyond their intended instructions. Last week, Anthropic disclosed that its Claude models had taken unauthorized actions on government websites, including submitting a fabricated homicide tip to a Philadelphia police website during testing in July. Other reported incidents have involved AI agents accessing restricted information, exploiting vulnerabilities, and attempting to breach government websites.
Trump has resisted calls to slow AI development, arguing that restrictions could allow China to overtake the US in the technological race, and dismissing fears of rogue AI as a “hoax.” Gates said he hopes to discuss the dangers directly with Trump and his senior advisers.
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has argued that the world must accept some “bad things,” including hacks and scams, in exchange for the benefits of AI and widespread access to the technology. In an interview published last week, he insisted that the “good stuff” would outweigh the harm by “orders of magnitude.”
Confronted with Altman’s remarks, Gates acknowledged that eliminating every risk is impossible, comparing AI to the automobile industry, where accidents persist despite decades of safety improvements.
“Those were a big deal, but nothing compared to this,” Gates said, referring to the personal computer and the internet. “This changes the world more than all previous technologies.”

Report: Saudi crown prince shuttles between bunker-equipped palaces as Houthi missiles hit Riyadh
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
07:18:45 UTC
16:18:45 KST

Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman is moving between heavily guarded palaces equipped with bunkers, protected by a handpicked security team, as escalating Houthi missile attacks disrupt daily life in Riyadh and threaten the kingdom's economic stability, The Wall Street Journal reported, citing officials familiar with his movements.
The 41-year-old crown prince has sharply tightened his security as the Saudi capital increasingly comes under fire from Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi militants. His last public appearance was Tuesday, when he donated blood as part of a national campaign, according to the report.
On Saturday, at least one Houthi missile struck King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, killing at least 12 people and injuring hundreds, many seriously. Two terminals sustained extensive damage, with sections of their roofs collapsing. Among the victims was a 28-year-old Egyptian flight attendant who bled to death after losing an arm, according to officials briefed on the attack.
Video verified by Storyful showed passengers evacuating the airport with their suitcases, passing a trail of blood on the floor. The attacks continued Sunday, when another projectile reportedly struck the closed airport, igniting a fire in Terminal 4 and causing further injuries.
The escalating strikes have transformed parts of Riyadh into a conflict zone. Residents have been forced to seek shelter as explosions echo across the capital. Workers in the city's financial district, students at several international schools and diplomats have been instructed to evacuate buildings or take cover.
On Thursday, debris from an intercepted ballistic missile struck a kindergarten and a medical clinic complex, highlighting the danger to civilian areas even when incoming missiles are successfully intercepted.
Saudi officials have warned that the kingdom is running low on missile interceptors, according to the Journal. With large areas to defend and attacks targeting multiple locations, Saudi Arabia has been moving air-defense batteries between strategic sites, including royal palaces and vital energy infrastructure.
The growing threat comes as Mohammed bin Salman faces mounting pressure over his ambitious economic transformation program. For years, the crown prince has sought to turn Saudi Arabia into a global destination for tourism, investment and technology, investing enormous sums in futuristic developments such as Neom and major new projects in Riyadh.
Those ambitions are now being threatened by the deteriorating security situation. Houthi attacks have targeted airports, refineries and the East-West oil pipeline, which allows Saudi Arabia to export oil through the Red Sea without passing through the Strait of Hormuz.
The militants have also threatened Red Sea shipping, undermining another vital economic lifeline.
According to the Journal, a major international investment conference scheduled for late October is increasingly in doubt as the attacks threaten international travel and investor confidence.
The economic outlook was already deteriorating. Foreign investment declined during the first half of the year, several flagship megaprojects have stalled or come under review, and the Saudi Finance Ministry now expects the economy to contract by 3.6% in 2026.
Mohammed bin Salman is also facing difficult military decisions. Although Washington has provided military advisers, the United States has so far resisted Saudi requests for direct assistance in reversing Houthi territorial gains in Yemen, the Journal reported.
President Donald Trump said over the weekend that Washington was communicating with the Houthis but could join Saudi strikes against the group. "What they did was very bad," he said following the airport attack.
Saudi Arabia has also sought assistance from Pakistan and is searching internationally for additional air-defense systems, while exploring possible diplomatic solutions to contain the confrontation.
For the crown prince, the crisis now threatens both the security of his capital and the economic transformation on which he has staked much of his leadership. With missiles reaching Riyadh, civilian infrastructure under attack and his own movements taking place between fortified palaces, Saudi Arabia faces a growing challenge to its efforts to present itself as a safe destination for international business and investment.

Mystery of La Navidad: site of first Spanish settlement in Americas unknown
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
07:10:02 UTC
16:10:02 KST

On Christmas Eve 1492, the Santa María ran aground off Haiti. Christopher Columbus used its timbers to build Fort Navidad, where 39 men died. More than five centuries later, archaeologists have yet to pinpoint the site.
Spain's history of maritime navigation in the 15th century is full of stories and an epic quality rivalled only, perhaps, by the Portuguese empire. One of those stories surrounds the first Spanish settlement established in the Americas.
On his first voyage to the Americas, Christopher Columbus sailed with three ships: the Pinta, the Niña and the Santa María; but only two of them returned to Spain. It is widely known that on 12 October 1942 land was sighted from the Pinta. It was the discovery of the New World.
At 23:00 on a cold 24 December 1492, Columbus went to sleep. As he recorded in his logbook, he had not closed his eyes for two days. The sea was, in his own words, "like a bowl", and the Santa María was making slow headway along an unknown stretch of coast in the north of Hispaniola. Around midnight, the ship ran aground on a reef.
Columbus, far from dwelling on the loss, decided to dismantle her and, using her planks and the nails that still did their job, he built the fort of Navidad, which could house almost 40 men and lasted less than a year.
When Columbus returned, no one was left alive and now, more than five centuries later, no one has been able to prove with precision and certainty exactly where stood this edifice in Spanish seafaring history.
The night of the disaster
The shipwreck was the result of a chain of errors. Columbus went to bed and left the ship sailing on in a light wind. The helmsman on duty did the same: seeing the calm coast, he handed over the steering of the vessel to a cabin boy, something Columbus had expressly forbidden throughout the voyage. This led to the Santa María's hull splitting open after running aground almost silently on a reef, near what is now the bay of Cap-Haïtien.
Around midnight, currents pushed the ship onto a shoal. She touched so gently that almost no one realised what was coming. The boy felt the rudder scrape the bottom, heard the sound of the sea, began to shout and Columbus jumped out of bed.
But it was already too late, so late that the tide had already fallen. He ordered the main mast to be cut down to lighten the ship and told Juan de la Cosa, master and owner of the vessel, to take an anchor out in the skiff. De la Cosa disobeyed, another link in the chain of errors: he took the boat to the Niña, which was sailing nearby. The Santa María listed and her planks sprang apart. Columbus transferred the crew to the Niña and waited for dawn.
The day of construction
With the first light, Columbus sent messengers to Guacanagarí, one of the five Taíno chiefs on Hispaniola.According to what they told him later, the cacique wept when he heard the news. He sent all his people out in large canoes and helped to unload the ship with his brothers and relatives. He ordered the goods to be stored beside the houses, and even emptied some so they would fit. Columbus wrote to the Catholic Monarchs that he did not believe there were "better people or better land" anywhere.
Everything that could be salvaged was saved, from supplies to deck planks and hull timbers. Columbus decided to leave a garrison there. He believed that gold was abundant on the island, and the loss of the ship made it necessary to leave men behind so that the rest of the expedition could return to Spain with only the Niña.
Around 26 December he began to build a fort from the timber and nails of the ship and called it La Navidad, after the night of the wreck. Historian Carlos Martínez Shaw recalls that the log itself records that the ship was beyond repair and was broken up, and that the fort was sufficiently large to house 39 people.
The chronicles relate that Columbus had artillery fired at what remained of the hull so that the Taínos could see his power. On 30 December, Guacanagarí seated him on a platform of palm and placed his own crown on his head.
The "39 of La Navidad" were placed under the orders of Diego de Arana, constable of the expedition. Among them were the king's pantry steward Pero Gutiérrez, Rodrigo de Escobedo, a surgeon, three craftsmen, a gunner and a tailor. Their mission was to trade with the Taínos and find out where the mine lay. Columbus set sail on the Niña in early 1493 on his return to Castile.
What happened to the first Spanish settlement in the Americas
The admiral returned on 27 November 1493, on his second voyage, with 17 ships and around 1,500 men. He found the fort burnt to the ground and the Spaniards dead, most of them disfigured. Guacanagarí blamed the attack on another chief, the lord of the mines. Historians still wonder whether the leader who had welcomed them might have had a hand in it. Columbus did not rebuild the fort but founded another settlement, La Isabela, elsewhere on the island.
The most serious find came from William Hodges, an American missionary doctor and amateur archaeologist. His patients showed him highly elaborate Taíno pottery and in 1977 he located the site of En Bas Saline, in northern Haiti. It was a major Taíno centre, very close to where the Santa María went down.
The Florida Museum of Natural History excavated there together with Haiti's Bureau National d'Ethnologie between 1983 and 1988, and returned in 2003. In total, 276 square metres were dug. The 2003 campaign confirmed that the central mound was a large structure burned at the end of the 15th century. Researchers identified En Bas Saline as Guacanagarí's village and as the probable site of La Navidad.
Among the animal remains, they found the first trace of the black rat from the Old World on the island. The definitive proof is still missing. Today there is no conclusive evidence fixing the exact location of the fort, and none of its timber has been identified in a way that is beyond dispute.
The wreck of the Santa María
The other piece of the puzzle is the ship. In 2014, underwater explorer Barry Clifford announced that he had found the Santa María in waters off northern Haiti. The Haitian culture minister, Monique Rocourt, said at the time that the evidence she had seen suggested it was not the ship.
The director of Haiti's National Bureau of Ethnology, Erol Josué, pointed out that the ship could not be lying on the seabed, because its planks had been used to build the fort.
Historian María Luisa Cazorla has put forward another hypothesis. The coastline has advanced because of sediment carried by rivers, and the remains of the ship would now lie on land, under some six metres of deposits. Her thesis argues that the wreck could be located within a radius of a few hundred metres by geophysical prospecting. In August 2026, 'History.com' was still referring to the Haitian wreck as a purported discovery.
For the moment, neither the ship nor the fort built from her timbers have turned up conclusively. Unwittingly, Columbus had laid the foundations of an empire that would last for centuries and where the sun never set.

When will El Niño peak and end? A full timeline of the weather phenomenon taking the world by storm
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
07:02:03 UTC
16:02:03 KST

A ‘Godzilla’ El Niño is still intensifying in the Pacific. When will we see the weather phenomenon peak – and when will it come to an end?
2026 will go down in history for what could become the largest El Niño in living memory, as the world scrambles to prepare for an onslaught of extreme weather.
The natural weather phenomenon (Spanish for ‘the boy’) occurs irregularly – roughly every two to seven years – when sea temperatures in the Eastern Pacific Ocean become unusually warm. Experts first started warning that a strong El Niño could form at the beginning of this year, supported by large amounts of heat in the subsurface ocean and the expected weakening of low-level trade winds.
In the first week of June, the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) confirmed that El Niño conditions were officially underway. Towards the end of summer, experts warned that the “unprecedented” El Niño could become the largest event since the 19th century – gaining the nickname of a ‘Godzilla’ or ‘Super’ El Niño.
Is El Niño getting stronger – and what are the impacts?
In its monthly bulletin on 12 October, Copernicus Climate Change Service announced that September's average sea-surface temperature reached 21.05°C – the highest on record for the month – amid strengthening El Niño conditions.
According to the WMO, sea-surface temperatures in the central and eastern tropical Pacific are also forecast to reach record levels during October, November and December.
Sea-surface temperature anomalies across the central-eastern equatorial Pacific, the region at the heart of El Niño, are measured by the widely used Niño 3.4 index. This increased markedly from an average +1.6 °C above normal in June 2026 to +2.5 °C above normal in August.
For October-November-December, the seasonal average Niño 3.4 sea surface temperature anomaly is forecast to reach approximately +3.7°C. This would be the highest since observations began and is stronger than the previous record of +2.6°C in November 2015-January 2016.
Previous El Niño events have contributed towards record-breaking heat, fuelling long-standing droughts, flash floods and deadly wildfires across the globe.
El Niño’s weather impacts are mainly felt in the tropics, but Europe can experience milder, wetter winters. An El Niño peak can also weaken the polar vortex, increasing the likelihood of a cold snap.
South America, the southern US, East Africa and Central Asia have all experienced heightened flood risks during previous El Niño events – while droughts and wildfire risks rise across large parts of Australia, northern parts of South America and in certain Asian countries such as Indonesia.
Extreme weather overseas will still have a knock-on effect for Europe. The IHE Delft Institute for Water Education in the Netherlands has been working in areas that are directly impacted by El Niño and warn that many staple foods that Europe imports could be at risk.
For example, in Nicaragua, crops such as maize and beans may fail in already fragile areas, leading to food insecurity and income loss in the country. A lack of rain and low flows in rivers also mean that irrigated crops in Colombia, Northeast Brazil and India will face severe restrictions or will need to rely more on groundwater, potentially causing overexploitation in the area – and export shortages.
A timeline of El Niño: When will it peak and end?
The WMO’s latest statement says that El Niño is forecast to peak in December, and will continue into next year.
“El Niño is firmly established and strengthening rapidly,” warns WMO Secretary-General Celeste Saulo. “WMO forecasts indicate a near-100 per cent likelihood that it will persist through February 2027, potentially being one of the strongest since at least 1950.”
The almost-certain figure isn’t from one climate model. The WMO has coordinated ocean buoy, satellite and radiosonde data from 13 national and international centres to make the prediction.
El Niño isn’t expected to end until spring 2027, but its impacts will likely stretch further. It’s why experts warn that next year could become the hottest on record.
El Niño clashes with climate change
Most El Niño events increase global average temperatures by around 0.2°C. While this is enough to trigger extreme weather conditions across the Global South, it is a fraction of the additional warming caused by climate change.
Human-caused global warming from the burning of fossil fuels has pushed global average surface temperatures 1.3°C to 1.4°C above pre-industrial levels. It is this that paved the way for Europe’s scorching summer, long-standing drought and deadly wildfires.
Nowadays, El Niño’s impacts are compounded by an already warming world – one that has a much stronger influence on the extreme weather we’re witnessing. 2025, for example, was the third warmest year on record – hotter than the El Niño year of 2016 – despite the naturally-forming cool drag of El Niño’s counterpart, La Niña.
Recent research suggests that climate change is turbocharging El Niño events too, by making them 36 per cent stronger than before the industrial era.
“El Niño doesn't add new heat to the planet. It releases heat the ocean has already been storing beneath the surface – which is why a strong event so often becomes one of the hottest years measured (as with 2024),” Saulo told the Global Heat Forum in Bangkok in October.
“The ocean it’s drawing from is the warmest we’ve ever measured it. There is simply more heat available to release.”

Roman fort found in Wales could prove myth of emperor’s camp is real
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
07:00:48 UTC
16:00:48 KST

Magnus Maximus, the Roman emperor who ruled Britain in the fourth century, led his troops against the Picts and Scots, but a theory that he also established a military camp near Frenni Fawr hill in Wales has so far been based on folklore.
Now fourth-century coins, among other finds at a newly identified Roman fort in Pembrokeshire, suggest the medieval tale was rooted in reality, to the excitement of archaeologists.
The fort was discovered by Dr Mark Merrony, a leading Roman specialist at the University of Oxford. He heads an excavation that is bringing to life a story about Magnus Maximus, as told in the Mabinogion, a collection of medieval epic tales of myth, magic and miracles.
Merrony expressed excitement that this landscape held the only Roman military site close to where the Mabinogion places the emperor. “If Magnus Maximus was there, there must have been an army there,” he said.
“It’s such a remote area but the tale mentions the easternmost peak of the Preseli Hills, which is where this site is. The presence of a heavily fortified Roman auxiliary fort may help unlock the mystery of a Mabinogion legend that has endured for nearly 1,700 years.”
In The Dream of Macsen Wledig, medieval storytellers used the emperor’s name in Welsh in recounting his rise to power. They described how on his military manoeuvres, he pitched his camp at Frenni Fawr, the 395-metre (1,300ft) easternmost peak of the Preseli Hills.
There had been no archaeological evidence for a Roman marching camp or fort on the summit of the Frenni Fawr or below it until now. Merrony discovered it about 2 miles (3.5km) south-west of the summit in 2024. Satellite imagery had shown a convincing outline in an overgrown field and, shortly after visiting it, his eye was caught by a Roman tile, which turned out to be the first of many.
With financial support from Oxford University and crowdfunding, one of several planned excavations has just finished, confirming his theory of the site and its significance.
Merrony said that before the dig, his brother, Nick, had jokingly asked him to find a couple of coins to prove the Magnus Maximus theory. “He came back and said ‘well, are these any good?’ I said ‘you’ve got to be kidding me’. He’d found two coins dating from the late 4th century.
“It is fascinating to consider that the two coins may be linked to the tale of Macsen Wledig – Magnus Maximus – in the Mabinogion, the Welsh equivalent of the Odyssey.”
Merrony is a leading specialist in the Romano-British period. His previous discoveries include two Roman villas, at Ford in Pembrokeshire and at Cutteslowe in Oxfordshire. He identified a Roman road along the southern shoulder of the Preselis in 2022, challenging assumptions that the Romans did not venture far into Wales.
His research will appear in Antiqvvs, a quarterly magazine dedicated to archaeology, ancient art and history. Magnus Maximus will also feature in Merrony’s forthcoming book, titled Lives of the Roman Emperors: From Augustus to Romulus Augustulus.
Measuring 180 by 150 metres, the fort is on a slope with a commanding view of the surrounding landscape. It is likely to have held about 500 troops, and its discovery overturns assumptions that the area’s Indigenous Celtic tribe was on peaceful terms with the Roman invaders.
It has “a characteristic playing-card form, with rounded corners” and a perpendicular road, Merrony said.
Finds at the site so far include an unusual iron stylus, many pottery shards, large quantities of Roman tiles and extensive compacted clay floors, a common feature on Roman military sites. Even rut marks left by wagons have been preserved.
The geophysical survey confirmed the presence of a rectangular building in the middle of the enclosure and a larger rectangular building immediately to the south.
“This arrangement is consistent with the placement of a headquarters building orientated east and thereby ‘facing the enemy’, and a commander’s house,” Merrony said.

SENSIVENEZIA WEAVES MATERIAL culture AND SPATIAL PERCEPTION

CHROMATIC PORTRAIT OF VENICE CRAFTED FOR CONTEMPORARY SPACES
