Why does the EU want a European Security Council? Take our poll
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
07:00:27 UTC
16:00:27 KST

The EU wants to build a new security mechanism to face hybrid threats, like drone incursions, cyberattacks and sabotage. But does it really need a new Security Council?
First proposed by European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen this September, the European Security Council is supposed to bring EU leaders and key allies together, including the UK, Norway, Ukraine and Canada. The goal is to coordinate faster on security threats that affect the continent.
Europe is facing a growing number of issues that fall below the level of conventional military attacks, like cyberattacks, sabotage, drone incursions and interference with critical infrastructure. Just last week, drones attacked two commercial vessels in Bulgaria's Black Sea economic zone, resulting in one ship sinking and a missing crew.
In practice, the ESC would give European leaders a regular forum to discuss emerging threats, agree on a common response, and coordinate action between EU countries and their partners. It would also work alongside an Emergency Security Protocol, designed to bring member states together quickly when one of them faces a serious hybrid threat. The wider plan also includes closer coordination on areas such as cyber security, air defence, space systems and other shared security capabilities.
Some officials and countries warn that the proposal could duplicate structures already in place within NATO. But the Commission says the new system is supposed to complement the alliance, and that NATO would remain responsible for collective military defence.
Is this ESC a good tool to boost European defence? Or does it risk alienating NATO allies? Our poll is anonymous and takes only a few seconds to complete. The competition to provide through-life support for the Royal Navy’s Type 31 frigates has been discontinued after the department concluded that the assumptions behind it no longer held, according to answers given in Parliament.
Ben Obese-Jecty, the Conservative member for Huntingdon, asked what plans the Secretary of State had to replace the abandoned requirement, and separately in what way the assumptions underpinning it no longer held. Both questions referred to the corrigendum to tender 707770451, entitled Type 31 Through Life Support, published on 22 July.
Luke Pollard, Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry, said:
“The Type 31 Through Life Support procurement was discontinued following a review of the proposed approach. The Department concluded that the assumptions underpinning that procurement no longer reflected the most appropriate route for delivering support to the Type 31 class. Those assumptions included the delivery context for the programme and the way in which future support arrangements should be structured. The requirement to provide effective through-life support for the Type 31 fleet remains unchanged.
“The Department is now considering the most appropriate arrangements to meet that requirement. Any future procurement activity will be taken forward in accordance with Defence requirements, value for money considerations and established commercial procedures.”
A third question from Mr Obese-Jecty turned to the programme’s budget, asking when the minister planned to reset the Approved Budgetary Limit to mitigate the impact of inflation, with reference to the National Infrastructure and Service Transformation Authority Major Projects Annual Report for 2025 to 2026.
Mr Pollard said: “The Ministry of Defence keeps the affordability of all major programmes under continual review. In common with other enterprises, the Type 31 programme is experiencing inflationary pressures, and the impact of possible costs is being assessed. Any changes to programme budgets and approvals will be considered through the Department’s established governance processes. It would therefore be inappropriate to speculate on the timing of any future decisions.”
The answers give no indication of what the revised support model might look like. Type 31 covers five Inspiration class frigates under construction by Babcock at Rosyth.

How can a new Security Council boost the EU's defence strategy? Ask the Euronews AI chatbot

The EU is reviving the idea of a European Security Council as Russia's hybrid attacks continue and reliance on US commitment to NATO remains risky. But how could this look like? Ask the Euronews AI chatbot.
The EU has significantly increased defence spending, including €8.8 billion for the European Defence Fund and €1.7 billion for military mobility. Member states’ defence investments rose by 158.7% between 2021 and 2026, according to the European Council.
Yet, according to the European Commission, Europe lacks a mechanism for rapid crisis response and coordinated defence efforts.
Proposed by the Commission President, Ursula von der Leyen this September, the European Security Council (ESC) would be Europe’s first permanent crisis-management forum, keeping security and defence on the agenda year-round.
The Security Council wants to improve operational unity, speed coordination, strengthen strategic direction, and unify crisis responses across member states.
The ESC reflects a broader effort to strengthen Europe's defence and strategic autonomy as concerns over Russian hybrid attacks, airspace violations, cyberattacks, and sabotage grow. Strained US ties and repeated threats to cut NATO funding have also pushed the EU to develop alternatives and rely more on its own security capabilities.
The proposal would bring together EU leaders and international partners, including Ukraine, Canada, Norway, and the UK. Through the emergency security protocol, modelled on NATO’s Article 4, members could call consultations when they believe their security, territorial integrity, or political independence is threatened, and plan a coordinated response.
The Commission's idea echoes a 2018 proposal by French President Emmanuel Macron and former German Chancellor Angela Merkel for an ESC, set out in the Meseberg Declaration, “Renewing Europe’s promises of security and prosperity”.

Is Switzerland’s decentralised democracy a helpful model for the Kurds?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
07:00:00 UTC
16:00:00 KST

Is Switzerland’s decentralised democracy a helpful model for the Kurds?
Could Switzerland’s federal structure suggest ideas for greater Kurdish autonomy? Some Kurdish activists and intellectuals in Switzerland believe it does.
The Kurds, whose population is estimated at 40 to 50 million, are one of the largest ethnic groups without their own country. After the First World War, their historical territory was divided – by a treaty signed in Lausanne, Switzerland – between four states: Turkey, Iran, Iraq, and Syria.
For decades, the Kurds have led political and military struggles to defend their status in these countries, with mixed results. Recently, Kurdish autonomy in northern Syria was dissolved after negotiations with the government in Damascus. This summer, Turkey passed a law aimed at ending the armed conflict with Kurdish militants.
Today’s debates about the Kurdish question are generally no longer limited to the expansion and protection of Kurdish minority rights. They also consider models of governance and democracy that would include and recognise the distinct identities of all citizens of a country.
Although Switzerland does not appear, at first glance, to be an obvious model for the Kurds, some Kurdish activists and intellectuals living in the country are intrigued by its example. Even if an independent Kurdish state is never established, they believe Switzerland’s multilingualism and elements of its federal system could inspire reforms in the countries where Kurds live as minorities, allowing greater autonomy.
More
When the Middle East was reinvented in Switzerland
Coexistence and decentralisation
Hüsnü Yılmaz is a lawyer, a member of the executive committee of the European Association of Lawyers for Democracy and World Human Rights, and chair of the foundation board of the Mesopotamia Observatory of Justice in Geneva. He believes coexistence is the key element of the Swiss model. “The country’s different languages and cultures are protected by constitutional guarantees, and the various interest groups participate in the functioning of the political system,” he says.
Decentralisation also plays a role, according to Yılmaz. Cantons, for example, enjoy extensive authority over education, health, and the organisation of certain public services. Cantonal and municipal autonomy allows for local solutions to local problems, which avoids having to rely entirely on the federal government. And in certain regions, he points out, education, public administration, and the courts are multilingual. He believes this fosters coexistence among the different language groups.
Multilingualism and unity
Ozcan Yılmaz, a historian at the University of Geneva, also emphasises the importance of daily coexistence among Switzerland’s linguistic communities. He feels the state’s formal recognition of language equality not only protects cultural rights but also reinforces citizens’ sense of belonging.
“But transferring the Swiss experience to Turkey, Iran, Iraq, or Syria is more complicated,” Ozcan Yılmaz explains. In his view, these countries embrace the idea of a nation-state with a single national language and identity as well as strong centralisation. Fundamental political change would be necessary to include governance principles comparable to those in Switzerland. As examples he cites administrative impartiality, secularism, a civic conception of citizenship, the separation of powers, and greater local autonomy.
In addition, both Hüsnü Yılmaz and Ozcan Yılmaz note that the Swiss federal system, which facilitates coexistence, is the product of a historical compromise developed over nearly two centuries. The success of this compromise rests not only on constitutional provisions, Hüsnü Yılmaz explains, but also on the way Swiss society embraced government institutions throughout the process. In a country like Turkey, he says, simple legislative and administrative reforms would not suffice: “Democratic change would require a new constitution as well as a fundamental [reconsideration] of the concept of a centralised state”.
Direct democracy and local autonomy
According to the Kurdish politician and lawyer Fırat Anlı, one of the key lessons of the Swiss model lies beyond multilingualism and federalism in the interplay between direct democracy and local autonomy.
Anlı sees interesting examples for Kurds in the powers given to local Swiss authorities and in Swiss citizens’ direct participation in democracy via referendums and popular initiatives. “Such principles have been championed for many years by the Kurdish political movement, especially a strengthening of local authorities.”
Anlı points out that the Kurdish governance model established in the Rojava region in northern Syria – an extremely politically fragile experiment – was largely inspired by principles also paramount in Switzerland, namely local democracy, cultural pluralism, and citizen participation. The Kurdish regions in Syria have an additional Swiss echo: they are called cantons.
To move towards fuller democracy in Turkey, Anlı believes a right to mother-tongue education must be recognised. As he points out, the Kurds cannot currently use their own language in public institutions. In addition, Anlı feels the state must uphold the rule of law and fully implement international human-rights standards. Lastly, in his view, local authorities must be strengthened, not only through administrative reform but by envisioning them as “a mechanism for addressing issues of political representation and social belonging”.
Role of women
Fatma Şık is a former co-mayor of the district of Sur in Diyarbakır province, Turkey. She has now lived in Switzerland for a number of years and is particularly impressed by the scope of its direct democracy. “The ability to make decisions via [referendums and popular] initiatives, and at the local level, is one of the defining features of the Swiss experience,” she says. In this she sees a similarity with the Kurdish concept of democracy: a recognition of cultural diversity.
Şık thinks that in matters of equality, however, the Kurdish women’s movement has developed an original approach that goes beyond certain Swiss practices. She points out that despite progress for women’s rights in Switzerland, women remain under-represented in the upper echelons of political and administrative hierarchies.
In contrast, Şık sees the Kurdish movement’s practice of co-chairing (a man and a woman sharing a leadership position), equal representation for men and women, and autonomous organisation as a model of advanced democracy. Citing her experience in Diyarbakır, she feels co-chairing has not only increased political representation of Kurdish women but has “also contributed to democratising decision-making processes, to power sharing, and to creating a space for challenging political practices traditionally dominated by men”.
In Şık’s view, comparisons should not be made only in one direction. While Switzerland can offer lessons for the Kurdish political movement, the Kurdish women’s movement has also developed political practices that could inform debate in Switzerland and other democracies.
Alternative to ‘one state, one people’
Although Switzerland’s political structure can offer inspiration to the Kurdish movement – especially to Kurds living in Switzerland – is it really likely to inspire concrete change?
Eva Maria Belser, professor at the University of Fribourg and expert on federalism, notes the importance of factoring in the historical, cultural, political, and geopolitical differences between countries. Nonetheless, she says, “vastly different historical contexts don’t make it impossible to transfer constitutional experiences”.
Switzerland itself was inspired by other countries when it built its federal structure in the 19th century, Belser points out. The bicameral system of the United States was a particular influence, although Switzerland did not create an exact copy. Instead, it adapted the idea to its own historical and political needs.
In the Kurdish context, Belser feels the Swiss federal system serves above all as a counter-example to the classic nation-state model of “one state, one people”. Switzerland shows that the individuality of different linguistic, religious, and cultural groups can be preserved, even as these groups live and participate peacefully within one political system.
Realistically, Belser says, Switzerland is more likely to act as a model for Kurdish coexistence in Turkey, Syria, Iraq, and Iran than as a model for a separate Kurdish state. “By allowing these historically established minorities to manage their own affairs autonomously, especially in cultural [matters], federalism can enable these communities to participate as full partners in the governance of the state as a whole,” she says.
Need for social consensus
Belser emphasises, however, that federal models based on the idea of a multinational state and on the principle of “unity in diversity” are rarely accepted immediately by the majority group. In this, she notes, Switzerland was an exception: it was the conservative rural German-speaking majority – not the linguistic minorities – that called for federalism. In general, she says, implementing federalism is not simply an administrative matter. “It also requires political will and social consensus,” she explains.
Where there is political deadlock, Belser believes it could be helpful not to limit debate over federalism to a “national question” or the “Kurdish question”. Instead, she recommends emphasising how decentralisation, in the sense of greater decision-making power for citizens, can offer advantages to the society as a whole.

Oil prices fell on Monday, October 12, amid expectations of increased supplies from Russia after U.S. President Donald Trump said there was an "energy truce" in the Russia-Ukraine war following the conclusion of a U.S. agreement with Moscow on diesel fuel supplies. UNN reports this, citing Reuters.
Details
Brent crude oil futures fell by $1.54, or 1.47%, to $103.18 per barrel by 01:54 GMT (04:54 Kyiv time), while the price of U.S. West Texas Intermediate crude fell by $1.54, or 1.68%, to $90.31 per barrel.
ICE diesel futures fell 3% to $1,436 per metric ton after President Trump said on Friday that Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 metric tons (2.25 million barrels) of diesel fuel to the U.S. and global markets.
Russia will supply another 500,000 tons in November and another 1 million tons "immediately afterward," Trump added. According to forecasts by the International Energy Agency, daily global diesel fuel consumption will amount to about 29 million barrels.
On Sunday, Trump also unexpectedly announced an "energy truce" in the Russia-Ukraine war, but Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he was still waiting for details of the agreement, while Russia declined to comment, the publication writes.
These statements somewhat eased immediate pressure on supplies, said Tim Waterer, chief analyst at KCM Trade.
"Questions remain regarding the validity and duration of any such agreement, and without clearer evidence that it will actually be honored, the scale of the pullback is likely to remain limited," he added.
IEA Executive Director Fatih Birol said on Sunday that all members of the organization should assess the need for additional diesel fuel supplies and that countries that have not yet fully met their volume commitments should accelerate their remaining deliveries, giving priority to diesel fuel.
The impact of the conflict in the Middle East persists
However, the conflict in the Middle East continues to support the price of Brent crude above $100 per barrel, the publication writes.
The Houthis claimed responsibility for Saturday's strike on Riyadh International Airport, which killed 13 people and injured more than 300, while Saudi authorities reported casualties from a new strike on the airport on Sunday.
U.S. President Donald Trump said on Saturday that the United States was considering joining Saudi strikes against the Houthis in the conflict, which is a consequence of the wider war with Iran launched by the U.S. and Israel in February.
In addition, new attacks on tankers passing through the Strait of Hormuz were recorded this month, threatening to slow the recovery of Middle Eastern oil exports that was observed in September.
The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) reported over the weekend that one tanker was struck by a drone near the Sohar anchorage in Oman, while another was damaged by an unidentified projectile while passing through the Strait of Hormuz.
What is the oil price forecast
In a note, Goldman Sachs analysts raised their December forecast for the price of Brent crude to $90 per barrel from $85 previously.
"We maintain our base case that further supply adjustments from the Middle East will ultimately lead to lower oil prices, while a potential renewed escalation remains a significant net upside risk to prices," the analysts said, estimating the risk premium at slightly more than $20 per barrel.
"We forecast that WTI oil prices, which are exceptionally low relative to Brent because of high transportation costs between the U.S. and Europe, will average $81 in December 2026 and $73 in 2027," they added.
In the Gulf of Mexico, energy giants Shell, Chevron, and BP were attempting to redeploy personnel and resume production at their platforms after Hurricane "Isaias" hit the coast on Saturday morning.

[Reminder: As we flagged earlier, Woodford was among the predicted winners – he’s one of the architects of modern forward guidance, the idea that central banks can control the economy through influencing public expectations about inflation, rather than just through interest rates.]
The Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel is worth 12 million Swedish kronor (£900,000), plus the glory of course, and the knowledge that every pronouncement you make now comes with the authority of a Nobel Prize winner.
Two US economists have won the 2026 Nobel economics prize for their work developing models that help central bankers and finance ministers to stabilise their countries, avoiding long recessions and runaway inflation.
The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences said it was recognising the pair for generating “a paradigm shift in stabilisation policy”, awarding them the prize worth a combined $1.2m (£900,000).
“New Keynesian models, a result of their research, allow us to explain and quantify how stabilisation policy affects business cycles and are now used by central banks and finance ministries around the world,” the academy said.

HMV to quit historic Oxford Street store, again....
Sarah Butler
Away from the Nobel economics prize announcement….HMV is preparing to exit its London flagship on Oxford Street in March - just over three years after reopening there with great fanfair – as the landlord proposed doubling the rent.
The entertainment retailer said it was now seeking alternative sites on the capital’s main high street, or another central location, as it had been trading strongly, my colleague Sarah Butler reports.
The latest closure comes after HMVreturned to the site in November 2023 after closing in 2019 leaving the store empty for an extended period before a brief stint housing one of many American candy stores that popped up on Oxford Street during the pandemic.
HMV, which currently has 114 stores under its own brand across the UK and a further six Fopp sites, said a proposed increase in rent which is already understood to be well over £1m a year – coupled with a requirement to fund substantial renovation works on the Oxford Street building – would make the store “commercially unsustainable”, leaving it with no choice but to seek an alternative site.
The store was HMV’s very first, and was opened in 1921 by Sir Edward Elgar, the British composer. Since then it has played host to a number of British bands, including a rooftop gig by Blur in 1995 and the Spice Girls’ Christmas lights switch-on the following year.
It is understood the Hong Kong-based landlord has signed a lease with an alternative tenant.
PhilHalliday, managing director of HMV, said:
“This is a special store, it’s where we began 100 years ago and bringing it back to life in 2023 was a big moment in our recent history. It’s frustrating that it has been made commercially unviable. However, we are looking ahead, and our focus is now on what we do to make exciting steps for hmv in 2027.”
He said sales were up by a quarter year-on-year at the Oxford Street store and 15% at established UK stores in the first nine months of 2026 as sales of both vinyl records and CDs continued to sell well and more shoppers came into stores.
“We have put together an offer that works across a number of generations,” Halliday added.
The retailer is expecting UK revenues to exceed £240m this year across the stores estate and website, up from £212m in 2025. The business now generates £50m of sales online and is upgrading its website backed by a new warehouse set to open next year.
“We’ve worked hard to make 363 Oxford Street a destination for pop-culture fans, bringing live performances, artist signings and a huge range of music and entertainment back to the heart of London. However, regardless of how much a location means to us, it has to make commercial sense.” Halliday said.
He said HMV intended to redeploy affected staff through other London stores and Head Office roles.
After learning of his success, Michael Woodford was asked during today’s press conference if any economic event or shock had ensured that his new framework had really stood up to the test.
Bloomberg has the details:
He cited how central banks adapted their toolkit to the global financial crisis of 2008 as they confronted a slump in demand that reductions in borrowing costs on their own couldn’t solve.
“Forward guidance about policy, so making more explicit statements about the likely future path of interest rate policy as opposed to relying on simply being able to cut interest rates further immediately — that was an important part of the policy response,” he said.
“It did contribute to better stabilization. It didn’t magically solve the problem, but I think it was an important contribution.”
Here’s how John Hassler, chair of the prize committee, announced Hall and Woodford’s success this morning:
“The laureates’ work has provided us with a stable theoretical foundation for the models that are now used by central banks and governments around the world,”
“With them, we are better equipped to deal with shocks in the economy, such as energy crises or sudden changes in how much households consume.”
Over at FT Alphaville, Toby Nangle has described Michael Woodford is “probably the most famous New Keynesian economist”.
Nangle (formally a senior asset manager at ColumbiaThreadneedle) writes:
If you’re friends with at least one econ nerd, you’ve probably heard either love or hate for Woodford’s Interest and Prices: Foundations of a Theory of Monetary Policy dropped into dinner-party conversations. This is his reputation-defining tome, named cheekily to echo Knut Wicksell’s Interest and Prices, written more than a century previously.
Woodford basically rebuilt Wicksell’s insights around the relationship between interest rates and the economy’s natural interest rate using modern general equilibrium economics.
And today, almost all central banks run dynamic stochastic general equilibrium models incorporating Woodfordian insights, including the Fed, the ECB, the Bank of England, and the mother of them all: Sveriges Riksbank.
Following today’s announcement, the Nobel prize for economics has now been awarded on 58 occasions.
That dates back to 1969, when RagnarFrisch and JanTinbergen won it “for having developed and applied dynamic models for the analysis of economic processes”.
The oldest winner was LeonidHurwicz, who was 90 in 2007 when he won alongside EricMaskin and RogerMyerson “for having laid the foundations of mechanism design theory”.
The youngest remains EstherDuflo, who was just 46 in 2019 when she shared the prize with AbhijitBanerjee and MichaelKremer. “for their experimental approach to alleviating global poverty” (as we blogged here).
Praise for Woodford and Hall is starting to pour in
Analytics company Clarivate, which had awarded both RobertHall and MichaelWoodford one of its Citations Laureate – given to those who are considered likely to win the Nobel Prize due to their research expertise – says today’s award is certainly merited.
DavidPendlebury, head of research analysis, institute for scientific information at Clarivate, explains:
“We are delighted to see both Robert Hall and Michael Woodford recognized with this year’s Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences. Hall was named a Citation Laureate in 2017 and Woodford earlier this year in 2026, reflecting the exceptional influence of their research. Their work has fundamentally shaped modern thinking about economic stabilization, productivity, economic fluctuations and the role of monetary policy in supporting economic growth and stability.
Looking at the publication record in the Web of Science, we see the enduring impact of their contributions. Their research has influenced generations of economists and helped inform economic policymaking around the world, demonstrating how foundational ideas can shape both academic understanding and real-world decision-making for decades.”
Economics professor CostasMilas of the UniversityofLiverpool says Woodford’s work has lessons for UK policymakers today, as they try to unwind the stimulus measures implemented since the financial crisis.
He tells us:
I am very pleased Robert Hall and Michael Woodford have been awarded the Nobel Prize in Economics.
In essence, this is a very useful scenario-type of analysis that my co-author Christopher Mahon (visiting fellow at the Open University Business School) and I are now advocating in our new LSE Business Review blog which argues that Quantitative Tightening policies in the UK should rely on scenario testing to assess how alternative balance-sheet strategies perform cost-wise if interest rates follow different paths.
How Hall created the fresh-water and salt-water economic divide
Robert Hall is also famous for coining the fresh water vs. salt water split in American macroeconomics.
This divide is both ideological and geographical.
A fresh water economist, Hall wrote 50 years ago, believes that economic fluctuations are largely attributable to supply shifts, and that the government is essentially incapable of affecting the level of economic activity. This leads to a belief in free markets, neoclassical price theory, rational expectations, and monetarism.
Freshwater economists tend to be based at inland universities located near the North American Great Lakes, such as the University of Chicago.
The salt water view holds shifts in demand responsible for fluctuations and thinks government policies (at least monetary policy) is capable of affecting demand, Hall argued.
Salt water economists thrive at the US coastal universities, such as Harvard, MIT, UC Berkeley, Yale, Princeton, UCLA, and Columbia.
In a 1976 paper, I introduced the distinction between fresh-water and salt-water economists. Bloggers using these terms are asked to contribute $1 to a fund that sends graduate students to MIT for one year and to the University of Minnesota for a second year.
Michael Woodford was born in 1955 in Chicopee, Massachusetts.
He’s based at Columbia University, New York, where he’s the John Bates Clark Professor of Political Economy.
According to Columbia:
Woodford has been a MacArthur Fellow and a Guggenheim Fellow, and is a Fellow of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences, as well as a Fellow of the Econometric Society, of the Society for the Advancement of Economic Theory, and of the Society for Economic Measurement, a Research Associate of the National Bureau of Economic Research (Cambridge, Mass.), a Research Fellow of the Centre for Economic Policy Research (London), and a Fellow of the CESifo Research Network (Munich).
He was the 2007 recipient of the Deutsche Bank Prize in Financial Economics, the 2018 recipient of the Banque de France/TSE Prize in Monetary Economics, and the 2024 recipient of the Erwin Plein Nemmers Prize in Economics.
Robert Hall, the older of the pair, was born in 1943 in Palo Alto, California (the birth place of Silicon Valley).
Hall is based at Stanford University, California, where he’s the Robert and Carole McNeil Joint Senior Fellow, Hoover Institution, and professor in the department of economics.
On Stanford’s website, Hall describes himself as “an applied economist with interests in employment, inflation, technology, competition, and economic policy in the aggregate economy and in particular markets.”
That work has included developing a framework for equitable and efficient consumption taxation, research into economic fluctuations and growth, and advising a number of government agencies on national economic policy.
Michael Woodford is now speaking to the Nobel prize commitee, by telephone.
He says he’s “elated”, as winning the prize is “a tremendous honour”.
“It’s a surprise, but I’m feeling very good about it,” he adds.
Woodford now explaining how the 2008 financial crisis stretched the limits of traditional monetary policy, as interest rates fell to record lows, while unemployment was too high and aggregate spending was too low.
This meant other tools were needed, and one was ‘forward guidance’ about policy – more explicit statements about the future path of interest rates.
How Hall and Woodford's work on microfoundations won Nobel Prize
Robert Hall and Michael Woodford, who are both Americans, have been recognised for their work helping global policymakers to smooth out the highs and lows of economic cycles, through a branch of economics known as the New Keynesian paradigm.
Their models have “significantly improved our ability to implement effective stabilisation policy”, the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences say.
This has allowed “well-timed fiscal and monetary policy measures” to reduce the economy’s peaks and troughs.
This work built on John Maynard Keynes’s work showing how policymakers could stimulate demand when it is too low and slowing it when it’s too high.
Keynes’s work struggled during the oil crises of the 1970s, which strained its assumption that the relationship between the macroeconomic variables was stable.
Hall and Woodford, though, showed that such models have to be built on microfoundations- ie, from the bottom up, based on the behaviour of individual actors.
The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences say:
Robert E. Hall’s and Michael Woodford’s research has made us better equipped to manage economic downturns. They laid the foundation of the New Keynesian paradigm, in which models are built upon microfoundations, which means from the bottom up.
Economic outcomes are the result of millions of decisions made at the microlevel by households and businesses. Using models based upon this approach, rather than simply studying the economy from a macro perspective, like a bird’s eye view, Hall’s and Woodford’s research has generated a paradigm shift in the theory of stabilisation policy.
Explaining why Hall and Woodford have won the biggest prize in economics, the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences say:
Economic development is characterised by alternating downturns and upturns. Stimulating or slowing down the economy at the right time can provide stability and allow us to avoid drawn-out recessions or runaway inflation. Robert E. Hall’s and Michael Woodford’s research has generated a paradigm shift in stabilisation policy.
New Keynesian models, a result of their research, allow us to explain and quantify how stabilisation policy affects business cycles and are now used by central banks and finance ministries around the world.

Newsflash: The Nobel Prize for economicshas been awarded to Robert E Hall and Michael Woodford, for their work on the “microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilisation”.
[Reminder: As we flagged earlier, Woodford was among the predicted winners – he’s one of the architects of modern forward guidance, the idea that central banks can control the economy through influencing public expectations about inflation, rather than just through interest rates.]
The Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel is worth 12 million Swedish kronor (£900,000), plus the glory of course, and the knowledge that every pronouncement you make now comes with the authority of a Nobel Prize winner.
The winner of the Nobel memorial prize in economics, the final award in this year’s cycle, is expected to be announced in around 10 minutes time.
You can watch the announcement, at the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences in Stockholm, here:
Reminder: The prize is formally known as the Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel. Sweden’s central bank established it in 1968 as a memorial to Nobel, the 19th-century Swedish businessman and chemist who invented dynamite and established the five Nobel Prizes.
AFP: Nobel watchers guess who gets economics' top prize
Monetary policy, technology, behavioural economics and development are among the fields tipped for this year’s Nobel economics prize, the AFP newswire report.
Last year, the economics award went to American-Israeli JoelMokyr, France’s PhilippeAghion and Canada’s PeterHowitt for research into how technology drives and affects growth.
That makes another prize for the same field unlikely this year, according to experts interviewed by AFP.
“There is obvious horse-trading between factions in the (Nobel) committee: ’I support your candidate this year if you support mine next year,’” Richard Tol, an economics professor at the University of Sussex, told AFP.
For Tol, the committee has been “signalling” that Americans ColinCamerer and GeorgeLoewenstein will win this year, “perhaps with MattRabin”, pioneers in behavioural economics and how we make decisions.
Another “strong candidate” is MichaelWoodford in the field of monetary policy, said David Pendlebury of research firm Clarivate, which predicts potential laureates by tracking highly cited academic work.
“It has been a while since that particular area has been recognised,” Pendlebury noted.
Looking at past laureates also shows that the Nobel committee tends to honour research about 20 to 25 years after publication, and Woodford’s key work was “a book published in 2003”.

By the end of August, the costs of this stage had reached 3.04 million euros.

financial, tax, legal, technical and commercial due diligence on the companies has been completed.

Registered unemployment falls below 40,000 as labor market improves
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
06:51:00 UTC
15:51:00 KST

Registered unemployment falls below 40,000 as labor market improves
Estonia's labor market showed signs of improvement in the third quarter, with fewer registered unemployed people, more job openings and less competition for available jobs.
Estonia averaged 38,000 registered unemployed in the third quarter of 2026, down 5,600, or 13 percent, from a year earlier. The share of the working-age labor force registered as unemployed fell from 6.3 to 5.5 percent.
The number of registered unemployed has remained below 40,000 for two consecutive quarters, reaching a level last seen in the first quarter of 2020.
The Estonian Unemployment Insurance Fund (EUIF) had an average of 5,250 job openings to fill during the quarter, up more than 25 percent on year. Vacancies grew most in manufacturing, professional, scientific and technical activities, trade and construction.
EUIF board member Brit Rammul said the figures point to a modest recovery.
"There are fewer registered unemployed people and more job offers," she said. But opportunities vary by sector, and finding work still depends on applicants' skills and which workers employers need.
Competition for jobs, meanwhile, has also eased. There were an average of seven registered unemployed people per vacancy in the third quarter, down from 11 a year earlier.
Registered unemployed profile largely unchanged
Competition was steepest in finance and insurance, with 255 registered unemployed people per vacancy, followed by information and communications at 66. By contrast, there were four unemployed people per vacancy in administrative and support services and three for craft and related trades jobs.
The profile of registered unemployed in Estonia changed little from a year earlier. The shares of older people, university graduates, managers and senior specialists rose slightly, while the shares of young people, those lacking vocational qualifications and unskilled workers declined.
There were also fewer registered unemployed who did not speak Estonian and fewer long-term unemployed. The gender breakdown, however, was largely unchanged on year.

Hurricane Simon batters Mexico's Pacific Coast
October 12, 2026
Hurricane Simon lashed vulnerable resorts and towns along Mexico's Pacific Coast on Sunday as it moved parallel to the shoreline, despite weakening to a category 3 storm.
"Additional weakening is forecast but Simon is still expected to be a strong hurricane as it passes near the coast of west-central Mexico tonight," the US National Hurricane Center's advisory said.
Simon is expected to move farther offshore on Monday before turning back towards Mexico's coast on Wednesday, it said.
On high alert
Mexican authorities have placed 28 municipalities across the states of Jalisco and Colima under the highest cyclone alert level. Another 93 municipalities were under high alert, according to civil protection bulletins.
The hurricane's center closed in on the Puerto Vallarta area, where its most damaging winds and rains were expected to hit around midnight and continue through Monday morning. Puerto Vallarta is a popular tourist destination in Jalisco. Apart from the resorts, several Mexicans live in communities inland and uphill, in houses that may not be able to weather the storm.
Experts believe the entire area between Mexico's western coast and the Sierra Madre mountains could be affected.
"We're expecting catastrophic wind and life-threatening storm surge impacts along that west-central coast of Mexico where the hurricane warning is currently in effect," senior hurricane center specialist, Philippe Papin said.
"They're also getting very heavy rainfall associated with the storm that's likely going to produce life-threatening flooding and mudslides in areas of higher terrain along the Mexican coastline, and there will be significant swells."
In Manzanillo, residents waded through flooded streets on Sunday morning as soldiers helped rescue locals from the overnight rainfall.
"The beds, the refrigerators, the stoves, all the furniture got wet. The whole house flooded," Cecilia Palomar told Reuters outside her home.
"My mother doesn't want to leave. We took her to my brother's, to higher ground. She's an elderly woman, but she doesn't want to leave. She doesn't want to be away from her home."
Airport closed, authorities urge caution
Puerto Vallarta International Airport was closed temporarily while authorities suspended non-essential activities.
They also established emergency shelters in threatened coastal communities.
Earlier on Sunday, Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum had urged residents of coastal communities in Jalisco, Colima, Nayarit and Michoacan to remain indoors ahead of the storm.
Hurricane Simon has come days after Hurricane Polo struck Mexico's Baja California Peninsula as a Category 2 storm, knocking down power lines and flooding the streets.

President Alar Karis loved by the people but foreign policy possibly a stepping stone
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
06:48:00 UTC
15:48:00 KST

President Alar Karis loved by the people but foreign policy possibly a stepping stone
President Alar Karis spent his final week as head of state at Kadriorg. Journalists say foreign policy was his weak point.
"Sometimes laws are drafted in great haste and certain things are simply overlooked. Sometimes the political desire to achieve something is so strong that the Constitution is forgotten. And that's what has led to all the decisions I've had to make," Outgoing President Alar Karis said, commenting on his decisions to initially refuse to promulgate 11 separate pieces of legislation.
"But I don't consider it something to boast about, saying, look how many laws I've rejected. Rather, it's a cause for concern. And I've always emphasized that parliament, the Riigikogu, could do its job better and examine things more thoroughly," Karis said in an interview to ERR.
Indrek Kiisler, deputy editor-in-chief of Postimees, said Karis did not come from a political background and therefore is not the kind of political operator that politicians tend to be.
"His primary aim was to guide the Riigikogu by sending a signal. He was doing exactly what the president is actually supposed to do," Kiisler added.
According to Kiisler, Karis tried to provide a counterbalance to the Riigikogu and the turmoil within it.
"That also applied to the legislation it passed, such as the motor vehicle tax," he noted.
Motor vehicle tax veto
President Karis initially refused to promulgate the motor vehicle tax law in 2024, arguing that it violated the principle of equal treatment. The Riigikogu amended the law and the president promulgated it six weeks later.
Erik Moora, head of Delfi's opinion section, said a debate emerged suggesting that every tax should have only one purpose.
"On the contrary, very few taxes have just one purpose and it is clear that the purpose of every tax is to raise revenue for the state budget," he said.
Critics began suggesting that there was something wrong with the motor vehicle tax having multiple objectives.
"It is clear that many taxes are intended to influence certain consumer behaviors and achieve other objectives, as was also explained in the case of this tax," Moora said. "Jumping on that bandwagon seemed a little populist to me."
The most politically contentious decision was Karis' veto of amendments to the Churches and Congregations Act, mainly concerning the status of the Estonian Christian Orthodox Church. The president referred the law to the Supreme Court, seeking to have it declared unconstitutional because it would not bring about any substantive change.
Karis said the law and the churches' statutes could be amended, but the ties would remain.
"That's why I repeatedly asked for the law to be reconsidered. And as you saw, when it reached the Supreme Court, quite a few judges there also expressed dissenting opinions," he said.
Karis said the case has now reached the European Court of Human Rights.
"I said, think through what the next steps will be and how this law is going to be implemented," he explained.
Tõnis Leht, an editor of the "Poliitikaguru" podcast, said Karis had not managed to change the approach toward the Russian Orthodox Church.
"Nevertheless, his criticism was fundamentally valid and substantive and the Supreme Court's ruling did take significant account of the arguments put forward by the president and his legal adviser," he said.
Russia's full-scale war
The defining event of Karis' presidency was Russia's full-scale war against Ukraine. Karis met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy just two days before Russia launched its full-scale invasion. He subsequently visited Ukraine several times and the two presidents also met at Kadriorg. Karis describes his approach to foreign policy as soft diplomacy.
Moora said Karis' presidency coincided with a period when Kaja Kallas, as prime minister, enjoyed an exceptionally high international profile, attracting considerable attention, airtime, quotations and media coverage. In his view, Estonia's message had an extraordinarily strong international presence.
"Karis was inevitably overshadowed by that," Moora said.
"I recently read that President Karis wasn't interested in foreign policy, which is an outright lie.," Karis said.
He noted that foreign policy can be conducted in different ways.
"In a sense, people are barking up the wrong tree here," he said. "Because the main responsibility, particularly in the context of the war in Ukraine, lies with the prime minister and the foreign minister."
Karis said they are the ones who take the lead because they attend NATO meetings and European Council summits.
Karis said he has always considered soft diplomacy important and believes its impact is much longer-lasting. He cited the Kazakhstan incident as an example.
"When I ask what actually happened there, I don't get an answer because nothing happened.," Karis said.
Kiisler said that once events had unfolded, Karis struggled to explain them clearly.
"He consistently had difficulty explaining his positions," Kiisler added.
"I can see how much the Kazakhstan scandal still weighs on him. He simply hasn't been able to move past it," Kiisler continued.
He noted that although considerable time has passed, Karis keeps returning to the issue because many people in Estonia still do not understand why he acted as he did.
"I get the impression that over those five years, he never really managed to develop a thick skin," Kiisler said.
Popular with the people
Despite the criticism of his foreign policy, Karis' greatest achievement was maintaining a high level of public support.
Leht said people like Karis because he comes across as smart and articulate, but also open and warm. He added that Karis is not dismissive, does not appear arrogant or condescending and never seems bored when interacting with people.
However, the mild-mannered Karis also showed that he could be quite sharp.
Kiisler said Karis did make pointed remarks, sometimes indirectly and sometimes explicitly, such as when he said Kaja Kallas should resign during the scandal over her husband's business ties to Russia.
Kiisler noted, however, that the kind of sharp rhetoric associated with former presidents Toomas Hendrik Ilves and Kersti Kaljulaid was largely absent during Karis' five years in office.
One of Karis' best-known quotes, however, comes from this year's Independence Day speech.
"We've overheated our beloved sauna and become dizzy from the intense steam."
Moora believes the remark will stick in people's minds. He said Karis often delivered good speeches, although they tended to be even better when read than when heard.
In closing, the president said it is ultimately the happy moments that he will remember most from his years in office.
"The occasions when I've presented state decorations have always been moving, seeing the emotions people experience. It's so wonderful to watch, all that surprise. It's genuine," Karis said.
President Ülle Madise will take over the presidency from Karis in the Riigikogu on Monday.
--
Editor: Marcus Turovski, Merilin Leetna

COLOMBO, Oct. 12 (Xinhua) -- Sri Lanka's financial system remains stable despite heightened global risks, while banking sector credit grew 23.6 percent year-on-year in the second quarter of 2026, up from 11.4 percent a year earlier amid strong private sector demand, the Central Bank of Sri Lanka said on Monday.
In its Financial Stability Review 2026, the central bank said the financial system remained stable during the first half of the year, supported by continued economic recovery, improved fiscal performance and adequate capital and liquidity buffers across banks and finance companies.
However, the bank warned that rapid credit growth, particularly household lending including vehicle financing and gold-backed lending, was creating potential systemic vulnerabilities. Rising household indebtedness, higher real estate prices and volatility in collateral values were also identified as emerging risks.
Household credit grew 25.4 percent year-on-year in the second quarter, compared with 14.8 percent a year earlier. Banks remained the main source of household financing, accounting for 62.5 percent of such credit.
Credit extended by finance companies expanded 45 percent year-on-year in the second quarter, driven largely by vehicle and gold-backed lending, compared with growth of 35.1 percent in the same period of 2025.
The central bank said geopolitical tensions, elevated energy and commodity prices, tighter global financial conditions and climate-related risks could spill over into the domestic economy through trade, tourism, remittances, capital flows and exchange rate movements.
The outlook for financial stability remains broadly positive, provided the economic recovery continues, fiscal consolidation progresses and prudent policies are maintained, the central bank said. ■

====================================================================================================

Letter from Mideast: Still waiting for peace near Gaza
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
14:43:44 CST
15:43:44 KST

This photo taken from an area near Israel's southern border on Oct. 6, 2026 shows Israeli military vehicles moving inside the Gaza Strip. (Photo by Gil Cohen Magen/Xinhua)
by Xinhua writer Wang Zhuolun
JERUSALEM, Oct. 12 (Xinhua) -- From a hill on the outskirts of Sderot, the Israeli city closest to the Gaza Strip, the devastation across the border is clearly visible. Shattered buildings form a jagged skyline just a few kilometers away, yet they seem worlds apart.
Three years ago, on Oct. 7, 2023, a Hamas-led attack on southern Israel triggered a new round of bloody conflict in Gaza. Militants entered Sderot and stormed the local police station, where fighting raged through the night. Israeli forces eventually demolished the building as they retook it.
I still remember crouching amid the ruins as I covered the war's early days: fighter jets roared overhead, fear emptied the streets, and acrid smoke hung in the air. Not far away, each Israeli strike on Gaza sent another plume into the sky.
Back then, no one knew how long the war would last, much less how its repercussions would spread across borders and engulf much of the Middle East.
Three years on, I returned. The ruins are gone. A memorial square now stands where the police station once stood, with newly planted greenery and paved walkways. Visitors stop to look around. Sderot is gradually reclaiming a sense of normalcy.
It took less than three years to turn ruins into a square. But how long will it take to turn war into peace?
In the West Bank city of Bethlehem, Ali Mansour told me he had been out of work since the war began. Before the conflict, he traveled daily to work in Israeli-controlled areas. Afterward, Israel sharply restricted work permits for Palestinian workers, leaving him without a job.
What he has been waiting for, Mansour said, is not just a job, but the chance to regain the dignity of an ordinary working life.
In Jerusalem's Old City, Palestinian souvenir seller Rami Hamdan has felt the war's toll in another way. In once-bustling shops, merchants now sit idle, waiting for customers who rarely come.
"I stopped watching the news long ago. I don't even want to know what's happening anymore," he said. "I just want to shut myself off from this world of endless war."
Perhaps this is war's most enduring consequence. An explosion has a time, a place, and a casualty count. It becomes a headline, then a photograph. But long after the smoke clears, war persists in less visible ways: in families mourning loved ones, workers waiting for jobs that never return, children growing up under air raid sirens, and ordinary people facing each day with uncertainty.
Over the past three years, the fighting has widened into a regional conflict.
It spread from Gaza to the Israel-Lebanon border and the Red Sea before escalating into large-scale direct military confrontations involving Israel, the United States, and Iran. Rockets, missiles, and drones repeatedly crossed Middle Eastern skies.
Over these three years, I have written "escalation" and "ceasefire takes effect" more times than I can remember. Again and again, just as a war seemed to be nearing its end, another round of fighting began.
The expanding battle fronts kept testing what I thought I understood about war. As a frontline correspondent, I have learned that the worst never stays the worst for long, and what looks like an ending can turn out to be the prelude to something worse.
Before leaving Sderot, I met Shalom Levi, a local resident. Now 60, he has lived his whole life near the Gaza border.
In Hebrew, "shalom" is both a greeting and the word for "peace." Levi told me his parents chose the name to express their hope for peace.
Behind him stood the memorial square built on the ruins of the police station. Beyond it lay Gaza, still scarred by war.
New monuments have risen from rubble. New grass has taken root in scorched earth.
But a man named "Peace" is still waiting for his name to become more than a promise. ■

"But if Russians agree to an energy ceasefire, Ukraine will agree," Zelensky said.

The dispute over the ceasefire comes as rising energy prices have become a growing political concern for Trump ahead of the U.S. midterm elections.

SYDNEY, Oct. 12 (Xinhua) -- The number of assaults on police officers in the Australian state of South Australia has surged by 25 percent, despite declines in several other categories of crime, according to official statistics released on Monday.
The latest figures released by South Australia Police showed that assaults on officers while on duty increased from 635 to 793 in the rolling 12-month period ending in August 2026, marking the 12th consecutive increase in such offences.
Meanwhile, the number of robberies fell by 13 percent, from 501 to 438, following a 16 percent decline in the previous reporting period.
Homicide and related offences dropped by 21 percent, from 53 to 42, while thefts from retail premises decreased by 3 percent to 21,757 incidents.
However, residential break-ins rose from 5,584 to 5,947, while non-residential break-ins increased from 3,391 to 3,513. Sexual offences also edged up from 2,704 to 2,718.
South Australia Police Assistant Commissioner David O'Donovan attributed the continued decline in robberies to police efforts targeting repeat offenders, including securing their detention or imposing strict bail conditions.
He said police remained aware of the trauma experienced by robbery victims and would continue working to reduce such offences. ■

World grain prices to continue growing in case of escalation in Black Sea — expert
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
06:39:16 UTC
15:39:16 KST

ASTANA, October 12. /TASS/. Global grain prices will rise if the escalation in the Black Sea region continues as exports from countries in this area account for about 40% of the global wheat trade, Evgeny Karabanov, head of the analytics committee of the Grain Union of Kazakhstan, told TASS.
"Based on wheat production, consumption, and stock volumes, a positive balance shaped up in the market for the 2026-2027 marketing year. However, the escalation evolving in the Black Sea destabilized the global market in terms of available wheat supply. Against this backdrop, and due to droughts in Europe and the US, global wheat prices have surged by 20-30% (depending on the markets) over the past three months, reaching their highest level since August 2023," Karabanov said.
The situation in the Black Sea region will directly impact the global grain market as this sea is just as important for the global wheat market as the Strait of Hormuz is for the oil market, the expert noted. "Exports from Black Sea countries make up around 40% of the global wheat trade, while oil exports through Hormuz account for about 20% of global trade. In the event of a further long-term escalation in the Black Sea region, global grain prices will continue to grow and poor countries that rely on wheat imports will find themselves in a difficult economic situation," he added.
According to estimates by the Grain Union, at the end of the previous marketing year (September 2025 - August 2026), Kazakhstan exported 14.7 million tons of wheat and processed products in grain equivalent, which was the best result in the country's history. Deliveries were mainly directed to the markets of Central Asian countries, Afghanistan, Iran, and China.
"Due to worsening logistics issues linked to the actual blocking of exports through the Russian ports of the Sea of Azov and the Black Sea, alternative routes for supplying Kazakh grain to the global market through the port of Poti (Georgia) and Baltic ports will be significantly more expensive -- the price will not be competitive," Karabanov added.

Meanwhile, Ukraine’s defence industry is developing its own propulsion systems for other weapons classes. In March, Fire Point announced that it had completed development of its own jet engine for the Flamingo cruise missile.

Trump turns the screws on Kyiv as EU budget talks hit a wall

Good morning. It’s Monday. I’m Mared Gwyn. Today: Europe braces as Trump turns up the heat on Zelenskyy, and Ireland’s EU budget compromise falls dead on arrival.
Kyiv under pressure: For Ukraine, the past few days have brought back the distinct taste of the Oval Office showdown: public pressure on President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, accusations that Ukraine is obstructing peace and a growing fear (again) that the aim is not compromise, let alone a just peace, but to force Ukraine to surrender, our correspondent Sasha Vakulina writes this morning.
Blindsided: US President Donald Trump made a surprise announcement on Sunday that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an immediate ceasefire on attacks against energy infrastructure. There was just one rather significant problem: at least one of those parties appeared unaware of the agreement.
“If President Trump negotiated it with Putin, please tell us when the ceasefire begins,” Zelenskyy said in response. Ukraine, he added, was ready.
It was not entirely clear Moscow got the memo either, Sasha explains.After Trump’s announcement, Russia struck a thermal power plant in Kharkiv, before targeting several other power plants overnight. And that was only Sunday.
Diesel deal rattles Europeans: On Friday, Trump had also announced a deal with Vladimir Putin to ease sanctions on Russian diesel exports, without informing Ukrainian or European negotiators who were in Miami for talks. It’s seen as an effort to bring down soaring diesel and gasoline prices, a major issue for American voters, ahead of the November 3 midterm elections.
Zelenskyy did not mince his words, branding the deal “weak” and warning it would hand Putin “billions” more to wage war. Trump told him he “better damn well stop” striking Russian refineries, before taking it further and saying Ukraine needed a “new leader”. Putin’s leadership, notably, did not come up for discussion.
Rallying around Zelenskyy: There is another irony for Trump: publicly berating Zelenskyy has hardly proven an effective way of weakening him at home - quite the opposite. EU leaders have also been rallying behind the Ukrainian leader – and Zelenskyy is now expected to join leaders when they gather for a summit in Brussels this Thursday and Friday, sources have told Euronews.
Hard reckoning: News of the Trump-Putin diesel deal and the subsequent energy ceasefire is also set to dominate the conversation today in Brussels and Luxembourg, where foreign ministers are gathering, Jorge Liboreiro writes.
Once again, the EU finds itself scrambling to close ranks behind Zelenskyy and push back, with calculated criticism, against Trump’s Russian-friendly diplomacy.
The US Treasury’s sanctions waiver to enable the diesel sales, set to last until April 2027, has particularly enraged Europeans, who see their own sanctions regime undermined by Trump’s out-of-the-blue decisions. It must be noted that the majority of vessels that Russia uses to trade its refined oil products are subject to the G7 price cap ($100 per barrel).
Foreign ministers will today make clear their pressure campaign on Moscow will continue unabated by formally blacklisting more than 1,600 people and companies accused of enabling the war, a record number in one go.
“We are of course continuing our path,” Kallas said on sanctions upon arriving in Luxembourg this morning. “Our message is clear. If we want to end this war, the only way we can do this is putting more pressure on Russia, and we would call on the US to put the sanctions in place so we can finish this war,” she added.
More is needed: Russia’s all-out escalation has forced EU officials and diplomats to admit that their multibillion-euro support for Ukraine will fall short next year. But there are no easy solutions, Jorge writes in his in-depth analysis.
Warsaw watches: The mounting tensions have also raised the stakes of the Warsaw Security Conference kicking off this morning, with President Zelenskyy expected to address delegates from Kyiv in around an hour.
Our chief EU editor Maria Tadeo, on the ground in the Polish capital, reports that security is tight and the mood tense after Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said on Sunday that a man had been arrested on suspicion of plotting to assassinate him and his defence minister. More from our Warsaw colleagues.
Dead on arrival: Meanwhile, a new pitch to trim down the EU’s next long-term budget – known as the Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF) – tabled by Ireland over the weekend has been met with immediate pushback from the so-called frugal countries, which are demanding a much smaller spending pot.
“The size of the new proposal is not a basis for agreement. The EU budget must be affordable for those who bear the brunt of financing it,” German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said in a statement on Saturday.
Dutch directness: Dutch Finance Minister Eelco Heinen was even more blunt. “The Netherlands cannot accept this proposal. At this rate, there will be no deal by the end of the year,” he said in a statement. Sweden also rejected the proposal, insisting that the “overall volume” needs to come down.
Ireland, which currently holds the rotating presidency of the Council of the EU, on Saturday pitched €141 billion in cuts to the previous proposal in an attempt to appease the frugals. The country’s EU affairs minister, Thomas Byrne, described the proposal as a “compromise designed to act as a catalyst” for wrapping up negotiations by the end of this year – a prospect that now looks increasingly remote.
Crunch time: EU leaders are set to tackle the budget issue when they gather for talks in Brussels on Thursday and Friday – and European Council President António Costa is pushing for a swift compromise. There has been a political push to wrap up the budget negotiations before the end of 2026 to prevent talks from being torpedoed by elections in major EU economies including France, Italy and Poland next year. Over the past few months, the EU has conducted six inspections as part of the fight against the shadow fleet. Each such inspection on board a vessel costs Russia time and money, the EU's foreign policy chief explained.
At the same time, she said, diplomatic measures exert the greatest pressure on Moscow. In particular, at the EU's request, African countries removed hundreds of vessels from their ship registries.
Losing its flag makes a tanker more vulnerable to inspections and detention, and also makes authorities, insurers, banks and traders hesitant to do business with it
The EU has so far imposed sanctions on approximately 670 vessels.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — President Lai Ching-te (賴清德) attended the closing ceremony of the Taiwan Bridges Project at National Taiwan University on Monday, praising the initiative for strengthening international academic cooperation and helping Taiwan develop future scientific talent, per RTI.
The project brought 31 Nobel laureates to Taiwan for lectures and academic exchanges in 2025 and 2026, connecting international researchers with Taiwanese universities and research institutions.
Lai said the initiative had built three bridges: a bridge of knowledge that brings world-class expertise to Taiwan and helps Taiwanese researchers engage internationally; a bridge between generations, through lectures and exchanges that inspire younger scientists; and a bridge of peace that promotes dialogue and encourages scholars to use their expertise to advance peace and prosperity, per CNA.
He said the project supports Taiwan’s ambition to cultivate three Nobel laureates in the sciences within 30 years. “I also firmly believe that a free academic environment encourages questioning, and a democratic society encourages dialogue,” Lai said.
He added that Taiwan would draw on its strengths in science, education, and democracy to work with international partners toward peace, prosperity, and a better future for humanity.
Academia Sinica President Chen Chien-jen (陳建仁) said the project’s most important achievement was using exchanges and dialogue to build bridges between research fields. These connections not only linked Taiwan with the world but also increased the international visibility of Taiwanese research, he said.
Chen said he hoped the project’s experience would lead to more cooperation across institutions, disciplines, and countries. He also expressed hope that the friendships and exchanges established through the initiative would continue to deepen and bring greater international attention to Taiwan’s scientific research.
The closing ceremony included a review of the project’s achievements and discussions about future cooperation. Participating institutions shared their experiences and presented digital records of the initiative’s activities.
Organizers said the project would provide a foundation for further international academic cooperation and exchanges across disciplinary boundaries.
The Taiwan Bridges Project was jointly organized by NTU, Academia Sinica, and partner academic and research institutions in collaboration with the International Peace Foundation. Nobel chemistry laureate Lee Yuan-tseh (李遠哲) helped initiate the program, which was supported by Lite-On Group founder Raymond Soong (宋恭源). Lai served as honorary chair.
The initiative reflects Taiwan’s effort to deepen international research connections and encourage young scientists to pursue ambitious research. Academia Sinica has emphasized that direct engagement with leading scholars can help researchers develop new ideas, strengthen long-term collaborations, and raise public support for basic science.

====================================================================================================

She vanished on a trip around the world. Did she end up a castaway in Australia's backyard?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
06:29:32 UTC
15:29:32 KST

in brief
- A new expedition is seeking to discover what happened to famous aviator Amelia Earhart.
- An object spotted on a Pacific island could be the remains of her plane.
A team of researchers is headed to a remote island they hope holds the secret to the disappearance of Amelia Earhart, an aviation pioneer whose feats made her one of the most famous figures in the early history of flight.
The researchers' primary target is the site of an unidentified object, first spotted in 2020 next to a lagoon off Kiribati's Nikumaroro island in the Pacific Ocean, located roughly halfway between Australia and Hawaii.
Nearly a century after Earhart's disappearance, a joint expedition between Purdue University, its research foundation, and the not-for-profit Archaeological Legacy Institute hopes to find out whether the object is the fuselage and tail of her plane.
After completing their final leg travelling by boat from Kiribati's capital to the atoll in the country's Phoenix Islands, the 17-person team will spend the following days searching the sandy landmass, stretching approximately 7.5km by 2.5km.
"There's something significant to flying over the Pacific Ocean," expedition member Sirisha Bandla said.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
"As we finally arrived at our point of departure here in Tarawa, it struck home that we'd flown over a majority of the portion that Amelia Earhart and Fred Noonan were attempting to traverse when they were lost.
"Now we hope to have a chance to bring closure to their story."
The flight that ended in mystery
Born in 1897, Earhart was forever changed by a 10-minute plane trip she took at the age of 23.
"By the time I had got two or three hundred feet off the ground, I knew I had to fly," she later recalled.
She later became the first person to cross the Atlantic twice by air, having made the first crossing as a passenger in 1928 and the second alone in 1932 — the first woman to complete a solo flight across that ocean.
In the same year, she became the first woman to make a nonstop solo flight across the United States and in 1935 she became the first person to fly solo and nonstop from Hawaii to the US mainland.
She also broke multiple speed and altitude records in the decade preceding those journeys.
Despite having been awarded the Distinguished Flying Cross — a US decoration for heroism or extraordinary achievements in aerial flight — Earhart still had her sights on a new record: a flight around the world at the equator.
Between creating her own clothing line and helping to establish a support network for the advancement of female aviators, Earhart started working at Purdue University in 1935, where she eventually purchased a Lockheed Electra 10E.
The aircraft was nicknamed the "Flying Laboratory" for its developed technological communication and navigation systems.
However, in 1937, the plane would become the vessel of her final voyage.
Earhart and her navigator Fred Noonan were last seen taking off from Lae, New Guinea, heading to Howland Island, an unincorporated territory of the US.
Radio operators on a US Coast Guard vessel received messages from the plane that it was running low on fuel and was struggling to locate the island.
After communication was lost and the pair failed to land, the US government began its largest-ever search for a missing aircraft. The 16-day mission, however, found no trace of the pair or the plane.
Several searches have been completed since.
The castaway theory
There are multiple conflicting theories about Earhart and Noonan's disappearance.
The US government's position is that, with limited radio communication and facing strong headwinds and cloud cover, Earhart and Noonan ran out of fuel before reaching their destination, crash-landing somewhere in the Pacific Ocean.
Another suggests the pair was running out of fuel but were able to land on Nikumaroro and lived out the rest of their lives as castaways on the remote coral island.
Human remains found on the atoll in 1940 have been the subject of ongoing academic debate.
While the original bones have been lost, measurements recorded by the doctor who examined them have been used by some to argue that they could be those of Earhart.
The clues left behind
The Taraia Object, a focus of investigations, has been visible on satellite imagery since 1938, the year after the pair went missing, according to Purdue University.
Remnants of a cosmetic jar of anti-freckle cream, as well as aeroplane-related materials and parts of a shoe, have also been found on Nikumaroro.
The researchers plan to heavily document the site, then complete a series of scans before any potential excavation work.
"We will start our remote sensing work using magnetometers and sonar to get a better idea of what is there before we actually uncover it. After that is all done, we will uncover it using a hydraulic dredge," expedition leader Rick Pettigrew said.
The team has visited a replica of the plane to study its parts and rivet patterns, to assist in identifying any potential wreckage.
They are scheduled to return to Kiribati's capital before the end of the month.
If the Taraia Object is the missing plane, the team hope for a full excavation next year, should they receive permission from the Kiribati government.
The mystery that refuses to die
Millions of dollars have been spent on several projects to search for the missing plane, despite none resulting in irrefutable evidence.
Competing Earhart explorer Ric Gillespie told news agency Reuters he believes the plane has been swept by tides into the sea, ultimately splitting apart and sinking.
Gillespie founded The International Group for Historic Aircraft Recovery. It's completed at least five expeditions to Nikumaroro over the last fifteen years.
He says the Taraia Object is more likely a fallen tree that has been swept into the lagoon.
"You can see the root ball. You can see the branches. It's a tree. People see what they want to see," he said.
The lack of definitive physical evidence has fostered a variety of speculations for what really happened to Earhart, ranging from being captured by the Japanese military to being returned to the US under an alias.

In Lviv, Ukraine’s oldest woman, former UPA liaison Olena Rybalko, has died at the age of 109

In Lviv, Ukraine’s oldest woman, former UPA liaison Olena Rybalko, has died at the age of 109
Kyiv • UNN
Olena Rybalko, a former UPA liaison and doctor, died in Lviv on October 9 at the age of 109. The farewell ceremony will take place on October 12.
In Lviv, at the age of 110, Olena Rybalko, Ukraine’s oldest resident and a former liaison for the Ukrainian Insurgent Army, died. The Lviv City Council announced this on the evening of October 11, UNN reports.
In Lviv, at the age of 110, the prominent Lviv resident and former Ukrainian Insurgent Army liaison Olena Rybalko died
"Olena Rybalko devoted her life to medicine, helped wounded insurgents, and survived the Holodomor. She was Ukraine’s oldest resident. According to her family, Mrs. Olena’s earthly journey ended on Friday, October 9," the city council reported.
Where the farewell ceremony will take place
The farewell ceremony will take place on Monday, October 12, at the Church of the Dormition of the Blessed Virgin Mary. The funeral service will begin at 12:00. Olena Rybalko will be buried at Yaniv Cemetery, in the family tomb.
What is known about Olena Rybalko
Olena Rybalko was born on June 2, 1917, in Vinnytsia region, where she received a medical education.
Her father, Kyrylo Rybalko, was a soldier of the Ukrainian People’s Republic and a founder of the Ukrainian Autocephalous Orthodox Church. In 1937, he was executed by an NKVD troika for activities aimed at reviving the Ukrainian Autocephalous Church. Her mother, the last descendant of the Ukrainian branch of the Potocki counts, died during World War II.
Olena Kyrylivna survived the Holodomor of 1932–1933. In 1946, she moved to Lviv, where she devoted her life to medicine.
She was assigned to work in Lviv region, where she took the position of chief physician at the Pustomyty District Hospital.
While working as a doctor, she helped wounded insurgents. She devoted nearly her entire life to medicine, retiring at the age of 89.
Her patients included prominent figures in Ukrainian culture, science, and the church, including Dmytro Pavlychko, Ivan Krypiakevych, and Yosyf Kladochnyi.
During those difficult times, she did not remain on the sidelines of the Ukrainian people’s struggle for freedom. Olena Kyrylivna provided medical assistance to Ukrainian insurgents and performed operations in Ukrainian Insurgent Army hideouts, risking her own life to save others, the Lviv City Council stated.

IEA urges faster diesel releases as supplies tighten
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
06:27:13 UTC
15:27:13 KST

The International Energy Agency (IEA) has urged member countries to accelerate pledged diesel stock releases and consider additional supplies as global markets tighten.
In an Oct. 11 statement, the agency said Executive Director Fatih Birol had written to member governments ahead of its Oct. 15 Governing Board meeting, calling on countries with outstanding commitments under a March agreement to speed up releases and prioritize diesel.
He also asked all members, including those that had fulfilled their pledges, to assess whether further diesel releases were needed and indicate possible volumes and timing.
Birol cited renewed attacks on civilian and energy infrastructure in Saudi Arabia, stressing the importance of cooperation among members to protect energy security and economic stability.
The agency’s 32 members agreed in March to make 400 million barrels of emergency oil reserves available following supply disruptions caused by the Iran war. It was the largest coordinated stock release in the IEA’s history.
G7 countries agreed on Oct. 2 to release up to 100 million barrels of crude oil and diesel over four months. The agreement followed a U.S. threat to halt diesel exports to Europe unless European governments took further action to curb record prices.
EU countries view the G7 agreement as the completion of March commitments rather than an additional release. The IEA said on Oct. 7 that about 100 million barrels pledged under the March agreement had yet to reach the market.
