Concerns that Türkiye could become a gateway for Chinese automakers are misplaced, according to Automotive Manufacturers Association (OSD) Chairman Cengiz Eroldu.
He noted that Türkiye’s Industry and Technology Ministry applies investment criteria similar to the EU’s.
Türkiye needs investments that bring technology and research capabilities rather than new assembly plants, Eroldu said.
Eroldu said China’s automotive exports rose 67 percent in the first eight months of the year to 7.1 million units, while Chinese brands increased their share of the European market to 10 percent despite additional tariffs.
He said the EU’s efforts to protect its automotive industry were understandable, adding that a stronger European automotive sector should include Türkiye as part of the same value chain.
Eroldu said that one of the biggest concerns voiced by his European counterparts is that Türkiye could become a gateway for Chinese manufacturers.
“One of the issues most frequently raised during our discussions is whether Türkiye will become China’s backyard,” Eroldu said.
“We are not opposed to foreign investment, including from China. However, such investments must create added value for Türkiye, enhance its competitiveness and contribute to the development of the existing industrial base,” he added.
“We support the continuation of the joint working model between Türkiye and the European Union, and we are continuing our engagement in this direction,” Eroldu said.
Responding to recent claims that imports of electric and plug-in hybrid vehicles (PHEVs) from China could resume, Eroldu said there was no reason to relax existing measures.
“In the automotive sector, the [foreign trade] deficit [with China], which stood at 3 billion euros last year, reached 1.2 billion euros in the first seven months of this year,” he noted.
“The figures speak for themselves. Expanding this deficit would not benefit us. However, if a manufacturer comes with a value-added investment backed by R&D activities, we would all support it,” Eroldu said.

Herzog: ‘I'll do everything I can to prevent repeat elections’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
06:26:19 UTC
15:26:19 KST

President Isaac Herzog vowed to do everything in his power to prevent Israel from heading into another round of elections if the upcoming vote fails to produce a clear political outcome. "I'm doing everything I can to ensure Israel has a stable government," he said in an interview recorded ahead of Monday's People of the Nation conference, hosted by ynet and Yedioth Ahronoth. "But I'll go further than that: I will do absolutely everything I can to prevent repeat elections."
Herzog warned that Israel faces enormous national challenges and cannot afford repeated election cycles. "We need to wait for the results rather than pass judgment in advance, but we must do everything possible to avoid going through this again and again and again," he said.
In the wide-ranging interview, recorded several days before the conference and just over two weeks before Israel's elections, Herzog also renewed his call for a plea agreement to end Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's criminal trial, warned that Israel's police force is overwhelmed and condemned violence by Jewish extremists against Palestinians in the West Bank as "an enormous moral stain" on the country.
During the judicial overhaul, you called for compromise. Three and a half years later, Israel is just as polarized, perhaps even more so. Do you think we've reached a point of no return?
"First of all, the danger is always there, and it remains very real. All it takes is one madman, and the danger becomes extremely serious. We're in an election period, and naturally, such a period is dangerous because it can lead to radicalization that could tear even deeper divisions into our society."
Are you concerned that one side might refuse to accept the election results?
"I believe everyone will accept the election results. I think Israeli citizens will go out and vote. I constantly urge Israelis to vote, and I remind everyone that elections are not a civil war. Elections are the way to resolve issues, make decisions and understand that the day after, we still go on together. Those who lose and those who win must all understand that they belong to the same people. Those who are elected must also look after those who were not."
If the election ends in deadlock, will you try to promote a unity government?
"I don't want to get into that right now. There are different opinions about the composition of the government and different political outlooks. Everyone understands which school of thought I come from, but it would not be right for me to say, two weeks before the election, what kind of government should be formed."
Do you think a pardon could help ease tensions in Israel and perhaps make it possible to form a government if there is a deadlock?
"The president has the full authority to task a member of Knesset with forming a government. That has nothing to do with pardons. After I hear from all the parties, in a process that the public will already be discussing because the results will come in about a week after the election, the consultations begin.
"As for the pardon issue, you're referring to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's trial. I've already said, and I keep saying, that this case needs to end, and it should end with a plea agreement. It needs to be resolved through a settlement.
"That's why I proposed mediation at the President's Residence a few months ago. Attorney General Gali Baharav-Miara hesitated but agreed to come into the room. I said it would take place under the auspices of the President's Residence. The prime minister has not responded to this day, and I repeat: I'm leaving the door open, all the time."
Are you calling on the prime minister to accept your proposal?
"I'm not issuing calls. I'm waiting for a response, but that's not the issue right now. We're in the middle of an election, and it's clear to me that this isn't relevant during the election process."
Are you worried about the integrity of the elections and attempts to disrupt them?
"I'm working closely with the Central Elections Committee. Just last week, I brought the heads of the major technology companies here, together with the committee's chairman, Justice Noam Sohlberg, and his excellent team. We assessed different situations, considered extreme scenarios and heard how each company is responding.
"Even so, we must always consider the possibility that someone will try to sabotage the elections, whether from within Israel or from abroad. That's exactly what they're constantly working on, and they're doing so in a very impressive way."
We're living through a period of apparent anarchy and a breakdown of law and order in so many areas: in the south, in crime within Arab society and in the Haredi community. Just in recent weeks, hundreds of Haredi activists came to free a military draft dodger and rioted in Modiin in the middle of the night, while about 100 Jewish extremists descended on a Palestinian home and set it on fire. They also try to attack IDF soldiers, who seem unable to stop them.
"It's a miracle nobody was killed and there was no bloodshed. First of all, our police force is doing its best, but this country is a bit too much for it. We need a stronger police force and a much larger one because there are so many challenges here.
"Crime in Arab society is a disaster. We're talking about more than 1.3 million citizens living under terror, morning and night.
"The violence we saw in Modiin is intolerable. And what worries me most, what keeps me awake at night, is the violence we're seeing in the West Bank. It is an enormous stain on the face of the country, a moral stain.
"I hear about it from everywhere in the world. People say to me, 'What's happened to you? Don't you know how to restrain groups of rioters?' These are groups of rioters. They don't represent the settlement movement itself or its values in any way. Yet, on the other hand, they're receiving tacit legitimacy.
"I know the state institutions are taking action. But I personally went to the IDF's West Bank Division two weeks ago and sat down with the division commander and the brigade commanders."
And what did you hear from them?
"Deep frustration. They're facing extremely complicated situations. As one particularly impressive commander told me, 'I don't know whether someone speeding toward me in a car at night is a Palestinian coming to carry out a terrorist attack or a Jew coming to stage a provocation.'
"The incident in Jalud was extraordinarily dangerous, and it wasn't an isolated incident. We're talking about rocks being thrown at commanders.
"Innocent Palestinians must not be attacked, and actions of this kind cannot be allowed. The main thing that must be stated clearly is that the IDF and the security forces have achieved remarkable successes in fighting terrorism.
"Their job there is to fight terrorism, yet they find themselves confronting an utterly intolerable reality. That requires all the relevant authorities to sit down together, develop a serious plan and bring the full power of the state to bear, including clear directives from the political leadership."
Do you think administrative detention should be reinstated?
"I think that possibility needs to be examined. There are certainly cases in which we need to know how to use that tool. If there's no alternative, there's no alternative.
"We cannot continue allowing this phenomenon. It's eating away at the State of Israel and destroying everything good about its image around the world.
"Last week, we marked three years since October 7. Around the world, people spoke about October 7, about the terrible disaster, what we went through and the barbaric, criminal terrorism. And then, inevitably, someone brings up an incident like this in the West Bank. That is unacceptable because this is not Israel. It's a phenomenon we can and must confront."
Israel is facing an unprecedented international campaign against it. In some places, Israel has practically become a pariah. This isn't confined to a small minority, and it isn't just antisemitism. How are we supposed to confront this wave of hostility?
"There's enormous antisemitism, so many engines of incitement and so much poison. But we have to confront this phenomenon by doing more than simply identifying the problems. We need to ask what the solutions are.
"We must reach out to countries and companies, speak, make appearances, explain and show the beauty of Israel, its extraordinary achievements and its contribution to humanity. And, of course, we have to develop better public diplomacy tools.
"We're the Startup Nation. We can do a much better job in this regard."
What are you hearing from Jewish communities around the world?
"I invest an enormous amount of effort in this, in maintaining connections, offering support and strengthening communities.
"We need to understand that everything said and every action taken here, in the nation-state of the Jewish people, directly affects our brothers and sisters in the Diaspora, Jewish communities, their security, their standing and their ability to make their voices heard.
"They are threatened and challenged. This is a very complicated period for the Jewish people. At the same time, the Jewish people are demonstrating strength and resilience and fighting back.
"I encourage everyone: Stand up, fight, make your voices heard. Don't be afraid."
Within a few years, the Haredi education system is expected to become the largest in Israel. Does that worry you? And do you have deep relationships of trust with the Haredi community?
"I cannot say that something relating to the composition of Israeli society worries me. This is Israeli society. It's a challenge we have the strength to address.
"Take the issue of Haredi military enlistment, for example. On the eve of Tisha B'Av, I had the privilege of visiting the IDF's Hasmonean Brigade for the reading of Lamentations. I was moved because I saw Haredi soldiers, and I saw them in large numbers.
"An interview with me was recently published in the brigade's newspaper, which was distributed to thousands of households. It's simply wrong to assume that the entire Haredi community thinks or acts the same way. But we have to talk.
"There are trends we're identifying. There's a demographic trend, and we need to address it. We need to understand that things must change. I believe that future generations of Haredim won't be exactly the same as those today, just as citizens in other groups will also change.
"We have no choice but to sit down together and build a shared future for our children and grandchildren. This is an amazing country, an amazing people, with extraordinary strength. I want to see everyone included, and that creates challenges.
"For example, we need as much service by women in the IDF as possible, alongside the challenge of Haredi military service. We'll need to find the right balance and hold a respectful, serious discussion.
"I think the people of Israel have had enough of the division and hatred within our society because it gets us nowhere. God forbid, it can lead to disasters.
"That's why we must do everything possible. I'm doing everything I can and putting my entire heart and soul into it. People from every part of Israeli society are constantly coming to these rooms at the President's Residence. Sometimes they begin by shouting and almost coming to blows, and the meetings end with tears and embraces."
There's a feeling in Israel that the very concept of taking responsibility has disappeared. That applies to the October 7 massacre and even to the attempted attack involving a flydubai aircraft.
"I said this in my speech at Mount Herzl, about the need to investigate thoroughly, without fear or hesitation, and provide all the answers."
Through a state commission of inquiry?
"That issue is now the subject of a debate on the eve of the elections, about the composition of the commission and what kind of commission it should be.

German labour minister quits Merz's fragile coalition
BERLIN, Oct 12 - Germany's labour minister and co-head of the centre-left SPD party resigned from both posts on Monday, citing the death of her stepdaughter and political attacks against her, adding to strain in Chancellor Friedrich Merz's coalition government.
"After my stepdaughter's death, I realised that I need time to come to terms with my grief," Baerbel Bas said in a statement, without giving further details.
Bas, whose ministry oversees large parts of Germany's welfare system, also said she had faced increasing "public attacks", including from members of the CDU/CSU conservative bloc, the SPD's coalition partners.
Bas had come under fire from lower ranks of the conservative party bloc over delays to a pension overhaul.
"The attacks against her during the past days of her mourning were inappropriate. That is unacceptable," said Vice Chancellor and Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil, the SPD's other co-leader, who cancelled a planned trip to India.
Merz's conservatives are seeking pro-business labour market deregulation to revive the economy amid a surge in energy prices and tough rivalry from China, while the SPD is pushing to preserve workers' rights and benefits.
STRUGGLING COALITION
Bas's exit adds pressure on the coalition, which trails the far-right AfD in opinion polls. It was shaken by major gains for both the far right and far left in regional elections last month.
Support for Merz will be further tested in five more regional elections next year that will impact his ability to get major legislation through the Bundesrat, a house of parliament filled by Germany's 16 states.
Nationwide elections are scheduled for 2029.
The SPD said that Alexander Schweitzer, the former state premier of Rhineland-Palatinate and one of the party's deputy leaders, would take over as labour minister.
Schweitzer lost his regional leadership role to a CDU rival after state elections in March. Under the coalition pact, the SPD does not need to consult with its CDU/CSU partners on who leads ministries that the party has been assigned.
The coalition partners have been working on changes to the nation's pay-as-you-go retirement system to address Germany's ageing society, a key element of a broader economic and social reform programme.
The labour market reform bill is under an initial review by the chancellor's staff.
Merz, whose party will wrap up a two-day strategy meeting in Berlin on Monday, struck a conciliatory tone on X, saying Bas's decision deserved respect and thanking her for her commitment.
It remained unclear who would succeed Bas as the SPD's co-leader or if Klingbeil would fill the role on his own. Bas said she would retain her seat in parliament. REUTERS

Scientists discover a hidden factor that can make or break chemical reactions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
06:24:46 UTC
15:24:46 KST

Scientists discover a hidden factor that can make or break chemical reactions
Scientists uncovered a hidden chemical variable and used it to boost reaction selectivity from 16% to 97%, potentially transforming how everyday materials are manufactured.
- Date:
- October 12, 2026
- Source:
- Seoul National University College of Engineering
- Summary:
- Researchers discovered a hidden factor that can determine whether chemical reactions succeed or fail, and then used it to boost the proportion of the desired product from 16% to 97%. By controlling acidity near electrodes, they developed a promising way to manufacture chemicals for plastics, medicines, and other products using oxygen and electricity instead of hazardous added oxidants.
- Share:
Scientists have identified a hidden factor that can determine whether a chemical reaction succeeds or fails. By controlling tiny changes in acidity near electrodes, researchers dramatically improved the production of valuable chemical ingredients, raising the proportion of the desired product from approximately 16% to 97%.
The breakthrough, led by Professor Jaeyune Ryu of the Department of Chemical and Biological Engineering at Seoul National University College of Engineering, could help make chemical manufacturing safer, cleaner, and more efficient. The researchers developed a method that uses oxygen and electricity to produce compounds used in plastics, medicines, adhesives, and other everyday materials without requiring the separate addition of peroxide oxidants.
Their discovery centers on a surprisingly overlooked factor called "local pH," which describes the acidity or alkalinity in the immediate surroundings of an electrode. By redesigning a chemical reactor to control the distance between electrodes and the movement of liquid through the system, the team found a way to manage these conditions and greatly improve the reaction's performance.
The work focused on two important families of chemicals: lactones and epoxides. Lactones are essential starting materials for biodegradable plastics and polyurethanes, while epoxides are used to manufacture adhesives, protective coatings, and epoxy resins found in electronic materials. Both also play important roles in producing pharmaceuticals and other specialized chemicals.
The findings were published in the Journal of the American Chemical Society (JACS), a leading chemistry journal published by the American Chemical Society (ACS).
The Hidden Chemistry That Can Make or Break a Reaction
The research builds on a technique known as organic electrosynthesis, which uses electrical energy to drive reactions that produce carbon-based chemical compounds.
This approach has attracted growing interest because it may reduce the need for some of the chemical oxidizing and reducing agents commonly used in traditional manufacturing. Such agents help reactions proceed by accepting or donating electrons, but some can be hazardous to handle and generate unwanted waste.
Until now, much of the effort to improve organic electrosynthesis has centered on familiar factors, including the electrical voltage, the materials used for electrodes, and the composition of the liquid in which reactions occur.
However, the researchers suspected that something important was being overlooked: the microscopic chemical environment directly next to each electrode.
This is where molecules exchange electrons and undergo chemical transformations. Although the surrounding solution may appear uniform, conditions within this tiny region can be dramatically different.
One particularly important factor is pH, a measure of how acidic or alkaline a substance is.
During an electrochemical reaction, hydrogen ions, also known as protons, can be produced or consumed at the electrodes. If these ions are generated or removed faster than they can move through the liquid, the pH near the electrode may become very different from the pH measured in the rest of the solution.
The researchers found that these local differences can influence several critical parts of a reaction. They can change how reactive oxygen species are produced, alter the behavior of the starting molecules, and even affect whether the finished products remain stable or begin to break down.
In other words, a reaction can fail even when the overall solution appears to have the right chemical conditions.
An Overlooked Problem May Affect Many Chemical Reactions
To determine whether this phenomenon might extend beyond their own experiments, the researchers examined more than 600 scientific papers on organic electrosynthesis published since 2010.
They found that approximately 89% of the studies involved reactions at one or more electrodes in which both electrons and protons were transferred.
This matters because the movement of protons can change local acidity. The finding suggests that overlooked pH differences near electrodes could influence a wide range of electrochemical reactions, rather than just a few specialized examples.
The team also measured how extreme these differences could become.
Even when the overall solution was essentially neutral, the researchers estimated that conditions near the cathode, the electrode where reduction occurs, could reach approximately pH 11, making the area strongly alkaline.
Meanwhile, the region around the anode, where oxidation takes place, could reach approximately pH 2.5, creating a strongly acidic environment.
These changes can have major consequences. Under such conditions, the reactive oxygen species needed to drive a reaction may become less available. Starting materials can change chemical form, and newly formed products may break down more rapidly.
Simply adjusting the acidity of the entire solution therefore may not solve the problem. What matters is the environment directly around the electrodes, where the chemistry actually happens.
Making Valuable Chemicals With Oxygen and Electricity
To demonstrate their discovery, the scientists investigated a well-established chemical process called Baeyer-Villiger oxidation.
This reaction adds an oxygen atom to a type of organic molecule known as a ketone, converting it into an ester or lactone. Lactones are ring-shaped compounds that serve as important building blocks for materials such as biodegradable plastics and polyurethanes.
Traditionally, Baeyer-Villiger oxidation often requires highly reactive oxidizing chemicals, including peroxyacids. Although effective, these substances can create difficulties involving safe handling, chemical waste, and the treatment of unwanted byproducts.
The Seoul National University team developed a different approach.
Instead of supplying these oxidants from outside the system, the researchers used electricity to activate oxygen gas at an electrode. This produced reactive oxygen species capable of transferring oxygen atoms into organic molecules.
To establish where the oxygen in the final products came from, the team conducted isotope-tracing experiments. These tests confirmed that the incorporated oxygen originated from oxygen gas rather than water.
The scientists also discovered that the two electrodes could work together in an important way.
At the cathode, oxygen reduction generates reactive oxygen species that initiate the oxygen-transfer reaction. Hydrogen peroxide formed during this process can then be converted back into reactive oxygen species at the anode.
This cooperation helps sustain the supply of reactive chemical species necessary for the reaction.
However, the entire process depends heavily on the acidity near the electrodes. If local pH becomes too extreme, the chemistry can become much less effective.
A Simple Reactor Redesign Boosts Selectivity From 16% to 97%
Once the researchers understood the importance of local pH, they investigated how to control it.
Using computer simulations and electrochemical measurements, they developed a reactor design that places the electrodes closer together while allowing the electrolyte, the electrically conductive liquid carrying the reaction ingredients, to flow between them.
The idea was to prevent extreme acidity differences from developing.
Because the area near the anode tends to become acidic while the area near the cathode becomes alkaline, bringing these regions closer together and circulating the liquid helps counterbalance their effects.
The results were striking.
Under conditions where local pH differences were not effectively controlled, approximately 16% of the relevant products formed were the desired target compound. With the improved reactor design, that selectivity rose to approximately 97%.
This increase in selectivity means the reaction became much better at producing the intended substance rather than unwanted products.
The researchers also discovered that changing the flow of the electrolyte had a powerful effect on production.
Across the flow rates they tested, the amount of product generated per unit time increased by approximately 14 times from the lowest to the highest flow rate.
Moving the electrodes closer together also made a difference. When the distance between them was reduced from 20 mm to 4 mm, the production rate increased by approximately 2.2 times.
Perhaps most revealing was what happened when the liquid was not allowed to flow.
Even though the applied voltage and the solution's composition remained unchanged, the researchers obtained almost none of the desired product.
This showed just how important the immediate chemical environment can be. The success of an electrochemical reaction depends on more than the ingredients, voltage, and electrode materials. The physical design of the reactor and the microscopic conditions it creates can be equally critical.
Applications for Biodegradable Plastics, Medicines, and Electronics
The researchers then explored whether their approach could be used to manufacture different kinds of useful chemicals.
Using their optimized conditions, they successfully synthesized lactones from 18 different ketone compounds.
One important example was ε-caprolactone, which they produced with an 82% yield.
This compound is a starting material for polycaprolactone, a biodegradable polymer used in medical applications such as surgical sutures and drug-delivery systems.
The researchers also applied their local pH control strategy to the production of epoxides, successfully obtaining products from six different alkene starting materials.
Epoxides are important ingredients in adhesives, surface coatings, and epoxy resins used in electronics. They are also valuable intermediates in the production of pharmaceuticals and fine chemicals.
Together, these experiments showed that controlling the microscopic environment around electrodes could have applications beyond a single reaction.
The findings suggest a potentially versatile way to improve the production of many commercially important chemical ingredients.
Toward Cleaner and More Sustainable Chemical Manufacturing
One of the most promising aspects of the technique is that it uses oxygen and electricity while reducing the need for externally added peroxide oxidants.
The reactions also take place at room temperature and normal atmospheric pressure, avoiding the need for separate equipment to heat or pressurize the system.
These characteristics could make certain chemical processes simpler and potentially safer.
Because electricity provides the energy needed to drive the reactions, the approach could eventually be combined with renewable energy sources to support more sustainable chemical manufacturing.
The researchers believe that pharmaceutical ingredients and other high-value specialty chemicals could be particularly promising applications.
These products often require careful control of reaction conditions and strict safety measures. Electrochemical methods may offer advantages by limiting the need to handle hazardous oxidizing agents and potentially allowing production in relatively compact equipment.
However, the technology is not yet ready for widespread industrial use. Further optimization and testing at larger production scales will be needed to determine whether the laboratory results can be reproduced economically and reliably in commercial manufacturing.
A New Way to Think About Chemical Reactions
Beyond its immediate applications, the discovery offers a different perspective on how electrochemical reactions should be designed.
Traditionally, researchers have concentrated on choosing the right starting materials, catalysts, electrode surfaces, voltages, and solution compositions.
The Seoul National University team's findings indicate that controlling the tiny environment where molecules actually react may be just as important.
This shifts attention toward "designing the environment in which molecules actually react."
Professor Jaeyune Ryu, who supervised the research, said, "This study transforms 'local pH' near the electrode from a hidden variable into a controllable design principle."
He added, "To improve the efficiency of organic electrosynthesis, we need to design not only the reaction substrates and catalysts, but also the environment in which the molecules actually react."
The researchers believe this principle could reveal opportunities to improve other electrochemical processes, particularly those involving the movement of both electrons and protons.
Rather than treating local acidity as an unavoidable side effect, future chemical reactors could be deliberately engineered to maintain conditions that favor the desired reactions.
The study's co-first authors were Seonghyeon Min and Junghoon Lee, both M.S. students in Seoul National University's Department of Chemical and Biological Engineering. Hanju Kim, an integrated M.S./Ph.D. student, participated as a co-author, with Professor Ryu overseeing the research.
Min and Lee plan to continue investigating how local reaction environments influence organic electrosynthesis, with the goal of extending the approach to a broader range of chemical reactions and manufacturing processes.
The research was supported by Seoul National University, the National Research Foundation of Korea, and the Institute for Basic Science (IBS).

Yemen's Houthis have struck Saudi Arabia several times in the past week, including an attack on Riyadh's international airport on Saturday that killed 13 people and wounded more than 300. It was the deadliest in the kingdom in more than a decade.

Global poverty index rises for first time since its 2010 creation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
06:21:20 UTC
15:21:20 KST

More than half of those in acute poverty were children. (AFP Photo)
A U.N. global poverty index has risen for the first time since its creation in 2010, bringing the number of people affected to 1.2 billion, the United Nations Development Program reported on Oct. 12.
In the 2026 edition of their annual report, the UNDP and the Oxford Poverty and Human Development Initiative research center counted 51.5 million more people living in "acute" poverty compared to the previous year.
UNDP Administrator Alexander De Croo said the increase in poverty should be a "wake-up call for the world."
"Behind these figures are 1.2 billion people facing hardships that reinforce one another: Hunger, missed schooling and a lack of clean water or electricity. This is unacceptable," he said in a press release.
However, UNDP said a major factor in the recorded increase was population growth, and new data was only available for 13 of the 108 developing countries covered by the report.
While the total number of people in poverty has increased, the report provides a mixed picture. Some 33 nations have halved the percentage of their people living in poverty as defined by the index in the past 15 years.
Those included six countries in sub-Saharan Africa. Among the countries that have made the most rapid progress were countries in Asia — China and Vietnam — UNDP said.
As in the previous year, the report found that the majority of the poorest people live in sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia, specifically the Indian subcontinent, the most densely populated region on Earth.
The poverty index used in the report includes indicators such as the lack of adequate housing, sanitation, electricity, cooking fuel, food and education.

German Social Democrats' leader and Labor Minister Bärbel Bas resigns, amid coalition friction
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
06:20:00 UTC
15:20:00 KST

Germany: Bas quits as SPD co-chair amid coalition friction
October 12, 2026
Bärbel Bas, a longstanding top official with the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD), resigned from her post on Monday, citing the death of her stepdaughter and continued "open attacks" against her personally at this time of mourning. She wrote that the attacks had come from within Germany's ruling coalition of the SPD and Chancellor Friedrich Merz's conservative bloc of Christian Democratic Union and Christian Social Union (CDU/CSU)..
"I am currently unable to muster the strength to fully carry out my government and party duties on short notice, I have decided to step down from both offices,” 58-year-old Bas said.
She is to be replaced as labor minister by Alexander Schweitzer, the former SPD premier of the western state of Rhineland-Palatinate and former Labor Minister in that state. Her successor as SPD party chair will be elected in a party conference expected for early next year.
Who is Bärbel Bas?
A member of the parliament since 2009, Bas' star began to rise when she speaker of the Bundestag in 2021 under the SPD-led coalition of former Chancellor Olaf Scholz.
Within her center-left party, Bas has been among its more progressive members.
Following the collapse of Scholz's government, the SPD became the junior coalition partners to Merz's conservatives, and Bas became a cabinet minister, as did SPD co-leader Lars Klingbeil.
Why is she resigning now?
After her stepdaughter passed away, Bas said she needed time to process her grief, and that her party deserved strong leadership.
She added that recent infighting between the SPD and CDU/CSU over various policy matters hastened her decision.
The CDU has accused Bas of delaying or blocking several reforms the conservatives are keen to pass, including changes to Germany's struggling pension system and employment laws.
Bas said that she informed both Chancellor Merz and Lars Klingbeil before issuing her public statement.
Merz thanked Bas for her "trustworthy cooperation" and said he respected her decision. Klingbeil, for his part, said that his colleague had been subjected to "outrageous" attacks, pointing out that such rhetoric was often unfairly leveled at women in power.
Vice Chancellor Klingbeil calls for SPD leadership vote
Klingbeil also warned that tension in the coalition provided fuel for the far-right who "want democratic forces to tear each other apart."
Klingbeil canceled a planned trip to India to deal with the upheaval within his party. He told reporters on Monday that the SPD's full leadership team, including himself, should face new internal elections at a party gathering in December or January.
The "most important proposition" is "ensuring that the government immediately regains the ability to act and achieves stability regarding key issues like labour market and pension policy," he said.
Edited by: Jenipher Camino Gonzalez

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12

The European Union plans to allocate around €3 billion in military aid to Ukraine next week.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky announced this on October 11 following a phone call with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen.
According to von der Leyen, the new funding will be directed towards drones and missiles to strengthen Ukraine’s defense and protect its airspace.

We had a very detailed discussion with @vonderleyen on virtually all the current areas of our work with the European Union and the decisions needed to support Ukraine. I thanked Ursula for the recent €1.24 billion tranche for defense, which Ukraine has already received. I am grateful for the confirmation that another approximately €3 billion in military support will be allocated as early as next week. These funds will strengthen us.

Just before our conversation, the Russians struck a power plant in Kyiv with a “shahed” drone, and many districts experienced power outages. Under these circumstances, reliable support from our partners means real protection for people’s lives and a guarantee that the Russians will not be able to break Ukraine. We deeply appreciate all the tangible steps taken to support our defense and our people.

Zelensky also thanked the European Commission president for the previous tranche of €1.24 billion, which Ukraine has already received, and for confirming further funding.
On October 7, the European Commission transferred €1.24 billion to Ukraine to purchase Ukrainian-made unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), interceptor drones, ammunition for them, and missiles.
By the end of 2026, a further €28.1 billion will remain available to Ukraine under the Ukraine Support Loan programme.
Of this amount, €15.4 billion has been allocated to the defense industry, while €12.7 billion will go towards budgetary support.
A further €4.4 billion in budgetary assistance remains available under the Ukraine Facility programme.

89 of the 121 drones launched by Russia neutralized overnight, including more than 70% of the jet-powered drones
Kyiv • UNN
On the night of October 12, Russia launched 121 drones at Ukraine, including 76 jet-powered ones. Air defense destroyed or suppressed 89 unmanned aerial vehicles.
Russia attacked Ukraine with 121 drones during the night of October 12, including 76 jet-powered ones. A total of 89 of them were shot down or suppressed, including 55 jet-powered drones (72%). UNN reports this with reference to data from the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine.
What Russia used to attack and where from
According to the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, during the night of October 12 (starting at 18:00 on October 11), the enemy attacked with a Kh-59 guided aircraft missile from the airspace over the waters of the Black Sea and 121 Shahed-type attack UAVs (76 of them jet-powered), Gerbera, "Banderol"/"Dan-T" drones, and Parodiya-type decoy drones launched from the following directions: Orel, Kursk, Primorsko-Akhtarsk — Russia, the temporarily occupied territory of Donetsk, and the temporarily occupied territory of the Autonomous Republic of Crimea — Hvardiiske.
How many were destroyed
The air attack was repelled by aviation, anti-aircraft missile forces, electronic warfare and unmanned systems units, and mobile fire groups of the Defense Forces of Ukraine.
"According to preliminary data, as of 09:00, air defense forces had shot down/suppressed 89 enemy Shahed-type UAVs (55 of them jet-powered), Gerbera drones, and drones of other types," the statement from the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reads.
Hits by the enemy's means of air attack were recorded at 15 locations, as well as the سقوط of downed targets (debris) at 4 locations.
The attack is ongoing; several enemy UAVs are in the airspace.

Addictive behaviour is falling among Portuguese teens but most vulnerable are still exposed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
06:16:48 UTC
15:16:48 KST

Portuguese teenagers are drinking and using drugs less and facing fewer problems, but risks are increasingly concentrated among those with multiple vulnerabilities, according to a new ICAD study on addictive behaviours.
There are fewer problems and lower levels of consumption among Portuguese teenagers, but the highest-risk behaviours are increasingly concentrated among young people who accumulate several vulnerability factors. This is the main conclusion of a new study by the Institute for Addictive Behaviours and Dependencies (ICAD).
The Study on Alcohol, Tobacco, Drugs and other Addictive Behaviours (ECATD-CAD 2024) examines the problematic dimension of addictive behaviours among pupils in Portuguese state schools aged between 13 and 18.
The findings point to an overall favourable trend compared with the picture observed in the previous edition of the study, carried out in 2019. According to ICAD, there has been "a consistent reduction in the experience of all the problematic situations analysed, including violent conduct, accidents, hospitalisations, risky sexual behaviours and other episodes with potential negative consequences".
This trend is unfolding in a context in which pupils report better academic performance, greater parental supervision and going out at night less often, factors which, according to the report, "appear to contribute to an environment that is generally more protective against risk behaviours".
Despite this positive development, ICAD warns that "in several indicators there is a growing concentration of the highest-risk behaviours in a relatively small group of adolescents, characterised by profiles of greater individual and social vulnerability, which makes it clear that the reduction in the overall number of consumers does not remove the need for intervention targeting specific groups".
Recent consumption of alcohol and, above all, illicit drugs remains one of the main factors associated with involvement in problematic situations. The report notes that, compared with 2019, this trend has become more pronounced.
"The group of pupils who use psychoactive substances show significantly higher prevalence of risky sexual behaviours, problems with the police, interpersonal violence, accidents and other potentially serious situations", ICAD states, while stressing, however, that most problematic situations do not occur immediately following an episode of consumption.
The report also distinguishes between drinking alcohol only and polyconsumption, identifying them as important factors in the likelihood of experiencing problematic situations.
Thus, adolescents who combine recent consumption of alcohol and illicit drugs "display substantially higher levels of involvement in accidents, problems with the police, cyberbullying and risky sexual behaviours when compared with those who consume only alcoholic drinks".
The analysis of the problematic dimension of the different addictive behaviours also shows that, in alcohol consumption, motivations linked to pleasure, fun and sociability remain predominant.
However, ICAD underlines that there is a significant proportion of young people who say they drink alcohol to forget their problems. According to the institute, this is an "indicator frequently associated with the development of harmful patterns of use and dependence".
The report also highlights that, in the case of cannabis, although most users do not present indicators of risk of dependency, "there is an increase in the proportion of users classified as high risk, alongside growth in the group without any identified risk".
Social media is a major concern among non-substance-related addictive behaviours
Among non-substance-related addictive behaviours, social media continue to emerge as the main concern, with a significant proportion of young people acknowledging that they spend too much time on these platforms.
In electronic gaming, including video games played exclusively online, indicators of problematic use remain broadly stable compared with the previous edition of the study. Gambling for money, meanwhile, although still involving only a minority of adolescents, shows an increase in prevalence, albeit accompanied by a slight decrease in indicators linked to the problematic dimension, such as the need to increase the amounts wagered.
There are also important differences between boys and girls. Male pupils continue to show greater involvement in problems with the police and in risky electronic gaming and gambling for money. By contrast, girls stand out for their higher prevalence of problematic use of social media and for resorting to alcohol consumption as a strategy for coping with emotional difficulties.
Social and family factors also have an impact. The profile most associated with problematic behaviours includes low academic achievement, weaker parental supervision, frequent nights out, and lower physical and emotional wellbeing. Conversely, good school performance, parental supervision and greater wellbeing act as protective factors.
Regional analysis also reveals changes compared with the previous study. Alentejo now appears as the region with the highest concentration of unfavourable indicators, followed by the Autonomous Region of the Azores, while Lisbon no longer occupies the position of greatest vulnerability observed in 2019.

designboom paris art week guide: what to see in and out of design miami and art basel 2026
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
06:15:45 UTC
15:15:45 KST

designboom paris art week guide: what to see in and out of design miami and art basel 2026
designboom maps the art, design, and cultural encounters worth seeking out across paris this october.
What to see across Paris during Art Basel Paris 2026
Paris enters its busiest art and design week with a program that looks as much to what has already existed as to what comes next. Across museums, galleries, historic buildings, and temporary spaces, the 2026 season brings together fashion archives, modernist furniture, contemporary sculpture, photography, craft, and experimental forms of hospitality, with many projects reconsidering how objects and images acquire meaning over time.
At the center of the week, Art Basel Paris returns to the Grand Palais while Design Miami.Paris takes over the Hôtel de Maisons. Beyond the fairs, museums and cultural spaces across Paris present projects that span art, fashion, architecture, and design: Ibrahim Mahama brings a network of artists and Ghanaian cultural histories to Fondation Cartier; Prune Nourry revisits the overlooked legacy of women sculptors at the Petit Palais; Jenny Holzer activates the Musée d’Orsay with texts and images; and the Musée des Arts Décoratifs marks 40 years of its fashion collections through four decades of exhibitions and 40 significant silhouettes.
Galleries turn to material memory and transformation, from Jean Prouvé’s architecture and Japanese ceramics to Wendy Andreu’s reworked furniture and Ais’s layered paintings. Temporary projects also blur the boundaries between disciplines, including WE ARE ONA’s collaboration with Rirkrit Tiravanija and chef Dalad Kambhu, where a shared meal becomes part of the artwork itself. From major institutional exhibitions to intimate gallery presentations, collectible design, food, and temporary interventions, this is designboom’s guide to what to see across Paris during Art Basel Paris and Design Miami.Paris 2026.
design miami paris / art basel paris 2026
Art Basel Paris 2026
Art Basel Paris returns to the Grand Palais from October 23rd to 25th, 2026, with its fifth edition that brings together 211 galleries from 41 countries and regions, while expanding beyond the fair through an extensive public program across Paris. Under new director Karim Crippa, the edition foregrounds the galleries, museums, institutions, and public spaces of the city as part of the fair’s wider cultural context.
The fair is organized across three sectors: Galeries, with 183 exhibitors; Emergence, with 16 solo presentations; and Premise, with 12 historically focused projects. This year, Premise moves into the larger Salon Seine, while Conversations relocates to the Grand Palais Auditorium for the first time. A record 12 joint booths will also bring together 24 galleries.
Outside the Grand Palais, the Public Program spreads across nine Parisian venues, including the Petit Palais, Palais d’Iéna, Cité de l’architecture et du patrimoine, Beaux-Arts de Paris, and several public squares and gardens. Highlights include Alice Diop’s Geste de Consolation at Palais d’Iéna, Tracey Emin’s sculptures at the Parvis des Droits-de-l’Homme, Kutluğ Ataman’s Küba at Beaux-Arts de Paris, and Robert Indiana’s LOVE Wall at Place Clemenceau.
 what: Art Basel Paris 2026
when: October 23rd–25th, 2026
where: Grand Palais, 3 Avenue du Général Eisenhower, 75008 Paris
Alice Diop – Geste de Consolation presented by miu miu
For her first exhibition project, French filmmaker Alice Diop transforms the Palais d’Iéna into a multimedia journey for Miu Miu’s 2026 Art Basel Paris Public Program commission. Geste de Consolation brings together film, photography, sculpture, poetry, dance, music, and live performance, centering acts of consolation conceived by Black women artists.
The project takes over four interconnected spaces. It begins with work by South African artist Zanele Muholi and a two-screen video installation by Diop, bringing together archival images and film excerpts that have shaped her own way of looking. This leads into Chambre à soi, a living room and library featuring carpets with a motif by Mary Lee Bendolph and books drawn from Diop’s intellectual influences. The central library opens onto a performance space where texts by writers including Penda Diouf, Zora Neale Hurston, June Jordan, Audre Lorde, Marie Ndiaye, and Zadie Smith are performed live. Choreography by Nadia Beugré and music by Angel Bat Dawid and her ensemble further extend the project beyond the conventions of a static exhibition. The journey ends with Simone Leigh’s monumental bronze Sentinel (Mami Wata), whose nearly five-meter-tall female figure references the West African water spirit whose image has travelled across Africa and its diasporas.
what: Alice Diop – Geste de Consolation
when: October 21st–25th, 2026
where: Palais d’Iéna, Paris
Tracey Emin brings three bronze figures to Paris
Presented by White Cube, Tracey Emin’s I Lay Here For You, I Followed You to the End, and I Will Not Be Alone occupy the Parvis des Droits de l’Homme outside the Cité de l’architecture et du patrimoine. The three bronze figures explore intimacy, vulnerability, and resilience through different poses of the female body. The works move from an elongated figure lying on the ground to a kneeling body and, finally, an upright seated figure, tracing, together, a shift from exposure and surrender toward strength and endurance.

Kutluğ Ataman brings Küba to the Chapelle des Petits-Augustins
Kutluğ Ataman’s Küba transforms the Chapelle des Petits-Augustins at the Beaux-Arts de Paris into a multi-screen portrait of a community shaped by migration, poverty, and survival. First created in 2004, the 40-screen video installation gives each television to a different resident of Küba, a former settlement on the outskirts of Istanbul founded in the late 1960s by people fleeing political persecution.
Set among mismatched armchairs and salvaged furniture, the screens show residents speaking directly to the camera about their memories, fears, beliefs, and dreams. Their stories overlap without one voice taking precedence, allowing visitors to gradually piece together a collective portrait while moving through the installation. Ataman uses individual testimony to consider how identity is formed through storytelling, giving the community’s own voices control over its representation.
 what: Küba, 2004
when: October 20th – 25th, 2026, 10am–7pm
where: Chapelle des Petits-Augustins, Beaux-Arts de Paris

Maison Parisienne
Pierre Renart and Maison Parisienne present a monumental wooden bench whose backrest unfolds into a curved ribbon, extending into a chaise longue. Made from a single flowing line of wood, the piece creates two facing seating areas designed for sitting and conversation.
Craftica Gallery
Craftica Gallery presents Korallion (2026), a birch plywood bench by Cyryl Zakrzewski that sits between sculpture and architecture. Designed for an outdoor setting, its fluid form responds to light, weather, and the passage of time while adding a sculptural element within the landscape.
Galerie Gastou
Galerie Gastou presents Irene Cattaneo’s Effi Briest, a group of monumental bronze swings inspired by the childhood swing in Theodor Fontane’s 1895 novel. Their weight and permanence contrast with the fleeting movement associated with swings, connecting the installation to the tension between childhood freedom and the social structures that shape adulthood.
Nilufar
Nilufar features a curated selection of vintage design alongside contemporary works, including Von Pelt Atelier’s Table Lamp Spring Fountain 2 (2025). Made in Spain, the lamp reinterprets the silver-plated decorative objects found in Spanish homes during the mid-to-late 20th century.
Galerie Patrick Seguin
 Galerie Patrick Seguin showcases furniture by Jean Prouvé, Charlotte Perriand, and Pierre Jeanneret alongside a 6×6 demountable house by Prouvé at Design Miami.Paris. The presentation brings together furniture and architecture to examine the shared ideas connecting the three designers’ practices.
The booth features Perriand’s Forme Libre low table from 1956, a Jeanneret sofa set from around 1955, and a Prouvé sideboard and Antony chair from around 1950. In the Hôtel de Maisons garden, Prouvé’s 1944 6×6 house is presented with a redesigned interior inspired by the chashitsu, the traditional Japanese tea pavilion.
Using natural materials including wood, the installation creates a dialogue between Prouvé’s architecture and Japanese approaches to living. It also draws on the designer’s connections with Japan, emphasizing affinities around simplicity, lightness, and material restraint.

Fondation Cartier pour l’art contemporain – Ibrahim Mahama
Ghanaian artist Ibrahim Mahama transforms the Fondation Cartier pour l’art contemporain into a collective space for art, research, and exchange with The Harvest Season. For his first major exhibition in Paris, Mahama occupies the institution alongside nine artists and collectives connected through long-term collaborations, research, and exchanges, bringing together site-specific works and new versions of existing installations. The exhibition takes inspiration from the three art centers Mahama has established in Tamale, northern Ghana, since 2019. These spaces combine artistic production, education, and transmission, providing a model for thinking about how cultural institutions can emerge from local networks rather than operate separately from them. At the Fondation Cartier, this approach extends into a program of exhibitions, performances, music, talks, workshops, and masterclasses.
Among the central works is Parliament of Ghosts, a circular parliamentary chamber made from traditional Asante wooden stools. The installation refers to Ghana’s 1966 coup and the dissolution of its government, while also functioning as a stage for performances and discussions throughout the exhibition. Mahama also presents Things Fall Apart, a monumental reconstruction of a former Ghanaian glass bottle factory, using original materials to connect industrial heritage with questions of education, infrastructure, and possible futures. The exhibition expands through works by Dorothy Akpene Amenuke, Gideon Appah, James Barnor, CATPC, Courage Dzidula Kpodo, Zohra Opoku, Postbox Ghana, Tjaša Rener, and Feda Wardak. Their practices bring together textiles, photography, painting, architecture, archives, agricultural materials, and inherited infrastructure, extending Mahama’s interest in how histories and forms of knowledge can be carried forward and transformed.
 what: Ibrahim Mahama: The Harvest Season
when: October 22nd, 2026 – February 28th, 2027

The Musée de l’Orangerie marks the centenary of Claude Monet’s death with Monet: Painting Time, an exhibition examining how the artist’s work evolved from capturing fleeting impressions to exploring the experience of duration. Nearly 40 paintings trace this progression, from his Impressionist works of the 1870s through the Haystacks, Poplars, and Rouen Cathedral series to the Water Lilies that occupied him until his death in 1926.
The exhibition brings together works from the Musée d’Orsay and Musée Marmottan Monet, alongside loans from French and international collections. Its final section focuses on the Nymphéas, connecting the series to the Musée de l’Orangerie’s permanent panoramic installation, which Monet conceived as an immersive environment.

The Grand Palais presents Cezanne et nous, an exhibition tracing Paul Cézanne’s influence from the late 19th century to the present through nearly 180 works. Bringing together artists including Paul Gauguin, Henri Matisse, Pablo Picasso, Piet Mondrian, Joan Mitchell, Bridget Riley, and Peter Doig, the exhibition examines how successive generations have interpreted, appropriated, and challenged Cézanne’s approach to painting.
The exhibition follows Cézanne’s growing influence from the artists and collectors who discovered his work in Paris in the late 1880s through the avant-garde movements of the 20th century. At Musée du Luxembourg, Andy Warhol: La ligne et l’image places drawing at the center of Warhol’s artistic practice. Around 150 drawings, alongside paintings, screenprints, photographs, and archival documents, trace how drawing remained a site of experimentation throughout his career, from his early work as a commercial illustrator to his late drawings for The Last Supper.
The exhibition is organized around five themes: Warhol’s beginnings in advertising illustration, his use of handwritten text, his fascination with faces and masks, his exploration of gay imagery, and his recurring preoccupation with death. Drawings reveal the techniques behind his images, including stamps, transferred lines, stencils, and collage, highlighting the relationship between hand and mechanical reproduction that runs through his work.

La MEP – Maison Européenne de la Photographie – Irving Penn: PENN & FASHION
Maison Européenne de la Photographie (MEP) presents a major survey of Irving Penn’s fashion photography from 1947 to 2008. Drawn primarily from the MEP and the Nicola Erni Collection, with loans from The Irving Penn Foundation and the Miyake Issey Foundation, Penn & Fashion, traces the American photographer’s six-decade relationship with fashion and his long collaboration with Vogue. The exhibition moves from his photographs of Parisian haute couture in the 1950s, including Dior and Balenciaga, through the work of the 1970s and 1980s for designers such as Ungaro, Courrèges, Yves Saint Laurent, and Karl Lagerfeld. It also highlights Penn’s collaboration with Issey Miyake, whose sculptural garments became a particularly strong match for his controlled photographic compositions.
The presentation continues through Penn’s later fashion and beauty work, including photographs of creations by John Galliano, Christian Lacroix, and Chanel. Across the exhibition, his attention to silhouette, volume, texture, and composition demonstrates how his fashion commissions operated between photography, art, and commercial image-making.

The exhibition traces the processes that turn fashion into museum objects, from the first sketch and couture atelier to photography, conservation, restoration, and display.
The presentation follows the two lives of a garment: its creation before entering the collection and its transformation into cultural heritage once it reaches the museum. Drawings, embroidery samples, patterns, model deposits, and archival material reveal the work behind the clothes, while photographs and fashion shows demonstrate how garments have been presented as artistic performances. The 40 silhouettes span the museum’s exhibition history, from Moments de mode and Madeleine Vionnet to Christian Dior, couturier du rêve and Les Mondes surréalistes d’Elsa Schiaparelli.
what: Look! 40 ans de mode au musée
when: September 30th, 2026 – April 4th, 2027
where: Musée des Arts Décoratifs, 107 Rue de Rivoli, 75001 Paris
PASSAGES: Pas sages
For PASSAGES: Pas sages, the Quai d’Orsay opens the historic Hôtel du Ministre to a contemporary art exhibition during Art Basel Paris. Co-produced by artist-designers Thierry Lemaire and Harry Nuriev and curated by Krystyna Winckler, the exhibition brings contemporary art, design, craftsmanship, heritage objects, and diplomatic archives into dialogue across the ministry’s historic salons.
The exhibition focuses on the idea of passage as a form of transmission, connecting artists who have participated in France’s international residency network with works from the Manufactures Nationales, the Centre National des Arts Plastiques, and the diplomatic archives. Artists include Louise Bourgeois, Zao Wou-Ki, Betty Woodman, Raphaël Barontini, Jeanne Vicérial, Pol Taburet, Nour Awada, and Nelly Saunier, alongside historical furniture, ceramics, textiles, and Cypriot antiquities.
Lemaire and Nuriev develop the scenography as part of the exhibition itself, introducing contemporary interventions into rooms such as the King’s Bedroom and a cabinet of curiosities assembled from diplomatic documents and objects. The presentation also connects the exhibition to France’s network of more than 80 international artist residencies, positioning artistic exchange as part of cultural diplomacy.
 what: PASSAGES: Pas sages
when: October 20th–23rd, 2026
where: Hôtel du Ministre, Quai d’Orsay, Paris
Carpenters presents Rick Owens Furniture and Japanese ceramics
Carpenters brings together two exhibitions for Paris Art Week, pairing Rick Owens Furniture’s Five Easy Pieces, curated by Michèle Lamy, with Master Pieces, a presentation of Japanese ceramics organized with De Biousse & West. The two shows approach material and craft from different perspectives, from Owens and Lamy’s use of rusted steel and wood to a century of Japanese ceramic practices.
Five Easy Pieces presents five new editions of functional artworks that continue Owens and Lamy’s interest in architectural form and primal materials. Rusted steel and wood foreground processes of transformation, with the materials carrying associations with resistance, nature, and time. Running alongside it, Master Pieces brings together 16 works by 11 leading figures in 20th- and 21st-century Japanese ceramics. Spanning a century of practice, the selection highlights different approaches to historical techniques, form, surface, pattern, and material, with works that are seldom exhibited outside Japan.
 what: Five Easy Pieces + Master Pieces
when: October 20th, 2026 – March 15th, 2027 (Five Easy Pieces); October 20th – December 19th, 2026 (Master Pieces)
where: Carpenters, 54 Rue de la Verrerie, 75004 Paris
Downtown+ – GHOSTS by Wendy Andreu and Ais
Downtown+ returns to 11 Rue Las Cases for GHOSTS, bringing together designer Wendy Andreu and artist Ais in an exhibition about how objects, bodies, and memories persist through transformation. Τhe show places reworked furniture alongside paintings that similarly use layers, erasure, and traces of what came before. Andreu transforms second-hand chairs by covering them with Regen, a composite material made from cotton rope and silicone. The original forms remain legible beneath the new surface, turning familiar furniture into objects that sit between functional design and sculpture. Ais’s paintings approach persistence through intimate figures partially concealed by superimposed layers and overpainting. Together, the furniture and paintings create an interior that shifts between the familiar and the surreal, questioning how objects and images retain memory even when their original forms are altered.
 what: GHOSTS
when: October 16th–24th, 2026
where: downtown+, 11 Rue Las Cases, 75007 Paris

UN global poverty index rises for first time, affecting 1.2 billion people
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
06:15:10 UTC
15:15:10 KST

A UN global poverty index has risen for the first time since its creation in 2010, bringing the number of people affected to 1.2 billion, the United Nations Development Programme reported on Monday.
In the 2026 edition of their annual report, the UNDP and the Oxford Poverty and Human Development Initiative research center counted 51.5 million more people living in "acute" poverty compared to the previous year.
UNDP Administrator Alexander De Croo said the increase in poverty should be a "wake-up call for the world."
"Behind these figures are 1.2 billion people facing hardships that reinforce one another: hunger, missed schooling and a lack of clean water or electricity. This is unacceptable," he said in a press release.
More than half of those in acute poverty were children.
However, UNDP said a major factor in the recorded increase was population growth, and new data was only available for 13 of the 108 developing countries covered by the report.
Multidimensional poverty rates
While the total number of people in poverty has increased, the report provides a mixed picture. Some 33 nations have halved the percentage of their people living in poverty as defined by the index in the past 15 years.
Those included six countries in sub-Saharan Africa. Among the countries that have made the most rapid progress were countries in Asia - China and Vietnam - UNDP said.
As in the previous year, the report found that the majority of the poorest people live in sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia, specifically the Indian subcontinent, the most densely populated region on Earth.
"In Egypt, Nepal, and Tajikistan, both the poverty rate and the number of people experiencing multidimensional poverty have decreased significantly," the press release said.
In Angola and Zambia, the poverty rate has also declined, but population growth has more than offset this decrease, resulting in an increase in the number of people living in poverty.
The poverty index used in the report includes indicators such as the lack of adequate housing, sanitation, electricity, cooking fuel, food and education.

Strauf told German newspaper taz that he had not called for annexations, saying he intended to refer to Germany and Austria’s shared history. The youth wing’s leadership also distanced itself from the post.
Alsace and Moselle changed hands between France and Germany several times before returning to French control at the end of World War II.

Smotrich calls on Netanyahu, Katz to defy High Court over return of Palestinians to Jenin, Tulkarm
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
06:15:00 UTC
15:15:00 KST

The High Court of Justice on Sunday ordered the state to provide a timetable for completing the measures it says are needed before Palestinians displaced from three refugee camps in the northern West Bank can return to their homes, and to say whether that work can be accelerated.
The justices also asked the state to address the petitioners’ claims about shortcomings in humanitarian aid to residents. The state must submit its response by November 23, 2026. The court did not order an immediate return or direct the IDF to withdraw from the camps.
The ruling came in a petition filed by six Palestinian residents and the Association for Civil Rights in Israel, which seeks to enable the residents’ return to their homes in the Jenin, Tulkarm and Nur Shams refugee camps and to establish a mechanism for the return of other displaced residents. The petition also asks the state to provide for residents’ humanitarian needs until they can return.
The decision prompted Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich on Monday to call on Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Defense Minister Israel Katz to instruct the IDF not to cooperate with the court.
Supreme Court President Isaac Amit and Justices Alex Stein and Khaled Kabub noted that about one year and nine months had passed since the start of Operation Iron Wall, the IDF operation launched in the northern West Bank back in January 2025. According to the state, the security conditions needed for residents to return had still not been met.
Court seeks timeline to return West Bank residents to refugee camps
The case has been before the court since September 2025. In its preliminary response, filed on February 3, the state argued that continuing security needs prevented residents from returning. It said the military had not ordered residents to leave and that most had left before the operation began. The response also acknowledged that residents could not return to the camps, except for limited purposes coordinated with the military. A Central Command officer filed an affidavit supporting the state’s account two days later.
At a hearing on March 30, the court heard from the parties and held a closed discussion with security officials. In a decision following the hearing, the justices noted that more than 400 buildings had been demolished in the camps on the military commander’s orders, in addition to buildings damaged or destroyed during fighting, and that some residents had yet to return. They asked the state to submit an update by July 1.
The state filed its update on August 24, after receiving extensions. It told the court that security conditions had not materially changed and that the military was continuing to find weapons and explosives in the camps. The state said the military needed to maintain operational control and that residents could not return under current conditions. It also said its review found that residents’ humanitarian needs were being adequately met.
In their September 17 response, the petitioners challenged both the state’s security justification and its assessment of humanitarian conditions. They argued that the state’s update described a continuing policy aimed at maintaining long-term security control and preventing future threats, rather than a need to keep residents away during active fighting. They also disputed the state’s account of the aid available to displaced families.
Smotrich called on Netanyahu and Katz to tell the IDF not to cooperate with the justices
After Sunday’s ruling, Smotrich accused the justices of endangering Israel’s security and warned that residents’ return would allow terrorist infrastructure to be rebuilt in the northern West Bank. He also compared the court’s involvement to its role in Gaza before the October 7 massacre and said the justices should themselves face investigation.
“I call on the prime minister and my colleague, the defense minister, to instruct the IDF not to cooperate with the court and not to allow the terrorist camps to be reestablished,” Smotrich said.
He argued that security decisions should rest solely with elected officials and reiterated his support for changes to Israel’s judicial system.

N12 publishes transcript of Braverman's alleged attempt to change PM's Oct. 7 call log - report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
06:14:55 UTC
15:14:55 KST

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s former chief of staff, Tzachi Braverman, allegedly asked a Prime Minister’s Office stenographer to change the recorded time of a call between Netanyahu and his former military secretary, Avi Gil, on the morning of October 7, 2023, according to a transcript published by N12 on Sunday.
The transcript, which N12 dates to January 2024, reportedly shows Braverman speaking to a PMO stenographer and asking her to change the recorded time of Netanyahu’s secure-line call with Gil from 6:40 a.m. to 6:29 a.m.
“Wow, how beautiful. Look how sharp he is, Netanyahu. Look how sharp he is. It was at 6:29, not 6:40. Change the time,” Braverman said, according to the transcript.
The stenographer reportedly refused despite Braverman’s insistence, saying she was not permitted to change the computerized record.
However, despite her explicit objection and the fact that the record was an official, digitally signed document, Braverman did not back down, N12 reported. He allegedly took the printed transcript and changed the time in blue ink, writing it himself. The stenographer left the room and went to Gil to tell him what had happened.
Following the report, the information was passed on to the police investigation.
According to N12, Braverman wanted to change the time of the call between Gil and Netanyahu to suggest the prime minister received a detailed report immediately after the attack began.
Gil accuses Braverman of changing call log times
The account appears to align with what Gil said in an interview published by N12 and Israel Hayom on Thursday, in which he charged Braverman with making the changes.
"In January, one of the stenographers approached me and told me she had been instructed to retrieve the transcript of that 6:40 a.m. phone call and had been instructed [by Netanyahu's then chief of staff, Tzachi Braverman] to change the time of the call from 6:40 to 6:29," Gil said in the interview.
A statement shared with N12 on behalf of Braverman argued that the transcript is false.
"The stenographer was never told that Tzachi Braverman participated in the call. No such transcript of a conversation with her exists, and no such transcript was presented to him during his police questioning," the statement read.
"We regret that it was not reported that the military secretary failed to mention during his police questioning a conversation he had with Mr. Braverman at 6:33 a.m., during which he informed Braverman about the call at 6:29 a.m."
"We understand that after more than a year in which the case has been in the hands of the State Attorney's Office, and with indications that it is heading toward closure, it has been revived as part of a political campaign of which Mr. Braverman is a victim."
Braverman suspected of collecting classified protocols without authorization after Oct. 7
Separately, N12 reported on Sunday that Braverman has also been suspected of systematically collecting around 30 classified protocols without authorization in the month after the October 7 massacre.
The protocols reportedly included sensitive security discussions concerning the period leading up to the October 7 massacre, including those about Gaza and meetings with senior security officials concerning Hamas, according to N12.
According to N12, investigators suspected the documents had been collected to help shape the public narrative surrounding the events leading up to the massacre.
Braverman allegedly removed the documents without the required authorization, according to N12.
N12 noted that the case has been transferred to the Attorney General’s Office to decide whether to indict Braverman for violating procedures.
Miriam Sela-Eitam contributed to this report.

Startups are betting on AI to predict the future
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
06:14:00 UTC
15:14:00 KST

Several startups are betting that they can leverage artificial intelligence (AI) to make better forecasts than even the most specialized experts when it comes to topics as varied as stock market movements, the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, or how a Shakira song will perform on music charts.
By 2030, "we're going to feel that what we were doing for our decision-making was complete Stone Age thinking," Dan Schwarz, cofounder of the forecasting company FutureSearch, said.
AI forecasting models are already on par with the best "superforecasters" — gifted individuals whose estimates are markedly superior to those of ordinary people — thanks to troves of data acquired from both public and private sources.
In early September, two AI models made history when they took the top spots in the Metaculus Cup, a competition among prediction champions, both human and nonhuman.
FutureSearch's in-house human wizard, superforecaster Tom Liptay, is aware that "he's not secure in his job" in the medium term, Schwarz said. "He knows that these things are going to surpass him."
Theo Summer, who cofounded Preseen with Veniamin Veselovsky, used AI tools to turn $35 into $1.9 million in just seven months on the American prediction-making site Kalshi.
The idea is not to guarantee a result but to define a probability of occurrence, with the ability to cross-check assumptions related to several interconnected events — for example, changes in the price of oil and the war in the Middle East.
"Right now, the quickest buyers are normally the hedge funds, just because if they think they can make money off something, they can move pretty fast," Veselovsky said.
Algorithms have shaped Wall Street for more than a decade, but the rise of AI forecasting is likely to further increase the automation of financial markets.
"I think it's probably already having a small impact because we already have customers who use it when making trading decisions," said Toby Shevlane, the cofounder of another forecasting startup called Mantic.
Now-famous prediction markets Kalshi and Polymarket, which are used by millions of Americans, are also becoming inundated by AI use.
It might soon be too late for retail investors, who don't have access to expensive AI tools, to profit on those types of consumer-oriented trading sites because "they will soon just be dominated by AI forecasting systems," Veselovsky said.
The most advanced models no longer just predict events, either.
They can also formulate their own questions about the future and then assign probabilities based on the different possible outcomes, Shevlane said.
Their sphere of influence is beginning to extend beyond finance, as well, with potential applications in government policy, corporate decision-making, scientific research, and insurance risk assessments.
Mantic provides a large American company with likely scenarios of regulatory developments in its sector and has also worked for the British government.
Companies "are interested in risks and how to monitor them," Shevlane said.
Meanwhile, other customers might be more interested in medical research, particularly to help make decisions around which types of treatments would be best to fund, Schwarz said.
Widespread access to these types of tools can come with costs, though.
"I think that good can be derived from this," Veselovsky said, but "I'm also a little bit scared because, you know, maybe Russia or China has better systems."
