Policymakers take on energy shock, rising debt at IMF-World Bank meetings
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
06:13:55 UTC
15:13:55 KST

The week of meetings in Bangkok will include closed-door and public events, and policy announcements from the world's top economic officials. (AFP Photo)
Finance ministers and central bankers meet in Bangkok this week for the annual gatherings of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank, with the global economy buffeted between the U.S.-Iran war's energy shock, rising debt pressures and the AI boom.
The meetings, which run through Oct. 17, will see policymakers tackle some stark choices, with the IMF calling on governments to rein in spending even as vulnerable citizens' needs may be growing in the face of surging inflation and climate risks.
On Oct. 13, the IMF will unveil its global economic forecast, along with detailed regional outlooks through the week, as policymakers set about tackling the challenges darkening the economic horizon.
Chief among the concerns will be the economic fallout of the U.S. war on Iran, which has seen energy prices skyrocket. Despite the crisis, the Fund has called on countries to curb spending on subsidies and instead build their fiscal buffers after years of shocks since the pandemic.
Critics say that approach is just not feasible for low-income countries, and that multilateral lenders need to do more.
Advanced economies have seen a boom in investment in artificial intelligence technology drive stock markets to new highs and bolster economic growth.
The IMF has said that the amount invested in AI will likely outstrip the capital put into building the railroads, the electricity grid or global telecommunications networks.
Several events through the week will focus on AI's impact, including in developing countries that may not be exposed to its economic benefits as they lie outside its supply chains.
The week will also see several key meetings on the sidelines, including of G20 finance ministers, where spiking bond yields will be high on the agenda.

Can you solve it? The treacherous riddle of the round table
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
06:10:47 UTC
15:10:47 KST

It’s made of wood, it’s in the shape of a circle, and it is the forum for many an important gathering.
It is also the setting for today’s puzzle.
The round table
Three people sit at a round table, facing inwards, towards the centre of the table. No two of them are the same age.
Each of them says “I am younger than the person to my left.”
1. What is the greatest possible number of people telling the truth?
2. What is the smallest possible number of people telling the truth?
Seven people sit at a different round table, facing inwards, towards the centre of the table. No two of them are the same age.
Each of them says “I am younger than the person to my left, and I am younger than the person two places to my right”.
3. At this table, what is the greatest possible number of people telling the truth?
4. At this table, what is the smallest possible number of people telling the truth?
999 people sit at a third round table, facing inwards, towards the centre of the table. No two of them are the same age.
Each of them says “I am younger than the person three places to my left, and older than the person three places to my right”.
5. At this table, what is the greatest possible number of people telling the truth?
6. At this table, what is the smallest possible number of people telling the truth?
I’ll be back at 5pm UK with the solutions.
PLEASE NO SPOILERS. Instead please discuss round tables.
Thanks to Daniel Griller, a longtime friend of this column, who wrote today’s puzzles. He is the author of the excellent puzzle books Elastic Numbers and A Ring of Cats and Dogs, and Other Curious Puzzles.
I’ve been setting a puzzle here on alternate Mondays since 2015. I’m always on the look-out for great puzzles. If you would like to suggest one, email me.

Police detain 10 illegal immigrants in Tallinn's Nõmme district
Police apprehended 10 illegal immigrants in Tallinn's Nõmme district on Sunday evening. Nine were taken directly to a detention center, while one was transported to a hospital by paramedics for further medical treatment.
At around 7:30 p.m. Sunday, police received a tip that two dark-skinned men who appeared lost were standing outside an apartment building on Valdeku tänav in Tallinn's Nõmme district. Police responded to the scene and detained both men. Checks revealed that they were Sudanese nationals staying in Estonia illegally. During conversations with the men, police learned that several other people were hiding in the area.
Kevin Kohver, field commander at the Lääne-Harju Police Station, said police launched a search of the area based on the information they had received, involving police patrols, service dogs and personnel from the Rescue Board.
"The area was searched using drones and ATVs. A drone also detected people moving in the forest and dog patrols and other search teams were dispatched to find them. Those hiding in the forest initially tried to flee from police officers, but with the help of service dogs and patrols, they were soon apprehended in various wooded areas. A total of eight additional men of Sudanese origin were found in the forest," Kohver explained.
He added that paramedics assessed the health of all 10 men after they were detained. "Nine of the 10 men did not require additional medical attention and were subsequently taken to a detention center. However, one of the men who had been hiding in the forest and attempted to flee from police had fallen while running away and injured his arm. He was taken to a hospital for further medical treatment. After receiving treatment at the hospital, he was also transferred to the detention center," Kohver said.
All of the detained men were in Estonia illegally and only one was carrying identification documents.

<p>Hot air balloons decorated with keffiyehs fly over the fairy chimneys in Göreme, Cappadocia, Türkiye. (AA Photo)</p>
Hot air balloons featuring keffiyeh patterns, a symbol associated with Palestinian identity, took to the skies over Cappadocia at sunrise, drawing attention to the humanitarian crisis in Gaza and calling on the international community to protect civilians and ensure the delivery of aid.
The “Peace Balloons” lifted off from Göreme, a town in central Türkiye known for its distinctive rock formations and hot air balloon tours. Flying above the region’s famous fairy chimneys, the balloons carried messages of solidarity with the Palestinian people and called for peace and international unity.
Sudanese student Mustafa Khaleel, speaking at the event, urged the international community to take stronger action on the situation in Gaza, where Israel’s military campaign since Oct. 7, 2023, has killed tens of thousands of people and injured hundreds of thousands, according to his remarks. He said many people were still believed to be trapped under rubble.
Khaleel said that despite ceasefire initiatives, conditions continued to threaten civilian lives. Women, children, older people and other civilians had been affected by the violence, while mosques, hospitals, schools and residential areas had also sustained damage.
He also highlighted the strain on Gaza’s health care system, saying shortages of electricity, fuel and medicine had made it increasingly difficult for patients to receive treatment. People with chronic conditions, including kidney failure, cancer and diabetes, faced particular difficulties accessing care.
Pregnant women had been forced to give birth without reliable electricity or adequate medical services, Khaleel said, adding that journalists had also lost their lives while trying to report on events in the enclave.
He urged the removal of all barriers to humanitarian aid, warning of the devastating toll hunger is taking on civilians. He called on international organizations and foreign governments to implement more decisive measures to bring the suffering to an end.
Khaleel warned against letting political interests or diplomatic calculations overshadow the situation in Gaza. He called on international institutions and decision-makers to fulfill their duties by halting the attacks and guaranteeing uninterrupted humanitarian access.
Furthermore, Khaleel called for safeguarding hospitals and medical staff, lifting restrictions on patient treatment and holding violators accountable under international law.
Addressing Türkiye and international mechanisms, he urged further action to end Israeli attacks in Gaza and other parts of the region, as well as to bring the occupation to an end.

A new dawn for Didim
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
06:01:55 UTC
15:01:55 KST

For centuries, the environs of Didim in Mid-Aegean Türkiye have carried the whisper of prophecy. It was here, at the monumental Temple of Apollo, that pilgrims once walked the Sacred Way from ancient Miletus to consult the oracle. Perched on a hill, overlooking the Maeander plain, Priene is one of the best-preserved sites of the Ionian league. Both Miletus and Priene still resonate with the impression of ancient times; one feels like walking through a time capsule. The mighty oracle of Apollon temple stands high and strong, as if whispering a secret, or maybe telling what will come next.
Only a few miles apart from each other, this magnificent trio of archaeological remains is not the only attraction of the Didim area; the natural park of Lake Bafa is another world to explore, from where the winding Meander River gently sweeps towards the Aegean through a verdant alluvial plain, and the picturesque villages like Doğanköy and Kayaköy are hidden gems to explore. Last, but not least, or maybe the foremost attraction is Altınkum beach, which literally translates as The Golden Sand. Strangely enough, despite having such a rich portfolio of history and natural beauty, Didim has never hit the stardom of other Aegean destinations. In modern times, as tourism swept across Türkiye’s western coast, the Mid-Aegean region (Orta Ege) found itself caught in a curious dichotomy. While Bodrum to the south became synonymous with flashy luxury and Alaçatı and Çeşme to the north with outgoing crowds, or in recent years, Urla as a gastronomy destination, Didim largely became associated with mass summer beach travel — its rich history and serene landscapes somewhat obscured by seasonal crowds.
New upcoming destination: Mid-Aegean
That narrative is now undergoing a profound transformation. The opening of Akra Didim — a visionary project by BHM Otelcilik, the group behind the 50-year legacy of Barut Hotels — signals a decisive turning point for the Mid-Aegean. It introduces an approach grounded not in ostentation, but in what they simply call “simplicity” referring to understated, subtle luxury rooted deeply in place, culture, and nature.
The property is gigantic, spreading to about 340,00 square-meter grounds, but the feel is not out of human scale. The architecture respects the coast rather than dominating it, with vast areas of open spaces, treating roofs as part of the landscape, creating a breathing environment which allows guests to slow down, enjoy the spatial atmosphere. The ‘Simplicity’ philosophy approaches comfort as the purest form of what is right, whilst creating a flow that allows guests to follow their own rhythm without having to organize anything. Based on six core principles – nature, harmony, balance, well-being, creation and production, and sharing – this approach ensures that diverse experiences come together as parts of a single whole at Akra Didim.
However, the term “simplicity” does not mean “simplistic” here. Everything is well-thought of, offering a diverse range of experiences for the guests. Coupled with world-class wellness facilities, extensive racket sports, including padel and pickleball, and a commitment to 12-month operation, the resort redefines Didim as a year-round haven for culture, sports, and well-being. Another emphasis is on intellectual and artistic enrichment. Through its Artist Residency Program and dedicated Art & Culture Village, the resort invites contemporary artists to reside, create, and display their work on site. Guests do not merely view art on hotel walls; they engage directly with creators in live ateliers.
Inspiration: The olive
Gastronomy is a strong tool that forms a vital part of the connection forged with the region’s natural environment and culinary culture. In Akra Didim, this is achieved by a special dining experience aptly named “Zeytin’lik,” which means “The Olive Grove” in Turkish, housed in a stone building nestled amongst olive trees. Here, the cooking is also in line with the philosophy of “simplicity,” featuring fire cooking only and reinterpreting the region’s culinary heritage through traditional methods such as open-fire grilling, stone ovens and pit fires. Zeytin’lik strongly emphasizes locality; it offers seasonal produce sourced from the region or grown in its own kitchen gardens and serves the day’s catch from the sea. Regional recipes collected from locals often feature in the menu, to be paired with wines made from indigenous grapes from the extensive wine cellar featuring only Turkish wines. Here, gastronomy transcends being merely a dining experience; it transforms into a journey experienced through the processes of production, cooking and sharing.
The Mid-Aegean possesses an extraordinary culinary heritage, anchored above all by the ancient olive tree. Didim sits in the heartland of the prized Memecik olive. Here, olive oil is not merely a cooking medium; it is the hero of the table. Zeytin-lik transforms regional gastronomy into an authentic story of place, where rustic Aegean heritage meets contemporary culinary finesse. If the oracle at Didyma were to speak today, it might well predict that the future of Aegean luxury lies not in extravagant grandeur, but in returning to the authentic, olive-scented soul of the region.

Mystery of 1950s wedding photo album found dumped in Wakefield solved
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
06:00:49 UTC
15:00:49 KST

When Andrew Bedford discovered an old wedding album dumped outside his city centre cafe in Wakefield, West Yorkshire, he considered chucking it into a nearby wheelie bin.
But when he opened the album, the vintage photographs of the happy couple on their wedding day in 1957 seemed too precious to throw away.
Unable to work out the identity of the bride and groom – their handwritten names had become too faded to read – he rescued the album and brought it back to his cafe, Eva’s Kitchen, for safekeeping.
His partner, Éva Lemperger, put out a plea on social media to help identify the couple.
Now the mystery has been solved after a local family historian took up the case and tracked down the couple’s 65-year-old son, Michael Dawson.
He revealed the album had been stolen from a storage unit near the cafe, along with other cherished family heirlooms, after his parents died.
It contains some of his only surviving photographs of his mother and father, Maxwell Dawson and Barbara Parr, and he now plans to “protect it with [his] life”.
Bedford said: “I was just so happy he got it back. I thought, if it had been mine, and I’d lost pictures of my family – and they were only pictures I had of them – I’d have been elated if somebody had found them and given them back to me.”
When the case of the mysterious wedding album was picked up by his local newspaper, the Wakefield Express, it caught the attention of a local historian and amateur sleuth, Anne-Marie Fawcett. “I run a local history group on Facebook with over 15,000 members, and I’m really interested in local history, particularly family history,” she said.
“I love researching. I love uncovering stories and finding connections. And I like getting to the bottom of mysteries … When I saw that nobody knew who the album belonged to, I thought, that’s something to get my teeth into.”
A clue in the birth certificate of another guest helped her to identify the church the couple were married in: Wadsley Parish Church in Sheffield. She then used a photo enhancing tool to decipher the name of the bride. “But there was more than one Barbara Parr in the records, so I had to follow them all.”
When she came across an electoral roll entry suggesting Parr’s husband, Maxwell, had lived near Wakefield, she guessed she had found the right couple and appealed for information about the family on social media.
An old school friend of Michael Dawson’s remembered him and helped Fawcett to find a photograph of him, enabling her to track him down on Facebook.
“I sent him a message, and he rang me,” said Fawcett. “He was absolutely made up.”
Dawson told her the album had been stolen from the storage unit where he and his brother had stored the cherished contents of his parents’ home after they died. “Someone had broken in and taken all the family treasure. He said he’d lost everything. So you can imagine how I felt to be able to reunite him with this [album] … I’ve got goose pimples talking about it. Everybody loves a happy ending, don’t they?”
Dawson told the BBC: “I’m absolutely elated because I am sentimental and it’s important for me to have these photos.
“I will protect it with my life now, based on the fact that it’s all I’ve got.”
Asked how he felt about Fawcett’s detective efforts, he joked: “I think she probably knows more about me than I do, which is a worry.”
But he added: “I thought I’d lost everything. I can’t thank her enough.”

UK van drivers face extra £2.5bn in diesel costs this year, figures show
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
06:00:49 UTC
15:00:49 KST

Millions of British van drivers face a combined £2.5bn cost to cover the rising price of diesel this year, according to figures, fuelling calls for the government to scrap its planned fuel duty rise.
The owners of diesel vans and pickups can expect to collectively spend almost £8.5bn at the pump this year, according to analysis for the Guardian, after diesel prices climbed to record highs due to a global fuel shortage caused by disruption to refineries in the Middle East and Russia.
The estimated fuel costs, calculated by analysts at Moneysupermarket, is significantly above the £5.95bn spent last year, raising concerns that the price of food and goods transported by road could rise sharply as retailers pass on increased logistics costs.
The comparison site warned last week that the average fuel bill for a van driver could reach £1,965 this year, up from £1,294 for the average van in 2025 based on typical mileage and fuel consumption.
The number of vans on British roads has grown significantly in recent years fuelled by the boom in online shopping, home deliveries and the rising number of self-employed people working in trades.
Although the adoption of electric vans has begun to increase, about 95% of light commercial vehicles are still powered by diesel. The average pump price climbed to a above £2 a litre for the first time this month, up over 40% since late February, when the US-Israel war on Iran began disrupting supplies of crude and refined oil products from the Gulf, leading to cost increases across the economy.
The rising cost burden has led to calls for government help in the upcoming budget, including abandoning plans to raise fuel duty from next year. The planned increase – postponed from September – will add 3p a litre in duty from 1 January, and another 2p from 1 March, in “a hammer blow” for costs, according to the Road Haulage Association (RHA).
Richard Smith, the RHA’s managing director, said: “Many of our members run on margins of around 2%. Surging diesel prices are impacting firms across the country, with some spending many thousands extra every week on fuel.
“Adding [fuel duty rises] on top of today’s fuel prices would be a hammer blow for many firms that move goods and the households that buy them. A fuel duty hike is a food price hike.”
Data from the motoring group RAC showed that, despite a recent dip in the cost of diesel, the price remains about 57p a litre higher than before the US-Iran conflict while petrol remains 42p higher. This means households are paying £31 and £23 more respectively every time they fill up a family sized car, according to the group.
The fuel duty rise “will only make prices at the pump even more expensive,” according to Simon Williams, the head of policy at the RAC.
“As things stand, this year is still set to be the second most expensive year on record for drivers,” Williams said. “The government has the power to take some of the sting out of higher fuel costs, either by extending and increasing the fuel duty cut or reducing VAT as they’ve done with domestic electricity.”
Smith added that the RHA was calling on the chancellor to bring in a 15p a litre rebate for British van, coach and haulage operators after Spain, France and Italy offered similar help for commercial vehicle businesses. “It’s time we caught up,” he said.
On Friday, the US president, Donald Trump, attempted to ease pressure at the pump for US drivers by announcing a deal for Russian deal, in a move which infuriated the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
The government was contact for comment.

The Gulf has entered a new era of instability. If its leaders think they can rely on old alliances, they are wrong | Nesrine Malik
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
06:00:49 UTC
15:00:49 KST

On Saturday, Houthi rebels launched a shocking and deadly attack on Saudi Arabia’s capital city, Riyadh. At the time of writing, the missile strike on King Khalid international airport has killed at least 13 people and left 300 injured, marking a significant turn in a regional conflagration that is only getting more intense. It was the single most deadly attack on any Gulf country since the US and Israel launched their war on Iran in February. In Saudi Arabia, a country that is unaccustomed to such fatalities, the death toll is bewilderingly high and likely to prompt a bloody response.
Over the past year, the Gulf has entered a new era of instability that is not temporary and cannot be reversed. This may feel like an overstatement – casualties have been relatively low, after all, compared with Gaza and Iran – but the gradual erosion of peace and security in places such as Saudi Arabia, Qatar and the UAE has changed the region more dramatically than its leaders would like to acknowledge.
The first audacious and unthinkable thing happened just over a year ago, when Iran fired missiles at an airbase in Qatar that hosts American troops, in retaliation for US strikes on Iranian nuclear facilities. Lighting up Doha’s skies and scattering shrapnel, it was a dismaying moment for the Qataris, who have tried to maintain good relations with Iran. But even then there was a degree of warning and coordination that signalled this was a face-saving measure on the part of the Iranians. Yet later in 2025, with no similar warning or choreography, Israel struck Doha, targeting Hamas members and killing five Palestinians and one Qatari. That was the beginning of the end of a longstanding norm and expectation – that there was a sanctity to Gulf lives and sovereignty, one secured by the management of the relationship with Iran and alliances with the US.
Then came Donald Trump and Benjamin Netanyahu’s war on Iran, which drew the Gulf once and for all into the fray. In retaliation for what Iran perceives to be political, military and logistical support for the offensive against it, Tehran struck Saudi Arabia, Qatar, the UAE, Bahrain, Kuwait and Oman. Iran targeted military sites, energy facilities, desalination plants – an entire infrastructure that underpins the economies of these countries. Much damage was inflicted by the suspension of normal life, the shuttering of schools for months, the closure of airports and airspace.
The most disastrous consequence of all, from the perspective of Gulf rulers, has been the way the attacks have disrupted the integration of these countries into the cosmopolitan international community as places for tourism, entrepreneurs, sports and entertainment. They spent billions in securing Formula One, golf and boxing franchises and tournaments, only for a flurry of cheap drones to put it all at risk.
The result is a fractious unravelling that has reactivated hostilities that had laid dormant. Yemen’s civil war began in 2014 when Iran-backed Houthi rebels, in aspiration to greater autonomy in the minority Shia homelands, took over the capital city, Sana’a. In 2015, a coalition of countries led by Saudi Arabia led a brutal campaign to dislodge the Houthis from territories they had gained, intensifying a grinding civil war that killed hundreds of thousands and triggered a humanitarian catastrophe. The war deescalated in 2022 with a de facto but unformalised division of the country between the Houthis and an internationally recognised, Saudi-backed government; the ceasefire was followed by rapprochement between Saudi Arabia and Iran.
But the 2026 war against Iran opened up strategic opportunities and stirred political loyalties, triggering a surge of Houthi advancement in Yemen. The closure of the strait of Hormuz, for example, shifted more commercial traffic along Yemen’s coastline, prompting the Houthis to make advances and seize territory in order to gain control of the now crucial Bab al-Mandab strait in the Red Sea. Tensions came to a head five months after the start of the war, with Saudi Arabia escalating strikes against the Houthis, and the Saudi-backed government bombing its own airport in Sana’a to prevent an Iranian plane from landing.
These developments are not just the result of a mischievous group seizing the moment, acting as spoiler in a bigger contest between Iran and the west. The Houthis are backed by Iran, but they are not empty proxies for Iran; they have domestic ambitions and sharp regional animosities, particularly against the House of Saud, which they see an imperious and arrogant master to whom they shall never submit. A senior Houthi official said that Saturday’s attack took place “so that the world understands” that Yemeni civilian infrastructure has been, and is being, targeted by the Saudis, gesturing towards that sense that Riyadh treats Yemeni lives as cheap.
From another perspective, what we are witnessing in the region is another consequence of Hamas’s 7 October attacks on Israel, and what followed in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran. The final piece that was stabilising the region’s tense equilibriums fell away when Trump decided that the safety and security of the US’s Gulf allies was secondary to his Iran “excursion”, as he called it. The limits of relying on the US security umbrella became clear both to allies and enemies.
Last month, the Trump administration refused to extend military assistance to Saudi Arabia to fight the Houthis, after a meeting of US officials with the Houthis, who assured them that they would not attack US ships in the Red Sea, only Saudi vessels. What is upon Saudi Arabia now is a long, intractable war with a resourceful and impassioned antagonist, one willing to sustain a high degree of pain in ways that Riyadh can’t match without orienting itself entirely towards war. If the 2015 campaign is anything to go by, it will claim thousands of lives with only a remote possibility of a decisive outcome.
And so Saudi, and the entire Gulf, are pulled further into the relentless storm. Trump cannot bring the Iran war to an end, Gaza remains an open wound, Israel continues to strike and occupy parts of Lebanon. The Houthi resurgence represents a new reality in a region that is bewildered and losing lives and capital, stuck between old alliances that no longer work and new hostilities that are too calamitous to confront.
- Nesrine Malik is a Guardian columnist

Drivers forced to use parking apps can pay up to 40% more
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
06:00:48 UTC
15:00:48 KST

Drivers are unwittingly paying up to 40% more to park as more councils switch to app-only payments and force customers to pick up the tab.
Many councils across England have removed pay and display machines and replaced them with app payments, including a number in London. Most local authorities encourage drivers to pay by app to beat queues, while apps are often the only way to pay when ticket machines are out of order. However, many car park signs fail to mention that app payments may incur an additional service fee.
Parking apps save councils money by removing the cost of installing and maintaining ticket machines, but while a few pay the app providers directly for their services, many leave drivers to foot some or all of the bill through “convenience fees” or “service fees”.
These typically range from 10p to 30p, but they are not included in the advertised parking tariffs in car parks, even when an app is the only payment option, and they are often not strongly flagged within the apps.
Of the parking apps tested by the Guardian, none clearly displayed the service fee until the payment stage, and even then, some required customers to click on an information symbol to find out why the price had increased.
These surcharges can push up the cost of an hour’s parking slot dramatically. In Harrogate, North Yorkshire, drivers who park in the town centre and pay by app are hit with a mandatory 30p service charge – a 38% rise on an 80p tariff.
Meanwhile, the price of two hours at the council’s Christleton Road car park in Chester soars by 40% when the 20p convenience fee is added to the 50p tariff.
Extra fees are added if drivers agree to receive booking confirmation and expiry alerts. They are typically between 10 and 30p per text.
According to the Advertising Standards Authority, quoted prices must include all mandatory fees for a contract to be valid. Drivers enter a contract with a council as soon as they accept the car park’s terms and conditions and park their vehicle.
However, few realise that they enter a separate contract with the app provider if they choose to pay online. App fees, therefore, may not legally have to be displayed on parking council signs.
Because service fees are agreed between local authorities and individual app providers, and since they can vary depending on location, drivers have no way of predicting what they will be charged.
The Guardian tested the apps by booking an hour’s parking at car parks around the country.
RingGo’s convenience fee added an extra 20p to the £2 tariff at Kings Yard in Lancaster. Drivers have to click on a small “see prices” link above the prominent “Next” button when they have chosen their location to see the charge. It is mentioned again on the payment page, but only when the “i” symbol beside the final price is clicked.
PayByPhone charged a 15p service fee on top of the £5.10 parking tariff at Dudley Street car park in Birmingham. The existence of the charge was not explained until the payment page and was hidden behind the Apple Pay button. Customers have to scroll down to the end of the page to see it.
Customers using JustPark have to click on a tiny pale grey “i” symbol beside the final price at the end of the booking process to discover its transaction fee. This added 12p to a £3.50 parking charge at Charmouth Road car park in Lyme Regis, Dorset.
MiPermit listed its 10p convenience fee above the final price at the end of the booking. This was levied on top of the £1.90 parking charge in Littlehampton, West Sussex.
RingGo said the fee funded the service it provided and that it was up to the councils it worked with whether or not to display it on car park signs. “In line with existing regulations, wherever pricing information is shown in the RingGo app, we also display any additional fees,” said Adam Dolphin at its parent company Arrive.
JustPark said mandatory fees were included in the price quoted during payment. “Nothing is added at the payment stage,” said a spokesperson. “The ‘i’ icon simply shows how that all-in price is made up, for drivers who want the detail.”
PayByPhone said its pricing was transparent. “The pricing elements related to parking, SMS options and service fees are presented before payment confirmation,” said a spokesperson. “Applicable pricing information – whether fees, parking rates or options – is available on the website and in the app.”
MiPermit was contacted for a comment.
The Local Government Association, which represents councils, said it was up to app providers to ensure their fees were clear and upfront.
The Department for Transport said parking tariffs and surcharges were a matter for councils. “Drivers should be able to see clearly what they will be charged before they pay for parking,” a spokesperson said.
A spokesperson for the AA said: “When a driver walks to the signs in the car park and sees £1 per hour, that’s what they should be charged, not £1 plus a 25p service charge.”

British Prime Minister Burnham stated that Russia interfered in the Brexit vote
Ukraine

British Prime Minister Burnham stated that Russia interfered in the Brexit vote
Kyiv • UNN
Andy Burnham stated that Russia interfered in the Brexit referendum.
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham stated that Russia interfered in the 2016 Brexit vote, warning voters in France and Germany about Moscow-backed attempts to influence their politics. UNN reports this, citing Reuters.
Details
Burnham, who took office as the UK's leader in July and said last month that the UK could consider rejoining the European Union in the future, is the first UK prime minister to openly state that there is evidence of Russian interference in the referendum ten years ago.
"When I came to Downing Street, I asked whether there had been Russian interference in the 2016 referendum. And I received a clear answer that yes, there had been," Burnham said in an interview with The Rest Is Politics podcast published on Sunday, October 11.
Burnham did not explain how he believed Russia had interfered in the referendum, nor did he provide details about what evidence the statement was based on.
The Russian Embassy in London did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Russia has previously denied interfering in the Brexit vote, describing Britain as gripped by anti-Russian hysteria.
Burnham's comments differ from those of former Prime Minister Boris Johnson, who campaigned for leaving the EU and said in 2020 that there was no evidence of Russian interference in the referendum, the publication notes.
Britons voted to leave the EU in 2016 by a margin of 52% to 48%, which, the publication writes, led to the biggest political crisis since the Second World War.
Burnham said that voters in European democracies should be better informed about attempts to undermine their political situation.
"What I mean is that it is important now to speak clearly about these things and, I believe, help voters in Germany and France understand that some of this policy is being initiated by our enemies, namely Russia," he said.
The UK government was unable to establish whether Russia interfered in the 2016 referendum on EU membership, according to a 2020 report by the parliamentary Intelligence and Security Committee. The report also stated that Russia had attempted to influence the 2014 Scottish independence referendum, in which voters rejected independence.
Last month, Burnham said he could campaign for Britain to rejoin the EU at the next election, reviving the country's contentious debate over its relationship with the continent.

Father was asked for DNA test to get a passport for his daughter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
06:00:47 UTC
15:00:47 KST

My teenage daughter is unable to see her grandparents because of the UK’s new requirement for dual nationals to hold a UK passport.
I’m a UK citizen, married to a French national, and we live in France. Our two older children have both French and UK passports. Our third child was born while we were living in Zimbabwe and only has a French passport.
I began her application for a British passport in February. I had to submit photos of my wife when pregnant, family photos from the birth to the present day, hospital records and official translations of French marriage and birth certificates.
During an official interview I was asked about my job, commute and the layout of my house, but very little about my relationship with my daughter.
I was then told that there was insufficient evidence to prove my paternity and was invited to consider a DNA test, which will cost £600 and take yet more time.
We need to visit my elderly father who is unwell in the UK but cannot risk it in case our daughter is denied boarding.
BN, France
Your daughter is a victim of new rules that came into force in February and effectively deny entry to the UK to dual national Britons who do not have a British passport.
Foreign nationals can enter freely on passports issued by their country of residence, but expats cannot unless they stump up £589 for a certificate of entitlement. The law has caused chaos, with children being stranded abroad or arbitrarily denied a passport granted to their siblings.
Since the UK government is not accepting that your daughter is a UK national, you asked if she could travel on her French passport. No one could answer the question.
As a result, you face Christmas apart from your parents. Home Office rules state that officials must consider a passport application on the “balance of probability” if an applicant refuses a DNA test. They must also explain why an application is refused. You have never been told why your copious proofs of paternity have been deemed inadequate.
The Home Office will not comment on individual cases, but it did tell me that additional evidence, such as the layout of a home, may be requested to add “credible authenticity”.
Soon afterwards, you were informed that the application had been accepted after all, despite no new paperwork having been sought since April. I can only assume that press scrutiny prompted the realisation that your domestic floorplan is credibly authentic.

iPhone 18 Pro Max review: Apple’s biggest, heaviest and longest-lasting superphone
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
06:00:47 UTC
15:00:47 KST

Apple’s largest Pro iPhone gets its biggest battery upgrade yet to make it a true two-day phone with new Siri AI and a variable aperture camera.
The iPhone 18 Pro Max is the supersized sibling of the regular 18 Pro and, though it is no longer Apple’s most expensive phone thanks to the £2,000 iPhone Duo, it has a similarly large price tag to match costing from £1,299 (€1,599/$1,299/A$2,299).
The 18 Pro Max follows the familiar formula of its Pro Max predecessors: take everything that’s great about the 18 Pro and supersize the screen and the battery. That means it has a first-class camera, the fastest performance and very long software support.
But it also means the 18 Pro Max is hard to use with one hand and pretty big to fit in a pocket. It weighs 249g, which is really heavy for even a very large smartphone, 23g more than its nearest rival, 38g more than its smaller sibling and heavier still than folding phones. It made my hand hurt after 10 days of use and is a two-handed phone needing some sort of handle or strap.
The 6.9in screen is a joy to behold. Super bright, crisp, smooth and with a very effective anti-glare coating it’s great for films, TV or games, and offers a similar level of real estate for video to most folding phones. It also has the new, smaller camera cut out and bigger dynamic island of the regular 18 Pro.
Specifications
- Screen: 6.9in Super Retina XDR (120Hz OLED) (460ppi)
- Processor: Apple A20 Pro
- RAM: 12GB
- Storage: 256, 512GB or 1TB
- Operating system: iOS 27
- Camera: 48MP + 48MP UW + 48MP 4x, 18MP front-facing
- Connectivity: 5G, wifi 7, NFC, Bluetooth 6, Thread, USB-C, Satellite, UWB and GNSS
- Water resistance: IP68 (6 metres for 30 mins)
- Dimensions: 163.4 x 78 x 8.75mm
- Weight: 249g
Battery life for days
The 18 Pro Max has the same new A20 Pro chip as the 18 Pro, which is one of the fastest chips you can get in a phone, plus a resigned cooling system that helps maintain peak performance during long gaming sessions.
It has the longest battery of any iPhone, lasting almost three days of light usage between charges, actively using the screen for seven hours for apps, browsing, messaging and photos. That is about four hours longer than its predecessor and almost a day longer than the 18 Pro. Even with heavy use, the 18 Pro Max still managed to end the day with about 50% left in the tank, meaning most people will have to charge it only every second or third day.
iOS 27
The 18 Pro Max runs the same iOS 27 as smartphones from the iPhone 11 onwards. The new software speeds up app launches and other parts of the system, refines the Liquid Glass redesign from last year and revamps Apple’s AI tools.
The new Siri AI chatbot is a significant step in the right direction, able to better understand you and perform tasks. It has its own app to review previous conversations and can see what is on your screen or through the camera. It can also suggest data from your various Apple apps, similar to Google’s proactive tools on the Pixels. But it relies on you using messages and mail, rather than third-party apps such as the WhatsApp or Gmail apps.
Sustainability
The battery will last in excess of 1,000 full-charge cycles with at least 80% of its original capacity, and it can be replaced for £119. Out-of-warranty screen repairs cost £389. The specialists iFixit awarded the phone seven out of 10 for repairability.
It contains more than 40% recycled material. The company breaks down the phone’s environmental impact in its report. Apple offers trade-in and free recycling schemes, including for non-Apple products.
Camera
The 18 Pro Max has the same camera system as its smaller sibling, which includes an 18 megapixel centre stage selfie camera in the screen and three 48MP cameras on the back.
The three rear cameras are some of the best on a phone, including a 4x/8x optical zoom and 0.5x ultra wide.
The big addition for the 18 Pro Max is a variable aperture on the main camera, allowing it to open wider than other iPhones for better low light performance or to narrow to preserve depth of field. But it also allows additional creative photography possibilities, including shooting starbursts.
The 18 Pro Max also has new AI-powered focus tracking, improved Photographic Styles for greater customisation, Apple’s new digital negative feature and automatic cinematic mode for video.
Price
The iPhone 18 Pro Max costs from £1,299 (€1,599/$1,299/A$2,299).
For comparison, the iPhone 17 costs £899, the iPhone Air £1,099 and the iPhone 18 Pro £1,199; the Google Pixel 11 Pro costs £1,279 and the Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra £1,359.
Verdict
The iPhone 18 Pro Max is Apple’s biggest, longest-lasting and most expensive slab phone for 2026.
It takes what is great about the regular 18 Pro and supersizes the screen and battery, giving it a run time of up to three days, which is a good half day more than its smaller sibling. That places it shoulder to shoulder with some of the longest-lasting phones available on any platform.
But similar to superphones from Google and Samsung, the 18 Pro Max is too big to use one-handed and tricky to pocket. It is also too heavy and made my hand hurt without using a Popsocket or a similar handle attached to it.
Otherwise, it is a fairly iterative upgrade on the 17 Pro Max, with the same design and feel. The screen is still one of the very best on a phone, and the improved dynamic island is a useful upgrade. The A20 Pro chip is seriously quick, the cameras are some of the best you can get on a phone and the variable aperture on the main camera opens up some new creative opportunities, even if its impact on image quality is fairly minor.
 Pros: fabulous 6.9in screen, better dynamic island, very long battery life, great cameras with variable aperture, USB-C, top performance, long software support, Face ID, better AI.
Cons: very expensive, very heavy, hard to use one-handed, small upgrade on last year, AI tools still lag top competitors.

United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher

Babcock International has appointed Royal British Veterans Enterprise as an approved signage supplier, giving teams across the defence company a route to buy standard and bespoke signage from a manufacturer whose workforce is largely made up of veterans and people with disabilities, according to the organisation.
Signage can now be ordered through the Babcock procurement portal and is manufactured at the enterprise’s social enterprise sites in Kent and Glasgow, which between them cover safety, compliance, wayfinding and project-specific requirements. The arrangement gives Babcock a single UK-wide service while putting measurable social value into its supply chain.
More than seventy per cent of the manufacturing workforce are veterans, people with disabilities, or both, so procurement spend feeds directly into sustainable employment, skills development and workforce inclusion.
Colin Harsant, managing director of social enterprise at Royal British Veterans Enterprise, said: “This agreement represents the best of purpose-led procurement. By choosing RBVE, Babcock is strengthening resilient UK supply chains, supporting sovereign manufacturing capability and helping to create sustainable employment opportunities for those who have served our country. We look forward to building a long-term partnership that delivers operational excellence alongside meaningful social value.”
Ewan Sime, global director of procurement and supply chain at Babcock, said: “At Babcock, we want our procurement decisions to deliver value well beyond the products and services we buy. Our new agreement with Royal British Veterans Enterprise gives our teams access to a high-quality, UK-wide signage service while helping to create sustainable employment and skills opportunities for veterans and people with disabilities. It is a great example of how we can work with our suppliers to strengthen our supply chain, support the Armed Forces community and deliver meaningful social value through the way we do business.”
Babcock’s involvement goes beyond the supplier agreement, and its colleagues raised £26,668 for this year’s Great Tommy Sleep Out, the campaign that funds housing, support services and routes back into employment for homeless veterans.
The organisation has supplied customers in the construction, infrastructure and defence sectors, and its manufacturing arms trade as Britain’s Bravest Manufacturing Company and Scotland’s Bravest Manufacturing Company.
Social value now carries weight in the scoring of British public contracts, and prime contractors have to show what their spending delivers beyond the goods themselves.

Gallery: Ülle Madise sworn in as president of Estonia
Former justice chancellor Ülle Madise was sworn in as the next president of Estonia on Monday, taking the oath of office in the Session Hall of the Riigikogu.
On Monday afternoon, President-elect Ülle Madise and her husband Lauri Madise arrived at the Office of the President in Kadriorg, where they were welcomed by President Alar Karis and his wife Sirje Karis.
From there, they traveled together to Toompea Hill, where the outgoing president greeted the Guard Battalion honor guard assembled in Lossi Square before Madise and Karis entered Toompea Castle.
At the ceremony, which began at 3 p.m., Karis delivered a final speech as head of state before President-elect Ülle Madise took the oath of office and delivered her first address as president of the Republic of Estonia.
The ceremony and speeches were broadcast live on ERR channels.
Born and educated in Tartu, 51-year-old Ülle Madise is a lawyer by training. She has previously worked at the Ministry of Justice, on the Riigikogu's Constitutional Committee, as chief auditor at the National Audit Office, as legal adviser to the president and, since 2015, as chancellor of justice. She was reappointed to the latter position for a second term in late 2021.
Ülle Madise is married to Lauri Madise, who works as a judge at the Court of Justice of the European Union in Luxembourg. The couple have no children. Ülle Madise's father is former politician and Supreme Court justice Tõnu Anton.
Madise was nominated as a presidential candidate by 75 members of the Riigikogu. Representatives of the Reform Party, Eesti 200, Isamaa, the Social Democrats and unaffiliated MPs submitted the relevant documents to the National Electoral Committee.
The Riigikogu elected Madise president in a secret ballot with 71 votes.

Although Likud publicly claims that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's bloc will win at least 61 seats in the 120-seat Knesset, citing internal polls that reportedly support that projection, conversations with party officials suggest a more modest target is being discussed behind closed doors: 55 to 56 seats. Such a result could be enough to form a blocking bloc and prevent Netanyahu's political opponents from forming a government.
If Netanyahu's bloc wins 55 to 56 seats, his opponents could struggle to assemble a governing coalition. In that scenario, Likud officials believe the party would either push for another election or attempt to recruit a coalition partner from the opposing camp. According to the officials, former prime minister Naftali Bennett is the only figure who might agree to such an arrangement.
The officials, who are familiar with Likud's efforts to mobilize voters, some having previously helped oversee those operations, stressed that this remains a political assessment being discussed privately within the party. They believe that if Netanyahu's bloc wins 55 to 56 seats, his opponents would need broad support from the Arab parties to form a government. Such an outcome could allow Netanyahu to block his rivals from taking power, even if he fails to secure the 61 seats needed to form a government himself. According to Likud officials, Netanyahu's main priority would be to prevent his opponents from forming a government, even if he cannot establish one of his own.
Likud officials see Bennett as potential coalition partner, without Lapid
Likud officials also believe Netanyahu would explore the possibility of bringing a partner from the opposing political camp into his coalition.
"If we manage to secure another partner from the change bloc, it can only be Bennett, without Lapid, of course," a right-wing source said.

Therefore, there is reason to believe that he might do it again, moving from one camp to another," the source added.
Likud officials believe another election could hurt Bennett politically, potentially making an agreement with Netanyahu a more attractive option. The scenario they envision would involve Bennett joining a Netanyahu-led coalition without Yesh Atid leader Yair Lapid.
However, the officials stressed that no talks have taken place between Netanyahu's representatives and Bennett or his associates.
Another election could weaken Gadi Eisenkot's standing as a leading candidate

The National Solidarity and Integration Coordination Board has defined the duties and powers of its subcommittees, while parliament’s monitoring commission will follow the process.
Foreign-policy discussions are expected to cover U.S.-Iran diplomatic contacts and the course of their conflict, Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, the Russia-Ukraine war and developments in Gaza.

Houthi missile strike in Saudi Arabia exposes growing regional threat, Yemen expert warns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
05:56:14 UTC
14:56:14 KST

The Houthis remain a significant threat to Saudi Arabia and other countries in the region despite recent territorial gains by forces backed by Riyadh, Yemen expert Inbal Nissim-Louvton told 103FM following a Houthi missile strike on a terminal in the Saudi capital.
Nissim-Louvton, a Yemen expert at Tel Aviv University's Moshe Dayan Center and the Open University, spoke with Ron Kofman and Aryeh Eldad on 103FM about the ongoing fighting between Saudi-backed forces and the Houthis, and the limitations facing countries seeking to weaken the terrorist organization.
Asked who was winning the confrontation between the Saudis and the Houthis, she replied: "It depends on whom you ask."
"I think we are still in the midst of it. Just a few weeks ago, the Houthis controlled the port of Mokha and Mayyun Island, overlooking the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. But now we can see that forces loyal to the internationally recognized government, which are backed by Saudi Arabia, have managed to regain control of those areas."
According to Nissim-Louvton, the fighting remains part of a broader conflict within Yemen.
Houthi control of Yemeni territory complicates Saudi military response
"There is still a certain dynamic to the fighting itself, which is part of the renewed civil war in Yemen and the collapse of the ceasefire between the Houthis and the Saudis, which had held up well until recently," she said.
"I think there is an asymmetry here that has worked in the Houthis' favor in the past and continues to play a role now," she added.
The expert emphasized that the Houthis' capabilities extend well beyond their missile arsenal, making them a persistent challenge for several countries in the region.
"The terrorist organization has more than just ballistic missiles. It is an organization that possesses the apparatus of a state, including the economic capabilities of a country, albeit a poor one like Yemen, but nevertheless," she said.
"They manage to control a considerable amount of territory in a country, with more than 50% of Yemen's population, and that makes them a major headache for the Saudis, the United Arab Emirates, and Israel."
Nissim-Louvton also explained that countries confronting the Houthis face significant limitations when attempting to strike infrastructure under the group's control, particularly ports essential to Yemen's civilian population.
"You can strike these ports only up to a certain point because they are the lifeline of most of Yemen's population. When you strike them beyond the limits that allow normal life to continue there, in the context of the civil war, you are effectively imposing a major humanitarian disaster on the population," she said.
Addressing the impact of the situation in Yemen and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait on Egypt, Nissim-Louvton noted that disruptions to maritime traffic have consequences beyond the countries directly involved in the fighting.
"Egypt was the main country harmed by the previous blockade or earlier rounds of fighting. This should be a headache for the international community because there is damage to and a violation of the security of freedom of movement along a maritime transport and trade route," she concluded.

A person inspects the damage at the site of a warehouse hit by Saudi-led airstrikes, in Sana'a, Yemen, Oct. 9 2026.EPA/YAHYA ARHAB
Türkiye, Egypt, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia strongly condemned on Oct. 11 “hostile” attacks by Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis against the Gulf kingdom, including the deadly strike on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport.
In a joint statement, the four countries condemned “in the strongest terms the ongoing hostile attacks perpetrated by the Houthi militia against the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, including the heinous attacks targeting King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh... which constitute a blatant violation of international law.”
The countries described the attacks as a “dangerous escalation” posing a direct threat to Saudi Arabia’s security and stability, as well as civilian safety.

The countries called for an “immediate and unconditional” end to the attacks.
The death toll from the Oct. 10 Houthi attack on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh rose to 13 after an injured Indian national died Oct. 11. The attack also left 309 people injured, according to Saudi authorities.
Türkiye and Pakistan agreed on Oct. 5 to activate collective deterrence measures under a mutual defense pact with Saudi Arabia and rapidly deploy military forces and capabilities to the kingdom.
The decision was announced after the three countries’ defense and foreign ministers held an emergency meeting in Riyadh. It marked the first time the alliance, known as the Mecca pact, has been invoked since it was signed Aug. 7.
The accord stipulates that an attack on any of the three countries will be treated as an attack on all three, echoing a central provision of NATO’s founding treaty.
The alliance emerged amid escalating regional tensions following the outbreak of war between the United States, Israel and Iran.

Countries warn against travel to Saudi Arabia following Houthi attacks
US, Australia, Canada, Japan, South Korea and New Zealand among countries urging citizens to avoid travel to Kingdom.
Several countries have warned their citizens against travel to Saudi Arabia following a series of Houthi attacks on airports in the kingdom.
On Monday, Australia and New Zealand became the latest to issue advisories against travelling to the kingdom, following similar warnings from the United States, Canada, the UK, South Korea, and Japan.
Australia’s Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade said Australians should avoid King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh and “reconsider” travel to other Saudi airports.
New Zealand’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade urged citizens not to travel to the Saudi capital’s main gateway and the provinces of Najran, Jazan and Asir for any reason, and to avoid “non-essential” travel to Saudi Arabia as a whole.
The US embassy in Riyadh on Sunday advised US citizens to reconsider travel to the kingdom, citing the threat of attacks by Iran and the Iranian-backed Houthis.
Global Affairs Canada issued an advisory against non-essential travel to any part of Saudi Arabia.
South Korea’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs recommended that its citizens in Saudi Arabia leave unless they are on essential business and advised anyone planning to travel to the kingdom to cancel their trip.
The UK’s Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office urged citizens to avoid travel to Jeddah and Dammam, and to all airports apart from Medina International Airport, except for essential reasons.
The warnings come as Saudi Arabia reels from five attacks on its airports in less than a week.
One person was killed and 11 others were injured on Sunday when a projectile struck King Khalid International Airport, according to Saudi Arabia’s General Authority of Civil Aviation (GACA).
A Houthi strike on the same airport on Saturday killed 13 people and injured more than 300 others, marking the deadliest attack on Saudi Arabia in more than a decade.
The Houthis claimed responsibility for all four strikes on Saudi airports before Sunday’s attack, which has yet to be claimed by any group.
King Khalid international airport and King Fahd international airport in Dammam remain closed following the attacks, causing significant disruption to aviation across the Middle East.
The attacks have also disrupted flights to and from King Abdulaziz International Airport in Jeddah.
More than 150 flights were cancelled and 374 flights were delayed at the Jeddah airport on Sunday, according to the flight tracking website Flightradar24.
Brendan Sobie, an independent analyst and consultant in Singapore, said it was too early to predict the ramifications of the attacks for aviation across the region and beyond.
“As has been the case with the Iran war and the impact from that crisis on the UAE, Kuwait and Bahrain, the impact of this latest crisis really depends on how long it lasts, how long Riyadh airport remains closed, and how long and to what extent are the restrictions once it reopens,” Sobie told Al Jazeera.

World Insights: U.S. sanctions relief on Russian diesel unlikely to cool fuel prices
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
13:52:04 CST
14:52:04 KST

by Ben Xie
NEW YORK, Oct. 11 (Xinhua) -- The United States on Friday temporarily lifted sanctions on Russia's export of diesel in a bid to ease a global fuel shortage and curb soaring domestic prices, but analysts warn that limited supplies and damage to Russian refineries could possibly blunt the impact.
U.S. President Donald Trump said on Friday that he had struck a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin during a phone call. On the same day, the U.S. Treasury Department's Office of Foreign Assets Control issued a temporary general license, authorizing Russian diesel transactions until April 7, 2027.
Under the phased schedule, Russia would deliver 2.25 million barrels in October, 3.75 million in November and 7.5 million "immediately thereafter," depending on the condition of Russian refineries. Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak confirmed the volumes.
U.S. diesel averaged 6.28 dollars a gallon on Friday, according to the American Automobile Association, down from a record 6.53 dollars on Sept. 22, but still far above 3.68 dollars a year earlier, and up about 70 percent since the U.S.-Israel war with Iran began on Feb. 28.
A Pew Research Center survey released Oct. 8 found that 74 percent of Americans were "very concerned" about energy prices, and 84 percent of registered voters said the economy was "very important" to their vote in the Nov. 3 mid-term elections.
On Saturday, the Russian government partially lifted its diesel export ban with immediate effect, allowing 500,000 tons to reach the global market, with Novak saying domestic supplies would not be affected.
However, analysts said that the U.S. relief on sanctions on Russian diesel is unlikely to help tame domestic diesel prices, which hover at close to record-high levels and threaten Republican control of Congress in the upcoming elections.
The International Energy Agency (IEA) says the world is short about 1.6 million barrels of diesel daily. Even if all 36 million barrels Russia promised arrived at once, they would plug the gap for only about three weeks.
The October release alone is roughly 10 percent of what Russia exported in a typical month before Ukrainian drone strikes battered its refineries, according to analysts.
"It's kind of shuffling deck chairs on the Titanic," a report by The Seattle Times quoted Michael Lynch of the Energy Policy Research Foundation as saying. Russian diesel sent to the United States simply means that other buyers must look elsewhere. At best, he said, Americans might see "a tiny dip in prices locally in places like the New York-New Jersey area."
"It's clearly not a fix, but another stream to aid a very tight diesel market," Jim Mitchell, director of oil trading analytics at consultancy Wood Mackenzie, was quoted as saying by Reuters.
"The biggest concern is the refiners being able to do it," Ryan McKay, senior commodity strategist at TD Securities, a Canadian multinational investment bank and financial services provider, was quoted as saying by the Business Times.
The November shipment amounts to roughly one day of U.S. consumption, noted Chris Kennedy, lead for Economic Statecraft at Bloomberg Economics. He questioned whether Moscow can deliver given refinery damage, logistics and legal hurdles, with the largest later tranches explicitly conditioned on the state of Russia's refineries.
To make matters worse, Hurricane Isaias in the Gulf of Mexico has now shut down about 1.3 million barrels a day of U.S. oil production, which equals nearly 63 percent of total U.S. production in the gulf.
The Iran war also continues to disrupt flows through the Strait of Hormuz, which carried about 20 percent of global oil and fuel shipments before the war.
As part of an accelerated IEA emergency-stock release, Germany will release up to 15 million barrels of diesel, heating oil and crude, while France has committed 10 million barrels of diesel. Moreover, Italy says it has completed its 10 million-barrel commitment.
The Russian barrels address the shortage from the output side, while the stock releases address it from the inventory side. However, analysts say neither is large enough to repair the market on its own.
Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis for GasBuddy, predicted that the deal could result in a short-term reduction of 10 to 20 cents for a gallon of diesel. However, he said, it would be "difficult to achieve" Trump's import goals. ■

====================================================================================================

Feature: Retracing the Long March: An Australian publisher's decades-long quest to understand China
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
13:52:01 CST
14:52:01 KST

by Xinhua writer Xiong Wenyuan
MELBOURNE, Oct. 12 (Xinhua) -- The Long March offers a key to understanding modern China, Australian publisher Harold Weldon has said, drawing on two journeys along the route and four decades of engagement with the country.
In a recent interview with Xinhua in Melbourne, Weldon compared the Long March, whose victory marks its 90th anniversary this year, to the spine of a body, saying it "goes right through the modern history of China."
Weldon, a writer and filmmaker who is also the founder and principal of Harold Weldon Advisory, first retraced the route in 1985, aged 19, and returned for the second journey in 2011.
A "WALKING UNIVERSITY"
His interest began at school. At 16, while studying Asian history, he read Edgar Snow's "Red Star Over China" and was drawn to its account of the Long March.
His father, also inspired by the book, later brought together international photographers to document China along the Long March route. Weldon had secured a university place, but his father encouraged him to join the family publishing company, describing the project as a "walking university."
Carrying Snow's book, Weldon joined a reconnaissance team that traveled by train and road and walked where vehicles could not go. On some stretches, donkeys carried their packs. He still keeps his diaries from the journey, with Polaroid photographs and pressed flowers.
At Jiaopingdu, a crossing on the Jinsha River, he met three surviving boatmen who had ferried the Red Army across. The elderly men came alive as they retold their stories.
On the climb back, Weldon ran out of water and became dizzy and exhausted. A girl of about 10 fetched her grandmother, who helped him rest in the shade of a mud-brick shelter and gave him spring water in a hollowed-out gourd.
The girl continued walking with him and, at one point, took his hand on the steep, narrow path.
"I've never forgotten her," he said. The demanding route he had walked just once was the children's daily journey to and from school.
ENDURANCE AND ADAPTABILITY
Weldon said his own hardships -- terrain, weather and fatigue -- had deepened his appreciation of what the Red Army endured while also facing pursuit and encirclement.
He believes the army's trials equipped it for later challenges. "Usually you say triumph over adversity, I say through adversity," he said.
Returning in 2011 also allowed him to revisit people and places from his first journey.
He recalled dozens of children crowding into the team's small room in Sichuan's grasslands in 1985 to sing simple songs. More than two decades later, Chinese colleagues tracked down one of those children, who was then working in the local tax bureau and helped locate the rest.
Weldon was reunited with eight of the former schoolchildren. He recalled crying when they met again.
He also recalled driving through unfinished tunnels in Sichuan in 2011, with only the headlights lighting the way. On a more recent visit, he saw elevated highways and tunnels threading through the gorges.
"Again, China just keeps going," he said.
For Weldon, adaptability connects the historical Long March with present-day development. The Red Army had to adjust to different environments and build relationships with local communities; the Communist Party of China must likewise respond to diverse regional conditions today.
Adaptability, he added, must go together with a clear purpose and a plan.
UNDERSTANDING CHINA THROUGH ITS PEOPLE
To introduce the Long March to overseas audiences, Weldon begins with human endurance, mutual support and perseverance. For Australian readers, he draws parallels with the spirit of the Australian and New Zealand Army Corps, emphasizing endurance and comradeship.
He then connects those qualities with the places where the Long March unfolded, helping readers move from a story of human endurance to an understanding of the Chinese revolution.
"And then they learn it's not a myth -- it actually happened," he said.
He called for "bridge builders" who could tell Chinese stories in ways that Western audiences would be open to hearing, while remaining faithful to those stories. The same, he said, applied to presenting Australian stories to Chinese audiences.
His own connections reach back to that first journey. The interpreter who accompanied him in 1985 still works with him between Australia and China, he said.
Weldon encouraged Australians to visit Chinese villages and meet local people to better understand the country.
"You need to connect on a human level," he said, warning against preconceived ideas about a country one knows little about.
Reflecting on his continuing engagement with China, he said: "Every morning there is a horizon. You have to keep going."
Weldon hopes to retrace the full Long March route for the third time.
He still thinks about the girl who held his hand on the path above the Jinsha River. He holds onto a few photographs from the journey and looks forward to a possible reunion with her one day. ■

Delhi police have again obstructed protests in India’s capital as thousands of people returned to the streets, led by opposition leaders, to demand the resignation of the election commissioner.
After mass unrest in the capital over the weekend, when thousands were detained and harassed by police as they attempted to take part in a protest led by the gen Z Cockroach movement, on Monday the main opposition leaders led another procession through Delhi, this time to the supreme court.
The leader of India’s opposition alliance, Rahul Gandhi, alongside other opposition figures and student groups, had declared their intention to march to the court and submit a petition calling for India’s chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, to step down.
Kumar has become a deeply controversial figure for his role in an exercise to verify and “purify” India’s electoral rolls, which has led to more than 130m names – more than the population of Japan – being deleted from voter lists since last year.
Opposition parties and civil society groups allege Kumar implemented this special intensive revision (SIR) to help entrench the power of Narendra Modi’s government and his Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata party (BJP). Muslim voters and other minorities who are traditionally not BJP voters have allegedly been disproportionately affected by the deletions.
The election commission has denied favouring any party and said wrongly deleted voters could re-enrol, while the BJP has accused its rivals of trying to undermine democracy by questioning legitimate electoral processes.
Several metro stations were closed on Monday in central Delhi and police barricades prevented thousands of protesters getting within 600m of the supreme court, forcing them to turn back.
However, lawyers confirmed they had submitted the petition on Gandhi’s behalf and by late evening, Gandhi had broken through the barricades and reached the court gates.
In a press conference before the march, Gandhi reiterated his allegation that the Modi government was using the commission to commit “vote chori” (cheating) and accused Kumar of being a “thief”.
Gandhi expressed support for the mass uprising of young people, led by the Cockroach Janta party (CJP) and student groups, who had tried to protest over the weekend but were met with police brutality and mass detentions.
“Till the constitution is upheld, till the chief election commissioner is removed, till the system of elections is revamped, till justice is served for India, the youth won’t stop,” he said.
The SIR and calls for Kumar’s resignation have galvanised support for beleaguered opposition parties, who are seen to have flailed in the face of the BJP’s electoral power. Gandhi was detained twice last week after the police refused to let him and other opposition leaders reach Jantar Mantar, the designated protest site in central Delhi.
Mahua Moitra, an opposition MP who was marching after being detained last week, alleged that in her constituency in West Bengal more than 10,000 voters had been unjustly removed from the electoral rolls.
“There’s no going back now. People know that their votes have been stolen and this government is finished,” Moitra said. “The police can detain us, they can use brute force and crack our skulls, but we are not going to get off the streets until Gyanesh Kumar resigns and this government is gone. If we don’t stand up to this, then there will be nothing left of our country.”
Moitra accused the supreme court of helping to validate the SIR process and disenfranchise millions of Indians. “When the history of this dark chapter of India is written, the supreme court will be the most disgraced,” she said. “It was the supreme court who put a stamp of approval on every illegality of this government.”
Gandhi has spent months accusing the BJP of fraudulently influencing elections, but his claims have been largely ignored. The issue exploded last month after the Indian Express newspaper reported multiple irregularities in the SIR process that had been pushed through by Kumar.
The protests are likely to continue this week. On Monday, leaders of the CJP approached the Delhi police to seek a date to be allowed to hold a protest without obstruction. They said that if the police refused to comply, their supporters would take to the streets again.

2026-10-12
13:51:19 CST
14:51:19 KST

HONG KONG/SHENZHEN, Oct. 12 (Xinhua) -- The redeveloped Huanggang Port opened at 6:30 a.m. local time on Monday, streamlining cross-border passenger travel between China's Shenzhen and Hong Kong Special Administrative Region.
The redeveloped port is positioned as the most important 24-hour passenger land boundary control point between Hong Kong and Shenzhen. It operates under a co-location arrangement with a new "collaborative inspection and joint clearance" mode, allowing travelers to complete both Hong Kong and Shenzhen immigration clearance in a single queue.
Under this new clearance mode, clearance time will be significantly reduced from around 30 minutes at the original Lok Ma Chau/Huanggang Port to approximately five minutes.
The design flow of the redeveloped port is 200,000 passenger trips per day, and could be further increased to about 300,000 upon the future commissioning of the Northern Link Spur Line of Hong Kong's MTR Corporation Limited.
The port has 134 "collaborative inspection" automated channels and 68 traditional manual counters set up side by side. In addition to the automated channels, travelers can also clear customs using the manual counters.
"It is very convenient and extremely fast," Ms. Wong, a traveler heading from Hong Kong to Shenzhen via Huanggang Port, said, adding that crossing the border previously required taking a shuttle bus, which was very time-consuming, but the new co-location arrangement has significantly improved efficiency.
"Officers from both sides work in the same area, allowing travelers to complete clearance procedures for both Hong Kong and Shenzhen in one go, which is highly efficient," Mr. Chen, a tourist visiting Hong Kong from Shenzhen, said.
The original Huanggang Port, which opened in 1989, was China's first large-scale land port with 24-hour clearance. It has served hundreds of millions of travelers, with daily passenger traffic peaking at over 60,000 and daily vehicle traffic reaching around 10,000.
Reconstruction on the original site began in 2019 to meet the surging demand for cross-border passage. ■

Eleven people were killed when a truck carrying timber collided with a tour bus near toll booths in the western province of Manisa on Oct. 11, authorities said.

Highway camera footage showed the bus reversing near the junction when the truck struck it from behind.

Medical, fire, disaster response and gendarmerie teams were dispatched to the scene. Rescue crews helped the injured, who were taken by ambulance to nearby hospitals.

Justice Minister Akın Gürlek said three prosecutors had been assigned to investigate the crash.
