Roti Jala: a golden net of Malaysian culture on Tehran’s guest table
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
04:14:59 UTC
13:14:59 KST

Roti Jala: a golden net of Malaysian culture on Tehran’s guest table
TEHRAN — The Embassy of Malaysia in Tehran on Sunday, October 11, hosted a warm and colorful gathering in which the aroma of Malay spices and hospitality, leaving a lasting memory of friendship between two cultures.
The event brought together foreign diplomats, officials from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Iran, Iranian graduates of Malaysian universities, and alumni of the Malaysian Technical Cooperation Program (MTCP). At its heart was one of Malaysia’s most beloved culinary treasures: roti jala.
At the beginning of the ceremony, Dato’ Wan Aznainizam Yusri bin Wan Abdul Rashid, Chargé d’Affaires and Head of Mission at the Embassy of Malaysia, delivered this speech:
“Distinguished guests,
Officials from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the Islamic Republic of Iran as well as other agencies, fellow diplomats, dear friends of Malaysia,
Ladies and gentlemen, good afternoon, and a very warm welcome — khosh amadeh — to the Embassy of Malaysia.
Thank you all for taking the time to join us today. Your presence reflects the strong bonds of friendship and cooperation that our nations, and indeed our diplomatic communities, continue to enjoy.
Today’s gathering serves a wonderful dual purpose. First and foremost, it is my distinct pleasure to officially introduce the Embassy’s new Head of Chancery, Mr. Muhammad Shahiran. Shahiran joined our team in Tehran a couple of weeks ago with a wealth of experience, having been posted previously in Turkmenistan and Peru. I know he is eager to get to know all of you, and I am confident he will find the same warmth, kindness, and cooperation from the officials here, the diplomatic community, as well as the Friends of Malaysia in Iran that I have enjoyed since my arrival last August. Please join me in welcoming him to his new home in Iran!
Mr. Muhammad Shahiran
Our second objective today is to share a piece of Malaysian culture with you through one of our greatest passions: our food.
The great Persian poet Rumi once beautifully captured the magic of gathering around food to feed the soul:
‘Sof-reh bee-aa-reed o fo-rood aa-va-reed’
‘Peesh ka-shee-dash keh kam lar-zand mo-reed’
‘Bring out the table spread, set it down, and bring the food,
For the lovers must be fed.’
Malaysia is known globally as a food paradise, where our diverse culture is reflected directly on our plates. Today, as part of our ongoing cultural diplomacy and efforts to promote Malaysia’s rich heritage, our Home-Based Staff have put together a special culinary showcase. Shortly, you will witness a live cooking demonstration of Roti Jala — which translates to ‘Net Bread’ due to its intricate, lace-like design. This traditional favourite is paired perfectly with our classic chicken and beef curries, rich with aromatic spices that I believe will resonate deeply with the sophisticated palates of our Iranian friends.
I would not want to take much of the time to bore you with my long speech. Let’s skip the formalities today. Enjoy the cooking demonstration, eat heartily, and let the food do what it does best — bring us closer together.
Thank you all very much, and kheyli mamnoon.”
After the speech, embassy staff demonstrated the art of making roti jala with skill and delicacy: a thin batter poured through a special funnel into fine, lace-like webs on the pan, turning in moments into golden, netted bread. Guests were also given the chance to try their own hand at it, shaping the batter and joyfully eating what they had made. A tahari — a spread of diverse Malaysian dishes — was then served, from aromatic curries to beloved Malay favorites, transforming the embassy into a small corner of Kuala Lumpur. Guests mingled, chatted, and deepened their friendships in the warm atmosphere.
And it was the incomparable hospitality of Dato’ Wan Aznainizam Yusri bin Wan Abdul Rashid and the Malaysian embassy team that made the pleasure of this gathering doubly memorable — a warmth felt from the very first moment and lingering, like the scent of Malay spices, long after the last bite. Roti Jala today was not merely a bread; it was a net that wove cultures together and proved that food is the most eloquent language of friendship among nations.

US Drops Sanctions on Daughter of Prominent Myanmar Businessman Thein Win Zaw
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
04:07:00 UTC
13:07:00 KST

The U.S. government has lifted sanctions on the daughter of a Myanmar businessman accused of supporting the country’s military, after she filed two lawsuits seeking her removal from the Treasury Department’s Specially Designated Nationals List (SDN List).
According to a Reuters report, Theint Win Htet’s name was removed from the website of the Department’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) on Friday. OFAC confirmed the deletion of her name from the SDN List in a statement the following day.
Theint Win Htet was added to the SDN List in January 2024 alongside her father Thein Win Zaw and his Shwe Byain Phyu Group of Companies. The Treasury Department said at the time that the company “has developed a historic relationship with Burma’s military to import and distribute petroleum,” including on behalf of Myanma Economic Holdings Public Company Limited (MEHL), a sanctioned military-linked conglomerate with tentacles in numerous sectors of Myanmar’s economy.
The listing announcement also stated that Thein Win Zaw has “provided fuel to Burma’s navy while using his companies to import petroleum and share profits with MEHL” and that he and his family members “own at least 20 companies in various sectors of the Burmese economy and are also closely associated with the regime.”
The following May, Theint Win Htet filed a lawsuit seeking her removal from the SDN List, claiming that President Joe Biden exceeded his authority under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act by listing the adult children of a designated individual. She also said that it had breached due process by not permitting her to contest her inclusion on the SDN List. Her case was dismissed in February 2025.
Theint Win Htet then filed a new complaint in July of this year, arguing that she has no active role in her father’s business affairs and that the sanctions had interrupted her studies in the United States. In the complaint, Reuters reported, Thein Win Htet stated that her “U.S. credit cards have been blocked, her foreign bank accounts have been restricted, closed, or refused, and she has been unable to complete her university studies.”
Her removal from the SDN List comes after the news agency reported that the U.S. had engaged in direct talks with the military-backed government for the first time since the February 2021 coup. According to the report, U.S. Assistant Secretary of State for Intelligence and Research Michael Vance “joined talks” with coup leader-turned-president Min Aung Hlaing in Naypyidaw on September 15-16. Numerous sources told Reuters that the talks were aimed at securing the release of detained American businessman Adam Castillo, but “also provided an opening for further engagement.”
Whether the removal of Theint Win Htet’s name is related to a possible broader diplomatic thaw remains unclear. A State Department spokesperson contacted by Reuters did not offer much explanation for the move, simply saying that the decision “reflects the administration’s determination that this designation no longer effectively supports U.S. policy objectives related to Burma.”
This is also not the first time since the coup that the name of a Myanmar individual or entity has been scrubbed from the SDN List. In July 2025, the U.S. government lifted sanctions on three Myanmar companies and a number of individuals linked to them, including KT Services & Logistics and its founder, Jonathan Myo Kyaw Thaung, who were sanctioned in 2022 for leasing Yangon’s port from MEHL. Also included on the list was Thein Win Htet’s mother Tin Latt Min.
As with last week’s announcement, OFAC did not offer a reason for the deletions, although The Irrawaddy noted that the move came after Min Aung Hlaing praised President Donald Trump in a letter responding to his threat of tariffs, in which he also commended him for shutting down U.S.-funded media outlets covering the country’s conflict. Trump administration officials said that there was “no connection between these decisions and the letter.”
Getting one’s name off the SDN List is hard even at the best of times, usually requiring the enlistment of one of a handful of specialist white shoe law firms. (Theint Win Htet was represented by Erich Ferrari, a prominent Washington-based lawyer who specializes in “economic sanctions, export controls, regulatory licensing, federal investigations, and prosecutions.”)
While the addition or removal of names from the SDN List is guided in part by legal criteria, OFAC’s decisions are often influenced by the broader policymaking climate. It is therefore plausible that a turn toward engagement with Myanmar would be accompanied by a loosening of U.S. sanctions on the country.
Whether or not this is the case here, any further shortening of the SDN List would suggest that the first steps toward engagement are evolving into a more substantial rapprochement.

India’s agri-seed sector accounts for the largest share of receipts under benefit sharing regulations during April-Sept
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
04:04:52 UTC
13:04:52 KST

ABS mechanism goes beyond monetary collection by linking the utilisation of biological resources with biodiversity conservation,
NEW DELHI: India’s agri-seed sector accounted for the largest share of receipts from users of the country’s biological resources during April-Sept period this financial year under the Access and Benefit Sharing (ABS) regulation -- a statutory mechanism which ensures that when local genetic resources create commercial value, a fair share flows back to states and communities to sustain that diversity.Though the amount of little over Rs 7 crore for the sector during that six-month period is not much, the receipts, at least, reflect working of the ABS mechanism in generating money by getting payment for utilisation of a diverse range of biological resources across agriculture sector.The other sectors that generate receipts include food, pharmaceuticals, biotechnology, medicinal plants, microorganisms and livestock. A total of around Rs 9.6 crore was received by the National Biodiversity Authority (NBA) towards access to biological resources from users in various sectors during the period.Contributions were received by the NBA from both domestic and international entities, including companies from Sri Lanka, Germany, France, the Republic of Korea and Bhutan.Union environment ministry’s records show that the NBA has realised around Rs 278 crore through ABS and disbursed more than Rs 200 crore towards biodiversity conservation and benefits for communities, farmers, institutions and other benefit claimers across the country since 2008.
The Authority, a statutory body under the Biological Diversity Act, 2002, regulates access to India's biological resources and associated knowledge and implements the Nagoya Protocol’s (a global convention) principle of fair and equitable sharing of benefits.Biological resources, used by different entities for developing seeds, include livestock genetic resources such as Mithun, Jersey cattle and frozen semen of Murrah buffalo, as well as Red Sanders wood sourced from cultivated sources and auctioned material. The range further includes agricultural crops such as chickpea, red lentil, green moong, horse gram, flaxseed, guar gum, tapioca, buckwheat, brown rice, cauliflower, okra, hot pepper, brinjal and ridge gourd.The biological resources also include medicinal plants such as Ashwagandha, Shatavari, Kalmegh, Vasaka, Licorice, Arjuna, Bacopa, Gotukola and Moringa, as well as soil microorganisms including Azospirillum, Azotobacter, Bacillus, Rhizobium, Trichoderma and Metarhizium.The ABS mechanism goes beyond monetary collection by linking the utilisation of biological resources with biodiversity conservation, sustainable use and equitable sharing of benefits.“Funds disbursed through the State Biodiversity Boards and Union Territory Biodiversity Councils support conservation of biological resources, preparation and updation of People's Biodiversity Registers, strengthening of Biodiversity Management Committees, biodiversity research and documentation, and benefits to local communities and other benefit claimers,” said the Union environment ministry on working of the mechanism and utilisation of the collected money.ABS-funded activities can complement relevant govt schemes and programmes, particularly those promoting tribal welfare, sustainable livelihoods and natural-resource-based enterprises, such as the Pradhan Mantri Janjati Adivasi Nyaya Maha Abhiyan (PM-JANMAN), Pradhan Mantri Janjatiya Vikas Mission and Pradhan Mantri Van Dhan Yojana.“Such convergence can strengthen community-led conservation, sustainable utilisation of biological resources and livelihood opportunities, while leveraging existing institutional mechanisms,” said the ministry in a statement.India’s ABS framework supports Target 13 of the Kunming–Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework on the fair and equitable sharing of benefits arising from the utilisation of genetic resources and associated traditional knowledge, as well as Target 19 on resource mobilisation. The framework also contributes to relevant Sustainable Development Goals, including SDG 2 (Zero Hunger), SDG 8 (Decent Work and Economic Growth), SDG 12 (Responsible Consumption and Production), SDG 15 (Life on Land) and SDG 17 (Partnerships for the Goals), through biodiversity conservation, sustainable resource use, livelihood support and institutional collaboration.
“As India prepares to participate in the seventeenth meeting of the Conference of the Parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity (COP 17), commencing on 19 October 2026 in Yerevan, Armenia, its ABS framework demonstrates the country’s continued commitment to biodiversity conservation, the sustainable use of biological resources and the fair and equitable sharing of benefits arising from their utilisation,” said the ministry.

Before switching over to explore sustainable development issues, Vishwa had covered internal security and investigative agencies for more than a decade.

MOSCOW, October 12. /TASS/. In 2026, Ukraine will repay $4.86 billion in a total debt to its foreign creditors, calculations by TASS based on data from Ukraine’s Finance Ministry showed.
Principal debt repayments will amount to €490 million ($550 million), $600 million and 1.26 billion in IMF Special Drawing Rights (XDR) ($1.7 billion, bringing the total to $2.41 billion. According to calculations by TASS, every Ukrainian citizen owes his country $8,622, given the nation has a population of 25 million and a public debt of $215.55 billion. If calculations are based on a population of 22 million, the national debt amounts to nearly $9,800 per person. While there are no accurate population numbers for Ukraine, the country’s Social Policy Minister Denis Ulyutin earlier mentioned population figures of between 22 million and 25 million.

Bunkers and Arks: Escaping the Future We Built Ourselves
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
04:00:00 UTC
13:00:00 KST

Inverting the conventional narrative, this story begins at the end. The day after the world's collapse. While almost the entire population struggles to survive flames and solar storms, a tiny fraction is greeted by a heavily armed guard at the entrance to the Survival Condo Project, a former missile silo in Kansas converted a few years ago into luxury apartments.
Forget, then, the hermit who stockpiles canned food in his basement or the end-times prophet. In recent years, survivalism has expanded into wealthier circles, taking root in Silicon Valley among technology executives and hedge fund managers. What could once be seen merely as an eccentricity has also become a way of thinking about the future and, for some, an investment.
The apocalypse is an idea we have grown accustomed to living with: as prophecy, literary genre, and business opportunity. It is not a static idea, but a construction that evolves with our anxieties, flourishing especially in moments of political insecurity or rapid technological change. Perhaps this helps explain the millions of dollars currently invested in structures designed to enable human survival.
Related Article
Architecture to Postpone the End of the World
But what, in all of this, is paranoia, and what is true? In The Rise of End Times Fascism, Naomi Klein and Astra Taylor identify three important factors accelerating the post-apocalyptic appeal of the end of the world. The first is the climate crisis. Although many people deny it, global elites living in beachfront properties are extremely vulnerable to rising sea levels and are well aware of the dangers of global warming. The second is Covid-19: the arrival of a global epidemic reinforced epidemiological predictions that a pandemic could indeed devastate our world. The third and final factor is the rapid advancement and adoption of AI, heading toward a path beyond our control.
According to the authors, none of this should be dismissed as paranoia. After all, many of us also feel the imminence of collapse, even if from the safety of our sofas, entertained by versions of life in a post-apocalyptic bunker, such as Silo, the hit series on Apple TV+. Perhaps also because we cannot afford to buy our own bunker. But how many of us would succumb to the idea of escaping global collapse into a private bunker?
In the book Notes from an Apocalypse, Mark O'Connell (2020) visits bunkers in South Dakota, refuges in New Zealand, and the Mars project in an attempt to understand why this idea flourished precisely in Silicon Valley, a place known for its unwavering confidence in its ability to change the world for the better. The author suggests that digital-media billionaires seem particularly fascinated by an impending apocalypse and by extravagant strategies for surviving it. Perhaps it is because their exorbitant fortunes give them obsessive dreams of immortality, or because they understand the darker implications of the monsters they have created. Technology brings with it the ability to imagine radically different futures, where utopia and dystopia coexist.
These escapist ideas, although they may seem benign at first glance, are permeated by assumptions about which parts of humanity deserve to be saved. They also share a remarkable lack of interest in urgently addressing the underlying causes of collapse. Douglas Rushkoff wrote the book Survival of the Richest in 2022, after giving a lecture to billionaires, where they asked him how to maintain authority over their guards after "the Event," when money would lose its value. He describes the idea of bunkers and arks as a naive and deeply antisocial response from those who prefer to optimize their bunkers rather than contribute to preventing the apocalypse.
Without making generalizations, it is important to note that a large portion of this population understands that the only real solution is to address the problems. Therefore, most donate significant amounts of money to good causes while also investing in their own escape plan. An architecture that is gaining ground in the luxury real estate market.
The place mentioned at the beginning of the article may seem as though it came straight out of a science-fiction novel, but it is real. Journalist Evan Osnos describes his visit to the Survival Condo Project in his article Doomsday Prep for the Super-Rich. As a former underground missile silo, the concrete structure housed a nuclear warhead between 1961 and 1965, when it was decommissioned. Built by the Army Corps of Engineers to withstand a nuclear attack, the complex has 15 floors, with enough food and fuel to survive five years off-grid. By raising tilapia in tanks and growing vegetables hydroponically under grow lights, powered by renewable energy, the site could operate indefinitely, CEO Larry Hall claims.
Osnos describes the private units as windowless ski apartments, with stainless-steel appliances and leather sofas. According to Hall, the most difficult part of the project is maintaining life underground while avoiding depression. To achieve this, the walls of the apartments are equipped with LED "windows" displaying live video of the prairie above the silo. Osnos reports that owners can choose forests or other views. One prospective resident from New York wanted a video of Central Park, day and night, complete with the sound of taxis and horns.
Another example that seems to have come straight from a science-fiction book is Vivos xPoint in South Dakota. It is part of a global network of underground shelters with units in the United States and Europe. The South Dakota site was developed from a former set of underground shelters built by the U.S. Army during World War II to store ammunition. It has 575 private reinforced-concrete bunkers, each measuring 205 m2, capable of accommodating more than 5,000 people, and is self-proclaimed as the largest survival community on Earth.
For those who are more claustrophobic, however, one option involves staying away from major centers of power. In this case, remote places such as New Zealand and Hawaii have been on the radar. New Zealanders used to speak of the "tyranny of distance," but now it has become their greatest asset. Requests for immigration permits from Americans have increased significantly in recent years, with Peter Thiel, co-founder of PayPal, as its most enthusiastic advocate.
There are also those who want to go even farther, seeing the Milky Way as an escape route, such as billionaire Elon Musk and the idea of space colonization as salvation for humanity. By viewing Mars as a "secular ark" essential to human survival, the illusion is also fostered that we can destroy Earth and still be fine.
From an architectural perspective, it is interesting to note that most of the structures being built emerged from the adaptive reuse of military equipment. Beatriz Colomina, in her book Domesticity at War (2007), states that "war does not end, but evolves, and so does architecture."When analyzing the Cold War era in the United States, she discusses how military technologies were incorporated into domestic environments as part of a new awareness of global geopolitics, which required the normalization (or domestication) of social conditions that would otherwise be frightening. Are we moving toward the normalization of living in bunkers and other structures originally designed for war?
From a broader perspective, the idea of the bunker goes far beyond the private refuge of the wealthy; it appears to be a global project. The bunker nation closes its borders to the world while violently claiming the land and resources it considers necessary to withstand the coming collapse.
Faced with a context that emphasizes individualism and class supremacy, trying to understand how we, as humanity, should respond to the imminence of global collapse may seem utopian if it were not necessary. Between accepting the end of the world as inevitable and striving to postpone it, Krenak advises the latter, drawing inspiration from Indigenous peoples who have resisted the end of their worlds for more than 500 years.
Bunkers, arks, and space colonies are responses produced by the same mindset that brought us here. Postponing the end of the world means, instead, addressing the causes that bring us closer to it, changing our relationship with the Earth, reconsidering the idea of unlimited growth, and recognizing that our survival depends on the life we share. It is not about finding a place to escape the future, but about changing the future we are building.
This article is part of the ArchDaily Topic: The Lure of Escapism in Architecture and Alternative Worlds. Every month we explore a topic in-depth through articles, interviews, news, and architecture projects. We invite you to learn more about our ArchDaily Topics. And, as always, at ArchDaily we welcome the contributions of our readers; if you want to submit an article or project, contact us.

Trump’s Targeting of Indian IT Firms Hits India-US Ties Again
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
03:51:00 UTC
12:51:00 KST

Ties between India and the United States hit another bump last week with the Trump administration freezing green card requests from eight technology firms, including those from India.
U.S. Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling announced on October 8 that Cognizant, Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services, Wipro, HCL Technologies, Capgemini, Microsoft, and Adobe have been suspended from participating in the Permanent Labor Certification (PERM), a program that is largely used by technology companies and outsourcing firms to sponsor a foreign worker’s permanent residency in the U.S. “We will not accept any new or process any pending permanent labor certification applications involving these companies,” Sonderling said.
The announcement came weeks before U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s visit to New Delhi.
Indian IT companies appear largely unperturbed by the U.S. policy change. Infosys, India’s second-largest IT firm, said it did not anticipate a material impact from the PERM application suspension. The National Association of Software and Service Companies (NASSCOM), India’s IT industry body, said that Indian companies had significantly reduced their dependence on H-1B visas in recent years and had expanded their local hiring in the U.S. Relatively few workers move from H-1B visas to permanent residency through PERM, it said.
Ajay Srivastava, who heads the Global Trade Research Initiative, a New Delhi-based trade and commerce think tank, said the U.S. move was a “warning for India’s IT industry.” “It covers four leading Indian IT firms and disrupts the permanent-residency plans of their employees, making long-term staffing in the U.S. more uncertain,” Srivastava told The Diplomat.
“The larger concern is India’s dependence on a market that accounts for 54.1 percent of its software and IT-enabled services exports. The measure signals a more protectionist U.S. approach to foreign technology workers. India should prepare for possible restrictions extending beyond green card sponsorship,” he said, adding that Indian firms should widen their export markets to reduce their vulnerability to sudden U.S. policy changes.
India’s software services exports to the U.S. fetched $221.4 billion in revenues in 2025-26, an 8.2 percent year-on-year increase.
Adding salt to injury was a comment by Vice President J.D. Vance. Speaking to reporters after Sonderling’s announcement, Vance said: “Our message to Microsoft is you’re a great American company, but you’ve got to hire great American workers. You cannot lay off American workers and then replace them with foreign indentured servants.”
In a sharply worded statement, India’s Ministry of External Affairs said that “talent mobility adds value to both economies.” The measures announced by the United States “do not advance the shared ambitions of both countries.” Recalling that the U.S. was a country built by immigrants, the statement said that “resorting to terminology that carries painful historical and colonial legacy connotations is deeply offensive.” The allusion was to India’s British colonial rulers transporting more than a million Indians to work as contract labor in British colonies abroad after the abolition of slavery by the British in 1833.
There is speculation in India that the U.S. policy change on green card requests is aimed at showing President Donald Trump’s domestic audience that his administration is tough on immigration. The U.S. will vote in mid-term elections in November. Voters are reportedly unhappy with the Trump administration’s performance, especially on the handling of the economy, with job numbers falling short of expectations.
Last week’s restrictions on Indian IT companies, together with Vance’s comments, have added to the chill in India-U.S. relations, especially since Trump returned to the White House in January 2025.
A trade pact negotiated between the two sides remains unsigned despite many rounds of talks. Washington’s courting of Pakistan, which India sees as instigating terrorism against it, has not gone down well in Delhi.
Speaking at the Asia Society in New York in September, India’s Minister for External Affairs S. Jaishankar highlighted the U.S. anti-immigration push affecting the movement of Indian workers to the U.S. as among the main causes for the current strain in bilateral ties.
Since returning to the White House last year, Trump has implemented several measures to rework American immigration policy. These include bestowing more powers on officials to enforce domestic immigration laws as well as increasing anti-immigration raids and deportations. Last year, India accepted the return of almost 400 of its nationals deported by the Trump administration. Their arrival in India in military aircraft and in shackles caused a domestic outcry.
The Trump administration has also been squeezing the H-1B visa program that allows foreign nationals to temporarily work in the U.S. in specialty occupations for a maximum of six years. In August, Washington proposed a regulation to raise the fee on new H-1B visas to over $100,000. The H-1B program offers 65,000 visas annually, allowing American employers to hire highly skilled workers with specialty training. The program permits another 20,000 visas for workers with advanced degrees for a three-to-six-year period. Fees for the two categories of visas were between $2,000 and $5,000 earlier.
Trump’s proposed regulation was struck down by a California court in September, blocking the $100,000 fee tag. India has been the largest beneficiary of the H-1B visas program for many years.
With the U.S. narrowing the options for skilled Indian workers, the Indian government could look at asking American companies to follow the examples of Microsoft and Adobe and set up Global Capability Centers in India. These centers are offshore units set up by companies to deliver services for their parent organizations.
India presently has more than 2,100 centers employing 2.36 million people and generating nearly $100 billion in revenue. The Indian government is also looking to attract Indian workers currently employed in the U.S. to return home.
The denial of green cards under PERM is likely to figure in talks when Rubio, the U.S. secretary of state and national security adviser, arrives in India later this month. Also likely to figure in the agenda is the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026,” which authorizes Trump to sanction countries that buy oil from Russia and Iran. India is among the largest purchasers of Russian oil. Given that the U.S. itself is looking to import diesel from Russia, India is likely to seek clarification on the provisions of the Lindsay Graham Act should it import fuel from Russia.
People-to-people relations have always been the strongest anchor of India-U.S. bilateral ties. Washington’s latest move hits this anchor. Rubio and Jaishankar have a challenging agenda before them.

North Korea fires multiple ballistic missiles towards the sea
South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff said one of the missiles launched from the Pyongyang area flew more than 900km.
North Korea has fired multiple ballistic missiles towards the sea off its east coast, South Korea’s military says.
South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff (JCS) said one of the missiles launched from the Pyongyang area flew more than 900km (559 miles) on Monday. The joint chiefs did not specify how many missiles were detected.
Japan’s Deputy Defence Minister Takashi Koyari said at least two missiles were launched 17 minutes apart and landed in waters outside of its exclusive economic zone.
Koyari said the first missile flew about 220 kilometres (137 miles) and the second more than 910 kilometres (565 miles), following an “irregular” flight path and suggested it may have been a hypersonic weapon.
South Korea’s presidential office said that Pyongyang’s repeated missile launches violate United Nations Security Council resolutions, urging an immediate stop.
Monday’s launches add to heightened tensions on the Korean Peninsula, as both countries have been conducting weapons tests.
Escalating tensions
JCS spokesperson Jang Do-young said the latest missile launch appears to be a show of force, days after South Korea tested its own hypersonic weapon.
On Thursday, South Korean President Lee Jae Myung oversaw the country’s first test-firing of a hypersonic missile, a rare public showcasing of a missile test by a South Korean president.
Lee’s office said the hypersonic weapon, once fully developed, would enhance South Korea’s ability to strike key targets by surprise in the “Korean Peninsula theatre of operations”.
On October 3, North Korea also tested a hypersonic intermediate-range missile designed to evade missile defences in South Korea and Japan.
Last week, Seoul demanded an apology after a landmine blast wounded three soldiers in the Demilitarized Zone between South and North Korea. A joint South Korean-UN investigation concluded that two landmines were planted by North Korean forces about a year ago. Pyongyang dismissed the claim and accused South Korea of provocation.
Prior to the border mine blast, Seoul said it was conducting “preliminary coordination efforts” to facilitate dialogue between Pyongyang and Washington.
Lee pledged to reopen dialogue with North Korea in his first speech after taking office in 2025.
North Korean leader Kim Jong Un continues to flaunt his nuclear weapons programme, while rejecting US and South Korean offers to resume stalled diplomacy.
Talks between Kim and United States President Donald Trump abruptly ended in 2019. Kim Jong Un’s government continues to demand that Washington abandon its “hostile” policy towards Pyongyang and drop demands for North Korea’s denuclearisation as a condition for talks.

====================================================================================================

To Rebuild the Nepali Congress, Gagan Thapa Must First Reform It
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
03:18:00 UTC
12:18:00 KST

Among the most charismatic political leaders of his generation, Gagan Thapa was long talked of as a prime minister-in-waiting. As he rose up the ranks of the Nepali Congress — the social democratic party that has been the country’s dominant political force for most of the post-1990 period — this advocate of value-based politics with unmatched oratory skills seemed destined to lead his party and country.
Then came the Gen Z movement. In just two days of protests in September 2025, the movement upended the old political order. K.P. Oli, the communist prime minister at the time, had to run for his life. The top Congress leader, Sher Bahadur Deuba, was beaten black and blue. Along with the homes of hundreds of other political leaders, Thapa’s Kathmandu home was torched and he too had to go into hiding.
The Gen Z movement would also act as a catalyst for change in the Congress. In its aftermath, a set of second-generation leaders under Thapa finally dared to revolt and wrest party leadership away from Deuba, then age 79. Yet most Nepalis saw this as too little, too late, and the Congress under Thapa performed dismally in the first post-uprising national polls held in March 2026.
Today, the Congress is a diminished force, occupying just 38 seats in the 275-member lower House. Meanwhile, with 182 seats, the new Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP), which took ownership of the Gen Z movement, garnered a near two-thirds majority.
When the Congress was trounced in the March 2026 polls, old party leaders put the blame for the defeat on Thapa and his “mistimed” revolt that was orchestrated on the eve of the March elections. But the RSP was riding a wave of discontent with the established political parties, and Congress under its old leadership would arguably have fared even worse in the elections.
Now Thapa, 50, has been re-elected party president by its just-concluded general convention. While asking for votes, he vowed to end the culture of nepotism and groupism in the party and to open the outfit to a new generation of leaders.
His other proposals include a system of primaries to pick the party’s electoral candidates and amending the constitution charter to limit any individual to two terms as prime minister. Thapa’s proposed reforms, if implemented, could open up new democratic space, both in the party and in the national polity.
This is in sharp contrast to the centralizing and power-hoarding tendencies of Sher Bahadur Deuba, the erstwhile party president, who did much to discredit the image of a party that was long associated with principled leaders like B.P. Koirala and Ganesh Man Singh.
But Thapa has a monumental challenge on his hands. The RSP has captured much of the political space once occupied by the Congress. Under party chair Rabi Lamichhane and senior leader Balendra Shah, who is also Nepal’s prime minister, the RSP remains very popular. It is thus expected to replicate its federal poll success in the local and provincial elections scheduled for 2027.
The old rivalry between Congress, the old champion of liberal democratic values, and the communists appears increasingly irrelevant to Nepali voters today. Now it is upon Thapa’s party to show the skeptical electorate what liberal democratic values mean in practice, and why a reformed Congress can uphold them.
The other big challenge for Thapa would be to bring back into the party’s fold the disgruntled leaders who still back former party president Deuba. If a big chunk of old Congress stalwarts continue to side with Deuba, Thapa will have a tough time rebuilding the party organization. His efforts to reinvigorate the Congress will be dealt a further blow if the Supreme Court, which is currently considering a case on the legality of the Thapa-led Congress, chooses to identify the Deuba faction as the authentic Congress party.
Gagan Thapa has many strengths. He has worked his way up the ranks of the Congress. However, Thapa’s rise came even as the party’s top leaders were openly engaging in self-centered politics and corruption. In the eyes of many young Nepalis, he preferred to play it safe and bided his time. But Nepali youths were less patient — and revolted. Many thus reckon Thapa’s time has passed.
Whether or not that is true, it is important for the Congress under Thapa to continue to be electorally competitive in Nepali politics. Besides its role as the champion of liberal democratic values, a strong Congress will also make the RSP accountable.
With the discrediting of the Congress under the old leadership, the RSP has come to occupy the liberal democratic space without doing much to demonstrate its commitment to liberal values. In just six months in office, the new RSP government has taken a number of questionable decisions — from removing squatters without due process to jailing political leaders on flimsy legal grounds — that make people suspect the party’s democratic credentials.
Thapa has proven his credentials as a fighter for democratic rights, as a competent administrator during his tenure as health minister, and as a voice of reason in the cacophonous Nepali political landscape. Now, for the first time, he will be tasked with rebuilding a party organization. But to do so, he will first have to dismantle the old, ossified structures and ways of thinking that have held the party back in recent times.

03:16:04 UTC
12:16:04 KST

After four years together in government, cooperation between Likud and Religious Zionism continues to deepen ahead of the upcoming elections. The parties have launched a joint campaign to "save the right-wing bloc," with the central goal of strengthening and expanding their political power.
Sources in both parties say personal ties between their leaders, Benjamin Netanyahu and Bezalel Smotrich, have also grown closer during the past term, particularly following Itamar Ben-Gvir's temporary withdrawal from the government over the hostage deal, while the finance minister remained loyal and paid a political price for doing so.
The strengthening alliance includes several measures: establishing a joint field campaign headquarters; mobilizing hundreds of activists, both volunteers and paid staff, to work on behalf of both parties; jointly mapping potential voter groups to increase turnout and maximize electoral opportunities; and preparing a detailed, coordinated schedule for Election Day.
The joint field campaign headquarters was recently established under the leadership of Yesha Council Chairman Yisrael Gantz, representing Likud, and Yesha Council Director-General Omer Rahamim, representing Smotrich.
The two are analyzing previous election results, identifying areas with untapped voting potential and working to significantly increase turnout in those cities.
With the help of numerous campaign workers and volunteers, they are dividing areas of responsibility among activists and plan to go door to door on Election Day to encourage people to vote and ensure that as many potential supporters of both parties as possible cast their ballots. The joint operation aims to help voters reach polling stations, including providing transportation when necessary.
Beyond their field operations, Likud and Religious Zionism also are cooperating on the parliamentary front, having signed a vote-sharing agreement.
"On the one hand, Likud and Religious Zionism appeal to different audiences, so their messages are also different," a source in Smotrich's party said. "On the other hand, we're all coming together for one goal: forming a broad coalition and winning the election."
Failed efforts to forge a broader alliance
Last week, Smotrich held his first major Religious Zionism conference, attended by yeshiva heads, rabbis, prominent activists and members of his grassroots communities.
He invited Netanyahu, who immediately confirmed his attendance to project a united front. During the conference, the two sat side by side and appeared closely coordinated.
This was particularly noticeable when it emerged that Itamar Ben-Gvir, their fellow member of the right-wing bloc, had not been invited to the event at all.
The national security minister also has complained that the prime minister refuses to be photographed near him or appear alongside him at public events.
As cooperation between Likud and Religious Zionism intensifies, the growing distance from Ben-Gvir has become increasingly apparent.
Officials in both parties blame Ben-Gvir, arguing that he has deliberately isolated himself.
Likud officials believe that while Shas and Religious Zionism are playing a coordinated bloc-wide game, the national security minister is pursuing a personal political strategy focused solely on his own success.
"Ben-Gvir wants to grow at Likud's expense, and that's what his entire campaign looks like," a senior Likud official said. "He isn't cooperating on anything related to winning the election for the bloc. He barely focuses on messages against the opposition and instead highlights internal conflicts within the bloc. He's deliberately creating a situation in which he is left out. That's his campaign."
Netanyahu's party says it held several discussions with representatives of Otzma Yehudit about cooperation, but claims Ben-Gvir showed no willingness to participate, either operationally or financially.
Because of that lack of cooperation, Likud officials believe many of the seats currently projected for Ben-Gvir in the polls represent voters whose support remains uncertain. They intend to try to win those voters back ahead of the election.
The Defense Ministry at the center of the dispute
Relations between Likud and Otzma Yehudit have become even more strained recently following Ben-Gvir's new campaign, which declared that "if Ben-Gvir had been defense minister, October 7 would not have happened."
The national security minister's coalition partners viewed the statement as provocative and interpreted it as further evidence that Ben-Gvir was focused on strengthening his party at their expense. This, in turn, further reinforced the Netanyahu-Smotrich alliance.
Likud's assessment is that Ben-Gvir is the only figure in Netanyahu's bloc competing directly for the same voters as the party. As a result, a political battle has developed between Likud and Otzma Yehudit over a large pool of undecided right-wing voters.
Throughout the recent period, Ben-Gvir's office has maintained that his support for Netanyahu is unconditional. In practice, however, from Ben-Gvir's perspective, the contest on the right is no longer about who will be prime minister, but rather who will serve as Netanyahu's defense minister.
Ben-Gvir has publicly identified the Defense Ministry as his next political goal.
Netanyahu understands that to prevent Ben-Gvir from achieving that ambition and force him to lower his expectations, he must weaken Otzma Yehudit and reduce the number of seats it wins in the election.
"Instead of directing his energy outward, Ben-Gvir is creating a situation in which the election is being fought within the right-wing bloc: Either Netanyahu or Ben-Gvir. That's completely unreasonable," a Religious Zionism source said.
"For two months, Smotrich talked about cooperation and coordination within the bloc. He wanted everyone together, but Winter and Ben-Gvir decided to go it alone. That's part of what led to the closer relationship with Likud."

Saudi Arabia, Israel have shared interests at stake, Houthi escalation highlights - editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
03:14:19 UTC
12:14:19 KST

A strike by Houthi terrorists on the international airport in the Saudi capital, Riyadh, has turned the desert kingdom’s efforts to mobilize security partners into an immediate test: Can new and existing ties protect the kingdom without widening the conflict? The attack killed 12 people and wounded an additional 309, according to Saudi civil aviation authorities. The Houthis have since warned airlines, passengers, and airport workers to avoid Saudi airports and airspace.
The consequences extend beyond the casualties. Riyadh’s airport remained closed on Sunday, and airlines canceled or suspended flights after the Houthis warned that Saudi airspace had become a theater of military operations. The October 10 strike was the third attack on the airport that week. Earlier attacks there killed three people, including a Saudi pilot. The Houthis have also threatened Saudi energy facilities.
The escalation is pulling Saudi Arabia back into a war it had spent years trying to contain. A 2022 truce between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia largely held until fighting resumed in July. Since then, the Houthis have advanced along Yemen’s Red Sea coast. At the same time, forces fighting on behalf of the internationally recognized government of Yemen have launched a counteroffensive with Saudi air support and other military backing.
The internationally recognized Yemeni government says its forces have retaken strategic positions near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait; the Houthis dispute those claims, and the extent of the government’s gains remains unclear. The coalition’s spokesman said 100 aircraft took part in the operation and claimed 324 high-value targets were destroyed; neither claim has been independently verified as of Sunday.
The Houthis have claimed control of territory and islands near the strait, including Perim Island, while government forces say they have pushed back.
Bab el-Mandeb connects the Gulf of Aden to the Red Sea and the Suez Canal. The Houthis’ positions near the strait give them greater ability to monitor and threaten shipping, though they do not control the passage in a way that lets them stop all traffic. Riyadh must protect its cities and energy infrastructure while backing a campaign to regain ground along a vital maritime route.
Saudi Arabia’s response presents a difficult choice. Restraint could leave the kingdom’s airspace exposed and weaken the deterrent message of its new partnerships. A deeper campaign could prolong the fighting and put Saudi forces and their partners at greater risk.
Saudi defense pact with Turkey, Pakistan faces test amid Houthi escalation
The Mecca Joint Defense Agreement with Turkey and Pakistan is one part of that calculation. The three countries signed it in August. On October 5, their joint committee said it would begin implementing collective-defense commitments and provide agreed military capabilities for rapid deployment in Saudi Arabia. The public statement did not identify the forces involved or give a timetable, leaving open how the commitment would work in practice.
Turkey has described the pact as defensive. Reuters reported, citing officials, that Turkish support would be mainly technical and defensive. The announcement left operational questions unanswered, including the size and command of any deployment. It is too early to judge what the agreement will deliver or whether either partner will join the fighting in Yemen. A collective-defense commitment does not itself establish participation in offensive operations.
Houthi threat to Red Sea shipping raises concerns for Israel's Eilat port
For Israel, the most immediate connection is the vulnerability of Red Sea shipping. Houthi attacks have kept international shipping lines from returning to regular direct sailings to Eilat. Recent advances near Bab el-Mandeb have renewed concern about the port’s recovery. Some activity has resumed through cargo unloaded in Aqaba, Jordan, but the direct route has not returned. The threat to shipping is already an Israeli economic and security concern, whether or not Saudi Arabia and Israel expand their contacts.
Israeli media have separately reported that Israel has provided or discussed intelligence assistance to Saudi Arabia through US Central Command. Those accounts rely on regional diplomatic or security sources; neither government has publicly confirmed the details. They do not establish a formal alliance or Israeli participation in the fighting.
The Riyadh strike is an early test of Saudi Arabia’s emerging security network. The broader question is whether Riyadh can protect its cities and trade routes while reversing Houthi gains without turning the renewed campaign into a deeper regional war. For Israel, the consequences will also be felt in terms of the safety and viability of the Red Sea routes on which Eilat depends.

North Korea launches multiple ballistic missiles, South Korea says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
03:14:15 UTC
12:14:15 KST

North Korea fired multiple ballistic missiles toward the sea off its east coast on Monday, South Korea's military said, marking Pyongyang'sfourth launch in a month and following Seoul's recent test of a hypersonic missile.
The ballistic missiles, which appeared to be of different types, were fired at around 9:20 a.m. local time from near Pyongyang, and one type flew more than 900 km, South Korea's Joint Chiefs of Staff said.
Earlier, Japan's coast guard said North Korea had fired two unidentified projectiles, believed to be ballistic missiles, adding that both appeared to have already fallen.
South Korea's National Security Office convened an emergency meeting, where it condemned the missile launches as violations of United Nations Security Council resolutions and urged an immediate stop.
North Korea has been under UN sanctions since 2006, aimed at halting Pyongyang's development of nuclear weapons and ballistic missiles.
South Korea tests hypersonic missile
The latest launches come at a time when tensions have been rising between the two Koreas in recent weeks amid weapons tests by both countries.
Last week, South Korean President Lee Jae Myung oversaw the country's first test-firing of a hypersonic missile, a rare public showcasing of a missile test by a South Korean president.
Monday's missile launches by North Korea appeared to be "a show of force in response to the successful test launch of our hypersonic missile, as well as an intentional demonstration of missile capabilities," a spokesperson for South Korea's Joint Chiefs of Staff said.
North Korea last fired a ballistic missile on October 3, with state media KCNA saying it was a hypersonic missile tested under the supervision of leader Kim Jong Un.
The tests followed a border mine blast last month that wounded three South Korean soldiers. Seoul said the landmines had been planted by North Korea and demanded an apology, but Pyongyang has dismissed this and accused South Korea of provocation.
Pyongyang has conducted missile tests on more than 10 occasions this year, including four in the last month.
The unusually frequent tests suggest Pyongyang wanted to increase its leverage ahead of a potential summit between leader Kim and US President Donald Trump, said Song Seong-jong, a professor at Daejeon University in Seoul and a former official at South Korea's Defense Ministry.
"They definitely need to raise the value of their status before meeting Trump," Song said.

Why Did the Industrial Revolution Not Start in India?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
03:06:00 UTC
12:06:00 KST

Historians often ask why the Industrial Revolution began in Europe and not elsewhere.
The classical framing of this question is the Needham Problem. Writing in 1969, the British historian of science, Joseph Needham, asked: “Why did modern science, the mathematization of hypotheses about Nature, with all its implications for advanced technology, take its meteoric rise only in the West…[and] had not developed in Chinese civilization?” After all, Needham noted, “between the first century BC and the fifteenth century AD, Chinese civilization was much more efficient than occidental in applying human natural knowledge to practical human needs.”
The Industrial Revolution refers to the transformation from agrarian, handicraft economies to machine- and factory-based industrial economies. It began in the 18th century and was the harbinger of the modern world, enabling Western dominance over most of the rest of the world, either through outright colonization, as in much of India and Africa, or by means of indirect control, as in China and Iran. The Industrial Revolution built on the preceding Scientific Revolution in Europe, which emphasized the acquisition of knowledge through reason and empirical research.
Needham sought to answer the question of why the Industrial Revolution did not begin outside Europe by examining the evolution of science in China.
But the issue ought not to be seen as merely a dichotomy between Western and Chinese civilization. In fact, India and the Islamic world would arguably have been better candidates than China for the emergence of industrial civilization. As in Europe, large swathes of India and the Islamic world engaged in long-distance trade, patronized universities, and were divided into competing kingdoms fighting against each other and against pastoralist peoples from the neighboring steppes and deserts. The Islamic world and Europe, especially, had to compensate for a lack of abundant labor. Incessant warfare led to the adaptation of gunpowder, while trade spread innovations such as the compass and paper beyond the region.
In India, there are two periods that stand out as optimal times for an industrial revolution to occur there. The first is in the 6ht century CE, when the Gupta Empire had disintegrated into a plethora of kingdoms and a shared elite culture across polities emerged. India thus experienced both political competition and was home to a pan-India culture. An exchange of ideas happened at a number of universities, such as Nalanda. These conditions were similar to those in early modern Europe. Some of India’s greatest advances in the arts, philosophy, and mathematics occurred in the centuries following the end of the Gupta Empire, with figures like mathematician Brahmagupta and philosopher Shankara living during this period.
A second period would have been in the Deccan peninsula during the early modern era. The topography and location of this region favored the persistence of several rival kingdoms seeking to gain an advantage over each other. They all had access to ocean-going trade and had a history of trade guilds, which allowed the easy flow of goods and ideas. In the early 16th century, the Deccan sultanates were some of the earliest innovators in cannon technology and military architecture. In the 18th century, the Kingdom of Mysore invented sophisticated rockets and other weaponry, whilst the Marathas established ordnance factories where skilled metalworkers created cannon and firearms adapted to local Indian conditions.
While it should be noted that the engine behind 18th-century Deccani manufacturing were skilled craftsmen rather than mechanization, the region had many of the right ingredients to commence industrialization around the same time as in Europe. The British conquest halted these initial local moves in that direction.
However, there were many other reasons the Industrial Revolution began in northwest Europe — and not elsewhere, such as in India — in the 18th century.
Industrialization is not inevitable. It is not the default outcome of human civilization. It takes certain institutions and worldviews as prerequisites and particular economic and geopolitical conditions — many of which came together by chance — to spark the process.
A great many factors must align, not least intense international rivalry in the state’s vicinity. For example, a polity ought to have enough labor to man its factories, but not too much labor — as China did — so as to make investment in industry more expensive than utilizing manual labor. A polity would ideally be sedentary rather than nomadic, stable enough internally to guarantee the continuity of institutions such as universities, companies, and land ownership, and home to a flexible labor market: the masses of peasants in many states were not permitted to move freely and offer their services anywhere. The polity must be strong enough to guarantee the rule of law, but not so bureaucratic so as to stifle private enterprise and innovation.
The historian Kyle Harper, speaking about the Roman Empire, noted that: “there [were] tinkerers and engineers, but they [were not] talking to the mathematicians and the physicists. If you were from on high to design self-sustaining innovation, I think you would want to bring those elements into proximity.” Harper argues that industrialization took off in early modern Europe because states funded scientific research and married the findings to the work of engineers and builders. Both groups seeded each other’s minds with ideas.
This process requires a state — or well-endowed institutions, such as corporations and universities — to facilitate scientific discoveries and its practical applications. This is a time- and capital-intensive process that was undertaken — more often than not — to improve the finances and security of the state through gains in efficiency and production. The benefits had to have been more than the costs.
On top of that, the state must overcome tradition and inertia: not an easy task. For example, after the victory of the Vijayanagara Empire against the Sultanate of Bijapur in 1520 at the Battle of Raichur, the two sides drew different conclusions on the efficiency of gunpowder.
Writing about the emperor of Vijayanagara, Krishadevaraya, historian Richard Eaton notes:
Though impressed with the matchlocks used by his Portuguese mercenaries, [Krishnadevaraya] failed to see firearms as the way of the future…there is no evidence that he followed up his victories by establishing an arsenal or a matchlock foundry in Vijayanagara. Nor did he or his successors ever mount cannon on the walls of their capital or provincial forts, or in other ways adapt their defensive systems to accommodate gunpowder technology…Bijapur, by contrast, responded quite differently to the battle’s outcome…[and] therefore launched an accelerated drive to pioneer new gunpowder technologies…from the small swivel guns that the Portuguese had placed on the gunwales of their ships, they took the idea of mounting a much larger cannon on a cubic block of granite set on an iron pin, enabling the gun to move horizontally.
Inertia is difficult to overcome. Research has found that in many parts of India, even when women are offered high-paying jobs in factories or offices, they decline due to family pressure and tradition that looks down on women working outside of the home. And for cultural reasons related to status, many Indians dream of becoming government bureaucrats or white-collar workers in the information technology industry, rather than seeking to work in factories or engaging in commerce or sales. These factors inhabit industrialization, development, and the spread of rational socioeconomic organization deriving from individualism.
For these reasons, for much of human history, it has been more efficient for most states — and most elites — to simply exploit land and people harder and harder. The Romans had a copious number of slaves and empires as diverse as the Ottomans and Mughals engaged in tax farming: the practice of a government contracting tax collection to private individuals, individuals who would often take a cut for themselves after fleecing peasants and merchants.
Many scholars have speculated that in India, mathematicians, artisans, scientists and builders were not often in the business of exchanging ideas, belonging to different endogamous jatis, or castes. According to economic historian Tirthankar Roy, “technology existed as tacit knowledge of artisan communities, and the evidence of partnership between diverse skills was rare. Scientific knowledge was often documented, but remained restricted within scholastic circles.”
Contrary to a widespread but incorrect belief, literacy was widespread amongst a number of castes, and was not restricted to just Brahmins. But different communities still interacted with and circulated texts mostly within their social milieu, and sometimes different jatis even used different writing systems. For example, in parts of North India, merchants used the Mahajani alphabet, scribes (Kayasthas) used the Kaithi alphabet, and Brahmins used Devanagari.
Another factor that may have inhibited industrialization in pre-modern India was its abundant quantity of specialized and cheap labor, which dampens the need for mechanization and labor-saving devices. China, too, had abundant labor, and thus, less incentive to mechanize in pre-modern times. The first Mughal Emperor Babur famously observed this phenomenon in his diary, the Baburnameh:
Another good thing in Hindustan is that it has unnumbered and endless workmen of every kind. There is a fixed caste (jam’i) for every sort of work and for every thing, which has done that work or that thing from father to son till now…680 men worked daily on my buildings in Agra and of Agra stone-cutters only; while 1491 stone-cutters worked daily on my buildings in Agra, Sikri, Biana, Dulpur, Gwalior, and Kuil. In the same way there are numberless artisans and workmen of every sort in Hindustan.
In fact, it was arguably not in the interests of a state to create a large number of unemployed people by introducing industry. Even today, if one were to observe construction in much of India, one would see a large number of individuals carrying and laying bricks with their bare hands instead of using machines or complex tools.
The historian Ada Palmer has noted that industrialization was less likely to begin in richer regions with more developed artisanal industries and vibrant trade, such as Italy. In fact, as per Palmer, even though Italians during the Renaissance had the technology for industrial looms, they did not want to pivot away from producing artisanal fabrics, which brought them wealth.
The parallels with India are striking. Due to its abundant labor, its social structure, and the inertia of an economic system that worked well enough, there was little incentive to initiate mechanization and the Industrial Revolution in India. The parts of India that came closest to industrialization — such as states in the early modern Deccan — did so when geopolitical conditions highly incentivized such an outcome. Survival trumped inaction in those cases. But more often than not, it was too late, or unnecessary, as the Industrial Revolution arrived fully formed from Europe in India.

Trump ‘really mad’ at Zelensky – media
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
03:02:34 UTC
12:02:34 KST

Trump ‘really mad’ at Zelensky – media
US President Donald Trump is furious with Vladimir Zelensky over Kiev’s continued attacks on Russian oil refineries, with Washington reportedly threatening to cut off weapons supplies and intelligence sharing unless Ukraine stops the strikes, according to Axios and the Financial Times.
The confrontation comes after Trump struck a diesel deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to ease a global fuel shortage that has sent American energy prices soaring.
Kiev has continued to target Russian refining facilities despite repeated warnings, with Trump accusing Zelensky of deliberately hurting American consumers and farmers while refusing opportunities to end the conflict.
“Trump is really mad. He feels Zelensky is taking the US for granted,” a White House official told Axios on Sunday. The source argued that Kiev’s attacks on Russian refineries are doing more damage to its relationship with Washington than to Russia.
US officials contacted Kiev and several European capitals over the weekend, threatening to suspend intelligence sharing and the NATO-backed Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List (PURL) mechanism, through which European countries purchase American weapons for Ukraine, according to the Financial Times, which cited officials familiar with the discussions.
Trump envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner also reportedly warned Ukrainian representatives during talks in Miami on Friday that Washington could stop sharing intelligence if Kiev continues to ignore the president’s demands, according to a Ukrainian official cited by Axios.
A US official, however, denied making direct threats, saying the negotiators instead reminded Kiev of Washington’s extensive military and intelligence support and urged it to stop taking actions that hurt American consumers.
The confrontation has threatened to derail broader negotiations aimed at ending the Ukraine conflict. Witkoff and Kushner have reportedly put their planned trip to Moscow on hold until Kiev and its leading European backers clarify whether they are prepared to support a unified peace proposal.
Trump reached a diesel deal with Putin on Friday after Zelensky ignored at least half a dozen requests to stop striking Russian refineries, according to earlier Axios reporting. The US Treasury subsequently eased sanctions on Russian diesel exports until April 2027, while Moscow pledged substantial fuel deliveries to help alleviate global shortages.
Zelensky called the move a “weak decision,” arguing that the agreement will provide Russia with additional revenue. Trump hit back, accusing the Ukrainian leader of creating problems for the world and suggesting that it is time for Ukraine to elect a new leader capable of reaching a deal.
On Sunday, Trump unexpectedly announced that Moscow and Kiev agreed to an immediate ceasefire covering attacks on energy infrastructure. “Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!” he wrote on Truth Social.
The announcement caught Kiev by surprise, with Zelensky saying it “was news for me.” Moscow has also yet to confirm the agreement.
A White House official described the proposed agreement as a “refinery for refinery” arrangement, under which both sides would stop attacking oil refineries, but not necessarily other energy infrastructure, according to Axios. Kiev has said the deal would disproportionately benefit Russia, since Ukraine has only one largely nonfunctional refinery and fully relies on imported fuel.

Officials said the redeveloped Huanggang port’s opening went smoothly on Monday morning, with Chief Secretary Eric Chan expecting a relatively quiet first day so staff can prepare to handle more travellers in future.
Speaking to reporters, Chan said he doesn't expect the port to be too busy on the day of its opening, which will give staff time to familiarise themselves with operations at the facility.
"There’s a reason we chose today to open. The National Day holiday has just ended. Today, we believe there will be fewer visitors, so everyone has time to get familiar with the operations. We hope that by the time the next peak arrives, our colleagues will be fully used to it. That’s the best approach," he said.
Chan added that if the new "collaborative inspection and joint clearance" model works well, the government will consider extending it to other border checkpoints.
Secretary for Security Chris Tang said more than 5,000 people used the redeveloped Huanggang port in the first two hours after it opened at 6.30am –  a 60 percent increase compared with before its renovation. 
Nearly 1,000 vehicles also passed through, up 30 percent. 
He said all the self-service "collaborative inspection" channels are working normally, and passengers can go straight through without waiting. 
As for vehicles using the joint one-stop lane, waiting times are under five minutes, he added. 
Tang said a joint command centre set up with Shenzhen authorities will help keep operations running smoothly on both sides of the border.
"For the joint operation room between Shenzhen and Hong Kong authorities, we will operate as long as it’s necessary, in particular during high peak season, for example on weekends or during the Apec conference. We’ll ensure that we’ll have sufficient manpower... We are ready to take the challenge," he said.
Transport chief Mable Chan said public transport carried more than 3,000 people to and from Huanggang port in the first two hours of operations.
The secretary for transport and logistics said contingency plans are in place ahead of the travel rush expected over the upcoming Chung Yeung Festival long weekend.
"We will not underestimate the challenge to be brought about in the coming long weekend. So, we have already agreed with the police to arrange a public transport cover area, which is very near to this new Huanggang boundary control point," she said.
"We can arrange some emergency and contingency arrangements and stacking of franchised buses, minibuses and even taxis in the buffer area. We can accommodate around 200 vehicles there."
As of 5pm, more than 42,200 passenger trips were recorded at the redeveloped port, with vehicle flow exceeding 5,700.

El Nino sets temperature record in key Pacific zone: EU monitor
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
02:40:00 UTC
11:40:00 KST

El Nino sets temperature record in key Pacific zone: EU monitor
PARIS – An intensifying El Nino broke a temperature record in a key zone of the Pacific in September, the EU’s climate monitor said on Oct 12, in another sign the weather pattern is gaining exceptional strength.
Global forecasters have been warning for months that the El Nino in 2026 will likely become the strongest ever observed and the latest record has tumbled even before the episode’s expected peak later in 2026.
The warming phase of a natural climate cycle, El Nino raises sea temperatures in the tropical Pacific, triggering changes in weather that can increase the risk of drought and flooding, and exacerbate man-made global warming.
The Copernicus Climate Change Service said sea surface temperatures in a tell-tale El Nino monitoring region of the Pacific, known as Nino3.4, had reached an “all-time high” of 29.70 deg C in September.
This exceeded the peak temperatures of previously strong El Nino events of 1982/1983, 1997/1998 and 2015/2016, “underscoring the exceptional intensity of the current El Nino”, the EU monitor said.
But in a statement to AFP, Copernicus said it “cannot yet say that the current El Nino is the strongest ever recorded”.
As climate change raises ocean temperatures, it can make recent El Nino events appear stronger than past ones, complicating historical comparisons.
Copernicus said it had adopted a new index, which accounts for the warming of tropical oceans, that suggested the current event is not yet stronger than past ones.
But the values observed in September “point to an already exceptionally strong El Nino, especially given that the event has not yet reached its peak”, Copernicus told AFP.
Not all forecasters use the same scale to interpret El Nino.
On Oct 9, Japan’s weather agency said that El Nino conditions had reached their “strongest intensity on record”, with temperatures in the phenomenon’s monitoring area 4 deg C above normal.
Record ocean temperatures
As El Nino gathers strength, global average sea surface temperatures hit a record 21.05 deg C for September, topping the previous high of 20.92 deg C for the same month in 2023, according to Copernicus.
Overall, the world experienced its second-hottest September on record, with surface air temperatures averaging 16.27 deg C, the EU service said.
September was 1.63 deg C hotter than the pre-industrial average, a period defined as 1850-1900.
Nations agreed at the 2015 UN climate talks in Paris to keep global warming “well below” 2 deg C above pre-industrial levels, while pursuing efforts to limit it to 1.5 deg C, in order to check the effects of climate change.
But the United Nations declared in September that the long-term 1.5 deg C target would be missed in a matter of years.
“We are in a new run of months above 1.5 deg C, and with a strong El Nino still intensifying it is likely to last into 2027,” Copernicus director Carlo Buontempo said in a statement.
“Crossing the Paris Agreement’s long-term limit is only a matter of time. How far we overshoot, and for how long, is still up to us,” he said.
Scientists say it is crucial to reduce greenhouse gas emissions from fossil fuels to limit the period of “overshoot” above 1.5 deg C and bring temperatures back down as quickly as possible.
Experts have warned that this El Nino would likely push global temperatures to a new record in 2027.
El Nino warms surface temperatures in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific Ocean, bringing worldwide changes in winds, pressure and rainfall patterns.
It typically takes place every two to seven years and lasts around nine to 12 months. AFP

Feature: Zheng Qinwen rediscovers inner fire with historic China Open triumph
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
10:31:22 CST
11:31:22 KST

by sportswriters Li Chunyu, Wang Chunyan and Hu Jiali
BEIJING, Oct. 12 (Xinhua) -- Sealing victory with an ace, home favorite Zheng Qinwen claimed her maiden WTA 1000 title at the China Open on Sunday, becoming the first Chinese player to win the tournament's women's singles crown amid roaring cheers on Diamond Court.
Known as "Queen Wen," Zheng defeated Russia's 19-year-old Mirra Andreeva 7-5, 6-4 to complete a remarkable comeback from injury.
Dressed in a red gown at her post-match press conference, the Olympic champion summed up her triumph in a few words: "I found my inner fire back."
As her winning ace landed, Zheng sank to the court in celebration, recalling the moment she captured Olympic gold on the red clay of Roland Garros at Paris 2024.
But the journey between those two moments of glory had been anything but smooth.
"I know how much I can inspire people after winning the Olympic gold. I keep trying to reach the best version of myself, but the injury changed my momentum," said Zheng, who reached the semifinals of the 2024 China Open.
The former world No. 4 underwent elbow surgery in July 2025 after a first-round exit at Wimbledon, beginning a frustrating period of recovery marked by setbacks and uncertainty.
"Sooner or later, I would have to go through this kind of surgery. But because of a lack of understanding of recovery, not enough visits to doctors or receiving advice from different doctors, I was making some wrong choices," she said.
Just over two months after surgery, Zheng returned to competition at the 2025 China Open, only to withdraw in the third round.
"I was really rushed. I wanted to play the matches, and my doctors told me I was able to play in those matches. But after these tournaments, the condition worsened, which took me longer to recover. This is a good lesson for me," Zheng reflected.
The prolonged absence brought pressure and doubts over whether she could regain the form that had made her one of China's brightest sporting stars.
Yet Zheng refused to let outside voices distract her, gradually discovering that the difficult period had also offered an opportunity for personal growth.
"The biggest takeaway is that lows are not necessarily bad. I rediscovered myself to see my shortcomings in skills and weaknesses of personality. Being positive every day is difficult. When I was in tough moments, I had an extra energy to make a breakthrough. The lows actually helped me improve," she said.
After falling outside the world's top 100 earlier this year, Zheng began her resurgence at the US Open, where she reached the quarterfinals as a qualifier.
Returning to Beijing, she strung together seven consecutive victories to make history on home soil.
"To play in China is like playing the fifth Grand Slam for me. They are the same important. I want to perform super well in front of the home crowd. This brings me extra pressure, but also helps me to put the efforts on court," she said.
The tournament also brought moments of personal celebration.
On October 1, China's National Day, Zheng wore red as she defeated compatriot Shi Han, explaining afterward that "red brings energy and power."
On Thursday, she celebrated her 24th birthday in Beijing wearing a blue-purple gown reminiscent of a wedding dress. Three days later, the China Open trophy arrived as a belated birthday gift.
"Now, at 24, I've become more mature. I am mentally more stable than I used to be. When I am making choices on and off the court, I am more clear-minded," she said.
"I want to be a more aggressive player. It has always been my dream and ambition."
Despite her latest achievement, Zheng says there is still more to come.
"If not for the surgery, I could keep going higher. The surgery stopped my progress somehow. I have to start from zero again. I really want to see what I can do in the future," she said.
Having endured months of uncertainty, Zheng said the setbacks had given her a deeper appreciation of every victory.
"There have been many chapters going through this journey. I just didn't expect that the lows this time continued that long. That is why I treasure the opportunities now. I know how much effort I have made behind each win."
For the newly crowned China Open champion, the journey is far from over.
"Honestly, I'm eager to know what's going to come next in my career," she said. "Tennis is a beautiful sport. I don't want to have a regret the day that I retire from tennis."
And as "Queen Wen" looked ahead to the next chapter, she had one reminder for herself:
"Be humble, keep my head up. Don't let the crown drop." ■
