Ceuta or Sebta? Why one city has two names and a disputed status
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
00:14:46 UTC
09:14:46 KST

Ceuta or Sebta? Why one city has two names and a disputed status
Felipe VI’s first visit to Ceuta and Melilla as king brings Spain’s territorial dispute with Morocco back into focus.
Spain’s King Felipe VI and Queen Letizia are due to visit Ceuta on October 13 and Melilla the following day, in Felipe’s first visit to either city as king since he ascended the throne in 2014.
The trip comes after a major migration crisis at the Ceuta border in July and as the long-running dispute between Spain and Morocco over the two cities on the North African coast remains unresolved.
Spain considers Ceuta and Melilla part of its territory, while Morocco regards both cities and several smaller Spanish-held territories in North Africa as part of its own territory.
The city that sits on the southern side of the Strait of Gibraltar also has different names in Spanish and Arabic.
In Spain, it is Ceuta. In Arabic, it is Sabta, commonly written as Sebta in Latin script.
So why does the same city have two names? And how did a city on the North African coast come under Spanish sovereignty?
Where does the name Ceuta come from?
The name is much older than either modern Spain or Morocco.
The city was known as Sabta in Arabic. Spain’s Ministry of Culture identifies Sabta with present-day Ceuta and traces its history through successive periods of Idrisid, Umayyad, Taifa, Almoravid, Almohad and Marinid rule.
The Spanish form, Ceuta, developed from earlier forms of the name. Sabta and Ceuta are different linguistic forms of the same city.
Who controlled Ceuta before Spain?
Ceuta passed through several political and dynastic systems in the Maghreb and al-Andalus.
Under the Idrisid dynasty, the city was in the hands of the Banu Isam before being taken by the Umayyad Caliph Abd al-Rahman III in 931, bringing it into the political sphere of al-Andalus.
In the 11th century, Ceuta became linked to the Taifa of Malaga. It later came under the Almoravids and Almohads. From the beginning of the 14th century, it became part of the Marinid sphere with periods when other local dynasties held power.
By the early 15th century, Ceuta was under Muslim rule.
That changed in 1415.
How did Ceuta become Portuguese?
On August 21, 1415, Portuguese forces led by King John I captured Ceuta.
The Portuguese conquest brought an end to more than seven centuries of Muslim rule in Ceuta. Ceuta’s own cultural heritage authority dates Muslim rule from 709 to the Portuguese conquest in 1415.
Ceuta remained Portuguese for more than two centuries.
Portugal and Spain were then ruled by the same monarchy from 1580 to 1640. When Portugal restored its independence in 1640, Ceuta remained under the Spanish monarchy rather than returning to Portuguese rule.
The 1668 Treaty of Lisbon, which formally recognised Portuguese independence, left Ceuta in Spanish hands.
That is how Ceuta came under Spanish sovereignty.
Why does Morocco claim Ceuta?
Morocco’s argument is rooted in the city’s history and geography.
Ceuta lies on the North African coast, surrounded by Morocco on its landward side. Morocco has claimed Ceuta and Melilla since gaining independence in 1956 and regards the two cities as occupied Moroccan territories.
Spain takes the opposite position.
Under Spanish law, Ceuta is an autonomous city. Its Statute of Autonomy describes Ceuta as an integral part of the Spanish nation and gives the city its own system of self-government.
The dispute, therefore, is not about who administers Ceuta. Spain does. It is about sovereignty.
Morocco says Ceuta should form part of Moroccan territory. Spain says its sovereignty over the city is established and Ceuta is part of Spain.
Neither side has accepted the other’s position.
Why doesn’t history settle the dispute?
Because the two sides interpret that history differently.
Morocco points to Ceuta’s long history within Muslim political systems in the Maghreb and its location on the North African coast. Spain points to centuries of Portuguese and Spanish control and to Ceuta’s present constitutional status as part of Spain.
The historical record does not provide a simple answer to a modern sovereignty dispute. The political systems that ruled Ceuta before 1415 were not nation-states with today’s borders, and the city’s current status is based on centuries of subsequent Portuguese and Spanish rule.
Morocco’s territorial claim dates from the period after independence in 1956, but Spain has continued to exercise sovereignty over Ceuta.
Why does Morocco call it Sebta?
Sebta, or Sabta, is the Arabic name for Ceuta and predates the modern sovereignty dispute.
In Morocco, Sebta is the Arabic name used for the city while Ceuta is the established Spanish form.
The choice of name can have political resonance because Morocco disputes Spanish sovereignty over the city. But using Sebta is not automatically a political statement. It is also simply the Arabic name.
What about Melilla?
Melilla’s history is different from Ceuta’s.
Spanish forces took control of Melilla in 1497 when it was incorporated into the Crown of Castile.
Ceuta, by contrast, was first Portuguese before remaining under the Spanish monarchy after Portugal regained its independence.
Today, both cities are Spanish autonomous cities, and Morocco claims sovereignty over both.
Why does Ceuta still matter?
Ceuta’s importance today goes beyond its size.
Ceuta is considered part of Spain, but it is not included in the European Union customs territory. Its border with Morocco is also an external border of the Schengen area.
That has made Ceuta a focal point for migration and border policy as well as a recurring issue in relations between Madrid and Rabat.
The issue returned sharply to the headlines on July 30 when more than 72,000 migrants entered Ceuta from Morocco, according to the Reuters news agency.
Now Felipe’s planned visits to Ceuta and Melilla are putting the two disputed cities back in the spotlight.

German opposition demands Trump-style diesel deal with Russia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
00:05:27 UTC
09:05:27 KST

German opposition demands Trump-style diesel deal with Russia
Two German opposition parties have called for restoring economic ties with Russia following US President Donald Trump’s example in striking a diesel deal with Moscow, challenging Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s sanctions policy as soaring fuel prices put further pressure on Europe’s largest economy.
The right-wing Alternative for Germany (AfD) and the left-wing Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW), which together command a majority in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt’s parliament, are preparing a joint resolution demanding an end to the sanctions on Russia and financial support for Kiev amid growing frustration over Berlin’s foreign policy and its economic consequences.
“Germany also needs a diesel deal with Russia,” Claudia Wittig, the deputy leader of the BSW parliamentary group, said, according to German media.
Wittig described fuel prices at German filling stations as “a scandal,” arguing that the sanctions have “failed across the board” and are primarily hurting Germany itself. She insisted that Berlin should go further than a one-off fuel agreement and resume regular imports of Russian oil and gas to help rescue German industry.
“We need policies that think more about Köthen than Kiev,” Wittig said earlier, referring to a German town in Saxony-Anhalt. “We can no longer afford this war.”
AfD co-leader Alice Weidel also hailed Trump’s deal with Moscow, accusing Merz of undermining Germany’s economy with sanctions and expensive liquefied natural gas imports.
“That’s how it’s done!” she wrote on X on Saturday. “While Merz ruins Germany with sanctions and expensive LNG, Trump practices realpolitik. German interests instead of escalation!”
The initiative comes after Trump reached a surprise agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin on Friday to ease the global diesel shortage. Washington subsequently suspended sanctions on Russian diesel exports, allowing the country to release hundreds of thousands of tons of fuel to the international markets.
Trump has repeatedly blamed Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky for exacerbating the global energy crisis by targeting Russian oil refineries despite his warnings. On Saturday, he suggested that Ukrainians should replace their leader, accusing Zelensky of rejecting numerous opportunities to settle the conflict.
The joint resolution is scheduled for a vote in the Saxony-Anhalt parliament in Magdeburg on October 14. AfD and BSW hold a combined majority following September’s regional elections, although the state legislature has no authority to lift federal or EU sanctions on Russia. The initiative also marks a further breach of Germany’s longstanding political ‘firewall’ against the AfD, which mainstream parties have sought to exclude from power despite its growing support.
Merz’s government has rejected any prospects of easing its anti-Russia stance and vowed to pursue even more sanctions. Government spokesman Stefan Kornelius insisted on Saturday that Berlin’s support for Kiev is “unwavering.” Green Party co-leader Franziska Brantner blasted Trump’s agreement with Putin, calling it the height of “unscrupulousness.”
The chancellor, whose popularity has sunk so low that he faces calls to resign from within his own party, has faced mounting criticism over the impact of his policies. Wagenknecht previously accused him of turning German citizens into “cash cows for Ukraine.” Moscow has accused Merz of acting more like a “Ukrainian chancellor” than a German leader.

Former Israeli army Chief of Staff Gadi Eisenkot has overtaken Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in a public opinion poll on who is best suited to lead the country, while Netanyahu's right-wing coalition remains short of the parliamentary majority needed to govern.
The poll, broadcast by Israeli public television network KAN, projected 22 seats for Eisenkot's Yashar party in the 120-seat Knesset, compared with 20 seats for Netanyahu's Likud—down one seat from the previous week's survey—ahead of national elections scheduled for October 27.
In head-to-head suitability, Eisenkot secured 43 percent backing against 38 percent for Netanyahu.
Netanyahu's broader right-wing and religious bloc gained two seats to 53, leaving the incumbent prime minister eight mandates short of the 61-seat majority needed to build a viable governing coalition.
Parliamentary arithmetic
Eisenkot's opposing bloc was projected to secure 50 seats, while the remaining 17 seats were distributed among parties classified outside both political camps.
Arab factions were projected to take 13 seats collectively, eight for the Joint List and five for Mansour Abbas's United Arab List (Ra'am).
Within Netanyahu's coalition, National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir's Jewish Power secured nine seats, United Torah Judaism eight, Shas seven, and the Religious Zionism–Zehut alliance five.
Amcha Yisrael, headed by former brigadier general Ofer Winter, cleared the electoral threshold with four seats after previously failing to do so.
The findings underline entrenched political gridlock, indicating that neither Netanyahu's bloc nor the Jewish opposition camp can form an independent government without reaching across factional divides.
The survey also revealed acute voter fluidity, with 30 percent of electors undecided and 21 percent considering boycotting the poll, whilst 54 percent supported a televised debate between the two main contenders.

US Homeland Security secretary sees no ‘risk’ from livestreamed execution
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
23:17:05 UTC
08:17:05 KST

US Homeland Security secretary sees no ‘risk’ from livestreamed execution
The decision to livestream Nidal Hasan’s execution has triggered harsh criticism and warnings that it could encourage radicalisation.
United States Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin has defended the planned livestreaming of Nidal Hasan’s execution, playing down warnings that images of his death by firing squad might be used as a propaganda tool for violent groups.
In an interview on Sunday with the CBS News show Face the Nation, Mullin framed the decision as part of President Donald Trump’s hardline approach to crime.
“I follow President Trump. He’s a commander-in chief of the country,” Mullin said, crediting the Republican leader with “restoring America values”.
Mullin also brushed aside concerns that the images of Hasan’s execution could be leveraged against the US.
“I don’t see an elevated risk at this point at all because of this,” Mullin said. “I think people need to understand, if you attack America, we will come after you, and we will make sure that the punishment fits the crime.”
Hasan, a former US Army major, was sentenced to death in August 2013 after being convicted of shooting and killing 12 unarmed active-duty soldiers and a retired serviceman at the Fort Hood military base in Texas.
The attack took place on November 5, 2009, when Hasan opened fire in a medical facility on the base where service members receive routine check-ups before deployment. The incident is considered one of the deadliest mass shootings to take place on a US military base.
Another 32 people were injured in the shooting. In the process of responding to the attack, police on the military base shot Hasan, leaving him paralysed from the waist down.
Critics have questioned the optics of broadcasting a firing squad killing of a man in a wheelchair. The livestreamed execution is scheduled for December 3.
But Mullin dismissed those concerns, arguing that viewership is optional. “Once again, no one has to watch it if they don’t choose to,” Mullin said.
Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth had announced plans last week to livestream the upcoming execution, triggering a wave of criticism. But Trump on Saturday suggested he may reconsider the decision.
“There are two thoughts: Don’t show it and show it. Because, you know, by showing it, maybe other people won’t be doing what he did,” Trump told reporters outside the White House.
“So I’ll make a decision, ultimately. I know what the military would like to do, but we’ll make a decision.”
Lawmakers on both sides of the aisle, however, have denounced the idea of a public execution.
In a Sunday morning appearance on NBC’s Meet the Press, Republican Senator Thom Tillis warned that broadcasting Hasan’s death would “put at risk” US lives.
“Terrorist organisations will use this as a recruiting tool. It will radicalise other people, and this is not who we are,” Tillis said.
“Look, the Fort Hood shooter should be put to death, but there’s a way to deal with this that’s proper, and there’s a way to deal with this that’s more improper than I have ever observed in my life.”
Tillis, whose term as senator ends in January, also directed criticism at Hegseth for what he suggested was reckless leadership.
“It’s another example of why Pete Hegseth and all of his bravado needs to get the hell out of the Department of Defense, because he is a failed leader,” Tillis said.
The senator was considered one of the deciding votes in Hegseth’s January 2025 confirmation vote, and he has since called his support for Hegseth’s cabinet nomination “the biggest regret” of his tenure.
Other Republicans echoed Tillis’s concerns about the livestream. Senator Lisa Murkowski of Alaska, for instance, compared the public execution with something she would expect “from terrorists and dictators”.
She also argued that Hasan has sought public attention, something he would receive in a broadcast execution.
“It would give this individual, who deserves no further notoriety, the martyrdom he seeks,” Murkowski added.
Republican Representative Tom Barrett of Michigan, a former military member, issued a statement on Friday explaining that he had trained at Fort Hood a year before the attack.
He also said he opposed the public execution, despite considering Hasan “evil”.
“Secretary Hegseth should seriously reconsider this decision,” Barrett wrote on X.
“Making a public spectacle out of an already tragic situation is unnecessary and does not serve a public interest.”
Military executions are extremely rare in the US and can only be approved by the president under the Uniform Code of Military Justice.
If the order against Hasan is carried out, he will be the first member of the US military to be executed since 1961.

Talk of Russian Regime Change Could Inspire a New European Peace Strategy
While Putin doubles down to defeat Ukraine and Trump calls for regime change in Kyiv, the NATO Allies should pitch an off-ramp to Putin’s potential successors.
A Russian-British critic of Putin now living in the UK, Vladimir Kara-Murza, said in September that as long as Putin is in power the Ukraine war is not going to stop. He added that political change in Russia is inevitable, that it may not be so far away, and that when it comes, it will be swift, sudden and unexpected. Kara-Murza is not alone in seeing the writing on the wall for Putin's presidency, and the prospect of regime change in Moscow could inspire Ukraine's European allies with an alternative strategy to Trump's Putin-leaning peace process.
The new Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act in the US is designed to increase sanctions on Russia, but there is no guarantee that President Trump will take advantage of it. His current preference is to coax Putin towards a Ukraine peace with the prospect of economic links with the US, and he has gone so far as to blame President Zelensky's attacks on Russian oil refineries for the global diesel shortage, and to make a deal with Putin to suspend sanctions on Russian diesel exports. When Zelensky described this as a 'gift' to Putin, Trump called 'for Ukraine to get a new President.'
Zelensky would back a ceasefire along current frontlines followed by talks about a definitive peace, but Putin insists he will not stop fighting unless Ukraine gives up territory which Ukraine still holds. Putin wants the strategically important Donbas, and he declares he will soon acquire it on the battlefield.
In the wake of the inevitable win for his United Russia party in the election to the lower chamber of the Russian parliament – an election from which Russia's only anti-war party was excluded – Putin is likely to double down to defeat Ukraine, however heavy the cost to Russia, and to his political support among the public and the elites.
European conditions for a fresh start with Russia would include a seat for Ukraine's allies in peace negotiations if Ukraine asked for it, a just outcome on Ukraine's sovereignty, and agreed Russian funding . . . for Ukraine's post-war reconstruction
The time seems right for Ukraine's allies to start talking over Putin's head to his potential successors – to let them know that a peace that respected Ukraine's sovereignty would bring Russia a major political and economic reset with Europe as well as an end to a war that is doing serious damage to Russia.
Regime Change in Russia May Not be So Far Away
Ukraine's resistance to Putin's invasion has led to deep drone and missile strikes into Russia, huge losses to Russia's military, and a burgeoning cost to Russia's economy. Commentators are saying that Putin's replacement is a real if not imminent prospect but certainly real enough for governments to start making contingency plans.
Tatiana Stanovaya, a political scientist who moved to France from Russia some years ago, wrote in July that the focus of the Russian ruling class has shifted from how to claim the spoils of the Ukraine war to 'minimizing the colossal damage being inflicted in the pursuit of even a semblance of victory'. She argues that it will soon have to choose between 'the path of escalation and radicalization, or one that leads to a process of internal restructuring and a post-Putin world'. Europe has a strong interest in nudging Russia along the latter path.
Europe Should Launch an Alternative Peace Strategy
Ukraine's European allies have so far been confined to the fringes of Trump's Putin-friendly peace process. Now Europe has the chance to launch an alternative peace strategy, in which it pitches an off-ramp from the Ukraine war, not to Putin, for whom anything less than a military victory seems off the table, but to his potential successor or successors, for whom a just peace for Ukraine might be an acceptable price to pay for ending the war and securing a reset in Russia's links with Europe. It would be in the UK's interest to launch or to join such an initiative. Canada – close to Ukraine and to Europe's NATO Allies, and now seeking a 'unique alliance' with the EU, might also join such an alternative strategy.
Messaging the Russian Elite
European leaders and EU officials could talk openly in speeches and interviews about a future when the war is over, Ukraine's sovereignty is guaranteed, and a reset of relations with Russia becomes possible. They might not come out and call for regime change, but would be clear that a reset in relations must await new policies in Moscow, and a new Russian regime representing a clean break with the leadership which had planned and executed the Ukraine war.
European conditions for a fresh start with Russia would include a seat for Ukraine's allies in peace negotiations if Ukraine asked for it, a just outcome on Ukraine's sovereignty, and agreed Russian funding – perhaps from Russia's frozen assets in the EU and the UK, if that has not in the meantime been expropriated to pay for Ukraine's war effort – for Ukraine's post-war reconstruction.
A just peace for Ukraine would mean a U-turn by a new Russian government on the denazification narrative peddled by Putin to justify his special military operation in Ukraine. Such a U-turn would need to come in a package which could be defended to ordinary Russians and enough of the ruling class to secure their backing.
The package would bear some resemblance to the partnership which Putin had been looking for in 2000 when he sought a Russian invitation to join NATO, and access to the prosperity of the West from which he thought Russia had been excluded. The partnership would need substance but appearances would matter too.
Europe could offer symbolic prominence to Russia in a post-war scheme of summits hosted alternately by Russia, NATO Allies and the EU, along with negotiations for free trade agreements with the EU and other partners, such as the UK, Norway and Canada.
How Would Trump React?
Europe's initiative might be its own project initially, but Trump, who currently seems keener to see regime change in Ukraine than in Russia, could seek to derail it or take it over. That argues for some astute Trump-handling by Ukraine's allies rather than giving in to Trump-induced paralysis. European leaders would need to include Trump's peace process in their narrative from the outset and pay tribute to it and tell Trump that a pitch to Putin's successors was more likely to push Putin into serious negotiations than to tip Russia into regime change – which might well be the case.
Europe's first priority must be support for Ukraine in a war upon which its survival depends. But a second front in the shape of unorthodox diplomacy could dispel misconceptions on the part of the Russian elite about the effects for them of a just peace for Ukraine, and nudge Russia towards a regime change that could bring that peace about.

Syria issues first letter of credit for Saudi Aramco petroleum deal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
22:23:56 UTC
07:23:56 KST

Syria's central bank said on Sunday it issued its first letter of credit in 14 years to facilitate a petroleum products supply deal between the Syrian Petroleum Company and Saudi Aramco (2222.SE).
The bank said the transaction was arranged in coordination with a major US bank, which it did not name, opening a channel to finance oil imports and settle payments through the formal banking system.
The move marks a step toward restoring Syria's access to international banking channels following the removal of US sanctions and its designation as a state sponsor of terrorism.
Saudi Arabia's energy minister signed three memorandums of understanding with Kuwait, Qatar and Egypt to strengthen energy cooperation, the Saudi state news agency said on Sunday.
The agreement with Qatar sets a framework for collaboration in petroleum, natural gas and petrochemicals, including exploring joint opportunities to develop pipelines for transport and exports.
Syria no longer classified as state sponsor of terrorism
The United States officially removed Syria from its list of state sponsors of terrorism at the end of August. Damascus claimed at the time that the step was the last major impediment for the country to bring in foreign investment.
Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad Al-Shibani told Reuters that the government hoped removing what he called the "last obstacle" would help reconnect Syria to the global financial and economic system and boost investment. "There is no longer any obstacle to investment, doing business and rebuilding economic life in Syria," he said.
“These actions were all taken in recognition of the positive actions taken and further commitments by the Syrian government under President Ahmed Al-Sharaa to fully distance Syria from acts of international terrorism,” US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in a statement.
Syria had been on the list since 1979, when Washington accused the government of former President Hafez al-Assad of supporting militant groups. The designation remained throughout the rule of his son Bashar Al-Assad, who was toppled by rebels led by current President Ahmed Al-Sharaa in December 2024.

At least 72 Sudanese miners killed in air strike: Rights monitor
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
22:08:26 UTC
07:08:26 KST

At least 72 Sudanese miners killed in air strike: Rights monitor
Emergency Lawyers blames Egypt for the deadly attack in northern Sudan.
An air raid at a gold mine near the disputed Sudan-Egypt border has killed at least 72 workers, according to a Sudanese rights group, after survivors described scenes of chaos in the mountainous region.
Emergency Lawyers, which documents atrocities in Sudan’s war, accused the Egyptian military of carrying out the attack.
“Egyptian fighter jets targeted civilian miners in the northern Wadi area inside Sudanese territory, resulting, according to preliminary information, in the killing of 72 civilians,” the Khartoum-based rights organisation wrote on X on Sunday.
The reported attack on Saturday cannot be independently verified, and Egypt has issued no official comment.
It was this year’s second attack on the mountainous border region of Jabal al-Uqaydat, a gold mining area. Similar strikes, also reportedly carried out by Egypt, killed 23 workers at the gold mining site in June.
The Egyptian military said at the time that it had conducted a “large-scale operation” against illegal gold mining within its borders.
The border between Sudan and Egypt is disputed, with both countries claiming the resource-rich Halaib Triangle.
Images shared on social media and by local rights groups, which could not be verified, showed dozens of bodies strewn in rubble and others wrapped in funeral shrouds. Miners described an air strike on the area.
Gold rush
Since April 2023, the war in Sudan between the army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) has killed more than 200,000 people and created a humanitarian crisis that has pushed many into the dangerous gold mining industry, which fuels both sides’ war efforts.
The rugged mountainous area, home to bountiful mineral deposits, stretches for hundreds of kilometres and includes the disputed Halaib Triangle.
Emergency Lawyers said the attack occurred within Sudanese territory.
“The repeated attacks on the gold and mineral-rich border regions reflect a desire by Egyptian authorities to expand and assert control over Sudan’s natural resources,” it said.
The Egyptian army said in June that it carried out its operation “within Egyptian territory”.
It said 223 people were detained, including 136 foreign nationals, and announced a campaign to counter “illegal gold mining and arms smuggling” in the area.
Despite backing Sudan’s army chief, Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, Egypt considers the war at its border – which stretches 1,200km (745 miles) from the Red Sea to Libya – a significant threat to its security.
East of the Nile River, the porous border has for years been a thriving conduit for gold, illicit trade and human trafficking, which Egypt has tried to stem, including by using mass deportations.

Breadcrumb
Netanyahu demands probe into Israeli whistleblowers cited in award-winning Gaza film
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu called on Sunday for an investigation into the anonymous sources featured in the award-winning Gaza war documentary "NAZA".
The film is based on testimony from 24 unnamed Israeli military whistleblowers who accuse the army of killing scores of civilians in Gaza with the use of AI-powered targeting systems.
"Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu this evening asked the chief of staff of the Israeli army, the head of the Shin Bet (domestic intelligence), and the state attorney to open a thorough investigation targeting the participants in the film 'NAZA' and to prosecute them," Netanyahu's office said in a statement.
"NAZA" takes its name from the Israeli military term for civilian casualties expected in airstrikes, an abbreviated form of the Hebrew phrase for "collateral damage".
Awarded a special jury prize at the Venice Film Festival, the film received a historic 25-minute standing ovation. The film has received praise around the world for revealing the extent of Israel's atrocities in Gaza, but has triggered a political storm in Israel.
"This film tells a false, misleading and biased story that defames the State of Israel and the army around the world," Netanyahu said, according to the statement.
He has previously declared his intention to back legislation to strip citizenship from people who "defame" soldiers.
Israel's war in Gaza, determined to be a genocide by scholars and rights groups, has killed more than 74,000 people, according to the territory's health ministry.
It has also devastated the enclave's healthcare system, displaced the majority of the population and levelled entire neighbourhoods.

An Israeli drone strike has killed three Palestinians and wounded several others in southern Gaza after targeting a tent near Nasser Hospital, medical sources confirmed, marking another breach of the fragile ceasefire.
A medical source at Nasser Hospital said the casualties were brought to the facility following the strike in the al-Buraq area of central Khan Younis.

Earlier on Sunday, medical officials at al-Shifa Hospital confirmed that six-year-old Jihad Iyad al-Ghandour died of severe wounds sustained on Saturday when Israeli soldiers opened fire inside Jabalia refugee camp in northern Gaza.
Ground incursions
Separately, Israeli forces expanded territorial control in eastern Gaza City early on Sunday, injuring two Palestinians—including a pregnant woman—and forcing dozens of families to flee.
Local sources reported that Israeli armoured vehicles, accompanied by armed Palestinian forces operating under army support, advanced tens of metres into the Shujaiya neighbourhood under artillery cover and quadcopter fire.
Troops fired heavily across the sector stretching from the eastern vegetable market to the Shujaiya intersection on Salah al-Din Street.
For roughly a week, eastern neighbourhoods including Tuffah and Shujaiya have faced night-time demolitions, artillery bombardment, and armoured patrols along the "yellow line", which demarcates Israeli-held sectors from civilian areas.
According to Gaza's Health Ministry, Israeli violations of the truce agreement enacted on October 10, 2025, have killed 1,488 Palestinians and injured 5,281 as of Sunday.
Since the wider war began in October 2023, more than 74,000 Palestinians have been killed, over 175,000 wounded, and roughly 90 percent of the enclave's infrastructure destroyed.

Greens leader seeks rule change after party declares Zionism is racism
Zack Polanski calls for internal rule reforms to give party leaders greater control over policy after Zionism vote.
Zack Polanski, the leader of the Green Party of England and Wales, has proposed a potential overhaul of his party’s democratic mechanisms, calling for the leader to have larger control over strategic direction.
The appeal came in an article published in The Guardian on Sunday after party members passed a motion declaring that Zionism is racism at their annual conference on October 4 in a divisive vote.
Polanski also failed to grab a parliamentary seat in the wake of the row with Israel in a by-election.
The Labour Party won the election for the parliamentary seat vacated by former leader Keir Starmer in Holborn and St Pancras on Friday, fending off a strong challenge from the left-wing Green Party in a boost for British Prime Minister Andy Burnham.
“Our party democracy must now evolve to meet that – creating wider engagement for members, giving leaders more responsibility to set the party’s strategic direction, and making our processes as robust and accessible as possible,” he wrote.
“Above all, that unity must be deployed in the service of changing this country for the better,” the Green Party leader added.
Criticism over vote on motion
Polanski also replied to the criticisms of him for not participating in the vote on the motion on Zionism.
“I have been asked why I was not present for the vote. The answer is that my priority was fighting a hugely consequential by-election for our party,” he said, adding that he put all his “energy into the race in Holborn and St Pancras”.
He admitted that some members feel “let down” by his decision not to make an appearance there.
The Green Party’s motion, which called for “Palestinian liberation, the right of return, Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions (BDS), and a full arms embargo against Israel” was criticised by Jewish groups, other parties and most Green Party MPs.
After conceding defeat in the fiercely contested by-election, Polanski answered his critics, saying he would stay on as leader.
He was barred from entering Israel after his party backed a motion to define Zionism as racism.

Two killed near Israeli-occupied area in south Lebanon
Despite a ceasefire agreement reached between Israel and Lebanon in June, Israeli attacks continue.
Two men have been killed in southern Lebanon’s Bint Jbeil district while taking part in an annual olive harvest, according to Lebanese state media and local authorities, as attacks by Israel continue.
One of the men died Sunday in the village of Froun from a munition left behind by recent fighting and the other in Yater as a result of Israeli shelling that “targeted the outskirts of the town while he was inspecting his land and olive harvest”, according to the official National News Agency (NNA).
The Lebanese army blamed Israeli tank fire and called the ongoing attacks “a flagrant breach of existing agreements”.
Afterwards, the Yater municipality urged residents “to avoid the outskirts of the town and refrain from crossing the earthen barrier separating some unsafe neighbourhoods” for fear of Israeli attacks.
In Froun, the NNA reported that “a foreign object” left over from previous Israeli operations exploded and killed the man, who was an engineer, as he and others tended their trees.
The engineer had come down from Beirut, where he lives, for the harvest, Froun mayor Hassan Bazzi told AFP.
The incident prompted local residents to call off the harvest and wait for “the Lebanese army to complete the decontamination of the village”, Bazzi said.
Displaced people
Since an agreement between Lebanon and Israel was struck in June, violence in the south has lessened, but not stopped.
Lebanon was pulled into conflict on March 2, when Hezbollah struck Israel in support of Tehran during the US-Israel war on Iran. Subsequently, Israel launched a bombing campaign and a ground invasion that authorities say have killed more than 4,300.
In August, Lebanon’s Prime Minister Nawaf Salam accused Israel of intentionally targeting homes and civilian infrastructure across the country. The International Organization for Migration (IOM) recorded nearly 350,000 internally displaced people in late August, a sign of the worsening displacement crisis.
Volunteers from the nearby town of Jebchit and locals came to help their southern neighbours with the harvest in an act of solidarity.
“From north to south, one people and one land,” said organiser Ahmad Chahhal.

Axios: Trump's "energy ceasefire" would cover only attacks on oil refineries
A White House official has told Axios that an "energy ceasefire", as understood by US President Donald Trump, means that Russia and Ukraine will stop attacks solely on each other's oil refineries, and that this is what Washington expects Ukraine to do. However, Ukraine has only one oil refinery, which is not operating at full capacity.
Source: Axios, citing sources
Quote: "President Trump's announcement Sunday about an 'energy ceasefire' between Russia and Ukraine referred to a potential deal that includes each side stopping attacks on oil refineries – and he expects Volodymyr Zelenskyy to abide by it, a White House official said.
The official said if attacks on oil refineries cease, a deal to stop hitting power plants and energy grids could come next."
Details: Axios said the "refinery for refinery" proposal, as the White House official described it, is not an equal arrangement.
A Ukrainian official told Axios that the country has only one oil refinery, which the Russians have attacked repeatedly and which is not operating at full capacity. Russia, by contrast, has an extensive network of oil refineries.
"We import diesel and gas. What we need is for the Russians to stop attacking our electricity grid," the Ukrainian official said.
"The Russians are thinking about it. We will know soon if they are ready," the White House official said.
Axios wrote that White House officials warn that Ukraine's attacks on Russian oil refineries are doing more damage to Zelenskyy's relationship with Trump than to Russia itself.
"Trump is really mad. He feels Zelenskyy is taking the US for granted," the White House official said.
The report also said that Trump's envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner have postponed their planned trip to Moscow amid the crisis with Ukraine, "at least until they get clarity on whether Ukraine and the Europeans are ready to agree to a new unified proposal for Putin".
Background:
- On 11 October, US President Donald Trump claimed that Ukraine and Russia had agreed to an immediate energy ceasefire.
- Barak Ravid, a journalist at American news portal Axios, stated that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy had been unaware of the "energy ceasefire" between Ukraine and Russia announced by Trump, but is willing to agree to it.
- Zelenskyy later said that, following Trump's statement, the Russians had struckCHPP-5 (a combined heat and power plant) in Kharkiv and a power station in Kyiv.
- Russia has yet to comment on Trump's statement.
- Meanwhile, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said that Russia had violated the "energy ceasefire" immediately after it was announced by Trump.

London Halal Forum kicks off second day with Palestinian breakfast
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
20:06:23 UTC
05:06:23 KST

The second day of the annual London Halal Forum, bringing together entrepreneurs, investors, and industry leaders, began with a traditional Palestinian breakfast, offering an authentic experience celebrating Palestinian cuisine and heritage.
The event, being held at the Queen Elizabeth II Centre in London and organised by Halal360, is a joint initiative of the Islamic Chamber of Commerce and Development (ICCD) and the Halal Products Development Company (HPDC).
The breakfast offers traditional delicacies to participants, including hummus, zaatar, labneh, and falafel.
'Genocide continues'
Speaking at the event, Bilal Erdogan, the deputy chairman of Ibn Haldun University’s Board of Trustees, said it is meaningful to be at the forum with a group of guests who care about Palestine, who care about the conscience of humanity, "that's been tarnished tremendously throughout the last three years."
Recalling a mass pro-Palestine rally in Istanbul that was held on January 1, 2026, he said people will once again stage a demonstration next year to remember Palestine.
"We will tell the world about the genocide, and we will show solidarity with our brothers and sisters in Palestine for what they have been suffering throughout, especially in these last three years, but obviously since 1948," said Erdogan.
He underlined that an immense humanitarian situation continues in Gaza despite "the so-called ceasefire situation."
"Unfortunately, every day genocide continues. Every day, we have attacks. Every day, we have killings, not only in Gaza but also in the West Bank."
Warning that the situation in the occupied West Bank and East Jerusalem is "getting worse", Erdogan stressed "we have to make sure" that resources that "we can put together" are strategically managed so that "we have better outcomes".
Referring to recent sanctions by some Western countries targeting trade with illegal Israeli settlements, he noted, "That's the beginning."
"Hopefully, they will extend that to hold (whole) Israeli products at some point."
"This breakfast is sort of a complete version of what we need to do about that, really empowering the producers, empowering the investors, and empowering any startups coming from the region."
Erdogan added that it should start from the ground, from food, but it should grow into "more valued sectors", in technology, in medicine, and in other fields.
Türkiye will continue to do whatever it can, he said, adding that the issue of Palestine transcends any political lines and issues.
"Inshallah, we can get together and do these meetings in Al-Quds, all together in peace and harmony," he added.
'Israel also pursuing economic war'
Also speaking at the venue, Palestinian Ambassador to the UK Husam Zomlot said the genocide is ongoing in Gaza and ethnic cleansing is ongoing in the occupied West Bank, noting "Israeli settler terrorists" attacks targeting the Palestinian olive harvest.
The ambassador said Israel is also pursuing an economic war against Palestinian people, which has continued for decades.
Türkiye's ambassador to London, Osman Koray Ertas, was also among the attendees.
A video about the Palestinian Museum, which aims to present and contribute to narratives on Palestinian history, culture, and society, was screened during the program.
Under the theme Halal Tayyib for Humanity, the forum is examining the halal economy’s expansion beyond certification and food products into investment, tourism, technology, supply chains, branding, and international trade.
The first edition of the forum was held in November 2025 at Excel London, bringing together over 1,500 participants, both in-person and virtually, highlighting London's emerging role as a key player in the growing global halal economy.

Ben Gvir left with a dilemma as Israeli parties seal election deals: How the system works
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
20:04:31 UTC
05:04:31 KST

Gadi Eisenkot with Yair Golan, Likud with Religious Zionism, Naftali Bennett with Avigdor Lieberman, Shas with United Torah Judaism, Ra'am with the Joint List, and perhaps Itamar Ben Gvir with Ofer Winter? Since Israel's founding, political parties have routinely signed agreements designed to maximize their electoral strength and prevent votes from going to waste in Knesset elections. 
Known as surplus-vote agreements, these arrangements allow two parties, usually ideologically aligned or belonging to the same political camp, to combine their votes for the final allocation of parliamentary seats. The goal is to ensure that votes left over after the initial count can help secure additional representation. So how does the system work, who benefits, and what could it mean for the October 27 election? Here's a guide.
Why are surplus-vote agreements necessary?
After polling stations close and all valid votes in a Knesset election are counted, seats are allocated among the parties that have passed the electoral threshold, based on the 120 seats in Israel's parliament. This begins the process of distributing Knesset seats.
The electoral threshold currently stands at 3.25% of valid votes, roughly equivalent to four Knesset seats. The number of votes needed to cross that threshold changes from one election to another, depending on turnout and the number of invalid ballots. In the previous election in 2022, a party needed at least 154,855 votes to qualify for representation.
The valid votes received by each qualifying party are then converted into a whole number of seats. The electoral quota represents the number of votes required for one Knesset seat. It is calculated by dividing the total number of valid votes cast for parties that crossed the electoral threshold by 120. In the 2022 election, the quota was 36,227 votes, meaning that approximately 36,227 votes were equivalent to one seat.
In most cases, however, parties are left with surplus votes that are insufficient to secure another full seat. These represent fractions of seats that remain unallocated after the initial distribution. This is where surplus-vote agreements come into play.
How does the system work?
Under the Bader-Ofer method, introduced in 1973, two parties that have signed a surplus-vote agreement are treated as a single list for the purpose of allocating the remaining seats. After all valid votes have been counted and the initial allocation of whole seats is completed, the remaining seats are distributed using a mathematical formula.
The calculation takes the combined number of votes received by the two parties and divides it by the number of seats they have already been allocated, plus one. For example, if two parties receive a combined 400,000 votes and are initially awarded 11 seats, their joint quotient would be 400,000 divided by 12, or approximately 33,333 votes.
That figure is then compared with the quotients calculated for all other parties or pairs of parties. The party or pair with the highest quotient receives the next available seat. The calculation is then repeated for the following seat, with the number of seats already awarded adjusted accordingly.
If a pair of parties that signed a surplus-vote agreement wins an additional seat, a separate calculation determines which of the two receives it.
That internal allocation is also carried out under the Bader-Ofer formula. In practice, the larger of the two parties often has an advantage, even if it does not have the largest number of leftover votes. However, the smaller party can also receive the additional seat, as has happened in previous elections.
The system generally favors larger parties, but a surplus-vote agreement can improve the chances of either partner securing an additional seat.
Which parties benefit from signing, and what happens to those that don't?
Surplus-vote agreements are signed between two electoral lists and may be submitted, under Israeli law, until 11 days before election day, subject to approval by the Central Elections Committee.
With the next election scheduled for October 27, just 16 days away, parties have until October 16 to decide whether to enter into such agreements. As a rule, the parties that sign these agreements are ideologically close or belong to the same political camp. Their shared objective is to maximize the number of seats their camp receives.
The electoral threshold is particularly important because a surplus-vote agreement is valid only if both parties cross it. Signing an agreement with a party that may fail to enter the Knesset therefore carries a significant risk.
If one of the two parties fails to cross the threshold, the agreement becomes ineffective, and the votes cast for the unsuccessful party are excluded from the allocation of Knesset seats.
The mechanism is not unique to Israel. Similar systems for distributing remaining parliamentary seats are used, or have been used, in other democracies. The Bader-Ofer method takes its name from former Knesset members Yohanan Bader of Gahal and Avraham Ofer of the Alignment, who initiated the legislation.
It replaced an earlier system under which the party with the largest remainder of unused votes received the next available seat, a method that tended to benefit smaller parties.
A party that does not sign a surplus-vote agreement can still compete independently for additional seats under the Bader-Ofer formula, but it cannot benefit from combining its votes with another party.
Such a decision can also expose a party to criticism from within its political camp, particularly if its refusal to cooperate is perceived as weakening the bloc's overall chances of gaining seats.
Who has signed with whom?
About a month ago, four parties opposed to another term for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu announced that they had signed surplus-vote agreements. The first agreement was announced by former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett, chairman of the Together party, and Avigdor Lieberman, chairman of Yisrael Beytenu.
Gadi Eisenkot, chairman of the Yashar! party, had preferred to sign an agreement with another party in the anti-Netanyahu camp but ultimately found himself paired with Yair Golan and his Democrats party.
In a statement, Eisenkot's party took credit for organizing the opposition camp, saying he had "worked in various ways to organize the camp of change and hope as effectively as possible."
"The camp's consolidation into four parties has, fortunately, created the possibility of signing mutual, internal surplus-vote agreements, drawing lessons from previous election campaigns," the statement said.
The Joint List and Ra'am, the United Arab List, subsequently signed their own surplus-vote agreement, seeking to prevent votes from being wasted in the election. As part of the agreement, the two Arab-led lists committed to conducting a "fair and clean election campaign, without personal attacks, defamation, incitement or falsification."
They also called on activists and supporters to maintain respectful political discourse despite their disagreements.
In the previous election, three Arab lists ran separately: Ra'am, Hadash-Ta'al and Balad. None signed surplus-vote agreements with the others, and Balad ultimately failed to cross the electoral threshold.
The next agreement was between Likud and Religious Zionism. The deal between Netanyahu and Religious Zionism chairman Bezalel Smotrich left Itamar Ben Gvir's Otzma Yehudit party with the option of signing an agreement with Ofer Winter's Amcha Yisrael party or remaining without a partner.
That dilemma comes as Likud has intensified its campaign against Winter. The party led by Yoaz Hendel and Yaron Zelekha also offered Winter a surplus-vote agreement, but he did not respond.
"Unfortunately, Likud refused to sign a surplus-vote agreement with us as part of an attempt to weaken our party and leave Ben Gvir outside the unity government Likud is planning with Eisenkot," Otzma Yehudit said after the Netanyahu-Smotrich agreement was announced.
The prospect of an agreement with Winter carries its own risk for Ben Gvir. If Amcha Yisrael fails to cross the electoral threshold, the agreement would have no effect.
Either way, the latest parties to sign a surplus-vote agreement were the ultra-Orthodox Shas and United Torah Judaism.
The two parties emphasized that their agreement reflected the "continuation of cooperation between the factions, in accordance with the instructions of the leading rabbis and sages of the generation."
In a joint statement, the parties led by Aryeh Deri and Yaakov Asher said: "In the next Knesset, too, we will continue to cooperate fully on the core issues concerning the preservation of the Torah world and the status of yeshiva students."

Scientists discover why a 100-year-old mushroom disease won't go away
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
20:01:25 UTC
05:01:25 KST

Scientists discover why a 100-year-old mushroom disease won't go away
- Date:
- October 11, 2026
- Source:
- University of Florida
- Summary:
- Scientists have uncovered a surprising secret behind a mushroom disease that has frustrated growers for more than a century: It involves more than 17 species of harmful bacteria, not just one. The discovery could explain why treatments have struggled to stop the disease and open the door to more effective, eco-friendly solutions.
- Share:
A disease that has troubled white button mushroom growers for more than 100 years is far more complicated than scientists previously believed. Researchers at the University of Florida have discovered that the problem involves a surprisingly diverse collection of harmful bacteria, rather than a single pathogen. The finding could help explain why the disease has been so difficult to control and lead to more effective ways to protect mushroom crops.
The discovery comes from a University of Florida study investigating bacterial blotch, a persistent disease that damages white button mushrooms and causes significant financial losses for growers.
White button mushrooms are a valuable specialty crop and a familiar ingredient in everything from salads and appetizers to everyday meals. Rich in nutrients and valued for their versatility, they are often promoted as an example of the "food is medicine" concept, which emphasizes the role of nutritious foods in supporting good health. Their nutritional benefits make them an important part of many healthy diets.
Despite their popularity, these mushrooms face a longstanding problem that can make entire portions of a harvest difficult or impossible to sell.
A Century-Old Mushroom Disease With Hidden Culprits
Bacterial blotch causes brown or yellow discoloration on mushroom surfaces, damaging their appearance and reducing their commercial value. The disease can also lower crop yields and shorten shelf life, making it a costly challenge for mushroom farms across the United States.
Adding to the difficulty, visible symptoms sometimes develop only after mushrooms have been shipped to grocery stores or purchased by consumers. This delayed appearance makes the disease especially troublesome for growers trying to ensure consistent product quality.
For many years, scientists primarily associated bacterial blotch with a single disease-causing bacterial pathogen. However, researchers at the University of Florida Institute of Food and Agricultural Sciences (UF/IFAS) have now found that the disease involves a much more complex collection of pathogenic bacteria.
These microorganisms can thrive in the carefully controlled, humid indoor environments used for commercial mushroom cultivation. Because several bacterial species may contribute to the same disease, methods designed to target a single pathogen may not be sufficient.
"For years, the industry has struggled with treatments that provide inconsistent results against bacterial blotch," said Samuel Martins, co-author and assistant professor in the UF/IFAS Department of Plant Pathology. "As part of a separate $7 million U.S. Department of Agriculture grant involving Penn State, University of Delaware and UF/IFAS, we are developing advanced diagnostics and sustainable solutions to strengthen mushroom farms nationwide."
DNA Analysis Reveals More Than 17 Bacterial Species
To investigate what was causing the disease, the research team collected affected mushrooms from several production facilities across the southern United States.
The scientists combined DNA sequencing, chemical profiling and conventional laboratory testing to identify the bacteria associated with the damaged mushrooms. DNA sequencing allowed them to examine the genetic identities of microorganisms present in the samples, while the additional tests helped characterize the bacteria and their disease-causing potential.
The results revealed a far more diverse group of pathogens than expected.
"We found more than 17 different species of pathogenic bacteria associated with the disease," said Sameerika Mudiyanselage, the study's lead author and a doctoral student of Martins and Romina Gazis at UF/IFAS Tropical Research and Education Center. "While two well-known bacterial pathogens dominated the known disease profile, we also detected a surprisingly high level of another group of bacteria that has not previously been linked to the mushroom disease."
The discovery suggests that scientists have been overlooking important contributors to bacterial blotch. Although two established pathogens remained prominent, the presence of additional bacterial groups indicates that the disease cannot be fully understood by studying those organisms alone.
This complexity may help explain why bacterial blotch has persisted for generations despite efforts to manage it. When several different microorganisms are associated with a disease, identifying the responsible bacteria, predicting outbreaks, and developing consistently effective treatments become more challenging.
The findings also suggest that growers may need more comprehensive detection methods capable of identifying a broader range of bacterial threats.
"We hope that expanding our research will lead to the development of better diagnostics and more effective treatments to address the full group of disease-causing bacteria in white button mushrooms," she said.
Natural Treatments Could Help Protect Mushroom Farms
The University of Florida researchers are now building on their findings with a follow-up study focused on more sustainable ways to manage bacterial blotch.
One promising approach involves testing plant-based essential oils, beneficial microorganisms, and other biological products as possible alternatives to conventional chemical treatments.
Essential oils contain naturally occurring compounds produced by plants, some of which have antimicrobial properties. Beneficial microbes may also help suppress harmful bacteria or make it more difficult for disease-causing organisms to thrive.
These approaches could eventually offer mushroom growers additional tools for controlling bacterial blotch while reducing their reliance on conventional chemical treatments. However, further research is needed to determine how well the potential alternatives work under real growing conditions.
"Ultimately, our goal is to provide growers with practical, science-based solutions that help strengthen mushroom farming systems," said Martins. "By understanding the complexity of bacterial blotch and the role of microbial communities, we can develop better eco-friendly management practices that reduce losses while improving sustainability."
The research changes the understanding of a disease that has affected white button mushroom production for more than a century. Rather than being the work of a single bacterial pathogen, bacterial blotch involves a diverse group of potentially harmful microorganisms, including previously overlooked species.
By uncovering this hidden complexity, scientists hope to improve disease detection, develop more reliable treatments, and reduce the crop losses that have long burdened mushroom producers. The findings could ultimately help make mushroom farming more resilient, productive and environmentally sustainable.
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of Florida. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Sameerika D. Mudiyanselage, Michelle Lee, Jose C. Huguet-Tapia, Romina Gazis, Samuel J. Martins. Genomic insights into a multispecies bacterial pathogen complex driving bacterial blotch in white button mushrooms. Microbiological Research, 2026; 309: 128532 DOI: 10.1016/j.micres.2026.128532

A chemical produced by gut bacteria may accelerate Alzheimer’s disease
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
20:00:56 UTC
05:00:56 KST

A byproduct produced by certain gut bacteria may directly accelerate the brain changes associated with Alzheimer’s disease. Elevated blood levels of this molecule, known as imidazole propionate, correlate with worse cognitive decline in humans and actively drive neurodegeneration in animal models. The findings were published in Nature Communications.
The human digestive tract contains trillions of bacteria that help break down food. During this process, microbes release chemical byproducts into the bloodstream. These chemicals, called metabolites, travel throughout the body and influence the function of various organs, including the brain.
Imidazole propionate is a specific metabolite generated when gut bacteria break down histidine, an amino acid found in many common foods. Previous research linked elevated levels of this molecule to metabolic conditions like type 2 diabetes and heart disease. Because metabolic problems often increase the risk of developing dementia, researchers suspected the chemical might also affect brain health.
Researchers Vaibhav Vemuganti and Jea Woo Kang from the University of Wisconsin-Madison led the investigation alongside senior authors Barbara B. Bendlin and Federico E. Rey. They aimed to test whether imidazole propionate directly influences the biological pathways involved in cognitive aging and Alzheimer’s disease.
The team began by analyzing blood samples from nearly 1,200 older adults, most of whom had no diagnosed cognitive impairment. They measured the concentration of imidazole propionate in each participant’s blood and compared those levels against the participants’ scores on standardized memory and problem-solving tests. To isolate the effects of the chemical, the researchers adjusted their calculations for age, sex, body mass index, and the APOE gene, a known genetic risk factor for Alzheimer’s disease.
People with the highest levels of the gut metabolite performed worse on cognitive tests at the start of the study. Over years of follow-up visits, these same individuals experienced an earlier and more rapid decline in memory and executive function compared to those with lower levels. Statistical models predicted that the cognitive performance of the high-metabolite group fell below that of the low-metabolite group roughly 15 to 18 years before the participants’ average age.
To look for underlying physical changes, the researchers measured molecular markers of Alzheimer’s disease in the participants’ blood and cerebrospinal fluid. Cerebrospinal fluid is the clear liquid that surrounds and protects the brain and spinal cord. High blood levels of imidazole propionate correlated with elevated amounts of tau tangles and neurofilament light chain, a structural protein that leaks out of damaged brain cells.
The researchers then analyzed the genetic material of gut bacteria from fecal samples provided by 294 participants. They specifically searched for a bacterial gene called urdA, which provides the biological instructions for making the enzyme that produces imidazole propionate. They identified this gene in several bacterial families, including certain strains of Streptococcus.
A higher abundance of bacteria carrying this gene was linked to lower cognitive scores and elevated Alzheimer’s biomarkers in the human participants. To investigate if this relationship is a direct cause and effect in humans, the team turned to large genetic databases. They used a statistical method that treats genetic inheritance like a randomized trial to evaluate whether naturally occurring biological traits lead to specific diseases.
The analysis revealed a specific genetic variant on chromosome 12 that causes some people to naturally accumulate higher levels of imidazole propionate in their blood. Carrying this genetic variant was associated with an increased risk of developing Alzheimer’s disease, suggesting the metabolite actively promotes the condition rather than acting as a harmless bystander.
The researchers then conducted small studies using two different mouse models genetically engineered to develop Alzheimer’s-like brain changes. One model mimics the buildup of amyloid plaques, while the other mimics the accumulation of tau tangles. The researchers added imidazole propionate to the animals’ drinking water for several months.
In mice predisposed to accumulating amyloid plaques, a sticky protein fragment associated with Alzheimer’s, the treated animals developed more plaques in their brains than mice drinking regular water. In a second group of mice predisposed to tau tangles, the treatment caused severe inflammation and triggered the hyperactivity of star-shaped support cells called astrocytes. By analyzing the entire spectrum of proteins in the mouse brains, the researchers also detected elevated levels of proteins linked to structural breakdown in the nerve fibers.
Because the metabolite originates in the gut, it must travel through the blood to reach the brain. The researchers tested how the chemical affects the blood-brain barrier, a tightly packed layer of cells that lines brain blood vessels and protects neural tissue from circulating toxins.
They exposed human brain blood vessel cells to the metabolite in a laboratory setting. The molecule reduced the electrical resistance of the cell layer, indicating a breakdown in barrier integrity. In a separate test, the researchers injected a blue dye into the bloodstream of treated mice. The dye leaked extensively into the brain tissue, showing that the chemical damages blood vessels and allows substances to abnormally enter the brain.
In a final set of experiments, the team applied the metabolite directly to isolated mouse neurons grown in culture. They also added a chemical inhibitor that blocks an enzyme called GSK3-beta. This enzyme is known to abnormally attach phosphate molecules to tau proteins, causing them to tangle and destroy brain cells.
Exposure to the gut metabolite caused the cultured neurons to rapidly accumulate damaged tau proteins. Blocking the GSK3-beta enzyme completely reversed this effect, outlining the specific molecular pathway the gut chemical uses to damage brain cells.
While the human observational data points to a strong relationship, it cannot definitively prove that lowering imidazole propionate will prevent dementia. The animal experiments relied entirely on male mice given the chemical in their drinking water, which may not perfectly replicate how the metabolite is naturally produced and absorbed in the human digestive system.
Future studies will need to test female animals to determine if the biological effects differ by sex. Researchers will also need to explore whether specific dietary changes or targeted medications can safely reduce the production of this metabolite in the human gut.
The study, “Gut bacterial metabolite imidazole propionate potentiates Alzheimer’s disease pathology,” was authored by Vaibhav Vemuganti, Jea Woo Kang, Qijun Zhang, Eric R. McGregor, James R. Hilser, Ruben Aquino-Martinez, Sandra Harding, Joseph Lawrence Harpt, Katharina R. Beck, Hailey Bussan, Jessamine F. Kuehn, Yuetiva Deming, Rachel Studer, Sterling C. Johnson, Sanjay Asthana, Henrik Zetterberg, Kaj Blennow, Corinne D. Engelman, Hooman Allayee, Rozalyn M. Anderson, Tyler K. Ulland, Fredrik Bäckhed, Barbara B. Bendlin, and Federico E. Rey.

Two killed near Israeli-occupied zone in south Lebanon
Two men were killed in south Lebanon on Sunday, one by Israeli fire and the other by an explosive remnant of war, as they took part in the annual olive harvest, according to state media and local officials.
South Lebanon has been the scene of two wars since 2023 between Israel and Hezbollah, and Israeli troops still occupy a band of territory 10 kilometres (six miles) wide running along the border.
The official National News Agency (NNA) said one of the men was killed in Yater, in Bint Jbeil district, when Israeli "shelling targeted the outskirts of the town while he was inspecting his land and olive harvest".
The Lebanese army blamed Israeli tank fire and called the ongoing attacks "a flagrant breach of existing agreements".
Afterwards, the Yater municipality urged residents "to avoid the outskirts of the town and refrain from crossing the earthen barrier separating some unsafe neighborhoods" for fear of Israeli attacks.
In the village of Froun, in the same district, the NNA reported that "a foreign object" left over from previous Israeli operations exploded and killed an engineer as he and others tended their trees.
The engineer had come down from Beirut, where he lives, for the harvest, Froun mayor Hassan Bazzi told AFP.
The incident prompted local residents to call off the harvest and wait for "the Lebanese army to complete the decontamination of the village", Bazzi said.
Since a framework agreement between Lebanon and Israel was struck in June, the violence in the south has diminished but not stopped.
Israel continues to carry out sporadic strikes and demolitions in and around the territory it occupies, while Hezbollah refuses to submit to government plans to disarm it.
About eight kilometres (five miles) away, in Jibshit, volunteers from the north came to help locals with the harvest in a show of solidarity.
"From north to south, one people and one land," said organiser Ahmad Chahhal.
As workers swatted at branches to make the olives fall, an AFP photographer saw drones and heard fighter jets overhead, and explosions could be heard in the distance.
Israel has ramped up its bombardment of Lebanon since March, with intense strikes and a ground invasion.
The framework deal between Israel and Lebanon involves Hezbollah's disarmament, a gradual Israeli withdrawal, and the deployment of the Lebanese army to the region.

A new Israeli election poll published by public broadcaster Kan Sunday shows former IDF chief Gadi Eisenkot's bloc shrinking by two seats, while Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's bloc rises two seats, bolstered in part by far-right Ofer Winter's Amcha Yisrael crossing the electoral threshold,
Eisenkot's bloc stands at 50 Knesset seats, down from 52 last week, while the governing coalition rose from 51 to 53. 61 members are necessary for a majority in the Knesset. The Arab parties, meanwhile, hold steady at 13 seats.
Eisenkot's Yashar party loses one seat compared with last week but remains the largest party, with 22 seats. Likud also loses one seat, falling to 20. Bennett's Together holds steady at 12 seats. Yisrael Beiteinu drops one seat to eight, while Otzma Yehudit gains one to reach nine.

Winter's Amcha Yisrael crosses the threshold, after failing to do so in Kan's previous poll, standing on four seats.
Blue and White remains below the electoral threshold, with just 0.9 percent of the vote, as does the Haredi Public party, also at 0.9 percent.
In a question about suitability for prime minister, Eisenkot leads Netanyahu by 43 percent to 38 percent. The poll also found that 30 percent of respondents have yet to decide whom they will vote for.
The poll was conducted by Kantar, headed by Dudu Hasid, among 552 respondents. The margin of error is 4.2 percentage points.

Mexican president urges residents to shelter as Hurricane Simon approaches

Mexican president urges residents to shelter as Hurricane Simon approaches
The Mexican community of Cabo Corrientes faces the risk of a direct hit as the Category 4 storm churns off Jalisco.
Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum has urged residents along the Pacific Ocean to stay indoors as Hurricane Simon’s powerful winds and heavy rains pound coastal communities.
As of Sunday, the hurricane’s eye was moving offshore of Mexico’s Jalisco state, with winds of at least 240km/h (150mph).
Torrential rain has already battered residents living between the Sierra Madre mountain range and the ocean. Communities in hilly and mountainous areas have been warned to brace for mudslides.
Simon reached Category 4 strength, on a scale of five, on Saturday, as part of an unusually active Pacific hurricane season.
“With the approaching impact of Category 4 Hurricane Simon, we urge residents of coastal municipalities in Jalisco, Colima, Nayarit and Michoacan to remain sheltered until authorities officially declare that the danger has passed,” Sheinbaum wrote in a post on the social media platform X on Sunday.
In a midday advisory, the United States’ National Hurricane Center (NHC) warned that Simon could produce “additional rainfall totals of 8 to 16 inches (20 to 41 cm) over portions of southwestern Mexico”.
Precipitation totals as high as 76 cm (30 inches) were possible in areas of Michoacan, Colima, and Jalisco until Monday.
It’s not clear whether the storm will make landfall. But the greatest risk of a direct hit lies at the moment with Cabo Corrientes, a town that sits on a cape in Jalisco, jutting into the Pacific Ocean.
Mexico’s National Civil Protection Coordination (CNPC) placed 28 municipalities in Jalisco and Colima under its highest cyclone alert level, while another 93 municipalities were under a high alert level, according to civil protection bulletins.
Classes were suspended in the affected areas, and efforts to evacuate residents were under way.
Businesses in popular tourist destinations like Puerto Vallarta boarded up windows and placed sandbags at entrances as the storm approached.
Jalisco’s Governor Pablo Navarro warned that the high-powered hurricane was creating “high-risk marine conditions” along the coast of his state, with waves reaching as high as eight metres (26 feet).
On Sunday, he also shared video on social media of the storm surge crashing onto sidewalks and flooding waterways.
“Here is the current state of Jalisco’s beaches this morning — from Barra de Navidad to Puerto Vallarta — as Hurricane Simon passes through,” he wrote in the video’s caption.
“I ask everyone to heed official instructions, take precautions and avoid putting themselves at risk. The safety of Jalisco’s families is the top priority.”

The hidden math of Alzheimer's could point to new treatments
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
19:24:25 UTC
04:24:25 KST

The hidden math of Alzheimer's could point to new treatments
- Date:
- October 11, 2026
- Source:
- Mississippi State University
- Summary:
- Mathematics may hold unexpected clues to understanding Alzheimer’s disease. Scientists have developed a model showing how common metals like copper and zinc may influence the buildup of proteins associated with the disease, while also exploring possible ways to stop the process. The findings could help researchers identify promising strategies for preventing harmful plaque formation.
- Share:
Could mathematics help uncover new ways to fight Alzheimer's disease? A researcher at Mississippi State University is using mathematical models to investigate how common metals influence the buildup of proteins associated with Alzheimer's and whether potential treatments could interfere with this process.
Shantia Yarahmadian, an associate professor in Mississippi State's Department of Mathematics and Statistics, is studying how metals such as copper and zinc may affect the behavior of amyloid-beta, a protein that can clump together and form plaques linked to Alzheimer's disease.
His research, published in the journal Bulletin of Mathematical Biology, builds on his ongoing efforts to use mathematics to better understand the complex biological processes involved in Alzheimer's.
Using Mathematics To Understand Alzheimer's Disease
Mathematical modeling allows scientists to explore complicated biological interactions by representing them through equations and simulations. Researchers can then test how different factors influence a process and predict what might happen when certain conditions change.
"Every biological phenomenon occurs in the physical world -- in space and time -- and involves changes in shape, quantity and matter," said Yarahmadian, a faculty member in MSU's Department of Mathematics and Statistics. "Because of its abstract power, mathematics allows us to uncover patterns, test hypotheses and make predictions that may not be possible through observation alone. Mathematics does not replace laboratory or clinical research; it complements it by helping us understand the larger system, identify the most influential mechanisms and guide future experiments."
This approach could be particularly valuable for Alzheimer's disease, which involves numerous interacting biological processes that are difficult to study individually.
How Copper and Zinc May Influence Alzheimer's Plaques
To investigate how Alzheimer's-related plaques develop, Yarahmadian created a mathematical framework that simulates the chemical reactions involved when metals such as copper and zinc interact with amyloid-beta.
Amyloid-beta proteins can stick together in a process known as aggregation. Over time, these clusters can contribute to the formation of plaques, one of the characteristic features of Alzheimer's disease.
The model examines how metal ions, which are electrically charged forms of metals, may influence this protein buildup. It also enables researchers to explore two potential therapeutic approaches designed to interfere with aggregation.
Rather than relying entirely on laboratory experiments, scientists can use the simulations to investigate how changes in these interactions might affect plaque formation and identify promising directions for further research.
Mathematical Predictions Match Laboratory Results
A mathematical model is most useful when its predictions reflect what happens in actual experiments. To evaluate his framework, Yarahmadian and his collaborators compared its results with laboratory measurements obtained through atomic force microscopy.
This imaging technique uses an extremely fine probe to examine structures at the microscopic scale, allowing researchers to study tiny clusters of proteins and other materials.
The mathematical model successfully reproduced the patterns observed in the experiments. This agreement suggests that the framework captures important aspects of how amyloid-beta proteins aggregate under the conditions studied.
The results provide evidence that mathematical simulations can help researchers investigate the mechanisms behind protein clumping and explore ways to influence the process. Although the findings do not establish an effective Alzheimer's treatment, they offer a promising tool for guiding future laboratory studies.
For Yarahmadian, the motivation behind the research extends beyond the mathematical challenge. He hopes that a better understanding of the disease's complex biology will eventually help scientists develop more effective strategies against it.
"What drew me to Alzheimer's research is the combination of its profound human impact and its extraordinary biological complexity," he said. "My goal is to use mathematical modeling to identify important mechanisms and generate insights that may help guide future experimental and therapeutic research."
Story Source:
Materials provided by Mississippi State University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Shantia Yarahmadian, Yasser Alzahrani, Vaghawan Prasad Ojha. Metal-Ion-Mediated Amyloid-$$\\beta $$ Aggregation in Alzheimer’s Disease: A Mathematical Model of Chelation and Inhibitory Therapies. Bulletin of Mathematical Biology, 2026; 88 (9) DOI: 10.1007/s11538-026-01732-1
