Syria between potential intervention in Yemen and domestic crises
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
18:25:07 UTC
03:25:07 KST

Syria between potential intervention in Yemen and domestic crises
TEHRAN – The costs and risks of Syrian intervention in Yemen could begin to mount from the moment a decision is made.
Following Syrian President Ahmad al-Sharaa’s visit to Riyadh a few days earlier, reports on October 7, citing U.S. officials, said Saudi Arabia and Syria were discussing the possibility of deploying Syrian forces to Yemen to participate in military operations against the Sanaa government.
According to reports, between 10,000 and 20,000 soldiers could be sent, with the 90th and 84th Divisions among the formations under consideration. Al-Sharaa was reportedly seriously weighing the proposal but has not yet made a final decision.
Meanwhile, Ahmad Mowaffaq Zaidan, an adviser to the Syrian presidency, denied that Riyadh had asked Damascus to send troops to Yemen. Syria’s official position has emphasized that rebuilding the country remains the priority and that any military cooperation must proceed through official channels and within existing bilateral frameworks.
The official denial, however, does not negate the existence of multiple reports suggesting that various options are under consideration. Nor do the leaks amount to a finalized agreement. To date, there has been no official announcement of a Syrian decision to intervene, no confirmed Saudi request, and no publicly disclosed agreement on the matter.
The significance of these reports, however, extends beyond the question of whether Syrian forces will ultimately be deployed to Yemen. The very fact that such a possibility is being discussed raises broader questions about the regional role Syria’s new leadership might assume, the limits of its commitments to its allies, and the criteria it will apply when deciding whether to intervene militarily beyond its borders.
Lebanon and Yemen: Why the different calculations?
The debate takes on greater significance when viewed alongside President al-Sharaa’s position on the possibility of intervening in Lebanon against Hezbollah, despite an explicit appeal from U.S. President Donald Trump himself. Al-Sharaa ruled out Syrian military intervention in Lebanon, arguing that such a move would require a request from the Lebanese government and that neither the Syrian army nor the country’s internal situation was ready for such a step.
These considerations are even more consequential in the case of Yemen. Geographically, Yemen is much farther away, and its conflict is exceptionally complex. Military intervention could expose Syria to security and political risks extending well beyond the battlefield.
If the Syrian army’s lack of readiness was sufficient reason to rule out intervention in Lebanon, what has changed to make sending thousands of troops to Yemen a viable option? Have Syria’s military capabilities improved sufficiently within a matter of months to support a large-scale overseas deployment? Or does Damascus’s relationship with Riyadh lead it to assess the risks differently?
What could Damascus gain and lose?
Reports suggesting that Syrian forces could be sent to Yemen are closely linked to the central role Saudi Arabia has played in supporting the new leadership in Damascus.
Riyadh has been one of al-Sharaa’s most prominent political backers and has helped advance Arab and international efforts to restore engagement with Syria. It has also played a role in efforts to lift sanctions and create conditions for the country’s reintegration into the region. For Damascus, relations with Riyadh extend beyond economic interests to encompass the pursuit of political and security support at an exceptionally sensitive stage of the country’s transition.
Damascus may view closer military cooperation with Riyadh as an opportunity to build political trust, secure economic and security assistance, and expand its room for regional maneuver. Through such cooperation, it could also seek to demonstrate that Syria is a capable partner able to contribute to a broader framework of Arab security, rather than simply a country seeking external assistance.
These potential benefits, however, are not enough on their own to justify sending thousands of troops into a foreign conflict. Military intervention abroad inevitably carries serious consequences. In addition to exposing Syrian forces to retaliatory attacks, it could expand the circle of Syria’s enemies and draw the country into a conflict whose outcome and terms of settlement it cannot determine independently.
The risks become even more pronounced if the proposed mission remains poorly defined.
Would Syria’s role be confined to protecting Saudi facilities and strategic sites, with its forces assigned clearly defined defensive responsibilities? Or would Syrian troops participate in offensive operations inside Yemen?
The distinction between these scenarios is fundamental. It would determine the legal, military, and political risks involved, as well as whether the mission would remain limited and time-bound or evolve into a prolonged military entanglement.
Domestic crises cannot be overlooked
These discussions are unfolding as Syria continues to face serious and deeply complex domestic challenges.
The integration of the “Syrian Democratic Forces” into state institutions has yet to produce a final settlement. Arrangements governing control, administration, and security in northeastern Syria remain contested, while ongoing protests and political mobilization in Hasakah Governorate underscore the depth and gravity of the unresolved issue.
The situation is even more precarious in the south, where much of Suwayda Governorate remains outside the Syrian state’s control. The far-reaching demands advanced by the community’s spiritual leader, Sheikh Hikmat al-Hijri, reflect the depth of the divisions confronting the government.
At the same time, Israel’s invasions and aggression continue across southern Syria. This is occurring alongside the resumption of excavation and fortification work aimed at completing the occupying regime’s so-called “Sufa 53” line inside Syrian territory, consolidating new realities on the ground at the expense of Syrian sovereignty.
Under these circumstances, the challenge is not simply to restore control over the territory facing aggression but to prevent the fragmentation of central authority in parts of Syria, at a time when the capital itself remains within the reach of the Zionist regime’s military aggression.
How, then, can a state facing a direct threat near its capital and struggling to preserve its territorial integrity in the south seriously consider sending thousands of troops to Yemen, thousands of kilometers away? What strategic imperative could justify diverting troops and resources to a foreign theater while the struggle to consolidate sovereignty within the country’s own borders remains unresolved?
Between a leak and a decision
Potential military involvement could offer Damascus an opportunity to strengthen its relationship with Riyadh and open the door to economic and political benefits. Yet these gains remain speculative unless they translate into tangible results, while the costs and risks of intervention could begin to mount from the moment a decision is made.
A state that has yet to complete the reconstruction of its army, economy, and institutions cannot afford to treat overseas military interventions as bargaining chips in a broader contest for regional influence.

Midterm panic pushes Trump to trade Zelensky for cheaper diesel
TEHRAN — With the 2026 U.S. midterm elections a month away and diesel at $6.28 a gallon, Donald Trump went looking for someone to blame and settled on Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelensky, whose official presidential mandate expired long ago and whose continued rule under suspended elections remains constitutionally questionable.
On Friday, after talks with Vladimir Putin, Trump announced that Russia would ship more than 300,000 tons of diesel immediately, 500,000 in November and a million after that.
U.S. Treasury’s General License 135 makes it legal, reportedly until April 7, 2027. Trump signed a Russia sanctions law last month. He thanked Putin anyway.
The fuel crunch traces to the war on Iran, which the United States and Israel opened on February 28 and which has throttled Persian Gulf supply since. Trump blames Ukrainian drones hitting Russian refineries instead. Analysts are unconvinced.
Analyst Tom Kloza called the announcement “more noise from Truth Social,” adding that Ukrainian drones have reportedly crippled about half of Russia’s refining. Ed Hirs of the University of Houston told Newsweek that he expects relief at the pump only well after the election, and only a temporary one, because the pledged volume is small next to the global market.
Saturday brought the insult. “I think it’s time for Ukraine to get a new president,” Trump told reporters, accusing Zelensky of wanting “to make problems for our farmers, our ranchers, with diesel fuel.”
The same day, Russian glide bombs reportedly hit Zaporizhzhia, where Ukrainian officials counted at least 21 dead, three of them children. Zelensky called Washington’s waiver “an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged.”
The timing was almost comic. Ukrainian and European officials were in Miami with Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner when the announcement landed, and a senior Ukrainian official told the AP that Kyiv had no warning.
A U.S. official gave Axios another version: Trump moved after Zelensky ignored roughly six requests to stop hitting Russian refineries. Ukrainian officials say Washington threatened to cut intelligence sharing.
Sunday’s Truth Social post claimed an “ENERGY CEASEFIRE,” effective immediately. “Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!” Zelensky said the announcement “was news for me,” and said Ukraine will comply if Moscow does.
Trump tried this on September 14. Neither capital confirmed it then, and both kept striking each other’s energy sites.
The pattern is hard to miss. Washington announces by social media post, informs its partner afterward and calls the result a deal.
Kyiv is asked to stop hitting refineries, absorb strikes on its power grid and, if Trump gets his way, hold an election under bombardment. Moscow may get sanctions relief and export revenue. Stockholm and Berlin claimed they are keeping their sanctions, even if Washington is not.

Yemen breaking the blockade and beginning a new phase

Yemen breaking the blockade and beginning a new phase
LONDON – How Ansarallah succeeded in breaking the Saudi-imposed air blockade on Yemen is worthy of attention. The process began with an Ansarallah delegation’s trip to Tehran to attend the funeral of Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, the Leader of the Islamic Revolution, who was assassinated in a joint U.S.-Israeli air raid on his office on February 28.
The delegation flew from Sanaa International Airport to Tehran but was forced to land at Hodeidah Airport on its return after Saudi jets bombed Sanaa airport.
The delegation’s journey to Tehran and its return marked the beginning of a new phase in line with broader regional developments. The message was clear: the emerging balance of power no longer allowed the Saudi-imposed air blockade on Yemen to continue.
Amid the war between the United States and Iran, the message was that any settlement must be comprehensive and include the entire Axis of Resistance, allowing it to exercise its rights without being denied recognition. The new equation became one in which a blockade would be met with a blockade, and the continuation of the blockade on Yemen would lead to countermeasures affecting the other side.
Developments then progressed to the point where the balance of power on the ground began to shift in favor of Ansarallah, representing the extension of the Axis of Resistance towards control of the Bab al-Mandab Strait. Ansarallah began advancing and taking control of the western coast of the Red Sea, reaching beyond Mokha. This advance extended to a point in the Bab al-Mandab Strait and the island opposite it.
This development was not coincidental. Rather, it formed part of a broader process aimed at changing the balance of power in the region. Ultimately, the situation developed to the point where the Axis of Resistance came to control the Strait of Hormuz, while the Bab al-Mandab Strait also came under the its control.
The combination of control and influence over the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab al-Mandab means that approximately 40% of global energy supplies have come under the influence of the Axis of Resistance. Having this degree of influence over the world's most important energy corridors makes the bloc a far more influential force globally. This shift in the balance of power is ushering all resistance fronts into a new phase.
We are facing a new situation unlike any previous one in terms of the scale of its influence and its capacity to alter existing equations. No previous situation has reached this level of influence. It could bring the Axis of Resistance to a level of influence equal to, or perhaps greater than, that of the U.S.-Israeli alliance, despite the latter’s military and intelligence superiority.
This American-Israeli superiority, which has severely struck the resistance fronts in Gaza, Lebanon, and the West Bank, has now been met by a corresponding counterweight. Control over the Bab al-Mandab is overturning the balance of power, with consequences for the Israeli occupation entity as a whole. The importance of these developments is that they do not concern military confrontation alone; they also affect strategic and economic interests connected to energy and global trade.
This is occurring alongside a transformation in the image of the Israeli occupation entity in global public opinion, where it has become increasingly rejected in the conscience of the world. One indication is that a British minister has declared that Gaza represents a reproach to the global conscience.
Similarly, the actions of settlers in the West Bank, including acts of destruction and violations, have come under condemnation, to the point that some Western officials have described them as terrorists. These developments are new, and they would not have emerged in the same form were it not for the changes that have taken place in the balance of power and influence in the region.
Control over and the ability to influence global energy supplies do not affect the military dimension alone; it also extends to the global economy. Influence over energy supplies affects energy prices and consequently the prices of consumer goods, including food items and metals. It may also have repercussions for global stock exchanges and financial markets. Therefore, control over the corridors that affect the supply of energy, metals, fertilizers, and food gives the Axis of Resistance greater capacity to influence the global economy and financial markets.
Taken together, these developments could constitute a turning point in the course of the world and in the nature of the balance of power that exists within it. We may be facing the possibility of building a new world in which the balance of power differs from that which prevailed during previous periods. In this new world, the resistance bloc could play an influential role. Accordingly, what began as steps to break the blockade on Yemen could extend beyond the borders of Yemen and the region, becoming part of a broader shift in the global balance of power.
The United States does not want to enter this war because direct American involvement would mean preventing US ships from passing through the Red Sea. Washington also does not want to become involved in two wars simultaneously.
The United States is therefore compelled to pursue a piecemeal settlement, one that does not encompass all fronts, including the Yemeni front. There may be a settlement to the U.S.-Iran conflict, but the Yemeni issue itself must ultimately be resolved through a Saudi-Yemeni dialogue.
However, acknowledging the Yemeni situation and the effective control that Ansarallah exercises over parts of Yemen entail an American recognition of the new reality. It would also form part of a broader recognition of Iran and the larger resistance bloc.
The strikes against Saudi Arabia’s oil and energy infrastructure are part of the Yemeni pressure campaign against the Saudi Kingdom. On the one hand, Saudi Arabia is being placed under pressure from the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea. On the other hand, pressure on global energy supplies creates additional pressure on Saudi Arabia to accept the situation in Yemen, including the role of Ansarallah.
Yemen is following a principle of responding to siege with siege. When the Yemeni capital is attacked, Yemen also strikes Riyadh’s energy infrastructure.
The persistence of the Yemeni position, combined with Saudi Arabia’s inability to overcome Yemen and the failure of other parties to enter the fighting alongside the kingdom, will ultimately give the Yemenis the upper hand. This could lead to a settlement that recognizes the existence and role of Ansarallah in Yemen. This, in turn, will serve the broader regional context: a U.S.-Iranian agreement that will acknowledges the new balance of power and recognize the right of the Axis of Resistance to exist and maintain its position in the region.

In its view, only concrete measures aimed at reducing tensions and addressing ecological challenges will ensure meaningful results for the region.
Arman-e-Emrooz: Looking beyond the West-East divide
Arman-e-Emrooz focused on the need to redefine Iran’s geopolitical position in a rapidly changing Asia. The newspaper argued that the rise of China, India, Indonesia, and other emerging powers demonstrates that Asia is no longer merely an arena for Western competition. Instead, it has become one of the world’s most significant centers of economic growth, political influence, and strategic power. The article suggested that these changes provide Iran with an opportunity to rethink its place in the international system. It argued that Iranian foreign policy should move beyond the traditional choice between the West and the East. Expanding strategic options, the newspaper said, requires a broader and more flexible approach rather than simply replacing one geopolitical orientation with another. Within this framework, Arman-e-Emrooz highlighted the concept of the “Global South” as a useful basis for foreign policy. It argued that the idea allows Iran to connect issues of national identity, geopolitical interests, and economic priorities. By emphasizing shared experiences of independence and development, benefiting from shifts in global power distribution, and expanding cooperation in trade, investment, energy, technology, transportation, and security, Iran could strengthen both its regional and international position.

Hive dwellers vs. screen players: The anatomy of two societies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
18:11:48 UTC
03:11:48 KST

Hive dwellers vs. screen players: The anatomy of two societies
TEHRAN - This question has puzzled many astute observers in the West — and echoed through the stunned minds of Trump and Netanyahu alike: Why, following the assassination of the leadership, did the Iranian government not collapse like governments in other countries?
In the first week, a thoughtful friend in the West posed this question to me by email. To answer it thoroughly by invoking Shia history and Imam Hussein might well prove incomprehensible to a Western mind. I therefore tried to frame my answer using concepts drawn from Western literature itself. I wrote to my friend about a book by Maurice Maeterlinck, titled *The Life of the Bee*, which a kind neighbor had gifted me in my youth, before the revolution.
The point I am about to share may make the question easier for a Western reader to grasp. Maeterlinck notes that before a real-world experiment, all researchers assumed that the sovereign ruler of the hive was the queen, and that everything existed to serve her and her desires. They therefore designed an experiment: they placed a ring at the entrance of a beehive through which worker and soldier bees could pass easily, but which the queen, owing to her larger body, could not pass through.
They then staged a mock attack on the hive. Following their natural instinct, the bees mobilized to save the queen first. Since the only exit from the besieged hive was through that ring, the queen became stuck in it while trying to escape. After some time, her protective guards assumed she was refusing to leave. They stung her to death, selected another larva capable of becoming a queen to replace her, and established a new hive with a young queen elsewhere.
The scientist's conclusion is profound and fascinating. From then on, he stripped the title of "God of the Hive" from the queen, redefining that supreme force as the "invisible spirit of the hive."
This is precisely what happened in Iran, with one difference: the executioners this time were real aggressors, yet once again their violent methods failed to conquer the invisible spirit of the hive.
I will elaborate on the difference between a nation whose god is the invisible spirit of the hive and the peoples of other countries, with more precise explanations. I have a filmmaker friend named Seyyed Reza Mirkarimi, the director of several monumental works of Iranian cinema, whose name and films you can look up. He offers a striking interpretation of those countries surrounding Iran that have been independent for only a few decades. He compares them to cinematic backlots during the production of grand Hollywood epics.
To better understand his analogy, imagine a film about the era of Alexander the Great being shot on a set at Cinecitta in Rome — thousands of extras, towering props, and magnificent scenery.
Viewed from the camera angle, on the big screen, or even in IMAX, we marvel at its grandeur. Even the actors, deeply immersed in their roles through rehearsal, believe in their characters for a time. Yet once the false glamour of the screening subsides, or filming concludes, they realize they merely stepped out of their true selves for a brief spell to live in someone else's skin.
Once shooting wraps, all those grand sets are dismantled and replaced by another set of deceptive facades. That is the sum total of a magnificent, dazzling life lived on a cinematic backlot devoid of true identity. Perhaps the very next day after filming ends, even the lead actor is not permitted to enter, wander around, or reminisce about the past.
The disparity between many newly established Arab states — filled with heterogeneous populations such as Pakistanis, Indians, and others — and the original indigenous Arab inhabitants precisely mirrors the role of these film extras. Their sole reason for being present is to collect a paycheck and grab a slice of that fleeting fame and profit for tomorrow, without leaving any lasting impact on the future of that cinematic backlot.
Yet the Iranian nation — and even the leadership that was assassinated — believes in the spirit of the hive. That is why, for two hundred and twenty days, men and women, young and old, have stood steadfastly in the public squares and streets.
In closing, I recommend that you, the reader of this essay, seek out and read the legendary Persian tale The Conference of the Birds by the Iranian poet Attar of Nishapur. The plot is briefly as follows: a flock of birds from across the world gathers to find a mythical bird named the Simurgh atop Mount Qaf and make him their leader. On the final day of the journey, atop Mount Qaf, only thirty diverse birds remain; the rest have fallen behind along the way, offering various excuses. They do not behold a mythical Simurgh; instead, they realize that the legendary Simurgh is, in fact, their own collective gathering. They no longer need to wait for a miraculous bird to lead them.

People who worry more tend to have more negative dreams, study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
18:00:53 UTC
03:00:53 KST

Among 389 Italian adults, stress emerged as the most central element in a web of connections linking worry, anxiety and depression, according to a study published in BMC Psychology. People who reported more worry and more depressive symptoms also tended to report more negative dreams, a pattern consistent with the idea that waking concerns carry over into sleep.
Dreams have long been associated with people’s emotional lives. The continuity hypothesis of dreaming proposes that concerns and feelings from waking life can continue into sleep and influence dream experiences. For example, people under pressure may dream about threatening or emotionally intense events.
However, it is difficult to determine how different dream experiences relate to different forms of distress. A person may remember dreams frequently without finding them upsetting, while another person may rarely recall dreams but feel strongly affected by the dreams they do remember. Research on dreams and research on worry, which has been linked to poorer sleep, have also largely been conducted separately.
Vittorio Lenzo of the University of Catania in Italy led a team investigating these relationships. The researchers surveyed 389 Italian-speaking adults recruited through university mailing lists, social media and online blogs. Participants were 18 to 64 years old, with an average age of about 24, and the sample included 330 women, 50 men and nine non-binary participants.
Participants completed an online survey containing three questionnaires. The Mannheim Dream Questionnaire asked how often people recalled their dreams, how emotionally intense their dreams were, how positive or negative their dreams usually felt, how often dreams affected their daytime mood and how often they told other people about their dreams. Each of these features was measured with a single question.
The Penn State Worry Questionnaire measured pathological worry, meaning persistent and difficult-to-control thoughts about possible future problems. Participants also completed the Depression Anxiety Stress Scale, which measures symptoms related to depression, anxiety and stress.
Lenzo and colleagues then used network analysis. In this type of analysis, each psychological feature is treated as a point in a network, and the connections between points represent how strongly two features are related after accounting for all the others. This approach can show which variables are most strongly linked to the rest of the network.
On average, participants reported high levels of worry, enough to be considered clinically elevated compared with normative data. Depression, anxiety and stress formed a closely connected cluster, with the strongest connection between anxiety and stress. Worry was most strongly associated with stress and only weakly with anxiety and depression, which the authors suggest may reflect worry’s role in sustaining prolonged tension.
Within the dream measures, people who recalled their dreams more often were also more likely to tell others about them, the strongest connection in the entire network. Frequent dream recall was moderately associated with more emotionally intense dreams, which were in turn linked with the feeling that dreams affected daytime mood.
The links between dreams and distress were weaker. People whose dreams tended to be more negative in tone reported more depressive symptoms and more worry, and people who felt their dreams affected their daytime mood reported more anxiety. The authors note that this pattern fits the continuity hypothesis, since people who worry a great deal may carry that vigilance into sleep.
Stress was the most central variable in the overall network, meaning it had the strongest total connections to the other variables, while depression, dream recall and dream intensity were among the least central. Dream emotional tone had what researchers call a negative expected influence, meaning its connections to the rest of the network ran mostly in the opposite direction from those of distress.
The authors concluded that “dream experiences are integrated components of a dynamic system of emotional functioning.” They suggest that more positive dream experiences might help dampen distress, while stress may amplify it. They also propose that worry and depression could lead to more negative dreams, which might in turn feed next-day anxiety, though both ideas require testing in studies that follow people over time.
There are a few things to keep in mind. Because the data were collected at a single point in time, the study cannot show whether dreams influence distress, whether distress shapes dreams, or both. The participants were a convenience sample of mostly young women recruited online, which limits how far the findings can be generalized.
All information was self-reported, and dream experiences depend on people’s memories, which may introduce bias. Each dream feature was measured with a single question, the connections between dreams and distress were small, and while the network was generally stable when tested using repeated statistical resampling, some individual connections were less certain.
The study, “Dream experiences and psychological distress: a network analysis of pathological worry, depression, anxiety, and stress,” was authored by Vittorio Lenzo, Chiara Fioretti, Alessandro Musetti, Raffaele De Luca Picione, Christian Franceschini, Patrizia Strano, Maria C. Quattropani and Alberto Sardella.

Araghchi calls for international accountability for environmental destruction in wars
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
17:54:24 UTC
02:54:24 KST

Araghchi calls for international accountability for environmental destruction in wars
TEHRAN — Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has called for stronger international mechanisms to prevent and address environmental destruction during armed conflicts, stressing that the international community must move beyond expressions of concern and ensure effective accountability for those responsible.
Addressing the international conference “Ecocide: The Silent War Crime” in Tehran on Sunday, Araghchi said large-scale environmental destruction during warfare was not merely an ecological concern but an issue directly linked to the right to life, public health, food security, international peace and security, and the rights of future generations.
“Environmental protection must move beyond declarations of commitment and enter the realm of accountability, responsibility and effective international action,” he said, warning that the consequences of environmental damage could persist for years or even decades after hostilities end.
Araghchi emphasized that warfare threatens not only human lives, cities and economic infrastructure but also water resources, soil, air quality, forests, agricultural land, energy infrastructure, natural habitats and biodiversity. The release of hazardous substances, contamination of vital resources and destruction of ecosystems can impose lasting costs on civilian populations long after the fighting has stopped.
Gaza, Lebanon and Iran face lasting environmental damage
Citing Gaza, Lebanon and Iran, Araghchi highlighted the far-reaching environmental consequences of military attacks across the region.
In Gaza, he pointed to the collapse of water and wastewater networks, damage to waste-management systems, contamination of water and soil, coastal pollution, and the accumulation of vast quantities of rubble and potentially hazardous materials.
He noted that the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) has reported unprecedented environmental damage in the Palestinian territory, warning that the destruction of essential infrastructure and contamination of natural resources could affect public health and living conditions for decades.
In Lebanon, Araghchi highlighted damage to forests and agricultural land caused by military attacks and resulting fires. He referred to reports submitted to the United Nations documenting the burning of millions of square meters of land and damage to tens of thousands of olive trees. He also recalled the extensive coastal pollution following attacks on oil-storage facilities, illustrating how damage to industrial infrastructure can generate environmental consequences far beyond the immediate site of an attack.
Turning to Iran, the foreign minister addressed the environmental risks associated with US and Israeli attacks on Iranian oil, refinery and energy facilities in March 2026.
He cited a UNEP assessment from that month concerning attacks on oil facilities in and around urban areas, including Tehran, where fires released hazardous compounds into the environment.
Such pollutants, Araghchi warned, can spread from the atmosphere into soil and water resources and ultimately affect the food chain, creating risks that extend well beyond immediate economic losses.
The consequences are particularly serious for civilians, children and future generations, who may continue to suffer the health and environmental effects of wartime contamination long after the conflict has ended.
International law must ensure accountability
Araghchi stressed that international law must not remain indifferent to environmental destruction and violations of fundamental human rights during armed conflicts.
He called for the effective implementation of international humanitarian law, particularly the principles of distinction and proportionality, alongside a thorough assessment of the direct, indirect and long-term environmental consequences of military operations.
The principle of distinction requires parties to distinguish between military objectives and civilian objects. The principle of proportionality prohibits attacks expected to cause incidental civilian harm excessively in relation to the concrete and direct military advantage anticipated. International humanitarian law also provides specific protection for the natural environment against certain forms of damage during armed conflicts.
Araghchi argued that no state or actor should consider itself above international responsibility. Extensive ecosystem destruction, severe contamination of water and soil, and lasting damage to natural resources must be addressed through effective mechanisms for prevention, independent documentation, damage assessment, compensation and accountability.
He said Iran supports legal and expert discussions aimed at strengthening international environmental protection, including consideration of recognizing ecocide as a distinct international crime.
The concept of ecocide broadly concerns exceptionally severe environmental destruction. Proposals to establish it as a separate international crime have gained attention in international legal discussions, although its precise definition, scope, and legal status remain subjects of debate.
For Iran, Araghchi indicated, strengthening international protection requires moving beyond general declarations and developing practical mechanisms capable of establishing responsibility and addressing the consequences of environmental destruction.
Iran warns against double standards in environmental protection
The foreign minister also warned against double standards and the politicization of environmental issues, insisting that environmental obligations must be applied fairly, transparently and without discrimination.
Environmental protection, he said, must not become a privilege for some countries and an obligation on others.
Araghchi further called for serious examination of the legal, humanitarian and environmental consequences of unilateral coercive measures that restrict countries' access to financing, clean technologies and essential equipment needed to protect the environment, manage ecological emergencies and address climate change.
He argued that environmental justice requires developing countries to have access to financial resources, scientific expertise and clean technologies necessary to respond to environmental challenges without unnecessary or discriminatory barriers.
He also stressed that independent documentation of environmental damage, scientific assessment of its long-term effects, and arrangements for compensation and rehabilitation should form an integral part of the international response to armed conflicts.
Three priorities for international cooperation
Araghchi proposed three priorities for strengthening international cooperation to prevent environmental destruction and address its consequences.
First, he called for stronger international legal frameworks and clear criteria for identifying, assessing, and responding to cases of extensive and severe environmental damage.
Second, he proposed the establishment of impartial, science-based mechanisms to document environmental damage caused by armed conflicts, assess its long-term consequences, determine applicable legal responsibilities and facilitate compensation.
Third, he urged expanded regional and international cooperation to prevent environmental destruction, restore damaged ecosystems and support countries and communities that lack adequate financial resources or technical capacity.
COP31 offers an opportunity to address the environmental costs of war
Araghchi also identified the 31st Conference of the Parties to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (COP31) as an opportunity to draw greater international attention to the environmental and climate consequences of military attacks.
He said Iran was prepared to contribute its scientific, legal and diplomatic capabilities to collective efforts aimed at preventing large-scale environmental destruction, strengthening regional cooperation and promoting international accountability.
The foreign minister emphasized that environmental damage caused by armed conflict cannot be treated as a secondary consequence of war. Its effects on public health, food security, natural resources and the livelihoods of affected communities make it an issue of international concern.
Concluding his remarks, Araghchi called on the international community to ensure that those responsible for environmental destruction do not escape accountability.
“Nature has no voice at the negotiating table or on the battlefield,” he said, stressing that collective action is necessary to prevent environmental devastation from coming at the expense of humanity's future.

Powers greater than US tried to conquer Iran but ended up in ‘dustbin of history,’ Rezaei says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
17:49:45 UTC
02:49:45 KST

Powers greater than US tried to conquer Iran but ended up in ‘dustbin of history,’ Rezaei says
TEHRAN — Iran’s top security official says Tehran will determine the outcome of its confrontation with Washington, rules out a return to previous diplomatic norms and warns of potential retaliation against US assets in the event of renewed aggression.
Major General Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council (SNSC), has warned that the United States will face the same fate as previous powers that attempted to subjugate Iran, saying even stronger empires ultimately disappeared into the “dustbin of history.”
In an exclusive interview with Press TV on Saturday, Rezaei said Washington had suffered repeated defeats in its confrontation with Iran and had increasingly resorted to economic warfare, which he characterized as a response to its failure to achieve its objectives through military pressure.
He stressed that Iran, rather than the United States, would determine when the confrontation ends, adding that Tehran would continue to resist until its demands were met.
Addressing the US military presence in West Asia, Rezaei pointed to the withdrawal of American forces from Iraq as evidence, in his assessment, of Washington’s failure to impose its military agenda on the region. He described the development as vindication of Iran’s longstanding opposition to the deployment of US forces in the region.
Rezaei also said more than 30 million Iranians had registered for the Janfada (Sacrifice for Iran) campaign, which was intended to mobilize volunteers prepared to take up arms in the event of US aggression.
On diplomacy, the SNSC secretary said Iran would not return to its previous diplomatic norms, while emphasizing that Tehran was not abandoning diplomacy altogether.
His remarks signaled that, although diplomatic engagement remained an option, Iran’s approach would be shaped by its assessment of the confrontation with Washington and the need to secure its demands.
Rezaei also warned that renewed US aggression could expose American assets to retaliation, including key data systems and artificial intelligence sensors.
Rezaei invokes ancient Rome to counter ‘civilizational war’ narrative
In a separate part of his remarks, Rezaei invoked the defeat of Roman forces by the Sasanian Empire under King Shapur I to challenge the framing of the confrontation with Iran as a civilizational war by US officials.
The reference draws on a significant episode in Iranian history. In 260 AD, Shapur I defeated the Roman emperor Valerian at the Battle of Edessa and captured him, marking a major setback for Rome in its eastern campaigns.
By invoking that episode, Rezaei placed the current confrontation within a broader historical narrative of Iran’s resistance to foreign powers and attempts at domination.
Hormuz tensions and the dispute with Washington
Rezaei also identified Washington and its regional allies as central to the tensions surrounding the Strait of Hormuz, one of the world’s most strategically important maritime corridors for oil and gas shipments.
Iran’s restrictions on passage through the strait followed the latest round of US-Israeli military aggression. The disruption affected a critical route for international energy trade and contributed to heightened concerns over global oil and energy supplies. The resulting market pressures also prompted the United States and the International Energy Agency (IEA) to draw on strategic reserves on multiple occasions.
Following the signing of an Iran-US memorandum of understanding in Islamabad in June, Tehran reopened the waterway. Iran subsequently said Washington had breached the understanding by imposing a blockade on Iranian ports, prompting the country’s armed forces to close the maritime corridor again.
The dispute over the strait has become a major point of contention between Tehran and Washington, linking military developments and diplomatic commitments to the security of international shipping and global energy markets.
Rezaei’s remarks underscored Tehran’s position that any resolution to the confrontation must take account of Iran’s security demands and its role in the region. His comments also made clear that Iran does not regard a return to the previous diplomatic framework as inevitable, even as it continues to leave the door open to diplomacy.

Bombs that pushed Iran across the rubicon
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
17:44:29 UTC
02:44:29 KST

Bombs that pushed Iran across the rubicon
Two wars launched by the US and Israel under the false pretext of stopping Iran's nuclear weapon may have made it more likely
TEHRAN – Donald Trump says he went to war to ensure Iran never gets the bomb — dozens of times and counting. Yet the war fought in the name of non-proliferation has acted like a boomerang: far from closing Iran's path to the bomb, it may have pushed Tehran closer to it.
The US and Israel say they attacked Iran twice to prevent it from acquiring a nuclear weapon. Yet at the time of both attacks, both US intelligence and the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) assessed that Tehran was not building one.
 
No evidence has emerged that Iran is currently racing to build a bomb. But a growing number of Western analysts argue the wars themselves have strengthened Tehran's incentive to do so — while inside Iran, calls to revise the nuclear doctrine and reconsider membership in the Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT) have moved from the margins to the mainstream.
 
The result is the central paradox of the current confrontation: a preventive war that may have produced the very outcome it claimed to prevent.
 
The justification vs. the assessment
Washington's stated rationale has been consistent: Iran must not be allowed to obtain a nuclear weapon.
But two key institutions directly contradicted the claim that Iran was actively pursuing one.
US intelligence: Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard testified to Congress in March 2025 that Iran was not building a nuclear weapon and that Ayatollah Seyyed Ali Khamenei had not reauthorized the weapons program suspended in 2003. A leaked US intelligence assessment reported by News24 on March 18, 2026, after the US operation known as Midnight Hammer, again found "no effort to rebuild enrichment" and concluded that Tehran had not moved to weaponize.
The IAEA: Director General Rafael Grossi said on June 19, 2025, amid the first war: "We found no indication of an active, systematic plan to build a weapon in Iran." He added that military strikes would only "delay the indispensable diplomatic work" needed for long-term assurance that
Iran does not acquire a weapon.
In other words, both attacks were launched not against an ongoing weaponization program documented by inspectors or spies, but against capabilities and intentions that Washington and Tel Aviv insisted could turn into one.
The second war removed a barrier: the fatwa
For two decades, Iran's principal political-religious barrier to a bomb was explicit: a fatwa by Ayatollah Seyyed Ali Khamenei declaring the production, stockpiling and use of nuclear weapons haram (forbidden).
Iranian officials repeatedly cited the fatwa as the reason Iran had the technical capacity but not the intent. Former Foreign Minister and former Atomic Energy chief Ali Akbar Salehi said in February 2024 that Iran possessed "all the pieces" needed for a weapon but had not assembled them — a restraint Tehran attributed to the Leader's ruling.
Ayatollah Seyyed Ali Khamenei was martyred in the joint US-Israel airstrike on the morning of February 28, 2026, in his office in central Tehran.
His successor, Ayatollah Seyyed Mojtaba Khamenei, has made no clear public statement on the nuclear fatwa. Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi acknowledged the uncertainty in an interview with Reuters on March 18, 2026, saying Iran's position against weapons would not undergo "significant change," but adding that fatwas depend on the issuing jurist and that he could not yet judge the new Leader's jurisprudential view. Any change, he said, would depend on the new Leader.
But that key religious prohibition that underpinned this doctrine for 20 years no longer exists — removed by those who coveted Iran's collapse and US domination over Iran.
In Washington and Tel Aviv, a quiet consensus: the bombing is making the bomb more likely
The most striking warning came, paradoxically, from inside Israel's own intelligence establishment. Danny Citrinowicz, who until recently ran the Iran branch of Israeli military intelligence, told The Times of Israel last summer that kinetic action would push Tehran "to cross the Rubicon on the nuclear file." The war, he said, would not prevent an Iranian bomb. It would accelerate it.
Citrinowicz was not alone, and what followed over the next year was something rare in the normally fractious world of arms control: agreement. From different capitals, disciplines and politics, analysts began describing the same mechanism — a state under existential bombardment, watching its declared, inspected sites destroyed, rationally concluding that only an undeclared deterrent could prevent the next round.
At Carnegie, James Acton argued that the premise of "obliteration" was an illusion. Iran, he noted, had almost certainly dispersed fissile material and key equipment before the strikes, and with what it retained it could, if it ever chose weaponization, move "in less than a year, even significantly less than a year." Eric Brewer, a former US intelligence analyst now at the Nuclear Threat Initiative, put it more bluntly to Reuters in May: as far as anyone knows, Iran still has all of its nuclear material, much of it in places American munitions cannot reach.
The institutional voices followed. Daryl Kimball of the Arms Control Association observed that the campaign had exposed the ceiling of force: bombing could neither erase knowledge nor permanently eliminate capability. Ellie Geranmayeh of the European Council on Foreign Relations noted that capability was "largely still in place," and that without inspectors — themselves now sidelined by war — existing stocks could be enriched to weapons grade with alarming speed. Even the press that had initially cheered restraint turned sombre. Time warned that destroyed centrifuges can be rebuilt but a changed strategic calculus cannot be undone; The Guardian editorialised that prevention by bombardment, absent any diplomatic endgame, historically hardens proliferation incentives rather than softening them.
The most systematic verdict arrived in August 2026 from Defense Priorities in Washington. In an explainer titled "A Security Dilemma Made Worse," it concluded that by waging a war that threatened the very survival of the Iranian state, the US and Israel had strengthened Tehran's motive to acquire the one weapon that might deter a third war. Proliferation was not inevitable, it wrote — merely more likely than before the strikes. Trita Parsi at the Quincy Institute and Ali Vaez at the International Crisis Group, neither of them hawks, reached the same destination by a shorter road: Tehran's determination to obtain a deterrent, they wrote, had been "dramatically increased," and rebuilding from under the rubble with an explicit weapons goal was now thinkable in a way it had not been before.
In short, deterrence theory was working — but in reverse. A country that finds conventional deterrence insufficient, and international verification incapable of protecting it, does what threatened states do: it reconsiders.
In Tehran, the unsayable is now said aloud
For years, even raising the question of a bomb in public in Iran was taboo. The fatwa of Ayatollah Seyyed Ali Khamenei stood like a wall around the debate: possession itself was forbidden, and that was the end of it. The wall is gone now, and the debate that has rushed into its place would have been unimaginable two years ago.
It began as a whisper. In October 2024, Kamal Kharrazi — the urbane head of the Strategic Council on Foreign Relations — said calmly that if an existential threat emerged, Iran would revise its doctrine. On April 1, 2026, during the US-Israel war against Iran, his house in Tehran was struck by US-Israeli aircraft. His wife was martyred in the attack and he was severely wounded, succumbing to his wounds eight days later. The capability, he noted, existed. Only the Leader's ruling stood in the way. That same month, 39 members of parliament wrote privately to the Supreme National Security Council asking for precisely such a revision.
Then came the first war, and the whispers grew louder. Ali Shamkhani, the veteran security official martyred on the first day of the second war, on February 28 of this year, appeared on state television in October 2025 and said, with the bluntness of a man who felt history had vindicated his doubts, that had he known then what he knows now, he would have supported building the bomb in the 1990s. By September 2025, the private letters had become a public petition: more than seventy MPs wrote to the president and the Council declaring an arsenal "necessary for nuclear deterrence" and openly asking for the fatwa to be reinterpreted — production for deterrence, they argued, was not the same as use.
What is remarkable is not merely the content but the setting. The argument is now made on camera, in parliament, and from the Friday pulpit. When Hojjatoleslam Haj Ali Akbari told worshippers in Tehran on October 9 that the nuclear program "belongs to the Iranian nation" and that there is a domestic demand to revise membership in the NPT, no one in the establishment criticized him. A month earlier, Nezamoddin Mousavi, a former MP close to the Revolutionary Guards, had told Ensaf News what many in the system now say privately: ambiguity did not prevent war.
It was time, he said, to review the doctrine, the worth of the NPT, and the meaning of deterrence after the strikes on Iran's own facilities.
Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi still holds the official line — no significant change, he told Reuters in March — but even his reassurance contained the seed of doubt. Fatwas, he acknowledged, belong to the jurist who issues them, and the new Leader, Ayatollah Seyyed Mojtaba Khamenei, has not yet spoken. In Tehran today, that silence is itself the story.
A 47-year-old dream turned nightmare
Seen from Tehran, the two campaigns were never really about centrifuges. The US and Israel knew better than anyone that Iran was not pursuing a nuclear weapon — their own intelligence services and the IAEA had told them so. What they pursued was a 47-year-old dream: regime change in Iran.
The calculation was that a heavy air campaign, combined with inciting street unrest, would finally realize that old fantasy. But aggression still needs a pretext. And what better pretext than the nuclear file — an issue they had spent more than two decades turning into a lever for global anti-Iran propaganda and for imposing wave after wave of sanctions?
Iran stood firm. The dream did not come true. Instead, it has curdled into a nightmare — one whose ultimate cost for Iran's enemies is still unknown, and still growing. The wars meant to foreclose Iran's nuclear options have instead opened the most serious national debate in its history about whether those options should be reconsidered, and have left Washington and Tel Aviv facing an Iran more convinced than ever that only its own strength can guarantee its survival.

Ángel Víctor Torres Pérez, Spain’s minister for territorial policy and democratic memory, said 12,000 people had returned to Morocco between 10 August and Sunday.
He described the returns as "voluntary", saying many had realised their cases would end in expulsion because they did not meet the requirements for asylum.
According to Spain’s Interior Ministry, nearly 25,000 migrants have arrived irregularly in the country so far this year. On Saturday night, a Maritime Rescue vessel rescued 96 people, including nine women and two children, from a small boat off Lanzarote.

Joint List head Jabareen lays out conditions on Eisenkot support in Israeli elections
The Palestinian majority Joint List has set out conditions for any support towards an anti-Netanyahu minority government in a move analysts tell The New Arab reflects "the significant amount of clout" they have going into the Knesset elections, where neither major bloc polls high enough to secure a government.
Yousef Jabareen, the new head of the Joint List, said in a statement that "after the election, we'll impose our conditions on any political constellation in Israel".
"We have the full freedom of action, with no limits, to replace the Netanyahu government, and we will use all the tools at our disposal," he added, according to the Times of Israel.
As it stands, most polls conducted show that neither the bloc under Benjamin Netanyahu nor the opposition bloc under Gadi Eisenkot will gain enough seats in the election, which could mean a hung parliament and another vote months later.
This would mean that, in order to oust Netanyahu's government, an Eisenkot bloc would have to negotiate support from Israel's Palestinian parties, which are polling to have enough seats to potentially bring the bloc over the line.
"It is a reflection of the fact that Palestinian citizens and the Arab parties have a significant amount of clout because of the fracture of the current Israeli electoral landscape," Amjad Iraqi, Senior Analyst for Israel and Palestine at the International Crisis Group, said of Jabareen's announcement.
"Whether it's the joint-list or Ra'am [the second Palestinian bloc], everyone can see that the seats that the Arab parties will take will kind of decide whether a coalition can come about," he told The New Arab.
Jabareen added that any support for the anti-Netanyahu bloc would not come without conditions, saying to get support the bloc would have to create a budget and plan to deal with crime in Arab Palestinian communities, stop demolitions of family homes of Palestinians convicted of terrorism, and commit to a roadmap for a two state solution.
"These are fateful elections here, in our country, which is the only one we have," Jabareen said.
Iraqi told The New Arab that this willingness to support an Eisenkot government comes from an assessment that Netanyahu's far-right government cannot be allowed to return to power.
An Eisenkot government could "give Palestinians on both sides of the green line a bit of oxygen to breathe after the intensity of this far-right government of the past four years."
However, questions remain about whether the outlines of the Joint-List, which are consistent with previous positions, could stop Eisenkot or members of his bloc from negotiating for the support, given there is widespread rejection of a two-state solution from most Jewish Israeli parties.
Iraqi added that the Joint-List should be mindful of Ra'am, the other main Arab Palestinian party running in the election, which has been more willing to put aside Palestinian statehood in order to join coalitions.
In an environment where Jewish-Israeli politicians in the Eisenkot Bloc have ruled out working with Israel's Palestinian parties, Iraqi said that there's also a question about whether Eisenkot would bring himself to seek the support of the parties, despite what polling shows.
"It's too difficult for Eisenkot to bring himself to ally with the parties or to ensure his other Jewish-Israeli coalition partners will also sit or be allowed to be propped up by the two Arab parties," Iraqi said, adding that they could be "quite resentful that they are beholden to the bargaining of these Arab parties, whether its because of racism or because they think it's a political handicap."
In September, Israel's Central Elections Committee banned the participation of the Joint List and Ra'am, as well as candidates for the Joint List Hadash MK Offer Cassif and Balad head Sami Abou Shehadeh, with widespread consensus among Jewish-Israeli political parties. The bans were later overturnned by the Supreme Court, while Abou Shehadeh withdrew his candidacy.
Among the plethora of different options, including a hung parliament resulting in fresh elections, or a deal between Netanyahu's Likud and Eisenkot, Iraqi said that "Israeli elections have a proclivity towards surprises, so I wouldn't write off anything".

IAI to unveil new tactical radar that seeks out low-flying drones at US's AUSA military expo
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
17:15:46 UTC
02:15:46 KST

Israel Aerospace Industries (IAI) announced on Sunday that it will unveil a new radar solution that can detect low-flying drones from its position suspended high above the ground.
The system, known as POINT@AIR, brings long-range radar detection and persistent surveillance to a compact, highly mobile aerostat platform. The unveiling was made at the Association of the United States Army (AUSA) Annual Meeting & Exposition in Washington, taking place this week.
The radar’s elevated position extends its line of sight beyond terrain and other ground-level obstructions, supporting earlier detection of low-altitude threats, while enabling forces to adapt surveillance coverage as mission requirements evolve.
In that sense, a heavy focus will be on anti-drone defense, an area where Hezbollah exposed IDF weaknesses during the 2026 conflict, leading to significant IDF losses.
The system will not replace MMR radar technology and other radars which are primarily focused on long-range detection, but will supplement them in certain specific areas where the threats, such as drones, are evolving.
Persistent operation, rapid relocation capabilities
Designed for persistent operation and rapid relocation, the system can operate without reliance on permanent infrastructure and can detect and track multiple aerial, maritime, and ground targets.
This is one of the new major issues, given that enemy threats have become more unpredictable regarding where and how they will attack from.
It supports multiple missions simultaneously, prioritizes targets according to operational requirements, and interfaces with command-and-control systems to contribute to an integrated operational picture, signaling the continued move toward greater integration of AI and the full network of sensors.
IAI's CEO Guy Bar Lev: 'Seeing the battlespace is the starting point for every effective defense'
Guy Bar Lev, president and CEO of IAI, said, “Seeing the battlespace is the starting point for every effective defense. The more persistent and comprehensive that view becomes, the better equipped forces are to understand what is unfolding, anticipate threats and act with confidence. IAI is increasingly developing next-generation capabilities that expand the boundaries of situational awareness and provide our customers with greater visibility, flexibility and time to respond.”
Dror Bar, CEO of ELTA Systems and EVP at IAI: “POINT@AIR reflects a fundamental shift in how persistent surveillance can be delivered - bringing sophisticated radar capabilities to an elevated platform that is smaller, more mobile and adaptable to the mission. Our goal was not simply to reduce the size of an existing solution, but to rethink what an aerostat-based radar could achieve. By combining advanced AESA technology, long-range detection and 360-degree coverage in a compact configuration, POINT@AIR gives operators the ability to establish persistent awareness where fixed infrastructure may not be practical.”
Based on the proven ELM-2083 radar family, POINT@AIR incorporates advanced Active Electronically Scanned Array (AESA) technology, with electronic scanning in both azimuth and elevation combined with mechanical rotation to provide 360-degree coverage.

Israel’s next leader should be chosen by Israelis, not Washington - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
17:15:36 UTC
02:15:36 KST

Israel owes an enormous debt of gratitude to the United States – to Democratic and Republican administrations, to president Joe Biden for standing beside us after the horror of October 7, to President Donald Trump for confronting Iran and advancing the Abraham Accords, to Evangelical Christians who have defended the Jewish state when others abandoned it, and above all to the American people.
Yet gratitude must never become submission, because Israel’s prime minister must be chosen by Israelis in Jerusalem, not by a president, donors, or political strategists gathered at Mar-a-Lago.
Trump has said that staying out of Israel’s October 27 election would be appropriate. He has also suggested that he might endorse someone. More recently, he shared an article highlighting a poll favorable to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc.
That may not constitute a formal endorsement, but in a close election, it is political intervention by suggestion. Our country is not a client state, an Evangelical political project, or a Trump-branded Middle Eastern property. Gaza is not an empty beachfront awaiting luxury towers, and Israel is not a corporation whose controlling shares belong to foreign patrons.
We are a sovereign democracy whose citizens bury the dead, send children to war, and live with the consequences.
Trump understands the power of uncertainty. By saying that he may endorse a candidate without naming one, he encourages every Israeli contender to seek his approval. Netanyahu can present himself as Trump’s natural partner. His challengers must assure Washington that they will protect the alliance.
Trump gains leverage before casting a single political coin. This is not merely affection for Netanyahu. Trump values loyalty, public credit, and the image of being the decisive dealmaker. He sees diplomacy through transactions, leverage, and visible victories.
That approach can produce breakthroughs, as the Abraham Accords demonstrated. But nations are communities of memory and responsibility, not properties to be acquired, redesigned, and branded.
Netanyahu understands this theater. For years, he has used photographs, speeches, and meetings with American presidents to reinforce the argument that only he can manage Israel’s most important alliance. His message is familiar: Without me, Israel will be isolated. Without me, Washington will turn away. Without me, the country is unsafe.
That is not democratic confidence. It is manufactured dependency. Israel’s future also cannot be managed by a narrow diplomatic circle embodied by Netanyahu’s longtime confidant Ron Dermer, despite his experience.
Dermer helped cultivate American and Gulf relationships. But diplomacy conducted mainly through leaders, billionaires, investment channels, and palace intermediaries leaves ordinary citizens outside the room. Israel needs institutions, public accountability and many voices, not one prime minister, one emissary, and one foreign patron.
Gadi Eisenkot's political rise
The rise of Gadi Eisenkot exposes the weakness of that argument. Israelis themselves have presented another credible leader: a former military chief with decades of security experience, personal sacrifice, and a reputation for sobriety. Recent polling has placed Eisenkot’s Yashar Party near or ahead of Likud, and one survey showed him leading Netanyahu as the public’s preferred prime minister.
Americans do not have to support Eisenkot. Trump does not have to like him. Evangelical donors do not have to agree with every decision he may make. But they must respect the possibility that Israeli citizens, after October 7, want a different kind of leadership less theatrical, less divisive and more accountable.
Trump should promise not to endorse a candidate. American political organizations and major donors should show the same restraint. They may support Israel and advocate for their beliefs, but money, access, and presidential prestige should not select its government.
Israeli candidates must also stop campaigning as applicants for American approval. They should tell voters what they will do about security, diplomacy, living costs, national service, social inclusion, and the failures of October 7. Their mandate must come from Israelis.
The next government should protect the American alliance as a relationship between democratic nations, not political personalities. Israel worked with Biden despite disagreements. It can work with Trump without surrendering its independence. Institutional alliances endure; personality arrangements collapse.
Eisenkot should make this principle central to his campaign. He can thank Trump for his contributions, honor Evangelical friendship, and recognize Biden’s support during Israel’s crisis while stating clearly that no outside leader will receive a veto over Israeli democracy. That position is not anti-American. It is the foundation of an alliance between equals.
I write as an Ethiopian-born Israeli-American who loves both countries. America taught me the importance of constitutional government and peaceful transfers of power. Israel taught me that Jewish sovereignty carries responsibility.
Those lessons lead to the same conclusion: Friends may advise, assist, and disagree, but citizens must decide. Israel’s election belongs to the nurse in Jerusalem, the reservist returning from Gaza, the struggling family in Beersheba, the Arab teacher in Nazareth, and the Ethiopian-Israeli mother whose children serve a country that still too rarely allows her community to represent it.
My teacher, Rabbi Jonathan Sacks, z”l, expressed this principle clearly: “Whoever governs in Israel does so only under the authority delegated by God on the one hand, the people on the other.” That covenantal principle applies equally to domestic politicians and foreign benefactors. Israel’s democratic authority comes from its people, not from Mar-a-Lago, royal palaces, billionaires, or political donors.
President Trump may be Israel’s friend. Evangelical Christians may be among Israel’s most loyal supporters. President Biden and millions of Americans deserve our gratitude.
But none of them is Israel’s kingmaker. Let the citizens of Israel choose. If they choose Gadi Eisenkot, Washington should respect that decision.
Israel’s future must be decided in Jerusalem, not at Mar-a-Lago.
The writer is a former New York City Supreme Court detective, an investigator and educator in conflict resolution and restorative peace, and a moral diplomacy expert. His upcoming book, Moral Diplomacy for a Broken World, is inspired by the late Rabbi Jonathan Sacks.

The world’s goodwill toward Israel was the exception, not the rule - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
17:15:22 UTC
02:15:22 KST

When I was 19, my father and I took my rabbi, Sinai Adler, to the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum in Washington because the rabbi was a survivor, and he refused to believe that the American government kept a permanent exhibition in which it admitted it could have interrupted the machinery of Auschwitz and chose not to.
He needed to see the admission with his own eyes. The gallery held a US War Department letter explaining the decision not to bomb the rail lines and a reconnaissance photograph of the camp taken from an American bomber. That photograph was made 17 days after Rabbi Adler had been brought through the gate.
As we walked out, my father tried to lift him. The halls were thick with school groups, and most of the children were not Jewish, which my father offered as proof that the world had learned something and that the next generation would not repeat the crime. Rabbi Adler answered that they were only coming to study their mistakes and to learn how to do it better the next time.
Years later, in a study hall in Israel, a student told him that German visitors were standing at the back of the room. They had come, they said, to see the miracle of the Jewish state. Students argued that these Germans had not been alive during the war and that six decades had passed. Rabbi Adler had them removed from the campus.
Those two scenes can be filed under trauma if you want an easy label. Rabbi Adler was a careful reader and a disciplined mind, and the conclusions he drew did not begin in shock.
He returned again and again to the Talmudic teaching that Esau hates Jacob. He treated that line as an operating instruction. Gentiles will persecute Jews, and a Jew who forgets that fact is unprepared for what history holds.
I hear the same complaint about Israel that I have heard for years. If only the country explained itself more clearly, if only the press operation were sharper, the world would grant the benefit of the doubt and perhaps even real support, especially after the massacre of October 7.
The evidence offered for that hope is the long stretch of Western backing that Israel enjoyed through most of its first seven decades. There were breaks in that pattern.
The West changes how it treats Israel
US President Dwight D. Eisenhower threatened Israel over the Sinai campaign of 1956. France embargoed arms on the eve of the Six Day War. Boycott campaigns gathered in universities and unions. Still, until about three years ago, the West as a bloc treated Israel as a partner more often than as a defendant.
The hope that better public relations will restore that climate misreads the record. Rabbi Adler and the sages were right about the ground under our feet. Antisemitism is the baseline we can count on. Support is the exception.
A common theory holds that the goodwill of those first decades was an aftershock of the Holocaust, a period in which even polished antisemites understood that Europe had gone too far and that open annihilation had become embarrassing.
That aftershock never erased the double standard. Friends still applied rules to Jerusalem that they would not apply to themselves. The pockets of hostility were the older pattern showing through the courtesy. The courtesy has worn off. The Holocaust survivor bump has ended. Baseline antisemitism has returned. We can argue about the date it faded.
But its end is no longer in dispute.
Support from Evangelical Christians is the large exception that still holds, and it grows out of their theology rather than out of a sudden affection for Jewish power.
Other help arrived from sources that were moral and strategic at once. US president John F. Kennedy approved weapons sales. US politician Henry M. Jackson tied aid for the Soviet Union to the release of Jews who wanted to leave. American president Richard Nixon ordered the airlift that kept Israel standing in the Yom Kippur War.
Those acts matter, and we should remember them with gratitude. They do not rewrite the longer pattern. Not all the gentiles hate us all of the time, but most gentiles will hate us most of the time. History is stubborn on this point for anyone who finds the sentence extreme.
Zionism began because that pattern would not dissolve. For two thousand years millions of Jews absorbed hatred and exile as a condition of life and waited for gentile mercy to improve.
Early Zionists first trusted emancipation and the Enlightenment to repair the Jewish situation from outside. When the repair failed, they concluded that the Jewish people needed a state of their own, a place that could shield them from persecution, let them work at full capacity, and for many restore a life of sanctity in their own land.
At eye level from Rabbi Adler’s seat in his study sat a set of Mishna books that he liked to take down for guests. The volumes had been printed in Berlin in 1936, three years after Hitler took office and three years before the first mass killings.
The publisher added an introduction that explained away the Mishna warnings about trusting gentiles. Those laws, the introduction said, belonged to an ancient world in which pagans hated Jews. The German gentile of the present was the most refined man civilization had produced. Jews could rely on him and did not need to apply the old suspicion. The books were still on the shelf when the refined men began the work the introduction had declared impossible.
The belief that Jews can talk the nations into permanent friendship treats 20 centuries of evidence as a public-relations problem. “Never again” was not coined to fund a better press office.
It was coined to remind Jews what happens when they rest their survival on the goodwill of people who have already shown them the limit of that goodwill.
The museum photograph, the German visitors at the back of the hall, and the Berlin Mishna of 1936 belong to one argument. Learn the baseline. Build as if the exception will not last. Keep the state strong enough that the next improvement in gentile technique never gets its laboratory.
The writer is a Zionist educator at institutions around the world and recently published a new book, Zionism Today.
