Iran at the threshold, Israel outside the room - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
17:15:11 UTC
02:15:11 KST

One justification for war with Iran was that time was running out. Tehran, Israelis were told, was “racing” toward nuclear weapons, “a step away” from a bomb.
Yet Iran has been near the nuclear threshold for years. Its distance from a weapon has never depended solely on centrifuges, enriched uranium, or the time needed to produce fissile material. US intelligence assessed that Tehran had acquired capabilities bringing it close to the threshold but had not decided to cross it. A crucial barrier was political.
Six months into the war, it is difficult to say that barrier has strengthened. Nuclear facilities have been damaged, but subsequent US intelligence assessments do not indicate a significant increase in the time Iran would need to produce a weapon.
Questions remain about its enriched uranium stockpile, while discussion in Iran about crossing the threshold has become more open. The war has also opened a front in the Strait of Hormuz and increased Israel’s diplomatic costs, particularly in the United States. Whether it has made Israel safer from nuclear threats remains unclear.
The only effort in the past decade that successfully imposed agreed, monitored, verifiable limits on Iran’s nuclear program was diplomatic. The 2015 agreement dramatically reduced its enriched uranium stockpile, restricted enrichment and centrifuges, and introduced extensive monitoring.
The International Atomic Energy Agency and Western intelligence assessments found Iran compliant with its core nuclear commitments. Missiles, proxies, and other security issues could – and still can – be addressed separately.
When the Trump administration withdrew unilaterally in May 2018 and reimposed sanctions, the IAEA was still verifying compliance. Iran began exceeding the limits afterward. Israel’s push for US withdrawal, followed by the shift from diplomacy to war, demands a sober assessment of this strategy’s costs.
A low-risk diplomatic option remains largely unknown to Israelis. Since 2019, regional states have gathered annually at UN headquarters in New York for the Conference on the Establishment of a Middle East Zone Free of Nuclear Weapons and Other Weapons of Mass Destruction. Its seventh session takes place this November. Iran and the Arab states participate. Israel is invited but stays away.
Israel has long argued that disarmament cannot be separated from regional security; that arrangements must be developed by regional states with their consent; and that states cannot relinquish capabilities considered essential while remaining in conflict with their neighbors.
It has rightly opposed focusing exclusively on its nuclear capabilities while ignoring missiles, chemical and biological weapons, and other threats. These concerns remain relevant.
They do not, however, require postponing disarmament discussions until peace, recognition, normalization, and extensive confidence-building measures have been achieved. Arab states see this approach as an endless series of prerequisites before weapons of mass destruction reach the table.
Peace, confidence-building, arms control, and disarmament can advance in parallel. War only increases the need for communication, escalation prevention, monitoring, and agreements.
Changing the regional landscape
Participation in November would not require Israel to relinquish weapons attributed to it, join the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT), abandon nuclear ambiguity, or accept a future treaty in advance. The conference operates by consensus: regional states participate, and decisions cannot be imposed on Israel.
Several longstanding Israeli demands are therefore already met. If Israel wants missiles, delivery systems, escalation prevention, regional security, and confidence-building on the agenda, it should make those demands inside the room.
Participation could itself build mutual confidence. Israel would discuss weapons of mass destruction directly with its neighbors without committing to an outcome. Arab states and Iran would have to accept Israel as a full, equal negotiating partner.
This would not constitute normalization: states conditioning full relations on ending the occupation and reaching an Israeli-Palestinian settlement could retain their positions. But accepting Israel as a legitimate participant would matter to a country that has long insisted recognition and regional relations are essential to disarmament.
The United States also stays away. Alongside its own reservations, Washington has linked its absence to incomplete regional participation and Israel’s opposition to the format.
An Israeli shift could enable an American one. The government formed after October’s elections could invite Washington to join it in November. After months of confrontation with Iran, this would be a significant diplomatic gesture without advance commitments to disarmament, NPT accession, or an unwritten treaty.
There are precedents. Israel participated in Arms Control and Regional Security talks with Arab states in the 1990s and consultations on a weapons of mass destruction conference in 2013–2014; Iran attended one meeting.
Beginning in 1980, Israel joined the UN General Assembly consensus supporting a nuclear-weapon-free Middle East for over two decades, while retaining reservations about how to achieve it. Attending November’s conference would revive a tradition of raising objections and demanding conditions while continuing to talk.
Meanwhile, the regional landscape is changing. Saudi Arabia is expanding its civilian nuclear program and security alliances, including the Mecca Agreement with Turkey and nuclear-armed Pakistan. Iran is reconsidering its nuclear future, and another confrontation remains possible.
Burying one’s nuclear head in the sand does not preserve freedom of action. It leaves others free to shape the reality Israel must confront.
The next government should arrive in New York with Israel’s security interests, reservations, demands, and proposals – and ask Washington to join it. It need not commit to disarmament. Entering the room does not endanger Israel’s security. In today’s regional reality, remaining outside requires an explanation.
The writer is a guest writer at the Mitvim Institute and an advocate for eliminating nuclear weapons and other weapons of mass destruction from the Middle East. She is the founder and executive director of the Middle East Treaty Organization (METO).

Bennett vows to shift 30 billion shekels from draft dodgers; Winter proposes 25% Haredi exemption
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
17:13:55 UTC
02:13:55 KST

Former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett unveiled what he called a "service revolution" on Sunday, promising extensive financial benefits for soldiers and reservists while cutting state support for those who evade military service. At the same time, Ofer Winter, leader of the Amcha Yisrael party, presented a competing conscription plan that would recognize up to 25% of each ultra-Orthodox draft-age cohort as full-time Torah scholars, effectively allowing them to avoid military service.
With just over two weeks remaining before Israel's October 27 election, the rival proposals place the contentious issue of ultra-Orthodox military enlistment at the center of the campaign.
Speaking at an election event, Bennett, chairman of the Beyachad party, outlined a package that includes free daycare for reservists, 50% discounts on certain payments and a housing subsidy of 1 million shekels for eligible service members.
"A vote for Netanyahu and Deri, who promise another four years of state-funded draft evasion, is a vote that guarantees the next disaster," Bennett said, referring to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Shas leader Aryeh Deri.
"For 17 years, Netanyahu has funded draft evasion in exchange for staying in power. Netanyahu is dismantling the IDF, and he knows it. The chief of staff has raised 10 red flags. Hamas is building up its strength along the borders, and the IDF is crying out for reinforcements. It is short 20,000 soldiers."
Bennett argued that the government could no longer continue providing financial support to those who avoid service while the military faces severe personnel shortages.
"As long as Netanyahu, Deri, Smotrich and Goldknopf keep paying people not to enlist, who exactly is going to provide our soldiers with the reinforcements they need?" he asked.
"We will take 30 billion shekels from the draft dodgers and transfer that money to those who serve. That is the service revolution: Anyone who does not serve the country will not receive a single shekel from the state."
Winter's plan: Higher military pay, but exemptions for up to 25% of Haredim
Winter's Amcha Yisrael party also released the main points of its proposed military service reform on Sunday, pledging to make combat soldiers and reservists a national priority.
According to the party, the plan rests on three elements: legislation and financial benefits, establishing military service frameworks adapted to different populations, and Defense Ministry supervision and enforcement of recognized religious study institutions.
The party said implementation would be anchored in a future coalition agreement and the state budget, including the necessary legislation, regulations and enforcement mechanisms.
Among its proposals is a substantial increase in salaries for soldiers performing mandatory service, with combat soldiers receiving double their regular pay toward the end of their service.
However, the proposal also creates a formal exemption mechanism for some Haredi men.
Under the plan, the number of yeshiva students eligible for recognition as full-time Torah scholars would depend on the IDF's operational requirements and its ability to absorb new recruits, with an upper limit of 25% of each Haredi draft-age cohort.
That would leave a significant share of eligible ultra-Orthodox men outside military service, despite Winter's repeated declarations that he intends to end widespread draft evasion.
The party said its model would establish a clear legal framework governing each citizen's obligations to the state and the benefits available according to their contribution.
"The guiding principle is clear: Those who give will receive. Those who do not give will not receive," the party said.
Every citizen reaching service age would be required to report to the authorities and establish their status through one of three tracks: military service in the IDF, national or civilian service, or enrollment in a recognized and supervised religious study program.
The party said the arrangement would ensure that every citizen has a defined legal status, an established service track and a corresponding set of rights and obligations.
It also pledged to pass the necessary legislation before the next government is sworn in, rather than settling for a general commitment to address conscription at a later stage.
Under the proposal, the defense minister and Defense Ministry would oversee the implementation of the different tracks, including eligibility criteria, enforcement and supervision.
The ministry would be required to submit a report every six months to the Knesset Foreign Affairs and Defense Committee detailing oversight of yeshivas.
According to the party, the framework would also help protect young ultra-Orthodox men who choose to enlist and their families.
Winter has previously declared that Amcha Yisrael will not join a government unless legislation integrating Haredi men into military service is passed before the coalition is formed.
"We intend to integrate the Haredi public into the IDF without compromises and without delays," Winter said previously. "No more of the same. What was will not be again. Those who have failed to integrate Haredim into the IDF until now will not succeed in doing so in the future. If Amcha Yisrael is strong in the next government, these things will happen."
Likud launches campaign against Winter despite his support for Netanyahu
While Winter has repeatedly stated that he would recommend only Netanyahu for prime minister, Likud is conducting an aggressive, paid social media campaign aimed at preventing Amcha Yisrael from crossing the electoral threshold required to enter the Knesset.
"He did say he would go with Netanyahu, but we're not sure that's true," a senior Likud official said.
The campaign uses targeted advertising aimed at specific voter groups, featuring dozens of videos and past statements by candidates on Winter's electoral list, including comments made several years ago.
Likud's goal is to drive voters away from Amcha Yisrael and keep it below the electoral threshold.
The campaign has focused particularly on Winter's second-ranking candidate, Arab Israeli activist Yoseph Haddad.
One widely circulated video features an interview Haddad gave approximately five years ago in which he expressed support for a two-state solution and the establishment of a Palestinian state.
Social media users pointed out that the interview took place roughly two months after Operation Guardian of the Walls, Israel's military operation against Hamas in May 2021, even though Haddad has said that his views changed following that conflict.
The dispute follows earlier attempts by Netanyahu's office to break up Winter's party before the deadline for submitting electoral lists.
According to sources familiar with discussions involving Netanyahu's aides and Haddad's associates, much of the effort focused on persuading Haddad to leave Amcha Yisrael in exchange for a reserved position on Likud's Knesset list.
The approaches reportedly continued until shortly before Amcha Yisrael formally presented its candidates.
Haddad rejected the offers, leaving Winter's party intact as it heads into the election while facing pressure from the very party whose leader Winter has promised to support.

At least 11 people have been killed and 27 injured after a tour bus and a tow truck collided in western Turkiye.
The crash happened near toll booths at Akhisar on the Gebze-Orhangazi-Izmir highway in Manisa province on Sunday morning.
According to a statement from the Manisa governor’s office, authorities received a report of the collision just after 11am local time.
The wounded were taken to local hospitals, including the bus driver, who was detained by police following his discharge.
Images from the scene showed blue body bags lined along the roadside next to the overturned bus, which sustained heavy structural damage to its rear section.
The tow truck, which appeared to be carrying wooden planks, had also overturned.
Writing on social media platform X, Turkiye’s Interior Minister, Mustafa Ciftci, referred to the victims as citizens, though authorities have not yet confirmed whether any foreign nationals were among the casualties.
The governor of Manisa, Vahdettin Ozkan, visited the crash site as emergency teams cleared the wreckage.
“Work at the scene is currently ongoing under the coordination of the Public Prosecutor’s Office,” Ozkan said. “We are experiencing, in a painful way, just how vital it is to strictly adhere to traffic rules.”

Overnight, the area between the towns of Mayfadoun and Zawtar al-Sharqiyah was subjected to heavy and concentrated Israeli artillery shelling.

At least 139 migrants dead after boat to Yemen capsizes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
17:01:46 UTC
02:01:46 KST

Breadcrumb
At least 139 migrants dead, including some children, after boat from Djibouti to Yemen capsizes
At least 139 migrants, including at least 15 children, have died and around 84 are missing after a boat carrying more than 300 people capsized while sailing from Djibouti to Yemen, the United Nations International Organisation for Migration said on Sunday.
The boat, carrying 305 people, capsized near Guhere, north of Obock, a port town in Djibouti, during the night of 8-9 October, the IOM said, citing survivor accounts.
Around 82 people survived the shipwreck, the statement said. An Ethiopian government spokesperson did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Photographs shared by the UN agency showed worn-out sandals and sneakers washed up on the shore.
"Our teams are on the ground alongside local authorities to provide emergency assistance," said Alexandre Coissac, IOM Chief of Mission in Djibouti.
"This tragedy is a stark reminder of the dangers faced by migrants along this migration corridor as they seek economic opportunities," Coissac said.
Djiboutian authorities are continuing search and rescue operations, the IOM statement said, adding that local authorities are also providing medical care to survivors and arranging burials for the deceased.
The Djibouti government could not be immediately reached for comment.
The migrants were heading to Yemen, with the hope of eventually making it to wealthier Gulf nations, even as Yemeni nationals themselves flee their country, which is experiencing the most serious escalation in fighting between Saudi Arabia-backed government forces and the Iran-backed Houthis since a UN-brokered truce in 2022. 
"Despite the violence in Yemen, migrants are still making the perilous journeys hoping to make it to the Gulf countries," the IOM statement said.
Fighting in Ethiopia
Fighting has also broken out in Ethiopia since last month in the biggest escalation of violence since the 2020-2022 Tigray war.
An IOM official told Reuters that the UN agency had documented heavy migrant traffic along the so-called Eastern Route through Djibouti for several years.
"People continue to use the route amid changing conditions in Ethiopia and Yemen, although the volume and direction of movement can shift over time," the official said.
Ethiopian migrants interviewed for the agency's most recent situation report on Djibouti from 20 September to 30 September said they left their country because of difficult living conditions, including the impact of drought.
"Some migrants also reported that they were fleeing conflict and forced recruitment by armed forces," the report said.
Multiple residents of Tigray, where fighting erupted on 23 September, have told Reuters that they had seen Tigrayan rebels forcibly recruit young men into the defence forces. The rebels have denied conducting forced recruitment.
The conflict has sparked fears of a return to all-out war, with Ethiopia and Eritrea severing relations over alleged Eritrean support for the rebel alliance seeking to overthrow Ethiopia's government. Eritrea has denied backing the alliance.
Severe risks
The so-called Eastern Route presents many dangers, including accidents at sea, trafficking and arbitrary arrests once on land. In 2025, more than 900 migrants died or went missing along the route, according to IOM's Missing Migrants Project, as the number of people undertaking the journey increased by 18 percent.
IOM has described the crisis sparked by the fighting in Yemen as alarming, with displacement figures surging to 200,000 from 76,000 in mid-September, according to data released by the agency last week.
More than 3,700 people have fled Yemen by sea to Djibouti as of last week, it said.

Two remembrance days in memory of October 7 - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
17:00:00 UTC
02:00:00 KST

One peculiarity of the State of Israel is the large number of formally celebrated remembrance days.
Remembrance days around the world frequently commemorate events connected to wars, joyous events (such as victories), or tragic events (such as the Holocaust).
One could argue that the multiplicity of remembrance days in Israel reflects the multiplicity of wars and tragic events that befell the Jewish people in general, and the Jewish state in particular, since biblical times and more specifically during the last 85 years.
The most recently added remembrance day – that commemorating the atrocities of October 7, 2023, and their aftermath – is unusual, in that despite the general agreement in Israel that the day should be marked, there are politically based disagreements as to how the commemoration should take place.
The differences, between those who support the government and those who support the opposition, are over who is directly responsible on the Israeli side for October 7, and whether more could have been done by the government to save at least some of the 41 hostages captured alive and returned dead.
Opposition spokesmen and some of the families who received their dear ones in plastic bags blame Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for this tragedy and for allegedly caring more about his political survival than the fate of the hostages.
Netanyahu and his supporters argue that this criticism is unfair and libelous and fails to take into account broader national security interests.
As a result, for the past three years there have been two separate commemoration ceremonies.
Two October 7 commemorations
The first one is organized by the state on 24 Tishrei, two days after Simchat Torah, which in 2023 occurred on October 7. This ceremony is called the Remembrance Day for the Fallen of the Swords of Iron War.
This year it occurred on Monday, October 5. The ceremony, which was held on Mount Herzl in Jerusalem and was attended by President Isaac Herzog, Netanyahu, Knesset Speaker Amir Ohana, Supreme Court President Isaac Amit, and IDF Chief of Staff Lt.-Gen. Eyal Zamir, was divided into two parts.
The first part was a state memorial for the casualties of the IDF and other security forces on October 7, and the three-year war that followed. The second part was a state memorial for the civilians who were massacred in the Gaza border communities on October 7, and civilian hostages killed after that in the Gaza Strip.
The second ceremony, held on October 7 in Tel Aviv’s Yarkon Park – the National Memorial Ceremony of October 7 Families – was organized this year by the Kumu movement.
Kumu is a nonpartisan organization of bereaved families, founded in 2024 by Yonatan Shamriz, whose brother Alon was one of three Israeli hostages who managed to escape their captivity in December 2023 but were accidentally shot by IDF forces in Gaza who failed to identify them.
Though Kumu is nonpartisan, it does not conceal the fact that it holds the government responsible for what happened on October 7. It is also critical of the fact that Netanyahu has so far failed to take personal responsibility and has avoided setting up any sort of inquiry committee to investigate who is responsible for Israel having been caught by surprise, and for some of the failures that followed.
The ceremony drew an audience of about 50,000, with no government representatives. Though the leaders of the five main Jewish opposition parties – Gadi Eisenkot, Naftali Bennett, Yair Lapid, Avigdor Liberman, and Yair Golan – were present, none of them participated officially.
The two hosts of the ceremony were actress Shani Cohen and former hostage Eli Sharabi, whose wife and two daughters were murdered by Hamas terrorists on October 7, after Eli was abducted from his home in Kibbutz Be’eri to Gaza. His brother Yossi was abducted to Gaza on the same day, but was killed while in captivity, apparently during an IAF attack on the area where he was held.
At the ceremony, survivors and bereaved family members briefly told their stories, while Cohen and Sharabi added commentary. Well-known Israeli singers also participated. It was a highly emotional event, but Sharabi distinguished himself by managing to keep a straight face throughout and concealing his emotions.
It should be noted that the National Memorial Ceremony was broadcast in full and in real time on Channels 11, 12, 13, 15 and 99. Channel 14 was the only Hebrew news channel that did not broadcast the ceremony.
During the ceremony, Channel 14 broadcast its program The Patriots, as usual.
Every once in a while, in the course of the ceremony, I switched over to Channel 14 to see whether it would show a modicum of respect for the feelings of the bereaved families and avoid attacking those attending the ceremony.
But, alas, these were false expectations. The panel members were their usual nasty, insulting, mocking selves.
One of the regular panelists stated that the supporters of the bereaved families of those killed as hostages, who could allegedly have been saved had the government acted differently, are hypocrites who don’t give a damn about the hostages, and are only interested in bringing down Netanyahu.
I expected the program’s host, Yinon Magal, to call the panelist to order in honor of the day. But he said nothing, and his facial expression indicated that he was pleased by the remark.
Then I suddenly remembered that the previous morning, on his talk show together with Ben Caspit on Radio 103fm, Magal had mentioned the names of 13 of over 282 contributors to a Hebrew book published in 2024, with a picture of Netanyahu on its cover, titled “Mr. Depriver – the heritage of he who abandoned the hostages.”
Yinon said of the 13: “All the names I have mentioned shall be remembered eternally in disgrace, on a pillory. These are the most despicable persons living in the State of Israel, who falsely accused Benjamin Netanyahu of a blood libel.”
Eleven of the names mentioned were of returned hostages, or of relatives of hostages who had perished in Gaza. They included Shamriz.
Magal finally apologized for mentioning the hostages, but the damage was done.
What are the chances of the two ceremonies being united next year? Well, that depends on who wins the election in two weeks.
The writer has written journalistic and academic articles, as well as several books, on international relations, Zionism, Israeli politics, and parliamentarism. From 1994 to 2010, she worked at the Knesset Library and the Knesset Research and Information Center.

India's 'cockroach' leaders vow to keep up election protests

India's 'cockroach' leaders vow to keep up election protests
Leaders of India's youth-led "cockroach" movement on Sunday pledged to press on with protests against the country's election commissioner, hours after they were released from detention, as authorities sought to thwart major demonstrations in New Delhi.
The rallies in the capital come after weeks of opposition mobilisation following allegations of misconduct during a nationwide voter roll revision that critics say could benefit Prime Minister Narendra Modi's ruling party.
The Election Commission of India, which oversees the voting process in the world's most populous nation, has denied wrongdoing.
Abhijeet Dipke, founder of the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), and two other leaders were released Sunday, one day after they were detained when they landed in New Delhi to take part in a protest at the Jantar Mantar site in the heart of the city.
Thousands of protesters have been detained since Saturday, according to the group and media reports.
"We will not back down," Saurav Das, another top CJP leader, told reporters after his release.
"We urge people to come out and carry out peaceful protests," he added, vowing to continue until Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar resigns.
Smaller rallies took place in Delhi on Sunday. Dozens of protesters were detained near Jantar Mantar, which remained blocked off, AFP journalists witnessed.
Police have not commented on the detentions.
Reporters Without Borders (RSF) said at least 16 journalists had also been detained, calling the police actions "unacceptable".
"Covering events of public interest is not a crime," RSF said in a statement. "It is their job."
In July, protests organised by the CJP over exam irregularities forced the resignation of the education minister, marking a rare climbdown by Modi's administration.
'Important to show up'
Ahead of Saturday's rally, authorities mounted a sweeping security operation across the capital, shutting down metro stations and more than 200 trains while imposing a ban on public gatherings in several areas.
Thousands of police and paramilitary personnel remained deployed on Sunday, but metro stations reopened and previously restricted mobile services were restored.
"I was detained for 10 hours yesterday," said Aarti, 37, who gave only one name. "I have come again today because it is important to show up."
The protest leaders were released on the condition that they would maintain "peace for one year", Ratna Singh, the CJP's head lawyer, said in a social media post.
The Supreme Court, hearing petitions challenging Saturday's detentions and other security measures, directed the authorities to ensure protesters gathering peacefully were not detained illegally.
"Detention shall only be after following a legal procedure," Justice Joymalya Bagchi said in oral remarks.
The court also ordered authorities to ensure there was no disruption to internet connectivity as seen on Saturday.
'An embarrassment to India'
The CJP has emerged as one of the most significant political challenges to Modi during his third term in power, winning millions of followers on social media since it was launched in May as a satirical party.
Soon after his release, the CJP's Dipke took aim at Modi, calling him "an embarrassment to India".
"Never has this country seen a bigger coward and bully," he said in a social media post.
The revision of voter rolls resulted in more than 133 million names being removed from electoral lists, according to media reports.
Critics say the measure has disproportionately affected minorities, particularly Muslims, potentially benefiting Modi's Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party.
Election authorities say the move was aimed at eliminating duplicate, deceased and fraudulent entries.
The detention of protesters on Saturday triggered sharp criticism and accusations that Modi's government was stifling dissent.
The UN human rights office called for the immediate and unconditional release of all those "arbitrarily detained" in Delhi -- a comment the Indian government called "misplaced".
Rahul Gandhi, leader of the opposition Congress party, said he was planning to march to the Supreme Court on Monday with "every single person who believes in democracy".
"There is nothing to fear," he said on social media. "These cowards can do absolutely nothing to us."

The Tigray People's Liberation Front joined six other opposition groups last month in an alliance seeking to oust Abiy.
UN Secretary-General António Guterres urged all parties on Friday to cease hostilities and resume dialogue. He warned that fighting risked further destabilising the wider region.
Ethiopia told the UN Security Council on Friday that it was taking self-defence measures, accusing Eritrea of sending troops across the border and occupying parts of northern Ethiopia.
Ethiopian authorities previously have accused Eritrea of supporting the TPLF, an allegation Eritrea has denied.
Ethiopian Foreign Minister Gedion Timothewos did not specify the measures being taken. His letter to the council did not identify the occupied areas or provide evidence supporting the allegations. The Associated Press could not independently verify the claims.
Eritrean Foreign Minister Osman Saleh urged the council to condemn what he called Ethiopia's "unprovoked declaration of war". His response did not confirm or deny the alleged troop crossings.
The dispute deepens a rift between the two countries whose armies fought together against the TPLF during the 2020-2022 war.

Nearly 2.97 million Palestinians are eligible to vote, including around 1.59 million in the occupied West Bank, 1.24 million in Gaza and 140,000 Palestinian residents in occupied East Jerusalem.
Palestinians last held legislative elections in 2006, when Hamas won a majority of seats.
The Palestinian political system has remained divided since 2007, with Hamas governing Gaza and the Fatah-led Palestinian Authority based in the occupied West Bank.

Saudis might step up strikes on Houthis even further after airport attack, experts tell 'Post'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
16:37:03 UTC
01:37:03 KST

Saudi Arabia is unlikely to back down in the face of the Houthis following an attack on Riyadh’s airport that killed 12 people and wounded 309, with the kingdom likely stepping up its military campaign against the Iran-backed terror group, regional experts told The Jerusalem Post.
The attack, which marked a significant escalation in the Houthis’ campaign against Saudi Arabia, has exposed the kingdom’s vulnerability to strikes against civilian infrastructure. Bernard Haykel, a senior fellow at the Foundation for the Defense of Democracies (FDD), said Saudi Arabia had long understood the Houthis’ ability to carry out such attacks, particularly with what he described as support from Iran and Iraqi Shiite militias.
“My sense is that they’re not going to buckle. They’re not going to just capitulate to the Houthis because of this,” he explained.
Haykel said Riyadh now faces a choice between reaching an accommodation with the Houthis or intensifying its military campaign against them, adding that he expects the Saudis will pursue the latter course and rely more heavily on Yemeni forces opposed to the group.
“I think that they’re going to ramp up against the Houthis,” he said.
The attack comes as Saudi Arabia faces the consequences of a broader regional conflict that Riyadh had sought to avoid. According to Haykel, Saudi leaders opposed the war against Iran and made considerable efforts to prevent it, but now recognize that they will have to bear some of its costs.
“They realize that they have to pay a price,” he said.
Former ambassador says attack shocked Saudis
Michael Ratney, former US Ambassador to Saudi Arabia and senior advisor at the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS), said the scale and audacity of the attack had shocked the Saudis, even though they were familiar with the Houthis’ military capabilities.
Ratney noted that the Houthis had already carried out several strikes against airports, including in Riyadh, during the preceding week, while the latest was the most serious of those incidents. “I think they were shocked, but in a way understood that this is what the Houthis are all about,” Ratney explained.
He identified the targeting of civilian airports as a particularly significant escalation. In the past, the Houthis had generally focused on military installations and energy infrastructure, including Saudi military bases and energy facilities.
“For them to target civilian airports with the expectation of civilian casualties is really a new escalation for the Houthis,” Ratney said.
The attacks put Riyadh in a difficult position as it seeks to achieve its military objectives in Yemen without triggering a wider escalation that could expose additional Saudi infrastructure to retaliation.
Ratney said Saudi Arabia’s immediate military priority was to help the Yemeni army retake positions along the coast near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait that the Houthis had seized the previous month.
“They’re determined to get the Houthis off of the Bab el-Mandeb,” he said, adding that Riyadh would probably then look for a way to de-escalate the conflict.
Riyadh growing concerns over lack of American assistance
Both experts pointed to Riyadh's concerns about the limits of American military assistance, especially as Washington deploys forces and resources across the region.
Haykel said Saudi Arabia was disappointed that the United States was not better prepared to help defend the kingdom against attacks from the Houthis and Iran, particularly given the potential shortage of missile-defense systems.
“I think there’s disappointment that the Americans are not better prepared and better able to help in fighting the Houthis and the Iranians,” he said.
At the same time, Haykel said Saudi leaders understand that American military power has limits, particularly when US forces are already heavily committed across the Persian Gulf.
Ratney said the United States was providing some assistance behind the scenes, including intelligence sharing, targeting and operational planning. But he added that Riyadh would prefer more direct American involvement in airstrikes.
“Clearly what they would like is US support on airstrikes, and I think there is some frustration,” he said.
The attack could influence Washington’s willingness to provide more overt military support, Ratney said, although he cautioned that Trump’s response was difficult to predict.
Still, Ratney said neither Saudi Arabia nor the United States appeared eager to escalate the conflict further.
Saudis worried about further strikes on civilian infrastructure
The concern is that intensifying military operations against Iran or the Houthis could provoke disproportionate retaliation, with civilian infrastructure rather than military targets bearing the consequences.
“None of them really want to escalate at this point because they see the result,” Ratney said.
The attack also raises questions about whether Israel could play a greater role in helping Saudi Arabia counter the Houthi threat, given Israel’s experience confronting Iranian-backed groups and its advanced intelligence and air-defense capabilities.
“The political risk of that outweighs any kind of military benefits that they might derive,” Ratney said, explaining that Saudi leaders are reluctant to see Israeli politicians publicly highlight or take credit for cooperation between the two countries.
Haykel was more skeptical about Israel’s ability to deliver a decisive military blow against the Houthis, particularly through intelligence-led operations targeting the group’s leadership.
He said Israel had developed extensive intelligence capabilities against Hezbollah in Lebanon, allowing it to target the organization’s senior figures and commanders. He does not believe Israel currently possesses a comparable level of intelligence on the Houthis in Yemen.
“If the Israelis had the intelligence on the Houthis to, say, destroy the leadership of the Houthis and the second-, third-tier commanders, you know, what they did to Hezbollah, basically, if they could do that in Yemen, that would be an incredible service and help in this war,” Haykel said.
For Riyadh, the immediate challenge remains how to deter further Houthi attacks without becoming trapped in another prolonged and costly conflict in Yemen. Both experts agree that it will be hard.

Hundreds join 'I'm not Jewish, I'm a Zionist' trend, 'Post' analysis finds - exclusive
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
16:37:00 UTC
01:37:00 KST

A social media trend in which non-Jewish users publicly declare themselves non-Jewish Zionists has spread rapidly across X/Twitter, with an exclusive analysis by The Jerusalem Post identifying more than 600 matching posts from nearly 550 accounts over the course of just over a week.
The posts follow a recognizable formula: “I’m not Jewish. I’m [nationality, religion or identity]. And I am a Zionist.”
The Post wrote a code to analyze X and ascertain where the trend started and who is amplifying it. This analysis uncovered 613 posts published between October 4 and October 11, with relatively little activity during the first several days before the trend accelerated sharply on October 9.
The dataset contained just three matching posts from October 4, followed by 13 on October 5, 10 on October 6, 22 on October 7, and 26 on October 8.
That figure then jumped to 131 on October 9, roughly five times the number captured during the previous day. Another 270 matching posts were published on October 10, followed by 138 captured on October 11 at the time the data was collected.
In total, 539 of the 613 posts analyzed, or approximately 88%, were published from October 9 onward.
From scattered declarations to a viral formula
Declarations of support for Zionism by non-Jewish users predate the current trend, and the earliest examples on social media located by the Post do not yet display the standardized format that has now become more widespread.
Among posts found on October 4 were broader declarations such as, “I’m not Jewish, but I am a Zionist.”
By October 5, however, users had begun inserting their national identity into the declaration. One early example read, “I’m not Jewish. I am Irish, and I am a Zionist.”
An October 6 post similarly stated, “I’m English, I’m not Jewish, but I am a Zionist.”
By October 7, the three-part structure began appearing more frequently, including variations identifying the posters as American, Canadian, or Iranian before declaring support for Zionism.
One example posted by Dutch writer Bart Schut on October 11 read, “I’m not Jewish. I’m a Dutch atheist. And I am a Zionist.”
The Post’s dataset included posts referencing a wide range of national identities, among others: Iranian, American, Canadian, German, Finnish, Irish, Italian, New Zealander, English, Polish, Australian, British, Dutch, Czech, Japanese, Portuguese and Nigerian.
Some users went further, combining national and religious identities. References to Christians, Catholics, atheists, Muslims, Hindus, and agnostics all appeared in the posts analyzed.
Hundreds of accounts join trend
The 613 posts collected by the Post came from 549 separate X accounts, indicating that the volume captured in the analysis was not primarily produced by a small number of accounts repeatedly posting the same phrase.
Most accounts appeared only once in the dataset.
The available data does not establish that the posts were centrally coordinated or part of an organized campaign. Rather, it demonstrates the rapid replication and adaptation of a common linguistic template across hundreds of accounts.
The timing suggests that the phenomenon changed significantly around October 9, just two days after the third anniversary of the October 7 massacre,
After the Post captured 74 matching posts between October 4 and October 8, another 539 appeared from October 9 onward.
The trend had also begun drawing attention from other X users by that point, with posts explicitly referring to the growing number of “I’m not Jewish, but I’m a Zionist” declarations as a trend. For example, on October 9, user Oren Barsky wrote: “the ‘I’m not Jewish, but I’m a Zionist’ trend is one of the most moving things I’ve seen on this platform.”
By October 11, Barsky said that the trend is “basically [his] whole feed.”
How the ‘Post’ analyzed the trend
The Post collected public X search results using multiple variations of the phrases “I’m not Jewish” and “Zionist,” covering posts published between October 4 and October 11. Duplicate post URLs were removed, leaving 613 posts from 549 unique accounts for analysis.

Scientists make stunning discovery that could help explain why life exists
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
16:35:58 UTC
01:35:58 KST

Scientists make stunning discovery that could help explain why life exists
- Date:
- October 11, 2026
- Source:
- Queen Mary University of London
- Summary:
- Scientists have discovered that the universe's fundamental physical constants may be finely balanced to make life possible. Even tiny changes to these constants could make liquids too thick or too thin for essential biological processes, potentially preventing life as we know it. Surprisingly, these life-friendly conditions existed billions of years before living cells appeared. The findings raise intriguing questions about why the laws of physics seem so well suited to life.
- Share:
Imagine a universe where stars still shine, planets still form, and water exists, but liquids are so thick that living cells can barely function. Even with the chemical ingredients for life, the conditions might make living organisms impossible.
Scientists have uncovered a remarkable connection between the fundamental laws of physics and the ability of life to exist. Their findings suggest that even relatively small changes to some of the universe's most basic physical constants could dramatically alter how liquids flow, potentially preventing essential biological processes from taking place.
The discovery, detailed in a study published in Science Advances, came from physicist Kostya Trachenko at Queen Mary University of London. His theoretical analysis identified an additional constraint on the values of fundamental physical constants: They must permit liquids to move in ways that support life within and between cells.
The work raises a profound question about the universe. Why do the fundamental laws of nature have values that appear so well suited to the existence of life?
The Fundamental Constants That Shape Our Universe
Fundamental physical constants are numbers that govern how the universe operates. Examples include the mass and electric charge of an electron and the Planck constant, which plays a central role in quantum mechanics, the branch of physics that describes matter and energy at extremely small scales.
These quantities are generally considered universal and unchanging over time. Their values influence everything from the behavior of atoms and chemical bonds to the nuclear reactions that power stars and produce elements essential for life.
Despite their importance, scientists still do not know why these constants have the particular values we observe.
An important clue emerged in 2020, when Trachenko and his colleagues demonstrated that fundamental physical constants place a lower limit on the viscosity of liquids.
Viscosity describes how strongly a fluid resists flowing. Water has relatively low viscosity and pours easily, while honey and tar are much more viscous and move slowly. The researchers showed that there is a fundamental limit to how freely a fluid can flow, with that limit ultimately connected to the basic constants of nature.
The 2023 study took this connection much further by examining its implications for biology.
Why Tiny Changes to Physics Could Make Life Impossible
Every living cell depends on the movement of molecules. Nutrients must reach the places where they are needed, waste products must be transported away, and countless chemical reactions must occur in a liquid environment.
Another important process is diffusion, the natural spreading of particles through a fluid. Diffusion helps molecules move around cells and enables many of the chemical interactions required for life.
If the viscosity of those fluids changed too much, these processes could become severely disrupted. Liquids that were too thick might prevent vital materials from moving efficiently, while excessively low viscosity could also interfere with the controlled flow necessary for biological functions.
Trachenko explained the surprising connection:
"Understanding how water flows in a cup turns out to be closely related to the grand challenge to figure out fundamental constants. Life processes in and between living cells require motion and it is viscosity that sets the properties of this motion. If fundamental constants change, viscosity would change too impacting life as we know it. For example, if water was as viscous as tar life would not exist in its current form or not exist at all. This applies beyond water, so all life forms using the liquid state to function would be affected."
The implications extend beyond water. Although all known life depends on water, hypothetical organisms elsewhere in the universe might rely on different liquids. The same fundamental physical constraints would still influence how those liquids behave.
Trachenko suggested that the range of constants compatible with cellular life could be surprisingly narrow.
"Any change in fundamental constants including an increase or decrease would be equally bad news for flow and for liquid-based life. We expect the window to be quite narrow: for example, viscosity of our blood would become too thick or too thin for body functioning with only a few per cent change of some fundamental constants such as the Planck constant or electron charge."
These predictions come from theoretical models rather than experiments in which scientists actually changed fundamental constants. The precise limits that different forms of life could tolerate remain uncertain.
A Cosmic Mystery Billions of Years in the Making
What makes the findings especially intriguing is that the same fundamental constants that influence liquid flow also govern the nuclear reactions responsible for creating heavy elements inside stars.
Long before the first living cells appeared, stars were producing elements such as carbon and oxygen that would eventually become essential components of living organisms.
Physicists have long investigated whether the constants governing these nuclear processes must fall within certain ranges for complex matter to exist. But the ability to create life's chemical ingredients does not necessarily guarantee that life can function.
Trachenko's analysis showed that some physical properties governing liquid flow could change without disrupting the combinations of constants needed to produce heavy nuclei in stars.
In other words, a hypothetical universe might still produce the elements necessary for life while having liquids so viscous that cellular processes could not operate.
That means the conditions needed to support life may involve more than the ability to form stars, planets, and complex chemistry. The physical properties of liquids could impose additional requirements on the universe's fundamental constants.
Follow-Up Research Reveals a Surprising Connection to Blood
The investigation continued beyond the original discovery.
In a follow-up study published in January 2025 in The European Physical Journal E, Trachenko and colleagues examined how fundamental physical constants influence more complicated biological fluids, particularly blood.
Unlike water, blood is a complex mixture containing plasma, red blood cells, platelets, and other components. Its viscosity depends not only on molecular properties but also on how these components interact.
For example, red blood cells can form clusters that increase resistance to flow. As the blood moves faster, those clusters can break apart, allowing it to flow more easily. This behavior makes blood considerably more complicated than a simple liquid.
The researchers found something unexpected. Despite the enormous complexity of blood and the relatively large size of red blood cells, its viscosity remains surprisingly close, on a fundamental physical scale, to a theoretical value derived from basic physical constants.
They proposed that interactions between closely spaced blood cells may help explain this connection. Even though red blood cells are vastly larger than atoms, the forces acting where their surfaces approach one another involve distances small enough for molecular and quantum effects to matter.
The 2025 analysis also emphasized an important complication. Estimating which fundamental constants are compatible with life requires accounting for both the intrinsic properties of liquids, determined by fundamental physics, and the additional effects created by interactions among cells and molecules.
These findings offer a more detailed framework for investigating the connection between the universe's basic physical properties and the biological processes that depend on them.
Could the Laws of Physics Have Evolved?
The research also points toward an even deeper mystery: Why do the fundamental constants have values that allow so many different physical processes to work together?
One speculative possibility raised by Trachenko is that multiple forms of fine-tuning may be involved. The values that allow stars to manufacture heavy elements and those that permit liquids to support cellular life may represent separate requirements.
He suggested an intriguing analogy with biological evolution, in which different useful characteristics can emerge through separate processes.
Perhaps some broader evolutionary principle could help explain how nature arrives at combinations of physical properties capable of supporting stable structures and increasingly complex systems.
For now, this remains a conjecture. Scientists have not established that fundamental constants evolve through such a mechanism, nor have they determined why those constants possess their observed values.
Still, the connection between liquid flow and fundamental physics opens another way to investigate one of science's biggest unanswered questions.
Something as ordinary as water moving through a glass, or blood circulating through the body, may hold clues to why the universe has the physical properties that make life possible.
Story Source:

Journal References:
- Kostya Trachenko. Constraints on fundamental physical constants from bio-friendly viscosity and diffusion. Science Advances, 2023; 9 (34) DOI: 10.1126/sciadv.adh9024
- K. Trachenko, P. G. Tello, S. A. Kauffman, S. Succi. Extrinsic and intrinsic effects setting viscosity in complex fluids and life processes: the role of fundamental physical constants. The European Physical Journal E, 2025; 48 (1) DOI: 10.1140/epje/s10189-024-00467-y

Skertsos said Greece aimed to become the first European country to introduce comparable legislation. He added that the proposal had been developed in consultation with relevant European authorities to ensure compatibility with the EU regulatory framework.
The legislation would be implemented under the European Union's Digital Services Act (DSA). Platforms found to be in breach of applicable rules could face fines of up to 6 percent of their global annual turnover, Papastergiou said.
The initiative comes as European policymakers consider broader measures to strengthen online protections for children. The proposed EU KIDS Act is still going through the EU legislative process.
The proposed social media ban follows other government measures to protect minors, including a ban on mobile phone use in schools and the development of digital tools to improve children's online safety. ■

Yvette van der Merwe, OIV's president, hailed China's important role and its growing contribution to the international vine and wine industry, highlighting Ningxia's significant development as a wine-producing region.
The experience of Ningxia, such as viticulture in specific environments, investment in technology and knowledge, and a vision to create a well-known wine culture and tourism brand, offers important opportunities for international exchange and mutual learning, she said.
With the goal of building a new landscape for the wine industry, the president called for deepening cooperation with relevant authorities, institutions, experts and the wine industry in Ningxia and across China.
That cooperation will include Ningxia-based experts joining OIV's international network and expert groups, exchanges on grape growing, winemaking, climate adaptation and emerging technologies, plus ongoing alignment with international standards and best practices, she said.

The congress, themed around building a new landscape for the global vine and wine industry, features an opening ceremony, a seminar on high-quality development of the Chinese vine and wine industry, a sci-tech sub-session, industry visits and a closing ceremony.
Over 400 academic papers from 35 countries will be on display at the sci-tech sub-session, introducing cutting-edge technologies that could help drive the transformation and upgrading of the vine and wine industry.
The 6th China (Ningxia) International Wine Culture and Tourism Expo opened alongside the congress, attracting 84 world-renowned wineries and enterprises from distinctive production areas in 16 countries. It has also drawn a total of 146 leading domestic wineries from Ningxia and other core production areas in China.

Namibia hosts first African nuclear test verification exercise
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
00:22:58 CST
01:22:58 KST

WINDHOEK, Oct. 12 (Xinhua) -- Namibia is hosting the first Integrated Field Exercise in Africa, with about 250 international experts to test procedures and equipment used to investigate suspected nuclear test explosions.
In a statement issued on Monday, the Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty Organization (CTBTO) said the exercise, running from Oct. 10 to Nov. 20 in Namibia's Erongo Region, is designed to assess readiness to conduct on-site inspections under the Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty (CTBT).
Participants include surrogate inspectors nominated by signatory states, national technical experts, CTBTO staff and external evaluators, the organization said, adding that about 150 tonnes of technical and support equipment have been transported to Namibia by sea and air for the exercise.
Namibia's Minister of International Relations and Trade Selma Ashipala-Musavyi said hosting the exercise demonstrates the country's commitment to nuclear disarmament and contributes to strengthening the international on-site inspection system.
CTBTO Executive Secretary Robert Floyd said the exercise allows participants to test and refine the operational readiness needed to conduct inspections when questions about compliance with the treaty cannot be resolved through diplomatic or other technical means.
The scenario-based activities include establishing a temporary base of operations in Swakopmund and conducting field activities in a designated inspection area in the Erongo Region.
According to the CTBTO, an on-site inspection is a verification measure provided for under the CTBT. Once the treaty enters into force, a state party may request such an inspection to clarify whether a nuclear test explosion has taken place. The request would require approval by the CTBTO Executive Council.
Namibia hosts two certified facilities near Tsumeb that form part of the treaty's International Monitoring System.
The exercise follows similar integrated field exercises held in Kazakhstan in 2008 and Jordan in 2014, the CTBTO said. ■

China to cut NEV export tax rebate for high-quality auto industry growth
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
00:22:31 CST
01:22:31 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 12 (Xinhua) -- China announced on Monday that it will cut the value-added tax (VAT) export rebate rate for new energy vehicles (NEVs) to 9 percent from 13 percent starting April 1, 2027.
VAT export rebates for e-cigarette devices and related products will be scrapped from the same date, according to a statement jointly issued by the Ministry of Finance and the State Taxation Administration.
Export consumption tax policies for products subject to the tax will remain unchanged, with existing tax refund or exemption arrangements continuing to apply, the statement said.
The adjustment comes as China has continued to optimize export tax rebate policies.
The country scrapped VAT export rebates for photovoltaic products from April 1, 2026, while cutting the rebate rate for battery products to 6 percent from 9 percent on the same date. The rebates for battery products will be eliminated from Jan. 1, 2027.
China is the world's largest market for NEVs, a category that includes battery electric and plug-in hybrid vehicles. The sector has expanded rapidly in recent years, with automakers increasingly looking to overseas markets for growth.
Luo Zhiheng, chief economist at Yuekai Securities, told business news network Yicai that cutting export tax rebates can, to some extent, reduce rat race competition and encourage companies to shift from low-price competition to technology and brand-based competition.
"China's NEVs are highly competitive internationally. Against the backdrop of tight global supplies of traditional energy, NEVs have met the needs of residents in Europe and the United States. Even with a partial rebate cut, they can retain sufficient competitiveness," Luo said. "Objectively, this also plays a positive role in stabilizing the macro tax burden and can better support the development of domestic demand."
During the January-September period, China's auto exports totaled 8.205 million units, including over 4 million NEVs, more than double the level a year earlier, according to the latest data.
"Despite a complex and severe external environment, exports have continued to grow rapidly, demonstrating strong resilience, while domestic new growth drivers are being steadily unleashed and the share of NEV sales is rising steadily," said Chen Shihua, deputy secretary-general of the China Association of Automobile Manufacturers.
Looking ahead to the fourth quarter, the industry is expected to maintain steady operation, Chen said. ■

- Harbinger’s uncrewed Praesidia hybrid truck is powering an AeroVironment LOCUST X3 30-kW counter-drone laser at American Rheinmetall’s AUSA 2026 booth.
- The companies have not said whether the laser-armed configuration is tied to any U.S. Army contract or test.
An uncrewed hybrid truck built by California’s Harbinger is powering a 30-kilowatt AeroVironment counter-drone laser at the Association of the U.S. Army’s annual meeting in Washington this week, shown at American Rheinmetall’s booth.
Harbinger CEO John Henry Harris said in a LinkedIn post on Oct. 12 that the company’s Praesidia vehicle is supplying power to an AeroVironment LOCUST X3 laser weapon mounted on the truck, with autonomy software from Forterra.
The display is at Rheinmetall’s booth, No. 2285. Harris pitched the combination as cheap, mass-producible equipment with “unlimited magazine depth,” a reference to the fact that a laser keeps firing as long as it has electrical power rather than running out of missiles or rounds. He did not say whether the system has been tested together in the field, whether any U.S. Army unit plans to use it, or what it would cost.
The Praesidia is a militarized version of the plug-in hybrid chassis Harbinger builds for commercial delivery trucks. It has no cab, is driven by wire so autonomy kits can control steering, braking and acceleration, and combines a large battery pack with a gasoline engine that acts as a generator. Harbinger says the vehicle can travel more than 800 km (500 miles) on a full tank and full battery, or about 170 km (105 miles) on electric power alone, and can export up to 350 kW of power to equipment it carries. That power is what a laser weapon needs: a high-energy laser draws electricity continuously while firing, and the vehicle carrying it has to supply it.
AeroVironment’s LOCUST laser family came from BlueHalo, which AeroVironment acquired in 2025. The U.S. Army has tested earlier LOCUST lasers mounted on Joint Light Tactical Vehicles as part of its effort to shoot down small drones without spending missiles. AeroVironment has not published detailed specifications for the X3 version beyond the 30 kW power level Harris cited.
The truck at AUSA comes from a program already under contract. In August, the U.S. Army gave American Rheinmetall an 18-month deal to build autonomous supply vehicles under Project Sustainment, using Harbinger’s chassis, Forterra’s autonomy software and Primordial Labs’ Anura control interface. Those vehicles are meant to haul supplies to company-sized units without a driver. Harbinger has also said it is configuring the Praesidia for battlefield communications, troop transport, perimeter security and counter-drone missions, and the CIA-backed venture firm In-Q-Tel invested in the company in June.

EU-China trade deal raises fears Brussels will go soft on Beijing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
16:22:22 UTC
01:22:22 KST

The EU's new trade deal with China has eased fears of an escalating trade war, but it could also weaken the political momentum behind Brussels' plans to take a tougher stance against Beijing's economic practices.
After four months of negotiations, Brussels and Beijing struck a deal on Friday under which China agreed to curb its hybrid car exports to the EU and ease restrictions on rare earths licensing.
The European Commission has framed the agreement as the first phase of talks launched in June to rebalance trade relations. The EU runs a trade deficit of more than €1 billion a day with China, whose exports are putting growing pressure on European industry.
The deal comes just a week after French President Emmanuel Macron and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz called for a new EU trade defence instrument to counter foreign economic distortions, potentially including measures to restrict access to the European market.
But with EU leaders due to discuss China at this week's summit, there are concerns in Brussels that the agreement could take the urgency out of efforts to develop tougher trade measures.
“It is quite a good deal, but I am afraid it might create relaxation at the European Council,” an EU official told Euronews, speaking anonymously. “If anything, the agreement shows that, when the EU flexes its muscles, it has an effect.”
Trade war averted. For now.
Friday's agreement appears to have shifted the debate among member states, easing the immediate threat of an escalating trade war with Beijing.
That risk had grown after the joint letter from Paris and Berlin signalled an unusual degree of alignment between the EU's two largest economies on the need to confront China's trade practices – a position that would have been difficult to imagine just months ago.
Spain, which like Germany has traditionally favoured a more conciliatory approach towards Beijing, faces snap elections in November.
The agreement also offers a reprieve for Merz and Germany's car industry, which has been struggling with fierce competition from Chinese manufacturers.
Under the deal, the EU will introduce country-specific quotas allowing 350,000 Chinese hybrid cars onto the European market annually over four years, with a fixed annual adjustment rate of 6%.
“This will cut by more than half the current exports to the EU, which we estimate are likely to reach up to 800,000 units in 2026,” a second EU official said.
According to Alicia García-Herrero, an expert at Bruegel, a Brussels-based think tank, Merz is in a weak position to reject the agreement.
“He will drag his feet when it comes to new measures because Germany will prefer to cash in this goody as the deal will reduce competition.”
“Not the end of the story”
The agreement could provide a model for combining trade pressure with diplomacy, with China making concessions before Brussels imposed safeguards it was already preparing.
Chinese car exports to the EU are worth around €15bn, small next to the EU’s €360bn bilateral trade deficit with China.
The EU also secured tariff liberalisation for car parts, footwear, ice cream and olive oil, saving at least €225 million in duties, according to the Commission. While welcome, those concessions will do little to close the wider trade gap.
EU trade chief Maroš Šefčovič is due to hold a video call with his Chinese counterpart in January, followed by another round of political talks in March.
“Last week’s deal shows that the Chinese are now beginning to take Europe seriously and realising that there’s a serious political issue, not just an economic issue,” Peter Chase of the German Marshall Fund told Euronews.
Even if EU leaders deem the deal good enough for now, all eyes are on the next chapter. “It’s not the end of the story,” an EU diplomat said. Some fear member states may now lower their guard.
Trade defence
The Commission promised EU ambassadors on Sunday that it would present proposals for the tool requested by Macron and Merz, to react systematically to market distortions, before the traditional December EU summit.
The proposed mechanism was already under consideration as part of a broader overhaul of the EU's trade defence toolkit.
Other measures under discussion include a diversification instrument to help companies reduce their dependence on single suppliers of strategic products, and a solidarity mechanism to support member states facing trade retaliation.
Yet some fear that, having secured concessions, member states may back down and withhold the strong political mandate needed to keep working on these tools.
“The Chinese well understood the message. They want to work with us on this. But because it showed it worked, we need to continue to keep the guns on the table,” the first EU official said.
Others within the Commission argue that Brussels already has considerable powers at its disposal, including the anti-coercion instrument, which has yet to be used, as well as anti-dumping measures and investment screening.
“We have a lot of instruments,” the second EU official said. “But as always, we can do more, and we can be better. And I think that is the discussion that will take place this week.”

In Mugla, southwestern Türkiye, participants will observe work under the Mooring Buoy Project, an environmentally friendly mooring infrastructure initiative implemented by the Turkish Environment Agency to protect sensitive seabed ecosystems and seagrass meadows in the bays of Fethiye and Gocek.

Greenland lawmakers signal support for Trump security deal
COPENHAGEN, Oct 12 - A majority of Greenlandic lawmakers signalled support for the Arctic island's recent security agreement with US President Donald Trump in a debate on Monday, although some opposition party members questioned the deal's economic value.
The United States, Denmark and Greenland last month signed the agreement, aimed at ending tensions after Trump's repeated threats to take control of the strategically located and mineral-rich island.
The agreement is subject to a second reading in parliament before being put to a vote, with lawmakers expected to pass the legislation.
The deal expands the US military's role in Greenland, paving the way for two new military bases and Trump's "Golden Dome" missile defence system, while reaffirming Danish sovereignty and Greenlanders' right to self-determination.
The chair of opposition party Naleraq, Pele Broberg, said many details still remained unclear on how the agreement would work in practice.
"The US is granted extensive rights in our country. The people of Greenland are not guaranteed any fixed payment for those rights," Broberg said in the parliamentary debate in Greenland's capital Nuuk.
The government parties, which have a majority of seats, defended the deal.
Former Foreign Minister Vivian Motzfeldt of the governing coalition's Demokraatit said Greenland had secured "massive" protection without having to pay for it, while winning recognition as an autonomous nation.
Foreign Minister Mute Egede said the deal was "a huge step forward" that could not be measured in terms of money.
Erik Jensen, chair of the Siumut party, said his party backed the deal.
"For several years, Siumut has been campaigning to ensure that agreements concerning Greenland are no longer concluded without Greenlandic participation... That is why we are satisfied," Jensen said. REUTERS

We have clear standards of conduct and expectations concerning the use of social media, that reflect our Trust values and our commitment to equality, diversity and inclusion. We take any concerns that may be inconsistent with those standards seriously and consider them through the appropriate processes. As a matter of policy, we do not comment on individual employment matters,” the spokesperson said, adding that “We recognize the distress that content of this nature can cause, and support is available for any member of staff affected.”

Combating Israel's 'brain drain': Inside Hebrew University's new medical education center
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
16:26:15 UTC
01:26:15 KST

Hebrew University of Jerusalem is launching a new Center for Advanced Medical Education, using a gift of $30 million from the family foundation of Steven H. Lavin, designed to revolutionize the way physicians are trained in Israel by incorporating new AI technology into education.
The new center aims to combat Israel's so-called 'brain drain', in which an increasing number of Israelis are receiving extensive education overseas and remain elsewhere just as Israel may need them the most. This has led to an increasing shortage of doctors in Israel, with the country projected to have only three doctors per 1,000 people by 2035.
Lavin told The Jerusalem Post that the October 7 massacre in 2023 highlighted the problem of this brain drain, specifically the element where highly qualified medical students are forced to go study abroad and often settle there just as Israel needs them the most.
"People are training abroad and staying abroad...they start to build their life, and they don't want to return," Lavin told the Post.
Lavin met up with a friend, Vice President of Hebrew University Ambassador Yossi Gal, with whom he discussed the problem, which led to the start of a concrete system to address the problem by partnering with Hebrew University to create a new system that would allow an increasing number of Israelis to study within Israel and begin to build their lives within the country.
In addition to retaining doctors within the country, Lavin stressed the benefit of having a generation of physicians trained in Israel, while immersed in the culture.
Professor Eli Pikarsky, Dean of the Faculty of Medicine at Hebrew University, underlined the importance of cultural immersion in patient care.
Pikarsky told the Post that the cultural preparedness of physicians and healthcare professionals will be an immensely important part of the program under development, as an essential, and yet one of the most difficult parts of the medical profession.
New training to utilize self-learning, group-learning systems to increase capacity
The system is designed to improve Israeli's medical education capacity without sacrificing the quality of education or the time and mentoring feedback from senior physicians.
Pikarsky explained that within the new system, a high proportion of the knowledge acquisition will be done using technology, both in self-learning and group learning. The new center envisions a future in which classes in large lecture halls can transition into modules that students will work individually and collaboratively to learn and work through.
Additionally, assessments of individual students will become more efficient, according to Pikarsky.
"Today, a physician, a mentor, meets a student next to a patient, and they do this simulated discussion of the patient case. They hear the patient, they examine the patient, and then this physician who is overworked, tired, has a family, has other obligations, and also wants a life has to sit at home at 10 o'clock at night and write the feedback. This is not the way to do it," he told the Post.
By using an automatic system during the discussion that will take notes and write a structured feedback outline for the mentor to use, the physician can then give more feedback sessions while also having an objective and online component.
Pikarsky said that the feedback itself will still come from the mentor, who will get an outline of what happened, suggested points for discussion with the student, and the general assessment.
"Then the mentor can then go over these and decide what he agrees with, what he doesn't agree with, and then provide that to the student," Pikarsky told the Post.
Pikarsky emphasized that the educational tools he'd described were just two of many under development.
Another tool Pikarsky suggested will use technology to assess medical students' ability to effectively communicate. While skill at communicating as a physician is one Pikarsky told the Post comes over time, the advantage that the system gives is the ability for students to strengthen their abilities without doing so in front of the patient.
They can then go over what happened, understand potential improvements, and implement them with another try in the system.
Tools will also be designed to help students collaborate and teach each other, which Pikarsky describes as an invaluable experience.
"It's really a very different way of learning something. And if all of our students had the opportunity to teach as part of their learning, they will learn more.
Embracing AI as the future of healthcare
Both Pikarsky and Lavin acknowledged that the idea of incorporating AI and additional technology into medical training concerns many who fear that this will lead to less personal connection within their education and then within patient care.
However, Lavin explained that while medical professionals will still be overseeing the work being done, tasks that are "inefficiently using highly trained people" will not have to be done by them.
Lavin told the Post that embracing these tools for training is the way forward to advance medicine and increase the quality of care.
"It's something that we will, as people have to adjust to. But I think that if we don't use the tools available to us for this training, we won't be getting the best medical service there is."
Pikarsky added on, explaining that contrary to the fear, the system is optimized to allow mentors more time to connect with students, observe them, discuss complex cases, and provide personal guidance without spending time on tasks students can complete with technological guidance.
