More than 20 fintech licences issued in 2026: LIAA representatives abroad prepare to attract more companies to Latvia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
16:24:02 UTC
01:24:02 KST

On 7 October in Riga, the FinTech Latvia Association (FLA) and the Investment and Development Agency of Latvia (LIAA) held a workshop for LIAA’s representatives abroad. They are often the first point of contact for foreign fintech companies choosing a base in the European Union. The workshop equipped them with facts and arguments explaining why obtaining a licence in Latvia offers a fast and reliable route to the European market.
The workshop came at an opportune time, as interest in Latvia as a fintech jurisdiction continues to grow. Since the beginning of 2026, Latvijas Banka, Latvia’s central bank, has issued more than 20 licences to fintech companies, including payment institutions, crowdfunding platforms, investment firms and crypto-asset service providers. Many other companies are currently undergoing licensing or taking part in pre-licensing consultations.
Tīna Lūse, Head of the FinTech Latvia Association: “We want Latvia’s fintech sector to grow and become stronger. That is why the association actively works to ensure that companies, the regulator and public institutions coordinate their efforts and work towards a common goal. A foreign company deciding where to enter the EU market often speaks to LIAA’s representatives first. If they can confidently explain that a licence can be obtained in Latvia within a few months and that the regulator is open to dialogue, Latvia becomes a serious contender.”
A sector that earns revenue globally and pays taxes in Latvia
Latvia is home to 127 fintech companies. At the end of 2024, they employed 3,644 people — 9% more than a year earlier. The sector’s combined turnover in Latvia reached almost €372 million, while profits totalled €97 million. These companies contributed more than €91 million in taxes to the state budget — 28% more than in 2023.
Latvia serves as a base from which fintech companies expand into global markets: they obtain their licences and build their teams here, while serving customers across Europe and beyond. More than 800,000 international investors, predominantly from Germany, invest through Latvia-licensed investment platforms. Over €13 billion has been invested through these platforms, which account for almost a quarter of Europe’s peer-to-peer lending market.
The largest fintech groups headquartered in Riga also operate across multiple countries, with the largest present in 17 countries on three continents. The combined revenue of the two largest groups exceeded half a billion euros in 2025. This is more than the entire sector’s turnover in Latvia, suggesting that, when overseas operations are included, the sector’s total turnover could be twice as high.
Latvia’s advantages compared with other EU jurisdictions
- An accessible regulator. Latvijas Banka offers an Innovation Hub, a regulatory sandbox and free pre-licensing consultations. With well-prepared documentation, a licence can be obtained within two to three months of submitting a complete application.
- A trusted jurisdiction. Latvia was the first country assessed under MONEYVAL’s sixth evaluation round. It received high or substantial effectiveness ratings in 10 of the 11 indicators.
- Local talent. More than 90 Latvian fintech companies are of Latvian origin, and the sector is built on local expertise in finance and technology.
Santa Purgaile, Deputy Governor of Latvijas Banka: “The requirements are the same throughout the European Union, but Latvijas Banka ensures that the licensing process is clear and efficient, providing all the necessary guidance and support. During pre-licensing consultations, companies learn exactly what we expect from them, which means we can assess a well-prepared application within a few months. A licence from Latvijas Banka allows a company to operate throughout the European Union, and its value is further strengthened by Latvia’s internationally recognised anti-money laundering framework.”
The workshop supports the implementation of Latvia’s Fintech Sector Development Strategy for 2025–2027. By the end of 2027, the strategy aims to increase the number of fintech companies by 30%, investment attracted by 15% and employment in the sector by 18%.
FLA and LIAA work closely together to promote Latvia internationally and develop its fintech sector. They jointly participate in numerous international events, including Latvian stands at industry exhibitions and trade missions, strengthening the global visibility of Latvia’s fintech ecosystem. Their next joint initiatives include Money20/20 Europe 2027 in Amsterdam and visits to Germany, Austria and France.
“Latvia has skilled finance and technology professionals, as well as companies that operate successfully in international markets. We also want new foreign fintech companies to establish and expand their operations here, creating well-paid jobs and increasing services exports. When choosing a European base, companies need to understand how to obtain a licence, recruit employees and grow their business. Our representatives abroad are often their first point of contact with Latvia. The more specific our answers to these questions, the greater the likelihood that a company will choose Latvia,” emphasises LIAA Director Ieva Jāgere.
FLA will publish the latest sector data in its annual report, Fintech Pulse 2026, which will be presented on 27 November.

Breadcrumb
Saudi's MBS 'shuttling between bunker palaces' amid Houthi attacks
Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman is reportedly moving between heavily guarded palaces equipped with bunkers in Riyadh as Yemen's Houthis intensify their missile and drone attacks on the Saudi capital.
The kingdom's de facto ruler has not been seen in public since last Tuesday and is travelling between fortified royal residences accompanied by a handpicked security team, according to the Wall Street Journal.
The reported movements come as the Houthis continue to bombard Riyadh with drones, cruise missiles and ballistic missiles, forcing the closure of King Khalid International Airport until 17 October following repeated strikes.
On Saturday, a ballistic missile struck one of the airport's terminals, killing 13 people and injuring hundreds. Another missile hit the airport on Sunday, killing one person, while four others were killed in attacks on Wednesday and Thursday.
The strikes have raised concerns over Saudi Arabia's ability to defend its capital, amid reports that the kingdom is running low on interceptor missiles used to shoot down incoming ballistic and cruise missiles.
According to the Wall Street Journal, Saudi Arabia's air defence stockpiles have been depleted by repeated attacks, leaving the kingdom increasingly vulnerable to further strikes.
Saudi Arabia, like much of the region, has expended large quantities of interceptor missiles defending against Iranian ballistic and cruise missiles launched following the outbreak of the US-Israeli war on Iran.
Saudi air defences under strain
Dr Burcu Ozcelik, a senior research fellow at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI), told The New Arab that Saudi Arabia faced significant challenges in countering Houthi attacks, particularly low-flying drones and cruise missiles that are harder to detect.
The kingdom's dwindling stockpile of interceptor missiles has further complicated its defensive efforts.
"It would be a mistake to say the Kingdom’s air defence systems are failing completely, they are under strain and stretched. But there are also reports of successful interceptions," Ozcelik said.
A report by the Associated Press in September revealed that Saudi officials had asked Britain, France, Pakistan and Egypt to deploy air defence systems to the country amid concerns over dwindling interceptor stocks.
The US has also deployed additional Patriot missile defence systems to Saudi Arabia and Qatar to protect energy infrastructure, according to Axios.
Other countries, including Greece, Britain and France, have provided air defence support, while Turkey and Pakistan, both partners in the Mecca Defence Pact, are also assisting Riyadh.
Ozcelik said Saudi Arabia was facing an asymmetric threat similar to tactics previously employed by Iran and its regional allies during the wider conflict.
Iran launched thousands of ballistic missiles and drones across the region, including against Gulf states, striking energy facilities and US military bases.
"What we are seeing is the familiar playbook the IRGC used against the Gulf - even a small number of missile or drones that gets through sophisticated air defences can create disproportionate damage and disruption," Ozcelik said.
"That's the asymmetric warfare logic that is working to the Houthis advantage."
Saudi Arabia vows decisive response
The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis has vowed to "respond decisively" to the attacks, having already resumed its air campaign against the group in support of Yemeni government offensives.
The renewed Saudi-led air campaign preceded the latest escalation in Houthi attacks on Saudi airports, with the group initially concentrating its strikes on energy infrastructure.
The repeated attacks have heightened security concerns in the Saudi capital, with the reported movements of Mohammed bin Salman between fortified palaces highlighting the growing pressure on the kingdom's leadership as the conflict intensifies.

Lebanon's Aoun hails EU security mission amid 'US objections'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
15:25:42 UTC
00:25:42 KST

Breadcrumb
Lebanon's Aoun hails EU security mission amid 'US objections'
Lebanese President Joseph Aoun welcomed the EU's decision on Monday to establish a new three-year security support mission in Lebanon, amid reported US objections to the bloc's plans for a greater security role in the country.
The mission, approved by the Council of the European Union, aims to strengthen the Lebanese army and Internal Security Forces as the country prepares for the withdrawal of UN peacekeepers from its southern border with Israel.
The decision, announced on Monday, establishes the European Union Support Mission in Lebanon (EUSM Lebanon) for an initial three-year period, with the aim of supporting the country's stability, sovereignty and state institutions.
EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said the mission would provide advice and assistance to Lebanon's security institutions to strengthen their control over the country's territory, border security and internal security.
"Europe is investing in Lebanon's future," Kallas said, describing the mission as a significant upgrade in security relations aimed at helping Lebanese state institutions restore full sovereignty and build lasting stability.
The mission will include civilian and military components operating under a unified political mandate, providing training and advice on border surveillance, intelligence gathering, reconnaissance, counter-smuggling operations, maritime security and cybercrime.
The military component will focus on strengthening the Lebanese army's capabilities in land border monitoring and control, maritime security and operational coordination.
The civilian component will provide specialised training and advice to the Internal Security Forces, including on cybercrime and counter-smuggling, while helping develop sustainable training structures.
It will also support security management at Lebanese ports, including the Port of Beirut.
The mission will contribute to the implementation of UN Security Council Resolution 1701, which calls for the deployment of Lebanese government forces in southern Lebanon and the withdrawal of armed groups from the area.
It will also complement existing EU assistance through the European Peace Facility and coordinate with EU member states, the United Nations and other international partners supporting Lebanon's security sector.
The decision formally establishes the mission, although its deployment remains subject to further operational planning and a separate decision by the EU Council.
The announcement follows a visit to Beirut on 8 October by Kallas, who outlined plans for a European mission to strengthen Lebanon's security institutions.
Kallas stressed that the initiative was not intended to replace the United Nations Interim Force in Lebanon (UNIFIL), whose current mandate is scheduled to end on 31 December, with a phased withdrawal expected over the following year.
US objections to European security role
However, the Lebanese news website Al-Modon reported on Monday that Washington had expressed objections in principle to the proposed European mission, citing sources familiar with discussions over Lebanon's future security arrangements.
According to the report, the US opposes establishing another international military arrangement resembling UNIFIL, preferring existing coordination mechanisms and a greater security role for the Lebanese army.
The reported disagreement reflects competing approaches to the international presence in Lebanon, with European governments seeking to maintain a role in supporting the country's security institutions as UNIFIL prepares to leave.
The reported American objections have not been independently confirmed, and there has been no indication that Washington has formally opposed Monday's EU Council decision.
Al-Modon also reported that discussions were underway over a separate monitoring committee potentially involving Italy, Switzerland and Jordan, although its composition and responsibilities had yet to be finalised.
The proposed committee would address questions surrounding the verification of security commitments, including the deployment of Lebanese forces, the withdrawal of Israeli troops and the monitoring of violations.
Israel has also opposed the deployment of a new international force to replace UNIFIL, favouring direct security coordination with the Lebanese army through US-backed mechanisms, according to Al-Modon.
The future of southern Lebanon's security arrangements remains contentious as Israeli forces continue to occupy positions inside Lebanese territory and carry out military operations despite agreements intended to secure their withdrawal.
Lebanese officials have repeatedly called for an international presence capable of monitoring violations and supporting the army's deployment across the south.
UNIFIL, established in 1978, has played a central role in monitoring the border area, documenting violations and coordinating with Lebanese forces.
Its departure raises questions about who will independently monitor the situation along the Blue Line, particularly as disputes persist over Israeli military activity, Hezbollah's weapons and the implementation of existing security agreements.
While the newly approved European mission is intended to strengthen Lebanon's security institutions, it will not assume UNIFIL's peacekeeping responsibilities, leaving the future of international monitoring in southern Lebanon unresolved.
